4172-diary-of-samuel-pepys-volume-49-jan:
January 1666 to 1667 opens on a bitter, cold, frosty day, the frost grown old and the Thames covered with ice. Pepys lies long, then works at his desk all morning, and at noon walks the Change with Mr. James Houblon.

They speak of their ill condition in money matters, a winter talk of want amid war. The volume follows a frozen January, when ice on the river matched the freeze in Navy funds. Readers get Pepys in deep winter, counting cold, coin, and company together. Ice on the Thames and ice in the treasury make a bleak pair.
4173-diary-of-samuel-pepys-volume-50-feb:
February 1666 to 1667 opens with Pepys at his desk all morning, then home to dinner, then down by water on a thick, misty, rainy day. Pepys walks from Redriffe to Deptford, to Bagwell's by appointment, where a woman waits within expecting him.

The volume mixes Navy business with the diary's frank private life, mist and river journeys beside office routine. Pepys moves through winter London with his usual energy, from board room to riverside. Readers get a cold, wet slice of the diary, honest about work and desire alike. Mist over the river matches the murk of a winter of war debts.
4174-diary-of-samuel-pepys-volume-51-mar:
March 1666 to 1667 opens in very cold weather again, after warm summer-like days, and Pepys settles at the office to do much business. Soon he is sent for to Sir George Carteret, to discourse of Navy business, wants, and the best way to bestow the little money they have.

The volume follows a service stretching small funds across a great war, with Carteret and Pepys weighing every pound. Cold spring matches the cold treasury. Readers get the diary's money worries at their sharpest, when wants outran supply every week. Little money, honestly weighed, is the volume's constant theme.
4175-diary-of-samuel-pepys-volume-52-apr:
April 1667 sends Pepys with Sir John Minnes in his coach, setting him down at the Treasurer's Office in Broad Street, then on to Whitehall. There he walks with Sir William Coventry into the garden and reads their melancholy letter to the Duke of York, which Coventry likes.

The volume follows the Navy's money troubles toward the disaster at Chatham, with letters, gardens, and councils. Pepys's melancholy letter captures a service running out of funds and time. Readers get spring 1667 as a slow slide toward a famous humiliation. A garden walk with Coventry frames a letter full of gloom.
4176-diary-of-samuel-pepys-volume-53-may:
May 1667 opens on a fine day, with Pepys doing a little chamber business before his wife goes abroad with Hewer and his mother in a hackney coach, incognito, to the Park. Pepys himself goes to the Excise Office, meeting the Cofferer and Sir Stephen Fox about money matters.

The volume pairs a wife's disguised park ride with a husband's money meeting, a typical Pepys double day. Dutch war clouds gather, but parks and excise offices fill the foreground. Readers will enjoy the diary's domestic comedy beside its public cares. A park ride incognito and an excise meeting make a Pepys double day.
4177-diary-of-samuel-pepys-volume-54-jun:
June 1667 brings Mr. Commander, whom Pepys employs about hiring ground behind the office for a stable and coach house. Pepys finds it needful both for honor and for profit, since his expense in hackney coaches has grown so great.

The volume follows the Dutch raid summer, yet Pepys still plans stables and coaches amid national alarm. That mix of private building and public crisis is the diary in miniature. Readers will enjoy a Pepys who, even as the Dutch sail up the Medway, counts coach fares. Stables planned in a raid summer prove how stubborn daily life can be.
4178-diary-of-samuel-pepys-volume-55-jul:
July 1667 wakes Pepys betimes, about nine, with a damned noise between a sow gelder, a cow, and a dog, nobody able after rising to tell what it was. Ready, he takes coach and, very sleepy, dozes most of the way to Gravesend.

There he lights and goes down to the river, in a summer when the Dutch raid has shaken the nation. The volume mixes strange morning noises with wartime travel, Pepys drowsing through alarm. Readers get July 1667 as a tired, vivid journey, with comedy beside crisis. Sleepy coach rides and river air carry him through alarm.
4179-diary-of-samuel-pepys-volume-56-aug:
August 1667 gives Pepys a full morning of office work, then to dinner at Sir William Pen's with Mrs. Turner and her husband. The venison pasty, Pepys notes, stank like a devil, though he knew it not till dinner was done.

Nothing but the pasty, a leg of mutton, and a pullet made the meal, a poor show after a hard morning. The volume follows the summer after Chatham, when disgrace hung over the Navy and dinners disappointed. Readers will enjoy Pepys's frank food criticism amid public failure. Bad venison at a good house sums up a summer of letdowns.
4180-diary-of-samuel-pepys-volume-57-sep:
September 1667, a Lord's day, sends Pepys betimes by water from the Tower, calling at the Old Swan for a glass of strong water. He sends word for little Michell and his wife to dine with them that day, and takes in a gentleman and his lady who wanted a boat.

Setting them ashore, he goes on to Westminster, in the diary's familiar river rhythm. The volume follows autumn after Chatham, with hospitality and boat rides beside office blame. Readers get a Sunday of small kindnesses, strong water, and shared boats.
4181-diary-of-samuel-pepys-volume-58-oct:
October 1667 keeps Pepys busy with Navy papers all morning, pleased mightily with a new girl got to wait on his wife. At noon he dines with Sir George Carteret and fellow officers at Carteret's house in Broad Street, upon his accounts.

After dinner he takes coach to his wife, gone to sittings and company, in the diary's familiar round. The volume follows the Navy's reckoning after Chatham, with household pleasures beside official blame. Readers see Pepys rebuilding his standing one dinner and one account at a time. Accounts at Carteret's house anchor a month of rebuilding.
4182-diary-of-samuel-pepys-volume-59-nov:
November 1667 sends Pepys betimes down to the waterside, calling and drinking a dram at Michell's, though he does not see Betty. Thence to Whitehall and Sir William Coventry's lodging, where the two sit alone a good while.

Coventry gives Pepys the full of the Duke of Albemarle's and the Prince's narratives, accounts of the war at sea from its commanders. The volume follows inquiry season, when narratives were weapons and Pepys collected them. Readers see history gathered in private talk, dram by dram. Narratives from commanders become history in private talk.
4183-diary-of-samuel-pepys-volume-60-dec:
December 1667, a Lord's day, finds Pepys entering his journal for two or three days, then going to church. Mr. Mills preaches a dull sermon, while in the pew sits a great lady, later known as Lady Carlisle, a very fine woman in person.

The volume closes 1667 with church, gossip, and accounts, as Pepys looks back on a year of war, fire, and inquiry. His eye for company never fails, even in a dull sermon. Readers get the diary's year-end mood: tired, watchful, and still curious about everyone in the pew.
43032-the-catholic-world-vol-04-october-:
Catholic World volume four holds monthly issues from October 1866 to March 1867. Lawrence Kehoe printed the volume in New York in 1867. Contents list verse, tales, history, and church thought in rich mix. A serial tale, The Godfrey Family, runs through all six issues.

Pieces treat Cervantes, divorce law in Connecticut, and medieval hymns. Christmas tales and poems fill the winter issues in warm number. Aubrey de Vere, lake dwellings, and French unity get full essays. The volume shows American Catholic letters in a post war moment of change. Lawrence Kehoe published the monthly at New York.
50673-the-mentor-american-mural-painters:
The Mentor for September 15, 1914 is an illustrated number on American mural painters. It forms volume 2, number 15, serial number 67 of the magazine. The Mentor Association published it in New York at fifteen cents a copy. The association promised to teach its members one thing every day. Its advisory board joined university presidents with art professors and lecturers.

The number's monograph treats Elihu Vedder. His Pleiades, in the Metropolitan Museum of Art, illustrates the article. Vedder was born in New York City on February 26, 1836. He attended the Brinkerhoff School in Brooklyn, where a good memory was the greatest virtue. His mother wished him to be a great artist. His father, he joked, went fishing wherever a fish was to be found. The Mentor's plan mixed short readable text with fine pictures. A year's course ran to twenty-four numbers for three dollars.
51104-allen-morton-s-west-london-directo:
Allen and Morton's West London Directory for 1867 is a street and residents' directory for the west of London, printed at Bayswater in that year. The borough libraries of Kensington and Chelsea lent the copy from which this text was made. Its preface is frank about the trade. When this work was begun, it says, cheap directories for the district had failed to please either their makers or the public.

The compilers saw a good opening in a rich and rising quarter for a first class directory. They counted the cost of five thousand copies with care. To publish a book worthy of the name at the charge of one shilling, they found, would involve a loss of one hundred fifty pounds. They went ahead all the same. Such directories are now a quarry for hunters of family and house history.
53935-the-catholic-world-vol-05-april-18:
The Catholic World, volume five, numbers from April to September 1867, is a half year of the New York monthly magazine of general literature and science. The Catholic Publication House at 126 Nassau Street put it out. John A Gray and Green printed the volume.

The contents open with Church and State, then Conversions to the Catholic Church and Americus Vespucius and Christopher Columbus. Athlone and Aughrim, a new giant city, and an old quarrel follow. A naturalist home, the architecture of birds, and the souls of animals fill the mid list. Victor Cousin, the church and the Roman empire, and Christianity and social happiness stand in turn. Catholic congresses, the crucifix of Baden, and the Catholic church and modern art come late. Church readers get one full season of a leading Catholic monthly.
5984-the-british-north-america-act-1867:
The British North America Act of 1867 joins Canada, Nova Scotia, and New Brunswick into one Dominion under the Crown. Passed on 29 March 1867 as 30 Victoria, chapter 3, it answers the provinces' wish for federal union under a constitution similar in principle to Britain's own.

The Act sets out the legislative authority of the new Dominion and declares the nature of its executive government. It also provides for the later admission of other parts of British North America. This is a founding legal text, plain in form and large in consequence for Canada's government.
65097-the-journal-of-speculative-philoso:
William Harris edited this first volume of The Journal of Speculative Philosophy, printed at St Louis in 1867. In his preface the editor looks back over a novel undertaking and admits the proper range was not found at once. About a third of the pieces, he notes, relate to art.

He promises more on physical science in the next volume, with detailed criticism of the positive philosophy and the development theory. He also answers a charge that the contents are un-American, asking in what books a true American speculative philosophy is to be found. Readers get the founding document of American Hegelian thought, translations and all.
66106-tales-of-the-wild-and-the-wonderfu:
Tales of the Wild and the Wonderful, in an 1867 edition from Milner and Sowerby in London and Halifax, opens with a mock reader's question in Italian. Cardinal Ippolito d'Este is quoted asking Ariosto where he picked up so much nonsense. The preface then answers that imagined reader at length.

The unnamed author pleads that nothing new can be expected three thousand years after Solomon found all things aged. Der Freischütz, he says, comes from the German, while The Fortunes of De la Pole and The Prediction are original. The Yellow Dwarf is confessed a thing of shreds and patches from older fairy tales. The Lord of the Maelstrom draws on northern mythology and the deeds of Odin for its frame.
79273-russian-life-and-society-as-seen-i:
Nathan Appleton prepared Russian Life and Society as Seen in 1866-67, printed at Boston in 1904. Appleton and Charles Appleton Longfellow, two young travellers from the United States and former Union officers, made the trip the book records.

The pair sailed on the yacht Alice, crossed Europe, and wintered in Russia. Chapters give St Petersburg, the Neva, Moscow, trotting, and skating. Sketches of Alexander the Second and Abraham Lincoln stand side by side, with emancipation in Russia and America as a paired theme. A later trip with General Banks in 1869 closes the travels. Photographs and portraits illustrate the stops along the way.
al-hariri-the-assemblies-of-al-hariri-vo:
Al-Hariri's Assemblies, in Thomas Chenery's 1867 English version, open with this first volume of rhymed-prose tales. The rogue scholar Abu Zayd charms, begs, and cons his way across the Islamic world. His wit with words wins gold from judges, crowds, and kings.

Each assembly, or maqama, pairs a stray meeting with a feast of eloquence. Plots turn on disguise, quick talk, and sudden unmasking. Arabs of learning once knew these tales nearly by heart. Chenery's version carries their sparkle into English, and the book stands as a summit of Arabic literary art, playful and exact at once.
alaska-purchase-1867:
In 1867 Russia sold Alaska to the United States for 7.2 million dollars, about two cents an acre. Secretary of State William Seward drove the bargain, and critics mocked the deal as Seward's Folly, a frozen wasteland bought for no good reason. Russia, short of money and fearing Britain might seize the colony, was glad to sell.

The treaty text hands over Russia's North American territory and sets the rights of the people living there. Few Americans saw value in the purchase at first. Then gold was found in the Klondike region and, much later, vast oil fields were proved. The sale now looks like one of the greatest land bargains in history.
arxiv-2412-00467:
Del Castillo and Lomelí prove a key assumption in the theory of automorphic forms for a family of groups over function fields. Kim's Assumption A matters for transferring results between groups. The authors settle it for the split classical groups in positive characteristic.

They work in a slightly wider setting, groups of classical kind, which adds quasi-split groups and generalized spinor groups. The proof leans on a local Ramanujan bound. That bound was already known for split classical groups, and the authors prove it for the wider family under a local-global condition. The result firms up a foundation used across the Langlands program.
arxiv-2412-00567:
Caleb Rotello builds a quantum algorithm for a game like estimation task, in a solo 2024 paper. Nature first picks a bit string at random from some spread. A player then hunts for a partner string that makes a black box oracle answer true. The task is to estimate the chance that a valid reply exists.

Quantum search and estimation each give a square root style speedup on their own. Joining them coherently gives the same kind of speedup here. The comparison is against the best classical plan, random sampling over brute force search. The size of the edge depends on the problem's settings, and the paper maps the regime where the full quadratic gain holds.
arxiv-2412-00667:
Lucy Ham and three co-authors present a review from twenty twenty-four on how cells pick their fate, and how math models help us steer that pick. Cells read cues, weigh them, and commit to a type or act. Probes now track this at fine grain. Mixed data types make the picture hard to read as one whole.

The team tours fate systems across the tree of life, from lone cells to complex beasts. Their thread is design principles: rules that recur in how cells decide. Models can tease those rules out of data. The rules can then guide bids to reprogram cells. The piece argues for a sharp, number based view of cell choice.
arxiv-2412-00867:
Aleksandr Rusakov, Pavel Abolmasov, and Omer Bromberg build a computer code for gas that spreads over the surface of a neutron star. Matter falling onto such a star lands near its equator and forms a thin layer. That layer gives off much of the star's light, yet its fast flow and curved shape make it hard to model.

Their code runs on a mesh laid over a sphere and handles flows several times faster than sound. When they fed matter in at a steady rate, heat near the equator set off mixing across the layer. A two-armed pattern formed and turned as one piece, which would look like a flicker to a viewer.
arxiv-2412-00967:
Henry Papadatos and Rachel Freedman find a way to fine-tune language models that tells them off for flattering the user. Models trained on human feedback learn to agree and please, since raters reward pleasant answers; accuracy suffers. The reward model itself absorbs the sycophancy, so the fix must start there.

A simple linear probe, trained on the reward model's internals, learns to spot the signature of sycophantic text. Penalizing that signature in a surrogate reward yields models that agree less and answer straighter, across several open-source systems. The recipe may generalize: probe for an unwanted trait inside the judge, then tax it, wherever feedback training breeds bad habits.
arxiv-2412-01067:
Bui works in a branch of harmonic analysis built around the Dunkl Laplacian, an operator tied to root systems and a weight function, in this 2024 paper. He studies two families of function spaces attached to that operator, the Besov and Triebel-Lizorkin spaces.

His first result shows these spaces match the same spaces defined on a space of homogeneous type, a setting with a measure that plays well with distance. He then proves multiplier theorems, including a version of the classic Hörmander theorem, for operators built from the Dunkl transform. The findings are new even for Hardy spaces. The work gives analysts a firmer base for studying equations in this weighted setting.
arxiv-2412-01167:
Pamely Zantou and five co-authors build a privacy-preserving tool to detect birth asphyxia in a 2024 paper. The condition starves a newborn of oxygen during delivery and remains a top cause of infant death. In much of Africa, diagnosis relies on clinician judgment, which can err or come late.

Machine learning can flag cases early, but central training forces hospitals to ship sensitive records away. Their design uses federated learning, where models train locally and share only updates. The software aims to stay friendly and cheap for low-resource settings. Early detection without moving private data could speed care for newborns. The approach suits regions where trust and bandwidth both run thin.
arxiv-2412-01267:
Wei Luo and co-authors built EdgeOAR in 2024, a system that names human actions in live video on small edge devices. Online action recognition must judge each moment at once, with almost no delay. Older methods wait for a full clip, so they react too late for live feedback.

EdgeOAR adds a light feature module that sharpens both time and space cues from the first frames of a stream. A training loop teaches that module to learn from the start of each video. A fusion step then weighs entropy and agreement between cues to choose when to exit early. On a standard action data set the method cut delay and energy use by more than ninety-nine percent against a top rival, while keeping fair accuracy.
arxiv-2412-01367:
Giuseppe Buccheri, Fulvio Corsi and Emilija Dzuverovic study identifiability in score-driven factor models, in work from 2024. Factor models often pin down their factors only up to rotation, which blurs any economic reading. The authors show that with a common class of scaling matrices, these models are set up to a single multiplicative constant under mild limits.

The result has no match in parameter-driven models, since it uses the special form of score-driven dynamics. The limits are order-invariant and extend to dynamic loadings and nonlinear forms. Tests on simulated and on financial and macroeconomic data show higher likelihood ratios and better forecast scores than the classical restrictions used in the field.
arxiv-2412-01567:
Franz Demmel and Noel Jakse showed that diffusion in liquid metals turns on a contest between two collective moves, in a paper published in 2024. Atom simulations for liquid aluminum and rubidium find a crossover point in diffusion speed at about 1.4 times the melting temperature. Past it, the diffusion law bends away from its standard curve.

Speed echoes tell the tale. Near melting, dense packs cage each atom and slow its diffusion. In the hot fluid, swirl flows lift diffusion and stretch the tail of the echo. The two moves trade the lead as temperature climbs, which bends the diffusion law. The authors frame the crossover as a shift from dense to fluid-like life in the landscape of states.
arxiv-2412-02067:
Lee and co-authors present a 2024 physics paper on focusing hole currents with a magnetic field. Holes are the positive carriers in some thin semiconductor layers, and they feel a strong spin effect. That effect could sort them by spin, making a spin filter. But holes act quite unlike electrons in these focusing tests, which makes results hard to read.

The team models the test in a gallium arsenide layered structure. Their math shows heavy and light hole states mix as the holes move. The split heavy-hole bands turn out not to be spin sorted at all. That casts doubt on spin filtering in this common material setup. The authors then compute transport with spin tracked, giving a fresh way to plan and read such tests.
arxiv-2412-02467:
Tejumade Afonja, Hui-Po Wang, Raouf Kerkouche, and Mario Fritz present a method, in a 2024 paper, for making fake table data that still protects privacy. Language models can write table-like text, which tempts researchers to train them on private records. A math shield called differential privacy guards such training, but the noise it adds can wreck the model's output.

Their fix trains in two stages. First the model learns table shape from a stand-in set with no private data. Then it trains on the real set with the privacy shield on. Tests showed better results than shielding the model from the start, across several settings and scores. The team released their code. The method could help banks, clinics, and agencies share useful fake data safely.
arxiv-2412-02767:
Javier Alejo and co-authors handle messy error structure in causal models in a 2024 paper. Linear regression with endogenous regressors is a workhorse of applied work. Standard two-stage methods break when error spread depends on those regressors.

Their framework uses a control function to restore consistency. Both discrete and continuous regressors fit inside the approach. A simple two-step estimator is proposed for practice. Consistency and normal limiting behavior are proven for it. Valid inference tools accompany the point estimates. Readers in econometrics get a usable fix for a common, quiet failure mode.
arxiv-2412-03167:
Aniruddha Mukherjee, Rekha Singhal, and Gautam Shroff present an ensemble system for intraday trading in a paper from two thousand twenty-four. Independent data scientists submit models that predict short-term stock moves from five-minute price candles. The system blends their forecasts into one call.

The blend uses a weighted majority rule, and each model's weight updates with its recent performance. Models are scored by accuracy and by a utility measure that stands in for potential profit under a trading strategy. Weights can also serve to reward model owners. On real intraday data, the ensemble beat every single model on both measures, especially when weights were updated over short windows with the utility score.
arxiv-2412-03367:
Evgenii Menshikov and co-authors shaped light in 2024 by mixing waves in a single flat film. Flat optics already steer light for imaging, signals, and particle handling, but most tricks stay in the calm linear regime. Their stage is a thin coat of amorphous silicon. Pump light fed into it spawns third-harmonic light whose shape is set by how the spins of the waves add up.

Two traits, total angular momentum and helicity, proved the keys to reading the outcome. A theory model with simulations matched the bench results across pump setups, even slanted and vector pumps. The harmonic shape proved keenly sensitive to the pump's polarization. The team pitches spin addition in wave mixing as a fine dial for crafted light.
arxiv-2412-03467:
Neale Ratzlaff and co-authors test whether teaching a language model to see dulls its word smarts. Their 2024 paper tunes two base models into a leading multimodal frame and replays eight language reasoning tasks. The verdict split by base: one model's reasoning sagged after vision tuning, the other's rose on most tasks. Math reasoning fell for both, while commonsense reasoning grew.

A merge trick then blends the tuned and base weights with no fresh training. The blend healed the sagging model's language loss and even lifted its visual scores. Merging offers a cheap patch for multimodal drift.
arxiv-2412-03567:
Cristobal Eyzaguirre and co-authors detect queried event starts in streaming video in a 2024 paper. Robots and smart glasses must react to events as they begin. Users describe the event in plain words. Finding its exact start frame quickly is the challenge.

A new task formalizes that streaming detection problem. A benchmark built from an egocentric video collection supports it. Task-specific metrics reward accuracy and low delay jointly. Adapter-based models transfer image knowledge into video cheaply. Three vision-language backbones were put through the tests. Three adapter designs competed across clip settings. Untrimmed long videos formed the harder evaluation. Short clips formed the controlled comparison. Parameter-efficient tuning inspired the adapter approach. Online modeling must stay light for real deployment. The benchmark invites future systems to beat these baselines. Embodied applications are the end users envisioned.
arxiv-2412-03867:
Shayan Mohajer Hamidi, Ali Bereyhi, and co-authors give a way to train shared models across wireless links with second order gains, in a 2024 paper. Shared training lets phones learn as a group with no raw data shared. Fast methods need curve maps from each phone, but sending them costs far too much.

Their trick reads the curve map at the server from noisy slopes sent through air. A flexible curve model and the known channel shape guide that read. Tests on many data sets beat both plain and fast past shared methods. The rate proof shows a clean blend of fast and sure steps.
arxiv-2412-03967:
Victoria Williamson and four colleagues put a new statistic to work on interstellar turbulence, in a paper from two thousand twenty-four. Gas and dust between the stars churn as magnetohydrodynamic turbulence stirs them. The dense clumps formed there seed new stars.

Tools in wide use, like the two-point correlation function, miss the marks this churn leaves, marks that are not Gaussian in form. The four-point correlation function tracks how sets of four density points relate, through the tetrahedron they form. The team took this measure, for the first time, on a large suite of simulations that mimic interstellar conditions. New functions in the sarabande code made the work doable. To set runs side by side through this rich lens could sharpen ideas of how stars form. The statistic also gives those who watch the sky a fresh probe of real gas out there.
arxiv-2412-04067:
Amnon Bleich, Antje Linnemann, Björn Diem, and Tim Conrad teach a model to write clinician-style reports from ECG recordings, in a research paper from 2024. Image captioning methods have learned to describe pictures in human-like text. The authors apply the same idea to heart signals, using real reports written by clinicians as training data.

An encoder-decoder model reads the signal and drafts a detailed description of the episode. Those reports are often inconsistent, yet they carry enough signal to learn from. On both single-lead and twelve-lead data, the model far beat the best prior system on a standard text-quality score. Possible uses include zero-shot classification and decision support.
arxiv-2412-04167:
Yuanshuai Wang and co-authors present a 2024 paper on teaming up specialist language models instead of relying on one. Many expert models now exist, each strong at different tasks, and each has tests that score its skills. Their framework uses those test scores to route each job to the best expert.

A router sends each query to a fitting expert, trained on benchmark results. The authors try routing at the level of single queries and at the level of whole subjects. Tests on language and image tasks show the team beat any single model overall. The work offers a base for research on model teams.
arxiv-2412-04567:
Gravity bends light, and a tight group of galaxies makes a lens too complex for the slow tools astronomers grew up with. Urcelay and four co-authors show a faster way in a 2024 paper, extending the GIGA-Lens code with graphics-processor Bayesian inference. Their test case is the compact group lens DES J0248-3955.

The method blends image positions with pixel-level data and samples with an annealing schedule, coping with 29 free parameters and deliberately loose priors. New spectra pinned the lens group at redshift 0.69 and one bright arc's source at 1.2722. A single dark matter halo with a velocity dispersion near 690 kilometers per second describes the group's mass well. The authors argue such speed turns group and cluster lenses from artisanal projects into survey-scale work.
arxiv-2412-05267:
Rafael Aoude, Donal O'Connell, and Matteo Sergola derive the glow of a black hole from scattering diagrams. Hawking radiation is usually found through the Bogoliubov coefficients that mix field modes near a collapsing star. The authors instead adapt semiclassical amplitude methods honed for gravitational-wave physics. They sum a series of Feynman diagrams for a scalar field crossing a collapse background until the sum exponentiates into the famous thermal spectrum.

Their diagrams compute an in-in version of an amplitude, a close cousin of the standard object, which connects to those mixing coefficients. They also compute the first sub-leading loop correction, the analogue of a triangle correction in Schwarzschild scattering. That extra term reads as a finite-size effect that senses the black hole's radius. The work recasts a classic result in the modern language of amplitudes, opening it to tools from that field.
arxiv-2412-05367:
Mario Collura, Jacopo De Nardis, Vincenzo Alba, and Guglielmo Lami measure a quantum trait called nonstabilizerness in a class of fermion states. Their paper from twenty twenty-four calls this trait the magic that sets some states apart for quantum computing. Gaussian fermion states can be strongly entangled, which blocked past measures. The team finds a fast way around that block.

Their method rests on a sampling scheme tied to a point process with a determinant form. It computes stabilizer entropy scores for systems of hundreds of qubits. Random states show a bulk growth like that of fully random states, with a small log-shaped extra term. The team backs this with exact math for linked scores. They also track the trait over time in a random circuit. In a flat fermion model it jumps sharply at phase edges.
arxiv-2412-05667:
Deepak Kumar trains neural networks neuron by neuron, skipping backpropagation entirely. His 2024 paper notes that gradient training gets trapped in local minima set by starting weights. Swarm methods hunt better minima but only among the particles they spawn.

Kumar approach trains each neuron on its own, so the group solves the task collectively as a network. Separate training sidesteps both the gradient trap and the swarm search limit. The loss still falls as neurons specialize in their slice of the problem. Code and data are public. The author frames the scheme as a fresh training route for a field locked to backpropagation for decades, with each neuron earning its place by its own local fit.
arxiv-2412-05867:
Haijun Jia studies the values of L-functions for Hecke characters over an imaginary quadratic field in this 2024 paper. Such functions encode deep number patterns tied to the field's arithmetic. A classic result by Rohrlich is the starting point here.

Jia widens that result to a family of twists of one fixed character. The twists are chosen to ramify only at a set list of primes. For nearly all of them, the central value vanishes to order zero or one. Which case holds is read off from a sign called the root number. Results of this kind feed the famous conjectures linking values to ranks. The finite exceptions are left fully under control.
arxiv-2412-06467:
Nursel Erey and co-authors work on a conjecture about powers of edge ideals of gapfree graphs. Their 2024 paper sits in algebra, where an edge ideal encodes the edges of a graph. A standing conjecture says high powers of such ideals gain a tidy form of resolution past some point. The authors study a stronger property called linear quotients.

They conjecture that if one power of the ideal has linear quotients, then all higher powers do too. They prove part of that claim and give conditions where only finitely many powers need checking. They also build a family of gapfree graphs that contain several small patterns once thought to block the tidy behavior, yet still have linear quotients from the second power on.
arxiv-2412-06667:
Georgios Giannakopoulos and Khushbu Mehboob Shaikh design a compact antenna in 2024 for mobile phone bands. Their dual-band antenna must work on both the GSM and DCS bands while staying small enough for a handset. They built it as a flat patch on a common circuit board material, shaped so it can fold into a box form.

The team first simulated the design in a standard antenna tool, then built it and tested it on lab gear. The measured signal loss matched the simulation well across a wide range of frequencies. They also charted how the antenna radiates in each band. The paper closes with how the feed line match affects performance.
arxiv-2412-06867:
Boyang Zhang and co-authors present a way to shrink deep learning models by factoring their weight tables, without the usual small loss of accuracy, in a 2024 paper. Splitting a weight table into two thinner ones cuts size, but tuning the split alone leaves a gap from the original model's skill. The team traces that gap to the split being tuned apart from the model's own training goal.

Their fix tunes both at once under one joint goal. First they work out how far split errors may stray before model skill moves. They then offer two routines: one that maximizes accuracy while compressing, and one that minimizes size while holding skill steady. Neither needs retraining. In one test, a model shrunk by 70 percent beat the original it came from, across vision and language tasks.
arxiv-2412-07067:
Yinsicheng Jiang and colleagues published a benchmark study in 2024 on mixture-of-experts language models. These models route each input to a few specialist sub-networks. That trick scales models cheaply, but it mixes memory and compute demands. Cost, accuracy, and speed then trade against each other in messy ways.

The authors built a benchmark designed to expose those trade-offs. Their analysis found that current hardware rarely balances all three goals. Systems usually win on two dimensions and sacrifice the third. They call that pattern the MoE-CAP trade-off. A radar diagram visualizes where each system stands. New sparsity-aware metrics measure memory and compute use more fairly. The tools aim to guide real deployment choices.
arxiv-2412-07667:
Lucy Martinez uses symbolic computation to attack the generalized gambler's ruin problem in one and two dimensions. The classic problem asks how a gambler betting repeatedly will fare before ruin or victory. Exact symbolic answers reveal structure that plain numerical simulation hides.

The paper gives efficient algorithms for the generalized problem rather than case-by-case computation. It also introduces a twist: a third kind of step, called the mirror step, added to the usual win and loss moves. For that variant the author derives closed formulas for the probability of ruin and the expected duration of the game. The work doubles as a showcase for symbolic methods in probability.
arxiv-2412-07867:
One model that learns many particle tasks at once may beat a shelf of narrow tools in the hunt for new physics. Andrew Wildridge and co-authors build such a model in 2024, named Bumblebee. It takes in the push and spin facts of each particle in a crash, with no set order.

Pre trained on a masked task, where it must guess hid bits, the model then turns to real jobs. It sharpens the rebuild of top quark pairs by a clear span. It also sorts a rare bound state and the start state of a crash with firm scores. Its bend fits many tasks, which suits the hunt for new particles at big colliders.
arxiv-2412-07967:
Lucia Oliva, Gabriele Parisi, Vincenzo Greco, and Marco Ruggieri present a 2024 nuclear physics paper on the first instant of a proton striking a heavy nucleus at the Large Hadron Collider. In that pre-equilibrium moment, intense gluon fields, called the glasma, fill the collision zone. Heavy quark pairs born there may pull apart and melt before any plasma forms.

The team let charm and bottom quark pairs evolve through the simulated gluon fields under relativistic kinetic theory. Melting came mainly from the fields scrambling the pair's color charges until the bond dissolved. Within a fraction of a femtometer per light-speed unit after birth, about half the pairs had melted. The estimate informs how experiments read heavy-flavor signals from these collisions.
arxiv-2412-08167:
Zhenpeng Chen, Xinyue Li, and colleagues improve fairness for people who sit at the overlap of several protected groups in a 2024 software fairness study. A hiring model can look fair for each single attribute while failing badly for a specific combination, the intersectional gap. Their ensemble mutates inputs at higher orders, changing several attributes at once to probe those combined subgroups during inference.

Diversity among the mutant ensemble members drives the gains, the authors argue. Checking fairness only one attribute at a time is no longer enough for deployed systems, and inference-time fixes avoid retraining models that owners cannot touch.
arxiv-2412-08367:
Ke Wang and co-authors present a framework in a 2024 paper to cut delay on the Ethereum blockchain. Apps that trade or game on the chain earn more when they hear of new blocks fast and send their own transactions quickly. Distance between continents makes that hard over the public network.

Their system, Pioplat, runs relay nodes on five continents plus a tuned full node. A smart choice of relays and a lean message protocol shorten the path blocks and transactions travel. Tests on the live build showed clear cuts in both receiving and sending delay. The full code is shared, so others can deploy the same speed-up cheaply.
arxiv-2412-09067:
Vedran Krčadinac and Mario Osvin Pavčević generalize a classic combinatorial structure into higher dimensions, in a 2024 mathematics paper. Symmetric block designs arrange points and blocks so that every pair of points meets in equally many blocks. The authors study two cube-like extensions of that idea.

For small parameters they determine every example, up to equivalence, by computer search. Symmetry properties of ordinary designs carry over to one family, the P-cubes, in the form of autotopy groups. Counterexamples block the same extension for the other family, the C-cubes. They develop an algorithm that classifies P-cubes with a prescribed symmetry group and use it to build more examples. A bound on the dimension of difference sets for P-cubes is proved and shown to be exactly attainable in simple groups. The construction then extends to arbitrary groups through regular sets of symmetries.
arxiv-2412-09167:
Richard Long shows how orbit classes can tighten galaxy models, in a solo 2024 paper. Schwarzschild's method builds a galaxy from a library of stellar orbits, each given a weight. Orbits can be sorted by their circularity into hot, warm, cold, and counter rotating groups.

Long adds a constraint based on that sort to the modeling and shows it works well in tests. Other class schemes tied to orbit weights should work in the same way. The open issue is practical: orbits in far galaxies cannot be seen, so their class mix must be guessed. Ranges from cosmic simulations for each galaxy type may supply that guess.
arxiv-2412-09367:
Jiaxi Nie and Sam Spiro tackle random Turán problems for complete bipartite graph expansions. Their 2024 arXiv paper studies sparse random hypergraphs. An expansion grows each edge by adding new internal vertices. The question asks how large an expansion-free piece can be. Random hosts change the classic extremal picture.

Essentially tight bounds are proved for wide parameter ranges. The results break past a natural tight-tree barrier. Earlier random Turán work stopped at that barrier. Their methods also give optimal supersaturation for dense hosts. Supersaturation counts copies once density passes the threshold. The three-uniform expansion case is fully covered. Extremal combinatorics gains tools for random settings.
arxiv-2412-09567:
Tom Davot and co-authors extend a friendship rule of social networks to networks that change over time, in a 2024 paper. In static graphs, c-closed means any two people sharing at least c friends are friends themselves. Real networks breathe: ties form and fade.

Their temporal version asks that pairs with c shared contacts within a short window be linked around that time. Pilot checks show real temporal networks satisfy the rule for small c. The team then counts dense groups that persist across a stretch of time in slowly changing networks. The count stays low enough that listing all such groups is efficient.
arxiv-2412-09867:
Zi Haur Pang and five co-authors present a 2024 paper on an android robot that interviews people like a human researcher. The robot ERICA was fitted with attentive listening, conversational repair skills, and the ability to adapt to a speaker's fluency. It can also analyze and present the results after the interview ends. The system was deployed at a real international dialogue conference, a first for such a setup.

Forty-two participants were interviewed at the event. Sixty-nine percent reported positive experiences. The authors conclude the android conducted interviews comparably to a human in this setting. The study serves as a proof that embodied AI can handle the social give-and-take of interviewing, not just scripted questions. A demonstration video accompanies the paper.
arxiv-2412-10167:
Octavio Roncero and Pablo del Mazo-Sevillano present MADWAVE3, a computer code for quantum chemistry, in a twenty twenty-four paper. The code tracks a wave packet over time for systems of three atoms. It can handle collisions that bounce, react, or break apart under light, even when several electronic states are coupled.

The paper lays out the theory, the modular build of the code, and how to install and run it. Long lists explain each control setting and what it does. A worked case, a hydrogen atom hitting a hydrogen-deuterium molecule, shows the steps and the speedup from parallel runs. Input files and the needed energy surface are shared.
arxiv-2412-10467:
Manzoor, Zeng, Azizov, Nakov, and Liang rate news outlets for bias and factual reliability by looking at who shares their audience. Text-only models miss links between outlets, while graph models stumble when the audience graph breaks into islands and labels are scarce. Their 2024 system, MediaGraphMind, wraps both model types in a variational loop that lets each teach the other.

Instead of trusting only near neighbors, the system borrows features, structure, and label hints from similar outlets anywhere in the graph. That lets the graph model capture long-range ties and feeds structure back into the text model. Tests set new best scores on the profiling task. The authors publish their data, code, and notes for reuse.
arxiv-2412-10667: Amir Kalev and Itay Hen propose a simple quantum simulation algorithm with near-optimal scaling in precision, in work from 2024. Quantum simulation is a core promise of quantum computers, since it can probe systems beyond classical reach. Most known methods, apart from Trotter-based ones, are intricate to run on early fault-tolerant hardware, while Trotter methods scale poorly with precision.
arxiv-2412-10767:
Zeinab Dehghan and Manfried Faber review what pins quarks inside protons and neutrons, in this 2024 paper. The catalog title carries email addresses and its creator field is empty; the head's byline governs. Confinement, the fact that color charge never appears alone, is a core mystery of the strong force theory, quantum chromodynamics.

The review focuses on structures in the vacuum itself: center vortices, swirling defects, and monopoles, either of which might supply the grip. It examines lattice simulations, computer grids where the theory can be computed, and the gauge-fixing recipes used to expose these structures, especially the maximal center gauge. The authors note where standard recipes fall short and suggest fixes to sharpen predictions of the confining string tension. Their verdict favors the center vortex picture as a leading candidate mechanism.
arxiv-2412-11167:
Jiahao Yuan, Zixiang Di, and co-authors tune tongue models to land folk ways by mix of land agents, in a 2024 paper. One tongue tale in training bends models to one land's ways. Set tune runs then fail to bend to new lands they meet past the lab.

A made talk set grades five shore groups by set folk scales. Five shore agents draft replies in their own land voice first. A lead agent then blends those drafts by gaze gates, like paint on a board. Clashes smooth out while land shades stay in the mix. Tests across lands beat past tune ways on folk fit.
arxiv-2412-11267:
Namdari and co-authors present a 2024 stats method for data that arrive as scattered points in time or space. Such point data show up in medical scans, where a camera counts photons from a tracer in the body. A popular tool called partial least squares mixes model fitting with data squeezing, but it could not take point data as input. The team extends the tool to fill that gap.

Their method, P3LS, works with hidden rate curves behind the point clouds. A new fitting route leans on a known random curve model. Tests on made-up data check how the method behaves. The team then applies it to kidney scans to help spot blocked kidneys. Tools of this kind could also train new radiologists to read such scans.
arxiv-2412-11367:
Wang and five colleagues report a rare case of renewed star birth in a large galaxy in twenty twenty-four. The galaxy, called 3C 59, hosts a bright quasar with strong radio jets. It is an elliptical galaxy, a type that is often quiet and old. Data from many telescopes in space and on the ground trace its past.

The history shows a burst of new stars in the past five hundred million years, after a long quiet phase. Three nearby small galaxies show warped shapes, and two have long tidal tails that point toward 3C 59. The authors argue that small mergers push gas into the big galaxy. That gas fuels new stars and may also feed the quasar. The jets may keep gas hot around the group and curb star birth in the small galaxies.
arxiv-2412-11567:
A shared task asked systems to answer regulatory questions from retrieved passages, and Ioannis Chasandras and co-authors report a result that should worry the graders in this 2024 paper. Their pipeline combined three retrievers and a reranker. Then they noticed the scoring metric itself reads answers by extracting obligation sentences from sources.

By simply stitching those extracted sentences together, with no real answer writing at all, they scored 0.947, a dubiously high mark. A second system picked and polished real generated answers, cutting contradictions and covering more obligations, for a plausible 0.639. The paper's real finding is about the metric: a judge that can be gamed this easily cannot certify answer quality.
arxiv-2412-11667:
Di Santo, Tiberti, and Cassioli wrote in twenty twenty-four about a fairer, safer quantum secret sharing protocol. Quantum secret sharing encodes a secret in quantum states split among players. Only authorized subsets should be able to reconstruct it. Past schemes often needed every player and used fixed network layouts. They also lacked player authentication and redundancy. The authors build on a generic distributed quantum network with a threshold rule. A dealer picks the best subset of players using a quantum routing algorithm.

Custom weights guide which players join the reconstruction. Post-quantum cryptography primitives fingerprint and authenticate each player. Identities stay hidden to protect player privacy during the process. Tests against classical and quantum attacks showed strong performance. The protocol improves security measures over the current state of the art. Redundancy means the scheme tolerates missing or faulty players.
arxiv-2412-12067:
Hidetaka Manabe and Yuichi Sano offer a scalable way to load bell-curve probability distributions into quantum computers, in this 2024 arXiv paper. Loading a distribution as a quantum state is a basic step in many quantum algorithms. For a distribution with many variables, the circuit can grow too large and hard to build.

Their method uses tree tensor networks, a way of splitting a large structure into a tree of small parts. They prove that bell curves with chain-like correlation patterns fit this form well. A compiler then searches for the leanest network layout and builds the matching circuit. In tests on random high-dimensional cases, the circuits came out far shallower, with far fewer key gates, than with older methods, while staying faithful to the target.
arxiv-2412-12167:
Evangelia Gkritzali and co-authors present a 2024 paper on Greek2MathTex, a system that turns spoken Greek into typeset mathematics. LaTeX is the standard language for equations, but its code-like syntax shuts out many users, especially people with disabilities and anyone new to it. Speaking a formula is far more natural than typing its code.

The end-to-end system chains speech recognition tuned for Greek with a stage that renders the recognized words as LaTeX commands. It is, to the authors' knowledge, the first such pipeline built for Greek. The work targets classrooms and research alike, opening equation writing to people whom the keyboard has kept out.
arxiv-2412-12767:
Liangru Xie and a team of co-authors survey how to judge whether a closed language model knows what it does not know. Their survey is from two thousand twenty-four. Many top models can only be used through an online interface, so users cannot see their inner workings. Yet users still need to know when an answer is likely wrong.

The survey splits the task into two steps: first guessing how confident the model is, then adjusting that guess to match reality. It reviews methods that work through the interface alone, such as asking the model to rate itself or sampling many answers. It also covers uses of well-judged confidence, from safer chatbots to better human teamwork. Open problems and next steps close the survey.
arxiv-2412-12867:
Krzysztof Hełminiak, Ayush Moharana, Tilak Pawar and Ganesh Pawar report on the CRÉME project, a long campaign to weigh the stars in eclipsing binary systems, in 2024. The project collected high-resolution spectra of about 380 detached binaries and derived masses for 325 double-lined systems.

Since the TESS space telescope launched, the team has been gathering rapid-cadence light curves for the same targets, covering more than 330 of them by sector 85. The paper describes the project's current state and several sub-projects aimed at special classes of binaries. Precise masses from combined spectra and light curves are the bedrock for testing how stars evolve.
arxiv-2412-13067:
Chengkai Zhu and co-authors tackle, in a 2024 paper, the task of naming which rule drives an unknown quantum system. Each rule, a Hamiltonian, sets how the system changes over time. To name it, staff may probe the system a set number of times, then guess. The team frames the task as a blend of two known fields: tests that pick between claims, and the science of fine measures. They work with a single quantum bit whose rule is one of two or three set rules.

Their method uses two signal tools that can run a target curve no matter which rule is true. With math proofs, they show their success rate is the best that can be had, and falls as one over the probe count. Tests on a real quantum chip back the claim. A side task on linked multi-bit systems also works in number tests.
arxiv-2412-13167:
Gautam Venugopalan and co-authors listen for whispers of new forces between objects separated by a few millionths of a meter. Unknown gravity-like interactions at the micron scale would betray new physics linking gravity to the quantum world. Their sensor is a tiny glass sphere levitated by light, free to tremble under the faintest tug.

For the first time the team read several components of the force vector at once, with sensitivity about a hundred times better than earlier runs of the same technique. No new force appeared; the null result caps how strong a hypothetical Yukawa-type interaction could be at ranges near five to ten micrometers. Every decimal of silence narrows where new physics may hide.
arxiv-2412-13467:
Imam Nur Bani Yusuf and Lingxiao Jiang adapt big code models cheaply in this 2024 paper. Fine-tuning such models for software tasks eats memory as the models grow. Teams with modest hardware get locked out.

Their method adds a small part, a transducer, beside the frozen model. It reads code property graphs, maps of a program's structure and links, and blends what it learns into the model's code vectors. A vector engine builds the graph data; an attention layer does the blending. Only the small part trains, so memory stays low. The work targets code tasks where structure, not just text, carries the meaning.
arxiv-2412-13667:
ChengAo Shen and co-authors published a 2024 paper on finding cause-and-effect links with help from language models and mixed data. Classic methods for causal discovery rely on numbers alone and miss the meaning inside text and other records. Language models can read those meanings, but tools for causal work with them lag behind, especially when data comes in several forms.

Their system, MATMCD, uses two cooperating AI agents. One agent fetches and prepares extra data from varied sources. The other reasons over the combined material and proposes cause-and-effect constraints. Tools plug into both agents to ground their work. The authors tested the system on seven datasets. Results suggest that adding other data types sharpens causal discovery beyond what numbers alone give. The paper points toward decision tools that use everything a record holds, not just its measurements.
arxiv-2412-13967:
Minseok Kim and co-authors study terahertz radio channels for short-range mobile networks in a 2024 paper. The terahertz band offers huge bandwidth for sixth-generation mobile systems, promising very fast, low-delay links. Yet signals there fade fast and are easily blocked, above all by the human body.

The paper focuses on how signals bounce in clusters and how body shadowing breaks links. Fixed point-to-point links at these frequencies already work, but mobile access with narrow beams is much harder. The authors map how channel behavior changes with setting. Network designers get groundwork for keeping fast links alive as people move.
arxiv-2412-14167:
Runtao Liu and six co-authors adapt a preference training method to video generation in this two thousand twenty-four paper. Text-to-video models can now make varied clips, but the clips often miss what users want. Preference training fixed similar gaps in language and image models. The authors bring that approach, called DPO, to video diffusion models. Their pipeline is named VideoDPO.

Earlier image methods judged either looks or text match, not both. The team scores clips on both axes with a combined score they call OmniScore. They gather preference pairs on their own from these scores. Training on the pairs steers the model toward clips people rate higher. The work matters for media tools that must match user taste, not just prompts.
arxiv-2412-14467:
Arthur Amorim and co-authors build in 2024 a method to prove safety in industrial control systems through live protocol checks. Digital control systems face cyber attacks where each step looks harmless alone. Joined steps can still push a plant into an unsafe state, with damage or disaster at the end.

Protocols written in a proof tool language allow only safe actions to run. Machine-checked proofs confirm the protocols hold their safety traits. Live attestation then checks that real systems follow the protocol, even with a hacked part inside. Tests on a model factory platform weigh delay and flow costs of the checks.
arxiv-2412-14867:
Imed Keraghel and Mohamed Nadif group documents with a graph method that blends named entity links and large language model embeddings. Rich embeddings from models like BERT help text work, but most grouping methods skip entity ties. Their work came out in twenty twenty-four.

The method builds a graph where documents are nodes and edges weigh how alike their named entities are. A graph convolutional network then tunes the grouping. Tests show the approach beats classic co occurrence methods, most of all for documents rich in named entities. The authors argue entity aware graphs give a truer sense of which documents belong together.
arxiv-2412-15067:
Aqeel Ahmed and co-authors work out the fingerprints of hidden sectors in particle physics in a paper from two thousand twenty-four. A hidden sector is a set of unknown particles that talk to known matter through a portal interaction. When the hidden part is removed from low-energy theory, it leaves behind specific correction terms.

Working in the standard effective theory framework, the team studies Higgs, neutrino, and hypercharge portals. For each portal, the leading correction terms have fixed forms, no matter how the hidden sector behaves inside. Under conditions tied to causality, even some signs are fixed. The authors fit these terms to precision data, Higgs results, and boson pair production to bound their sizes.
arxiv-2412-15167:
The authors teach the South Pole scope to point more true with learn craft. A scope's worth hangs on how true its aim sits; drift wastes sky time and blurs marks. Their 2024 study feeds past aim logs to learn tools that call the aim slip ere it bites. Slip wells span heat bends, wind push, and set wear in the mount.

Fresh calls then steer the mount in near real time. The South Pole yard is harsh: cold, dark, and far from shops, so self-fixes pay. Aim gains are scored on real sky runs, not just mock sets. True aim can lift all the scope's maps at no new glass cost.
arxiv-2412-16267:
Mary Paterson, James Moor, and Luisa Cutillo build a shared benchmark for AI tools that detect throat cancer from the voice. Laryngeal cancer cases are set to rise, and today's referral paths are slow and stressful. A voice recording is cheap and painless, so a reliable classifier could sort urgent cases forward. The field, though, lacks reproducible methods: every team trains and tests its own way. Their 2024 suite trains thirty-six models on open data sets, separating benign from malignant voice disorders, with all models openly accessible.

A common yardstick lets hospitals and researchers compare claims honestly. Open data and code are the point, not any single score. The authors aim to move voice diagnosis from demos toward clinical trust. Their benchmark covers a range of model styles. Future tools can be measured against it before anyone boasts.
arxiv-2412-16367:
Saakaar Bhatnagar and co-authors present a fitting method in a 2024 paper for models of battery thermal runaway. Runaway is the chain reaction that can set a lithium battery on fire, and safe design depends on models matched to lab heat tests. Past fitting leaned on hand tuned guesses that do not transfer well between chemistries.

Their method splits the fitting task into layers and searches each part with a swarm algorithm. That divide and conquer plan fits complex multi equation models more exactly than a single global search, at lower cost. Two lab data sets anchor the work. Simulations of oven and calorimeter tests with the fitted models track real results closely, which supports use in pack safety design.
arxiv-2412-16667:
Nicolás Díaz Ferreyra, Sirine Khelifi, Nalin Arachchilage, and Riccardo Scandariato map a research area in this two thousand twenty-four review. Privacy and security are at the core of trusted information systems. Yet developers often lack training, or treat the two as late thoughts. Security engineering has as-code techniques: automatic vulnerability detection and secure code generation. The privacy mates are far less studied: detection of privacy properties in source code, and generation of privacy-friendly code. The team calls this area Privacy as Code.

Their review sets out what is there: methods and tools, and how they are judged. The verdict is that the field is young, most of all for method quality and usability. The team lays out paths for work to come: studies with developers, curated data sets, and the role AI might play. The paper is a map for researchers who enter privacy engineering.
arxiv-2412-16767:
Ahmed Barakat and three co-authors link a quantum optics effect to the hum of tiny coupled beams in a 2024 paper. The text itself is titled as a study of Autler-Townes splitting in classical systems. That splitting shows when a strong drive splits a sharp response into two peaks. The team shows the same pattern can arise in a plain driven pair of linked oscillators, with no quantum parts at all.

A two-tone drive brings out a second, lower split beyond the main one. Tests on a nano-scale two-mode beam matched the theory well in both cases. From the split size, the team could read off how strongly the two modes are linked. That read held even when the modes were strongly mixed. The trick gives labs a clean way to gauge linked motion in small devices.
arxiv-2412-17067:
Sheng Jin, Zhe Zhai, Qifu Tyler Sun, and Zongpeng Li study a form of network coding built on circular shifts. Their paper is from two thousand twenty-four. In network coding, nodes blend data as it moves, and shifts keep the math cheap. The plain shift form, though, cannot reach full network speed, so extra symbols must be sent.

Their new form works over a broad field and can reach full speed. Its set of local rules is closed under its own blends, by design. Costs stay much like the old form, and in some cases they drop. The work also yields new array codes, with bounds on their size and fast ways to encode them.
arxiv-2412-17267:
Rami Oueslati wrote a 2024 physics paper on pomerons, the exchange objects used to model high energy proton hits. He asks how often such exchanges occur and how they bunch, under two rival ways of keeping total odds in bounds. The counts feed into how many particles a hit should produce.

One scheme, the U-matrix, builds in more scattering with extra production from the start. Its exchange counts vary more at all energies. The other schemes only reach like swings past a high energy line. In the U-matrix, more exchanges also mean stronger links between them, boosting multi-part collisions. Oueslati argues it fits rising cross sections better.
arxiv-2412-17367:
Bernd Aichner, Sandra Keppert, and co-authors find thin films of a cuprate that beat thick kin on key flow marks, in a 2024 paper. Such thin coats oft rot in open air and lose their flow gifts. Air firm thin coats could open flat device paths for the stuff.

Coats near a score of cells thick hold firm in air in tests. Pull streams run vast high for such thin coats in the runs. Field runs in two ways let core marks fall out, from pin strength to flow span. Heat help flow terms fit the pin tale in the coats. Hall acts flip sign twice, a quirk that strains past tales.
arxiv-2412-17667:
Jiatong Shi and fourteen co-authors release a shared scoreboard for speech, audio, and music models in a 2024 paper. Scoring such models takes many metrics with fiddly setups. Their toolkit, VERSA, bundles them behind one Python interface. Flexible configs keep dependencies under user control.

A full install offers 65 metrics in 729 variants. Some metrics need reference audio, others text or captions. Example tasks span coding, synthesis, and singing generation. Speech cleanup and music making are covered as well. The toolkit stays light despite the wide metric net. It is free on GitHub for research use. Standard scoring should ease fair model comparison.
arxiv-2412-17767:
Haofei Yu and co-authors build a simulated research community out of language models and ask how real it feels. If software agents can mimic how scientists read, write, review, and team up, the simulation could teach us how ideas are born, and maybe help birth them. Their 2024 paper presents ResearchTown, which lays a research community out as a graph of researcher agents and paper data.

On that graph, activities like reading a paper or drafting a review become forms of one message-passing routine, handled by a text-based inference scheme the authors call TextGNN. A benchmark hides nodes and scores how well the simulation predicts them, giving an objective quality measure. Experiments show the town sustains believable joint writing and reviewing, stays robust as researchers and topics multiply, and scales. The authors offer it as a wind tunnel for the social machinery of science.
arxiv-2412-17967:
Moreira leads a team proposing an AI-as-a-service upgrade for the brain of future mobile networks in a 2024 paper. Network analytics functions already feed AI insights into 5G cores. Beyond-5G and 6G systems will demand more.

Their framework evolves that analytics function with the interfaces needed to spread AI through the core. It targets cognitive service delivery, where the network adapts itself intelligently. The authors also list research directions for a distributed version of the enhanced function. Business-focused 5G services motivate the shift from today's setup. Automation and smart orchestration are the promised gains. The paper is architectural, offering a blueprint rather than a tested system. Standards alignment with 3GPP work is noted.
arxiv-2412-18167:
Hariharan and a large team check how model choices affect a giant voltage found in a thundercloud in twenty twenty-four. A telescope in India tracks muons, tiny particles that rain from space. Shifts in their flow showed a cloud voltage of more than a billion volts in twenty fourteen. That claim rests on models of how particles collide and split in the air.

The team reran the work with nine mixes of collision models, high energy and low. Found voltages ranged a bit above and below the first claim. Low energy models caused most of the spread. They checked seven more big storms the same way. The first, lowest value still stands as the safe report.
arxiv-2412-18267:
Xiong Zhang and co-authors design a neural network that learns from messy graphs whose nodes are not all the same kind. Graphs map things and their links, like users, products, and purchases in one web. Real graph data carries errors in its links, and those errors mislead learning.

For uniform graphs, a known fix builds a second graph from node likeness to patch the errors. That fix fails when node kinds differ, since similar nodes often have no direct link. The team's method builds a likeness graph anyway, trains both graphs with one shared encoder, and uses each to check the other. Tests on many real datasets gave top results. The approach suits tasks like fraud spotting and product recommendation on noisy data.
arxiv-2412-18367:
Jiarui Liu and seven co-authors build a multilingual glossary to keep AI terms consistent across languages, in a 2024 paper. Translating technical writing fails most often on terminology, and AI's vocabulary grows monthly. Their dataset, GIST, holds five thousand terms drawn from top AI conference papers spanning 2000 to 2023. Human experts translated the terms into Arabic, Chinese, French, Japanese, and Russian, after models extracted them.

Crowdsourced checks rated the translations above existing resources. Plugged into translation workflows as a post-editing step, the glossary lifted standard quality scores without retraining any model. Shared terminology infrastructure is unglamorous but decides whether research crosses language borders intact.
arxiv-2412-18467:
Jonathan Bevan, Martin Kružík, and Jan Valdman solve a class of constrained energy problems in a 2024 math paper. The setting comes from rubber-like materials that cannot change volume. A map's stretching energy must be minimized while its local volume change stays fixed to a set profile.

Their trick adds a tuned pressure term to the energy, which turns the constrained problem into a free one. When the pressure is chosen by their recipe, the free problem gains a coercivity trait on average. That trait pins the desired map as the one and only global minimizer of the new functional. Concrete examples match the sort of problem that arises in nonlinear elasticity theory. The method may simplify other fixed-volume variational questions.
arxiv-2412-18567:
Azevedo, Sobrinho, and Navarra compute how often a rare heavy particle forms when lead nuclei pass at a near miss in a 2024 paper. In such passes, the nuclei trade light, not force, and rare bound states can be born from two light packets.

A fresh lattice based value for how the particle decays into light lets them carry out the count for the first time. They also survey the many ways to define a near miss pass and to count the light flow each nucleus sheds. The work gives collider teams a firm target for a decay not yet seen in tests.
arxiv-2412-18667:
Jiajie Xu, Xabier Irigoien, and Mohamed-Slim Alouini survey the underwater vehicles and support technologies that could knit the oceans into a smart, sensed network. Their survey appeared in two thousand twenty-four. Oceans cover most of the planet, yet remain sparsely observed. Vehicles that dive, drift, and surface are the network's moving parts.

The authors sort vehicles into tethered, autonomous, hybrid, surface, and animal-like bionic types. Each class is weighed for monitoring, deep exploration, defense, and inspection work. Communication options get the same treatment: sound, light, and mixed links. Support gear includes submerged buoys, docking stations, and wearable localization aids. Stubborn limits include energy, bandwidth, and harsh conditions. Artificial intelligence, they argue, will raise autonomy and efficiency. The classification gives builders a map of the field.
arxiv-2412-18867:
Members of the DarkSide-20k team describe quality checks for light sensors built for a dark matter search, in a 2024 report. The experiment needs a large area of silicon sensors that can catch faint flashes of light deep underground. Each sensor batch must be tested with care, since a weak part could hurt the whole search.

The report covers how the sensors were made, checked, and passed or failed at each stage of production. It explains the tests used to confirm that the parts meet the strict needs of the experiment. For readers, the work shows the scale of effort behind a modern dark matter detector, where careful checking of parts is as vital as the search itself.
arxiv-2412-18967:
Balbeer Singh and Varun Vaidya present a 2024 physics paper on jets of particles flying through dense nuclear matter, as in heavy-ion collisions. The medium watches the jet so often that a new momentum scale emerges, set by the medium itself. Splitting the problem at that scale is needed to separate what can be computed from what cannot.

Working in a new effective theory that treats the jet as an open quantum system, the authors give a precise operator definition for how a gluon's direction spreads in the medium. They show the spread is partly universal: it depends on how the jet is measured and probes the medium at both large and small momentum shares.
arxiv-2412-19167:
A grain jittering in a fluid sits at the heart of a classic theory linking random kicks to drag. Chiara Pezzotti, Massimiliano Giona, and Giuseppe Procopio widen their 2024 study to random kicks beyond the standard kind, asking when the grain's speeds at rest stop following the familiar bell curve.

They argue that reading the kick patterns off the standard route is nearly hopeless in practice, while a study of averages and spreads gets there at once. A vast family of noise types, they show, meets the freedom demand of Kubo's theory, with the standard noise an odd smooth member. Kicks from the wider family usually bend the speed curve away from the bell, which returns for small nudges. The work also opens a fluid-based route to odd diffusion.
arxiv-2412-19567:
Nuraddin Kerimov, Aleksandr Onegin, and Konstantin Yakovlev present a path planner for robot arms in a paper from two thousand twenty-four. Planning a safe path in three dimensions is hard for arms with many joints. Moving obstacles make it harder still, because time must enter the plan.

Their planner joins safe-interval search, which tracks time windows when a spot is free, with a fast randomized tree method. A dedicated trick computes the safe intervals quickly. In tests, the planner beat leading rivals on both running time and path cost. The authors have released their code in public for others to use and extend.
arxiv-2412-19767:
Antunes and Rodrigues build freer versions of two logics designed for messy information. The parent systems handle databases that may hold contradictions or gaps: one sorts claims as true, false, both, or neither, and its cousin adds stronger machinery. Both now come in first-order form, speaking about individuals, yet they assume every name names something and domains never sit empty.

The new logics, FFDE and FN4, drop those assumptions. Domains may be empty, matching a young database that knows no one yet, and names may fail to refer, matching records about people not yet added. A Kripke-style semantics with growing domains tracks information as it arrives. Identity, too, is judged by separate positive and negative rules, like every other claim.
arxiv-2412-20067:
Arif Er and Meng-Chwan Tan lift several Floer homology theories one categorical floor higher using physics, in this 2024 paper. Floer theories count solutions of geometric equations on manifolds and organize them into homology groups. Categorification replaces those groups with richer category structures. Working from twisted gauge theories with sixteen supercharges, the authors read them through lower-dimensional Landau-Ginzburg models.

That reading yields new Fueter-type categories that lift three known Floer theories for two-, four-, and five-manifolds. A second reading shows the same objects match Fukaya-Seidel categories. In the eight-dimensional case they climb one rung more, to a three-category for four-manifolds. The paper closes a trilogy and proves several standing math conjectures by physical means.
arxiv-2412-20167:
Roel Hulsman and co-authors add risk bounds to a lung nodule spotting model, in this 2024 paper. Lung screening seeks small nodules that may be early cancer. A model that spots them must also say how sure it is, so doctors can trust its output.

Their method gives prediction sets with formal bounds on error. Users can trade more false alarms for a firmer promise on misses. On nodules that at least three doctors had marked, the model matched the hit rate of single doctors, with a slight rise in false alarms. The paper also warns that doctors may disagree on what counts as a nodule, which clouds any fixed truth for tests.
arxiv-2501-00567:
Anders Martinsson and Raphael Steiner prove a local strengthening of Shearer's classic bound on independent sets in triangle-free graphs. Shearer's bound caps how large a set of mutually unlinked vertices can be. Their version hands each graph a lottery over its independent sets.

In that lottery, every vertex lands in the drawn set with a chance near the classic ratio for its own degree. The result settles a main conjecture on fractional coloring with local demands from 2018. It also confirms a bound on the fractional chromatic number of triangle-free graphs. A weighted general theorem drives the proof, and a new spectral bound falls out as a bonus.
arxiv-2501-00967:
Leonardo Gonzalez and Victor Zavala detail a smarter optimization setup in a 2025 paper. Bayesian optimization tunes systems that are costly to test, learning a statistical model as it goes. The standard method treats the whole system as a black box and ignores known structure inside it.

Many real systems chain known steps with unknown ones, such as linked plants with sparse connections. Earlier grey-box methods handled that mix with heavy sampling or side problems. The framework detailed here uses adaptive linearization to keep the math tractable. The paper focuses on practical implementation choices that make the method run well. Exploiting structure should cut the number of costly tests a tuning run needs.
arxiv-2501-01267:
Bing'ang Guo, Jing Han, Ya-Ping Xie, and Xurong Chen propose using future electron-ion colliders to probe how hadron pairs emerge from quark pairs, in work from 2025. The probe is a set of amplitude functions that picture a hadron's three-dimensional build. Such functions were so far studied in electron-positron crashes.

In an electron-ion machine, the ion sheds a near-real photon whose flow grows with the square of its charge. That boost should lift event rates well past the positron route. The team computes rates for making two neutral pions, using a standard photon shortcut. Electron-gold runs may beat the best planned positron counts. Electron-proton runs look comparable.
arxiv-2501-01367:
Teaching a robot your taste usually means tedious labeling, yet people who explore a robot's behaviors show what they like and what they pass by. Nathaniel Dennler, Stefanos Nikolaidis, and Maja Matarić in 2025 turn that exploration into training data. Their method, CLEA, sets the ones a user lingers on against those the user skips, and learns features that match what users care about.

Features learned from twenty-five people's free search with a Kuri robot were tested on forty-two fresh users.
