They beat self-supervised features on completeness, simplicity, minimality, and explainability when drawing out preferences. Used this way, that search cuts the time it takes to teach a robot to suit one user.
arxiv-2501-01467:
Martin Erinin and colleagues built a laboratory cloud chamber in a paper published in 2024. Clouds form when humid air cools and water condenses onto tiny seed particles, but field conditions are hard to control. Their chamber, called REACh, triggers droplet birth with a sudden pressure drop that cools the air, mimicking rising air in the sky.

The mid-sized chamber tightly controls starting humidity, seed type and amount, temperature, pressure, and mixing by turbulent flow. Fast instruments track droplet sizes and counts as the cloud lives and dies. Tests showed the coldest point of each expansion follows dry or moist theory well across humidity levels. Cloud physicists gain a repeatable test bed for nucleation studies.
arxiv-2501-01567:
Christian Haesemeyer and Charles Weibel revisit a question in algebraic geometry: when does good behavior in K-theory force a space to be geometrically tame? K-regularity is a stability property of algebraic K-theory, a tool that tracks vector bundles and related data. Normality is a mild health condition on a scheme's local rings.

They prove two results. First, affine algebras over fields of characteristic zero that pass the second-level K-regularity test are always normal. Second, for spaces built as complete intersections, they sharpen a classic bound by Vorst linking K-regularity to plain regularity. The improvement connects with recent work on higher du Bois singularities, a topic in modern singularity theory.
arxiv-2501-01767:
Er Jin and co-authors build LogicAD, a system that flags logical flaws in factory images and explains them in words. A part can look fine pixel by pixel yet break a rule, such as a missing piece in a set. Older detectors need heavy hand labeling and training data, which the team hoped to avoid.

Their approach pairs a vision language model, which turns image content into text features, with a format embedding and a logic reasoner. On the public MVTec LOCO AD benchmark, the system reached 86 percent on the AUROC scale and about 84 percent on its best F1 score. That beat the prior best method by a large margin. Each flagged flaw comes with a written reason, which inspectors can check.
arxiv-2501-02067:
Many functions in math and optimization are too rough for ordinary calculus, so analysts build second-order tools that act like curvature for jagged cases. Pham Duy Khanh, Boris Mordukhovich, Vo Thanh Phat, and Le Duc Viet study two such tools, proposed very recently by Rockafellar: a generalized form of twice differentiability and objects called quadratic bundles. Unlike older tools, these live in the same space as the problem itself.

The team develops fresh ways to handle these ideas for a broad class of well-behaved rough functions, called prox-regular. They prove new characterizations of the generalized derivative. They also show the quadratic bundles are never empty for these functions, which clears the ground for using them in optimization.
arxiv-2501-02367:
Clarence Protin reads the philosophy of Hegel through modern topology in a 2025 paper. He argues that core concepts of topology, and also of logic and category theory, can be understood in the light of Hegel Science of Logic. At the same time, those modern concepts can serve as concrete illustrations of Hegel own deductions.

Protin presents the paper as a preliminary sketch, not a full treatment. It continues his earlier work arguing that prototypes of many topology notions appear already in Aristotle Physics. Used carefully, he suggests, modern math can be a rigorous reading tool for Hegelian concepts, while philosophy can enrich math in return. The note makes a case for a two way, disciplined exchange between the fields.
arxiv-2501-02567:
Mrinal Kanti Debnath and co-authors map the phases of a lattice model for liquid crystals in a 2025 study. The model places two-axis molecules on a grid, with a set rule for how pairs interact. Theory had predicted two kinds of ordered fluid states, plus a special point where the shift between them changes character.

Computer runs that sample many random states were used to draw the phase map. The results confirm both ordered states and the special point on the border between them. A score built from energy patterns helped show which shifts are sharp and which are smooth. The broad map matches theory, though the point where all three states meet sits in a different place than theory first placed it.
arxiv-2501-02867:
Rezkellah Noureddine Khiati and co-authors address a snag in reading lung CT scans by computer. Software must outline diseased tissue types such as fibrosis and ground-glass opacity, but sick tissue is rare next to healthy tissue, so training data is lopsided. Their fix uses a diffusion model to make extra training images.

The model creates fake patches of each disease type while keeping the shapes and fine textures that mark real tissue. Added to training, these patches raised accuracy across all disease types, with the biggest gains for the rarest patterns. Better outlines of diseased lung tissue could help doctors measure illness spread and track change over time. The method needs no extra patient scans to work.
arxiv-2501-02967:
Shashank Singh and co-authors report a hidden ionization effect in atomic collisions in a 2025 paper. Neon ions were fired at an aluminum target at two energies. Bright bremsstrahlung, braking radiation, flooded the spectra. Careful sorting pulled the true lines out of that glare.

Lines show one- and two-photon paths from inner shells. The double-photon lines in the beam ions appear only at the lower energy. Aluminum lines are oddly faint while double lines flare. The cause, the team argue, is photoionization by the braking radiation itself. It converts most singly stripped atoms to doubly stripped ones at the higher energy. The silent effect may lurk in many plasma events.
arxiv-2501-03767:
AutoFish, a data set for fine fish study, is shared by Stefan Hein Bengtson and co-authors in a 2025 arXiv paper. Auto fish records could aid fair fishing and fight overfishing. The set holds 1,500 photos of 454 look-alike fish laid on a white belt in mixed groups. Each fish is marked with an outline mask, an ID, and a length.

Marks began as hand points, grew with help from a segment tool, and were fixed by hand. Base scores from two mask models top out high. Two length tools were also tested, with the best erring by well under a centimetre when fish lay clear. The set is public.
arxiv-2501-03867:
Nicolas Fournier gives a short proof that a classic equation of clumping particles must lose mass in finite time. The Smoluchowski equation describes particles that stick together when they meet, a model for aerosols, polymers, and planet formation. Gelation, the sudden birth of an infinite cluster, shows up mathematically as mass leaking out of the solution.

Fournier revisits a two thousand two proof and sharpens a recent result by other authors. For a broad family of sticking rates, every weak solution gels, meaning it loses mass within finite time. The family covers rates that grow steeply with particle size, plus a borderline case sweetened by a logarithmic factor. In that borderline case, how much logarithm is needed turns out to depend on the rate's shape.
arxiv-2501-03967:
Satchel French and co-authors classify the viewing angle of newborn heart ultrasounds from video rather than single frames, in a 2025 paper. Knowing which standard view an echocardiogram shows is a first step in screening, and clinics without expert sonographers could use automated help. A still image discards the motion that human experts unconsciously use.

Their network pairs a convolutional front end with a recurrent unit and a new temporal feature weaving step that mixes information across frames. Using only four consecutive frames, it beat image-only classification by 4.33 percent in accuracy, at little extra computing cost. The team also released a professionally annotated neonatal dataset with sixteen viewpoints to spur further work in this underserved area.
arxiv-2501-04067:
Jamie Todd and co-authors present a 2025 paper on forecasting tire wear energy in Formula One racing. Pit stop timing and tire compound choice can decide a race. Both hinge on how fast each tire degrades, which follows from the energy pushed through it lap by lap.

The team trained deep learning models on historic telemetry from the Mercedes-AMG PETRONAS team. A tree-based method, XGBoost, was fitted to the same data for comparison, and both approaches performed strongly. Two explainability tools, feature importance and counterfactuals, revealed what drives each forecast. Strategists could see not just the number but the reasons behind it. The authors offer an automated, explainable aid for race-day decisions under pressure.
arxiv-2501-04567: Martyn R Dixon, Leonid A. Kurdachenko, and Igor Ya. Subbotin study a class of algebraic objects called left braces. Their 2025 paper gives a detailed account of some nilpotent left braces that are generated by one element. The abstract is brief, and it states the aim and scope of the work rather than listing findings.
arxiv-2501-04667:
Tâm Le Minh and co-authors introduce a 2025 method for finding many good peaks of a hard function at once. Such searches matter when a task has several strong answers, not one. Their method, Natural Variational Annealing, keeps a spread-out guess that can hold many peaks, then slowly shifts from broad search to fine tuning as the run goes on.

Updates use natural gradients, which makes them look like well-known, simple rules. The team also adds fitness shaping, an idea from evolution-based search. In tests, the method matched or beat gradient and evolution rivals, and the authors apply it to a real inverse problem in planetary science.
arxiv-2501-04867:
Serge Tabachnikov, writing alone in 2025, studies curves traced by bouncing light in odd geometries. The setting is a billiard table whose distance rule is a Finsler metric with straight-line paths. A caustic is the bright curve that reflected rays outline as they bounce. Tabachnikov fixes the number of bounces and asks about the curve's sharp points, its cusps.

He proves that such a caustic always has at least four cusps. The question descends from Jacobi's last geometric statement about shapes on an ellipsoid. Recent work had settled the claim for ordinary Euclidean billiards. This note extends the result to the wider Finsler setting. The proof adds a piece to the long study of how light and geometry meet.
arxiv-2501-05167:
Oleksandr Baziei and co-authors build a mesoscale simulator for active polar fluids in a 2025 paper. Dense living suspensions, like swarming bacteria, act as fluids that are never at rest. Nematic active fluids have good mid-scale simulators, but polar ones were stuck between tiny and huge scales.

The team adapts multi-particle collision dynamics, a coarse-graining method, to three active particle models. One variant follows the classic Vicsek flocking rules, while others allow richer rules. The result is a solvent-like polar fluid that can flow around shapes and carry other particles. Complex lab and body settings become open to simulation. Biologists gain a middle lens between single swimmers and smooth flow laws.
arxiv-2501-05367:
Marco Vona and Eric Lauga compute how a particle spins in place inside a spherical membrane in this 2025 paper. Membranes are the skin of every cell, and how inclusions drift and rotate in them shapes biology. A classic 1975 result for flat membranes showed the surrounding fluid rescues the math from blowing up.

The authors move the problem onto a sphere, treating the particle as a rigid cap on the surface. They solve the flow in semi-analytic form, tracking how spin mobility depends on the cap's size and on the ratio of membrane to solvent thickness known as the Saffman-Delbrück length. The flat result falls out as a limiting case. The formulas fit questions from rotating protein channels to raft drift, and they offer a way to measure a membrane's viscosity by watching big inclusions rotate, where flat theory fails.
arxiv-2501-05467:
Work from 2025 extends a physics account of musical harmony to systems beyond the Western twelve-tone scale. The base idea borrows from heat theory, where order can arise from disorder as free energy falls. A past author used that path to explain how ordered pitch sets emerge from raw sound.

The authors study that method in depth and apply it to Gamelan instruments, whose tuning differs from Western norms. They also clear up points in the first account to make it firmer and better known. Readers see how one math frame can span varied music systems. The work builds a bridge between physics and art with testable form.
arxiv-2501-05567:
Benjamin Kiefer, Yitong Quan, and Andreas Zell tackle distance guessing for robot boats in a 2025 paper. Boats that run on their own are growing more common at sea. Yet their sensors cost a lot and need careful setup. Radar and laser tools can also give thin or noisy data.

The team offers a cheaper route based on photos. They built a data set of images with boxes drawn around objects and the true distance to each one. Their model branch both spots an object and calls out how far away it sits. The style is closer to how a person judges distance by eye. They show the method in a help system that warns crews about boats, buoys, and other hazards near the craft.
arxiv-2501-05767:
You Li and ten colleagues build the first model that can point to objects across many images from free-form text. Multimodal models read single images well and grasp groups loosely. Precise pointing inside a group, though, has lagged. Chain-of-thought tricks that chain single-image pointing prove shaky.

Their model, Migician, learns the skill end to end. A new data set of over six hundred thousand examples covers many multi-image pointing tasks. It adds fresh free-form instructions generated for this purpose. A dedicated benchmark, MIG-Bench, scores the skill directly. Migician beat the best existing models by a wide margin on it. It even passed models many times its size. Code, model, data, and benchmark are all released openly.
arxiv-2501-05967:
Mihaescu, Isar, and Macovei study a tiny chip trap paired with paired electron dots in this twenty twenty-five paper. The dots act like small gates for charge, and the trap holds a wave field that links to them. The team tunes the pair so the dot beat is twice the trap beat.

Inside, that tuned link gives rise to a rich set of joint acts in the pair. The flow of charge through the dots ties to the wave field in the trap in a bent, non-plain way. Both parts show sharp shifts at key points as the settings change. The light-like flux from the trap can bunch or spread, and at some points the trap acts like a tiny laser at wave-band rates.
arxiv-2501-06367:
Hassan Nassar and four co-authors design a hardware fingerprint that resists both wear and learning attacks. Their work appeared in twenty twenty-five. Such fingerprints, called PUFs, turn tiny manufacturing quirks of memory chips into unclonable keys for authentication.

Non-volatile memory cells that hold several levels give rich, hard-to-model responses. But frequent writing wears the cells out, shortening the device's life. The team first models how wear degrades response quality. On that model they build a design that spreads writes evenly and eases stress per cell. The result lasts sixty-two times longer than the best prior design. Protection against machine learning attacks stays intact.
arxiv-2501-06467:
Rui Liu, Zhenqi Jia, Feilong Bao, and Haizhou Li published a computing paper in 2025 on making synthesized conversation sound more expressive. Systems usually look only at the current dialogue, ignoring stored past chats that hold useful style knowledge. Their scheme retrieves similar stored dialogues by both meaning and style from a purpose-built database. A graph structure then blends style cues from old and new exchanges.

The merged style knowledge feeds the speech synthesizer. On a standard conversation dataset, both measured and human-judged scores beat baseline systems for expressiveness. The authors release code and audio samples. They argue remembered conversations make agents sound more empathetic.
arxiv-2501-06567:
Yuru Li, Jiawei Tan, and Qingying Xue prove weighted bounds for commutators of singular integrals in a 2025 paper. These operators sit at the heart of harmonic analysis and partial differential equations. They measure how multiplication and averaging fail to commute, a gap with deep bounds attached.

Working under flexible integral conditions of Young type, the authors first pin the operators down with sparse domination. Dyadic methods then deliver two classic bounds with general weights. A version with numbers sharpens the second bound. Their proof splits a link between the count and a small parameter that earlier work kept fused. The results cover a wide shelf of such tools, from Calderon commutators to Fourier multipliers.
arxiv-2501-06667:
Andrew Diggs and co-authors compute why light slowly degrades hydrogenated amorphous silicon, the coating that passivates many solar cells, in a 2025 paper. The damage comes from silicon-hydrogen bonds snapping. Using density functional theory with path-sampling methods, the team measured the energy barrier for that snap in p-type, intrinsic, and n-type material.

The barrier dropped asymmetrically: about 0.3 electron volts for p-type and 0.1 for n-type, matching experiments. A model based on local electric interactions fingers the cause, a high-energy donor state created by the freed hydrogen at the transition point. Adding simulated sunlight, electron-hole pairs shaved another 0.4 or so off the barrier, again matching measured degradation.
arxiv-2501-06867:
Alice Nardelli and co-authors give a robot arm a personality and test whether people can sense it, in a paper from 2025. Personality shapes how humans read each other, and robot makers use it to smooth teamwork. Past work is scattered and built mostly for human-shaped robots. Factory arms, though, are set to work beside people more and more.

The team loaded a full cognitive model of personality into a Kinova arm. The model rates the arm on traits like care, openness to people, and ease. Those ratings steer how the arm moves, picks acts, and reacts. In a joint game study with many sessions, users played with arms set to unlike traits. Some arms also spoke, while others used only gestures. The study asks whether shape-free robots can still project a clear character.
arxiv-2501-07067:
Irin Babu Vathachira, Yael Hillman, and Amit Kashi map, in a 2025 paper, how mass moves between the two stars of a symbiotic system. In such a pair, a white dwarf draws matter from a larger companion star. The wind from the companion is the key stream, and how that wind behaves decides the route the mass takes.

The authors split the settings into two regimes. If the wind is still slow when it reaches a key balance surface, it gets trapped and funneled toward the white dwarf. If it speeds up enough to escape first, it spreads out in all directions, and only a fraction lands on the dwarf. They worked through 375 combinations of white dwarf mass, donor mass, and donor size. For each, they found the spacing at which the trapped route takes over.
arxiv-2501-07367:
Jean-Pierre Gazeau and Hamed Pejhan unite three fields in one symmetry frame, in a 2025 physics study. The fields are the graviton, the photon, and a middle case called the partially massless graviton. All are set in de Sitter space, the curved spacetime of a universe with steady expansion. The frame rests on conformal symmetry, which keeps angles while stretching lengths.

The authors build on Dirac's six-cone method and a group-based view in Wigner's sense. The method first served flat space; here it stretches to curved de Sitter space. Massless and partly massless fields of any spin above zero get one shared treatment. The authors say the unity clarifies core parts of gravity theory.
arxiv-2501-07567:
Cosima du Pasquier and co-authors build a design framework for knitted fabrics that predicts how they stretch. Their 2025 paper starts at the yarn level with detailed finite element models. Such models are accurate but far too slow for design work.

A simplified energy model compresses the yarn results into three numbers that forecast behaviour in minutes. The forecasts matched bench tests, so new knits can be screened without fresh trials. Mixed fabrics are handled as patchworks joined like springs in line or side by side. A compression sleeve with even pressure shows the method in action. The authors aim at faster custom textile design.
arxiv-2501-07867:
Benjy Marks, Shivakumar Athani, and Itai Einav offer a new way to model sand and grain flows in a 2025 paper. The two standard paths track each grain or treat the pile as a smooth bulk. Both tell a fixed story of motion. Their model instead tracks the empty spaces between grains as they shift under gravity.

The model weaves in known grain tricks: sorting by size, mixing, and the rest angle of a pile. It can show both a still pile and a flowing one, split by how full the space is. Grain size steers flow and sorting in the model. Tests on a falling column and a draining silo matched the model's claims.
arxiv-2501-08167:
Rewina Bedemariam and co-authors test whether language models can judge the summaries that other language models write. Their 2025 paper starts from a boom in model-made summaries of open survey text. Such summaries promise fast themes and moods from rich feedback, yet they can drift from what people truly said. One top model wrote theme summaries of survey replies. Three other models then judged how true those summaries stayed to the source.

Human ratings gave the yardstick, checked with known agreement scores. Model judges scaled well and scored near human raters overall. Humans still caught fine, context-bound shades that models missed. The authors close with advice for safe use of model judges on loose text.
arxiv-2501-08267:
Mosab Alfaqeeh finds named people, places, and groups in social media posts by fusing text, image, and hashtag cues, in a paper from 2025. Social posts are short, slangy, and vague, so text only tools miss or misread many names.

The TriMod frame joins all three cue types with transformer focus, which maps image objects to text names with more care than past fusions. It also evens out gaps in how each cue type spreads. On a mixed media test set, the frame beat top past tools on precision, recall, and their blend by clear margins.
arxiv-2501-09067:
Eunmo Ahn and nine co-authors weigh an invisible galaxy cluster by the way its gravity smears distant galaxies, and rebuild the crash that made it. The cluster is low in mass yet sports two radio relics, shock glows, flung unusually far apart, about 2.7 million parsecs. Their 2025 weak-lensing study, the first for this system, uses deep Subaru telescope images. It finds two dark matter clumps, north and south, about five hundred thousand parsecs apart. Simulations then test merger stories that fit.

Radio relics mark the shock fronts of cluster collisions, cosmic crashes in slow motion. Lensing gives the mass map that light alone cannot. The authors pair the map with simulations to rewind the crash. Their cluster's relics sit oddly far out for its size, which the merger story must explain. The paper is the third in a series on this one system.
arxiv-2501-09167:
Weizhen Wang, Chenda Duan, Zhenghao Peng, Yuxin Liu, and Bolei Zhou build a benchmark that tests whether vision-language models understand scenes well enough to act in them. Their 2025 paper notes that such models are promising as embodied agents for driving and mobility, but no standard closed-loop test measured their spatial reasoning and step-by-step decisions.

MetaVQA generates question-answer pairs automatically from two large driving data sets, using marked top-down views with ground-truth labels. Questions target object relations and scene dynamics in real traffic situations. Fine-tuning on the benchmark sharpened models' spatial reasoning and produced safer driving behavior in simulation. Skills learned in simulation also transferred to real-world observation, the team reports.
arxiv-2501-09267:
Abdalwhab Abdalwhab and co-authors ask whether flexible vision-language models are ready to spot pipes, ducts, and wiring parts on real construction sites, in a 2025 paper. Robots with cameras could one day check mechanical, electrical, and plumbing work on their rounds. Open-vocabulary models can look for anything named in words, with no special training, which makes them tempting for messy sites.

The team filmed sites with a ground robot and labeled the parts by hand. They then raced the open models against small detectors fine-tuned on the labeled set. Flexibility did not win: the tuned lightweight models beat the open ones by a wide margin in this special setting. The authors conclude that, for now, site robots still need training on the exact parts they must find.
arxiv-2501-09467:
Tundulyasaree and co-authors design taxes and subsidies to push city freight off trucks in a 2025 paper. Buses, trams, metros, and barges run on schedules with spare capacity. A city can tax road freight and subsidize line services to shift the balance.

Their two-level model lets authorities set the prices while forwarders pick routes in response. Fully funding the line service turns out to be the optimal, budget-wise policy. A worked Berlin case cut driving distance by about three percent, with line usage jumping sharply from a tiny base. Denser line schedules and clustered deliveries deepened the shift, though operating costs rose with the tax.
arxiv-2501-09567:
Tong Liu, Ying-Hai Wu, Hong-Hao Tu, and Tao Xiang bridge two ways of building wave functions for exotic spin states. Their paper is from two thousand twenty-five. Chiral spin liquids are magnetic states whose spins swirl in a fixed handedness. They are close cousins of the fractional quantum Hall states of electrons, and some host particles prized for quantum computing.

The authors start from a field theory model and turn its wave functions into a second form based on fictitious particles. That form can be converted into a network layout that computers handle well. In one dimension, the states match known critical spin chains. In two dimensions, they sort the states into their topological sectors in a systematic way. Parent Hamiltonians are derived for one series of these liquids.
arxiv-2501-09767:
Tuowei Wang and five co-authors present LeMo, a system for teaching language models to handle longer texts, in a 2025 paper. Longer context windows are in demand, but training for them eats memory, mostly through stored intermediate values. Existing shortcuts cut the cost of weight updates rather than this memory load.

LeMo rests on a pattern the authors call contextual token sparsity: many tokens add little in long texts. The system drops dull tokens layer by layer, predicts the drop pattern cheaply in advance, and uses tuned low-level code to cash the savings. Model quality is preserved while memory use falls. The work opens a path to long-context training on more modest hardware.
arxiv-2501-09867:
G-functions are power series with deep ties to geometry, and Yves André, a solo author, surveys their role in arithmetic geometry, the field where number theory meets shapes. These functions solve the equations that govern how the periods of a family of shapes change as the family bends. Where two such functions meet in an algebraic relation, the meeting point often has extra hidden symmetry.

A principle from Bombieri caps how special such points can be, an idea that fed into a famous conjecture on unlikely meetings in geometry. André closes with the method's recent revival around the Zilber-Pink conjecture, a sweeping claim about when special points can appear. The survey links old results to the newest work.
arxiv-2501-09967:
Fuseini Mumuni and Alhassan Mumuni survey explainable artificial intelligence, from transparent models to explaining the biggest black boxes, in a 2025 paper. Powerful models often hide their decision logic, which breeds distrust and slows adoption in high-stakes fields like healthcare and self-driving cars.

The survey covers inherently interpretable models first, then methods that pry open opaque ones, including large language models themselves. A newer twist uses language and vision-language models as explainers of other systems, producing high-level explanations in words people grasp. The authors weigh principles, strengths, and weaknesses across the field, with side-by-side comparisons where data allows. They close with the open challenges: explanations can be unfaithful, fragile, or hard to evaluate. Future directions aim at explanations users can trust and test.
arxiv-2501-10167:
Simulating two fluids that do not mix, like oil and water, means tracking a moving interface that can stretch and break. Jing-Wei Chen and co-authors improve a phase field model for this task. Their version adds a diffusion term whose strength adapts to how far the interface sits from its ideal profile. They also analyze the model's mobility so it approaches the sharp-interface limit as the interface gets thin.

They also generalize the smoothed spike functions used to compute surface tension, keeping the total tension exact even off equilibrium. And they prove that small under-resolved structures do not shrink away as they do in the classic method. Tests from rising bubbles to droplet breakup matched experiments and theory, and the recommended mobility range worked across all of them.
arxiv-2501-10867:
Gonzalo Herrera shows how dark matter detectors, now fine neutrino catchers too, can probe new physics through neutrinos. The paper from twenty twenty-five offers three ideas. Each turns a low-energy neutrino signal into a test of physics past the Standard Model. The detectors in view were built for dark matter but see solar neutrinos well.

First, solar neutrinos can trigger the Migdal effect through coherent scattering on nuclei, leaving a set mark. Second, a radioactive source near a liquid xenon tank could reveal the neutrino anapole moment by electron scattering. Third, neutrinos tied to a light dark sector may carry boosted electromagnetic traits from loop effects. Herrera weighs how well near-term detectors can test that case. The paper recasts sunk-cost rigs as broad physics probes.
arxiv-2501-10967:
Zhanpeng Chen and five co-authors published a paper in 2025 on how vision-language models number the parts of an image. These models read pictures as a stream of patches, and the usual numbering runs in reading order from one corner. That scheme buries the center, where the subject usually sits, under fading attention from a common position trick.

Their method numbers patches from the edges inward, widening the sharp central zone step by step like a pyramid. Related patches and the instruction text end up closer in the numbering, so attention lands more sensibly. Tests across model sizes showed steady gains in general image understanding. The code is public, so other teams can adopt the scheme directly.
arxiv-2501-11067:
Elad Levi and Ilan Kadar build a testing ground for conversational AI systems. Their paper appeared in two thousand twenty-five. Chatbots built on large language models must hold multi-turn talks, call the right tools, and obey strict policy rules. Old test methods are fixed sets of cases made by hand. They miss the mess and variety of real use.

Their framework, IntellAgent, is open source and uses several agents working together. It builds varied test cases on its own from policy-driven graphs. It also creates realistic events and runs live talks between a fake user and the system under test. The output gives fine-grained reports on where a system fails. That detail helps builders fix weak spots that coarse scores would hide.
arxiv-2501-11167:
Mustafa Ghaleb and co-authors propose FedTest, a testing scheme for federated learning that speeds convergence and blunts adversarial attacks, published in 2025. Federated learning trains models in parallel at many users' sites, preserving privacy and using distributed computing power. Standard strategies struggle to judge the quality of received models, handle uneven models, and limit the harm from bad ones.

Under FedTest, each user's local data trains that user's model and also tests the models of the others. Users can then score each model accurately. Those scores drive efficient aggregation and expose malicious models. Numerical results showed faster convergence and a reduced influence of malicious users, the authors report. They argue the scheme makes federated systems both more efficient and more robust overall.
arxiv-2501-11367:
A measure is called spectral when the functions living on it can be rebuilt from a tidy set of pure waves, like notes making a chord. Kolountzakis and Wu study a simple shape: two unit line segments, one on each axis, starting at the same offset point t. Earlier work had settled many values of that offset. This paper pushes the classification close to complete.

The authors show the measure is not spectral whenever the offset lies between minus one half and zero, and also whenever the offset is irrational. One case, the offset of exactly minus one half, remains undecided. In every known spectral example for this shape, the wave set lies along a single line. The paper gives a simple test for when such line spectra can occur. The result narrows a long-running question in harmonic analysis to a single point.
arxiv-2501-11467:
Krishnendu Chatterjee and five co-authors build proof slips that let anyone check a model checker's answer cheaply. Checkers can err, and a wrong pass on a safety claim is a grave risk. Their 2025 work gives slips for chance-based models that mix choice and odds, the Markov decision processes.

The slips rest on plain fixed-point math and work for any finite model of the kind. Stock methods can mint them with little extra cost. The team proved the slips sound in a proof assistant and built a checked checker for them. A standard checker was taught to mint slips too. The first formal check of a known benchmark set caps the work. Trust can now be earned line by line.
arxiv-2501-11767:
Pelin Çiloğlu and four co-authors make the math of drying solar cell ink solvable at real-world scale. Printed organic solar cells form their light-catching pattern as a wet mix of polymer, acceptor, and solvent dries. Their 2025 model couples a phase field equation for the separating mix with fluid flow equations and an evaporation law. The result is a huge, coupled system of equations at every time step. The paper's core is a preconditioner, a solver setup that makes those systems tractable for iterative methods.

Without such solvers, the model stays a theory nobody can run. Morphology decides a printed cell's efficiency, so simulating the drying is designing the device. The authors use finite elements with a semi-implicit time march. Their contribution is numerical craft in service of a materials question. Faster solves mean more recipes can be tried in silico.
arxiv-2501-11867:
Heidarpur, Mirhassani, and Chang build chip hardware that multiplies large polynomials twice as fast as the best prior designs. Polynomial multiplication sits at the heart of many modern encryption schemes, including ones built to resist quantum attacks. Their 2025 design runs on programmable FPGA chips and uses a number theoretic transform, a number-based cousin of the fast Fourier method.

Data flows through first-in, first-out buffers so every stage works at once, letting the chip finish two polynomials of degree n in about n over two clock cycles. That halves the processing time of the fastest reported work. The design also uses fewer chip resources than that fastest rival. The authors target faster encryption hardware.
arxiv-2501-11967:
Xiaochuan Xu, Zeqiu Xu, Peiyang Yu, and Jiani Wang propose a hybrid attention framework for fake news detection with large language models in a 2025 paper. The flood of online news has made fake stories a grave social risk, and text alone holds both counts and deep meaning that can flag them.

Their method blends textual statistical features with deep semantic features read by a language model. A hybrid attention step homes in on the feature mixes that count most for spotting a fake. On a large fake news data set, the model beat past tools. Heat maps and value checks aid trust in its calls.
arxiv-2501-12067:
Hamid Nasiri and Peter Garraghan present in 2025 EDoRA, a lean way to fine-tune large models by splitting weights into size and direction parts. Lean tuning cuts trainable weights, but past forms can lag full tuning in how they learn. Scale across tasks has also been a weak point.

EDoRA freezes low-rank parts set by a value split method and adds one small trainable block between them. On a standard language test set, it matches or beats top past methods. It does so with up to thirty times fewer trainable weights. The gain suits teams that tune models on tight memory budgets, and code is shared in public.
arxiv-2501-12267:
Chaohao Xie, Kai Han, and co-authors fill missing regions in videos with a diffusion model that needs no extra training, in work from twenty twenty-five. Flow guided inpainting copies pixels from other frames, but big holes have no matching pixels at their center. Diffusion models invent rich content, yet naive use breaks time consistency.

Their framework steers the denoising process with valid pixels pulled along optical flow paths. Those pixels constrain the random noise the model starts from. Filled frames then feed further propagation and generation rounds. Different noise seeds give varied but coherent results. Tests beat leading video inpainting methods on both time coherence and fidelity, the authors report.
arxiv-2501-12567:
Cuellar and five co-authors report on gas near distant quasars that also show strong molecular and neutral hydrogen absorption. Their study from two thousand twenty-five uses the X-shooter tool on the Very Large Telescope. They look for absorption from highly ionized nitrogen close to the quasar's own redshift.

Nitrogen lines showed in nine of thirteen quasars, a far higher rate than in systems far from quasars. The ionized gas moved over much wider speed ranges than the neutral gas, so the two seem split in motion. Bluer, outflowing parts showed higher ionization. The team reads these systems as key stages when a quasar still sits in rich gas, before or as outflows start.
arxiv-2501-12667:
Wenbin Zhou, Liyan Xie, Zhigang Peng, and Shixiang Zhu wrote this paper in two thousand twenty-five. It spots the moment a data stream's pattern shifts, by way of score matching with noise.

Classic change-point tools lean on set forms for the data before and after the shift. That fails on rich, high-dimensional streams. Here the score of the data law is learned by adding noise, then cleaning it back, a trick called denoising score matching. A CUSUM test runs on those scores, in both offline and online forms. Theory shows the noise scale can be tuned to sharpen the catch. Tests on fake data and on quake precursor hunts back the claim.
arxiv-2501-12967:
Serena Dipierro and co-authors study when a population survives in a hostile region under mixed forms of spread. Their paper appeared in 2025. The model is a logistic diffusion equation, where growth is limited by crowding. Spread is driven by a blend of fractional operators, covering both normal wandering and long jumps. Outside the region, conditions are lethal.

Survival hinges on the spectrum of the region, its size and shape in effect. The authors prove ranges where steady living states exist and where only extinction remains. A striking example shows both normal and jumpy spread alone would kill the species. Yet adding even a tiny amount of a concentration pattern lets it survive. The work clarifies how nonlocal spread changes the fate of populations in poor habitats.
arxiv-2501-13067:
Studzinski and co-authors construct in 2025 special matrix units for the walled Brauer algebra, a structure tied to partly transposed permutation operators. The algebra matters for quantum information, above all for fast circuits that run the mixed Schur-Weyl transform. Past work used basis paths akin to family trees.

Their units are built explicitly in one ideal layer and adapted to a paired symmetric group action. The approach hints at a recursive route through the remaining layers. A second method uses tensor networks of coupling coefficients, but needs certain counting values. Tests apply the results to a special case in the paper.
arxiv-2501-13167:
Juan Cruz-Martinez, Alexander Huss, and Christopher Schwan speed up particle physics forecasts in a 2025 paper. Collider studies need theory predictions under many input settings. Precomputed grids let those predictions be rechecked almost instantly. One key process, Drell-Yan production, lacked grids at the highest precision order.

That process makes electroweak bosons when quarks collide. It tightly constrains the quark content of the proton. The team linked a precision event generator to a grid library. They release grids spanning the measurements used in global fits. With them, they probe a curious cancellation between quark channels. They also test a shortcut approximation long used in place of full results. The grids should sharpen future maps of the proton's insides.
arxiv-2501-13567:
Jeonghun Cho and Gary Geunbae Lee improve medical question answering by teaching the system what background it needs first, in a 2025 paper. Retrieval-based answering fetches outside documents, but medical texts are dense and long, and readers may mistrust or misread them. Their compressor, K-comp, first writes down the prior knowledge a question requires. It then squeezes the fetched passages while weaving that knowledge in.

The result is a short context aligned with the question's intent. Reader models guided by that context answer more accurately and lean on the passages instead of guessing. The authors frame knowledge injection as the fix for two failures at once: overload from thousand-token documents and hallucination from stray, off-topic content. The method targets closed expert domains where readers lack background.
arxiv-2501-13767:
Mingzhao Wang and a team of co-authors solve the traveling salesman problem with a diffusion model that guesses whole tours at once. Their work appeared in twenty twenty-five. Step-by-step solvers are slow; parallel ones are fast but sloppy, and tours suffer.

Their system, DEITSP, denoises many candidate tours simultaneously in a single step, steadied by a self-consistency trick. A dual graph transformer reads both city points and the roads between them, with fewer layers for speed. Iterations alternate adding and removing noise, widening the search beyond earlier diffusion attempts. A noise schedule refines the solution space as it goes. On real and large synthetic instances, the solver matched or beat rival neural methods on quality, speed, and generalization.
arxiv-2501-13867: Antonino Ficarra wrote a 2025 paper in algebra presenting the theory of cotangent functors in the approach of Palamodov. Cotangent functors are tools that measure how algebraic structures deform. Alongside the theory, Ficarra presents a conjecture of Herzog tying the vanishing of certain of these functors to a prized property of rings called being a complete intersection. The abstract is brief, so this account stays at the level of what the work sets out to do.
arxiv-2501-13967:
Haoxuan Che, Yifei Wu, Haibo Jin, Yong Xia, and Hao Chen wrote this machine learning paper, published in 2025. It trains medical image models across hospitals that cannot share their scans, in a way that still works on scans from new places.

In federated learning, each hospital trains locally and only model updates travel. The hard part is handling the style gap between hospitals' images. Older methods remix the traits of known sites, which may never mimic a truly new site. The authors' framework instead invents fresh image styles by pushing generated pictures away from the originals at the feature level, then trains the task model to close that gap. They also note that sites contribute unevenly to the shared model's toughness. The paper builds on that observation to balance the training.
arxiv-2501-14267:
Xing-Jian Lv and co-authors propose reading the gamma rays from nearby gas clouds to settle whether a local cosmic ray source shapes the particles reaching Earth. Their 2025 paper starts from a puzzle: cosmic ray proton and helium spectra show a bump, and their arrival directions wobble, both hinting at one nearby accelerator.

Giant molecular clouds near the solar system work as passive detectors: cosmic rays striking their gas produce gamma rays that reveal the local particle flux at each cloud. A nearby source would stamp different spectral features on different clouds; a galaxy-wide cause would stamp them uniformly. The authors show upcoming observatories can detect the difference, and that the energy trend of the gamma-ray spectrum can even locate the source. The proposal turns the solar neighborhood into an instrument nature already built.
arxiv-2501-14467:
Surya Peravali and co-authors improve the simulation of aerosol injectors used in X-ray imaging. Such injectors spray nanoparticles into a tight stream for single particle snapshots. Better design means denser streams, less stray gas, and sharper patterns. Trial and error in the lab is slow, so sound simulation matters.

Their framework tracks both the carrier gas and the particles through the injector and into the vacuum chamber. A hybrid method blends molecule level and fluid level math to span the flow's many scales. First benchmarks of the coupled parts are shown. The whole chain is checked against lab data, giving designers a trusted sandbox for tuning.
arxiv-2501-14567:
Dominika Burešová builds a small, countable algebra in which every pair of linked events has a shared cause inside the system, in work from 2025. The demand comes from a principle of Reichenbach: when two events rise together, a common cause should explain the link. Philosophers and logicians have tested the principle in many settings.

Whether a countable example could meet the demand stayed open. Large algebras were known, but small ones were not. The note constructs one directly. The example keeps the event structure modest while still supplying a common cause for every positive correlation. It answers a standing question in the logic of causation, with a construction others can inspect and vary.
arxiv-2501-14667:
Robert Mihai Amarinei reports in 2025 the status of an experiment in Switzerland hunting for a muon decay that standard theory forbids. The decay, one muon turning into three electrons, should occur at a rate near one in 10 to the 54th power even in theories that give neutrinos mass. Seeing it at all would prove new physics.

The detector, now under construction, aims first at a sensitivity near one in 10 to the 15th power, then ten times finer after upgrades. Novel silicon trackers must catch the faint triple electron signal amid a storm of normal decays. The talk lays out the build's progress and near term plans. Rare decay hunts like this one probe mass scales no collider can reach.
arxiv-2501-14867:
Kaili Cao and Marc Pinsonneault model red giant stars in a paper from two thousand twenty-five. They focus on two signs of what happens inside such stars. One is the first dredge-up, when surface material mixes with processed matter from inside. The other is a bump in brightness along the red giant path.

They compare survey data on real giants with models built by a standard star code. The models match the broad trends with mass and metal content, but the observed surface change is smaller than predicted. The brightness bump also sits higher in the data than in models. The authors discuss fixes and propose lithium as a sharp test for telling them apart.
arxiv-2501-15067:
Yuntong Hu and co-authors present CG-RAG, a system for research question answering, in this 2025 paper. Answering research questions needs exact search across scientific papers. Standard retrieval methods can miss how papers link to each other through citations.

CG-RAG builds a graph view of the citation network that holds both direct and hidden links. A search step mixes word-based and meaning-based signals inside that graph. A final step uses the graph context to help a language model write a precise answer. Tests on several research benchmarks beat strong prior methods. Both search accuracy and answer quality rose under this design.
arxiv-2501-15367: Guangjun Zhu, Jiaxin Li, Yijun Cui, and Yi Yang wrote a 2025 paper in commutative algebra on the depth of powers of edge ideals for a special family of cycles. Depth measures how far a module is from being Cohen-Macaulay, a central quality gauge. For edge weighted cycles whose ideals are integrally closed, the authors derive exact formulas for the depth of every power of the edge ideal. The hosted text gives only this one sentence summary, so the result is described at that level.
arxiv-2501-15667:
John Campbell extends a classic matrix measure to a broader family tied to richer symmetry tools, in a math paper from 2025. The classic measure weights permutations by character values for a chosen shape. Prior work replaced those weights with values from symmetric functions, which opened a more general view.

Campbell goes one step further using quasisymmetric functions, whose bases are indexed by ordered splits rather than shapes alone. He defines the new family through a recent power sum basis in that setting. He then proves a counting formula for the weights in a key special case linked to a Schur-like basis, giving the new objects a firm combinatorial footing.
arxiv-2501-15767:
Muhammad Maaz and Timothy Chan tackled a new check task for chance based models. Their paper, from twenty twenty-five, deals with Markov processes whose rates come from machine learning. A learned rate is not a fixed number, so plain checks fail. For a wide set of models, from linear to neural nets, they cast key checks as a two part math program. Those checks ask if a state can be reached, how long it takes, and what total gain accrues.

Their solve scheme breaks the program and spreads bounds to speed the search. Tests showed solves up to one hundred times faster than top tools. They show use in a real health care case and share a free tool for the work.
arxiv-2501-15867:
Alexey Maltsev studies the level lines of layered potentials on a plane, in a paper from 2025. Such potentials arise in the physics of two-layer systems, where electrons move in a near-regular but not repeating field. The lines where the potential holds a fixed value trace how particles can travel.

The setup is a special case of a classic problem named for Novikov, with four repeating rhythms in the field. That problem's tools apply here, but the layered case has its own clear traits. Maltsev sets out those traits and what they imply for line shapes. The work speaks to transport in layered materials, where line topology can switch behavior sharply.
arxiv-2501-16067: Joop Niekus traces the path of Brouwer's use of free choice chains in the base of math, up to the year a way to use them well was found. The paper, from two thousand twenty-five, is a work of history and close reading. From the rules of that first good use, Niekus draws a small set of base rules. With just those, he rebuilds Brouwer's work from that year on. The rebuild matches the source with care, and makes clear why the proofs work.
arxiv-2501-16167:
Onur Alican and a team of co-authors built an index to grade how like a true voltage source a power device acts. Their paper, from twenty twenty-five, deals with power systems now ruled by electronics. New devices crowd in with wild dynamics. Grid staff need to know how close each acts to the classic source models they trust. Their index is scored per tone band, so gaps show where they live.

Both makers and grid operators can use the score. It flags in which tone ranges a model under study will part from the reference. Readers who plan the new grid get a shared gauge for a mixed fleet. One number per band beats a vague claim of like acts.
arxiv-2501-16267: Vikulova constructs an example in algebraic geometry, published in 2025, reaching the largest symmetry group a certain surface can have. She builds a smooth del Pezzo surface of degree two over a field where the surface has no points, yet its automorphism group matches the biggest one known over friendlier fields. The group is a specific simple group times a two-element factor. The construction shows the extreme case survives even when the surface carries no points at all.
arxiv-2501-16567:
Marcin Szyniszewski and co-authors compute how graphene sticks to boron nitride in a 2025 physics paper. Stacks of these atom-thin sheets form van der Waals structures with prized electronic traits. How the layers grip and relax against each other shapes those traits.

They used quantum Monte Carlo methods, which treat the weak grip forces with high accuracy, to map grip strength against layer shift. Feeding that map into elasticity theory gave the relaxed shapes of the layers, with no hidden alternate forms. Simple pair formulas fit the grip map well. In wrapped stacks, new moiré patterns arise whose size depends on twist angle, and their bands shift if one wrapping layer flips.
arxiv-2501-16967:
Julien Dörner and co-authors measure how much doubt in proton-proton cross sections clouds the gamma-ray and neutrino skies. Cosmic ray sources hide because charged rays bend in magnetic fields. Gamma rays and neutrinos travel straight, so they carry the clues. Both are born when cosmic protons collide, and the rates of those collisions come from tuned models.

Their 2025 paper spans energies from the GeV to the PeV range. Different cross-section models, each fit to accelerator data, spread the predicted fluxes by amounts the authors quantify. That spread limits how firmly a bright spot can be tied to proton acceleration. Multimessenger astronomers get an error budget for the very signals they hunt sources with.
arxiv-2501-17067:
Sara Doan and co-authors present, in a 2025 paper, the first systematic survey of coronal lines in the spectra of nearby type 1 quasars. Coronal lines come from highly stripped atoms near a feeding black hole. The team examined eleven such lines in Sloan survey spectra.

Strong coronal emission proved rare: only 885 of 19,508 galaxies showed even one line. Lines needing the most energy were rarer still. The most common line tracked closely with the quasar's total power output. The authors suggest dust in the emitting region suppresses most of these signals. They also measured how often ionized outflows appear alongside. A full catalog gives black hole researchers a new census to mine.
arxiv-2501-17167:
Yaojie Hu and eight co-authors present, in a 2025 paper, a team of AI agents that writes computer programs under quality control. Given a problem stated in English plus a set of unit tests, the system must produce code that passes. Its agents play the roles of a software team: writing code, testing it, and debugging their own work.

The new piece is a quality checker that imagines running the code against the tests before anything is run for real. Its verdicts steer the flow: send the answer, restate the problem, or step back and redo earlier work. The checker accepts correct programs reliably and shields the team from faulty self-made tests. The system set top scores on four standard coding benchmarks.
arxiv-2501-17467:
Riku Kuze, Shigeo Kimura, and Ke Fang model black hole systems in this 2025 paper. The systems pair a black hole with a normal star that feeds it gas. Some of them shine at extreme gamma-ray energies, and the source of that glow is debated. The team proposes a two-part picture based on how the gas disk behaves.

In their picture, a strongly magnetic disk heats protons and electrons to high speeds. Fast protons then clash with disk gas and light, making very high energy gamma rays and neutrinos. Jets from the black hole add lower energy gamma rays of their own. Added up over many quiet systems, the glow may explain part of the galaxy's diffuse high-energy light.
arxiv-2501-17567:
Emmanuel Irabor, Mariam Musavi, Abhijit Das, and Sergi Abadal wrote a 2025 paper on linking AI chips without wires. AI work keeps demanding more compute, and makers now split jobs across many small chiplets. The links between chips are still stiff and waste power, which caps how far the design can scale.

Wireless links could free chips to talk across a package with less loss. The team weighs what such links can offer multi-chip AI accelerators. Flexible links may let builders mix chip types for each new model family. Their study maps the gains and the hard parts, from signal noise to layout. The work feeds the search for scalable AI hardware.
arxiv-2501-17767:
Ankush Agarwal, Ganesh S, and Chaitanya Devaguptapu answer questions that span tables and prose in a 2025 study. Real questions often need numbers from a table joined with facts buried in text, across several hops. Fine-tuned systems need costly human-made training sets, and language models alone handle single-source text better than mixed sources.

Their hybrid graph approach links table cells and text passages into one structure that a language model can reason over. Building the graph replaces heavy training data with explicit connections. Multi-hop aggregation then follows those links. The design targets accurate answers where evidence is split between structured and unstructured homes.
arxiv-2501-17867:
Naoya Ozaki and five co-authors plan the flight path of DESTINY+, a Japanese mission that will spiral out from Earth on a weak electric engine. Their 2025 paper designs the long climb from Earth orbit to a lunar transfer orbit, a trip of many loops. Weak thrust makes the path sensitive to errors in thrust, timing, and navigation, so the plan must hold up under real-world sloppiness.

The team shapes the path with a method that adjusts the route step by step, using a change of variables tied to the orbit angle. They then run many simulated flights with random errors mixed in. The feedback rules from the same method steered the craft to its target in the tests. The work supports a mission meant to prove deep-space flight on small, cheap launchers.
arxiv-2501-18267:
Georges Neaime gives new presentations for elliptic Artin groups in a 2025 math paper. These groups grow out of braid-like structures and play a role in algebra. Older presentations for the matching monoids had a known flaw: terms could not always be cancelled cleanly.

Neaime shows that the monoids built from his new presentations are cancellative. That result repairs the flaw found in the older forms in print. The work also opens a path toward richer Garside structures for these monoids and groups. Readers in algebra get a firmer base for later study of how these objects are built and compared.
arxiv-2501-18667:
Evgeny Moerman and co-authors test a costly method for computing energy gaps in solids, in a 2025 paper. The method, called EOM coupled cluster, promises steady improvement but suffers large errors when the simulated cell is small. Real cells large enough to avoid those errors are too costly to run.

The team pairs the method with a cheaper approach called GW to estimate gaps for several insulators and semiconductors. The hybrid cuts the needed cell size while keeping accuracy close to measured values. They also find that errors grow when the excited states have less single excitation character. The work offers both a practical route and a clue about why the method errs.
arxiv-2501-18867:
Jianke Zhang and co-authors present a training method for robot control models in a 2025 paper. Models that join vision, language, and action can steer robots, but they lean on high-level meaning and often miss fine spatial detail and how scenes change over time. Those gaps hurt precise tasks such as grasping.

Their model, UP-VLA, trains on two goals at once: grasping the meaning of scenes and words, and predicting what the scene will look like next. The second goal forces attention to space and motion. On a standard robot test set the model beat the prior best by a third, and on real robot tasks it raised success rates, above all where exact position mattered. The authors argue the joint training is the key.
arxiv-2501-19067:
Hossein Zakerinia, Dorsa Ghobadi, and Christoph H Lampert present a 2025 paper on why deep networks that learn several tasks at once still generalize, despite having far more knobs than data points. One leading account says the real learning happens in a small hidden subspace of the full weight space. The authors test that account in multi-task learning.

They build the network directly inside the small subspace, using random expansion tricks to do so. High-accuracy shared solutions then appear with far fewer free parameters than single-task learning needs. From that low intrinsic size they derive generalization bounds that are not vacuous, meaning the promised error ceiling sits below blind guessing.
arxiv-2501-19367:
Mahendra Verma reviews turbulence as a nonequilibrium field theory. His 2025 arXiv paper gathers key results from decades of work. Equilibrium theory treats a truncated Euler system at rest. Its Fourier modes share energy evenly and pass none along. Real hydrodynamic turbulence sits far from that quiet state.

Field theory here yields a scale-dependent viscosity for the flow. Energy flux through scales comes out nonzero, as it must. The energy spectrum also follows from the calculations. Methods extend to passive scalars and magnetized fluids. Weak turbulence and intermittency get brief coverage in the review. The synthesis serves physicists modeling flows from labs to stars. It frames turbulence as a field theory success story.
arxiv-2502-00267:
Jonathan Owens, Bojun Feng, Jie Liu, and David Moore study how water changes carbon capture in a sponge-like crystal, in a 2025 paper. The crystal is a metal-organic framework fitted with amine arms that grab carbon dioxide in a chain reaction. Its uptake curve has a sharp step, which makes it attractive for capture work.

Using atom-level calculations, the team shows how nearby water molecules twist the chain behavior and the energy of capture. They predict a new arrangement in which water and carbon dioxide braid together down the pore. A simpler grid model, adjusted for water, then reproduces the sharp shift in uptake at low pressure. The braid hints that capture may flip into a phase change, a finding that could guide drier or wetter capture designs.
arxiv-2502-00367:
Shin-ichi Matsumura, a solo author, proves a structure theorem for a class of complex spaces in a 2025 paper. The spaces are compact Kähler manifolds whose holomorphic sectional curvature is nowhere negative. Such spaces were known to split nicely when they are projective. Matsumura asks whether the same split holds in the wider Kähler world, where fewer tools apply.

The answer is yes, the author shows. Each such space fibers over a flat base, a finite cover of a torus, with rationally connected fibers. A key step studies directions along which the space is truly flat. The fundamental group turns out to be abelian, tying shape to symmetry.
arxiv-2502-00667:
Maezawa and Saito study an ordering between graphs built from rainbow patterns in colored networks. A rainbow subgraph uses a different color on every edge. One graph sits below another in their order when banning its rainbow form in richly colored complete graphs forces the second form out too.

When one graph contains the other, the order is automatic. Earlier work covered the strange case where a bigger graph still sits below a smaller one. This study turns to pairs where neither graph contains the other. The authors prove many such ordered pairs exist. They also map how those pairs arrange themselves inside the overall order.
arxiv-2502-00867:
Cooper and Okur study how to split a directed network with balanced flow into loops, in a paper from twenty twenty-five. Such a network is called Eulerian when flow in and out match at each point. They count splits of full tours into a given number of smaller loops. They show a signed sum over all counts cancels to zero.

The only case that escapes the rule is a single directed cycle. Their proof uses heaps of pieces, a picture tool for stacked items. They link heaps to splits and to maps of shared edges. A classic inversion step on the split lattice then gives the result. The proof also ties a key graph polynomial to color counts of shared-edge maps.
arxiv-2502-01167:
Daniel Sliwowski and Dongheui Lee teach robots to learn what must be true before and after an action in 2025. A robot that works in daily settings must spot when a task goes wrong. Their system, called ConditionNET, learns these before and after facts from data alone. It uses a vision and language model trained with extra goals for stable features.

The system models how actions link to their before and after facts. That link lifts scores on two tasks: spotting odd events and naming the phase of a task. Tests used two data sets of a robot arm pouring and wiping. One set was made for this work. A live robot trial shows the method in real use.
arxiv-2502-01267:
Alvarez and Ruggieri build a counterfactual test for unfair machine decisions in a 2025 paper. The legal question is sharp: would this person have fared better with a different protected trait? Older situation testing compares similar people, which can miss how traits ripple into other fields.

Their method builds each complainant's counterfactual twin, where the trait flip flows through linked attributes. Test and control groups then compare like with like around that twin. The frame covers single traits and combined ones. For combined traits, testing each trait apart missed the joint harm that scholars feared. Law and causal math meet in one audit tool.
arxiv-2502-01367:
Tom Banks wrote a 2025 physics note on shock wave rules proposed by 't Hooft near black hole horizons. He builds a finite model of those rules from a bold guess about what counts the states in a region of space. The guess treats them as a thin field theory with a cutoff.

In his model the count of states matches the known area law for black hole entropy. The field is a slight shift of free light fermions. Two cutoffs in the model smooth out the sharp clashes that appear in the raw rules when space is finite. The note ties horizon physics to a wider space-time programme Banks has long pursued.
arxiv-2502-01567:
Deqian Kong and co-authors proposed a new class of language models built around latent thought vectors in two thousand twenty-five. In these models, hidden thought vectors follow a stated prior model and guide a Transformer decoder as it writes tokens. Thought is thus an explicit part of the model, not just a by-product.

Training uses variational Bayes with two speeds: fast updates for each text's thought vectors, and slow updates for the shared decoder. The models add new scaling knobs, like more thought vectors or more inference steps. With them, the models beat standard autoregressive and diffusion models on perplexity and zero-shot tasks. They also showed early few-shot reasoning that grew with model size.
arxiv-2502-01667:
Jie Ren and co-authors improve how image diffusion models learn what people like. Their twenty twenty-five paper takes up direct preference methods, now common for tuning such models. Past work gave the same like or dislike label to a final image and its noisy mid-steps.

The authors show that move is flawed in two ways, in slope direction and in rank order. Their method, TailorPO, ranks noisy mid-steps by their own step-wise reward. A simple design then fixes the slope problem while tuning runs. Readers who align image models get a clear case for scoring each step on its own merits.
arxiv-2502-01867:
Anastasiia Soboleva and co-authors present a 2025 arXiv paper on the cold start problem in online advertising. New ads have almost no click history, so click-through forecasts start shaky, and early weak showings can drag an ad down for good. The team builds an upper-confidence-bound algorithm within a multi-armed bandit frame, tuned to position-based auction systems that charge per click.

They derive theory bounds on wasted budget and test the method on synthetic and real platform data. It held up in practice. Alongside long-term gains, they propose a control on how much exploration is allowed, so short-term profit does not bleed while the system learns.
arxiv-2502-02067:
Shivam Singh and co-authors give household robots a way to learn new chores without fresh training data. Their framework, AdaptBot, starts with a large language model's generic plan for a task. Such plans often break on the real limits of a body, a home, or a task, so a knowledge graph of the robot's world steps in to ground each step.

When the graph and the plan disagree, the robot asks a human for help and folds the answer back into its knowledge. Tests in simulated cooking and cleaning worlds show the three-way interplay beating the language model alone by a wide margin. The authors offer the design as a route to assistants that adapt on the spot.
arxiv-2502-02367:
Alexander Kolesov and three co-authors make and move data by use of charge on plates. Their method sets a source spread on one plate of a capacitor. A target spread sits on the other plate, with charge of the flip sign. A neural net learns the field of force between the plates. Points then ride the field lines from one plate to the next.

Points that land, the proof shows, match the target spread. That one trick serves two jobs. It can make new data, and it can move data from one form to next. Toy tasks and image tasks show the method at work. The physics does real work here, not just a nice image. The field's shape moves the points where other plans lean on learned maps or noise steps. Their code is free for all to use.
arxiv-2502-02667:
Amit Kumar and Gojko Vujanovic compute a piece of jet physics in twenty twenty-five. When a fast quark plows through hot QCD matter, it loses energy. Some of that loss comes out as real photons, a process called bremsstrahlung. The authors focus on quarks with very high virtuality and energy.

They work within the higher-twist formalism and build improved emission kernels. Their account includes heavy-quark mass effects and processes that swap fermions and bosons. It also includes coherence effects that older treatments missed. A generalized factorization step, like one used in electron-nucleus scattering, shapes the derivation. Diagrams are sorted by the final particles produced. Readers get sharper kernels for how jets shed energy as light.
arxiv-2502-02767:
Computer science research often involves a kind of honest deception: fake accounts that audit a platform, scraped pages, or probes of a login system. Madelyne Xiao, Andrew Sellars, and Sarah Scheffler argued in 2025 that anti-fraud laws, less studied than hacking statutes, quietly shadow all of that work. Fraud law targets misrepresented identity and false information, which many standard research methods involve.

The authors sort the fraud and deception issues that arise across fields from penetration testing to user studies and AI audits. Two areas get special attention: attacking or auditing AI systems, and research that uses legal identification. They aim to give researchers and lawyers a shared map of a risk both literatures had largely ignored.
arxiv-2502-03067:
Stavros Orfanoudakis, Peter Palensky, and Pedro Vergara argue that pairing large language models with graph neural networks can improve how electric vehicles charge without straining the power grid. As EV adoption grows, uncoordinated charging threatens grid stability. Classic optimizers and reinforcement learning struggle with the size and fast change of the problem.

In their study, language models handle the sequence side of charging decisions, while graph networks extract the relational structure of the grid and vehicles. Together they beat conventional smart charging methods in their tests. The authors present the pairing not just as a performance gain but as an opening for new research directions in energy management.
arxiv-2502-03167:
Shrish Roy and Bernd Ulmann describe a 2025 experiment with an unconventional computer built from oscillators. Interest in non standard computing is rising as classic digital chips hit limits in energy use and speed. An Ising machine is one such design. It links many oscillators so their phase patterns settle into the answer to a hard problem, such as the max cut task. Information lives in how the phases line up against a reference.

The authors built a working oscillator based machine in the lab. They present its design and report results from running it. The paper walks through how the oscillators are coupled and how problems are loaded onto the hardware. Their results add hands on evidence on what these analogue machines can do, beyond theory and simulation.
arxiv-2502-03567:
Luca Cocconi, Yihong Shi, and Andrej Vilfan study information-optimal mixing at low Reynolds number, in a research paper from 2025. At such scales, flow is smooth and reversible, so mixing is hard to gauge. Mutual information between particle positions before and after mixing gives a universal, assumption-free score of how well mixing erased the starting pattern.

For a planar shear flow with a time-varying rate, the authors derive a compact formula for that information. They solve exactly for the best shearing schedule under limits on total shear or on energy loss. The best schedules are universal and symmetric in time in both cases. A minimum energy cost of erasing information follows for a broad class of systems.
arxiv-2502-03667:
Ruiming Cao, Guanghan Meng, and Laura Waller use natural sample motion to reach super-resolution in structured illumination microscopy, published in 2025. That microscopy method normally captures a set of images under different light patterns and computes an image sharper than the diffraction limit allows. Their approach takes a different route.

Instead of many patterns, they use a single speckle illumination pattern and rely on the sample's own motion to encode the fine detail across multiple raw images. From those frames, they jointly estimate both the motion and the super-resolved image. Simulations and experiments both showed the method works, they report. The idea trades controlled illumination hardware for computation, using movement that is already present in many imaging setups.
arxiv-2502-03867:
Kay Barshad, Yair Censor, Walaa Moursi, Tyler Weames, and Henry Wolkowicz examine a widely used optimization approach in a 2025 mathematics study. The method starts from an algorithm that seeks a feasible point for convex constraints. Small extra steps then try to lower an objective value without losing feasibility.

The authors ask when those extra steps are guaranteed to end at a better feasible point than the plain algorithm would reach. They give a condition under which steps based on negative gradient descent fail to deliver that improvement. Knowing the failure case matters because any future guarantee must rule it out, and users can avoid the condition in practice.
arxiv-2502-03967:
Walter Wuensch and co-authors review what sparks vacuum breakdown in high field gear in a 2025 paper. A vacuum arc can wreck devices pushed to fierce electric fields. The review pools lab, theory, and simulation work on how such arcs start.

Conditioning, burn rates by field and heat, and the fields a shape or metal can bear fill the lab side. Stage by stage theory then ties those marks to one spark path. Most of the base work fed the CLIC collider push for steep gradient parts. Links reach out to the wider high field crowd.
arxiv-2502-04067:
Matthew Penn and co-authors speed up family tree building for the genome era. Full likelihood and Bayesian tree methods strain under whole-genome data sets. Distance methods are fast but less trusted, since their scores were seen as weaker. The team builds a Bayesian form of distance methods on an entropy-based score for pairs of species.

They show that score ties closely to the classic likelihood of Felsenstein. Tree estimates on three benchmark sets matched past results well. The method then ran on sixty million sites from 363 bird species in a fair time. It exposed deep doubt about bird splits right after the asteroid impact that killed the dinosaurs. Fast Bayesian trees can now serve genome-scale work.
arxiv-2502-04367:
Kiran Sharma, Ziya Uddin, Adarsh Wadal, and Dhruv Gupta build an image classification system for kidney disease in this two thousand twenty-five paper. Their hybrid deep learning model sorts kidney CT scans into four categories: normal, stone, cyst, and tumor. The design fuses a pre-trained ResNet101 network with a custom convolutional neural network. Feature fusion is meant to sharpen the accuracy of automated diagnosis.

Trained on a dataset of over twelve thousand CT images, the hybrid model reached very high reported accuracy, including perfect testing accuracy in the authors' experiments. It outperformed a standalone ResNet101 on precision and recall while reducing testing time. The authors present the architecture as a robust, efficient candidate for clinical use in automated kidney disease diagnosis.
arxiv-2502-04467:
S Martínez-Rozas and co-authors speed up planning for tethered robot teams in a 2025 paper. A marsupial setup pairs a ground robot with a drone that carries it or powers it through a hanging cable. Planning their joint path means guessing the cable's sag thousands of times, and the accurate curve model is slow.

The team derive a fast analytic stand-in for the hanging tether's shape, plus a compact way to describe its state that avoids collisions. Planners can then test many routes without drowning in curve computations. Faster planning widens where such drone-and-rover teams, useful in collapsed buildings and mines, can be deployed.
arxiv-2502-04567:
Zhuotong Chen and co-authors rethink how language models are trained from human preferences. Standard preference training pairs a favored answer with a disfavored one, chosen by rough rules of thumb with no firm theory behind them. The team instead frames the task as fitting a probability model, where the hard part is estimating a normalizing constant.

Their fix borrows a sampling trick called contrastive divergence to draw hard negative examples straight from the reward model. The samples then serve as the disfavored answers in training. A second version extends the method to online training, where fresh examples arrive as the model learns. On popular alignment benchmarks, the new method beat leading baselines, and the online version improved results further.
arxiv-2502-04667:
