Xinhao Yao and co-authors analyze how chain-of-thought training builds reasoning in language models in a 2025 paper. Models trained to show their steps reason far better, but why that training generalizes was not well understood. The authors argue the core is composition: models combine simple learned skills into solutions for harder, new problems.

Their theory splits generalization error into familiar and novel parts. Models without step training fail on novel compositions, while step-trained models compose old skills and succeed. Controlled tests and real-world checks back the account, including faster convergence. The frame may guide how reasoning data are built.
arxiv-2502-04867:
Oliver Maclaren, Ruanui Nicholson, Joel Trent, Joshua Rottenberry, and Matthew Simpson study how to shrink math models when some settings can not be told apart from data, in work from 2025. Such blur is common when models meet real records. It drives methods that rewrite or cut models down.

Their approach asks when a symbolic rewrite can be swapped for a number check at one reference point. The key object is a reduced picture of which setting mixes drive what the model shows. They prove that, under a clean change of variables, one slope table at that point fixes the whole reduced space. The same checks split strongly and weakly informed setting mixes in near-blur cases.
arxiv-2502-05067:
Tabares and four co-authors programmed a quantum simulator in this paper from twenty twenty-five. Cold atoms in light grids naturally mimic the Fermi-Hubbard model of interacting electrons. New controls let experimenters steer the grid in time, turning the setup into a programmable device. The team built algorithms to prepare ground states on it.

Their variational circuits are pre-compiled for the native model and beat slow adiabatic recipes. The same style reaches extended models with extra hopping terms tied to superconductivity. A second method mimics imaginary-time cooling to refine energies further. Tests used ladder-shaped grids, but the protocols fit flat two-dimensional setups. The authors aim them at regimes classical computers cannot reach.
arxiv-2502-05267:
Ron Belyansky, Cheyne Weis, Ryo Hanai, Peter Littlewood, and Aashish Clerk wrote a 2025 theoretical physics paper on phase transitions in condensates where influence runs one way. Their system is a line of nonlinear bosons, driven and leaking energy, described by a quantum master equation. Neighboring sites interact nonreciprocally, a setup now reachable in superconducting circuits.

With periodic boundaries, the system always settles into a traveling wave condensate that moves at a set speed and rhythm. Open boundaries change everything. The phase diagram gains static and dynamic phases, transitions where a symmetry breaks at a critical exceptional point, and phases where the bulk and the edges behave differently. Mean field analysis maps the terrain. No post selection tricks are needed, aiding experiments.
arxiv-2502-05367:
Almuthanna Alageel and Sergio Maffeis present a 2025 computing paper on spotting the quiet chatter of advanced persistent threats. Such intruders hide command traffic inside ordinary web browsing and can lurk for months. Signature-based alarms largely miss them, since each campaign looks different.

Their system, EarlyCrow, starts from how these campaigns actually behave, the tactics cataloged from recent tools. It summarizes each capture not flow by flow but in pairs, bundling behavior, statistics, and protocol facts into a format called PairFlow. Context around a suspicious connection does the discriminating. On campaigns the system had never seen, it scored a macro F1 of about ninety-three percent with a false positive rate under one percent. The authors aim it at the earliest whisper of an intrusion.
arxiv-2502-05467:
Jingheng Ye and co-authors argue that large language models can be good English tutors, in this 2025 position paper. Schools have begun using such models, but mostly in old drill shapes that ignore how languages are best learned. The authors claim the models fit language teaching far better than that.

They assign the models three roles: enriching lesson materials and simulating students; grading learners and shaping their study paths; and acting as personal tutors that widen access. The paper calls for joint work across fields, weighing risks alongside promise, to fold the models into English teaching with care.
arxiv-2502-05567:
Xiaoyang Liu and seven co-authors present ATLAS, a framework for autoformalizing theorems, in work from 2025. Autoformalization turns plain mathematical text into machine-checkable formal language. Progress is held back by a lack of paired examples, so ATLAS builds such data from a concept repository, with expert iteration and knowledge distillation to improve a student model.

Two new augmentation methods exploit the structure of formal languages. After ten rounds, the team built a dataset of 117k theorem statements at undergraduate level. A translator fine-tuned on that data set a new state of the art over prior systems on all benchmarks. Dataset, model and code are shared in a public repository.
arxiv-2502-05867:
Language models hallucinate facts and slip on arithmetic, so giving them tools helps, but teaching tool use usually needs hand-made example traces. Ne Luo and co-authors ask in 2025 whether models can teach themselves instead. They first probe prompting tricks that coax tool use with no examples, then let the model generate its own practice traces from question-answering and math datasets.

Fine-tuning on those self-made traces lifted scores on a long-tail knowledge test by 3.7 points, on a set never used in training. Results on other test sets were mixed. The study shows both the promise and the limits of demonstration-free tool learning, and where curated examples still earn their keep.
arxiv-2502-05967:
Saaketh Narayan and co-authors present a 2025 computing paper on training large language models in cheap 8-bit arithmetic. The FP8 format promises big speed gains, but low precision makes training touchy. Today's recipes need careful tuning, dynamic scale factors, or smaller models to stay stable.

Their method, µnit Scaling, removes those crutches. It rests on a first-principles look at the operations inside a transformer and makes a few minimal, fixed changes. Settings then carry across model widths, and training numbers match inference numbers. The team trained models from one to thirteen billion parameters with all hidden layer math in FP8. Quality matched the high-precision baselines, and training ran up to a third faster.
arxiv-2502-06067:
David Burt, Renato Berlinghieri, Stephen Bates, and Tamara Broderick build honest error bars for spatial health and environment studies, in a 2025 paper. Officials often need an association, say between air pollution and illness, not just a prediction. Standard machine learning predicts well but says little about such links. Worse, the authors show existing interval methods can miss their promised coverage when the model is wrong and locations are not random, the normal case in spatial work.

Their method constructs frequentist confidence intervals that stay valid under minimal assumptions, driven by how smoothly the association can vary. Policy built on a spurious pollution effect, or a missed real one, is expensive either way. Trustworthy intervals are the difference between evidence and decoration.
arxiv-2502-06167:
Yifang Chen, Xiaoyu Li, Yingyu Liang, Zhenmei Shi, and Zhao Song wrote this 2025 theory paper asking whether the image generators called visual autoregressive transformers can, in principle, express anything. These models build pictures coarse to fine, predicting the next scale rather than the next token, and they have beaten diffusion rivals on quality. The question is their ceiling.

Even a stripped-down version clears it. A single-head model with one self-attention layer and one interpolation layer is already universal: it can approximate any image-to-image Lipschitz function to any accuracy. Flow-based autoregressive transformers inherit the same guarantee. The authors read the theorems as design guidance. The power sits in the bones of the architecture, so engineering effort can go to efficiency and scale instead of rescuing expressiveness that was never in danger.
arxiv-2502-06267:
Nir Gavish and Guy Katriel study optimal regulation under periodic forcing in a 2025 arXiv paper. A controller must choose an effort profile that repeats over time. The forcing from outside also follows a cycle. The problem matters in direct uses and as a model for harder ones. The natural setting uses periodic non-negative measures.

The authors prove a unique best solution exists in that space. Under smooth data, the solution has a density with an explicit formula. The measure is then absolutely continuous in the math sense. When the data has jumps, the solution can include point masses as well. Computer runs fill out the picture for varied cases. They show the rich ways best effort profiles can look.
arxiv-2502-06667:
Shahar Hod, writing alone, derives the survival chances of a biased random walker who can restart. His 2025 paper studies a Sisyphus-like walk. At each step, the walker has a set chance to step toward an absorbing trap at the origin. With the complementary chance, it jumps back to its start instead. The question is how long the walker survives.

Hod solves the time-dependent survival probability in closed form. He proves it decays in an exponential way at late times. A critical starting distance emerges: beyond it, the restarting walker outlives a standard random walker at late times, despite the trap's pull. Below it, restarting hurts. The result is a neat case where a restart rule flips from harmful to helpful at a sharp threshold.
arxiv-2502-07067:
Siddharth Gandhi, Luyu Gao, and Jamie Callan build a code search tool in a 2025 paper. Their task is to find the files in a large code repository that best fit a bug report or question. Commit histories, often ignored, hold clues about which files change for which reasons. The system mines those histories.

A first pass uses BM25 search over commit messages. A neural model based on CodeBERT then reranks the results. Tests on seven popular open projects show large gains over the BM25 baseline, up to eighty percent on key scores. The authors hope the tool will help language model agents fix bugs.
arxiv-2502-07167:
Li-Juan Li and co-authors ask how much quantumness survives in the curved spacetimes of an expanding or contracting universe, in work from 2025. A detector moving through such a space, coupled to a quantum field, acts as a probe of the local quantum weather.

Modeling the detector as an open system, the team tracked its uncertainty and coherence in de Sitter and anti-de Sitter space. Acceleration in one and boundary conditions in the other shaped the early evolution, and both quantities oscillated when the detector started in a superposition. High temperature damped the oscillations. In the long run both spacetimes settled to the same values, set only by the ratio of the detector's energy gap to temperature.
arxiv-2502-07267:
David Senjaya and co-authors probe the inside of an exotic black hole for signs of instability. The extremal dyonic Kerr-Sen black hole is a charged, spinning solution whose interior holds closed timelike curves — paths that loop back in time. Their 2025 paper asks whether scalar fields inside would blow up and wreck the spacetime, or stay tame.

Exact solutions to the wave equation come out in double confluent Heun functions. From those, the team extracts quasiresonance frequencies for heavy and light scalars alike. Both branches of frequencies fail to propagate in a way that would enable time travel. That fits Hawking's chronology protection idea. A new mass scale also emerges from the math. Relativists get exact tools for a spacetime that tests the rules of time.
arxiv-2502-07367:
Li Wang, Jiaqun Wei, Haicheng Zhang, and Panyue Zhou widen a corner of representation theory in this 2025 paper. They introduce extriangulated length categories, a setting that covers both abelian length categories and bounded derived categories of algebras with finite global dimension.

The team proves such a category is a length category exactly when it admits a simple-minded system, a tidy generating set. They then study its torsion classes, special subcollections closed under key operations, as a lattice. That lattice turns out complete, semidistributive, and algebraic, with brick labels marking its arrows. Finally they pair support torsion classes with support tilting subcategories in a one to one match, extending a known bijection to the new setting.
arxiv-2502-07467:
A team of engineers proposes a 2025 plan for guiding swarms of drones with less radio room. Each drone in a swarm needs control signals, and giving each one its own band wastes scarce space. Their plan lets a base station sense the area and steer the swarm at the same time.

Signals sent up from the swarm blend in the air, and the station shapes them into one control signal. The team gives two ways to clean up that blend, plus a way to send the signal back down. Tests show control near as good as a top method, with sharp sensing kept.
arxiv-2502-07567:
Jean-Paul Brasselet and co-authors revisit an old way to define a class of measures for singular shapes. Their paper from 2025 deals with Chern classes for shapes with singular points. Such classes were guessed by Grothendieck and Deligne and first proved by MacPherson, with many later definitions.

The first definition, by Marie-Hélène Schwartz, used obstruction theory and has been largely forgotten. Its core ideas are simple, but the build needed fine and hard work with layered decompositions. The authors show that in a Lipschitz frame, with its control on stretching, her ideas lead to a simpler definition and build. The result is a clean path to Chern classes for complex analytic shapes.
arxiv-2502-08067:
Han-Jia Bi and Sheng-Wen Li present a 2025 physics paper on using tiny multi-level atoms as refrigerators to quiet microwave resonators. Thermal noise in such resonators limits quantum devices and precision sensors. Their scheme couples the resonator to many three- or four-level systems, then pumps those systems with light.

Pumping herds the systems into their ground states, from which they steadily swallow thermal photons out of the resonator. The authors compute the cooling process precisely and find its limits. For three-level systems, too strong a pump warps the energy levels and breaks the resonance that cooling needs, so the drive must stay in a sweet range. Four-level designs relax the trade-off.
arxiv-2502-08267:
Lars Rohwedder, Arman Rouhani, and Leo Wennmann present a rounding method for allocation problems, in this 2025 arXiv paper. Rounding turns a fractional plan into whole assignments while keeping hard limits. Earlier dependent rounding schemes could let the total cost creep up. Their scheme promises the final bill never tops the fractional one.

The method keeps the sharp concentration behavior of random rounding. It applies to a class of assignment problems much like those older schemes handled. As a payoff, the authors pair it with known linear programming tools. Together they build an approximation for a budgeted Santa Claus problem. There, gifts of varied value go to players under a cost cap, while the worst-off player's share is lifted as high as possible.
arxiv-2502-08367:
Peter Hochs and Hemanth Saratchandran wrote a 2025 mathematics paper that generalizes a known trace formula to settings where a group also acts on the space. Guillemin's trace formula gives the trace of an operator that pulls back functions along a flow on a compact manifold. Such traces summarize how the flow carries values around the space.

Their equivariant version holds when the group action is proper and the space remains compact once the action of the group is taken into account. The result is not an end in itself. It lays the foundation for an equivariant form of the Ruelle zeta function, which counts closed paths of a flow, and which the pair construct in a companion paper. To get there, they first had to generalize the trace itself in the same group-aware way. The paper is pure mathematics, aimed at researchers who work on flows and geometry.
arxiv-2502-08567:
Anna Gallo, Fabio Saracco, and Tiziano Squartini offer a stricter way to simplify two-layer networks, in a 2025 paper. A bipartite network links two kinds of nodes, and projecting it onto one layer guesses which same-kind pairs are truly tied. Their method keeps a link only when the pair shares far more agreeing or opposing ties than chance allows, and it stamps each candidate link with a p-value.

After checks on synthetic networks with known structure, the team ran the method on real data. The surviving links formed patterns that the benchmark models could not explain, signs of genuine self-organization. The tool serves anyone who mines layered data, from markets to social ties.
arxiv-2502-08867:
Jade Ducharme and Jonathan Pober present a way to locate interference sources in a 2025 arXiv paper. Radio-frequency interference can swamp the faint signals that radio telescopes seek. Knowing where an emitter sits could let astronomers subtract it instead of discarding data.

Their method applies near-field corrections to bring a moving source into focus. In a two-minute observation with an Australian array, an unknown object crossed the view. The focus method put it at about 11.7 kilometers up, moving near 792 kilometers per hour. That profile fit an airplane. Two more observations confirmed the method by again pointing to airplanes.
arxiv-2502-09567:
Negru and co-authors present MorphNLI, a step-by-step method for judging how two sentences relate. The task sorts pairs into entailment, contradiction, or neutral. Their system asks a language model to edit the first sentence, step by step, into the second.

A standard inference model then tracks how the label shifts after each small edit. Those step labels are pooled into the final call. In cross-domain tests, the method always beat strong baselines, with gains up to 12.6 percent. The edit trail also explains the verdict, since each atomic change can be inspected.
arxiv-2502-09667:
Jairo Diaz-Rodriguez presents a text grouping method in a solo 2025 paper. Clustering sorts documents into piles by topic. Classic tools name each pile's center with a point in number space. That point means nothing to a human reader.

His variants swap the number point for a written summary. The summary serves as the pile's center and can be read at a glance. One version uses light, rule based summarizers that run offline. The other calls a language model under a fixed budget per round. A streaming version handles text that arrives live. Tests across many data sets beat classic baselines. A new benchmark built from StackExchange posts supports the streaming case.
arxiv-2502-09767:
Yangtian Zhang and co-authors loosen a core limit on diffusion models that write text. Such models build sequences step by step, but each step sees only the current draft, so early slips can never be fixed. Their model, CaDDi, instead conditions each step on the whole path the draft has taken so far.

One transformer then handles both the step-by-step logic of language models and the revise-and-refine logic of diffusion. Standard language models fall out as a special case of the design. Pretrained language model weights drop in with no change to the architecture. On language benchmarks, CaDDi beat the best discrete diffusion rivals. The result narrows much of the gap to large autoregressive transformers.
arxiv-2502-10167:
Yun-Chih Chen and a large team of co-authors walk readers through a toolkit for testing new kinds of computer memory in a 2025 tutorial. The new memory types keep data when power is off, unlike the chips in wide use today. Real parts are scarce, so teams test designs in software first.

Four worked case studies show the toolkit in action. They cover main memory that mixes old and new chips, chips that compute where data sits, and schemes that spread wear so parts last longer. Each study gives hands-on tips for shaping the tools to a team's own task. The full code is open for anyone to use.
arxiv-2502-10267:
Szabolcs Borsányi and co-authors used lattice models in 2025 to fence in one of the most wanted locations in nuclear physics: the key point of quantum chromodynamics. There the shift between normal matter and quark-gluon plasma changes character. They hunted it by following lines of constant entropy density from imaginary chemical potential, where model is safe, toward real values, keeping the matter strangeness-neutral as tests need.

Supporting the search is a new equation of state at zero density. Extrapolated to the continuum from models at four lattice spacings with markedly boosted precision, plus fresh data at imaginary chemical potential. Watching whether the entropy contours converge on a meeting point, the authors find their current precision already excludes. At the two-sigma level, any key point below a baryon chemical potential of about four hundred fifty million electron volts, narrowing the territory where tests should look.
arxiv-2502-10667:
Sijie Dong, Soror Sahri, Themis Palpanas, and Qitong Wang wrote this 2025 paper on catching bad data before it poisons machine learning. Hand-written validation rules are brittle: too strict and they cry wolf, too loose and errors slip through, and hidden tangles between columns defeat them entirely. The team replace rules with learning.

Their framework, DQuag, reads a table as a graph and lets a graph neural network learn how features depend on each other. Two decoders split the work: one flags rows that break the learned patterns, the other proposes repair values. Multi-task training sharpens both jobs at once. Because nothing is hand-specified, the system spots subtle inconsistencies that rule-based checkers miss. Experiments back the design on detection and repair alike.
arxiv-2502-11067:
Aronsson, Rahbar, and Chehreghani surveyed in twenty twenty-five ways to buy facts one by one for each case, trading truth against cost. A test or sensor fact can cost time or cash, so blind full reads waste both. They give the first joint frame for the field as a hid-state choice chain.

That frame ties the field to known plan tools for hid-state tasks. Four method kinds are sorted, from cost-wise trees to sim-trained plans. Most past work lacks proof of sound bounds, they note. Ties to step-wise stochastics point to where proofs can come from.
arxiv-2502-11167:
Bohan Lyu, Siqiao Huang, and Zichen Liang ask if large language models can stand in for a code runner and predict how a run ends. Stand-in models save time in data work, and the new models shine at reading and writing code. Their 2025 bench, SURGE, holds 1,160 tasks in eight groups. Groups span code in many languages, hard contest problems, whole-store analysis, and costly science sums.

Retrieval and proof tasks join bug hunts and runs bound to one tool set. The team grades 21 models, open and commercial, on growth laws, data thrift, and prediction accuracy. Readings show where the models can fake a run well and where they slip. The bench and its grading frame sit open for all. Fast fake runs could cut the cost of code tests, if accuracy holds.
arxiv-2502-11267:
Zeyu He, Saniya Naphade, and Ting-Hao Huang studied in 2025 how well people write prompts for language models when no gold labels exist to check progress. Their case was data labeling, where users revise prompts again and again hoping accuracy improves. They built a spreadsheet add-on, PromptingSheet, for this task.

In a study with twenty people, only nine improved their labeling accuracy after four or more rounds of revision. The rest stayed flat or got worse without knowing it. An automated prompt tuning tool also struggled when few gold labels were on hand. The authors stress the value of gold labels and warn of risks in blind prompt work.
arxiv-2502-11367:
Jack Gallifant and five co-authors test sparse autoencoders in 2025 as a lens on language models for safety-critical sorting tasks. These autoencoders tease a model's inner activity into sparse features that humans can name. The study asks which layers, widths, and pooling choices yield features that classify well.

The derived features beat raw hidden states and word-count baselines, topping a strong F1 mark. They even transferred from a small model to a larger sibling, and crossed to other languages for toxicity spotting and to image tasks. Switching features on or off in binary form worked as well as careful selection, simplifying the pipeline.
arxiv-2502-11467:
Naoki Takeshita and Masaaki Imaizumi ask how well transformer networks can copy a special kind of formula, in a 2025 theory paper. Transformers are the networks behind most modern language tools. The formulas here take tables of numbers as input and give the same answer when columns are swapped. Such symmetry shows up in many data tasks.

The authors build transformers that copy these formulas and track how network size affects the error. Their proof uses traits of symmetric formulas, a classic topic in algebra. The link they find is explicit, tying size to accuracy in a clear way. Results like this help explain why these networks are so flexible in practice.
arxiv-2502-11567:
Jing Sun, Xavier Trias, and Roel Verstappen extend a turbulence modeling approach in a 2025 paper. Large-eddy simulation models only the big swirls of a flow and estimates the small ones. Their minimum-dissipation model is prized because it shuts off where it should: at walls, and in smooth or changing flows, without extra wall rules. The gap was handling a carried scalar, such as heat, alongside the flow.

The new scalar form of the model lets the carried quantity feed back on how turbulence grows or fades. Paired with a symmetry-preserving numerical scheme, it was tested in a heated cavity using open software. The scheme clearly sharpened predictions of flow and heat transfer, even on meshes stretched far from uniform. The authors present the pair as a robust tool for turbulent transport problems.
arxiv-2502-11667:
Camila Navarrete, Alejandra Recio-Blanco, Patrick de Laverny, and Ana Escorza published this astronomy paper in 2025. It uses data from the Gaia space mission to study red giant stars in pairs. A fresh Gaia release listed about one thousand long-period pairs, the largest sample of its kind with both light and motion records.

The team matched those pairs against the main Gaia catalog and derived sizes, masses, and brightness for 243 of one class and thirty-nine of another. In the main class, the giant often swells nearly to the edge of its allowed space, and orbits grow rounder as the star grows. The unseen partners look like small, dense remnants. At least fourteen pairs match forecasts for the systems that later explode as type Ia supernovae. The two classes seem to differ in age as well.
arxiv-2502-11867:
Yun Li, Neil Yorke-Smith, and Tamas Keviczky present a study from twenty twenty-five on robust plans when the unknown comes in many clumps. In data driven robust design, the set of possible bad cases is key. A union of many subsets gives a tight, flexible set. Two gaps block its use in control: hard math, and plans that play too safe.

They give one mixed integer form for the whole union set. The worst case then falls out of a single solve. A new aim blends robust and distribution robust views to trim the safe bias. A column and constraint method makes the sums run fast. Three case studies back the scheme.
arxiv-2502-12267:
Xi Zheng, Ziyang Li, Ivan Ruchkin, Ruzica Piskac, and Miroslav Pajic set out a frame for trustworthy autonomous systems in this two thousand twenty-five paper. Cyber-physical systems use AI for seeing, planning, and control, but their built-in doubt blocks safety sign-off. The neurosymbolic path swaps some random neural layers for symbolic AI whose steps can be read, bringing back fixed behavior where it counts. Hard spots stay in fusing sensors, adapting, and checking.

NeuroStrata is the team's neurosymbolic frame, built to help design, test, and check self-running systems. The paper lays out its parts, reports results, and sets out plans ahead. The aim is autonomy that can earn sign-off: systems whose choice paths can be inspected and checked, not just sampled. For fields where safety is key, like self-driving cars and medical tools, that is the gap between shippable systems and lab demos.
arxiv-2502-12367:
Cracks near the corner of a wedge-shaped elastic body create stress patterns that are hard to compute. In this 2025 paper, the author analyzes two model cases: a crack buried inside the wedge and one cutting in from an edge. The buried case turns into a matrix equation problem of a known hard type, with entries that grow and shrink exponentially.

When the buried crack runs along one face, the paper gives an efficient solution path. It splits the matrix kernel into a simple dominant part and a smoother part that factors more easily on a computer. Formulas follow for the stress peaks at the crack tips and the energy freed as a crack grows. Limit formulas cover a tip approaching the corner.
arxiv-2502-12667:
Ryan Keeley and co-authors find fresh hints that dark energy changes over cosmic time. Their twenty twenty-five paper fits distance data from the DESI survey, the Planck satellite, and two supernova sets. A flexible formula lets the dark energy pressure shift fast or slow across eras.

With one supernova set the evolving model beats the constant model by a strong margin; with the other, the edge shrinks but stays. The result echoes the DESI team own fits. If dark energy truly drifts, the standard cosmic model needs revision, and the fate of expansion reopens. Growth of structure data may soon confirm or kill the hint.
arxiv-2502-13067:
The curl operator, which measures how a vector field rotates, has a spectrum: a list of vibration-like values tied to the shape of the region it acts on. Josef Greilhuber and Willi Kepplinger ask in 2025 whether those values can repeat on a smoothly bounded three-dimensional domain. For a typical such domain, they prove, the answer is no — every eigenvalue is simple, standing alone.

The heart of the proof is a new formula describing how curl eigenvalues shift when the domain's boundary is nudged. The formula mirrors a classical one for the Laplace operator under fixed boundary conditions. The authors put it to work at once, simplifying the derivation of a known condition that any domain minimizing the first curl eigenvalue at fixed volume must satisfy. They extend the same reasoning to conditions for domains that extremize higher eigenvalues.
arxiv-2502-13167:
Jun Kevin and Pujianto Yugopuspito present a language model system for auditing smart contracts, in a 2025 paper. Smart contracts run decentralised finance, but coding flaws and complex attacks leave them open to theft. Standard static tools miss dynamic flaws and raise many false alarms.

Their system, SmartLLM, fine-tunes an open language model and pairs it with retrieval of domain knowledge from token standards. A low-cost tuning method keeps training efficient. In tests, it caught every known flaw in its set, with seventy percent overall accuracy, beating two leading static tools and plain prompting of large commercial models. Flaws found included re-entry attacks and weak access control. The authors offer the system as a scalable audit aid for safer decentralised apps.
arxiv-2502-13467:
Yu Chen and co-authors prove regret bounds for a continuous bandit problem in a 2025 paper. In K-Max bandits, a player picks several arms and is rewarded by the best outcome among them, seeing only that maximum and which arm won. Continuous outcomes add discretization error and biased estimates.

Their DCK-UCB algorithm adapts its discretization and corrects its confidence bounds, achieving the first sublinear regret guarantee in this setting. A special case with exponential outcomes gets a near-optimal rate from a likelihood method. Picking portfolios, channels, or sensors by their best performer fits this frame exactly.
arxiv-2502-13767:
Abhik Roychoudhury, Corina Păsăreanu, Michael Pradel, and Baishakhi Ray argue that AI coders must earn trust in a 2025 opinion piece. Language models now write code snippets with surprising skill. That skill promises to automate much of software engineering. But deployment needs trust at least equal to human practice.

The recent turn to LLM agents offers one path forward. Agents pair code generation with analysis tools that check the code. The authors ask if such agents will dominate future workflows. They also ask how the craft itself may change. Programming at scale may yield to programming with trust.
arxiv-2502-13967:
Roman Bachmann and eight co-authors published this paper in 2025. It introduces FlexTok, a way to compress images into token sequences whose length adapts to the picture. Image generators work on tokens, and fixed-length tokenizers waste effort on simple images while starving complex ones.

FlexTok squeezes an image into anywhere from one to two hundred fifty-six ordered tokens, arranged coarse to fine like a summary that keeps adding detail. A flow-based decoder rebuilds a plausible image from any prefix of the sequence, trained by randomly dropping token tails. In generation tests with a transformer, quality scores stayed strong from eight to one hundred twenty-eight tokens, beating a fixed tokenizer with fewer tokens. Text-conditioned generation worked too. The authors note the tokens behave like a visual vocabulary, describing scenes from gist to detail. Adaptive length, they argue, should be the default for image tokenization.
arxiv-2502-14267:
Akshaan Bandara builds a banknote reader in 2025 to help blind people in Sri Lanka handle cash with confidence. Telling notes apart by touch is unreliable, and errors can cost money and independence. Past aids were often awkward to use, so Bandara aims for a stand-alone system with a simple interface.

A custom image set of Sri Lankan notes was used to fine-tune an object-spotting model. The model scored very high accuracy on held-out images and worked well in real-world trials. Blind users could identify note values quickly and accurately with the device. Bandara presents the system as a step toward safer, more independent daily payments.
arxiv-2502-14667:
Özgür Akarsu and co-authors build a 2025 model of dark energy, the force that speeds up the growth of the universe. Their model lets its strength slide smoothly from a negative value in the young universe to a positive one today. Such a shift could ease a known clash over how fast space now expands.

Math checks show the model fits both early-universe data and the local speed measure, and it does so without wild side effects. The change from negative to positive lasts longer than the raw math shape suggests. A twin version built on a normal field also works, the team reports, which widens the options.
arxiv-2502-14767:
Priyanka Kargupta and co-authors let papers debate each other through language model personas in a 2025 paper. Science grows fast and scatters across fields, so judging what is truly new in one paper against a cousin paper is hard. Their framework, Tree-of-Debate, turns each paper into a persona that must defend its novelty.

The debate grows as a tree, so each novelty claim gets its own branch of attack and reply. Expert judges rated the output as rich in usable points and fair in contrasting the papers. The authors pitch the tool as help for literature review, where scholars must sort real advances from repeats across communities.
arxiv-2502-15067:
Cañizares and co-authors track radio waves from a solar burst in a 2025 paper that uses data from five spacecraft. Fast electrons from the Sun make radio waves as they travel outward, but scattering blurs where the waves seem to come from. The team used a burst from December 2021 to trace the true path of the waves through the inner solar system.

Their tracking method placed the sources along a spiral path set by the solar wind, and ground-based images backed up the result. Checks with a probe near Earth also matched. Their measures of scattering fit current models well. The work gives firm proof that scattering explains why electron counts far from the Sun once looked too high.
arxiv-2502-15267:
An Insight-HXMT team reports fresh timing and spectra from the Rapid Burster, a neutron star famous for firing X-ray bursts in volleys. Its type II bursts, driven by unstable inflow rather than nuclear burning, still puzzle theorists. China's Insight-HXMT telescope and the Swift observatory caught the latest outburst across a wide energy band.

Stacking the long bursts revealed a first: hard X-rays trail the soft by three seconds. Short bursts showed no clear lag, likely a matter of faint counts. Every burst spectrum came out non-thermal. The team reads the delay as a corona that shows up late, a clue any model of these bursts must now explain.
arxiv-2502-15567:
Ganghua Wang, Yuhong Yang, and Jie Ding build a shared frame for a growing risk in machine learning in their 2025 paper. Thieves can try to copy a trained model by asking it many questions and watching its replies, as with cloud services or chips that run such models. Past work on attacks and guards lacked a common base for fair tests.

The authors set out clear terms for the threat, for what each side wants, and for how to score an attack or a guard. They study the trade-off between keeping a model useful and keeping it private. Tests in several learning settings back their claims. One lesson stands out: guards work best when they shape their noise to the exact form of the attack they face.
arxiv-2502-15667:
Diyou Liu and Mohammad Khosravi tackle system identification when sensors mix signals in a paper from 2025. Many systems have linear dynamics but nonlinear, bilinear readouts. The goal is to recover the model parameters from input and output data alone. The authors build two probabilistic frameworks for the task. The first maximizes a likelihood function with a fast first-order optimizer.

The second uses an expectation-maximization approach with a specially shaped cost function. That shape guarantees a single best solution, and the authors derive it in closed form. They also prove the procedure stays feasible step by step. Simulations compare both methods and show accurate parameter recovery. The work targets control problems with bilinear sensing.
arxiv-2502-15967:
Abbas Mohammadian and co-authors redraw a graph built from a group, sorting its elements by symmetry in a 2025 paper. The enhanced power graph links group elements that share a common power source. Their new version folds the picture by the group's own symmetries, so each node stands for a whole class of elements that those symmetries swap among themselves.

The first results reassure: the new graph's connectedness and diameter behave much like the old one's, so the character survives the folding. The authors then study the universal nodes, the ones joined to all others, and settle when the graph comes out complete. At the far extreme, they classify when the graph is empty, with no edges at all. The paper extends a small trade of turning algebra into networks, where graph tools, paths and cliques, answer algebraic questions.
arxiv-2502-16467:
Rami Atar and Masakiyo Miyazawa prove a heavy traffic limit for a queue with jumping rates in a 2025 paper. In a busy single-server queue, arrival and service rates may switch abruptly as the line grows. Classical diffusion limits assume smooth rates, so this case needed new tools.

The authors show the scaled queue length converges to the unique solution of a stochastic equation with discontinuous drift and diffusion. Their key device is a semimartingale decomposition for point processes that differs from the standard one. The method may serve many other queueing limits. Service systems, from clinics to call centers, live in this heavy traffic regime.
arxiv-2502-16567:
Guo, Wu, and Zhang work out the math of a tiny, fast instability that grows where two streams of plasma slide past each other at electron scales. This Kelvin-Helmholtz instability matters in several astrophysical settings, but a background magnetic field is almost always present, and no good formula covered the relativistic case. The authors derive a general dispersion relation for magnetized shear flows with few assumptions, then compute growth rates for key cases.

A background field usually trims the fastest growth rate, though at very high shear speeds it can raise it slightly. The field also widens the band of unstable waves and shifts the most unstable wavelength. Computer simulations confirm the predictions, and they show the field suppressing a secondary effect, the build-up of steady magnetic fields from electron gyration. For plasma physicists, the paper fills a long-standing gap between theory and magnetized space plasmas.
arxiv-2502-16767:
Jhon Rayo, Raul de la Rosa, and Mario Garrido built this 2025 hybrid search system for regulatory texts. Rules and standards run long and tangled, and compliance officers need exact answers fast. Word matching alone misses meaning; meaning search alone misses exact terms. Their system blends a tuned sentence-embedding model with the classic BM25 word ranker.

Retrieved passages then feed a language model that drafts the answer, the retrieval-augmented pattern. In tests, the hybrid beat either approach alone on recall and ranking quality at the top ten results. The authors share their tuned model and method openly. The goal is practical: trustworthy tools that help officers find the clause that decides a case.
arxiv-2502-16867:
Momammad Ali Ranjbar presents a 2025 study on controlling a robot arm so it follows a set path quickly and smoothly. Standard sliding mode control is tough against disturbances but can make the arm chatter, jittering around the path. The proposed method uses a fast terminal form of the control, designed to settle in finite time without the chatter. It was built on the arm's Newton-Euler dynamics and checked with a Lyapunov stability proof.

Simulations on a three-joint arm compared the new controller with two standard rivals. The new method tracked paths more accurately, settled faster, and held steadier. The author presents it as a strong fit for high-precision robot work where both speed and smoothness matter. The study is a single-author simulation paper, so hardware tests remain future work.
arxiv-2502-17167:
Mazandarani, Shokrnezhad, and Taleb design in 2025 a smarter way for devices to share the airwaves in mixed wireless crowds. Virtual worlds will flood networks with twinning and presence traffic, and the shared band must be rationed fairly. Their agent must live beside older devices whose counts, rules, and habits it cannot see.

The agent learns by deep reward play, doubled and dueled for stability, and keeps learning as the crowd changes rather than freezing after training, they report. A symmetry-aware memory trick helps it reuse what it learns. Math backs the gains: top throughput for the smart agent with fairness held. Networks that never sit still need manners that keep learning too.
arxiv-2502-17467:
Behnam Afshar and Reza Ameri write a 2025 algebra paper on systems where sums can give sets of values, not just one value. Such systems extend normal algebra and model cases where results are not fully fixed. The paper works with a well-behaved class of these systems and with links between their parts.

The authors first show that two ways of sorting the links form matching grid structures. They then build step-by-step tools that carry structure from one system to another in a clean way. With those tools they define free objects and a way to pair systems inside their class. The results give algebraists a firmer base for work in this less-charted branch.
arxiv-2502-17667:
Axel Álvarez and Sebastián Donoso develop a cube-based approach to nilsystems in work from 2025. Nilsystems are structured dynamical systems used to understand patterns in number theory and dynamics.

The authors study cube structures tied to the universal minimal system and its extensions. They give new proofs for saturation traits of maps to maximal nilfactors in cubes, plus fresh results for the structure theory of topological systems. One proof shows a key relation is an equivalence relation, with an algebraic description that is new even in the simplest case. The work adds tools for this abstract field.
arxiv-2502-17967:
Chat models read charts better than raw numbers in a virtual stock market, Tianmi Ma and co-authors find in a 2025 paper. Language model traders compete in a zero-sum arena where their own bids move prices, unlike backtests on frozen history. Bid and ask orders meet as in a live exchange.

Given plain text numbers, the agents reason poorly and chase recent values. Swap the same data into charts and both number sense and profit jump. A reflection step adds further gains. The arena gives a fair test bed for machine investors and exposes a plain truth: format shapes machine judgment.
arxiv-2502-18067:
Zhen Zhang and co-authors wrote this 2025 paper on shrinking the building blocks of smart radio surfaces. A reconfigurable intelligent surface steers wireless signals with many small metal elements, and smaller elements pack in more functions. The trick is knowing which parts of each element actually carry the current of the signal.

The team map current flow across an element in its working states, then use an image method called Otsu segmentation to pick out the strong-current zones. Those zones, mapped back onto metal, become the new, smaller patch shape. A Quasi-Newton optimizer then tunes the parameters of the design. The recipe keeps performance while cutting size, using the physics of the current itself as the stencil.
arxiv-2502-18667:
Top quarks rarely switch flavor without changing charge, and such flavor-changing interactions would signal new physics if seen. The authors use machine learning to hunt four-fermion interactions in which a top quark decays to an up or charm quark plus an electron pair, giving a three-lepton signal at the LHC. They study top pair and single top production, folding in both reducible and irreducible backgrounds and realistic detector effects.

Machine learning classifiers sharpened event selection and signal sensitivity against the heavy backgrounds from top pairs and boson production. For 3000 inverse femtobarns, the expected 95 percent limits on the interaction scale reach 5.5 TeV and 5.7 TeV in the top pair channel. The single top channel reaches about 2 TeV. The authors also translate the bounds into limits on a heavy neutral Z prime boson in a sample model.
arxiv-2502-18867:
Akhil Penta, Vaibhav Adwani, and Ankush Chopra adapt transformer tracking for skiing events. Their 2025 arXiv paper tackles multi-camera race coverage. Accurate tracking feeds performance analysis and injury prevention. Occlusions and fast motion defeat many standard trackers. The team tuned the STARK transformer tracker for snow sports.

Architecture and settings were adjusted for the ski domain. Camera movement and sudden camera switches were handled explicitly. Changing light and weather add further strain on tracking. The adapted model follows skiers through those disruptions. Coaches could extract cleaner motion data from race footage. Training plans may improve with reliable tracking output. The work extends vision transformers to a hard outdoor sport.
arxiv-2502-19067:
Ujjwal Singh and co-authors build a code generation test across Indic languages in a 2025 paper. Most coding benchmarks use English prompts alone. Their test covers six major Indic languages spoken by a large share of the world. Twelve programming languages pair with those tongues in the frame.

Models take a prompt in an Indic language and write working code. The gap matters for India, home to a vast pool of new developers. Public release of data and tools invites wider use. The authors aim to make AI coding help fair across tongues. Richer tests can push vendors to serve users far beyond English first markets.
arxiv-2502-19267:
Rodrigo Dourado, Martin Leijnse, and Rubén Seoane Souto map the sweet spots of a three-link chain built to host Majorana particles in this 2025 paper. Two-site chains of quantum dots linked by a superconductor already show these prized states at special settings. A third site promises sturdier states but multiplies the knobs.

The authors find three kinds of sweet spot. In the genuine kind the states sit tightly at the chain's ends. In the second the middle dot acts as a wall, faking a two-site chain. In the third the states sprawl and meet in the middle. The genuine spots shrug off disturbances best. Energy spectra, current flow, and microwave absorption each carry fingerprints that can tell the three apart in the lab. The work guides builders toward the settings worth hunting.
arxiv-2502-19467:
Nina Coyle, Shirley Li, and Pedro Machado study how shaky neutrino interaction models affect oscillation measurements in a 2025 paper. Neutrinos change flavor as they travel, and measuring that change needs a good model of how they hit atomic nuclei. That model is a known weak point.

Using setups modeled on the NOvA and DUNE experiments, the team swapped in several event generators to span the uncertainty. For current, data-limited experiments the bias stayed small. For DUNE, which will be limited by systematics, the bias could grow large even with near-detector data. The result argues for better interaction models before DUNE's precision arrives.
arxiv-2502-19567:
Marcin Spoczynski, Marcela Melara, and Sebastian Szyller present a frame that makes each step of a machine learning pipeline provable, in a 2025 arXiv paper. Open data and models spread fast, and with them the risks of poisoned data and supply chain attack. Rules now press vendors for clear records, yet secrets must stay shut.

Their frame, Atlas, borrows open specs from data and software chain proof. It gathers signed records of where each model piece came from and how it was changed. Trusted hardware and public logs guard the records, while locks keep data private and bar stray hands. A test build weds several open tools, and two case pipelines show the frame can run in real work.
arxiv-2502-19967:
Vimala Soundarapandian and co-authors wrote a 2025 computer science paper on checking copied data types for a strong form of correctness. Copies of data across machines give fault tolerance and fast access. Users gain when each copy's state can be read as some clean order of the updates it has seen.

The authors give a fully automatic way to check that property for mergeable data types. They find new algebra rules for the update and merge steps that are enough to prove the property. Those rules go past the classic trio of rules used in past work. A bottom-up proof method checks the rules on its own. The team proved the method on many complex types, plus a new one for a common data format.
arxiv-2502-20467:
María González-Calderón and co-authors build statistical methods for testing one-shot devices. These are products that work only once and are then destroyed or rebuilt. Because such a device can only be checked at one inspection moment, testers know only whether it failed before or after that moment. These devices are usually very reliable, so labs stress them harder than normal use to learn how long they would last.

Plain estimates can be thrown off by a few odd results, so the team develops robust estimators based on a weighted divergence measure, along with matching tests. Their setting is lifetimes that follow a log-logistic curve under several stresses. They derive the formulas and the large-sample behaviour of the new estimators. Computer simulations then check how well the methods hold up in practice.
arxiv-2502-20567:
Richard Lebed and Steven Martinez test whether exotic four-quark states are pairs of mesons in disguise. Their paper appeared in two thousand twenty-five. Tetraquark models often picture two quarks bound against two antiquarks. Meson-meson molecules are the rival picture. The authors join both in one model. A diabatic formalism, generalizing Born-Oppenheimer ideas, does the joining.

Simple molecular potentials are added to an established diquark model. Mixed states emerge, part diquark pair and part molecule. Sweeping the potential's parameters maps the possibilities. Some settings reproduce the masses of two famous candidate states exactly. Other regions yield a pure molecular state. The study shows how both pictures can share one spectrum.
arxiv-2502-20667:
Ojonugwa Ejiga Peter, Md Mahmudur Rahman, and Fahmi Khalifa report their lab notebook from a medical imaging challenge at CLEF 2024. The 2025 report tackles the MedVQA-GI task, generating medical images from text to support diagnosis in gut medicine. Most earlier systems only analyzed fixed images; this one must create them on demand.

Their pipeline fine-tunes Stable Diffusion, adds DreamBooth personalization and low-rank adapters, and uses CLIP to judge the results. The challenge splits into image synthesis and optimal prompt production, writing the text that yields the needed picture. Synthetic imagery could stock training sets and teaching files where real cases are scarce or sensitive.
arxiv-2502-21067:
Chahine-Nicolas Zede and co-authors speed up search in large collections of 3D point clouds for place recognition. Their 2025 paper tackles the task of finding the stored scans most similar to a query scan. Past methods compare descriptors one by one, a slow step at large scale. The team adapts a transformer based index first built for text search.

Their method turns point cloud descriptors into short 1D identifiers, so retrieval can run in constant time. Vision transformers map the descriptors to those identifiers, with position and meaning cues added. Tests on a public benchmark compared both quality and speed against leading methods. The catalog byline is garbled with address text, so the head byline governs the author names.
arxiv-2502-21267:
Alexander Scarlatos and co-authors build a live music jamming partner in a 2025 paper. AI music tools write fine tracks, yet live duet play needs low lag, clear plans, and fast flex to human turns. Their rig, ReaLJam, pairs a person with a transformer agent tuned by reward drills. The agent plays ahead in its head and shows its plan on screen as it goes. That preview lets the human steer the jam.

Seasoned players jammed with the agent in a user study. Sessions felt fun and music-rich, the team report. Players read the plan view to time their moves. Fault lines showed too: lag and plan trust shape play. The authors list rules for the next live jam builds.
arxiv-2503-00067:
Abhishek Mallick and Siddhartha Biswas analyze Rayleigh waves in a porous thermoelastic layer in their 2025 arXiv paper. The medium is orthotropic and nonlocal, and the layer also allows mass diffusion. Their theory combines Eringen's nonlocal elasticity with a three-phase-lag model of heat conduction.

Using normal mode analysis, they derive the frequency equation that governs the waves and examine special cases in detail. The interplay of Fick's diffusion law and Fourier heat law under the hyperbolic framework is central to the study. They also identify and compute the elliptical paths traced by surface particles during wave propagation, including the eccentricity of those paths.
arxiv-2503-00267:
Xinwei Luo, Songlin Zhao, Yun Zong, Yong Chen, Gui-shuang Ying, and Lifang He guide an eye-disease classifier with anatomy maps, in a 2025 paper. Retinal photos reveal many diseases, but a plain image network may miss the thin vessels and layers where signs live. Outlining those structures first gives the classifier a map to reason with.

SegImgNet builds segmentation maps at several scales, then reads the photo and its maps through two encoders. A special attention block lets the maps steer the reading of the raw image toward telling regions. The two streams merge for the final diagnosis. Anatomy-guided reading mimics how human graders work and can sharpen accuracy on hard cases.
arxiv-2503-00567:
Samita Rani Pani, Pallav Kumar Bera, and Rajat Kanti Samal use machine learning to predict when a power grid failure will start to cascade, in a 2025 paper. One fault can trip the next, and blackouts can spread in minutes. The onset time, the window before the chain starts, is a key number for operators who want to act fast.

The team framed onset guessing as a class sorting task and tried several classic algorithms on public data from a 150 bus test grid. A random forest sorted best, and a Bayesian search tuned its settings. The authors offer the result as a base for stronger, more failure proof grids.
arxiv-2503-01067:
Swamy and four co-authors ask in twenty twenty-five why the best way to tune large chat models is a two-step route. First a score model learns from human picks, then the main model learns by trial with that score. A plain one-step fit on the same picks looks more direct.

They test a few views on why the two-step route wins, with both math and trials. The best-backed view rests on a gap: checks are easy to learn, but good replies are hard to write. The trial step then picks from a small set of replies that pass the easy check. That cuts the data the full task needs.
arxiv-2503-01167:
Li and Li make synthetic training pairs that teach vision-language models to notice small wording swaps. A model that truly grasps composition should tell apart people holding surfboards from people holding shovels. Their 2025 method, SPARCL, forges such near-twin image and caption pairs with a fast image generator steered by features from a real photo.

A style transfer pass then keeps the forged image close to the real one outside the changed spot. A self-adjusting loss drops suspect pairs and leans on hard, informative ones. Across four composition tests, training with the forged data lifted a standard model's average score by more than eight points. It also beat prior methods on three of the four tests. The authors frame forgery as cheap teaching data.
arxiv-2503-01267:
Engui Fan, Gaozhan Li, and Yiling Yang solve a wave equation exactly using curve-based methods, in a paper from two thousand twenty-five. The equation is a modified form of a known shallow-water wave model, with an added spread term. Exact solutions are rare for such nonlinear wave models.

Their route builds a Riemann-Hilbert problem tied to the equation. A special function, built from a family of hyperelliptic curves, solves that problem in closed form. A rebuild formula then yields the wave solution in full. The curve family carries a genus set by two size parameters in the setup.
arxiv-2503-01467:
Jens Emil Christensen, Søren Fuglede Jørgensen, Andreas Pavlogiannis, and Jaco van de Pol compute the exact sizes of the smallest CNOT circuits. CNOT gates are basic building blocks in reversible and quantum computing. Algebraically, CNOT circuits on n qubits match the general linear group over the field of two elements, and finding a minimal circuit means finding distances in its Cayley graph. That graph grows super-exponentially, which blocked past searches.

A new distance method lets the team synthesize optimal circuits that were out of reach, covering all circuits on seven qubits. Two theory results support the method: a full account of the graph's isometries, and polynomial formulas for sphere sizes at fixed distance.
arxiv-2503-01567:
Michael Björklund and Mattias Byléhn study spread and fluctuation of random measures on symmetric spaces, in work from 2025. They define a Bartlett spectral measure for random measures that stay unchanged under isometries. Commutative spaces give the right frame for that definition and its tools.

For spaces tied to higher rank matrix groups, number variance grows slower than volume squared for all such measures. On flat and curved standard spaces, a heat kernel form of hyperuniformity extends the classic notion to distributions. The authors show that well behaved spectral measures can be realized by Gaussian random distributions. They also compute spectra for determinantal point processes, giving a spectral proof of hyperuniformity for one complex ensemble.
arxiv-2503-01767:
Xiuqi Tommy Zhu and co-authors design a virtual reality simulator where trainee clinicians practice talking with patients who talk back. Fixed scripts have kept VR training stiff and hard to adapt. Their 2025 paper starts with interviews of advanced health professions students, asking what makes communication practice fail them now.

Students wanted scenes that feel real, controls that stay simple, and dialogue they cannot predict. The team built the Virtual AI Patient Simulator on those rules. Large language models drive embodied virtual patients, so each conversation can wander like a real one. Professors get simple forms to author new cases and tune the patient's manner. Health educators gain a rehearsal stage that never tires and never judges.
arxiv-2503-01867:
Phuong-Nam Nguyen sets out a mathematical framework for how artificial networks might consolidate memories, much as a brain does, in a 2025 paper. The model blends three parts. First, neural activity drifts on low-dimensional manifolds. Second, the hippocampus sends out sharp wave-ripple bursts that replay experience during rest. Third, a balance energy, drawn from Heider's theory of consistency, keeps beliefs from clashing.

In tests, the model copies the key traits of those ripple bursts. The balance term forces synaptic interactions to stay coherent, so the network is far easier to read. Nguyen aims at neuromorphic machines that learn in a robust way and adapt well. The frame is a proposal backed by early tests, offered as a bridge between neuroscience and machine learning.
arxiv-2503-01967:
Peter Goldreich, Yoram Lithwick, and Jing Luan model Saturn's moon Enceladus as a world caught in a repeating cycle, in a 2025 paper. The moon sprays water geysers through cracks, wobbles in its ice shell over a global ocean, glows with unusual heat, and is migrating outward fast. The team coupled the moon's orbital evolution to its interior.

Their model settles into a limit cycle of about ten million years with three stages. First the shell freezes and thickens, squeezing the ocean until it cracks the ice and feeds the geysers; the orbit grows more eccentric meanwhile. Then tidal heating melts the shell back. In the third stage the shell hovers near three kilometers thick, where its wobble resonates with the orbit and tidal heating peaks. Predicted eccentricity, wobble size, shell thickness, and brightness all match observations. Today's heat, they say, is leftover from the last resonant stage.
arxiv-2503-02067:
Alexander Doudkin, Pat Pataranutaporn, and Pattie Maes test whether AI chatbots can persuade in a 2025 study on green behavior. Fighting climate change needs people to act on what they know, a step that often stalls. The team compared chatbots' sway over three groups of 1,200 each: real people, simulated people built from real data, and fully synthetic personas.

Chatbots used personal or standard scripts and four persuasion styles. Synthetic and simulated agents shifted their stated stance a lot, while real humans barely moved, a gap the authors call the synthetic persuasion paradox. Simulated testers thus overstate how well AI persuasion works on people.
arxiv-2503-02267:
Sourav Mishra, Shreya Hallikeri, and Suresh Sundaram design a new activation curve for physics-informed networks. Their paper, from twenty twenty-five, presents REAct. Such networks solve physics problems by learning, but training often stalls. The activation curve inside each unit shapes how well learning travels across problems.

Their curve bends a classic shape with four learnable dials. That lets one curve fit many physical systems. On heat problems, error fell to a thousandth of the classic curve's level. It also held up on finer grids and points beyond the training zone. Inverse tasks with noisy data gave cleaner parameter guesses as well.
arxiv-2503-02367:
Aida Abiad and Benjamin Jany extend, in a 2025 paper, classic bounds on graph coloring to a quantum version played across distance. In the quantum coloring game, separated players use shared entanglement to color a graph's vertices. The quantum chromatic number can dip below the classical one.

The authors define a distance version: vertices within k steps must differ, generalized to graph powers. They show three eigenvalue bounds known for the classical distance number hold for the quantum one too. Some graph classes then have equal quantum and classical values. The result maps where quantum advantage in coloring simply cannot appear, sharpening the boundary between classical and quantum strategies.
arxiv-2503-03067:
Shuning Zhang and Shixuan Li explore whether young adults accept love between humans and artificial companions, in a 2025 paper. Their focus is Chinese women in romantic or close bonds with AI partners. Fourteen interviews trace how these relationships start, how they are kept up, and how they are seen by others. Comfort and relief from social pressure drew the users in.

Companions played many roles: friend, mentor, or partner. Being customizable and always available counted as major strengths. Users still felt the limits of machine emotion and understanding. The authors call for ethics rules and safeguards on privacy and over-immersion. Long-term mental effects of such bonds remain an open research question.
arxiv-2503-03367:
Xiaotong Zhang and co-authors present a method to outline liver blood vessels in 3D scans, in this 2025 paper. Surgeons need that map before cutting out part of the liver. Standard methods read scans slice by slice and can lose the vessel tree's overall shape. The team borrows a trick from how CT scans themselves are built.

Their projections keep only the top few brightest points along each view line, mimicking the scan physics. Those projections guide a diffusion model that grows a full 3D vessel tree. On a public liver data set, the method earned the best scores on the three main overlap and detection measures, ahead of prior work. The authors say physics-aware priors help keep vessel structure whole.
arxiv-2503-03567:
Timothee Mathieu builds visual hypothesis tests from safe confidence intervals in a 2025 paper. Deciding if two means differ usually needs numeric test machinery. A visual rule based on interval overlap would be intuitive. Safe intervals built from e-variables make that rigor possible.

The framework lets users see the confidence region and test at once. Overlap or its absence decides equality or direction. Both sequential and fixed-sample versions are proposed. Finite-time error bounds accompany each test. Those bounds hold without asymptotic assumptions. An application compares sequential learning algorithms in practice. The method suits settings where data arrive over time. Anytime-valid inference is the broader movement behind it. The author offers statisticians a transparent testing display. Error control stays explicit on the plot itself.
arxiv-2503-03967:
Soya Park, Zamfirescu-Pereira, and Chinmay Kulkarni present Visionary Tuning, a system that helps people write clear behavior rules for chatbots. Telling a model how to act in plain words sounds easy, yet people struggle to state what they want. Their system lets the chatbot play-act talks with itself, which surfaces patterns a user can then name.

In a study with twelve users, self-play helped people spot more behavior patterns and write better prompts than working alone. A larger crowd check with sixty people found the tuned chatbot followed the rules without losing quality. A second test on movie ratings showed the method can also learn one critic's taste, from low to high scores.
arxiv-2503-04167:
Yufang Liu and eight co-authors ask whether multimodal AI models really look at the picture when they solve math problems, in this 2025 paper. Most benchmarks pair word problems with diagrams. The team found that top models barely use the images: change or remove them, and scores hardly move, because text and answer options leak the answer.

To force honest looking, they built a new dataset where the image is essential and where near-twin images flip the correct answer. Leading models failed to catch those subtle visual differences. Stacking more image encoders, a common trick from general visual question answering, did not help math scores either. The authors conclude that current models see too coarsely for math, and they release their benchmark and code to push better visual grounding.
arxiv-2503-04467:
Xiang Zhang and two colleagues wrote a 2025 survey on the two-dimensional Burgers' equation. This equation models a flow where the fluid pushes itself along while friction smooths it out. It is a classic test case for the math of fluids.

A model is well-posed if it has exactly one solution and that solution behaves in a stable way. The authors show such results using tools from the study of dynamical systems. Their proof leans on the Galerkin method, which turns the flow problem into a set of simpler equations. Energy estimates and compactness arguments close the case. The survey gathers the key ideas in a short, clear form for new readers.
arxiv-2503-04867:
Alaa Mazouz and co-authors build a full path for learned image compression that is both secure and fast enough for hardware. Learned compressors beat standard codecs on efficiency, but running them live on chips, with protection, is hard. Their 2025 paper prunes and quantizes a model inside its training loop until it fits hardware limits. They add a new watermarking step done during quantization training, which marks the compressed stream for ownership and tamper checks.

The workflow runs from training to deployment on FPGA hardware. Security and speed are treated as design inputs, not afterthoughts. The authors aim at real uses, such as cameras and drones, where streams must be small, instant, and provably theirs. Their platform lets other teams repeat the whole chain.
arxiv-2503-04967:
Ossenkopf-Okada and co-authors map atomic carbon glowing around molecular clouds in a quiet corner of the Milky Way. Theory says a skin of loose carbon atoms wraps clouds as they form. Its faint lines could clock that formation, if the skin's shape is known.

The team pointed a desert telescope at a five-arcminute strip in the little-studied third quadrant. They compared the carbon line with several carbon monoxide lines and older gas maps. The atomic carbon spread most smoothly of all, with the gentlest gradient. It outshone the rarer monoxide form everywhere along the strip. Quiet regions may be the galaxy's norm. Their carbon skin now has a measured profile.
arxiv-2503-05067:
Thomas Hsiao and Lance Waller weigh a light fix for place-based reads when spots were picked with bias. The work dates to 2025. Map stats oft rest on the guess that read spots stand free of the field read. When spot picks lean to high zones, that guess fails.

Their fix first gauges how thick spots sit cross the map, then weights each read by the flip of that gauge. A fast near-form keeps the math quick at scale. In tests, the fix beat stock bias tools when the spot plan was off. Sharp gauge work tied weak to sharp calls, a point the team flags. Two real maps ground the proof.
arxiv-2503-05267:
Amal Alphonse, Ana Djurdjevac, Emil Engstrom, and Eskil Hansen extend a parallel computing method to heat problems on moving domains in a 2025 math study. Parabolic equations on evolving shapes model processes such as molding heated material. Splitting a fixed domain across processors is routine, but a domain that changes shape breaks the usual structure.

Their variational setup carries domain decomposition to the evolving case. Transmission conditions govern how neighboring pieces exchange information across their shared boundaries. The authors prove the structure is sound, opening the way to large simulations on parallel hardware for manufacturing and materials problems with moving fronts.
arxiv-2503-05367:
Jing Zhang and four co-authors tackle dose planning for a cancer treatment in this 2025 paper. The treatment sends radiation straight to tumor cells with targeted drugs. Doctors need a dose estimate tuned to each patient, yet labeled data for training models is scarce.

Their fix learns from many scans that lack dose labels and a few that have them. The method creates likely labels for the unlabeled scans, in a style drawn from a known training scheme. Tests used fake data built with physics simulation. Adding the extra scans improved organ dose estimates over training on labeled scans alone.
arxiv-2503-05467:
Christian Ikenmeyer and Jakob Moosbauer give a strikingly short proof of a famous counting result in matrix multiplication. Their 2025 paper revisits Strassen's theorem that multiplying two-by-two matrices needs a tensor rank of at most seven, the fact behind the first fast multiplication algorithm. Standard proofs involve clever but heavy verification, checking that a proposed scheme really computes every entry.

Their proof needs none of that. It rests on properties of one specific group action of order six, combined with recent flip graph techniques that search among equivalent schemes while respecting symmetry. The argument is calculation-free and pattern-free: the structure of the symmetry group does the work. The authors offer it as a model of proving rank bounds by reasoning about orbits, rather than by exhibiting and checking an explicit decomposition.
arxiv-2503-05567:
Tchuiaga and Dor Kewir build a theory of Weil bundles over p-adic manifolds, in a math paper from 2025. Weil bundles lift a space by an algebra of infinitesimals, a classic tool over real numbers. The p-adic world, central to number theory, lacked a systematic version.

They show the lifted space carries a natural analytic structure. Functions, vector fields, and connections lift from the base, and a Galois symmetry acts when the bundle is defined over a number field. A comparison links bundle cohomology to crystalline cohomology. Applications include a geometric view of p-adic modular forms and deformations of elliptic curves.
arxiv-2503-05767:
András Benczúr, Tibor Gyimóthy, and Balázs Szegedy survey artificial intelligence research in Hungary in this 2025 article, published in Hungarian with an English summary. The field has surged since the mid-2000s on the back of big data and cheap computing. Hungarian groups joined early and scored in both theory and practice.

The survey first recalls the years before deep learning took off. It then covers major theory advances from Hungary after 2010. A final part sketches applied wins of the same period. The authors present the piece as a compact map of a national research scene.
arxiv-2503-05867:
Erica Sawczynec and co-authors open a public archive of ten years of starlight spectra from the IGRINS instrument. IGRINS is a compact near-infrared spectrograph that captures a wide band at high sharpness in one shot. Its data came from three telescopes in Texas, Arizona, and Chile.

The archive, called RRISA, gives open access to raw files and cleaned data for all non-private runs. Targets are cross-matched with five major sky catalogs, so users can pull known facts fast. The release ships a third version of the reduction pipeline. It cleans cosmic ray hits better, strips pattern noise, and adds a flexure fix that cuts Earth-air glow leftovers. Open archives like this let any team mine a decade of sharp infrared spectra without booking telescope time.
arxiv-2503-06067:
Designers often argue their case with example user flows, sequences of app screens that show a task being done, but finding a good example is slow. Daeheon Jeong and Hyehyun Chu tackle that search problem in this 2025 paper, after interviewing practitioners about how they communicate design ideas.

They train a model that links the visual look of screens to written descriptions of flows, using contrastive learning. A survey then confirmed that the system retrieves flows people judge relevant. The authors discuss what their results mean for how software should represent user flows, aiming to make example-based design talk faster and better grounded.
arxiv-2503-06167:
Mohammadreza Doostmohammadian, Zulfiya Gabidullina, and Hamid Rabiee propose a faster way for networks of agents to share resources, in a 2025 paper. Think of many machines that must split a limited supply while each follows its own cost. Their method adds momentum, an extra push toward the best split, and tracks the slope of the cost so the group settles quickly.

The authors prove the shared limit is respected at every step, so the method can stop at any time with a valid answer. That beats older tools that only meet the limit at the very end. The method also copes with coarse, rounded data sent over links, with networks whose links change over time, and with delays in messages. The team notes this bundle of traits had not been shown together before.
arxiv-2503-06267:
Higinio Serrano, Bernardo Uribe, and Miguel Xicoténcatl present a 2025 paper on magnetic equivariant K-theory. K-theory sorts bundles of vector spaces by their traits, and the magnetic form adds group actions that fit crystals in magnetic fields. Such groups give markers for gapped states in magnetic materials.

The authors show the groups form a full cohomology theory and work out its base values. They prove forms of three classic results for this setting and build a staged tool for computing the groups. Two worked cases show how the theory applies in practice.
arxiv-2503-06367:
Jiaming Zhang and co-authors present a 2025 physics paper on an electronic circuit that mimics exotic non-Hermitian systems, where gain and loss are balanced. Two resonators, one amplifying and one damping, are linked by a capacitor. In ideal versions of such systems, two vibration modes merge at a special point and then one grows explosively.

Real inductors always waste some energy as heat, and that small loss changes the story. The team shows, in both bench tests and theory, that the mode merging no longer happens. Instead, the circuit flips from fading to growing oscillations near the expected special points. The work warns that textbook pictures of these systems need the loss term kept in.
arxiv-2503-07067:
Ko and a team of colleagues presented DistiLLM-2 in twenty twenty-five, a method for distilling large language models into smaller ones. Distillation trains a compact student model to mimic a big teacher. Most past work used the same loss rule for teacher-written and student-written training data, ignoring how the two interact.

Their contrastive method raises the chance the student gives teacher-like answers while lowering the chance of its own weaker answers. Extensive tests built strong student models across tasks such as following instructions and writing code. The method also supported preference alignment, tuning toward human choices, and a vision-language extension.
