The authors argue matching the loss rule to the data type is the key to better distillation.
arxiv-2503-07267: Hervé Henry, writing alone in 2025, simulates how cracks run through uneven materials. Real materials often mix a stiff base with soft inclusions scattered at random. Henry uses a phase field model, which smears the crack over a small zone so a computer can track it in three dimensions. The random mix barely changed the overall stiffness. But it changed the cracking a lot. The less even the spread of soft spots, the more force the material withstood before the crack took off.
arxiv-2503-07467:
Zetao Cheng, Haoyu Li, and Lei Zhang build in 2025 multi-bubble solutions for Liouville systems on a flat torus. Such systems pair growth terms with balance rules across a grid of fields. A central open question asks whether solutions with many bubbles can exist at all in the broad case.

The authors give a full construction of multi-bubble solutions in the most general setting. Their setup keeps weights positive and fields repeating around the torus edges. The matrix that couples the fields meets set conditions that the proof leans on. The result closes a long-standing gap for this class of equations.
arxiv-2503-07567:
Nithin Raveendran, David Declercq, and Bane Vasić set design rules for a promising family of quantum error-correcting codes. Their 2025 paper studies lifted product quantum LDPC codes built from cyclic classical base codes. For a quantum computer to run reliably, its codes must catch errors whose weight clears a floor called the minimum distance.

Degenerate codes can beat that floor even when their parts are light, but only under the right conditions. The authors spell out those conditions as simple constraints on the rows and columns of the base matrix. Small worked examples show the rules in action. Because the constraints are cheap to state, they can slot into existing design software for both classical and quantum codes.
arxiv-2503-07667:
Wei Dai and co-authors introduce CLIMB in 2025, a large benchmark for clinical AI that spans many data types. Progress in medical AI has clustered on a few kinds of data, which blocks models that judge a patient's whole state. CLIMB unifies imaging, language, time series, and graph data into one test bed for training and evaluation.

The benchmark holds 4.51 million patient samples totaling nineteen terabytes, across flat images, 3D video, signals, graphs, and mixed data. Broad multitask pre-training lifted results on neglected areas by up to twenty-nine percent for ultrasound and twenty-three percent for ECG tasks over single-task learning. Pre-training also transferred well to new tasks, and strong single-type encoders paired well with the right fusion methods.
arxiv-2503-07867: Roberto Aloisio reviews cosmic ray tests of new physics in twenty twenty-five. The Pierre Auger Observatory is the world's largest cosmic ray detector. Its ultra-high-energy cosmic rays probe two scenarios beyond the standard model. Super heavy dark matter, born in the early universe, could decay into photons and neutrinos that Auger can search for. Lorentz invariance violation, suggested by quantum gravity ideas, would alter particle dispersion and interaction thresholds with background light. Auger data constrain both possibilities.
arxiv-2503-07967:
Researchers propose a Code Digital Twin as a knowledge base for AI coding help in this 2025 paper. Large software systems in big firms grow step by step under many design rules, and much of their know-how is tacit, spread across code, settings, talks, and version history.

Current AI tools fetch context at task time, but the needed context is scattered and tangled over time, past what a model can reliably gather and fuse. The proposed twin keeps long term knowledge work apart from task time fetching, acting as a context engine behind coding assistants. It models both the code and the reasons behind it, so answers can rest on a kept, growing record.
arxiv-2503-08067:
Ali Veisi, Hamidreza Amirzadeh, and Amir Mansourian improve, in a 2025 preprint, how transformers handle texts longer than any they trained on. Models usually learn position from added bias signals tied to relative distance. Fixed or globally learned biases cannot adapt to what a given passage is about. The authors' method, CABLE, learns a bias per token and per attention head. The bias bends with the input's context. That flexibility targets the sharp failure of models on over-long inputs.

A mid-size GPT-2 fitted with CABLE scored better on long texts than rivals with standard encodings. Tests ran on two large public corpora. A BERT model with CABLE also did better at long-context retrieval. The gains stacked on top of the strongest existing relative encodings. The authors release their code openly. They pitch context-aware biases as a general patch for length limits in deployed models.
arxiv-2503-08167:
Salvatore Capozziello, Sara Cesare, and Carmen Ferrara wrote a 2025 paper on the three ways gravity can be described with the same results. One view uses curvature, one uses torsion, and one uses a third trait of space called non-metricity, yet all three match the predictions of general relativity.

The authors ask what happens when each view is stretched by swapping its core term for a general function of that term. They show the stretched forms do not stay equal on their own. Adding the right boundary terms restores the match for the torsion and non-metricity forms. The result maps out which extended theories of gravity truly agree and which part ways.
arxiv-2503-08267:
Asmaa Abdallah, Ahmed Eltawil, and co-authors train a clear auto coder to probe beams and set mix beams for fast wave links, in a 2025 paper. Such links need keen beam aim but can spare just few test chirps. Past beams waste probe strength on dead zones in the room.

Their coder learns from past room reads to aim probes at hot zones. It then calls free beam forms from few strength reads with no set code book. End to end train runs with no hand marks and a strength max loss. Code size at the neck is checked by math to keep reads rich.
arxiv-2503-08467:
Oana Balmau and co-authors speed up mixture-of-experts models by slicing experts across graphics cards in a 2025 paper. The catalog title carries pasted conference classification text. These models route each token to a few specialist sub-networks, but routing is lopsided: some cards idle while others drown.

Their system, MoEShard, splits each expert's matrices by rows and columns across all cards, so every card shares every expert's work. No tokens are dropped and balance is perfect by construction. Fusing the sliced computations cuts kernel launch overhead as well. Against a leading baseline on encoder models, time to first token improved up to 6.4-fold. The authors argue sharding, not luck, should carry expert parallelism.
arxiv-2503-08567:
Christian Kading and Mario Pitschmann discuss density matrices in quantum field theory in a 2025 paper. Density matrices describe both closed and open quantum systems. Recent methods compute their elements directly for a scalar field using two established formalisms. The article gives a fuller discussion of those methods and derives expressions for both system types.

For closed systems, the authors show the dynamical map is divisible and give a path integral expression in Fock space. For open systems, after tracing out the environment, the map is not divisible, which makes the dynamics non Markovian, meaning memory effects persist. Their expressions lead to master equations without the artificial time integrals found in many others. Readers get a careful foundation for open field theory.
arxiv-2503-08767:
Joshuah Heath and six co-authors study a noise source that plagues superconducting qubits. Their twenty twenty-five paper deals with two-level systems, tiny flaws inside the Josephson junction at a qubit's heart. These flaws soak up energy and shorten the qubit's useful life, a process called decoherence.

The team treats each flaw as a soft bosonic mode pinned in place, in the oxide skin or in the bulk. They find one flaw can create a local hot spot where the Josephson energy is amplified. That amplification measurably shortens the qubit's energy lifetime, even when the flaw is not on resonance with the qubit. The source of decoherence is specific to the superconducting part itself.
arxiv-2503-08967:
Adrien Gregorj and co-authors measured in 2025 how walking partners fall into step without being told to. The data came from an underground pedestrian network, where uninstructed walkers were recorded going about their day. Groups were annotated for relationships, interaction level, and physical contact. The team first devised a way to pull the body's gait wobble out of plain trajectory data.

Frequency tools measured how well stride rhythms aligned between companions. Nonlinear tools then judged the stability of the paired motion. Closer distance and richer social interaction strengthened synchronization and steadied stride timing. Three-person formations and each walker's position inside the group also mattered. The authors conclude social bonds literally shape how crowds move. Urban designers and robot builders both rely on such findings.
arxiv-2503-09167:
Mateusz J Samsel, Agata Fronczak, and Piotr Fronczak study how epidemics unfold over time on networks, in this 2025 physics paper. The shape of the contact web, they argue, decides the whole rhythm of an outbreak, not just its start. They pair theory with large simulations of the simplest spread model, where the healthy catch the disease from the sick and stay infectious.

Two universal patterns emerge. On small world webs, where shortcuts link distant corners, case counts follow a Gompertz style curve with a fast early rise. On fractal webs, growth follows the slower Avrami pattern known from crystals spreading in constrained space. The team gives formulas for the overall course under each pattern and for how the infection rate bends it. The common claim that outbreaks always start with exponential growth, they show, fails on fractal webs.
arxiv-2503-09267:
Enrique Pérez-Montero and four co-authors extend in 2025 an infrared diagram that reads the hardness of radiation bathing gas clouds, now aimed at the cores of active galaxies. Line ratios in the mid-infrared encode how harsh the central engine's light is. High-excitation lines available in the same range sharpen the tool for narrow-line regions.

A large sample of active galaxies with space telescope spectra was run through their code, which returns ionization level and continuum shape together. Ratios built from neon and oxygen lines proved sturdy stand-ins for the continuum's slope. Both the slope and the excitation split into two humps across the sample, hinting at two families of central engines. Sorting engines by their light helps trace how black holes feed and shine.
arxiv-2503-09567:
Qiguang Chen and co-authors survey long chain-of-thought reasoning in large language models, in a 2025 paper. New reasoning models, such as the ones named in the survey, solve hard maths and coding tasks by thinking in long steps before answering. No full survey of that long style existed, and debates about overthinking and test-time scaling lacked a shared frame.

The survey separates long from short chains and offers a taxonomy of reasoning styles. It names three traits of the long style: deep reasoning, wide exploration of options, and reflection that checks the path. It then studies how such behaviour emerges, including cases where models think too long for the task. Gaps and future directions close the paper, among them multi-modal reasoning, efficiency, and better knowledge support. The authors aim the survey at researchers building reasoning systems.
arxiv-2503-09667:
Annu Bura and co-authors study tiny loops in the Sun's lower atmosphere in this 2025 paper. Telescopes have spotted small, bright loop shapes that change within minutes, but how they form was unclear. The team examined two such loops with data from three space and ground instruments that watch the Sun in many kinds of light.

The loops stretched a few thousand kilometers across and stood much lower than tall. Above them the team saw jets shooting upward and spectra that point to magnetic lines snapping and rejoining through small blobs of plasma. Heat measures showed gas hotter than a million degrees at the loop sites. The authors argue the loops and jets fit the same burst pattern known from tiny filament eruptions, scaled down from larger solar jets.
arxiv-2503-09867:
Stefan Wagner and Stefan Harmeling probe what self taught vision models keep and lose about objects, in a 2025 paper. Such models learn from images without labels and show a sound grasp of scenes. The pair test them on finding a set object in a cluttered picture.

The models read shape and size well, since edges carry those cues. They fare poorly on color, material, and texture, which are key when two objects share a shape. The authors add a small learned space over image patches that restores those traits. Retrieval rose across all traits with the add-on. The work points to a fix for tools that must pick exact objects.
arxiv-2503-09967:
Jiahua Tian and Xin Wang read hidden symmetries of five-dimensional theories off a mirror of their geometry, in a 2025 paper. The theories are superconformal field theories built by geometric engineering. Their exotic symmetries act not on points but on lines and surfaces, the one-form and two-group kinds. Such charges are counted by defect groups, which should live in the shapes the theory is built from.

Defects become branes wound on paths in a curved six-fold space. Their groups can be read from the values of line operators, taken at leading order. The mirror map then ties both symmetry kinds to how the mirror model twists at its wide-radius point. For some theories the pair even win closed forms for those line values where older methods had none. A closing conjecture ties the two-group symmetry to a torsion count in the theory's master geometry.
arxiv-2503-10167:
Hyunbin Jin and co-authors coax language models to reason longer by a decode-time nudge. The work dates to 2025. Prompt tricks can wake step-by-step thought, but they take hand craft to build. The team asks whether the wake can come from the read-out step alone.

Their plan watches the model's output as it forms. When a close seems near too soon, it slips in a set phrase that urges more thought. That nudge keeps the chain of steps from end in a rush. Tests on a range of thought tasks showed clear gains in right calls. The work backs decode tweaks as a swap for prompt craft.
arxiv-2503-10267:
Burchell and co-authors release a vast text trove in 2025 for training language tools across many tongues. Top models need huge, clean, varied text, and building that in many languages at once is hard. Their set, HPLT version two, grows an earlier project of the same name.

The single-language part holds eight trillion tokens across 193 languages. The paired part holds 380 million sentence pairs across fifty-one languages, fit for translation work. The team logs every step of how the data was built and shares the code to redo it. Wide checks cover quality and mix. An open trove of this size helps smaller language communities build tools that only big labs could make before.
arxiv-2503-10967:
Vasiliev presents equations for a supersymmetric higher-spin gauge theory in any dimension, in work from 2025. Higher-spin theory extends gauge ideas to fields of every spin at once. Adding supersymmetry brings matching boson and fermion fields into one system.

The nonlinear equations cover symmetric massless fields plus hook-shaped bosonic fields of all spins. A key move recasts symmetry and factorization demands inside the BRST formalism. That step greatly simplifies the nonlinear system as written. The theory is expected to carry endless independent coupling constants. Vasiliev conjectures those constants flow from locality limits on the factorization ideal. The work targets mathematical physics specialists.
arxiv-2503-11067:
Bin Liu and co-authors reformulate recommendation ranking as variational inference in a 2025 paper. Pairwise learning drives most implicit-feedback recommenders, yet sparse, noisy clicks and popularity bias corrupt it. Popular items get shown more, then clicked more, in a loop.

Their VarBPR treats the hidden index variables behind each comparison probabilistically. Training splits into an inference stage and a learning stage, with closed-form posteriors. A prior sets the target exposure pattern, and a temperature knob controls debiasing strength. The design gives operators principled control over how much popularity should count. Recommenders could serve long-tail taste without abandoning statistical rigor.
arxiv-2503-11167:
Haonan Wang, Qixiang Zhang, Lehan Wang, Xuanqi Huang, and Xiaomeng Li rebuild videos, in a 2025 preprint, from brain scans of people watching them. Reading moving pictures from fMRI data is hard: the signal is coarse, and motion must stay smooth. Their framework, NEURONS, copies the layered design of the human visual cortex. It splits the job into four linked tasks. These are picking out key objects, naming concepts, describing the scene, and drafting a rough video. Each task feeds the next, much like stages of real vision.

At run time, those outputs become guiding signals for a pre-trained text-to-video diffusion model. The model paints the final clip from that guidance. Against leading rivals, NEURONS raised video consistency by about a quarter and scene accuracy by about a fifth. The authors point to brain-computer interfaces and clinics as future users.
arxiv-2503-11467:
Jose-Luis Holgado-Alvarez and co-authors train a legged robot's navigation policy against adversarial moving obstacles, in this 2025 paper. Steady walking is largely solved; dodging surprise obstacles in new places is not. Their setup splits control into a walking layer and a navigation layer. The navigation layer learns while obstacle agents actively try to block it, like opponents in a game.

Unbounded opponents would make training hopeless, so the adversaries follow bounded rationality, modeled with quantal response equilibria. A curriculum raises their cleverness step by step. The method, called Hi-QARL by the authors, is tested in unseen random mazes with several moving obstacles. It holds up well there and transfers to a simulated Unitree GO1 quadruped.
arxiv-2503-11667:
Zhenyu Wang releases a toolkit for peeking inside large language models, in a 2025 paper. The logit lens method reads a model's half-finished thoughts by decoding its inner layers as if they were final answers. Older tools for this trick no longer fit modern model designs.

The new toolkit, LogitLens4LLMs, works with current models such as Qwen-2.5 and Llama-3.1. Special hooks grab signals from both the attention parts and the feed-forward parts of each layer. The tools run inside the popular HuggingFace library with low extra cost. Users can explore one run interactively or process many runs in batches. The author shares the code openly to support deeper study of how these models work. Such tools help researchers check what a model seems to represent at each stage.
arxiv-2503-12067:
Amir M Mansourian and co-authors survey, in a 2025 paper, the full landscape of knowledge distillation, a method for shrinking big neural networks into nimble ones. Modern vision and language models are too large for many phones and edge devices, costing too much time and memory. Distillation trains a small student model on extra guidance from a large teacher. The field has grown fast, and older surveys no longer cover its newest branches.

The authors sort methods by where the knowledge comes from, how the transfer runs, and which algorithm drives it. They also organize work by data type and by use, from diffusion models to three-dimensional inputs and giant foundation models. Head-to-head comparisons help readers pick a method for their setting. The survey claims a fresh structure rather than a simple update of earlier reviews.
arxiv-2503-12667:
Jacob Chmura, Jonah Dauvet, and Sebastian Sabry test if the stored knowledge of large language models can lift a tool that judges whether an event sounds plausible. Their paper is from two thousand twenty-five.

Tools that learn word sense from co-use fail to split events that could happen from those that could not. The team draws out facts held in large models, with light fine-tuning. They train twelve small add-ons, each for a type of fact, such as traits of things or strength of links. They then fuse the add-ons on top of a base model's word codes. The mix is trained across two sets of plausibility tasks. Their code is shared in the open.
arxiv-2503-12867:
Materials that fold in designed ways can absorb shocks or even compute, and a 2025 paper by Wenfeng Liu and co-authors offers a recipe book for their moving parts. The prized features are floppy modes, motions that cost almost no energy, and frustrated loops, rings whose parts cannot all be satisfied at once.

The team's combinatorial method builds chains carrying as many of these features as desired, with chosen shapes. Adding a deliberate mismatch turns a floppy chain into a frustrated loop. A buckling trick lets the modes fold one after another in a set order. As a showpiece, the structures perform matrix-vector multiplication in the material itself. The work supplies design rules for soft machines and mechanical logic.
arxiv-2503-13267:
Shoupan Liu, Yunqi Liu, Yan Peng, and Cheng-Yong Zhang study rotating black holes in 2025 in a modified gravity theory. Their framework adds a squared Gauss-Bonnet term and a scalar field coupled to it. Such setups can produce black holes with scalar hair around them.

Using a spectral method to solve the field equations, they map where the new solutions exist. Both spin and the squared coupling term narrow the space for these hairy solutions. Over a wide range, the new black holes have higher entropy than standard ones of the same mass and spin. That suggests they are thermodynamically favored.
arxiv-2503-13767:
Two ultracold gases that refuse to mix can tear at their shared border in ways that echo fluids and even astrophysics. Kishor Kumar and co-authors simulate a pair of rubidium condensates in a flat circular trap in this 2025 paper, stirring them into three classic instabilities. Heavy-over-light layering gives Rayleigh-Taylor plumes; sliding layers give Kelvin-Helmholtz rolls.

A third route needs no push at all: flip the gases from unmixing to mixing and watch the border dissolve unevenly. Every case bred vortices and sound waves, with vortices winning late in the sliding case and sound elsewhere. Energy spectra sometimes matched the classic Kolmogorov turbulence laws, with a bottleneck kink in the quench case.
arxiv-2503-13867:
Wentao Cao, Jonas Hirsch, and Dominik Inauen wrote this 2025 mathematics paper stretching a classic theorem on bending surfaces without stretching them. The Nash-Kuiper theorem says a squeezed-short shape can still be embedded with its distances intact, wrinkled at fine scales. How rough that wrinkled map may be has a famous threshold tied to Borisov.

The team push past that threshold: for any short immersion of a bounded, simply connected region, they build an isometric immersion as close as desired, with smoothness up to the weaker exponent. In two dimensions their bound meets the Onsager exponent known from fluid turbulence. Three new devices power the proof: a fresh corrugation pattern, an integration-by-parts step, and a tailored split of the error terms.
arxiv-2503-14067:
Chipmakers keep adding tiny number formats for AI, and the instruction set groans under the variety. Laslo Hunhold argues in 2025, through Intel's AVX10.2 vector extensions, for swapping the whole shelf of float formats for one tapered-precision design called takum. Takum promises the exactness where values cluster and reach where they spread, under a single consistent rule set.

Rebuilding the extension on takum, he finds, yields a cleaner, more readable instruction set with room for honest eight- and sixteen-bit general arithmetic, not just deep learning niches. The case study invites a rethink of how processors should count.
arxiv-2503-14167:
Christian Poelitz and Nick McKenna wrote a 2025 paper on fake dialogues that train AI helpers for data tasks. Real chats about tables go off script when user facts are missing or wrong. Building data sets of such chats by hand is slow. Their frame makes the chats from ready-made table questions.

Each made-up chat solves one table question in a joint way. Two scenes are modeled: the AI asks for clarity, or the user corrects the AI. A strong teacher model checks each chat for correctness. Tests on two data sets showed even large models struggle to ask good clarifying questions and to absorb corrections well.
arxiv-2503-14467:
Dietmar Ferger published a paper in 2025 on the long-run behavior of estimators defined by minimizing U-processes. Many statistical estimators are exactly that: the value that makes some averaged objective smallest. Classical theory promises a neat bell curve at the square-root rate, but many real estimators break that promise.

Ferger gives necessary and sufficient conditions for such minimizers to settle into a stable limit law, with a broad family of allowed normalizing sequences beyond the standard one. Every possible limit falls into exactly one of four classes from Smirnov's classic theory. The domains of attraction, the estimator families feeding each class, get fresh characterizations. The results extend Huber's famous theory and cover higher-degree U-statistics in one frame.
arxiv-2503-14667:
Pablo Ochoa, a mathematician, proves that a broad family of elliptic systems has real solutions inside bounded regions. The systems live in Orlicz-Sobolev spaces, a flexible setting for problems whose growth is not a neat power law. Their source terms sit at the critical edge set by the space's embedding rules, where standard methods often break.

Ochoa joins two heavy tools. A Mountain Pass Theorem that drops the usual Palais-Smale compactness demand does part of the work. The second Concentration Compactness Principle of Lions, moved into Orlicz-Sobolev spaces, does the rest. Together they yield nontrivial solutions for very general systems. The result widens the reach of variational methods to nonlinearities without polynomial growth.
arxiv-2503-15167:
Fujian Yan, Hui Li, and Hongsheng He present a method that lets robots plan task suited grasps from partial views of an object. A good grasp depends on the task: lifting, holding a handle, wrapping, or pressing each demand different contact. Depth scans alone show only part of the shape.

A recurrent generative network rebuilds the full volume from a varying number of scans. Candidate grasps are drawn from a knowledge data set and matched by volume and action similarity. A reinforcement learning step then refines the chosen grasp for the task. On a dual arm mobile robot, the system reached eighty-nine percent grasp accuracy across four tasks.
arxiv-2503-15567:
Yanchen Luo and co-authors introduce a 2025 model that designs three-dimensional molecules for drugs and materials. A molecule mixes atom types, bonds, and exact positions in space. Past models kept separate inner codes for the flat facts and the spatial ones. That split slowed both training and generation. Their model squeezes all of it into one shared code. The code keeps the symmetry of space and rebuilds the molecule with almost no error.

A standard diffusion model then makes new codes in that shared space. Tests on two public molecule sets set new marks for quality. On the drug-like set, one error score fell by nearly three quarters from the prior best. Shape accuracy also rose by a large margin on average. The team shares its code in public. They argue one code beats split codes for this task.
arxiv-2503-16167:
Hong Yi Lin and four co-authors present CodeReviewQA, a test set for how well large language models grasp code review notes. Their study appeared in twenty twenty-five. Review notes are often brief, vague, and loose in tone, so a model has to grasp both code and human intent. Past tests score fixes by word match, which hides where a model fails.

The test set breaks a fix into three steps, each posed as a choice task. Steps cover what kind of change is asked, where it goes, and which fix is right. Nine hundred hand-picked cases span nine code tongues. Tests of many new models showed clear weak spots that fix scores alone had masked.
arxiv-2503-16267:
Samik Basu, Ramesh Kasilingam, and Ankur Sarkar count smooth structures in a 2025 math paper. They study a space formed by a complex projective space times a sphere. Two smooth forms can share the same shape yet differ in fine structure, and the team sorts those cases.

They compute a group that measures how much a smooth form can twist along the sphere factor. The work uses known values for stable maps between spheres. For sphere sizes from two to seven, with one gap, they pin down that group. They also classify all smooth forms for sizes one to seven.
arxiv-2503-16367:
Saifollahi and the Euclid team read early shots from a new space scope, aimed at dwarf galaxies in the Perseus crowd. Dwarfs and their star balls, called globular clusters, trade mass and stars in ways that tell how each was born. Their 2025 release study uses the scope's first free data to map that trade in the crowd. Sharp, wide shots let faint dwarfs and their small balls be counted in one sweep.

Counts and hues of balls per dwarf form the core read. Rich ball kin can flag dwarfs that lost their gas or merged in the past. The crowd's harsh yard makes it a keen test bed. Early data thus serve as a proof of the scope's reach. Full survey years will stretch the same read to the far sky.
arxiv-2503-16467:
Anargh Viswanath, Lokesh Veeramacheneni, and Hendrik Buschmeier want robots that can explain themselves by truly taking in the scene around a conversation, in this 2025 workshop paper. A robot that hears speech but ignores vision, or the reverse, will misunderstand its human partner and lose trust. The challenge is fusing the streams into one usable context.

Their framework builds a joint representation of speech and vision, then aligns the two in time. The test case is relevance: judging whether what the user just said matches what the robot currently sees. A multimodal joint representation module merges the inputs, while a temporal alignment module lines up words with the visual moments they refer to. The authors close by mapping how such context representations support different flavors of explainability in human-robot collaboration.
arxiv-2503-16567:
Laurits Dixen, Stefan Heinrich, and Paolo Burelli test deep learning models at reading object ideas from brain waves, in this 2025 paper. Neural decoding tries to recover what the brain represents from recorded activity. Their data set holds EEG recordings from forty-six people watching images flash by.

The decoding target was simple: living versus non-living things. Fifteen deep models across five designs were compared with a top linear method. The linear model failed the task, while nearly all deep models succeeded. Results split further by object category, showing where each design shines. The authors suggest such networks can double as tools for probing the brain itself.
arxiv-2503-16667:
Oriol Vendrell-Gallart and co-authors test whether data fusion can support foundation models for metal printing. Their 2025 study deals with laser powder bed fusion, a method that builds metal parts layer by layer. Large foundation models could speed process tuning and new material design. Data scarcity is a major block, though. The team runs controlled experiments on transfer across materials and properties.

Lab data sets were made for two stainless steels. Five process settings were varied, and porosity and hardness were measured. Statistical models called Gaussian processes were fit in many configurations. The tests ask if knowledge of one steel or property helps predict another. Results stress data size, complexity, and noise. The authors call for structured learning that uses domain knowledge.
arxiv-2503-16967:
Konstantin Grotov and Dmitry Botov stretch the data science notebook into a two-dimensional canvas in this 2025 paper. Notebooks line code up in one column, which fights the branching way analysts actually think and makes teamwork and AI help awkward. Their Computational Canvas lets cells float freely on a plane.

Features include arrangeable cells, separate working environments, and cleaner output handling, all built as a plugin for a popular code editor. The spatial layout supports visual exploration and natural collaboration among people and AI agents. The authors argue the shift from line to plane suits modern data work, where experiments fork, merge, and get revisited rather than marching straight down a page.
arxiv-2503-17167:
Huy Truong, Andrés Tello, Alexander Lazovik, and Victoria Degeler present a large data set for water networks in a 2025 paper. Real water network models are hard to share because they can expose private details. That lack of data holds back machine learning work, which needs many examples to learn from.

Their data set, DiTEC-WDN, holds 36,000 unique cases run over one day or one year. An automated pipeline tunes key values such as pressure, flow, and demand, then checks that each case stays realistic. In total the set holds 228 million graph based states. It can support tasks such as forecasts over time and estimates at the graph, node, or link level. The set is shared under a public license for open study.
arxiv-2503-17367:
T Zalialiutdinov and D Solovyev build a coupled cluster method to study light two atom molecules in strong magnetic fields. Fields warp the energy math, tangle the wave function, and add a gauge origin quirk that standard tools handle poorly. Their 2025 study pairs two open chemistry packages to do the job.

They compute energy curves, steady and shifting dipole moments, and vibration spectra for three molecules: hydrogen, helium hydride, and lithium hydride. Field strengths vary across the runs. Special atomic orbitals that carry the gauge fix the origin problem inside the code. The authors say the setup lifts accuracy for coupled cluster work in fields and opens wider studies.
arxiv-2503-17467:
Yuxuan Wei and co-authors add a Wiener filter stage to MPEG's point cloud compression to clean up decoded quality, in a 2025 paper. Point clouds pack scenes into huge point sets, and the lossy side of the G-PCC standard leaves visible damage at low bitrates. The filter sits inside both encoder and decoder and is sharpened by inherited coefficients and a brightness-based sorting of points.

A fast neighbor search built on Morton codes keeps the added cost down. Tested under a standard lossless-geometry setup, the method saved roughly 6 to 8 percent of bitrate across color channels at equal quality. The gains target immersive media that streams detailed scenes.
arxiv-2503-17967:
Zeyu Wang computes the murmuration pattern for a family of L-functions tied to imaginary quadratic fields. The work appeared in twenty twenty-five. Murmurations are ripples in averages of arithmetic data, first spotted with machine learning in modular forms.

Wang finds the density for Hecke L-functions attached to nontrivial characters of these fields. The density shows the same universality seen in the modular form case. Its averages also agree with a famous conjecture about low zeros of L-functions. The fresh feature here is an almost repeating wave in the pattern. That wave lets the murmuration be described without averaging over primes, a shortcut no other family had shown. The result widens a fast-growing topic.
arxiv-2503-18067:
Shahaf Bassan and co-authors build neural networks that explain themselves for business process monitoring in a 2025 paper. Such monitoring predicts what a running case will do next, like its next activity, from logs of past cases. Deep sequence models lead the field but act as black boxes. Explanations bolted on after training can be unfaithful, costly, and brittle on odd cases.

Their approach weaves the explanation into the model itself, so the reasons come out with the prediction, not after it. The design targets the trust problem head-on: a manager who can read why the model expects a delay can act on it. The paper sets out the self-explaining design and tests it on the standard next-activity task. Faithful, cheap explanations are the prize.
arxiv-2503-18167:
Suman Adhya, Avishek Lahiri, Debarshi Kumar Sanyal, and Partha Pratim Das test whether negative sampling helps neural topic models learn better topics, in a paper from 2025. Topic models sort large text sets into themes with no labels given. Negative sampling, which trains a model by contrast with wrong examples, had not been well tested in this label-free field.

The team added negative sampling to the decoder of several autoencoder-based topic models. Tests ran on four public data sets. Topics grew more coherent and more diverse, and document sorting improved as well. Human raters also judged the topics to be of higher quality. The authors present the trick as a cheap way to lift topic model performance.
arxiv-2503-18267:
Minh-Tuan Tran and four colleagues wrote a 2025 paper on dataset distillation, compressing a large training data set into a small synthetic one that trains models almost as well. Features in data come in two kinds: instance-specific details unique to each example, and class-general patterns shared across a category. Good distillation must keep both.

Earlier approaches tended to favor one kind and lose the other. The authors propose refining the non-critical regions of distilled images, the areas that carry instance detail without disturbing the class pattern. This refinement rebalances the two feature types. Better distilled data sets mean cheaper model training for everyone who reuses them, from research labs to production teams.
arxiv-2503-18667: Acharya and a very large team of co-authors in the KATRIN collaboration wrote this 2025 paper reporting a search for sterile neutrinos based on 259 days of data from the KATRIN experiment. Sterile neutrinos are a proposed extra kind of neutrino that would barely interact with matter. A find would rewrite the standard picture of particle physics. The paper is one of the collaboration's main data releases, with the full author list of the project, and it rests on the long 259-day run rather than a short test period.
arxiv-2503-18867:
Juan Guillermo Garrido characterizes a strong form of monotone behavior for set-valued maps, in this 2025 math paper. Monotone maps are a core tool in the study of equilibria and optimization. The strong local form he studies is harder to pin down than the basic one. Garrido works in Hilbert spaces, where geometry aids the proofs. His results were backed by several Chilean science grants.

His main tool is the graphical derivative, which reads a map's local slope from its graph. He shows that strong local maximal monotonicity matches a stated property of that derivative. A payoff follows for a second-order account of variational convexity. That account no longer needs a side condition on how smooth the underlying function must be.
arxiv-2503-18967:
Semra Gurtas Dogan, Abdullah Guvendi, and Omar Mustafa present a 2025 physics paper on how light bends and waves travel through an optical wormhole. The setting is a curved two-dimensional space linked to the BTZ black hole, with constant negative curvature. Its optical metric forms a hyperbolic wormhole for light rays.

In the ray picture, an effective barrier pushes light paths away and blocks circular photon orbits. In the wave picture, the authors recast the wave equation into a form like the Schrödinger equation. A position-dependent critical frequency separates waves that pass from waves that fade out. At high frequency the medium turns clear. The setup acts as a curvature-tuned filter. The authors suggest uses in analog gravity rigs and graphene-based light platforms.
arxiv-2503-19567:
Peter Boyvalenkov and Sergii Favorov published this mathematics paper in 2025. It concerns crystalline measures, special patterns of point masses spread through space. Such a measure has a remarkable property: its Fourier transform, which rewrites the pattern in terms of waves, is again made of point masses. The authors ask how fast the total mass of these patterns can grow inside large regions.

They prove two results. First, take the transform's masses, square them, and build a new measure from those squares. That new measure cannot pile up too fast anywhere; it stays translation bounded. Second, if the wave positions inside any fixed-size ball are independent in an integer sense, the transform itself is also translation bounded. These results give concrete conditions a crystalline measure must meet to count as a Fourier quasicrystal. Such patterns matter in the study of ordered materials that are not simple crystals.
arxiv-2503-20267:
Jiabin Wang and co-authors show how a cold atom gas can mimic two universes at once in this 2025 paper. The system is a Bose Einstein condensate with two spin components. Sound waves in each component feel their own curved spacetime metric. That lets one lab system host two expanding or shrinking analogue universes side by side.

By ramping the interaction between the components, one universe expands while the other contracts. The sizes can be read from oscillation frequencies in density patterns. The expansion history shows up in the pattern amplitudes. Both signals are within reach of current cold atom setups. The work opens a lab route to questions about multiple universes that astronomy cannot test directly.
arxiv-2503-20467:
Graphs can be treated as a language, and some graph families can be checked as fast as reading a sentence. Mattia De Rosa and Mark Minas describe a tool for that job, GrappaRE, in this 2025 paper. Users write a regular expression over typed symbols, and the tool turns it into a trimmed deterministic automaton.

The automaton then tests whether a graph belongs to the family, with no backtracking detours. Timing measurements confirm the check runs in time proportional to graph size. The work builds on a recent result showing which graph languages automata can define this way. Convenient specification is the selling point: describe the family in one expression, and recognition follows mechanically.
arxiv-2503-20667:
Chenjing Bu builds a new branch of a counting theory in 2025 for objects that carry a mirror like symmetry. The base theory counts stable objects in a category and is a tool in geometry and physics. Bu extends it from the general group of symmetries to the two groups that keep a form fixed, the orthogonal and symplectic cases.

The counts are defined with a motivic algebra and its new partner module for the symmetric case. He proves wall crossing formulas, which say how the counts change when the rule for what counts as stable shifts. As cases, he defines counts for symmetric perfect complexes on a special three dimensional shape, and for self mirror views of a quiver. The work is pure math, aimed at experts in this fast growing field.
arxiv-2503-21067: Enzo Baraldi de Onofre, Leonardo Mauro Pereira Moraes, and Cristina Dutra de Aguiar present a web app that answers sports questions in plain words, in a paper from 2025. A user types a question and gets back the three best matched answers, with linked facts and source pages. Sample cases show the app can return both names and number values. The app and its code are open to the public on the HuggingFace site.
arxiv-2503-21667:
Davide Tebaldi and Roberto Zanasi offer a direct way to sketch asymptotic Bode plots, in a 2025 control engineering paper. These plots summarize how a system responds across frequencies, and a rough sketch often suffices for first analysis. The standard recipe, though, dissects every factor of the transfer function one by one, which grows slow and error-prone as systems gain parts.

Their method computes generalized approximating functions for the whole transfer function and draws the magnitude and phase sketches in one pass, using a small set of firm rules. The authors compare it with the classic approach and claim gains in orderliness, precision, and time, especially for functions with many factors. The paper targets students and practicing engineers alike.
arxiv-2503-21767:
A robot that hears "hand me the red mug" must find that object inside its three-dimensional map of the room. Hairong Yin, Huangying Zhan, Yi Xu, and Raymond Yeh improved that skill in 2025 for scenes built from Gaussian splats, a fast rendering format. Labels painted onto the scene from camera views often disagree with each other, blurring the map's meanings.

Their method tracks segmentation masks across views to build one consistent set of labels for teaching the scene. It then answers queries by first finding that trusted ground truth and using it to pick the matching points. Scores on three benchmark datasets beat prior methods, with one dataset gaining over twenty points.
arxiv-2503-21867:
Cuomo, Firat, Nardi, and Ricci study energy correlators at large charge in conformal field theories in a 2025 paper. The states are created by operators with a large global charge. A superfluid effective theory describes this sector in many theories.

The authors build a systematic way to compute event shapes inside that effective theory. At leading order, shapes split into products of classic values set by symmetry, as known before. The next order is a true prediction, and they compute it for energy and charge correlators. A sharp boost appears when detectors are nearly aligned, caused by sound waves. Results extend to a wide class of event shapes.
arxiv-2503-21967:
Agustin Munoz Gonzalez, Juan Ignacio Sequeira, and Ariel Dembling wrote this finance paper, published in two thousand twenty-five, on a hidden cost in crypto markets. People who add coins to automated trading pools can lose value when prices move, a loss known as impermanent loss.

The authors work out the math of that loss for constant-product pools, the kind used by Uniswap and Balancer. They show that a pool's value can be copied exactly with a fixed mix of standard call and put options. Within a set price range, that mix fully covers the loss. A worked example uses real option prices from Deribit, a large crypto options market, to show a strangle strategy in action. The paper gives pool providers a concrete way to hedge a risk many only meet after the fact.
arxiv-2503-22067:
Sergey Kitaev and Philip Zhang wrote this 2025 arXiv paper in enumerative combinatorics, counting permutations by their descents and their sortability. A permutation is stack-sortable if a simple stack machine can rearrange it into order; restricting the number of stacks gives families whose counting is partly understood. The authors work near the top of the range, with almost as many stacks as elements.

They find the full distribution of descents, packaged in Eulerian polynomials, for permutations sortable with all but three or all but four stacks. They extend the count to permutations that also avoid any chosen pattern of length three, across three stack levels. The distributions double as enumerations of the families themselves. Two conjectures close the paper, one linking the work to restricted stacks and another claiming a hidden symmetry between two pattern classes at every stack count.
arxiv-2503-22267:
Charalampos Passalidis studies heavy-tailed probability laws that live in more than one dimension, in a two thousand twenty-five math paper. He brings in a new class, the multivariate strong subexponential ones. Such laws fit rare, huge events, like extreme insurance claims. In them, one big jump can swamp the sum of all the rest.

He proves a few basic facts for the new class. One is a form of Kesten's inequality for this case. One says the class stays closed when sums are formed. He then shows the single big jump rule for sums stopped at a random time. The terms he needs are weaker than for the old class of this kind. He also finds sharp bounds for large moves away from the mean. A use in a nonstandard insurance risk model ends the work.
arxiv-2503-22367:
Shakul Awasthi, Hyunggyu Park, and Jae Sung Lee study small random systems whose heat level changes over time. Their paper is from two thousand twenty-five. Such systems matter for tiny engines, yet the common over-damped shortcut drops the speed of the parts from view. That shortcut then gives wrong values for heat loss and entropy growth.

The authors name these gaps thermodynamic anomalies and derive exact forms for them. One sharp point is that thick fluid and small mass lead to the same motion laws but unlike anomaly laws. Their forms let users judge engine yield without measuring speed. They also give a simple way to gauge the kinetic energy of such a system.
arxiv-2503-22467:
Networks of who depends on whom, among genes or species, are usually read as flat webs, yet the entities fall into natural groups. Jeanne Tous and Julien Chiquet build the groups into the model itself in 2025 with the Normal-Block model. Variables are clustered first in the mathematics, and the network is then drawn between clusters, smaller and easier to read.

Extra penalties prune false edges, and a zero inflated variant absorbs the quirks of real count data. Two fitting routes are offered, one quick and one rigorous, the second learning clusters and network together. Tests span simulated webs, protein data, and word counts on web pages. The authors supply a public software package for the method.
arxiv-2503-22567:
Josh Millar and four co-authors present the first head-to-head benchmarks of micro neural processing units, tiny chips that run neural networks on very little power, in a 2025 paper. Running AI on the device itself cuts delay, protects privacy, and lowers cost compared with the cloud. Several commercial chips now target this niche, but independent comparisons were missing.

The team built and released an open compilation pipeline so the same trained models could run fairly across very different hardware. Their tests confirmed some expected trends but also exposed surprises: some chips scaled oddly as models grew more complex, and spec sheets did not always predict real performance. The authors offer guidance for both chip and software designers.
arxiv-2503-22667:
Young discs of gas around newborn stars can grow heavy enough that their gravity stirs them into spirals, moving matter inward and building planets. Starlight heating should calm that unrest, especially in the outer disc. Caitriona Leedham, Richard Booth, and Cathie Clarke ask how much the answer depends on the way heating is put into the model, comparing two recipes in two-dimensional simulations.

When heating was spread by mass, the unrest died out once starlight became the heat source, as expected. When heating was spread evenly by area, the unrest survived under strong starlight and high stability readings, matching theory. Discs could still break into fragments in that regime, though the cooling had to be faster as the heating rose. The team caps the viscosity in that state at roughly 0.03 to 0.09. Their point is practical: the recipe chosen for starlight can flip what a simulation predicts.
arxiv-2503-23167:
Zewen Liu and co-authors survey the marriage of graph neural networks and differential equations in a 2025 paper. Networks learn on graph data; equations describe how things change continuously in time and space. Together they promise models that respect both structure and dynamics.

The survey sorts methods by principle and shows where each fits. Uses span molecules, traffic forecasting, and epidemic spread, all systems that are networks in motion. Open challenges and future directions close the review. For researchers entering this fast-growing borderland, the paper serves as both map and compass.
arxiv-2503-23967:
A famed toy of quantum chaos pairs chance links with odd bits that are not quite fermions. Tingfei Li probes one slim case of that toy in a 2025 note, where each bit talks to just one mate. The links are drawn from a chance pool with a known shape, which makes the sums tractable.

Heat marks of the toy settle in a self true way, he finds. A form test of its tune spread shows a ramp that grows with a fast, e based climb. The climb's rate runs to a fixed mark or to no bound as the toy grows, by the bit count rules in play. The note adds a fresh view on toys with odd bit kinds.
arxiv-2503-24167:
Changying Ding and Daniel Drimbe prove that certain product groups keep their shape under a loose notion of sameness, in a 2025 paper. Measure equivalence groups groups whose actions can be matched in a measured way, a soft cousin of isomorphism. Their solidity result concerns products built from biexact groups, a class with strong rigidity traits.

The payoff is a clean decomposition: if a two-factor product matches a many-factor product of such groups, the factors must line up after splitting the list once. Results like this tell algebraists which group blueprints can be heard through static, and which are truly distinct.
arxiv-2504-00167:
Sinico, Boschetti, and Neto present a 2025 robotics paper on touch reading without extra sensors. Collaborative robots already carry torque sensors in their joints. The team used those built-in signals to read digits that people draw by hand. Users traced numbers zero to nine on a plain pad fixed to the robot arm.

Their data set pairs joint torque traces with forces at the tool tip from many writers. A trick that flips and rotates samples guards against odd drawing styles. A memory network sorted the digits online with ninety-four percent accuracy, even for new writers. A real robot then used the skill in a fruit delivery task for people with limited movement.
arxiv-2504-00267:
Daniel Irving Bernstein and Nathaniel Vaduthala study flag matroids, layered structures built from matroids of rising rank, in a paper published in two thousand twenty-five. Their central question is which of these structures can be written with numbers from a given field.

They give a new axiom system that defines flag matroids from scratch. For uniform flag matroids, they pin down exactly when a numeric form exists. For full flag matroids, they list the blocked smaller patterns that rule out a form over the two-element and three-element fields. They also treat the regular case in several matching ways. The results sort out which of these layered structures algebra can actually build.
arxiv-2504-01067:
Zhiyuan Ji and co-authors photograph a young galaxy whose starlight is leaking the photons that once reionized the universe. The galaxy Ion1, seen as it was when the cosmos was young, lets Lyman continuum light escape, and the team imaged it with two James Webb cameras plus older Hubble views. For the first time in such a leaker, they caught warm dust glowing in the mid-infrared.

The dust lies in a porous pattern, thin exactly where the ionizing light and the hydrogen glow peak. The escaping region also shines far bluer than the rest of the galaxy, a gradient the team traces to uneven dust dimming. Their picture: a compact starburst near the galaxy's heart blows clear channels through gas and dust, and photons slip out where the cover is thinnest.
arxiv-2504-01367:
Hanxi Fang and co-authors add two-way version control to data notebooks in this 2025 paper. People explore data in loops and branches, undoing and forking as they go. Standard notebooks, though, march in a straight line.

Their system, Kishuboard, versions code and data together as one space. Two knobs let users roll back runs or branch the data state with ease. It plugs into the popular Jupyter notebook tool. A user study checked whether the design works in practice. The authors argue exploration tools should match how analysts actually wander. Rollback and branching become first-class acts, not hacks.
arxiv-2504-01667:
Cedric Lothritz, Jordi Cabot, and Laura Bernardy wrote this 2025 paper testing language models in Luxembourgish, a small language the industry mostly ignores. Evaluation data for such languages barely exists, so the team borrowed a ready-made yardstick: official language proficiency exams, the kind used to certify human learners.

Run through the exams, the big frontier models, Claude and DeepSeek-R1 among them, scored high, while smaller models flopped. More useful still, exam performance predicted how the same models did on other Luxembourgish language tasks. The authors argue proficiency tests are a cheap, credible benchmark for low-resource languages, no custom data set required. The case study doubles as a warning about which languages get left behind.
arxiv-2504-01867:
Gennady Stupakov, a solo author, revisits how particles scatter inside relativistic beams, in a 2025 paper. Standard theory treats scattering as pairs of particles colliding one at a time. In reality each particle interacts with many partners at once, a collective effect the simple picture misses.

A plasma physics framework from the 1960s already handles such many-body collisions. Stupakov applies it to the growth of energy spread in a relativistic beam. His early conclusion is that the standard theory may understate the effect of long-range correlations between collisions. The work suggests beam heating estimates in accelerator physics could need revision.
arxiv-2504-02567:
Pavel Peterka and co-authors show that a flash of light fired just before the main pulse can throttle the high harmonics an atom-thin crystal emits, in a 2025 paper. The crystal is a single layer of molybdenum disulfide, driven by mid-infrared light into producing ultraviolet harmonics, copies of the drive at multiplied frequencies. A weaker prep pulse, tuned on or just below the material's exciton resonance, seeds carriers in the layer first.

With resonant prep, the harmonics dimmed, which the team blames on ultrafast dephasing as the seeded carriers scatter. With near-resonant prep, a fast extra dip appeared only while the two pulses overlapped, matching two-photon absorption that theory predicts. The work shows harmonic output in two-dimensional materials can be steered on ultrashort time scales, a knob for future light sources and switches.
arxiv-2504-02667:
Thomas Dooms, Ward Gauderis, Geraint Wiggins, and Jose Oramas design neural networks that can explain themselves in this two thousand twenty-five paper. Their build, chi-net, fuses the compositional multilinear structure of tensor networks with the expressivity and efficiency of deep neural networks. The compositional structure is the interpretability hook. Tensor networks split computations into pieces whose ways of acting on each other can be looked at, unlike plain weight matrices.

The team also brings in a diagonalization method, ODT, showing linear low-rank structure in a model, shown on a multilayer model for the SVHN digit data set. That shown structure is then used two ways: toward formal, weight-based interpretability, arguing in a strict way about what the network computes. The other way is toward model compression, shrinking the network with its shown low-rank form. The paper sets compositionality as the bridge between performance and interpretability.
arxiv-2504-02867:
Hongliu Cao, Ilias Driouich, Robin Singh, and Eoin Thomas automate the design of language model judges, personalized to each evaluation job. Judging generated text with models is now standard, since overlap and embedding scores miss nuance. Existing judge frameworks, though, adapt poorly to different text and ground-truth styles. Their scores also skew oddly and correlate weakly with human judgment.

The proposed multi-agent system designs a bespoke judge for each application. Agents iteratively refine the evaluation prompts, balancing task fit against alignment with human perception. Experiments show better evaluation accuracy than existing methods. Scores come out better behaved as well as better aimed. The system treats judging as a design problem with a client, not a fixed instrument. Personalized evaluation, the authors argue, is what open-ended generation always needed.
arxiv-2504-03467: Wonjun Chae and co-authors study sums of squares with one forbidden value in this 2025 paper. The question: if squares of one chosen integer may not be used, how many squares does it take to build every reachable positive integer? Dubouis settled the case where zero is the forbidden value. This paper handles a general fixed exclusion.
arxiv-2504-03767:
Brandon Radosevich and John Halloran audit the security of the Model Context Protocol, the open standard that lets language models call external tools and data sources. The protocol's convenience comes with risk: chained tool servers let a model act on a developer's machine. The authors show leading models can be coerced through such tools into running malicious code, opening remote access, and stealing credentials.

As a countermeasure they built MCPSafetyScanner, an agent-based auditing tool that examines any MCP server before deployment. It generates adversarial test cases from the server's own tool list, hunts for matching vulnerabilities and fixes, and writes a security report. The tool is freely released. The authors argue agentic workflows need this kind of proactive auditing as standard practice.
arxiv-2504-03967:
Ziqing Guo, Jan Balewski, and Ziwen Pan built a translator between quantum software frameworks in a 2025 paper. Simulating quantum circuits on classical machines verifies algorithms before hardware runs them, but mainstream tools run on CPUs and crawl, while graphics processors need code written for entirely different frameworks. Their Q-GEAR system converts circuits written in the popular Qiskit toolkit into kernels for NVIDIA's CUDA-Q platform automatically.

Converted circuits then run far faster: about two orders of magnitude on CPUs and tenfold on GPUs, with little coding effort, per their benchmarks. Linking memory across several GPUs lets oversized circuits fit. Container images tuned for a national supercomputer's scheduler reached near-full GPU use, easing adoption for large simulation campaigns.
arxiv-2504-04067:
Pranab Sen proves new concentration bounds, which are math guarantees that random averages stay close to their expected values, for quantum information tasks. Earlier results for a covering problem in quantum communication gave guarantees only on average, and a classic theorem handled independent samples. Writing in twenty twenty-five, Sen extends the picture in two directions. One result covers several parties at once and gives an exponential strength guarantee. The other covers samples drawn by a random walk on an expander graph, a sparse network that mixes quickly.

The expander result rests on a new proof tool that adapts a classical bounded-difference method to walks, which the author expects to be useful elsewhere. Notably, the bounds avoid any explicit factor for the size of the quantum system. Applications include new one-shot limits for sending private messages over quantum wiretap channels with many separate eavesdroppers.
arxiv-2504-04167:
Abhishek Sadhu, Aritra Sarkar, and Akash Kundu present a framework for running large quantum circuits on small hardware in a 2025 paper. Near term quantum devices have few qubits, sparse links, and short stable times, which limits chemistry methods that need big circuits. Cutting a circuit into smaller parts helps, but finding the best cuts is hard and affects cost and accuracy.

Their framework joins circuit cutting with a search over circuit layouts. A learning agent first explores layouts to find a good structure. A second agent then refines that structure by choosing the best cuts. Tests with numbers show gains in accuracy and resource use. The authors offer it as a scalable path for quantum chemistry.
arxiv-2504-04567:
Carlos Hernandez-Suarez finds a way to gauge sample reach when data pour in as a stream. Reach says how like it is that the next case drawn falls in a class the sample has seen. The count of classes is unknown, and stream tools can hold just a set few past cases. His 2025 fix bends a stock stream tool that counts how many kinds have passed.

The bent tool yields a reach gauge on the fly, with no full store of the stream. Ease and speed top the pitch. Such gauges serve fields from word counts to beast hunts, where kinds outrun lists. A stream-fit gauge can warn when a sample still misses most of the world it claims to speak for.
arxiv-2504-05067:
Abughalwa and co-authors design wireless secrecy that covers every user, not just the lucky ones. Their 2025 paper uses smart reflecting surfaces to boost real users and foil a hidden eavesdropper. The setting is strict: short packets for urgent, low-delay traffic, where secrecy is hardest to promise. They aim to lift the weakest user's secrecy rate as high as possible.

The plan tunes both the sender's beams and the surface's reflections. With perfect channel knowledge, they split the hard problem into steps that close in form. With flawed knowledge, a smoothing method turns endless constraints into solvable ones. Simulations show all users stayed secure under tight delay limits, even with rough channel data.
arxiv-2504-05367:
Soumyadip Sarkar teaches neural networks to solve a basic quantum problem: a particle trapped in a one-dimensional well. The governing equation, Schrödinger's equation, has exact answers for simple wells, which makes them good test cases. Sarkar's networks are physics-informed, meaning the equation itself is built into their training.

The setup tries three cases: an endless well, a finite well, and a finite barrier. Built-in trial shapes force the wave to vanish at the edges, and for two cases the energy itself is learned during training. The learned waves matched the known solutions closely, and energies settled near the true values. Sarkar discusses weak spots, such as sensitivity to starting settings, and concludes the method is a workable route to quantum energy problems.
arxiv-2504-05667:
Yuki Kambara and Eiichiro Kokubo simulate protoplanet growth when planetesimals form in a narrow ring, not across a whole disk. Recent gas and dust work shows planetesimals gather at pressure bumps and snowlines. In a ring, scattered bodies leak from the edge, so the ring spreads as growth proceeds.

N-body runs show oligarchic growth still explains how the protoplanets grow, even as the ring widens. The largest protoplanets form near the ring centre, and bodies far from the centre stay smaller. Final ring width depends on total ring mass, not on the starting width. Peak protoplanet mass also depends strongly on total mass and only weakly on starting width.
arxiv-2504-05767:
Zhang Dong and co-authors present a method to resolve references across documents inside knowledge graphs. Their 2025 paper tackles coreference: the same entity can appear under many mentions in many texts, and matching them is key to clean extraction. Knowledge graphs add structure that plain text methods cannot use.

Their approach links graph entities to text mentions through a dynamic mechanism that updates as context builds. Contextual embeddings carry the sense of each mention, while graph-based inference traces how entities relate. Tests on several benchmark data sets showed gains in both precision and recall over standard methods. The authors argue that graph context sharpens our grasp of tangled links across documents.
arxiv-2504-06267:
Arrays of Rydberg atoms linked to a single light cavity form a rich test bed for quantum physics. The authors of this 2025 study follow how such a system settles over time, using diagram methods that track wiggles beyond simple averages. Short-range forces between atoms compete with long-range forces carried by the cavity light.

From that contest, a prethermal stage appears. In it, the atoms and the light each settle at their own effective temperature, and the two can even run opposite. The stage lasts before full balance sets in. The authors argue that platforms like this can probe deep questions about how quantum systems thermalize, well beyond one dimension.
arxiv-2504-06367:
Olga Garcia-Gallego and co-authors use the light of far quasars to test mixed dark matter, a blend of cold and warm forms. Warm particles would smooth out small clumps, and that smoothing leaves a mark in the Lyman-alpha forest, the pattern of gas shadows in quasar light. The team reads that mark at high redshift.

Their runs draw on the Sherwood-Relics simulation suite to build flux spectra for many cosmos setups. A neural network emulator speeds the fit between model and data. New spectra from the UVES and HIRES tools on large telescopes then set tight caps on the warm share. For light warm particles the warm share must stay small, and caps ease as particle mass grows. The bounds hold even after patchy reionization and fixed grid effects are counted.
arxiv-2504-06467:
Brenner Rego, Joseph Scott, Davide Raimondo, Marco Terra, and Guilherme Raffo release ZETA, a software library for tracking systems and catching their faults, in a 2025 paper. Engineers who estimate a machine's hidden state must handle uncertainty honestly. Zonotopes — tidy geometric sets that wrap the possible states — do this rigorously, but tooling was scattered.

The MATLAB library implements zonotopes in three flavors plus interval arithmetic, with the operations each needs. It propagates sets through nonlinear behavior, shrinks set size without losing safety, and supports reachability checks, state estimation, and active fault diagnosis for linear, nonlinear, and descriptor systems. Worked examples show the routines in action. A shared toolkit spreads set-based methods beyond their home labs.
arxiv-2504-06667:
Yashar Deldjoo, Nikhil Mehta, Maheswaran Sathiamoorthy, Shuai Zhang, Pablo Castells, and Julian McAuley argue for wider tests of AI recommenders, in a 2025 paper. New recommenders do not just rank items; they write explanations and hold conversations. That freedom brings risks that classic scoreboards miss, from inventing products that do not exist to leaking private data.

The authors sort the evaluation problems into two kinds. Some are old concerns, like bias and privacy, made worse by open-ended output. Others are new, such as checking factual correctness and content safety in generated text. They propose judging these systems across accuracy, fairness, safety, and fit to user intent at once. Richer scorecards can keep helpful recommenders honest.
arxiv-2504-06767:
Paolo Angella and co-authors remove motion blur from brain scans without needing clean training pairs in a 2025 paper. Patient motion degrades MRI quality and can force repeat scans, yet paired sharp and blurred images are rare in clinics. Their framework, DIMA, learns the look of motion artifacts from unpaired blurred scans alone.

A diffusion model trained on those scans then paints realistic artifacts onto clean images, manufacturing the pairs a correction network needs. The method avoids k-space tricks and sequence details, so it adapts across scanners and protocols. Across several data sets and scan planes, correction matched supervised rivals and generalized better to real clinical data. The authors aim to cut repeat scans and sharpen diagnosis.
arxiv-2504-07167:
Joheen Chakraborty and co-authors present a 2025 astronomy paper on flickering outbursts from a supermassive black hole. Quasi-periodic eruptions are repeating soft X-ray flares whose cause is still debated. The source nicknamed Ansky shows shifting absorption features during each flare, giving a rare handle on the gas involved.

The features match dense, ionized plasma rushing outward at a fair fraction of light speed. Their strength tracks the flare's heat and brightness closely. Sharp spectra also reveal emission lines that point to far more nitrogen than usual. The authors model the pattern as a uniformly expanding shell, which explains how the features evolve within one eruption. The work tightens ideas about what collides or falls near the black hole.
arxiv-2504-07467:
Ruiyi Zhang and co-authors proposed in 2025 a defense for language models against prompt injection attacks. Such attacks hide malicious instructions inside outside text the model reads, bending its answers. Encoding the input in Base64 was known to blunt these attacks, but it also degraded normal task performance. The new defense mixes several character encodings instead of relying on one.

Across experiments the mixture reached one of the lowest attack success rates recorded. At the same time it kept performance high across standard language tasks. Rival encoding defenses could not hold both ends at once. The authors present the method as a practical shield for systems that read untrusted content. It needs no retraining of the model itself. Security teams deploying retrieval-fed models are the natural audience.
arxiv-2504-07767:
Shung-Ichi Ando reviews a key nuclear reaction for starlight in this 2025 paper. In the reaction, a helium nucleus joins carbon-12 and emits a gamma ray, forming oxygen-16. Its rate at stellar energies helps set how stars burn and what they leave behind.

Ando works within cluster effective field theory, a low-energy framework tuned to the burning temperature of real stars. Elastic scattering data fix the theory's range parameters first. One transition's strength factor is then estimated cleanly at the key energy. The second transition resists the same treatment, since a needed normalization cannot be read off the scattering data. The review lays out the resulting uncertainty honestly.
arxiv-2504-07867:
Joshua Li and co-authors built in 2025 a system that turns first-person kitchen videos into scene graphs describing objects and their relations over time. Training such systems usually needs large labeled datasets. Large vision models can label single frames without training, but they lose track of which object is which as the video moves. Their pipeline pairs a strong segmentation tracker with a large vision-language model.

The tracker follows each object across frames with accurate masks. The language model names objects and relations in each frame. A matching step links the two, producing a scene graph that stays consistent through the video. On two standard kitchen datasets, the system beat the language model alone by over eight points in mean recall.
arxiv-2504-07967:
Md Ferdous Pervej and co-authors built a content-making model in 2025 for wireless channels, the math accounts of how radio signals travel between transmitter and receiver. Builders need true-to-life channel models to design and standardize communication systems. Machine learning makers exist. But most either predict single channel snapshots or cover only signal loss, while a complete account must be double-directional, tracking angles at both ends of the link.

Their maker combines a hybrid Transformer, changed to use a cheaper low-rank focus calculation, with a bidirectional memory network that makes full double-directional channel data. Training is guided by domain knowledge so the generated channels match the figures of real ones. Models showed the generated samples' figures aligned closely with the truth and mostly beat earlier predictive methods.
arxiv-2504-08267:
Borboruah, Malhotra, Patel, Patra, and Sankar build a left-right symmetric neutrino mass model without a scalar bidoublet, in a paper from twenty twenty-five. The model mirrors left and right forces with two separate doublets. Charged fermion masses arise through a universal seesaw mechanism. Three singlet neutral fermions carry TeV-scale masses.

Light neutrino masses appear only at one loop, staying naturally small. Careful coupling choices enable resonant leptogenesis at the TeV scale. The lightest right-handed neutrino becomes a warm dark matter candidate. Its mass of a few keV fits that role. Double beta decay signals stay observable in reach.
arxiv-2504-08367:
Recep Akif Tasci, Ibrahim Yildirim, and Ertugrul Basar introduce Flip-KLJN, a variant of noise driven secure key exchange. The classic Kirchhoff law Johnson noise protocol shares bits at intermediate wire noise levels only, discarding the matched resistor cases. Security rests on physics rather than computation.

In the new scheme, a pre agreed intermediate level triggers a flip of the bit mapping during the exchange period. To an eavesdropper the flips look random. The formerly discarded high and low levels then also carry pre agreed bit values that flip together with the original mapping. The key rate doubles, and all three wire levels become indistinguishable to Eve. Error probabilities are handled by analytic calculation and simulation.
arxiv-2504-08567:
Kumar Bondada and co-authors study joint sending from phones to a base station in a 2025 paper. In their setup, a served user and near users send data to the station as one team. The aim is more data per slice of airwaves for sixth generation networks.

Sharing data among the phones costs airwaves too, and the team count that cost in full. They match linked and unlinked sending styles at many power levels. They also give a pick rule that finds the best helper phones for top speed. Even with sharing costs, joint sending won on speed, which marks it as a strong path for new networks.
arxiv-2504-08967:
Rana Elnaggar and co-authors published a research paper in 2025 on a language-model tool that fuzzes cross-platform compilers to shake out bugs. Compilers that target many chip types have endless code paths, and hand-writing tests for each path eats expert time. Their tool pairs a language model with a retrieval system stocked with compiler knowledge.

Let loose on Intel's SYCL compiler, the tool drafted tests on its own. Within hours it found eighty-seven cases where code gave wrong answers or crashed the compiler across different chips. The testers needed no prior knowledge of the compiler passes involved. The authors say retrieval-guided fuzzing can give small teams the reach of large ones.
arxiv-2504-09467:
Pal, Lahiri, and Saha studied tiny heat engines in twenty twenty-five that run inside flowing fluids. Their engine is a single colloidal bead held in a trap whose stiffness pulses in time, a standard design for a stochastic heat engine. Around it, the fluid shears steadily, and the flow's shape — circular, elliptic, or hyperbolic — can be tuned from outside.

Over long times, the flow's own work swamps the trap's thermodynamic work whenever the flow strays much from circular. Only a perfectly circular flow lets the trap do all the work. A second model tethers a spinning particle near the bead, so its wake stirs the bead's motion. At high spin rates the flow work again dominates, and the engine stops producing useful thermodynamic work.
arxiv-2504-09567:
Chenxuan He and co-authors wrote this 2025 statistics paper on a classic hard problem: testing whether two sets of variables are independent once a third is held fixed. Such tests matter in causal work, but tangled conditional patterns make them slippery, above all with many variables and no assumed shapes.
