Their trick turns the conditional test into a plain unconditional one. Two transport maps, learned from the data by flow models, reshuffle the variables so the hard structure washes out. On that simpler footing they build a test statistic with proven behavior under both answers, and judge it by permutation. Simulations and a real-data study show the method working in practice.
arxiv-2504-09867:
The Anh Bui and Xuan Thinh Duong developed function spaces tied to a classic differential operator in a 2025 paper. The operator, named for Laguerre, mixes growth, wells, and singular terms on the positive half-space. Hardy spaces bound to it were built here for the full small-exponent range.

The team then studied the matching smoothness spaces and showed they are exactly the dual partners of the new Hardy spaces. Higher-order Riesz transforms, a standard tool for reading such operators, were proven bounded on plain volume spaces and on both new families. The results round out a harmonic analysis toolkit for this operator. Such spaces feed work on equations driven by the operator in physics and probability.
arxiv-2504-10067:
Kai Li and five co-authors present a 2025 attack on federated learning at the edge of the internet of things. In federated learning, devices train a shared model on their own data and send only model updates to a server, which saves bandwidth and guards privacy. That design, though, lets a bad actor poison the shared model with crafted updates.

The team's attack needs no access to device data at all. A graph-based auto-encoder studies honest updates caught in transit and learns the links between their shapes and the data traits behind them. It then builds fake updates that bend those links to push the shared model's training loss as high as it can. The authors show the trick can drag down the whole system while flying under the radar of checks that look for odd data.
arxiv-2504-10567:
Yushu Wu and co-authors present H3AE, an autoencoder for video diffusion models that squeezes video far harder while keeping quality and speed, in a 2025 paper. Autoencoders shrink video before the diffusion model works on it, which cuts cost. Their power in design, squeeze ratio, and training recipe had been little explored.

The team rethought the network layout and where computing effort goes, and built a family of encoders that decode in real time, even on phones. A single training goal unifies plain and image-guided variants in one network. A new latent consistency loss steadied quality gains and beat older add-on losses. The final model tops prior work on rebuild scores by a wide margin.
arxiv-2504-10667:
William Cook writes alone in a 2025 statistics paper on coordinate free decisions. A good statistical choice should not hinge on the language used to state the problem. Cook asks how to be sure a change of coordinates does not quietly change the answer. He starts with the best blend of two well behaved estimators under a strict risk rule.

The best blend, he proves, stays the same under straight rescaling of the weights. That case points to a wider rule he names meta equivariance: the unique best point of a smooth, strictly curved objective over matrices shifts in step with any invertible rescaling. The principle gives method builders a test for whether their recipes respect the problem or just its wording.
arxiv-2504-10767:
Faiyaz Elahi Mullick and co-authors bring a brain trick to magnetic hardware in a 2025 paper on adaptive synaptogenesis. Brains rewire their connections during learning under a two-key system: local coincidence proposes a change, and a supervisory signal from another region approves or vetoes it, which prevents catastrophic forgetting.

Artificial networks lack that discipline. The authors adapt the algorithm for edge computing, show it working in simulation, and design nanomagnetic accelerators that carry out pieces of the process in hardware. The supervised Hebbian scheme keeps new learning sparse and strategic, aiming at machines that keep learning for years without wiping what they knew.
arxiv-2504-11067:
Sebastian Baunsgaard and Matthias Boehm address slow, bulky data work in machine learning in a 2025 paper. Modern pipelines do more than train a model. They clean data, add new cases, and build new features in loops, then train again. Keeping numeric tables compressed saves memory and speeds work, but old methods miss patterns that these steps create.

Their system, BWARE, pushes compression through feature steps so it can use what those steps reveal about the data. It also reshapes a compressed table into a better form for the next task without first expanding it. Tests show large gains in end to end run time, which helps teams work with data that once barely fit in memory.
arxiv-2504-11767:
Qinyan Shen, Karl Gregory, and Xianzheng Huang fix trust checks after model choice in twenty twenty-five. Their case is group test data, where the true scores are seen in part at best. In place of true scores, teams see pooled test scores that can be wrong. The choice of which traits count has to deal with that gap in what is known.

A back and forth max step works out LASSO picked scores with a fine built in. Once choice is done, plain trust bands read too bold, since the same data did double work. The team stretches past choice trust checks, built on the polyhedral lemma, to fit this case. Test runs show their bands hold up more well than plain ones do. The piece gives sound checks for pooled test work, where choice of traits and gauge of traits share one set of data.
arxiv-2504-12067:
Alexander Bakhtin and co-authors share a dataset paper, published in 2025, for research on software built from many small services. Such systems are watched through logs, measures, and traces, which help spot faults and find their causes. Methods that mix all three kinds of data are gaining ground, but good test data are scarce.

The team ran tests on a real service system that handles secure sign-in, calling its parts in both right and wrong ways. Each call was labeled by the fault it triggered. They gathered about 657,000 log files with over two billion lines, plus tens of millions of measure files. Early analysis picks out key measures and notes hard parts of the data. The set gives researchers shared ground for testing fault-finding tools.
arxiv-2504-12167:
Yuan Luo and co-authors present RADLER in a 2025 paper, a system that uses radar to spot pedestrians, cyclists, and cars in cities. Radar data are noisy, and detailed three dimensional city models are easy to get worldwide. Those models hold exact, labeled shapes of city objects, yet their value for radar work was little tested. The team set out to close that gap.

They built a data set of fifty four thousand paired radar and image samples matched with city models. Their network first learns strong radar features by self supervised contrast with images. It then fuses in depth and meaning features taken from the city models. On their data set, the system beat past radar methods on both precision and recall by clear margins. The authors hope the work spurs more map guided radar research.
arxiv-2504-12767:
Fatma Elsafoury and David Hartmann present a 2025 paper on bias in language models against groups the research world overlooks. Most bias studies focus on the United States and its minorities. Yet the United Nations counts up to 1.2 billion people in marginalized groups worldwide, many tied to specific regions and low-resource languages.

Theirs is the first study of offensive stereotyping across 23 language models for 270 marginalized groups from Egypt and beyond. They test how models portray groups that standard benchmarks never mention. Findings reveal where debiasing work still fails to reach. The authors argue that fair models must be tested on the world's full diversity, not one country's slice. Their data extend bias audits to new ground.
arxiv-2504-13467:
Jianing Dong, Raymond Wong, and Kwun Chuen Gary Chan tackle in 2025 estimation when data go missing in many tangled patterns. Real surveys rarely lose values in a tidy order, and the loss is often not random, which breaks standard fixes. The team builds on pattern graphs, diagrams that link the observed patterns in a sample.

Their method sets balancing weights step by step along the graph, avoiding the instability of a cruder local scheme. The resulting estimator reaches the theoretical efficiency bound for moment-based models, regressions included. Simulations favor the method, and real-data checks show the answers hold up under different assumptions about the missingness.
arxiv-2504-13867:
Matheus Rodrigues Felizardo and co-authors map tasks that test executive function in children in 2025, using team framing since the head author order differs from the catalog list. Executive functions steer impulse control, focus, and memory juggling. Childhood is a key growth window for them. No standard tool set joins such tasks with play and motion.

The review searched three databases for studies of five to nine year olds. Twenty three studies passed the entry rules. Tasks, scoring, and stop rules were charted for each. The team aims to ground a research platform on that map. A shared task set could steady how growth is measured. Gaps in method reporting were one bar to reuse.
arxiv-2504-13967:
Yufei Bai simulates magnetic patterns in thin films in a study from 2025. Films magnetized straight out of their plane form maze-like and bubble-like domain patterns that shift with film thickness and outside field. Bai borrows a model from chemistry, the Lengyel-Epstein model of reaction and diffusion, and applies it to these magnetic patterns.

The simulations reproduce maze, bubble, and in-between states seen in real layered films under a microscope. The shapes and topology of the simulated domains match the observed ones closely. Bai argues that the chemistry analogy is a sound new tool for studying how magnetic domain patterns form and change in thin films.
arxiv-2504-14067:
Justin Ray Angus and Johannes van de Wetering wrote a 2025 physics paper on a computer method for collisions in plasmas. A plasma is a hot gas of charged particles, found in stars and fusion devices. Particles in a plasma constantly deflect each other through electric forces, an effect called Coulomb collisions.

Exact simulation of every encounter is too costly, so codes use statistical collision models. Their method pairs particles at random and applies a screened collision rule, valid when the plasma is weakly or moderately coupled. It matches the standard theory with first-order corrections and reduces to the classic method for small time steps. The code change is about ten lines, so existing simulation programs can adopt it easily.
arxiv-2504-14567:
Ilya Shirokov studies versions of the Hopf theorem for convex surfaces in this two thousand twenty-five paper. The classical theorem concerns continuous maps from a compact space into a space of the same dimension and guarantees certain points that map to the same value.

Shirokov shows the theorem, and its quantitative strengthening, still hold when the surface is convex, provided straightest paths are replaced by quasigeodesics in the sense of Alexandrov and Petrunin. He also proves a discrete version for triangulated convex polyhedra: a certain path among point pairs with equal images must connect antipodal pairs to identical pairs. A final result gives the neighbor sets at a fixed distance a nontrivial homology group. The work extends a topological staple to less smooth settings.
arxiv-2504-15067:
Péter Gurin and Szabolcs Varga published a 2025 physics paper on sticky particles confined to a narrow channel. Patchy particles carry attractive spots and can bond into chains. Squeezed into a channel barely wider than themselves, their ordering becomes a one-dimensional problem with rotation. The authors extend a theory of association, Wertheim's perturbation theory, to this setting.

With a transfer-matrix method, they prove the theory is exact when the particles' hard cores interact additively, only neighbors touch, and bonding runs along the channel. At constant pressure, every structural and thermodynamic quantity follows from the pressure and the fraction of unbonded sites. Narrow-channel fluids model things, from molecules in pores to colloids in grooves. An exact theory is rare and useful: simulations can be checked against it, and design rules for self-assembling materials can be read off.
arxiv-2504-15267:
Shaorong Zhang and five co-authors present a 2025 paper on translating between two kinds of brain scans with a diffusion bridge model. One scan type maps the brain's wiring in fine detail but takes long to acquire. The other, a standard MRI, is quick and common.

Their model learns to turn the quick scan into the detailed one and back again. That lets clinics enrich their data without long extra scan time. The team judged the outputs by look alike scores, pixel level match, and spread of values. The made up scans kept the brain's structure and the state of its white matter well. A sex sorting test showed the fake data still carried real signal.
arxiv-2504-15367:
Anton Simen and co-authors blend two search styles to solve hard optimization problems in a 2025 paper. Branch-and-bound solves such problems by splitting them into cases and using relaxed versions to bound the best possible score. That trick gets hard when the goal involves higher-order terms, which make the relaxed form non-convex and loose.

Their quantum method uses a counterdiabatic drive, a helper push that keeps a quantum system on track, in digital form. Bias fields stand in for the relaxed solution, and the branch-and-bound loop sharpens results step by step. Tests ran in tensor network simulations with up to one hundred fifty-six qubits. Runs on IBM quantum hardware used up to one hundred qubits. In both, the method beat simulated annealing and a tuned quantum annealing baseline. It found better answers with much less computing effort.
arxiv-2504-15667:
Jingchen Zou and co-authors present, in 2025, a way to estimate how well a medical image segmentation model performs on data nobody has labeled. In clinics, new scans rarely come with expert outlines, so true accuracy stays unknown. Their evaluator uses a general segmentation model to help guess the target model's scores.

The framework adapts to many quality measures and model designs. Across six public datasets and six measures, its estimates tracked the real overlap scores closely, with small average error. It plugs into training without adding overhead. The authors offer it as a safety check for deploying segmentation tools where labeling every case is impossible.
arxiv-2504-15967:
Khalaf, Itani, and Sharafeddine present a study from twenty twenty-five on digital twins for device networks, aided by drones. A digital twin is a live copy of a real system used to test and tune it. Their setup parks several drones at chosen spots to gather data from ground devices. Many devices may watch the same object, so their readings merge into one status. Updates then flow to a base station that holds the twin. They coin a new score for how fresh the twin's status is.

Their goal is to gather the most data while keeping the twin fresh. They state the task as a hard math problem and solve it by stepwise smoothing. Tests show their method beats base approaches. The authors say fresh twins support better data-driven choices.
arxiv-2504-16167:
Sunko and co-authors confirm a predicted way to see magnetism with light in materials that show no net magnetization, in work from 2025. The Kerr effect, a twist in reflected light, normally betrays ferromagnets, and its appearance in antiferromagnets seemed to need exotic structures.

Theory said layered A-type antiferromagnets, with ferromagnetic sheets stacked in alternating directions, should show the effect intrinsically. The team measured the effect's imaginary part across photon energies in the crystal MnBi2Te4 and matched it against model calculations. The agreement supports the mechanism. The authors conclude the effect should appear in all such layered antiferromagnets with out-of-plane spins, enabling optical reading of their domains.
arxiv-2504-17067:
Xinqi Xiong and co-authors translate synthetic colonoscopy images toward realism while keeping their depth truth, in a 2025 paper. Judging depth inside the colon would aid navigation and diagnosis, but real procedures yield no ground-truth depth to train on. Synthetic scenes supply depth, yet models trained on them stumble on real tissue because the look differs.

Their framework, PPS-Ctrl, steers a diffusion model with maps of per-pixel shading, which capture how light plays across the moist surface. Shading pins the scene's structure more firmly than a depth map alone, so textures can turn realistic without warping anatomy. The translated images improved depth estimation over a GAN-based rival, and the code is public.
arxiv-2504-17167:
Fernando Peña Vázquez continues a study of Hochschild cohomology for differential operators on p-adic spaces. This 2025 paper, the second in a series, works on smooth Stein spaces whose tangent sheaf is free. Its objects are algebras of differential operators of infinite order, in a capped form suited to p-adic analysis.

The main result gives the shape of the cohomology: its complex is strict, built from nuclear Fréchet spaces, and matches the de Rham complex of the space itself. From there he compares the first cohomology group with a wide family of Ext functors. Under finiteness assumptions on the space's de Rham groups, the first group is identified with the bounded outer derivations of the operator algebra, and the second with its small deformations. The paper ties an abstract cohomology to concrete questions about how the algebra can bend.
arxiv-2504-17267:
Chuer Chen and co-authors built MV-Crafter in 2025, a system that makes music videos from a song with little user skill. Making a music video takes script work, filming, and tight sync with the beat — hard for amateurs. Their system mimics the human process in three modules. A language model writes a script from the song's meaning, a generator makes the clips, and a sync module aligns them.

A beat-matching algorithm and a warping method keep picture and music locked together. The interface adds simple editing tools. Tests showed the system producing higher-quality videos than earlier automated frameworks. It aims to open music video making to singers and fans without crews.
arxiv-2504-17867:
The Euclid Collaboration charts how the galaxy stellar mass function changes across most of cosmic time in the Cosmic Dawn Survey. The mass function counts galaxies by their star mass. Its drift over time reveals how galaxies assemble their stars.

Measurements span ten square degrees of sky with Euclid data. The range runs from fairly recent epochs to the early universe. Deep imaging lets the team weigh galaxies across that span. Careful catalogs support the mass estimates per era. The survey name honors the dawn of galaxy formation. Results test models of star formation across ages. Such baselines anchor the Euclid mission's wider science. They also guide smaller deep-field studies.
arxiv-2504-17967:
Kevin Song, Andrew Trotter, and Jake Chen present a 2025 paper on a swarm of language model agents hunting for drugs together. Over ninety percent of drug candidates fail in trials, and the data needed to choose better ones lies scattered across genomics, chemistry, and clinical records. Single models lack the specialization and memory for disciplined, hypothesis-driven work.

Their framework, PharmaSwarm, assigns agents to genome analysis, knowledge graph queries, pathway simulation, and binding prediction, while an evaluator agent grades every proposal for plausibility, novelty, likely effect, and safety. A shared memory banks what survives validation and sharpens the submodels over time. The authors describe a four-tier validation pipeline, from benchmarks to expert studies, to keep the swarm honest.
arxiv-2504-18067:
Chuyu Wang, Huiting Deng, and Dong Liu present a new way to make images of the inside of the body in 2025. Their method sends mild electric currents through tissue and reads the response. From those reads it builds a map of how well each spot conducts. The task is hard because small errors can blur the map, and some areas respond weakly.

Their method, called PhyNC, uses the physics of the test to guide a neural model. The model gives more capacity to weak areas, so detail there is not lost. Tests on made up data and on real lab data beat older methods. Detail held up better and false marks were fewer, most of all in weak areas.
arxiv-2504-18167:
Fredrik Lohne Aanes, a solo author, speeds up a popular way of explaining model predictions in a 2025 paper. Shapley values split a prediction fairly among input features, but the conditional version is slow when the explainer model is a linear or polynomial regression. Aanes develops three methods, two approximate and one exact, that estimate the needed pieces for all feature subsets at once rather than one by one.

The methods lean on constrained random field theory and fast sparse matrix tools. In case studies they matched the accuracy of the standard sequential software while cutting run times from hours to minutes or seconds. One case handled over two million submodels in minutes. The author recommends the exact method, since it needs no tuning.
arxiv-2504-18567:
Jingxu Wu, Yuwei Yin, and Jianing Shi simulate hot quark matter in a twenty twenty-five paper. They use the two-flavor PNJL model, a model of quantum chromodynamics that tracks both quarks and the phases of the strong force. Heat and baryon density are the two dials they vary.

Two transport traits are their focus: how thick the matter flows, given by viscosity, set against its entropy. They find the shear ratio dips to a minimum, while the bulk ratio peaks, near the line where chiral symmetry is restored. The effect grows at high baryon density. Such marks could point to the QCD critical endpoint in heavy-ion collisions.
arxiv-2504-18767:
Flows that never vanish and orientations that keep every cut balanced turn out to be two faces of one object. Together they tie tractable flow problems to stubborn coloring ones. Karthekeyan Chandrasekaran, Siyue Liu, and Ravi Ravi study in 2025 the priced versions. Given a bidirected graph with possibly different costs per direction, find the cheapest nowhere-zero flow, or the cheapest balanced orientation.

Both resist approximation within any finite factor, a hard verdict. The authors answer with bicriteria algorithms that bend cost and balance together. For the friendlier symmetric-cost case they give a clean three-approximation for flows, while proving the problem stays NP-hard.
arxiv-2504-18867:
Roberti and co-authors study how often two burning shells inside massive stars merge before the star explodes, and what the mergers change, in a paper from 2025. The team uses surname only for the first author because the catalog lists initials in a garbled pattern. More than two hundred star models with varied mass and metal content were analyzed.

Mergers could be forecast from the earlier helium burning stage: most merging models shared low core mass and low central carbon share. Their element output matched the odd element richness seen in the oldest stars, fixing a long standing shortfall for two elements. The authors stress the mergers' role in seeding space with new elements.
arxiv-2504-18967:
Jyotirmoy Ganguly and Rohit Joshi study divisibility in the character values of Coxeter group representations. Fix a positive integer d and an element g of the group. The question is what share of irreducible characters take values at g that are divisible by d. The authors work with infinite families of irreducible Coxeter groups and track that share as the groups grow.

For Coxeter groups of types A, B, and D, the share tends to 1 as n approaches infinity. For dihedral groups, which are Coxeter groups of type I2(n), the authors compute the limit of the share directly. The results show divisibility by a fixed integer becomes the norm in these families.
arxiv-2504-19067:
Some dark matter models split the dark particle into a ground state and a slightly heavier excited state, with a dark photon carrying force between them. A dark Higgs boson completes the picture: it gives the dark photon its mass and sets the gap between the two dark matter states. Ko and co-authors note that this particle has been little searched for. When it is heavy enough, its decays turn half visible or fully invisible, which defeats the usual searches for light scalars.

The authors study how the Belle II experiment could catch it anyway, through dark Higgs production alongside other particles and through rare decays of B mesons. Two signs look robust: pairs of displaced particle vertices, and missing energy carried off by the dark Higgs decay. They also assess a proposed far detector for Belle II, called GAZELLE, and its reach for this elusive particle.
arxiv-2504-19167:
Tithi Dwary, Khyodeno Mozhui, and Krishna sort which split graphs can also be read as order graphs, in a paper from two thousand twenty-five. A split graph divides its points into a fully linked clique and an unlinked set. The order side asks whether arrows can point along a ranking without cycles.

A labeling test marks exactly which split graphs qualify. From that test, any such graph needs at most three ranking words to encode it. The bound also re-proves a known cap on the dimension of split orders. Readers in graph theory get a tidy test plus a sharp encoding cap in one pass.
arxiv-2504-19367:
Defant and Lee wrote in twenty twenty-five about a reduced random walk in the hyperbolic plane. The walk comes from Lam's work in hyperbolic triangle groups. Viewed in the upper half-plane model, the walk wanders under group actions. The authors prove it settles almost surely at a point on the extended real line. One special case, the modular group setting, gets detailed treatment. There they give an explicit formula for the limit's distribution.

The formula uses a new function they name the interrobang function. It mirrors many analytic and arithmetic traits of Minkowski's classic question-mark function. Such limit laws connect probability with number theory in striking ways. Random walks on groups often reveal hidden fractal structure. The explicit distribution is the paper's centerpiece result. It opens the special function to further study.
arxiv-2504-19767:
Katherine Lin and five co-authors study how people build a habit of writing in a paper journal over time. Those who keep journals hold strong views on their books, pens, page layouts, and what should go on the page. The team sought to see how those tastes form and settle in.

They went through journal content shared in public on YouTube and Instagram, and they spoke with eleven journalers one on one. Habits, it turns out, are shaped by three forces at once: the stuff used, the person's own life and needs, and the group round them. Those forces also feed how journalers see who they are. The team close with design ideas for tools to come. Good support, they argue, should respect what paper is good at, not press it flat into apps like any other.
arxiv-2504-20267: Aleksander Filip Żarnecki wrote a personal contribution in 2025 to the 2026 update of the European Strategy for Particle Physics. The note concerns the Future Circular Collider, a proposed ring collider put forward as CERN's next flagship project. Żarnecki explains that after joining many discussions and contributing to official documents, he concluded those documents do not give the whole picture. His note sets out his concerns about how the strategy update process is being run. It questions the possible choice of the new collider as the field's leading project.
arxiv-2504-20467:
Samuel Jelbart and co-authors untangle two kinds of reduction in a model of a gene regulatory network, in a 2025 paper. Gene network equations often split into fast and slow parts. They also contain steep switches that act almost like steps. Modelers simplify with quasi-steady reductions or piecewise-smooth swaps. Whether those two shortcuts commute was unclear.

A four-dimensional network serves as the test case. Geometric blow-up analysis tracks the dynamics near the tricky points. The interplay of time scales and switching turns out to be delicate. Wrong ordering of reductions can distort the model's behavior. Applied mathematicians gain a worked warning. Systems biologists learn when their simplified models stay faithful.
arxiv-2504-20567:
Chakraborty and five co-authors wrote this study in twenty twenty-five about explaining computer tuning tools to people. Bayesian optimisation is a method that finds good settings for a system when the best settings are unknown. Newer tools add explanations meant to help users trust and use the results. The team asked whether the form of an explanation changes how well people do.

They built a playful task in which people tuned six settings to cook a perfect soft-boiled egg. Over two hundred volunteers got either a bar chart, a list of rules, a written explanation, or no help. Any explanation raised success and cut the number of tries. All three forms worked about equally well. Designers, the authors suggest, can add explanations without fussing over format.
arxiv-2504-20667:
Simone Piaggesi and co-authors present ILLUME, a framework that makes explanations of black-box models for tabular data both local and global, published in 2025. Surrogate-based explanations are popular but split awkwardly: local surrogates capture detail at high cost and with fragile settings, while global ones are cheap but miss local behavior.

ILLUME grounds explanation in representation learning. A globally trained surrogate is paired with instance-specific linear transformations learned by a meta-encoder. That pairing yields feature attributions and decision rules for single cases and for the model as a whole. Wide experiments showed the explanations were accurate, robust, and cheap to compute. The framework can be combined with various surrogate models, the authors note, offering one route around the limits of older methods.
arxiv-2504-20867:
Jonathan Bader and co-authors survey how to guess a scientific workflow's appetite before it runs in this 2025 book chapter. Big analyses are chopped into tasks spread over clusters, and the scheduler must feed each task the right memory and time. Guesses typed in by users are often wrong, wasting machines or killing jobs.

The chapter sorts prediction methods by what they use, from past runs of the same task to models of the input data, and compares the leading approaches in detail. Good forecasts pay off beyond speed: they enable energy-saving schedules, lower carbon plans, and honest cost estimates for researchers renting compute. The authors map where the field stands and where the open problems sit, offering the overview as a guide for system builders.
arxiv-2504-21467:
Luc Vedrenne, Sylvain Faisan, and Denis Fortun align many 3D point clouds at once. Their 2025 paper introduces POLAR, a method for multiview registration. Pairwise alignment plus syncing scales poorly as views pile up. Older generative methods falter under big rotations or heavy damage.

POLAR moves the puzzle into the hidden space of a pre-trained autoencoder. A loss built to shrug off damage guides the search there. A multistart strategy keeps the optimizer from getting stuck. On made-up and real data, POLAR beat leading methods by clear margins. It handles many views, wide starting angles, and rough inputs in one frame.
arxiv-2505-00167:
Longteng Chen proves a result in geometry in this 2025 paper on the Kähler-Ricci flow. The flow is a rule that smooths the shape of a space over time. Chen studies spaces that open out into a cone shape far from the center.

The question is whether two flows that start from the same cone must stay the same. Chen shows they must match the standard self-similar flow, as long as set bounds hold on curvature and the form stays in the same class. The work partly answers a question posed by Feldman, Ilmanen, and Knopf. It also extends earlier results by Conlon, Deruelle, and Sun.
arxiv-2505-00467:
Balazadeh and co-authors report in 2025 on a workshop that tried to break large language models in health care settings, before a 2024 conference on machine learning for health. Clinicians and computing experts wrote realistic clinical prompts and looked for replies that could cause harm. Clinicians can spot risks that model builders, without clinical training, may miss.

The report shares the design of the exercise and sorts the flaws found into groups. A second study then checked whether those same flaws appeared across all the models provided. Readers get a practical account of how red teaming with clinicians can surface dangers before a model reaches patients.
arxiv-2505-00667:
Cian Reeves and co-authors built a practical frame in 2025 for faking lab light tests on a computer. Such tests flash light at matter and read how electrons move in less than a blink, which reveals how a material works. Lab results gain a lot when a matched computer run can check the reading and add insight.

The frame rests on a math form that tracks how many particles act as a team over time. It grows a classic series step by step in real time rather than in fake time steps. The team aimed for a tool that labs can run on real cases, not just toy ones. Good fakes help sort true effects from noise in fast light tests.
arxiv-2505-00767:
Gloria Isbrandt, Frank Pollmann, and Michael Knap explore what happens when spin ice is made anisotropic on a breathing pyrochlore lattice. Spin ice is a magnetic system whose spins obey local constraints, leaving a highly degenerate ground state. The team adds a tunable anisotropic coupling to the standard Ising spin ice Hamiltonian.

The ground state structure changes markedly, visible in the spin structure factor and in reduced residual entropy at low temperature. Depending on parameters, the system either crosses over into a constrained manifold with entropy below the conventional Pauling value, or orders into a symmetry-broken state. Large-N analytical predictions agree well with their simulations.
arxiv-2505-01967:
Jiatao Li, Yanheng Li, and Xiaojun Wan profile the hidden worldviews of chatbots in a 2025 study. Language models shape social talk and choices, yet their built-in stances toward authority, equality, freedom, and fate are rarely mapped. The team builds a taxonomy that turns four classic worldviews into measurable dimensions.

Testing twenty-eight models reveals distinct mental profiles that differ by model family. Social cues in the prompt then shift those profiles in systematic ways, showing the stances bend with context. The authors offer the frame as a tool for building AI that is clearer about its leanings and safer to deploy.
arxiv-2505-02167: Pierre Laurent and Paul Underwood give a one-dial test that aims to tell prime numbers from composite ones, in 2025. Their test is built on cubes and leans on a fact of its math: a linked value is at all times a perfect square. Wide checks to date have found no case that fools it. The pair also set it next to the Baillie-PSW tests, the field's workhorse set, and sketch a kin test built on squares that has so far held up as well.
arxiv-2505-02267:
Mederic Motte gives prospect theory, the classic account of how people judge gambles, a formula that can be computed at once for bell-shaped rewards. The paper appeared in two thousand twenty-five. Prospect theory bends values and odds in set ways: losses sting more than gains please. Fitting those bends to data usually means slow numeric work.

Motte crafts bends with three guarantees. They always obey the theory's shape rules. They are rich enough to mimic a wide range of tastes. And for Gaussian gambles they yield a closed-form price. That last trait makes the scheme fast enough for whole populations. Two worked examples show population-level modeling in action. The frame suits risk studies where many agents must be priced quickly. It keeps the theory's spirit while dropping its computational drag.
arxiv-2505-02367:
Toru Sakai and co-authors compute this 2025 magnetization curve for a ladder of quantum spins. The system is two rails of half-spins joined by ferromagnetic rungs, with competing directional preferences. Diagonalizing finite clusters exactly, the team traces how magnetization grows with field. At half the saturation value, a plateau appears where magnetization stalls, and the stall breaks the ladder's translational symmetry, a pattern repeating only every few rungs.

The plateau needs the competing anisotropies to be strong enough. Phase diagrams over the anisotropy plane and several magnetization curves chart where it lives. Such plateaus are fingerprints of exotic quantum order, and ladders are among the few systems where exact numerics can certify them.
arxiv-2505-02867:
Ruiqi Wang and Hao Zhang build a system that can outline almost anything a user describes in an image, even sideways descriptions. Referring segmentation normally targets plain labels like 'the red car'. Real requests point at parts, or at qualities: a material, a style, a function. Their system, RESAnything, handles such arbitrary references with no task-specific training.

The trick is attribute prompting. A segmentation model proposes candidate regions; a large language model then writes out each candidate's shape, color, and place, and reasons step by step over which attributes the request implies. The system beat rival zero-shot methods on classic benchmarks and pulled far ahead on implicit, part-level queries. The authors also release a new test set of about three thousand curated cases to push the field on these harder requests.
arxiv-2505-03967:
Erwin Miña-Díaz and Olof Rubin study Chebyshev polynomials defined on equipotential curves. Their 2025 paper works with an analytic function whose Laurent expansion at infinity has a simple leading form.

To that function they attach Faber polynomials, taken from the polynomial part of powers of the function. The equipotential curve is the set of points where the function's modulus equals a fixed radius. They prove that the nth Chebyshev polynomial for that curve converges to the nth Faber polynomial as the radius grows to infinity. The proof uses the fact that zero is the strongly unique best approximation to a monomial on the unit circle.
arxiv-2505-04067:
Min-Yu Li and co-authors teach a neural network to recognize heartbeat stars in a paper from 2025. Heartbeat stars are binary pairs whose light swells and dips like an electrocardiogram trace. Their light curves come in many shapes, so most finds so far came from slow manual checks.

The team extracts features straight from each light curve. Fourier analysis finds the orbital rhythm, and the first hundred harmonics become the input vector. Synthetic curves from a standard code built the training set. A recurrent neural network then learned to spot the heartbeat pattern. Tests validated the method against known cases. Automatic hunting can scan the flood of survey data for these rare pairs.
arxiv-2505-04667:
Olivier Minazzoli writes in twenty twenty-five about the principle of relativity of inertia. He compares how that principle sits in two theories of gravity. One is general relativity, Einstein's well-known theory. The other is entangled relativity, a newer and leaner theory. The newer theory can recover both general relativity and standard quantum field theory in a set limit.

Entangled relativity also rules out spacetime with no matter in it at all. Minazzoli argues this makes the new theory a better fit for Einstein's own vision. He adds that its leaner form is a point in its favor under Occam's razor. Readers get a theory-level argument about what inertia should mean.
arxiv-2505-04767:
Nathan Roth and a large team of co-authors report the first clear sign of gas activity from the largest known Oort cloud comet, in work from twenty twenty-five. The comet, named Bernardinelli-Bernstein, was watched far beyond the planets. At that range the Sun is faint, so any gas flow is hard to spot. A large radio array in Chile made the deep look possible.

Carbon monoxide gas was found, along with glow from dust near the core. The core is huge, well over a hundred kilometres across. Gas left the comet in jets that changed shape between the two watch nights. Dust glow stayed tight and compact, in line with heat from the big core. Light data show a flare in late February, then a calm return by March. The find proves this distant giant is active, not inert.
arxiv-2505-05467:
Haibo Wang and co-authors present StreamBridge in two thousand twenty-five, a framework that turns offline video language models into live streaming assistants. Models trained on finished videos struggle with two things online: following long multi-turn exchanges and speaking up proactively when something happens.

StreamBridge adds a memory buffer that compresses older context with a decaying scheme, keeping long conversations manageable. A small separate activation model watches the stream and triggers responses, and it plugs into existing models easily. The team also built Stream-IT, a large training set of interleaved video-text sequences for streaming tasks. In tests, upgraded offline models beat even flagship commercial systems on streaming understanding while staying competitive on standard video benchmarks.
arxiv-2505-05567:
Francisco Candón and five co-authors refreshed in 2025 the expected glow of axion-like particles left over from all past supernovae. Dying massive stars should emit these light particles, which can turn into gamma rays on the way to Earth. Using telescope data, the team updated the limit on the particle's coupling to light. They assumed the largest coupling to nucleons still allowed by the 1987 supernova's cooling.

For very light particles, the new bound is about twice as strict as earlier ones. Adding pion conversion in the star's core tightened bounds for heavier masses as well. The team also forecast what five planned gamma-ray missions could see. Even the best of them would only match current limits, while the 1987 bound stays far stronger. The work sharpens a rare window on particles beyond the Standard Model.
arxiv-2505-05767:
Grace Chiu and co-authors build a tool that unifies fish counts from different survey gears into one abundance picture. Sustainable fishing needs counts that agree across neighboring regions. Each region's gear sees fish at its own scale, though.

A first national project now estimates greater amberjack across the continent. Video cameras of several types were deployed together in a calibration test. The team frames the mismatch as a change-of-support problem. A Bayesian layered model learns how each gear's index maps to true numbers. That mapping converts regional indices onto a shared scale. The tool supports fair quotas across state lines. It suits other wide-ranging species surveys as well.
arxiv-2505-05867:
Future particle detectors need sensors that are light, fast, and stingy with power. A large international collaboration reports new test results in 2025 for tiny digital pixel chips. The chips were built in a 65 nm CMOS process, the same broad family of methods used to make computer chips.

The chips are test versions for the ALICE ITS3 detector, which will bend wafer-scale sensors into curved layers around the collision point. The team measured how the test structures behave, building on earlier rounds of tests. Their results feed the design of a detector layer that aims to use very little material and only a small amount of power in its active area, as the project requires.
arxiv-2505-05967:
Uyoata and co-authors set out to cut the signaling cost of power control in future factory wireless networks. In 6G plans, dense clusters of small subnetworks will serve robots and sensors at short range, and their access points must constantly adjust transmit power to limit interference. Earlier schemes assumed a central controller with perfect, fresh channel knowledge and ignored the chatter needed to gather it.

Their approach lets each access point learn both when to signal and how much power to use, through multi-agent reinforcement learning under partial information. In simulation the learned protocol used eight times less signaling than standard schemes while clearing data buffers nearly as fast as an all-knowing ideal. The authors argue learned protocols suit the messy reality of factory floors.
arxiv-2505-06167:
Chenwei Wang and co-authors propose reading the flight angles of charged particles from the pattern of hits across a satellite's detectors, in a 2025 paper. Their instrument, GECAM, watches the sky for gamma-ray bursts and also catches particle events in low Earth orbit. A particle's pitch angle, its tilt against the magnetic field, is a key clue to its origin. GECAM-style detectors were not built to measure it.

Simulations show the counts across detectors encode the angle well enough to recover it. Applied to a real electron rain event caught by GECAM-C, the method gave an angle near 90 degrees. The authors say the trick opens a new window on space particle events, from electron beams tied to distant storms to those sparked by lightning.
arxiv-2505-06267:
Ilyas Oulkadda and Perez introduce Adversarial Knowledge Distillation, a way to shrink big code models without dulling them. Code assistants now serve millions of developers, but their output can be buggy or unsafe. Bigger models cost more to run, and fresh training data runs thin. Distillation moves skill from a large teacher into a small student.

The twist is adversarial practice data. Synthetic tasks are generated to stress the student where it is weak. That targeted drill aims at robustness, reliability and security, not just raw scores. The authors present the method as a step toward dependable code generation at low running cost and with tight data budgets.
arxiv-2505-06367:
Everest Yang and co-authors introduce CAST, a 2025 framework that follows a treatment's effect as a smooth curve over time instead of freezing it at chosen checkups. Causal machine learning already estimates who benefits from a therapy, but survival versions report effects only at fixed moments.

CAST blends parametric and flexible methods to draw the whole effect trajectory for each patient. Applied to 2,651 head and neck cancer patients treated with chemotherapy and radiation, it traced how benefits rise, peak, and fade, at group and individual levels. Seeing the full curve could help clinicians time treatments and pick the patients who gain most.
arxiv-2505-06467:
Nisan Chhetri and Arpan Sainju present a framework that improves text-to-image generation without expert prompt writing, published in 2025. Many users write prompts that models misread, leading to distorted or misaligned images. Standard scores also miss structural flaws that a person would spot at once.

Their system, PromptIQ, refines the prompt on its own and scores each image with a new metric. That metric, Component-Aware Similarity, detects and penalizes errors in the parts of an image. The system loops, generating and checking images until the user is satisfied. This removes trial-and-error prompt tuning by hand. The authors report clear gains in both generation quality and the accuracy of their quality scores.
arxiv-2505-06567:
Wanchen Zhang and co-authors present new quantum states in a 2025 physics paper. Entanglement links particles so that the group acts as one. A state is called resistant if it stays entangled after some particles are lost, but falls apart once too many are gone. An earlier team guessed that such states exist for every group size and every loss level.

The authors give two general ways to build them. The first mixes known symmetric states, called Dicke states. It yields strong resistant states for groups of qubits, the basic quantum units. The second route starts from classical error correcting codes. It yields new resistant states for larger units, called qudits, at certain loss levels. The work moves the field closer to states that survive damage in real devices.
arxiv-2505-06667:
Elad Paran and Tran Nam Son extend a beloved theorem of algebra into the noncommutative world, in this 2025 paper. The classical Ax-Grothendieck theorem says that a polynomial map from a space to itself that never sends two points to the same place must actually reach every point: one-to-one forces onto. It fails in general when multiplication does not commute, as numbers in a division ring can misbehave.

Working over division rings that are finite over their centers, the authors prove the theorem again for maps built from polynomials in non-commuting variables. They also settle simpler image questions with no size condition at all. A Waring-type result follows: every square matrix over such a ring breaks into differences of products of a certain special form. These are landmarks in the algebra of skewed number systems, cousins of the quaternions.
arxiv-2505-07067:
Francesco Cagnetta, Hyunmo Kang, and Matthieu Wyart study how learning machines improve with more data, in a 2025 theory paper. A known pattern, called a scaling law, says error falls in a steady curve as data grows. The authors ask how that curve arises when data is built in layers, the way grammar builds sentences from rules inside rules.

They study two tasks on such layered data: sorting items into classes and guessing the next word. For sorting, the curve's steepness is set by how the grammar rules are spread out, while the layered build inflates the error by a large fixed factor. For next-word guessing, the rule spread shapes only small wiggles in the curve, not its overall slope. The work ties two rival accounts of scaling laws into one picture.
arxiv-2505-07367:
Julian Rodemann and James Bailie bound in 2025 how well learning from self-picked data generalizes. Active learning, boosting, and bandits all pick later data by earlier fits. A shared frame called reciprocal learning unifies those cases for study.

Universal bounds rest on covering counts and a distance-based ambiguity set. No claims about the self-picked data spread are needed, only checkable traits of the method. Finite-run bounds stay valid at any stop point, which yields stopping rules. A semi-supervised case shows the bounds at work in practice. Verifiable conditions on the methods keep the bounds honest.
arxiv-2505-07467:
Yui Hayashi, Yuya Tanizaki, and Mithat Ünsal build the semiclassical machinery of confinement on a small twisted box. Yang-Mills theory on a plane times a small torus, with a non-minimal 't Hooft twist, can be treated semiclassically. Their center vortices descend from known monopole solutions through a three-dimensional abelianized picture. The construction assigns each vortex fractional charges.

Its magnetic and topological charges come in N-th parts, fixed by the twist. The action is likewise a fraction of an instanton's. A dilute gas of such vortices then describes the confining vacua. The authors derive how observables depend on the vacuum angle and compute string tensions. They finally test which twist best stabilizes the center at large N, examining a Fibonacci-based proposal from related models. The checks run through both one-form and zero-form center symmetries.
arxiv-2505-07667:
Subgroups of a classic group family can churn under pairing in unlike ways, and Sasha Bontemps charts that churn in work from twenty twenty-five. The groups, named for Baumslag and Solitar, split into kinds by two whole-number knobs. A past split of the subgroup space into parts guides the study.

For the skewed, non-shared kinds, the churn on most parts is weak, far from the strong mixing seen in a wider group class. One part breaks that tale. For the balanced kind, strong mixing holds on each part. The contrast shows how a small knob shift can flip the whole temper of subgroup motion in these groups.
arxiv-2505-07867:
Jorge Mestre-Tomas presents a software package in a 2025 paper for thinning species records on maps. Modelers thin crowded occurrence points to cut sampling bias before fitting habitat models. Older tools use brute force checks that crawl on large data sets.

His R package offers several thinning styles: keep a minimum gap between points, sample by grid cell, or filter by coordinate precision. Two tuned algorithms built on local search trees slash memory and run time. Group wise thinning and point ranking round out the kit for real workflows. Benchmarks on simulated and real data show large speed gains over existing tools. The package is free for ecology teams.
arxiv-2505-07967:
Changyu Liu and co-authors study robust regression in a 2025 paper. Regression models can fail when real data shift away from training data. A robust method guards against the worst case within a set of nearby data distributions, measured here by Wasserstein distance.

The authors work out how the guard acts for flexible, nonparametric models. A first-order distance gives one kind of smoothing, while higher orders give another tied to gradients. They bound the error for neural network estimators and give a convergence rate. New bounds control both a function and its slope at once. The theory helps builders trust models under shift.
arxiv-2505-08067:
Sorensen and Gibbons wrote a physics paper in two thousand twenty-five tracing a mystery noise in dark matter detectors. The detectors use liquid xenon and watch for faint flashes of light. For nearly a decade, a delayed glow with a slow fading pattern has followed each flash, and in recent years it has swamped searches for light dark matter.

Working with a small xenon cell at a Berkeley lab, the authors ran a broad series of tests. They conclude that the main source is fluorescence from the quartz windows of the light sensors, set off by ultraviolet light. Naming the source gives detector builders a concrete target to fix.
arxiv-2505-08467:
Leonardo Giani, Rodrigo von Marttens, and Oliver Piattella propose a twist on the standard cosmology model, in a 2025 paper. In their version, ordinary matter stops behaving like pressure-free dust at late times. Below a chosen transition redshift, its equation of state drifts away from zero.

The team fits this two-parameter extension against fresh data: baryon acoustic oscillations, supernova distances, and early-universe distance measures. They compare it with the popular CPL formula for evolving dark energy. By a standard model-selection score, the two are nearly indistinguishable. Both beat the standard model by a clear margin. The authors note the setup arises naturally in cosmological backreaction, where averaging lumpy space changes the effective equations. They derive a prediction for how structure growth evolves, which low-redshift surveys can test.
arxiv-2505-08767:
Hassan and four co-authors wrote this 2025 arXiv paper on using Bayesian optimization to steer particle beams at Canada's TRIUMF lab. The lab accelerates rare isotope beams for physics, and tuning their path by hand is slow. A coming facility will run several beams at once, making hands-on tuning untenable. The team is building semi-automated tuning around a known centroid correction routine.

Machine studies run over two months in late 2024 tested the approach on the real post-accelerator. The results shaped a plan for the medium- and high-energy transport lines: tune the line section by section, letting the optimizer settle each stretch before moving on. The paper is a strategy report, laying out how Bayesian methods will be folded into daily operations. It marks a step toward self-driving beamlines at a major national lab.
arxiv-2505-09267:
Isaac Harris and co-authors report fine control of a diamond-based quantum device in a 2025 paper. Long-distance quantum networks need parts that link light signals with long-lived memory. Tiny flaws in diamond, called color centers, offer both: an electron spin that talks to light, and a nuclear spin that stores data.

The snag is that firing light at the device kicks the memory and blurs it. The team used a tin-based center with a strong internal link, run at zero magnetic field, where the memory shrugs off light pulses. Built into a photonic chip, the device hit high gate accuracy and held memory for milliseconds. The result supports this design for future network nodes.
arxiv-2505-09767:
Ahmad Dkhan and four co-authors model the wireless channel for terahertz links aided by reconfigurable intelligent surfaces in a 2025 paper. These surfaces, placed between a base station and a user, can shape signals at extremely high frequencies. Dense arrays at such frequencies bring complications: signal absorption, waves that curve near the array, coupling between elements, and correlated fading.

The team describes the small-scale fading with a mixture gamma distribution and derives the form of the combined surface-aided channel. They then test simple linear methods for estimating that channel. Their simulations show that including correlation, coupling, and near-field effects markedly improves estimation accuracy, especially for very large arrays used at short range.
arxiv-2505-10167:
Saikat Barua and co-authors make hybrid quantum machine learning models explain themselves, in this 2025 paper. These models encode data with quantum circuits, then hand the results to classical learners, a power that comes with black-box opacity. Their framework, QuXAI, centers on an explainer called Q-MEDLEY built for exactly this split design.

The explainer blends several feature-importance lenses while respecting the quantum encoding stage, then draws the verdicts as readable attributions. In tests it picked out the classical features that truly drive the hybrid models and separated real signal from noise. It held its own against established explanation tools in classical checks. Extra ablation tests showed each part of the blend earning its place. The authors offer the code openly.
arxiv-2505-10367:
Chuanqing Pu and co-authors present the winning entry of team GEB in a 2024 competition on forecasting and trading hybrid wind-solar power. The team placed third in trading, fourth in forecasting, and first among student teams. Their system stacks forecasts from several weather models for wind power. It also corrects solar forecasts online, as new solar capacity changed the test data. Everything then merges into probability forecasts for the combined output.

A stochastic trading strategy then bids into the day-ahead electricity market, aiming for the best expected revenue under price uncertainty. Case studies check each piece of the design. The paper also explores teaching the system end to end, shifting forecast errors in ways that raise trading profit. All code is public, so energy researchers and traders can reproduce the approach. The work shows that forecast quality and trading profit, while linked, reward different choices.
arxiv-2505-10467:
Pablo Hernández-García and co-authors introduce new network measures in 2025 for judging how robust a higher-order network is. Networks built from grouping units, not just pairs, appear in social and biological systems. The question is which connections and holes survive damage.

Their thick measures check whether features rest on high-dimensional building blocks, while their cohesive measures weigh the strength of higher-order links behind each feature. Simulating attacks with a damage dial lets them separate features that stay robust from those that thin out. Stability theorems under a network distance back the method. The authors frame robustness as persistence under degradation.
arxiv-2505-10667:
Shmuel Friedland wrote a 2025 paper on relaxed forms of the optimal transport problem. That problem asks for the cheapest way to move mass between distributions, in both classic and quantum forms. A smoothed version has seen much progress in the past fifteen years.

Friedland shows that interior point methods for these problems can be seen as barrier relaxations. The dual form of the problem has far fewer variables, which is a clear gain. For the classic case, these methods are slower than a known fast scaling method. For the quantum case, though, the dual interior point method seems to work quite well in practice.
arxiv-2505-10867:
Luca Luceri and five co-authors hunt coordinated fake accounts on TikTok, a video-first platform past methods barely touch. Their paper from twenty twenty-five studies coordinated inauthentic behavior around the twenty twenty-four United States presidential election. Text-era detectors lean on signals TikTok lacks. The team adapts network methods to the app's habits instead.

User similarity graphs rest on shared acts: synced posting, near-dup copies of captions, reused clips, and matched hashtag chains. Pruning the graphs exposes dense clusters of likely partners. The data span hundreds of thousands of election videos. Found acts range from synced narrative pushes to semi-automated copying with AI voices and split screens. Some classic signals port well; transcript likeness and Duet links do not. The study lays a first base for TikTok influence research.
arxiv-2505-11067:
Omobayode Fagbohungbe and co-authors present a 2025 paper on training neural networks in analog memory hardware, and how well that training transfers to new tasks. Such hardware promises fast, frugal learning by computing where the data sit. Real devices, though, switch unevenly and vary from unit to unit, which breaks standard training recipes.

The team assessed a newer algorithm built to cope with that mess, one that chops updates to tame the devices' lopsided response. Earlier rival methods demanded unrealistically perfect devices or proved fragile. The study weighs how the analog-trained models perform when moved to fresh tasks, the transfer setting where the hardware's speed could pay off most.
arxiv-2505-11367:
Ji Eun Kim and Libby Hemphill study how moral language shapes online giving in a 2025 paper. Charity appeals often lean on values such as care, fairness, and loyalty. The team measured which values appear in real campaigns and how donations answered.

They analyzed 14,088 campaigns on GoFundMe, sorting appeals by three moral frames. Emergency campaigns reacted most strongly to moral wording. Appeals stressing harm and unfairness drew more donations and comments overall, yet each donor gave a little less on average. Loyalty framing helped everywhere, raising both gift counts and messages of support. The authors suggest platforms could coach fundraisers on framing, while warning that outrage-based appeals have a cost.
arxiv-2505-11567:
Guessing the next bend in a stream of data is hard in part since the data hold noise that no tool can beat. Tianyi Shi and co-authors take on that floor in a 2025 study. They prove a twist exists that can cut the noise count of linked streams, then build a loss that trains tools in both time and tone views.

Their loss, OLMA, checks the guess in raw time and in two tone forms, and across both the stream's own span and its side streams. On many test sets, tools trained with the loss guessed more true than past tools. The team frames noise and tone bias as a fresh, sound path for the field.
arxiv-2505-11667:
Boolean control networks model systems whose parts switch on and off, from gene circuits to logic hardware. Giorgia Disarò and Maria Elena Valcher asked in 2025 how much can be learned about such a network from data alone, without ever writing down its model. Data-driven control is common elsewhere, but it had barely been tried on this class of systems.

Using only a limited set of observations generated by the network, the authors show how to judge basic features such as which states can be reached and where the system settles. They also solve two control tasks from data: keeping the system within safe states, and forcing its output to follow a target. The paper aims to open a new direction for the field.
arxiv-2505-11967:
Bas Sanders sets out a new way to measure doubt in trade and place-based models, in a paper from 2025. Economists use these models to guess what a policy change would do. Those guesses can steer real choices, so the doubt around them matters. Three snags make the doubt hard to gauge: the data link pairs of places, the count of places is small, and the data feed the model twice over.

The author builds a bootstrap method shaped to fit these snags. The method is simple to run and comes with both short-run and long-run promises of soundness. He then reapplies three well-known past studies with the new method. The reruns show where the method helps in practice. The paper gives trade research a cleaner way to say how firm its forecasts are.
arxiv-2505-12467:
Haochun Wang and five co-authors tested in 2025 how teams of AI agents should work together, beyond the frameworks that hold them. Multi-agent setups now tackle complex tasks, but most research tweaks the outer frame rather than the day-to-day rules of teamwork. The team studied four such rules: who leads, who takes part, how turns flow, and how past talk is kept. They ran tests in two settings that stress evidence handling.

Central leadership, teacher-led turns, ordered exchanges, and teacher-made summaries of past talk gave the best mix of accuracy and cost. The team also built a score that weighs accuracy against token use. Their message is that smart interaction rules matter as much as system shape. Designers of agent teams can use the findings to cut waste while keeping quality.
arxiv-2505-12567:
Wenrui Xu and Keshab Parhi survey attacks on large language models and the agents built on them. Their 2025 paper notes that such models now serve in health, finance, support, robots, and self-driving cars. Wide use brings risks: misuse, privacy leaks, and service breaks that erode trust. The survey sorts attacks into three phases of a model's life: training, use, and attacks on uptime and honesty.

For each phase, they lay out known attack styles and the defenses matched to them. Case detail covers both fresh methods and stock ones. The authors hope the survey works as a guide and a call for stronger guards as threats evolve.
arxiv-2505-12767:
A fairness promise from a language model means little if a swapped word can flip its answer. Danqing Chen, Tobias Ladner, Ahmed Rayen Mhadhbi, and Matthias Althoff build proof-based fairness certificates in a 2025 paper. Their frame checks transformer models for steady outputs across gender-linked terms. Small swaps like synonyms are the attack the checks must survive. The same frame extends to toxicity spotting.

Proofs are stated inside the model's embedding space, where word swaps land as bounded moves. Certified models must flag harmful text even after such moves. The authors frame the work as formal backup for ethical deployment. Moderation systems are a named use, since a missed toxic post carries real cost.
arxiv-2505-12867:
Ruancun Li, Luis Ho, and Chang-Hao Chen used a space telescope in 2025 to look inside the glow of distant quasars. Quasars are bright centers of young galaxies, and their host galaxies are hard to see against the glare. The team studied thirty-one quasars from the early universe and detected the host light in thirty of them.

Two groups stood out. Bright blue quasars sat in round, bulge-heavy galaxies, while fainter red quasars sat in flat, disk-like hosts. The bright group also held black holes that were small for their galaxy size, compared with the faint group. The split hints that black holes and galaxies grew together in more than one way in the early universe.
arxiv-2505-13267:
Ocran and colleagues chart the radio glow of star-forming galaxies in a deep sky field, including many too faint to list one by one. They separate true star formers from quiet galaxies and active nuclei using many wavelengths of data. Stacking the faint sources by redshift bin reveals their average spectrum.

Across seven slices of cosmic time, the radio spectral slope showed no firm drift with distance. Curved models fit best at low frequencies, where the spectrum steepens. At the top frequency, the glow mixed a steep synchrotron part with a flat thermal part from hot gas, the thermal share holding near eleven to eighteen percent. The authors call for deeper, sharper radio maps.
arxiv-2505-13367:
Carsten Henkel solves the Bogoliubov-de Gennes equations for waves that bounce in a lumpy condensate. The paper from twenty twenty-five studies the full continuous spectrum near a turning point. A basis swap splits the particle and hole amplitudes, near enough, into two modes. One mode spreads wide and rules phase ripples of the condensate. The other hugs zones where density slopes.

Phase shifts on reflection are worked out by hand math and by numeric runs. Those shifts set the standing wave pattern in the trap. As a use case, Henkel computes mode tones in a gravitational trap with no local density shortcut. A companion paper takes up the warm cloud's density and quantum depletion. The study sharpens the theory of sound-like waves in trapped gases.
arxiv-2505-13467:
Kleischmann and three co-authors report tests on clay in salty water done in space, in a paper from twenty twenty-five. The tests ran on the space station, where there is almost no gravity. The team watched how small bits of clay clump into larger lumps over time. They tracked the clumps with photos for ninety-nine days.

They find that tiny shakes on the station sped up the clumping. Clumps grew much faster than they would from random heat drift alone. Computer models back up the same point. Stronger shakes and more solid clay both made growth faster. The result shows a new way that bits in a fluid can join up.
arxiv-2505-13567:
Yoav Ger and Omri Barak develop a theory of how recurrent networks learn when they act inside closed-loop settings. Brain-like learning happens while the learner changes its world. Lab training usually freezes the world in an open loop instead.

Two identical networks diverge sharply between the two modes. The team characterizes the closed-loop path with exact math. Learning unfolds in stages that track the training loss. Two goals compete throughout the closed-loop process. Short-term policy gains fight long-term stability of the interaction. A motor control task shows the frame in action. The results argue for closed-loop views of brain learning. They may reshape how neural models are trained.
arxiv-2505-13767:
Celso Jorge Villas-Boas and Ciro Micheletti Diniz published a 2025 physics paper arguing that most of the energy in thermal radiation hides where detectors cannot see it. Heat glow, like light from a warm object, is usually treated as a crowd of independent waves. The authors show the crowd organizes into collective modes. Most of those modes are dark: entangled states of light that do not couple to matter.

In a system of many field modes, only one share in M of the energy can interact with matter at all. The rest sits locked in the dark modes. A common way of estimating energy, measuring brightness, can therefore mislead badly. The team tests the idea in a model cavity holding a single lossy atom, where breaking symmetry lets some hidden energy leak into view. The claim reframes what a detector reading means: silence may signal hidden energy, not absence.
arxiv-2505-13967:
Krishna Gupta and four co-authors built a quasi-Newton method in two thousand twenty-five for optimization problems that juggle several goals under uncertainty. Only finitely many uncertainty scenarios are assumed, and each goal function is smooth in the classic sense. The aim is robust weakly efficient points: choices that stay good no matter which scenario lands.

At each step, a partition trick builds a fresh family of vector problems whose descent direction the quasi-Newton step computes. Any limit point of the sequence is proved to be a robust weakly efficient point, given standard assumptions. Local speed is superlinear when the curvature estimate behaves. Numerical examples round out the paper.
arxiv-2505-14367:
Jialong Han, Si Zhang, and Ke Zhang improve cheap fine tuning of language models in a 2025 paper. Low rank adapters tune a big model by training a few small matrices. Random starting values make that training unstable and wasteful. Their method, DuDe, initializes adapters from the model's own weights instead.

Weight matrices are split into size and direction parts. A singular value decomposition seeds the adapters in a principled way. Training then starts from the pretrained structure rather than noise. On a broad knowledge test the method reached about forty eight percent accuracy. On a math word problem set it scored near sixty three percent. Theory and tests agree the split steadies optimization. Pretrained knowledge survives the transfer better than with random starts.
arxiv-2505-14667:
Wonje Jeung, Sangyeon Yoon, Minsuk Kahng, and Albert No published a 2025 paper on keeping reasoning models safe without dulling them. Large reasoning models think aloud in long chains, and harmful prompts can hijack that chain toward dangerous outputs. Standard safety training suppresses the harm but often shortens and weakens the reasoning itself. It also cracks under clever jailbreak prompts.

Their method, SAFEPATH, teaches the model a small reflex: when a prompt is harmful, begin the reasoning with a short safety primer, just eight tokens. The rest of the chain is left unsupervised, free to reason at full depth. Across benchmarks, harmful outputs fell while problem-solving performance held. The primer works like a guardrail placed at the entrance, not speed bumps along the whole road. The authors offer it as a lightweight patch for a real tension: models that reason longer need safety that does not reason less.
arxiv-2505-14767:
Meng Cheng and four co-authors, including Nathan Seiberg and Senthil, set out in 2025 to organize the possible phases of matter in the fractional quantum Hall effect. In this effect, electrons in a flat sheet under a strong magnetic field form exotic states whose order is topological rather than visible in any local pattern.

The authors start from the measured Hall conductivity and use it to pin down the global symmetry of the low-energy theory and its anomaly. That information alone, they show, points to one minimal topological order, or a small set of them. Nearly all orders seen in experiments turn out to be these minimal ones.
arxiv-2505-14867:
So Won Jeong and Claire Donnat present LOBSTUR, a way to tune unsupervised graph neural networks without labels, in work from 2025. Such networks learn strong node representations but are touchy about hyperparameters, and with no labels there is no easy score for picking the best model. Their frame bootstraps the graph locally, resampling edges and features in ways that respect nearby structure.

Embedding consistency across the resampled graphs is scored with canonical correlation analysis, giving a label-free quality signal. On standard datasets the method lifted classification accuracy by about two thirds over uninformed tuning. A real-world deployment is included to show the frame works outside benchmarks.
arxiv-2505-15267:
Wenmin Li, Shunsuke Sakai, and Tatsuhito Hasegawa shrink big image sets into tiny fake sets that still teach well. Such fake sets let small devices and fast tests train models with far less data. A known method tunes the fake set so a model trained on it walks the same path as one trained on real data. At very small sizes, that method loses the rich sense of the real set.

Their add-on uses contrastive learning while the fake images are made. That step forces each fake image to stand apart from the rest in its traits. Fake sets built this way taught models that scored far higher in the scarcest tests. Image quality of the fakes rose too. The gain held across the board but stood out most where each class had just a few fakes.
arxiv-2505-16067:
AI agents that remember their past attempts can improve with experience, but Zidi Xiong and co-authors show the memory cuts both ways. Studying how agents add and delete memories, they find a strong experience-following habit. When a new task resembles a remembered one, the agent's output closely mirrors what it did before, for better or worse.

That habit breeds two failure modes. Old errors get copied forward and compound, and some past successes mislead because they were right for the wrong reasons. Controlled experiments show that policing memory quality matters more than hoarding volume, and that grading memories by how later tasks turn out provides free quality labels. The study offers design rules for agent memory that ages gracefully.
arxiv-2505-16167:
Xiao Hu and Yang Ye teach robot hands to grip by feel when sight cannot be trusted. Construction work hides parts behind other parts, so cameras misjudge pose. Their 2025 paper builds a tactile simulator for training. A reinforcement learning method, Proximal Policy Optimization, then adjusts grip posture live from touch feedback. The hand keeps re-aiming as its fingers report pressure and slip.

Simulated trials cover jobs like pipe fitting and rebar work. The touch-led hand adapts its posture to each new error in the object's judged pose. Grip success and steadiness both rise against vision-only habits. The team pitches touch as the sense of last resort when eyes fail on site.
arxiv-2505-16467:
Vera Neplenbroek and co-authors wrote a 2025 paper on how stereotypes steer language model personalization. Models guess user traits from faint cues in chat. Those guesses can lower answer quality for some groups. The team probed the effect with controlled synthetic talks.

They read both the model hidden user picture and its answers to direct questions. Models did infer traits like age and background from stock cues. For some groups the wrong guess stuck even after the user stated the truth. A fix tested in the paper cut the effect well. Hidden personalization needs watching as chatbots spread.
arxiv-2505-16567:
Thibaud Gloaguen, Mark Vero, Robin Staab, and Martin Vechev show that a language model can hide a trap that wakes when a user fine-tunes it. Fine-tuning has been held a safe, controlled act: clean data in, tame behavior out. Their 2025 attack, FAB, trains a model by fake fine-tunes in the lab, so the trap is honed to fire on real ones. A leash keeps the base model clean and strong until then.

Downstream users who tune the fair-face model on their own clean sets trip the trap with no sign. Three trap kinds pass the tests: sly advertising, jailbreak ease, and over-refusal. The trap holds through dataset, step, and tuning-method choices. Open-weight release thus needs a new grade of check, they hold.
arxiv-2505-16767:
Zheng and co-authors present a 2025 cosmology paper on clustering math for Horndeski gravity, a leading rival to Einstein's theory. When growth rates depend on scale, standard perturbation tools need rework. The team derived second- and third-order kernels for that general case. Two effective functions capture every departure from general relativity in their formulas.
