A Wronskian method solves the growth functions, leaving kernels analytic up to one time integral. Galaxy bias and redshift-space distortions are folded in. Once the linear growth is known, the full one-loop galaxy power spectrum follows. The authors built the toolkit for survey forecasts and real data fits in modified gravity tests.
arxiv-2505-16867:
Lydia Makrygianni and a large team report a twin star-shred flare in a 2025 paper. A black hole tore a star in 2022, then flared again 700 days on in near twin form. Lens tricks and chance pairs fail to tell that tale, they show. The first flare thus reads as a part shred: the star lived, swung back, and shed more. A capture path may have set that loop.

Both flares match the stock optical class in heat, light, and spectra. So part shreds may hide in that class at large, or the whole class is part shreds. Past full-shred models then want a rework, the team say.
arxiv-2505-16967:
Nandan Thakur, Crystina Zhang, Xueguang Ma, and Jimmy Lin showed in two thousand twenty-five that trimming bad training data can make search models stronger. A leading training set held one point six million query-passage pairs from fifteen sources. Dropping eight sources shrank the set more than twofold, yet search quality rose on a standard test.

The culprit was false negatives: passages wrongly labelled as irrelevant. The team used language models as a cheap judge to find and relabel them as true matches. Retrained retrievers and rerankers gained clear points on two benchmarks. Human checks backed the relabelling. Their cleaned data and code are shared in public.
arxiv-2505-17167: Ibrahim Ethem Hamamci and co-authors present a 2025 arXiv paper on a fairer score for AI-written radiology reports. Word-overlap metrics miss clinical truth, while model-based judges wobble, and clinical checklists reward lazy all-normal answers when diseases are rare. Their CRG score grades only the abnormalities the reference report actually names, in binary or structured detail. Penalties are weighted by how common each label is, so rare findings count properly. Any language model can drive the feature extraction.
arxiv-2505-17267:
Odysseas Chlapanis and co-authors introduce GreekBarBench, a test set for language models in Greek law. Their paper appeared in 2025. The questions come from Greek bar exams across five legal areas. Answers must reason in free text and cite the right statutes and case facts. Grading free text is hard, so the team built a scoring system with three dimensions, judged by a language model.

They also built a second benchmark to check the judges against human experts. Simple rubrics tied to text spans made the model judges agree better with experts. They then graded thirteen leading models. The best beat the average expert score but fell short of the top five percent of experts. The work gives Greek legal AI a demanding, well-checked measuring stick.
arxiv-2505-17367:
Zichuan Yang and Yongzhi Wang present EVM-Fusion in a 2025 paper, an explainable vision model for medical image classification across organs. Clinic use demands accuracy plus a clear view of how a model decides.

The design runs several paths in parallel: two neural paths boosted by Vision Mamba blocks, and a classic feature path. A two-stage fusion joins them, first with cross attention, then with a learned fusion block that adapts its recipe. Explainability is built in through attention maps from each path and fusion weights. On a nine-class multi-organ data set, test accuracy neared perfect. The authors pitch the model as a trustworthy aid for diagnostic support.
arxiv-2505-17567:
Denisa Qosja, Kilian Barth, and Simon Wagner use generative models to sharpen radar pictures in this 2025 paper. In a range-Doppler map, fine detail along the Doppler axis lets a radar separate slow-moving targets from clutter and still objects. Hardware and physics cap how sharp that axis can be at capture time, so processors try to add sharpness afterward.

The authors start from a zero-padded Fourier transform and then refine the map with a diffusion model, the class of neural networks behind modern image generators. The refined maps pull apart targets that sit close together in Doppler, which the plain transform smears into one blob. The team presents the method as a way past the usual resolution limits without new hardware.
arxiv-2505-17967:
Training a large language model is cheaper when its gradient updates are squeezed into a low-rank space, but the usual tools for that squeeze are themselves costly. Ionut-Vlad Modoranu and co-authors replace those tools with a fixed transform borrowed from signal processing, the discrete cosine transform. For each layer they pick the transform columns that line up best with the current gradient, building the projection with one matrix multiplication plus a sort.

Because the transform is fixed, it is computed once before training starts, and fast Fourier methods speed it further on large layers. In trials on pretraining and fine-tuning, the method matched the accuracy of the costly standard approach while running faster and using up to a quarter less memory.
arxiv-2505-18667:
Elise Sanger, writing alone in 2025, tests Einstein's theory of gravity with a gravitational wave signal from a merging pair. One object was most likely a neutron star, and the other a compact object in the lower mass gap.

Sanger ran tests in two frameworks that let the signal drift from what the theory predicts at each stage of the spiral inward. The signal matched the theory for every drift measure. Limits on dipole radiation, an extra form of energy loss some rival theories allow, were very tight. She notes traps in the analysis, such as a clash between drift measures and tide effects. A test of one rival theory gave its best limits to date.
arxiv-2505-18867:
Ming Cheng and co-authors build a system that rewrites science in plain words in a 2025 paper. Most past tools were trained on one field, such as biomedicine, yet modern research often spans many fields at once. Their system, Sci-LoRA, blends small tuned modules, each raised on a distinct field of science.

For each new text, the system sets the blend weights on the fly, with no need for a field label. It joins field facts at both the data and model levels to keep depth and range in balance. Across twelve fields and five test sets, it beat large rival models and flexed well to new mixes of topics.
arxiv-2505-19267:
Javier Cacheiro and co-authors describe in 2025 QMIO, a hybrid system that tightly couples a supercomputer with a quantum processor. Quantum units could speed up specific simulation kernels, cut energy use, or add new capability to high-performance computing centers. Loose coupling wastes that potential, so integration depth matters for real workloads in scientific computing today.

The paper lays out QMIO's hardware and software parts, plus the middleware that links them. It also shares lessons from designing, building, and running the system. The work offers a reference design for centers planning their own hybrid quantum-classical installations in coming years.
arxiv-2505-19367:
Iskander Azangulov and co-authors put the guidance of diffusion models on firm theoretical ground, in a 2025 paper. Guidance steers these image and text generators toward desired outputs. Choosing the guidance strength over time is now mostly guesswork. Poor schedules waste quality or diversity.

The authors first pin down how guidance strength relates to classifier confidence. They then cast scheduling as a stochastic optimal control problem. Guidance becomes a decision made step by step, not a fixed dial. The framework adapts strength as generation proceeds. Tests show the payoff of that adaptivity. Model builders gain a principled alternative to hand-tuned schedules. The theory may extend to other generative settings.
arxiv-2505-19867:
Yavar Taheri Yeganeh, Mohsen Jafari, and Andrea Matta build a deep active inference agent for slow, long tasks in a 2025 paper. Active inference unites sense, learn, and act in one chance-based frame. Most agents of this kind need sharp short forecasts and full plan search. Both break when rewards come late and plans run to hundreds of steps. The team test their agent in a mock plant with such delays.

Four tricks drive the design. A multi-step jump lets the inner model forecast a whole span at once. A policy net sits inside the model and learns from the same aim score. Training swaps steps between model and policy from a shared memory bank. One gradient step then plans the span, so no full search runs at act time. Tests show the agent steers well with no hand-made rewards.
arxiv-2505-20067:
Isabelle Augenstein and co-authors examine crowd fact-checking on social media in 2025. Platforms once relied on staff teams and outside checkers to flag false claims. Some large platforms now use notes written and rated by users themselves.

The authors map current approaches across major platforms and weigh the promise of crowd checks. Such notes could fight false claims at greater scale and speed. Yet views of truth are shaped by bias, politics, and culture, so crowd agreement is hard. The paper argues that crowd efforts can aid, but not replace, skilled fact-checkers.
arxiv-2505-20367:
Sen Yan and co-authors present, in a 2025 paper, a deep learning method that repairs spotty magnetic resonance spectra. NMR spectroscopy reads a molecule's surroundings, structure, and motion. The machines are costly and the scans slow, so faster sampling methods are prized.

Random sub-sampling cuts scan time but leaves artifacts that mar the result. The authors explore diffusion models, little tried for this task, to fill in the missing pieces. Their method aims to lift reconstruction quality back toward full-scan levels. Clean spectra from shorter scans would ease costs across drug research and industry. The paper tests whether a fashionable generative tool earns its place in a precision science.
arxiv-2505-20667:
Tianwa Chen and co-authors study how experts read combined diagrams of business processes and rules in this 2025 paper. Firms often draw workflows and the rules that govern them in one integrated model, to avoid the confusion of split documents. The question is how skilled workers make sense of such dense displays.

The team paired spoken think-aloud records with eye-tracking data while experts worked through tasks. They traced two phases: hunting for the right information, then working through what it means. Experts differed in style, the study found. The authors argue that support tools should adapt to the person, not offer one fixed view to everyone.
arxiv-2505-21267: Hung, Martínez and Navarro study the sum of the squares of irreducible character degrees that are not divisible by a given prime in 2025. They relate this quantity for a finite group to the matching quantity inside the normaliser of a Sylow subgroup. Their work addresses a recent conjecture by Giannelli, which they prove when the prime is 2 and in several other cases. The result adds to a line of research connecting global character data of a group with the structure of its local subgroups.
arxiv-2505-21367:
Micha Christoph and Raphael Steiner settle a conjecture about which directed patterns must appear in every dense directed network. Extremal graph theory asks what structures are forced by sheer density. For undirected graphs many answers are known; for directed graphs, arrows make the same questions stubborn.

An earlier team had shown that any forced directed pattern must be an oriented forest of a special shape. They conjectured the converse: every forest of that shape is forced, appearing inside any directed graph whose minimum out-degree is large enough. Christoph and Steiner prove the conjecture in full. Their 2025 paper closes the KAMAK tree problem, named for the earlier team's initials. The proof is a compact capstone to a short line of work.
arxiv-2505-21467:
Hu and co-authors speed up a new breed of language model in this 2025 computer science paper. Diffusion language models write by cleaning up a rough draft of the whole text over many passes, which gives quality but slow runs. Each pass normally recomputes everything, and cutting passes hurts coherence.

Two training-free tricks fix this. One caches stable internal values across passes instead of recomputing them. The other lets a small standard model guide which tokens to reveal, slashing the pass count. Together they sped up generation about twelvefold on reasoning tests with almost no quality loss. For the first time, these models run as fast as the standard kind.
arxiv-2505-21667:
Soham Mitra, Praveer Tiwari, and Archana Pai show how the ringdown of merged neutron stars could pin down the matter inside them, in this 2025 paper. After two neutron stars collide, the hot remnant vibrates, emitting gravitational waves that encode the equation of state, how pressure and density relate at extremes no lab reaches.

Today's detectors are nearly deaf at those high frequencies, so single events say little. Building on an earlier injection study, the team extends a hierarchical Bayesian method to four reference radii at once and threads them through a flexible equation-of-state model. With the planned A+ detector sensitivity, combined events could fix neutron star radii to about a kilometer, or half that under astrophysically informed priors. They also probe biases from the empirical relations the method leans on. The work maps a route to measuring ultra-dense matter.
arxiv-2505-21767:
Xiaoyan Li and co-authors rebuild the heart's electrical trace from a fingertip pulse signal, in a 2025 biomedical paper. Turning PPG into ECG is attractive for wearables, but fine waveform details are easy to lose. Their method feeds a vision transformer a four-channel picture of the pulse. The channels hold the raw signal, its two rates of change, and the area beneath it, so both timing and shape cues survive.

The transformer's attention links beats to each other and to their own parts. Across tests the method cut reconstruction error by up to 29 percent against strong one-dimensional baselines. New error measures on clinically meaningful intervals backed the gain, pointing to more faithful traces.
arxiv-2505-21967:
Juan Ren, Mark Dras, and Usman Naseem study attacks on vision-language models in a paper from two thousand twenty-five. These models take in images as well as text, which opens new attack surfaces. The authors ask why standard adversarial attacks can slip past the safety tools built into such models.

They carry out a systematic analysis of the models' internal representations. They also propose a two-stage scheme for grading attacks, first sorting outcomes into non-compliance, refusal, and true exploitation. The second stage scores how fully the output serves the harmful intent, and sorts refusals by type. A normative schema then sets out ideal model behavior against harmful prompts, as a target for safety work.
arxiv-2505-22167:
Weilun Feng and co-authors shrink video diffusion transformers with a framework called Q-VDiT. These models make striking video but carry huge parameter counts that bar them from edge devices. Quantization cuts the bit width of the weights, yet image-born methods bend when frames must stay in step.

Their 2025 paper names two faults: information lost in the squeeze, and training aims that ignore video's own needs. A token-aware estimator pays back quantization error along both token and feature axes. A temporal distillation step then guards the links between frames while each frame is tuned in full context. At very low bit width, their model sets a fresh scene-consistency mark.
arxiv-2505-22367:
Aswathy Menon Kavumpadikkal Radhakrishnan and her four co-authors, publishing in 2025, ask whether the inner structure of oxygen nuclei leaves a fingerprint on particle flow at the Large Hadron Collider. Oxygen nuclei are known to hold clusters of helium nuclei inside them. Colliders have begun smashing oxygen into protons and into itself to study tiny drops of quark-gluon plasma. Flow patterns in the debris reflect the shape of the colliding nuclei.

The team simulates both collision types with a hybrid model that chains several standard codes. They compare clustered nuclei against a smooth standard profile. Clustering barely matters when oxygen hits a proton. In oxygen-oxygen collisions it changes every flow measure they study. The size of the helium clusters also shifts the effect. The work gives experimenters a way to read nuclear structure out of collision data.
arxiv-2505-22667: Julius Ross writes a short guide on accessibility for working mathematicians. Its single message is stated up front. Creating accessible documents requires authors to hold a working understanding of accessibility. They must also write with accessibility in mind from the start. The guide presses that accessibility is an author's responsibility, not an afterthought applied at the end.
arxiv-2505-22767:
Vasilaki asks how chat with a big tongue tool sparks fresh sight in this twenty twenty-five piece. A chat can jolt a mind to see a snag in a whole new way. She frames that spark as fruit of a two-way loop, not tool wit lone.

Inside, each made word turns back as feed for the next word in line. Each reply also loops through the mind, whose fresh read re-shapes the next ask. The tool's part swings tween stock lines and frame breaks that open new paths. A spine of kept past bits could call back the best modes on cue. Past chats, open tools, and brain math make the claims test-ripe.
arxiv-2505-22967:
Plans made by language models often break when a computer tries to run them, since free text sets few hard rules. Chengqi Zheng and co-authors tackle that flaw with a graph-based frame in work from twenty twenty-five. Workflows are drawn in a chart language that people can read and machines can check.

Change steps drawn from breed-style search swap, tweak, add, and drop graph parts while guarding sense and structure. The search stays inside a space of plans that can be checked before they run. Tests on an agent test set showed higher success rates and faster arrival at plans that run. The team frames the method as a base for agent systems that stay clear and safe to inspect.
arxiv-2505-23067:
Rongli Huang, Changzheng Qu, Zhizhang Wang, and Weifeng Wo study how convex surfaces evolve under a curvature-driven flow with a fixed boundary rule, in a 2025 paper. The flow, driven by a Hessian curvature measure, reshapes a surface over time. The boundary rule here is the second boundary value condition, tying the surface gradient at the edge to a target.

First the authors explore translating solutions, shapes that move without changing form, under this boundary rule. Then they prove the flow exists for all time and settles onto such a translating solution. The hard step is controlling second derivatives at the boundary. Their trick uses the orthogonal symmetry of the problem to get those estimates. The result extends classic work on the Gauss curvature flow with the same boundary rule to the wider Hessian family. The paper closes a gap in the theory of such flows.
arxiv-2505-23267:
Jianlin Ye and co-authors guide drone path planning with a vision-language model in this 2025 paper. Drones must reach targets or sweep areas while dodging obstacles. The classic random tree method plans such paths but can wander and settle slowly.

Slow, crooked paths are a real problem in disaster response work. Their method lets a vision-language model steer the tree's growth. The model reads the scene and biases sampling toward promising routes. That guidance aims for faster convergence and cleaner paths. Tests judge how much the guidance helps in complex spaces. Rescue and inspection drones both need plans they can trust at speed. The method needs no retraining of the underlying planner.
arxiv-2505-23367:
Jeonghyeok Do and co-authors sharpen satellite images in a 2025 paper through a method called PAN-sharpening. It fuses a sharp black and white image with a coarse color image to yield a sharp color result.

The catch is that the two images seldom line up pixel by pixel, due to sensor placement, timing, and scale gaps. Older deep learning methods assume a perfect match and so produce color shifts, double edges, and blur. The new framework rebuilds both image types in one network, using the sharp image's detail as a self check. An attention step aligns texture and structure in both directions. Tests beat the best rival on all measures, far faster and with less memory.
arxiv-2505-23467:
Adolfo Cisterna, Mokhtar Hassaine, and Ulises Hernandez-Vera study heat laws of regular black holes in a gravity theory with endless corrections in 2025. The theory stacks many curvature terms in a regularized way. For flat horizons they find two branches. One is a regular black hole held up by a scalar field. The other is a standard gravity answer with a flat scalar.

Both branches share the same free energy at a set heat. That tie stems from the flat base's symmetry and scale traits. For round horizons, the tie holds when one term is left out. With that term in, either branch can win. The winner rests on the theory's coupling values.
arxiv-2505-23667:
Lang Cao and co-authors train language models to answer table questions by writing spreadsheet formulas, in a research paper from 2025. Models reason well in words but slip on numbers in complex tables. Formulas offer an exact, checkable path from data to answer.

Their method, called Fortune, rewards the model when its formula runs and lands the right answer. No hand-labeled formulas are needed for training. Across seven table benchmarks, the approach lifted performance sharply, above all on multi-step numeric tasks. The trained model, Formula-R1, shows that executable answers beat mental arithmetic for table work. The framework opens a practical route to reliable data assistants.
arxiv-2505-23767: Mostafa Najafi and Ali Morassaei study functions that stay fully monotone on the plus half-line, in a short math note from twenty twenty-five. A fully monotone function keeps a strict sign pattern through all of its rates of change. The note states key traits of such functions. It then builds fresh classes of them. Worked special functions show the tests in use.
arxiv-2505-23867:
Under the head title "InfiMed: Low-Resource Medical MLLMs with Advancing Understanding and Reasoning", Zeyu Liu and co-authors build medical vision-language models that reason well on a small budget. Medical image-and-text data is scarce and often thin, which limits how deep such models can think. The team also notes that reward-based fine-tuning, reliable in general domains, does not transfer cleanly to medicine.

Their recipe mixes rich text reasoning data and general image data into the first training stage, restoring the base model's reasoning while adding medical skill. For thin medical sets, they add chain-of-thought samples with a reflective pattern that teaches the model to check its own steps. The resulting 3-billion-parameter models led seven medical benchmarks, and the tuned version averaged 59.2 percent accuracy, ahead of a larger rival at 57.3. Training used 188,000 samples in stage one and 36,000 in the reward stage.
arxiv-2505-23967:
Anders Aamand and co-authors design faster rough answers for hard graph problems in this 2025 paper, with help from predictions. Many core graph tasks, such as cutting a network or covering its points, have no fast exact method. Their twist is to feed the method hints learned from past data. Each edge gives two bits of hint about whether its ends belong in the best answer. Even hints that are only weakly right prove useful in their tests.

With those weak hints, their methods beat the classic best-known ratios. Gains cover MaxCut, Vertex Cover, Set Cover, and Independent Set problems. A shared pattern runs through the designs for each problem. Constraints tied to high-value parts are handled apart from the rest. The work joins a growing line on learning-aided methods. It shows predictions need not be sharp to break old barriers.
arxiv-2505-24267:
Liancheng Fang and co-authors introduce MUSE, a watermarking method for tabular data generators, in their 2025 arXiv paper. Watermarks prove ownership of synthetic data, but older methods for tabular diffusion models relied on inverting the model, which works poorly for tables. Tables are cheap to generate, though, which opens another route.

MUSE generates many candidate samples and picks one by a special scoring rule, embedding the watermark by selection rather than inversion. Theory links detectability to candidate count and dataset size, letting users tune strength. Experiments show top detection and robustness with far less distortion of data fidelity than rivals, and the method works with any generator that can sample repeatedly.
arxiv-2505-24867:
Ujjwal Upadhyay and co-authors expose a time blindness in video-language models in this 2025 paper. Modern models read space and time in videos well when scenes look normal. Their skill collapses when all meaning sits in the order of frames alone.

Their benchmark, SpookyBench, hides shapes and text inside sequences of noise-like frames. People spot the patterns with near perfect accuracy. Top models scored zero on the same task. The gap points to a heavy lean on single-frame spatial cues. When training data had weak spatial signal, model time sense decayed faster than human sight. The authors release the set to push new designs.
arxiv-2506-00267:
Cihan Xiao and co-authors release CASPER, a dataset of natural spoken conversation, in this 2025 paper. Speech tools need real talk to learn from, yet most datasets hold scripted dialogue that sounds stiff. Their recording pipeline was designed to draw out free, flowing chats on many topics.

The first release holds more than one hundred hours of spontaneous speech. Each recording pairs people in genuine exchanges rather than read lines. The team also describes its collection method in full, so other groups can repeat it and grow the dataset. They plan further stages that will expand the resource for speech research.
arxiv-2506-00367:
Andrew Laeuger and co-authors compute the ringdown of a black hole wrapped in a thin shell of matter in a 2025 paper. After a merger, a black hole rings with characteristic tones, and distant bumps in spacetime were recently shown to destabilize that tone spectrum.

Here the bump is physical: a far shell with surface tension that itself can oscillate and couple to the gravitational waves. The basic tone can drift gently or be displaced by wholly new modes. Shell coupling also births weakly damped tones found only in the polar wave sector. Standard fitting tools were tested on mock signals. Early ringdown ignores the shell; its fingerprints, late echoes and those weak tones, emerge only later.
arxiv-2506-00567:
A Aguilera and co-authors study frames built by repeating one operation on a starting set of vectors, in a math paper from 2025. Such frames, called dynamical frames, arise in sampling problems where a signal is probed over time. The head of the paper gives it the title Optimal Dynamical Frames.

The team first settles when an operation can generate a frame of a special balanced kind, called a Parseval frame. Past work gave conditions that were known to be enough; the authors show they are also required. They then define the frame index of an operation: the fewest starting vectors needed to build a frame by repetition. A formula is given for the balanced case. Last, they show that an operation and its adjoint share the same index, by an explicit build.
arxiv-2506-00667:
Vasilii Korolkov presents a unified system for splitting videos into scenes and picking key frames, in a 2025 paper. Scene cuts and good stills underpin search, summaries, and previews. Older methods often fail across varied video types and lengths. His system adapts its policy to the video at hand. Short clips get adaptive thresholds, mid-length ones a hybrid method, and long recordings interval splitting.

Frame choice uses a light scoring mix. Sharpness, brightness, and time spread decide which frames represent each scene. Heavy saliency models are avoided on purpose. The system runs inside a commercial analysis platform. It has processed media, education, research, and security footage at scale. Throughput and interpretability are design priorities. Future upgrades include sound-aware cuts and learned frame scoring. The paper reports deployment lessons alongside the method.
arxiv-2506-00867:
Kyowoon Lee and Jaesik Choi fix this 2025 weakness of diffusion-based planning. Diffusion planners dream up long action sequences from offline data and shine on sparse-reward tasks. Their dreams, though, can wander off the manifold of feasible behavior, producing impossible trajectories, a real hazard in safety-critical uses. The authors trace the fault to guidance error during sampling and bound that gap.

Their method, LoMAP, needs no retraining: it projects each guided sample onto a low-rank subspace fitted to the offline data, snapping dreams back to the feasible sheet. On standard offline planning benchmarks it improved reliability, and it also plugged into a hierarchical diffusion planner for further gains. The fix treats feasibility as geometry: stay near the data's surface.
arxiv-2506-00967:
Zhang, Vorobyov, and three co-authors design a learning system that sets transmit power in cell-free massive antenna networks. Classic optimization methods iterate too slowly for real-time use. Graph neural networks work faster, but earlier versions assumed clean, separate pilot signals for every user.

In real networks, users outnumber the clean pilots, so signals contaminate each other. The proposed graph attention network handles that contamination directly. It also adapts when the number of active users changes, and it trains without costly precomputed answers. Tests show it performs well even against a strong optimization baseline. The authors frame the work as a step toward practical real-time power control.
arxiv-2506-01067: Bruce Reed and Yelena Yuditsky describe what a typical graph looks like when one fixed tree pattern is banned as an induced subgraph. For every tree except the single edge, they prove that almost all graphs avoiding the tree split into a set number of parts that certify the avoidance. Each part is free of a small four-vertex path and carries extra structure set by the tree. The result yields strong counts of how many such graphs exist.
arxiv-2506-01167:
Alper Bozkurt, Calin Belta, and Ming Lin speed up robot learning from formal rules in a 2025 paper. Safety rules written in temporal logic say what must happen over a whole run, not just at one instant. Such rules give sparse feedback, so learning crawls, and hand-shaped rewards can break the rule's meaning.

Their framework pipes the rule's automaton into a differentiable simulator, softening its switches so gradients flow. Theory bounds the gap between the soft and exact objectives in both steady and random settings. On hard continuous control tasks, training sped up greatly and returns doubled over discrete baselines. The method also plugs into reward machines unchanged.
arxiv-2506-01367:
Kensuke Mitsuzawa and Damien Garreau present a test-time method to flag made-up answers from language models, in this 2025 paper. False claims slip into agent systems with no ground truth at hand to check them. Their method watches how steady a model's answers stay as its randomness dial turns.

A distance measure tracks the path between one answer and a batch of sampled ones across heat settings. True and false claims leave paths of different shapes. Tests ran on claim-checking sets in several languages with two modern model families. The authors offer the flagger as a label-free guard for live systems.
arxiv-2506-01467:
Dorian Gailhard and co-authors present a stepwise generator for graphs and hypergraphs that keeps node and link features, in a paper from two thousand twenty-five. Graph generators handle small structures well but stall on large, complex ones. Layered methods scale better, yet often drop the features that real uses need.

Their frame grows a sample scale by scale, through local expansion and polish. A node budget knob controls grain and keeps scales consistent with each other. Tests spanned fake data, three-dimensional meshes, and point clouds. Scores matched or beat the best rivals, while scaling to far larger featured structures.
arxiv-2506-01567:
Marcin Kroczek, Justyna Zawalska, and Katarzyna Rycerz split big scheduling problems so a quantum device can chew them piece by piece. Their 2025 paper addresses workflow scheduling, the assigning of linked task chains to machines. A hybrid solver that pairs a D-Wave quantum device with classical machinery has size limits, and real workflows blow past them.

Their heuristic, built for series-parallel workflows, decomposes an oversized problem into pieces the solver can accept, then reassembles a schedule. Tests used real workflow descriptions from a public standardization repository, run in an execution environment the authors describe alongside the algorithm. The claim is practical: the split extends the hybrid solver's reach to jobs that would otherwise not fit. The authors present the method as infrastructure for a period when quantum hardware helps at the margins of classical scheduling.
arxiv-2506-01767:
Sobati-Moghadam proposes in twenty twenty-five a light defence for split-packet attacks in low-power Internet of Things networks. In these networks, packets are routinely cut into fragments to fit tiny radio frames. Receivers store fragments before checking them, so attackers can flood memory with fake early fragments at little cost.

Her system scores each node's behaviour over time, rewarding steady success and punishing suspect patterns fast. A chained hash checks fragment integrity early, catching tampered sequences before they waste memory. Simulations of injection, replay, and flooding attacks kept delivery rates and energy use steady. The author pitches behaviour-based defence over heavy cryptography for tiny devices.
arxiv-2506-02167:
Tiwari and co-authors (2025) introduce Fire360, a benchmark for testing AI perception and memory in firefighting video. Models struggle most where reliability matters most: smoke, poor light, and damaged structures. Firefighters are injured by the tens of thousands each year, often when awareness of the scene breaks down. The dataset holds 228 panoramic videos from professional training sessions, labeled with actions, object positions, and notes on image degradation.

The benchmark sets five tasks, from answering questions about a scene to reasoning about safety. One task, transformed object retrieval, asks a model to match a clean exemplar to its fire-damaged counterpart in a different scene. Human experts score 83.5 percent on it, while a leading model lags far behind, exposing weak reasoning under degradation. The authors release the dataset and its test suite to push models that can see, remember, and reason in such conditions.
arxiv-2506-02267:
Xue Xia and co-authors present a recommendation model used at Pinterest in a paper from two thousand twenty-five. Ranking a user's home feed depends on predicting clicks from past actions. Most industry models read only short recent histories, missing long-term taste.

Their model, TransAct V2, reads very long action sequences to improve click prediction. It also adds a next action loss, training the model to forecast the user's coming action within the ranking task. The third advance is serving: the system is built to run these heavy sequence models at scale with low delay. The authors describe the model as a production system, not a lab prototype.
arxiv-2506-02667:
Gabriele Digregorio and co-authors present a Python library for building custom debuggers. Their 2025 poster paper notes that stock debuggers serve human users, while scripted ones tend to aim at kernel code, leaving user programs thinly served. The library gives building blocks for a scripted debug flow with a friendly interface.

Case studies span software building, reverse work, and security tasks. In tests, the library handled system calls and breakpoints three to four times faster than the standard GDB tool, by median delay. Code and docs are open for public use and joint growth. The authors pitch it as base gear for automated debug work.
arxiv-2506-02767:
Marco Cali and co-authors wrote a 2025 paper on speeding up a learning method for robot control, where the name Cali appears with a grave accent in the byline. The base method, MC-PILCO, learns a model of how a system moves and then works out a good policy, but that step can be slow. The team pair it with a fast method that improves a path step by step.

Their combined method uses the fast path step to make useful trial paths and to start the policy off well. On the cart pole task, it cut run time by nearly half when both methods solved the task in four trials. It also kept a perfect success rate across trials. The gain held even in cases where the base method took fewer rounds to settle.
arxiv-2506-03067:
A team of researchers introduces EDITOR in a 2025 paper on text-to-image models such as Stable Diffusion. Prompt inversion works backward from a picture to guess the text that created it. The task helps with crediting data, tracing a model's sources, and checking watermarks.

EDITOR starts by using an image captioning model to seed word embeddings for the picture. It then refines those embeddings by reverse work in the model's latent space. A final step turns the embeddings back into plain text. Tests on MS COCO, LAION, Flickr, and DiffusionDB show the method beats earlier ones. It aims to give prompts that are both faithful to the image and easy to read.
arxiv-2506-03167:
Long Tan Le and co-authors harden meaning based wireless communication against noise and meaning errors with a worst case training method, in work from twenty twenty-five. Semantic systems send task relevant content instead of raw bits, a draw for sixth generation networks. Two failure modes haunt them: garbled features at the source and channel noise in transit.

Their framework trains against a ball of plausible data shifts, using a distance measure borrowed from optimal transport. Theory gives firm bounds on how well the system holds up on fresh data. Image and text transmission tests showed better survival under noise and crafted attacks than prior designs. The authors stress that meaning stayed intact across varied wireless conditions.
arxiv-2506-03567:
Hermann Edlbauer and a large team of co-authors built in 2025 an eleven-qubit processor from phosphorus atoms set in silicon. Atom spins in silicon hold their state for seconds, a prized trait. Groups of atoms share one electron, which lets them act as one multi-qubit register, but registers must be linked without losing accuracy.

The team joined two registers through electron exchange and steered all eleven qubits as one device. New tuning routines kept every qubit measure high at once. The chip is a step toward linked atom registers large enough for error correction, the stage quantum machines need to become reliable.
arxiv-2506-03667:
Joji Joseph, Bharadwaj Amrutur, and Shalabh Bhatnagar shrink 3D scene models so phones can locate themselves faster, in a 2025 paper. Structure-from-motion pose estimation is accurate but heavy, a problem for augmented reality and robots. Their preprocessing picks a dominating set of reference views. That is a small crew from which every other view is close, and the model is trimmed to match.

On the OnePose dataset, pose estimation ran one and a half to over fourteen times faster. Reference images were cut by a factor of up to twenty-three and point clouds shrank several-fold, at little accuracy cost. The authors offer the trade as a practical route to real-time 3D tracking.
arxiv-2506-03767:
Loïc Foissy builds algebraic machinery for random equations in a 2025 paper. Stochastic partial differential equations describe systems buffeted by noise, from fluids to finance, and modern solution methods expand their answers over decorated trees. The algebra of those trees, how trees graft onto each other, decides whether the expansion works.

Foissy defines grafting rules that also rewrite the labels on the new edge and the receiving vertex. He finds the exact condition on the relabeling map that makes the result a pre-Lie algebra, then extends it to a post-Lie one. One known construction from the literature falls out as a special case, anchoring the abstract result to a tool analysts already use.
arxiv-2506-03867:
Jacqueline Rowe and co-authors build EuroGEST, a data set that probes gender stereotypes in language models across thirty languages. Bias testing has leaned heavily on English alone. Europe's languages carry their own gendered patterns.

Sixteen classic stereotypes anchor the test items. Translation tools, quality checks, and grammar rules expanded them. Human judges confirmed the translations and labels hold up. Twenty-four models from six families took the test. The same few stereotypes scored strongest almost everywhere. Women were cast as beautiful and empathetic most often. Men were cast as leaders and professionals in reply. Bigger models held the stereotypes more firmly. Fine-tuning did not reliably wash them out.
arxiv-2506-03967:
Sebastián Daza and João Nuno Mestre study deformation problems with symmetry in a mathematics paper from twenty twenty-five. A deformation problem asks how a structure can be bent or varied while keeping its core rules. The authors work with the algebraic system that controls such problems when a symmetry group acts on them.

Using special operators tied to that algebra, they give a smooth way to list the nearby structures around a given one. Along the way they offer new proofs, both algebraic and fully explicit, of known results on rigidity. Those results say when a structure cannot be deformed at all, and when no obstacles block a deformation.
arxiv-2506-04667:
Osayamen Aimuyo, Byungsoo Oh, and Rachee Singh present in 2025 FlashMoE, a single-kernel system for expert-mix models spread across graphics chips. Such models grow cheaply in size, yet past code wastes chip time on launches and host-run scheduling. Idle gaps and padded transfers cap real speed.

FlashMoE fuses expert math and chip-to-chip transfer into one steady kernel that runs on the device. Fine stages for send, compute, and merge overlap inside that kernel. Tests on an eight-chip node show up to nine times the chip use and six times lower delay than top baselines. Throughput and overlap gains round out the case.
arxiv-2506-04967:
Claudianor Alves, Rui Ding, and Chao Ji study solitary waves for a generalized wave equation in this 2025 paper. The equation is the Kadomtsev-Petviashvili equation in two dimensions. The waves sought have a fixed total mass, called normalized solutions. An unknown parameter acts as a multiplier to enforce that mass condition.

For a pure power response, the authors prove ground state solutions exist in both the subcritical and supercritical ranges. For a mixed power response, a solution appears as a local minimum of the energy. A second solution with positive energy is also shown for a sequence of small masses. The authors note these are the first such results for this setting.
arxiv-2506-05367:
Aakash Garg, Libing Zeng, Andrii Tsarov, and Nima Khademi Kalantari teach an image generator to make stereo image pairs from a text prompt. Their 2025 paper notes that stereo pairs with wide spacing between views are rare in training data, so a new model cannot be trained from scratch. Instead they start from Stable Diffusion, a strong text-to-image model, and fine-tune it for the stereo task.

Fine-tuning alone was not enough: the two views must agree with each other and with the prompt. The team added tuning driven by reward functions. One reward scores how well the pair matches the prompt, and rewards of their own design score how consistent the two views are. Tests across varied scenes show the method beating earlier ones on quality. A general image model, they show, can be repurposed for a task its makers never targeted.
arxiv-2506-05467:
Alex Vañó-Viñuales built in 2025 starting data for simulating a neutron star on a hyperboloidal slice of spacetime. Such slices reach out to future null infinity, where gravitational waves are cleanly read. Working in spherical symmetry with a simple matter model, the author solved the constraint equations for a lone neutron star. A second setup placed a black hole at the star's center.

The author states these are the first full hyperboloidal slices of a neutron star spacetime ever constructed. The data satisfy the Einstein constraints and suit time evolution codes for gravity and fluid flow. Starting simple keeps the method checkable before harder cases are tried. Later work can drop the symmetry and chase mergers or collapse. The result opens a cleaner path to wave signals from neutron star events.
arxiv-2506-05667:
Yuhan Hao and a large team build DriveAction, a benchmark for human-like driving calls by vision-language-action models. Their paper is from two thousand twenty-five. Such models steer self-driving cars, but past tests lack scene range, trusty action labels, and scoring tied to human taste.

The set holds over sixteen thousand question pairs drawn from more than two thousand real driving scenes. The scenes were logged by drivers of self-driving cars, and action labels come from what those drivers truly did. A tree-shaped scoring frame links sight, words, and action. Tests show top vision-language models need both sight and words: drop either and accuracy falls, drop both and it falls most.
arxiv-2506-05967:
Katarzyna Kobalczyk and Mihaela van der Schaar reframe preference learning for AI alignment through causality in a 2025 paper. Reward modeling from human preferences is a central step in aligning large language models with human values. The learned reward must generalize to new prompts and responses it never saw.

Viewing the problem causally exposes traps such as causal misidentification, preference heterogeneity, and confounding by user-specific factors. The authors list the assumptions reliable generalization needs and contrast them with common data collection practice. The gap between the two explains many brittle reward models.
arxiv-2506-06867:
Today's quantum computers are small and noisy, so big circuits must be cut into pieces that fit. Awad Wehbe and co-authors present Fidelipart, a cutting method that reads the error rates of each gate before choosing where to slice. Their 2025 paper turns the circuit into a weighted hypergraph and hands it to a partitioner that avoids cutting through error-prone steps.

On test circuits of 6, 10, and 24 qubits, Fidelipart cut the number of added SWAP gates by 77 to 100 percent and reduced cut qubits by up to half. Estimated fidelity, the chance the answer comes out right, rose by 27 percent to more than 250 percent. The price was a modest 8 to 13 percent longer run time, which the authors gladly pay for more reliable computing.
arxiv-2506-06967:
Evan Wilson, Jian-Xin Zhu, and Jason Haraldsen computed in 2025 exact energy levels for small spin clusters with Heisenberg-Kitaev interactions. Clusters studied were a three-spin trimer, a four-spin star, and a tetrahedron, all with spin one-half. Such Kitaev terms are sought in magnetic materials but are hard to detect.

Adding a strong Kitaev term creates a second Schottky anomaly in the heat capacity, a clean thermal signature. It also bends the energy levels in a magnetic field and drives quantum phase transitions of first and second order. The exact solutions are offered as guides for experiments on molecular magnets and on wider lattices such as honeycomb and Kagome forms.
arxiv-2506-07667:
Prarabdh Shukla and five co-authors audit Twitch's automated chat filter and find it misses most hate while blocking teaching content, in a study from 2025. Live chat moves too fast for human moderators, so platforms lean on automation whose real accuracy is rarely tested. The team built isolated test streams to probe it.

Over one hundred seven thousand comments from four datasets were sent through the filter. Up to ninety-four percent of plainly hateful messages slipped through on some sets. Adding slurs to those messages caused total removal, exposing a slur crutch. Meanwhile up to about ninety percent of benign educational uses of sensitive words were blocked.
arxiv-2506-07767:
Zhong-Wen Feng and co-authors wrote this 2025 paper asking what a tweaked uncertainty principle would do to gravitational waves from the young universe. If quark matter changed phase sharply in the first moments, the event would have left a background hum of waves. A higher-order generalized uncertainty principle, a proposed fingerprint of quantum gravity, alters the heat physics behind that hum.

The sign of the key deformation parameter decides everything. Negative values make entropy and pressure vanish past a ceiling temperature and blow the spectrum up, so the team discard that branch. Positive values slide the wave peak to lower frequencies and lift its height slightly. For natural parameter sizes the shift at quark-era temperatures is tiny, but allowed larger values could one day let a detection bound the principle itself.
arxiv-2506-07867: Alexis Tchoudjem and Vikraman Uma described a symmetry-respecting K-ring for a family of group embeddings in a 2025 paper. The shapes studied wrap a complex algebraic group in a torus-friendly way and can be singular. Their cell structure allows a full accounting of topological K-theory with the group acting twice over. Earlier work covered only smooth, regular embeddings, so the result reaches a wider class and mirrors a known algebraic version.
arxiv-2506-07967:
Zvonimir Bujanović, Matija Kazalicki, and Domagoj Vlah improve in 2025 a classic guess for the rank of an elliptic curve, a key number in number theory. Such sums, built from prime counts, have long been used to guess rank, yet much room was left to sharpen them. Rank is famously hard to pin down by direct means.

Their first trick uses two unlike sums at once, read over several ranges. That paired view sorted curves far better than one sum alone. Their second trick lets a neural network learn the best weights for the sums from data. Learned weights gave a small extra edge over the classic sums.
arxiv-2506-08067:
Roberto Baviera and Michele Domenico Massaria wrote a 2025 finance math paper on option price curves. In the Bachelier model, the implied volatility curve is called the smile. Its far edges, or tails, hold clues about the asset's returns. The authors study how those edges behave at large strikes.

They use a theory of steady tail change to write clear formulas for the far edges. The formulas tie the edges straight to how fast return tails fade. They also link the slope of the smile to a math trait of the price process. Their results let a reader judge which models are valid from the smile alone.
arxiv-2506-08167:
Sunny Gupta, Nikita Jangid, and Amit Sethi present a federated learning scheme that keeps local training honest when each site's data look different. Their paper appeared in two thousand twenty-five. Federated learning trains one model across many sites without pooling data. Skewed local data bias each site's classifier and drag the shared model down.

Their method, UniVarFL, fixes the bias at the client, with no help from the global model. One penalty aligns each class's predicted odds with what balanced data would give. Another spreads feature points evenly over their sphere, which aids generalization. Together they mimic training on pooled, balanced data. Tests across several benches beat existing methods in accuracy. The scheme stays light, suiting phones and other weak devices. Code is shared in public.
arxiv-2506-08267:
Mansooreh Montazerin and co-authors recover plain math formulas from data using a small, readable neural network. Their 2025 paper deals with symbolic regression, which seeks formulas rather than black box predictions. Past methods search huge populations or generate formulas token by token, which scales poorly. Their network has a fixed design with four interpretable building blocks: log, identity, exponential, and sine units.

Training uses oversampling and a custom loss that rewards sparsity and steadies gradients. After training, pruning trims the network down to a compact formula. On standard benchmarks, the method beat all baselines in both accuracy and sparseness. Tests removing each design piece showed each one matters. The authors argue readable formulas give insight that fitted curves cannot. Such formulas can be checked, reused, and built upon by hand.
arxiv-2506-08467:
Prakash Shukla and co-authors ask how students should cite AI help in design coursework. Standard citation rules rest on stable sources, clear authors, and the chance to look a source up again. AI output fits none of those well, since it changes each time and has no single author.

The team studied thirty-five team projects and reflections from 175 undergraduates in a user experience design course who could use AI tools freely. Citation habits ranged from careful credit to vague hints or none at all. The authors argue citation should become a reflective habit that makes students weigh how AI shaped their work. They suggest tools such as AI contribution statements and process-aware citation forms for design classes.
arxiv-2506-08767:
Shaoshi Chen, Yiman Gao, Hui Huang, and Carsten Schneider present telescoping algorithms for a class of summation extensions. Their 2025 paper rests on complete reductions in a difference field, a tool for splitting a term into a summable part and a remainder.

A term is summable exactly when its remainder is zero, which makes the method a test as well as a tool. Their complete reduction works in a tower of extensions and gives a new, efficient frame for the parameterized telescoping problem. Such extensions cover sums like the harmonic numbers and versions used in combinatorics and particle physics. Structural theorems link the method to Karr's theorem on symbolic summation.
arxiv-2506-08967:
The Step-Audio team at StepFun presents a large audio model that answers spoken questions with speech of its own, in a 2025 paper. Most audio-language models still reply in text, which breaks the natural flow of a voice conversation. Their model, Step-Audio-AQAA, handles the full loop from audio in to audio out. It pairs a two-stream audio tokenizer, capturing both meaning and sound detail, with a 130-billion-parameter language core and a voice synthesizer.

Training after the main build mixed text and audio tokens in one stream so the spoken answers stay coherent. A preference-tuning step, combined with merging model versions, polished quality and expression. The team positions the system for the audio query, audio answer setting, where a user speaks and expects a spoken reply. They frame it as a step toward voice assistants that converse in voice throughout, with feeling intact.
arxiv-2506-09067:
Xue, Abbasi-Asl, and Pedarsani present a 2025 paper on shielding medical vision-language models from jailbreak prompts. Such models write reports from scans and clinical questions, yet they can be tricked into harmful answers. Blocking tricks too hard brings the opposite flaw: refusing honest clinical queries. Their defense works at answer time, priming the model with synthetic clinical demonstrations.

Tests spanned image sets from nine medical modalities. Safety rose against both image and text attacks while normal performance barely moved. Feeding more demonstrations eased the over-refusal problem. A mixed demonstration recipe balances the two goals when examples must stay few. The authors frame the trade as tunable, not fixed.
arxiv-2506-09167:
James Williamson and four co-authors estimated deep belly fat from wrist motion data in a 2025 paper. Visceral fat, packed around the organs, tracks closely with diabetes and insulin resistance, and it also responds fast to activity. Imaging can measure it, but the authors asked whether movement itself carries the signal. They used national survey data from over 4,800 adults with a week of wrist accelerometry each.

Two methods were tried. One built hand-crafted features from gait and sleep and mapped them by regression; the other fed raw day-long traces through a foundation model and a transformer. Body measures and demographics sharpened both. Combined, the estimates matched imaging-based values with a correlation of 0.86. Daily movement, it turns out, says a lot about hidden fat.
arxiv-2506-09667:
Jan Goedgebeur, Jorik Jooken, Michiel Provoost, and Carol Zamfirescu disprove a long standing graph theory conjecture in a strong form. In 1976 Faudree and Schelp guessed that in a highly connected graph, any two vertices are joined by paths of every length above half the graph size. Thomassen later gave counterexamples, but not for cubic planar graphs.

The authors build cubic planar counterexamples with a count of vertices that grows in steps of six times a parameter plus sixteen. In each graph, one pair of vertices has no path of any odd length in a wide range. They also give an endless family of graphs with many gaps in the short half of their cycle lengths.
arxiv-2506-09767:
Ali Mohammadian, Milad Poursoltani, and Behruz Tayfeh-Rezaie wrote a 2025 math paper on lean networks that just avoid a given pattern. A saturation number counts the fewest links in a network that lacks a target shape but gains it if any missing link is added. Such minimal-but-ready networks are a classic topic in graph theory.

The team work out how that count grows for two targets: complete multipartite graphs, which split nodes into fully linked groups, and even cycles long enough to behave well. Their results extend a 2010 finding and partly settle a 2013 conjecture by Füredi and Kim. The paper is proof-based, giving growth rates rather than exact counts for every size.
arxiv-2506-09967:
Shangshang Wang and six co-authors show how to move reasoning skill from one language model to another at very low cost. Their paper appeared in two thousand twenty-five. Their family of small reasoning models is called Resa. The trick is to first train a sparse autoencoder on a strong source model.

The autoencoder learns to spot the inner patterns tied to reasoning. It then guides normal fine-tuning of a target model on checked question-answer pairs. No worked reasoning traces are needed for that step. The tuned models kept nearly all of the skill of far costlier trained peers. Training took minutes and cost about a dollar. Skills lifted from one data set still helped on bigger ones. They could even be bolted onto a third model at test time with no new training.
arxiv-2506-10067:
Andrew A Allocca, Devesh K Verma, Sriram Ganeshan, and Justin H Wilson study, in a 2025 paper, whether the control of quantum chaos follows universal rules. Their test bed is the quantum Arnold cat map, a classic model of chaotic motion. Inspired by classical tricks, their protocol flips at random between the system's own instability and steering steps that push it toward a target.

Exact quantum simulation and a semi-classical shortcut agreed closely on how control takes hold. To explain the pattern, the authors built a simpler stand-in model, an inverted harmonic oscillator, which can be solved on paper. All three lines of work pointed the same way: the shift into control is shaped by the fuzz that quantum uncertainty itself sets, not by interference effects. The authors frame this as a universal feature of such transitions.
arxiv-2506-10367:
Zhi-Lei Zhang, Guo-Jian Qiao, and C. Sun present a 2025 paper on exotic particles that may hide in a pair of quantum dots linked to a superconductor. Peaks in electrical readings at such setups have been read as signs of Majorana fermions, prized for future quantum computers. Those signs, though, appear only at finely tuned sweet spots, which clouds their meaning.

The team models the superconductor's effects inside the dots in full detail, rather than folding them into two summary values. The resulting dressed particles spread as mixtures of dot and superconductor excitations. They can sit at one end of a wire across a continuous range of settings, which eases detection.
arxiv-2506-10467:
Felix Härer reports exploratory research from 2025 on systems where several language-model agents work as a team. Such teams can mix reasoning, code writing, and running software to handle tasks in a single field. Yet teams are often judged piece by piece, and how to specify and grade the whole system is poorly understood.

Härer offers two linked pieces: a schema language for writing down how a multi-agent system is built, and an architecture with a working prototype that runs those specifications and scores the results. Test cases in cybersecurity, covering question answering and server and network defense, were completed correctly by agents using models from two major providers. The work shows the approach is workable.
arxiv-2506-11167:
Cheng Wang and a large team of co-authors present in 2025 a foundation model for brain scan analysis. Functional MRI reveals brain activity and aids diagnosis, but current tools need complex preparation and are built task by task, which hurts repeatability. Their model, NeuroSTORM, learns straight from full 4D scan volumes.

It was pre-trained on more than twenty-eight million scan frames from over fifty thousand people aged five to one hundred. A lean design for space and time plus light task tuning let it transfer fast. Across five tasks, from disease diagnosis to state sorting, it beat prior methods. On hospital data with seventeen diagnoses it led the field.
arxiv-2506-11467:
Carlos Rafael Catalan turns translation evaluation into a game that also recruits its players in a 2025 language technology study. Machine translation for low-resource languages cannot be judged by string matching alone; human judges are essential, yet hard to find for small language communities. A platform that makes evaluation playful can draw in the very speakers whose judgment is scarcest.

Players assess translations as part of the game, and strong players become the recruited evaluator pool. The design treats evaluation and recruitment as one problem. Low-resource communities gain both a scoreboard for their translation systems and a crowd to improve them.
arxiv-2506-11567:
Jens Lucht, Paul Meyer, Leon Merten Lohse, and Tim Salditt present HoToPy, a free Python toolbox for X-ray holo-tomography, in a 2025 paper. The method images tiny objects by reading how X-rays bend and spread through them, then rebuilding the volume slice by slice. Phase retrieval, the hard step, has many competing algorithms. HoToPy gathers them behind one simple interface, for both deep holographic and direct contrast imaging.

The box also handles alignment of the stack, image cleanup, and simulation of experiments. The team shows it on a catalyst nanoparticle imaged at a Hamburg synchrotron beamline. Its modular build suits both quick tests of new algorithms and full reconstruction pipelines at other light sources. The authors offer it as shared infrastructure for the phase imaging community.
arxiv-2506-11667:
Matthew Stover, a solo author, settles a question in geometry in a 2025 paper. He shows that the complex projective plane can serve as the base space of a closed hyperbolic four-dimensional orbifold. An orbifold is like a manifold that allows a few well-tamed singular spots.

No such case with a symplectic base was known before. That gap matters because a long-open question asks whether closed hyperbolic four-manifolds can carry such structures at all. Stover's case does not close that question, since orbifolds allow singular spots that manifolds do not. Still, it gives the first proof of its kind, and it sharpens where the true border may sit.
arxiv-2506-11867:
Hanchen Wang, William Legrand, Richard Schlitz, and Pietro Gambardella show that an electric current can switch a coupling between magnons on and off. Their paper from twenty twenty-five works with an ultrathin film of bismuth-doped yttrium iron garnet. Two platinum nanostripes bound a region where cavity modes form. Edge traits from the metal contact reshape the magnon spread there.

Cavity modes mix with boundary modes trapped under the capped film, opening a gap where they cross. A spin-wave model with dipole and exchange terms fits the seen modes well. Spin current from a stripe's spin Hall effect breaks the cavity's edge terms. Past a threshold, modes and mixing fade. Microwave power offers a second knob, shifting the gap. The build suits chip-scale magnonic parts that can be set by current.
arxiv-2506-12167:
Marcin Pęski and Colin Stewart study when a researcher can ask about a belief without warping the choice it ties to, in 2025. A researcher may want to learn how sure a decision maker was about a past pick. Offered payoffs for honest reports can skew that pick. The question is when truth can be bought without bending the act.

The authors find exact conditions for this kind of elicitation. They sort all questions that can be safely asked in three standard problem types. For those types, they show how to draw out beliefs. The tool is a variant of a known bidding mechanism. The results give survey design a firm base.
arxiv-2506-12267:
Jarrod Reilly and co-authors design an atomic laser that shrugs off the shaking of its own cavity. A continuous superradiant laser, atoms emitting in lockstep, could serve as an active atomic clock of extreme precision. The blocker has been the repumping step, which heats atoms through random emission. Their 2025 paper replaces that randomness with coupling to a second cavity, making repumping a collective act.

Collective two-level systems famously lack a lasing threshold, but the authors show multi-level atoms escape that ban, since pumping and decay can run on separate transitions. With realistic atomic numbers the design yields a steady laser with a linewidth near a hundred microhertz. Better still, a working regime exists where sensitivity to cavity length vibration drops below a tiny bound, and at one locus of settings it vanishes entirely.
arxiv-2506-12367:
Erica Cai and Brendan O'Connor ask in a 2025 paper how errors in machine built knowledge graphs skew later study. Such graphs map who belongs to which group and aid work from social science to health. Large models now pull these graphs from huge text sets, but the cost of their slips is unclear.

The study checks errors at two levels, single links and whole graph shape, on graphs of person membership pulled from social register books. There is a band of pull quality where bias in most graph measures stays near zero. Below that band, bias grows and each measure drifts in its own steady way. Fake error tests show common error models miss that drift, which warns users to check quality first.
arxiv-2506-12467:
Fang Qin and Rui Chen set out a frame to steer small states that sit at the corners of a class of materials with special wave traits. Their paper is from two thousand twenty-five.

In these materials, corner states can be trapped at set spots. The team shows that long-range hops of waves let a user tune where the states sit in a round form. Hops in unlike paths shift them in unlike ways. They then test forms with many sides. A corner holds a trapped state when the signs of a mass term on its two edges clash, and holds none when the signs match. The work gives a broad tool to place such states by design.
arxiv-2506-12667:
Alexis Tudor and co-authors wrote this paper, published in two thousand twenty-five, on how to make AI systems worthy of trust. Large language models can sound sure while making things up, and their choices cannot be audited; pure rule systems can explain themselves but are heavy and complex.

The team proposes a middle path built on s(CASP), a goal-directed reasoner that answers queries with a visible chain of steps. They test it against a well-known list of sixteen traits that trustworthy AI should have, plus two of their own: spotting clashes and weighing other possible worlds. Worked examples include a chatbot and a reasoner inside a virtual body. The authors argue that plain, checkable reasoning can meet the trust list without a giant rule base.
arxiv-2506-13267:
Subbotin and eleven co-authors present a 2025 paper on steering the plasma in a fusion device with a learned controller. A tokamak needs tight control of the plasma's shape and place to run safely. Standard control first rebuilds the plasma state from sensor data, then applies fixed models, which limits speed and flexibility.

The team trained a deep learning agent in a simulator of the DIII-D tokamak. The agent reads raw magnetic signals and sets the coils directly, with no rebuild step. This was the first use of such learning for magnetic control on this mid size device. The authors report stronger and more flexible control across several plasma setups.
arxiv-2506-13367:
Utkarsh Bajpai and co-authors help indoor robots search for objects named in plain words. Their 2025 paper uses vision-language models that read camera views for semantic cues. Word choice in the prompt can sway what the model sees, yet past search methods ignore that wobble.

The team builds a sensor model that scores doubt from prompt phrasing, then folds that doubt into a map that joins shape and meaning. A search planner picks frontiers with a bandit-style rule that weighs doubt as well as gain. In tests the method matched top rivals on finds, without heavy hand-tuning of prompts. Doubt-aware search, the authors argue, makes robot perception more honest.
arxiv-2506-13767:
Chenpeng Feng presents a 2025 mathematics paper on the surface formed by all planes inside a general cubic fivefold, a five-dimensional shape cut out by a cubic equation. He studies this moduli surface and how it deforms as the fivefold varies. The surface turns out to be smooth and projective, with an ample canonical bundle, placing it among surfaces of general type.

For a particular family of such surfaces, the variation of their degree-one Hodge structures is maximal, meaning the family explores the full possible range. The main tools come from hyper-Kähler geometry and a detailed computation of the surfaces' Hodge numbers. The paper is a specialist contribution to the geometry of cubic hypersurfaces and their moduli.
arxiv-2506-14167:
Prithvi Raj wrote a 2025 paper on a new generative model that aims to be fast, clear, and exact at once. Common models either use simple hidden priors and stay limited, or sample step by step at high cost with little insight. His model, KAEM, rests on a classic theorem that breaks functions into one dimensional parts.

The hidden prior is built from one dimensional curves, so exact sampling runs in a single pass. On small data sets, a one pass method gives unbiased posterior reads. For harder cases, a staged cooling method fixes poor mixing. Image scores match rival prior based models at lower cost. The prior stays readable by design.
arxiv-2506-14467:
Nico Zevallos and co-authors report a robot system that placed catheters into the large femoral vessels of pigs in hemorrhagic shock, in a 2025 paper. Fast central access saves lives in trauma care, allowing heavy fluid replacement and advanced procedures. Yet threading a line into a deep vessel under ultrasound guidance takes rare skill, so it is seldom done before hospital arrival.

The team's system combines robotic ultrasound with automated needle work, moving beyond earlier semi-autonomous attempts at femoral access. Its main result is successful cannulation of both the femoral vein and the femoral artery in the animal shock model. The authors frame the work as a step toward full automation of emergency vascular access.
arxiv-2506-14767:
Li-Wei Chen and four co-authors improve the naturalness of computer generated speech in a 2025 paper. Spoken language models work on discrete speech tokens, but those tokens capture words while dropping tone, rhythm, and other expressive traits, so output sounds flat. Earlier fixes hand added pitch features, which cover only part of what makes speech sound human.

Their method instead learns, end to end, a compact code for the continuous expressive traits and feeds it alongside the word tokens. No manual feature picking is needed. Human raters preferred the speech continuations the system produced over the alternatives tried. The authors release code, samples, and models for others to build on.
arxiv-2506-14867:
Isabel Garcia Garcia, Marius Kongsore, and Ken Van Tilburg build a new kind of instanton, a lump of field with a twist count, out of purely electric-magnetic parts. Their paper appeared in two thousand twenty-five. Instantons are key events in quantum field theory, but they were thought to need non-Abelian fields. The team shows an Abelian field can carry the twist too.

Each of their setups grows from a closed loop of magnetic charge in four-dimensional space. The field must wind in a nontrivial way along that loop. The result is a dyon loop, part electric and part magnetic, with a nonzero twist count. They place the loops inside a classic unified model to show the setup is complete. There, the whole charge sits in the plain photon sector. Numerically, the loops deform smoothly into the classic small instanton.
arxiv-2506-15267:
Yu-Ting Lan and co-authors tackle the cold-start problem for new items in a computing paper from 2025. Online shops and apps must show brand-new items to someone, yet new items have no clicks or ratings yet. If no one sees them, their makers get no feedback and may quit.

Lookalike methods find users who resemble an item's early fans. Older versions use fixed rules or weak models of those users. The new approach builds a generative model of the next user to reach. It blends many signals about users and items. Better first exposure can turn good new items into hits and keep creators active on a platform.
arxiv-2506-15467:
Mohammad Rowshan and Vlad-Florin Dragoi published a computing paper in 2025 on improving the weight distribution of polar codes. Polar codes are built from how reliable their sub-channels are, a method that leaves a poor weight profile. Added pre-transforms can fix that, but the team studies plain polar codes without them. Their design is guided by a partial order based on weight contribution.

The methods need no search or optimization routines. Tests show gains over a range of codes, both with and without pre-transforms. The authors present the work as a direct route to polar-like codes with better weight distribution.
arxiv-2506-15967:
Dan-Dan Hu and colleagues work out a rare semileptonic decay of the Ds meson with QCD light-cone sum rules. The decay yields the scalar meson f0(980). That meson is thought to be a mix of two energy states. The states join light-quark and strange-quark parts. To grasp such decays tests both the structure of the meson and the method of work.

The team first works out the f0(980) decay constant with sum rules in background field theory. They then find the first two moments of its leading-twist light-cone distribution amplitude. The mixing-state amplitudes are included. With those inputs they work out the transition form factor for the decay. They extend it across the full region with a series expansion. That gives decay widths and a branching fraction.
arxiv-2506-17267:
Jusheng Zhang and co-authors present a 2025 training method for vision-language models, the systems that link images and words. Such models often lean on surface word-image links and miss the cause behind a scene. They can fail when a small change flips the sense of a picture. The team set out to teach finer and more causal reading.

Their method, CF-VLM, trains models on near-miss fake scenes built to clash with the real one. Three training goals work as a team: keep the base image-word match, hold the true scene steady against fakes, and sharpen care for tiny but key edits. Tests showed steady gains over strong rival methods on reasoning and new-case tests. The models also made fewer made-up claims about images. Stronger causal reading matters for high-stakes uses of such systems.
arxiv-2506-17567: Yoshioka, writing solo in twenty twenty-five, studied whether sheaf stability survives a Fourier-Mukai transform built from the Poincaré line bundle. Sheaves are bookkeeping tools for geometric data on a surface, and stability decides which ones behave well in moduli problems. Working on abelian surfaces, he shows Gieseker stability is preserved under this transform. He also adds remarks on the weak Brill-Noether property, which concerns how many sections certain bundles carry.
arxiv-2506-17967:
Hendriksen and seven co-authors tune sight-tongue tools to grade fake world films in this twenty twenty-five paper. World tools dream films of acts in fake rooms for plan work. No stock grade can tell if a dream film's acts ring true.

Inside, two grade tasks test act reads and face reads in three ask forms. Their tuned judge reads a film's time line, not lone still frames. Drill forms from full to light tune paths met at one judge build. That one judge tied task-tuned kin on each grade task in the runs. Folk grade rounds in seven fake rooms matched the judge with faith.
arxiv-2506-18267:
Haseeb Ullah Khan Shinwari and Muhammad Usama introduce a dynamic rank method for efficient fine-tuning of foundation models in 2025. Standard low-rank adaptation uses one fixed rank for all layers and heads, though they learn in very different ways.

Their method learns scaling factors that set rank per head, guided by a goal that balances task score against parameter cost. Sparsity and smoothness terms keep ranks low and stable as they shift. Tests on a large language model and a vision-language model reached near full fine-tuning quality with a tiny share of trainable parameters. It also cut memory use for multimodal adaptation sharply.
arxiv-2506-18967:
Juarez Saborio, Vialla, and their team show a new way to fold thin sheets of graphene in a controlled way, in work from 2025. Graphene is a sheet just one atom thick, with prized strength and odd fold traits. Folds are hard to place and size with care, though.

The team cut tiny pits in a stretchy base with a fast laser. A sheet laid on top folds once over each pit when the base is stretched. Fold size can be tuned, and folds flatten back with little harm. Rows of neat folds can also be made for new devices.
arxiv-2506-19467:
Ni and eight co-authors test whether reasoning helps language models capture how human annotators disagree, in a paper from twenty twenty-five. When labelers disagree, the split often flags a task that is a matter of taste or a case that is not clear. Keeping that split can matter. Sixty setups span three tasks, model sizes, and ways to steer the models. Reasoning trained with checked rewards is set against plain chain-of-thought prompting.

To the team's surprise, reasoning trained with checked rewards makes the fit to human splits worse. Plain chain-of-thought makes it better for models trained on human feedback.
