Swapping human labelers for reasoning models risks loss of this useful spread of views. The results warn against the view that reasoning always helps when models judge work. On tasks of taste, the split may need to be kept, not reasoned away.
arxiv-2506-19667:
Ethan Ackelsberg presents a 2025 math paper on patterns inside large sets of fractions. A question from four other scholars asked which shapes must appear in any big chunk of the rational numbers. Ackelsberg proves two such results. In any finite coloring of all fractions, one color holds an endless set whose squares and sums stay in that color. Any set of fractions with positive share holds a shifted copy of the same shape.

Twin claims for whole numbers are both false, so fractions behave in a richer way. The proofs move the puzzle into dynamics, the study of systems over time. New tools there handle averages twisted by polynomial paths. The work gives a clean case where two close number systems split in their pattern rules.
arxiv-2506-19867:
Robert Reynolds offers a math study from 2025 on a family of hard integrals that run out to infinity. The integrals mix a log-type function with fraction-type terms in the bottom part of the expression. Such integrals show up in work on area, chance, and physical amounts, but many have no simple closed form.

Reynolds works out the integrals as finite sums that involve a named zeta-type function. He then draws out special cases that link to other known functions and to well-known constants. The paper gives other researchers ready-made formulas they can use in place of slow numeric work. It also ties the results to the wider study of sums, limits, and common transforms used in science.
arxiv-2506-19967:
Travis Thompson and co-authors improve question answering over knowledge graphs in a 2025 paper. Language models reason well but lack direct access to structured facts. Standard retrieval hands them text passages, yet multi-step questions need chains of linked facts that flat retrieval misses. Graph-based retrieval helps, but often loses the links between nodes.

Their method, Inference-Scaled GraphRAG, spends more computing at answer time. One route deepens the step-by-step walk across the graph. Another runs several walks in parallel and takes a majority vote. Reasoning and graph calls alternate in a loop. On a standard benchmark, the method beat both plain graph retrieval and earlier traversal systems by wide margins. The authors present inference-time scaling as a practical, model-free upgrade.
arxiv-2506-20067:
Muhammad Zeeshan Mumtaz and co-authors maximize harvested energy in near-field wireless power with extra-large antenna arrays in a 2025 paper. Users close to a modular array see only parts of it, and channels vary across its surface.

The design problem mixes switching sub-arrays on or off with setting each one's power share. A multi-tier optimization built on fractional programming handles both choices together. Tests show the algorithm nearly matches exhaustive search at a fraction of the effort. Against the naive scheme, all sub-arrays on at equal power, harvested power efficiency more than doubled. The gains matter for powering sensors and wearables that cannot be plugged in or reached easily.
arxiv-2506-20667:
Louis Legrand and colleagues design a safer way to reconstruct how gravity from cosmic structure bends the oldest light in the universe. The bending, called lensing of the cosmic microwave background, is recovered from telescope maps whose noise is uneven because of scanning patterns and atmosphere. If that noise is modeled even slightly wrong, the lensing answer comes out biased. Writing in twenty twenty-five, the team reshapes the best-fit reconstruction so it only trusts correlations between map splits with independent noise, sidestepping the auto-correlations where modeling errors bite. With many splits, the method stays close to the statistically optimal reconstruction.

Simulations show the recovered lensing measurements stay immune to noise mis-modeling while losing almost no signal. The authors present the estimator as preparation for the next generation of background surveys, where precision goals leave no room for noise-driven bias.
arxiv-2506-20767:
Richard Sarmento and Evan Scannapieco simulate the earliest galaxies in a 2025 paper. They ask how the mass spread of the first stars shapes what a new space telescope can see. Two large simulations are compared, one with detailed light transport and one with a cheaper approximation. Both include a model of turbulent mixing needed to track first-star formation.

Light transport changed little, and both runs matched observations and other simulations fairly. They predict far fewer detectable galaxies at the earlier epoch than the later one. Even with a top-heavy first-star mass spread, those stars contribute almost none of the light of detectable galaxies, because their mass recycles too fast.
arxiv-2506-21067:
Vahid Asadi and co-authors test in 2025 whether machine learning can weigh a galaxy as well as the standard method, but much faster. The standard method fits a model to how a galaxy's light spreads across colors. That fit gives traits like the mass in stars, but it is slow and heavy when a survey holds millions of galaxies.

The team tried a range of learning methods, both guided by labeled data and not. They included grouping methods, tools that shrink data to its main traits, and tools that lay data out in a flat map. Each method was judged on how close its mass values came to the standard fits. A fast method that stays accurate would let astronomers work through huge sky surveys in far less time. That speed opens the door to new studies of how galaxies grow.
arxiv-2506-21167:
Dylan Sechet and colleagues present a hierarchical deep learning approach for detecting rare instruments in audio. Their 2025 arXiv paper serves music information retrieval. Knowing which instruments play in a clip aids cataloging and discovery. Past models focused on common instruments with plenty of training data. Rare instruments have few labeled examples to learn from.

The method builds on the Hornbostel-Sachs classification of instruments. A hierarchy lets the model predict broad instrument groups as well as fine classes. The team tested ways to build that structure into the model. They used the MedleyDB dataset, known for its range of instruments and genres. Results showed more reliable detection at the coarse level. The approach narrows the gap between fine identification and group recognition.
arxiv-2506-21267:
Gracie McGill and nine co-authors read the Andromeda galaxy's accretion history in the horizontal branches of its outer halo star clusters. Their paper from twenty twenty-five presents deep Hubble photometry of forty-eight clusters, many tied to tidal streams. New empirical relations, calibrated on Milky Way clusters, yield consistent metallicities and extinctions from the color-magnitude diagrams. One correlation jumps out of the data.

Clusters with very red horizontal branches sit almost always on substructure. Stream-free clusters show extended blue branches instead. The split is the first direct proof that red-branch halo clusters arrive via satellite accretion, an idea fifty years old. A few metal-poor red-branch oddballs suggest recent, young arrivals. Andromeda's merger past looks longer than our own galaxy's.
arxiv-2506-21367:
Sam Lerman and Jing Bi present a 2025 add on for teaching game playing agents from raw pixels. Such agents learn from trial and error, guided by value scores for each move. The team's method, rQdia, keeps those scores consistent across altered views of the same image. A simple extra loss term pulls the score patterns for an image and its augmented copies toward each other.

The plug in was tested on three well known agents. On robot control tasks viewed through pixels, it improved two of them on most tasks. On classic arcade games, it improved a third agent on most of the twenty six games. Gains showed up both in how fast the agents learned and in final performance after long training. The authors note the method finally pushed pixel based control past a rival that reads the true game state.
arxiv-2506-21567:
Persian medical text has no large language model of its own, a gap for a language spoken by over a hundred million people. Baqer Merzah and co-authors fill it with BioPars in this 2025 paper, pretrained on a benchmark corpus drawn from more than ten thousand Persian articles, textbooks, and medical websites. They also built a question set of over five thousand Persian medical questions.

Tested against general models including GPT-4, BioPars produced better long answers on Persian medical questions across standard scoring measures. The authors are candid that models, theirs included, remember facts better than they reason through real cases. They release the project openly as a continuing effort.
arxiv-2506-21667:
Dimitri Veras, writing solo in 2025, asks how dead stars that are billions of years old still show fresh rock dust. White dwarf stars often bear signs of ground-up planets, yet their stock of loose rock should drain away far sooner. Some top-up route must exist, and Veras tests one: blasts from dying stars nearby.

A blast wave could shove far-out dust, sand, and stones inward from a star's cold outer cloud. Veras works out the shapes such blasts must take and the kicks each grain size needs to land on a long-lived inner path. Dust and small pebbles, he finds, are almost sure to be sent in or thrown out by each blast. Rocks above a set size almost never move. Mid-size boulders may arrive at least once in a star's long cooling life.
arxiv-2506-21867: Isamu Iwanari studies stable infinity-categories, a higher form of the structured categories used in modern algebra, fitted with t-structures that sort objects by degree. He proves that the Hochschild cohomology of such a category governs how it can be deformed, for deformations that respect left complete t-structures. In short, a category's own cohomology controls the ways the category itself can bend.
arxiv-2506-21967:
Language model agents that call tools look strong on final answers, yet a tool call can fail at many quiet steps. Reading the manual, picking the tool, filling its fields, or digesting the reply can each go wrong. Seven researchers stress-test that whole chain in 2025. They inject errors at each stage and watch how agents cope. Open-source agents break more often than those built on commercial models.

Bigger models, surprisingly, do not fix the weakness. They can even grow easier to fool with attacks dressed as normal instructions. The authors argue that stability deserves its own scorecard beside accuracy. Their results warn builders that a smooth demo can hide a fragile agent. They also sketch what future evaluations should measure.
arxiv-2506-22267:
Junaid Ahmed Khan and co-authors build a chatbot for data center exhaust in a 2025 systems paper. Industrial sensors pour out telemetry that only specialists can query. Answering a plain question takes domain knowledge plus fluency in database languages.

Their design pairs a language model with a virtual knowledge graph assembled on the fly for each question. The model translates the user's words into formal graph queries. On their tests accuracy jumped from a quarter of questions to over ninety percent, while answers arrived in seconds instead of twenty. The whole service runs on premises, keeping operational data inside the building.
arxiv-2506-22367:
Zacharegkas and co-authors tie galaxy mass to dark matter halo mass using Dark Energy Survey data in a 2025 paper. The stellar-to-halo mass relation anchors how galaxies populate the invisible scaffolding of the universe. Clustering patterns plus weak lensing distortions measure it from two sides at once.

A fresh sample of galaxies sorted by stellar mass feeds a halo occupation model spanning tiny to huge scales. The joint framework reaches deep into the one-halo regime, where satellites crowd a single halo. Resulting constraints agree with earlier lensing studies. A validated sample and sharper modeling are the paper's main advances for the next survey rounds.
arxiv-2506-22567:
Shansong Wang and co-authors build a general biomedical vision-language model in a 2025 arXiv paper. Models like CLIP link images and text, but biomedicine lacks the huge paired datasets used for natural images. Their model, MMKD-CLIP, learns instead by distilling knowledge from nine expert models.

Training ran in two stages. First came standard pretraining on 2.9 million image-text pairs across 26 imaging types. Then the model matched features from its teachers on over 19 million pairs. The team tested it on 58 biomedical datasets covering millions of images. The aim is one generalist model for many medical image tasks.
arxiv-2506-22767:
Hao Wu and four co-authors report a 2025 method for telling apart two electric fields whose frequencies sit very close together. Old views held that a system's linewidth sets the best possible resolution, so tiny gaps would need very long measurement times. The team argues that random noise, not linewidth, sets the real limit.

Their protocol uses a Walsh modulated sequence to encode the frequency gap into a quantum state. In tests, they split two fields near 100 megahertz that differed by only five hertz, using one millisecond per run. That result beat the old limit by a wide margin and sped up data taking greatly. The method may help sensing tasks that need fine frequency detail.
arxiv-2506-22967:
Amir Aghdam, Vincent Tao Hu, and Björn Ommer present ActAlign, a way to name very specific actions in video without any training examples. Sorting a windmill dunk from other dunks, sight unseen, strains normal video models. Image-language models read single frames well but miss how actions unfold over time.

For each candidate class, a language model writes the ordered steps of the action. ActAlign then matches that step list against the video's frames using dynamic time warping in a shared embedding space. No video training or fine-tuning is involved. On the ActionAtlas benchmark it reached about thirty percent accuracy, beating models with eight times more parameters. Human accuracy there is only about sixty-two percent.
arxiv-2506-23167:
Pol Benítez and seven co-authors propose a new way to tune the band gap of semiconductors with electric fields. Fine control of optoelectronic traits matters for photodetectors and photovoltaics. Their strategy excites low-energy polar optical phonon modes that couple strongly to electronic states in anharmonic materials. A screening of more than 10,000 compounds hunted for centrosymmetric candidates with imaginary polar phonon modes and suitable band gaps.

The screen found 310 promising candidates, and three perovskite-like compounds got deep study. Polar distortions cut the band gap of Ag3SBr by up to 70% and raised that of BaTiO3 by nearly 23% at ambient conditions. PbHfO3 barely changed, which sharpened the contrast.
arxiv-2506-23267:
Shrikant Utagi and Prateek Chawla test two recent witnesses for non-Markovian behavior in quantum systems, where the environment feeds information back into the system. Both witnesses rest on forms of temporal correlation. Through counterexamples drawn from the literature, the authors show cases where these witnesses flag memory effects that standard distance and entropy measures miss.

The paper then turns one witness into a measure. The pseudo-density matrix behind it links directly to the Choi matrix of the process. That link lets the authors quantify total quantum memory in any process that cannot be split into steps. One witness family, based on temporal steering, may miss a class called eternal non-Markovianity. The pseudo-density approach catches that class faithfully. The authors close by distinguishing weak and strong forms of quantum direct cause in open-system dynamics.
arxiv-2506-23367:
Paige Tuttösí and four colleagues build a speech system tuned for second-language listeners, in a 2025 paper. English tense vowels last longer than lax ones, and learners often miss that contrast. The team added a clarity mode to a text-to-speech system that stretches tense vowels while leaving the rest natural.

French-speaking learners of English transcribed speech in tests. The clarity mode cut their errors by at least nine percent compared with normal output. Listeners also found it more encouraging and respectful than speech that is simply slowed down. Oddly, listeners still believed full slowing helped most, even though their scores said otherwise. An automatic speech recognizer did not use the same cues as the learners. The authors warn that machine scores cannot stand in for learner listening tests.
arxiv-2506-23467:
Chenlang Yi and co-authors build a fairer vision language model for chest X rays in 2025. Models that pair images with text score well at reading scans. They can also absorb bias tied to race and gender, which skews diagnosis for some groups. Their framework, AdFair-CLIP, fights that bias during training.

An adversarial step suppresses traits that reveal sensitive group membership. That cuts false links between group traits and disease signs. Tests on chest X ray sets show fairness and accuracy both rising. The work matters because biased tools can quietly widen health gaps at scale.
arxiv-2506-23767:
Every public company files a yearly report thick with risk, and reading thousands of them by hand is hopeless. Xue Wen Tan and Stanley Kok build a small, transparent model to do the reading in this 2025 paper. TinyXRA judges a firm's risk from its annual filing, using a compact transformer suited to long documents and modest hardware.

Unlike older gauges that punish stock swings in both directions, theirs folds in asymmetry and tail shape, plus a ratio that counts only downside pain. A dynamic word cloud, steered by the model's attention, shows which terms drove each verdict, with filler filtered out. Trained to sort firms into risk quartiles, the model topped prior accuracy across seven test years in data from 2013 to 2024. Speed plus explanations aim it at real screening desks.
arxiv-2506-23967:
Geerd-Dietger Hoffmann and Verena Majuntke present, in twenty twenty-five, a tool to measure the resource use and carbon cost of software. As computing demand grows, so does interest in software's environmental footprint. Measuring is the first step to cutting it. The Green Metrics Tool runs software in containers, in a controlled and repeatable way. It assesses resource use across key phases of a program's life. The pair argue for fact-based metrics to guide decisions on efficiency.

The tool adds views of the data, cross-run comparison, and rule-based and AI-based tips for savings. Those features can guide developers and researchers to lower-impact software, they say. The talk version came from a workshop on low carbon computing held in Glasgow in late twenty twenty-four.
arxiv-2507-00167: Simone Coccia and Daniel Litt prove a density result for integral points in character varieties, in a math paper from 2025. The setting is a smooth variety with a simple normal crossings compactification. The varieties parametrize SL2 local systems whose boundary traces are fixed algebraic integers. The authors show integral points are potentially dense there. Their proof uses work of Corlette and Simpson to cut the claim down to Riemann surfaces. There, they build an integral point whose orbit under the mapping class group is Zariski dense.
arxiv-2507-00767: Abedennour Dib, Aymeric Garnier, and Alessandro Spallicci extend a classic result about fast light particles in this short 2025 physics paper. The Aichelburg-Sexl solution describes the gravity field of a massless particle moving at light speed. The authors broaden it to cover particles that also spin as they move, using spherical harmonics in tensor form. They also take first steps toward a notion of self-force for photons, which could show up as a shift in the light's frequency.
arxiv-2507-00967:
Gregory Scholes asks whether a system built from ordinary classical parts can behave in ways that resemble quantum states. His tool is a network graph, which does two jobs at once. It sets the wiring of the classical network, and it defines a space of states built from sums of states in a product basis. Scholes reviews how such graphs are built and what they can do, and then extends the theory.

He adds a way to shrink the graph while keeping the features that make its states look quantum. The smaller graph gives a clear picture of how links between parts mirror the correlation pattern of a quantum state. He also asks, with care, whether these systems can show anything like entanglement, and contrasts that question with the separate idea called classical entanglement in optics.
arxiv-2507-01167:
Atsushi Inoue and two co-authors prove that a classic test for economic models stays valid under wide conditions, in a 2025 econometrics paper. The Anderson-Rubin test checks a subset of model parameters while leaving the rest free. The version here rests on a criterion from a continuously updated estimator. The team treats the data spread in a flexible way, with set rules imposed only under the null claim.

They show the test keeps the right error rate even when parameters are weakly or not at all pinned down. The result covers data with uneven spread, cross-sections, and time series that need not sit still. A fresh proof trick, based on small nudges and smoothing of the estimator's core equations, drives the result. The authors say applied workers can trust the test in more settings than before.
arxiv-2507-01267:
Michelle Si and Jian Pei tackle a puzzle in data markets: why one owner's data are worth more than another's. Their 2025 paper uses the Shapley value, a fair-division score from game theory. They seek a counterfactual account: the smallest set of entries whose move from one owner to another would flip their ranking.

They show such an account always exists, but finding the exact one is NP-hard. A direct sampling route is also too costly, since each trial needs fresh value estimates. Their algorithm, SV-Exp, speeds the work with three tricks: tracking value changes, scoring single entries, and shifting sets greedily. Tests on real data show the method is fast and that the accounts help explain value gaps.
arxiv-2507-01467:
Teaching an image machine to clean noise from a picture is slow, and a known trick lends it eyes: align its inner views with a trained model's clean views. The authors of a 2025 paper argue that trick stops too soon. The lent eyes guide training, then vanish at use, when the machine works from pure noise.

Their fix tangles the loan into the work itself. Low-level picture codes are woven with one high-level class token from the trained model, and the pair is denoised as one. The machine then births matched picture-and-class pairs from noise alone. Birth quality and training speed both jump, at near-no added cost in use. Simple tangles beat side lessons.
arxiv-2507-01567:
Patrick Benito Eberhard and four co-authors wrote a 2025 paper on steering teams of agents to cover areas that change over time. Fleets of taxis and search-and-rescue teams face this problem: the spots that matter most shift, while each agent has nonlinear motion and hard safety limits. The authors build a shared-control framework for the task.

Each agent pairs a trajectory planner with a tracking controller, running at two different rates. For patterns that repeat in cycles, the team proves the fleet settles into the best layout and respects all limits, with no collisions. A faster algorithm handles patterns that do not repeat. Hardware tests with four miniature race cars back the method. The work suits real fleets that must adapt coverage on the move.
arxiv-2507-02067:
Nikolaos Papanikolaou and six co-authors review advanced printed sensors for environmental monitoring as a path to sustainable solutions. Printing techniques create flexible, low cost, and highly customizable sensing devices. That range of uses fits wide roll out where fixed tools cost too much or are too stiff to scale.

The sensors track air and water quality, soil conditions, and atmospheric change among other factors. Sensitivity and accuracy are high for pollutants, temperature swings, humidity, and other parameters key to judging and guarding the state of nature. Because printed devices can be tailored to each setting and produced cheaply, dense nets of such sensors become practical. The review maps how this technology could widen the watch on the world around us while lowering its footprint.
arxiv-2507-02267:
Katlego Machethe and co-authors forecast top quark measurements at a planned collider in a 2025 paper. The Large Hadron Electron Collider would smash electrons into protons, giving a clean stage to probe how the top quark talks to the Z boson. The team studies one decay channel and a key angle between particles.

With modest data, coupling limits would reach a tenth of the standard values. With full data, limits tighten to a hundredth, a few percent of the expected size. Exotic dipole couplings are also bounded. Two-parameter fits widen the ranges but stay competitive. Readers get a case for the machine as a top physics tool.
arxiv-2507-02367:
Christian Salomonsen and colleagues teach a network to read a PET scan's input curve so mice need no arterial line. Dynamic PET tracks a tracer through the body, and kinetic models need the tracer's blood concentration over time. Drawing that curve means cannulating an artery, an intricate, terminal procedure in small animals. Longitudinal studies die with the subject.

Their fully convolutional model watches the scan's volumetric frames, extracts spatial features, then reads them over time to predict the arterial input function. It trained and validated on a common glucose tracer's scans with real blood curves. Two further tracers, for dopamine and prostate targets, test its range. Shortened and time-shifted scans probe robustness. The model predicted the input function reliably throughout. Blood-free kinetics could spare animals and unlock repeat imaging.
arxiv-2507-02467:
Vincent Runge, Charles Truong, and Simon Querné speed up the exact hunt for change points in long time series, in a paper from twenty twenty-five. Dynamic programming finds every shift in a series' behavior, but slowly. Pruning rules that discard hopeless candidates made it fast, yet each existing rule has a blind spot: one fades when changes are sparse, the other suits only simple models.

Their framework, DUST, judges candidates through a dual function weighed against a threshold. Strong duality holds for the pruning problem under mild assumptions. For single-parameter models it pairs one rival's simplicity with the other's speed, and it shines for non-Gaussian data. A mouse monitoring series shows it recovering the true change structure efficiently.
arxiv-2507-02567:
Maarten van Dijk and colleagues take a census of the particles flowing down a CERN test beamline. The T10 line in the renovated East Area feeds experiments and school competitions alike. Knowing its particle mix at each momentum is basic housekeeping. The team measured it four independent ways.

Pressure scans on a threshold Cherenkov counter vary the gas until species switch on one by one. A lead-glass calorimeter and time-of-flight measurements add cross-checks. A paired-counter method brackets a species' threshold from above and below. The measurement began as a Beamline for Schools proposal, carried out in twenty twenty-three and expanded with more scans into twenty twenty-five. Overlapping data sets are compared into one comprehensive account. The work is metrology in service of everyone downstream of the beam.
arxiv-2507-02667:
A hot Jupiter that orbits backwards is a clue mishandled by tidy theories of planet formation, and Steven Giacalone and co-authors present a fresh one in a 2025 paper. Watching the planet KELT-23A b cross its sun-like star with the Keck Planet Finder, they measured the orbit's tilt against the star's spin.

The projected tilt came out near one hundred eighty degrees: the planet circles retrograde, against the spin. Cool stars like this one usually realign their hot Jupiters into tidy prograde orbits through tides, so a backward survivor is a genuine outlier. The authors note the true orbit may sit closer to polar. They offer a toy model: a wide companion star, an M dwarf five hundred seventy AU away, may have delivered the planet late, after the tides had done their calming work.
arxiv-2507-02767:
Conditional logic studies if-then reasoning, and its intuitionistic branch asks what such reasoning looks like when proof, not truth, is the standard. Dalmonte and Girlando give this young field a proof-theoretic treatment. In the intuitionistic setting the would and might conditionals split apart and can no longer be defined from each other, which forces fresh machinery.

They build a nested calculus for the intuitionistic system and a sequent calculus for its constructive sibling. From the sequent calculus they then define a wider logic that adds the might operator back in, conservatively extending the earlier system. For that logic they supply a class of models and an axiomatization, and they carry the results over to several further extensions. The paper gives the field the calculi it needs to test proofs mechanically.
arxiv-2507-02967:
Pragya Dhungana and co-authors (2025) test object detection models for inspecting underwater pipelines. The sea floor is a hard place to see: turbidity, bent light, and decayed images defeat ordinary inspection cameras. The team compared two recent YOLO generations, version 8 and version 11, in three sizes each. The task was image segmentation, outlining the pipeline structures in frames shot beneath the seabed. Artificial intelligence enhancement steps supported the detection pipeline.

YOLOv11 beat YOLOv8 overall in their comparisons. The authors report the newer model delineated target structures more accurately under the poor visual conditions. They frame the study as groundwork for autonomous fault diagnosis on subsea lines. Reliable outlining is the first step toward spotting corrosion, cracks, and leaks without divers. The work also gives operators a practical ranking of model variants for this niche, where most published benchmarks use clear land images instead.
arxiv-2507-03267:
Networks that change over time and carry text on their dots and links show up in feeds, chats, and trade, but test sets for making new ones are thin and messy. Jie Peng and co-authors fix that in a 2025 paper with a benchmark of eight cleaned dynamic graph data sets. Their texts on nodes and edges are rich enough for models that must write as well as link.

On top of the data they set two tasks: grow a graph among known members, or grow one that also invents new members. Scores judge build, timing, and text quality together. The team adds a team-of-agents system, run by a large language model, as a shared test driver. Early runs show that build and text trade off in sharp ways, a clue for the next round of model design.
arxiv-2507-03767:
Pouriya Torkinejad Ziarati studies when polynomials can generate a whole function space in a 2025 solo maths paper. The spaces are Poletsky-Stessin weighted Bergman spaces. They live on domains like the unit ball and the bidisk. A polynomial is cyclic if its shifts span the full space.

Ziarati widens the parameter range for these spaces on a broad domain class. The new family resembles Dirichlet-type spaces on the unit ball. Cyclic behavior on the bidisk departs from a prior known case. Those contrasts are drawn out in the paper. Open problems on the shape of cyclic polynomials close the work. The study maps fresh ground in complex analysis.
arxiv-2507-03867:
Yu Xiang Zhu and co-authors design a programming type system keeping a prized guarantee: the computer can always decide whether one type fits inside another. Their system, Nominal Wyvern, belongs to a family fusing object-oriented and functional ideas, gaining power such as self-referential type bounds. In older systems of this family, that power breaks decidability, or easy use is sacrificed to save it.

The new design separates two jobs that others merge. Types are declared by name, in the style programmers know, and refined structurally only at the point of use. That split steers users away from the recursive shapes that cause undecidable cases, and lets the authors adapt a known separation trick to prove decidability. The result keeps the expressiveness programmers use, including bounded polymorphism and modules. The authors pitch the system as proof usability and decidability need not trade off.
arxiv-2507-04667:
Hahyeon Choi, Junhoo Lee, and Nojun Kwak ask what makes that sound right now in a 2025 paper. Sound-source hunts in video have long worked frame by frame, which misses how a sound grows and moves. Past sets also kept sources in view and lone, a far cry from real clips.

Their test set, called AVATAR, is built on video with fine time marks. Four cases span lone sounds, mixed sounds, many sources, and sounds from off screen. Their model reads time as a first-class clue. Stock methods stumble on the moving cases, which shows the gap the set names.
arxiv-2507-05167:
Nestor Guillen and Luis Silvestre explain a breakthrough on the Landau equation in an expository note from 2025. The equation describes how particles in a plasma collide and spread. A feared outcome is blow-up, where values grow without bound in finite time. Their recent work rules out blow-up for the case of Coulomb forces, and the note lays out the ideas for a broad math audience.

The key step tracks a quantity called Fisher information along a solution. They show it does not increase over time, which blocks blow-up. A lifted helper equation, built in twice the variables, makes the proof work. For this equation it becomes a family of heat equations on a sphere. Background links round out the note.
arxiv-2507-05267:
Markus Böck reports a full strong solution for the game Connect-Four on its standard board. His paper is from two thousand twenty-five. The game was solved in the sense that the best move can be found by search. But a full look-up table, giving win, draw, or loss for each state, was thought to be too big to build.

Böck uses a symbolic search based on binary decision diagrams, with a fast code build. On a single core of home-grade hardware, the work took about two days and made a large table. His open tool also adds a search that finds the fastest win or the slowest loss. Game fans and code users can check the result freely.
arxiv-2507-05367:
Nadia Zakamska and a large team report a candidate circumplanetary disk occultation of a main sequence star, ASASSN-24fw. Dusty disks around planetary companions can eclipse their host star for months when geometry aligns. The star dimmed by four magnitudes for eight and a half months, and spectra were taken with three major telescopes.

Multiple low ionization metal emission lines appear, narrow and blueshifted relative to the star, plus complex sodium absorption. If tied to the occulter, the gas signals suggest a gas rich disk. A broad hydrogen line likely comes from the inner circumstellar disk instead. Historic plates show prior occultations in 1981 and 1937, which fix a long orbital period for the occulter and make the system a rare laboratory for giant planet disk studies.
arxiv-2507-05467:
Gnabasik and seven colleagues measure temperature at the nanoscale with electron patterns in twenty twenty-five. Tiny devices need precise heat maps, but optical and probe methods have limits. Their method reads temperature from electron backscatter diffraction patterns in a microscope. Heat blurs the pattern's bands in a measurable way.

Simulations set sensitivity limits for four semiconductor materials. A Fourier analysis captures the subtle blurring across the whole pattern. On silicon, experiments matched the predicted sensitivity closely. They reached thirteen kelvin uncertainty with a ten second capture. Temperature maps under a heat gradient were also produced. The authors offer the method as a practical tool for device diagnostics.
arxiv-2507-05567:
Among codes that all meet the same best-possible length bound, some still fail less often than others. Chaofeng Guan and co-authors study that tiebreaker in a 2025 paper. The measure is the error coefficient, the count of lightest codewords, which sets the error floor on a noisy channel under best decoding.

Proving how small that count can be is hard, and the standard linear programming bound often falls short. The authors build several iterative lower bounds for codes that meet the Griesmer bound. For binary codes of dimension up to five, the bounds are tight in most cases. Where they are not, the gap to the true value stays at two or less.
arxiv-2507-05667:
David Baraglia proved in 2025 a genus bound for surfaces that respect a symmetry of a four-dimensional space. A Real structure is a smooth flip of the space that preserves orientation, and a surface counts as Real when the flip sends it to itself while reversing its orientation. First he showed a cohomology class can be carried by such a surface exactly when it lifts to an equivariant class. That test sorts which classes are even candidates.

When the space's Real Seiberg-Witten invariants do not vanish, the genus of these surfaces obeys an adjunction inequality. Two versions cover nonnegative and arbitrary self-intersection. Examples show the least genus for symmetric surfaces can exceed the least genus for surfaces with no symmetry demand. The result extends a classic four-manifold tool into the symmetric setting. It gives obstructions specialists can apply directly.
arxiv-2507-05867:
Nikita Savin, Elena Ambrosovskaya, Dmitry Romaev, and Anton Proskurnikov assess linear control for zero speed fin roll damping in two thousand twenty-five. Ships at rest or slow speed lose the lift that damps roll. A Navis system uses two fins that drag and oscillate to push back. That drag based act works even when the hull stands still.

Their control design stays linear in its core structure. Nonlinear drag forces and actuator limits are still counted in the loop. A high fidelity vessel model built for hardware tests hosts the runs. Simulations show the scheme damps roll well in that setting.
arxiv-2507-06067:
Maximilian Tschuchnig, Lukas Lamminger, Philipp Steininger, and Michael Gadermayr improve synthetic CT images made from cone-beam scans. Cone-beam CT is used a lot in surgery for its speed and low dose. But its images have flaws and look worse than standard CT. To turn cone-beam scans into the CT form is a strong fix.

The team uses learning that joins cone-beam data from surgery with standard CT taken before surgery. The two sets are not lined up by nature. So they add a registration module that can learn, inside the build steps. They test the model on a controlled fake data set and on two real clinic data sets. Adding registration lifted image quality past base methods in most test settings. Gains were largest when cone-beam quality was low.
arxiv-2507-06267:
Fitting a model to data breaks when the outside signal driving it jumps suddenly, and a 2025 arXiv paper by Hyeontae Jo, Krešimir Josić, and Jae Kyoung Kim fixes the jump first. Their method, HADES-NN, alternates two steps: a neural network smooths the jagged signal, then the smooth version feeds standard parameter fitting.

The estimates came out accurate and tight across test cases. Two came from real biology: the body clock driven by light recorded on wearables, and yeast answering a mating signal. The authors say the trick widens the range of real systems that can be fitted at all.
arxiv-2507-06367:
El Mehdi Achour, Kathlén Kohn, and Holger Rauhut study the geometry behind training for a simple class of neural networks in this 2025 paper. Their networks apply learned filters across images but stay linear, which keeps the math tractable. Training moves the filters downhill on an error surface, a path called gradient flow.

For fully connected linear networks, earlier work showed the training path can be rewritten as a flow measured by a curved geometry on the space of functions. That result needed a special balanced start. The authors prove the rewrite holds for convolutional networks no matter how training starts. The result covers multi-dimensional filters, and the one-dimensional case when the filter strides exceed one. The geometry itself still depends on the starting point. The findings give a cleaner picture of how these networks learn.
arxiv-2507-06467:
Luyu Qiu, Jianing Li, Chi Su, and Lei Chen build a database helper that asks before it guesses, in a 2025 paper. Turning plain questions into database code trips on vague wording: one phrase can mean several queries. Most tools bet on one reading at once and risk a wrong answer. This system keeps a spread of candidate queries, each with a chance weight, and talks with the user to thin the spread.

At each step it picks the fork where a question would teach it the most. That pick follows a classic rule that weighs how much a reply should cut the doubt on average. The user answers, the spread updates, and the code firms up. The authors say the back-and-forth suits real business data, where terms are loose and the cost of a wrong table is high. The frame turns guessing into guided choice.
arxiv-2507-06967:
Sebastien Andre-Sloan, Anirbit Mukherjee, and Matthew Colbrook prove in 2025 that noisy training data force physics-informed networks to grow. Such networks solve equations in high dimensions, yet real data carry noise that caps how low error can go. When a network can still beat the noise floor was unknown.

A size bound ties sample count and target error to the least weights needed. More noisy labels alone do not grant a free drop in error. Tests on three equation families show a sharp size threshold in practice. Below that size, training stalls above the noise floor in every run.
arxiv-2507-07067:
Clement Ruah, Houssem Sifaou, Osvaldo Simeone, and Bashir Al-Hashimi review ways to close the gap between simulated and real telecom networks in a 2025 paper. AI models for networks starve for local data, since collecting it live is costly. Digital twins can synthesize site-specific data, but their output never quite matches reality.

Two complementary fixes are surveyed. Calibration tunes the twin itself against real measurements. Gap-aware training instead teaches the model to live with the mismatch. The review weighs two such training styles: one models the gap in the environment through Bayesian learning, the other corrects the training loss using real samples. Both help models trained on twin data survive deployment.
arxiv-2507-07267:
Saharian and Asatryan study the vacuum of a massive vector field between two plates in a 2025 physics paper. The setup is the Casimir setting, where boundaries change the zero-point energy of a field and can pull the plates together. Their field, the Proca field, describes a vector particle with mass. The work is set in a space with extra dimensions.

The authors compute the basic correlation functions and the average values of field strengths and energy flow for two ideal boundary types. In the zero-mass limit most results match those for a massless field. The energy flow under one boundary type does not, and they trace the gap to how that boundary treats the lengthwise wave mode. The force between the plates pulls inward under both boundary types.
arxiv-2507-07467:
Juyeop Han, Lukas Lao Beyer, Guilherme Cavalheiro, and Sertac Karaman wrote this robotics paper, published in 2025. It plans drone flight paths that actively help the drone know where it is, indoors, where GPS cannot reach.

Map-based localization needs heavy pre-built maps that scale poorly. Instead, a learned estimator predicts 3D scene coordinates for each pixel, giving position directly, and an uncertainty-aware version says how much to trust each patch of view. The planner steers the camera toward trustworthy scenery while a smoother blends the slow visual fixes with fast motion-sensor data. In simulation, position error fell by at least five percent and orientation error by over thirty percent against baselines. Hardware-in-the-loop tests showed the system could run in near-real conditions.
arxiv-2507-07567:
Reza Ghasemi Alavicheh and three co-authors turn amplifier distortion into a shield for wireless links. Their 2025 paper works on physical layer security. Amplifiers bend signals as they near saturation, a flaw engineers usually fight. Bent signals, steered well, could jam eavesdroppers instead.

Their Z3RO precoder flips some antennas so distortion cancels at the true user. Elsewhere, the distortion lands as interference. Eavesdroppers then face a dirtier channel than the intended receiver. Simulations show secrecy rates up to two and a half times the standard method. The gain holds at a ten percent outage level. Dirt in the signal becomes a feature, not a bug.
arxiv-2507-07667:
Amanda Marques de Lima, Erico Souza Teixeira, Eivson Darlivam Rodrigues de Aguiar Silva, and Ricardo Luiz Longo published a paper in 2025 on sharpening quantum calculations by polishing more than the energy. The variational quantum eigensolver estimates a molecule's energy on a quantum device. But properties like charge distribution come from a related object, the one-particle reduced density matrix, which energy-only tuning can leave sloppy.

Their two-step method first lowers the energy, then adds a weighted penalty that drags the density matrix toward convergence too. On two standard circuit designs the polish barely moved already-good energies, yet electron density, dipole moments, and atomic charges all improved markedly. For the weaker design, energy accuracy itself jumped. Better properties for free, in effect, from the same quantum runs.
arxiv-2507-07767:
Jerome Brender and co-authors test whether a structured chat interface helps students learn with AI in a 2025 education study. How students prompt large language models affects their problem solving and understanding of course material. The team built a platform that guides students toward better, more thoughtful prompting habits during coursework.

Fifty-eight students in a graduate robotics course took part in the study over the term. One group used the structured platform, while a control group used ChatGPT freely with no guidance. Comparing the two groups shows whether light guardrails on prompting improve learning outcomes, a question facing any course that lets students learn with AI help.
arxiv-2507-07967:
De Wilde and a large solar team synthesized in 2025 what a flaring Sun would look like if it were just another star, a point of light with no surface. Solar telescopes resolve flares in rich detail, but stellar astronomers see only whole-disk spectra. Bridging the two views tells each side what the other can know.

Nineteen small-field flare observations from a one-meter Swedish solar telescope, gathered between 2011 and 2024, were stitched into synthetic full-disk spectra. The team then asked what can and cannot be inferred about a flare from the star-like view alone. The byline is a long collaboration list, framed here by its lead author. Readers get a translation test with stakes for exoplanet weather: how much flare physics survives the trip to point-source light.
arxiv-2507-08167:
Md Saif Hassan Onim, Andrew Kiselica, and Himanshu Thapliyal read the feelings of older adults from wrist sensor signals alone. Their paper is from two thousand twenty-five; the pack row gives no title or year, so the text head is the source. Knowing mood helps care in hospitals and assisted homes, but cameras feel intrusive and miss some states.

Forty older adults wear two wristbands while face-based reads give the truth labels across twelve feeling kinds. Classic learning models then guess feeling strength from body signals alone. The best fits the labels well with tiny error. The path suits people with dementia or trauma stress, and keeps the read private and cheap to run.
arxiv-2507-08267:
Hiroshi Yoshihara, Taiki Yamaguchi, and Yuichi Inoue share in 2025 a two-stage plan for training models that solve math problems. Strong math skill is a key test for large models. Two training styles lead the field, but how to blend them for both accuracy and speed was not clear.

The plan first trains with guided examples for many rounds to push accuracy to its peak. A second stage then uses reward-based learning from live answers to cut answer length while keeping that peak. The team did well in a strict math contest with more than two thousand teams. Code will be shared so others can repeat the work.
arxiv-2507-08567:
Preslav Aleksandrov and nine co-authors present AbbIE, an encoder that loops over its own latent states to model sequences with adjustable effort. Their paper from twenty twenty-five reshapes the encoder-only transformer into a recursive form. Standard scaling buys skill with more weights and tokens. AbbIE adds a third dial: iterations at test time.

The loops run in latent space, with no special data or training scheme needed. Trained with just two loops, it generalizes to any loop count at use. Perplexity beats a standard transformer at matched size. Zero-shot in-context learning gains show up as well. Harder tasks can spend more loops, easy ones fewer. All tests stay at modest model sizes. The authors open a fresh axis for transformer scaling.
arxiv-2507-08767:
De la Varga, Morales, and Pineda tackle in 2025 state estimation for power distribution grids with scarce live data. Live measures are often too sparse to pin the grid state, while past data go stale as conditions shift. Both gaps hit at once in daily grid work.

A neighbor-based estimator first guesses the spread of delayed measures from current context. A robust version then guards against errors in that guess by reweighting neighbors under set rules. The guard problem rewrites as one level with like cost to the base tool. A data-driven rule picks the guard strength online, and grid tests check the gains.
arxiv-2507-08867:
Machine learning has sharpened the hunt for new physics, but it leans on simulations, and gaps between simulation and real data can quietly bias results. Malte Algren and co-authors present a calibration method based on optimal transport, applied for the first time to high-dimensional simulations. They test it on jet tagging with data modelled on the CMS experiment at the Large Hadron Collider.

Inside a strong classifier, each jet is summarised by a 128-number representation. After the team calibrates that representation with transport maps, the many quantities built on it for later tasks come out properly calibrated too. That opens the door to using jet flavour information in collider analyses without the old bias worries. The authors frame the method as a step toward foundation models that particle physics can trust, and as a general fix for correcting rich simulations across the sciences.
arxiv-2507-08967:
Rongyi Zhu and co-authors present SIMS, a steering method that lets a language model improve its own guidance data, in a paper from 2025. Steering nudges a model's behavior toward human preferences while it runs. Standard steering leans on hand-labeled data, which ties its quality to the labels and limits how it adapts.

SIMS needs no outside labels. It makes and refines pairs of contrast samples in rounds of self-improvement. Two added tricks, prompt ranking and contrast sampling, sharpen the effect. Tests across several models and benchmarks showed SIMS beating prior steering methods on both strength and adaptability. The authors offer self-improving steering as a fresh path for aligning models at run time.
arxiv-2507-09067:
Serhan Bahar sets out a coin on screen built to live through quantum screens while it fights the watch risks of coins from chief banks. The ledger named in the title is a token based build. It joins set post quantum locks with hash based proofs that show a fact with no leak of the fact. Its aims are rule by the user, growth, and pried deals.

Parts of the design are short lived proof chains for deals that can not be linked. It has a stake vote that weighs pried use to spread who takes part. A proof way with no leak lets users pick what to show. They can prove facts on a deal with no show of all. Block times of ten to twenty ticks of the clock weigh guard and flow. The design is in thoughts; builds to test it are set as work to come.
arxiv-2507-09367:
Shiva Azimi and Arash Tavakoli publish a recipe book for traffic simulators in a 2025 paper. Cities run ever more mixed traffic, but most simulators treat each road user type separately, script their behavior, ignore transit riders as decision-makers, and shut out non-technical researchers. Their platform is built to fix all four flaws.

Inside immersive virtual environments, transit users, pedestrians, cyclists, drivers, and automated vehicles interact in real time. Hardware modules include a treadmill that allows walking in any direction, a bike trainer, and a moving car cockpit. Sensors record physiology, brain activity, eye movements, and behavior together. The design is modular and the scripts are open source, aiming at accessibility for researchers without deep engineering support. Three use cases show it working. The authors argue human-centered simulation should be a shared instrument, not a boutique one.
arxiv-2507-09767:
Ofir Itzhak Shahar, Gur Elkin, and Ohad Ben-Shahar score, in 2025 work, how well pairs of odd-shaped image shards fit, with no bets on their shape or paint. Such pair scores are the heart of shard rebuild tools, from jigsaws to dug pasts. Past scores lean on neat shard shapes that real finds lack.

Their score blends shape and paint to find a pair's best join. A new shard set, cut by a fresh method and worn by a set wear law that apes true field wear, gives the test bed, with marks for the task. Set in a dig-past solver, the score topped the field on near-shard truth and miss counts.
arxiv-2507-09867:
Jun-Hao Wei and co-authors propose a cheap way to map the wiring of a quantum network, in work from 2025. Knowing a network's structure decides how well quantum applications can run on it. So does knowing how much entanglement each link holds.

The method needs only two local measurements per qubit. Judging uncertainty and shared information together lets them count the entanglement sources between any two nodes. Neither measure achieves that alone. Two error-correction tricks clean up the estimates under noise. One removes bias in correlation readings. The other stretches the tolerable noise for certifying entanglement from about 9 percent to over 26 percent. The scheme fits many hardware platforms.
arxiv-2507-10067:
Yagub Aliyev (2025) solves optimization problems about cevian simplices, a classic figure from triangle geometry lifted into higher dimensions. Draw lines from a point inside a triangle to the three opposite sides; the feet of those lines form the cevian triangle. Its area is at most one quarter of the triangle's area, and the maximum occurs when the point is the centroid. Aliyev works with this construction for simplices in any dimension.

Using barycentric coordinates, he shows the bound becomes one over n to the power n in n dimensions, again reached at the centroid. He then turns to the parts of the figure. The simplex is divided by the construction into smaller pieces, and he finds the maxima of their volumes as the interior point varies. The paper completes the picture: one special point, the center of mass, extremizes the whole and its parts alike.
arxiv-2507-10267:
Novruz Amirov and co-authors tackled in 2025 the detection of DNS tunneling, a trick that hides stolen data or commands inside normal-looking name lookups. Rule and signature methods miss many of these secret channels because the traffic mimics honest queries. The team instead trained learning models on features drawn from the traffic itself.

Their combined approach sorted tunneled traffic from clean traffic with high accuracy in testing. Because it learns patterns rather than fixed signatures, it can catch new tunnel styles as they appear. The work offers network defenders a stronger watch on a quiet back door.
arxiv-2507-10367:
Jingwei Xu leads a team in a 2025 paper that presents FalconFS, a distributed file system built for large-scale deep learning pipelines. Such pipelines pull huge sets of small files, again and again, as they train. The store that feeds them can be the choke point of the whole run.

Most systems cache file paths on the client to speed that work. The team found that client state is not just weak help here: it eats prized memory. FalconFS keeps clients stateless. Paths are solved on the server by a hybrid index and lazy copies of the tree. Like requests merge to lift server pace.
arxiv-2507-10767:
Mathias Drton and co-authors tackled causal learning in 2025 for models where causes can feed back in loops. Loops make cause hard to read from data, since the usual rules based on links between facts no longer hold. The authors study straight-line models where the noise is not shaped like a bell curve.

First they show when two loop diagrams give the same model. Then, for diagrams whose loops do not share points, they use simple relations among data spreads to find source loops. Sorting the loops in blocks leads to a fast method that they argue learns the true structure over time. That order is what lets the method move from loops to full structure.
arxiv-2507-11667:
A large team measures three scarce elements in stars of the galactic bulge in this 2025 astronomy paper. The elements are phosphorus, sulphur, and potassium, and the sample is fifty-eight spheroid stars already studied for other elements with the APOGEE survey.

The authors derive the amounts by spectral synthesis, using star parameters from the survey's data release, and they recommend the best spectral lines for these elements in the infrared H band. Results are checked against the survey's own analysis and the few past studies. Chemical evolution models are compared as well, with a neutrino process added to fit the odd numbered elements. The work sharpens the record of how the bulge was enriched.
arxiv-2507-11767:
Xingzhuo Chen and co-authors speed supernova light simulations with AI in a 2025 paper. Modeling how light fights through an exploding star is slow, above all the atomic physics part. Their code, SEDONA-GesaRaT, swaps that part for trained neural networks.

The networks learned from 119 one-dimensional runs of type Ia supernovae. They solve atom level counts fast and accurately. The team then ran a full three-dimensional explosion model end to end. Polarized light data cubes came out with clean signal. The whole run cost about three thousand core-hours, a budget that once bought only flat or simplified runs. Wide surveys of explosion structure now come within reach.
arxiv-2507-11967:
Yuchi Ishikawa and five co-authors teach a model to learn from sound, images, and words at once. Their paper appeared in two thousand twenty-five. Masked autoencoders learn by hiding parts of audio and video and guessing them back. Adding language guidance can sharpen what they learn. The catch is training data: matched sound, image, and text triples are scarce.

The team makes those triples on its own from raw videos. An image captioning model writes frame-level captions first. A filter based on CLAP then keeps only triples where sound and caption align well. No hand labels are needed. Their model, LG-CAV-MAE, adds a pretrained text encoder to the audio-visual setup. It beats prior methods on retrieval and classification tests. The gains show the value of clean auto-made triples.
arxiv-2507-12167:
Walraven and Karman describe a new kind of force between polar molecules that carry an unpaired electron, at temperatures near absolute zero. Normally, molecules in states that differ by one rotation step attract strongly and are lost in collisions. Their 2025 paper shows that, for certain fine states, rules block that path.

Flipping a single nuclear spin can switch the strong force off. What remains is a weaker force that can push molecules apart, which slows their loss. The team focuses on calcium fluoride, a molecule that can be cooled with lasers. They show the effect also holds for several other such molecules, and propose a tweezer based test.
arxiv-2507-12367:
Diganta Misra and a large team test whether AI coders can write for the exact library version a project pins. Libraries change fast, and code that ignores version shifts breaks. GitChameleon 2.0 holds 328 Python completion problems, each tied to set library versions with runnable unit tests. Models, agents, assistants, and retrieval systems all face the same check: the code must pass when executed.

Even the strongest enterprise systems landed only in the 48 to 51% success band. Version-conditioned generation is thus a live weakness, not a solved chore. The benchmark aims to guide builders toward coders that adapt as libraries move.
arxiv-2507-12667:
Siyuan Yao and Chaoli Wang make time-varying simulation data explorable on an ordinary laptop. Scientists drowning in volumetric time series cannot interactively carve out and follow the features they care about with reconstruction-only tools. VolSegGS represents a dynamic volume with deformable three-dimensional Gaussians that render new views in real time.

Segmentation starts from the Gaussians' view-independent colors for a coarse cut, then an affinity field network refines the boundaries. Because the labels ride inside the Gaussians, their deformation carries the segmentation forward through time, giving continuous tracking for free. Tests on several time-varying data sets beat state-of-the-art alternatives. The authors pitch the framework at exploratory analysis where bandwidth and hardware are scarce.
arxiv-2507-12767:
As populations age, AI agents are being offered as helpers for older adults, from reminders to care coordination. Jiaxin An asks a design question that is easy to miss: how much independence should such an agent take, and how much should it leave with the person? Earlier work mapped the stages of a task and the agent's role in each. An draws on ideas of autonomy from several fields and splits it into four parts for older adults.

The four parts are choosing for oneself, setting one's own goals, staying in control, and carrying social responsibility toward others. An argues the last of these is under studied: an agent used in shared spaces affects family and community, not just its owner. The paper proposes research directions: tackle social responsibility, define agent independence task by task, and build ways to measure autonomy.
arxiv-2507-13267:
Igor Araujo and Zimu Xiang study two properties of oriented graphs in two thousand twenty-five. An oriented graph has edges with a set direction. One property asks if big near tournaments must hold a copy of a given graph. The other asks if they must hold a perfect tiling by that graph.

The pair disprove a guessed full account of the first property. The guess came from a team of six named authors in past work. They also show the two properties can split apart. Some graphs have the first property but not the second. They give a fresh case of a graph with the tiling property as well.
arxiv-2507-13767:
Daniele Giachini and six co-authors add lobbying to models of how opinions form, in a research paper from 2025. Lobbyists plainly shape public opinion and policy, yet standard opinion models leave them out. In the new model, lobbyists have limited budgets and can plan complex campaigns.

People in the model update their views from signals sent by others, filtered through habits like under-reacting and favoring what they already think. Computer runs show two regimes. In one, lobbyists can sway the whole network. In the other, peer pressure splits the public into camps. When rival lobbyists compete, spending early wins in one regime and spending late wins in the other.
arxiv-2507-13967:
An excitonic insulator is an unusual state where bound pairs of electrons and holes reshape a material's behavior. Golosov studies it through the extended Falicov-Kimball model, a standard model for such pairing. Most work sticks to half-filling, where the material's sites are half full. Golosov instead scans all filling levels, focusing on settings where the excitonic state is stable at half-filling.

Using Hartree-Fock calculations, Golosov maps the possible uniform phases and finds wide regions where the material prefers to split into mixed phases. The excitonic insulator can survive as one part of that mixture well away from half-filling. In one range, a doped excitonic metal is the lowest-energy uniform state, though it may need long-range electric forces to keep it from splitting. The work shows excitonic effects reach further from half-filling than usually assumed.
arxiv-2507-14067:
Shuliang Liu and co-authors design a watermark for vision-language models that survives where text-only marks fail. Owners of these models need proof of authorship embedded in generated text. Existing text watermarks pick tokens in biased ways that fight the image content, and fixed strategies leave key concepts exposed.

Their method, VLA-Mark, coordinates the mark with the picture at several scales: local patch affinity, global meaning, and attention patterns. An entropy-sensitive dial strengthens the mark when the model is confident and eases off when meaning is at risk. No retraining is needed. The result aims to protect model property without bending what the model says about an image.
arxiv-2507-14267:
Ziqi Wang and his six co-authors, publishing in 2025, build a team of AI agents that runs materials simulations under strict guardrails. Language model agents can drive long calculations, but their numbers are hard to trust. The team's engine, DREAMS, wraps a standard physics method in a layered safety guard. Every value must trace to a registered source, and checks run both as tools are called and when the final report is written.

The guarded system landed within 1 percent of reference values on a standard lattice benchmark. It also reproduced an expert-level result on a classic surface puzzle. An unguarded twin reached a nearly right answer while a fifth of its essential steps quietly failed. The guard costs about thirteen times more input text. The authors let users switch layers off to trade trust for cost, and frame the design as a path to autonomous labs.
arxiv-2507-14567:
Jasmin Imran Alsous and co-authors study the physics of giant fruit fly sperm in a 2025 paper. A male fruit fly makes sperm about 1.8 millimeters long, thousands of which pack into a storage sac two hundred micrometers wide. Evolution's reasons for such length are debated, but the physical fallout of packing those filaments was unstudied. The team imaged the stored sperm in three dimensions and filmed them live.

Stored sperm form a dense, highly aligned material with slow, system-wide flows and wandering defects. Single sperm still race through the pack in either direction along the alignment lines. The authors model each sperm as sliding in a tube formed by its neighbors, driven by its own bending waves. Their theory yields a material stress that keeps the pack aligned, matching experiments and simulations.
arxiv-2507-14767:
What-if questions land differently on different people, and Yanming Zhang, Krishnakumar Hegde, and Klaus Mueller build a visual tool for that fact in a 2025 paper. Most causal tools report average effects across a whole population. Real groups are mixed, so an intervention can help one subgroup and harm another.

Their framework simulates and explains personal-level effects inside subgroups, side by side. Two case studies demo the flow: opioid deaths in health data and voting lean in an election. Users can probe why a result flips between groups. Planners gain a guard against one-size policies that quietly backfire on minorities within the data.
arxiv-2507-14867:
Zhaoqiang Xia, Hexiang Huang, Haoyu Chen, Xiaoyi Feng, and Guoying Zhao wrote this paper in two thousand twenty-five. It reads feelings from micro-gestures, the small body moves people make without knowing, using a hypergraph-enhanced transformer.

Micro-gestures are a fresh cue for feeling, but past work on them is thin. The frame has an encoder and a decoder, each built from hypergraph attention blocks that link skeleton joints in groups, plus time-based convolution at many scales. The decoder rebuilds the motion as a self-taught task, which sharpens the subtle moves. A light head then names the feeling. Joint training on both tasks tops past methods on two public data sets.
arxiv-2507-14967:
Pratik Ingle, Kasper Stoy, and Andres Faina show how a soft surface can move varied objects without gripping them, in a 2025 paper. The surface carries many small actuators that change its shape and tilt objects along. Dense arrays are hard to control, and learning-based control needs much training and can fail on new objects.

Their method uses a simple feedback controller that maps a tilt angle directly to actuator commands, with a geometric step in between. No large training set is needed. In simulations and on a real textile surface with fewer actuators, the method moved objects of unlike shape, weight, and texture. Fragile items such as eggs and apples were handled safely. The authors present the approach as a practical path for soft robotic surfaces in real use.
arxiv-2507-15067:
Bing He and co-authors build a detector for bad actors on online platforms in a 2025 paper. Platforms need to spot abusive or fake accounts, yet attackers tweak their posts slightly to slip past automated detectors. Earlier deep learning models break under such small changes, so the authors aim for a detector that stays steady when inputs are nudged.

Their model, ROBAD, first reads each post in both directions to capture its local meaning. A second stage then reads the whole sequence of posts, watching for signs that the text was tampered with. This local-plus-global design builds a user profile that resists evasion tricks. The work targets safer platforms where banned actors cannot simply rephrase their way back in.
arxiv-2507-15467:
Daniel Grieser, Álvaro Sánchez-Hernández, and Boris Vertman wrote a 2025 survey paper on a family of curved spaces that pinch into cusps. The catalog title carries a funding note, but the paper itself reviews math for spaces that run off to infinity in a pointed, fibred way. Such spaces appear when smooth spaces break down at a seam, and they pose hard questions about waves and heat on them.

The survey gathers results on spectra, torsion, and index theory for these spaces, in both complete and incomplete forms. It explains the shared tools, which track how heat and waves behave near the cusp in fine detail. It also sketches how the main proofs work and where the forms differ. Surveys like this give newcomers one map of a scattered field.
arxiv-2507-15567:
Zhongshan An and Michael Anderson prove that Einstein's equations with a certain boundary rule form a well-posed problem, in a 2025 paper. This is the second work in their series on geometric boundary data for general relativity. The setting is a finite region of spacetime with a timelike edge, where physics must be told what happens at the boundary. Their rule fixes the conformal shape of the boundary metric plus a scalar density mixing bulk and boundary volumes.

Well-posedness means solutions exist briefly, are unique, and depend smoothly on the starting data, the minimum sanity check for any simulation. The proof handles the vacuum equations under these twisted Dirichlet conditions. The authors place the result in a program to make bounded-region relativity as rigorous as the whole-universe case. Numerical relativists need exactly such guarantees when they cut a finite box out of spacetime.
arxiv-2507-15767:
Adam Michael Bauer, Cristian Proistosescu, and Kelvin Droegemeier ask how fast future data can pin down how much the Earth warms, in a 2025 paper. Climate sensitivity has stayed uncertain for about forty-five years, since a landmark report. Two shifts may help: carbon dioxide will grow as a share of forcing as particle cooling fades, and the warming signal will stand taller above natural swings.

Their model folds in the full spread of parameter doubt and the way yearly swings link together. They find the short-run warming response can be pinned down no matter its true value. The long-run equilibrium value is harder, with low values easier to confirm than high ones. Most warming this century rides a fast mode that speaks to the short-run value, they explain.
arxiv-2507-15867:
John Wu, Adam Cross, and Jimeng Sun present a software system in 2025 that hunts for rare diseases in health records. Rare diseases affect one in ten Americans, yet records often miss them. Standard disease codes have no match for over half of the known rare disease codes. Patient notes hold the clues, but they are long, messy, and full of short forms.

Their system gives a language model tools to expand short forms, reason about hidden signs, and match terms to two disease catalogs. It needs no training on labeled examples, which are scarce. A small, cheap model matched or beat larger tuned systems in their tests. Costs fell sharply, and hospitals could run it on site to keep patient data private.
arxiv-2507-16267:
Xinyue Yang and six co-authors present SFNet, a deep learning system that reads brain MRI scans in two domains at once to diagnose Alzheimer disease. MRI data are gathered as frequency signals and then rebuilt into pictures, so scans carry both spatial and frequency information. Most diagnostic models use only the spatial picture, and earlier two-domain attempts were limited to flat, two-dimensional scans.

SFNet is built for full three-dimensional scans. One branch pulls local spatial features with a dense network, another captures global frequency patterns, and a multi-scale attention module sharpens the spatial side. On the standard ADNI dataset, the system beat existing baselines while using less computation. It reached 95.1 percent accuracy at separating healthy brains from those with Alzheimer disease. The authors argue dual-domain reading captures signs that single-domain models miss.
arxiv-2507-16567:
Adith Sai Aramthottil and four co-authors warn that some signs of odd behavior in messy quantum systems can be false alarms. Ordered quantum systems are expected to settle so that local reads match a heat based forecast. Their work came out in twenty twenty-five.

The issue is how reads spread when many messy cases are averaged. A non bell shaped spread can look like a break in the settling rule, the authors argue. Across mess types, the spread of a local spin read mirrors the spread of the mess itself. They trace this to overlap between the read and powers of the system's energy rule, and show how to set the energy window right.
arxiv-2507-16867:
Yunyi Zhao and five co-authors run communities of microgrids with a learning agent that watches both the bill and the carbon ledger. Their 2025 paper introduces an algorithm that fuses a diffusion model into deep reinforcement learning. The diffusion machinery generates action distributions by a denoising process, giving the policy a richer repertoire than a standard learner brings to shifting, uncertain conditions.

Tested against classic methods and recent learning rivals, the system cut operating costs by margins from a few percent to about thirty. Against its own carbon-blind variant it cut emissions by nearly twenty-nine percent, and its performance varied less from run to run. The design is meant to retarget easily to new system layouts and goals. The authors present it as a practical scheduler for renewable-heavy local grids that must answer for cost, emissions, and risk at the same time.
arxiv-2507-16967:
How fast sound moves through a thick liquid sounds like a niche question, until the liquid sits deep inside a planet where no probe can go. Sergey Khrapak offers a simple rule for that speed in a 2025 paper. The rule ties sound speed to heat, mass motion, and the point where the liquid would freeze.

For a standard model liquid, the rule's numbers come out nearly fixed, with one part drifting a bit with heat. The same shape fits real liquids such as argon, krypton, xenon, nitrogen, and methane once their own numbers are set. Khrapak tests the rule against a fresh lab measure of methane under planet-like squeeze and finds a fair match. Until more lab data arrive, the rule gives a quick way to fill gaps in models of deep worlds.
arxiv-2507-17167: Gerardo Gonzalez Robert and three co-authors extended classic results about continued fractions in a 2025 math paper. They looked at numbers whose fraction parts are, again and again, both large and prime. They fixed both the size and the fractal dimension of those sets, building on theorems from the late 1990s and from 2020. New estimates for a sum tied to near-prime numbers made the proofs work.
arxiv-2507-17467:
Elena Pitta, Tom Kouwenhoven, and Tessa Verhoef present a study from twenty twenty-five on a test task for models that mix sight and words. The task asks if a claim about a photo is true, false, or unclear. The team used one vision model as their test case. They ask how far scores on this task show real grasp of sight and words.

They tried no-shot, few-shot, and fine-tuned runs. Three prompt cases beat none, but more cases added noise. The order of labels in the prompt swayed the calls a lot. With no photo, the model made up content, which hints it leans on word habits. Fine-tuning scored high and gave sound reasons. Yet like scores with weak sight cast doubt on the task.
arxiv-2507-17867:
Felipe Navarro and five co-authors release in 2025 Spatialize, an open-source software library for estimating values across a map from scattered measurements. Their method, ensemble spatial interpolation, blends the plainness of basic interpolation with the strength of geostatistics, the field behind the classic Kriging method.

Many random runs of simple interpolators are averaged into one estimate, and the spread of the runs doubles as an uncertainty measure, giving full probability distributions rather than single numbers. The library is written in Python with a C++ core for speed and built for large datasets. It targets miners, environmental scientists, and anyone mapping sparse data.
arxiv-2507-18067:
El Kabid and co-authors present neural operator models that stand in for the equations governing ocean currents. Satellite products give current data at moderate resolution, too coarse for many coastal tasks. Their framework learns surrogate solutions of partial differential equations that can be queried at any resolution. That supports both prediction and downscaling of current fields.

They applied the method to Copernicus ocean current data and to synthetic fluid simulations. The models aim to deliver fine local detail from coarse global inputs. Such tools could serve coastal management, environmental monitoring, and maritime safety, where current detail matters.
arxiv-2507-18467:
