Pradeep Singh and two co-authors give a unified treatment of echo state networks in this 2025 paper. These networks keep a fixed, richly connected reservoir and train only a simple readout on top. The design mirrors a brain insight: fixed circuits plus an adaptive output can handle time based data well. Yet core questions about stability and memory were scattered across fields. The authors pull them into one dynamical systems frame.

They prove that the echo state property, where start conditions wash out, forces a fading memory of past inputs. Algebraic tests turn network traits into certified bounds for both kinds of activation. They also show such networks can approximate a wide class of causal filters. A memory capacity analysis links topology and leak rate to trade offs at the edge of chaos. The paper closes with design rules for reservoir size, input gain, and activation choice.
arxiv-2507-18667:
Police sketches turn witness memories into faces, and drawing them takes scarce expert time. Nicholas Fidalgo and co-authors test whether image-generating AI can help in this 2025 project, comparing three pipelines built on a popular diffusion model.

One plain pipeline was tested against versions that align text and image with a matching model, one of them fine-tuned for the task. Careful tuning of the matching model improved text fit, yet the plain pipeline still scored best on image quality measures and produced the clearest faces by eye. The study suggests simple setups remain hard to beat for sketch generation, at least for now.
arxiv-2507-18767:
Mia Gabriella Escobar, Valentin Garcia, and Anastasiia Minenkova settle an open case about special quantum spin chains in a 2025 mathematics study. Early state exclusion describes chains where a starting state becomes unreachable after the first step. Infinite families of matrices with and without that property were known for even chain lengths, but odd lengths from seven upward stayed open.

For a chain of seven qubits with nearest-neighbor coupling and environmental effects, the authors present infinite families of the relevant matrices in both flavors. Closing the smallest odd case suggests the pattern extends, and gives quantum walks research a complete small example.
arxiv-2507-18867:
Xuefei Wu and co-authors teach teams of learning agents with rewards shaped by human expertise, in this 2025 paper. Multi-agent learning struggles when only a shared team reward is given. Sparse rewards make exploring the world slow and blind.

Hand-made individual rewards can guide each agent, but they lack deeper smarts. The team's framework, LIGHT, learns each agent's inner reward instead. It folds in broad human expertise to guide that learning. Agents then explore with denser, smarter feedback. The approach aims at complex tasks where teams must split work. Games and robot fleets are natural test beds for the idea. The design keeps human input broad, so it need not be coded per task.
arxiv-2507-19067:
Mohammad Naeimi and Mostafa Haghir Chehreghani tackled popularity bias in graph-based recommenders in a 2025 paper. Such systems lean toward items that are already popular, which cuts personal fit and fair exposure for the rest. Past fixes act before, during, or after training, each with flaws.

Their fix adds a penalty term to training that charges the model for leaning on popular items. Two sampling plans and two ways to mark what counts as popular make it flexible. It plugs into leading graph models without change to their shape. On three data sets it cut unfairness measures by up to a tenth while holding accuracy steady. The authors present it as a simple, model-free add-on.
arxiv-2507-19167:
Shaun Davey, Callum Atkinson, and Julio Soria compare two ways to pull traveling patterns from turbulence in a 2025 paper. Behind a sphere, the wake churns yet hides orderly structures that drift downstream. A classic decomposition finds spatial modes, and a Hilbert-based variant finds moving ones, at the cost of filtering artifacts.

The study ran both methods on the same wake velocity data. Mode pairs from the classic method that match the moving structures were pinpointed. A cheaper shortcut emerged: applying the Hilbert transform to the classic modes alone reproduced the special modes well. That trick avoids the artifacts of transforming the raw data first. The result sharpens how engineers read turbulent wakes.
arxiv-2507-19367:
Weihao Chen and co-authors secure modular firmware updates for internet-of-things devices without giving up user customisation, in work from twenty twenty-five. Updates defend devices, yet the update channel itself invites attack. Two hundred devices from dozens of vendors are audited first. Five new vulnerabilities trace directly to customisation practices. Half of recent update flaws share that customisation origin.

Their platform chains integrity checks across every firmware module. Clever hashing keeps per-module verification cheap on weak hardware. Server-side work offloading and caching cut the heavy costs. Forging an image stays hundreds of times pricier than serving one. Update generation speeds up nearly threefold in device trials. Downtime shrinks almost sixfold against package-manager baselines.
arxiv-2507-19467:
Nikita Leppenen and Alexander Poddubny study in 2025 how groups of tiny light emitters share energy with a single light mode. In such systems, some collective states decay very slowly, a trait called subradiance, but random shifts in each emitter's tuning usually destroy those states. Their theory work uses a classic model of driven, leaky emitters with disorder in their frequencies.

They identify a different kind of long-lived pattern: correlations between emitters that decay slowly and can also swing in time. Unlike the usual slow states, these patterns survive the frequency disorder. In small systems they can outlast even the exotic time-crystal phase of the model. The result points to a hardier form of collective behavior in messy light-matter systems.
arxiv-2507-19867:
Anshul Chavda and five co-authors make made up in car chats full of the stops and self fixes that real drivers make. Sets that live now miss these breaks in speech. Bots trained on them deal poor with real speech. Their frame builds DiscoDrive, with 3,500 chats of more than one turn. The chats span seven car fields, with breaks in speech wove in as they are made.

Models trained on the made up data tied or beat models trained on a stock set took from folk. That held on test sets that fit the task. As a boost with just ten per cent of that stock set, the data gave more gains. Folk who scored the chats judged the made up chats a bit more plain to the ear and more sound as one than the set took from folk.
arxiv-2507-19967:
Filippo Bracci and Ahmed Yekta Okten pose in 2025 a set of open maths questions on curved domains in complex space. The note deals with bounded convex domains, which are rounded regions with no dents. Two themes run through the note: how far one can see across such a region, and what repeats do over time.

Rather than prove a main claim, the authors list gaps and guesses for others to test. They set out what is known, what stays unclear, and where a proof might go next. The note serves as a map for work on how maps act inside these rounded regions.
arxiv-2507-20067:
Bobbili and co-authors introduce in 2025 PITA, a method that aligns language model output with user preferences at inference time, with no retraining. Guidance model methods steer token choices but lean on a separate reward model fit to human feedback, an unstable step. PITA removes that dependency.

A small guidance policy learns from preference feedback and shifts token probabilities as text is generated. The task is framed as finding a hidden preference distribution, solved by stochastic search and repeated refinement. Tests cover math reasoning and sentiment classification. Results show aligned output at lower compute cost than fine tuning routes, which is the practical appeal.
arxiv-2507-20167:
Taekyun Kim and Dae San Kim study special polynomial families in a 2025 mathematics paper. Sheffer polynomials form a wide class with many known members. Degenerate versions twist the classic rules with a small parameter. The paper first blends those twists with higher order Bernoulli and Euler types.

From that blend, the pair derive fresh identities and properties. They then attach the polynomials to a random variable. Its moment generating function shapes a new family member for each distribution. Uniform and Bernoulli cases are worked out in detail. Related results for the higher order families follow. The paper sits in combinatorics and special functions. It offers formulas other researchers can apply to sums and generating functions.
arxiv-2507-20767:
Alexander Metelkin, Sam Jacob, and Bernhard Vowinckel use learning models to predict forces on round particles in a flow, in a paper from two thousand twenty-five. Fine-grained flow tests are exact but costly, while fast methods need good force rules. Their model reads the space around each particle, not the exact spots of its neighbors.

Local fill fractions on a fine grid serve as the input. Training data came from exact flow runs through random fixed particle arrays. The new model beat models fed with raw particle spots on force and twist accuracy. It also handles mixed particle sizes and shapes more readily.
arxiv-2507-20867:
Džuklevski wrote in twenty twenty-five a short note constructing a set of convex tiles with a rare tiling property. A tile set is called sigma-morphic if it tiles the plane in countably infinitely many truly different ways. Whether a single such tile exists remains an open problem. All known sigma-morphic sets used bumps and nicks on their tiles. Those features force the tiles to be non-convex, with dents in their outlines. Džuklevski instead builds the set entirely from convex tiles.

The construction cleverly splits tiles from a known set into convex pieces. The pieces behave just like the originals when tiling the plane. So the new set inherits the countably many distinct tilings. Convexity makes the result surprising to tiling specialists. It shows dents are not required for this kind of flexibility.
arxiv-2507-21067:
Jan Kapusta presents a manifesto, published in 2025, for a new way of thinking with AI systems. Today's systems reason in the dark, and the write ups bolted on later rarely make them true partners. Kapusta proposes symbiotic epistemology, a stance that treats the AI as a reasoning partner whose confidence should be openly calibrated against its reliability.

The companion protocol, SynLang, gives the partnership a grammar: patterns for high level reasoning, a detailed factor by factor mode, declared confidence numbers, and rules for passing context between agents. The paper backs the pitch with real dialogues where a model adopted the protocol and accepted mid course corrections. The aim is collaboration that strengthens human judgment rather than replacing it.
arxiv-2507-21267:
Wilbur Shirley, Carolyn Zhang, Wenjie Ji, and Michael Levin challenge a belief about quantum symmetries in this two thousand twenty-five paper. Folklore said a symmetry that cannot be gauged or made on-site must be anomalous. Anomalous symmetries block simple gapped ground states. The authors build lattice models in two dimensions whose symmetries resist both gauging and on-site form. Yet the models have calm, unique, gapped ground states, the mark of no anomaly.

They sort such symmetries by an index drawn from a cohomology group. The labels come from one-dimensional quantum cellular automata, rules that shuffle quantum data along a line. The counterexamples redraw the map of possible symmetries. Condensed matter theorists who classify quantum phases are the audience.
arxiv-2507-21367:
I-Hsiang Chen, Hua-En Chang, Wei-Ting Chen, Jenq-Neng Hwang, and Sy-Yen Kuo help segmentation models survive new environments in this two thousand twenty-five paper. Domain generalized semantic segmentation must label images from places the model never trained on, where appearance shifts can wreck performance. Recent methods align features back toward the source domain but neglect the latent priors describing how domains vary. Their framework, PDAF, adds probabilistic diffusion modeling to existing segmentation networks.

A latent domain prior captures domain shift and conditions the alignment of source and unseen target features. Three modules cooperate. An extractor predicts the prior by supervising domain shifts on paired real and pseudo-target images. A compensation module adjusts features to cancel shift. A diffusion-based estimator recovers the prior without paired samples. The design iteratively refines features, and extensive experiments across diverse urban scenes validated the gains in generalization.
arxiv-2507-21467:
Selimhan Dagtas, Mert Can Cakmak, and Nitin Agarwal built in 2025 a faster way to gather YouTube recommendations and compared the bias of its short and long video feeds. The platform's own data tools throttle research, so the team used parallel scraping to harvest suggestions at scale.

Short-form feeds swung sooner toward gripping but narrower picks, while long-form feeds diversified more slowly. A probe of political topics added fresh bias evidence. The dataset and method give outside researchers a way to audit a recommender that shapes what billions watch next.
arxiv-2507-21967:
Adina Feinstein, John Noonan, and Darryl Seligman report early images of 3I/ATLAS, the third known object from outside our solar system, in a 2025 paper. The object was found on July 1, 2025, and telescopes rushed to measure it. The team instead mined older data from TESS, a NASA planet-hunting satellite, which had watched the object's sky area from May 7 to June 2, 2025.

By stacking many faint images, they recovered the object and measured its brightness. Those values match the brightness reported after discovery. Set beside size limits from the Hubble telescope, the brightness hints the object was already active far from the Sun, near six times Earth's distance. The team also built a twenty-day light curve and found no clear sign of a spin period.
arxiv-2507-22267:
Owen Hoffman and four co-authors teach online safety by letting two chatbots act out a scam while learners coach the victim. Their work appeared in twenty twenty-five. Language models make fraudulent chats cheap and convincing, so the public needs practice spotting them.

One model plays the scammer, another the target. Users watch the exchange unfold and feed advice to the target along the way. Learning research says feedback on hypothetical choices sticks better than lectures. Earlier work had shown models can simulate scams realistically enough to train on. The system turns that unsettling skill defensive. The authors presented the design at a conversational AI workshop on ethical agent personalities.
arxiv-2507-22567:
Weicheng Gao explores a low-cost radar method for telling which way a walking person is moving. Motion direction shapes the micro-Doppler signature radar picks up from a gait, and knowing it helps later tasks like gait recognition. The catch is boosting weak features and reading direction at one and the same time.

Gao first builds Doppler-time maps of human gaits, then links features to enrich them. A hybrid model, part Vision Transformer and part convolutional network, reads the maps quickly and lightly. Tests on an open dataset check the method, and the code is released for others to try.
arxiv-2507-22767:
Dhar, Fong, and Motani smooth the teacher so the student can learn. Symbolic regression can turn a neural network's knowledge into a readable formula, but the formulas usually predict badly, because networks learn jagged functions while formula search prefers simple ones. Their fix works upstream: train the network with penalties on its Jacobian and Lipschitz constant so the function it learns stays smooth.

Across twenty data sets and fifty trials each, formulas distilled from smoothed teachers score significantly better than the standard pipeline produces. Ablations check which parts of the student algorithm matter. The authors conclude that aligning the teacher's complexity with the student's reach is the missing ingredient in symbolic distillation.
arxiv-2507-22967:
José Lima, Raydonal Ospina, Michelli Barros, and Antônio Macêdo build a diagnostic check for models of extreme wind gusts, in this 2025 arXiv paper. Rare, violent gusts cause damage and deaths, and regression models help assess that risk. Yet a single unusual event can bend a model's results, so analysts need ways to spot such events.

The team applies a local influence method to a class of extreme-value regression models. By curving the model's fit surface, they measure how much each data point pulls the parameters. A trial run on simulated data worked as hoped. Applied to real gust records from Itajaí, Brazil, the method flagged one severe storm event, one that caused damage and deaths, as strongly influential. The tool can help scientists judge how much trust a fit deserves.
arxiv-2507-23067:
Zhenyu Pan and co-authors chart the tug-of-war between reasoning skill and social bias in multimodal language models. Sharper reasoning drills often leave bias untouched or worse. Their 2025 study first races three bias fixes under one rule set: fine-tuning, distillation, and rule-based reinforcement learning. Then it varies the mix of fairness and reasoning samples inside each. The goal is a map of the trade-off, not a single trick.

A sweet spot shows up. A mix near one part fairness data to four parts reasoning, trained by reinforcement learning, cut stereotype scores by a tenth. It kept most of the model's reasoning strength. The team offers the ratio as field guidance for teams tuning such models.
arxiv-2507-23267:
D T Braithwaite, Misael Cavalcanti, and a large team of co-authors apply transformer models to personal spending records. Their 2025 paper notes that banks use predictive models for risk, fraud, and personal advice, where small performance gains are worth large sums. Most bank models still rely on hand built features from tidy tables, leaving raw data underused.

Transformers, by contrast, learn rich representations straight from raw sequences in other fields, without manual feature work. The team tests whether the same self supervised approach works on transaction streams. Bank data are messier and larger than text, so the transfer is not obvious. The study asks whether learned spending representations can beat engineered features at the tasks banks care about.
arxiv-2507-23467:
José Luís da Silva and Mohamed Erraoui wrote a mathematics paper in 2025 on a way to split certain random quantities into parts. Some laws of chance have a neat property: a quantity can be written as a product of a shrunken copy of itself and an independent leftover part. The gamma law has this property, and so does the simpler exponential law inside it. That fact has been known since work in 1977.

What was missing was the exact law of the leftover part. The authors find it and write it out using a special function from advanced analysis. For the exponential law, the leftover follows a law known as the M-Wright law. For the wider gamma family, and for the size of a centered bell-curve variable, the leftover follows a related law with different settings. The result completes a picture left open for decades.
arxiv-2507-23567:
Yung-Hsu Yang and eight co-authors bring 3D object detection to unfamiliar scenes in a 2025 paper. A single camera is cheap, but teaching a system to locate objects in 3D from one image usually assumes the test world matches training. New rooms and new object types break that assumption.

Their system starts from a 2D detector that already handles open-ended categories, then lifts its finds into 3D with a dedicated box-estimation head. Both stages train together. Geometry cues condition the lifting, and a canonical image space makes training across data sets cleaner. On standard indoor and driving benchmarks, including cross-dataset tests where scenes change entirely, the system set new records. Robots and augmented reality headsets both need this skill: seeing an object once, in a new place, and knowing where it sits in space. Code and models are public.
arxiv-2508-00067:
Limberg and co-authors present a 2025 find of one of the most metal poor stars ever seen. Stars born from near pure early gas carry a fossil record of the first star generations. The team mined a space survey's low grade spectra for a red giant whose iron sits near one sixty thousandth of the sun's share.

Sharp spectra confirmed the star as a far red giant, about 24 kiloparsecs out in the galaxy's halo. Its carbon level is capped very low, even after a fix for burn off as the star aged. That low carbon hints its birth gas cooled by dust grains, not by the usual fine line glow. Its motion hints at a shove from a falling dwarf galaxy.
arxiv-2508-00467:
Samratul Fuady, Danesh Tarapore, and Mohammad Soorati present a 2025 arXiv paper on letting only part of a robot swarm vote. Swarms usually decide as a whole, which ties up every robot and wastes effort on easy calls. Their method, SubCDM, picks a subset of robots to decide for all, formed on the fly from local information alone.

The subset grows or shrinks with the hardness of the question: close calls recruit more voters, easy ones fewer. In simulations with one hundred robots, the subset's verdicts matched the full swarm's accuracy while freeing the rest for other work. No central controller directs the choice of voters. The authors offer the method as an efficiency upgrade for swarm missions, from environment monitoring to disaster response, where robots are always short-handed.
arxiv-2508-00667:
Mingtao Yang and co-authors present a 2025 astronomy paper on reading a dark matter halo's past from the brightness gap inside it. The gap between a central galaxy and its brightest satellite records how the halo gathered mass. The team tests that code with weak gravitational lensing, which weighs halos by how they bend background light.

They stacked lensing signals for isolated central galaxies from a large sky survey, sorted by central brightness and gap size. In the middle brightness band, halos with smaller gaps proved heavier and less concentrated. At the bright end the link vanished, and at the faint end it blurred. This is the first lensing test of gap-based halo reading. Surveys can now use the gap with known limits.
arxiv-2508-00967:
Massoud Pourmandi, a solo author, proposes a cooperative perception system for swarms of drones, in two thousand twenty-five. Drone teams that rebuild a scene in three dimensions face tight computing limits and low-bandwidth links. Sending all raw images to one place is too costly, and privacy matters as well.

The proposal has each drone extract scene meaning with a light detection model and update a local neural scene model. A shared diffusion model is trained in a federated way, so drones learn together without pooling raw data. Meaning-aware compression trims what must be sent. The author plans validation in simulation and on real drone testbeds, and frames the system as a step for multi-agent autonomy.
arxiv-2508-01267:
Rose Waugh and Moira Jardine model what happens when spiral shock fronts in a star's wind crash into orbiting planets. Where fast and slow wind streams collide, they squeeze into corotating interaction regions that sweep around the star like water from a lawn sprinkler. These fronts can crush a planet's magnetic shield and spark outflows of its air.

Where the fronts form depends sharply on how fast the star spins, which fades as the star ages. Planets at Earth-like or Mars-like distances can be hit at any age, while closer worlds are struck only when the star is young and spinning fast. When the hits come often enough, the pulses merge into near-constant pressure. At middling rates, the planet breathes in pulses, and the storm-driven outflow can exceed half the air it loses. The work ties stellar youth to harsher weather for young planets.
arxiv-2508-01367:
A supercurrent that grows instead of fading after a light flash is explained by Qinghong Yang and co-authors in a 2025 paper. Laser pulses heat superconductors and thin their superfluid, which then recovers as electrons cool. If a probe pulse starts a current during that recovery, the current can grow as the superfluid rebuilds.

Kinetic math traces the growth to quasiparticles scattering off impurities and lattice waves. That defies the usual view that impurities only weaken currents. Signs of the effect include a fast magnetic response and light reflection above the normal cap. The find could reshape how ultrafast superconductor tests are read and how fast switches are designed.
arxiv-2508-01667:
Zhixiang Wei and seven co-authors present Rein++, a framework that adapts large vision foundation models to semantic segmentation, the task of labeling every pixel in an image. Foundation models train on huge data, but segmentation data sets are small and real scenes shift away from training conditions.

One part of the system tunes less than one percent of the model's parameters through small trainable tokens, giving strong generalization from little data. A second part adapts the tuned model to new unlabeled scenes, using a segment anything model to sharpen boundaries. Tests across settings beat prior methods with lean training. The pipeline moves from day scenes to night scenes without new labels.
arxiv-2508-01967:
Okan Köksal computes how lowering a crystal's symmetry switches on a Rashba spin effect in a layered oxide sandwich. The paper appeared in two thousand twenty-five. The Rashba effect splits electron spins by direction when symmetry breaks and spin-orbit coupling is strong. It is a prized knob for spintronic devices.

The stack pairs strontium hafnate with lanthanum aluminate on a buckled honeycomb frame. In the lopsided phase, a clear Rashba splitting appears near two key points, with a helical spin texture. In the symmetric phase, the bands stay spin-degenerate and the effect vanishes. A simplified model built from localized orbitals reproduces the full calculations. Phonon checks confirm the lopsided structure is stable. Measured strengths place the material among solid oxide Rashba candidates.
arxiv-2508-02167:
Yuxuan Wang and four co-authors present a 2025 arXiv paper on compiling programs for coarse grained reconfigurable arrays, a kind of chip whose parts can be rewired for each task. Such chips are fast and flexible, but writing a compiler for them is hard. Older tools handle data flow well yet give little help with control flow, the branch points that steer a program.

The team builds its tool on MLIR, a shared compiler base, as a set of passes that reshape and improve code. A new back-end mapping step fits programs onto a plain grid model of the chip, even when chip space is tight. Tests report speed gains of up to 2.1 times over older tools, won from compiler work alone.
arxiv-2508-02267:
Gal pays tribute to Toshimitsu Yamazaki, the Japanese physicist who died in 2025 after a career chasing exotic forms of hadronic matter. The talk highlights two themes that ran through Yamazaki's research.

The first is his discovery of deeply bound pionic-atom states, atoms where a pion sits in tight orbit around a nucleus. The second is his search for kaonic nuclei, especially a form he called Kaonic Proton Matter, where antikaons bind groups of protons. Gal closes with his own recent work on a related puzzle: whether a deeply bound H dibaryon, a six-quark object, can exist given observations of double-lambda hypernuclei. He finds it is not ruled out, though its lifetime is far too short for it to serve as dark matter.
arxiv-2508-02367:
Federico Viola studies how the symmetry group of a regular tree can act on spaces with a special kind of form in two thousand twenty-five. These actions, called representations, must be continuous and cannot be split into smaller parts. Each one has an index that counts how far it sits from the standard unitary case.

Cases with index zero and index one were already fully known. Viola shows that no such actions exist for any index above one. That result closes the list: the known cases are all there are. Work of this kind maps the full range of ways a large group can act while keeping a fixed form.
arxiv-2508-02567:
Lloyd, Abanin, and Gopalakrishnan show that a recently proposed measure of quantum states also grows under plain classical dynamics. The measure, called Markov length, was meant to flag phase changes in quantum mixed states. The team quenched a low-temperature ordered state into the high-temperature phase.

Ordinary measurements show no growing length scale during that heating. The Markov length, though, grew exponentially with time. That means the heating state drifts ever further from a simple thermal form. The authors built a matrix-product method to compute the measure and tested it on the classical Ising model. Simple information arguments explain the growth in every case they tried.
arxiv-2508-02867:
Hannes Jakob offers a set theory paper from 2025 on approachability, a way of judging how well large infinite sets can be reached by smaller steps. The work deals with successors of singular cardinals whose cofinality is countable, a case where the pattern has been unclear.

Working from an assumption of many supercompact cardinals, Jakob builds a model that also keeps the generalized continuum hypothesis. In that model, for each such singular cardinal and each smaller regular cardinal, there are stationarily many points that cannot be approached. The paper answers a question posed by Mitchell and settles a related question from Foreman and Shelah, in the negative direction for approachability.
arxiv-2508-03167:
Charles Tapley Hoyt and thirteen co-authors present Y0, a Python package for causal identification. Before estimating how strong a cause is, researchers must know whether the effect can be estimated from their data at all. Y0 applies interventional, counterfactual, and transportability queries to trial data, observational data, or a mix of both. It then guides users to a symbolic estimand that can be estimated non-parametrically.

The package offers a domain-specific language for causal queries and estimands as symbolic probabilistic expressions. It also represents causal graphs with unobserved confounders, such as acyclic directed mixed graphs. Many identification algorithms from recent literature are implemented, and the code is open under the MIT License.
arxiv-2508-03367: Sreenath Manikandan and Frank Wilczek show in 2025 how paired detectors can test a core claim about light fields with no vacuum noise in the way. The claim treats such fields as coherent states, a clean base case in quantum optics. Counts of links between two tuned detectors form the base of the test. Right pick of read plan can bare squeeze in count or in phase, two twin traits of the field.
arxiv-2508-03467:
Mehdi Dabirnia, Hamdi Joudeh, and Albert Guillén i Fàbregas write on source coding in this 2025 theory paper. Source coding squeezes data for sending or storage; here the decoder also holds side information about the source. The authors study how fast error chances fall as codes grow long. They work in the dual domain, where the math runs over a few settings.

They present a trimming method that yields two new error exponents for two styles of random codes. The setup even allows a decoder tuned to the wrong statistics. The better of the two exponents matches a known classic result. Number examples show how the two exponents differ in practice. With no side information, their exponent matches the best possible code's error rate.
arxiv-2508-03767:
MERAI, a record-matching pipeline for huge firm data sets, is set out by Sandeepa Kannangara and co-authors in a 2025 arXiv paper. Matching the same person or firm across messy files is called entity resolution. It gets hard at firm scale. MERAI was built to dedupe and link files with millions of rows, and it was checked on real firm work.

Two known tools faced it in tests. One stalled past two million rows for lack of memory. MERAI cleared more than fifteen million rows and kept top match scores in both dedupe and link tasks. The tool suits banks and other large data holders.
arxiv-2508-03967:
Mamadou Keita and co-authors present a method for spotting AI generated images in a 2025 paper. Older detectors often lean on low level artifacts tied to one generator, so they fail on new generators or damaged images. The team instead borrows retrieval, a trick that has improved text systems, and applies it to pictures.

Their framework, RAVID, encodes a query image with a tuned vision encoder and pulls the most relevant images from a database. A vision language model then judges the enriched input. On a benchmark covering nineteen generators, the method reached the best average accuracy. It also held up far better than rivals when images were blurred or compressed. The authors present retrieval as a new base for fake image detection.
arxiv-2508-04167:
Hiroki Kojima, Ivan Yevenko, and Takashi Ikegami published a paper in 2025 deriving an equation that decides which patterns in a continuous Game of Life can glide. Lenia smooths Conway's classic cellular world into continuous space, and it breeds self-propelling blobs called gliders. In the variant studied here, the rules are partial differential equations, so calculus can attack what simulation only shows.

The authors derive the glider conditions exactly and name them the Glider Equation. Used as a loss function, the equation lets gradient descent hunt stable gliders on purpose, including faster variants, and a speed-free version widens the search to any velocity. Many finds eventually destabilize, yet the method surfaces formations blind search would miss. Links to neural field models close the paper.
arxiv-2508-04867:
Jose Antonio Moreno and co-authors confirm robust superconductivity living on the surface of a layered crystal that is also a Weyl semimetal, a material with exotic electronic states. Earlier work had hinted that the surface turns superconducting at a far higher temperature than the bulk. Without seeing vortices, though, doubts remained about whether the phase was truly coherent.

Using a scanning tunneling microscope at very low temperature, the team measured a clear superconducting state tied to the surface's special electron arcs. They imaged quantized vortices, the tiny whirlpools that prove true superconductivity, and observed the Josephson effect between regions. The surface state held up to a stated magnetic field. The result firms up a platform where topology and superconductivity meet.
arxiv-2508-05367:
Newton Mwai, Emil Carlsson, and Fredrik Johansson present a 2025 paper on bandit learning for personal choices. Bandit methods learn by trying actions and watching rewards. Learning from scratch is too slow when one person faces few choices, as in care or tailored offers. Latent bandit models speed things up if a hidden state model is known. In practice that model is hard to find, and few hidden states may not fit everyone.

People with the same hidden state may rank treatments alike yet rate symptoms on unlike scales. The team relaxes the model to need only the ranking of actions in each state. Rankings survive scale gaps that break raw reward models. Care and product teams get faster personal learning with weaker demands on the model. The paper reframes what a latent model must supply: order, not exact numbers.
arxiv-2508-05467:
A large DESI collaboration paper, with H. Zou among its authors, shows how to merge two kinds of galaxies into one measuring tool. The DESI survey maps the universe using a frozen sound wave from the early cosmos as a yardstick. In one slice of cosmic time, its two galaxy types — heavy red ones and light-emitting young ones — overlap, and using both raises the density of markers and cuts noise.

The team built a pipeline that weights each galaxy by its clustering bias and tested it on simulated universes. On real first-release data, the merged catalog tightened the yardstick measures by about 11 and 7 percent on its two main numbers, matching the simulations.
arxiv-2508-05767: Cho-Ho Chu widens a fixed-point law in a 2025 note on maps of the disc. The old law says a self-map of the disc with no fixed point drives all starts to one edge point. Chu lifts that law to shaped domains of set rank in wide number spaces. The note is short, and its claim is the lift itself.
arxiv-2508-05867:
Mario Brcic, a solo author, warns that AI assistants with long memories could shift power over minds, in a 2025 paper. New assistants learn without pause and build deep personal memory of each user. That bond goes far past old privacy worries, Brcic argues. He names the stake cognitive sovereignty: the power of a person or nation to think freely and keep its own identity.

Value in such systems grows with the depth of memory held, which locks users in hard. The paper links that pull to mind risks, such as leaning on the tool to think and tying one's self to it. At world scale, he sees a new digital colonialism and quiet steering of public talk. His policy frame rests on memory portability, openness, home-grown systems, and alliances. The essay recasts AI help as a contest over who holds the mind's archive.
arxiv-2508-06367:
Antonio Beltrán studies a containment question in finite group theory, in a 2025 math paper. Take a group G, a normal subgroup N, and an element outside N. The coset of that element is a shifted copy of N. Beltrán asks when such a coset fits inside the union of just two conjugacy classes of G, the sets of elements that mirror each other by conjugation.

He shows N need not be solvable and can even be a non-abelian simple group. In those cases the two classes must share the same size, and the shape of N is tightly limited. Its key building blocks must be repeated copies of one simple group of Lie type in odd characteristic.
arxiv-2508-06467:
Making a language model forget specific data, for legal or safety reasons, often either leaves traces or damages unrelated knowledge. Ameya Anjarlekar and Sandeep Pombra propose GRIN, a targeted unlearning framework. Its core metric compares gradients to find the parameters most responsible for memorising the data marked for forgetting. Noise is then injected into just those parameters before a fine-tuning pass.

The selective disturbance aims to erase the unwanted material while sparing the rest of the model's skills. The authors also propose fresh evaluation measures suited to language models, and they test the approach on standard forgetting benchmarks covering fake biographies, hazardous knowledge, and safety data. The modular design lets each stage be swapped or audited separately.
arxiv-2508-06767:
Fleets of robots need routes that respect both each other and the networks carrying their data. Arman Dogru, Irem Bor-Yaliniz, and Nimal Gamini Senarath introduce a framework in 2025 for multi-agent path finding inside digital twin systems, virtual copies of real operations. Their method trains agents together but lets each act on its own, with priority rules that account for network load.

In simulations, the framework beat existing benchmarks on accuracy, speed, and scale. The authors also draw out data-sharing strategies meant to keep automated systems resilient in complex settings. They present the work as a bridge between network-aware choices and sturdy coordination for embodied machines.
arxiv-2508-06867:
Muhammad Awais Khan, Jérôme Droniou, Kim-Ngan Le, and Iuliu Sorin Pop studied solvers in twenty twenty-five for stochastic Stefan problems, which model phase changes like melting under random forcing. Simulating them requires repeatedly solving a nonlinear equation at every time step and for every random scenario, so solver efficiency dominates the cost.

The authors compare a standard Newton method against linearized solvers. The linearized versions reuse one coefficient matrix across all iterations, time steps, and noise realizations, so it can be factored once and for all. Convergence is slower per step, but the total cost can win. Sensitivity analysis with adaptive tolerances, in deterministic and stochastic settings, guides which solver to pick for a given scenario.
arxiv-2508-06967:
Shintaro Hokada, Shunsuke Iizuka, and Satoshi Takada propose in 2025 a faster way to compute contact between two elastic bodies, a classic problem set out by Hertzian contact theory. When two curved solids press together, the contact patch is an ellipse, and finding its shape usually takes heavy computation.

The authors give an incremental formula that updates the ellipticity of the contact disk step by step. It reaches good accuracy in only a few rounds, and it works from nearly round patches to very stretched ones. Faster contact math helps engineers who simulate gears, bearings, and wheels at scale.
arxiv-2508-07067:
Honghao Lin and three co-authors design sampling tools for huge data streams in this two thousand twenty-five paper. A stream passes once, too fast to store, so algorithms must sketch it on the fly. One key task is drawing a random item with chance tied to its frequency raised to a power. The authors give samplers that use nearly the least possible memory. One version updates its sample at every moment of the stream.

They then tackle streams where items can be forgotten, resetting their counts. That twist breaks older estimators with heavy bias. Their near-unbiased estimators cover the full range of powers in this harder model. The results serve the theory of data streams and the systems built on it.
arxiv-2508-07367:
Bilal Ghermoul presents near-complete progress on a number puzzle from 1956 in a paper from 2025. The puzzle asks whether five divided by any whole number can be split into three unit fractions. Unit fractions have one on top, like one half or one third. For most remainder classes modulo five, direct formulas were already known.

The hard class leaves remainder one when divided by five. Ghermoul gives explicit formulas for most of that class, using polynomial expressions. One subcase, tied to multiples of two hundred fifty-two, rests on a stated conjecture. Computer checks confirm the pattern up to about ten billion. The author includes the checking code with the paper.
arxiv-2508-07467:
Boris Altshuler derives spectral formulas for spinor and scalar loops in curved space in a 2025 paper. The setting is de Sitter space, the expanding geometry used in cosmology, with anti de Sitter space treated alongside. Products of harmonic functions there admit a standard expansion whose density weights carry the physics.

Compact formulas give those densities directly, and the flat space limits check out. Poles in the density line up with late time divergence of a loop in a Yukawa model with a light scalar field. Simple representations for the real parts of one loop self energies are proposed. Spectral equations for conformal dimensions follow in the chain approximation.
arxiv-2508-07667:
Wenkai Li and four co-authors present a 2025 arXiv framework for keeping private details private when language models juggle mixed information. A model summarizing a meeting must repeat the public decisions while swallowing the personal asides, and single models leak. Their design splits the privacy work among specialized agents: some extract candidate details, others classify them, with rounds of checking between.

By shrinking what any one agent must hold in mind, the framework adheres to context-specific privacy norms more reliably. The team also mapped how mistakes cascade, showing when an early miss becomes a later leak. On two benchmarks, their best setup cut private information leakage by about eighteen to nineteen percent with a leading commercial model, while keeping public content intact. The lesson is architectural: privacy improves when the plumbing of information flow is designed, not hoped for.
arxiv-2508-07767:
Marc Martí-Sabaté and four co-authors recast in 2025 the physics of topological waveguides as leaky cavity modes. Such guides carry waves along edges that shrug off defects, thanks to topological protection. Theory usually treats them as endless, yet every real device ends somewhere.

A quasinormal mode method describes the finite, open guide directly. Its spectrum is discrete and complex, and it matches the endless-ribbon picture closely. The edge states behave like light bouncing in a Fabry-Pérot cavity, steered rather than trapped. The frame gives engineers a sharper tool for designing finite topological devices, from acoustic chips to photonic circuits that route waves around damage.
arxiv-2508-07967:
Haijia Jin and co-authors map out how to run wireless networks that fly low, in a survey from 2025. Drones and other craft near the ground need links that both carry data and feed control loops. The team calls these systems low-altitude wireless networks, or LAWNs for short.

The survey lays out the parts of such a network and the scores used to judge it. It then weighs trade-offs across control, data links, and state estimation, the work of guessing what a craft is doing from afar. A case study shows craft working as a team while wireless limits bite. The authors close with open needs, such as growth to large fleets and strength when links fail. The piece aims to guide both design and field use.
arxiv-2508-08067:
Francesco Dell'Accio and co-authors present a numerical method for fractional derivatives, in a 2025 paper. Fractional derivatives extend the classic idea of a rate of change to non-integer orders. The Caputo form is widely used for systems with memory. The Bagley-Torvik equation is a standard test case for damped motion.

The method builds on the multinode Shepard scheme, paired with a Gauss-Jacobi quadrature rule. It first approximates the fractional derivative of a given function. The team then applies it to boundary value and initial value problems. Tests on the Bagley-Torvik equation confirm the method works well. Engineers who model such systems may find it useful. The approach is simple to adapt to other problems.
arxiv-2508-08267:
Clark introduces a new math idea called grationality in a 2025 paper, first shown at a 2025 meeting of a national math group. The idea mirrors rational numbers, but for shapes. A nice polygon is a regular shape whose side lengths are whole numbers. A number is grational if one nice shape has the same area as that many copies of a smaller nice shape.

Clark gives examples of numbers that are grational and numbers that are not. Theorems then link this trait to how numbers divide. The proofs use plain tools such as tiling, cutting shapes apart, and step by step descent, with many pictures. Readers see how simple tools, jokingly called math with a spoon, can still prove sharp results.
arxiv-2508-08467:
Lei Zhang and co-authors built a programming playground that lets children create their own augmented reality experiences with AI help, in a 2025 paper. Most children's AR and AI tools cast kids as consumers. Their system, Capybara, flips the role: children invent 3D characters, dress them with accessories, and overlay them on the real world through the camera.

Text-to-3D generative models turn a child's description into a character. Auto-rigging and body tracking make it move, and vision models recognize real objects so children can program interactions between their characters and the physical room. User studies with twenty children in the United States and Argentina showed the system could support rich, personalized creations. The authors argue the findings show children can harness generative AI as authors, not just audiences, and they present Capybara as evidence that creation-first design works for this age group.
arxiv-2508-08567:
Brendon McBain and Emanuele Viterbo study how much data can be stored in DNA and read back with nanopore sensors in a 2025 paper. Reading DNA strands gives a noisy signal, and common decoders first convert that signal into bases, which can lose information. The authors instead decode from a tractable model of the raw signal itself.

They derive message passing decoders for that model and a rate bound that can be applied to public sequencing data. Coding across strands of one hundred bases reached at least a set rate range per base in their tests, with a stated average. The rates use single reads only, so they call them cautious.
arxiv-2508-08867:
Lin Zeng, Boming Zhao, Jiarui Hu and colleagues present GaussianUpdate, a way to keep 3D scene models current as real places change in 2025. Scenes built with 3D Gaussian Splatting look sharp, but rebuilding them from scratch whenever furniture moves or objects vanish is wasteful.

Their method updates the Gaussian scene with new data while keeping what is still valid from before. A multi-stage strategy handles different kinds of change explicitly, and a visibility-aware learning scheme with generative replay refreshes the model without storing old images. Benchmarks showed high-quality, real-time rendering, plus the ability to visualise how a scene looked at different times.
arxiv-2508-08967:
Kuan-Tang Huang and four co-authors study why speech recognition falters on new recording channels in a 2025 paper. Pre-trained recognizers do well until the microphone or channel changes, when accuracy can drop sharply. Past work blamed mismatch between training and test collections. This study argues the channel itself changes speech traits in ways that fundamentally hurt recognition.

Their fix normalizes the model's internal features toward those of a clean reference channel. That alignment sharply improved performance on unseen channels and even unseen languages. The authors present the method as a general defense against channel variation, a common real-world deployment problem for speech systems.
arxiv-2508-09567:
Guo, Zhou, Bao, and Zhang study group velocity inside superradiant condensates around rotating black holes in a 2025 paper. Superradiance lets scalar fields draw energy and spin from a black hole, forming a cloud system. Past work focused on phase velocity, which moves around the hole.

The authors show the cloud has a rich group velocity pattern. Far from the black hole, the outward velocity follows a wave-like form over time and angle. The sideways and vertical speeds fade with distance. This local velocity map adds detail to how such clouds behave. The work extends knowledge of black hole and condensate pairs. It may inform future signal models.
arxiv-2508-09767:
Shuhei Kato proposed UtterTune in twenty twenty-five, a light method for fixing pronunciation in multilingual text-to-speech systems. Modern speech systems built on language models sound natural, but they often lack an explicit step that maps letters to sounds, so pronunciation control is weak. UtterTune uses low-rank adaptation, a small trainable patch, to steer one language's pronunciation without disturbing the others.

The test case is Japanese, where both segment sounds and pitch accent can be adjusted at the phoneme level. Evaluations, both measured and human-rated, confirm the edits work. Naturalness and speaker similarity hold up in a zero-shot setting, where the voice was never trained on. The method offers precise control for one language at a time inside a shared multilingual system.
arxiv-2508-09967:
Xiang, Li, Zhang, and Li present a study from twenty twenty-five on sorting tissue slides with very few labeled cases. Whole slide images are huge, and expert labels are scarce in clinics. New image-and-text base models can sort slides with no labels, but they trail classic methods. Few-label methods help, yet their fixed sorter designs crack under data scarcity. The team's sorter picks and tunes its own design from a bank of sorter types. A guide part learns how to blend those options.

Their sorter beat prior methods on several few-label test sets. On one lung cancer set, its score rose by a clear margin over the best rival. Gains were largest when just one case per class was given. The authors say the tool suits clinics with very little labeled data.
arxiv-2508-10167:
Rayan Trabelsi builds in a 2025 study a route from a neat class of physics matrices to quantum circuits that mimic their motion. The matrices, called Toeplitz, repeat along their diagonals and show in wave and heat problems. He splits them into diagonal parts and sorts those parts into a few families.

That sorting yields deep simplifications, above all when indices are powers of two. As a capstone he writes out the full circuit for a classic equation of spread, the discrete Poisson case. The work grew from a master's internship, and it maps a tidy bridge from matrix form to circuit form.
arxiv-2508-10367:
Pablo Hernandez-Camara and colleagues borrow a classic test of human eyesight science to probe how vision-language models actually see. The contrast sensitivity function charts the faintest contrast a viewer can detect at each spatial scale, from broad stripes to fine ones. Writing in twenty twenty-five, the team treats each model as a test subject. It views filtered noise patterns and answers structured prompts, and its yes-no answers are fitted into psychometric curves that yield thresholds, with no peeking inside the model. Several current models were put through the full procedure.

Some models matched the human curve in shape, others in overall scale, but none matched both. Answers also swung with small changes in prompt wording, a fragility the authors flag. The measured curves predicted how models coped with blurred and adversarial images, which the team offers as evidence the test is a useful diagnostic.
arxiv-2508-10567:
Philipp Wolters and co-authors add radar to self-driving car perception in this 2025 paper. Systems that drive end to end, from sensors to steering in one model, promise better results, but camera-only setups struggle in bad weather, blocked views, and judging speed. Radar answers some of those gaps, since it senses motion directly and cares little for rain or fog.

Their system, SpaRC-AD, fuses camera and radar in a query-based design. Sparse three-dimensional feature matching and radar-based speed estimates build a scene model used to refine object anchors, map lines, and motion forecasts. Against camera-only rivals it lifted detection, tracking, and mapping scores and cut prediction and planning errors. Tests covered city driving data and a closed-loop simulator.
arxiv-2508-10667:
Xu and a team including Zhang, Fan, and Zhou teach image models to find a street address from a street photo in this twenty twenty-five paper. Big image-language models can name a town or land, but they often fail at the exact street spot inside a city. Street photos alone give only small local clues.

Inside, the method adds sky-view maps as wide clues and trains the model to match the two views. The team built question-and-answer sets from street photos in Pittsburgh and San Francisco to test it. Their model beat rival models by wide gaps on both sets. The work points to maps as a strong aid for fine place finding.
arxiv-2508-10767:
Miyagi, Heinz, and Schwenk count from first laws a high bend in the charge spread of two key atoms, in a study from 2025. The bend, the fourth charge span, may tell how thick the neutron skin of a rich core runs. Skins tie cores to neutron star stuff, so the stakes are wide.

First-law counts for the calcium and lead cores show the bend locks hard to charge and neutron spans. That lock lets the team call the bend for both cores. The tie to skin, though, proves weak. Fine charge reads, they warn, can not name the skin sans a model crutch. A hoped clean probe turns out to need help.
arxiv-2508-11067:
Sourojit Ghosh and Kyra Wilson review ten years of research on bias in artificial intelligence and large language models, in work published in 2025. They read 189 papers from four major venues in the field. Their aim is to map what bias research has covered, what it has left out, and how often its ideas reach real systems.

Most of the papers, they find, never define bias in human terms and give only a math or technical sense of the word. Nearly four in five focus on gender, while race, age, faith, and nationality get far less attention. Only about one paper in ten tells builders how to use the findings in practice. The authors call for wider coverage of groups outside the West.
arxiv-2508-11167:
Jianhong Han, Yupei Wang, and Liang Chen present a detector for objects in remote sensing images that adapts to a new domain without access to the source data. Their 2025 paper notes that privacy and transmission limits often block source images in real work. Self training methods fill the gap but can collapse when their auto-generated labels are noisy.

Their system, VG-DETR, brings in a vision foundation model to check those labels, using a small set of labeled target images. It rescues good predictions hidden among low confidence ones. A two level alignment step matches detector features to the foundation model's features, for single objects and whole images alike. Tests showed top results on source-free tasks.
arxiv-2508-11667:
Bryan Tuck and Rakesh Verma present a way to spot adversarial text attacks on transformer models by testing how stable their internal representations are, in a 2025 paper. Their method, Guided Perturbation Sensitivity, first ranks the words in a text by importance, then masks the top few and watches how much the model's embedding shifts. A small detector network reads the resulting pattern.

Tampered words turned out to react far more strongly to masking than honestly important words. Across three data sets, three attack types, and two victim models, the detector topped 85 percent accuracy, often at lower cost than rivals. It also carried over to new data and attacks without retraining, which the authors stress as its practical edge.
arxiv-2508-11767:
Kasmanoff and Zalkikar wrote in twenty twenty-five about using imitation learning to spot bad behavior in chat models. Imitation learning copies expert examples when no clear reward exists. Applied to conversation, it yields both a talking policy and a judge. The judge learns to tell expert chats from machine-made ones. The talking policy worked well enough on its task.

The judge's results were the more telling part for the authors. Its scores exposed limits in how dialog models behave. They argue the same trick can audit other data models built for chat tasks. Any flawed pattern the judge catches can guide fixes. The work reframes a training tool as a safety check. It needs no hand-built list of bad behaviors.
arxiv-2508-12167:
Ali Rostami-Shirazi and co-authors ask why Milky Way star clusters hold so much mass in dark stellar remnants, in a 2025 paper. Comparing a cluster's moving mass with its starlight mass shows a gap of more than two times, and the hidden mass sits at the center. Most of it is thought to be white dwarfs. Yet giving over half a cluster's mass to white dwarfs would strain accounts of how clusters evolve, unless black holes change the story.

The team ran a grid of direct simulations of clusters, varying the kick that newborn black holes receive. Only runs with low kicks matched the dark remnant share seen in real clusters. Held black holes gather at the center and act as an energy source, throwing energy into the whole cluster through close encounters. That energy pushes out bright stars and remnants at different rates, raising the dark share.
arxiv-2508-12367:
Vandana Rajpal and Arpit Kansal study the ideal spaces of a tensor product used in operator theory, in a short paper published in 2025. The product joins a ternary ring of operators, a structure from functional analysis, with a C-star algebra. Ideals are special subsets that help reveal how such a product is built.

The authors characterize three kinds of ideals for this product: primal, factorial, and Glimm ideals. Giving a clear account of these spaces helps other workers tell when products built in this way share the same deep structure. The paper is brief and proof-focused, aimed at readers who already work with operator algebras and tensor products of this special kind.
arxiv-2508-12467:
Umesh Shankar proves that the rows of a broad family of triangular number arrays always bend the right way. The family is defined by a super-recurrence, a powered version of the rule behind Stirling, Lah, and Eulerian numbers. Many recent generalizations of those classics obey the powered rule. Writing in twenty twenty-five, Shankar gives sufficient conditions for every row to be log-concave, meaning each entry squared dominates the product of its neighbors. The proof reads the array as weighted lattice paths and builds a weight-increasing injection.

The single condition covers the classical examples at once, a unified route to their log-concavity. It also confirms a conjecture about generalized Lah numbers. The paper closes by introducing a two-parameter generalization of the Eulerian numbers, shown palindromic, with remarks on deeper positivity properties.
arxiv-2508-12767:
Altangerel Gereltsetseg and Tejfel Mate survey ways to speed up the data plane of software-defined networks, in a 2025 paper. Such networks split control from the hardware that moves packets. Control has been studied for years, while programming the moving layer is newer. A 2019 seminar of leading researchers set the open problems for the decade.

The authors review those problems and papers in the field. They suggest four fixes: richer language features for outside tasks, compression based on packet size, caching inside the network, and offloading work to extra threads or machines. Each fix targets packet speed or better link use. The paper maps options for a young, fast-moving area.
arxiv-2508-13267:
Hugo Tranin and a large team of co-authors merge the sky's galaxy lists into one deep catalog in a 2025 paper. Sky watchers who chase flashes and gravity-wave events need sure distances, sizes, and star masses for galaxies, yet old lists fade past a short range or mix in stars. The new list draws on major surveys and cleans the set with star data.

Near eighty million galaxies sit in the list, reaching far past prior lists. Star masses come with most entries, and shape fits with most as well. In trials the list found many more hosts for known star blasts than older lists could.
arxiv-2508-13367:
A bundle of fibers under load fails fiber by fiber, and heat can trigger those failures over time, a slow process called creep failure. The four authors build an equal load sharing fiber bundle model in which transition state theory sets the rate of elementary failures. For uniform fiber thresholds they derive the lifetime distribution, its mean and variance, and their asymptotic limits, all matching simulations closely.

The scaling with fiber number matches earlier analytical results for a Gaussian noise breakdown model at low temperature. For random fiber strengths the lifetime distribution becomes a multi-dimensional integral with no closed form, yet simulations show similar large-bundle scaling. Failures come in avalanches set off by single thermal events, and the avalanche size distribution matches theory for quasistatic loading.
arxiv-2508-13567:
Wenji Zhou and co-authors present in 2025 ENCODE, a two-stage method that models long user behavior strings for click prediction. Long histories hold rich taste clues, but serving systems need fast answers. Past tools drop parts of the string or pull weak matches, which loses key signals.

ENCODE first clusters the full history offline and pulls exact taste points from each cluster. A lean distance learner cuts the cost of that clustering step. Online, the stored tastes then score the current target item fast. The design keeps full use of the string and high match to the target, breaking the usual trade-off.
arxiv-2508-13667:
Kun Fang introduced in 2025 a light software tool for modeling the gamma-ray glow around pulsars, spinning dead stars that shed energetic particles. Those particles scatter background light up to gamma-ray energies, forming a halo. Halos can probe how cosmic rays spread over short galactic distances.

Standard models assume smooth, even spreading, but real transport is likely messier. The new tool includes several transport models tied to different ideas about where halos come from. Users set up runs through a plain config file, with no code edits. Its grid method stays stable on uneven grids and where spreading jumps sharply. The tool is aimed at a growing set of sharper halo data.
arxiv-2508-13867:
Mingliang Zhong and co-authors add an uncertainty module to OpenLB, an open-source library for lattice Boltzmann flow simulation. Simulations of fluid flow rest on input values that are never exact, so honest results need error bounds. Their 2025 paper, written for a mathematical software journal, builds that check into the library itself.

The module uses non-intrusive stochastic collocation, with polynomial chaos and Monte Carlo sampling of the inputs. Tests cover a Taylor-Green vortex with up to four uncertain inputs and flow past a cylinder. Convergence matched theory, and the method scaled well on large machines. Flow modelers get a toolkit that reports not just the flow, but how much to trust it.
arxiv-2508-14067:
Sonakshi Chauhan and four co-authors present a 2025 study of where language models gather and move information, starting with punctuation. Earlier work flagged punctuation tokens as attention sinks and memory aids. Using interventions that remove or swap parts of the input, the team tested whether punctuation is necessary and sufficient for performance across layers in GPT-2, DeepSeek, and Gemma.

The answer split by model: in GPT-2 punctuation was both necessary and sufficient in many layers, less so in DeepSeek, and not at all in Gemma. The team then asked whether models freeze early summaries of sentence parts or stay sensitive to changes layer by layer. Conditional and universal statements turned out to be processed very differently. The findings warn against generalizing one model's internals to all.
arxiv-2508-14267:
Mihai-Silviu Lazorec and Marius Tărnăuceanu study counts of conjugacy classes of subgroups in two thousand twenty-five. Two ratios gauge how near a finite group sits to a Dedekind group. In Dedekind groups all subgroups are normal, a rare tidy trait. One ratio weighs subgroup classes against the full subgroup lattice.

For nilpotent groups, that ratio fills the whole unit interval densely. A high floor on the second ratio forces a group to be nilpotent. A still higher floor forces an Iwasawa group structure. A final result pins when p groups count as Dedekind. Structure facts ride along with each bound.
arxiv-2508-14567:
Walter Zimmer and co-authors present a data set of real highway crashes in a 2025 paper on road safety. Rare, severe events are the hardest for safety systems to learn, since normal driving data contains almost none. Their TUM Traffic Accident set fills that gap with recordings of actual high-speed collisions.

The set holds ten crash sequences filmed by four roadside cameras and laser scanners. Nearly 300,000 two-dimensional boxes and 93,000 three-dimensional boxes are labelled across more than 48,000 frames, covering ten object classes. The team also built a detection model that mixes fixed rules with learned ones. Tests in the paper show the model is robust, and the data, model, and code are shared in public for other teams.
arxiv-2508-14767:
Fabian Holst, Emre Gulsoylu, and Simone Frintrop build a vessel pose data set from cameras and transponders in a 2025 paper. Ships broadcast identity and position signals automatically. Those feeds suffer delays, manipulation, and dropouts. Camera images alone lack the scale for 3D pose.

Fusing both sources yields labeled poses without manual annotation. A detection network finds vessels in ordinary photos. Broadcast messages supply position and heading for matching ships. Two alignment methods competed for projecting data into images. The geometry-based method clearly beat homography on projection error. Detection quality reached a solid average precision score. The resulting public data set holds thousands of annotated harbor images. Each carries a full 3D bounding box pose. Training pose estimators is the intended use. Maritime autonomy and harbor monitoring both need such data. The fusion recipe transfers to other camera networks.
arxiv-2508-15167:
Mónica Clapp and Carlos Culebro prove sign changing solutions exist for a field equation in a 2025 paper. The equation pairs a wave spread term with a pull from a fading field. Its push term is tame far out and wild near the start.

On outer domains that stretch to infinity, they ask for warps that cross zero set times. Mild shape rules on the domain give the room they need. In four or more dimensions, rich domain shapes meet the rules. For each such shape, any set count of sign flips can be forced. The work widens the map of still wave shapes.
arxiv-2508-15267:
Ruilin Zhou, Jinglei Cheng, Yuhang Gan, Junyu Liu, and Chen Qian address a hard step in shared quantum computing in a 2025 paper. A quantum program must be split across linked machines, each with its own layout. Poor splits waste the weak links between machines and slow the whole run.

Their method first groups the program's bits by how the circuit is built. It then places those groups on machines and fine-tunes the map with a slow-cool search. In tests, the method cut the cost score by up to 88.40 percent next to a base method. The gain helps large programs fit mixed machine sets.
arxiv-2508-16067:
Teddy Koker, Mit Kotak, and Tess Smidt train a foundation model for materials science on a shoestring, in a paper published in two thousand twenty-five. Such models predict how atoms arrange and vibrate, but training the leaders costs so much compute that most research groups cannot compete.

Their model, Nequix, is a compact potential that respects three-dimensional rotations and reflections by design. It simplifies a known architecture and adds modern training practices, including a specialized layer normalization and the Muon optimizer. The whole model has seven hundred thousand parameters. Training took one hundred hours on a single class of high-end GPU. On two public benchmarks it ranks third overall, at about a twentieth of the training cost of most rivals. It also runs about a hundred times faster than the top-ranked model. Weights and a reproducible codebase are released openly.
arxiv-2508-16267:
Alina Fastowski, Bardh Prenkaj, and Gjergji Kasneci measured how sturdy a language model's facts are under changed decoding in a 2025 paper. Past tests judged fact strength by score alone or by tweaked prompts, which miss what happens inside generation. Their score pairs a fact's starting uncertainty with how much heat in the sampling choice shakes it.

Across five models and three question sets, strength varied widely. Small models scored lower than large ones, and accuracy fell by about three fifths as uncertainty rose. The gap shows that a fact can be right yet fragile. The authors lay the ground for models that hold facts more firmly.
arxiv-2508-16567:
Shay Gilpin questions a quiet assumption behind ensemble methods in weather and climate forecasting. Forecasters run many model copies, called an ensemble, and use the spread among them to estimate forecast error. Because the same model moves both the forecast and its error estimate, it is usually assumed that an accurate forecast means an accurate error estimate, apart from sampling noise.

Through math and computer tests, Gilpin shows that this assumption fails when the features being tracked shrink toward the size of the model grid. In flows governed by simple movement, the forecast itself stays accurate while the error estimate can be off by ten times more than expected. Standard fixes such as inflating the spread or limiting its reach do not repair the gap. The work warns that the problem is built into the method itself.
arxiv-2508-16867:
David Beauchemin and Richard Khoury introduce a 2025 dataset of language judgments for Quebec French. Big language models do well on many tasks, but how much grammar they truly grasp is less clear. Judgment sets, where each sentence is marked as sound or not, help test that grasp. The new set holds more than 25,000 in-domain sentences and a smaller out-of-domain set.

The pair also tested seven models on this and seven other judgment sets. Tuned transformer models were strong baselines for most languages. Large models asked with no training did poorly on the task. Cross-language models showed no sign of having picked up Quebec French judgment in pre-training. The set is built from rule examples, not speaker feelings.
arxiv-2508-17067:
Good and co-authors derive particle creation from entanglement entropy in this 2025 paper. They work out explicit links between entropy and the spectrum, count, and total energy of radiated particles. Test cases span fast-accelerating motion, black hole evaporation, and beta decay.

Known results are matched where they exist and extended elsewhere. The team focuses on the low-entropy limit, akin to slow motion, then checks bursts from harmonic cycles. The upshot is a working bridge between information flow and matter creation. They frame it as a concrete case of the slogan that things come from bits.
arxiv-2508-17267:
Bingang Guo, Wei Kou, and Xurong Chen model photon condensation in a cold electron gas in a 2025 paper. High energy photons bouncing off cold electrons lose energy by inverse Compton scattering. The team tracks the photon spread over time with a modified Kompaneets equation, starting from a black-body spectrum.

Photon counts pile up at the low energy tail, a sign of Bose-Einstein condensation, they find. Entropy tracking backs the picture: the condensed state matches the entropy peak reached during cooling. The work frames photon condensation in cold electron settings as an entropy driven process, with a full theory outline.
arxiv-2508-17367:
Régis Mélin, Asmaul Smitha Rashid, Romain Danneau, and Morteza Kayyalha revisit the adiabatic limit in large multi-terminal Josephson junctions. Their paper from twenty twenty-five responds to fresh experiments that probe new size and voltage ranges. As bias voltage grows in big devices, the electrochemical potential nears the level spacing of the core. New effects then enter the current.

A counting result anchors the model: correlated pairs from colliding Floquet-Kulik quartet levels form a fixed share set by the channel count. The team then treats the central metal as a continuum under slow-change rules. Andreev modes move through populations tuned by voltage and flux. Set voltage scales emerge for the wobble of critical current. Those scales touch quartet, topology, and Floquet readings alike. Recent Harvard and Penn State tests inspired the frame.
arxiv-2508-17467:
Krishna Teja Chitty-Venkata and seven co-authors benchmark mixture-of-experts models in a paper from two thousand twenty-five. Such models reach huge parameter counts while staying efficient, by routing each input to a few expert subnetworks. At inference time, they face load imbalance across experts and extra routing cost.

Their bench study varies batch size, sequence length, and key model settings across several model families. They test optimization tricks on high-end Nvidia GPUs, including pruning, fused operations, speculative decoding, and quantization. Parallel strategies were also compared. Results show how performance shifts across configurations. The authors aim to guide efficient deployment of these models in practice.
arxiv-2508-17767:
Guangwei Zhang and co-authors built ISACL in 2025, a guard that spots when a language model is about to leak training text. Models can learn text that is under copyright and then spit it back out. Most guards check the output after it is made, which is too late to stop a leak. This team reads the model's inner state before it writes a word.

A classifier trained on known guarded works flags risky inner states. The host system can then halt the reply or steer it aside. The tool is wired into a search-aided setup that checks rights as it works. The authors say the early read cuts leak risk at scale while the text stays strong.
arxiv-2508-17967:
Mona Bhukta and co-authors film tiny magnetic whirlpools as they bump into each other in real time, in work from twenty twenty-five. The whirlpools, called skyrmions, sit in a material where spins cancel out. How they scatter shapes plans for fast, small magnetic devices.

The team used X-ray movies to watch a skyrmion grid driven by current pulses. At low drive, free skyrmions hit pinned ones and bounced back over a few billionths of a second. At higher drive, the whole grid moved as one clean sheet. Math fits gave the force range between skyrmions, which matched computer models. The grid ran well at high speed over billions of cycles. Control held even in the messy flow mode.
arxiv-2508-18167:
Deep Patel, Iain Melvin, Christopher Malon and Martin Renqiang Min teach language models when to speak in group discussions, in their 2025 arXiv paper. Models usually answer only when prompted, which limits them as collaborators. Their framework, DiscussLLM, trains models to judge the moment, not just the message.

A two-stage pipeline synthesizes realistic multi-turn human discussions, each tagged with an intervention type such as factual correction or concept definition, and a trigger point where help adds value. Models learn to emit a silent token when no intervention is needed. Two designs are compared: one integrated model, and a split classifier-generator built for low latency. Timing and helpfulness are both evaluated.
arxiv-2508-18367:
Minchev and co-authors warn that wandering stars distort galaxy histories in a 2025 paper. Astronomers rebuild a disk galaxy's star formation history from where stars sit today, region by region. That habit assumes stars stayed near their birth radius. In real disks, stars migrate inward and outward over billions of years.

Using zoom-in simulations of galaxy formation, the team measured the bias this creates. In inner disks, early star formation is understated by a quarter to a half, while late formation is overstated. In outer disks, mid-age stars are overstated by up to two or threefold, since many were born inside and drifted out. History peaks flatten and spread, and inside-out growth looks slower than it was. The authors say surveys of nearby galaxies must correct for this drift, using disk mass, bars, and motion as clues.
arxiv-2508-18467:
Olivia Long and Carter Teplica study how language models act when they think they face themselves in a 2025 paper. As AI agents take on long tasks, they meet other agents more often. Most past work looked at human and AI pairs, not AI with AI.

The team adapted a classic public goods game played in rounds. Four models played either against an unnamed AI or against what they were told was themselves. That framing shifted how much the models cooperated. Though the game is a toy, the result hints that labels alone can sway agent teamwork in real multi-agent systems.
arxiv-2508-18567:
