Darin Tsui, Kunal Talreja, and Amirali Aghazadeh test sparse autoencoders for protein work with few labels in 2025. Protein scores from sequence alone stall when lab tags are scarce for a new task. Sparse codes split rich model codes into clear trait units that may carry more signal per tag.

With as few as 24 tagged strings, sparse codes match or beat their base model on score forecasts across tasks. Steering the strong trait units yields top-grade builds in 83 percent of design cases tried. The gains beat builds steered by the raw base codes alone.
arxiv-2508-18867:
Oleg Stepanyuk and Kamen Kozarev follow one solar eruption across four instruments to settle how its front should be defined. A coronal mass ejection is a huge cloud of gas and magnetic field blown off the Sun. Its shape seems to change with each telescope and wavelength, which fuels debate about where the front, the shock, and the core sit. Their 2025 study tracks a large event from May 7, 2021, seen at the Sun's eastern edge.

Images came in sequence from a space telescope suite, a ground coronagraph in Hawaii, and two telescopes on a solar observatory craft. The team traces the front from the low corona outward without gaps. Their step-by-step map gives other researchers a shared reference for what each bright rim in an image really is.
arxiv-2508-19267:
Sai Teja Reddy Adapala and Yashwanth Reddy Alugubelly present a 2025 paper on a security frame for self running AI agents. As agents act on their own and talk to each other, new risks appear. Old security tools were not built for hijacked control flow or failures that cascade across agents.

Their frame, called Aegis, stacks three parts. The first gives each agent an ID that cannot be faked, based on a web standard. The second guards messages with math that should resist future quantum computers. The third checks that agents follow policy, using proofs that hide private data. The authors test the frame against a standard list of threat types.
arxiv-2508-19367:
Alex Cuellar, Ho Chit Siu, and Julie Shah teach robots to infer how people want objects arranged, from watching examples. Their 2025 paper notes that robots are getting better at pick-and-place work like packing and sorting. What lags is a rich way to express human rules about relative position, such as what counts as beside, inside, or apart.

They introduce a formal logic framework that extends a known calculus of region connections with position details. An inference algorithm learns such rules from demonstrations. In a human study, the learned rules captured what people intended. Learning from demonstration also beat asking people to write the rules themselves.
arxiv-2508-19467:
Picking out harm reports in social posts on opioid use is the task set by Sumon Kanti Dey and co-authors in a 2025 arXiv paper. People share drug use stories online that clinics never hear. The team built a data set of first-person posts marked for health harms, like withdrawal, and social harms, like job loss. Their marked set refines an older one with tighter rules.

A tuned mid-size model beat big chat models on exact picks and rule fit. It also did well with far less marked data. Yet its scores still sat well below the match rate between human experts. Deep field knowledge still sets humans apart in this task.
arxiv-2508-19767:
Star clusters make good clocks, since all their stars share one age, but reading that age well is tricky. Brogaard and seven co-authors aim for a firm age for the open cluster NGC 6633. Their 2025 study mixes data from the Gaia space mission with older data from the CoRoT mission.

The team picks out five giant stars that belong to the cluster, using light data, Gaia measures, and past spectra. For those giants, tremor-like waves in the star reveal mass and size. Set next to model tracks, those values pin down the cluster age in a way that stands apart from the usual colour plot method. The work also tests how mixing inside a star, spun by rotation, shifts age estimates.
arxiv-2508-19967:
Grainge and co-authors present a 2025 study grading how well vision-language models can guess where a photo was taken. Pinpointing place from visual clues helps rescue work and teaching, but it also endangers privacy. A model that reads street signs and skylines could stalk people from casual posts. The team tested twenty-five top models on four image sets from varied settings.

Generic street photos fooled the models badly. Social-media-style images, though, were placed correctly about sixty-one percent of the time at the tested precision. The paper probes how the models reason their way to a guess. The authors urge quick safeguards as the skill sharpens with each model generation.
arxiv-2508-20367:
Luke Bhan, Miroslav Krstic, and Yuanyuan Shi present a 2025 control study on systems whose actuators respond only after a delay of unknown length. Predictor feedback cancels such delays by forecasting the system's future state, but the forecast has no exact formula for nonlinear systems. The authors replace the forecast with a neural operator, a learned map trained once offline and then run fast online. They build the theory on the delay's description as a transport equation.

A Lyapunov-style proof shows the closed loop settles near the target, with the slack set by the learning error and the delay bounds. Tests on a biological switch system ran about fifteen times faster than standard numerical methods. The work gives learned predictors a firm stability footing for real control tasks.
arxiv-2508-20567:
Yangfan Wang and co-authors introduce in 2025 a sampling method that widens the variety of multi hop questions a system can generate for question answering training. Such questions need facts from several places, and sparse data lets models learn false patterns. Past fixes varied wording or planned content, but often made simple questions and skipped key knowledge in the source text.

Their method samples varied sets of knowledge pieces from a context, framed as predicting the next most relevant sentence, trained with a contrastive style loss. A random decoding step balances accuracy and variety. The picker improved by about four points over rivals, and questions built with it raised scores on two standard multi hop test sets.
arxiv-2508-20767:
Teresa Bister reviews what cosmic ray data can tell us about the sources of the most energetic particles known, in work from 2025. These particles arrive from space with huge energies, yet their origin is still unknown. Two large observatories now give rich, exact data.

Patterns in energy and mass above a bend in the spectrum fit distant sources spread evenly through space. The particles are mostly mid-weight nuclei. Arrival directions show a broad tilt and a few warm spots at the highest energies. Those clues limit how many sources there can be and where they sit. Puzzles remain, such as why the sources look so alike and why some events point to empty regions.
arxiv-2508-20867:
Rohan Phanse and co-authors built benchmarks for AI that must weave answers from many sources in this 2025 paper. Retrieval-augmented systems fetch documents before writing. Most tests let one document hold the whole answer, but real questions scatter facts across sources that no single page covers.

Their framework spins up such tests at scale. Two benchmarks came out of it: one on story synthesis, one on meeting summaries, both pulling from large collections. Trials with varied fetchers and top language models show answer quality riding on fetch quality. Even with perfect fetching, weaving stays hard. Reasoning models, though, clearly out-wove standard ones at that step.
arxiv-2508-20967:
Ernesto Birgin, Geovani Grapiglia, and Diaulas Marcondes design in 2025 faster ways to minimize bumpy functions whose variables must stay within bounds. Such problems appear across engineering and data work. Their methods combine active-set logic, which fixes variables sitting at their limits, with Newton steps solved cheaply by an iterative solver.

Two escape routes from flat faces are studied: a spectral gradient method and a cube-regularized Newton variant. The authors prove how many function calls each needs to reach a near-stationary point, with the second scaling better in accuracy. Computer tests against existing methods favor their approach, and the cheap solver beat the standard one for Newton directions.
arxiv-2508-21067:
Aaron Kleger and Rufus Boyack examine physical limits on effective non-Hermitian systems in work from 2025. Open and interacting quantum systems are often modeled with a Hamiltonian that is not Hermitian, but the model must obey strict rules.

A common shortcut inserts the anti-Hermitian part straight into the Green function. The authors show that shortcut clashes with the standard theory for interacting systems. They give a consistent description instead, in terms of pseudo-Hermitian quantum mechanics. They also characterize low-temperature distributions and apply the results to the light response of a model system.
arxiv-2508-21167:
Lee and co-authors build RARR, a system that reads daily activities from floor and surface vibrations inside a real home. One in four people with dementia lives alone, and remote monitoring could ease the load on distant family caregivers. Vibration sensors are discreet and protect privacy, but home setups usually demand large amounts of labeled data for each new user.

RARR sidesteps that burden by learning first from sound. The team pretrains its model on synthetic data made from near-surface audio, which mimics the signals activities produce. A small amount of real labeled data then fine-tunes the model for a given home and person. The result aims at robust tracking of daily routines that holds up across new users and new rooms. That design targets the gap between tidy laboratory results and messy real-world deployment.
arxiv-2508-21567:
Tan Van Vu, Ryotaro Honma, and Keiji Saito derive, in a 2025 preprint, universal limits on how precise any observable can be in an open quantum system. Such systems leak into their surroundings at any coupling strength. Known uncertainty relations tie precision to thermodynamic cost, but mostly for memoryless, Markovian settings. Memory changes the game, and bounds there were missing. The authors measure each process against its time-reversed twin. The gap between forward and backward paths becomes an asymmetry term in the bound.

For currents that flip sign under time reversal, precision is capped by entropy production plus that asymmetry. For general observables, a floor on relative fluctuation is set by an activity term describing environmental change. The framework covers arbitrary coupling and two-point measurement schemes. The authors present it as the broad map of precision limits that the Markovian results only sketched.
arxiv-2508-21667:
Abhishek Setty presents a new way to load sparse matrices into quantum algorithms, in a 2025 paper. Block encoding is the step that lets a quantum computer work on a matrix, and it feeds methods for simulation and solving linear systems. The costly part is often the oracle that maps matrix positions to circuit controls. Setty's framework centers on coherent permutation, a way to shuffle quantum states in a controlled fashion.

The method unifies shift, delete, and insert moves on indices and squeezes down the control logic needed. It also ties amplitude permutation to combinatorial optimization, so control states can be assigned with hardware limits in mind. Tests on IBM quantum backends showed large cuts in circuit depth for the examples tried. The gains are strongest for matrices with regular structure.
arxiv-2509-00167:
W. F. Lamberti, S. R. Lawrence, D. White, S. Kim, and S. Abdullah run a pilot study in 2025 on generative AI and critical thinking in college classes. Such tools spread fast in education, yet their role in growing critical thought is little studied. Past work casts the tools as tutors or as assignment helpers, not as objects of critique.

Their classes in computational and data science ask students to analyze, critique, and revise AI-generated solutions. The tasks stress that AI output is often flawed in context or plain wrong. Early findings show how well students apply structured critical thinking to those outputs. The pilot lays groundwork for larger studies in future terms on teaching with AI present.
arxiv-2509-00267:
Axel Gross, Samuel Cupp, and Matthew R. Mumpower calculate the particle signals from decaying r-process nuclei in 2025. The r-process, rapid neutron capture, forges heavy elements in extreme cosmic events. Its nuclei decay by beta decay, shedding electrons, gamma rays, neutrinos, and neutrons as they settle.

The team computes emission spectra from first principles, using detailed nuclear structure and decay data for each particle kind. A reaction network simulation then tracks how those spectra evolve over time. The distributions shift strongly with time and are non-thermal, with substantial average energies. Such signals could probe heavy element formation directly, across many messenger types at once.
arxiv-2509-01467:
A tool called NMR reads the states of atomic nuclei. Reading those spins with light could push fine sensing toward single molecules. Evgenij Vasilenko, with eight co-authors, reports optical readout of nuclear spins in a europium-based crystal. Very narrow optical lines let the team prepare and detect the spin states with light.

Radio waves drove two nuclear resonances. Those lines were narrow and clearly linked to the optical line in use. The team ran standard spin tools: Rabi oscillations, spin echo, and decoupling pulses. These steer the spins and shield them from noise. Nuclear coherence lasted up to two milliseconds. The results mark a step toward light-based NMR in precisely built molecular systems for quantum technology.
arxiv-2509-01667:
Adam G Riess leads eleven authors who test whether crowded star fields bias a key cosmic distance measure. Their study uses new James Webb Space Telescope views of Cepheids, which are stars that pulse in brightness on a steady rhythm. The team targets NGC 3447, a supernova host galaxy whose young companion has almost no old stars behind the Cepheids.

Inside, the authors compare telescope data under crowded, clear, and nearly empty background conditions. They find no shift between the parts of the system and much tighter scatter where the background is empty. Combined with other hosts, their value for the Hubble constant stays well above the early universe prediction. The result supports the view that crowding does not explain the gap.
arxiv-2509-02167:
Jing Wang leads four co-authors with AudioRWKV, an efficient bidirectional architecture for audio pattern recognition. Transformer audio models scale poorly with sequence length due to quadratic cost. State space rivals can turn unstable when scaled up. Their design inherits a stable recurrent form from a recent RWKV generation with linear cost.

A two dimensional depthwise convolution replaces the one dimensional token shift to catch local time frequency patterns. The core kernel becomes bidirectional, letting each point see global context while keeping linear complexity. The smallest variant matches a much larger rival model on performance. Long audio over five minutes processes many times faster than the transformer baseline. Throughput stays more stable than competing designs in tests.
arxiv-2509-02867:
Christian A. Schröder, Reinhard Kienberger, and Stephen R. Leone introduced a 2025 physics paper about software for planning a special kind of light source. The source uses high-harmonic generation, where a strong laser pulse makes a gas emit much higher energy light. Such beams support very fast spectroscopy, the study of matter through its light.

Their program is free for anyone to use and change. It models both the tiny single-atom response and the way light builds up across a whole gas target. That breadth lets it fit many setups, from extreme ultraviolet light to soft X-rays. The team checked its output against four common laboratory arrangements. Labs can use it to design and improve these demanding light sources.
arxiv-2509-03067:
Lukas Freter and 5 co-authors developed a 2025 theory of dynamical superradiance in organic materials. Superradiance happens when many excited emitters release energy together into one light mode, faster and brighter than they would alone. In organic matter, electronic states constantly interact with molecular vibrations, which complicates that shared release.

The team studied two models: vibrations as a surrounding bath that scrambles phase, and vibrations built directly into the system. Using symmetry, they solved one model exactly for well over a hundred emitters. That check let them test faster approximations for truly large groups. Vibrational coupling did more than scramble phase; under some tunings it even strengthened the burst. A lopsided rise time across tunings could let experiments spot that help.
arxiv-2509-03167:
Jorge Sanchez Almeida, Angel R. Plastino, and Ignacio Trujillo explored in 2025 how dwarf galaxies can grow broad stellar cores. Many dark matter dominated dwarfs show stars spread in a flat central core rather than a sharp peak. Some dark matter theories say the invisible halo itself slowly softens from a peaked cusp into a core.

As the halo expands, its gravity weakens and the stars it holds drift outward. The authors model stars on purely sideways, purely radial, and mixed orbits under that slow change, using adiabatic invariants, quantities that stay fixed under gentle drift. Cores formed easily in many setups, though their sizes depended on starting conditions. Circular-orbit systems made cores for a stated range of starting slopes. Radial systems made none, which gives observers a useful discriminant.
arxiv-2509-03467:
Soukeina Elhassen and four co-authors wrote a 2025 research paper on recognising continuous Saudi Sign Language from video. Sign language is the main communication route for many deaf people in Saudi Arabia, yet most computer systems focus on other sign languages or on single signs. Their work targets full signed sentences instead.

The team introduces KAU-CSSL, a dataset for continuous Saudi signing built around complete sentences, described as the first of its kind. Their model first extracts picture features with a pretrained ResNet-18 network, then tracks timing with a transformer and a bidirectional memory network. Accuracy reaches high levels when the same signers appear in training, and drops when new signers are tested. The dataset gives later researchers a shared base to improve on.
arxiv-2509-03567:
A 2025 research paper by Alexandre Journeaux and seven co-authors asks how short-range correlations build up in an ultracold Bose gas. Their gas sits near a Fano-Feshbach resonance, a tuning point where atoms interact especially strongly. Watching pair correlations form in real time tests theories of quantum gases.

Using fast optical control, the team jumps the energy of a molecular channel onto resonance in under a microsecond. They then track the two-body contact, a measure of close pair encounters, through losses caused by photodissociation, where light breaks molecules apart. Repeated pulses sharpen sensitivity to early losses from atom pairs. Atom pairs and molecular states stay in long-lived coherence with each other. A two-channel theory with zero-range interactions reproduces the behaviour, explaining how narrow the resonance is and how long the closed channel lives.
arxiv-2509-03667:
A 2025 research paper by Vivek Vasan and four co-authors asks whether entanglement purification still works when classical communication takes real time. Quantum networks distribute entangled particle pairs to distant nodes, but stored pairs lose quality through decoherence, the fading of quantum behaviour. Purification trades several weak pairs for fewer strong ones, yet its coordination messages travel over ordinary networks and impose idle waiting.

Two standard protocols, BBPSSW and DEJMPS, are evaluated under realistic internet protocol delays in city-scale networks. Quantum dynamics are modelled microscopically with a Lindblad treatment, and memory parameters come from current testbeds. Break-even curves map where purification succeeds or fails across network and memory conditions. The authors also count how many pairs a multi-round protocol consumes overall. Resulting memory quality targets, latency budgets, and overhead estimates guide deployment on present and near-future networks.
arxiv-2509-03767:
In a 2025 research paper, part of the ODYSSEUS survey, Caeley V. Pittman and six co-authors examine how young T Tauri stars exchange spin with their surrounding disks. Classical T Tauri stars are young stars fed by gas disks, varying strongly from minutes to decades. Much theory assumes stable spin states, an assumption this work tests directly.

For 47 stars from a space telescope sample, the team measures spin periods and corotation radii. Each corotation radius, where disk material orbits at the star's spin rate, is compared with where the star's magnetic field truncates the disk. Most stars fall in the spin-up regime, hinting at efficient angular momentum loss. Outflows and episodic accretion both appear, consistent with accretion-powered winds. The truncation point varies over days, pushing some stars across stability boundaries. Inclined systems near equal radii show dipper light curves, though dippers occur at all ratios.
arxiv-2509-03967:
A 2025 mathematics paper from Aida Abiad and one co-author examines the Zq-forcing number of graphs. Zero forcing is a colouring game modelling how influence spreads through a network. A player seeds a few blue vertices, and colour spreads by fixed rules until, ideally, the whole graph turns blue. The goal: the smallest seed set that succeeds.

The q-analogue adds an oracle that pushes back, forcing the player toward larger seed sets during play. The structure of several graph families drives the paper's two kinds of results. A SAT-based algorithm computes the exact Zq value and yields optimal strategies for both player and oracle, by encoding the game for a satisfiability solver. For cactus graphs, where cycles share at most one vertex, a polynomial-time algorithm handles the q equals one case. Exact values are proved for further classes, including block graphs, extending earlier tree results.
arxiv-2509-04167:
Peng Zhao and one co-author, Xiaoning Wu, prove that solutions exist for a coupled gravity-and-matter system in a 2025 mathematics paper. The Einstein-Dirac system joins Einstein's gravity equations with Dirac fields, which describe particles with spin, such as electrons. Their setup starts from data given on two crossing sheets of light-like surface, a harder starting style called a characteristic problem. No symmetry is assumed about the solution.

Following a strategy due to Luk, the authors promote certain spinor derivatives to independent variables. That move removes curvature terms from the energy estimates, the bookkeeping that keeps solutions controlled. Smooth solutions then exist across a rectangle-shaped region ahead of the starting sheets. The proof closes at the best possible derivative level.
arxiv-2509-04267:
Masahico Saito and one co-author, Emanuele Zappala, build knot invariants from a cohomology theory for Yang-Baxter operators in a 2025 mathematics paper. Knots and their invariants, numbers that identify knot types, connect deeply with quantum physics through these operators. Cocycles, special bookkeeping functions inside cohomology, earlier produced invariants for a related structure called quandles. The authors reinterpret those building blocks as deformations, gradual bendings, of the operators themselves.

Two construction routes are developed, one through traces and one through pairings between algebraic pieces. The older quandle invariant fits inside the new frame, and the quantum version sometimes separates knots the older one cannot. Even the famous Jones and Alexander polynomials arise as special cases.
arxiv-2509-04567:
Archishman Khasnovis and three co-authors count atomic hydrogen in Green Pea galaxies to explain why some leak ionizing light in a 2025 astrophysics paper. Green Peas are small, furiously star-forming galaxies thought to resemble the universe's early reionizers. The Green Bank Telescope searched thirty of them for the 21-centimeter hydrogen line, finding seven, and literature data widened the sample to sixty. A spectral ratio called O32 flags likely leakers of Lyman continuum light, the radiation that reionized the cosmos.

Galaxies with low O32 were detected in hydrogen over half the time; strong leakers almost never were. High-leaker systems hold less hydrogen, with lower gas fractions and faster depletion times. Their starbursts likely consumed the gas, opening escape routes for ionizing light.
arxiv-2509-04667:
Real-time speech can hide who is speaking without badly garbling what is said. Waris Quamer and one co-author present DarkStream, a streaming speech synthesis model for speaker anonymisation, in a 2025 paper. The system must work under strict latency limits in live communication.

DarkStream encodes content with a causal waveform encoder and transformer layers for context, aided by a short lookahead buffer. It generates waveforms directly with a neural vocoder, skipping slower intermediate steps. A fake speaker embedding, produced by a generative model, replaces the real voice identity. Tests show near-chance speaker verification while keeping words largely intelligible.
arxiv-2509-04967:
Fuzzing a program without its source code often misses bugs hidden in data flow. Kai Feng, lead author with two co-authors, present FuzzRDUCC in a 2025 software security paper. Traditional grey-box fuzzers follow control flow edge coverage, which can overlook how data propagates through a binary.

Their framework uses symbolic execution to reconstruct definition-use chains directly from executables. A heuristic algorithm selects relevant chains without excessive computational cost. Evaluated on a standard utilities benchmark, the fuzzer finds unique crashes that leading fuzzers miss in their tests. The authors present dataflow guidance as a feasible next step for vulnerability discovery.
arxiv-2509-05367:
Safety training that sorts requests into safe or unsafe breaks down on moral dilemmas, Shei Pern Chua and five co-authors demonstrate in a 2025 paper on language model security. Dilemmas force trade-offs, and that reasoning skill itself becomes an attack surface.

Their red-team method, TRIAL, hides harmful requests inside ethical framing over several turns and succeeds against most models tested. In response they propose ERR, a defence that separates answers enabling harm from answers that merely explain an ethical view. It uses a layered, harm-gated tuning design. The defence held up against reasoning-based attacks while keeping the model useful, the authors report.
arxiv-2509-05967:
Teaching a model three-dimensional medical imaging without labels, in a way doctors can follow, is the aim of a 2025 paper by Yiqin Zhang and two co-authors. Self-supervised learning eases the scarcity of labeled medical data, but most designs come from flat image work and hide what the model learns about space. Their method uses tasks a human can observe directly.

Three sub-tasks train the model on spatial relationships inside scans, at several levels of detail, so learning stays stable and interpretable. Results match current methods while making the learning process visible. The authors argue that the extra dimension of medical scans, handled openly, can supply the semantic depth self-supervision usually lacks.
arxiv-2509-06167:
City data fused into one latent picture reveal more than each source alone, test Ximena Pocco and four co-authors in a 2025 paper. Urban analytics mixes static data, like land use, with dynamic data, like movement, at street-level detail, and the mix is granular and multimodal. Their visual analytics framework uses autoencoders to fuse the sources and asks whether the fused representation finds deeper patterns.

The analysis says yes, mostly: combined latent representations produce more structured patterns than separate ones, though separate views still win in particular cases. The framework lets analysts explore those latent spaces directly. The authors frame the result as guidance for when fusion is worth its complexity in city-scale data work.
arxiv-2509-06467:
Can a vision model trained only on everyday photos handle medical scans? Che Liu and twenty-three co-authors test that idea in a 2025 benchmark report on DINOv3, a large self-supervised image model. The team asks whether it can serve directly as a shared encoder for medical tasks, with no special medical training.

They run DINOv3 on two- and three-dimensional classification, segmentation, meaning outlining regions in an image, and registration, meaning aligning images, across many scan types. Sizes and resolutions vary to check scaling. The model sets a strong baseline and even beats some medical models on several tasks. Weak spots remain in whole-slide images, electron microscopy, and PET scans, and bigger versions do not always help. Even so, its features look like a solid starting point for medical tools.
arxiv-2509-06567:
When does an energy functional lose its Lavrentiev gap? Michał Borowski answers more broadly in a solo 2025 analysis paper. The gap is a mismatch between the lowest energy found among smooth functions and among rougher ones. Double phase functionals mix two growth rates, weighted by a function that varies across the domain.

Borowski shows that the smoother that weight is, the wider the range of exponents with no gap. When the weight is infinitely smooth, no extra restriction on the exponents is needed at all. For weights with a finite number of smooth derivatives plus a Hölder condition, he establishes the optimal exponent range, extending earlier results that covered only Hölder weights. The pattern is clean: each gain in smoothness buys a matching gain in allowed exponents, closing a question about how regularity controls this gap.
arxiv-2509-07067:
Sara Rastello, Giuliano Iorio, Mark Gieles, and Long Wang model micro-tidal disruption events in young star clusters in a 2025 paper. In a dense young cluster, stars pass close to stellar-mass black holes again and again. A star that strays inside the black hole's tidal radius gets torn apart.

The team ran a suite of direct N-body simulations with a specialised code, adding new recipes for handling the disruptions themselves. Their cluster models were built to look real, with primordial binaries drawn from the Milky Way population as observed. The runs include how stars and binaries change over time, kicks from supernovae, and stellar winds, plus the pull of the Galactic tidal field. They find three routes that make the events: lone star and black hole meetings, contacts helped along by binaries, and messier systems with several stars at once.
arxiv-2509-07767:
Nai-Bo Zhang and 4 co-authors show in 2025 how weighing and sizing one heavy neutron star can limit the dark matter inside it. Some theories let dark matter build up inside neutron stars. That changes their mass-radius relation. Paired mass and radius measurements are stronger than either one alone. The pulsar PSR J0740+6620 gives exactly such a paired measurement, for a massive star.

The dark matter model is fermionic and interacts only through gravity. The nuclear equation of state is well constrained. In that setup, the joint measurement cuts the uncertainty on one quantity by more than half. That quantity is the dark matter central energy density. Other dark matter parameters stay unconstrained. The dark matter fraction is bounded below two percent by maximum mass alone. With the joint measurement, the bound falls below about 0.3 percent. The result supports only a small dark matter admixture in such stars.
arxiv-2509-07967:
Gravity can bend light from a distant galaxy into several images, and the same trick can delay a gravitational wave signal. Sourabh Magare, Anupreeta More, and Shasvath J. Kapadia explore the warning time that creates, in a 2025 research paper. If the first signal from a neutron star merger arrives, lensing may guarantee a repeat performance hours or days later. Telescopes could then watch the merger live.

The team tests whether optical images of the lensed host galaxy can predict that delay. They built mock lenses matching Hubble Space Telescope and ground-based Hyper Suprime-Cam quality. For double images, both telescopes gave similar uncertainty. Four-image systems predicted delays accurately with Hubble, less so from the ground. A real lens case showed day-scale differences between the two. The authors argue high-resolution imaging is essential for this early-warning scheme.
arxiv-2509-08167:
Gene regulatory networks route information most efficiently when their parts decay at matched rates, argue Miguel Ángel García-Ariza and 3 co-authors in a 2025 paper on biological information flow. Cell state changes are driven by networks where deterministic chemistry mixes with molecular noise. To study information transfer, the authors recast a Boolean network model as motion through a space of Gaussian distributions.

That space carries the Fisher information metric, a natural ruler for statistical models. In the new picture, optimal information transfer trajectories become gradient flows of the Kullback-Leibler divergence between distributions. Efficiency demands isotropic decay rates, equal in all directions across nodes. Geometric reframing of this kind can reveal design principles that simulations of single networks would never state plainly.
arxiv-2509-08367:
Jochen Harant and Ingo Schiermeyer bound the independence number of subcubic graphs from below in a 2025 combinatorics paper. An independent set is a group of vertices with no edges among them, and its maximum size is a central graph parameter. Subcubic graphs, where every vertex has at most three neighbours, appear in network design and scheduling.

Their bounds weight vertices by degree: counts of degree-one, degree-two, and degree-three vertices each contribute with their own coefficient, minus a constant. Families of graphs are exhibited showing the bounds are sharp, unimprovable in general. Degree-aware bounds beat one-size formulas because leaves and branching vertices play very different roles in how large an independent set can grow.
arxiv-2509-08567:
Chains of self-driven particles can form a living interface that crawls, bends, and flickers with fluctuations. Arvin Subramaniam, Tirthankar Banerjee, and Rajesh Singh study such an interface in a 2025 research paper. The particles interact through chemistry, and their motion couples spin with drift. The authors map every steady shape the interface can take across its parameter range.

One regime stands out: the interface settles into a curved, C-shaped form and propels itself nonstop. Its height flickers follow a classic scaling family but with wholly new exponents, including super-ballistic growth. Meanwhile, the particles' alignment flickers grow smoother as the system gets bigger, defying intuition. Together, the results point to a new non-equilibrium class. Such classes help physicists predict how whole families of active materials behave from a few shared rules.
arxiv-2509-08667:
Amirali Rayegan and 1 co-author introduce EZR, a framework for explainable optimization in software engineering, in a 2025 paper. Engineers face huge configuration spaces, and labeling examples is costly and error prone. EZR aims to use fewer but better labels.

Active sampling guided by Naive Bayes picks informative examples first. The learned logic is then distilled into short decision trees that explain global and local choices. Across sixty real datasets, EZR reaches over ninety percent of the best known result in most cases. Its explanations beat standard tools on clarity. Code and materials are shared for checking and reuse.
arxiv-2509-08867:
Every large language model answer burns electricity, and developers rarely know how much their choices matter. K. Pronk and Q. Zhao introduce the LLM Efficiency Benchmark in a 2025 research paper. Earlier energy studies often used setups unlike real production serving. Their benchmark runs on vLLM, a widely used, production-ready serving system.

The benchmark varies model size, architecture, and the number of simultaneous requests. It then measures how each factor changes energy efficiency during inference. The point is realism: numbers gathered under production-like conditions can guide real decisions. Developers choosing between models, or tuning request batching, get evidence instead of folklore. The authors hope such benchmarks build climate awareness into everyday AI engineering, where small efficiency choices multiply across millions of daily queries.
arxiv-2509-09067:
Recognizing that someone is using an ATM, not just standing near it, defeats skeleton-only action recognition. Hesham M. Shehata and Mohammad Abdolrahmani add scene awareness in a 2025 research paper. Graph networks reading body poses perform well on general actions. They fail on human-object interactions because the object and its place in the scene are missing from the input.

The authors feed fixed object information from the environment into the model. A multi-task learning setup trains recognition jointly with interaction-area information. They collected real data in public spaces, covering interactions with fixed machines and plain walking or standing. Accuracy rose well above the skeleton-only baseline, reaching near-perfect scores on their dataset. Surveillance, assistive monitoring, and smart buildings all need machines that understand not just how people move, but what they are engaging with.
arxiv-2509-09367:
Li-Jun Zhou and 5 co-authors work toward precise gauge fixing for lattice QCD in a 2025 paper. Lattice QCD solves quantum chromodynamics from first principles on a spacetime grid. Work on off-shell partons has mostly stayed in the Landau gauge, since precise fixing in other gauges is hard.

A universal power law link between parton matrix elements and gauge fixing precision motivates an empirical extrapolation method. Proper definitions of bare coupling and effective gauge parameter support the procedure. The method reproduces gauge dependent renormalization constants for quark operators at a fraction of a percent level. That accuracy holds up to a gauge parameter near one. Wider parton studies may follow.
arxiv-2509-09867:
Yago Romano Matinez and Jesse Roberts ask, in a 2025 paper, whether a language model agent can truly help a partner reach a goal, rather than only answer questions. Their test bed is UNO, the turn-based card game. The model agent is told not to win itself, but to help another player win, which makes cooperation the measured skill.

The authors built a tool that lets decoder-only language models play inside the RLCard game environment, reading full game state from text prompts. Models from one billion to seventy billion parameters were tried under two prompting styles. Every model beat a random player when playing for itself, but few could lift a partner's results by much, and scale alone did not fix that gap.
arxiv-2509-10067:
Georgi Baklicharov and 2 co-authors propose a fairer way to judge treatments when some patients die or switch therapy mid-trial in a 2025 biostatistics paper. Such intercurrent events tangle intention-to-treat analysis, and standard fixes aim at hypothetical worlds or survivor-only effects that rest on claims nobody can verify. Sensitivity to hidden differences between groups then haunts every conclusion.

Their PLOT estimands compare matched treated and untreated patients at the last moment before either one hits an intercurrent event, using only information gathered earlier. In randomised trials those contrasts are identified with no structural assumptions, even when overlap between groups is severely broken. Tests and estimators built on the idea stay efficient and model-free, and simulations show leftover selection bias shrinking to a negligible size.
arxiv-2509-10167:
Lénaïc Chizat asks what really limits very deep residual networks in this solo 2025 paper on machine learning theory. Residual networks, or ResNets, are trained by gradient methods from random starting points. Chizat shows that as depth grows, a network behaves as if it were also infinitely wide, whatever its true width is.

Training settles toward a limiting process described by an ordinary differential equation, and he gives explicit error bounds for the gap. Depending on how the residual steps are scaled, the limit either keeps rich, genuinely nonlinear feature learning or slips into a lazy regime where features barely move. For the common two-layer block design, he identifies the exact scaling that keeps feature updates at their strongest and proves matching rates.
arxiv-2509-10267:
Daria I. Markina and 8 co-authors study how sound, electrons, and magnetism interact in the layered material CrSBr in this 2025 paper. CrSBr is a magnet whose layers stack loosely. Its three kinds of behavior are linked. That link makes odd combined states. The team tracked the link across a wide range of heat and cold.

They used Raman scattering at several laser energies. They also ran tests on how the material takes in and gives off light. Near the point where magnetic order sets in, the main vibration modes changed shape. Light-emitting states also gained or lost strength. Each mode answered to a different electronic state. The authors hold up CrSBr as a useful test bed for such linked behavior in thin magnets.
arxiv-2509-10367:
Shrinking a dataset while keeping its teaching value is Tong Chen and Raghavendra Selvan's topic in this 2025 machine learning paper on dataset condensation. The aim: build a tiny synthetic dataset so that a model trained on it alone performs about as well as one trained on the full data.

Recent work connects condensation to approximating a data distribution with fewer points. The authors turn that insight into a unified framework based on discrepancy, a formal distance between distributions, which covers existing condensation methods and gives the task a cleaner definition. The broader framing matters because it stretches condensation's goals beyond raw accuracy. Robustness, privacy, and other properties a small dataset might need to preserve can now be stated in the same language.
arxiv-2509-10967:
Chenghan Li and Garnet Kin-Lic Chan present a layered learning scheme for reaction free energies in this 2025 paper. Free energies decide how chemical reactions behave in liquids and cells, but computing them with top-level quantum methods costs far too much. Their framework distills a few high-fidelity quantum calculations into a ladder of machine-learned quantum Hamiltonians, each simpler than the last.

Because the models keep explicit electronic degrees of freedom, quantum and classical parts of a system can be embedded together faithfully, including long-range electrical effects. As a check, the team computed acid strengths and the rate of an enzyme reaction entirely from first principles. Both matched experiments within chemical accuracy or the stated uncertainty.
arxiv-2509-11067:
Liangxuan Guo and 7 co-authors present Agentic Lybic, a team of AI agents that operates a desktop computer, in this 2025 paper. Single agents fumble long, multi-step tasks through poor coordination and weak checking. This system's whole structure runs as a finite-state machine, which routes work between parts as conditions change.

A controller and a manager direct three workers: one writes code, one clicks through graphical interfaces, and one supports decisions. An evaluator gates quality, and the state machine picks the route for each subtask, allowing replans after errors. On the OSWorld benchmark the system reached a success rate above half of tasks within fifty steps, which the authors report as the best result at the time.
arxiv-2509-11167:
Pouria Mahdavinia and three co-authors wrote this 2025 machine learning paper. It concerns model merging. Several fine-tuned copies of one language model are combined into a single model. Each copy is good at a different skill. No retraining from scratch is needed.

Their first method is called OTA Merging. It weights each model's edits with leftover optimizer statistics. Those statistics map which parameters matter most. Clashes between skills shrink as a result. A companion step is Fast Fisher Grafting. It trims conflicting or unimportant edits. The surviving changes concentrate in early attention layers and word embeddings. Together, the two methods beat strong baselines. The merged models cover math, code, instruction following, and knowledge recall. Code and checkpoints are public.
arxiv-2509-11367:
Chang-Hwan Lee and Alexander Shim tackle a blind spot in how learning agents are trained, in this 2025 machine learning paper. Agents are taught as if the world's rules never change. In health care, in robots, and in finance, the rules do drift. A policy trained on last year's rules can go wrong in silence.

The pair detect drift by watching what the agent does. They score how much one run of acts differs from the next. The score counts the edits needed to turn one run into the other. Added steps count. Dropped steps count. Swapped steps count too. In tests, runs made under changed rules scored far from the old norm. Runs under the old rules did not. The split held at each noise level tried. The score can serve as an alarm for agents in the field.
arxiv-2509-12267:
Christian Zhou-Zheng and 8 co-authors argue for a traditional approach to generating piano music in a 2025 paper. Their entry targets the MIREX 2025 Symbolic Music Generation challenge, which asks systems to continue a piece of symbolic piano music. Recent work has favored large foundation models with complex designs.

The team instead returns to a simple next-token prediction objective on tokenized raw MIDI, the digital format that records notes. They claim simpler methods remain more effective for constrained, single-instrument tasks when the data and fundamentals are better. No architectural augmentation is added. The authors release their model weights and code publicly. Their case is that careful basics can outperform scale for this narrow musical task.
arxiv-2509-12567:
Synthetic turbulence, a random flow with the statistics of the real thing, is a cheap stand-in for costly simulations. Matthieu Chatelain and seven co-authors develop one such field in 2025 and devote the paper to its Gaussian backbone, the structure on which everything else rests.

In space, the field is a divergence-free fractional Gaussian field matching known turbulence statistics up to second order at a fixed Reynolds number. In time, each Fourier mode follows an Ornstein-Uhlenbeck process whose clock runs faster for smaller eddies. The authors derive the statistics analytically, build fast numerical schemes, and check both against a standard turbulence database.
arxiv-2509-12667:
Ziyun Liu and Chris Donahue turn a rhythm game into a music research dataset in a 2025 paper. Beat tracking needs annotations for where beats and downbeats fall in songs. The community game Osu! contains beatmaps created and refined by a large, diverse community, covering underrepresented genres such as anime, Vocaloid, and video game music.

The authors built a pipeline that extracts beat annotations from those beatmaps and partitions them into meaningful subsets. Manual analysis found that beatmaps with a single timing point, or with widely spaced timing points, provide reliable annotations, while closely spaced points often need extra curation. Annotations for the same song were highly consistent across creators. They release the pipeline and a high-quality subset to support music information retrieval research.
arxiv-2509-12867:
Yabo Zhang and 5 co-authors present Tool-R1 in a 2025 paper on teaching language models to use tools efficiently. Language models reason well about text but remain limited on real-world tasks needing up-to-date knowledge, precise operations, or specialized tools. Reinforcement learning offers a way to train for such multi-step tool use.

Tool-R1 enables general, compositional, multi-step tool use by generating executable Python code. It integrates user-defined tools and standard libraries, sharing variables across steps to build coherent workflows. Its reward combines a language-model judgment of the answer with whether the code executed successfully. A dynamic sample queue caches and reuses high-quality training trajectories, cutting costly online sampling. Experiments on the GAIA benchmark showed substantial gains in accuracy and robustness.
arxiv-2509-13267:
Alexander Dombowsky and David Dunson learn discrete Bayes nets in 2025 with hierarchical shrinkage toward low-size latents. Table nets need many parameters via interactions or cell chances. Sparse counts strain both classic paths and invite overfit.

Node-parent chances shrink to latent parameters after the fact. Sampling uses Langevin steps inside Gibbs rounds. Full conditionals prove log-concave under mild rules, which speeds sampling. Structure learners keep the acyclic trait while using the prior. Fake tests cover sparse counts and graph choice. A breast cancer set reveals prognostic links among clinical traits.
arxiv-2509-13967:
Guangzhao He and four co-authors introduce a dilated coordinate method in a 2025 nuclear physics paper. The target is lattice effective field theory calculations. Weakly bound few-body nuclei are a numerical headache. Their interactions act at short range, demanding a fine grid. Their wave functions trail off slowly, demanding a huge box. A uniform lattice pays for both at once.

Their approach stretches coordinates analytically. The mesh refines itself where the physics is sharp. It coarsens where the wave function only tails away. Demonstrations on two- and three-body systems converge to the infinite-volume answer faster than uniform lattices. The biggest gains come for highly excited states and shallow bound states near the continuum threshold. The method lays groundwork for exotic nuclei near the dripline and for scattering calculations.
arxiv-2509-14267:
Piyushkumar Patel, writing alone in 2025, designs a support assistant for online shops that answers from product facts and past cases. Shoppers need fast replies, but a fluent answer that invents details erodes trust. His system grounds replies in a knowledge graph, a network of linked product facts.

Patel reviews recent graph based retrieval systems, then proposes a method that merges a relevant subgraph with text pulled from support archives before writing the answer. The full design, data flow and tests are set out for real time use. In the reported trial the system improved factual accuracy by a clear margin and left most users satisfied. The gain comes from letting structured facts check free text generation.
arxiv-2509-14367:
Alexei Bazavov and twenty-five co-authors set a precise distance scale for lattice QCD in 2025, the grid based study of the strong force. Lattice results come out in grid units, so a known physical mass must fix the scale. The team uses the Omega baryon mass.

Nine simulated ensembles span a range of grid spacings, most with near physical light quark masses. Electric charge corrections define a pure strong force Omega mass for comparison. The gradient flow scale, a standard ruler in such work, comes out with an uncertainty under half a percent. The central value agrees well with earlier calculations. A shared, precise scale lets different lattice groups compare results without a hidden ruler mismatch.
arxiv-2509-14467:
Gunter Schutz and Ali Zahra study a variant of the exclusion process in 2025, a lattice model where masses hop but cannot share a site. A hop across a bond is allowed only when the site just before it stands empty. That next neighbour rule sharply enriches the dynamics.

Long range links in the data appear, plus a mixed order shift tuned by hop asymmetry. At half filling the system falls into two ergodic parts, each tied to its own reversible balance law. The balance law links to q-Catalan numbers, a warped counting family. That link lets the pair derive firm long size laws for key heat values in the strongly asymmetric case, and conjecture more. Tight local rules can thus breed rich global phases.
arxiv-2509-14667:
Ritesh Pandey and four co-authors study light bending in 2025 around black holes in a cosmology inspired modified gravity. Changes to the Schwarzschild like spacetime alter photon paths, lensing and shadows. Finite distance effects matter when space is not asymptotically flat.

The deflection angle is computed with the Rindler-Ishak method, which handles finite distances consistently. The effective potential for light shows a single unstable peak at the photon sphere. Orbits split by impact parameter into capture, escape and unstable circular cases. Deflection falls as key parameters vary in the reported analysis. Comparing predicted bending and shadows with observations offers a route to test this modified gravity family.
arxiv-2509-15167:
Pak-Hei Yeung and four co-authors borrow knowledge from everyday photographs to segment medical volumes with little labeled data, in a 2025 medical imaging paper. Three-dimensional medical segmentation normally needs many hand-labeled scans, which are expensive expert work. Their setting keeps only a few labeled volumes beside a large unlabeled pool.

The framework, called M&N, progressively distills knowledge from a model pre-trained on two-dimensional natural images into a 3D segmentation model trained from scratch. The two models co-train in rounds, each generating pseudo-masks that teach the other. A sampling rule guided by learning rates adjusts the mix of labeled and unlabeled data in each batch, limiting damage from wrong pseudo-masks. Across several public datasets the method tops thirteen existing semi-supervised approaches.
arxiv-2509-15567:
Hongyu Kuang leads a team that writes better commit notes for code changes. A commit note tells why a change was made, and good notes ease upkeep. In practice, coders often skip or skimp on them. Past auto writers focus on fancy ways to encode the change. This team instead squeeze the change into a brief text form first.

Their form has three parts: a summary of the change, comments drawn out of it, and key code names stressed. A rule based tool builds the form, and a code language model is then tuned to turn forms into notes. The brevity helps the model use its pre-training well. Tests support the plan.
arxiv-2509-15667:
Dimitrios Damianos leads a team that joins speech and language models in a smooth space. Their aim is speech ready language models that can listen as well as read. Instead of feeding raw sound codes to the language model, they use a middle space shaped by sound yet built of text like states. The fusion runs through cross attention between hidden states.

Their system supports both full clip and streaming modes. They build VoxKrikri, the first Greek speech language model, on this frame. Greek speech to text scores reach the best known level, with gains of about a fifth over rivals. The team argue the smooth fusion path suits low resource languages well.
arxiv-2509-16267:
Abandoned underground mines hold key raw materials, but their tight, unstable tunnels are unsafe for people and standard machines. Victor V. Puche, Kashish Verma, and Matteo Fumagalli propose a team of specialized robots that work together in such mines. Each robot runs its own layered state machine for step-by-step tasks, and robots trigger each other through direct messages to stay in sync.

Unlike prior work that stops at mapping, this system is built to extract minerals through physical work. Local control, rather than one central brain, keeps the team flexible in confined spaces. The design aims at full task chains underground.
arxiv-2509-16367:
Moving a cloud of ultracold atoms through a light lattice without smearing its momentum is a delicate trick for quantum sensors. Raja Chamakhi and four co-authors simulate a fast protocol that loads the cloud into the lattice, speeds it with a smooth ramp, and releases it, all without slow adiabatic care. The cloud's breathing motion inside each site turns out to govern how pure the final momentum stays.

At special magic times matched to that breathing rhythm, the momentum stays nearly single-toned even with very fast loading. Speed gains of three to six times come with high transfer fidelity, a practical route for timed sensors.
arxiv-2509-16667:
Sen-Peng Eu, Tung-Shan Fu, and Yu-Ren Pan study a playful shape in combinatorics in a 2025 math paper. The shape, called a fighting fish, is a branching form that extends a known class of stacked shapes. Past work built these shapes from cells. The team offer a new way to build them from tree-like parts.

Their tree method rests on special cells at the shape's stem. With it, they count fighting fish of each size in a clean way. The count matches a pattern from trees where each node has three branches. Variants with marked tails or mirror symmetry are counted too. The work ties two branches of counting math together.
arxiv-2509-16867:
Motohiko Ezawa studies tunneling in a family of magnets in a 2025 solo physics paper. The magnets differ by a wave pattern labeled with letters p, d, f, g, and i. Some of them are altermagnets, a newer class with no net magnetization. A junction of two such magnets resists current based on their alignment. That effect is tunneling magnetoresistance.

Ezawa derives a universal formula for the resistance ratio. The ratio in these magnets can trail ferromagnets when coupling is strong. Still, zero net magnetization promises fast, dense memory. The formula gives device designers a quick way to compare the whole family before building samples.
arxiv-2509-17167:
Seungjun Yi leads a team of ten co-authors on a 2025 arXiv paper about automating thematic analysis. That method reads texts such as clinical interview transcripts and reports the main themes it finds. Doing it by hand is slow, and large language models alone do not yet match human coders well.

The team's system, called SFT-TA, places fine-tuned agents inside a multi-agent setup built from large language models. Each agent was trained with supervision for its own role in the workflow. The full system matched human reference themes better than earlier frameworks and a GPT-4o baseline. Fine-tuned agents on their own did worse, which shows that the role each agent plays inside the group is what makes the setup work.
arxiv-2509-17667:
Arafat Ahsan, Vandan Mujadia, Pruthwik Mishra, Yash Bhaskar, and Dipti Misra Sharma build a better judge for machine translation into Indian languages. Their 2025 arXiv paper notes that grading translations is hard: the languages involved are rich in script, word shape, and sentence structure, and they diverge widely. String-matching scores such as BLEU miss much of that, and learned metrics starve for gold human ratings outside the big language pairs.

The team first created a large human ratings data set covering many Indian languages and translation directions. On it they trained COMTAIL, a neural metric tuned for pairs with at least one Indian language. The best variants beat the prior state of the art by clear margins at judging such pairs. Ablation studies then map what the metric is sensitive to. The work gives low-resource pairs a grader trained on their own ground.
arxiv-2509-17967:
Ruben Campos Delgado shows that a known quantum trait, contextuality, can depend on the viewer's frame. His 2025 paper uses the operational sense of the trait set out by Spekkens. That sense asks if a hidden-state model can explain what spin measures show.

Delgado takes states that hold both spin and motion, then boosts them to a moving frame. After motion is traced out in both frames, one viewer gets a contextual model and the other does not. Spin-only contextuality is thus frame-bound, he argues. A side result gives a moving viewer a better shot at telling two quantum states apart.
arxiv-2509-18067:
Boyang Zhang and 4 co-authors train ranking models that are fair where it counts most: at the top. Their 2025 paper deals with lists that assign scarce goods, such as aid or jobs. Past fair rankers balance group exposure across the whole list, yet users most often act on just the top few.

Their frame scores exposure gaps in the top slice alone, at training time. A smooth stand-in for the hard top-cut choice makes the goal trainable. Fast random methods keep the cost low at scale. Tests show the method beats past fair rankers on both score and top-slice fairness.
arxiv-2509-18267:
Ashland Knowles and R Ganesh explain the crystal shapes of group-15 elements from a boundary theory. Their 2025 paper deals with pnictogen solids, such as antimony, grey arsenic, and phosphorene. Each atom holds three outer electrons in p orbitals, shared with neighbours as bonds.

Their model puts a trivalent net on a cubic grid, with three bond stubs at each site. A rule that bans twin parallel bonds forces a tripod shape at each site. Lines of the grid must then swap bond and blank in turn. Bulk bonds are set by spins on three edge planes, a bulk-boundary map.
arxiv-2509-18367:
Edge devices like sensors can learn together without sending raw data to one center. Zhuoyu Yao and five co-authors study swarm learning for such edge networks. Their 2025 paper tackles a known snag: each device holds different data, so local training pulls the shared model in clashing ways. The team first measures how that data mismatch affects learning.

They define a new score for how uneven the local data sets are. That score links data mismatch to how well the swarm model trains. Based on it, they design M-DSL, a method that picks the workers whose updates help the shared model most. Math analysis shows the method settles toward a stable result. Tests on varied data sets beat standard benchmarks. The authors say smart worker choice is key when edge data cannot be made uniform.
arxiv-2509-18567:
A star in graph theory is one hub joined to many leaves, and a star-forest is a set of such stars. Jiaxi Nie, Yibo Ren, and Hehui Wu study how few star-forests can cover every edge of a complete graph. Their 2025 paper defines a number for the least forests needed when each forest may hold at most k stars. Prior work had settled the case of two stars per forest.

The team shows that with three stars per forest, the count takes a clean value when the graph size is a multiple of 27. For four or more stars, they find an exact formula in a stated size and remainder range. The value sits just above half the vertex count. These results disprove a conjecture from the earlier paper on the two-star case. The work closes several cases of a tidy decomposition problem.
arxiv-2509-18667:
Retrieval systems that search knowledge graphs can answer hard questions, but building the graph with a language model burns tokens. Qiao Xiao, Hong Ting Tsang, and Jiaxin Bai present TERAG, a graph retrieval framework built to cut that cost. Their 2025 paper borrows a ranking trick from HippoRAG, a prior system. The trick spreads importance through the graph at search time instead of build time.

TERAG builds leaner graphs up front and lets the search step do more of the work. In tests, it reached at least eighty percent of the accuracy of widely used graph systems. It did so while using only three to eleven percent of their output tokens. That gap makes graph retrieval viable at much larger scale. The authors pitch TERAG for cost-sensitive deployments. They present it as a simple change with outsized savings.
arxiv-2509-18967:
How faithfully do galaxies trace the mass around the emptiest and densest spots in the sky? Q. Hang leads a large Dark Energy Survey team that compares galaxy counts with weak lensing mass maps from the survey's third-year data. They stack the regions around troughs, called voids, and peaks, called clusters, in the projected galaxy density. Then they measure how galaxy density and lensing strength fall off with angle around each spot.

The ratio of the two profiles changes only mildly with angle, which means their shapes agree well. The team models that ratio with templates from large simulations dressed with realistic noise. From it they extract the galaxy bias, the factor linking galaxy clustering to mass clustering, in three distance slices. Bias comes out broadly consistent between voids and clusters, though peaks give somewhat larger values.
arxiv-2509-19167:
Chin-Yu Hsiao and two co-authors settle a long-open question about heat flow on CR manifolds, spaces that mix complex and real geometry. The heat kernel of the Kohn Laplacian describes how heat spreads under a diffusion tied to the complex structure. Its small-time behavior had resisted proof in general. For compact manifolds whose Levi form, a key curvature-like object, never degenerates and keeps one signature, the authors now establish the asymptotics, under a standard side condition.

Where that condition fails, they handle a corrected operator instead. The results let them define analytic torsion for these manifolds and track how it changes when the metric changes. They extend the analysis to high powers of a line bundle and to manifolds with a circle symmetry. Applications include equivariant versions of the torsion and of the Quillen metric.
arxiv-2509-19567:
Speech recognition stumbles on rare words, names, and terms it has never seen in training. Dimitrios Siskos and five co-authors use retrieval to fetch helpful context for the recognizer on the fly. A compact embedding search pulls likely context from a store of text. They compare it with two language-model routes: one that invents context from a prompt, and one that fixes the transcript after the fact.

Tests span three speech sets: talks, earnings calls, and financial speech. The retrieval route cut word errors by up to about a sixth versus no context. Perfect hand-fed context did better still, which marks the headroom left. The gains come at low cost, since embedding search is cheap to run. The work suits live captioning and voice tools that meet new names daily.
arxiv-2509-19767:
Search systems increasingly must honor filters, such as newest documents in one category, without losing speed. Alireza Heidari, Wei Zhang, and Ying Xiong present FusedANN, which fuses attributes into the search geometry itself. Hard filters become soft, weighted penalties inside a convexified space built with transformer methods. Top results then respect the penalties while staying semantically near.

The authors prove the method collapses to exact filtering when matches are plentiful. When they are scarce, it relaxes gracefully toward near-matching attributes instead of returning nothing. Approximation quality for downstream search is preserved in their analysis. Product search, document retrieval, and recommendation all mix vectors with attributes. A principled fusion could replace the fragile index hacks now common in production.
arxiv-2509-19867:
A review by Oriol Artime and seven co-authors surveys how complex networks hold up under damage. Cells, brains, societies, and the internet share one trait: local failures can cascade into systemic collapse. Power grids overload in chains; ecosystems slow critically near extinction. The review frames both local and global failures as perturbations that reshape a system's function.

The authors organize theory and computation by that perturbation lens. Robustness names resistance to damage; resilience names recovery after it. Keeping the two apart clarifies decades of mixed usage. The synthesis spans mathematics, physics, biology, and engineering. Readers get a map of measures, models, and open gaps. Such maps help grid operators and ecologists alike ask sharper questions about the networks they guard.
arxiv-2509-20567:
Diagnosing disease from clinical text gets harder when the text is not in English. Ayan Sar and four co-authors present SwasthLLM, a framework for cross-lingual medical diagnosis, in a 2025 arXiv paper. It works across English, Hindi, and Bengali with no language-specific fine-tuning. A multilingual encoder with language-aware attention reads the text, and a classification head names the disease.

A Siamese contrastive module pulls matching texts in different languages toward similar representations. Translation consistency training reinforces that invariance. Meta-learning then prepares the model to adapt to new languages or tasks from tiny data. Supervised accuracy reached about ninety-seven percent in their tests. Zero-shot diagnosis scored about ninety-three percent on Hindi text and seventy-three percent on Bengali. The phased design targets clinics where annotated data in local languages barely exists.
arxiv-2509-20667:
Chemistry calculations on supercomputers can waste large amounts of costly machine time. Tanzila Tabassum and seven co-authors tackle that planning problem in a 2025 paper on parallel computing. Their tools use machine learning to predict what a huge chemistry job will need before it runs.

The methods forecast how long a coupled-cluster calculation will take. From that forecast, users can pick settings such as the number of nodes and the tile size. The authors frame two user needs. One is the fastest finish for a given machine. The other is the cheapest run, measured in node-hours used. Good forecasts help researchers avoid guessing before they commit expensive resources.
arxiv-2509-21067:
Beginners learning to program often accept an AI's fix without understanding their bug. Oka Kurniawan and five co-authors design against that habit in a 2025 pilot study for the Koli Calling 2025 conference on computing education. Their tool is CodeHinter, an AI-assisted debugging assistant.

CodeHinter combines classic debugging tools with language-model techniques aimed at semantic errors. Rather than handing over a repair, it hints and prompts so students stay engaged in finding the fault. The paper reports findings from the second design iteration, tested with undergraduate students. The authors examine whether the tool helps novices fix code while still learning the debugging process itself. The study speaks to educators wary of AI shortcuts in programming courses.
arxiv-2509-21167:
Deleting an unwanted concept from a text to image diffusion model can be framed in many mathematical ways. The work is by Nicola Novello and 4 co-authors. Diffusion models can make images of concepts that users want removed. Most removal methods shrink a squared error loss between outputs for a target and an anchor concept. That loss hides a known divergence measure between two Gaussians. The paper widens that view.

The authors extend the loss to any f-divergence, a family of ways to measure gaps between distributions. Some members give cheap closed form training goals. Others need a min max form, which they provide. They study how each choice changes gradient size and convergence. One closed form based on Hellinger distance beat the squared error baseline across many tests.
arxiv-2509-21267:
Language models give strikingly similar answers, and whether that sameness is harmful depends on the task. Behind the work are Shomik Jain and 6 co-authors. Models often give very similar answers. Whether that is bad depends on the task. For maths, answers should agree on the final value but may differ in strategy. For creative writing, plots and settings should vary. Past work rarely made that distinction.

The authors build a task taxonomy with clear notions of functional diversity. That means differences a user would find meaningful for that task. A small user study checked that the taxonomy matches human views. They add a sampling method that raises diversity only where sameness is unwanted. Their evidence questions the claimed trade off between diversity and quality.
arxiv-2509-21367:
Yu-Kai Shih and You-Kai Kang wrote a 2025 paper on a secure tourism chatbot for Hsinchu, Taiwan. Smart tourism chatbots give travellers personal, real time help. They face prompt injection attacks, where users craft inputs to force bad behaviour. Such attacks can leak private data or produce harmful content. The paper presents a case study of a defended system.

The chatbot uses retrieval augmented generation, which grounds answers in retrieved documents. It also calls external APIs for live services. Defences include multi layered language analysis and injection guardrails. Intent is split across lexical, semantic, and pragmatic levels. A tiered response strategy and gatekeepers judge intent before answering. The authors report high contextual awareness and security.
arxiv-2509-21467:
Radio observations reveal how stars work, evolve, and interact with their surroundings. Lynn Matthews summarizes a 2024 conference on radio stars in a 2025 paper. The meeting was held at MIT Haystack Observatory in April 2024. More than sixty researchers from around the world attended. New observatories frame the summary, as radio facilities enter a new generation.

Topics ranged widely across stellar radio science. Talks covered cool and ultracool dwarfs, extrasolar space weather, and stellar masers. Thermal emission from evolved stars and circumstellar chemistry were discussed. Low frequency solar observations and hot star emission also featured. Sessions treated explosive stellar events and very long baseline interferometry. Widefield sky surveys and their radio star detections closed the programme. The summary gives a snapshot of a field in rapid change.
arxiv-2509-21567:
Brain waves recorded by EEG carry signals about how consumers decide. Mohammad Parsa Afshar and Aryan Azimi compare prediction methods on such data in a 2025 paper. The setting spans marketing, cognitive neuroscience, and human computer interaction. Features were extracted and cleaned from the NeuMa data set. Brain connectivity features were built for graph based models.

Classical machine learning models were compared with graph neural networks of several architectures. Ensemble models feature among the classical approaches. Graph models use connectivity between brain regions as their structure. The comparison aims to show how each model family performs on the same data. Such a benchmark helps researchers pick tools for EEG based consumer behaviour prediction.
arxiv-2509-21667:
Relativistic superfluids with a conserved charge may keep their coherence forever, a 2025 paper argues. Lasha Berezhiani and 2 co-authors analyse a uniform superfluid in a complex scalar field theory. Zero charge condensed states undergo quantum loss through internal number changing steps. Charged superfluids behave in other ways in their analysis. Stability holds to all orders in perturbation theory, despite the states not being Hamiltonian eigenstates.

Constructing the quantum state explicitly shows how the dynamics works. Naive coherent state constructions are insufficient for stationarity. Specific non Gaussian corrections are essential for a stationary state. The resulting state is the interacting vacuum of the superfluid fluctuations. It also serves as the ground state of a modified Hamiltonian with a chemical potential term. The state does not fade with time. It stays set, and that calm hold is what lets the flow act as one piece.
arxiv-2509-21867:
Cleaning noise out of speech as it arrives, with almost no delay, is the job of streaming speech enhancement. Sunghwan Ahn, Jinmo Han, Beom Jun Woo, and Nam Soo Kim present FastEnhancer in this 2025 paper. Neural methods clean speech well but often run heavy, and clever designs can still lag on ordinary hardware. Their model is built from the start to cut real-world delay.

FastEnhancer uses a simple encoder-decoder shape with efficient blocks that mix recurrence and attention. On standard quality and clarity measures, it reached top-level results. At the same time, it ran faster than rivals on a single ordinary processor thread. That mix matters for live meetings, smart home devices, and hearing aids, where the cleaning must keep up with the speaker. The code and trained weights are shared in public.
arxiv-2509-22367:
Tanise Ceron and 3 co-authors ask how much political content sits in the data used to train large language models. Models often give slanted replies, yet no one had measured the politics of the training text itself. The team sampled open pre-training and post-training sets at large scale. They sorted texts by leaning and by stance on key issues.

Every set leaned left, and pre-training text held more political content than post-training text. Stances in the data also tracked model behavior closely. That link showed up in base models and stayed after later training. The authors call for more open data records so such links can be tracked.
arxiv-2509-23267:
Monsoon rain feeds India's farms, yet fine-scale forecasts stay hard with sparse ground gauges. Swaib Ilias Mazumder, Manish Kumar, and Aparajita Khan built a multimodal deep learning framework for that task. Their new data set maps five Indian states at one-kilometer resolution. Seven geospatial inputs join, from soil moisture to land use. The season covered is the June to September 2024 monsoon.

An attention-guided U-Net reads spatial patterns and time links across inputs. Focal and dice losses handle the skewed rain classes. The multimodal model beat single-input baselines and prior deep methods. Gains were clearest in extreme rainfall classes, the hardest to catch.
arxiv-2509-23867:
Finding the video moment a sentence describes should suit detection transformers, yet standard tricks for improving them backfire here. Jiajin Tang and 6 co-authors diagnose why, then build Sim-DETR. Two faults emerge: queries for similar moments fight each other, and each query is torn between global meaning and local placement. Their fix makes two small changes inside the decoder layers.

Self-attention between queries is limited by how much they overlap in meaning and position. A query-to-frame alignment step then bridges global and local context. Experiments show the simple baseline unlocks the transformer's full strength for temporal sentence grounding.
arxiv-2509-23967:
Long chains of thought make reasoning models accurate and expensive at the same time. Ken Deng leads the team behind HiPO, a hybrid policy optimization framework that teaches models to choose when deep reasoning is worth it. A hybrid data pipeline pairs detailed Think-on replies with direct Think-off ones. A hybrid reward balances accuracy against efficiency, discouraging needless deliberation.

Across math and coding benchmarks, models trained this way cut token length substantially while holding or improving accuracy. The authors offer selective reasoning as a principled route to deploying reasoning models where resources are tight. The team frames the method as a step toward reasoning models that spend compute only where it pays.
arxiv-2509-24067:
Qiushui Xu and 6 co-authors tackle value learning from fixed logs of past actions, where a learner cannot try new moves.
