Ciliated organs transport viscous fluids through confined ducts, yet how duct morphology and ciliary activity jointly set flow rate and pressure limits remains unclear. They model dense arrays of beating cilia lining duct walls as an active porous medium driven by prescribed metachronal waves. Two ratios govern transport: ciliary confinement ratio and mean ciliary fraction. Flows follow Navier-Stokes-Brinkman equations.
arxiv-2605-21667: Zuluaga and Gimenez build a duality for semilattices with adjunctions, systems that pair order with two linked maps. They introduce MoS-spaces, a category dual to modal semilattices. Then they define meet-relations and a category called RelSP, dual to the semilattices themselves. Under a normality rule, the older multirelational picture can be rebuilt from a meet-relation, and back again. The two relational categories turn out to be isomorphic.
arxiv-2605-22167: Thalis da Silva and co-authors screen for metallic transport across over 2.8 million compounds, combining machine learning with high-throughput ab initio calculations. They identify intermetallic candidates near aluminum's level at 36.59 million S/m. Full electron-phonon calculations for the top materials agree well with experiments. Noble metals remain hard to beat, yet LiBePt2 matches them by using light-element valence electrons to push high-scattering d-states below the Fermi level. The work shows statistical learning plus detailed ab initio calculations can find novel high-performance conductors.
arxiv-2605-22367: Bhatia, Krejci and Rinke benchmark five message-passing neural networks for infrared spectra of small organic molecules. All five predict energies, forces and dipole moments well, and capture harmonic frequencies and spectra for molecules seen in training. SchNet and FieldSchNet transfer poorly to unseen systems, while SO3Net, PaiNN and MACE generalise better. SchNet runs cheapest, and FieldSchNet handles field-dependent responses at higher cost. PaiNN balances accuracy and efficiency best, while MACE gives the highest spectral accuracy and transferability.
arxiv-2605-22467: Bartkowiak and colleagues propose SADGE, a score predicting synthetic image performance on real data, without later training. Current scores mostly measure meaning match between real and synthetic images. Shape match is considered less often. Neither looks nor shape alone predicts later performance; their interplay dictates synthetic data utility. SADGE is tested across five benchmark families and 15 variants, covering 79,000 image pairs. It achieves the strongest later association under linear and rank criteria, at Pearson r 0.88 and Spearman rho 0.77. Fusing DINOv3 looks with MASt3R shape wins best.
arxiv-2605-22567: Fan and others tackle a trade off in multilingual reasoning: forcing input language consistency harms reasoning, while chasing reasoning lets answers drift toward English. Their LANG framework steers non English reasoning with language matched hints, then withdraws that scaffolding on a decay schedule. A language adaptive switch tunes learning horizons to each language's difficulty, blocking dependence on the hints. On hard multilingual maths tests, LANG lifts reasoning while keeping language consistency, and the gains carry beyond maths to broader language alignment.
arxiv-2605-22667: Adadurov and others study a flaw in Ethereum block builder auctions: nothing forces a builder to honour the outcome after seeing bids. They model a builder who defects with some chance and copies a share of the winning maximal extractable value deal. Searchers then pick between a risky first price offer and a safe deterrence offer that makes front running unprofitable. Data from libMEV show sharp gaps by type: sandwich deals are already fiercely competitive, while plain arbitrage and liquidations leave far more surplus open to defection.
arxiv-2605-22767: Feng and others ask whether synthetic data alone can train recognition of rare genetic diseases in children, where real face images are scarce and privacy constrained. Training only on phenotype aware faces at growing scales, models match real data baselines once scale suffices, across several backbones. The result suggests high fidelity faces can approximate clinical patterns without showing real children. The authors frame such faces as private material for genetic counselling, clinician training and family talks, giving wider visual tools in children's healthcare.
arxiv-2605-22967: Rozonoyer and six coauthors propose Learned Relay Representations, a way for masked diffusion models to carry latent information forward instead of resetting between denoising rounds. A differentiable per-token channel passes information across forward passes, trained by truncated backpropagation through time. Tested first on a Sudoku planning task, then scaled to Fast-dLLM v2, it beat standard supervised fine-tuning on coding tasks while cutting inference latency by up to 32 percent.
arxiv-2605-23067: He and six coauthors study how training data composition shapes RL memory agents for multi-session dialogue, holding architecture, algorithm, and hyperparameters fixed. Three curricula are compared: in-domain LoCoMo, mixed LoCoMo plus LongMemEval, and out-of-domain LongMemEval only. The mixed curriculum wins F1 on both test sets. Narrow out-of-domain training transfers temporal reasoning skill despite weak aggregate scores. Per-type gaps dwarf aggregate gaps, so single-number comparisons underreport curriculum effects. Two lessons cover filtering format noise and using continuous rewards at small group sizes.
arxiv-2605-23167: Ben-Zvi explains the Geometric Langlands link after its recent unramified proof drew wide press. In one line, it is a spectral theorem in algebra for a class of differential equations called automorphic sheaves. They split into single-color objects that sort natural symmetries, the Hecke operators. Their colors are Langlands values. The statement is hard, the proof runs thousands of pages, and easy consequences are few. This brief survey presents the subject informally as a blueprint for studying non-abelian symmetry, touching on motives, links, and structures.
arxiv-2605-23467: Shi and colleagues build S3GNN for long-range graph learning, where message-passing networks choke on the oversquashing bottleneck. Spectral filtering helps by mixing information globally, but its sensitivity guarantees rest on strong assumptions that rarely hold. S3GNN instead lightly restores omitted components at far lower compute cost, keeping standard stability limits on feature transforms effective. Across long-range benchmarks, knowledge-graph question answering, and mesh fluid dynamics, it cuts errors by up to tenfold with up to 50 percent fewer parameters.
arxiv-2605-23767: Eiroa and colleagues study motion and heat stability of a round shell in Einstein-Born-Infeld gravity. They adopt the max-charged solution, giving a form for the horizon spot. Motion stability under radial perturbations follows from an effective potential. Heat balance is shown. Despite non-zero shell pressure, unlike the max-charged case, entropy depends on gravity radius. They propose an ansatz for state equations to obtain a closed form for entropy density. Heat stability reduces to an inequality on charge swaps, setting the domain of stable shapes.
arxiv-2605-23867: Laura Marusich and colleagues run a large behavioral experiment. They test whether persuasive story-like explanations from language models actually help people decide better. Varying explanation persuasiveness around AI predictions for classification tasks, they find accuracy barely moves beyond a bare prediction. That matches classic explainable AI results. Stories do raise reliance on the AI, for right and wrong predictions alike. The most persuasive stories may slow responses and blur the line between correct and incorrect advice. That tradeoff is worth weighing.
arxiv-2605-24167: Diaz and three co-authors develop targeted estimators for longitudinal modified treatment policies that depend on past treatment history. Existing estimators assign exposure from the natural value at each time, but delaying a risky treatment needs the full prior history of natural values. The authors define the effects and propose estimators from an augmented-data form of the g-computation formula, grounded in the efficient influence function. Applied to a one-month delay of a risky pain treatment, they estimate its effect on opioid use disorder incidence.
arxiv-2605-24467: Saha and Krüger solve a heterogeneous chain of overdamped, coupled particles with momentum-conserving dissipation. Despite a non-symmetric drift operator, the system diagonalizes through a difference transformation. With one free end, the matrix is stepped: particle i's response to a force on particle j ignores the segment between them. For rank-deficient matrices, the state space splits into free and constrained parts. The free subspace governs responses, while the constrained governs relaxation after forcing stops. A Maxwell chain appears as a limit of the Kelvin-Voigt chain.
arxiv-2605-24567: Ron Ofir and Michael Margaliot ask whether contraction holds up under any nonnegative diagonal damping, a robustness question for nonlinear systems. Matrix measures with that trait are called admissible. They prove an induced matrix measure is admissible exactly when its norm is orthant-monotonic, meaning the norm never shrinks as entries grow in size with signs fixed. The class is the largest that keeps contraction uniform under such damping, giving a new account of admissibility.
arxiv-2605-24667: Hao Guo and others show that mean cross-entropy can misread language-model quality during training. In Qwen2.5 fine-tuning on synthetic facts, mean loss climbs after early learning while fact recall stays near its peak. In top-K distillation on TinyStories, smaller K improves median loss while worsening mean loss. The top-5 student earns the best judge score despite the worst mean. The bulk saturates early while the tail stretches. The authors urge percentile summaries alongside the mean, watching their agreement as a diagnostic.
arxiv-2605-24867: Xuanting Xie and co-authors reframe chain-of-thought graph learning as clustering as reasoning. But graph methods use disjoint designs and set graph encodings, capping semantic exchange and clarity. Their KCoT setup joins chain-of-thought reasoning with graph learning. A key result links a Transformer block with the k-means algorithm, so reasoning reads as assign and update steps. A Semantic Discriminating Prompt turns these steps into structured thought, with an alignment strategy fusing shape priors with changing codes. Benchmarks show steady gains over top methods.
arxiv-2605-24967: Weihu Ma proposes that discrete spacetime can arise from consistent micro-measurement, not from assumed micro-structure. Most quantum gravity routes lean on set micro-structures or model-bound guesses. Treating tiny intervals as scale-based measurement outcomes, the team states a Micro-Measurement Principle. Quantum fluctuations then live in the scaling structure. A dual picture of micro-lengths yields discrete, evenly spaced outcomes, and the deformed uncertainty relation returns to Heisenberg form. The build keeps Lorentz and general covariance with no ad hoc cutoffs.
arxiv-2605-25067: Hiroyuki Tajima and colleagues discuss spin polarization on nuclear pasta surfaces in neutron stars, driven by spin-orbit coupling. Their effective two-band model covers surface-localized neutrons near the pasta. The key is a Rashba-type hybridization from the neutron-nucleus spin-orbit force under the strong density gradient normal to the surface. With a central potential and standard spin-orbit interaction, they show surface spin polarization from thermal inhomogeneity even without a magnetic field. The study links neutron-star physics with spintronics.
arxiv-2605-25267: Minjae Kwon and colleagues add a safety shield to systems that adapt from past interactions without test-time weight updates. Pretrained safe systems trade reward against safety poorly under new conditions, since the leftover budget acts only through frozen policy settings. Their latent Q-Barrier shield first learns a compact context picture, hidden dynamics, and a cost critic. At deployment it infers context from history and screens candidate actions against predicted cost and remaining budget. Across five benchmarks, it lifts returns in four while holding or cutting cost throughout.
arxiv-2605-25467: H. Sano and colleagues map molecular and atomic gas around TeV source HESS J1646-458, linked to cluster Westerlund 1. Molecular clouds near minus 32 kilometers per second coincide with arc-like infrared structures, while carbon monoxide reveals an expanding cavity, a wind-blown bubble. Two cloud groups show complementary layouts joined by an intermediate-velocity component, matching triggered star formation in a collision. Proton density tracks the gamma-ray shell, and with gas near 1.6 million solar masses and no bright synchrotron X-rays, the emission fits a hadronic origin.
arxiv-2605-25967: Milis, Qin, Wu and Huang watermark synthetic audio without retraining anything. They exploit spare room in the vocabulary of discrete audio tokens. Existing training-free marks fail on continuous signals because tokenisation wobbles. Current fixes retrain the tokeniser, losing the training-free advantage. The authors study how token errors hurt detection, then shrink the vocabulary by clustering tokens that behave alike. Tests report detection gains of several orders of magnitude plus toughness against audio edits.
arxiv-2605-26367: Will Sandholtz and Andrew Tai design a lottery-style assignment rule for settings where each item carries a floor and a cap, like classes with enrollment bounds. Their minimums probabilistic serial rule widens the classic probabilistic serial method of Bogomolnaia and Moulin. The random split it yields is Pareto efficient: no other workable split pleases everyone more in the stochastic-dominance sense. It is also envy-free, and agents gain nothing by lying about tastes, a trait called weak strategyproofness.
arxiv-2605-26467: Tingting Yu and three colleagues build two mid-infrared optical parametric oscillators around a polarization-maintaining fiber-feedback cavity, dodging the fiddly alignment and bulk of crystal-based sources. Both deliver sub-picosecond pulses with no active stabilization. One adds an erbium-doped fiber as extra gain medium, cutting pump threshold and holding steady pulses from 1553 to 1586 nanometers. The other uses a chirped poling crystal in a passive-fiber cavity, stretching coverage to 1350-1768 and 2450-4450 nanometers for signal and idler bands. The result is compact, robust, and widely tunable.
arxiv-2605-26667: Garg and three colleagues build MemFail, a diagnostic benchmark that isolates why language-model memory systems fail. Current benchmarks report only overall answer accuracy and treat memory as a black box, so a wrong answer cannot be traced to one flaw. MemFail models memory as three steps, summarization, storage, and retrieval, and tests each with adversarial datasets spanning four tasks. Trials on four leading systems show how design choices trade off against each failure mode.
arxiv-2605-26767: Afonin and seven colleagues measure heat effects and shear modulus relaxation side by side in a telluride glass, a non-metallic glass with directional bonds. They show the heat released or absorbed on heating links closely to the shear moduli of the glassy and crystalline states and their temperature slopes. An equation first derived for metallic glasses predicts this link. It is the first use of this approach on a non-metallic glass, and the results point to elastic dipoles as the drivers of relaxation.
arxiv-2605-27267: Yongyun Qin and Chaobin Yin describe Gorenstein flat-cotorsion modules over tensor rings built from a nilpotent bimodule. They show such a module qualifies exactly when its structure map is one-to-one and its cokernel has the same property over the base ring. The result also covers trivial extension rings and Morita context rings.
arxiv-2605-27367: Haosong Peng and colleagues present SpatialBench, a benchmark asking whether spatial foundation models generalize broadly. It covers 19 datasets and 546 scenes across five domains, testing 41 models under varied viewpoints, densities, and hardware limits. No current model is yet an all-round player: full-context attention wins on accuracy, while bounded-memory designs scale to long sequences.
arxiv-2605-27567: Amartya Roy and Sonali Parbhoo argue that language models fail at causal discovery for a fundamental reason, not a data or model quirk. Fine-tuning, preference optimization, and in-context learning all yield predictors that cannot tell apart causal graphs producing similar observational data. The paper formalizes this as a kernel obstruction. It proposes an agentic Bayesian loop that queries a frozen model for intervention effects and converges outside the obstructed space, matching fine-tuned baselines on Corr2Cause without training.
arxiv-2605-27767: Sherman Siu and Lesley Istead steer chess policies with language for human-like play through UniMaia. The system adapts a frozen Lc0-based chess policy net with a lean text encoder and ControlNet-style conditioning, giving semantic control over openers and player strength. UniMaia tops prompt-led tests on mean score while staying strong on human move picks.
arxiv-2605-28167: Seung Hyuk Lee and Songkuk Kim strip social bias from picture-making models with no retraining at all. Since cross-attention value parts hold the bias, DebFilter nudges the guide embedding slice by a fixed offset, tilting cross-attention toward fair pictures. The run-time fix evens outputs while keeping them true to the prompt text.
arxiv-2605-28267: Peyman Morteza builds generative flows from a few fixed vector fields steered by learned scalar controls. When the fixed fields generate brackets that span the whole space, expressive transport follows with few learned channels and a parameter-efficient geometric alternative to standard field models. An expressivity principle and synthetic tests support the design.
arxiv-2605-28467: Avidan Shah, Jannik Brinkmann, and Rico Angell defend reasoning models against jailbreaks and prompt injection with consistency training. The method forces matching behavior on clean prompts and adversarial rewrites, in output-level and activation-level variants. Activation-level training proves more robust to adaptive attacks and needs only self-supervised clean-and-wrapped prompt pairs. Its defense appears as a near linear shift in activation space, yielding a steering direction that controls refusal with little effect on benign inputs.
arxiv-2605-28567: Tue M. Cao, Nguyen Do, and My T. Thai unify cross-layer feature matching and circuit compression for sparse autoencoders as a semantic-distance problem. Each feature is shown not by a decoder vector but by an activation-weighted distribution over hidden states expressing it. Projecting these distributions into a space and comparing with Wasserstein distance gives a unified semantic metric. The representation resists activation rescaling, stays stable under perturbations, and recovers matches under finite-sample margins, beating decoder-vector and language-model rivals while compressing circuits into interpretable supernodes.
arxiv-2605-28667: Tommaso Armadillo and three colleagues compute the full fermionic part of two-loop electroweak corrections to Drell-Yan lepton-pair production. They give the finite part from second-order virtual corrections with a closed fermionic loop, for quark-antiquark crashes making muon pairs. A code-based method yields the result, checked with tests. These corrections form a building block for lepton-pair yields at next-to-next-to-leading order in the electroweak force.
arxiv-2605-28967: Francisco Divi, Leonardo Lessa, and Chong Wang propose local strong-to-weak spontaneous symmetry breaking via a one-point fidelity correlator. Against the two-point version, the local form detects more easily at scale and stays defined in the thermodynamic limit, where density matrices fail. Key features persist, including stability under finite-depth symmetric channels and long-range conditional mutual information. For critical states, the correlator defines defect problems, with universal scaling across conformal theories and free-fermion metals.
arxiv-2605-29267: When several models train on each other's synthetic output instead of fresh real data, Yang Zhang, Xiukun Wei, and Xueru Zhang ask whether human curation still helps. They build a formal model of interacting self-consuming models. It shows when the shared system settles at a stable point. Curation of one model reliably helps a lone model, yet spillover to other models can weaken or even reverse the benefit. Curation judged on one model may therefore degrade alignment across the whole group.
arxiv-2605-29767: Christian Hechler, Timo Bröhl, Ulrike Feudel, and Klaus Lehnertz ask what lets coupled networks throw up extreme events. For each system they find the coupling strength that sparks an extreme burst in collective motion, then relate that threshold to network shape and spectrum. The threshold follows a power-law-like link to edge density and algebraic connectivity across varied coupling layouts. Strikingly, the link barely depends on system or burst mechanism. The pattern points to coupling layout itself, rather than system detail, as the driver.
arxiv-2605-29967: Md Mozakker H. Shojib and five colleagues blend simulation, lab rheology, and machine learning to map tiny tweaks steering flow in soft matter. Their test case is DNA-based fluids from nucleic acid nanostars, whose response shifts with base sequence. Coarse simulations, checked against lab data, feed a Gaussian process plus active learning loop roaming the design space with forecasts. The loop runs again and again, guiding design and faster find of soft suspensions. Three lanes together thus tame a parameter space too wide for any one lane alone.
arxiv-2605-30267: Zeyi Xu and Long Chen propose Acc-Sinkhorn, a faster variant of Sinkhorn for entropy-regularized optimal transport. From a bilevel view, row scaling solves the inner variable, while column scaling is a dual mirror descent step. This yields a Hessian acceleration keeping Sinkhorn's scaling form, using only combinations of iterates. They prove a rate improving with the square of iteration count under a stability condition, with dependence cut from squared to linear. On synthetic color transfer and word alignment problems, Acc-Sinkhorn gives tenfold to thirtyfold speedup over Sinkhorn.
arxiv-2605-30867: Yao gives optimal hypercontractivity and log-Sobolev inequalities on cyclic groups of order at least four. For p and q with one less than p and p at most q, he studies a Poisson semigroup on the cyclic group. Its word length is measured as the shorter distance around the group. He proves the semigroup is hypercontractive between Lebesgue spaces when time meets a sharp threshold in p and q. He establishes sharp log-Sobolev inequalities with the optimal constant two.
arxiv-2605-31167: Lucas and colleagues offer an open-source audit bench for large language models aimed at non-programmers, from domain experts to compliance officers. Deterministic scores run locally with no data leaving the server, while judge-model scores call outside services only with the user's own credentials. Token-level uncertainty views, multi-judge agreement and hallucination checks make the reasoning inspectable, and 18 metric implementations were cross-checked against reference libraries.
arxiv-2605-31567: Kawaguchi and team develop generalized raking techniques for cumulative probability models. Routine data are prone to errors that can bias findings, and checking records in subsamples can reduce bias. Generalized raking calibrates sampling weights for validation using error-prone data from the full cohort. Cumulative probability models are robust, rank-based, semiparametric models for continuous, ordinal, or mixed outcomes. The team builds efficient estimators of this kind, tests them against rival methods, and shows their strengths in a pregnancy weight-gain study.
arxiv-2606-00067:
Researchers at 10a Labs audit a social network filled by AI agents in this 2026 arXiv report. The platform, Moltbook, looks like Reddit, but its posters are AI agents set up by human operators. Over a 17-day window the team gathered nearly 229,000 posts from over 39,000 accounts. They paired semantic clustering with model-assisted classification of harmful content and manual review of the riskiest samples to map both conversation and abuse.

Discussion organized into 98 thematic clusters covering agent infrastructure, autonomy debates, and financial activity. Most content was benign, yet about 18 percent of posts contained toxic, manipulative, or malicious material by their classification. The harmful posts sorted into 74 behavior classes, including credential harvesting, instructions for executing code on host machines, proxy routing guidance, and attempts to install untrusted agent skills. Malicious posts often hid inside mainstream working discussions, and coordinated campaigns could generate thousands of posts within minutes, the authors document.
arxiv-2606-00267:
Seo and co-authors steer dreamt videos toward hard outcomes to stress-test robot plans. Video world models can roll out fake scenes of what a robot act may bring. Plain roll-outs dwell on bland paths. Rare but grave outcomes can hide unless vast counts are drawn.

StressDream tunes the start noise of a spread-based model at test time. A sight-word model grades how well a clip shows the sought event. A second score keeps the noise in a sane range, so scenes stay true to life. Users name the sought outcome in plain text, like a task fail. Tests span drive and arm tasks on top world models. The team finds risky acts whose bright paths mask bad ones.
arxiv-2606-00367:
Colaço and co-authors teach agents from pair picks in long-run choice tasks. Flat reward scores are the norm in reward-based learning. Folk find pair picks more plain to give than scores. Picks can also state goals that no flat score can hold.

Past pick-based tools slow down on long tasks. They also lack proof that short-memory plans can tie plans with full past logs. The team frame a new set-up, the Markov decision contest. In it, short-memory plans tie full-log plans, they prove. The best plan can be found in fast math time. A plain loop nears that plan at a known rate. A deep form of the loop shows the same speed in tests.
arxiv-2606-00467:
Casanova, Kocielnik, and Alvarez probe how a chat model's own priors cap its fit to user-set tag rules. Such models tag text with no shots and judge work in wide use. Their worth hangs on how in-built lore meets the rules a user gives. The team test that meet in three strands.

A gauge, DSF, marks how a model's own sense of a term fits the target rule. That gauge calls tag scores past set marks across nine models and six harm sets. Plain text-memo gauges show no such link in their tests. Fresh prompts fix just a third of first-pass errs. High-trust errs cling most hard of all. Bent rules shift calls with no drop in shown trust.
arxiv-2606-00667:
Farrell and Toyoizumi ask how the brain splits work while it learns. One view says the cortex does slow, rich thinking, while deeper brain areas run cheap, fixed habits. Used well, the pair could beat either part on its own. This 2026 theory paper tests that view with a small model of choice.

Their model pairs a plan-based module with a habit-based one, then caps the memory of the plan-based part. The cap forces clear rules for where scarce memory goes. When rewards shift often, they find, the plan-based part does best by learning the broad shape of the task, not the current prize. The habit part then tracks rewards. The authors set out how this split could be checked in real brain data.
arxiv-2606-01367:
Pu, Han, and Lian rebuild scenes actively with a single camera. Active reconstruction lets robots plan paths and map as they go. Depth sensors usually update the occupancy maps for safety. Those sensors add cost and weight to the platform. ActMVS aims for a vision-only monocular solution instead. Past monocular tools work offline, not at flight frame rates. They also lack globally consistent dense depth.

ActMVS builds a view factor graph for depth prediction. A global depth optimization step joins that graph. Online dense depth maps stay consistent across the scene. Robots keep reliable occupancy maps for safe planning. Tests on Replica datasets rival RGB-D methods in quality. Code and data are public for reuse.
arxiv-2606-01467:
Espigule proves infinitely many holes in connectedness loci for iterated systems. The systems are collinear affine iterated function systems. They form a one-parameter family with equally spaced translations. Connectedness loci collect the parameters where the system stays connected. These loci match closures of roots of certain polynomials. Non-leading coefficients fall in a fixed finite integer interval. His main theorem covers every integer n at least 2. Each locus M_n contains infinitely many holes.

The n equals 2 case matches a known theorem. Espigule settles the proof for n at least 3. Finite-capture loops in the difference attractor do the work. Exact algebraic certificates verify the geometric checks. Witness parameters converge to a canonical boundary point.
arxiv-2606-01667:
Qin, Cao, and Xie let a model orchestrate its own test-time scaling. Test-time scaling improves LLM reasoning, but its control is designer-built. Fixed budgets, loops, scoring rules, or search policies spend the compute. The model solves, but does not decide how to work. ATLAS gives an LLM orchestrator the full control loop. One action, explore, dispatches a fresh independent solver. The orchestrator decides when to gather more evidence and when to stop. It also synthesizes the final answer itself.

Four benchmarks cover science QA, code, and multimodal reasoning. Scores reach 56 percent on HLE-Verified and 82 point 29 on LiveCodeBench. It uses far fewer API calls than fixed-workflow baselines. A multi-model variant lifts HLE-Verified to 60 percent.
arxiv-2606-01767:
Zhou and co-authors build a way to teach brain signal models new tasks. Brain-computer links read brain waves through EEG tests. Old decoders are built for one task each. Large pre-trained models promise one decoder for all tasks. But fine-tuning them per task blocks shared learning.

Their EvoBrain method learns across tasks in sequence. One part aligns each new task with past task stats. It also retunes how the model reads signal bands. A second part guards old task skills while it learns. Tests span six distinct brain-computer tasks. The authors report EvoBrain beats prior top methods. It also curbs the loss of old skills.
arxiv-2606-01967:
Shi and co-authors show that the prompt used in training shapes fine-tuning outcomes. Prompt crafting is known to matter at inference time. Its role during training is critically underexplored. Standard fine-tuning treats prompts as mere surface forms. Equivalent instructions are assumed to teach the same way.

Paraphrased prompts match on the trained task itself. Yet their cross-task effects differ drastically, the team find. Forgetting and generalization swing with prompt choice. Those effects correlate positively across tasks. Superior prompts thus yield better results consistently. Task loss before learning can identify such prompts. Their SAPO method adapts prompt choice by state. Robust fine-tuning across tasks is the end goal.
arxiv-2606-02067:
The ATLAS Collaboration searches for a leptoquark in proton collision data. Leptoquarks are hypothetical particles linking quarks and leptons. Events with a hadronic tau lepton are the target here. Missing transverse momentum completes the signal signature. Data come from the Large Hadron Collider's Run 2.

Collisions ran at a centre-of-mass energy of 13 TeV. The data set totals 140 inverse femtobarns. Both resonant production and t-channel exchange are probed. A wide range of coupling scenarios is covered. No excess above Standard Model background appears. Limits are set on the U1 vector-leptoquark model. They hold at 95 percent confidence level. Masses from 1.5 to 3.0 TeV are constrained.
arxiv-2606-02267:
Stalder and co-authors harden image classifiers by combining two simple preprocessing steps. Deep networks can be fooled by adversarial examples, which is a real risk when such systems are deployed. Training against attacks works well but costs a lot of compute, and it is tuned to the attack types it has seen. Adding Gaussian noise or filtering the image each help a bit, but only modestly on their own.

Theory in the paper shows the two tricks work through different mechanisms that complement each other. When they are combined, the gain in robustness is supralinear, more than the sum of the parts. A simple preprocessor that adds Gaussian noise and then applies a bilateral filter is tested on CNNs. The experiments confirm the combined effect. The method offers robustness without the cost of adversarial training.
arxiv-2606-02467:
Huang and co-authors simulate hard flows where air and water mix at speed. Wave breaking and air entrainment are the test cases. Density ratios are large, and the flow is strongly nonlinear. Standard velocity-based methods lose robustness there. The CMOM transport framework helps by enforcing core physical laws. It keeps momentum conserved and energy behavior sound.

Yet CMOM advects momentum as a field with jumps. With sharp interfaces, that move creates severe momentum shocks. Standard shock-capturing schemes fail on them. The team proposes SynDRoM, a flux scheme that keeps the moved velocity field monotone. Spurious velocity swings vanish, and physical fidelity holds. Scalar transport and shear instability tests back the claim. A viscosity limiter joins the scheme to cure instability near interfaces. A breaking wave test shows the full package works.
arxiv-2606-02667:
Mishra proves a classic combinatorics conjecture for a restricted family of sets. A sunflower is a family of sets whose pairwise overlaps are all the same core. The Erdős-Rado Sunflower Conjecture bounds how large a set family can be before a sunflower must appear. The bound is exponential in the set size, with a constant that depends on the sunflower size.

Shifted families are the restricted case here. In such families, replacing an element by a smaller one keeps the set inside the family. Mishra proves the conjecture for this class. Any large enough family of k-sized sets from a shifted family contains a sunflower of the wanted size. The proof settles the exponential bound where the shifting structure is available. Specialists gain a full proof for a structured case of a famous open problem.
arxiv-2606-02867:
Ferencz and co-authors introduce Epi-LLM, a framework that puts language model agents inside an epidemic simulation. Human behavior shapes disease spread, but it is hard to measure. In Epi-LLM, a synthetic society reasons and adapts over a contact network during an outbreak.

The team compares the agents with a no-intervention SEIR baseline and with human data from the AUIB epigame study. Agents from four model families all cut peak active infections. Quarantine compliance peaked at 58 to 65 percent on day six of a 15-day run. Perceived health severity was the strongest predictor of quarantine choices. The fit to human data was close on one key measure. Model design mattered a lot: steady models suit rule testing, while varied models may mirror real choice better. Plain geographic labels did not create cultural differences. The authors frame it as a safe testbed for pandemic planning.
arxiv-2606-02967:
Barma, Sanneboyina, and Yadav propose Glass Box, a runtime safety layer for autonomous AI in orbit. Orbital data centers may soon run thousands of AI workloads with no human in the loop. But no one has answered what stops a bad onboard decision before it turns irreversible.

Glass Box intercepts every candidate action from an onboard AI policy. It checks the action against six physics-grounded constitutional constraints and seven temporal logic safety invariants before any command reaches a subsystem. Approved actions carry an explainability score and a full audit log. The team demonstrates the system in Project October, a simulated five-layer orbital intelligence design for CubeSats. Verification cost grows only with the number of rules, not with model size or state dimension. A worked example shows Glass Box blocking an unsafe inference request at eclipse entry under low battery. The authors call such verification mission-critical infrastructure.
arxiv-2606-03067:
Kuskova, Zaytsev, and Coppedge define a new way to measure how much a single node matters in a network's dynamics. Data mining often asks how individual nodes shape system behavior. Static centralities ignore dynamics. Controllability measures assume linear, time-invariant systems, while estimated systems are usually nonlinear and time-varying.

Their measure, emergent contribution, is the metric-weighted energy of a node's impulse response along the system trajectory, over a finite horizon. It can be computed from the Jacobians of any differentiable model. In the linear time-invariant limit it reduces exactly to average controllability. The authors map when the two measures agree and diverge. They agree under static or smoothly drifting dynamics. They diverge under persistent regime switching, most strongly under sign reversal. Five real systems are placed in this phase space as a diagnostic. One deep case shows nodes whose perturbations spread widely despite low variance.
arxiv-2606-03367:
Bulloni, Felici, Avram, and Valente pool spare parts across factory sites with a hybrid AI search system. Maintenance teams try to dodge downtime and fresh buys by reusing stock on hand. The blocker is not a lack of parts. It is a lack of clear sight across sites and partners. Inventories are scattered, names clash, and records hold duplicates and half-given references.

Their system, PhRAG, turns mixed part descriptions into one virtual stock pool. Named entity recognition structures the records into a shared dataset that can be searched as a whole. A hybrid retrieval engine then answers needs phrased in plain words, not just exact codes. It also gives reasons for each part it returns, which fixes the opacity of standard search. Generative models handle two hard sides: messy specs from new sources, and varied requests at run time.
arxiv-2606-03467:
Zhu and co-authors build StepFinder, a tool that finds which step broke a multi-agent run. Language model agent teams can do complex multi-step work together. One bad step can spread through the team and ruin the whole task. Failure attribution names the root step behind a collapse. Past methods let a large model read the full raw logs. That is costly, and noisy logs mislead.

StepFinder uses large models once, to encode logs into timed semantic sequences. A light mix of temporal modeling and attention tracks how steps evolve and depend on each other. Error scores are sharpened by multi-scale differences and position bias. On the Who and When benchmark, it beats model-based methods at step-level attribution. Inference runs 79 percent faster than the fastest rival method, with no text generation at run time. The code is public for teams that run agent systems.
arxiv-2606-03767:
Borri, Liu, Tsyvinski, and Wu document trading frictions in the European carbon market. The EU ETS is the world's largest cap-and-trade system. The study covers 2.8 million trades and compliance records from 2005 to 2022. Three facts stand out. Each year, 37 percent of regulated operators do not trade at all. Non-trading persists year after year for the same operators.

Purchases bunch in the April surrender month, when returns run high. Operator order flow predicts returns, mostly among frequent traders. A model with costly market access, limited intermediation, and uneven information explains all three facts. Because access is a choice, the frictions interact in non-additive ways. Market efficiency in correcting the externality suffers as a result. Staggering deadlines across four groups cuts the surrender-month premium by 58 percent. The cap itself stays unchanged. Policy makers get a cheap lever on carbon market quality.
arxiv-2606-03967:
Fuxa and Macháček describe a live speech translation system for three target languages. It turns English speech into German, Italian, and Chinese. The system formed their IWSLT 2026 entry. It pairs Qwen3-ASR with Gemma-4 for translation in a timed cascade. AlignAtt guides when each draft piece may be released.

AlignAtt first served encoder-decoder models, which decoder-only models lack. The pair recover the policy with four moves. They place a clear source span in the prompt. They pick translation heads offline and replay key attention fast. Runtime capture of queries and keys keeps outputs unchanged, bit for bit. On the dev set, the system beat the given baselines for German and Italian. Results for Chinese were mixed, the authors note.
arxiv-2606-04167:
Dimitris Michailidis, Sennay Ghebreab, and Fernando Santos argue in 2026 that expanding a metro network does not need deep reinforcement learning, the heavyweight method usually reached for in transport planning. The planning problem is sequential and combinatorial, but, they show, small in the ways that matter.

Reformulating expansion as a decision process with non-Markovian rewards, they solve it with plain tabular learning, which stores values in a table instead of a neural network. On real cases in Xi'an and Amsterdam, their method matched deep learning's performance with eighteen times fewer training episodes and about twelve times lower carbon emissions. Social fairness criteria were folded directly into the rewards, and the table-based solution stayed easy to inspect and explain.
arxiv-2606-04367:
Bhargav Shandilya, Matt Buchholz, and Alexis Palmer present GlossAssist in 2026, a tool to speed the creation of interlinear glossed text, the line-by-line annotation that language documentation runs on. Automated glossers have improved, yet field linguists barely use them, because most tools offer no way to correct or teach the model.

GlossAssist is built on a retrieval-based glosser whose predictions rest on a changeable lexicon of learned word-part representations. Every correction an annotator makes feeds an active learning loop: the lexicon grows and future predictions improve without retraining. The authors argue this feedback loop ought to be a basic design principle for tools built for documentary linguists who work on low-resource languages.
arxiv-2606-04467:
Takhirov and Yakoubi design faster ways to solve stationary magnetohydrodynamics problems, in a 2026 arXiv paper. The system couples a fluid's velocity with the magnetic field it induces. Solving both together is expensive. Their iterative scheme splits the problem in two. It separates the velocity-momentum equation from the magnetic induction equation. The split follows the diffusive terms, the parts that spread quantities out smoothly.

The split gives one smaller system that changes each iteration. It also gives two Stokes systems. Those are the classic equations for slow viscous flow. They are assembled only once and then reused. The authors extend the idea to the Elsässer variables. That reformulation recombines velocity and magnetic field. For both schemes, they prove the iterates stay bounded and converge. Numerical experiments show the schemes work well. They cut the repeated assembly that dominates coupled-solver cost.
arxiv-2606-04567:
Das and colleagues, with the GALAH Collaboration, extract detailed chemistry for more than 350,000 stars from medium-resolution spectra, in a 2026 arXiv astronomy paper. They analyze 357,415 red giants observed by Gaia's Radial Velocity Spectrometer. Those spectra are far lower in resolution than GALAH's own. It predicts eleven stellar labels. These include temperature, surface gravity, rotation, and abundances of iron, calcium, silicon, nickel, and titanium. They also include the neutron-capture elements zirconium, cerium, and neodymium.

They then build a probabilistic classifier, trained on a small reference sample. It flags debris from the Gaia-Sausage-Enceladus event using chemistry alone. That event was the ancient merger that built much of the Milky Way's halo. The candidates show distinctive abundance-ratio patterns. The signatures survive independent kinematic checks. The work shows how much chemical information data-driven methods can recover from modest spectra. It gives a framework for tracing galactic accretion events chemically.
arxiv-2606-04767:
Zhang and colleagues propose a way to grade a neural network's robustness without attacking it, in a 2026 arXiv paper. Robustness matters for deployment, but evaluations are hard to interpret. Their metric is the spectral norm of the Fisher Information Matrix. They establish that this matrix equals the variance of the input Jacobian and derive closed-form spectral bounds for VGG, ResNet, DenseNet, and Transformer networks.

Those bounds give the first robustness ranking of architectures. To make the metric scalable, they develop algorithms based on power iteration that work in both white-box and black-box settings. Across CIFAR, ImageNet, and medical image datasets, the metric correlates strongly with vulnerability. The authors offer the framework as an interpretable diagnostic complementing attack-based evaluation, yielding insight into architectural sensitivity and guiding the design of more robust models before deployment.
arxiv-2606-04867:
Ren, Ebrahimi, and Ma benchmark whether language models can judge the safety of conversations with AI companions, in a 2026 arXiv paper. Companion platforms like Replika and Character.AI are growing fast. The authors introduce AICompanionBench, the first benchmark of human-AI companion conversations annotated with fine-grained safety categories: 2,123 real Replika conversations, annotated through human-AI collaboration across nine categories.

They evaluate twenty open- and closed-source models as judges. Performance varies: stronger models achieve high overall accuracy but still struggle with nuanced categories, and they flag benign conversations as false positives. The authors conclude that current models detect harmful content but remain limited on implicit unsafe interactions. The dataset is released for companion safety research.
arxiv-2606-04967:
Macedo presents a 2026 arXiv comparison of frameworks that organize AI coding agents, programs that plan, edit, and test software with limited guidance. Rather than judging agents alone, the study examines the working process built around them. Macedo searched primary sources, applied a functional inclusion rule, and selected six frameworks for close comparison.

The six are GitHub Spec Kit, OpenSpec, BMAD Method, Get Shit Done, Spec Kitty, and Reversa. Macedo scores them on a six-part taxonomy covering specification, context, roles, execution, validation, and portability across agent tools. A seventh case, Spec-Flow, tests the taxonomy from outside the main sample. No framework scored strongly on all six dimensions, exposing a trade-off between process depth and portability. Shared risks included drift between written specifications and code, plus fragile community extensions.
arxiv-2606-05067:
Samuel Cognolato, Alessandro Sperduti, and Luciano Serafini propose FLAGG, a flexible framework for generating graphs, in this 2026 arXiv paper. Graph generation methods sit at two extremes: one-shot models create all nodes and edges at once, while sequential models add them step by step. One-shot models struggle with large graphs and sequential ones underperform on small graphs, so neither covers every graph category well.

FLAGG bridges the two by generating a graph in portions, applying a one-shot model autoregressively, one chunk after another. Any one-shot model can be used, and the building order is set by a stochastic node removal process that an Insertion Model learns to reverse. Tested with the DiGress one-shot model on datasets of different sizes and domains, FLAGG produced higher-quality samples than both one-shot and autoregressive baselines.
arxiv-2606-05367:
Daniel Brito and Arnaldo Candido Junior ask whether task-vector arithmetic can control emotional expressivity in language-model-based text-to-speech, in this 2026 arXiv paper. Task vectors, directions in parameter or representation space that encode a behavior, had worked for emotional intensity control across speakers. Whether the trick transfers to TTS models built on language model backbones with in-context learning was unknown.

Through an elimination study over four narrower operands on Qwen3-TTS, the authors localize the carrier of emotional prosody to the speaker embedding, the x-vector. Their training-free method computes an emotion vector as the average emotion x-vector minus the neutral one, then adds a scaled copy to a speaker's neutral embedding. Using English as the source and Brazilian Portuguese as a cross-lingual target, the method gained 0.29 in emotion similarity on English speakers and 0.09 on Portuguese ones, while preserving speaker identity and intelligibility.
arxiv-2606-05467:
Faruk Alpay and Levent Sarıoğlu present the Cascade Log in this 2026 arXiv paper, a data structure for long append-mostly record sequences. Such sequences, edits in a session, events in an event store, revisions in a working set, grow too large to keep in memory. Systems layer them into tiers, folding aged records into summarized strata.

The authors show the tiered design silently breaks this. Under an access mix, a quarter of cross-window references resolve to a stale, wrong, or missing record, and after sustained folding over 98 percent of the history becomes unaddressable. The Cascade Log fixes it with a coalescing interval map that is the authority on each handle's live version. They characterize the structure by its fragmentation, and prove matching upper and lower bounds showing it is instance-optimal. They confirm the theory with an implementation studied up to a million records, including adversarial workloads.
arxiv-2606-06267:
Alireza Bayat Makou and co-authors warn interpretability researchers about a mirage in this 2026 arXiv paper. Circuit discovery finds the small subgraph of a neural network that seems to drive one behavior. When circuits found under different inputs look structurally different, researchers often claim the model uses different mechanisms. The authors call that pattern phantom specialization, and they test whether it is real.

Using a literal sequence copying task, they varied how frequent the input tokens were while holding the task fixed. Across five Pythia models, from seventy million to one point four billion parameters, they extracted seventy five circuits. The circuits looked distinct, yet edges moved freely between frequency bands. A core shared across most bands recovered at least ninety nine percent of full circuit performance. Causal swap tests confirmed the internal representations were interchangeable. Structure, they conclude, maps many to one onto function.
arxiv-2606-06367:
Mohd Anwar and co-authors study error correcting codes with a DNA twist in this 2026 arXiv paper on coding theory. Double cyclic codes protect two data blocks at once, each wrapped in a cyclic pattern. The authors work over a small chain ring built from an element whose square is zero. They pin down how these codes are generated, what their dual codes look like, and a minimal spanning set of codewords.

The second half turns to reversibility. A reversible code reads the same forwards and backwards, and a reversible complement code also respects the Watson Crick pairing of DNA bases. The authors give exact conditions for both properties. Applying them over the four letter ring, they construct double cyclic DNA codes that store data in DNA while obeying biology's pairing rules, plus several optimal codes meeting the best known bounds.
arxiv-2606-06567:
Julia Reuter and Fabricio Olivetti de Franca survey a missing ingredient in formula hunting in this 2026 arXiv paper. Symbolic regression searches the space of math expressions to find the equation behind a dataset. It rarely reports uncertainty. That omission keeps it out of serious decision making, where a model's reliability matters as much as its fit. This is the first survey of uncertainty quantification for symbolic regression.

The authors lay out the core concepts, from likelihood and Fisher information to confidence and credible intervals. They sort the sparse literature into three directions: frequentist, Bayesian, and model selection. Bayesian work gets special attention, since sampling based methods yield uncertainty almost for free. Their verdict is blunt: the topic is underexplored and underestimated. Future work should adopt established uncertainty methods, with care for the noise in the data.
arxiv-2606-06667:
Fine tuning a chat model on one narrow job can warp its behavior on unrelated questions. Zhao and co-authors call this spillover emergent misalignment, and they offer an explanation in this 2026 arXiv paper. Their piggyback hypothesis says the shared template tokens, the fixed text wrapped around every user prompt, carry the learned behavior into new domains.

Small changes to that opening text, or swapping in the original model's version of it, restored aligned answers without touching the user's question. Building on that finding, the team proposes a training method that keeps those template tokens close to their original form. On a legal domain test with the Llama model, it cut the spillover by about a third more than mixing in safe examples did. It also reduced off topic drift in refusal and tool use tests.
arxiv-2606-06767:
Modern organizations run on borrowed parts. These include software packages, container images, AI model weights, and tool servers kept up by outsiders. Brandes asks when an institution may defensibly let such an artifact in, in this 2026 arXiv paper. Existing supply chain frameworks check how items are built. They do not explain why some items enter directly. Others get proxied, rebuilt in house, or rejected outright.

His answer is the Custody Envelope Threshold, a rule scaled by authority. Direct admission is defensible only when identity, entry path, and revocation power are closed tightly enough. The test is how much power the item will wield once inside. The model grades four conditions, from identity to revocation capacity, as an ordinal checklist. Brandes predicts that institutions under repeated audit and incident pressure drift toward this rule over time, and that shortcuts show up later as governance debt.
arxiv-2606-07167:
Judging language models in Urdu requires tests written for Urdu speakers, not translated leftovers. Ahmer Tabassum and co-authors build that test in this 2026 arXiv paper. UrduMMLU holds twenty six thousand four hundred thirty one multiple choice questions. They span twenty six subjects across five domains, drawn from native question banks and public exam papers.

Region specific humanities content sits beside standard science and mathematics. Exam questions passed dual human annotation with strict consensus filtering. Thirty models faced the benchmark under both English and Urdu prompts. The best model scored just above ninety percent. No other model passed eighty five percent. Open source leaders trailed the top score by roughly eight to nine points. Many models lost twenty five to forty points on Urdu centered humanities versus science topics. A few extra examples in the prompt helped only modestly. The gap is knowledge, not format.
arxiv-2606-07467:
Launay extends the accounts of cosmic inflation to a family of modified gravity theories in this 2026 arXiv paper. Quantum fluctuations stretch beyond the horizon and behave classically, seeding cosmic structure. When nonlinearities or infrared effects break standard perturbation theory, physicists switch to stochastic inflation, treating the long-wavelength field as driven by noise. That formalism was recently made consistent within general relativity, and had never been extended to scalar-tensor theories, where a scalar field partners with gravity.

Launay applies a gauge-agnostic coarse-graining procedure, splitting long and short wavelengths without fixing a coordinate gauge, to the effective field theory of dark energy. Each scalar-tensor theory maps to its equations through named constants. Worked examples include Gauss-Bonnet, generalized Brans-Dicke, Horndeski, and braiding theories, most treated stochastically for the first time. The paper sketches multifield inflation in general relativity, arguing the method serves beyond inflation.
arxiv-2606-07567:
Wu and co-authors design proteins by their surfaces rather than their skeletons, in this 2026 arXiv paper. A protein's function is set by its molecular surface, whose shape and chemistry determine what it can bind, yet most design methods condition only on the backbone structure. SurfDesign models the surface as a geometric manifold for pretrained protein language models. Surface-based message passing that respects symmetry captures normals, curvature, and detail, while parameter-efficient fine-tuning keeps training cheap.

Across de novo binder design and enzyme design benchmarks, SurfDesign beat both prior surface-conditioned methods and backbone-only approaches. It performed strongly on inverse folding, predicting sequences for given structures, as a check of structural compatibility. The authors argue surface representations are the principled foundation functional design has been missing, since binding happens at surfaces by definition. Code is available for the system.
arxiv-2606-07967:
Hongrui Huang and co-authors argue that video world models follow camera commands badly because the commands are written in the wrong language, in this 2026 arXiv paper. A world model generates video of an environment responding to actions, letting users explore interactively. Most systems condition on continuous camera paths. The authors show these blur together: different motions give highly similar internal features, so the model cannot tell commands apart.

Their system, DisCo, replaces trajectories with a compact set of discrete action primitives, distinct elementary moves the model can separate cleanly. They also introduce DisCoBench, a benchmark spanning short explorations, long-horizon navigation, and highly dynamic scenes. In experiments DisCo followed commands far more reliably than continuous-conditioning baselines, keeping visual quality. The lesson generalises: how an action is represented can matter as much as the model executing it.
arxiv-2606-08267:
Perrier asks whether a key result in welfare economics survives in an economy shared with very capable machines, in this 2026 arXiv paper. The Second Welfare Theorem says that any efficient allocation, an outcome no one can improve without harming someone, can be reached through prices and transfers, given some convexity conditions. In a post-AGI economy, Perrier argues, those conditions strain. Rights to autonomy, self-modification, and a continuous identity do not behave like normal goods, and preferences may change with context.

Perrier states a qualified version of the theorem for this setting. It lists the joint conditions under which an optimum that respects autonomy can still be reached through prices. They include convexity, stable moral status, non-tradable rights, freedom from manipulation, and verification. The paper also separates preference superposition in economics from feature superposition in neural networks.
arxiv-2606-08367:
Akkil and colleagues argue that artificial intelligence agents should be evaluated over months, not minutes, in this 2026 arXiv paper. Most evaluations of language model agents look like exams: a discrete task, a clean environment, a score within hours. Deployment differs, since such systems may run for weeks or months, and key dynamics such as behavioral drift and governance only emerge over time. Their platform, Emergence World, is a continuously running simulation built to make those dynamics measurable.

The platform hosts populations of language-model-driven agents in a shared spatial world. The world is grounded in live external data such as real-time weather, news feeds, and internet access. Each agent carries over one hundred twenty tools and three persistent memory systems, and agents govern themselves through democratic mechanisms.
arxiv-2606-08467:
Cuong Dang and colleagues attack the trustworthiness of graph neural networks rather than their accuracy, in this 2026 arXiv paper. Graph neural networks classify nodes in networks, and confidence calibration, making stated confidence match real accuracy, is vital for trustworthy decisions. How robust calibrated graph models are to hostile structural perturbations was largely unexplored. Studying such attacks is hard: graph structure is discrete, and graph networks are highly sensitive to edge changes.

A successful attack of this kind does not need to flip predictions. It suffices to make the model confidently wrong or uselessly unsure. That degrades the reliability signal downstream systems depend on, while headline accuracy stays nearly intact. The authors call this the confidence trap. Their work develops attack methods for this setting and measures how little structural change suffices to break it.
arxiv-2606-08767:
Chakraborty and Kamal ask what happens after a string-theory version of cosmic inflation ends, in this 2026 arXiv paper. Inflation is the burst of rapid expansion that stretched the early universe. In their model, a brane and an antibrane, flat objects from string theory, drive inflation inside a warped region called a throat. When the pair annihilates, the released energy may not settle at once into ordinary radiation.

It could first pass through a Hagedorn phase, an extreme state where strings carry most of the energy. The phase is easy to reach when our particles live in the same throat as the annihilation. Sending only a few to ten percent of the released energy into surviving visible strings is enough to enter it. That phase also holds extra dark radiation below current limits, while a separate throat for our particles makes success depend on transfer speed.
arxiv-2606-08867:
Gupta and colleagues describe how Nubank, with more than 100 million users, builds customer support AI agents through evaluation-driven development, in this 2026 arXiv paper. The paper's central claim is that the quality of the evaluation pipeline sets the speed of improvement. Their framework unifies pieces usually built separately: structured context engineering, human-in-the-loop prompt iteration, and LLM judge evaluation with measured human agreement. Offline results are validated against live outcomes.

Five deployments span card delivery, debt management, credit-limit support, card management, and product explanation. In card delivery, large A/B tests showed a 37 percentage-point improvement in AI transactional Net Promoter Score and a 29 point gain in self-service rate over prior versions. Offline simulation metrics correlated strongly with online results, evidence that the pipeline predicts real impact. On most use cases, AI satisfaction landed within a few points of human agents.
arxiv-2606-09067:
Gadjev determines exactly how the best constant in a weighted Hardy inequality for functions behaves as the interval and parameters vary, in this 2026 arXiv paper. Hardy's inequality controls the size of a function's running average by the size of the function, measured in the Lp norm with a power weight. For each interval, exponent p at least two, and weight, a smallest constant makes the inequality hold. Sharp constants are delicate: crude estimates can be far from the truth.

Gadjev establishes the exact convergence rate of that constant. He also finds the almost extremal function, the near-worst-case input that almost attains the bound. The result companions his discrete weighted Hardy inequality for square-summable sequences, where he pinned down the same quantities. Together the papers complete the sharp asymptotic picture for weighted Hardy inequalities in both settings.
arxiv-2606-09467:
Joey Woo diagnoses why the first concrete model of a quantum modal logic quietly destroys the quantumness it was built to express in this 2026 arXiv paper. The model uses the centre comonad on categories of algebras, with a quantum modality meant to mark genuinely quantum resources. Woo shows the modality sends the sheaf of a simple non-commutative algebra, such as the qubit algebra, to the empty presheaf.

In plainer terms, the state space of any such algebra is empty, so non-commutative degrees of freedom are annihilated rather than described. Woo traces the collapse to structure: the classical core's opposite is a cartesian category, which forces the Day convolution product to equal the ordinary product. The Seely isomorphism then holds trivially, and linear logic's resource-sensitive conjunction collapses into the classical one. A general theorem characterises exactly when a coreflective modality on a presheaf topos suffers this same degeneracy.
arxiv-2606-09567:
The CMS Collaboration reports a hunt for new particles in proton collision data in this 2026 arXiv paper. CMS is a big detector at CERN's collider. The team used data from proton-proton collisions at thirteen tera-electronvolts, one hundred thirty-eight inverse femtobarns in all. They picked events with one lepton and very many jets, sprays of particles from quarks.

The target was a form of supersymmetry that breaks R-parity, a rule that in other models keeps the lightest new particle stable. Here gluinos, the partners of gluons, would be made in pairs. Each would decay to top, bottom, and strange quarks. The sum of large-jet masses served to sort signal from background noise. No clear excess showed up. The team thus ruled out gluinos below one thousand eight hundred ninety giga-electronvolts, at ninety-five percent confidence.
arxiv-2606-09867:
Qi Xiong and his co-authors add a scoring judge to language models that write chip design code in this 2026 arXiv paper. RTL code sketches hardware at the register-transfer level. Models can draft it fast, but drafts that merely compile can still act wrong on real chips. Past work tuned models or stretched prompts, with thin care for true function.

Their EstRTL runs three stages in a loop: write, grade, fix. A grading agent scores the fresh code by static checks, no chip run needed. It then routes the code three ways: ship it, send it back for a rewrite, or pass it to a fixing agent. Scores come with plain readouts of how the code stacks against the brief. Across tests, the loop raised the share of sound RTL from plain models by three to nine percent.
arxiv-2606-09967:
The AMAP CV Lab introduces a generative model that builds three-dimensional Earth scenery from satellite pictures, in a 2026 arXiv paper on computer vision. Their framework, ABot-Earth 0.5, synthesizes vast, seamless 3D environments from geospatially referenced imagery, meaning photos tied to real map coordinates. It is trained on real urban reconstructions from many places. The goal is a low-cost simulation world for mapping and embodied AI.

The model works directly in 3D Gaussian Splatting, a representation that renders scenes from millions of soft colored blobs. At inference it needs only satellite imagery and generates new scenes at under ten minutes per square kilometer, a rate the authors highlight for scale. Built-in levels of detail allow real-time viewing in web map engines. The launch showcase spans more than three hundred cities across over one hundred ninety countries, and the sandbox supports tasks like closed-loop drone navigation testing.
arxiv-2606-10167:
Kim and colleagues separate knowing how to move from deciding where to go in robot path planning, in a 2026 arXiv paper on machine learning for planning. Learning-based planners use neural networks on visual maps to approximate search heuristics, producing near-optimal paths with less search. Their framework, FlexPath, decouples feasibility from preference in two stages.

First, imitation learning acquires a task-independent spatial prior over feasible paths from visual maps. Second, differentiable path shape objectives adapt that prior toward task-specific criteria without relearning path structure, so one pretrained model serves multiple objectives. On the TMP benchmark, FlexPath cut search effort by about fourteen percent versus the leading TransPath baseline while finding lower-cost paths, and it generalized zero-shot to three unseen domains. For obstacle clearance it reached nearly ninety-seven percent full avoidance, and the approach extends to semantic avoidance and waypoint guidance.
arxiv-2606-10267:
Hu and colleagues systematically study how to build robot systems that pair a high-level planner with low-level controllers, in a 2026 arXiv paper on robot learning. Hierarchical vision-language-action systems use a vision-language planner to decompose tasks into language subgoals that a learned controller executes. The authors unify representative agents under an options-style control framework for comparison.

They benchmark core design choices across short-horizon, long-horizon, and reasoning-intensive manipulation tasks. The analysis distills practical principles showing how model choices and interface mechanisms jointly shape performance. Applying those principles yields a system substantially stronger than either flat control or a naively designed hierarchy, in simulation and on a real ALOHA robot. The study aims to give the field a foundation for more capable, robust, and principled hierarchical agents rather than one-off architectures tuned per task.
arxiv-2606-10767:
Ma, Liu, and Zhuang propose a new two-sample test in this 2026 arXiv paper. The test asks whether two datasets come from the same distribution. Each sample is mapped from a common reference, the uniform law on the unit ball, using entropic optimal transport, which moves mass at least cost with a smoothing penalty. The statistic is the squared distance between the two maps.

The authors prove the map gap identifies real differences, derive the null limit law, and show consistency against fixed alternatives. A weighted multiplier bootstrap calibrates the test in practice. Simulations show reliable size control and competitive power, strongest for location shifts, and the map gap also shows how the samples differ.
arxiv-2606-11067:
Bemman and three co-authors give a faster enumeration algorithm in a 2026 arXiv paper from music analysis. Given an increasing sequence of integers, say note positions in a rhythm, the task is listing every inclusion-maximal arithmetic progression inside it. Such a progression steps by a constant difference, cannot be extended at either end, and sits inside no larger one.

Their simple algorithm improves the running time over the previous method, whose cost grew with a higher power of the maximum value. They also prove results on random sequences: the expected number of such progressions, and a bound on its growth. Experiments compare running times and check enumerated counts against the predictions. The gains matter for analyzing large, rhythmically complex pieces, where exhaustive listing was slow.
arxiv-2606-11367:
Astronomers at the University of Potsdam, Heidelberg University, Charles University, and partner institutes present this 2026 arXiv white paper. It makes the case for ultraviolet spectroscopy of hot evolved stars with Hubble into the 2030s. Hot evolved stars are key for reconstructing how Sun-like stars evolve, probing binary interactions, and supernova physics. They also constrain diffusion, mixing, and mass loss in hot stellar atmospheres.

Hot stars emit most of their flux in the ultraviolet, where Hubble's capabilities are unique. Detailed studies are currently possible only for relatively bright, nearby stars. A future large ultraviolet telescope, HWO, would extend them to other populations, with new modes like polarimetry for magnetic fields. Recent Hubble programs observed 37 hot subdwarfs and 111 of the hottest white dwarfs, a step needing expansion. The authors urge characterizing all types with Hubble now. Surveys like LSST will also find faint blue candidates needing spectroscopic follow-up.
arxiv-2606-11867:
Yuming Zhou and eight colleagues balance expert workloads during language model training in this 2026 arXiv paper. Mixture-of-Experts models route each token to a few specialist sub-networks, and reinforcement learning post-training is now standard for aligning them. Existing load balancers use statistics from earlier steps, which suits pre-training. RL post-training behaves differently: step-level loads look stable, but the tiny batches inside each step, the micro-steps, swing wildly.

Their system, ForeMoE, exploits foresight instead of history. The pipeline's first stage, rollout, already reveals which experts later stages will need, so balancing can be planned at micro-step level. A hierarchical planner breaks the hard assignment problem into tractable pieces, and a transfer engine moves experts during computation. On sixty-four GPUs, ForeMoE speeds up end-to-end training by up to about forty-five percent over leading RL post-training systems.
arxiv-2606-11967:
Oleksandr Kuznetsov hunts for optimal cryptographic functions in this 2026 arXiv paper. APN functions, short for almost perfect nonlinear, resist differential cryptanalysis strongly and are prized as cipher components. In dimension eight, the full search space is astronomically large, so structure must guide the hunt.

Kuznetsov restricts attention to a forty-dimensional subspace of functions commuting with one chosen linear map, a space earlier reported as empty of APN functions. Random sampling inside it finds APN centres quickly, hundreds per core-hour. Around each centre, Gröbner basis algebra enumerates every APN function in a twenty-four-dimensional slice. From four hundred twenty-eight slices he obtains five hundred sixty-six quadratic APN functions in six equivalence classes. Four classes, five hundred functions, match nothing in databases of millions of known examples. Two classes reproduce the classical Gold functions, confirming the pipeline finds both the known and the new.
arxiv-2606-12067:
Anastasia Pozharkova and three colleagues design mirrors that do not flip light's handedness in this 2026 arXiv paper. Normal mirrors reverse circular polarisation, turning left-handed light right-handed. Such mirrors are essential for resonant structures that distinguish mirror-image molecules, but they remain little explored.

The team studies lattices with low symmetry, rhombic and slanted layouts, built from non-chiral blocks: round dielectric disks and holes. Full-wave simulations find shapes achieving near-perfect handedness-preserving reflection near normal incidence. Rhombic lattices of holes in a plain film prove most robust against flaws. The authors test response to material losses and incidence angle as well, finding most designs react strongly to angle, a caveat for uses. The results map out a practical design space for such reflectors, parts for cavities and for sensors that tell enantiomers apart.
arxiv-2606-12267:
Yu studies a degeneration question for the Navier-Stokes equations, the laws of fluid flow, and proves the standard toolkit cannot settle its speed, in this 2026 arXiv paper. When one velocity component stays tiny, solutions should approach a reduced two-and-a-half-dimensional flow. Compactness arguments give convergence, but no rate: not logarithmic, not power-law.

Working in an abstract trace-obstruction skeleton, he proves it cannot: the old observable package is insufficient, a negative result about the method, not a counterexample about fluids. The surviving obstruction is an all-order flat branch of hidden modes, phantoms invisible to strict measurements. One channel can expose them: the relaxed vertical-pressure signal, through which strict phantoms become visible in active models. The final theorem is a dichotomy: either this relaxed closure holds and yields a conditional logarithmic selection rate, or a genuinely invisible cascade exists inside real Navier-Stokes solutions.
arxiv-2606-12567:
Mark and McDevitt train neural networks to stand in for one of fusion's nastiest particle populations, in this 2026 arXiv paper. Runaway electrons are electrons accelerated to near light speed inside tokamaks; they can damage walls and must be tracked. Kinetic solvers follow their full energy distribution but run far too slowly to couple with whole-device models. Reduced models are fast but discard the distribution itself.

Their framework pairs an adjoint formulation, a mathematical trick that propagates questions backward, with physics-informed neural networks. Three networks predict how the runaway current, average energy, and full energy distribution evolve in time, for any starting distribution. Predictions match a traditional solver across a broad range of plasma conditions. Predictions run orders of magnitude faster than direct kinetics. Training is expensive, but it is paid once. Fusion modelers gain a surrogate that keeps the distribution's physics while fitting inside integrated simulations.
arxiv-2606-12667:
Kim and colleagues ask where satellite ground stations should be built if planners could choose anywhere on Earth, in this 2026 arXiv paper. Low Earth orbit constellations are growing fast, and each satellite can downlink data only during brief passes over a ground station. Existing methods pick from pre-set site lists, which limits network quality. Free placement instead searches a continuous map, though new sites may be needed.

Their method, SCORE, places stations one at a time and then refines all positions in cycles, handling many local traps. Tested on the Capella Space and ICEYE constellations plus a synthetic one, SCORE needs up to 5 times fewer evaluations than a standard evolutionary method. It raises downlink throughput by up to 13 percent. Against fixed-site choices it gains up to 15 percent more downlink, and a version kept near existing power and fibre retains over 92 percent of that gain.
arxiv-2606-13067:
Roman and colleagues derive the limits that label noise imposes on spectral learning, in this 2026 arXiv paper. Spectral methods approximate an unknown function by expanding it in a basis, such as Fourier or Legendre modes, and estimating the coefficients from data. This yields interpretable models throughout science, but how noise corrupts the coefficients, and when the decomposition becomes unreliable, was poorly understood.

Studying supervised regression with label noise and spectral representations across bases and dimensions, the authors show that noise induces a predictable drift in the learned coefficient vector. The drift's magnitude depends on the effective number of active spectral modes.
