Systems from Illumina, Life Sciences, and Roche each carry distinct strengths and quirks in speed, accuracy, and cost. The comparison walks through sample handling, the runs themselves, and the computing that follows. It closes by surveying what the technology is used for, from decoding genomes to tracking germs. For labs choosing a platform, the review offers rare experience-based guidance.
europmc-pmc3404667:
Lepeule, Laden, Dockery, and Schwartz extended a famous air pollution study in 2012, following the Harvard Six Cities cohort through 2009. The study links fine particle pollution to earlier death, but critics questioned model choices and low exposure levels. Eleven extra years of follow-up brought cleaner air and a longer record to test those doubts.

Each standard step up in fine particles came with a clear rise in overall death risk, and larger rises for heart-related and lung cancer deaths. The relationship stayed straight down to quite low particle levels, with no safe floor in sight. Results held across different statistical approaches. Cleaner air, the team concludes, should keep paying public health dividends.
europmc-pmc3417167:
Lahnakoski and colleagues mapped the brain's social perception network in 2012 using movies instead of still pictures. Most earlier work used static faces, leaving real-life social reading poorly charted. Nineteen volunteers watched well over a hundred short clips inside a scanner while raters scored each clip for social features such as faces, speech, emotion, and pain.

One groove along the side of the brain, the superior temporal sulcus, answered every social feature and no non-social one. Four wider networks split the work: one for bodies, motion, and pain; one for faces and speech; one for pain and feeling; and a broad front-to-side system. The study shows naturalistic scanning can chart the social brain efficiently.
europmc-pmc3439967:
Shao and colleagues presented MAnorm in 2012, a method for comparing genome-wide binding maps between cell types fairly. The technique behind the maps, ChIP-Seq, shows where gene-control proteins sit on DNA, but comparing two maps quantitatively had few good tools. Without them, claims about cell-specific binding rest on shaky ground.

Their model normalizes two datasets against each other and calls true differences in binding strength. Those calls lined up strongly with changes in the target genes' activity and with the binding of cell-type-specific regulators. The method handles epigenetic marks as well as transcription factors. Simple and sturdy, it gives researchers a common ruler for a measurement the field makes constantly.
europmc-pmc3469467:
Comeron, Ratnappan, and Bailin mapped recombination across the fruit fly genome at fine scale in a 2012 PLoS Genetics paper. Recombination shuffles genes when sex cells form, and its rate varies along chromosomes. Past maps were too coarse to test how that variation shapes evolution. The team tracked the products of thousands of female meioses using millions of genetic markers.

They charted more than one hundred thousand recombination events, some narrowed to very short DNA stretches. Crossing over rates spiked and crashed sharply along chromosomes, and the hot spots differed between flies. Gene conversion, the second outcome, spread more evenly and appeared even where crossing over was absent. Comeron's group says future models of selection must build in these layers of variation.
europmc-pmc3474767:
Schellong and co-authors pooled studies on birth weight and later overweight in a 2012 PLoS ONE meta-analysis. Doctors have long claimed that conditions before birth shape adult weight, with birth weight as the handy sign of those conditions. No global test of that claim existed. The team gathered studies from many countries covering people from early childhood to old age.

Their pool held 66 studies and well over six hundred thousand people. Risk rose in a straight line with birth weight: babies born light carried lower later risk, while babies born heavy carried clearly higher risk. The pattern held after adjusting for other factors. Schellong's group argues that preventing overfeeding before birth could be a true route to preventing overweight.
europmc-pmc3483167:
Krstic and colleagues tested whether body-wide infection can set mice on a path like Alzheimer's disease, in the Journal of Neuroinflammation in 2012. Inflammation inside the brain is a hallmark of Alzheimer's, but no one had shown that infections elsewhere in the body can start the process. The team gave pregnant mice and adult mice a mimic of viral infection that stirs the immune system.

Mice exposed before birth developed brain changes with age: lasting inflammation, buildups of a protein tied to Alzheimer's, altered forms of a second protein, and failing memory. A second immune hit in adulthood made the pattern far worse. In mice already prone to Alzheimer's, deposits formed right at the inflammation-driven buildups. Krstic's group suggests repeated infections may be a real risk factor for the disease.
europmc-pmc3510067:
Where do HIV transmissions among men who have sex with men actually happen? Steven M. Goodreau and nine colleagues model the United States and Peruvian epidemics in 2012, using dynamic network simulations fed by large surveys, with partnerships split into main and casual types.

Two model variants disagree on early infection's share: acute-stage partners account for 4 to 5 percent of transmissions in one, 22 to 29 percent in the other. Both agree chronic-stage partners drive the plurality or majority. Main partnerships carry much of the spread, a corrective to casual-only thinking. The breakdown by infection stage, testing, and treatment history is meant to guide combination prevention design.
europmc-pmc3526467:
Enzyme family GH5 cuts many kinds of sugar chains, and Henrik Aspeborg, Pedro M. Coutinho, Yang Wang, Harry Brumer, and Bernard Henrissat reorganize it in 2012. With over 3,200 known sequences, up from 21 in 1990, the family's diversity defeats simple function prediction from sequence alone.

Their global analysis assigns about 80 percent of sequences into 51 subfamilies. One third of subfamilies with known activity are monospecific, doing a single job; twenty subfamilies have no characterized member at all. Mapping known functions onto the family tree shows where experiments are missing. The classification gives enzyme hunters a knowledge-based shortcut from sequence to likely specificity.
europmc-pmc3539067:
The nose is a tempting drug route with a catch, and Per Gisle Djupesland reviews delivery devices and their clinical performance in 2013. Nasal dosing treats local disease like rhinitis and sinusitis directly, offers needle-free vaccination, and can deliver drugs body-wide with fast absorption and no liver first pass.

The catch is anatomy. The nasal airway evolved to filter and condition air for the lungs, not to accept medicine. Its narrow valve, twisting passages, and cycling tissue states fight consistent dosing. Devices have grown more reproducible in laboratory tests, yet clinical gains lag. Djupesland explains which device traits matter and why the nose's defenses deserve respect in design.
europmc-pmc3645767:
Melatonin, the night hormone, works as a two-way buffer for the immune system in a 2013 review by Carrillo-Vico, Lardone, Alvarez-Sánchez, Rodríguez-Rodríguez and Guerrero in the International Journal of Molecular Sciences. Made from a food building block in the pineal gland, melatonin is found across nearly all life forms. Its immune role had long drawn doubt, but hard study has since made the link firm.

On the account given here, melatonin stirs the immune system when it runs low or is held down, and calms it when it flares too high, as in sharp swelling. The review then tests that picture against real cases: infection, self-attack diseases, vaccine response and immune ageing. That breadth makes the piece a guide to when the hormone might help, and when it might hinder, in care.
europmc-pmc3744067:
Kira Holmström and nine co-authors reported a study in Biology Open in 2013 on Nrf2, a factor that switches on protective genes in cells. Nrf2 and its brake, Keap1, control a network covering over one percent of the genome, best known for defense and drug-handling genes. The team tested its effect on cell energy in mouse nerve cells and fibroblasts.

Cells lacking Nrf2 had weaker mitochondrial voltage, less ATP, and poorer respiration, while cells with Nrf2 switched on showed the reverse. The respiratory machines themselves were normal in amount and in test-tube activity, but they worked poorly in living cells without Nrf2. The reason was supply: without Nrf2, the fuel molecule NADH was rebuilt too slowly. The authors conclude that Nrf2 guards energy supply as part of its protective role.
europmc-pmc3754967:
Xiuying Zhang and eight co-authors published a study in PLoS ONE in 2013 on gut microbes and how glucose intolerance progresses. Type 2 diabetes develops through stages, and gut bacteria may play a part.

The team mapped gut microbes in 121 people: 44 with normal glucose tolerance, 64 with prediabetes, and 13 with newly diagnosed Type 2 diabetes. Microbe groups differed by stage, and the mix shifted as tolerance worsened. Twenty-eight bacterial units were tied to diabetes status, most of them more common in the diabetes group. Bacteria that make butyrate, a helpful gut fuel, were more common in the normal group, while one major genus fell to half its level in the diabetes group. A microbial class called Verrucomicrobiae dropped in both prediabetes and diabetes, which the authors flag as a possible early marker.
europmc-pmc387267:
Hajime Hirase, Lifen Qian, Peter Barthó, and György Buzsáki image star-shaped brain cells in living rats in PLoS Biology in 2004. Astrocytes, the brain's support cells, show big slow calcium surges in dishes and slices. Whether such surges happen in the intact brain, and what they do there, was unknown.

A glowing dye laid on the cortex let a two-photon microscope watch calcium in surface astrocytes of sleeping rats. Single cells surged much as they do in a dish. Neighbor cells often surged in sync, shown by broad timing links. When neurons fired more, astrocyte surges grew stronger and more in step. The findings give the first live proof that astrocyte networks hum along with neuron activity, a hint of two-way talk in the working brain.
europmc-pmc3893567:
Denis P. Shamonin, Esther E. Bron, Boudewijn P. F. Lelieveldt, Marion Smits, Stefan Klein, and Marius Staring speed up brain image alignment in Frontiers in Neuroinformatics in 2013. Aligning brain scans to a common frame is vital for measuring shrinkage in Alzheimer's disease, yet the math runs slowly. Their work speeds a known alignment package.

They split the work across many CPU cores and onto the graphics chip, and they exploit tricks in the bend model the package uses. The faster tool then powered a study that sorted Alzheimer's patients from healthy controls by gray matter volume from MRI scans. Two sorting styles, by tiny cube and by region, both leaned on heavy alignment work. The gain shows how raw speed can widen what imaging studies can attempt.
europmc-pmc3894167:
Mireille Bétermier, Pascale Bertrand, and Bernard S. Lopez question a textbook claim in PLoS Genetics, with the record dated 2014. Broken DNA ends can be rejoined by a fast path called non-homologous end-joining. That path has long been branded sloppy and error-prone.

The authors argue the main path is in fact careful but flexible. Errors blamed on it often come from a backup joining path that truly is sloppy. The main path also adapts to ragged ends, and many breaks arrive with chemical damage that must be trimmed before joining, which can cost bases. On this view, the ends set the error rate, not the joining machinery. Flexibility pays off in immune diversity and radiation survival.
europmc-pmc3908367:
Krijn P. Paaijmans and six colleagues argue in Global Change Biology in 2013 that daily swings in temperature change how cold-blooded animals will fare as the climate warms. Climate studies usually work with monthly or yearly averages. Real insects, the authors note, live through hot afternoons and cool nights, not averages, and their bodies respond to that daily range.

Using a mosquito as a test case, they show that daily fluctuation slows development in warm settings, speeds it in cool ones, and lowers both the best temperature and the heat limit. Extending the analysis to other land insects, they find that daily swings shrink the safety margin species have before heat harms them, so warming may bite sooner than average-based forecasts suggest.
europmc-pmc3964967:
Milton H. Saier and three colleagues describe the Transporter Classification Database in 2014. Their paper appeared in Nucleic Acids Research. The database is the reference point for transport proteins. Those proteins move molecules across cell membranes. It holds more than 10,000 proteins, with no duplicates. Every known family of membrane transport systems is covered. The proteins come from all kinds of living things.

Entries sit in a five-level filing system. Broad class sits at the top. The single transport system sits at the bottom. Superfamilies are cross-linked between levels. Each family carries hand-written notes. The notes cover shape, function, mechanism, and evolution. The database links out to many other resources. It is the only scheme of its kind backed by the world biochemistry union. The paper reports the update and its software.
europmc-pmc3965067:
A. Patricia Bento, Anna Gaulton, and colleagues update ChEMBL in Nucleic Acids Research in 2014, the open database of drug-like molecules and their measured biological activity. ChEMBL's data are largely extracted by hand from the medicinal chemistry literature: the compounds tested, their structures, the assays run, and the protein targets hit. Since the 2012 description, the resource has grown in both sources and functions.

New data track compounds from early research through clinical development to the market, using United States drug naming applications. A richer data model now represents drug targets, and checks were added to help users spot unreliable measurements. Access widened too: beside the website, downloads, and web services, ChEMBL is offered in a linked-data format for machine querying.
europmc-pmc3974867:
Tanay M. Desai and colleagues pin down exactly where a flu-fighting protein stops the virus, in PLoS Pathogens in 2014. IFITM3 is switched on by interferon and blocks many enveloped viruses, including influenza A, which enters cells through internal compartments called endosomes. Earlier work suggested it jams the virus's membrane before the two membranes can merge, possibly by piling up cholesterol. Using direct fusion assays and live imaging of single virus particles, the team watched the entry step by step.

Merging of the outer membrane layers proceeded normally in IFITM3's presence. What failed was the next step: opening the pore that lets the virus's contents into the cell. Forcing cholesterol high by other means did not block fusion, so cholesterol is not the weapon. IFITM3, the authors conclude, freezes fusion halfway.
europmc-pmc3978367:
Marc-André Bellavance and Serge Rivest review the two-way traffic between stress hormones and the brain's immune system in Frontiers in Immunology in 2014. When the body meets physical or mental stress, the hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal axis releases glucocorticoids. These steroid hormones reach nearly every cell, and their power to suppress immunity has been exploited in medicine for seventy years against allergies, autoimmune disease, and inflammation.

Yet the story is not one-way suppression. Under some conditions glucocorticoids prepare or even boost immune responses, and the brain shows the paradox most clearly, with evidence pointing both to protection and to harm. The review weighs that evidence and the genomic and non-genomic routes the hormones use, aiming to explain when stress hormones calm brain inflammation and when they feed it.
europmc-pmc4055767:
Erin K. Sully and eleven colleagues test a molecule that disarms Staphylococcus aureus without killing it, in PLoS Pathogens. This bacterium causes most acute skin infections. Its quorum sensing system, agr, switches on tissue-damaging toxins when the population is dense. Blocking the signal could help the host while sparing friendly skin microbes.

A large screen found savirin, a small molecule that jams agr in the pathogen but leaves the same system in a harmless skin relative untouched. It works by blocking the regulator AgrA, so toxin genes stay off. Unlike antibiotics, it barely slows growth and triggers no stress response. In two mouse skin infection models it reduced tissue damage and helped clear the bacteria, even given after abscesses peaked. Repeated passage produced no resistance, a sharp contrast with antibiotics run in parallel.
europmc-pmc4066267:
Roberto Romero and colleagues asked whether the vaginal bacteria of pregnant women differ between those who later deliver early and those who deliver at term. Their nested case-control study appeared in Microbiome in 2014. Preterm birth is a leading cause of newborn illness and death, and infection is one suspected trigger.

The team collected vaginal fluid samples over time and read bacterial genes to survey the microbes present. Cases delivered spontaneously before thirty-four weeks; controls delivered at term. Community make-up changed with pregnancy stage in normal cases, with several Lactobacillus types rising. Yet overall, bacterial types and amounts did not differ between women who delivered early and those who delivered at term.
europmc-pmc4111867:
Eneko Larrañeta, Ryan F. Donnelly, and colleagues proposed a standard model membrane and test for microneedle insertion studies. Their paper appeared in the International Journal of Pharmaceutics in 2014. Microneedle arrays pierce the skin's outer layer to deliver drugs through tiny channels, and reliable penetration is the first requirement for them to work.

Testing penetration was hampered by limited techniques, mostly based on measuring water loss through skin or on direct visualisation. The authors identify a film material as a suitable stand-in for skin in insertion tests. Their proposed procedure is simple enough for routine use in comparing needle designs and checking batch quality during scaled-up production. It complements existing physical tests for factors such as needle height, tip sharpness, and fracture force.
europmc-pmc4154667:
Gary W. Beecham, Gerard D. Schellenberg, Thomas J. Montine, and the Alzheimer's Disease Genetics Consortium hunted genes behind the brain changes of Alzheimer's disease, using autopsy data rather than symptoms alone. Their genome-wide study appeared in PLoS Genetics in 2014. Tissue measures can separate true disease features from look-alike dementias.

Data came from nearly five thousand brain autopsies with standardised scoring of plaques, tangles, vessel amyloid, Lewy bodies, and other changes. The strongest signals clustered around the APOE gene for diagnosis and for most individual features. New associations included a sugar-transfer enzyme gene and a transporter gene for plaque score, and a region between genes on chromosome nine. The study shows pathology-based genetics can sharpen the search for Alzheimer's mechanisms and treatments.
europmc-pmc4159567:
Yong-Jie Zhang, Leonard Petrucelli, and a team of peers showed that a rogue protein built from the C9ORF72 gene repeat harms nerve cells. Their study came out in Acta Neuropathologica in 2014. This repeat is the most common root of the nerve-wasting ill ALS and of one form of dementia, when passed down in a family.

By an odd route of protein building, the long repeat is read into plain chains of two amino acids. These chains clump in the brains of the sick. The team made the glycine-alanine form in lab cells and in nerve cells. It formed light and heavy clumps and lumps of waste. It proved toxic to nerve cells. It also set off stress in the cell's folding shop. The work adds this protein path to the harm once pinned on the repeat's RNA alone.
europmc-pmc4168567:
Alain B. Labrique, Garrett Mehl, and three co-authors laid out a framework for mobile health tools in Global Health, Science and Practice in 2013. Phone-based health projects had spread fast, mostly as small pilots, and health ministries lacked clear guidance on which ones could strengthen a whole health system.

The framework names 12 common uses for mobile tools across reproductive, maternal, and child health care. They range from client education and reminders to data collection, provider training, and supply tracking. Each use is tied to a known weak point in health systems, such as missed visits or slow reporting. The authors also stress that scale-up needs hard proof on cost and health gains, which most pilots had not yet produced.
europmc-pmc4190567:
Genevieve Housman, Sibaji Sarkar, and five co-authors surveyed how cancers resist drugs in Cancers in 2014. A tumour that first shrinks under treatment often returns in a form the same drugs cannot touch. Resistance is a main reason cancer therapy fails.

The review walks through the known escape routes. Cells can break drugs down, pump them out, repair the DNA damage they cause, or change the drug's target so it no longer binds. Some cells dodge death signals by switching form, and tumours hold mixed cell types, so treatment can leave the hardiest behind. Gene-silencing marks can also switch resistance on without any mutation, and may help form stubborn cancer stem cells. The authors close with treatment ideas meant to block or delay these escapes.
europmc-pmc4223067:
Christine Burkard, Peter J. M. Rottier, and nine co-authors traced the entry route of coronaviruses in PLoS Pathogens in 2014. To infect a cell, a coronavirus must merge its envelope with a cell membrane, using its spike protein as the fuse. Where in the cell that merge happens decides which defences can stop it.

Working with mouse hepatitis coronavirus, the team silenced genes one by one and found late endosome and lysosome machinery strongly promoted infection. Tracking the virus confirmed it rides the endocytic path to lysosomes, where lysosomal proteases must clip the spike to arm it. A broad protease blocker stopped fusion cold. Adding a furin cut site to the spike let the virus skip the lysosome step. A feline coronavirus behaved the same way.
europmc-pmc4270067:
Oliver H Miller leads a team studying why the drug ketamine lifts depression so fast. Their study appeared in eLife in 2014. A single low dose can help patients who resist other drugs within hours, and the team tested whether one part of the NMDA receptor, the GluN2B unit, drives that effect.

In mice, blocking GluN2B in the front of the brain copied ketamine's fast effect and cut despair like behavior. Removing GluN2B also raised protein building in key brain cells and added new inputs to them. The findings point to GluN2B as a core target for new fast acting treatments for depression.
europmc-pmc4365767:
Benjamin Lehne and a team of co-authors built a full workflow for a widely used DNA methylation chip, in Genome Biology in 2015. Methylation, a chemical mark on DNA, helps control the genome, and the Illumina 450K chip lets labs measure it genome-wide. Yet labs lacked one agreed way to clean and analyze the data. The team built their pipeline on 2,687 people, with 36 samples measured twice, and tested it against existing approaches.

The workflow adds new steps for quality checks, data scaling, and batch fixes that lean on the chip's own control probes. It also sets a fair null model for genome-wide scans using shuffled tests. The pipeline beat existing methods on data quality and on finding sites where gene variants move methylation levels. Cleaner data of this kind sharpens studies that link methylation to disease.
europmc-pmc4404667:
Ceara Cunningham and co-authors measured how often specialist doctors answer web surveys, in BMC Medical Research Methodology in 2015. Surveys are a standard tool for studying health care, but doctors respond poorly, and specialists were little studied. As part of a project on physician pay plans in a large Canadian city, the team sent an online billing survey to 904 physicians across specialties. Personal invitations, several reminders, and a prize draw for gift certificates were all used to lift the response rate.

The overall response rate was 35.0 percent. Neurologists and neurosurgeons answered most, at 46.6 percent, followed by internal medicine at 42.9 percent. General surgeons, pediatricians, and psychiatrists answered least, all under 30 percent. Non-respondents most often blamed lack of time and survey burden. Even with every standard lure, two-thirds of the specialists stayed silent, a warning for anyone planning such a survey.
europmc-pmc4417567:
Marta Castro-Manrreza and Juan Montesinos reviewed how mesenchymal stem cells regulate immunity, in the Journal of Immunology Research in 2015. These multipotent cells, isolable from many tissues and easy to grow, can mature into bone, cartilage, and fat lineages. Their stronger clinical lure is immune control: they dampen the very cells that drive immune attack. The review concentrates on their effects on T cells, the principal effectors of immune responses, and on the signals behind those effects.

Suppression runs through secreted soluble factors and through contact molecules on the cell surface, shifting T cells toward tolerance. The authors describe the mechanisms in detail, then their roles in autoimmune diseases, where misdirected immunity is the problem. The flagship clinical use is graft-versus-host disease, where donor immune cells attack the patient and these stem cells can calm the assault.
europmc-pmc4522567:
Peter U. Diehl and Matthew Cook built a brain-like computer network that learns digits with no teacher, reported in Frontiers in Computational Neuroscience in 2015. Spiking neural networks mimic nerve cells that fire in pulses, a step toward understanding how the cortex computes. Most such systems cheat: they train a normal network first, then convert it, which real brains cannot do.

Their design uses only brain-plausible parts: conductance-based connections, learning rules keyed to spike timing, sideways inhibition between cells, and thresholds that adapt. No labels or teaching signals were shown at all. The network still scored 95% on the MNIST benchmark of handwritten digits, beating earlier spiking systems. The result suggests local timing rules alone can support real pattern learning.
europmc-pmc4593167:
Martin J. Johnson and Carl R. May published a 2015 overview of reviews on changing professional behaviour in health care. Getting research evidence into routine practice is slow and uneven. The authors wanted to know which kinds of interventions work, and why. Their analysis used normalisation process theory, a framework for how new practices become routine.

They searched major databases and found 67 systematic reviews that met their rules. The interventions fell into three broad groups: persuasive, educational, and action or monitoring approaches. Approaches built on action and feedback, such as audit with feedback, reminders, and outreach visits, tended to perform well. The review helps planners pick change strategies that staff can actually adopt and sustain in daily care.
europmc-pmc4622167:
Peter Hedden and Valerie Sponsel published a 2015 history of a century of gibberellin research. Gibberellins are plant hormones that drive growth and flowering. The story began in nineteenth-century Japan with a rice disease caused by a fungus. Infected seedlings grew too tall and stayed sterile. The review appeared in the Journal of Plant Growth Regulation.

Chemists later traced the effect to substances the fungus secreted, named gibberellins, and by the late 1950s plants were shown to make their own. The review tracks how the making of these hormones was mapped gene by gene. It also covers the 2005 discovery of the gibberellin receptor and the current focus on DELLA proteins, growth brakes that gibberellins remove. The arc shows how a crop disease opened a whole field.
europmc-pmc4686867:
Michelle A. Lawson, Michelle M. McDonald, Natasa Kovacic, and a large team tracked dormant myeloma cells in Nature Communications in 2015. Multiple myeloma often returns after treatment, and doctors suspect sleeping cancer cells hidden in bone. Using live imaging in mice, the team watched single myeloma cells settle in the bone-lining niche, switch off, and later wake to form colonies. They asked which bone cells control the switch.

Contact with bone-lining cells or bone-building cells turned dormancy on. Bone-eating cells, the osteoclasts, turned it off by remodeling the niche. Sleeping cells also shrugged off chemotherapy aimed at dividing cells, which fits the pattern of relapse. The work shows relapse may be fought from outside the cancer cell, by guarding the niche. That opens a treatment angle beside drugs that attack the tumor itself.
europmc-pmc4691067:
Navin Rauniyar and Laszlo Prokai reviewed parallel reaction monitoring in the International Journal of Molecular Sciences in 2015. Protein studies often need to measure a few chosen proteins again and again across samples. Broad scans find candidates but can miss the same protein from run to run. Parallel reaction monitoring, or PRM, is a targeted method run on high-resolution instruments. It watches preset protein fragments with very exact mass readings.

The review explains what makes PRM selective and specific, using hybrid quadrupole-Orbitrap machines as the main example. It also walks through counting methods that use labeled standards and methods that need no labels. Compared with the older targeted approach, PRM is easier to set up and checks all fragments at once. The authors present it as a strong route for testing candidate disease markers with the consistency that medical claims require.
europmc-pmc4699467:
Ying Dang, Gengxiang Jia, Jennie Choi, and five colleagues improved the guide RNA used in CRISPR editing, reporting in Genome Biology in 2015. The editing system pairs the Cas9 cutter with a single-guide RNA that steers it. The standard guide was shortened compared with the natural bacterial version, and it carries a run of four thymines that can pause the enzyme that copies it into RNA. Both features looked like drags on performance.

The team tested guide variants one change at a time. Lengthening the paired stem region by about five bases and changing the fourth thymine to another base raised knockout efficiency, sometimes sharply. The better guide also improved hard jobs like deleting whole stretches of DNA, which matters for silencing non-coding genes. The fix is simple: any lab can adopt the new structure. Small design care, the study shows, can rescue editing experiments that would otherwise fail.
europmc-pmc4702867:
Geoffrey L. Winsor, Emma J. Griffiths, Raymond Lo, Bhavjinder K. Dhillon, Julie A. Shay, and Fiona S. L. Brinkman upgraded the Pseudomonas Genome Database, reporting in Nucleic Acids Research in 2016. Pseudomonas bacteria thrive almost anywhere; some infect people, animals, and plants. The database grew famous for its community-checked annotation of one reference strain. Thousands of new genome assemblies, complete and draft, demanded a bigger design.

The upgrade integrates curated annotations with isolate details and stronger tools for comparing many genomes at once. Computed analyses flag possible drug targets and vaccine candidates, and help find matching genes across strains. A community push is assigning high-quality function terms to genes. Plans point toward pan-genome and population views as holdings keep climbing. The paper shows a specialist database retooling for the age of thousands of genomes per species.
europmc-pmc4728667:
Trisha A. Jenkins, Jason C. D. Nguyen, Kate E. Polglaze, and Paul P. Bertrand reviewed tryptophan, serotonin, mood, and thinking in Nutrients in 2016. Tryptophan, an amino acid from food, is the raw material for serotonin, a brain chemical deeply tied to mood. Experiments that raise or drain tryptophan shift serotonin levels, and low serotonin tracks with poor memory and depressed mood in those studies. The review pulls this experimental literature together.

A second thread reaches downward: the gut-brain axis. Gut microbes influence behavior, and they also handle tryptophan, so gut changes could ripple into brain chemistry and mental state. The authors weigh how much of that chain is proven and how much is promise. For readers, the piece links diet, microbes, and mind through one measurable molecule chain, while marking where the evidence thins. It frames several testable ideas for mood and cognition research.
europmc-pmc4746267:
Guo and five colleagues review the heat stress transcription factors, the HSF family that switches on protective genes when plants face heat, drought, or salt. Rooted plants cannot flee bad weather, and abiotic stress cuts global crop productivity by an estimated half, so these genetic switches matter for food security.

The review describes the conserved structure that lets HSFs bind DNA, catalogues the family in different plant species, and maps how their activity is regulated at several levels. Despite the shared structure, plant HSFs have diversified widely and plug into many stress networks. The authors suggest this wiring could be exploited to breed hardier crops.
europmc-pmc4815767:
Nikolaos Diamantis and Udai Banerji review antibody-drug conjugates in the British Journal of Cancer in 2016. A conjugate welds a tumor-seeking antibody to a cell-killing drug. The poison rides to the tumor and spares the rest of the body. Early versions failed. Their drugs were weak, their links shaky, and their targets poor. New linkers and far stronger payloads revived the idea.

Two conjugates had won licenses by the time of the review. One treats breast cancer. One treats lymphoma. A crowd of others filled early trials. The authors lay out what makes one succeed. The target must sit on the tumor and not on healthy tissue. The link must hold in blood and break in the tumor. The payload must work in tiny doses. The focus falls on solid tumors.
europmc-pmc4820667:
Emma E. Davenport leads a twelve-author team in The Lancet Respiratory Medicine in 2016 splitting sepsis patients by their gene activity. Sepsis care has no targeted drug, partly because patients' immune replies differ wildly. The team read the full gene activity of blood cells from 265 intensive care patients with sepsis from lung infection, then checked the pattern in 106 more.

Two response signatures emerged. One, found in about four in ten patients, showed a suppressed immune system: tolerant to bacterial toxins, with worn-out T cells and dimmed display molecules. Those patients died at about two and a half times the rate of the other group within two weeks. A seven-gene test could sort patients, and gene variants that tune the response were also mapped. The split, the authors argue, is the map targeted sepsis therapy needs.
europmc-pmc4855267:
Renan Corrêa-Oliveira and co-authors reviewed in 2016 how short-chain fatty acids steer immune cells. Gut bacteria ferment fiber into these small fats, chiefly acetate, propionate, and butyrate, named for their two, three, and four carbon chains. Gut lining cells burn some for fuel. The rest act as signals between microbes and the immune system.

The fats switch on surface receptors on gut and immune cells and also tweak gene-control marks inside them. Through those routes they shape cell growth, survival, and action across many immune types. The review pulls the routes together, showing how a food breakdown product helps set gut peace and defense.
europmc-pmc4891567:
Ujjal J. Phukan, Gajendra S. Jeena, and Rakesh K. Shukla reviewed WRKY transcription factors in plants in 2016. Plants face many stresses at once in the field, and single-stress defenses fall short. WRKY proteins switch whole gene sets on or off by gripping DNA spots called W-boxes, so one factor can coordinate answers to drought, salt, and germs together.

Control of WRKY action runs at gene, protein, and domain levels, with gene marks, cell signals, and protein shredding all in play. Boosting single WRKY genes often helps one stress while hurting growth, a trade-off the review weighs. Their network reach makes them prized targets for crops that must shrug off combined stress.
europmc-pmc4914367:
Anton Goloborodko, Maxim V. Imakaev, John F. Marko, and Leonid A. Mirny showed in 2016 that one mechanism, active loop extrusion by condensin proteins, can pack and sort sister chromosomes for division. How meters of DNA compact, separate, and untangle is a core puzzle. Polymer simulations let loop-growing machines reel DNA into loops on both sister copies at once.

The single mechanism robustly compacted the copies, kept them apart, and stripped tangles, ending with clean individual chromatids shaped like those seen in cells. The paradox of simplifying knots while condensing dissolves: loops sort as they grow. The team proposes loop extrusion as a universal folding tool, used in rest phases for gene contacts and in division for packing.
europmc-pmc4944467:
Jayu Jen and Yi-Ching Wang review zinc finger proteins and their part in cancer growth. Their review appeared in the Journal of Biomedical Science in 2016. Zinc finger proteins form the largest family of transcription factors in the human genome. Their small zinc held motifs come in many forms, which lets them serve in development, cell division, metabolism, and waste recycling. Evidence over recent decades ties some members to cancer progression.

The same protein can help or hinder a tumor depending on cancer type and cell stress. The review lays out how these proteins control gene reading in general. It then sums up recent work on the C2H2 class in tumor growth, cell death, migration, and invasion. Layers of regulation explain the conflicting results in the field. The authors press for deeper mechanism work before these proteins can serve as drug targets or cancer markers.
europmc-pmc4975467:
Samuel E. Jones leads a large team hunting genes behind morningness and sleep length. Their genome wide association study appeared in PLoS Genetics in 2016. Being a morning or evening person, and how long one sleeps, run in families and link to obesity and diabetes. The team scanned the genomes of more than one hundred and twenty-eight thousand white British adults in UK Biobank, using self reported chronotype and sleep duration.

Sixteen variants tied to chronotype, including spots near the known clock genes RGS16 and PER2. A second dataset from 23andMe confirmed most of the signals. The study also found new loci for sleep duration. Each variant shifts the odds of morningness only slightly, which fits a trait built from many small effects. The authors offer the loci as entry points into the biology of circadian rhythm in humans.
europmc-pmc5062467:
Edoardo Gaude and Christian Frezza analyze cancer metabolism across tumor types in Nature Communications in 2016. Cancer cells rewire how they burn and build fuel, but whether that rewiring follows set rules, and whether it matters for patients, was unclear. The team read the activity of metabolic genes across twenty cancer types in a large public tumor collection and linked the patterns to spread and survival.

Each cancer kept metabolic traces of its tissue of origin, yet all converged toward a shared landscape. One pattern stood out everywhere: cancers that turned down their mitochondrial genes fared worst. That same shutdown tracked the gene signature of the invasive, spread-prone cell state, and it marked metastatic melanoma and kidney cancer and metastatic cell lines. The authors propose the mitochondrial signature as a tool for sorting patients by risk and for aiming future metabolic therapies.
europmc-pmc5082667:
Linda Truebestein and Thomas A. Leonard review the coiled-coil, a protein structure built from helices wound around each other, in BioEssays in 2016. Coiled-coils appear in proteins across all kingdoms of life. Some are near-identical in sequence and length wherever they occur, hinting every part of them works. Others vary freely in sequence but keep their length, acting as pure spacers.

Those spacers shape cell structures such as centrioles and the Golgi, and tether transport vesicles at the right distance. In motor proteins, coils pass shape changes along their length to govern cargo handling. In enzymes they serve as rulers, holding the active site a fixed distance from its target. The authors note that claims of coils scaffolding large complexes still lack structural proof, and that few full-length structures exist. Their survey argues length itself is information: evolution tunes these rods to set the cell's geometry.
europmc-pmc515367:
Joshua M. Akey and six co-authors read human evolutionary history in 132 genes, reporting in PLoS Biology in 2004. Finding which genome regions natural selection shaped is hard, because population history alone can mimic selection's marks. Comparing many genes at once offers a way to tell the two apart.

They resequenced all 132 genes in 24 African-Americans and 23 European-Americans and modeled both demography and repeated testing. Many apparent selection signals dissolved into population history, yet eight genes still bore strong signs of positive or balancing selection in European-Americans, and none in African-Americans. One stretch of chromosome 7 with four genes in a row showed a sharp recent selective sweep. The pattern fits adaptation as humans spread out of Africa, and it matters for hunting disease genes.
europmc-pmc5171767:
Mathis Loïc Messager, Bernhard Lehner, Günther Grill, Irena Nedeva, and Oliver Schmitt estimated the world's lake water in Nature Communications in 2016. Lakes shape carbon cycles and ecosystems, yet global data on their depth, volume, and water age were patchy. The team built a statistical model that infers volume from the terrain around each lake.

Their database covers 1.42 million natural lakes of at least ten hectares, spread over 2.67 million square kilometers, with shorelines together about four times longer than the ocean coasts. Total stored water came to about 181,900 cubic kilometers, under one percent of Earth's non-frozen land water. Water stays in a lake for about five years on average, though the typical lake turns over in roughly fifteen months.
europmc-pmc5178767:
E. S. Phipson wrote a thesis on the 1918 influenza pandemic in India, published in The Indian Medical Gazette in November 1923. Phipson, lately assistant health officer for Bombay, examines a catastrophe he helped investigate: within two months the epidemic killed, at the latest computation, no fewer than eight million people in India.

He argues the disaster was overshadowed by the war and its aftermath, though for sheer virulence it had no parallel in India's history and probably none in any other country. The thesis traces earlier influenza epidemics since Hippocrates, then studies the 1918 visitation in detail, above all in Bombay City, where he was responsible for much of the inquiry. He closes by asking what lessons the epidemic teaches for handling future outbreaks.
europmc-pmc5222067:
F. J. Waldo, coroner for the City of London and Southwark, lectured on the ancient office of coroner before the Medico-Legal Society, in an abstract printed in The Hospital in 1911. The talk corrects older writers who placed coroners in Anglo-Saxon times under kings Alfred and Athelstan, a claim Waldo traces to unreliable sources that misled even Lord Coke.

The first firm record comes from September 1194. A royal circuit then required each county to elect three knights and a clerk as keepers of the pleas of the Crown, though some evidence points to the year 1100. Waldo stresses that the early coroner's real job was guarding chance revenues owed to the King, such as felons' forfeited goods, wrecks, and treasure trove, more than pursuing justice. Inquests on sudden deaths began largely to learn whether property passed to the Crown.
europmc-pmc5273367:
James W. Dawson summarized the histology of disseminated sclerosis in the Edinburgh Medical Journal in 1916, work begun with the late Alexander Bruce, who had gathered most of the tissue material. The full study, with case histories and 456 figures, appeared in the Transactions of the Royal Society of Edinburgh the same year. Its question is how the plaques of this disease, now called multiple sclerosis, form and spread.

Plaques, the pair found, scatter with no respect for nerve tracts, as if seeping outward from a central source. In the cord they wedge inward from the surface coverings. In the brain they follow the veins and the walls of the ventricles, and sections point to spread along the lymph channels that wrap the veins. The cerebellum and pons show the same venous pattern, which the authors take as the road map of the disease's advance.
europmc-pmc5372567:
Ramón Cacabelos reviewed Parkinson's disease from its roots to gene-based drug choice in the International Journal of Molecular Sciences in 2017. The disease is the second most common slow nerve disease of age, after Alzheimer's. Its call signs are stiffness, shaking at rest, and slow movement. The nerve loss that drives it starts decades before those signs show.

Rates climb steeply with age, from rare in the forties to common past eighty. Risk may come from toxins, farm sprays, head knocks, small strokes, and gene flaws. The core harm is the loss of dopamine-making nerve cells in a dark midbrain zone, with protein clumps tied to failed waste clearing, worn powerhouses, and oxygen stress. Care leans on dopamine stand-ins and kin drugs that ease signs but do not halt the loss. The review ends with gene tests that may tune drug picks.
europmc-pmc5401767:
A. H. Ashok and six co-authors review the dopamine account of bipolar disorder in a 2017 paper in Molecular Psychiatry. Bipolar disorder swings between mania and depression. For more than four decades, one leading account has blamed faults in dopamine, a brain signal tied to reward and drive. New brain scans and wider use of dopamine-blocking drugs made a fresh review timely, so the team searched brain, drug, and tissue studies.

Proof points to too much dopamine action in mania, with more free receptors of one type and an overactive reward network. In depression, scans show more of the pump that clears dopamine, but other signs clash. Both dopamine-raising and dopamine-blocking drugs can ease depression, a puzzle the authors flag. They sketch a model of failed balance and list drug ideas it suggests.
europmc-pmc5408367:
Na Shi, Na Li, Xinwang Duan, and Haitao Niu review the two-way talk between gut germs and the gut's immune system in a 2017 paper in Military Medical Research. The gut holds the body's largest germ community, and its lining holds a guard system of lymph nodes, lining cells, and immune-rich tissue. Each side shapes the other: friendly germs train the guard system as it matures, while the guard system keeps germ shares in balance.

When that balance breaks, harmful germs gain ground, immune responses go astray, and gut diseases can follow. Swelling from a faulty response in turn warps the germ mix further, locking in the problem. The review lays out this loop and the main players on both sides. The authors offer it as a base for later studies of gut disease.
europmc-pmc5411767:
Koren and co-authors present Canu, a genome assembly program built for noisy long reads. The research article appeared in Genome Research. Canu succeeds the Celera Assembler. It targets single-molecule data from PacBio and Oxford Nanopore machines. Such reads are long but carry high error rates. That mix makes repeats and near-identical haplotypes hard to resolve.

Canu uses an adaptive overlap method based on weighted MinHash. It also builds a sparse assembly graph. The graph avoids merging repeats that have diverged. The authors report that Canu needs half the coverage of older tools. It also runs far faster on large genomes. They show complete microbe genomes and near-complete chromosomes. On human and fruit fly data, contig NG50 passed 21 million bases. Canu can also emit assembly graphs in GFA format.
europmc-pmc5440667:
Balzergue and co-authors untangle how low phosphate quickly halts root cell elongation in Arabidopsis. Their study appeared in Nature Communications. Phosphate shortage plagues about 70 percent of farm land. Roots respond by stopping primary growth. The sensing machinery behind that stop was unknown. The team worked at the root apex. They separated two response pathways genetically. One acts fast on cell elongation. The other acts slowly on cell division.

The fast path runs through the factor STOP1. STOP1 switches on ALMT1, a malate channel. Malate leaves the cells into the wall space. With the ferroxidase LPR1, it stiffens walls. Stiff walls block expansion in the transition zone. The slow path shrinks the stem cell niche. Iron and callose build up there instead. That path leans on LPR1 but largely skips STOP1. Malate emerges as a surprise wall-expansion brake.
europmc-pmc5453967:
Chen and co-authors test how two gut community types ferment the same dietary fibers. Their study appeared in Scientific Reports. Human guts sort into broad enterotypes. One is ruled by Prevotella bacteria. The other is ruled by Bacteroides. Both groups ferment fiber into short-chain fatty acids. Those acids feed the colon and calm inflammation. The team asked whether enterotype changes the output.

They fermented three fibers in stool samples. The fibers were fructooligosaccharides and two arabinoxylans. One arabinoxylan came from sorghum, one from corn. In Prevotella guts, all three fibers boosted one Prevotella strain. Total acid output ran high, with propionate on top. In Bacteroides guts, each fiber enriched different strains. Acid amounts and ratios differed by fiber. The same fiber can thus yield different health signals. Personal gut type may shape fiber advice.
europmc-pmc5467167:
Cortes-Ciriano and co-authors paint a molecular portrait of microsatellite instability across 23 cancer types. Their study appeared in Nature Communications. Microsatellite instability reflects broken DNA mismatch repair. Short repeats mutate at runaway rates. Sequencing data now allow fine-grained fingerprints. The team analyzed about 8,000 tumor exomes. Roughly 1,000 whole genomes joined them. Patients spanned 23 cancer types in total.

Instability frequency varied widely within and across types. Recurrent targets emerged from the catalogue. DNA repair and oncogenic pathway genes recurred. Non-coding loci displayed frequent instability too. The team built an exome-based prediction model. It calls the instability phenotype with high accuracy. Clinical testing can use the locus catalogue. Panel assays could flag likely immunotherapy responders. High mutation loads raise neoantigen burden. That burden links to checkpoint therapy response. Better prognosis also marks many unstable tumors.
europmc-pmc5507767:
Byrne and co-authors report a cohort analysis in The Lancet Neurology on a blood marker for Huntington's disease. Dying neurons leak a protein called neurofilament light into body fluids. Trials need cheap ways to track that damage over time. Spinal fluid works but is hard to collect. The team tested blood samples from the TRACK-HD study instead.

Blood levels ran far higher in mutation carriers than controls, they report. Levels climbed with each disease stage. High starting levels predicted later mental decline and brain shrinkage. They also flagged who would develop symptoms within three years. Blood and spinal fluid values tracked each other closely.
europmc-pmc5580567:
Akombi and co-authors present a systematic review on child undernutrition in sub-Saharan Africa. One third of the world's undernourished children live in that region. The review asks which factors link to stunting, wasting, and underweight in young children. Answers can guide better programs.

Five databases were searched, and 49 studies met the rules for inclusion. The most steady factors were low mother's education and poor household wealth. Male sex, low birth weight, and young mother's age also mattered. Unsafe drinking water, diarrhea, and rural residence raised risk too. Long breastfeeding past twelve months appeared as well. The authors call for a broad, community-based response across sectors. Readers get a clear list of where action counts most.
europmc-pmc5612167:
Thomas Laycock argues that the brain works by reflex action, in a paper read at York in September 1844 and printed in The British and Foreign Medical Review. Reflex action was already accepted for the spinal cord. A pinched frog, even with its brain removed, still tries to escape. Laycock extends the same law upward.

His logic starts from anatomy. The ganglia inside the skull continue the spinal cord. So they should answer outside stimuli under like rules. He backs this with cases from lower animals. Cut centipede segments still move when touched. An isolated stretch of frog spinal cord still pulls back a stimulated limb. Four years earlier he had printed this view; now he lays out the proofs in full. The stakes, he says, lie in grasping insanity and its treatment. Readers meet an early claim that the mind's organ is not exempt from reflex law.
europmc-pmc5636267:
Nakagawa and co-authors revisit two summary measures for mixed-effects models. Their methods paper covers the coefficient of determination, R2, and the intra-class correlation coefficient. Earlier work handled only Poisson and binomial models. This paper extends both measures to other kinds of data. The focus falls on negative binomial and gamma models, which biologists use often.

The authors explain two tools that help readers grasp the math. One is Jensen's inequality, and the other is the delta method. They also give special notes for binary and proportion data. Worked examples from ecology and evolution show the method in R. The result is a guide that works across fields and software.
europmc-pmc5650667:
Alexander and co-authors present the receptor section of a pharmacology guide. It appeared in the British Journal of Pharmacology. This section covers G protein-coupled receptors, or GPCRs. They form the largest class of membrane proteins in humans. About 800 such receptors have been identified in man. Roughly half serve senses like smell and taste. The rest respond to signals from small molecules to large proteins.

The Concise Guide to PHARMACOLOGY 2017/18 spans nearly 1,800 drug targets. Entries give nomenclature, key properties, and top research tools. Links point to a fuller open access knowledgebase. The section follows official IUPHAR naming where appropriate. Its landscape layout helps readers compare related receptors side by side.
europmc-pmc5657867:
Shah, Hayes, and Martin present a federal analysis in MMWR. It asks how first opioid prescriptions lead to long-term use. Records came from a large commercial insurance database. The sample held over 1.29 million opioid-naive adults. None had cancer diagnoses. Patients were followed from their first prescription onward. The team measured odds of still using opioids at one and three years.

About six percent still used opioids at one year. The sharpest risk jumps came at clear thresholds. Passing five days and thirty-one days of therapy mattered most. A second prescription also raised the odds sharply. So did a cumulative dose of 700 morphine milligram equivalents. First supplies of ten or thirty days carried added risk.
europmc-pmc5660367:
Bell presents an early paper on how muscles connect with the brain through nerves. Charles Bell, the sole author, builds on his prior work on the nerves of the face. He had shown that cutting one nerve removed feeling but not motion. Cutting the other stopped motion but left feeling intact.

Bell argues that each muscle needs two nerves with distinct jobs. One nerve carries motion, and the other carries sensation back to the brain. He traces the sensitive fifth nerve deep into muscle tissue. Dissection showed it spread there more richly than in skin. The two nerves thus form a circle linking brain and muscle.
europmc-pmc5817867:
Butti and co-authors focus on receptor tyrosine kinases in breast cancer. Breast tumors grow through tangled, faulty signaling. Growth factor receptors sit near the top of those webs. Their signals feed cell division, spread, and stem-like traits.

Pathways below the receptors include MAPK and PI3K/Akt. They also shape how tumor and support cells talk. That reach makes the receptors tempting drug targets. Mutations, extra copies, and side pathways blunt the drugs, though. The review weighs each receptor family and its drugs. Readers get a breast-cancer lens on a broad drug strategy.
europmc-pmc5854467:
Grant and co-authors describe cisTEM, free software for single-particle image processing. Their article appeared in eLife. The software handles data from electron cryo-microscopy, a method that images frozen particles. It runs the full pipeline from raw movies to 3D maps. Steps include particle picking, 2D grouping, and fine 3D refinement. A graphic interface lets users send jobs and watch progress.

The authors say a typical dataset can finish in half a day. That speed comes from a standard CPU workstation, not graphics cards. Jobs can also run on large clusters through flexible profiles. Some tools in the package are new, and others adapt older methods. The package can be downloaded from cistem.org.
europmc-pmc5909567:
Aitken reported a case of doubling of the great intestine in a newborn. The case report appeared in the Glasgow Medical Journal in 1912. The patient was a female child with a large birth hernia at the navel. She was seen about seventeen hours after birth. No operation was attempted, and she died the next day. The finding came from the post-mortem exam.

The lower bowel split into two complete channels, he reports. Each channel had its own opening to the outside. Wall layers differed between upper and lower parts of the split. No other major organ showed the same doubling. Kidney and womb defects were noted, though. The case records a rare birth defect in detail.
europmc-pmc5927767:
Croset and co-authors reveal cell diversity in the fruit fly midbrain by single-cell methods. Their article appeared in eLife. They profiled thousands of single cells with Drop-Seq. Wiring maps alone cannot show how brain cells signal. Gene profiles add the missing molecular layer. Profiles were assigned to major regions and cell types.

Each neuron could be typed by its transmitter, they report. Some peptide signals clustered with certain fast transmitters. Receptor patterns hint at rich circuit modulation options. The atlas links molecular traits to brain regions. It covers hubs for memory and navigation. Researchers get a resource for circuit-level questions.
europmc-pmc5979367:
Basu reviews DNA damage, mutagenesis, and cancer in a compact survey. His mini-review appeared in the International Journal of Molecular Sciences. Many chemicals and physical agents are tied to human cancer. UV light and gamma radiation are among them. DNA damage is an early step toward cancer. Cells hold repair tools that fix most lesions in time.

If damaged DNA is copied first, mutations can result, Basu explains. Changes in oncogenes or tumour-suppressor genes can then spread. A cell line gains a growth edge and expands. Initiation, promotion, and progression may unfold over years. Tobacco and lung cancer give the classic long-exposure case.
europmc-pmc5986467:
Rauber and co-authors link ultra-processed food intake to a worse dietary nutrient profile in the UK. Their study appeared in Nutrients. They used National Diet and Nutrition Survey data from 2008 to 2014. Four-day food diaries were classified with the NOVA system. Ultra-processed foods supplied 56.8 percent of energy on average. Fresh or minimally processed foods gave 30.1 percent.

As ultra-processed intake rose, free sugars and sodium rose too, they report. Protein, fibre, and potassium fell across the same range. Free sugars climbed from 9.9 to 15.4 percent of energy. Cutting these foods could improve diet quality a lot, they argue.
europmc-pmc6010767:
Argelaguet and co-authors present Multi-Omics Factor Analysis, a framework for unsupervised integration of multi-omics data sets. Their paper appeared in Molecular Systems Biology. Multi-omics studies profile several molecular layers at once. Methods to merge such mixed data without supervision were lacking. MOFA infers hidden factors behind the variation. It separates axes shared across data types from private ones. The factors support subgroup finding, imputation, and outlier detection.

On 200 leukaemia patient samples the method found major disease axes, they report. Known drivers and an oxidative stress response emerged. A single-cell application traced coordinated changes during differentiation. The framework turns layered data into interpretable structure.
europmc-pmc6048167:
Kang and co-authors reveal the structure of a fungal cell wall. Their research article appeared in Nature Communications. The wall is a tempting drug target. Its sugars are absent from human cells. Yet its detailed arrangement stayed unclear for years.

The team studied the pathogen Aspergillus fumigatus. They used solid-state NMR with sensitivity boosts. Linkage analysis of wall sugars added support. Chitin and one glucan form a stiff inner scaffold. That scaffold resists water strongly. Softer glucans form a wet matrix around it. Proteins and more glucan cap the outer surface. One glucan type serves two roles at once. It adds rigidity and supports virulence too. Readers get a high-resolution model for drug design.
europmc-pmc6105267:
Bøtker and co-authors set practical guidelines for rigor in cardioprotection research. Their guidelines appeared in Basic Research in Cardiology. Heart protection ideas have flourished in labs for decades. Almost none improved patient outcomes in trials. Weak study habits share the blame.

The authors lay out design rules step by step. Randomization and blinding come first. Power analysis and sound statistics follow. Reporting standards for animal and human work are covered. Registries for early-stage trials are proposed. The aim is proof strong enough to justify patient trials. Readers get a checklist for believable protection claims, from bench to clinic.
europmc-pmc6113867:
Beghain and co-authors present a methods article in Microbial Genomics on a computer tool for typing Escherichia bacteria. The genus holds E. coli and several close kin. E. coli itself splits into seven main groups. Knowing the group helps track disease, since groups differ in hosts and habits.

The tool, called ClermonTyping, works from a strain's genome sequence. It copies the logic of well-known lab PCR tests. It matched those tests in 99.4 percent of cases. It also matched a genome clustering tool almost as well. The authors offer the tool free online for other researchers to use.
europmc-pmc6130467:
Afonine and co-authors present a methods article in Acta Crystallographica Section D on new tools for checking cryo-EM maps and models. Cryo-electron microscopy now yields many near-atomic structures. Each map must be fit with an atomic model. Both the map and the fit need careful quality checks.

The tools sit inside the PHENIX software suite. They judge map quality, model quality, and how well the two match. The team applied them across many high-resolution maps. They discuss what the scores show and where errors hide. The work aims to keep a fast-growing field honest about its structures.
europmc-pmc6292067:
Forbes and co-authors compare gut microbes across four immune-mediated diseases. Their study appeared in Microbiome. The diseases were Crohn's disease, ulcerative colitis, multiple sclerosis, and rheumatoid arthritis. The team asked whether these conditions share a common gut imbalance. Stool samples came from patients and from healthy controls.

The team used gene sequencing to profile the gut bacteria. Microbe mixes differed clearly between the groups. Diversity was lowest in Crohn's disease and highest in healthy controls. Some bacterial groups were higher in all patient groups. Others were lower across the board. A machine learning test sorted Crohn's cases from controls best. The authors say the shared shifts may point to common roots of these diseases.
europmc-pmc6296767:
Vatanen and co-authors trace the early gut microbiome in the TEDDY study. Their analysis appeared in Nature. TEDDY follows children at risk for type 1 diabetes. That disease is an immune attack on insulin-making cells. Stool samples came from 783 young children. Samples were taken each month from three months of age.

The team read over 10,000 stool metagenomes in all. Gut mixes in control children held more genes for fermentation. Those genes help make short-chain fatty acids, key gut fuels. No single microbe marked later diabetes across all sites. Function mattered more than which species were present. Infant gut mixes also changed fast and differed by child. One of three Bifidobacterium species often ruled the first year.
europmc-pmc6318667:
Chai and co-authors review hydrogels and the mechanisms behind their behavior. The review appeared in Gels. Hydrogels are water-loving networks that soak up large fluid volumes. They suit biosensors, drug delivery, and tissue engineering. Some respond to heat, acidity, light, or chemicals.

The authors explain two ways hydrogels swell. They also cover how gels form and how mesh size is figured. Natural gels from sugars and proteins are surveyed. Synthetic gels from recent papers join them. Uses include cell culture, self-healing materials, and drug release. Strength remains a weak point for many gels. The review helps readers pick and design gels for medicine.
europmc-pmc6324067:
Vita and co-authors report the 2018 update of the Immune Epitope Database. The article appeared in Nucleic Acids Research. The database stores lab data on immune epitopes. Entries span infectious, allergic, and autoimmune diseases. Transplant-related data are included too. Over 1.6 million experiments fill the system. They were curated from 19,500 publications.

The resource has been public for over ten years. Recent work improved search and reporting tools. Data keep growing in size and complexity. The team queries PubMed every two weeks for new papers. Outreach gathers needs and feedback from users. Daily traffic runs near 300 unique visitors. The update sets future goals for the service.
europmc-pmc6325267:
Wolff and Vann argue that the thalamus does far more than relay signals. Their viewpoint piece appeared in the Journal of Neuroscience. Older views cast the thalamus as a passive switchboard. It was said to pass data to cortex and hippocampus. New lab evidence points to a richer role. Studies of distinct thalamic nuclei keep finding active work.

The authors link the thalamus to learning and memory. They also link it to flexible adaptation when rules change. They propose one shared job behind these roles. The thalamus helps build and update mental representations. Two-way paths with the cortex fit that job well. So does its place joining signals from below the cortex. The piece ends with open questions for future tests.
europmc-pmc6331567:
Wang and co-authors find that a common epilepsy drug helps resistance genes spread. Their study appeared in The ISME Journal. The drug is carbamazepine, found widely in water systems. Antibiotic resistance spreads fast when bacteria trade genes. Such trades happen on small DNA rings called plasmids. Past blame fell mainly on low antibiotic doses.

Even low, environment-level doses of carbamazepine boosted gene transfer. Transfer rose within and across bacterial genera. The team traced how the drug achieves this. It raised reactive oxygen inside the cells. It also made cell membranes more leaky. Gene and protein scans backed the same story. Non-antibiotic drugs thus may aid resistance spread too. The finding widens what pollution controls should watch.
europmc-pmc6337067:
Pulgar reviews how drugs can cross the blood-brain barrier by hitchhiking. His mini-review appeared in Frontiers in Neuroscience. The barrier guards the brain from the blood. It blocks most medicines from entering. That limits treatment for brain diseases. One route exploits a natural cell process.

Cells can ferry cargo across themselves in small bubbles. That process is called transcytosis. Receptors on vessel walls can drive it. Recent work clarifies how cargo moves inside cells. Better binding designs and new materials help too. Protein engineering adds sharper targeting tools. The review covers these advances and their limits. It shows a path for drugs that the barrier now blocks.
europmc-pmc6341167:
Zhang and co-authors sequence the genome of the Pacific white shrimp. Their study appeared in Nature Communications. The shrimp thrives on the sea floor and in farms worldwide. It molts often, shedding its shell to grow. The genome spans about 1.66 billion letters. It holds 25,596 protein-coding genes.

Repeats make up an unusually large share of the genome. Gene families for vision and movement are expanded. Those expansions fit life on the sea floor. The molting hormone pathway also shows expansion and selection. That may explain the shrimp's frequent molting. Thirty years of farm breeding left marks as well. The authors say the genome aids both biology and breeding.
europmc-pmc6383267:
Qiao and co-authors survey gene duplication in plants, writing in Genome Biology. Plant genomes grow by copying single genes or whole genomes. Over time many extra copies are lost, in cycles that shape plant diversity.

The team built a tool to sort copies by how they arose in 141 plant genomes. Whole-genome copies differ from small tandem copies in fate and use. They face distinct pressure from selection and diverge in activity at distinct rates. Counts of old genome-wide copies fall off sharply with age. The survey gives rules for how duplicate genes are kept or lost.
europmc-pmc6383867:
Williams and co-authors set out a global strategy against snakebite in PLoS Neglected Tropical Diseases. Snakebite poisoning hits up to 2.7 million people a year. Most victims live in remote, poor regions with weak care.

Kofi Annan called snakebite the most important tropical disease most people have never heard of. The strategy calls for joined global action on prevention, treatment, and recovery. Better antivenom supply and trained local care sit at its core. The authors argue the burden can be cut with steady funding. The plan follows the World Health Organization naming it a priority.
europmc-pmc6397467:
Li and Nabet review exosomes and cancer therapy resistance in Molecular Cancer. Exosomes are tiny vesicles that cells release. They carry proteins, lipids, and genetic material between cells in and around a tumor.

Both tumor and support cells send exosomes, and the messages can blunt therapy. Resistant cells can pass their resistance to cells that once responded. The review also covers ways to measure exosome cargo in patients. Exosomes may serve as warning markers, drug targets, or drug carriers. Reading them well is key to using them, the authors argue.
europmc-pmc6416167:
The GBD 2016 Brain and Other CNS Cancer Collaborators present a systematic analysis in The Lancet Neurology. Brain and central nervous system cancers demand costly, advanced care. Past counts covered single regions or short spans, which made global comparison hard.

The analysis estimates cases, deaths, and health loss from 1990 to 2016. It covers meninges, brain, and spinal cord cancers under one scheme. Burden differed widely between countries, they report. Such numbers help governments plan scanning, surgery, and treatment capacity. The authors note that survival gains have been slow for many of these cancers.
europmc-pmc6421967:
Kourtis and co-authors present a Vital Signs report in the Morbidity and Mortality Weekly Report, on staph bloodstream infections in the United States. Staphylococcus aureus is a common cause of sepsis in hospitals and in the community. Resistant forms, called MRSA, get most attention.

The team joined population surveillance from 2005 to 2016 with large hospital record sets. They tracked resistant and drug-sensitive infections side by side. Hospital MRSA had fallen, but community patterns needed a fuller count. Their report gives that national picture. It aims to guide prevention in both settings.
europmc-pmc6432667:
Planas-Riverola and co-authors review brassinosteroid signaling, the steroid hormone pathway that steers plant growth, cell division, and stress adaptation. Most knowledge comes from Arabidopsis, where the membrane receptor BRI1 catches the hormone and starts a relay that switches on growth genes. Recent root studies complicate that single-pathway picture.

Different root cell types appear to run distinct versions of the pathway, tuning growth locally and helping the plant respond to harsh conditions. Stem cell renewal and death in the root tip receive detailed treatment, as does cross-talk with other hormones. Plant biologists get a current map of where signaling is uniform and where it is surprisingly local.
europmc-pmc6450067:
Glasgow and co-authors revisit RE-AIM twenty years after its launch, a planning and grading framework in a field where proven programs often fail to reach the public fairly. RE-AIM scores programs on reach, effectiveness, adoption, implementation, and maintenance. The first paper on it has been cited over 2,800 times, and the framework shows up in more than 450 applied studies.

Use spread from public health into clinic, community, and workplace settings, though applying every dimension in full proved heavy. The authors urge a plain focus on the key elements. Newer stress falls on cost, on adapting programs as they run, and on interview work that explains how results came about. Packaging the tool for non-researchers and pairing it with other frameworks come next.
europmc-pmc6453967:
Zheng and co-authors turn rhein, a herbal compound, into a self-delivering hydrogel for treating brain inflammation, with no carrier material at all. Natural drug molecules often dissolve poorly and degrade fast, and added carriers bring their own compatibility problems. Rhein instead assembles itself through noncovalent bonds into a three-dimensional nanofiber network.

The gel proved stable, released its payload slowly, and responded reversibly to stimuli. Inside microglia inflamed by lipopolysaccharide, it entered cells, engaged toll-like receptor 4, and blocked the NF-κB pathway, keeping the p65 subunit out of the nucleus. Relief lasted longer and hurt cells less than the same dose of free rhein.
europmc-pmc6495367:
Gazzard and co-authors report the LiGHT trial, a head-to-head test of selective laser trabeculoplasty against daily eye drops as the first treatment for open angle glaucoma and ocular hypertension. Seven hundred eighteen treatment-naïve patients at six UK hospitals were randomized, 356 to laser and 362 to drops, and followed for three years with quality of life as the main outcome.

Quality-of-life scores ended identical, but the paths differed. In the laser-first group, 74.2 percent of patients needed no drops at all to hold target pressure at 36 months. Their eyes were on target at more visits. None required glaucoma surgery, against 11 in the drops group. Laser first carried a 97 percent probability of being more cost-effective, and the authors say it should be offered first-line.
europmc-pmc6544567:
Ittisoponpisan and co-authors ask whether computer-predicted protein structures can judge disease variants, writing in the Journal of Molecular Biology. A protein's 3D shape can reveal whether a single-letter change damages it. Measured structures cover only a slice of human proteins, but modeled ones roughly triple that reach — if they can be trusted.

The team checked nearly 2,000 disease-linked missense variants and over 2,100 harmless ones. Forty percent of the disease set caused structural damage, against just 11% of the neutral set. Predicted structures from Phyre2 models gave near-identical verdicts, even when a model was built from a distant relative. Their Missense3D pipeline, released openly, applies the check to any variant.
europmc-pmc6558367:
Pende and co-authors review killer Ig-like receptors, the switches that govern natural killer cells, writing in Frontiers in Immunology. Part history and part survey, the article honors Alessandro Moretta, whose clone work in the early 1990s uncovered these receptors. KIRs read the HLA class I badges on healthy cells and hold NK cells back; when a tumor drops those badges, the brake releases.

The review covers KIR genetics and their extreme variety, how NK cells are educated to spare the self, and the partner receptors that trigger killing. It then follows the science into the clinic. Donor NK cells in half-matched stem cell transplants can attack leukemia. Checkpoint blockers aimed at KIR, NKG2A or PD-1 open further cancer strategies.
europmc-pmc6579767:
Tsurusaki and co-authors identify the cell death that ignites fatty liver inflammation, writing in Cell Death and Disease. A fatty liver often sits quiet for years before turning into steatohepatitis, with inflammation and scarring. Which kind of hepatocyte death pulls the trigger was unknown. Using a diet model that produces the disease quickly, the team timed the deaths as they began.

Necrosis came before apoptosis at onset. Blocking necroptosis, genetically or with drugs, did not stop it. Blocking ferroptosis, the iron-driven death that rusts membrane lipids, protected liver cells almost completely and kept immune cells from flooding in. Oxidized membrane lipids, ferroptosis's fingerprint, had risen in the liver. The authors nominate ferroptosis as the trigger, and a target for prevention.
europmc-pmc6602467:
Shi and co-authors present CPGAVAS2, a server for annotating plastid genomes. Their article appears in Nucleic Acids Research. Plastomes help classify plants and trace their evolution. Sequencing now produces them by the thousand. Fast, accurate annotation has become a pressing need.

The upgrade tackles errors that spread from flawed reference records. Two curated reference sets anchor the new annotations. One holds 43 plastomes checked against RNA-seq data. The other holds 2,544 plastomes curated by alignment. New algorithms handle small exons and the trans-spliced gene rps12. The server also flags repeat elements and SNP sites. Case studies show it annotates better than rival servers.
europmc-pmc6662567:
Kang and co-authors present MetaBAT 2, an adaptive tool for binning metagenome assemblies. Their paper appears in PeerJ. Binning groups assembled fragments into single genomes. It unlocks study of uncultivated microbes. The first MetaBAT needed careful parameter tuning. Poor choices hurt accuracy on weak assemblies. The new version removes manual tuning entirely. Its algorithm adapts to each dataset itself. Engineering work also cut compute and memory use.
