Benchmarks covered over 100 real-world assemblies. MetaBAT 2 beat rival tools on accuracy and speed. A typical assembly bins in a few minutes. That timing holds on a single commodity workstation. The software is open source online. The authors recommend it as the community standard.
europmc-pmc6679067:
Bunte and Beikler review Th17 cells and the IL-23/IL-17 axis in periodontitis and kin diseases. Their review appears in the International Journal of Molecular Sciences. Innate and adaptive immunity normally act in tight balance. When that balance breaks, chronic inflammation and autoimmunity follow. Th17 cells and their cytokine IL-17 sit at the centre. IL-23 keeps their harmful activity going. The axis features in psoriasis and rheumatoid arthritis. Inflammatory bowel disease shares the same wiring.

Periodontitis links to these body-wide conditions. A skewed oral microbiome starts the gum inflammation. Left alone, it destroys attachment and jaw bone. The review traces Th17 cell growth step by step. It then maps shared illness patterns across diseases. Drugs that tune the axis close the survey.
europmc-pmc6712367:
Daviu and co-authors reviewed the brain links between stress and anxiety. Stress and anxiety share behavior and brain wiring, and each can feed the other. Knowing how they interact could improve care for many mental health conditions. The review draws mostly on studies in rodents.

The authors trace circuits in the amygdala that set emotional tone and anxiety-like behavior. They show how a stress chemical from the locus coeruleus drives anxiety after acute stress. Other sections cover mitochondria in the nucleus accumbens, reward coding, and hormone neurons in the hypothalamus. Together the work maps several paths by which stress turns into lasting anxiety.
europmc-pmc6735367:
Xian and co-authors tested stem cell exosomes as a treatment for inflamed astrocytes. Exosomes are tiny packets released by mesenchymal stem cells. They calm inflammation in brain diseases such as epilepsy and stroke. Astrocytes, the brain's support cells, may carry much of that effect. The team studied them in cell culture and in mice.

A bacterial toxin inflamed cultured astrocytes from the hippocampus. Exosome treatment reduced their reactive swelling and inflammatory signals. It also fixed faulty calcium signaling and mitochondrial strain. In mice with induced seizures, the exosomes had similar calming effects. Blocking a protective gene pathway called Nrf2 undid the benefit, pinning down the mechanism.
europmc-pmc6819567:
Waters and Ley review a family of gut bacteria in BMC Biology. The Christensenellaceae live in the human gut and belong to the Firmicutes group. They drew notice because people with more of them tend to weigh less. That link with body mass index has held up across many groups and studies. It is among the most consistent microbe-health links yet found.

The review sums up what is known about where these bacteria live and what they do. Their levels also track with health in gut disorders such as inflammatory bowel disease. Strikingly, how much a person carries runs in families, so host genes play a part. The pair note that the exact genes and the bacteria's role remain open questions.
europmc-pmc6859567:
Dodson and co-authors review a master switch against oxidative damage, in Redox Biology. The transcription factor NRF2 turns on genes that neutralise harsh reactive molecules. Many diseases involve a redox balance gone wrong. Among the damage products, peroxidised lipids stand out as drivers of illness. They also power ferroptosis, a form of cell death that depends on iron and fat damage.

The review sets out how NRF2 and the genes it controls block lipid peroxides from forming. Some of its target enzymes can themselves be disabled by those same reactive lipids. That two-way link makes the pathway a focus for cancer drug design. Both triggering and blocking ferroptosis are under study.
europmc-pmc6914667:
Pabst and Slack review secretory IgA, the chief antibody of the gut. Their review appeared in Mucosal Immunology. IgA is made in vast amounts each day. Yet experts still dispute what it does. Some cite the mild effects of IgA loss. Others stress its abundance and long history.

The pair revisit old disputes in IgA biology. They start with antigen specificity in the gut. They then set out clear terms for induction and function. Next they map the cell and molecular pathways that shape IgA. They also explain how IgA acts on microbes. On that basis, they propose how IgA helps build and keep helpful links with gut microbes.
europmc-pmc7033067:
Baltzer and co-authors present a consensus and mission statement in European Radiology. They write for the EUSOBI International Breast Diffusion-Weighted Imaging working group. Diffusion-weighted imaging, or DWI, is an MRI method that can help tell benign breast lesions from cancers. Practice varies widely, though, and results are hard to compare.

The group gives its first shared recommendations. They cover scan settings such as b values, fat saturation, and image resolution. They define levels of diffusion restriction in breast lesions from published data. They also advise how to measure the ADC value in a small, well-chosen region. The group stresses standard methods and quality checks. It aims to move breast DWI into routine clinical use at many sites.
europmc-pmc7136167:
Anderson and co-authors lay out a framework for developing drugs that specifically fight metastasis, in Nature Reviews Clinical Oncology. Spread to distant organs causes most cancer deaths, about 90% by their estimate. Yet drug development still leans on responses of the primary tumor, and metastases differ biologically from it.

A working group formed by Cancer Research UK and Cancer Therapeutics CRC Australia brought together academic, industry, government, and regulatory voices. They identified the main challenges: most seeded cells die, survivors grow in foreign tissue, and trials rarely measure spread directly. The paper recommends lab models and trial designs aimed at blocking metastatic growth itself, rather than assuming primary tumor shrinkage will do the job.
europmc-pmc7145667:
Rodchenkov and co-authors update Pathway Commons, a merged library of biological pathway data, in Nucleic Acids Research. The resource collects reactions, complexes, transport steps, and molecular interactions from 22 source databases and blends them into standard formats. At the time of writing it held 4,794 detailed human pathways and about 2.3 million interactions.

Users can search the collection, download bulk interaction tables and gene sets, or query it through programming libraries in Java, R, Python, and JavaScript. Pathway diagrams follow a standard graphical notation. The team is also building text-mining tools and author curation aids, since hand-curated sources can only cover a small part of the fast-growing literature.
europmc-pmc7184167:
Cai and co-authors describe a prodrug that kills senescent cells in aged mice. Their study appeared in Cell Research. Senescent cells are worn cells that stop dividing but stay alive. They build up with age and stir low-grade inflammation. That build-up harms tissue repair and physical function. Clearing these cells is a hoped-for route to healthier aging. Past drugs killed only some cell types.

The team's compound, SSK1, stays inert until an enzyme switches it on. That enzyme, beta-galactosidase, runs high in senescent cells. Once active, the drug turns into a cell-killing agent. The authors report it cleared senescent cells in mouse and human samples. In aged mice, it lowered age-linked gene patterns across tissues. It also calmed inflammation and restored physical function. The authors offer the approach as a new anti-aging strategy.
europmc-pmc7268667:
Crawford and Serhal argue that the rapid shift to digital health care during COVID-19 could widen health gaps if equity is ignored. Their commentary appeared in the Journal of Medical Internet Research. Video visits and remote monitoring kept care going while people stayed apart. Yet poverty, poor internet access, and low digital literacy can shut people out.

They present a Digital Health Equity Framework for spotting those barriers before a tool is rolled out. Equity, like person-centered care, should be built into provider training and defended at personal, institutional, and social levels. The authors call for ways to measure digital health equity, so new tools can be checked against the goal of fair access rather than assumed to help everyone equally.
europmc-pmc7276767:
Bourgonje and co-authors review the role of ACE2, the cell protein SARS-CoV-2 uses to enter the body, in the course of COVID-19. Their review appeared in The Journal of Pathology. ACE2 sits in many organs and normally counterbalances another enzyme in the system that controls blood pressure and fluids.

Age, sex, ethnicity, medication, and conditions such as heart disease and metabolic syndrome have all been linked to both ACE2 levels and disease severity. Yet organs rich in ACE2 do not all suffer equally, so other mechanisms must shape the damage. The authors gather fast-growing pathology reports from patient tissue to explain how infection unfolds. That understanding, they argue, is the base for treatments grounded in evidence rather than guesswork.
europmc-pmc7278967:
Zorena and co-authors review adipokines, hormone-like signals released by fat tissue, and their links to obesity and its complications. Their review appeared in the International Journal of Molecular Sciences. The World Health Organization counts obesity among the top threats to human health, and overweight people now outnumber the undernourished worldwide.

Fat tissue is not inert storage. Its adipokines travel in the blood and act on receptors across the body, steering metabolism in many organs. Some of these signals reduce insulin sensitivity and feed inflammation, setting up chronic complications such as diabetic foot problems and psoriasis. The authors searched major medical databases on white, brown, and perivascular fat. They argue adipokines will grow in importance for diagnosis and treatment as obesity spreads.
europmc-pmc7297667:
Gopalaswamy and co-authors set tuberculosis side by side with lung disease from its lesser known kin, the non-tuberculous mycobacteria. Their review counts more than 170 of these species in soil and water. Only a few cause human lung disease, chiefly the Mycobacterium avium complex and M. abscessus.

The two ills share early steps. Inhaled germs are eaten by lung immune cells, and the body walls them off in clumps called granulomas. But the kin germs come from the world around us, not from sick people. Who falls ill, and how, differs too. The kin favor people with a lung flaw called bronchiectasis, and in HIV they spread through the body. Tests and drug checks are far ahead for tuberculosis, a gap the team stresses.
europmc-pmc7306967:
Mukhtar and co-authors explore how teachers and students in Pakistan experienced the sudden move to online learning. Their qualitative case study appeared in the Pakistan Journal of Medical Sciences. When COVID-19 closed institutions, the University College of Medicine and University College of Dentistry in Lahore switched to online teaching almost overnight.

From March to April 2020, the team ran four focus groups with 12 faculty members and 12 students. Remote learning's comfort and accessibility were the praised advantages. Inefficiency and difficulty keeping academic work honest were the main complaints. Recommendations included training faculty in online methods and redesigning lessons with lower mental load and more interaction. Even with flaws, the authors support online learning as manageable and student-centered during lockdown.
europmc-pmc7349567:
Battaglia and co-authors present a review in Cells on ferroptosis, a form of cell death. This death is driven by iron and by damage to cell fats. The review centers on mitochondria, the cell parts that use iron and make reactive oxygen species. Cancer is the main setting.

The authors pull together work on how mitochondria shape this death path. Ferroptosis comes with clear harm to mitochondrial form, energy use, and metabolism. Cancer cells carry high iron and high reactive oxygen levels to fuel growth. That load can leave them open to ferroptosis. The review asks whether mitochondrial failure alone can start the process. It also weighs using this path to kill stubborn cancer cells. Readers get the case for and against a new treatment angle.
europmc-pmc7399967:
Elizabeth and co-authors review ultra-processed foods and health in Nutrients. Ultra-processed products, factory formulations of refined ingredients, now dominate diets worldwide. The authors searched for studies in healthy participants linking how much of these foods people eat with health outcomes, and appraised study quality.

Of 43 studies, 37 tied higher ultra-processed intake to at least one adverse outcome. In adults the list ran from obesity and heart and metabolic risk to cancer, type 2 diabetes, depression, frailty, and earlier death. In children it covered metabolic risk and asthma. No study found a benefit. Most evidence is observational, the authors note, though plausible mechanisms keep accumulating. The review arms nutrition policy with a broad, careful summary.
europmc-pmc7460667:
Luo, Ma, and Lu review mitochondrial dysfunction and its place in cancer. Mitochondria run energy production, redox balance, and cell death control. Faults in them appear across many human cancers.

Defects can arise in cycle enzymes, in mitochondrial DNA, or in the electron transport chain. Stress from oxidation and faulty growth signals adds more harm. These faults rewire how cells use fuel and upset redox balance. They also help cells resist death signals and treatment. The review gathers current knowledge on each fault type. It ties each one to the growth of specific cancers. The authors frame mitochondria as both a cause and a target in cancer care.
europmc-pmc7490367:
Rieke and co-authors explore how federated learning could shape the future of digital health. Machine learning thrives on medical data, which modern systems collect in huge volumes. Yet most data sit locked in silos, and privacy rules limit sharing.

Without enough data, models fall short of their promise in clinics. Federated learning trains models where the data live, so raw records need not move. The paper weighs what drives the current data block. It then maps how federated setups could free model building while guarding privacy. Technical hurdles and design choices get a full airing. The authors see a path from research models to bedside tools. Governance and trust, they stress, must grow with the math.
europmc-pmc7498167:
Olsen and co-authors report a sharp drop in influenza activity during the COVID-19 pandemic. Four countries anchor the report: the United States, Australia, Chile, and South Africa. Flu indicators began falling in late February 2020.

United States lab data showed a 61% decrease in specimens submitted and a 98% decrease in flu activity by positive share in the spring period. Summer flu circulation sat at historic lows. Southern Hemisphere countries had very low flu in their winter season of June to August 2020. Masks, distancing, school closures, and remote work likely helped. The authors still urge full flu vaccine plans for the fall. Both viruses may circulate at once, so vaccine cover stays the best guard for the season.
europmc-pmc7541367:
Liu and co-authors review gut microbiota and dysbiosis in Alzheimer's disease. Brain and gut talk through metabolic, immune and nerve routes. Changes in gut microbes link to many brain disorders.

The review asks whether gut imbalance helps drive Alzheimer's disease. Evidence ties dysbiosis to amyloid-beta buildup in the brain. It also ties it to inflammation and oxidative stress. Insulin resistance may play a role as well. A direct cause is not yet proven. The authors outline ways to shift gut microbes for prevention. They also outline treatment ideas. Readers get a clear survey of the gut-brain link in dementia.
europmc-pmc7558467:
Joubert, Beck, Dumontet and Denevault-Sabourin review antibody-drug conjugates over a decade of progress. An ADC links a toxic drug to a targeted antibody. That design aims chemo at tumor cells.

In 2009 only one ADC was in clinical use. By 2020 there were 9 FDA-approved ADCs available. More than 80 others were in active clinical studies. The review focuses on approved and late-stage agents. It covers toxicity and resistance that limit benefit. New designs try to widen the treatment window. Pairings with chemo or checkpoint drugs are discussed. Uses beyond oncology are also explored in the review.
europmc-pmc7768267:
Zheng and co-authors show how a SARS-CoV-2 protein shuts down the cell's interferon alarm. Weak interferon output is a hallmark of COVID-19. The culprit here is the viral membrane protein, M. It targets the cell's RNA sensors, RIG-I and MDA-5, which spot viral RNA and call for interferon.

The M protein binds three parts of this alarm chain, including RIG-I and the relay MAVS. This blocks the team of proteins that must form to fire the signal. A key switch then stays off, and interferon of types I and III is not made. Adding M helped another test virus copy itself more freely.
europmc-pmc7809767:
Du and co-authors review Aurora kinase A as a cancer drug target. AURKA is an enzyme needed for cell division. It helps run the process of mitosis. Cancer tissues show far more AURKA than normal tissues. This holds across many tumor types in the TCGA database.

Active AURKA feeds a wide range of cancers. Many of its target proteins are now known. Some are tumor suppressors, and others drive tumors. Partner proteins cluster in classic cancer pathways. Small drug molecules that block AURKA have been found. Some entered clinical trials alone or with standard drugs. The authors weigh the mechanisms and the treatment chances.
europmc-pmc7854667:
Daly and co-authors build dense tissue models by printing cell balls into self-healing gels. Lab tissue models help study development and disease. They also screen drugs for effect and harm. Most models lack real tissue density and cell mix.

Their printer places tiny cell spheroids at fine detail. The gel support closes around each ball. Balls then fuse into one tissue with a set layout. The team printed heart tissue from stem cells. Heart muscle and fibroblast shares were set by design. The model copied scarred heart traits, with weak, uneven beating. Gene-silencing drugs were then tested for repair. The method suits many precision disease models.
europmc-pmc7861967:
Liu and co-authors gauge how well non-drug measures cut SARS-CoV-2 spread across 130 countries and territories. Closures, travel limits, and aid programs rolled out worldwide. Proof of which ones worked was patchy. The team assessed each class of measure against transmission data.

Measures were grouped into types. Internal closures and containment formed one group. Border rules formed a second. Economic support and health system steps filled out the list. The authors compared timing and strength across places. Effects on the spread rate were then estimated. Such pooled evidence guides the next emergency playbook. It also shows where single-country studies can mislead.
europmc-pmc7940067:
Rolleston presents a lecture on William Harvey's predecessors and contemporaries. The lecture was delivered at the College of Physicians in Philadelphia on 22 March 1928. Harvey's book of 1628 set out a wholly new idea of how blood circulates. That idea challenged the teaching of Galen, which had ruled medicine for more than thirteen centuries. Rolleston asks what the world Harvey worked in looked like.

Opponents called Harvey a bold disturber of the peace of physicians. Some even branded him a quack. Rolleston sets that hostility in context. He surveys the men who came before Harvey and those who worked beside him. Their partial insights show how the ground was prepared. Their resistance shows what a new truth costs. The lecture is both a tribute and a study in how medicine changes its mind.
europmc-pmc7953067:
Cristofori and co-authors present a review of probiotics and their calming effects on gut inflammation. The gut hosts millions of microbes and is the body's main site of contact with them. That community helps train the immune system from early life. When its balance breaks, inflammation can follow. Probiotics are live microbes given to restore the balance. Their exact ways of helping are still being worked out.

Studies in animals and humans show real effects on immune and inflammatory paths. The review explains how probiotics can firm up the gut wall and raise mucus cover. They can also cut the bacterial toxins that trigger immune alarms. Diet, age, weight, drugs, and stress can all blur the gains. The authors sort the evidence by mechanism. They frame the gut as a door through which local microbes sway the whole body.
europmc-pmc7955067:
Pacini and co-authors present a study that merges the two largest CRISPR screens of cancer cells. Such screens switch off genes one by one across many cell lines. Genes a cancer needs to survive show up as its weak points. Two big public screens had been run apart, at the Broad and Sanger institutes. Joining them promises a fuller map of cancer's weak spots.

The team compared methods for cleaning the merged data. They corrected for uneven guide strength, side effects of DNA cutting, and batch differences. The merged sets kept the findings of each screen alone. They also added power for cancer-type and subtype checks. New markers of gene need appeared, and shared vital genes stood out more clearly. The result is the largest merged resource of its kind, offered as a base for future screens.
europmc-pmc7986567:
Schaffer and co-authors present a guide to interrupted time series analysis with ARIMA models for judging health interventions. Such studies track an outcome before and after a policy lands. The common method, segmented regression, can fail when data carry seasons or echo their own past. ARIMA models handle both problems. The guide explains when to reach for them.

The authors walk through the theory in plain steps. They cover picking the shape of the impact, choosing the model, and checking its fit. Reading the results gets equal care. A worked example anchors the lesson: an Australian policy of January 2014 that cut refills for one strength of an antipsychotic drug. Code in R and SAS lets readers copy the full analysis.
europmc-pmc8010267:
Ayoubkhani and co-authors measure the health burden people carried after leaving hospital with covid-19. Their retrospective cohort study covers NHS hospitals in England. It followed 47,780 patients discharged alive by 31 August 2020. Each patient was matched to controls drawn from about 50 million people. Follow-up ran a mean of 140 days.

The authors report that 14,060 patients were readmitted within that span. A further 5,875 died after discharge. Readmission ran at four times the control rate, and death at eight times. New respiratory, diabetes, and cardiovascular diagnoses were all sharply raised. The excess risk was larger in people under 70 and in ethnic minority groups. The authors urge joined-up care for post-covid syndrome.
europmc-pmc8016467:
Huang and co-authors present DeepPurpose, a deep learning library for predicting drug–target interactions. Knowing which proteins a drug binds is basic to drug discovery. Deep learning models predict such binding well, but they are hard to use. Each published tool has its own interface and code style. Newcomers from computing and biology both struggle with them.

DeepPurpose wraps many models behind one easy framework. It implements 15 encoders for compounds and proteins. Over 50 neural architectures sit behind them. Users can train custom models with little code. The authors report state-of-the-art results on several benchmark datasets. The library also supports ensembles across methods, which older tools made awkward.
europmc-pmc8078867:
Balali-Mood and co-authors compare how five heavy metals poison the human body. A century of industry has raised exposure to them all. Mercury, lead, chromium, cadmium, and arsenic lead the list of culprits. They reach people through water, air, and food. Once inside, they build up and harm many tissues at once.

The review traces each metal's route of attack from animal and human studies. Shared routes stand out across the five. All five stir up reactive oxygen species and wear down antioxidant defenses. Enzymes get switched off, and cell growth and repair go astray. Some metals grip specific proteins by name. Lead locks onto two enzymes of blood making. Chromium, cadmium, and arsenic also break DNA repair. That damage helps explain their cancer risk. Chelation therapy is flagged for a future review.
europmc-pmc8081667:
Rhie and co-authors report lessons from building complete, error-free genomes for vertebrate species. Top-grade reference genomes exist for only a few species. The Genome 10K consortium spent five years testing cheaper ways to build them. The team produced assemblies for 16 species across six vertebrate lineages. Each assembly was checked hard against older references.

Long-read sequencing proved essential for top quality. Complex repeats and mixed haplotypes caused most remaining errors when mishandled. The new builds fixed real faults in famous older genomes. False gene duplications vanished, and gene sizes grew. A shared chromosome breakpoint turned up twice in bat genomes. Protein-coding genes showed a rich GC pattern with their control regions. The authors now aim at all roughly 70,000 vertebrate species. The Vertebrate Genomes Project carries that plan forward.
europmc-pmc8102467:
Blood Pressure Lowering Treatment Trialists' Collaboration pooled patient-level data from 48 randomized trials to test who gains from blood pressure drugs. The analysis covered 344,716 participants in total. Some had prior cardiovascular disease, many had none. Baseline pressures ranged from under 120 to over 170 mm Hg. Whether treatment helps at normal starting pressures was the open question.

Follow-up ran a median of just over four years per participant. In that span, 42,324 participants had at least one major cardiovascular event. The benefit of treatment scaled with how far pressure fell. Bigger drops in systolic pressure bought bigger risk cuts. The pattern held across the baseline pressure range. It held for people with and without past disease alike. Gains appeared even among those starting below 130 mm Hg systolic. The authors read this as a case for treating risk, not just high readings. Fixed drug plans could suit most adults.
europmc-pmc8121667:
Stephenson and co-authors map the blood immune response to COVID-19 cell by cell. They profiled over 780,000 peripheral blood cells from 130 patients. Illness severity in the cohort ran from mild to critical. Each cell gave up its gene activity, surface proteins, and receptor code. The joint view exposed a coordinated, shifting response. Several cell states stood out as severity markers.

One monocyte type, rich in complement genes, expanded and grabbed platelets. Early blood stem cells leaned toward making platelet parents. Platelet activation rose alongside that push. Severe disease carried clonally expanded killer T cells. Mild disease instead showed more follicular helper T cells. Antibody-making cells swelled, yet one class, IgA2, thinned out. The lost class guards the airways' lining. Each discrete cell state is a drug target candidate. The atlas gives therapy a wiring diagram.
europmc-pmc8333067:
Li and Wu review pattern recognition receptors in health and disease. These receptors spot set molecular patterns directly. Patterns mark pathogens, dying cells, and damaged tissue.

They bridge the fast innate response and the tailored one. Binding can spark defence against infection and tumours. Most fall into five families by protein structure. Toll-like and NOD-like receptors lead the list. RIG-I-like and C-type lectin receptors follow. The review covers each family's signals and jobs. Faults in this early warning system echo through many diseases. Absent in melanoma-like receptors complete the five families named.
europmc-pmc8470767:
Krawczyk and co-authors ask how close the Enterococcus group sits to full pathogenicity. These bacteria live in the gut of people and animals. Two species, E. faecalis and E. faecium, are the most common in humans. Strains have long served as probiotics in food.

That use has grown controversial in recent years. Enterococci pick up virulence genes and drug resistance with ease. In hospitals they act as opportunistic pathogens and cause outbreaks. They can slip from the gut into other tissues. The review weighs their good, probiotic face against their harmful one. Genome flexibility is the thread that links the two.
europmc-pmc8475767:
Takata and co-authors show how a failing blood-brain barrier fans brain inflammation. The barrier is built from vessel lining cells locked by tight junctions. It guards brain balance and shields neurons. In many brain diseases, this barrier breaks down.

Damage signals and germs can trigger brain inflammation. Glial cells wake and release signals that harm neurons. A leaky barrier lets immune cells and blood proteins slip into brain tissue. That inflow then feeds the inflammation further. Glial cells also act back on barrier strength. The review traces cell events inside the barrier's lining cells. It aims at ways to prevent or treat barrier failure.
europmc-pmc8645667:
Gavas, Quazi, and Karpiński review nanoparticles as tools for cancer therapy. Standard care includes chemotherapy, radiation, and immune therapy. These can lack precision and harm healthy cells. Drug resistance adds a second wall. Tiny particles, from 1 to 100 nanometers, offer a new route.

Particles can target tumors and release drugs where they are needed. Their traits include good stability and low added toxicity. The review sorts particles into main types. It covers how each type uses tumor traits to reach cancer cells. It also notes a limit: most work stays in lab and animal studies. Few nano drugs have won approval so far.
europmc-pmc8647967:
Nie and co-authors review a gut bacterium, Roseburia intestinalis, and its links to human health. This anaerobic bacterium lives in the colon and makes butyrate, a useful fuel for gut cells. It has been tied to gut inflammation control and energy balance. Levels of the bacterium shift in several diseases.

The review covers bowel disease, type 2 diabetes, and artery disease. In bowel disease, patients show clear changes in the bacterium's abundance. Its products help guard the gut wall and tune immune cells. New tools, such as single-cell sequencing, have deepened work on this group. The authors weigh its promise as a future therapy.
europmc-pmc8706767:
Zhang and co-authors review NF-κB signaling in inflammation and cancer, thirty-five years after the factor was found. This protein family switches on genes for immune and stress responses. Faulty control of it links to many human diseases. That makes it a tempting drug target.

The review sums up the family members and how the pathway turns on. It then traces what faulty signaling does in inflamed tissue. Tumor growth and the tumor setting get their own account. Drug work aimed at the pathway is reviewed next. The authors note blocks that still slow this work. They call for finer knowledge of its roles in health and disease.
europmc-pmc8786667:
Perin and co-authors update the causes of death in children under five across the world from 2000 to 2019. Cause data guide child survival programs in every health system. The team rebuilt estimates for newborns and children up to 59 months. Their new methods use a Bayesian frame that handles unreported causes in verbal autopsy data.

In 2019, 5.30 million children under five died. Preterm birth complications led at 17.7 percent of deaths. Lung infections, birth events, and diarrhoea followed. Infectious causes made up 49.2 percent of deaths. Deaths fell a lot since 2000, led by drops in lung infections and diarrhoea. Trends varied widely by region.
europmc-pmc8799467:
Bulten and co-authors report the PANDA challenge, a global contest to build AI for prostate cancer diagnosis and Gleason grading. Prior AI results came from single studies without broad validation. The contest drew 1,290 developers, the largest of its kind in tissue imaging. They trained on 10,616 digitized prostate biopsies.

Top algorithms reached expert pathologist level on blinded test sets. Agreement scores hit 0.862 on a United States set and 0.868 on a European set. Many distinct approaches generalized well across labs and patient groups. The authors argue this success warrants clinical trials. Reproducible methods were a core design goal of the challenge.
europmc-pmc8824567:
Schmitz, Grotewold, and Stam review cis-regulatory sequences in plants. These DNA stretches control when and where genes switch on. They include enhancers and silencers, grouped into cis-regulatory modules. Gene sequencing has raced ahead of regulatory mapping. Plant scientists still know far less about these control regions. The review asks how that gap can close.

The authors describe what these modules are made of. They cover methods to find and test them across whole genomes. They compare where modules sit relative to their target genes in different species. Transposable elements earn a section as a source of new modules. The authors close with open challenges. Their aim is better grasp of gene control for plant science and crop gains.
europmc-pmc8938267:
Xie, Xu, Bowe, and Al-Aly chart heart and vessel outcomes in the year after COVID-19. Acute COVID-19 harms the cardiovascular system in known ways. The post-acute picture was far less clear. The team used US Veterans Affairs health databases. The COVID-19 cohort held 153,760 people. Two control groups held over five million each. Outcomes were set in advance. Follow-up ran a full year past infection.

Survivors faced raised risks across many categories. Stroke, rhythm disorders, and heart failure all rose. Clotting disease, pericarditis, and myocarditis rose too. Risks appeared even in people never hospitalized. They climbed with the severity of the acute illness. Intensive care patients carried the heaviest burden. The authors call the total burden substantial. They urge care pathways that watch the heart. Recovery, in their data, is not the end of risk.
europmc-pmc9300467:
Garcia-Alonso and co-authors build a single-cell roadmap of human gonad development. They profiled gonads from the first and second trimesters using single-cell and spatial gene readouts. Chromatin access assays and microscopy added more layers. Matching mouse stages were profiled to pick out human-specific programs.

The map names the cell states present when sex is set. A shared early supporting population can turn toward testis or ovary fates. In females, two waves of granulosa cells shape the growing ovary. In males, two fetal testis macrophage types signal inside and outside the cords. The atlas should guide lab-grown gonad models. It may also clarify disorders of sex development and infertility causes.
europmc-pmc9409667:
Filip and co-authors review the strain the COVID-19 pandemic placed on health care systems worldwide. From December 2019, SARS-CoV-2 spread fast across countries. Hospitals had to treat pandemic cases and keep up normal care at once. Many systems proved unready for that double load.

The authors compare how countries responded to the surge. Wards not on the front line were remade for COVID-19 care. Staff safety and workflow changes get close review. A large part looks at digital care as a fix. Telemedicine and mobile health apps let patients reach care without exposure risk. The authors argue such tools can ease crowded emergency rooms. They urge a broad overhaul before future outbreaks hit.
europmc-pmc9410767:
Ihim and co-authors review interleukin-18, a strong pro-inflammatory cytokine in host defense. Many cell types make IL-18, from monocytes and macrophages to skin and tissue cells. It guides both innate and acquired immune responses. High blood levels show up in several immune diseases.

The review sums up the biology of IL-18 first. It then maps its role disease by disease. Rheumatoid arthritis, lupus, and type 1 diabetes get chapters. So do psoriasis, bowel disease, and muscle inflammation. A later part covers antibodies and drugs that target IL-18. Most such drugs gave only partial gains, the authors note. They suggest pairing IL-18 blockade with drugs against other cytokines. That mix may work where single drugs failed.
europmc-pmc9465867:
Zheng and co-authors review elesclomol, a copper carrying drug that targets mitochondrial metabolism in cancer. The drug was first known as a source of oxidative stress. It is now linked to cuproptosis, a copper driven form of cell death. Its power depends on how much a cancer leans on mitochondrial energy.

Cancer stem cells lean hard on that energy supply. So do cells that resist platinum drugs or proteasome inhibitors. The review shows elesclomol hit all such cells hard. Its toxicity rides on moving copper ions into the cell. Past trials failed to show clear gains, yet safety was confirmed. The authors urge new trials in cancers with high mitochondrial metabolism. Pairing the drug with platinum or glycolysis blockers is a key plan.
europmc-pmc9499867:
Milà-Alomà and co-authors test plasma p-tau231 and p-tau217 as early markers of amyloid pathology in Alzheimer's disease. Trials of disease-changing drugs need cheap screens for preclinical cases. Blood tests could fill that role before brain scans. Which marker wakes earliest was not settled.

The work drew on the ALFA+ cohort of people without symptoms. All tested plasma markers shifted in preclinical disease. P-tau231 turned abnormal at the lowest amyloid burden, though. P-tau231 and p-tau217 linked most strongly to amyloid PET signal. The link held in brain regions that gather amyloid first. Both also tracked later rises in amyloid PET uptake. The authors pitch the pair as tools to enrich trial cohorts. Such screening could cut the cost of early stage trials.
europmc-pmc9605867:
Yengo and co-authors build a saturated map of common genetic variants tied to human height. Common variants were tipped to explain 40 to 50% of height variation. Naming the exact variants takes enormous sample sizes. Height is easy to measure and richly heritable, so it suits the hunt.

The genome-wide study pooled data from 5.4 million people of diverse ancestries. It found 12,111 independent variants with firm links to height. Together they account for nearly all common variant heritability. The variants cluster in 7,209 genome segments that cover about 21% of the genome. In European ancestry groups they explained 40% of height variance in fresh samples. In other ancestry groups they explained only about 10 to 20%. The authors blame linkage patterns and allele shares for the gap. More work is needed to saturate the map outside Europe.
europmc-pmc9640667:
Kline and co-authors run a scoping review of multimodal machine learning in precision health. Machine learning has long worked on one data type at a time in health. Real clinical calls blend many data types at once. Fusing streams aims to match that expert habit.

The team searched three databases for work from 2011 to 2021. A final set of 128 articles entered the review. Neurology and oncology used fusion methods the most. Early fusion was the most common way to merge data. Studies that compared fusion with single stream models did better with fusion. The gain averaged 6.4% in predictive accuracy across those papers. Clear paths to clinic use were mostly missing. Approvals and bias checks for mixed groups were also rare. Scale and slow data joining are the named costs.
europmc-pmc9757867:
Bytyçi and co-authors pool studies to measure how common statin intolerance really is. The problem matters for public health and heart risk. Patients who cannot take statins face higher event rates. Loose claims may inflate how often true intolerance occurs.

The team gathered 176 studies with over four million patients. Trials and cohort studies both entered the pool. Fewer than one in ten patients met intolerance marks overall. Rates matched across the three main rule sets used. Cohort studies showed 17% intolerance in their samples. Trial rates ran much lower than the cohort figure. Older age and female sex raised the odds somewhat. Obesity, diabetes, and thyroid trouble also raised risk. Some heart drugs and higher doses added to the risk. The authors say full intolerance is rarer than often claimed.
europmc-pmc9799367:
Mannar and co-authors solve the structure of the Omicron spike locked onto its human cell receptor. Omicron was set to pass Delta as the top variant worldwide. Its spike carries 37 mutations versus the first strain. Fifteen of those changes sit in the receptor binding zone.

Cryo-electron microscopy showed the spike gripping ACE2 in fine detail. Mutated spots formed fresh salt bridges and hydrogen bonds. Those new grips offset changes that weaken binding alone. One change at position 417 is known to loosen the hold. Net binding strength ended near Delta's level in the end. Tests with pseudoviruses showed stronger antibody evasion too. The pair of traits helps explain Omicron's fast spread. Strong grip plus antibody escape is a potent mix. The authors map the exact residues behind both effects.
findelkind-pg1367: A novel by Ouida, the flamboyant Victorian bestseller, about a foundling child and the fortunes that swirl around him. Romantic, sentimental, and lushly written in her inimitable style, it is pure Ouida: emotion at full flood. Popular fiction from an author who never did anything by halves.
frus-1861-d167:
On 22 June 1861, William H. Seward wrote to Carl Schurz as Spain set its neutral course. The letter is document 167 in the Foreign Relations volume for 1861.

Seward's June letter reached toward Madrid as Spain set its neutral course. Cuba made Spain a sea power near the American coast. Clear orders to Schurz helped keep Spanish ports and Cuban waters from aiding the South by stealth. Spanish cruisers and Cuban ports both fell under the watch Schurz had to keep. The watch he kept ran from the court's doors to the docks of Cadiz. The watch ran from court doors to Cadiz docks.
frus-1861-d267:
The home office spoke to James Shepherd Pike on 11 November 1861, through a letter from Seward. It stands as Document 267 in the volume of foreign papers laid before Congress with the President's message. It belongs to the autumn of the war's first year, when keeping Europe out of the war was a core task for Washington.

Seward's letters in this run set out Washington's line for the man on the spot to follow. For students of the war, the value lies in the sequence: one dated step in a long exchange. The Foreign Relations series, kept by the State Department's Office of the Historian, preserves the full run.
frus-1861-d67:
Writing on 12 August 1861, William H. Seward kept up his steady stream of letters to Charles Francis Adams. The letter is document 67 in the Foreign Relations volume for 1861.

Mid August found the Union cause in Europe at a low point. Seward kept his letters short, plain, and free of despair. For Adams, each such page was both an order and a sign of trust. Their steady tone did much to hold Britain's respect through a bleak season. Adams answered each order in turn, which kept the London file in neat pairs. Neat pairs in the file let readers trace each point from order to answer.
frus-1862-d167:
Document 167, dated 25 October 1862, is one of three Seward dispatches to London printed under that date in the 1862 Foreign Relations volume. All three went to Charles Francis Adams, the American minister to Britain.

A cluster of same-day letters usually means a mail steamer was about to sail and the Department cleared its desk at once. Orders, war news, and copies of other papers could all leave on the same tide. For historians, clusters like this one mark the rhythm of transatlantic diplomacy, driven by ship schedules as much as by events. British backing for the South would have brought Richmond credit, ships, and fresh hope at once.
frus-1862-d267:
In Washington, Secretary of State William H. Seward wrote to William L. Dayton on 16 April 1862, a day after his previous Paris dispatch. The letter is Document 267 in the 1862 Foreign Relations volume.

Two letters in two days from the Secretary usually means fresh news to send or a point to underline twice. The spring mails to Paris carried the Union's case at a moment when New Orleans was about to fall to a Union fleet. That prize, a great port and cotton outlet, spoke loudly in Europe, and Seward made sure his envoy could speak to it. French public opinion ran warmer for the Union after the emancipation news arrived.
frus-1862-d367:
Document 367, dated 31 May 1862, is a memorandum of a conversation between Henri Mercier. The French minister in Washington, and Secretary of State William H. Seward. Such memoranda were written up after talks to fix what had been said.

A recorded conversation differs from a letter: it captures diplomacy done aloud, with questions, hints, and warnings that formal notes avoid. Memoranda in this file are among its most revealing papers. This one comes from the weeks after Mercier's Richmond trip, when face-to-face talk between the two men carried more weight than paper. The French legation's notes were written in French and printed here in the Department's English.
frus-1862-d467:
George Perkins Marsh, the American minister in Turin, sent this report to Secretary of State William H. Seward on 6 January 1862. It is Document 467 in the 1862 volume of Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs, the first Italian paper in the file.

Marsh opened the year reporting from a kingdom barely ten months old, where the American war was followed with fellow feeling. Italy's leaders had just fought to unite their own country and saw the Union's cause in that light. His early report gave Washington a measure of Italian sympathy and of the new kingdom's standing among the powers. The letter starts a file that stands out in the volume for its genuine cordiality.
frus-1862-d567:
Henry Shelton Sanford reported from Brussels to Secretary of State William H. Seward on 26 August 1862. The dispatch is Document 567 in the 1862 volume of Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs, laid before Congress with the annual message.

Late August 1862 was a low season for the Union, and Sanford's reports that summer did not hide it. From Belgium he could watch French policy hardening in Mexico and British opinion swinging with the battle news. He also pursued his standing hunt for Confederate agents and purchases in Europe. Seward needed such reporting most when times were worst, and Sanford supplied it without varnish. The letter belongs to the hard summer file that precedes the turn at Antietam.
frus-1862-d667:
On 7 August 1862, Secretary of State William H. Seward sent a formal note to the ministers for foreign affairs of Japan. It is document 667 in the Foreign Relations volume for 1862, the last of his direct notes to the court in this file. Robert H. Pruyn was by then running the American legation.

Notes sent over an envoy's head were rare, and they marked points Washington wanted stated in its own voice. This one belongs with the two earlier notes to the same ministers, in 1861 and in March 1862. Together the three show a young tie kept up by set forms, long waits, and great care on both sides.
frus-1862-d67:
The home office spoke to Charles Francis Adams on 20 May 1862, through a letter from Seward. It stands as Document 67 in Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs, the volume sent to Congress with the President's yearly message. The letter comes from the spring of 1862, a year into the war, a time when each foreign capital watched the war with care.

Seward's letters in this run set out Washington's line for the man on the spot to follow. Read in order with its neighbors, it shows diplomacy as daily work rather than grand speeches. The State Department's Office of the Historian keeps the series, called Foreign Relations of the United States.
frus-1863p1-d167:
For the first of his three letters of 24 April 1863, Charles Francis Adams wrote to Secretary of State William H. Seward from London. Three Adams letters in the volume bear the date, and two Seward letters share it too. Adams was the American minister in London; this letter is document 167 in part one of the 1863 volume.

Five sheets in the file bear 24 April, a peak day for the exchange. Adams's three took the London heads in turn: talks, yards, and press. This one opens his set. The pile for one date shows both capitals at full work on the same brief, in the spring the ship fight turned.
frus-1863p1-d267:
From his London post on 21 August 1863, Charles Francis Adams, the American minister in London, reported home to Secretary of State William H. Seward. The dispatch is document 267 in the Foreign Relations volume for 1863. It appears in the Foreign Relations series, where the State Department printed the papers it sent with the President's yearly message to Congress. It was one of 4 letters between the same men dated that day.

Public meetings across Britain, many of them backing the Union and emancipation, formed part of the picture Adams reported. He tracked opinion as carefully as he tracked ministers. The letter's value lies partly in its place in the sequence: it shows the conversation between the two capitals continuing without a break.
frus-1863p1-d367:
In Washington on 20 January 1863, Secretary of State William H. Seward addressed this note to Lord Lyons, Britain's minister in Washington. It is document 367 in the 1863 Foreign Relations volume. It survives in the 1863 volume of Foreign Relations of the United States, the State Department's official record of its work abroad.

Lyons was the man Seward had to persuade, warn, or answer in person in Washington. Notes to him carried the American side of each dispute between the two governments. It dates from the month the Emancipation Proclamation took effect, which changed the politics of the war in Britain at once. Read alongside its neighbors in the volume, it shows the daily grind behind the war's big diplomatic crises.
frus-1863p1-d467:
One entry in the 1863 papers is a 17 April 1863 letter from William H. Seward to Lord Lyons. Lyons was Britain's minister in Washington, and Seward was the American Secretary of State. It appears in Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs, the State Department volume printed with the President's annual message for 1863. Readers meet it in the first part of the 1863 Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs, the government's own record of its dealings abroad.

Confederate warships built in British yards were a sore point all year. Washington pressed London to stop them, and letters like this carried that pressure. Students of the war use this mail to see foreign policy as the men on the spot lived it, page by page. Readers who work through the file in order will find this letter where the clerks of 1863 left it, in the middle of the stream.
frus-1863p1-d567:
On 16 June 1863, Lord Lyons, Britain's minister in Washington wrote to William H. Seward, the Secretary of State. The two men at the ends of this channel, Seward in Washington and Lyons speaking for Britain, wrote to each other almost daily. The letter sits in the published record of how the Lincoln government handled foreign affairs in the early summer of 1863.

Single letters rarely settle anything here. Their worth is in the chain they form, which lets a reader watch a dispute rise, cool, and fade in real time. A reader gets the feel of diplomacy done by hand: formal greetings, careful wording, and hard points pressed without open threats. That is the use of such a page: not a famous text, but a firm rung in the ladder of the record.
frus-1863p1-d667:
From Charles Francis Adams, America's minister in London to William H. Seward, the Secretary of State: a letter dated 19 November 1863. At the time, the Union government was fighting the Confederacy at home and working to keep foreign powers neutral. It forms part of Foreign Relations of the United States, the official printed record of American diplomacy.

That autumn the sharpest issue was the pair of ironclad rams built for the Confederacy at Birkenhead. Britain held them back, and this mail ran while that fight played out. Single letters rarely settle anything here. Their worth is in the chain they form, which lets a reader watch a dispute rise, cool, and fade in real time. The volume's editors printed it without comment; its meaning comes from the company it keeps in the file.
frus-1863p1-d67:
Charles Francis Adams dated this dispatch 30 January 1863 and sent it to Secretary of State William H. Seward. Adams was the American minister in London. The letter is document 67 in part one of the Foreign Relations volume for 1863.

Adams wrote at the end of a full month of London work. His January mail had covered the freedom edict's welcome in Britain and the cabinet's watchful calm. Reports like this one let Seward weigh whether the tide across the sea ran for or against the Union. The dispatch is a quiet, workmanlike piece of the file, of the kind the whole record is built from.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d167: American members of the Moscow Conference's committee on Iran answered their British colleagues with a memorandum dated October 26, 1943. It is Document 167 of the Cairo and Tehran volume. Paired papers like these show allied drafting at work: two delegations shaping one text on a country both used and neither ruled. The record gives the source and the date. The memorandum is printed in the Foreign Relations series.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d267: An editorial note in the Foreign Relations volume states that no record of the substance of this Cairo meeting has been found. The only facts the editors can give about it, namely that the meeting took place and who took part, are taken from the President's Log. The note stands in the volume in place of a document, marking a gap in the surviving record of the conference.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d367:
Minutes kept for the Combined Chiefs of Staff record the same second plenary session at Tehran. It met on 29 November 1943 at four in the afternoon. This is the staff version that parallels the Bohlen minutes. The emphasis falls on General Marshall's figures and Stalin's sharp questions.

Marshall insists the American problem is not troops or equipment. It is ships, landing craft, and airfields near the fighting. The Overlord build-up runs on schedule, with a million tons assembled in Britain ahead of the troops. Voroshilov confirms the morning's technical talks. Stalin then asks who commands Overlord and who carries its moral and technical responsibility. Told that General Morgan plans for a commander not yet named, he answers flatly that nothing will come of these operations on that basis.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d467:
A second message from Secretary of State Cordell Hull reached President Roosevelt on December 2, 1943, as the President moved from the Tehran Conference toward the second meeting at Cairo. Two Hull cables on one day speak to the pace of business that December. The State Department included both in its Cairo-Tehran conference volume.

Roosevelt was running American diplomacy from conference rooms in Iran and Egypt, while Hull ran the department from Washington. Messages in this channel carried reports, requests, and advice between the two men. Read with its companion cable, this one shows the steady administrative thread behind the dramatic summit photographs and communiqués.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d567:
Prime Minister Churchill wrote to President Roosevelt on October 18, 1944, while Churchill was in Moscow for talks with Stalin. The message appears in the State Department's Cairo-Tehran volume, among the later papers tracing the conferences' consequences.

Churchill's Moscow visit produced the famous percentages discussion about influence in the Balkans, and he kept Roosevelt informed as it unfolded. A message from Moscow in that week belongs to the alliance's most delicate balancing act: holding Soviet cooperation while spheres of interest hardened in Eastern Europe. For readers, it shows the Prime Minister reporting to Washington from inside the Kremlin's orbit.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d67: Roosevelt wrote to Secretary Hull on October 28, 1943, as the Moscow Conference closed. His letter is Document 67 of the Cairo and Tehran volume. The president and his secretary had exchanged letters all through the Moscow days, an unusual closeness for two men who often kept their distance. The record gives the date and the names and no subject. The letter is printed in the Foreign Relations series.
frus-1944-quebec-d167:
The Combined Intelligence Committee estimated the enemy situation in the Pacific and Far East on September 9, 1944. The study ranges over Japanese politics, economics, and military strength. Japan, it says, hoped to avoid war with the Soviet Union and to hold successive defense lines until war weariness divided the Allies into accepting a satisfactory peace.

Economically, Japanese shipping was barely adequate, sinkings exceeded launchings, and fuel oil stocks might last only about nine months. Militarily, her air force had declined and her navy suffered serious losses, though ground forces kept their strength. The committee expected fierce resistance along the inner line from Japan through Formosa and Luzon to Mindanao, and a strong defensive posture in Manchuria against the Soviet threat.
frus-1944-quebec-d267:
The United States Chiefs gave their formal answer on British Pacific participation in C.C.S. 452/27, dated September 13, 1944. They would welcome a British naval task force in the Pacific to take part in the main operations against Japan. Two qualifications followed, and they were the sentences London would spend the next day's meeting trying to remove.

The force's initial use, the Americans considered, should be on the western flank of the advance in the Southwest Pacific. They also assumed the force would be balanced and self-supporting. The paper repeated acceptance of the separate British Empire task force under MacArthur. Brooke told the Combined Chiefs the British were disturbed by the statement, which predated the plenary session's warmer assurances.
frus-1944-quebec-d67:
President Roosevelt wrote to the War Shipping Administrator, Emory Land, on September 12, 1944, at Quebec. The catalog heading misspells the title as “War Shinning Administrator.” The message appears in the State Department's Quebec 1944 volume.

Land's agency allocated the merchant fleet on which every Allied plan depended, and Quebec took up the shipping terms of continued aid to Britain. A presidential message to the shipping chief during the conference ties the summit's grand questions to hulls and cargoes. For readers, it shows the President reaching from the conference table to the administrator whose numbers bound them all.
frus-1945-50-intel-d167:
A letter from the President’s Chief of Staff (Leahy) reached the Director of the Federal Bureau of Investigation (Hoover) on 4 September 1946. The editors of Foreign Relations of the United States placed it as document 167 in the 1945 to 1950 intelligence volume. At the time, a new National Intelligence Authority oversaw central intelligence, and the Central Intelligence Group did its daily work.

Writers chose a letter when they wanted a stance to count. The text gives the sender's side in full. Many of the big fights of these years can be followed letter by letter. Read next to the papers around it in the volume, it helps show how the postwar intelligence system took shape step by step.
frus-1945-50-intel-d267:
On 26 April 1948, the Executive Secretary (Souers) sent a memorandum to the Members of the National Security Council. The editors of Foreign Relations of the United States placed it as document 267 in the 1945 to 1950 intelligence volume. The Cold War was turning harder that year, and the new Council and CIA were being tested by it week by week.

Such notes moved business along: they told a busy reader what had happened, what it meant, and what should come next. Kept in sequence, such memos form the true diary of the office that sent them. Alone it is a page; in sequence it is evidence of how a state taught itself a new trade.
frus-1945-50-intel-d367:
On 14 February 1949, the Assistant Director for Policy Coordination (Wisner) sent a memorandum to Director of Central Intelligence Hillenkoetter. The State Department prints it as document 367 in Foreign Relations of the United States, in the intelligence volume for 1945 to 1950. An outside survey team led by Allen Dulles was then reviewing the CIA, and its findings would drive a round of reform debate.

The form is plain on purpose: a named sender, a named reader, and a short statement of the matter at hand. The note's brevity hides its weight: men at this level did not write to each other for practice. For a reader of the period, the piece fills one link in the chain between the war's end and the settled Cold War system.
frus-1945-50-intel-d67:
McCormack wrote to Secretary Byrnes on 7 January 1946, as the intelligence settlement reached its final fortnight. McCormack's research and intelligence office at State stood to gain or lose much by the outcome. Foreign Relations of the United States prints it in the later volume covering American intelligence between 1945 and 1950.

A special assistant writing to his secretary at such a moment usually pleads a last point or reports a last danger. McCormack had built the State office from the OSS's research branch in four months, and its fate hung on the directive being drafted. Readers should read his January papers as the work of a man near the finish line. His own place beyond it was growing less sure. The new system, when it came, owed his office much and kept it little.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d167:
“General Balkan Policy” is the heading of a briefing book paper written for the President's trip. It is printed in the Malta and Yalta volume. The paper argues that the three chief allies should weigh the problems of Southeastern Europe against the welfare and safety of Europe as a whole.

Old lines are fading, the paper notes, as beaten satellite states pass under Allied Control Commissions and near the rank of co-belligerents. The danger is that one ally plants its own sway in a single country, or that the allies parcel out fields of sway between them. Merely standing apart from such deals is no policy, the paper warns. Washington must press the others to hold back, so each people can freely choose its own form of rule.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d267:
The Joint Chiefs told the President what they needed from Russia on 23 January 1945. Their memorandum, printed in the Malta and Yalta volume, sets out the principles guiding them toward Soviet entry into the war against Japan. It also reports how the Moscow talks stand.

Russia's entry, at the earliest date her forces can attack, is necessary for the Pacific operations. America will give the fullest support that does not weaken her own main effort. Russia's tasks are named. She is to defeat the Japanese forces in Manchuria. She is to join in air operations against Japan from eastern Siberia, and to cut Japan's sea traffic with the mainland. The supply project is moving well. Of 750,000 tons of dry cargo for the Siberian stockpile, a quarter million should be in American ports by 1 March.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d367:
Five subjects crowd the foreign ministers' table in Edward Page's minutes of February 7, 1945. Stettinius opened by asking whether any Dumbarton Oaks points needed clearing up. Molotov replied that the world security body had not been sent to the ministers for debate. He had a few questions, but was not ready to press them.

The ministers then turned to dismemberment. They weighed the surrender formula, and a commission to study how Germany might be broken up. France's place in the control machinery followed, tied to a French zone. Reparations closed the list. Page records a working lunch where the conference's hardest files changed hands.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d467: Only the handling of a telegram survives here, in notes attached to a message from press secretary Stephen Early to Jonathan Daniels, dated February 11, 1945. A notation in the Hiss Collection copy records that Early took the original at 10:30 that morning and said he would send it. By 1:30 p.m. the Map Room reported it sent. A copy from the Roosevelt Papers adds one change: release was to come twenty-four hours after the communiqué appeared, not forty-eight. The fragment documents the conference's news management rather than its diplomacy.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d67:
Writing from the cruiser Quincy at sea on 28 January 1945, President Roosevelt updated Churchill on the hard journey still ahead. The telegram is printed in the Foreign Relations volume on the Malta and Yalta conferences. Roosevelt was already traveling toward the meeting code-named Argonaut.

The approaches to the conference, he says, look much harder than first reported. His advance party will recommend how he should travel after Malta. He also agrees that Stalin should be told the schedule as soon as it can be fixed. The editors' notes add that earlier messages dealt with the Malta to Yalta flight and with poor travel conditions from the Crimean airport.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d167:
Ambassador Alexander Kirk reported a plea for a quick Trieste settlement in a telegram from Caserta on June 23, 1945. The message is document 167 in the Foreign Relations volume on the Potsdam Conference. General Morgan, the Allied commander on the spot, had sent the embassy a memorandum about Venezia Giulia, the disputed region around Trieste.

Morgan argues that now a military agreement on occupation is in place, a final settlement should be arranged as soon as possible. If the region stays reserved for late settlement, he warns, the Allies face a long stretch of Yugoslav penetration and propaganda west of the Morgan Line, with rising incidents. A prompt settlement by joint Allied action would impress European opinion, he holds, and ease similar problems later. He recommends taking the question up at the Big Three meeting.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d267:
The British Embassy proposed reviving the European transport conference in an aide-mémoire dated July 11, 1945. The note is document 267 in the Foreign Relations volume on the Potsdam Conference. The Lancaster House conference on European inland transport had stalled, largely because the Soviet delegation would not sit with an unrecognized Polish government.

Now that Britain, the United States, and France have recognized the Polish Government of National Unity, London argues, the way is open. As host, Britain would tell Moscow it is urgent that the conference resume and finish its work. London is ready to invite a Polish delegation at once. But it wants assurance first. It wants to know the Soviet delegation, still in London, will be ordered back to full participation. That would happen once the Poles can take their seats. A similar note went to the other governments concerned.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d367:
Agreed reparations principles are announced in Pauley's top secret cable from Moscow of July 6, 1945. Weeks earlier, at the first meeting of the Reparations Commission's steering group, he had proposed a set of principles drawn from his instructions. After long talks, he reports, every delegate had now agreed to recommend them to their governments.

The first principle holds that removals for reparations should chiefly end Germany's power to make war. They would take out the factory capacity that counts as war potential. The next holds that reparations should speed recovery and rebuilding in the lands Germany had laid waste. The cable, relayed to Secretary Byrnes at sea, marked a rare three-power agreement in Moscow.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d467:
Future allied policy toward Italy is transmitted in Ambassador Kirk's despatch from Rome of June 27, 1945. He sends a report prepared in the Allied Commission for the Supreme Allied Commander, Mediterranean Theatre. Kirk suggests it be read with his embassy's reports urging a simple interim arrangement in place of the present armistice regime, and a Tripartite Economic Advisory Council.

The enclosed report, signed by Ellery Stone, opens by calling Italy a country at the parting of the ways. Defeated in 1943, she had been fought over and occupied for two years, and had suffered civil war in the north. Neither domination by the western allies nor a harsh peace, it concludes, fits a policy of preserving Italy as a bastion of democracy in the Mediterranean.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d567:
An extract from a Belgrade wire of June 22, 1945, forms document 567 in volume one of the Foreign Relations papers on Potsdam. U.S. charge Harold Shantz sent it to the Acting Secretary of State. It quotes words Marshal Tito spoke the day before to a group from Trieste.

Tito told the group, in town for an anti-Fascist women's congress, that he had done all in his power. Yugoslavia, he said, was forced to submit to a great sacrifice with a heavy heart. The problem of civil government, he added, was still open. He vowed to fight for the rights of the people of Trieste and the Slovene coast. He also said Slovene and Italian anti-Fascists had a moral right to resist a return of fascist courts by lawful means.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d667:
Secretary of State Byrnes told Ambassador Caffery in Paris that Russia should be invited into the Tangier talks at once. The urgent secret wire of July 5, 1945, is document 667 in volume one of the Foreign Relations papers on Potsdam. It reverses the earlier plan to keep the talks to three powers.

Byrnes argues the present talks have a narrow task only. They are to prepare the speedy replacement of Spanish control by a temporary regime. A later conference of all interested powers would settle the zone's future. Small nations, he says, have no reason to seek seats now, though their joining would draw no strong U.S. objection. It must stay clear that no plan for a permanent government of Tangier is to be drawn at these talks. Russia, he adds, could hold a position much like the one the U.S. sought for itself.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d67:
Edward Page, first secretary at the American embassy in Moscow, wrote up a June 15, 1945 meeting with Soviet official Andrei Vyshinsky. His memorandum of conversation is document 67 in the Foreign Relations papers on the Potsdam Conference. Ambassador Harriman came to raise the groundwork for the Berlin meeting of the Big Three.

Harriman told Vyshinsky that General Deane had orders from Eisenhower to get permission for an advance group to reach Berlin on June 17 and start the arrangements. He left a copy of Deane's letter on the subject and said he was ready to discuss the matter at any time. The short memo records the first formal American approach to Moscow about the conference's practical setup.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d1067:
George Kennan cabled Washington from Moscow on July 24, 1945, about a Soviet letter on Greece. Vice Commissar Dekanozov had written to the British chargé, answering a British protest over Soviet press and radio attacks on the Greek government. Moscow sees no grounds for the charge, he wrote, since the journal in question is not an official Soviet organ.

Dekanozov then turns the complaint around. He cites a July 8 meeting in Athens where speakers attacked the USSR and crowds shouted slogans about marching on Sofia, Belgrade, and Moscow. Such speeches, he claims, grow more frequent and more extreme. Moscow calls the situation improper in a country hosting its British ally's troops.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d1167:
The Soviet team set down this memorandum on 30 July 1945, in the summit's final stretch. Late Soviet papers tended to fix Moscow's terms as the bargaining closed. Once written and passed to the other teams, a memorandum became part of the formal record.

A paper of this kind could restate a demand, offer a draft, or mark a line that would not move. Readers can set it beside the final protocol to see which Soviet words survived. It is Moscow's stand, stated in Moscow's phrasing, days before the leaders went home. The American files kept it whole.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d1267:
On 17 July 1945, the summit's opening day, the United States Chiefs of Staff issued this memorandum. A staff paper from day one set the armed forces' view before the team as the talks began. The chiefs' office worked in step with the conference from its first hours.

Opening-day papers framed the questions as the soldiers saw them. Later notes would react to the bargaining; this one preceded it. That gives it a clean value: the military view before the trades began. It is the first of the long chiefs-of-staff run in this part of the volume, and it sets the tone for the rest.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d1367:
Edwin Wilson, the American ambassador in Turkey, cabled the acting secretary of state on 19 July 1945. Turkey had stayed out of the war until its final months, then joined the winning side. The text comes from the second Potsdam volume of Foreign Relations of the United States, the State Department's official history series.

Ankara's post mattered because Turkey guards the straits between the Black Sea and the Mediterranean, a passage Russia had coveted for ages. Soviet pressure on Turkey was rising in 1945, and Wilson reported from the front of that squeeze. His cable shows how a regional strain reached Washington during Potsdam, where the straits question sat on the leaders' own table as well.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d710a-67:
Cavendish Cannon, an embassy secretary in Portugal, reported a subcommittee's evening session to James Dunn on July 22, 1945. The memo is an unnumbered item in volume two of the Foreign Relations papers on Potsdam. The subcommittee was working on the Yalta declaration paper's second and third sections.

Ambassador Gromyko and Mr. Golunko sat for the Soviet side. They said they were not prepared to discuss point 3 that evening. A Soviet paper on changes in the control commissions in Rumania, Bulgaria, and Hungary would circulate the next morning. It had to be taken into account on the subject, but it was not yet ready. The group therefore agreed to work on point 2 only, the press question. No report would go to the foreign ministers until point 3 had been considered. On the press point, the Soviets tabled a draft on easing entry for press and radio.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d767:
Document 767 is a working paper of the United States delegation dated July 24, 1945. It comes from the day the conference reached its midpoint. Staff used such papers to frame choices for the sessions ahead. The paper remained in the delegation files and entered the second Potsdam volume.

Midpoint drafts show a negotiation taking stock. Early claims have met resistance; new shapes are being tested. Readers can trace a topic's movement by its papers. The document adds one clear step in that chain. It also shows the quiet industry of the American staff, whose writing filled the hours between the leaders' meetings.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d867:
Robert Murphy, the political adviser in Germany, sent this report to the Secretary of State on July 21, 1945. It passes on findings from the Intelligence Section of SHAEF's Psychological Warfare Division. The findings rest on a wide field survey of German opinion. The subject is how ordinary Germans viewed Nazis and Nazism right after the war ended.

The survey found that many Germans saw a Nazi as an outsider sent in by the Party. Blame thus shifted away from the person's own town. It also records the label Muss Nazis for people who joined from fear of losing jobs. On war guilt, answers ranged from true believers to people who blamed Himmler and the SS.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d967:
Britain's delegation drafted this reparations text at Potsdam on July 31, 1945. A note on the paper says the drafting committee was still at work on it at 11 p.m. Soviet claims would be met from the Soviet zone, and the USSR would settle Poland's claims from its own share.

Western claims would be met from the western zones and from German external assets, two points the Soviet delegate reserved. The USSR would also receive 15 percent of surplus western equipment in trade for eastern goods, plus 10 percent free. Removals must finish within two years. The amount to remove must be fixed within six months at the latest.
frus-1950v07-d67: An editorial note in the 1950 Korea volume reconstructs the first hours of the war. In the small hours of June 25, Ambassador Gross phoned Secretary-General Trygve Lie. He read the American request for an urgent Security Council meeting. North Korean forces had crossed into the South that morning. Pyongyang radio had declared war. Washington called the attack a breach of the peace. The note also records a call to Tokyo at four that morning for news of the fighting.
frus-1969-76v32-d267: An editorial note in Volume XXXII of the 1969-1976 series draws on Haldeman's diary for April 24, 1972. Kissinger, back from Moscow, reports to Nixon at Camp David. Nixon backs down on both a briefing fight and the arms announcement. Kissinger's memo of the same day sums up 13 hours of talks with Brezhnev and Gromyko. Moscow, it says, agreed to count submarine missiles in the deal. Nixon wrote on the memo: superb job. The note catches relief after a tense day.
gao-gaoreports-b-297367:
A joint venture of Hera and Synthesis protested a Navy award in GAO decision B-297367, dated December 20, 2005. The winner was Ergodomi. The site was Souda Bay on Crete, in Greece. The work was to tear down an old sewage plant and build a new one. The plant would be of cast concrete with a high grade clean step.

GAO denied the protest. Marks for both bids fit the scheme in the call. Broad past skill of the firm was weighed as the scheme set it. It did not have to count past the scheme. When marks track the set scheme, a firm that wants a new scheme will lose. The award thus stood.
gao-gaoreports-b-298767:
Omega Systems, Inc. protested the rejection of its proposal as late. A Marine Corps buy sought a data distribution system for tactical networks. The work spanned design, build, and papers for the system. GAO ruled in B-298767 on November 6, 2006.

The firm invoked a rule for late revisions that aid the government. That rule helps only an otherwise winning proposal. GAO found the firm's bid did not meet that test. The agency had already judged its price not fair before the last round. A late filing cannot revive a bid that was not set to win. The rejection stood. GAO denied the protest.
gao-gaoreports-b-307767:
A price break on government oil and gas is rejected in this GAO opinion, B-307767, dated November 13, 2006. The United States takes oil and gas as rent for leases on its lands. A 2005 energy law lets the Interior Secretary grant a preference in selling that take. The aim is to aid federal low-income energy aid plans.
