Two senators asked if a preference could mean a sale below market price.

GAO sided with Interior's reading of the law. The same clause tells sales to fetch not less than market value. Nothing shows Congress meant preference to mean a price cut. The close call went for full price.
gao-gaoreports-b-309267:
Relief for a hospital cashier is split in this GAO letter, B-309267, dated January 15, 2008. Joan C. Jackson was chief cashier at the veterans hospital in Washington. She held cash that patients left for safekeeping. Two sums went missing on her watch. One sum was $3,280 in 2001. The other was $123 in 2003.

GAO refused relief for the $3,280 loss. The Veterans Affairs Department sought relief for both sums. GAO has let agencies settle small losses on their own since 1991. The cap for that path is $3,000. So the department may settle the $123 loss itself. It must do so in line with GAO's past rulings.
gao-gaoreports-b-310667:
Silynx Communications, Inc. lost its protest under GAO decision B-310667, dated January 23, 2008. The buy sought gear that had to meet firm base specs. Silynx said its gear was scored wrong. The agency found the gear fell short of the base specs. The call warned that award could rest on first bids. No talks were held with the firms.

GAO denied the protest. A miss on a must-meet spec makes a bid unfit. Award on first bids was fair since the call warned of it. The price test drew on past cost facts in a sound way. A low price for unfit gear proves no flaw. A bias claim on a judge of bids fell for lack of proof.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-267:
Information Technology, GAO-05-267 of March 14, 2005, checks a long, costly build of a new trade data system. The Automated Commercial Environment would speed true trade through ports and stiffen border guard work. It is a multi-year, multi-billion-dollar build at the Department of Homeland Security. Congress set rules for each spend plan, with a GAO check among them.

GAO tests the fiscal year 2005 plan next to those rules. It tracks what has been done with past GAO advice on the build. It adds notes on the plan and on how the work is run. Gains stand, but the call for firmer control runs on.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-667:
Child care help for working families is updated in GAO-05-667, dated June 29, 2005. All states open subsidies to welfare families, those leaving welfare, and other low-income workers. Thirty-one states say they can serve every eligible family that applies, six more than in the last report. When money runs short, most states put welfare families first. Since 2001, 35 states have changed entry rules: 19 tightened access, 8 widened it, and 8 did both.

On average each month the main fund serves about 1.75 million children. Yet Washington knows little about families aided straight from welfare funds, a gap GAO flags for Congress.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-767:
War funding is audited in GAO-05-767, issued September 28, 2005. GAO is running a series of checks on the cost of the global war on terrorism. Past work raised doubts about the defense cost data itself. Here GAO counted war funds for fiscal years 2004 and 2005. It matched extra war funds against what the services said they spent.

GAO found the services got about $52.4 billion in extra war funds in fiscal year 2004. The next year brought about $62.1 billion. On top of that, $7.9 billion and $7.6 billion in yearly funds were meant for the war. The department does not track those yearly sums apart. So the funds lose visibility, and the department does not count them when it weighs war needs. GAO urged that all war funds be counted.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-867:
Amtrak's food service contract is audited in full in GAO-05-867, a report from August 24, 2005. Amtrak runs 11 commissaries that stock its trains. Since January 1999, a contractor has run them and ordered all food and drink. Amtrak paid the firm $59 million to $64 million a year from fiscal years 2002 through 2004. The deal runs to September 2006.

GAO concluded that basic management steps were ignored or set aside. Agreed contract terms were not carried out. Oversight the contract itself calls for was not done. Amtrak did not make sure it got products at the most reasonable price. The service is a small part of Amtrak's budget, GAO noted. But it shows why the railroad must get its operations in better order, and it promised recommendations to that end.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-967:
Recovery of sealed radioactive sources is reviewed in GAO-05-967, dated September 22, 2005. Such sources sit in many medical and industrial devices. Loose control of them raises safety and security fears. The Energy Department must ensure a disposal path for the hottest class of this waste. It also works to recover unwanted sources. GAO checked recovery work, disposal planning, and how sources are identified.

The department has raised the project's priority and sped recovery, GAO found. It beat an earlier goal and has collected over 10,800 sources. In May 2005, it opened study of disposal options for the hottest waste class. No date exists for when a disposal site might open. The recovery net now covers lower classes too. That could raise costs. One job took 443 sources from a bankrupt firm for about $581,000.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-167:
Staffing strategy at the Office of the U.S. Trade Representative is examined in GAO-06-167, dated December 6, 2005. The office leads trade talks and frames disputes for presidential choice. Its workload has swelled with new regional and bilateral free trade deals. A fresh round of world trade talks adds more strain. GAO asked whether the office leads and plans its workforce well.

GAO found that the office would gain from fuller use of strategic human capital practice. Its small size and lead role in trade policy raise the stakes for planning. GAO urged the Trade Representative to build a full strategic system for its people. The system should cover leadership, planning, hiring and retention, and performance review. The office said it shared GAO's stress on planning. It also held that it already performs these tasks well enough.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-267:
Computer security at the health department is faulted in GAO-06-267, a report issued on February 24, 2006. The Department of Health and Human Services is the nation's largest health insurer and its largest grant maker. Its Medicare and Medicaid arm serves about one in four Americans. Those programs run on networks stuffed with private medical and money data. GAO tested how well the department's security program guards that data. The review leaned hardest on the Medicare agency's systems.

GAO found deep flaws in the controls that guard access. Network management, user accounts, and passwords all showed weak spots. The department has a security program on paper, but it is not fully in place across its divisions. GAO urged the Secretary to have the chief information officer finish the rollout. The department backed GAO's stress on reform. It argued that the report shortchanged the progress it had made.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-367:
A network of 18 linked systems was the Army's bold plan for future combat. In GAO decision form GAO-06-367, dated March 14, 2006, GAO reviews the Future Combat System. The Army said the system would change how troops move, shoot, and communicate. GAO calls the concept bold and the program one of the most complex ever tried. Law requires a yearly review.

GAO tested the program's business case. It checked whether needs were stable and technology was mature. It also weighed the buying strategy and whether costs were sound and affordable. The verdict is in the title. A better business case was needed for success.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-567:
If census counts were adjusted, would grant money move? Simulations here test that question. Report GAO-06-567, issued June 23, 2006, models use of statistical population estimates for some federal funding. Census data guide grants to states and local areas. The Census Bureau used statistical methods to judge the accuracy of the 1990 and 2000 counts. It found the estimates unreliable and did not adjust results. The question is how sensitive grant formulas are to such estimates.

GAO names the top 20 formula grant programs by targeted funds. It simulates effects on Medicaid and the Social Services Block Grant. The analysis only simulates reallocations, GAO stresses. Data are from fiscal years 2004 and 2005.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-67:
A federal tool for rating programs is evaluated in GAO-06-67, a report GAO released on October 28, 2005. The Office of Management and Budget built the Program Assessment Rating Tool to judge program results and push improvements. The ratings drew on performance data and program evaluations. GAO was asked to check whether the reviews had improved the evidence base behind them. GAO examined agency progress in finishing evaluations that the budget office had called for.

GAO found that about half the programs had completed evaluations, and three more were being planned. Where budget office recommendations caught managers' attention, agencies overcame measurement and funding barriers. But where the two sides did not share expectations, evaluations could miss what the office needed. The report shows how a rating tool can focus agency attention.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-967:
Recovery after the Biscuit Fire is analyzed in GAO report GAO-06-967, dated September 18, 2006. The 2002 fire burned almost 500,000 acres of the Rogue River-Siskiyou National Forest in southwest Oregon. The Forest Service reply ranks among its largest and most complex postfire projects. Its sales of dead trees drew sharp debate.

GAO set the project beside the agency's broad postfire approach. It tracked the state of the salvage sales, and set their results beside first estimates. It checked other project work, plus claims of improper logging and the agency reply. The report gives both sides a shared fact base.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-167:
One-stop centers were built to match job seekers with employers in one place. GAO asked employers how well that works in GAO-07-167, dated December 22, 2006. The Workforce Investment Act of 1998 created the centers. The law also pushed centers to serve employer needs, not just workers. GAO surveyed employers who had used the centers. It visited eight centers and spoke with labor officials.

Employers hired only a small share of staff through the centers, GAO found. About 9 percent of their 2005 hires came that way. That was roughly 1,300 of 14,500 workers hired. Two-thirds of those hires were low-skilled workers. Most employers used just one service: posting job openings. They rated the services they used as helpful. But many did not know other services existed. GAO said the Labor Department barely measures employer involvement. It urged the department to track and report it.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-67:
Katrina health aid of $2 billion is traced state by state in GAO-07-67, a GAO report dated February 28, 2007. The Deficit Reduction Act of 2005 set the money aside in February 2006. It flows through Medicaid and the State Children's Health Insurance Program. The Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services split the fund among states hit by the storm and states that took in evacuees. Initial shares came out on March 29, 2006.

GAO worked under the Comptroller General's own authority. It checked how the split was made and how much of the money states had spent. Four states with the largest shares got deep reviews: Alabama, Louisiana, Mississippi, and Texas. State Medicaid offices shared enrollment and claims tales. The last question looks ahead: will those states need more once the fund runs dry? The report gives Congress a spend-down ledger for emergency health cash.
gao-gaoreports-gao-08-167:
Market regulator finances are audited in GAO report GAO-08-167, dated November 16, 2007. The Securities and Exchange Commission was set up in 1934 to enforce securities laws and protect investors. A 2002 law requires it to file audited financial statements. GAO agreed to run the audit for fiscal years 2007 and 2006.

GAO found the statements fairly presented in all material respects. Yet a material weakness marred the reporting process itself. In GAO's view, the agency lacked effective internal control over financial reporting as of September 30, 2007. Faults in closing the books and in tracking receivables fed that judgment.
gao-gaoreports-gao-08-367:
Vehicle donations to charity after a tax rule change are studied in GAO report GAO-08-367, dated February 15, 2008. From January 1, 2005, donors could generally deduct only the price a charity got for selling the car, not its estimated fair market value. GAO asked 10 charities how the change had hit them.

The charities gave mixed reports. Comparing 2003 with 2006, 6 saw fewer vehicles donated, 3 saw more, and 1 gave no data. Six took in less revenue from the programs, while 3 took in more. Some charities cut services or changed how they sell cars, using steps like online sales and minimum auction bids. All 10 said new reporting rules added paperwork, but all coped with it.
gao-gaoreports-gao-08-567:
The tax agency's budget and filing season are what GAO takes up in report GAO-08-567, dated March 13, 2008. The President's fiscal year 2009 request for the Internal Revenue Service is $11.4 billion, up 4.3 percent from the 2008 enacted level. It adds 7 percent for enforcement and under 1 percent for taxpayer service.

Mid-season, the agency had processed 51.2 million returns and sent 46.5 million refunds worth $122.7 billion. New stimulus law calls may force hundreds of collections staff onto phones, at a revenue cost of up to $681 million. Systems upgrade funding falls by over $40 million with little detail on effects. Paid preparers lack a single ID number, which limits oversight. GAO urged return-on-investment data for big enforcement programs.
gao-gaoreports-gao-08-67:
Immigration officers choose whom to arrest and remove, a choice that shapes lives. GAO-08-67, dated October 15, 2007, looks at how Immigration and Customs Enforcement guides those choices. Reviewers asked when officers and lawyers can use judgment, and what controls keep choices fair and sound.

Judgment matters most at the start: whether to open a case, make an arrest, or hold a person. Officers said rules bind them tight for target cases, less so for others they meet. Kindness factors, like care for kids or health needs, count too. Training is being updated. But written guidance still lacks the factors officers should weigh, GAO found.
gao-gaoreports-gao-08-967:
Letting more countries join the Visa Waiver Program is moving fast, and GAO-08-967, a September 2008 report, urges better control of the process. The program lets citizens of member countries visit the United States without a visa. The report reviews how the executive branch is expanding it and whether the homeland security department has tools to judge and reduce the risks, such as travelers who overstay.

GAO found the expansion process lacks transparency when set against the department's own standard procedures. Risk tools are also unfinished: plans for an air exit system leave out travelers who stay in the country, and overstay rates are not well tracked for current or hopeful member states. GAO recommends a clear, open expansion process and better overstay monitoring. The department generally agreed.
hard-cash-pg3067:
Charles Reade called this novel a matter-of-fact romance, a fiction built on truths, and his preface of December 1868 defends the method at length. He lists his sources like a barrister: reports, blue-books, journals, letters, and living witnesses cross-examined. The prologue settles into the villa of the Dodd family outside the seaport of Barkington.

Mrs. Dodd, a well-born lady married to a merchant captain, is raising her son Edward and daughter Julia there. From that household the plot spreads to sea, to money, and to the book's famous battleground, the private lunatic asylum. Reade's madhouse chapters, drawn from evidence he offers to show any visitor, made the novel a campaign document against asylum abuses. Two chapters are both numbered XLI in the text, as the transcriber notes.
hughes-manual-of-pharmacodynamics-1867:
Richard Hughes sought to put homeopathic drug study on a firm footing in A Manual of Pharmacodynamics, first issued in 1867. Hughes, a leading British homeopath, asked a plain question: what does each drug actually do in the body? His answers bridge the remedy lists and daily practice.

Drug by drug, he sets out actions and effects in an order made for study at the desk. He weighs proving reports against wider medical knowledge of each substance. The manual shaped British homeopathy's more scientific wing, and its calm, testing tone still sets it apart from more dogmatic works of the school.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-aaron-markovich: Aaron Markovich of Wilna was agent, or court Jew, to King Ladislaus IV of Poland in the seventeenth century. One letter, dated January 11, 1638, is the only known record of him. In it the king asks the czar to let Aaron visit Moscow free of custom duties. He was to buy goods for the royal household and sell some precious goods of his own. The czar refused the request.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-abraham-son-of-:
Abraham, son of Samuel the Pious, was a noted Talmudic scholar and elegist of the Kalonymus family. Brother of Judah the Pious, he was born at Speyer in the second half of the twelfth century. He reached a very old age by the entry's account.

Eliezer ben Nathan of Mayence, who died before 1170, ranked him a rabbinical authority of the first order. Isaac of Vienna, flourishing about 1250, knew him in person. Abraham wrote elegies on Jewish suffering in the First Crusade of 1096 and the Second of 1147. He also wrote penitential poems and worked as a defender of Judaism, as the Nizzahon shows.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-adams-john-767: John Adams was the second president of the United States. He was born at Braintree, Massachusetts, on October 19, 1735. He died at Quincy on July 4, 1826. In his late years he gave much thought to the past of faiths. He wrote at length on it with Jefferson. In February, 1809, he wrote that the Hebrews had done more to civilize men than any other nation. He said fate had set the Jews to keep and spread faith in one wise, almighty ruler. He voiced like views in 1818.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-ahasuerus-967:
Ahasuerus was a Persian king, identified in the entry with Xerxes, who reigned from 486 to 465 B.C. The Book of Esther tells his story. He ruled one hundred and twenty-seven provinces, from India to Ethiopia. After a feast of one hundred and eighty days, he set Queen Vashti aside. Esther then became queen in the seventh year of his reign.

Mordecai uncovered a plot against the king and was later honored. Haman, the chief adviser, plotted to destroy all the Jews of the kingdom. The king first agreed, then reversed himself through Esther. Haman was put to death and Mordecai raised in his place. The entry's critical section argues that the name, the Persian court, and the dates all point to Xerxes.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-alba-jacob-di-1: Jacob di Alba was an Italian rabbi of the late sixteenth and early seventeenth centuries. He held the rabbinate at Florence. His one known work is a set of homilies on the Pentateuch. It is called "Toledot Ya'akob," the Generations of Jacob. The book was printed at Venice in 1609. Nothing more of his life is given in the entry.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-alexandra-salom:
Alexandra Salome was, with one exception, the only Jewish queen who ruled in her own right. She was born in 139 B.C. and died in 67 B.C. She was the wife of Aristobulus I., then of his brother Alexander Jannaeus. On Aristobulus's death in 103 B.C. she freed Alexander from prison. In his reign she held little open power. Yet on his deathbed he left the government to her, not to his sons.

She took the reins in 76 or 75 B.C., at the camp before Ragaba. She hid the king's death until the fortress fell. Then she made peace with the Pharisee leaders Alexander had hunted. Prisoners were freed, and exiles came home by the thousand. She set her son Hyrcanus II. in the high priesthood. The Sanhedrin was rebuilt on Pharisee lines, as a supreme court. Her reign marks a great epoch in Jewish self-rule.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-allon-strong-12: Allon is a name borne by two men in the Bible lists. The entry reads the name as meaning strong, with doubt. The first Allon was a son of Jedaiah. He stands in the family line of Simon. That line is given in First Chronicles. The second Allon came back with Zerubbabel. Other versions of the lists spell the name Allom. He may be the same man as Amon or Ami in two other lists.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-amasia-amasieh-:
Amasia is a city in Asia Minor on a river. The river is the Yeshil-Irmak, the Iris of old. In 1900 the city held 23,000 souls. It counts for little now, the entry says. In the 1500s it drew many Spanish exiles. That flow marks a time of wealth for the town.

A grim tale fills the rest of the entry. A Christian guest in a Jewish house went missing. Jews were seized and forced by pain to confess. They were hanged for a murder that never took place. Days later the Christian walked back into the city. The sultan then set a new rule for such charges. Royal courts alone would hear them from then on.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-ananias-1467: Ananias is a Greek form for more than one Hebrew name. Three men come from names with one first sound. One put aside his foreign wife in Ezra's list. One was a Levite who taught the Law. Three more come from names with a second sound. One stood by Ezra as he read. One heads the line of Judith. A last Ananias shows in Acts. He cheated the apostles and fell dead.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-aristo-of-pella:
Aristo of Pella, in the Decapolis, was a Christian writer who argued against Judaism in the second century, between 135 and 170. He wrote a Dialogue Between Jason and Papiscus. In it a Jewish Christian debates an Alexandrian Jew, who is won over in the end and accepts Christianity. The work was widely read for centuries, yet it has now completely disappeared.

Fragments of its thought survive in a similar Latin dialogue and in later writers. Eusebius drew from Aristo the report that Hadrian barred Jews from the soil of Jerusalem. Jerome found in the dialogue a claimed Hebrew reading of the first verse of Genesis. The entry explains that reading as a mistaken rendering of the Targum, whose opening words mean with wisdom.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-arzareth-1867:
Arzareth names the far land beyond the great river where, in Fourth Esdras chapter 13, the Ten Tribes of Israel will live under the laws of Moses until the restoration. Columbus, the entry notes, took America to be that land. The name itself may come from Deuteronomy chapter 29, where God casts a disobedient people into another land, eretz aheret, and the Mishnah reads the verse as speaking of the Ten Tribes.

Whether the tribes will return split the sages. Akiba and Eliezer read the phrase as this day in opposite ways. One took it to mean that, as the day goes and does not return, the exiles will not return. The other read it as night turning to daylight, so banishment ends in brightness. Fourth Esdras took the hopeful view.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-ashi-12467:
Ashi, a famed Babylonian teacher, was born in 352 and died in 427. Tradition in the academies says he was born in the year Raba of Mahuza died. He was the first great teacher in the Babylonian colleges after Raba. His father Simai was rich and learned, a student at the college of Naresh near Sura. Ashi's own teacher was Kahana, later head of the academy at Pumbedita.

While still young, Ashi took charge of the academy at Sura, closed since Hisda died in 309, and raised it to its old standing. A saying of the time held that learning and high rank had not met so fully in one man since Judah the Patriarch. The likeness is the point: as Judah compiled the Mishnah, Ashi began the editing of the Babylonian Talmud.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-ashkenazi-isaac:
Isaac ben Jacob Ashkenazi was rabbi at Byeltzy in Bessarabia in the middle of the eighteenth century. He is the reputed author of a cabalistic book, Berit Olam, Everlasting Covenant. It gives cabalistic readings of the letters of the alphabet and closes with chapters on ethics. The work was found among his papers after his death.

Isaac Hayyim of Byelostok published it under Ashkenazi's name at Wilna in 1820. The entry's wording is careful: reputed author, a book found in his papers, another man's editing. Two catalogues, Walden's Shem ha-Gedolim and Zedner's list of Hebrew books in the British Museum, are the sources named. Nothing of the rabbi's life beyond his town and century is recorded.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-baanah-2267: Baanah is the name of three men in the Bible. The first was a son of Rimmon of Benjamin, an officer under Ishbosheth. With his brother Rechab he killed Ishbosheth as he slept. They carried the head to David, hoping for a reward. David had both brothers put to death instead. The second Baanah was the father of Heleb, one of the thirty men of David's bodyguard. The third came back from exile with Zerubbabel. He was among those who sealed the covenant with Nehemiah.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-bahya-behai-ben:
Baḥya ben Asher ben Halawa was a Spanish Bible scholar, born at Saragossa about the middle of the thirteenth century and dead in 1340. He was a pupil of Solomon ben Adret but gave his strength to Bible study, not Talmud. He served as a preacher at Saragossa on a small shared salary. Want and hardship, the entry says, did not lessen his zeal.

His chief work is a commentary on the Pentateuch, first printed at Naples in 1492. It uses four ways of reading at once: the plain sense, Midrash, reason, and the Cabala, which he calls the path of light. The entry also covers his "Kad ha-Ḳemaḥ," sixty chapters on faith and conduct, and his "Shulḥan Arba'" on meals. His many quotes from lost works give the books lasting worth.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-baruch-2567: Baruch is presented in this short entry as a Jewish pioneer settler in Spain. The tradition of the Ibn Albaliah family regarded him as the ancestor of their house. No dates, places, or deeds are given for him here. The notice points onward to Ibn Daud's "Sefer ha-Ḳabbalah," in Neubauer's "Medieval Jewish Chronicles," and to the entry Albalia. The whole record is those few lines: a name, a role as first settler, and a family's claim of descent from him.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-behar-jacob-jos: Jacob Joseph Behar, called Ha-Rofe, was chief rabbi of Bagdad about the year 1843. The short entry credits him with two Hebrew works. One is a commentary on the Song of Solomon, printed at Calcutta in 1843. The other is a commentary on the Psalms, printed at Jerusalem in 1845. No birth or death dates, teachers, or other acts are given for him in this notice.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-ben-durand-2867: Ben Durand was a diplomat who served as a go-between for Abd-el-Kader and the French government. He died at Algiers in September of 1839. Two French governors of Algeria, named Clauzel and Valée, also made use of his services in their dealings. That is the whole of this short entry. No birth date, birthplace, or earlier post is given for the man who linked the two sides.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-benjamin-b-jehi: Benjamin ben Jehiel ha-Levi, a Polish Talmudist, lived at the start of the seventeenth century. He wrote Gib'at Benjamin, or Benjamin's Height, printed at Lublin in 1617. The work is a list in alphabetical order of the contents of Jacob ben Asher's four Ṭurim. The entry calls it an excellent index to that code. It also notes the book is very rare, since it was never reprinted after that first issue.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-berger-oscar-30: Oscar Berger, a German doctor who treated by electric means, was born at Münsterberg, in Silesia, on Nov. 24, 1844. He died at Ober-Salzbrunn on July 19, 1885. He took his medical degree in 1867 and set up practice at Breslau in 1869. There he taught at the university from 1873, the first to lecture on nervous diseases. He studied joint pain, face pain, and the ties of pain to other ills. A busy writer, he helped edit a journal of neurology and wrote on many nerve themes.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-bertensohn-lev-:
Lev Bernardovich Bertensohn, born at Odessa on August 10, 1850, was a Russian physician, son of Bernard Bertensohn and nephew of Joseph. He graduated from the St. Petersburg Medical Academy in 1872 and lectured at the Rozhdenstvenskaya Hospital from 1876 to 1887 on diagnosis and treatment.

The entry highlights his chief work on balneology, the study of mineral waters, published in 1873 with Dr. Voronikhim, and his 1887 appointment to head a commission improving the Caucasus mineral springs. It also mentions his study of pseudoleukemia, an 1883 article on Turgenef, whom he treated in the writer's closing years, and works on Caucasian waters.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-bles-david-s-33: David S. Bles was a communal worker at Manchester. He was born at The Hague in 1834. He died at Vienna on October 14, 1899. He was senior partner in a shipping firm. He retired from it in 1897. Philanthropy then claimed his full time. He had served as city magistrate for thirteen years. He was also Dutch vice-consul for many years. Holland's queen gave him the Order of Orange and Nassau. He led Manchester's Jewish Board of Guardians. He founded a Hebrew scholarship at Victoria University.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-boethusians-346:
Boethusians were a Jewish sect close to the Sadducees. A Midrash tale traces both sects to pupils of Zadok and Boethus. In that tale a saying on serving God without thought of wages was misread over time.

The entry says the tale is legend, though both sects did deny resurrection. Boethusians fought the Pharisees over the Passover sheaf and the date of Pentecost. They also clashed over new moon sightings and Day of Atonement incense. The name may come from the priestly house of Boethus under Herod. The tale adds that its members lived in splendor, using silver and golden vessels all their lives, and drew their followers chiefly from the wealthy.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-bordeaux-3567:
Bordeaux, capital in medieval times of Guienne and now of La Gironde in France, has a long Jewish past. Legend places Jews there soon after the Second Temple fell. Free trade was allowed under Louis le Débonnaire in 828.

Charges that Jews betrayed the city to Normans and Saracens lack proof, the entry says. Firm evidence comes in a deed of 1077 naming a Jewish hill at Saint-Seurin. Jews lived outside the walls in that age. Later, Portuguese and Avignonese Jews formed a large community. By 1734 about 350 families, near two thousand people, lived openly as Jews there.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-breastplate-366: Breastplate renders the Hebrew shiryon or siryon. The entry says coat of mail or cuirass would be more exact. Kings of Israel wore such body armor in war, as their neighbors did. Goliath's coat of mail is the best known Bible case. Monuments of Egypt, Assyria, and Rome show its form. It was made of overlapping metal plates at varied lengths. It guarded breast and back and could reach the knees. Isaiah and Paul both used the piece as an image in their writing.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-budapest-11667:
Budapest, capital of Hungary, joined the older communities of Buda, Ó-Buda, and Pesth. Jews are first mentioned at Pesth in 1406, and they owned houses there by 1504. After the Turks were driven out in 1686, no Jews could live in Pesth for nearly a century. Travelers paid a toll just to pass through or stay overnight.

Settlement opened under Joseph II, whose decree of March 31, 1783, let Jews settle slowly. Worship began in rented rooms, and the great Tabaksgasse temple opened in 1859. The entry traces cemeteries, schools, and community government in detail. By 1900 the Jewish population stood at 166,198. Its closing notes name congregation presidents and the Orientalist Ignaz Goldziher as secretary.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-buzaglo-william: William Buzaglo was an English inventor and medical empiric who died at London in 1788. He first won notice with stoves built on a new plan, meant to heat large public buildings. Later he practiced medicine and claimed he could cure gout with no drugs, by muscular exercise alone. The entry likens his method to modern massage, while leaving its real worth open. His bold advertising, full of self praise, made most people class him as a quack. Captain Grose mocked his manifesto in a parody handbill.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-carpentras-4067:
Carpentras, a town in the department of Vaucluse, France, had Jewish settlers from a very early period. A twelfth-century rabbinical source already names its rabbis beside those of Troyes, Paris, and the Rhine. Jews were expelled early in the thirteenth century, then returned in 1263.

In 1276 sixty-four heads of families signed an agreement with Bishop Pierre III Rostaing. They accepted the bishop as their lord and listed their taxes, from a yearly rent of 18 Tours pounds to a share of synagogue seat rent. In return the bishop promised fixed taxes, protection of property, and defense against violence. Pope John XXII expelled the Jews in 1322 and their synagogue was torn down. Clement VI reversed that order on his accession in 1342, and twelve families returned the next year.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-celsus-k-4167:
Celsus was a Greek writer against Christianity who flourished in the second century. He was the first pagan to denounce the new faith. His book, The True Word, sought to refute Christian doctrines and to ridicule them as well. The book itself is lost.

Large parts of it survive inside Origen's reply, Contra Celsum, written in eight books. Origen was unsure who Celsus was and wrongly tagged him an Epicurean. The entry places him about 180, under Marcus Aurelius. In his first two books, Celsus puts his case in the mouth of a Jew. That Jew, though, knew his own religion poorly, so the figure is a device. Celsus had mixed with Jews and drawn Jesus stories from them. Yet he was no friend to Jews. He called them slaves escaped from Egypt and mocked their laws.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-chattels-4267:
Chattels are personal or movable property, set against real or landed property in English and American law. Jewish law makes the same split with its own terms: ground on one side, movables on the other. Slaves count with the ground class. Claims on other persons count with movables, though bonds follow rules of their own in part.

Under Talmudic law, a proper bond, once delivered, became a lien on all the debtor's lands, but not on his goods. After a debtor died, only lands and slaves answered to his creditors. In the Middle Ages, need forced a change, and goods and money were made liable too. Since the Jubilee lapsed, land and chattels descend by the same rules. A sale of chattels, unlike land or bonds, can be corrected for a bad price under the law of overreaching.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-christina-augus:
Christina Augusta, queen of Sweden, was born at Stockholm on Dec. 7, 1626, and died at Rome on April 19, 1689. A daughter of Gustavus Adolphus, she reigned from 1632 to 1654. The entry stresses her warm stance toward Jews. She studied Hebrew literature eagerly as a girl and welcomed Hebrew scholars at her court.

Menasseh ben Israel was kindly received, and his pleas met sympathy. She also backed Jewish settlement in the West Indies with England. Her financial agent at Hamburg, the Portuguese Marano Isaac Manoel Texeira, drew her repeated defense against that city's senate. She even lodged at his home. Her bid to stop the banishment of Vienna's Jews in 1670 failed.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-coro-4667:
Coro is a town in Venezuela, five miles from its seaport, La Vela de Coro, on the Caribbean Sea. In the early days of the republic it had many Jewish residents. They had come from Curaçao, in the Dutch West Indies, about sixty miles away. Worship later centered at the home of Mordehay Abraham Senior and then of his son Isaac.

In 1855 the Jews of Coro, about 300 in number, were plundered and driven to refuge in Curaçao. Dutch warships won them redress and an indemnity, paid in 1859. A cemetery was set up in 1858. A fresh outbreak in June, 1902, sent them to Curaçao once more.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-criminality-476:
Criminality means the average tendency to commit crime. The entry opens by answering a charge. Critics had claimed that Jews showed lower morals and more crime than Christian neighbors. One writer said Jews were one twenty-fifth of Prussia's people but half its criminals. The article calls that false in every respect. David Friedländer, from official records, counted only 22 Jews among 1,703 Prussian convictions in 1789.

The hard part, the entry says, is fair comparison. Jews were few, so small shifts swing the rates. Trade, schooling, and political standing all shape the figures. Closed careers push some men toward the offenses open to them. Records are patchy in place and time. From what exists, the Jewish share of crime sits below the Jewish share of population.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-dan-ashkenazi-4:
Dan Ashkenazi was a German Talmudist and exegete of the second half of the thirteenth century. He ranked among Germany's leading Talmudists and taught Mordecai ben Hillel. Late in the century he emigrated to Spain, likely fleeing persecution. In Spain he was called Ashkenazi, the German. Its top rabbis thought highly of him. Trouble came when he gave a letter of recommendation to a youth who claimed to be a prophet.

Solomon Adret scorned the German rabbi in a circular letter on the false prophet. The two had clashed before. Dan had ruled at Saragossa that slaughter by Christians could pass strict law, since Christians were not pagans. Adret's five responsa show Dan could not be overlooked. Nissim b. Reuben and others still honored his learning, the entry notes.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-david-tevele-be: Moses's son David Tevele was a Russian rabbi and author born in Turetz, in the government of Minsk, in 1792. He studied at Volozhin and graduated as rabbi. At twenty-five he became rabbi of Stouptz, serving from 1817 to 1849, when Minsk elected him chief rabbi. He held that post until his death there on April 27, 1861. His "Bet Dawid" holds responsa and sermons. Two more books of his responsa and novellae appeared after his death, at Wilna in 1864 and 1882.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-delmedigo-elija: Eliezer's son Elijah Delmedigo was a Cretan rabbi and Talmudist who flourished in Candia in the second half of the sixteenth century and the first of the seventeenth. He was widely known in his time as a Talmudic scholar. One legal decision of his survives in Joseph Samega's "Derek Yemin." The short entry adds his most noted family fact: he was the father of Joseph Solomon Delmedigo, the famous philosopher and writer. Two printed sources are cited, and no dates are given.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-dias-felix-5167: Felix Dias was a French painter born at Bordeaux in 1794 who died on May 29, 1817, and the entry on him is short. From his earliest youth he showed marked talent for painting. He was sent to the Academy, where he won several academic honors. In 1817 he took the first prize for composition. The few works he left behind, the entry says, show a skillful blending of colors, a fine taste in arrangement, and great vigor of design. He died at only about twenty-three.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-dominico-irosol:
Dominico Irosolimitano was a Talmudist, physician, and censor of Hebrew books born at Safed about 1550. He trained at the rabbinical college in his home city, in medicine as well as Talmud. His skill as a doctor reached the Sultan of Turkey. The Sultan called him to Constantinople as court physician. He died in Italy about 1620.

Dominico later converted to Christianity and taught Hebrew at the College of the Neophytes in Rome. Under the Inquisition he became a busy expurgator of Hebrew books. He worked at Venice and then as chief reviser at Mantua in 1595-97. His own works include a Hebrew rendering of the New Testament. He also compiled the Sefer ha-Zikkuk, a book of expurgation still in manuscript.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-ehud-5467:
Ehud was the second judge of Israel, a Benjamite son of Gera. He hid a two-edged sword under his clothes. With it he carried a gift to Eglon, king of Moab. Eglon had held Israel down for eighteen years. Ehud asked for a private audience, and got it.

Being left-handed, Ehud drew the sword without suspicion. He drove it through the fat king's body. Then he fled to Seirath and raised an army. His men slew the whole Moabite force, 10,000 men in all. Critics, the entry adds, treat the tale as an old folk story. They still accept Ehud himself as a real man of history.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-englisch-bertho: Berthold Englisch was an Austrian chess player of note. He was born in 1851 at Hotzenplotz in Austrian Silesia. He died on Oct. 19, 1897, in Vienna. In 1879 he took first prize at the Leipsic tourney. In 1883 he placed fourth in the London tourney. At Frankfort in 1887 he took the seventh prize. There he won games from Alapin, Gunsberg, and Zuckertort. In 1896 he won first prize at a Rothschild tourney. Those results mark the whole of his record here.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-ezra-the-scribe:
Ezra the Scribe was a priest descended from Seraiah the high priest, and his name likely shortens Azaryahu, God helps. In Greek and Latin he is Esdras. The entry warns that his life must be rebuilt from scant scraps, in part from his own memoirs. His first firm record is a royal order letting him lead exiles back to Jerusalem. The order came in the seventh year of Artaxerxes, matched here to 458 B.C.

The entry defends that date against scholars who would move Ezra to 397 B.C. or to Nehemiah's second visit in 433. It finds no cause to doubt the order's core, though its wording may carry Jewish coloring. The king named is Artaxerxes Longimanus, the entry holds. Later sections weigh the order in which Ezra and Nehemiah reached the city.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-felix-antonius-:
Antonius Felix was procurator of Judea, a freedman of the empress Antonia who first ran Samaria under Cumanus. When Samaritan and Galilean clashes near split the two rulers into war, Claudius recalled Cumanus. In 52 C.E. Felix became sole procurator, with full army command, at the high priest Jonathan's urging.

Tacitus, quoted here, says Felix used royal power with a slave's temper, with cruelty and excess. He lured Drusilla, sister of Agrippa II, from her husband. He shipped the Zealot leader Eleazar to Rome in chains and crucified his followers in great numbers. Yet he used the Sicarii for his own ends, even in Jonathan's murder. An Egyptian-led rising against the Jerusalem garrison was crushed under him. His term is called a reign of anarchy.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-franchetti-augu:
Augusto Franchetti was an Italian lawyer and historian born at Florence on July 10, 1840. He studied law at Pisa and was admitted to the bar in 1863. He then settled at Florence. As a drama critic he gave much time to the stage, above all to Aristophanes. He translated that poet's works into Italian verse. In 1874 he became professor of modern history at an institute of social sciences.

Franchetti sat on Florence's town council from 1872 and on its municipal council from 1886. For forty years he was a director of the Florence Jewish community. He was its president from 1870 to 1899, while the new synagogue was being built. His books include a verse translation of the Clouds of Aristophanes, printed in 1881. His large history of Italy from 1789 to 1799 reached a second edition at Milan in 1903.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-friedjung-heinr:
Heinrich Friedjung was an Austrian journalist and author born at Rostschin, Moravia, on January 18, 1851. He studied at Prague, Berlin, and Vienna and took his doctor's degree. In 1874 he became a professor at the Vienna business academy. He had to give up that post in 1881 for reasons of politics. In 1883 he became editor of a German weekly he had founded himself.

In 1886 he took charge of a German daily in Vienna. From 1891 to 1895 he sat on the Vienna town council. He wrote often for a great Munich paper. His chief books treat the emperor Charles IV and the settlement with Hungary. His best-known work is a two-volume fight for the mastery in Germany, printed in 1896.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-galante-6467:
Galante was a Jewish family that rose in Rome early in the sixteenth century. Its head Mordecai was a Spanish exile of the Angel family. Roman nobles called him Galantuomo, the gentleman, for his fine manners. The family kept that name and later settled in Palestine. There it produced authors and noted men.

Abraham ben Mordecai Galante was a cabalist who died in 1560. He wrote comments on Lamentations and on the Zohar. Wealth let him build a grand tomb shrine over Simon ben Yohai grave at Meron. Moses Galante the Elder studied under Joseph Caro and was ordained at age twenty-two. A younger Moses wrote works that sort out clashing Bible verses.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-geller-peter-is: Peter Isaacovich Geller, a Russian painter born at Shklov on December 10, 1862, studied at the Odessa School of Design. In 1878 he entered the St. Petersburg Art Academy. He won two silver medals in 1881-83 and a gold medal in 1885 for a canvas of Saint Irene healing Saint Sebastian. In 1887 he gained the rank of artist of the first degree. His 1889 canvas of Jewish conscripts taking their oath was bought by the academy.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-gifts-6667:
Gifts were a common custom among early Israelites in daily life and at family feasts. A lesser man gave to a greater to win favor. Gifts calmed anger and opened the gates of nobles. No one came before God, a prophet, or a king with empty hands. Yet a proverb warned that he who hates gifts shall live.

Conquered peoples sent gifts as tribute, so to bring presents often meant to submit. Kings traded gifts at treaties and scattered them among subjects. Gifts marked weddings too, from Abraham servant coins to the groom mattan. The law barred gifts as bribes to judges. In rabbinic law a gift is property passed on freely, with rules set by the giver health and mind.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-goldsmith-milto: Milton Goldsmith was an American merchant and author. He was born at Philadelphia on May 22, 1861. In 1877 he went to Europe and studied three years at Zurich. His novels are two: "Rabbi and Priest" (1891) and "A Victim of Conscience" (1903). He also wrote several librettos for comic operas. Several dramatic pieces came from his pen as well. Beyond those, he placed short stories in newspapers. His poems appeared in magazines. The entry is very short and gives no facts about his business career or later life.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-guzikov-michael:
Michael Joseph Guzikov, born at Shklov in 1806, was a Russian musician who died at Brussels on Oct. 21, 1837. Born into a family of talented musicians, he became skilled on many instruments while still young. He toured Russia with his father and relatives and played before Emperor Nicholas in 1828.

After concerts in Moscow, Kiev, and Odessa, Guzikov toured Europe on Lamartine's advice. He spent five months in Vienna, honored by the emperor and Prince Metternich, then played in Prague, Dresden, Berlin, and Paris. The entry remembers him best as inventor of the straw violin. He played it with such skill that audiences greeted him with great enthusiasm everywhere.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-hanameel-the-eg:
Hanameel the Egyptian was a high priest who flourished in the first century B.C. Herod, fresh in power in Palestine, picked him for the office left empty by Antigonus's shameful death in 37 B.C. The Mishnah calls him an Egyptian, Josephus a Babylonian. He was of priestly stock but not of the high priests' family.

His first tenure was short. Herod removed him for the Hasmonean Aristobulus in 35 B.C. When the popular youth was drowned at Herod's order that same year, Hanameel came back. No source says how long his second term ran. He is credited with preparing one of the seven red heifers provided in all the centuries from Ezra's restoration to the final dispersion.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-harris-sir-augu:
Augustus Glossop Harris, born in Paris in 1852, was an English actor, playwright, and theater manager. He left trade for the stage in 1873. In 1879 he took over Drury Lane Theater in London, a house known for losses. His bold staging and sharp management made it pay.

Harris also revived grand opera in London, first at Drury Lane and then at Covent Garden. He wrote many plays, some with partners, and staged a grand Christmas pantomime each year. He sat on the London County Council and was knighted in 1891. Work wore down his health, and he died on June 22, 1896.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-henriques-david: David Quixano Henriques, born May 13, 1804, was an Anglo-Jewish reformer and a son of Abraham Q. Henriques. He directed the City Bank and the Bank of Australasia. Early on he served the Portuguese synagogue as a manager. Later he helped found the West London Synagogue and held high office in it. He was its treasurer from 1847 to 1862. He died in London on March 6, 1870.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-heymann-paul-76: Paul Heymann, born at Pankow, near Berlin, in 1849, was a German laryngoscopist. He studied medicine at Berlin and Heidelberg, taking his degree at Berlin in 1874. After further study in four cities, he settled in Berlin in 1878. He became a lecturer there in 1894 and assistant professor in 1899. His many essays dealt mainly with laryngoscopy, tuberculosis, and diseases of the nose and throat. He also edited a handbook of laryngology and rhinology, printed from 1896 to 1900.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-hirshman-leonar: Leonard Leopoldovich Hirshman, born at Goldingen, Courland, in 1839, was a Russian eye doctor. After graduating from the University of Kharkof, he worked in the labs of Graefe, Helmholtz, Jäger, Knapp, and Pagenstecher. In 1868 he became a lecturer at Kharkof. In 1872 he rose to professor there. Three main works are listed, dated 1863, 1868, and 1873. Their German and Russian titles concern drug-caused pupil changes, the physiology of light sense, and treatment of trachoma, as given in the entry.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-house-2667:
House in ancient Palestine is described from the ground up. Warm weather let people live much of life outdoors, so a house meant little more than shelter for sleep and meals. Wood was scarce. Plains homes used sun-baked clay bricks, while mountain homes used limestone.

Many dwellings grew out of caves, first enlarged, then hewn, then walled at the front. Most houses had one room shared by people and animals. Flat roofs served for evening rest and summer sleep, and law required a rail around the roof edge. Rich homes added hewn stone, paneling, and ivory inlay. The basic style, the entry says, barely changed over the ages.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-hyneman-7967:
Hyneman is an American family of remote Spanish and later German roots. Its early record is thin. The first firm trace is Henry Hyneman signing an oath of loyalty to Pennsylvania in 1779. Elias Hyneman, born in Holland, settled in Philadelphia and fathered thirteen children.

His son Leon, born in 1808, made a name in freemasonry. He founded the Order of Druidesses in 1849 and ran a masonic journal from 1852 to 1860. Rebekah Gumpert Hyneman, born a Christian, embraced Judaism and wrote tales and poems. Elias Leon Hyneman died at Andersonville prison in the Civil War after giving his horse and shoes to wounded comrades. Later kin include a painter and a Philadelphia lawyer.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-ibn-gabirol-sol:
Solomon ben Judah ibn Gabirol, known in Latin dress as Avicebron, was a Spanish poet, philosopher, and moralist born in Malaga about 1021. He died about 1058 at Valencia. Orphaned young, he found a patron at seventeen in Jekuthiel Hassan. At barely twenty he wrote a Hebrew grammar in verse, 400 lines in acrostic form.

Gabirol was the first teacher of Neoplatonism in Europe. His Fons Vitae carried Greek and Arabic thought back to Christian schools, where it shaped medieval debate. Jews of his age largely ignored his philosophy, as they had ignored Philo. His ethics book, written at Saragossa in 1045, guides the moral qualities. A legend tells that a jealous rival killed him and hid the body under a fig tree.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-ibn-shoshan-heb:
Ibn Shoshan, also read Ibn Susan and meaning lily, was a Spanish family of Toledo. It can be traced from the twelfth century into the seventeenth. Its first known head, Solomon, bore the nickname the Mighty Hammer and served as nasi at Toledo. His son Joseph led the town after him and died in 1205.

Joseph stood high with Alfonso the Eighth and built a fine synagogue at Toledo. Later kin served as judges, physicians, and community agents across the centuries. One Samuel fed oil to schools in Cairo and Jerusalem. Isaac, a physician born in 1324, died of plague in 1399. Issachar ben Mordecai made calendar tables spanning the years 1539 to 2240, printed at Salonica in 1564. Another member died a martyr at Seville in 1481.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-isaac-ben-elija: Isaac ben Elijah Sheni, also written Shani, was a Turkish rabbi who lived at Constantinople in the first half of the sixteenth century. He wrote "Me'ah She'arim," a double commentary, plain and cabalistic, on one hundred of the six hundred and thirteen commandments, printed at Salonica in 1543. He also revised and edited Menahem Recanati's "Ta'ame ha-Mitzwot," printed at Salonica in 1544. Steinschneider suggested that he may be the same person as Isaac ibn Farhi.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-israel-bruna-be: Israel Bruna ben Hayyim was a German rabbi of the fifteenth century. He served first at Brünn. When the Jews were expelled from that city in 1454, he settled at Ratisbon and opened a yeshibah, against Rabbi Anshel's claim that it trespassed on his rights. Leading rabbis, among them Jacob Weil and Israel Isserlein, backed Bruna and praised him. In 1474 enemies had him jailed, possibly on a ritual-murder charge; after thirteen days he was freed. He wrote a volume of responsa.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-jabbok-8367: The Jabbok is one of the Jordan's chief tributaries. Scripture names it at Jacob's meeting with Esau and his night struggle with the angel. It marked the line between Reuben and Gad on one side and Ammon on the other. Sihon's land runs from the Arnon to the Jabbok. Eusebius places the river between Gerasa and Philadelphia. It is identified with the Wadi al-Zarka, rising in Mount Hauran and reaching the Jordan between Gennesaret and the Dead Sea. Its name is tied to its bluish water.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-jacob-ben-zabda: Jacob ben Zabda was a Palestinian amora of the fourth generation, a younger contemporary and likely pupil of Abbahu. He repeats several of Abbahu's rulings and sermons, and halakot in the names of Jeremiah and Jose II as well. He was a firm believer in magic's powers. Food found lying on the road must not be touched, he taught, since it may have been laid there for a spell. He also read one verse strictly: to speak against one's teacher is to insult the majesty of God.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-jehoshaphat-val: Valley of Jehoshaphat is a valley named by Joel, who says God would gather all the heathen nations after Judah's return and judge them for their wrongs to Israel. Since the name means that God judges, some readers have taken the valley as a figure of speech, not a real place. From the fourth century on, Jews, Christians, and Muslims have matched it with the Kidron valley beside Jerusalem and hold that the Last Judgment will occur there. A Midrash remark denies that any such valley exists.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-jonathan-ben-da: Jonathan ben David ha-Kohen of Lunel was a French thinker of the twelfth and thirteenth centuries. He defended Maimonides against the sharp attacks of Abraham ben David of Posquières. At Jonathan's urging, Maimonides sent his great Guide to Lunel, where Samuel ibn Tibbon turned it into Hebrew. Jonathan also wrote a commentary on a work by Alfasi. About 1210, just before leaving for Palestine with two companions, he traded letters with a Talmud master of Dampierre on a question about the Holy Land.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-joseph-joslein-:
Joseph Joslein ben Moses was a Bavarian Talmudist born at Höchstädt about 1420 who died after 1488. He studied for five years under Israel Isserlein. At the request of his fellow students he wrote down his teacher's rulings, with Isserlein checking the text. That record became his book Lekket Yosher.

He began arranging the material in 1463, three years after his teacher's death, and finished in 1488. The book follows the order of the four Turim. Beyond its legal value, the entry says, it shows the lives of Isserlein and his students. It also paints the manners and customs of the rabbinic schools of that age. One copy alone survives, in manuscript at Munich.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-judah-ben-abrah: Judah ben Abraham was a pupil of Rashi who flourished at the start of the twelfth century. He studied beside Shemaiah, the father-in-law of Rashbam, and worked with him on written tasks. Together the two sorted the writings Rashi left at his death. They also edited a work on the Passover rite, following notes Rashi had given them by word of mouth. That work is cited in the Tosafot to Pesahim. It is credited there to Rashi and Shemaiah as its authors.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-judge-10267:
Judge in Hebrew is most often shofet, a word akin to the Phoenician sufet, the title of chief rulers in Sidonian colonies. The later word dayyan became the standard term in Talmudic times. Other words, such as pelilim and even elohim, also stand for judges in some verses.

The long entry traces how justice was run. Elders judged at first; then Moses, on Jethro's advice, set heads over thousands, hundreds, fifties, and tens, keeping hard cases for himself. Later parts set the marks of a fit judge: for a high court, wisdom and freedom from bodily blemish; for a court of three, seven traits from wisdom to a good name. Kin could not judge together, and no friend or foe of a party could sit.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-kalomiti-abraha: Abraham ben Moses Kalomiti was a Turkish scholar of the fifteenth century. A commentary on Job in a Bodleian manuscript is credited to him. The work takes a reason-based line. In it the author cites his own book on Aristotle's "Ethics." The entry notes a doubt raised by Steinschneider. He thought Kalomiti may only have copied the commentary, not written it. The surname was borne by other noted Turkish Jews as well.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-keller-naphtali:
Naphtali Keller was an Austrian scholar born at Tarnow, in Galicia, on Jan. 25, 1834. He died at Rožnau, in Moravia, on Aug. 5, 1865. His father was a well-to-do innkeeper. As a youth Keller spoke Hebrew with a friend for practice. He began to write poems in that tongue. Hebrew books on modern themes filled out his schooling.

Keller lost his wife's marriage portion in business. He moved his family of six to Vienna. There he scraped a living as a broker. In 1864 he brought out the first volume of a Hebrew journal, "Bikkurim." He edited it with care and fairness. Illness sent him to a watering place in 1865, but he died there. The entry names his two tales of Galician Jewish life.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-koranyi-friedri:
Friedrich Korányi, a Hungarian physician and medical writer born on Dec. 20, 1828, at Nagy-Kallo, took his doctor's degree at Budapest in 1851. After two years in a Vienna surgical clinic he practised in his home town. In 1865 he became privat-docent for nervous diseases at Budapest. A year later he was made director of the internal clinic and full professor.

Honors followed in a steady line. The Order of the Iron Crown came in 1881, Hungarian nobility in 1884, and a seat in the House of Magnates in 1891. His German works treat anthrax, lung disease, and consumption in Hungary. The entry ends by noting that Korányi embraced Christianity.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-lautenburg-sigm: Sigmund Lautenburg, a theatrical manager born at Budapest on Sept. 11, 1852, left school at twelve for a bank job when his parents grew poor. The stage pulled harder than banking. An uncle took him to Vienna for more study, but plays won again. He acted from 1871, starting in Schiller at Neusohl. Berlin, Elberfeld, and Barmen followed. He then directed theaters in Amsterdam, Bremen, and Lübeck. Since 1887 he has run Berlin's Residenztheater as general manager.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-leviticus-9867:
Leviticus is the book of the Bible whose English name comes from the Latin "Liber Leviticus." Jewish writings cite it by its first word, Wa-yikra. The book holds laws on the work of the priests. The entry calls it, in truth, a body of priestly law.

The laws are shown as spoken by God to Moses early in the second year after the Exodus. Chapters one to seven give rules for burnt, meal, peace, sin, and trespass offerings. Some rules speak to the people, and some to the priests. The entry walks through the book part by part, from altar fire to the priests' share of each gift.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-liebermann-matt: Mattathias ben Asher Lemle Liebermann was a rabbi and preacher in Prague. He served in the second half of the seventeenth century and died there in 1709. He wrote "Mattat Yah," a set of sermons on the Pentateuch. The set reaches only as far as Numbers chapter thirty-three. It was printed at Frankfort-on-the-Oder in 1696. A second set of his sermons, "Peri Megadim," survives only in manuscript.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-lob-ben-samuel-: Samuel Zebi Hirsch's son Löb was a Russian rabbi born probably at Pinczow about 1630, and he died at Brest-Litovsk in 1714. He studied under leading teachers and served as rabbi in many towns, ending at Brest-Litovsk from 1701 to 1714. In 1669 he was sent to Constantinople to look into the claims of Shabbethai Zebi. His legal replies were printed at Neuwied in 1736 by his grandson, with more replies by the grandson added.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-lublin-10167:
Lublin, a city of Russian Poland southeast of Warsaw, is the subject of a Jewish Encyclopedia entry from 1906 by Herman Rosenthal, Judah David Eisenstein, Joseph Jacobs, and Bernhard Friedberg. Jews lived there by the fourteenth century, confined to a suburb assigned in 1396. From the mid-1500s to the mid-1700s, Lublin was a center of Jewish life.

The article details special taxes, trade limits, and the licenses of 1596, when one hundred Jewish houses stood in the Podzance quarter. Lublin hosted meetings of the Council of Four Lands, the central body of Polish Jewry. It also records a riot in 1648 and the Cossack massacre of 1656, which killed most of the city’s ten thousand Jews. A protective charter of 1675 and later royal restrictions follow. Readers get a rich period history of a major Polish Jewish community.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-manne-mordecai-:
Mordecai Zebi Manne, a Russian Hebrew poet and painter, is profiled in the 1906 Jewish Encyclopedia. Born at Rodzkowitz, in the government of Wilna, in 1859, he had the usual Talmudic training. His father taught him Hebrew grammar. At thirteen he entered the yeshivah at Minsk. He died in his home town in 1886.

The article follows his turn from study to art. At Wilna he entered the school of painting and design while still at the yeshivah. In 1880 he enrolled at the Imperial Academy of Fine Arts in St. Petersburg. Two years later the grand duke Vladimir gave him a silver medal for extraordinary progress. His poems placed him among the foremost Hebrew poets of his day. One, Mas'at Nafshi, is still sung at Zionist gatherings. He also wrote a pioneering series of essays on painting and Jewish art. His collected writings filled two volumes, printed at Warsaw.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-massarani-massa:
Massarani is the name of an Italian Jewish family traced from the fifteenth century. Richard Gottheil and Ismar Elbogen wrote its Jewish Encyclopedia entry in 1906. The name comes from Massarano, a small town near Novara in Piedmont. Members of the family appear first as manuscript copyists. They then appear in Mantua, and later in Milan.

The most vivid figure in the entry is Bezaleel ben Samson Massarani. He worked to save Hebrew books when the Inquisition threatened them with destruction. He chaired the Mantua deputation that agreed at Padua to censor the Talmud in advance. He then went to Rome and won from Pope Sixtus V the right to print and own it in censored form. Around him the article gathers copyists, rabbis at Cento and Salonica, and a Milan lawyer of about 1850.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-meir-b-david-10:
Meir ben David was a grammarian of the last third of the thirteenth century. Crawford Howell Toy and Wilhelm Bacher wrote his Jewish Encyclopedia entry of 1906. He survives only in the books of other men. His one known work, “Hassagat ha-Hassagah,” was a criticism of the grammatical treatise of Ibn Janah, “Kitab al-Mustalhak.” The work itself is lost; what remains is the passages Profiat Duran quoted in his own grammar, the “Ma'aseh Efod.”

Two more traces follow him. Joseph ibn Kaspi, who knew Meir personally, records in his supercommentary on Ibn Ezra an explanation heard from the lips of Meir himself. The editors judge him probably identical with a grammarian called simply R. David. Abraham Bedersi quotes a note of his on a verse of Job in his book of Hebrew synonyms. The entry is a small lesson in how medieval scholarship is recovered, quotation by quotation.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-mendes-10667:
Mendes is one of the oldest Sephardic families. The Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906 traces it across four continents. Cyrus Adler, H. Pereira Mendes, Joseph Jacobs, and Frank H. Vizetelly wrote the article. The family held on in Spain and its possessions long after the expulsion of 1492. Branches reached Aquitaine, Holland, Italy, and Turkey. The French branch was rooted at Bordeaux and Bayonne. It intermarried with the Pereiras, Da Costas, and Fonsecas. It produced municipal councilors and a president of the tribunal of commerce. Its earliest Bayonne tombstone dates to 1637.

The Holland branch produced writers. It produced the editors of the Sephardic ritual as well. Modern prayer-books still rest on that ritual. The American line runs through David Pereira Mendes. He fled Spain for Bayonne and reached Jamaica in 1786. The article follows his descendants onward. It ends with Abraham Pereira Mendes, the Kingston-born rabbi who died in New York in 1893.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-meyuhas-10767:
Meyuḥas was an Oriental Jewish family that produced a line of rabbis and writers for Jerusalem and Constantinople, traced in a Jewish Encyclopedia entry by M. Seligsohn, M. Franco, and Joseph Jacobs, published in 1906. Four members get their own sketches, spanning the eighteenth and nineteenth centuries. Most of their books were printed at Salonica.

Abraham ben Samuel wrote homilies on the Pentateuch and responsa printed between 1784 and 1798. Raphael ben Samuel, chief rabbi of Jerusalem, published Talmudic and legal novellae at Salonica in the 1750s. His descendant Moses Mordecai Joseph, Jerusalem's chief rabbi from 1801, rallied the city's Jews to dig defenses as Bonaparte's army approached in 1799. Samuel Ḥayyim closes the line as chief rabbi of Constantinople in the 1830s.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-miphkad-r-v-ham:
Miphkad is a name in Nehemiah's wall-building list that may not be a gate of Jerusalem at all, as Isidore Singer and M. Seligsohn explain in the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. Nehemiah iii. 31 mentions it between the Horse Gate and the Sheep Gate, but the catalogue of gates in chapter twelve omits it. In Ezekiel the word marks the place by the Temple where the sin-offering was burned.

The name seems to mean an appointed place. Jerome translated it porta judicialis, the gate of judgment, which led Lightfoot to guess at the Prætorium's judgment hall or the Temple's east gate. Barclay identified it instead with the high gate of Benjamin at the Tyropæon bridge. A one-verse toponym that kept scholars guessing for centuries, in one compact note.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-monticelli-1096:
Monticelli, a small town in the province of Piacenza, got its Jewish community from a catastrophe elsewhere, as Richard Gottheil and Ismar Elbogen write in the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. When the Jews were expelled from the duchy of Milan in 1597, the Soavi and Sforni families of Cremona settled here. They brought the German ritual from Lombardy and kept it ever after.

A society for nursing the sick and for study, founded in the sixteenth century, was still alive when the article was written. The numbers tell the later story: 143 Jewish inhabitants in 1865 had fallen to 32 by 1901. Flaminio Servi served as rabbi in 1863. A six-line entry, sourced to the Corriere Israelitico, for a community fading in place.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-moses-botarel-c:
Moses Botarel of Cisneros was a Spanish scholar of the fourteenth and fifteenth centuries with a reputation for wonders. Joseph Jacobs and Jacob Zallel Lauterbach wrote his Jewish Encyclopedia entry. He studied Cabala under Jacob Sefardi, and also medicine and philosophy. To him philosophy and Cabala taught the same truths in different words.

Botarel believed in amulets and claimed he could join the names of God for magic, so many took him for a sorcerer. He even let it be believed that Elijah had appointed him Messiah, and he wrote to the rabbis asking for their hard questions. Yet he also attended the Tortosa disputation of 1413 and 1414. His commentary on the Sefer Yezirah, made for a Christian scholar, was printed at Mantua in 1562.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-moses-zeeb-wolf:
Moses Zeeb Wolf ben Eliezer was a Lithuanian rabbi born at Grodno at the start of the nineteenth century. Wilhelm Bacher and M. Seligsohn wrote his Jewish Encyclopedia entry. He first headed the yeshiva at Grodno. In 1813 he was called to the rabbinate of Tiktin, and in 1824 to Byelostok, where he died.

His Mar'ot ha-Zobe'ot treats the chapter of the Eben ha-Ezer on the agunah, the wife whose husband is missing. His Aguddat Ezob gathers homilies for holy days, with nine funeral orations added. His novellae on the Shulhan Aruk came out after his death, one part printed by his son at Warsaw. Three volumes of his responsa followed at Wilna in 1886.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-nagari-moses-be:
Moses ben Judah Nagari was a philosophical writer who, by Steinschneider's reckoning, lived at Rome about 1300. Gotthard Deutsch and S. Mannheimer wrote his Jewish Encyclopedia entry. Even his name is in doubt: Steinschneider reads it Na'ar, from the Ne'arim family. Later bibliographers mangled it into Nagara, Najara, and Nigdi.

His one work is the Ma'amar ba-Ma'areket, an index to Maimonides' Guide with explanations of its philosophical terms. It was printed at Venice in 1574 together with Saul Cohen's questions to Isaac Abravanel. Because it looks like part of a larger work, it was wrongly called Kezat Bi'ure ha-Moreh. The entry spends much of its space untangling him from men of similar names.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-nathan-mordecai:
Nathan Mordecai was a French doctor at Avignon. Isidore Singer and S. Kahn wrote his entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. He lived in the middle of the fifteenth century. Joseph Colon praised his medical skill in their letters. Colon gave him the honorific title of mori.

Between 1450 and 1456 Nathan ordered a full Talmud copy. The work copied was Meiri's Bet ha-Behirah, with his own marginal notes. Scholars identify him with several men of like names. One is the mathematician Mordecai Nadi. Another is an astronomer called the great luminary. Scribes copied Alfasi and Averroes for him in those years. The entry also warns against confusing him with Isaac Nathan.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-neumann-angelo-:
Angelo Neumann was an Austrian director of opera. Isidore Singer and Edgar Mels wrote his entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. He was born at Vienna on Aug. 18, 1838. He went on stage in 1859 as a barytone. He sang at Cologne, Cracow, Presburg, and Danzig.

From 1862 he sang at the Vienna court opera. In 1876 he became operatic director at Leipsic. There he staged Wagner's full Ring in 1878. No company had yet performed the cycle entire. The feat seemed impossible until he achieved it. In 1882 he formed a traveling Wagnerian company. Three years later Prague took him as theater director. Berlin also owes him its first Cavalleria Rusticana.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-nizza-solomon-b:
Solomon Nizza was a rabbi of Venice. Isidore Singer and J. S. Raisin wrote his entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. He served in the seventeenth and eighteenth centuries. Sage, Talmudist, and liturgical poet describe him alike. He succeeded his father Isaiah in the post.

His father wrote on ethics and on the Zohar. His grandfather had been rabbi of Padua earlier. Great Talmudists wrote to Nizza and printed his decisions. His formal approbations were sought after widely then. He taught Moses and Gershon Ḥefeẓ in Venice. A eulogy for Gershon came from his pen. His penitential poem holds eight rimed stanzas. The Roman rite sings it on New-Year's morning still.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-orion-11767:
Orion is a group of stars seen in the night sky. The board and Ludwig Blau wrote its entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. The Hebrew word Kesil is held to name this group. Old Greek and Aramaic texts so render that word. They render it in Isaiah and in the book of Job.

In the Targum, the word is Nefila, which means giant. In the Peshitta, it is Gabbara, which means hero. Both names are held to point to Orion as well. The Talmud reads Kesil as Orion, the piece says. Jerome reads it that way in Amos and Job too. Some later sages read the word as the star Canopus. New scholars lean to the old view of the word. In Amos and Job, Orion stands by the Pleiades stars.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-palestine-holin:
The holiness of Palestine is its rank as a sacred land. Joseph Jacobs and Judah David Eisenstein wrote the entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. Jews hold the land dear as the land of their fathers. It was the cradle and the grave of the Patriarchs. It was the Promised Land of the old tales.

Many laws of Moses could be kept in that land alone. The holiness of those laws shone on the land itself. The Bible calls it a land God cared for at all times. God calls it my land, in the words of Joel. The phrase holy land stands just once in the Bible. The Mishnah calls Palestine the most holy of all lands. In law, that holiness may have ceased with the Temple's fall.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-peach-prunus-pe: Peach trees came late to the Jewish sources of Palestine. Emil G. Hirsch and Immanuel Benzinger wrote the short entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. The fruit first shows up in the Mishnah. The plum, its kin, appears even later, in the Gemara. The entry gives just two source notes and stops there. It names no use, law, or story tied to the fruit.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-pethahiah-b-jac:
Pethahiah of Regensburg was a Jewish traveler of the twelfth century. He was born at Prague and traveled between 1175 and 1190. Wilhelm Bacher and Schulim Ochser wrote his entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. His book is called the Sibbub, or Circuit.

He set out from Ratisbon toward the East. His road crossed Poland and southern Russia. It ran through Armenia, Persia, and Babylon to Palestine. Part of his notes were lost in Bohemia. Judah the Pious gathered what remained of them. The book was printed at Prague in 1595 and often after.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-pinheiro-moses-: Moses Pinheiro was a leading follower of Shabbethai Zebi. Joseph Jacobs and M. Seligsohn wrote his entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. He lived at Leghorn in the seventeenth century. His learning won him great esteem there. He urged the Jews of Leghorn to believe in Shabbethai. Even after the apostasy came, he clung to the false Messiah. He taught Cardoso the Kabbalah and the Shabbethaian mysteries.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-pontoise-12267:
Pontoise is a French town in the department of Seine-et-Oise. Richard Gottheil and S. Kahn wrote its entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. A Jewish community lived there as early as the eleventh century. The entry follows that community through two hard centuries.

In 1179 the Jews of Pontoise were charged with killing a Christian boy. The boy, Richard, was honored as a martyr at Paris. A paper of 1294 names Jews of the town in a house sale. Their names were Sanson, Meuns, and Abraham. In 1296 Philip the Fair gave one Jew and his children to his brother. That same man later served as agent for the crown. He dealt with Jews of Amiens, Senlis, and Champagne.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-rapa-elijah-b-m: Elijah b. Menahem Rapa was an Italian Talmudist of the sixteenth century. The Executive Committee of the Editorial Board and A. S. Waldstein wrote this short Jewish Encyclopedia entry, published in 1906. He is also called Elijah Rapoport. He wrote Be'er Mayim Hayyim, printed at Corfu in 1599. That book treats Talmudic and other subjects. A second work, Erez Hefez, covers Bible and Talmud topics. No date is given for that second book.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-reischer-jacob-:
Jacob b. Joseph Reischer was an Austrian rabbi born at Prague. Isidore Singer and Jacob Zallel Lauterbach wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article, published in 1906. He was also called Jacob Back. He died at Metz in February 1733.

The article says his teacher Simon Spira gave him a wife. She was the daughter of Spira's son. Reischer served as judge at Prague, then rabbi at Rzeszow. That city's Jewish name, Reische, gave him his surname. Later posts took him to Anspach and Worms. From 1719 he served at Metz until his death. His many books comment on the Shulhan Aruk. They also include responsa, or legal answers, in three parts. The entry shows a working judge across central Europe.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-rings-12767:
Rings served Jews as ornaments and as signs of rank. Cyrus Adler and Albert Wolf wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article, published in 1906. Finger, ear, and nose rings appear in the Bible. Seal rings and dignity rings were known then too.

The article notes that neither Bible nor Talmud links rings to marriage. Betrothal once used money, a valuable object, or a document. The groom spoke a hallowing formula at that moment. About the seventh century the ring became frequent in betrothal. Roman influence in Palestine may explain that change. Betrothal and wedding were then split apart in time. Later both rites joined on the wedding day. The groom placed a ring on the bride's right middle finger. Jews did not exchange rings as Romans did. The entry traces one symbol's slow path to the wedding.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-rosenthal-herma:
Herman Rosenthal was an American author, editor, and librarian born in Courland, Russia, on October 6, 1843. Cyrus Adler and Frank H. Vizetelly wrote his entry for the 1906 Jewish Encyclopedia. He began as a printer and poet in Russia.
