Özkurt and Eskiler studied why elite wrestlers in Turkey plan to stay in their sport in a 2026 paper. More than three hundred seventy wrestlers answered scales on goals, basic needs, motivation, and enjoyment. Sixteen wrestlers also gave interviews about what keeps them going or pushes them away.

Enjoyment carried part of the effect of motivation onto plans to continue. Interviews added outside supports such as coaches, role models, and social backing, plus drags such as failure, unfairness, and scarce resources. Keeping elite wrestlers engaged thus depends on more than inner drive. Federations that protect enjoyment and fairness may hold talent longer.
plos-pone-0353167:
Piersol, Colangelo, and Buckman began building a broad inventory of women's bodily experiences in a 2026 study. Older tools focus on negative feelings around monthly cycles, yet body states span good and bad feelings across many systems every day. Three hundred young women students rated how often varied body experiences occur and how pleasant each feels.

Items gathered from past research were trimmed by grouping methods, then tested for a sound structure. Early results supported a multi-part inventory rather than a single score. A fuller measure could help researchers link daily body experience with mood and health across the whole life span, not only around periods. Later work will refine and validate the tool.
plos-pone-0353267:
Barkha Yadav-Samudrala and seven colleagues give cannabidiol to aged mice carrying an HIV protein gene, in this 2026 PLOS ONE study of brain ageing with HIV. The viral protein Tat lingers in the body and harms the brain even when infection is controlled. Fifteen-to-eighteen-month-old mice, male and female, received the cannabis compound daily for twelve weeks, then faced memory and anxiety tests.

Recognition memory improved, but only in females carrying the viral gene. Pain responses shifted in all treated mice, and body temperature and weight changed without harming movement. Brain chemistry measurements showed the compound reshaped the body's own cannabis-like signalling differently by sex and region — a warning against one-size dosing.
plos-pone-0353367:
Ajmi Blout and colleagues compared childhood hardship and mental health in two Tunisian prisons in a 2026 study. One held men and one held women, with more than five hundred prisoners answering anonymous surveys on early adversity, substance use, mood, and self-worth. Women reported far more anxiety and depression than men.

Nearly half the women reported suicidal thoughts while inside, clearly more than the men. Men, in turn, more often reported low self-esteem. The authors call for rehabilitation programs that treat trauma and mental health inside prisons. Gender-specific support matters, since the heaviest burdens differed so sharply between the two prisons.
plos-pone-0353467:
Hongliang Ma and seven co-authors compare ways of farming salty coastal land in this 2026 PLOS ONE field study from Tangshan, China. Over two years they tested three patterns against ordinary single-crop farming: rotating fresh peas with rice, raising crabs inside rice paddies, and rotating wheat with rice. They measured money earned alongside soil and chemical use.

Each pattern beat its comparison crop on income, and the rice-and-crab system earned the most. Salt in the soil eased slightly, organic matter rose, and sprays dropped by roughly a fifth to a half. The results show coastal farmers need not choose between profit and healthier soil.
plos-pone-0353667:
Hannah Pearl Glucksman and four colleagues put a new eye-scanning device through its paces in clinic, in this 2026 PLOS ONE study. The machine uses scattered laser light to measure how stiff the cornea and the eye's lens are, properties tied to diseases such as keratoconus. Thirty-three volunteers, some with that condition and some with normal vision, were scanned repeatedly on three machines by different operators.

Readings agreed closely: repeated measurements on one machine varied by only about one to two percent, and machines matched each other nearly as well. No one was harmed during testing. Consistent stiffness readings are the first requirement before such a scanner can guide eye care.
plos-pone-0353767:
Nor Diyana Hani Ghani led a team of six authors on this 2026 study of MyKidEye, a phone app teaching parents about children's eye problems. Parents from two schools either used the app, which explains common vision problems, warning signs, and treatments, or served as a comparison group, answering knowledge, attitude, and practice surveys before and after.

Practice scores improved clearly in the app group, while knowledge and attitude gains did not reach clear significance in this short trial. Ghani presents the app as a useful support for lasting eye care habits at home.
plos-pone-0354267:
Haitham Abu Khadija led a team of eight authors on this 2026 study of a simple blood ratio that may flag risk after a heart valve procedure. More than seven hundred patients received a replacement aortic valve through a leg artery. Beforehand, the team split them by their AST to ALT ratio, two routine liver enzymes, and tracked thirty days of complications.

Patients with a high ratio faced clearly greater risks of kidney injury, stroke, and new heart rhythm problems, though not of death. Abu Khadija suggests adding this cheap marker to pre-procedure checks.
plos-pone-0354367:
Patria Rojas and co-authors searched for social drivers of non-medical sedative and opioid use among Latino adults in the United States. Misuse is rising, and Latino-specific evidence was thin. Their 2026 analysis used a national research dataset covering more than twenty-two thousand Hispanic and Latino adults with complete records.

Recent non-medical use was rare in the sample, well under one percent for each drug class. Odds of opioid misuse rose with older age, male sex, depression, reported discrimination, and neighbourhood disorder. More schooling, higher income, being foreign-born, and speaking a language other than English at home were protective. Rojas and colleagues call for culturally fitted prevention aimed at the highest-risk subgroups.
plos-pone-0354467:
Forero and colleagues, in a 2026 paper, automate the counting of tumor cell colonies in radiation experiments. To judge whether radiation kills cancer cells, researchers grow surviving cells into colonies and count them, a slow and subjective chore by eye. Their tool, built as a plugin for a common image program, was tested on colon cancer cells.

The method finds round colonies using a shape-hunting technique, cleans the image with standard operations, and sets the smallest true colony size from a performance curve. On test images, it matched human counters closely, with sensitivity and agreement scores in the low nineties and a strong overall reliability rating. It also allows manual edits, so a researcher can fix doubtful spots. The authors say the tool can stand in for hand counting in colony survival assays, speeding a routine step in radiation biology.
plos-pone-0354667:
Chuanmin Zhang and four colleagues published this 2026 comparison of soccer policy in China and Japan. Using text analysis software and a policy scoring model, they examined thirty-one official football policy documents from both countries, rating the tools used, the content covered, and overall policy quality.

Both nations back development, public participation, and club building, but China leans on school football while Japan targets elite players and league strength. China's policies scored better on system design, Japan's on clear implementation and community ties. Zhang aims the lessons at improving Chinese football policy.
plos-pone-0354967:
Bingjie Wang and colleagues describe in 2026 what happens to eyes where blood stains the clear front window after a severe open injury. Records came from a large eye injury study, covering a few dozen eyes that had inner eye surgery without an immediate donor cornea transplant. A washout came first, with a temporary artificial window used when the view stayed too cloudy.

Most corneas cleared at least in part on their own over time, leaving a usable edge view. Vision and eye pressure both improved by final follow up, and only one eye later needed a donor transplant. Saving the patient's own cornea is favoured.
plos-pone-0355167:
Pia Pennekamp and three colleagues use eye tracking to test a theory of how witnesses pick faces from a lineup, in PLOS ONE in 2026. The theory says witnesses compare features across lineup members. They lean on features the suspect does not share with the fillers, since shared features cannot distinguish anyone. The researchers digitally pasted one feature, eyes, nose, or mouth, from a target face onto every member of some lineups, then watched where one hundred participants looked.

Gaze allocation to the supposedly diagnostic features did not differ between doctored and control lineups, nor did it track whether identifications were right. Witnesses simply did not visibly weigh shared features the way the theory proposes. The authors conclude the mental comparison, if it happens, is not carried out through overt eye movements. The result trims one proposed mechanism from lineup science, leaving the accuracy question open for other explanations.
plos-pone-0355367:
Chisho Takeoka and colleagues test in 2026 whether brain wave recordings from the scalp can sort a rare prion disease from Alzheimer's disease and healthy ageing. The prion illness, in its sporadic form, damages thinking as abnormal protein builds up in the brain, and early diagnosis is hard. Their sample was small, with only a handful of prion cases.

Measures of wave power, synchrony, and network shape fed a sorting model that reached very high accuracy in first checks and stayed well above chance in stricter tests. The authors treat the signals as promising candidates only, since larger outside samples must confirm the result before clinic use.
plos-pone-0355467:
Xing He and colleagues probe in 2026 how a low oxygen response factor affects gut inflammation and gut microbes in rats modelled with diarrhoea dominant bowel syndrome. Stressed rats developed the bowel condition, while other groups had the factor raised by thin air or lowered by a blocking drug. Colon tissue, symptoms, and stool microbes were tracked over four weeks.

Raising the factor calmed a key inflammatory pathway, while lowering it worsened symptoms and raised that pathway's signals. Microbe mixes shifted in the model, with some helpful groups falling. The authors note a link between the factor and microbes, but direct cause remains unproven.
plos-pone-0355867:
Jan Schleicher, Doreen Klingler, and Manfred Claassen release a software fix for a quiet error that can derail single-cell gene studies, in this 2026 paper. A popular technique predicts where a cell's gene activity is heading by comparing freshly made, unspliced transcripts with mature, spliced ones. Yet the field's standard counting tool was built for older sequencing chemistry. Newer protocols read from the other end of the transcript, and the old tool silently assumes the wrong direction there.

Their new command-line program, tidesurf, counts both transcript types correctly for both chemistries. On four public datasets it recovered the right counts where the old tool performed well and, crucially, where it quietly failed. The authors warn that continuing to use the legacy tool on the newer data invites wrong biological conclusions, and they position tidesurf as its up-to-date replacement.
plos-pone-0355967:
Chen Zhang and coauthors published a 2026 engineering paper in PLOS ONE on a web-based simulator. It tests the control systems of pumped storage hydropower plants before they ever run a real turbine. These plants, giant water batteries for the grid, depend on control software whose full logic is hard to validate. The platform combines physics-based plant models with a browser drag-and-drop modeling environment, so engineers assemble control logic graphically.

A governor case study showed the simulator tracking commands with tiny error. More importantly, it also exposed a dangerous overspeed weakness when a faulty actuator was injected, exactly the drills the platform exists for. Its trajectories matched an established commercial simulator almost perfectly. It ran in real time for many simultaneous sessions, and passed a hardware-in-the-loop trial. Users rated it highly. It is presented as risk-free rehearsal space that can cut commissioning failures.
plos-pone-0356267:
Chloe Meewes Lewis and four colleagues search blood samples for molecular hints of who will catch chlamydia again, in this 2026 study. Reinfection is common and raises the risk of reproductive harm, yet no test predicts it. The team profiled tiny regulatory molecules called microRNAs, collected from women's blood at a treatment visit, both inside tiny released vesicles and free in serum. They then checked who tested positive again three months later.

One vesicle-carried molecule found at baseline was linked to later reinfection, while three serum molecules were linked to staying clear. The molecules' predicted targets cluster in immune T-cell pathways, with different molecules leaning toward different T-cell types. The authors stress the findings are preliminary: the candidates now need validation in larger groups before any predictive test for reinfection risk can be built.
plos-pone-0356367:
Fayyaz Ahmad and four colleagues apply machine learning to a humble factory problem in this 2026 study: predicting how much sewing thread a garment will consume. Ordering too much thread wastes money; too little stalls production. The team focused on a common industrial stitch class. They compared six algorithms, including tree ensembles, support vector machines, and a neural network, on predicting consumption from simple inputs such as the number of fabric layers and stitch length.

An ensemble method called Extra Trees won clearly, predicting thread use with an average error of only a few centimeters and explaining the great bulk of the variation. Repeated cross-validation showed the model was stable rather than overfitted. The authors propose their prediction formula as a ready tool for garment manufacturers who want to order precisely and cut stock waste.
plos-pone-0356467:
Rashedul Hoque and three colleagues explore cheaper ways to measure the electrical state of living cells, in this 2026 study. The standard tool, patch clamp, reads a single cell through a fine glass pipette; it is accurate but slow, costly, and demands rare skill. The team instead used two techniques that read thousands of cells in under a minute, one based on how cells move in an electric field and one based on light scattering.

Working with a human bladder cancer cell line, they applied three drugs known to alter cell electrical behavior and compared the cheap methods' readings with published patch clamp results. The field-based technique matched patch clamp values closely for membrane voltage and conductance. The authors argue such methods could open routine electrical testing of cells to ordinary labs and speed up drug screening.
plos-pone-0356767:
Ally Motta de Matos and A L B Cruz test whether dogs and cats will actually eat food made with microbial protein, in PLOS ONE in 2026. Fermentation grown protein could ease pressure on meat supply chains, but a nutritious kibble that pets refuse is worthless. Thirty dogs and thirty cats took part in home based two bowl tests over four meals, choosing between a diet with ten percent microbial protein and a matched diet with ordinary protein.

Both species preferred the new diet by a clear statistical margin. Dogs ate a substantially larger share of the microbial bowl, and cats did the same on a smaller scale. Pets also approached and started on the new food first more often. Laboratory checks of the diets supported the preference readings. For pet food makers, the result removes the most basic obstacle: the animals themselves seem to like it.
plos-pone-0357267:
Yang Li and a team of engineers rebuild the software that checks earthquake sensor data for gaps and faults using modern cloud tools. Seismology networks now produce data faster than older server setups handle comfortably. Their design runs the quality checks in small software containers that grow or shrink with demand, guided by a scheduling method that watches processor and memory load plus task timing.

Under the same hardware budget, the cloud version answered requests about twice as fast as the older server version at both load levels tested, without changing the quality math itself. Li and colleagues are careful to limit the claim to the tested workloads. Still, the result suggests observatories can scale data checking up and down with quake activity.
plos-pone-0357367:
Netrang G. Desai and coauthors published a 2026 neuroscience paper in PLOS ONE on a structural detail braking the brain's main inhibitory receptor. GABA-A receptors, targets of sedatives, open when the messenger GABA binds, but how binding becomes opening is still murky. One amino acid, proline, sits in a linker segment of every subunit; only one subunit type carries a second proline nearby. The team inserted or removed that second proline in frog egg cells and recorded currents.

Adding the proline to the alpha subunit made the receptor far more sensitive to GABA and let channels open spontaneously with no messenger at all, as if a brake lifted. The same change in the gamma subunit did little. Removing the natural proline from the beta subunit produced mixed effects rather than simple loss. That subunit's linker proline, they conclude, acts as a molecular brake on activation.
plos-pone-0357467:
Michael O. Adu and David O. Yawson published a 2026 bibliometric study in PLOS ONE on a stark mismatch: crops feeding much of sub-Saharan Africa get little research on the organs they are harvested for. Cassava, yam, sweet potato, taro, and cocoyam supply a large calorie share, yet their root systems, which become the food, are barely studied. The authors paired food supply data from forty-six countries with nearly nine hundred publications spanning eight decades.

The region produces most of the world's cassava and nearly all yams but accounts for under a tenth of root research, clustering in Asia and North America. Potato attracts a fifth of the papers for a small calorie share; yams feed far more people for a sliver of attention, and taro and cocoyam are near-invisible. The most root-dependent countries publish almost nothing. Scenario models suggest fixing the imbalance could lift yields substantially.
plos-pone-0357567:
Tzu-Lan Chang and colleagues published a 2026 virology study in PLOS ONE on a workhorse of gene therapy: HIV-based lentivirus particles dressed in an envelope protein borrowed from another virus, VSV. The question was practical: how do the envelope's sugar chains change how virus particles behave in solution, and does behavior change infectivity? The team tracked particle clumping with light scattering and checked the picture with microscopy, filtration, and antibody tests.

The virus flipped between three states depending on serum, acidity, and calcium: clumped on its own, spread out, or clumped by calcium. Strikingly, the switching points sat right at the levels found in the human body, so small shifts in conditions could swing infectivity, and the three states infected cells at clearly different rates. Removing the envelope's end sugars destroyed the switching ability. Handling conditions near body-like values, they warn, can silently change a batch's potency.
plos-pone-0357667:
Tian-Qi Li and coauthors published a 2026 genetics study in PLOS ONE on tooth agenesis, the most common developmental dental disorder, in which some teeth never form. Known genes explain only part of cases. The team sequenced the protein-coding DNA of eighteen patients with the non-syndromic form. Two kinds of cluster analysis then hunted for unknown genes that keep known company.

Both clustering methods agreed, and one gene, EPB41L4A, landed in a cluster crowded with well-established tooth agenesis genes. That gene takes part in the Wnt signaling pathway, a master control system in embryonic development, which strengthens the suspicion. The authors are careful about what clustering can prove: genes grouped together tend to share functions, so EPB41L4A earns candidate status, not a verdict. It becomes a priority for follow-up experiments that could sharpen genetic counseling and diagnosis for families missing teeth.
plos-pone-0357767:
Qian Liu and coauthors published a 2026 study in PLOS ONE on malignant melanoma, the dangerous skin cancer, among East Asians aged sixty and older. Using the Global Burden of Disease 2023 dataset, they traced deaths and disability from 1990 to 2023 They then projected rates to 2040 with a multi-model forecasting system. It picked the best of seven candidate models for each place and measure.

Deaths among older adults more than doubled across the three decades, and years of healthy life lost rose steeply too, even though age-adjusted death rates barely moved. That gap points to population aging itself as the engine of the rising burden. Women showed higher incidence and prevalence, while men carried higher mortality and disability. Forecasts varied by location, with several places expected to plateau. The authors call for early-detection efforts and fair access to diagnosis and care aimed squarely at older adults.
plos-pone-0358267:
Gemechu Ameya led a team of five authors testing a traditional Ethiopian plant in the lab, published in PLOS ONE in 2026. Rumex abyssinicus roots have long been used in local medicine in southern Ethiopia. The team analyzed the roots' chemistry and tested their extracts against microbes in vitro.

Ameya's results support the folk remedy's germ-fighting power and identify the compounds likely responsible. Lab validation matters because it separates remedies that work from those that merely persist. It also guides safe dosing and further testing. Ethiopia's plant wealth is a national resource for drug discovery, and studies like this document it with modern methods before traditional knowledge is lost. The work stops at the lab stage, as it should, with clinical claims left for later evidence.
plos-pone-0358467:
Théo Dessier led a team of six authors who compared two ways of choosing health measures for pigs, published in PLOS ONE in 2026. Health indicators for farm animals are often picked by experts far from the barn. Dessier's proof-of-concept work instead asked the people involved, focusing on breathing health in pigs.

The team ran two participatory approaches side by side and compared what each produced. Their comparison shows which approach yields indicators that staff can actually use day to day. Farmers and vets gain a practical lesson: involving barn-level users early leads to measures that get recorded, not ignored. That matters because health checks only protect herds when they fit real routines.
plos-pone-0358567:
Pei-pei He leads a team of eight building a nanoparticle that turns tumor friendly immune cells against liver cancer, in PLOS ONE in 2026. Macrophages inside tumors often settle into a healing mode that shields the cancer. The team's particle is a hollow manganese shell carrying a drug that alarms the immune system, wrapped in a coat. In the tumor's acidic, antioxidant rich interior the shell dissolves, freeing both the drug and manganese ions that stimulate immunity and double as an MRI tracer.

In dishes, macrophages flipped from the tumor friendly mode to the attacking mode, with the proteins to prove it. Two immune pathways fired together. Injected into mouse liver tumors, the particles suppressed growth by about four fifths, with no poisoning of the animals. Treated tumors filled with attacking macrophages and emptied of the friendly kind. The strategy treats the tumor's guards as the drug's first target.
plos-pone-0358767:
Saisai Hou and three colleagues published an operations research paper in PLOS ONE in 2026. They dealt with demand for services that arrives in uneven bursts and in several types at once, such as patients reaching an emergency service on a bad night. Planners must set staffing before they know how heavy that demand will be.

Hou's team proposed a simulation method that strengthens decision checks under this kind of spread-out demand. Better calibration means plans hold up when real demand runs hotter or cooler than the average. Managers of clinics, call centers, and repair services face this same planning trap, so a method that respects messy demand can prevent both idle staff and long queues.
plos-pone-0358867: Chen and three co-authors published a 2026 PLOS ONE paper on car and vehicle suspension systems with two goals at once. The system should both hush road vibration and harvest energy from that shaking. Their controller mixes two control standards to balance comfort against power recovery. A suspension that powers its own sensors while riding smoothly would suit electric vehicles well.
plos-pone-0358967: Carmona-Rosado and seven co-authors published a 2026 PLOS ONE study on children in Madrid, Spain. They measured three linked things: whether homes had steady access to food, what children ate, and their weight status. The design was cross-sectional, a snapshot at one point in time. Linking food access with diet and weight can guide school meals and aid programs aimed at city families.
plos-pone-0359167: Liu and four co-authors published a 2026 PLOS ONE paper on a light object detector for drone cameras that see heat, not light. CAS-YOLO is built to be small and efficient on infrared images from unmanned aircraft. Spotting people or vehicles by heat helps rescue and patrol work at night. A light model can run on the drone itself instead of a distant server.
plos-pone-0359867: Liu, writing alone, published a 2026 PLOS ONE study on how to plan surveys about depression. The work uses decision theory, a formal way to weigh costs against the value of information. It covers both hiring enough of the right people to take part and checking that the survey plan is sound. A worked example uses a Chinese setting. Careful planning matters because weak samples can mislead mental health policy.
plos-pone-0360067:
Dikshya Adhikari, Hari Prasad Kaphle, Ramesh Ojha, and Chiranjivi Adhikari published this research article in PLOS ONE in 2026. It studies burnout among health workers in Pokhara, Nepal. The work is cross-sectional and hospital-based, gathering data from staff at one point in time.

Beyond measuring how common burnout is, the authors examine the factors associated with it, such as workload or role. Naming those factors tells hospital leaders where changes might protect staff. Health workers in stretched hospitals carry heavy emotional loads, so evidence from a Nepali setting adds to a largely Western literature on burnout.
plos-pone-0360667:
Abdullah Alshehri and colleagues compared adults living in high traffic and low traffic areas in 2026 to test links between environmental noise and jaw and dental problems. The conditions under study are temporomandibular joint disorders, which cause jaw pain and clicking, malocclusion, a poor bite alignment, and bruxism, the grinding of teeth often done in sleep. Chronic noise is a known stressor, and stress is a known driver of teeth grinding and jaw tension.

Their cross-sectional study measured these conditions in both groups of adults and examined the associations with noise exposure. If traffic noise truly raises rates of jaw disorders, the finding would add a quieter, less noticed item to the health bill that busy roads present to the people living beside them.
pmc-10652467:
Florence Jaguga and co-authors test a peer led substance use program for youth in Kenya in this 2023 paper. Young people in sub-Saharan Africa face high substance use risk. Few can reach professional services. The program used trained peers to screen youth and give a single brief counseling session.

Two peer providers served 100 youth aged 15 to 24 years. All sessions were recorded and rated for fidelity to the plan. Surveys measured whether the program was feasible and welcome. Focus groups with 25 youth and interviews with staff added depth. Scores supported both feasibility and acceptability. The model could widen access where clinics are scarce, using workers drawn from the community itself.
pmc-10655267:
Takeshi Tsuda, Kimberly Davidow, Gina D'Aloisio, and Joanne Quillen used exercise tests to sort childhood cancer survivors by heart risk, in a 2023 study. Survivors often show weak exercise capacity with no symptoms, a possible early sign of heart trouble. The team tested seventy-eight survivors aged ten and up, all off treatment. Each exercised under rising effort while the team tracked breath, heart rate, and oxygen use, then split the group by peak oxygen score.

Drug doses from cancer care were alike in both groups, so they do not explain the gap. The weak group carried a bit more weight and showed lower peak work and oxygen marks. Paired charts pointed to two culprits: less muscle mass and a heart that cannot raise its stroke volume on demand. Breathing efficiency dipped slightly too. The authors say the test pattern flags hidden heart weakness and shows where training could help.
pmc-10655367:
Jiana Lin and co-authors report, in a 2023 study, doubling the chromosome set of paper mulberry, a hardy tree valued for forage, ecology, and medicine. Plants with doubled genomes often outgrow their normal kin in nutrients and stress tolerance. The team wanted those gains for this species.

Leaves, callus tissue, and seeds were treated with colchicine, a chemical that blocks cell division's sorting step. Early shape, chromosome counts, and DNA measurements confirmed the doublings. The best recipe soaked leaves in a stated solution for three days, yielding success in about nineteen percent of attempts. A working protocol gives breeders raw material for tougher, richer mulberry lines.
pmc-10655467:
Lingke Liu and seven co-authors report a case in 2023 of a rare blood vessel tumor in a two year old boy. The tumor type usually appears in infants and young children, and can range from small surface growths to large invasive ones. This child also had low platelet counts and fingers that turned red or blue in the cold.

Scans found a mass near the spine, and a biopsy confirmed the tumor type. Tests showed shifts in signals that control blood vessel tone, which may explain the cold sensitivity in his hand. Treatment with a steroid drug and sirolimus led to steady improvement over follow up. The authors say this is the first reported case with this mix of signs.
pmc-10656467:
Viruses that infect soil bacteria remain poorly known, even in a model host studied for decades. Véronique Ongenae and co-authors describe two new such viruses in a 2023 paper. Both were found using a common Streptomyces strain as host. Each virus infected a wide range of related strains, but neither could infect a close sister group. Their genomes run just under fifty thousand letters.

Each genome holds seventy-two likely genes and a tool for slipping into the host's own genome. That tool points to a quiet lifestyle in which the virus hides inside the host. Both stayed stable across wide heat and acid ranges. The pair are classed as new species in a known genus. The work widens the map of viruses in this bacterial group.
pmc-10656567:
Xiao Liang, Lianjing Liang, and Yuchao Fan test whether fine dust in the air causes heart and vessel disease, in a 2023 study. The dust, known as PM2.5, is a major part of air pollution. The team used a genetic method that mimics a trial: gene variants linked to dust exposure served as tools. Data came from the UK Biobank, focused on people of European ancestry.

Across twenty-five diseases, higher dust exposure raised the odds of hardened arteries, angina, and long-term heart strain. It also raised odds of high blood pressure, palpitations, and stroke. Extra checks with other methods backed the main finds. The authors urge policy steps to cut dust levels for heart health.
pmc-10657367:
Kellianne Alexander and co-authors show how a gene switch directs the removal of young synapses in this 2023 study. As brains mature, some early links between nerve cells are pruned away. Working in a tiny worm, the team found that a regulator called DVE-1 runs this pruning in one class of nerve cells.

In worms lacking the regulator, young connection sites stayed in place into adulthood, leaving the motor circuit over-connected. The regulator works from the cell nucleus, which fits a role in switching genes on and off. Its target genes point to the cell's protein disposal system as the tool that clears the old links.
pmc-10657467:
Chang Zhao, Parker Webster, Alexis De Angeli, and Francesco Tombola describe a plant ion channel in 2023 with an odd two-step switch. Ion channels are gates in cell membranes; most open to either voltage or force. The channel found here, in the model plant Arabidopsis, needs both, in order.

A mechanical nudge must prime the channel before voltage can open it. The channel sits in the plant's vascular tissue and has cousins across vascular plants. Cousins outside flowering plants need no priming. Guided by AI-built models, the team found the residues that lock the channel shut. Force loosens that lock, they propose.
pmc-10657567:
Magdalena Łukowiak and co-authors read ancient sponges from a seaway that no longer exists in a 2023 paper. The Messinian Salinity Crisis nearly dried the Mediterranean and battered its sea life. The sample comes from late Miocene layers in southwest Spain, in the basin that then linked the Mediterranean to the Atlantic.

Isolated sponge spicules, the glassy needles that brace a sponge, made up the find. The community proved rich: at least thirty-four soft and stone sponge types, plus six glass sponge types. Eight species-level matches still live in the area today, and others now survive only in far refuges, from the Red Sea to Japanese waters. The authors argue the crisis shrank once-wide ranges into scattered pockets, and that this corridor fauna catches the world just before the cut.
pmc-10670667:
Alturkustani and co-authors take a fresh look in 2023 at how doctors pin down a rare brain tumor in children. The tumor has a long name and can be hard to tell apart from other growths under the microscope. A newer test sorts tumors by the chemical marks on their DNA, and its answer can clash with the classic look based answer.

Rather than ask which answer wins, the team studied the gaps between the two. They drew cases from a children's brain tumor database and sorted them into three groups by how the two methods agreed. One gene pair's status was checked in each case. The gaps revealed traits that may sharpen the rules for naming this tumor. Clearer rules mean a surer diagnosis, which shapes surgery and follow up care for each child.
pmc-10674467:
Patrick Hinsen and co-authors study in 2023 robotic swarms that explore and locate gas sources in moving air. Multi-robot systems offer redundancy and resilience in hazardous settings. To find leaks efficiently, robots must sample where measurements are most informative, using a model of how gas spreads.

Their method builds a spatial uncertainty map from a dispersion model that now includes wind-driven flow. A potential field guides robots across that map. Wind direction swings make the task fundamentally harder, simulations show. Still, the swarm recovers source candidates within seconds and rivals systematic sampling, with larger swarms cutting uncertainty faster.
pmc-10687167:
Guanghua Che and co-authors validate a Chinese scale for the urges that precede tics, in this 2023 study. Many children with tic disorders feel a building urge before a tic, and gauging that urge can guide care. The team translated and adapted a scale that rates each child's own urges by number, frequency, and strength, then tested it on a clinic sample.

The scale proved reliable and sound. Urges clustered at the head, face, and throat, and stronger urges tracked with worse tics. Urge scores also rose alongside compulsive symptoms, anxiety, and attention problems, which the authors say can sharpen treatment choices.
pmc-10690967:
Ding and co-authors build a new food swap system to guide healthy eating in pregnancy for women in China. Swap systems let people trade one food for another of like value, but the older Chinese system was made for patients, not for pregnancy. Their 2023 system covers about 500 foods in ten groups, with finer portion sizes and a guide score for picking foods.

Dietitians used both the new and the old system to rewrite the same sample meals, making 40 menus each. Menus from the new system held more whole grains, beans, fruit, fish, and eggs, landing closer to national guide targets. They also supplied more of several vitamins and minerals, such as folate and calcium. Portion errors shrank as well, so the authors judge the new tool fit for pregnancy care.
pmc-10691067:
Five researchers find a leaf shape that flags haploid rice plants early in a paper from 2023. Doubled haploid breeding speeds up crop improvement, but half the plants stay haploid and useless unless treated. Growers normally raise every plant to maturity just to find the fertile ones. The team compared haploid and doubled plants across growth and flower traits. Photosynthesis and water loss differed, as did flower part shapes.

One marker stood out: haploids always had sharply pointed leaf tips, while doubled plants had drawn-out tips. Checks with a DNA content instrument matched the leaf calls perfectly. The authors say the cheap visual test can rescue haploids for treatment early. It also cuts the cost of raising unwanted plants.
pmc-10691467:
Jacques Bughin argues that whether AI cuts jobs hinges on a firm's posture toward the technology, in work from twenty twenty-three. What matters is how mature its AI use is, and whether AI aims at new products or mere automation. Debate on AI and jobs fixates on task replacement. Strategy, he notes, decides what firms do with the freed power.

A game theory model frames firms weighing innovation against automation for profit and edge. Its prediction: job change after AI adoption is not doomed to be negative, and rides on innovation success and profit sharing. A survey of three thousand large firms in ten countries matched the model. Employment grew where AI maturity and product innovation bias ran high.
pmc-10692067:
Jaewook Lee and co-authors review the role of missing oxygen atoms in hafnium oxide in this 2023 paper. The material is known as HfO2. It is promising for ferroelectric and resistive switching memory. It also fits well with standard chip making methods. The missing atoms are called oxygen vacancies, and they are its most common defect.

Vacancies shape which crystal forms appear and how strong the ferroelectric effect is. They also affect switching speed, endurance, and variation between devices. In resistive devices, their motion and grouping form the main switching mechanism. The review explains how vacancies form and how they change chemical, physical, and electric traits. Device makers can use it to tune performance.
pmc-10692267:
Anders Bech Jorgensen and three co-authors reviewed bacteria and surgical leaks in a 2023 paper. After bowel surgery, the rejoined ends sometimes leak, a dangerous complication. Some gut bacteria make enzymes that dissolve collagen, the protein that holds the healing join together, and they are suspects in these leaks.

Following standard review rules, the team gathered fifteen studies covering nearly fifty-three thousand patients, of whom about seventeen hundred had leaks. Samples came from stool, bowel lining, removed tissue, or drain fluid. In ten of the fifteen studies, collagen-dissolving bacteria turned up in leak patients. Yet no study counted the bacteria or measured the enzyme itself, and methods varied widely. The authors conclude the suspects are commonly present but not yet proven guilty. Sharper studies that quantify the germs are the needed next step.
pmc-10693067:
Jinquan Liu and co-authors compare two surgical choices for gout-driven carpal tunnel syndrome, in a 2023 study. Gout can deposit stony crystals inside the wrist tunnel, squeezing the median nerve. Surgeons clearing the tunnel must decide what to do with the diseased finger tendon inside. One option trims the damaged part, and the other removes the tendon outright. The study covered ten patients with thirteen affected wrists.

Nine wrists were trimmed and four had the tendon removed. All wrists were cleared of gout stones, and numbness eased in every case. At follow-up near fourteen months, finger movement and standard hand scores showed no clear gap between the groups. Both groups improved a lot over their pre-surgery state. One trimmed wrist saw the lesion return after a year. The authors present trimming as a sound default, with removal held in reserve.
pmc-10693167:
Ine Cockerell and a large team read a drug's real-world worth in a gene ill in a 2023 study. The ill grows benign lumps in brain, kidney, and skin and sparks seizures. Trials had shown the drug everolimus helps, but ward proof ran thin. The team tracked 64 patients in Norway and Denmark, mid age 19. Seizure, kidney lump, and brain lump reads came from live care charts.

Of 45 seizure patients, near a third halved their fits. Youth beat adults on that mark by a wide span. Kidney lumps shrank in near four of ten and held in most of the rest. Brain lumps shrank in three tracked cases. Side harms hit 95 percent, led by mouth sores. Nine quit the drug. The authors call the drug sound but watch-heavy.
pmc-10693567:
Tyler Hornsby and co-authors model in 2023 how sound waves shake a cancer drug loose from gold nanoparticles. Ultrasound can trigger drug release on demand, and the group's earlier work freed the drug doxorubicin from gold particles under gentle pulsed sound. What was missing was the timing: how fast the drug leaves, and by what mix of heat and force.

A new membrane setup measured release at body temperature and at a warmer, fever-range level. Non-heat effects, such as the push of the sound field, accounted for about a third to two fifths of the release. The release curve fit a known model that points to a mixed diffusion process, neither purely still nor purely stirred. A computer model estimated the sound's pushing force inside the test bag. The authors offer the kinetics as a base for tuning such treatments.
pmc-10693867:
Roeland Lameris and co-authors study how a small antibody changes what the immune protein CD1d shows to T cells. CD1d presents lipid antigens and sits on some tumor cells, including multiple myeloma. A single-domain antibody that targets CD1d was known to boost binding of annexin V, a marker read as a sign of cell death. Their 2023 paper asks what really drives that signal.

Cell assays and gene editing showed the antibody does not kill the tumor cells. Instead, it boosts how much phosphatidylserine CD1d presents, and that lipid drives the marker binding. Crystal work revealed the antibody and CD1d joined with a natural lipid inside. Immunology readers get a corrected story with a new immune link.
pmc-10694867:
Marta Gariglio and a team of co-authors tested whether live insect larvae make life better for Muscovy ducks, in a 2023 farm study. Ducks in pens can turn aggressive, and giving them something to forage may calm that behavior. The team offered larvae of black soldier fly or yellow mealworm on top of normal feed.

They raised 126 young female ducks in 18 pens, split among plain feed and the two larva diets. Growth, weight gain, and feed use were tracked for about eight weeks, along with stress markers in droppings, filmed behavior, and blood tests. Growth did not differ across groups. The ducks ate both larva types at much the same speed, with one age window where fly larvae went faster. The design lets the team weigh welfare gains against plain performance.
pmc-10694967:
Irene Novo and co-authors test when a popular tool for past population size gives skewed answers, in a 2023 study. The tool, GONE, reads one DNA sample to trace how a group's breeding size changed in recent history. Breeders and conservation teams lean on it for rare species. Its math, though, assumes the group stayed sealed off from others.

The team ran computer worlds that break that seal in four ways: merged ancient groups, steady migrant swaps, inflow from a big source, and flipped chromosome blocks. Deep past mergers skewed the size reads the most. Slow steady migration and common flips also bent the results. Two fixes helped: split the sample by true subgroup first, or drop the flipped zones from the read. The authors urge a structure check before any history claim.
pmc-10695467:
Sara Zarei and co-authors report a severe case of raised pressure inside the skull in a 2023 paper with a literature review. The condition, idiopathic intracranial hypertension, builds pressure with no tumor or fluid blockage to explain it. Their patient was a thirty-two-year-old woman whose chronic headaches led first to a polycystic ovary diagnosis.

Despite top medical treatment and a surgical window cut into the optic nerve sheath, she lost vision in both eyes completely. Nearly five years later she came to the authors' clinic with ringing in the ears, hearing loss on one side, joint pain, and high inflammation markers. The paper walks through how each companion condition may link to the pressure disorder, a cautionary tale about guarding vision early.
pmc-10696067:
Heba Abunahla and co-authors build a memory device from carbon nanotubes for brain-like computing, in a 2023 paper. In spiking neural networks, doing the math inside the memory itself saves the energy of shuttling data around. Their memristor uses a single layer of single-wall carbon nanotubes as its switching film, laid out in a flat structure.

The device switches smoothly through many levels rather than snapping between two, and its states stay stable, with both conductance and capacitance open to tuning. Wired into a spiking network, it carried out the core multiply-and-add work at ninety-five percent classification accuracy. Each spike cost only a few femtojoules, the team reports, pointing to very frugal learning hardware.
pmc-10696767:
Kishore Garapati and co-authors present a 2023 methods paper on sBioSITe, a sensitive way to catalogue the proteins sitting on a cell's surface. Surface proteins run immunity, signalling, and movement, and their pattern defines what a cell is; disease rewrites the pattern. Yet fishing them out cleanly has stayed hard, since they are scarce and sticky.

The method tags surface proteins with biotin while cells are intact, digests everything, then pulls out exactly the tagged fragments for identification. Skipping several lossy steps keeps more of the rare material. The authors show the direct route finds surface proteins with high sensitivity, giving cell biologists and drug hunters a cleaner census.
pmc-10698967:
Paulo Andrés Cano and five co-authors published a study in 2023 on a device that lets surgeons work on one lung while the other rests collapsed. Chest operations need that still, open view, and a bronchial blocker tube is one way to get it, though many anesthetists still prefer older double-lumen tubes. The team reviewed their center's experience across seven years of chest surgery.

They analyzed 134 patients, most operated for lung cancer, across lung, pleural, and chest wall procedures. Collapse was rated excellent or good in about ninety-seven percent of cases. More than ninety percent of patients had no complications during or just after surgery. Video-assisted operations and side positioning gave the best collapse. The record supports the blocker as a safe default.
pmc-10699067:
Awoke Mihretu and co-authors study how the COVID-19 pandemic hit mental health care in Ethiopia in a 2023 paper. People with existing mental health conditions faced added risk, yet low-income countries drew little research focus. The team combined several methods to get a fuller picture.

They mapped public reports, tracked monthly visits at the main psychiatric hospital, and interviewed key informants. Visit data from 2019 and 2020 were compared with a segmented model. Early in the pandemic, services shrank and patients struggled to reach care. The study shows why mental health services need protection during crises. Its lessons apply to other low-resource health systems as well.
pmc-10699167:
Glyphosate is the world's most used weed killer, yet how much of it reaches pregnant people living near farms is poorly known. Cynthia Curl and co-authors follow forty pregnant people in southern Idaho through 2021 in this 2023 study, testing their urine about every two weeks.

For those living close to fields, the chemical showed up more often and at higher levels during spray season than outside it. For those living farther away, levels stayed flat across the year. Outside spray season, near and far homes looked the same. The pattern points to farm spraying as a real source of exposure for nearby residents.
pmc-10700467:
Min Huang and ten co-authors report a real-world study of two COVID vaccines used widely in China, BBIBP-CorV and CoronaVac, in a paper published in two thousand twenty-three. Clinical trials had set their value, but long-term blood data from daily use were thin. The team drew blood from one hundred eleven vaccinated donors in the Nanjing area, plus six volunteers tracked in depth, and compared them with recovered patients.

Nine in ten vaccinated donors had made neutralizing antibodies. Levels peaked about four weeks after the shots, fell fast at first, then eased slowly and could still be found about nine months on. Five of the six tracked volunteers held strong levels; one barely responded at all. The authors say both vaccines work well for most adults, but personal response varies a lot.
pmc-10701867:
Zhenzhen Guo and co-authors build a power sheet from spent battery waste that runs on water drops in 2023. Ambient energy harvest needs cheap stock and steady output. Their sheet has an uneven build drawn from battery residue. A tenth of a milliliter of water triggers about half a volt. Ions in the water boost the effect.

Seawater drops pushed output higher still. Power density reached a solid level for such small inputs. The design is simple and the stock is waste. The authors see supply for low power gadgets as the use case. The work turns a disposal problem into a power source. Field life and scale up remain to be proven.
pmc-10701967:
Yanrong Wang and co-authors compare two families of immune drugs for advanced small-cell lung cancer, using real hospital records rather than a trial. Both drug types are combined with the same chemotherapy and given as first treatment. One family blocks a protein called PD-1, and the other blocks its partner, PD-L1.

The study covered 194 patients treated at three centers of one hospital system between 2017 and 2021. Time before the cancer grew again was nearly the same in both groups, at roughly six to seven months. Overall survival also matched closely, and about three quarters of patients in each group saw their tumors shrink. Side effects severe enough to stop treatment were rare in both groups. The authors conclude that the two drug families perform alike in real-world care. Choice between them can rest on other factors, such as cost and availability.
pmc-10704767:
Alongside their normal genomes, coronaviruses churn out many broken copies called defective viral genomes. Whether those fragments can actually build proteins was unknown. Ching-Hung Lin and co-authors combined nanopore direct RNA sequencing with mass spectrometry to find out. The sequencing mapped the defective genomes in infected cells. Protein databases built from those maps then guided the search through cell extracts.

The team identified six proteins encoded by defective genomes. Each was betrayed by a fusion peptide, a joined stretch created when the defective copy was stitched together during synthesis. The result shows defective genomes are not dead ends but can carry working protein recipes. Understanding what those proteins do could clarify how coronaviruses cause disease and suggest antiviral strategies.
pmc-10705767:
Takumi Sato, Yasumasa Kakei, Takumi Hasegawa, and a team of co-authors test whether gold nanoparticles can make standard treatments hit head and neck cancer harder. The antibody drug cetuximab targets a growth signal these tumors carry, but it works weakly and brings harsh side effects, while gold particles were known to amplify radiation's local punch.

In dishes, the triple combination of particles, drug, and radiation killed far more cancer cells than any single or double treatment. In mice carrying human tumors, the same trio shrank tumors the most, and microscopes confirmed the particles reached the tumor tissue. Safety checks found no harm to normal tissue. The authors stress the particles alone did nothing; their value is as sensitizers that make the other treatments count.
pmc-10707367:
María Luna-Luna and co-authors test how the kidneys handle cholesterol carried by HDL, the so-called good cholesterol particles, in rabbits. Their 2023 study starts from a puzzle: earlier work suggested kidneys help manage these particles, but their role is disputed. The team reduced kidney mass by three quarters in a rabbit model to see what changes.

They tracked labeled cholesterol esters moving through the blood. With less kidney tissue, HDL particles grew richer in those esters. Exchange with other lipoprotein types did not change much. Total outflow of the esters from plasma fell when flows from both particle types were combined. The results support a kidney role in cholesterol balance.
pmc-10707567:
Mingzhi Wang and four co-authors built a computer method to help spot autism from brain scans, in a 2023 paper. Current diagnosis rests on observed behavior and can be a matter of judgment. Brain scans offer a more direct measure of brain activity. Past scan-based models have not reached the accuracy doctors need.

Their method, MAACNN, mixes two kinds of learning in stages. First, a noise-removing network pulls features from scans at several scales without labels. Then labeled learning sorts people into groups, with an attention step to blend the scales. Tests used a large shared autism data set in two parts. The method scored above seventy percent accuracy on both parts. The authors say it could aid clinical diagnosis, though it is not a stand-alone test.
pmc-10708767:
Fatema Kaladari and co-authors build a glowing sensor for vitamin B7. Their 2023 paper deals with biotin, a vitamin mammals must take in, so supplement levels need checking. Stock assays crawl and cost. Their compound ties biotin to a quinone that glows through a redox cycle with a helper and luminol. When avidin, biotin's partner protein, grabs the compound, the glow dims.

Free biotin then fights for the seat and frees the compound, and the glow returns. That contest forms the assay, which read vitamin tablets with sound recovery and tight spread. A no-biotin quinone proved the contest real.
pmc-10709267:
Yusuke Uchinami and co-authors report, in a 2023 study, results for a gentler chemotherapy rhythm in older patients with advanced head and neck cancer. The standard pairing of radiation with cisplatin every three weeks can be too harsh for older adults to finish. A weekly, lower-dose rhythm promises milder side effects. The team reviewed patients aged seventy and over who began that weekly plan over sixteen years.

Forty-nine patients formed the study group, with a median age in the early seventies. Their cancers sat in the throat or voice box, at stages three or four, with no spread to distant sites. Radiation reached the full planned dose in most cases. The paper weighs three-year survival and the factors that shaped it, aiming to show when the weekly rhythm serves older patients well.
pmc-10709367:
Nicolaj Hackert and seven co-authors compare immune cells in mice and people in this twenty twenty-three study. Neutrophils, the most common white blood cells, are often studied in mice, but it is unclear how far mouse findings carry over to human care.

The team merged data from many mouse and human studies, covering both calm states and states of swelling and infection. Gene activity in the cells matched well across the two species. Swollen tissue brought wide variety, yet a shared core program stood out, with genes for alarm signals and surface markers. Tests in lab-grown cells confirmed two gene switches help drive that core program, which supports using mouse work to guide human study.
pmc-10709567:
Mohamed and five co-authors published this study in twenty twenty-three on finding key genes in lung cancer. With thousands of genes active in a tumor, the hard part is picking out the few that matter most. The team built a new selection tool that pairs a search method modeled on virus spread with voting among several classifier models. They applied it to a large public lung cancer gene dataset.

The tool flagged ten hub genes tied closely to lung cancer. Network analysis confirmed these genes sit at busy crossroads in the cell. The study also highlighted pathways for calcium signals and saliva production as notable in the data. The authors say the method can sharpen diagnosis research and guide future work on how the disease develops.
pmc-10709667:
Dams on the upper Yangtze River can leave water loaded with too much dissolved gas. Quan Yuan and co-authors test what that gas load does to young fish of one migratory kind in their 2023 study. Fish face four gas levels, from normal to well above normal, while water speed runs from still up to fast flows. Too much gas can cause bubble harm in fish and cut their odds of living and swimming well.

Deaths start once flow passes set speeds, and the speed that kills shifts with the gas level. At the two high gas levels, mid-range speeds give the longest life span, while still water and fast water both do worse. Jointly, gas level and flow speed shape the risk. The results help judge the harm dam releases pose to fish on their runs.
pmc-10709867:
Mohammadreza Mehryar and co-authors study the enzymes that help join cut DNA ends when the CRISPR tool Cas9 is used to rearrange chromosomes. Such edits come out exact and easy to predict, thanks to the tool's tidy cuts, yet the join work behind that result was not well understood.

The team built a program to read the join sites fast and an assay that uses cell growth to flag edits. Large cuts back at the joins were common. Turning down one enzyme shifted the balance: more large cuts, fewer small losses. Two enzymes acted in opposed ways on losses of one base versus more, a split the team map out.
pmc-10709967:
Mengyuan Fu and twelve co-authors count risky drug use in older Parkinson's patients in China in a 2023 paper. Some drugs harm older adults more than they help. Parkinson's patients have complex drug needs across motor and mind symptoms. How often risky drugs reach them in China was unknown.

The team read a national insurance database from 2015 to 2017. It held 14,452 patients aged 65 and over with the disease. About 58 percent got at least one risky drug in that span. About 43 percent got a drug that can dull the mind. Use rose with age and ran higher in women. Younger patients got more motor-risk drugs, though. The authors urge targeted work on safer prescribing.
pmc-10710567:
Taijun Hana, Satoshi Takahashi, Yuki Kawaguchi, and Soichi Oya test, in a 2023 study, if ChatGPT can advise brain tumor patients on when to seek care. Brain tumors hit about 20,000 people a year in Japan, and some need fast care. Lay knowledge is thin, though, so people may wait in spite of clear nerve signs. A wise adviser who urges a clinic visit could cut that wait. ChatGPT holds wide knowledge and can be reached at all hours, which makes it a candidate for that role.

The team played patients with set tumor signs and asked the tool for advice. It urged a hospital visit in all cases, with the right sense of speed and the right ward. When patients balked and said no, it kept up its push to go. Noise facts mixed in did not throw it off.
pmc-10710967:
Dina Sweed and co-authors studied why some hydatid cysts can breed and others cannot. The cysts come from a tapeworm that spreads between animals and people and is common in Egypt. Their 2023 study covered fifty-eight patients whose cysts were classed as fertile or non-fertile by whether they held young tapeworm heads. The team stained cyst tissue for granzyme B, a protein immune cells use to kill targets, and for two immune cell markers.

Granzyme B ran higher in non-fertile cysts and rose with the level of swelling in the cyst wall. It did not track the wall's scar tissue. The protein also rose alongside both cell markers. The authors suggest it fuels swelling and may block cyst fertility.
pmc-10711867:
Virtual doctor visits grew fast, but Indigenous patients say the tools for judging those visits were not built with them. Pamela Roach and nine co-authors worked with Indigenous patients and an advisory group to build such a tool, in a 2023 study. Earlier interviews had set four themes: access, relationships, quality, and safety. The team then tested draft statements with five patients and refined the wording with advisors.

The finished tool has twelve statements that patients can use to rate virtual primary care. Because Indigenous people shaped it at every step, the authors say it reflects their view of good care and is ready for clinic use.
pmc-10712067:
A family of enzymes called carotenoid cleavage oxygenases cuts carotenoids into scent compounds and two plant hormones. Jannat Akram and co-authors mapped this gene family across the whole cucumber genome for the first time, and compared it with the matching family in a well-studied model plant. They found ten such genes, mostly sitting in the cytoplasm and chloroplasts of cells. The family splits into seven branches, including the groups that make each hormone.

Control regions next to the genes carry switches for growth, hormone signals, and stress responses, and 84 small RNAs help regulate the family. Two genes, CsCCD7 and CsNCED2, switched on hardest when cucumbers got a cold-protecting treatment. Others were most active in organs tied to sap flow. The authors say the map lays groundwork for breeding and gene studies.
pmc-10712167:
Gupta and co-authors review in 2023 trials of a calming drug given as a mist before surgery. Placing a breathing tube can spike heart rate and blood pressure, which may harm weak patients. The mist form spreads over a wide surface and may avoid the slow heart rate seen with drip delivery.

The team searched six databases up to March 2023 for trials in adults under full sleep for surgery. Two reviewers screened the work on their own against set rules. Trials had to report heart rate and blood pressure around tube placement. The pooled results aim to show if the mist is safe and works well enough for routine use.
pmc-10713667:
Md Shawon and co-authors measured psychological distress and unhealthy eating among adolescents in sixty-one countries in two thousand twenty-three. Data came from a global school-based health survey. Distress was counted when a student reported at least two of loneliness, anxiety, or suicidal thoughts, plans, or attempts.

Among two hundred twenty-two thousand four hundred one students, distress prevalence was about eighteen percent, higher in girls than boys. The African region was highest and South-East Asia lowest. Half the students drank soft drinks daily, and over half ate fast food weekly. Distress linked to each unhealthy habit, from low fruit and vegetable intake to soft drinks and fast food. The authors note wide regional variation.
pmc-10714067:
Adélie Antoine and nine co-authors follow mother Weddell seals hunting under Antarctic sea ice in a 2023 study from Terre Adélie, East Antarctica. Feeding a pup is the most costly part of a seal's life, yet fine detail on how mothers hunt was scarce.

In 2019 the team fitted three nursing females with sonar tags for seven days. The seals spent most of their time hauled out on the ice. Dives were shallow compared with other seasons, and all feeding lunges took place on the seafloor. The tags logged 331 prey capture attempts, with 125 prey sized on the sonar echoes. Half the prey fought back or fled. The study gives a close view of how these mothers balance feeding themselves and their pups.
pmc-10715767:
Eszter Csibra and Guy-Bart Stan introduce a web tool for lab data in a 2023 paper. Labs use plate readers to run many small tests at once. These machines export results in odd formats with little labeling. Analysis software, by contrast, wants neat tables with clear labels.

Their app, Parsley, bridges that gap without any coding. Users point to the parts of a file that hold each kind of data. The app then extracts a tidy table ready for analysis. It handles more than ten machine types and over fifty data kinds. No install is needed, since the tool runs in a web browser. The authors aim to speed up lab work and help staff who do not code.
pmc-10716167:
Yicun Liu and seven co-authors build a competing RNA network to probe how liver cancer forms, centered on circular RNAs that sponge small RNAs. Liver cancer is a top cause of cancer death worldwide. The study came out in twenty twenty-three.

Profile scans found thousands of changed circular RNAs in tumor tissue. The top risers were checked in a fresh patient group by a gene copy test, and five were picked for network work. Database hunts traced their down stream small RNAs and target messages, which formed the network maps. Five chains in the network link to worse outlook for patients, the authors report.
pmc-10716667:
Ivan Dvoyashov and co-authors trace the family history of rock voles in a 2023 paper. The voles form a subgenus of Central Asian mountain voles with two species. Their relationships were murky because samples were few and single-gene trees disagreed with each other.

The team sequenced thousands of nuclear markers in twenty voles from five species, and dated splits in a mitochondrial gene. Nuclear data showed each species is a clean group of its own. The mitochondrial mismatch was best explained by ancient cross-breeding rather than by sorting noise. The authors link the mixing to wide migrations during the late ice age, when populations split and met again. They frame the study as a start for work on the whole genus.
pmc-10716967:
Marjolein Stip and co-authors wrote this 2023 review on turning the tumor's own guards into attackers in neuroblastoma. This childhood cancer surrounds itself with myeloid cells, white blood cells that build a suppressive web shielding the tumor. High-risk cases lean on that shield hard.

The review first maps what each myeloid type does for and against the tumor. It then sorts the counter-strategies into three plays: recruit the cells as effectors, as already happens with anti-GD2 therapy; block their arrival or remove them; or reprogram them from guards into attackers. A warning threads the survey: draining the swamp also drains potential effectors. The most promising routes sharpen existing antibodies, for instance by blocking the don't-eat-me signal. The authors chart a crowded but hopeful front.
pmc-10717267:
Tatton and Lloyd review smoking cessation services for pregnant women in the United Kingdom, in work from twenty twenty-three. Smoking in pregnancy raises risks of miscarriage, stillbirth, low birth weight, preterm birth, and childhood asthma. Quitting rates through services have stayed disappointingly low.

Less than half of pregnant women who accessed services in England over a decade reported quitting. The rapid realist review asks for whom services work, under what conditions, and how. Realist methods look for context and mechanism, not just average effect. The findings can help redesign services around the women who currently fall through.
pmc-10717767:
Haiqing Zheng and co-authors link vegetable habits to kidney function in very old Chinese adults. Kidney function was gauged by a rate that estimates how well the kidneys filter blood. Data came from a long-running survey of healthy longevity in China, with waves in 2011 to 2012 and 2014. Diet reports split fresh vegetables from salt-preserved ones at each wave.

People who ate fresh vegetables only now and then had lower filter rates than near-daily eaters. The gap held after checks for other traits of the group. People who rarely or never ate salt-preserved vegetables had higher rates than daily eaters of them. The authors back diets rich in fresh vegetables for kidney health in the oldest adults.
pmc-10718267:
A December 2023 obituary listing records the deaths of Canadian physicians, in the style of a medical journal's monthly notices. Each entry gives the doctor's name, home city, medical school and graduation year, and field of practice. Most entries add the date and age of death and the close family who survive.

The entries run in alphabetical order and link out to fuller obituaries. Early entries include an internist from Orangeville who trained at the University of Toronto. A child psychiatrist from Kingston and an anesthesiologist from Victoria also appear. So does a family doctor in Nova Scotia who trained in Cairo. Ages at death in the visible entries range from the late fifties to the mid eighties. The listing serves as a record of service for the profession and a notice board for colleagues.
pmc-10718467:
Greta Tuckute and co-authors test whether audio neural networks mirror the hearing brain in a 2023 study. Networks that predict brain responses offer one yardstick for understanding a sense. Such models lead in vision research but were little checked for hearing.

The team scored public audio networks plus in-house models trained on four tasks. Most beat classic filter models at predicting auditory cortex responses. Middle network stages matched early cortex best, while deep stages matched later regions. A few top models, though, predicted poorly. Training on speech in noise helped more than speech in quiet, and multi-task training gave the best overall fits.
pmc-10719267:
Nilesh Satpute and co-authors published this nanomaterials study in 2023. They made magnetic nanoparticles of a lanthanum cobalt oxide using a green recipe. Extract of Jatropha curcas leaves served as the natural agent in a water-based synthesis. The team probed the particles with tools covering structure, shape, composition, and light behavior. Magnetic measurements came from a sensitive SQUID instrument.

The grains were small spheres, with crystal units near eleven nanometers and grains near twenty-four. Spectroscopy confirmed the intended mix of lanthanum and cobalt in the right charge states. The material behaved as a semiconductor with a wide band gap near 4.95 electron volts. As a catalyst under sunlight, it broke down methylene blue dye fully within about two hours, faster than three rival dyes. Magnetically, the particles showed antiferromagnetic coupling and single-molecule magnet traits. The authors pitch the green-made particles for cleaning dyed water.
pmc-10719367:
David Yardeni and co-authors question a score used to rank liver patients for care, in a 2023 study. The score, MELD-Na, helps judge how sick a patient is and who should get a transplant first. The team focus on fatty liver disease tied to metabolism, called MASLD, where high pressure in liver veins can arise early.

They reviewed 326 patients found to have swollen veins in the throat or stomach, a sign of that pressure. The MASLD group bled from those veins more often than groups with liver harm from viruses or alcohol, about 36 percent against 26 to 30 percent. Their MELD-Na scores near the first bleed ran lower, yet at mid-range scores their survival was worse. The score may thus rank these patients as less sick than they are, which could delay the care they need.
pmc-10720467:
Esohe Fawole and William Ristenpart report a surprising charge effect in this 2023 paper. A metal electrode held at high voltage normally takes a capacitive charge that drains away at once when the voltage is removed.

The team found that in moist air, when the wire linking the supply to the electrode joins two different metals, extra charge builds up slowly on top of the expected charge. Stranger still, that extra charge stays after the voltage is switched off, and even after the electrode is lifted out of the measuring cup. They report charge amounts and rates across voltages, metal pairings, and humidity levels, explain the effect through a proposed water ionization process, and discuss what it means for high voltage fluid systems.
pmc-10721167:
Agrippa Dube and co-authors review in a 2023 paper how heat shapes the snails that host a liver fluke. The fluke ill is a left-out tropic ill borne by snails in fresh water. A warming world shifts snail life, and with it the reach of the ill.

The team swept lab and model work on heat and the host snails: how fast they grow, breed, and die at each grade. Such life marks set where the fluke can ride. The sweep pulls a loose field into one place. Health and farm teams in warm lands gain a clear view of a risk that climbs with the heat.
pmc-10722267:
Jianli Zhou and Linyuan Qin studied caffeine in urine and metabolic syndrome in United States adults in two thousand twenty-three. Past work looked only at how much caffeine people drink. Urine levels of caffeine and its breakdown products may tell a different story.

They used a national health survey from two thousand eleven to two thousand fourteen, with two thousand three hundred ninety-four adults. Fifteen caffeine-related measures were grouped into two main components that explained most of the variation. Both components linked to higher risk of metabolic syndrome and central obesity after adjustment. One also linked to lower risk of raised triglycerides, and one showed a U-shaped link with that risk. Patterns differed by component.
pmc-10724367:
Vijendra Ramlall and co-authors teach a machine learning model to guess which hospital visits involved COVID-19, then use those guesses to hunt the disease's long shadow. Records often fail to say clearly whether a visit was a COVID visit, which muddies studies of after-effects. Their 2023 study trains a random forest on electronic health records to score each visit with a probability.

Higher probabilities of a past COVID visit tracked with later diagnoses of heart attack, urinary tract infection, acute kidney failure, and type 2 diabetes. The authors offer the scoring trick as a cleaning tool for the endemic era, when research must squeeze truth from messy routine records. The associations line up with reported long COVID burdens, though the method shows correlation, not proof of cause.
pmc-10724867:
Prasanna Sonar, Aarati Panchbhai, and Aachal Lande report a 2023 case of Ludwig angina, a fast spreading infection of the floor of the mouth and neck. The infection swells both sides of the jaw area and can close the airway, which makes it life threatening. It often starts from a tooth infection and lifts the tongue, causing noisy breathing as the airway narrows.

The report stresses fast diagnosis and a clear plan as the steps that save lives. Securing the airway comes first, in this case by a planned surgical opening in the neck. Draining the infected spaces and giving strong antibiotics through a vein follow. The authors offer the case to sharpen clinical knowledge of this rare emergency and to add a detailed patient account to the record.
pmc-10725967:
Maryam Alabbad and co-authors published a 2023 bibliometric analysis of research on early signs of language-based learning disabilities. These disorders include dyslexia, dyscalculia, and dysgraphia, which affect how children handle spoken and written language. The team mapped studies that used brain and cognitive measures to find early predictors. Their source was the Web of Science, covering work from 1991 to late 2021.

The search gathered 921 publications. Output grew slowly in the 1990s, then rose in recent years. Neuroimage and Neuropsychologia led the journal list, and the United States led by country. Hot topics included neuroimaging, fMRI, and cortical thickness. The authors argue that early predictors could anchor prevention programs for very young children. Combining brain measures with cognitive tests may sharpen future work.
pmc-10726967:
James Bates and co-authors show that a cysteine-based compound both prevents and reverses physical dependence on morphine in rats, in a 2023 study. Dependence may grow as morphine blocks cysteine transport into neurons. That transport feeds the brain's antioxidant defenses. Restoring cysteine supply could break the chain.

Male rats received a morphine depot for a day and a half. The test compound slips easily into cells. A blocking drug then triggered withdrawal signs in untreated animals. Treated rats showed far weaker dependence, and reversal as well. Opioid dependence treatments today are themselves opioids. A non-opioid shield would change addiction care. Human trials remain distant but the mechanism is fresh.
pmc-10729167:
Marianne Saragosa and co-authors asked young carers how health care treats them and what help they want in 2023. Young carers give regular, heavy care, often more than an adult helper would. Their dealings with clinics and hospitals were little known.

Interviews and focus groups with eight young carers ran in 2022, then a co-design workshop built on their words. Three themes emerged: finding their way in the system as carers, being kept out of the loop, and care slowly becoming normal life. The workshop sorted wishes into supports aimed at carers and moves to raise awareness inside the system. The study argues carers should help design the services meant for them.
pmc-10729267:
Nine authors lay out a scope plan for gain-risk reads in health tech calls in a 2023 protocol. Gain-risk math weighs good ends against bad in drug and tech life spans, yet its use in value boards is dim. The plan hunts guide and method works on the theme by set rules. Two big banks plus board sites form the hunt field.

Set forms screen the finds by two lone reads in the plan. Counts and charts will sum the field in the end work. The read needs no ethics pass since all data are in the open. Gains aim at boards and rule shops.
pmc-10729967:
Peptides that self-assemble into fibers are candidate materials for growing cells and carrying drugs, and swapping one ingredient's acid changes the fiber's shape. Five researchers simulate a two-peptide system in 2023 at the level of moving molecules. One partner stays fixed, rich in positive charge. The other carries negative charge from either glutamic acid or aspartic acid, two acids that differ by a single carbon in their side chain.
