The aspartic version builds flatter sheets, grips its partner harder across the sheet faces, and assembles more slowly. The glutamic version forms faster and rounder fibers. The authors say such small chemical choices give designers a dial for tuning fiber form to each medical job.
pmc-10730367:
Advaitha Madireddy and Jeannine Gerhardt wrote a 2023 lab protocol for watching DNA copy itself, one molecule at a time. Their method is called single-molecule analysis of replicated DNA, or SMARD. It lets scientists see copying at chosen spots on a chromosome in fine detail.

The steps begin with pulse labeling, where new DNA is tagged as it forms. Next, the DNA is pulled out and stretched flat. Stains and probes then mark where copying began, how it moved, where it stopped, and where forks stalled. Few tools show these events at such fine scale. Labs that study DNA copying can follow the steps to run the method themselves.
pmc-10731267:
A pea aphid drinks plant sap, a diet too thin to live on, and a lodger germ makes up the lack. Hui-ping Liu and nine co-authors ask how the plant itself steers that lodger in 2023. The germ brews key nutrients for its host, and the host can raise or thin its numbers.

Aphids were raised on unlike host plants, and their growth, breeding, germ counts, and nutrient churn were read side by side. The plant's stamp runs through all three: body, lodger, and diet. How the germ mediates the plant-aphid tie was the open gap. The answer feeds pest craft, since a crop that starves the lodger may tame the pest.
pmc-10731667:
Xiaofen Tao and co-authors report a missed diagnosis in a nine-year-old boy in a 2023 case paper. Children often breathe in small objects, and a stuck object can cause lasting lung harm if it is missed. This boy's chest scan showed a hollow lesion in his left lower lung lobe. The image looked like a birth defect of the lung airways.

A camera passed into the airways told a distinct story. A peanut sat lodged in one branch of that lobe. Doctors pulled it out with forceps, and the boy was spared an operation to remove the lobe. The authors review past reports and stress that a breathed-in object can mimic many other diseases. They urge doctors to keep this cause in mind for children with lung problems, even when no choking event is recalled.
pmc-10732667:
Patrícia Deps and co-authors set out steps to end the stigma around Hansen's disease, the infection long known as leprosy. People affected can develop lasting disability and psychological harm when care comes late. The authors argue that stigma is complex and needs several parallel moves, not one campaign. Their list starts with a human-rights approach and the repeal of laws that discriminate against patients.

Training health workers comes next, so diagnosis and treatment improve and side effects shrink. Better tools to catch and cure the disease early would cut the disabilities that feed prejudice. Finally, they call for dropping stigmatizing words from medicine and law. The short piece is a position statement rather than a study, addressed to health systems still shaped by the disease's history. Its point is that stigma is a policy problem with named, actionable fixes.
pmc-10733767:
Patricio Lopez Turconi studies how Argentine courts fill the legal void on surrogacy, in work from twenty twenty-three. Argentine law holds no clear rules on whether surrogacy deals are legal or binding. That gap has not stopped intended parents; it has pushed them into court.

Turconi reviews thirty-two court rulings on altruistic gestational surrogacy claims. The study profiles who sues, what legal arguments courts use, and what orders they issue. Courts lean on human rights law and the best interests of the child to grant access. The author then makes the case for real legislation. Judge made rules bring tangles and uneven access that a statute could fix.
pmc-10735367:
Liat Ayalon and Karl Pillemer introduce a symposium on climate change and aging in a 2023 paper. Older people face high risk from extreme weather, through body frailty plus isolation, digital exclusion, and age bias. Yet climate policy often skips them, and youth-led action can cast them as the problem.

Talks in the set cover heat exposure as the world ages, and long mental shadows after one versus two weather disasters. Other talks turn to action: older people already act green and gain from joining climate work. The set argues for plans that shield elders and enlist them as partners in the response.
pmc-10735567:
Joshua Armstrong, Saskia Sivananthan, and Josée Guimond report forecasts of dementia in Canada from 2020 to 2050 in 2023. Canada's dementia group is growing fast. The team built a model that uses traits of the population and known risk factors. They focus on sex, ethnic origin, and age at onset.

Women made up just over six in ten cases in 2020, and that share should hold. Cases among Indigenous peoples are set to rise sharply. The share among people of Asian origin should grow from a small part to near a fourth. More than 40,000 people under age 65 may live with dementia by 2050. The shifts will shape care needs across the country.
pmc-10735767:
Samaneh Farsijani, Ziling Mao, and Anne Newman study how daily food energy links to death rates in United States adults. Their paper appeared in two thousand twenty-three. The team used a large national health survey with more than thirty-three thousand adults. Food intake came from day-long diet recalls. Deaths were tracked through a national index.

Over a follow-up of about eight years, more than four thousand people died. Adults eating very few calories each day died at higher rates than those eating a mid-range amount. Very high intake also pointed to higher risk, though less clearly. The low-intake risk held for most groups by age, sex, and body weight. One group differed: among Black adults, lower intake linked to lower risk. The overall pattern forms a U shape.
pmc-10735867:
Gabrielle Pfund and co-authors test whether sense of purpose and mind power feed each other in old age in a 2023 study. Four long United States studies, with tens of thousands of older adults in all, were run through one shared lens. Waves spanned up to eighteen years.

Shifts in purpose came before shifts in mind power, and the trade ran the other way too. Over long spans, the two changed in step. The team reads this as a two-way street: purpose guards the mind, and a fading mind can drain purpose. Boosting purpose may thus aid sound mind aging.
pmc-10735967:
Anthony Bardo and Takashi Yamashita present a 2023 study of despair in the United States. They use survey data from the mid-1990s and from 2011 to 2014. The study looks at pain, distress, and misuse of drugs and drink. It asks whether links between these problems and poor mental health grew over time. Hope, or the lack of it, is also part of the picture.

The authors compare trends by age, race, and social and income status. Poor mental health at the low end of a health scale stands in for despair. The work cannot prove that these problems caused the deaths in the deaths of despair story. It can still guide health plans by showing which groups lost ground in health and hope across the two survey waves.
pmc-10736067:
Rose Lin, Jingjing Su, and Kathi Heffner pool trials of mindfulness training for adults with mild memory loss. Mild cognitive impairment marks an early stage before dementia for many people. Past trials of mindfulness for thinking skills gave mixed results. The team searched six data bases for randomized trials on the topic.

Twelve trials with 530 people met the bar for pooling. Mindfulness gave a small to mid gain in overall thinking scores. Gains also showed for space skills and long-term memory. Short-term memory, planning, and focus showed no clear gain. Study quality and program traits did not shift the effect in checks. The authors call for larger trials to firm up the claim.
pmc-10736167: Dana Bradley introduces the faculty award presentations of the Academy for Gerontology in Higher Education for twenty twenty-three. The session features an address by Lisa Borrero of the University of Indianapolis, recipient of the Distinguished Faculty Award for exemplary teaching. A second lecture comes from Nasreen Sadeq of the University of South Florida, co-recipient of the Rising Star Early-Career Faculty Award. Her co-recipient, Berenice Benayoun of the University of Southern California, will lecture later.
pmc-10736267:
Daniela Belen Sosa Cifuentes and Jonathan Guillemot ask why few medical students choose geriatrics in a 2023 study from Ecuador. The country lacks specialists for older adults, yet training slots alone are not the fix. Thirty-two students in Quito were interviewed by trained peers about their specialty dreams.

None ranked geriatrics first, and only two entertained it at all. Most barely knew older adults beyond their own relatives, and fears of death and decline loomed large. Many felt the field cannot save lives, despite calling it important. Readers get a diagnosis: exposure comes before vocation.
pmc-10736467:
Aditi Durga and co-authors describe how they reshaped a dementia care app with the people who would use it, in this 2023 paper. More than sixteen million Americans care for family or friends with dementia without pay. The existing app, Aliviado Dementia Care, needed tailoring for caregivers from varied cultural backgrounds.

The team drafted screen layouts based on needs caregivers had named, then watched eight care partners try them. The testers came from six states and varied in race, age, and background. They found the screens easy to move through and were glad the app would be substantial. Their feedback led to plainer, more inclusive wording, a rebuilt home screen, and new features like drug reminders and a summary care profile. The caregivers liked that the app guides them through judging symptoms and planning care without drugs, and helps them work with their doctors.
pmc-10736667:
Timothy O’Connor and three co-authors ask nursing students why they skipped a survey after a class on age-friendly care, in a 2023 study. Nurses are in short supply, above all in long-term care. Teaching students a framework built on four Ms, covering mind, mobility, medication, and what matters, may draw some toward elder care careers.

When few students filled out the feedback survey after the joint teaching session, the team switched to focus groups to learn why. Answers covered survey length, timing, and students’ sense of the task’s value. Honest feedback of this kind is what course designers need to fix response rates. The study models how to evaluate geriatric teaching by listening first.
pmc-10736767:
Ji Yoo and Jay Shen weighed a training-plus-telehealth program for dementia care in a shortage area, in a 2023 study. The program, begun in 2020, coached primary care teams across professions and added remote visits for older patients. The team compared 244 clinic patients aged sixty to ninety-seven with mild to moderate dementia, half under trained providers and half not, matched for health and background.

The trained group's patients landed in hospital far less often, and returned within ninety days half as often. Savings averaged about twenty thousand dollars per patient. Federal quality measures, like caregiver teaching and care plans, also improved by 2021. The study ties workforce training to cheaper, better dementia care.
pmc-10736867:
Ann Reddy and co-authors share partner engagement strategies from an embedded pragmatic clinical trial, in a 2023 case study. Such trials rely on providers, not research staff, to carry out the study steps in daily care. That makes the partnership with the practice a thing to manage with care. Their trial aimed to improve advance care planning for people with dementia in assisted living.

The setting was a large physician practice serving 160 assisted living centers. Research and provider teams co-designed the work and co-led its rollout. Communication and project tools kept both teams accountable and set clear expectations for time and resources. At the start they agreed how effort would shift across the planning, execution, and monitoring phases, and how often to meet.
pmc-10737367:
Fred Kobylarz and five co-authors study how often doctors billed Medicare for advance care planning talks. Their 2023 paper looks at people who died in 2019. Such talks let patients state what care they want if they can no longer decide for themselves, and new billing codes from 2016 let doctors charge for them.

The team linked claims and other files for more than two million people who died. About one in six had a billed planning talk in the last two years. Talks were a bit more common under fee-for-service care than under Medicare Advantage plans. Most talks were short, and most took place in hospitals. The paper also tracks how use varied by race, place, and type of care.
pmc-10737567:
Sam Molli and Stephanie Wilson study how spousal support interacts with daily rumination and sleep in a 2023 paper. The cognitive model of insomnia holds that mental arousal harms sleep, and rumination, the replaying of worries, is a prime suspect. Social support may buffer that effect, but most studies treat rumination as a fixed trait.

Using data from a national daily experiences study, the authors separated day-to-day rumination from person-level tendencies. They tested how support and a spouse's perceived responsiveness changed the link with sleep and negative affect. The daily view shows when a partner's support matters most: on the worst rumination days.
pmc-10737667:
Natalie Chong and Joseph Caldwell study whether planning that centers on the person links to better lives for care users in 2023. The care is home and community based help for adults on Medicaid. Good planning should reflect each person's choices and needs. Past proof of a link to outcomes was thin.

Data came from a survey of near seven thousand adults in twelve states. Most users said they were fully part of choices. Fewer said their plans showed their choices. Each sign of high grade planning linked to less unmet need. Each also linked to more taking part in community life, more control, and more contentment. The authors say plan quality is a real lever for better outcomes.
pmc-10737767:
Laura Zahodne, Kristine Ajrouch, and Cerise Elliott introduce a 2023 symposium on dementia research in groups that studies often leave out. The talks cover African American, Latino, and Arab American older adults across the full course of the disease.

One talk links early-life hardship to later thinking skills in Latina women. Another finds that rough neighborhoods and poor sleep harm thinking in Black men. Later talks cover a care program shaped for Arab American immigrants with mild memory loss, and gaps in support use among caregivers from minority groups. A final speaker from the National Institute on Aging adds policy context for the set.
pmc-10737867:
Mei-Ching Chang, Yu-Tai Lo, Wei Lee, and Sheng-Yu Fan find a simple cut-off that flags frailty and disability risk in older clinic patients, in a 2023 study. A World Health Organization scale grades six inner capacities: thinking, moving, nutrition, hearing, vision, and mood. The team tested 397 outpatients aged 65 and over at a medical center. They compared the scale against standard frailty and daily-living measures.

Three or more failing capacities marked the danger line for both frailty and disability. Thinking, mobility, and nutrition problems drove frailty risk. Hearing joined that trio for disability. The scale discriminated well in both cases. The authors urge clinic staff to watch elders with failing capacities closely, since those failures arrive before the frailty they predict.
pmc-10738067:
Joseph Gaugler and co-authors mapped in 2023 how dementia caregiving weighs on public health across United States states. Care for a person with dementia is heavy, yet state-level reads were thin. The team mined a 2021 national risk survey from the thirty-nine states that ran its caregiver module. They compared dementia caregivers with other caregivers on health and hours.

High blood pressure among dementia caregivers ran from under thirty percent in South Dakota to over half in Arkansas, above the non-dementia caregiver mean. In most states at least a third of dementia caregivers gave twenty-plus hours a week, a mark few states hit for other caregivers. The team offers the state map for local service and policy aims.
pmc-10738167:
Hyunjin Noh, Haelim Jeong, Denise Kan, and Lewis Lee ask rural older adults in Alabama how they view trimming pain drugs and trying drug-free care, in a study from two thousand twenty-three. Phone talks reached elders with lasting pain and several health issues. Views on cutting back meds were mixed and wary.

Many feared losing drug gains while also fearing side effects. Doubt about drug-free options ran high, and cost plus travel blocked access. Plain lack of word about what exists was also common. The authors urge teaching and advocacy to build know-how and trust. Readers get the elder view that any pain plan must answer first.
pmc-10738267:
Xueqing Wang, Xuezhixing Zhang, and Emma Zang measure how older Americans of different backgrounds spend their later years, in marriage and in living arrangements. Family life after fifty has grown more varied, but the years spent in each state had not been tallied by group. They used a national study running from 1992 to 2018.

At age fifty, White adults could expect significantly more years married than Black or Hispanic adults. The gap came from more years spent divorced or never married in the other groups. White adults also spent more years living with a spouse. Black and Hispanic adults spent more years living with people other than a spouse. The authors say these patterns deepen inequality in old age, since a spouse is often the first source of care and support.
pmc-10738667:
Rupal Parekh and Christine Tocchi studied re-engagement of Black older adults with churches and senior centers. Their 2023 focus group study is set around Hartford, Connecticut. Such sites serve as social hubs that support well-being. Attendance has not returned to pre-pandemic levels since reopening. The team used a community-based participatory approach to learn why.

Three focus groups heard leaders from senior centers and churches. Staff described what engagement means since the sites reopened. They named barriers that keep older adults away. They also named factors that draw people back in. The long-term goal is a behavior program to lift re-engagement. Better return rates could cut depression and disability risk in this group.
pmc-10738767:
Dahye Hong, Jennifer Kim, and Bada Kang studied older Korean adults in a 2023 paper on mood and mouth health. They asked how signs of low mood link to oral health in people aged 65 or older who live with long-term illness. Their work used data from a Korean aging study that ran from 2018 to 2020.

Women and men were looked at apart, and the team counted pain, limits on use, and felt effects on daily life. Having three or more long-term illnesses and loss of clear thinking tied to worse oral health in both groups. The link with low mood was stronger in men, while in women worse mood meant worse oral health step by step. The authors say easing low mood could help oral health in this group.
pmc-10738967:
Dokyung Yoon, Eileen Crimmins, and Jennifer Ailshire studied neighborhood ties and well-being in older adults with dementia, in a paper from twenty twenty-three. They used a national survey of adults aged sixty-five and older in the United States. The question was whether a strong sense of trust and closeness nearby softens the harm dementia does to well-being.

People with likely dementia reported lower well-being than others. People in close-knit areas reported higher well-being. The gain from close local ties was larger for those with dementia than for those without it. The authors say building trust among neighbors may help protect people living with dementia.
pmc-10739167:
Mark Monane and co-authors present this 2023 conference abstract on a blood test for Alzheimer likelihood. The QUIP study enrolled 347 older adults with memory complaints. The test returns an amyloid score that estimates the chance of a positive brain scan. Clinicians logged their judgment and drug plans before and after seeing results.

Scores swung decisions hard: low scores dropped disease probability and drug use, high scores raised both. The key question was whether age or sex bent that response. They did not: shifts in certainty and prescribing matched across age and sex groups. The authors say the test's sway holds evenly across older adults in clinic pathways.
pmc-10739267:
Family carers for people with dementia face a hard load as end-of-life care begins, and Hannah Cho and co-authors asked how social support shapes that load, in work from twenty twenty-three. Twenty carers of hospice patients with dementia gave long talks. Most were women, and the group spanned two ethnic groups.

Three themes framed their tales: shifts in social life, chances to connect, and ways of staying in touch. Carers told of being home-bound, of stress, and of family rows. They also told of help from kin and friends that kept them going. The authors argue carers need planned breaks and steady links, not just thanks, and they call for more work on contact tools and rest care.
pmc-10740567:
Liyin Lian and co-authors review, in a 2023 paper, how single-celled parasites keep host cells alive during early infection. These apicomplexan parasites live inside host cells and cause many diseases in people and animals. If the host cell dies on cue, the parasite loses its home, so it blocks that death.

The review sorts the key parasite proteins and host paths used to stall cell death in the first stage of infection. Each trick helps the parasite survive and multiply inside the cell. Knowing the tricks gives drug and vaccine makers clear targets to aim at. The authors frame the early host-parasite tug of war as a weak point worth attack. The paper gathers a scattered field into one map for future work.
pmc-10740867:
Iris Heinsoo and co-authors review chest infection treatment in dogs in this 2023 paper. The condition, pyothorax, is pus in the chest cavity. Common bacteria include mixed anaerobes and several named species. Guidelines suggest certain first choice antibiotics while culture results are pending. The team checked whether those choices match real culture data.

Records covered 53 dogs treated at two referral centers between 2014 and 2020. Just over half had a positive fluid culture. Pasteurella species were the most common isolate, followed by Escherichia coli. Sensitivity of each isolate to tested drugs was tallied. The results were compared with a national poster guide and other published guides. Mismatches point to where first choice advice may need updating.
pmc-10740967:
Peri Colino-Gallardo and co-authors measure in 2023 what a jaw widening treatment does to the bones and teeth of growing children. The treatment stretches the upper jaw with a screw device over a short time. Its effects have been studied for years, but clear three dimensional proof of the changes has been thin.

The team treated 20 patients, with a mean age near eleven years, using a fixed expander. They took 3D scans before and after treatment. The scans measured the width of the nose and upper jaw, the height of the palate, the curve of the tooth row, and the tilt and span of the back teeth. Hard numbers on each change help dentists predict what the treatment will do. They also help set fair hopes for families before work begins.
pmc-10741767:
Oleksiy Myronyuk, Denys Baklan, and Aleksej Rodin compare water-repellent steel finishes in a 2023 paper. A femtosecond laser can texture stainless steel so droplets bead and roll off, either by letting the surface develop repellency on its own or by adding a chemical treatment. Which route survives sunlight better was the question.

Surface shape mattered enormously. Fine laser ripples alone repelled poorly; adding engraved microgrooves, forty-five micrometers wide on a sixty-micrometer pitch, with rough protrusions on top, worked best. The team used a two-liquid surface energy method to score repellency, treatment quality, and ultraviolet stability on one scale. The spontaneously repellent surface degraded under ultraviolet light much faster than surfaces treated with stearic acid or a silane modifier. The practical verdict favors chemical finishing for outdoor use, with topography still doing half the work.
pmc-10741967:
Mierzwa and co-authors report a 4-year-old boy found by chance to carry two rare gene changes. One change sits in the RET gene and causes MEN2B, a syndrome with early thyroid cancer. The other sits in the RyR1 gene, linked to muscle disease and a risk with anesthesia.

Testing began because of short stature and slow motor growth, and the mixed signs slowed diagnosis. Scans of his thyroid looked normal, but a blood marker was high at 34, far above the normal limit. Surgeons removed the thyroid, and lab checks confirmed medullary thyroid cancer.
pmc-10742267:
Moustafa Aldaly and co-authors compare radiation plans for left-sided breast cancer, where the heart sits dangerously close to the target. Radiation saves lives after breast surgery but can scar heart and lungs years later. Their 2023 study weighs older conformal therapy paired with a deep breath-hold, which inflates the lung and pushes the heart away, against intensity-modulated therapy planned on four-dimensional scans that track breathing. Doses to organs at risk are the deciding numbers.

Breath-hold is a low-tech shield; modulated beams are a high-tech one. Comparing them on the same patients' anatomy tells clinics which investment pays. The authors come from the planning side of radiotherapy, where these choices are made daily. Their endpoint is dose, the proxy for late harm. The work helps smaller centers judge whether technique or equipment matters more.
pmc-10742567:
Ibtissam Bouhzam and co-authors extract useful compounds from spent coffee grounds with two solvent families in this 2023 study. Brewing leaves mountains of grounds that are rich yet mostly thrown away. Those grounds still hold polyphenols, chlorogenic acid, and caffeine worth recovering.

Water mixes of ethanol and of acetone were compared from the same grounds. A weak acetone mix recovered all three targets best at once. The team report yields for each compound under each mix. First-of-its-kind comparisons remove guesswork for processors. Turning a waste stream into ingredients suits both profit and planet. The study gives the coffee chain a tested recipe to start from.
pmc-10742867:
Natalia Mena-Vazquez and co-authors compare sleep in arthritis patients with and without lung disease in a 2023 study. Rheumatoid arthritis can scar the lungs, a complication called interstitial lung disease. Sleep trouble is common in arthritis but its link to lung involvement was unclear. Thirty-five patients in each group were matched by age and sex.

Sleep questionnaires showed worse quality in the lung disease group. Insomnia was twice as common and more severe, and sleep satisfaction ran lower. That group also showed weaker resilience and more anxiety and low mood. Fatigue and life quality scores are reported as well. Lung disease itself was the key factor tied to insomnia. The authors urge sleep checks in this subgroup.
pmc-10743067:
Ahmad Mansour and co-authors report river blindness eye disease far from its home range in a 2023 study. Onchocerciasis scars the back of the eye, yet young eye doctors in rich states rarely see it. Travel and migration now bring cases to clinics in North America, Europe, and the Middle East.

Four cases met the presumed label through life near fast rivers in endemic zones, layered imaging, slow worsening, and clean tests for other causes. Signs ran from optic nerve swelling to worm tracks under the retina and patchy pigment scars. Skin signs were often absent, which hides the cause. Ivermectin drew a response.
pmc-10743567:
Barbara Carrese and co-authors test tiny drug-carrying particles against breast cancer grown as three-dimensional balls of cells, in a 2023 paper. The particles are built from a blood protein and loaded with doxorubicin, a standard cancer drug. Such balls of cells mimic real tumors better than flat cell layers, so the team used them to judge how well the particles enter, kill, and show up on imaging.

The particles entered cancer balls more deeply than healthy breast cell balls. The drug spread through the cells over a day, and the balls died mainly at the highest dose. Adding laser light, which heats the particles, killed cells at lower doses and shorter times. The particles also gave off a sound-based imaging signal that grew with dose. The authors argue the mix of drug, heat, and imaging could cut the drug dose patients need.
pmc-10743667:
Chen Liang and co-authors review conversion therapy strategies that turn inoperable liver cancer into cases surgeons can remove. Liver cancer is among China's most common malignancies. Most patients arrive too late for curative surgery.

Conversion treatments aim to reopen that door. For early cases, they grow the healthy liver remnant. For advanced cases, they shrink tumors and lower stage. Drugs, radiation, and vessel procedures all play roles. Success can lead to resection or even transplant. The review sorts the latest strategy combinations. It weighs which patients gain real survival benefit. The field moves fast as new drug pairs emerge. Careful selection decides who should attempt conversion.
pmc-10743967:
Jacob Schoffl and colleagues report the first test of heart rate variability biofeedback in adults with spinal cord injury. The therapy trains self-control of cardiac autonomic activity and has helped other clinical groups, but spinal cord injury disrupts the autonomic pathways it acts through. The article sets out a lab framework and a case series of two adults with chronic injuries at different levels and degrees.

The program ran ten weeks, mixing face-to-face and telehealth sessions with daily home practice. Body measures included heart rate and blood pressure variability and baroreflex sensitivity. Both people showed some improvement in the body measures. They also reported gains in mood, fatigue, pain, and quality of life. With two participants nothing is proven; what it gives is feasibility and a measuring framework ready for a powered trial.
pmc-10744767:
Silviu Constantin Latcu and co-authors give a photo rich guide in 2023 to a rat model for erection loss after prostate surgery. Nerve harm during that surgery is a top cause, and rat studies have hinted at ways to restore function that have not yet carried into clinic.

The essay walks through each step of the model: freeing the key nerve, harming it in set ways, and sparking it to test response. Blood pressure in the neck and pressure inside the organ must both be logged. Fine surgical detail fills the guide. The authors push for shared, strict methods so results can travel further.
pmc-10744967:
Teng-Kuan Wang and six co-authors test two ways to ease pain after total knee replacement surgery. Pain control in the first days of rehab is a must for good results. Yet opioids and spine based drips can cause dizzy spells, nausea, and weak legs. Their mixed plan joins a nerve block, a joint shot, and a pain pump the patient runs by vein.

The study looks back at 118 patients run under spinal numbing. On day one, the spine drip group had weaker legs. The rate was twenty two point nine eight percent, against six point four five percent for the mixed plan. Numbness was also more common with the spine drip. Its rate was forty three point three three percent, against eighteen point five two percent. Pain was scored on a number scale. The mixed plan eased pain as well, with fewer early side effects to slow rehab.
pmc-10745067:
Jungim Lee and colleagues published a 2023 survey of worm infections in northwestern Tanzania. Two parasite groups burden the region. One spreads through contaminated water contact. The other spreads through soil. The team tested schoolchildren and adults across many villages.

Urine and stool samples were examined with standard methods. Thousands of children took part in the survey. Questionnaires explored exposure risks at home and school. Infection in adults ran near one in twelve for one parasite. Results guide where mass treatment should focus. Knowing risk factors helps target water and sanitation efforts.
pmc-10745467:
Pamela Vocale and co-authors simulated gas flow and heat transfer in diamond-shaped microchannels, in a study published in 2023. New fabrication methods have made such channels practical, but thin gas inside them behaves oddly: it slips at the walls and its temperature jumps there. The team solved the flow and energy equations with a commercial code, checking results against published data. They varied the diamond's side angle to test geometry effects.

The simulations covered fully developed laminar flow. How rarefied the gas is, and the channel's shape, both strongly shifted the Nusselt number, the standard heat transfer measure. Their checks matched known velocity profiles in the slip regime and known heat values in the normal regime. The authors offer the results as design guidance for micro-devices that move heat with gas.
pmc-10745667:
Ali Khaghani, Atanas Ivanov, and Kai Cheng simulate the making of curved optical lenses to learn which forces at the cutting tip decide the finish. Ultraprecision diamond turning sculpts freeform optics, and its accuracy depends on the machine's bearings as much as on the tool. Their 2023 paper proposes building the linear bearings from metal matrix composites instead of traditional materials, and tests the swap in simulation.

A dynamics package modeled the slow-tool-servo machining mode while the software tracked the forces where tool meets workpiece. As the surface's curvature changed along the cut, the interfacial forces changed with it, and the composite bearings cut the pressure along the toolpath significantly. The slideway joints, in turn, felt those cutting forces directly. The authors argue lightweight bearing materials are not a structural nicety but a surface-quality lever, and that the forces at the interface deserve design attention.
pmc-10746967:
Silvia Gabrielli and a team of co-authors describe building a virtual reality game with, not just for, teenagers with autism. Their study appeared in twenty twenty-three. The game, called Zentastic, aims to train social skills through shared adventure play.

Small groups of teenagers play together online while therapists guide the sessions. Teenagers and therapists joined the design work from the start. They reacted to an early version in an acceptability study, then tested the finished game over several sessions. The players took to the game well. Their social skills also rose from the start of training to the end. The authors offer early proof that such games can help, while noting the study was small and exploratory.
pmc-10747067:
Daniele Murra and co-authors review how Arduino boards can run arrays of optical sensors, and they build an accurate solar compass from them, in a 2023 paper. Sensor arrays range from lines to camera-style matrices with thousands of tiny elements. They need electronics with precise timing and fast, accurate digitizing.

The authors show that, with proper settings, a simple Arduino board can handle both one- and two-dimensional optical sensors. They then describe a solar compass coupling the board to a tested array sensor. The compass gives the north direction with a very high degree of accuracy. The paper serves hobbyists and instrument builders alike.
pmc-10747667:
Cong Shi and co-authors upgrade in 2023 spiking neural networks with learnable leak and onset attention. Spiking nets mimic brain firing and promise lean compute. Deep versions still struggle to weigh key signals across space and time in a balanced way.

Their neurons learn their own leak rate to fit modern tasks. Attention fires at the first time step to lock focus early. A new norm rule tied to the leak rate joins a local loss scheme for training. Tests on three image sets reach high accuracy in just eight time steps, a strong speed for spiking models.
pmc-10748267:
A feed toxin from fungi, zearalenone, and a bacterial toxin, lipopolysaccharide, often reach farm animals together, yet most studies test them one at a time. Wang and five co-authors study their combined hit on pig gut cells grown in the lab, and whether quercetin, a plant flavonoid, can soften it. Dose tests picked working levels of each toxin and of quercetin for the main experiments.

The toxin pair cut cell survival and loosened the gut barrier's seal proteins. Adding quercetin restored survival, lowered a damage marker, and switched on the Nrf2 defense pathway and its protective genes. The barrier proteins rose again, and fewer cells died by apoptosis, with a key death gene turned down. The authors conclude quercetin shields gut cells from the paired toxins, largely by waking the cell's own antioxidant command system.
pmc-10748367:
Qiong Wu and co-authors teach a network controller to keep sensor data fresh while saving battery in this 2023 paper. In dense Internet of Things systems, many devices share channels through multi-antenna, overlapping transmission schemes. Data freshness, measured as age of information, matters as much as speed for live uses, and both sampling choices and transmit power move it.

The team framed the base station's decisions as a learning problem. A deep reinforcement learning agent sets sampling orders and power per device, while the station untangles the overlapping signals. In simulation the learned policy kept information younger and burned less energy than rival methods. Its total reward beat a genetic algorithm approach and a random one by clear margins. The authors present the scheme as a practical route to fresher, cheaper sensing in crowded device networks.
pmc-10749367:
Yangjian Dong and co-authors rank traditional Chinese exercises for easing anxiety and depression in older adults, in a 2023 analysis combining trials with a network comparison. Thirty trials with 2,806 participants fed both a standard meta-analysis and a ranking of therapies against each other.

Taken together, the exercises clearly improved both anxiety and depression scores versus controls. Tai Chi came out on top for both conditions, with Yi Jin Jing second for anxiety and Ba Duan Jin second for depression. The authors recommend Tai Chi as the leading option while calling for larger, stricter trials to firm up the ranking. The study gives clinicians a graded menu rather than a single prescription.
pmc-10749967:
Liu and seven co-authors improve a deep learning network for coconut scan segmentation, in work from twenty twenty-three. Coconut breeding relies on manual experience because the fruit inner structure is hard to observe. Seeing internal traits accurately and in time would speed breeding decisions.

Computed tomography scans give cross sections of the whole coconut. Their model, based on the DeepLab network, replaces one pooling module with a denser version and adds an attention module. Image segmentation then labels tissue regions automatically. Better segmentation turns slow expert reading into repeatable measurement for breeding trials.
pmc-10751567:
Siqi April Li and co-authors share a lab protocol from 2023 for fruit fly research. Their method turns existing fly lines that carry gene markers into split-GAL4 driver lines, which let scientists switch genes on in chosen tissues. The protocol replaces one kind of inserted marker line with another using breeding crosses rather than costly injections into eggs.

The steps run through four rounds of in vivo crosses inside living flies. After that, the team checks the flies with DNA tests and glowing marker imaging to confirm the new piece sits in the right direction. Only then do they set up stable fly stocks for long-term use. The authors note the method is cheap and can be adapted by fly labs that study many kinds of tissue.
pmc-10751767:
Geun Wan Kim and Ji Won Ha showed in 2023 how to watch gold nanorods inside cells without the image ambiguity that plagued earlier tracking. A rod's symmetric shape made its tilt unreadable in standard contrast microscopy. Their imaging method breaks that symmetry for rods held in focus inside silica shells. Large scattering from the rods paints a doughnut pattern with two lobes.

Turning the sample rotated the lobes in step, revealing spin direction directly. The team then tracked coated rods as cells pulled them inside during uptake. At the necking stage, rods twisted once or twice as the pocket pinched off. The movies even showed a right-handed twist matching the dynamin helix that cuts the neck. The method promises sharper views of cargo motion in living cells at full speed and detail.
pmc-10753667:
Selim Sanel, Serdar Demiroz, and Tamer Coskun report a rare knee injury in a healthy man aged 28 years. The back inner part of the top of the shin bone broke on both sides after a low force fall. He fell on his knees while playing leapfrog, when a friend jumped on his back.

Scans showed breaks on both knees in the same spot. The team fixed both sides in one operation with screws and plates, working from the back of the knee while he lay face up. He could move the knees at once but bore no weight for two months. At six months he had full motion, full weight bearing, and no pain.
pmc-10755667:
Ellis Paintsil and co-authors review Campylobacter infections from an African viewpoint, in a 2023 article. These bacteria cause gut illness worldwide and can trigger later nerve damage. The African picture has its own traits, from strain mix to drug response. The team searched the medical literature for Africa-focused work.

The review covers human and animal medicine plus food hygiene. It maps how common the gut species are in north and sub-Saharan Africa. Drug susceptibility patterns are charted. The gravest after-effect, a paralysis syndrome, is reviewed in African populations. A chapter treats a species of animal health concern. The authors argue that control plans must fit African settings, not imported templates.
pmc-10761067:
Haichao Yuan, Senmao Li, Zhengping Zhao, and Yan Wang test whether engineered stem cell vesicles can slow prostate cancer in this 2023 paper. The vesicles, called exosomes, come from umbilical cord stem cells and are loaded with interferon-beta, a protein tied to cancer control. Cancer cells readily took up the vesicles in lab tests.

Vesicles rich in the protein slowed cancer cell growth, held more cells in a resting phase, and raised cell death rates. Vesicles with the protein knocked down had the opposite lean. In mice, the enriched vesicles shrank tumor size and weight. The team concludes that loading these vesicles with interferon-beta suppresses prostate cancer growth and promotes cancer cell death. They present the approach as a candidate cell-free therapy.
pmc-10765067:
Daiki Ikarashi and co-authors report lasting control from a drug plus radiation pairing in a 2023 paper. Enfortumab vedotin treats advanced urothelial cancer after earlier lines fail. Two patients gained long control when radiation joined the drug at the main tumor.

The first, a man of seventy-eight, had lung and lymph node spread from a ureter tumor. Six months on the drug shrank his lesions, but the primary tumor regrew. Radiation plus continued drug then held the disease in check. A second man of sixty follows a parallel course in the report. Pairing local radiation with a systemic drug may stretch its reach.
pmc-10771967:
Nikhila Chelikam and co-authors reviewed the rise of point-of-care ultrasound, the practice of scanning patients at the bedside during examination and treatment. The method is fast, radiation-free, and repeatable, and it began as a way to find internal bleeding in trauma patients. It has since spread through emergency rooms, intensive care units, and operating theatres as a life-saving diagnostic habit.

The review traces that history and surveys where the scans help most today. It also names barriers inside general internal medicine, including training gaps, while noting that new pocket-sized probes put the tool within easy reach. The authors recommend a focused, binary decision style of scanning and proper training in medical curricula to spread its benefits.
pmc-10773567:
Four authors, led by Manal Alohali, build in 2023 a framework to spot attacks on cyber physical systems, the linked sensors and controls in smart cars and plants. Data flows over open networks in such systems, so guarding it is vital. Past detection tools left clear gaps in speed and accuracy.

Their design pairs a deep network with an ant colony search method that tunes it. Bagging, a vote across many model copies, steadies the calls. Tests showed higher detection rates than rival methods, the authors report. The work targets safe data flow in systems that mix computing with the physical world.
pmc-10784767:
Samuel Dada and six co-workers wrote a 2023 study in rats on kidney harm from diclofenac, a common pain drug. The drug can hurt the kidneys even though it eases pain and swelling. Vitamin E is known to guard kidneys against some harms. The team tested if it could guard against this drug too.

They split male rats into six groups, with drug doses with or without vitamin E. The drug raised waste levels in the blood and signs of harm in kidney tissue. Rats given vitamin E as well showed lower swelling signals and less cell damage. Their kidney tests and defense enzymes also looked better.
pmc-10784867:
Ahmad Kamil Ahmad Fahmi and co-authors report two adults with a rare, aggressive cancer hiding in the nose, in a 2023 paper. Alveolar rhabdomyosarcoma is a soft-tissue malignancy seldom seen in adults, where outcomes run worse than in children. Both patients arrived with local pressure effects and signs the disease had spread.

The first woman bled spontaneously from one nostril; tests showed a crashed platelet count and tumor cells filling her bone marrow. A scope found a mass beside the middle turbinate. The second patient had a bulging eye and blurred vision, with a pale mass on the other side of the nose. Staining of tissue confirmed the diagnosis in both. The authors stress fast workups.
pmc-10826867:
Rajeshkrishna Bhandary and co-authors give a close critical read of India's National Mental Health Survey of 2016. Their 2023 appraisal notes the survey was a landmark effort by a top national institute. It aimed to fix flaws of older, smaller surveys.

The appraisal finds real strengths but also clear gaps. The private sector, a major care provider, took no part. The chosen interview tool misses common illness groups such as somatoform disorders. Rate math for single disorders is hard to pin down from the design. Rich interview data were not shared. The authors urge a fuller, culture-fit tool, private sector input, and better funding for later survey rounds.
pmc-10827867:
Héctor Martín-Cardoso and co-authors show how phosphate fertilizer aids rice blast fungus in this 2023 study (the catalog lists 2024). Rice feeds half the world, and blast disease slashes yields. Heavy phosphate feeding was known to worsen blast, but the mechanism was murky.

Live imaging of infected sheaths showed the fungus invading faster in phosphate-loaded leaves. Its attack genes and cell-death tools switched on harder there. On the plant side, early alarm chemistry failed to build, and defense genes woke weakly. Phosphate thus boosts the pathogen while muting the host, the authors conclude. Both partners in the infection shift under high feeding.
pmc-10845067:
Cancer leaks traces of itself into the blood, and reading those traces without surgery is the promise of liquid biopsy. Mariya Levkova, Trifon Chervenkov, Lyudmila Angelova, and Deyan Dzenkov review how a pocket-sized sequencing technology, Oxford Nanopore, fits that promise in this 2023 paper. The method reads long DNA strands directly, in real time, from a device that shrugs off the lab.

Applied to tumor DNA floating in blood, it can flag cancer, spot spread, steer precision drugs, and watch whether treatment works. Two traps dominate: tumor molecules are vanishingly scarce in a blood draw, and harmless age-related blood mutations can masquerade as cancer signatures. The authors searched the literature under strict rules and weigh where the method stands. Portability is its trump card; sensitivity its open question.
pmc-10847267:
Michael Malek-Ahmadi and co-authors sell robust regression for brain studies in a 2023 paper, per its head. Line fits are the work horse of brain science stats. Yet brain data oft skew hard, and lone wild points can drag a line far off.

Squashing skewed data helps at times, but brings its own traps. Robust fits make no shape grant on the data spread. Their reads match line fit reads when data behave. The team show the method on human brain decay data tied to Alzheimer disease. Skew safe stats can save sound studies from bum fits.
pmc-10849767:
Spencer Greatorex and co-authors report a study, given in the head as a 2023 paper, on a self-guard loop that slows fatty liver disease in obesity. Most people with obesity get a fatty liver, but only some go on to the inflamed, scarred form that harms health. What holds the line for the rest was not clear.

The team found two partners in liver cells that rise early in the disease and work as a pair. One makes a mild oxidant that switches on the other, a master guard that lifts cell defences, which in turn makes more of the first. Cutting the first partner in mouse liver cells weakened the guard and let damage grow. Mice with it cut, fed a high fat diet, went on to the inflamed form. Boosting it held the disease back.
pmc-10894067:
Giesbrecht and co-authors test whether ground penetrating radar can find drowning victims trapped under ice. Each year people fall through ice on lakes and rivers and drown. Bodies may float up under the ice sheet, where divers face risk and poor odds of success. A contact-free search tool would keep rescue teams off thin ice. The team placed three euthanized pigs under ice as stand-ins for human victims.

Radar units at 500 MHz and 1 GHz were dragged across ice from 5 to 26 cm thick. Both units picked out the rough shape of the targets through ice up to 42 cm. A signal matching method helped flag the buried shapes. The results support radar as a safer first search step.
pmc-10901167:
Masahiro Ohara and co-authors show that pausing during vapor deposition lets engineers dial the built-in electric polarization of organic films up, down, or even backwards, in a 2023 study. Such films run organic screens and lights, and their molecules settle into a slight common tilt that creates the polarization. A spinning probe measured the surface voltage of two common film materials right after coating.

The voltage sagged over time as the surface layer relaxed. By opening and closing the deposition shutter in a rhythm, the team stacked relaxed layers and set the polarization size at will. In one material the direction flipped entirely. The trick works for ordinary molecules, not just polar ones.
pmc-10905367:
Masaki Odahara and six co-authors build a system for delivering genes into plastids, the green compartments inside plant cells. Their 2023 paper notes that plastids are prized targets for making valuable molecules in plants. The team had a peptide carrier that ferries DNA into plastids of leaves and seedlings. Here they grow a better source tissue for the job: masses of young shoots rich in stem cells.

A liquid culture method produced those multiple shoots in two model plants and in strawberry. The carrier then delivered a cassette holding a resistance gene and a glowing reporter gene, flanked by plastid-matching sequences. Tests days later showed the cassette woven into plastid DNA in all three species, and microscopes plus protein tests confirmed the reporter shining inside plastids. The authors present shoot masses as promising material for this route to plastid engineering.
pmc-10905567:
Ryszard Zamorski and co-authors present a 2023 study of why some rice varieties store a wall sugar called glucomannan in their grains while others store none. Cell walls shape plant growth and the quality of food and materials made from plants. How wall makeup varies within one species was poorly understood.

Under the microscope, grain walls from many varieties fell cleanly into two groups: with the sugar or without it. The sugar made up a tenth or more of the starchy walls where present and sat close to cellulose fibres. Gene comparisons pointed to one gene whose form differed sharply between the two groups. Finding the exact gene could guide breeding for grain quality.
pmc-10937467:
Zhao-Han Zhang and three co-authors build a layered model to forecast outcomes for liver cancer patients, in a study published in 2023. This cancer is complex, and a fair personal forecast can steer hard treatment choices. The team mined two large sources: a national cancer genome atlas and a long-running population registry.

From the atlas data they found genes whose activity tracked with survival. A regression model turned those genes into a risk score for each patient. Clinical facts were then folded into the score to form the full multilevel model. The aim is a forecast that speaks to one patient’s odds, not just group averages. Such a tool could help doctors weigh surgery, drugs, and watchful care.
pmc-10984667:
Ajay Kumar Jain leads a large clinical research network team asking whether what children with fatty liver disease actually eat tracks with how severe the disease is. Pediatric fatty liver is spreading, and lifestyle change is the main treatment, yet rigorous diet measurement has been missing. One hundred nineteen children from ten tertiary centers had their diets scored with the Healthy Eating Index.

Children averaged about thirteen years old, and most were boys and Hispanic. Those in the healthiest diet tier weighed less and had better blood lipids: triglycerides fell steadily from the lowest to the highest diet-quality group, while protective cholesterol rose. The pattern supports diet quality as a measurable lever in pediatric liver disease care.
pmc-11019967:
Collins, Moons, Dhiman, and co-authors publish TRIPOD+AI, updated guidance for reporting clinical prediction models. Such models estimate a patient's risk or likely outcome, and they may use plain statistics or machine learning. A first TRIPOD statement in 2015 set minimum reporting rules for these studies.

The update extends those rules for an era when learning algorithms are common in medicine. Authors are told what to report so readers can judge if a model was built and tested fairly. Clear reporting helps hospitals avoid weak models and helps good models earn trust faster.
pmc-11090167:
Yu-Jie Guo and eight co-authors develop a scale in 2024 to measure how ready cancer patients feel to return to work. Research on this topic in China is still new, and no tool existed for this specific skill. The team built draft items from theory and prior studies, then refined them through expert rounds and a pilot survey.

A large survey of three hundred seventy six patients was used to test the scale. The final version has twenty four items in three groups: focusing on recovery, rebuilding confidence, and adjusting plans. Scores were highly consistent and held up over a two week retest. The authors say the scale can guide support for patients who plan to work again.
pmc-11225467:
Rita Nassanga and eight co-authors describe chest scan findings in Ugandan patients thought to have COVID-19 lung infection, at a time when lab test kits ran short. Fine chest scans were used to guide care in place of the gene test. The study came out in twenty twenty-three.

The team reviewed scans of hundreds of patients and the gene test results where they existed. Cloudy patches in both lungs were the most common find. Only a part of patients had the gene test, and few of those tested positive, yet most who tested negative still had scans classed at the highest COVID like level. Scan exactness beat the gene test, the authors conclude.
pmc-11390067:
Ersin Ergül and co-authors follow patients with lung blood clots for a year and tally outcomes and costs. Their 2023 study ran at a tertiary care center with checks every three months. The disease is life-threatening, with hard follow-up and high costs.

More than one hundred and forty patients on blood thinners took part. Bleeding risk did not split by drug choice. Three upkeep regimens matched on sticking to therapy, clot return, and bleeding. About one patient in four died within the year, most in the first three months. One regimen cost far more per year than the rest. The authors weigh cost as the main split among like-performing options.
pmc-11532267:
Duoping Zhu and six colleagues published a 2024 study predicting where an endangered plant, Pyrethrum tatsienense, can grow in China as the climate changes. The plant is critically endangered, and protecting it requires knowing which habitats suit it now and in the future.

The team used a computer model called Maxent, tuned for accuracy, with records of 127 places where the plant occurs. They fed in climate data for the distant past, the present, and future scenarios. The model identified the main factors that limit the plant's range and mapped how suitable habitat may shift. Such maps help conservation planners choose reserves and decide where replanting efforts are most likely to succeed.
pmc-11532367:
Old age brings oral disease, and for tribal elders the burden can be heavy. The three authors surveyed 486 members of the Irula tribes of Tamil Nadu aged 65 and over, chosen by multistage sampling in the northern district. They used the Geriatric Oral Health Assessment Index to score oral health-related quality of life, alongside demographics, medical history, and oral complaints.

Most respondents were 65 to 69, three quarters were women, and two thirds could not read. Many reported trouble eating and speaking and oral discomfort. Education stood out: more schooling went with better oral quality of life scores, while arthritis went with worse ones. Other conditions showed no clear link. The authors call for targeted oral health programs and awareness drives in tribal communities, plus larger studies of elder oral health.
pmc-11533267:
Xiaoli Xu, Wansheng Zang, Anken Wang, and Chenhao Yang check a new eye-measuring method in schoolchildren, before and after relaxing drops, in a 2024 study. Multispectral refraction topography maps how focus varies across the retina, center to edge — data that may predict which children will turn nearsighted. A map is only useful if repeated maps agree.

Sixty children aged seven to eighteen were measured three times each way, with standard refraction checks alongside. Agreement and repeatability statistics judged the device, using a summary value for peripheral refractive error. Trustworthy retinal maps could move myopia screening from a single center number to a whole-retina risk picture.
pmc-11535067:
Li and co-authors reshape how magnetic powder cores for power electronics get their insulation. Pressing the powder cold leaves air gaps and stress that wreck its soft magnetic behavior. Their method, ultrasonic rheomolding, forms a lens-shaped insulation layer that adapts to each grain.

The molded cores beat cold-pressed ones on both fronts that usually trade off. Permeability rose from about 32 to about 43, and bias performance jumped from 69 to 88 in a hundred. Core losses fell to about a twentieth of the pressed cores. The lens layer cushions grains against stress, so magnetization stays efficient. The result suits next-generation power devices.
pmc-11535567:
Four researchers examine magnesium composite parts made by stir processing with added ultrasound, in a research paper from 2024. The base alloy gains strength from hard titanium carbide particles stirred into its surface. Ultrasound during stirring adds energy that may spread the particles better.

Parts made with vibration had no voids in the stirred zone and showed finer grains. The particles spread evenly and pinned the grain edges, raising dislocation counts. Hardness and tensile strength rose clearly over plain stir processing. The grain size shrank as well. The study shows vibration-assisted stirring as a route to tougher light-metal parts for transport use.
pmc-11536667:
Hongyu Mao and co-authors read the full chloroplast genome of a plant in a 2024 report. The plant is Bidens aurea, first from warm parts of the Americas and now spread through Asia and the Americas. Chloroplasts hold the green parts that catch light in plant cells.

The genome forms a ring with two large zones and two repeat zones, each sized in the report. Family tree work split nineteen Bidens types into five main groups. Bidens aurea sat closest to two named kin. The full read gives a firm base for DNA barcodes that tell Bidens types apart. It also helps trace how the group spread and split.
pmc-11536767:
Aboalsamh and co-authors tell of a rare in-gut loop post a one-cut kidney gift. Scope gift cuts took the place of open cuts from 1995 on. One-cut work trims four cuts to one for the gift pull. Known risks span blood hits, in-cut organ harm, and gut stalls. Rare snags past those have gone less probed in print. In-gut loops are one such rare snag in that set. They can block the gut, starve it, and kill its wall.

Their case is a through-web loop post the one-cut gift work. The host was sound in the main, with no grave past ills. One past mark stood out: an irate bowel call years prior. The team flags how such loops form post the cut.
pmc-11538267:
Sarto i Monteys and co-authors report on an invasive beetle spreading through Catalonia, Spain, in a paper published in 2024. The beetle mimics a wasp and bores into mulberry trees, which can die from the damage. It was first found in Europe in 2018. In Catalonia it grew from one district and 44 square kilometers that year to seven districts and over 1,100 square kilometers by late 2023. Its flight season is also stretching at both ends as temperatures climb.

The authors expect the infestation to keep spreading, likely along the Mediterranean coast toward Greece. They also test a control treatment, injecting a standard insecticide into infested trees. Results on how well that treatment works guide town councils facing dying street trees. The paper pairs a spread map with a practical control check. Both are tools for slowing a pest that climate change is helping.
pmc-11540067:
Xue-Feng Liang and co-authors measure how well flu shots in pregnancy prevented flu-like illness in Gansu, China, in this 2024 paper. Province records from the 2019 to 2021 seasons formed a large comparison group. Vaccinated and unvaccinated mothers were followed for illness rates.

Illness struck about four point seven percent of the vaccinated group and about six point nine percent of the unvaccinated. After adjustment, the vaccine's protection came to roughly twenty-two percent. Timing within pregnancy made no clear difference. The authors conclude the shot gave real, if modest, protection, and they report the finding for maternal health planning.
pmc-11561767:
Zhongyi Zhang and nine colleagues test a traditional Chinese herbal mix against fatty liver disease in mice. The decoction, called Qinlian Hongqu, had shown hints of easing the metabolic troubles tied to the disease. How it works was unknown, so the team combined animal tests with computer analysis.

Treated mice showed better blood fats, less liver fat, steadier blood sugar, and improved insulin response. Network analysis pointed to bile acid pathways. Lab checks then confirmed the mix acts through a signaling chain: the FXR and TGR5 receptors raise GLP-1, a gut hormone that aids insulin control. The authors present this chain as the decoction's main route of benefit.
pmc-11568167:
Jeong Mo Han and eight co-authors teach a neural network to forecast eye treatment results in a 2024 paper. Wet macular degeneration, a leading cause of blindness, is treated with injections that block blood vessel growth. Scans of the retina guide care, yet even experts struggle to predict who will improve.

The team trained a deep network on over two thousand scan images from 517 Korean patients. Two training setups were compared: scans taken before treatment alone, or scans from before and during treatment. The model was then measured against ophthalmologists. It beat the doctors at predicting anatomical improvement, with high sensitivity, catching most improvers, though its specificity was modest. The authors see such tools as decision support for planning injections and counseling patients. They are careful to frame the model as an aid, trained on one population, not a replacement for clinical judgment.
pmc-11570267:
Sukjoon Jung and co-authors study how daily gene rhythms change as plant leaves age, in work from 2024. A body clock sets the daily pattern of gene activity in the plant Arabidopsis. Aging was known to shorten the clock's free-running period, but what happens under normal day-night cycles stayed unclear.

In old leaves, the core clock genes shifted their timing and changed their wave shapes. The shift ran genome-wide, not just in clock genes. In effect, old plants live a shorter day and longer night than young ones on the same cycle. Plants with broken clock genes aged with their own distinct rhythm changes. The authors frame the rhythm shift as a programmed part of aging.
pmc-11571667:
Feng and co-authors review how chemical tags added to proteins after they are built — posttranslational modifications — steer fat metabolism in cancer. Tumors rewire how they make and burn lipids to feed fast growth, and these tags can switch the enzymes of that machinery up or down, move them, or change their partners. The review gathers what is known about the main tag types and the lipid pathways they control.

The authors argue that the tagging enzymes and their target sites are promising places to intervene. Blocking or boosting a tag could starve a tumor's lipid supply lines in ways that spare normal cells. Much of the evidence is still basic, and the review is candid that this corner of cancer metabolism is under-mapped. For researchers hunting new drug targets, the paper lays out where the tags sit and which ones look most actionable.
pmc-11572667:
Uchenna Okpete and Haewon Byeon review a study of teen depression in China in a 2024 commentary. Teen depression affects about one in seven adolescents worldwide. It can lead to school failure, drug use, and suicidal thoughts. The study under review covered nearly eight hundred Chinese teens.

Bad life events and distorted thinking both tracked with symptoms. Social support softened the blow of bad events. It did not blunt the effect of distorted thinking, though. The commentators urge therapy that targets perfectionism and rigid self reliance. They also back stronger support systems in schools and neighborhoods. Culture aware, whole person care is their main call. More work is needed on peer and parent roles over time.
pmc-11574467:
Acute myeloid leukemia starts in blood-forming stem cells, so no surface marker is found only on the cancer and not on healthy stem cells. Volta and co-authors build a two-headed antibody that links T cells to CD117, a protein found on both leukemia cells and healthy blood stem cells. The idea is short-term shared targeting, followed by a stem cell transplant to rebuild the blood system.

In lab tests the antibody killed leukemia lines and patient cells at very low doses, and in mice it held back leukemia growth and lowered CD117 cells. The authors suggest it could clear cancer and stem cells before a transplant.
pmc-11575067:
Naghmeh Abbasi Kasbi and seven co-authors survey what patients believe triggered their multiple sclerosis in a 2024 study from Iran. The disease inflames and strips nerves in the brain and spinal cord. What sets off the first attack remains disputed among scientists.

A questionnaire went out through a hospital research center and social media channels. Patients reported stress events, infections, vaccines, pregnancy, head injury, surgery, and weight loss around onset. Answers split by whether diagnosis came before or during the COVID-19 pandemic. Comparing the eras shows whether pandemic conditions changed the trigger mix. Patient-reported patterns can guide deeper studies of true causes. The survey also captures how a crisis era reshaped illness experience.
pmc-11576967:
Léo-Paul Tricou and seven colleagues study how the germ Staphylococcus aureus gets inside bone cells, in a twenty twenty-four paper. The germ's usual door uses a bridge of proteins that ends at docking spots called beta-1 integrins. A membrane protein, caveolin-1, was known to slow entry in skin cells. The team asked what happens in bone cells when the usual door is missing.

Entry needed recycling of the docking spots plus three helper switches. To their surprise, germs still entered cells that lacked the usual door, as long as caveolin-1 was also gone. Backup docking spots then took over the bridge role. The work shows the cell's membrane order decides which door the germ can use.
pmc-11579267:
Muhammad Arif Asghar and four co-authors review infectious uveitis, a swelling inside the eye caused by germs, in a paper published in twenty twenty-four. Viruses, bacteria, fungi, and parasites can all trigger it, and it harms sight worldwide. The team mapped trends over fifteen years and traced how the disease works at the molecular level.

They searched five databases for studies from twenty oh nine to twenty twenty-three, keeping ninety-seven. Reports rose over time, above all for viral cases. Viruses caused the largest share, then bacteria. Rates ran highest in poorer regions with more body-wide infections and fewer test tools. Network analysis of linked proteins flagged a few immune signals as hubs. The review ties germ types to immune pathways.
pmc-11580267:
Yiqun Luan and co-authors track world aid for early child care and schooling in a 2024 study. Poor and mid-income lands spend little of their own funds here, so donor aid can fill gaps. The team mined an aid log for projects across well over a hundred such lands over fifteen years.

Aid for this field made up under two in a hundred parts of all school aid, far below a ten-part share urged by a UN body. One large bank gave over half the total. Lands at war got a fourth of the per-child aid of calm lands, a gap the team flags.
pmc-11585267:
McDermott and co-authors explored how older adults in an underserved community experience chronic pain, and how clinic staff see the same problem. Using the socioecological model, they looked beyond the body to relationships, community, and society. They ran focus groups and interviews with 25 medical staff and 18 older patients at a diverse primary care clinic in the greater Boston area, then analyzed the transcripts for themes.

Patients described complex care needs, wide effects of pain on body, mood, work, and identity, and the ways they cope. Relationships with family and with staff could help or strain care. At the community level, people wanted more resources and culturally informed care, while income shaped what help was reachable at all. The authors call for pain treatments that act at every level, not only the individual one.
pmc-11585567:
He Yang and co-authors trace a molecular path from mental stress to heart disease. Their 2024 study centers on a protein that binds RNA and helps control heart growth and rhythm. Stress switches on a mark on this protein through a chain of signals in heart cells.

In mice with a blocked switch site, stress led to weak heart pumping, rhythm faults, poor blood fats, and sudden death. The blocked mark cut output of a key fat-carrying protein in the heart. Restoring that protein in heart cells fixed rhythm and pumping faults by easing cell stress and energy failure. Blood levels of the mark also flagged chronic stress in people. The work ties stress to heart harm step by step.
pmc-11586967:
Daniel Halloran and co-authors test a sugar-ring compound that may restore bone-building signals in aging mice. With age, bone marrow stem cells can stop responding to a key growth signal, BMP-2, which helps drive the bone loss of osteoporosis. Earlier work showed the signal's receptor rises in old mouse cells, yet signaling still falters.

Using marrow cells from fifteen-month-old mice, the team tagged the growth signal with glowing dots to watch it bind its receptor. They then treated the cells with a compound that disrupts how cells pull material inside. After treatment, bone mineral tests showed signaling had recovered in the old cells. The authors suggest fixing the receptor's handling may open a new route to treat age-related bone loss.
pmc-11588067:
Shravan Pradeep and five colleagues published a materials study in two thousand twenty-four on baseball's famous Rubbing Mud. For nearly a century, mud from a secret New Jersey river site has dulled new baseballs for Major League play. What makes it work was a mystery of soft matter physics.

Multi-scale tests of flow and friction revealed three mechanisms. The cohesive mud fills leather pores, evening the surface, thanks to strong shear thinning. Its residue doubles sticking contact on the ball. Sparse angular sand grains, glued on by clay, stud the surface and raise grip friction. The authors say the mix could inspire sustainable geomaterials. They also note lessons for mudslide modelling and moving through mud.
pmc-11589767:
Masafumi Hayashi and co-authors asked in 2024 how bacteria that lack a cell wall can still keep a set shape. They worked with a form of Escherichia coli that grows without a wall and tends to look uneven, like an ameba. Normal rod-shaped cells need a wall, so these cells pose a clear puzzle.

The team found that building just the wall across the middle, as the cell splits, was enough to make the cells mostly oval and even in size. A protein called FtsZ drove this split. The cells also needed at least one of two systems that place that split at the right spot.
pmc-11590267:
Yan Yang and co-authors model what makes a nurse ready for disaster in a 2024 study. When floods, quakes, or epidemics hit, nurses form the surge workforce, and their disaster literacy, knowledge plus judgment plus critical sense, decides how well wards cope. Which personal and social factors feed that literacy was the question.

Fifteen hundred seventy-three nurses across fifteen hospitals in one Chinese province answered questionnaires on five traits. Overall literacy sat at a middling level, weakest in its critical dimension. Structural modeling traced the wiring: collectivism fed literacy directly, and also indirectly, flowing through social support, psychological resilience, and self-efficacy in sequence. Each trait lifted the next. The authors translate the chain into management advice: training programs should build teams and support, not just drill facts, because a nurse's readiness grows from the whole ecology around her.
pmc-11590367:
Jane Foo and co-authors published this drug discovery study in 2024. Up to forty percent of patients with estrogen receptor positive breast cancer eventually resist standard hormone therapies. Resistance often comes from changes that keep the receptor switched on. Rather than block the usual hormone pocket, the team targeted a second site on the receptor called AF2. Partner proteins must dock there for the receptor to drive gene activity.

Using AI-guided deep docking, they screened over a billion small molecules in the computer. About 290 candidates went into cell-based and cell-free tests, ranked by how well they cut receptor activity and cancer cell growth. One lead compound, VPC-260724, worked at low doses. Tests confirmed it binds the AF2 site directly and breaks the receptor's grip on a key partner protein. It also slowed resistant cancer cells. The authors suggest pairing such a blocker with current treatments.
pmc-11590467:
Ariane Gobel and co-authors present a 2024 study on two questionnaires that measure how a mother bonds with her new baby. A strong early bond is a key part of the mother-child relationship. Both tools are widely used, but their measurement quality has been unclear, and translated versions need fresh checks before results can be compared across studies.

The team used data from three German studies, in Hamburg and Dresden, with samples from a few hundred to nearly two thousand mothers. They checked the German versions' item behavior, score patterns, and proposed factor structures. The aim was to learn whether the two tools measure bonding in a sound, repeatable way.
pmc-11590567:
Lisa Sangkum and co-authors ran this 2024 randomized trial on stretching spinal anesthesia in older men having prostate surgery. Spinal blocks for this operation wear off quickly, leaving a pain-management gap. Thirty-eight patients aged sixty to eighty received either a low intravenous dose of dexmedetomidine, a sedative known to deepen blocks, or saline, right after the spinal injection.

The block faded measurably slower with the drug: the two-level regression time stretched from about eighty-one to one hundred four minutes. Peak block height also rose. Low blood pressure, slow heart rate, and pain scores over the first day did not differ between groups. The authors conclude a small sedative dose safely buys extra anesthesia time in elderly patients.
pmc-11591367:
Jacqueline Poblete and co-authors mine pisco grape pomace, the skins and seeds left by distilling, for antioxidant and enzyme-blocking molecules using green extraction. Winery waste is cheap and rich, and molecules that block acetylcholinesterase or cyclooxygenase carry real therapeutic interest. The team wants the useful names, not just bulk activity.

Their 2024 study layers the extract on chromatography plates, sprays bioassays directly on the bands, and reads the active spots by mass spectrometry. Three antioxidants are identified, among them quercetin glycosides and gallic acid. Gallic acid doubles as the cyclooxygenase blocker, and a kaempferol glycoside blocks the cholinesterase. The authors pitch the waste stream as feedstock for functional foods, closing a loop in the pisco industry.
pmc-11591667:
Ji Woo Yang and co-authors build a rapid test for drug-resistant gut bacteria in a 2024 paper. Resistant strains spread worldwide and raise death rates. Standard tests are too slow and complex for bedside use.

Their platform joins rapid amplification with a CRISPR-based readout. Two key resistance genes are the targets. The full test takes about fifty minutes, including extraction. Fluorescence signals give the answer without heavy equipment or long culture waits in the lab. Readers in diagnostics learn how CRISPR tools can move resistance checks from central labs to the point of care, where fast answers guide first treatment choices.
pmc-11592067:
