Wenyi Tang and co-authors review two hormone families in a 2024 paper. Activins and inhibins were first known for opposed effects on a pituitary hormone. Wider roles across many tissues have since emerged. They signal mainly through a classic pathway, with other routes in play. Their action is complex and depends on context.

Recent work ties both families to heart and vessel disease. Signals from other organs also track with heart disease growth. The review sums biological roles, mechanisms, and heart findings in one place. Heart researchers get a map of two factors long filed under reproduction. Cross-system signals are easy to miss in organ-siloed research. If these factors drive part of heart disease, they offer fresh drug targets. The authors frame the field as young, with mechanism gaps still open.
pmc-11592567:
Likan Zhan, Andrei Khrennikov, and Yingce Zhu test in 2024 whether the math of quantum theory can describe a quirk of human perception. Some objects can be seen in two ways, like a cup that flips between views depending on context. The study belongs to a field that borrows quantum methods for use outside physics.

In their tests, the way people saw cup-like objects depended on what came before, showing memory effects and a kind of lag when the view flipped. The order of questions changed the answers, much as order changes results in physics tests. A standard bound used to check for fixed, context-free answers was clearly broken. The authors stress this does not prove anything deep about nature. It shows that answers from different contexts cannot be forced into one shared table of random outcomes.
pmc-11594467:
Grigorios Kyriakopoulos and three co-authors review farm pesticides, legal and banned, in a 2024 paper. Pesticides drive modern yields but are criticized for harming soil, water, and sometimes people, so greener options are in demand. Their review catalogs dozens of distinct chemicals, alone or in mixes and residues. Most target insects, with smaller groups against weeds, fungi, and mites.

They sorted the chemicals by structure into simulated marketable and banned pools and computed adjustment measures that grouped them into four clusters. Crystal analysis worked only for the marketable set. The authors frame the catalog as a base for judging which chemistries deserve replacement.
pmc-11595067:
Hikosaka-Kuniishi and a team of colleagues studied a signaling helper protein, TRAF5, in mouse immune responses in twenty twenty-four. Germinal centers are lymph node hubs where B cells refine antibodies. TRAF5 connects to CD40, a key switch in that process, but its exact role was unclear.

Mice lacking TRAF5 were immunized with a model antigen plus adjuvant. Their germinal center B cells formed poorly, and antigen-specific IgM and IgG1 antibodies fell sharply. Genes that CD40 normally switches on for center formation also dropped. In lab tests, TRAF5-free B cells made less antibody, grew less, and answered CD40 stimulation weakly. Giving a CD40 activator to deficient mice still failed to rescue center growth. The authors call TRAF5 crucial for CD40-driven, T-dependent immunity.
pmc-11595267:
Yuxin Chen and co-authors sequence stick insect genomes in a 2024 paper. Stick and leaf insects are famed for mimicry, but their family tree is still debated. Mitochondrial genomes offer markers to settle the branches.

The team sequenced five mitogenomes and built trees with two methods and two data sets. Their results place the leaf insect family at the base of a major group. Two subfamilies held together as single branches, while one family proved polyphyletic, drawn from mixed lines. A time tree put the origin of living stick insects in the Jurassic, with most lines splitting after the dinosaur-killing extinction.
pmc-11595367:
In hot closed-die forging, metal is hammered into shape between dies that wear out fast under heat and pressure. Grzegorz Ficak and co-authors review in 2024 what wears the tools down and what can be done about it. Wear arrives by several mechanisms, and die life stretches when makers choose the right hot-work steel, heat-treat it well, engineer the surface, and manage lubrication and cooling.

When dies do wear, shops can regenerate them by re-profiling or by laser rebuilding. Predicting wear is its own field: the review covers the classical Archard model and its fit to experiments, high-temperature low-cycle fatigue, and a newer route using artificial neural networks. The authors aim the survey at practitioners who need dies to last longer in one of manufacturing's harshest jobs.
pmc-11595967:
Georgy Lazorenko and four co-authors tested flax waste as a soil strengthener in a 2024 paper. Expansive soils swell and shrink as their moisture changes, which cracks roads and foundations. Usual fixes are costly and hard on the environment, so the team tried fibers left over from flax processing.

Mixed into clay soil, the flax tow raised strength by up to 29 percent at a dose of 0.6 percent. Cracking fell sharply at a slightly lower dose. Adding more fiber backfired, because the fibers clumped and gripped the soil less well. The authors present flax waste as a cheap, green way to steady problem soils.
pmc-11596267:
Zeki Gunsoy and co-authors ask what makes a shoulder break during its own repair in a 2024 study. Putting a dislocated shoulder back can, rarely, fracture the bone near the joint. The team reviewed eighty-nine first-time front dislocations in patients without loose joints. A displacement ratio measured how far the ball sat from its socket rim.

Ten patients suffered the treatment-caused fracture during closed reduction. Others split into failed reductions and clean successes for comparison. Extra fractures of the socket-side bump appeared in over forty percent of all cases. Bone quality scores and injury details were weighed alongside head position. Pinpointing which positions snap would let clinicians choose safer techniques for risky shoulders.
pmc-11597267:
Elana Bosch, Jorg Sporri, and Johannes Scherr review genetic variants that affect iron handling in healthy adults. Their review came out in 2024. The goal is to support nutrition advice that is tailored to a person's genes.

The team searched three large databases for studies in English and German over a long span. Twenty-one papers met their rules, and all of the variants found affected iron measures. One gene showed the strongest link to iron levels. Two variants in another gene appeared to protect against low iron. Eleven other variants raised the risk of iron shortage, which suggests those carriers may gain from extra iron in the diet.
pmc-11597367:
Khursheda Parvin and co-authors present a 2024 study of a plant acid that helps tomato seedlings ride out drought. Water shortage cuts seedling growth, drains leaf water, and lets reactive molecules damage cells. The acid, a natural compound from plant cell walls, is known to tune stress responses.

Seedlings grown in water culture were pretreated with the acid for two days, then put under four days of drought stress, both by withholding water and with a drying agent. The team tracked growth, leaf water, green pigments, and the antioxidant defense system, plus a detox pathway for a harmful byproduct. Pretreated plants kept more growth and suffered less oxidative damage than untreated stressed plants.
pmc-11597767:
A Brazilian plant known as espinheira-santa has long been used for stomach trouble. Maitê da Silva and co-authors tested its leaf extract against the standard reflux drug omeprazole in 2024, in a double-blind trial with eighty-six patients with reflux symptoms. One group took the drug; two others took the extract at 400 or 860 milligrams, all for four weeks.

Every group improved: reflux symptom scores and heartburn's drag on daily life fell sharply, with no differences between the groups after treatment. About three quarters of patients stuck with the schedule. The authors conclude both extract doses performed no worse than omeprazole in this preliminary trial, a result that supports further study of the traditional remedy.
pmc-11598967:
Yang Liu and co-authors show how a heat shock protein helps a cattle virus enter cells, in a 2024 paper. The head byline omits one catalog author, so team framing is used. The virus causes breathing disease in cattle and enters cells through a common uptake route that uses a protein coat.

The protein raised the coat protein's levels through a signal path and boosted a partner protein's enzyme work. Both steps made the uptake route run faster, so more virus got in and copied itself. Tests with other viruses suggest the protein can aid entry for a range of viruses. That breadth makes it a point of interest for antiviral work.
pmc-11600067:
Blue-green algae in lakes and reservoirs can release toxins that reach drinking water and farm ponds. Siddharth Rajput and co-authors review how those toxins may start or push cancer, in a 2024 paper. They focus on three well-known toxins, plus two nerve toxins whose role is less clear.

One toxin blocks enzymes that keep cell growth in check, so cells can grow out of turn. A second toxin acts in much the same way. A third halts protein making and can damage genes. The nerve pair may add risk through cell stress and gene damage, though proof is thin. The review pulls the evidence into one place for health and water staff.
pmc-11600567:
Ida Rahmqvist and co-authors test a personal blood test to track a childhood cancer, in a 2024 study. The cancer, neuroblastoma, can return after treatment. Bits of tumor DNA float in the blood and can signal its presence. Older tests used a fixed set of known changes, which misses some children.

Each child's test was built from that child's own tumor. Panels targeted ten unique changes per patient. The team ran the tests on 136 blood samples from 13 children over time. Very deep sequencing read the samples. A personal approach widens who can be monitored and may catch relapse earlier. Blood tests of this kind spare children some scans and biopsies.
pmc-11600667:
Melker Johansson and four co-authors ask in 2024 whether physical work and leisure activity pull blood pressure in opposite directions for men and women. Heavy work activity is suspected of raising pressure, unlike leisure exercise. Using a Danish aging cohort, the team treated the day as a fixed pie: sleep, sitting, and light and hard activity at work and at leisure.

Pressure readings were modeled as time was notionally shifted between pie slices. The compositional method lets each swap show its own association, separately by sex. The study speaks to the activity paradox debate, where the same movement seems to harm at work yet help at play, with patterns that may differ for women and men.
pmc-11600767:
Lung tumors that stop answering to platinum chemotherapy need new weapons, and a compound from orchids is one candidate. Lingxue Tang and five co-authors tested erianin, a natural product from Dendrobium orchids, on drug-resistant lung adenocarcinoma cells and in animals, in a 2024 study. They measured cell growth, movement, invasion, and programmed death with a battery of standard assays.

Erianin slowed the resistant cells and cut their ability to spread. It worked through a major growth pathway, quieting the Wnt signal chain, and switched on an executioner enzyme that drives cell suicide. The authors present erianin as a promising lead against resistant lung cancer, pending much more testing.
pmc-11600867:
Tiina Savikangas and four co-authors published an aging study in twenty twenty-four on how mood and movement related during COVID restrictions in Finland. Two population cohorts, one around age sixty and one spanning the seventies and eighties, reported activity frequency, changes in activity, and three facets of mental well-being.

Feeling more positive affect tracked with moving more often in both cohorts, and with having increased activity in the younger one. Negative affect and depressive symptoms showed their own, separate associations, examined independently rather than as one mood score. The authors argue well-being's bright and dark sides are distinct levers on older adults' activity. Pandemic-era data make the snapshot historically specific.
pmc-11600967:
Mehdi Karim and co-authors pool trial results on saffron for people with diabetes in this 2024 review. Saffron is a spice with a long history in traditional medicine. Interest has grown in whether it can improve the blood markers that drive heart and metabolic risk.

Fifteen trials with eight hundred sixty-nine overweight patients with diabetes or prediabetes were combined. Saffron clearly lowered fasting blood sugar, a long-term sugar marker, blood fats of one kind, and top blood pressure. It also lowered a liver enzyme linked to strain. No clear effect appeared for insulin output, cholesterol measures, or kidney markers. The authors judge saffron a helpful add-on for some markers. They call for more trials with longer follow-up to firm up the picture.
pmc-11601067:
Catarina Cardoso and colleagues test for sleep apnea in patients whose lungs are scarring from interstitial disease other than the idiopathic kind, in this study from twenty twenty-four. Fifty patients took home sleep tests. The yield was striking: seventy-six percent had obstructive sleep apnea, a rate echoing the idiopathic fibrosis literature.

Two measures predicted it independently: lower total lung capacity and lower waking oxygen saturation. Twelve patients started positive airway pressure therapy. Within three months, over ninety percent were well controlled, sleepiness scores fell significantly, and night-time low oxygen was corrected in every patient. Emotional well-being trended upward. The authors argue for a low suspicion threshold in fibrotic lung clinics: ask, test, and treat, because the mask quietly fixes the nights of most who wear it.
pmc-11602067:
Zhendong Gao and six colleagues review whether social capital lifts student physical activity, in a paper from twenty twenty-four. Students often move too little, harming health and grades. Social ties might push them toward exercise. The reviewers searched four databases under standard guidelines.

Ten studies covering twenty-seven hundred students qualified, mostly from North America and Europe. Study quality scored high across the set. Strong networks, family and friend support, and social cohesion all tracked with more activity. Emotional support, role modeling, and social norms were the proposed mechanisms. Most evidence was self-reported and cross-sectional, limiting causal claims. The authors still see social capital as a real lever. They urge objective measures and longitudinal designs next.
pmc-11602667:
Firoozeh Gerayeli and co-authors map airway cells one by one in a 2024 study of pulmonary long COVID. Some patients keep new or worsening breathing symptoms long after their first infection. The cell-level drivers of that lingering illness were unclear. The team built a single-cell gene map of the airway lining to find them.

Adults with and without long COVID were recruited around Greater Vancouver in Canada. The long COVID group had new or worse respiratory symptoms at least twelve weeks after infection. Bronchial brushings gathered cells from the airway wall, and each cell's gene activity was read on its own. The map shows which cell types shift in number or state in the sick group. Such shifts point to the pathways that keep lungs inflamed and suggest where treatment could aim.
pmc-11603067:
Zhiqiang Wang leads a team that tests a spine fusion setup in the lab. Their study from twenty twenty-four deals with oblique lateral interbody fusion. The surgery treats lumbar degenerative diseases with small cuts.

A side plate adds stability in normal bone cases. Whether it works in weak bone was unclear. Calf spine samples were split by bone condition. Normal, thinned, and osteoporotic groups were compared. Loads were applied in many directions for the tests. A camera system tracked segment movement in three dimensions. States ran from intact spine to cage plus plate.
pmc-11603167:
Hakan Gem and co-authors link a spit bacterium to worse mouth sores after stem cell transplant, with the effect split by sex. Their 2024 study tracks oral mucositis, a painful toxicity that lengthens hospital stays. Chemo and radiation cause the sores directly, but host factors may tune their depth.

Mouth microbes were profiled at several sites while trained examiners scored sores over time. One harmless resident, found in saliva before transplant, foretold harsher sores two weeks later. Its sex lean matched higher uric acid in men. The authors call it the first sex-tied microbe path found for this injury. They point to prevention targets that follow from the link.
pmc-11603267:
Fuhui Yan and co-authors profile tiny blood-borne packets in 2024 to find markers and drug leads for delirium after surgery. Diagnosis today rests on bedside observation alone. The team compared proteins and metabolites inside plasma exosomes from patients with and without the condition. Clear differences emerged, pointing at brain inflammation and blood-brain barrier damage.

Five candidate markers stood out, including an enzyme called MMP9. A drug-matching database then suggested compounds that might block it. Computer docking showed two of them binding strongly. The authors present these as fresh treatment avenues. The study shows how multi-layer profiling of exosomes can guide targeted care.
pmc-11603667:
Moritz Lodde and seven co-authors test two ways of plating a difficult pelvis fracture in the laboratory, in this 2024 study. T-shaped fractures of the hip socket are hard to fix, especially when bone is thin. Locking plates, whose screws grip the plate itself, promise a steadier hold. Sixteen synthetic pelvis models received the same simulated fracture and a two column plate.

Half were fixed with locking screws, half with conventional ones, then loaded repeatedly while markers tracked movement at the fracture. The locking constructs moved less, both at rest and under cycling. Overall stiffness, though, did not differ significantly between the groups. The authors conclude that angular stable plates buy positional stability where bone is scarce, even if the whole construct is no stiffer.
pmc-11603767:
Christiane Horwood and co-authors report, in a 2024 World Health Organization study, how heavily baby formula marketing reaches mothers across seven countries. Formula promotion is well funded and has eroded breastfeeding, despite laws in many places modeled on an international marketing code. The team surveyed pregnant women and mothers in Bangladesh, Mexico, Morocco, Nigeria, South Africa, the United Kingdom, and Viet Nam. Over eight thousand women described the marketing they had seen.

About four in ten women reported exposure, but the spread was huge, from a trickle in Morocco to nearly everyone in Viet Nam. Television was the top channel everywhere, with shop displays and print ads also common. Social media and video sites played a smaller role in most countries. The authors argue the findings show how unevenly marketing rules bite around the world.
pmc-11603867:
Hailing Huang and co-authors study a family of genes called PIWIL in liver cancer, using mice and many layers of gene data. The family helps silence genes, and its members were suspected of playing split roles in this cancer. Tissue from cancerous and healthy livers was compared with sequencing, computer analysis, and lab checks.

Two family members ran high in cancer and one ran low. A web of RNA sponges and blockers seemed to drive that split: some members were freed from their blockers while one stayed blocked. Partner proteins tied the family to gene control and metabolism. The authors read the pattern as two members pushing the cancer on, and one holding it back.
pmc-11603967:
Meng Zhang and co-authors searched blood samples for a marker of a serious lung vessel disease in a 2024 study. The disease, pulmonary arterial hypertension, strains the right side of the heart. A simple blood test that flags it early would help doctors act sooner.

The team compared blood proteins in patients and healthy controls, then checked the best leads with a second test. Three proteins stood out, and one, called HGFA, split patients from controls with the best accuracy. Low levels of that protein tracked with worse heart function. Gene-based checks and rat studies backed a real link to the disease, which makes the protein a strong lead for a future blood test.
pmc-11604667:
Kakade, Bote, and Pawar test whether two plant compounds can shield liver cells from a common food additive. Butylated hydroxytoluene, an antioxidant in packaged foods, paradoxically stresses cells with reactive oxygen. The pair, Boeravinone B and Chebulinic Acid, was applied together to human liver cells in culture.

The additive alone spiked reactive oxygen and nitrogen, raised stress-enzyme activity, and pushed a fifth of cells into programmed death and nearly three-quarters into self-digestion. The compound pair cut the reactive species roughly in half, lowered the damage markers, and kept far more cells growing normally, a rescue confirmed by gene tests. The authors propose the pairing against additive-driven liver harm.
pmc-11604967:
Zong-jie Wang and Tian-hua Lin analyzed hospital data in 2024 on brain bleeding and sedation. The condition is subarachnoid hemorrhage, a sudden bleed around the brain. Sedative choice may affect how patients fare. The team drew cases from a large intensive care database. They compared three sedatives on predictive value. They then matched patients who got one drug, dexmedetomidine, with similar patients who did not. Later models weighed death and length of stay together.

Dexmedetomidine predicted outcomes better than the other two sedatives. After matching, the two groups were equal in size. Use of the drug tied to lower risk of death in hospital. A competing-risk model treated death as the rival outcome for stay length. In that model, the drug still protected against death. It showed no clear link to length of stay. The authors call the drug a promising sedative choice here.
pmc-11605067:
Guangpeng Xu and five colleagues published a computer vision study in two thousand twenty-four on finding tyre defects in X-ray images before tyres leave the factory. Tyre structure is complex and defects slender and varied, defeating manual inspection and older algorithms.

Their detector, built on the YOLOv5 model, adds a snake-like convolution that follows curved, thin features such as cord cracks and overlaps. New fusion modules blend image scales while attention blocks suppress busy backgrounds. A softer box-selection step sharpens final calls. Accuracy rose about six percentage points over the base model on standard measures. The authors claim it beats current mainstream detectors on this task.
pmc-11605867:
Five authors, led by Dawan Hawezy, surveyed medical students and examiners about a new exam format in this 2024 paper. Clinical skill exams called OSCEs, where students rotate through set tasks, reached most medical schools only in the last decade. The grand version, GOSCE, stretches that format into a bigger, mixed test of specialties.

The study asked fourth- and sixth-year students, plus their examiners, how they saw the format, its features, and its quality. The aim was twofold. First, to judge whether the grand exam readies students for real wards, where cases from many specialties mix. Second, to see how its design differs from older assessment habits in the eyes of those who take and run it. Such feedback guides schools that are weighing the new format against the standard one.
pmc-11605967:
Prashant Nasa and a large international team of co-authors published a survey study in 2024 on dangerous pressure build-up inside the abdomen. Raised pressure can starve organs of blood, and a society of specialists last set shared definitions in twenty thirteen. The team asked clinicians worldwide whether they accept the current wording and proposed updates.

The online survey, run across twenty twenty-two and twenty twenty-three, gathered views on measuring pressure, defining the conditions, and managing them. Agreement levels were compared across specialties, training, and years of experience. Results will feed the next round of guidelines. For a condition where minutes matter, shared definitions help intensive care teams act the same way everywhere.
pmc-11606067:
Beatriz Böger and co-authors audit weight-loss surgery costs in a 2024 Brazilian study. Grouping patients by diagnosis-related groups lets a health plan compare cost and care fairly across hospitals. The team reviews over 1,400 patients who had metabolic and bariatric surgery across four hospitals over four years.

Most patients are women in their late thirties with severe obesity, and nearly nine in ten receive a gastric bypass. In-hospital complications are uncommon, though bleeding and leaks appear, and one patient dies. About five percent return within a month. The authors total the full cost of care to guide plan management.
pmc-11606167:
Zhu and four co-authors test an iron-cheat drug as a cure for gum rot in rats in this twenty twenty-four study. Gum rot eats the bone that holds teeth and is fed by swelling in the gum. The drug fakes low air in cells, a state known to curb such swelling.

Inside, cells dosed with the drug made far less of the scent marks that call swelling in. The drug also blocked a key swelling path by holding its switch out of the cell core. Bone-eat cells formed in far lower counts when the drug was on board first. Sick rats on the drug lost less jaw bone and had calmer gums. The team backs it for more cure work.
pmc-11607067:
Zheng Fang and co-authors weigh a hard trade-off in panda country: dogs living near giant panda habitat are vaccinated against canine distemper to protect the pandas, but the vaccine itself may spread. They tracked 69 dogs in panda areas, testing blood for virus defenses and swabs for virus shedding after shots.

Vaccinated dogs did shed virus, mostly starting around day nine. Unvaccinated dogs kept in shared kennels caught the virus from them, as family-tree tests of the virus confirmed. Dogs that started with stronger defenses shed less and for fewer days. Dog ranges also overlapped wild panda ranges in two reserves. The authors advise keeping vaccinated dogs restricted for at least three weeks, with local officials, reserve staff, and villagers managing shots together.
pmc-11607367:
Long noncoding RNAs, gene-like stretches that never become proteins, help steer bladder cancer, and Jing Zhou and eight co-authors hunted for ones tied to a fresh form of cell death. That death, ferroptosis, is driven by iron and damaged fats. The team screened patient data for ferroptosis-linked RNAs whose levels differed in tumors.

Statistical sieves narrowed the field to an 18-RNA signature that forecasts patient outcomes. Lab tests on two bladder cancer cell lines showed two of the RNAs at work: raising one or silencing another pushed the cells toward death. The silenced one, AL136084.3, binds a protein called NUPR1, and the two track together in tumors. The authors offer the signature as a prognostic tool and the RNA-protein pair as a lead for treatment research.
pmc-11607867:
Khadivi, Mirheidari, Saeidifar, Moradi, and Tunç measure in twenty twenty-four the shape diversity of tamarind trees grown in southeast Iran. Tamarind is a valued fruit tree across the tropics, but its local variation was poorly charted. The team scored fifty-five local types on dozens of leaf, fruit, and tree traits and analysed them with several statistical tools.

Most traits varied widely between types, which signals rich diversity for breeding. Leaf size tracked together, as did fruit length with fruit weight. The types fell into four clusters, and the team ranked the top twenty by trait performance. The authors offer the results as a resource for breeding tougher, better tamarind varieties.
pmc-11608067:
Emmanuel Abiola Babington, Cletus Amedu, Ebuka Anyasor, and Ruth Reeve review ultrasound methods that trace blood flow without injected contrast, in this 2024 paper. Ultrasound has served clinics since the nineteen forties, and flow imaging has passed through generations. Color and power Doppler came first, but both miss slow flow.

Newer modes changed that. One mode renders flow directly in brightness rather than by the Doppler shift. Microvascular imaging, using a clever wall filter, catches the slow signals in tiny vessels that older modes lose. Advanced dynamic flow, popular in obstetric scanning, maps fetal vessels and heart chambers in fine detail. The authors walk through each method's principles, strengths, limits, and clinical uses, with the supporting literature.
pmc-11608267:
Hossein Poorhemati and Svetlana Komarova build in 2024 a unified math model of how bone turns hard. Mineralization is ruled by two masters at once: biology, as the collagen scaffold matures, and chemistry, as acidity and ion levels shift in the fluid around the bone.

Earlier models handled one side or the other. A biological model tracked the matrix but ignored ion supply, which diseases of phosphate balance can disturb. The authors merge the two older models into one that carries both regulations together. The combined model should predict bone hardening under conditions neither parent model could reach alone.
pmc-11608367:
Genes are switched on and off by proteins called transcription factors, and the GATA family guides growth and stress responses in plants. Mangi Kim compares the protein makeup of GATA factors across the plant kingdom. The study gathers 5,335 of these proteins from 165 species listed in a public plant database, spanning many branches of the plant family tree.

By lining up the amino acid sequences, Kim maps the parts that stay the same across species and the parts that change. The shared core includes the zinc-finger grip that holds DNA. The changing parts hint at how different lineages tuned the factors for their own needs. The author says these patterns can guide work on crops that handle stress better, since GATA factors help plants react to drought and other hardships.
pmc-11610167:
Christine Pacitti and co-authors review pain medicine use in adults with intellectual disabilities, in this 2024 systematic review. These adults feel more pain than most, take many medicines overall, yet may get less pain relief. The team screened over twenty-six thousand papers and kept twenty-seven sound studies.

Simple painkillers were prescribed more than stronger classes, while mind-acting drugs were prescribed more than any pain drug at all. Patients and caregivers alike reported pain being missed and undertreated. The authors call better pain assessment and treatment a research priority for this underserved group.
pmc-11610567:
Runlu Chen and co-authors find that a DNA repair protein also acts as a brake on a yeast's power to cause disease, in a 2024 study. The yeast, Candida albicans, lives on human skin and gut but can turn harmful. Its Rad18 protein helps fix gaps left in DNA after copying. Whether that repair work ties to virulence was unknown.

Yeast stripped of the Rad18 gene grew weak under DNA damage, as expected. Two inner parts of the protein proved key for that defense. To the team's surprise, the stripped yeast survived better inside immune cells and killed more wax moth larvae. Gene reads showed the loss freed two virulence genes, HWP1 and ECE1, to run hotter. Muting those genes with a gene-silencing tool reversed the extra virulence. Repair and attack, it seems, share one switch.
pmc-11611567:
Jinbo Zhao and co-authors ask how a local pig breed thrives on coarse feed while pregnant. Songliao Black sows in China are known for toughness on rough diets, yet the body pathways were vague. Their 2024 study fed 40 sows, each 30 days pregnant, one of four diets. The base corn-soy diet got none, a tenth, a fifth, or three tenths of alfalfa meal in swap for part of the base.

Meals with a tenth or a fifth of alfalfa gave the best litter results. Stool gene readings showed the tenth group held the richest gut microbes, with more helper kinds. Blood and stool scans found 239 shifted body compounds, tied to three paths: a cell signaling path, building-block making, and hormone making. Set microbe pairs rose and fell with set compounds. The team maps how fiber, microbes, and compounds act as one.
pmc-11611967:
Giovanni Rubeis and Andrew Sixsmith introduce a journal collection on the ethics of AgeTech in a 2024 editorial. AgeTech covers tools built to improve older adults' lives, from communication apps and robots to wearables and smart homes. These tools can empower older people, yet they raise hard ethical questions.

The collected articles examine those questions, with special focus on artificial intelligence and robotics. Topics run from autonomy and privacy to fairness in how such systems treat their users. The editors aim to supply frameworks and strategies for building technology that respects dignity while supporting health and quality of life. The editorial frames the stakes for designers, caregivers, and policymakers in ageing societies.
pmc-11612167:
Carbon monoxide from a faulty heater can injure a child's brain for years, and which children carry lasting harm is hard to foresee. Tuoying Wen and four co-authors followed 113 poisoned children in China in 2024, for an average of three and a half years after discharge. Most poisonings traced to gas water heaters used in closed bathrooms.

Thirteen children, about one in nine, showed lasting cognitive problems. Longer unconsciousness, higher inflammation markers, and seizures during the stay marked the higher risk group. Brain swelling was the commonest scan finding. The authors say the pattern can guide which children get long follow up. Prevention, they add, starts with the heater and the room.
pmc-11612867:
Moa Wolff and co-authors test cooling the nose to treat migraine at home, in a 2024 feasibility study. Many migraine patients get too little relief from current drugs. Blowing evaporative coolant through the nose eased attacks in an earlier clinic study, likely by cooling blood bound for the brain.

The Swedish team asked patients with episodic migraine to use the device themselves at home when attacks struck. The single-group trial checked whether people could manage the device, follow the steps, and tolerate the treatment outside a clinic. Results from this dry run shape the design of a planned full randomized trial. A drug-free option patients can self-administer would widen migraine care.
pmc-11613367:
Faaiz Ali Shah surveys clinical teachers about a hospital computer system in Peshawar, Pakistan, in a 2024 study. The system handles hospital records and management tasks at Lady Reading Hospital. Happy end users are a fair test of whether such a system earns its keep on busy wards.

A standard twelve-item satisfaction survey went to the orthopaedic division's consultants, and one hundred forty-two replied. Most said the system gave precise information and met their content needs most of the time. Large shares found the output clear, timely, and up to date. Overall, most consultants were satisfied with the system. The study gives hospital managers a user-side verdict to guide further upgrades.
pmc-11613867:
Nancy Sabry Ellethiey and co-authors study how skill care for nurses links to how well they feel their job deal is kept. The study appeared in 2024. It covers three hundred seventy-five nurses in three private hospitals in Egypt. More than half of the nurses were in the young adult group.

Nurses rated skill care as fair, trust in the job deal as low, and warm ties at work as fair. Warm ties helped pass the good effect of skill care on to trust in the deal. Age group changed the link, and in a weak way. The authors say fair skill care and warm ties help nurses trust that work will honor its side of the deal.
pmc-11613967:
Junaid Zafar Sheikh and four co-authors describe a rare illness showing up in an even rarer place, in a case report published in twenty twenty-four. The illness, Kikuchi-Fujimoto disease, causes fever and swollen lymph nodes and usually fades on its own. It nearly always strikes the neck nodes; only two past cases involved chest nodes alone.

Their patient was a twenty-nine-year-old Indian man with fever, mouth and skin sores, weight loss, and swollen chest nodes on a scan. Tests ruled out cancer, infection, and immune disease. A needle sample taken through the airways showed the dying node tissue typical of this illness. He was treated for symptoms and reassured. The authors stress that knowing this illness spares patients harsh care meant for look-alike diseases, and that long follow-up matters since it can pair with immune conditions.
pmc-11616267:
Mormone and co-authors compare two bone marrow sources for knee arthritis care, in work from 2024. Marrow holds rare stem cells and healing factors, and shots of it can ease joint pain. It is most often drawn from the hip crest, and rarely from the shin bone. The trial set both sources against platelet-rich plasma in thirty patients.

Half-year checks on half the patients showed hip marrow held far more key cells than shin marrow. Yet pain and function gains at six months were alike across all three arms. Hip marrow led on pain change, shin marrow on function change, but neither lead was firm. Full results are still to come.
pmc-11616367:
Mari Storli Rasmussen and co-authors tally the full first-year cost of moderate to severe trauma in Norway, in a 2024 study. Most earlier counts stopped at the hospital bill, missing rehabilitation and social support. Registry data followed 601 patients hurt in 2020 for twelve months after injury.

Health care averaged about 847,000 kroner per patient and rehabilitation about 251,000 more, with secondary care in the first six months dominating. Severely injured patients used more care and cost more than moderately injured ones, and injury severity, head, spine, and limb injuries drove the totals. The authors offer the fuller picture to planners who arrange services for patients with complex needs.
pmc-11616867:
Luis Genaro and co-authors test ways to measure hand skill in dental students in a study from two thousand twenty-four. Fine finger control matters for cavity work, and schools want tests that predict who will struggle in preclinical training. Five assessment methods were compared in ninety-five fifth-year students.

Scores on real cavity and filling work served as the standard. A dentistry-specific dexterity test performed best, with clear significance and acceptable discrimination. Two classic pegboard and finger tests did not reach significance. The authors recommend the dental test for early screening, so students with motor difficulties can get targeted help sooner.
pmc-11618067:
Ye Mu and co-authors trace how Pacific climate patterns steer low-level wind jets that feed South American summer rains, in a 2024 paper. The jets run north along the eastern Andes and carry moist air. They come in three types, Central, Northern, and Andes, each tied to different flood patterns. Two slow Pacific rhythms, the El Niño cycle and a decadal swing, may set how often each type blows.

Looking back sixty-five years, the authors found both rhythms matter. The Central jet shows up more in El Niño years and warm or neutral decadal phases, bringing heavier extreme rain to the continent's south. Cool decadal phases with La Niña favour the other two jets, shifting extremes toward the western Amazon and the southeast. Some jet types also last longer under certain phases. The results aid seasonal flood outlooks.
pmc-11618467: Melvin Lee Qiyu, Amna Ahmed, and Tom Dawson report a toddler whose scurvy fooled his doctors at first, in a case report from twenty twenty-four. The three-year-old boy could not bear weight for four weeks. Fine red spots marked his lower legs. Scans showed swollen bone and soft tissue, raising fears of worse disease. Blood tests and his picky diet pointed instead to vitamin C lack. Vitamin C and pain relief, plus diet and physio help, set him right.
pmc-11618667:
Sepsis in children is dangerous and hard to spot early, so hospitals are testing computer tools that predict it. Ryan Tennant and co-authors reviewed the field in 2024, gathering studies on data-driven prediction tools for children outside the newborn period. They found twenty-seven studies and mapped how the tools were built, tested, and reported.

Most studies came from a single hospital, and most used a classic statistical method rather than newer machine learning. Reported accuracy varied widely, and many studies used data where sepsis was rare. Details about real-world use, such as fit with staff workflow, were often missing. The authors urge builders to involve clinical users early and to report human factors more fully.
pmc-11618767:
Teppei Matsui and co-authors asked how the primate brain keeps real signals apart from its own background chatter, in a 2024 study. In mouse sight areas, patterns from real sights and from idle activity point in different directions, which helps sort signal from noise. Primate sight areas, built in columns, seemed to break that rule.

In marmoset monkeys, the first sight area indeed showed alike patterns for idle and driven activity. Higher sight areas, though, pulled the two apart step by step up the chain. At the top, the split matched what mice show in their first area. The authors say this sorting is a general rule of brain work. In primates, the work is spread across levels rather than done at the first step.
pmc-11619167:
Ping-Zhen Lin, Li-Hui Yang, Jing Su, and Jiao-Mei Xue wrote this 2024 study on stress, coping styles, and depression among nurses in China. Stress is known to track with low mood in nurses, but two kinds of stress may work in unlike ways: hardship in childhood and the stress felt day to day. The team surveyed 737 nurses at a large hospital.

The nurses' coping styles fell into four groups, from active coping down to low coping. Both kinds of stress tracked with higher depression scores. One style, holding feelings in, carried part of the effect of childhood hardship on depression. That style, plus the low coping group, carried part of the effect of daily stress. The authors urge hospitals to cut stress and coach better coping to guard nurses' mental health.
pmc-11619467:
Juan Yao and co-authors compare two myopia corrections by what they do to the eye's surface. SMILE reshapes the cornea with a laser, while an implantable collamer lens slips inside the eye, leaving the surface nearly untouched. Thirty-two SMILE patients and thirty-five lens patients were examined before surgery and three times over three months.

Tear measures dipped then recovered in both groups, but SMILE patients stayed drier, with higher symptom scores and more meibomian gland loss at three months. The lens group bounced back faster, with objective measures normalizing sooner after the first month. The authors advise warning SMILE patients about a longer dry-eye stretch and watching their oil glands.
pmc-11620767:
Braces need fixed anchor points, and tiny screws placed in the jaw now provide them without relying on the patient's cooperation. Snehaa Selvaraj and six co-authors review what decides whether these mini implants hold, in a 2024 paper, with attention to implant length and type. The devices are small, easy to place and remove, and can bear force right away.

Longer implants tend to hold more firmly. Self-drilling designs grip better than self-tapping ones, and titanium implants succeed more often than stainless steel. For patients with gum disease, bone loss, or low cooperation, the authors present mini implants as a dependable anchor choice.
pmc-11621567:
Xiangyu Ma and colleagues present a two thousand twenty-four structural study of a receptor that keeps hearing working. The receptor, GPR156, lacks the large outer part most relatives carry. It stays unusually active even without a trigger.

Frozen-electron microscopy revealed the receptor alone and joined to its partner protein. A small loop region forms its outer face. Paired receptor units touch through a shared surface in both states. The tail of one unit both helps partner binding and blocks a second partner. The structures explain its constant activity and guide future hearing research.
pmc-11622467:
Kirstie Herb Neff and co-authors set out a trial plan in 2024 to link pregnancy care with food aid. Poor rural mothers-to-be face high risks in birth and later heart ills. Yet less than half of those who can join the main food aid plan for mothers and small children do join.

The trial tests ways to weld birth care to that plan inside the clinic visit. One path links women straight to the plan, and one adds a diet coach. All runs in real wards, not a lab set-up. The aim is more sign-ups and a fairer start for rural families. Clinics gain proof on a weld that could be copied wide.
pmc-11623067:
Justina Michael and Thenmozhi Manivasagam build a feature extraction frame that names weeds in crop images, plus a field app on top. Weed calls need the right features from images where the span of the weed shifts wildly. Their 2024 frame, HierbaNetV1, pulls features with split-size filters and makes 3,872 feature maps per image, from fine to coarse. Low and high features mix in the learning.

A new sorghum-weed dataset, built for this work, tests the frame next to pre-trained peers. It won at 98.06 percent accuracy. Component cuts show each piece earns its place. Side datasets across crops and weeds back its spread. The app, HierbaApp, puts the call in the hand of a farmer in the field, live.
pmc-11623267:
Michaela Kosticova and three co-authors report interviews in 2024 with teens about why they go to bed late on school nights. Late bedtimes cut sleep and harm health, yet most prior work did not ask teens for their own view. The team interviewed twenty four teens aged fourteen to seventeen, alone and in groups, as part of a wider school health study.

School demands and free time, in particular chatting with friends online, pushed bedtime later. Teens often saved both homework and leisure for late evening and put them ahead of sleep. Worry at bedtime also kept some awake. Teens said less homework, more activity, and parent set bedtimes would help them sleep earlier.
pmc-11624167:
Raoull Hoogendijk and co-authors check whether a commercial stool preservation kit keeps children's gut microbes true in the tube. Cancer trials increasingly read the gut microbiome, and three pediatric brain tumor trials collect samples with OMNIgene-GUT tubes that hold samples at room temperature. The kit was proven in adults but not in children. Their 2024 study compares tube-kept samples against the gold standard of instant deep freezing.

Diversity measures, both within samples and between them, showed no meaningful differences between methods. Pairwise tests of which microbes grew or shrank told a sharper story: unpreserved storage distorted community structure, while the kit held it steady. Combined with the ease of mailing a tube instead of shipping frozen samples, the authors endorse the kit for pediatric trials.
pmc-11625267:
Pariwat Imsa-ard studies boredom in foreign language classes through the eyes of Thai university students, in a solo paper from 2024. Boredom can drain effort and hurt results, yet it is often treated as a minor mood. Hearing how learners themselves sort the causes can help teachers design classes that hold attention better.

Thirty six students sorted 44 statements about boredom in language learning, and six were later interviewed. The sorting grouped views into three main factors. Tasks that fail to engage came first, followed by teacher related factors and unhappy feelings about the learning setting. Imsa-ard urges teachers to shape tasks and class settings with these factors in mind, so that students stay engaged and learn more.
pmc-11625567:
Wang and co-authors review two enzymes that chew through tissue scaffolding and their role in keloid scars, in a 2024 paper. Keloids are overgrown scars that resist current treatments. The enzymes, MMP-2 and MMP-9, belong to a family that breaks down the extracellular matrix, the mesh holding tissue together. Their balance against their regulators decides whether collagen piles up or clears.

The review maps the signaling chains that switch these enzymes up or down, including growth factor and microRNA routes. When the balance tips, collagen deposits in excess and the scar tissue thickens and spreads. The authors gather the evidence into one picture of keloid formation. They close by pointing to targeted drugs against these enzymes as a promising direction for a stubborn condition.
pmc-11625667:
Drugs that unleash the immune system on cancer can also trigger immune side effects, and Anna Rudzińska and co-authors asked whether smoking history shapes those effects or survival. They followed 151 patients at a Polish hospital receiving checkpoint inhibitors, alone or with chemotherapy. Just over a third developed immune side effects, most often thyroid trouble or skin reactions.

Smoking turned out not to predict side effects: patients with similar smoking histories fared alike on toxicity, timing, and number of sites affected. Yet each added pack-year of smoking slightly worsened both overall and progression-free survival. Smoking status also did not change how side effects related to survival. The authors caution that other routes by which smoking could sway treatment cannot be ruled out.
pmc-11626967:
Three researchers in China studied how social support links frailty and depression in older cancer patients, in a paper published in 2024. Frailty and low mood often feed each other in old age, and support from others may break the cycle. The team surveyed 448 patients aged sixty or more in cancer wards of three hospitals. They measured frailty, depression, and support with standard scales.

Depression tracked with lower support of every kind, while frailty rose alongside depression. Support sat between the two: part of depression's link to frailty ran through support, about sixteen percent of the total effect. Income changed the first leg of that chain, so the support effect differed by earnings. The authors conclude that strong support can ease depression and lower frailty risk. They urge care teams to treat social backing as part of cancer care for older adults.
pmc-11627167:
Suzane Shiyun Chin recounts her stint on the science team of a family medicine conference in Malaysia, in a personal essay from two thousand twenty-four. She had just returned to work after a long break when her home state hosted the national meeting. It was her first time as an organizer rather than a guest.

Her team reviewed over two hundred research abstracts, shortlisted entries, and kept authors, judges, and vendors in loop. A highlight was briefing the health minister at the electronic poster board. Judging day talks showed her how experts weigh posters. She closes by hoping to stay in primary care research.
pmc-11628767:
Muzaffer Keklik and co-authors report, in a 2024 letter, a case of a skin lymphoma that raced into its tumor stage. Mycosis fungoides is the most common skin T-cell lymphoma, making up forty percent of primary skin lymphomas. Once tumors form, the outlook turns poor.

The patient was a 58-year-old man first diagnosed abroad with painful, itching lesions on his right leg. Topical steroids failed, so the lesions were cut out and grafted. Still, his disease advanced very fast into the tumoral stage. Letters like this flag how quickly a usually slow disease can turn. Clinicians reading it gain a warning to escalate care when skin lesions defy first-line treatment.
pmc-11628967:
Elliott-Sale leads a large team building a classification tool for ovarian hormone profiles in female athletes, in work from twenty twenty-four. Hormone profiles shape training response and health in athletes, yet they are rarely classified in a standard way. A fit for purpose tool was missing.

The study developed and evaluated step one of a two step process: classifying the ovarian hormone profile itself. Athletes from post puberty to perimenopause are the target group. Reliable classification is the base for later work linking profiles to performance, injury, and contraceptive use. Sports science has long under served female physiology, and tools like this help close the gap.
pmc-11629267:
Marginal zone lymphoma usually creeps, but in some patients it transforms into an aggressive large-cell cancer. Côme Bommier and co-authors reported in 2024 how often that happens, from a prospective cohort of 529 patients plus a pooled analysis of the literature.

Transformation struck twenty-one cohort patients, a ten-year risk of about 3.6 percent, and it nearly quadrupled the risk of death. Having cancer at two or more sites outside the nodes, or a high prognostic score, predicted it. The wider literature put the ten-year risk nearer eight percent, highest in spleen and nodal subtypes. Transformed patients still lived years, but the authors call for better prevention.
pmc-11629667:
Bowen Zhou and co-authors build a risk chart for chest pain patients in a 2024 study. The patients have unstable angina and mid-level artery narrowing seen on scans. Swelling in the body is a known driver of artery disease and sudden heart events.

Records covered patients seen from early 2019 to mid 2021 at one hospital. The team split seven hundred seventy-three patients into training and test groups. A screening tool picked key swelling markers and other risk factors. From those, they built a chart that scores the chance of staying free of major heart and brain events. Such a chart could help doctors plan care for this group.
pmc-11632367:
An invasive thistle that races across American grasslands evolved bigger size after crossing the ocean. Bryan Reatini and co-authors map the genes behind that jump in a 2024 study. They build the weed's full genome at chromosome scale.

Crosses between home and invader plants yield a gene map. Thirteen trait zones tie to the size gains. Big zones carry signs of structural DNA swaps between the lines. One swap lifts several invader traits at once. Old genome doublings also cluster under two zones. Structure, not just spelling, may drive fast invasion.
pmc-11632767:
Eisenhardt, Fiorentini, and Williams compare metal choices in two-metal catalysts that turn carbon dioxide and ring compounds into plastics in this 2024 study. The best-known catalysts rely on scarce cobalt, while cheaper aluminum and iron versions often lag. The team built aluminum and iron catalysts paired with potassium and raced them against the cobalt one.

The aluminum catalyst set a speed record for its class at ordinary pressure in one key reaction, while the iron version suited a different pairing better. Careful measurements tied speed to the electron richness at the metal site. Weighing speed, abundance, and cost together, the authors give clear design rules for catalysts built from plentiful metals.
pmc-11634167:
Mushood Ahmed and co-authors pool trial data on two ways to replace a narrowed aortic valve: a catheter route and open surgery. The surgical route is standard for patients at low or middle risk, but the catheter route has grown more common. The team asked how the two compare over time.

They gathered 17 reports from nine trials, covering 9,092 patients. Death rates matched at 30 days, one year, and two years. Past five years, though, the catheter group showed a slightly higher death risk, about 13 in a hundred more. Other harms, such as stroke, tilted the other way at some time points. Timing, the authors stress, changes the verdict.
pmc-11634867:
Wang and co-authors test a simple blood ratio as a warning sign in a hard-to-treat infection. The germ Klebsiella pneumoniae, when resistant to carbapenem antibiotics, kills many of the patients it infects. The team reviews 190 such patients, of whom 73 died in hospital, and checks the neutrophil-to-lymphocyte ratio measured on the day the infection began.

A higher ratio independently predicts death, alongside intensive care admission and co-infection with other resistant germs. A ratio above about 10.7 marks the danger zone with moderate accuracy. Getting appropriate treatment within three days, by contrast, protects. The authors offer the cheap, routine ratio as a quick prognostic tool for these cases.
pmc-11634967:
Simon Hadjaje and colleagues studied how fruit fly wings unfold in 2024. A fly leaves its pupal case with folded wings. Within minutes, the wings open into stiff flight blades. Rising body pressure drives the change. Fluid then flows into the wing structure. The team imaged the wing inside and out. They filmed unfolding at the whole organ scale. They also tracked fluid flow during opening.

Opening proved to be more than simple unfolding. The wing also expands in area as it opens. Surface cells stretch, and the outer skin smooths its wrinkles. A computer model joined material measures into one account. The model predicted a working point for successful opening. It also matched the timing of the real process. The authors say flies exploit material quirks for speed. The lessons may inform soft deployable designs, they suggest.
pmc-11635067:
Yunhao Sun and co-authors build a nano system that helps cisplatin work better against esophageal cancer. Cisplatin is the main first drug for this cancer, but resistance limits it. Curcumin can drain glutathione, a shield that helps tumors resist the drug.

Curcumin alone dissolves poorly and reaches tumors weakly. The team loaded curcumin and cisplatin into framework nanoparticles with copper. Tiny gold particles on the shell mimic a glucose-burning enzyme. The system makes peroxide that feeds extra chemical attack on tumors. Glutathione loss then leaves cancer cells open to cisplatin. Tests support the combined design in lab settings. The work joins two attack routes in one carrier.
pmc-11635167:
Michelangelo Certo and colleagues show that a little-known metabolic enzyme, CARKL, steers T-cell behavior by resetting metabolism. How immune cells use fuel decides how they work. The pentose phosphate pathway branches off glycolysis, giving molecules for defense against oxidants and for building. CARKL is a sedoheptulose kinase in that pathway, known to count in macrophages.

The study looks at CARKL in T cells, where its level shifts in a dynamic way as cells switch on. When CARKL was raised, big metabolic shifts came, hitting mitochondrial respiration, ATP production, and the mix of inflammatory cytokines. Changes to CARKL also shaped how T cells move, by guiding chemokine receptor levels. In one key case, CARKL cut the receptor CXCR3, hurting movement toward its chemokine signals. The finds set one enzyme as a dial for both what T cells give off and where they go. Such control points draw drug work.
pmc-11635467:
Nikos Delikoukos and co-authors detail a recipe for dosing graphene with nitric acid vapor in a 2024 paper. The vapor settles on grown graphene sheets as charge sharing clusters, pulling electrons out and leaving holes behind, a p type doping that tunes the sheet for devices.

Light and photoelectron probes track carrier counts and energy shifts step by step. A polymer coat step keeps the doping stable and permanent while the sheet's structure stays intact. The protocol gives labs a controlled way to set graphene's charge without wrecking the crystal.
pmc-11637367:
Elizabeth Anna Banyas and a team study views on starting HIV pre-exposure prophylaxis during incarceration, in research from 2024. HIV rates are higher in the United States correctional system than outside it, yet access to this prevention drug stays poor. Thirteen in-depth interviews were held with recently released people in a transition program in the southern states.

Interviewees wanted more education about the drug while inside, and more on HIV prevention in general. They saw starting it in prison as a smooth bridge to post-release programs. Barriers after release were expected, which strengthens the case for beginning inside. The authors back in-prison starts as one route to reach an underserved group.
pmc-11637767:
Squire and co-authors describe a specialist clinic for a distressing delusion in a 2024 article. Some patients hold a fixed belief that their skin is infested with parasites or fibers, a condition called delusional infestation. Sorting real tropical disease from delusion takes two kinds of expertise at once, which few clinics offer under one roof.

Their clinic, hosted at the Liverpool School of Tropical Medicine, pairs tropical medicine doctors with psychiatrists in joint sessions. Between 2018 and 2023 the service saw 208 patients; most could be fully assessed, and just over half were confirmed to have the delusion. Women outnumbered men two to one. The authors lay out how the clinic runs, step by step, as a template for other centers and as a guide for doctors who meet such patients in ordinary practice.
pmc-11638167:
Yinan Wang and co-authors present a network that reads imagined movement from brain signals in patients with one sided weakness, in work from 2024. Brain computer links can drive rehab devices for the upper limb. Brain signals vary a lot from person to person, so decoders often fail on new patients.

Their network pulls features from many frequency bands at once, using filters of varied size. An attention step keeps the most useful band features. A graph attention part then captures how the sensor sites relate in space. The design aims for decoding that holds up across patients, a key need for real rehab use.
pmc-11638367:
Lu Tian and colleagues hunt a vanishing fish by the DNA it sheds in river water, in this study from twenty twenty-four. The fish, Bangana tungting, is endangered and lives in a protected stretch of the Yuanshui River in Hunan, China. Net surveys can miss rare fish and harm them, so the team filtered water instead and read the traces left behind.

Over two years, the fish's DNA turned up at eight of sixty sites in the first survey and four of forty-four in the second, proving it still holds on there. Where it appeared, the water carried enough dissolved oxygen; below a clear threshold, it vanished. Sites near hydroelectric dams showed fewer traces, and more dams meant fewer finds. The authors say water testing gives rangers a gentle, sharp tool for tracking rare fish, and they urge cleaner, freer-flowing water in the reserve.
pmc-11639767:
Kuźnicki and co-authors review how macrophages, a type of immune cell, might be turned against cancer, in a review paper from 2024. Macrophages that gather in tumors can help or hinder growth, and the mix of their subtypes links to patient survival. The review sets out their traits and roles in tumor growth.

The authors explain how these cells affect the main treatments: immune therapy, radiation, and chemotherapy. New ideas include tiny particles that carry drugs to the cells and reshape the tumor setting. Lab-made receptor macrophages, called CAR-Ms, show early promise. The review also covers training the cells with magnetic fields, plasma, and electric pulses. It closes with prospects for pairing these cell-based plans with other care.
pmc-11639867:
Giorgio Barbera and co-authors review a diagnostic trap in a 2024 paper on head and neck cancer follow-up. Surgeons use absorbable blood-stopping material during operations, and leftover material can form a lump that mimics a returning tumor on scans. The team surveyed past reports and added two cases from Verona.

Across cases, ultrasound showed stable, uneven lumps, while CT scans showed a liquid core with little or no dye uptake. One scan type lit the lumps up like real tumors, a misleading sign. Needle samples showed inflammation with no cancer cells, and removed lumps confirmed trapped material fibers. The authors urge surgical teams to keep this mimic in mind before ordering invasive steps or delaying cancer care.
pmc-11640167:
Schreieder and co-authors study how many skin lesions must be removed to find one melanoma, in a 2024 analysis from a German hospital. That ratio, the number needed to treat, shows how precise doctors are when they cut out pigmented moles for testing. The team reviewed records of 118,668 lesions treated from 2004 to 2013 and linked the ratio to patient age and the referring doctor's field.

The overall ratio was 17.2 lesions per melanoma found. It fell steadily with patient age. After national skin cancer screening began in 2008, fewer lesions were removed and the ratio improved from 20.3 to 14.7. Hospital dermatologists were the most precise, while office-based ones removed the most lesions per find. The authors argue age should shape how removal thresholds are set.
pmc-11640267:
Arianna Di Napoli and co-authors gather reports of lymphomas tied to implants other than breast implants. The breast implant lymphoma is now a recognized disease, but scattered cases link joint replacements, meshes, and other devices to blood cancers too. The team searched four databases under PRISMA rules and pulled out the primary studies.

Forty-three reports covered fifty-two patients in all. Most of the cancers, about eighty-five percent, were B-cell lymphomas, led by one type that grows in fibrin near a device. That type clustered around biological tissue implants and metal ones. The review sorts cases by sex, age, site, material, and cancer type. It argues that device-linked lymphoma is a wider family than the breast implant story alone.
pmc-11640367:
Juanxiang Zhang and eleven co-authors, plus Maria Luisa Dettori, hunt for DNA markers that predict growth in Ashidan yaks. Two genes were the suspects: TXK, a signaling kinase, and PLCE1, an enzyme important for muscle cell development. Both had been tied to economically valuable traits in other animals.

A liquid microarray genotyped two hundred thirty-two yaks at one variant in each gene. Both variants correlated significantly with weight, height, length, and chest circumference at various ages. Animals carrying the CC form of the TXK variant, for example, grew significantly heavier than their herdmates. Such markers could let breeders select for growth genetically instead of waiting to measure each generation.
pmc-11640467:
Ivan Ramos-Martínez and colleagues pool studies from around the world to gauge how much flu circulates in dogs, in this meta-analysis from twenty twenty-four. Influenza A crosses between species, and dogs can catch strains named for other hosts. The team gathered every study that measured antibodies or active infection in dogs for three subtypes.

Past exposure ran at about eight percent for the horse strain H3N8 and seven percent for the dog strain H3N2, and about three percent for the pandemic H1N1 strain. Active infection told a split story: the horse strain was rare, while H3N2 showed in nearly a fifth of tested dogs in prevalence studies. The authors place dogs as a reservoir where human, swine, horse, and bird flu viruses can meet. That mixing is exactly why vets and doctors watch this species closely.
pmc-11640667:
Yi Xue and co-authors teach computers to tell goats apart by sight, in a 2024 study. Knowing each animal's identity is basic to careful farm management. Most past work used face photos only, leaving other views untried.

The team built a rig that photographs each goat from five angles: both sides of the face, the front, the back, and the side of the body. They tested four standard vision networks on 54 white goats. A single side-body view with one network reached over ninety-nine percent accuracy. Mixing two views beat any single view, and three views helped further. The results give farms a practical recipe: side shots and fused views identify goats with very few mistakes.
pmc-11640767:
Xueli Zhu, Weilong Tian, and their co-authors studied how fatty acids shape the quality of backfat in Beijing Black pigs. Their 2024 study notes that backfat traits steer pork quality and buyer choice. The team compared the fatty acids in pigs whose backfat differed in firmness, seeking both the key acids and the genes behind them.

Four acids stood out by statistical tests: caproic, stearic, linoleic, and alpha linolenic acid. A genome wide scan in 413 pigs found 22 DNA variants tied to these acids or their ratios. Four genes, including PLPP3 and CYP27A1, were named as candidates for the traits. The findings give breeders markers for firmer, better backfat in this prized local breed.
pmc-11640867:
Junkun Pan and co-authors review plant-sugar packaging films loaded with phenolic compounds for keeping produce fresh in a 2024 paper. Biodegradable wraps from polysaccharides are gaining ground as plastic alternatives.

Phenolics, natural plant chemicals, add antioxidant and antimicrobial punch to these films and coatings. The review catalogs how phenols are blended in and how they change film strength, barrier behavior, and appearance. Field uses follow, from slowing rot and browning in fruits and vegetables to smart packaging that signals freshness. Gaps remain: how the protection works in detail, safety testing, and pairing with other steps along the supply chain. The authors map a design path toward factory-ready films.
pmc-11641167:
Daniela Berardinelli and co-authors review nurse-led efforts to help patients take medicines as prescribed, in this 2024 systematic review. Poor adherence worsens health and raises costs for people with chronic disease, yet how well nurse-led programs work was unclear. The team searched five major databases with no date limits.

They included twenty-two studies with nearly six thousand participants. Face-to-face nurse visits helped in most heart failure studies and in single studies of leukemia, hypertension and multimorbidity. Mixed programs that added phone follow-up helped in some cases, while remote-only programs rarely worked. Tablet-based education showed no edge over nurse-led teaching, a sign that personal contact may matter most.
pmc-11641367:
Jin Young Nam and Soojeong Shim measured the medical cost burden of severe maternal illness in South Korea in a 2024 study. Severe complications around childbirth cause lasting health loss and drive up care costs. Past work rarely separated the cost of the complications themselves from the cost of blood transfusion, which often travels with them.

Using a national insurance delivery database, the team compared delivery care costs for patients with and without severe morbidity, and with and without transfusion. The design isolates what each factor adds to the bill. Cost clarity helps planners fund prevention, since avoiding one severe case saves both health and money. The study gives Korean policy a firmer price tag for maternal safety work.
pmc-11641467:
Špela Golubović and co-authors asked family caregivers about cancer prevention for people with intellectual disabilities, in a 2024 study. Many cancers can be stopped with screening and healthy habits. These people face steep barriers to those services. Caregivers often bridge the gap to care. Forty-one of them filled out a survey, and fifteen gave interviews.

Three quarters had never been given facts on prevention for their role. Most did not arrange screenings on a routine basis. A lack of clear information topped the barrier list. Planning and emotional strain came next. Four fifths wanted more training for the task. The talks stressed lifestyle support, access, health literacy, and mental support. The authors call for resources made to fit caregivers. Health systems must link services better, they argue. Fair prevention starts by giving the people who help each day what they need.
pmc-11641667:
Huaming Xi and co-authors test a natural sugar as a shield against ovarian aging. Their 2024 paper studies trehalose, a sugar known to switch on the cell's cleanup system and fight oxidation, in a mouse model where a second sugar, D-galactose, ages the ovaries early.

Mice given trehalose kept more ovarian weight and showed far fewer dying egg-support cells than untreated aged mice. Cleanup markers rose, and the machinery that recycles worn mitochondria grew stronger. In dishes, trehalose cut aging markers and cell death in the same support cells and lowered their reactive oxygen. The authors suggest trehalose could serve as an anti-aging aid for ovarian health, acting through cleaner mitochondria.
pmc-11641767:
Corneliu-George Coman and colleagues test chitosan nanofibre dressings carrying an antibiotic on burn healing in rats. Their 2024 study measures biochemical, oxidative, and immune effects of the wound coverings.

Two fibre formulations were spun with different antibiotic amounts, and some received a surface coating treatment. Burns were made with a heated steel rod on male rats. Dressings were compared against untreated controls and a standard commercial silver dressing using wound size, tissue analysis, and blood inflammation markers. Chitosan dressings significantly accelerated healing. The high-antibiotic coated group showed best wound closure and least inflammation, with higher protective enzyme levels and lower stress hormone levels than other groups.
pmc-11642167:
Matteo Matteucci and co-authors review gentler ways to remove pelvic lymph nodes in skin melanoma in this 2024 paper. When melanoma reaches the groin and pelvic nodes, surgeons must clear them, but the open operation carries heavy risks. Camera-guided and robot-assisted versions promise smaller wounds and easier recovery.

The pooled literature covered sixty-four robotic cases, one hundred eighty-seven camera cases, and eighty-three open cases. The robotic route proved workable, with complication rates and cancer outcomes much like the other methods, and shorter operating time linked to lower hospital costs. Surgeons gain from three-dimensional views and wrist-like tools. The authors are blunt that the evidence is too weak for firm conclusions. Randomized trials would settle the question, but few patients qualify for the surgery in an era of drug therapy, so trials fill slowly.
pmc-11642267:
Ryosuke Yamamoto and co-authors track what drives walk skill at hospital exit after stroke in a 2024 study. Stroke leaves long gait loss in most who have it, and rehab aims to lift that loss before discharge. Past work had not mapped how the drivers of walk skill shift with time since the stroke first struck.

Ward records of stroke patients with one-side brain harm feed the checks. The team sets traits next to walk grades at exit across time bands since onset. Their bet is that the driver set shifts by band, which would shape rehab plans by stage and by need.
pmc-11642367:
Amy Whitbread and co-authors test a new way to check vitamin levels in a 2024 pilot study. Instead of a standard blood draw, they used menstrual blood, which can be gathered with a cup and needs no needle. No past study had checked whether vitamin levels can be read from such samples.

Thirty healthy volunteers gave menstrual blood and matching finger-prick blood. Both sample types were dried on cards and measured with a precise lab method. Levels of vitamin A and vitamin D in the two samples tracked each other closely, though the exact values differed. The authors call the result a proof of concept and say larger studies must confirm the method before routine use.
pmc-11642667:
Gian Paolo Azzena and co-authors test a dye based scan for judging skin blood flow during breast removal surgery, in a study from 2024. Rebuilding the breast with an implant is now the common path after such surgery. Success depends on the skin left behind staying alive, which needs a sound blood supply.

Fifty patients in a row were split into two groups. In one, surgeons judged the skin flap with a glowing dye scan that shows flow in near infrared light. In the other, they used standard clinical judgment. The team recorded risk factors for each patient and compared rates of skin death and other problems. They also checked which risk factors tracked with skin loss. The aim was to see if the scan cuts problems after surgery.
pmc-11643367:
Arshad and six co-authors linked a brain-healthy diet to mood in this cohort study from twenty twenty-four. The MIND diet blends Mediterranean and blood-pressure eating patterns. Nearly five thousand British civil servants reported their diets in the early two thousands. Their depressive symptoms were then tracked across thirteen years of follow-ups.

About thirteen percent had symptoms return at least twice. Those eating closest to the MIND pattern had about a quarter lower odds of that recurrence. Three foods carried the signal on their own: leafy greens, other vegetables, and berries. The links held after accounting for income, habits, and prior health. The authors present diet as a plausible lever against repeat depression.
pmc-11643567:
Alexander Saenko and co-authors fabricate transparent memory devices from zinc oxide films in a 2024 paper. Memristors, resistors that remember their state, are building blocks for new computing hardware. The team studied how magnetron sputtering power changes the structure and electrical behavior of nanocrystalline zinc oxide films.

At seventy-five watts in argon at room temperature, the films came out smooth and uniform. On that basis they built transparent device stacks and tested their resistive switching. They also fabricated crossbar arrays, the grid layout such memories need. Transparent electronics could one day merge displays with memory.
pmc-11643667:
Kinga Szentner and co-authors test a common polymer as a helper for turning cellulose into sugars, in a study published in 2024. Cellulose, the main fiber in plants, can be broken down by enzymes for fuels and chemicals, but the process is often slow. Adding soapy helpers is a known trick, and the team tried polyethylene glycol on several cellulose types.

The additive clearly raised how much cellulose the enzymes could digest. The gain was largest for a mostly loose, disordered cellulose, and smaller for a tightly packed crystal form, where enzymes and helper alike reach the chains poorly. X-ray, infrared, and liquid analyses backed the pattern. The authors say the results clarify how such helpers act and can guide cheaper enzyme use in biofuel plants.
pmc-11643767:
Francesca Filannino and co-authors tested whether irisin, a muscle messenger released during exercise, can calm brain inflammation, in a 2024 study. Inflammation in the brain is driven largely by microglia, its resident immune cells, and by a protein assembly called the NLRP3 inflammasome that releases fiery signals. The team treated lab-grown microglial cells with a bacterial trigger, with and without irisin.

Even at low doses, irisin kept the cells closer to their resting state and slowed their migration. It raised a marker of the calming cell mode and lowered the inflammasome's parts and its main output signal. The authors present irisin as a possible protective mediator, and a candidate tool for preventing diseases driven by brain inflammation. The work was done in cells, so animal and human tests remain ahead.
pmc-11643867:
