Kang and Wang build a laser pulse device from tiny cubes of palladium, in a 2024 paper. The metal cubes, about twelve nanometers across, sit on a D-shaped fiber. There they act as a saturable absorber, a part that lets a laser fire in ultrafast bursts rather than a steady beam.

Placed inside an erbium-doped fiber laser, the device produced pulses centered at 1.56 micrometers, repeating about twenty-seven million times per second, each lasting under two trillionths of a second. The absorber proved sturdy and worked across a broad band. The authors present it as a flexible building block for high-energy ultrafast fiber lasers.
pmc-11643967:
Chen-Che Hsieh and co-authors test seaweed extracts for skin repair in 2024. The red alga they study holds compounds that fight oxidation and swelling. They ask whether its extracts can shield skin from sun harm, boost collagen, and slow scar growth.

Two extracts were made, one with alcohol and one with an alkaline mix. The alcohol extract restored a key collagen building block past its starting level in sun-harmed cells. It also cut signals that drive scar-like growth by large shares. Both extracts lowered harmful oxygen byproducts. The alcohol one was stronger against scars, the other better for repair.
pmc-11644067:
Medical image classifiers starve for data, and one remedy is to shift images in feature space, inventing new examples with the same label. Yaoyao Zhu and co-authors warn that shifting too far silently changes the label. Their fix, BSDA, treats the shift amount with Bayesian care, sampling it in a way that respects the data's own spread.

The module plugs into ordinary networks without surgery. Across two- and three-dimensional datasets and several imaging types, it beat rival augmentation schemes and lifted baseline models it was attached to. For small, precious medical datasets, a principled nudge beats a random one.
pmc-11644167:
Dolores Termini and co-authors test a way to find flaws inside printed plastic parts without cutting them open, in a paper from 2024. As printed parts move into real use, shops need checks that leave the part intact. The team used waves in the terahertz range, both as scans through the part and as timed signals, to build images of resin parts.

The team then scored how round and even each image slice looked, and used shifts in that score to flag flaws. Parts with added flaws scored far worse than clean parts, and blocked paths in one part were also caught. One flaw raised the score by about one seventh. The work shows the scan plus score method can find and size flaws in even, round printed parts.
pmc-11644367:
Baoshan Kang and co-authors found a plant protein that helps a watermelon virus spread in a 2024 study. The virus causes yellow mosaic disease and cuts yields. One of its proteins, P3, plays roles in copying, moving, and harming the host, but its chemical job was unknown.

The team showed that P3 grips a watermelon protein with two cutting jobs, housed mostly in the leaf's green parts and outer skin. The grip sits at one end of P3. When the two met in tobacco leaves, they clumped as a pair. That plant protein boosts the infection, so blocking the grip could breed or spray for hardier melons.
pmc-11644467:
Lijun Hu and co-authors build a modified fiber that pulls uranium from seawater in this 2024 study. The oceans hold vast uranium, but at vanishing low levels. Fibrous adsorbents are seen as the most promising way to harvest it.

Their fiber starts from a tough polyethylene base, reshaped by radiation grafting. A branched helper layer speeds uranium ions through the fiber's depths. The design also resists fouling by sea life, a common failure. In lab solution the fiber loaded far more uranium than in fake seawater tests. A month-long seawater trial gives the realistic rate. Such fibers could one day make ocean uranium a real fuel source.
pmc-11644567:
The authors coat wheat seeds with silk protein to guard them in a greener way than chemical fungicides. Their 2024 study uses silk fibroin, a natural polymer that films well but fights microbes weakly on its own. Two partners fill that gap: a commercial seed agent and a natural antimicrobial peptide.

The silk blend formed stable sheet structures that stiffened the coat. Coated seeds sprouted up to sixty-five percent better, with taller shoots and longer roots, above all under cold stress. The peptide added lasting bacteria control. Dose mattered: too thick a coat chokes the seed's air supply. The team frames silk coats as a workable green swap for farm use.
pmc-11644767:
Iwona Traczyk and co-authors measure excess weight among Polish adults using a national health survey from 2016 to 2020. The 2024 study drew on body measures from 3,735 adults. It tracked general overweight and obesity by body mass index, plus fat carried around the belly. Social traits such as age, sex, schooling, and place of residence were weighed as well.

Over half the adults, about fifty-seven percent, carried excess weight. Belly obesity hit about thirty-two percent and was far more common in women than men. Risk rose with age, and men faced higher odds than women. The typical profile was a rural resident with modest schooling. The authors urge teaching efforts aimed at rural areas.
pmc-11644867:
Satellite photos of the Tibetan Plateau are often spoiled by clouds, just where scientists most need clear views of snow. Guoqiang Zheng, Tianle Zhao, and Yaohui Liu present a cloud removal model for that region in this 2024 paper. The plateau's snow feeds major rivers and shifts fast, so gaps in the record hurt climate and water studies.

Their model, called MATT, mixes attention at several scales with a local module that rebuilds fine detail. A cloud mask inside the local part helps it tell cloud from snow, two bright surfaces that are easy to confuse. The design reads both the broad scene and small textures at once. Tests in the paper compare the model's cleaned images against other methods. The authors aim the tool at snow monitoring over rough, high terrain.
pmc-11644967:
Mehrabi, Martulli, Bernasconi, and Carboni compare ways to watch a crack creep inside a glued joint under repeated sideways loading, in a 2024 study. Adhesive joints lighten aircraft and cars, but hidden cracks in the glue line threaten safety. Finding the crack tip precisely, without cutting the part open, is the practical challenge.

In interrupted fatigue tests, four methods went head to head. The contenders were plain visual reading, digital image correlation, optical backscatter reflectometry, and an analytical beam formula based on stiffness. Their estimates were checked against each other as cracks grew. Knowing which cheap method tracks truth lets inspectors schedule repairs before a joint lets go.
pmc-11645067:
Xiaocui Chen and co-authors design a geostress-adaptive blast charge for a machinery room excavation in a 2024 engineering study. Blasting is fast and cheap, but its vibrations can harm nearby buildings and residents.

A 3D simulation model of an underground pumped storage plant tested three charge layouts. The optimized layout cut damage to the protective rock layer by about two fifths. Harm to side walls also fell, with no loss in the main blast zone. Remote vibration readings dropped in several directions. Field use of the plan then met its goals for rock integrity and structure safety. The study backs simulation-led blast design for tight sites.
pmc-11645467:
Alexander Tamalunas and eight co-authors survey what patients with lower urinary tract symptoms think about plant-based medicines. Their study came out in 2024. These symptoms, often tied to an enlarged prostate, are commonly treated with prescription drugs whose benefits are limited and side effects are common.

Three hundred patients at a specialist center answered the questionnaire. Most were taking prescription medication, led by one main drug class. Plant medicines were the second most common treatment, used by about four in ten of those on medication. Patients rated plant medicines as only modestly effective, but almost nine in ten praised how well tolerated they were. Two thirds thought health insurance should cover them. The authors say such medicines may keep patients on treatment where prescription drugs fail.
pmc-11646367:
Jiayun Ling and co-authors look back at five children treated for Kawasaki disease in 2024. The illness can harm the heart, and the usual first treatment does not work for some children. In this small series, all five children had that hard-to-treat form. Each child got one dose of a drug that blocks a signal called IL-6.

The authors draw on records from a children's hospital in China from early 2023 to early 2024. They track signs, lab tests, and heart checks for each child. They also watch for side effects from the drug. The series gives doctors a close look at how the drug fared in a few real cases where the standard care had failed.
pmc-11646467:
Anne Wand and co-authors ask why mental health clinicians skip advance care planning with older psychosis patients, in work from 2024. Planning future care matters for people with schizophrenia as they age. Clinicians, though, rarely open that conversation with this group.

Fifteen clinicians from Sydney public services joined online focus groups. Two themes emerged from the recorded discussions. Clinicians valued planning and wanted to do it more. Complexity stopped them anyway, in their own accounts. Barriers spanned patient, family, and system levels. Naming the blockers is the first step toward training and tools that clear them.
pmc-11646667:
Raquel Garcia Rocco da Silva and co-authors tested whether two gene variants link to nerve damage in young people with type 1 diabetes, in a 2024 study. The damage, a symmetric nerve injury in the limbs, hits some patients harder than others, and genes may explain part of that gap. The variants sit in a folate-handling gene and an immune signal gene.

Seventy children and teens had a nerve test on the leg and gave spit samples for gene typing. About 16 percent showed the nerve damage. Those with damage had higher blood sugar and fat levels on average, and their nerve signals were weaker. One gene form also tied to slower nerve speed, while family history played a role.
pmc-11646867:
Alexander Podgorski and four co-authors manage a heart invaded by lymphoma, with no playbook to consult. A 39-year-old woman arrived with a fever syndrome first read as a returned traveler's illness. Workup found stage IV peripheral T-cell lymphoma inside her heart muscle, with ventricular tachycardia. The team had to weigh sudden death risk against an antibody-drug chemotherapy plan and a later stem cell transplant.

No direct evidence base existed for such a case. Decisions grew from team discussion, careful risk scoring, and lessons borrowed from cardiac sarcoidosis care. The report stresses the patient's youth and prior health in each call.
pmc-11647367:
Yuichi Iida and Mamoru Harada test a cell therapy that turns donor stem cells into beacons drawing immune fighters into tumors. Their study appeared in 2024. The stem cells are engineered to release CCL19, a signal that attracts dendritic cells and T cells. An earlier version used the host's own cells, which is slow to prepare for each patient. The new version uses cells from a donor line, ready off the shelf, and was tried in several mouse tumor models.

The donor cells shrank tumors strongly. Part of the effect came from the host reacting to the foreign cells themselves. The therapy packed tumors with a rare dendritic cell type that makes interleukin-12 and primes killer T cells, and it worked without the lymph nodes that such priming usually needs. The authors see a practical path toward ready-made immune cell therapy.
pmc-11647467:
Lok Shrestha and co-authors compare two COVID booster styles head to head. One shot held only the original strain, the other added an Omicron variant. Blood drawn a month later showed both raised neutralizing antibodies against five variants, even one that had not yet appeared when samples were taken.

The two strain shot lifted antibodies against the Omicron branch more strongly. It also grew a broader pool of memory B cells, the reserves that answer future infections. That breadth tracked with the antibody breadth. T cell boosts mostly matched, with the two strain shot ahead on one variant. The authors credit the wider B cell pool for the edge.
pmc-11647967:
Biao Qi and co-authors present a 2024 journal article on a magnetized string that turns pull into commands for wearable interfaces. Inspired by tendons, the device reads the string's natural vibration tone: stretch changes the pitch, and a coil picks the tone up electrically as a fading ringing signal. Each tone stands for one command, so many commands share a single channel.

Designers can tune the tone library by string size, material, or tension, and even retune one string mid-use by changing its stretched length. Demonstrations ran touch addressing, identity checks, and robot control. The authors offer the scheme as a simple, high-capacity wearable link.
pmc-11648167:
Solomon Gebereyowhans, Shuwen Zhang, Xiaoyang Pang, Kidane Workelul, Jing Lu, and Jiaping Lv published a 2024 food science study on spiced goat milk cheese. They made a Camembert type cheese and added cumin, Sichuan pepper, or a mix of both. The aim was to see how the spices changed quality and health related traits.

The basic makeup of the cheese stayed the same with any spice. Texture, microbe counts, taste scores, and antioxidant power all shifted, though. Tasters liked the spiced cheeses more than the plain one after 40 days of ripening, with cumin scoring highest. All spiced cheeses showed stronger antioxidant activity and higher phenolic content than the control. The results suggest spices can lift both flavor and keeping quality in goat cheese.
pmc-11649767:
Franziska Stoller and co-authors published this neuroscience study in 2024. A European research project had linked social dysfunction across diagnoses to the integrity of the default mode network, a set of brain regions active at rest. The team tested cause and effect in mice by damaging the forceps minor, a fiber tract tying together the network's frontal hubs, using focal loss of myelin insulation.

Brain imaging confirmed the damage weakened the network's connectivity. The mice then interacted less socially and showed more anxiety in automated behavior tests. Strikingly, the effects reversed as the tract recovered. The authors present this as direct evidence that default mode integrity drives social behavior, not merely correlates with it. They argue the finding supports treatments aimed at network repair in precision psychiatry.
pmc-11650267:
George Wanjala, Lenox Omondi Pius, Péter Strausz, and Szilvia Kusza argue for advocacy to save farm animal diversity in East Africa. Their paper, from twenty twenty-four, centers on Kenya and Tanzania. Local breeds carry genes that help livestock cope with heat and drought. That diversity is shrinking, which threatens future protein supply.

East Africa historically spread domesticated herds across the continent. The authors outline roles for advocacy and management groups. Their framework runs from farmers up to regional associations. Regional promotion, they argue, can sway national policy. Saving breed variety is pitched as climate insurance. The paper offers a structure others could adapt.
pmc-11651067:
Wenrui Xia, Xiaoang Li, Ruixuan Han, and Xiaoke Liu review how the gut's microbes may shape athletic performance through the gut-brain axis, in a 2024 narrative review. Elite athletes carry different gut communities from sedentary people, and diets shift those communities, feeding back on fitness. Exercise changes the microbes; the microbes change how food energy is harvested and spent.

The review sorts the evidence three ways. First, it covers three supplement families and their effects on gut microbes and athlete fitness. Second, it lays out how supplements act through gut changes along the gut-brain axis, the two-way signaling between bowel and brain. Third, it argues that supplement plans should be tailored to the type of exercise, since endurance and power sports stress the system differently. The authors combine diet, microbes, and training in a framework for athletes seeking health and performance.
pmc-11651767:
Xirui Lin and co-authors use a large United States cancer registry in this 2024 study to settle a staging question in early lung cancer. Tumors two to three centimeters wide that invade the lung's inner lining may be worse than their stage suggests. The team pulled 10,452 patients with node-free tumors of two to five centimeters, diagnosed from 2010 to 2019, and compared survival across stage groups and treatments.

Patients in the two-to-three band with invasion fared worse than both nearby stage groups at five years. Chemotherapy after surgery lifted their outlook to match a higher stage group that also got it, and one lower group gained clearly from it. The authors back post-surgery chemotherapy for these patients.
pmc-11652267:
Jin-Ok Lee and co-authors build KTED, a web database of jumping genes in the Korean genome, in work from twenty twenty-four. Transposable elements move within genomes and shape health in many ways. Once dismissed as junk, they now show diverse biological effects. Population-scale resources on them, though, remain surprisingly scarce. Whole genomes from thousands of Korean study participants feed the database.

Element counts and positions are organised for easy web browsing. Five common disease groups get distribution comparisons inside KTED. Blood fat, blood pressure, diabetes, thyroid, and cancer groups are covered. Location and class of each element frame its likely impact. Researchers can inspect patterns without wrangling raw sequence files. Korean population genetics gains a specialised public resource.
pmc-11652367:
Han Chen and colleagues published a data-driven study in 2024. They studied diabetic retinopathy, a serious eye complication of diabetes. The disease can badly damage vision over time. The team focused on a cell death process called PANoptosis. They hunted for related genes that change in the disease. Public gene datasets supplied the patient data. Gene databases supplied the PANoptosis gene lists. Several computer methods narrowed the candidates down.

Three machine learning methods selected key hub genes. The team built a diagnostic scoring chart from them. Lab tests then checked the chosen genes directly. Cell experiments tested what silencing two genes does. Blood vessel cells behaved differently after that silencing. Immune cell patterns in tissue were also analyzed. The work offers candidate markers for earlier detection. It also suggests targets for future treatment research.
pmc-11652667:
Saleh and co-authors test in 2024 how well a white filling resin sticks to two glass based dental cements in the lab. Strong bonds matter when layered fillings are used to repair teeth. They made 240 samples and split them by cement type, wait time, surface grit, and glue method.

Samples were checked at one day and at three months. The resin rich cement beat the plain cement at both times. A total etch glue beat a self etch glue in most groups. Smooth surfaces bonded best for the resin rich type. The results guide dentists on surface prep and glue choice for layered repairs.
pmc-11652767:
Johanna Mosquera-Moscoso and co-authors review hands on procedures for easing a severe chronic pain condition in children, in a paper from 2024. The condition, complex regional pain syndrome, brings lasting, disabling pain, often after injury but sometimes with no clear trigger. No treatment guidelines exist for children, so care leans on team based therapy, medicines, and physical rehabilitation.

When those fall short, doctors turn to procedures such as targeted anesthesia near nerves. The review, built on a librarian guided search of work since 2000, gathers which interventions are used in children and which have shown benefit. Compiling scattered case experience is a step toward the pediatric guidance the field lacks.
pmc-11653567:
Philipp Kaufmann and co-authors test whether gene expression shows sex-specific dominance in seed beetles, in a 2024 study. When different gene versions are favored in different settings, the favored version may dominate in that setting, which can preserve variation. The sexes are two such settings, and clashing selection between them is well known.

They use three crosses between inbred lines from a beetle population where fitness showed dominance reversal between sexes. Dominance effects on expression were positively correlated between sexes overall. Yet hundreds of transcripts showed significant sex-specific patterns. The study probes a poorly understood layer of how sex differences in expression evolve.
pmc-11653767:
Nicola Farrar and colleagues studied how the way health professionals talk shapes patient choices about joining a clinical trial. Recruitment is a known weak point of randomized trials, and recruiters clearly sway decisions, but the mechanism was murky. Writing in twenty twenty-four, the team embedded data collection in three British trials from different specialties. They recorded recruitment consultations and interviewed patients who had agreed or declined, linking the two sources for the same patient where possible, and analyzed the material thematically.

Professionals across the whole care pathway, not just recruiters, influenced how patients judged their need for and benefit from the treatments on offer, often by signaling a personal preference for one option. Patients still drew on family and other support and framed the final call as their own. Willingness to be randomized hinged on expected benefit and on access outside the trial.
pmc-11653867:
Redoy Ranjan and co-authors present a 2024 study on body measures and bleeding strokes in Bangladesh. Simple measures like weight and waist size predict heart and vessel disease, but most cut-off values come from people of European ancestry. The MAGPIE study set out to build values that fit the Bangladeshi population.

The case-control study enrolled 1,491 matched people nationwide between 2022 and 2024. Of these, 918 had a haemorrhagic stroke, and women made up just over half of that group. Body mass index, waist size, and hip size were all higher in the stroke group. Curve analysis set local cut-off points for each measure. The results give doctors in Bangladesh thresholds grounded in their own population.
pmc-11653967:
Santana Silver and co-authors ask when a new clinical practice stops being new and becomes the normal standard, in work from twenty twenty-four. Health groups need a clear way to tell that shift, so care stays in line with the best proof. The team spoke with leaders who run quality and change work.

Seventeen leaders from varied health settings took part in deep interviews. They named four signs of a settled practice: it fits the workflow, spans the whole unit, has staff buy in, and needs no watch to last. Plans that worked started slow, built staff ownership, and kept measuring progress. The findings can guide tools to track the change process in a firm way.
pmc-11654167:
Gilson dos Santos and co-authors dissect why arthritis pain outlives arthritis inflammation, using a mouse model where the immune receptor TLR4 is deleted from chosen cell types. Their 2024 study uses serum-transfer arthritis, in which pain sensitivity persists after swelling resolves in normal mice but not in mice lacking TLR4.

After the arthritic serum, normal mice grew nerve fibers in the joint lining and lost trabecular bone density, changes absent without the receptor. Deleting TLR4 in immune cells of the bone marrow line, or in the spinal cord's microglia, partly reversed the chronic pain; deleting it in sensory neurons did not. One microglia-targeted deletion softened the arthritis itself. The map that emerges is distributed: a pain that lives in joint, bone, and cord, gated by one receptor. For rheumatoid patients whose pain survives remission, that map suggests where to aim.
pmc-11654267:
Chau and co-authors report a 2024 study of a low-cost plan to treat depression in Vietnam. In the plan, trained helpers who are not specialists give clients a workbook and steady coaching. The study sits inside a larger trial held in eight provinces, and it asks how clients themselves felt about the care.

The authors spoke with forty-five clients and sorted their answers into themes. Warm ties with the helper and support from family and neighbors helped clients stay with the plan. Heavy duties at home, poor health, and shame about mental illness got in the way. Since visits in person are hard to keep up, the team is now moving the plan into a phone app.
pmc-11654367:
Minjae Lee, Sujin Shin, Miji Lee, and Eunmin Hong reviewed trials in two thousand twenty-four on digital serious games for nurse training. Such games promise to beat limits of short training time and scarce gear. Yet few strong reviews had looked only at randomized trials of these games in nursing.

They searched six databases and judged bias with a standard tool. Eleven studies entered the review and eight entered the pooled analysis. Students who learned with games gained more knowledge than control groups, with gains sorted by a model that tracks learning and behaviour change. The findings support games as a real teaching aid.
pmc-11654967:
Taddese Alemu Zerfu and co-authors assess what a widely used health data platform did for data quality and access in Ethiopia's primary care units. Their 2024 study deals with DHIS2, a system that has reshaped health data handling worldwide. Its effect at the primary level in Ethiopia was little documented.

The team ran interviews and group talks with providers and administrators across the country's primary units. Sampling mixed convenience groups with hand-picked experts. The answers were sorted by theme, covering the system's reach, its wins, and its snags. Participants reported clear gains in how fast and how completely data arrived. The study maps where the platform helps most and what still blocks it, from skills to infrastructure.
pmc-11655667:
Alexis Hargadon and ten colleagues show that a baby squid uses stomach-style acid to choose its glowing bacterial partner, in a 2024 paper. The bobtail squid recruits Vibrio fischeri from seawater into a light organ, ignoring countless other microbes. How such specificity arises was poorly understood.

Young organs sweep bacteria in with ciliated fields coated in acidic mucus laced with antimicrobials that work best at low pH. The team traced the acidity to a conserved proton pump, the V-type ATPase. Blocking the pump neutralized the mucus and wrecked colonization by the right partner. The pump thus links the host's immune chemistry to partner selection. The authors propose microenvironment control as a general strategy animals use to pick symbionts. The squid, long a symbiosis model, now shows one of its gatekeeping tricks in molecular detail.
pmc-11655867:
Teofila Seremet and co-authors build a molecular map to tell skin diseases apart and guide care, in a 2024 study. Many skin conditions are driven by the immune system. Targeted drugs exist for several pathways. But doctors lacked a way to read those pathways in a single patient.

The team compared gene profiles across many inflammatory skin diseases. Seven modules stood out, each tied to a known immune path. The modules form a map with strong power to sort diseases. It also helps in cases where clinic and lab views disagree. A map of this kind could match each patient to the drug that fits their pathway, rather than relying on trial and error.
pmc-11655967:
Daniel Costa and co-authors share two decades of seal tracking data in a 2024 paper. Female northern elephant seals along the west coast of North America wore sensors each year from 2004 to 2020. The seals helped birth the field of bio logging, and their dive records are a rich trove for ocean study.

The set holds near four million dives and hundreds of thousands of fixes from 475 seals, with many seals tracked more than once. Cleaning and curation steps are laid out in full, and the code sits in public stores. Two public repositories hold the data for any team to mine for seal biology or new analysis tricks.
pmc-11656367:
Yuhan Jiang and six co-authors present a 2024 study on a drug-loaded gel meant to calm inflammation in cartilage implants. Implants for cartilage repair often fail through poor bonding, swelling, or infection. The team loaded a soft gel with soyasaponin Bb, a compound from traditional Chinese medicine. They tested the gel on human cartilage cells in the lab and in implants placed in rabbits.

The compound lowered levels of three swelling-related markers in cartilage cells stressed by an immune signal. It acted through a known control pathway inside the cells. The loaded gel did the same in lab tests. In rabbits, stained tissue showed the gel cut the local swelling response around implants. The authors conclude the gel is a promising aid for cartilage repair. It could help implants settle with less reaction from the body.
pmc-11656767:
Hazel Jenkins and seven co-authors studied imaging for low back pain in older adults in a 2024 paper. About a quarter of back pain patients in primary care are sent for scans, but older adults are often left out of the counts. The data come from an Australian cohort study of people aged 55 and over seeing chiropractors.

Of 217 patients with a new bout of back pain, about 61 percent got some form of imaging over twelve months. X-ray was the most common choice. The paper describes who was sent for imaging and what the images showed. The findings help clinicians weigh when scans are truly needed in older patients.
pmc-11656867:
Wenrui Zang and a large team study treatment resistance in a deadly brain tumor in a 2024 paper. The tumor, called glioblastoma, often stops responding to both drug therapy and radiation. The team created resistant tumor cells by exposing them to the standard drug over a long period, then checked resistance in lab and animal tests.

Gene activity checks pointed to amino acid handling as a key factor. A transporter protein called LAT4 rose after drug exposure and boosted use of the amino acid leucine. That in turn switched on a growth pathway and made cells resist radiation. Blocking the transporter, paired with radiation, improved outcomes in animals. The work names a target for future combination therapy.
pmc-11657267:
Esophageal cancer often grows quietly through stages that doctors can see in tissue long before it turns deadly. Rutao Li and co-authors mapped gene activity in place, across normal tissue, two grades of precancer, and early cancer from patients with the squamous form of the disease. The spatial maps showed steady rewiring of cell signals and a build-up of macrophages as tissue worsened.

Two markers stood out: a protein called DTX3L rose in the surface cells, and one called BST2 rose in the supporting tissue, each climbing step by step toward cancer. Silencing either gene in the lab slowed cancer cell growth and movement and calmed a pro-tumor state in macrophages. The pair could help flag the disease early.
pmc-11657567:
Changlong Hu and Lin Wang review tiny parcels shed by stem cells as a liver therapy, in work from 2024. The parcels, called exosomes, come from mesenchymal stem cells, which can also grow into liver cells and aid repair. Fresh proof casts the parcels as the main healing cargo the cells release.

The review explains how the parcels form and what they carry. It then walks through their roles in liver harms of many kinds, from scarring and organ failure to cancer, oxygen strain, and fat buildup. The parcels also join the regrowth process after injury. The authors weigh what must be solved before clinic use.
pmc-11657867:
A small virus best known for a mild childhood rash can do far more harm in some patients. Silvia Bloise, Enrico Cocchi, Lorenzo Mambelli, Caterina Radice, and Federico Marchetti review parvovirus B19 in children in a 2024 paper. The virus causes fifth disease, a red-cheek illness in children. In people with blood disorders it can halt red cell making for a time. In pregnancy it can cause severe fetal anemia and loss.

The review covers joint, heart, nerve, liver, and kidney effects as well. Care ranges from simple symptom relief to antibody infusions and steroids. No vaccine or direct antiviral drug exists for the virus yet. The authors stress early spotting and fast care for the worst cases. The paper gathers a wide field into one guide.
pmc-11657967:
Jingyang Li and co-authors present a 2024 journal article on sleep length and lung function in United States adults. The team drew on national survey data for 9,284 people aged 20 to 64, grouping sleep into four bands with seven hours as the reference. Breathing tests measured air volume, flow, and two kinds of impairment.

Both short and long sleep went with weaker lungs. Six hours or less, and eight hours, cut the main volume and flow measures; nine hours or more cut peak flow too. Short and long sleepers also faced higher odds of restrictive impairment. The links ran stronger in men. The authors place seven hours as the sweet spot.
pmc-11658367:
Xiaolei Lin, Can Li, and Yulan Wang report a late sight shift case in a 2024 note. A 52-year-old woman with high short sight and past laser care lost sight in her left eye five years post lens surgery. Her left eye grade had swung to plus 6.63 in the check.

Full checks led to a stack lens set in the eye's rear groove as the fix. The fix gave high joy marks from the patient in the note. Late far shifts are rare post lens work, and the case maps cause hunts.
pmc-11658967:
Hao Ji and co-authors test a root fungus for guarding plants against heat and drought. Their paper from 2024 deals with Piriformospora indica, a fungus shown to lift stress strength in other plants. Work on rose, jasmine, and azalea cuttings was thin, so those three were put to the test.

Plants with and without the fungus faced a week without water or a day at forty five degrees in a growth chamber. Under drought, fungus plants survived at rates thirteen to seventeen points higher, with less cell damage marks and more green pigment. Under heat, a leaf health value rose in the treated plants. The fungus lifted stress enzymes as well, the team reports.
pmc-11659767:
Hume Douglas and co-authors report the first North American records of a Eurasian flea beetle that eats garlic mustard, in this 2024 paper. The beetle was once weighed as a weed-control agent against the invasive plant and rejected, for fear it would also harm native mustard kin. Specimens turned up across five states, from Illinois to Maryland, with photo records wider still.

DNA barcoding hints the European beetle may hide look-alike species. The authors give marks to tell it apart and model where it may spread, mostly humid eastern regions. They note that known finds sit in spots the model rated poor, a sign of sampling bias.
pmc-11660067:
Hossam Alhawatmeh and three co-authors report a 2024 trial of mindfulness meditation for people with end-stage kidney disease. These patients live with high levels of inflammation, which worsens their health. Meditation has cut inflammation markers in other chronic illnesses, but it had rarely been tried in this group.

Patients at a hospital in northern Jordan were split by chance into two groups of 31. The meditation group practiced for half an hour during dialysis, three times a week for eight weeks. Blood tests tracked three markers of inflammation. The study tests whether a calm-mind practice can move the body's chemistry.
pmc-11660967:
Henil Upadhyay, Jonathan Barnes, Anna Beattie, and John Reicher review two clot busting treatments for pulmonary embolism in this 2024 paper. A clot in the lung arteries is the third most common acute heart and vessel emergency, and severe cases need the clot cleared, not just thinned.

One route gives clot dissolving drugs to the whole body, with bleeding risk everywhere. The other threads a catheter to the clot and treats it locally. Trials over a decade show the catheter route improves heart chamber ratios and brings fewer bleeds and deaths than expected. Still, no large trial has pinned down which mid-to-high risk patients gain most, whether ultrasound assisted devices beat plain ones, or what the approach costs health systems. The authors call for those trials and for shared guidelines.
pmc-11663667:
Sakina Abbas and co-authors published this wheat study in 2024. Stripe rust, a fungal disease, threatens wheat harvests worldwide, and the fungus keeps evolving past existing defenses. The team examined 349 wheat lines from Pakistan and southwest China. They screened them for thirteen known resistance genes using DNA markers. Field trials then measured how each line actually withstood current rust races.

Over sixty percent of the Chuanyu lines from China resisted, against half of Pakistan's recent varieties and a fifth of its historic ones. Some genes appeared everywhere, while one useful gene was missing entirely from the Chinese set. Certain historic genes still worked well against today's fungus. Four gene pairings stood out for strengthening resistance when combined. The authors urge breeders to stack such genes deliberately. Rotating and combining defenses should slow the fungus and protect yields longer in both regions.
pmc-11663867:
A rare inherited disorder scrambles fat handling so badly that a waste product builds up in tendons, eyes, and brain, yet it can be treated if caught in time. Anthony Matta and co-authors review the condition in a 2024 paper and add a case of their own. Stubborn diarrhea, early cataracts, and nerve trouble on top of cholesterol lumps form the classic warning pattern.

Blood tests for the waste product and the missing bile acid, plus a gene check, settle the diagnosis, and a replacement bile acid is the standard care. Their patient was first misread as a common cholesterol disorder despite major early heart events. The review also backs one gene variant as likely disease-causing.
pmc-11665167:
Mohsen Meidani and co-authors report a tongue infection that looked like tongue cancer in a 2024 case study. Actinomycosis is caused by a common mouth bacterium and mostly strikes the face and neck. In the mouth it can cause pain, swelling, hardening, and pus, a picture that closely mimics benign and malignant disease alike.

That overlap matters because the cancer it imitates, squamous cell carcinoma, is highly invasive with a poor outlook, and the two call for very different treatment. The paper presents a patient with a suspicious tongue mass that raised concern for that cancer. After partial tongue removal and lab study, the diagnosis proved to be actinomycosis instead.
pmc-11665267:
Andrey Frolov, Stuart Atwood, Miguel Guzman, and John Martin report an unusual brain malformation case in a 2024 medical article. Polymicrogyria, the most common malformation of cortical development, folds the brain's surface into many tiny gyri separated by shallow grooves. It usually surfaces early in life through developmental delay, intellectual disability, epilepsy, or language and motor trouble, with severity varying widely between patients.

Finding the condition in an elderly individual is rare, and the authors describe a distinctive polygenic background in their patient. Late-presenting cases stretch the known spectrum of the disorder and remind clinicians it can hide behind decades of milder symptoms.
pmc-11665467:
Joseph Femia and Tom Gieroba report a hip swap through the front route in a woman whose far thigh had been cut high, in a case report from 2024. Loss of a leg loads the far hip and wears its joint down, a double blow with limb loss itself. Hip swaps in such patients are rare, so past tales are few and thin.

The patient was a woman of fifty two whose left hip had worn to bone on bone pain. The team chose the front route for its soft tissue gains and picked the joint parts with her one leg stance in mind. Care steps and early course are set out in full. The authors claim the first tale of this route with a high far cut, and draw rules for like cases.
pmc-11666567:
Jing Lu and co-authors ask, in twenty twenty-four, whether blood iron levels predict death in people with cardiovascular disease. Heart disease is a leading global killer, and iron may play a role, but data in patients were thin. The team used a national United States survey from nineteen ninety-nine to twenty eighteen, with mortality follow-up. The cohort held one thousand nine hundred three cardiovascular patients, mean age about sixty-four. Survival curves, adjusted hazard models, and flexible curve fits linked iron levels to all-cause and cardiovascular death. Subgroups split by age, sex, weight, blood pressure, diabetes, and smoking.

Survival differed clearly across iron quartiles. After adjustment, lower serum iron tied to higher risk of both death outcomes. The study flags iron status as a prognostic marker in this population.
pmc-11666767:
Five authors, led by Max Chen, compare surgery results in 2024 for patients from Northern and Southern Ontario in Canada. Northern residents face known health gaps, yet no one had checked if their surgery results were worse. The team used linked health records for planned, mid to high risk operations from 2009 to 2022.

Over half a million patients were included, about seven in a hundred from the North. Deaths within thirty days were much the same in both regions after fair adjustments. The study also weighed days at home, hospital stays, costs, and readmissions. The results ease fears of a large surgery gap, while other gaps remain.
pmc-11667067:
Hung-Chou Kuo and co-authors seek start rules for a preventive drug in a rare disease in 2024. Acute intermittent porphyria causes attacks of severe belly pain from a heme building fault. True attacks can be hard to tell from chronic pain. The drug givosiran can prevent attacks, but who should start it needs clear signs.

The team reviewed two patients from a Taiwan trial of the drug. Both had raised urine levels of two heme precursors plus clear attack signs before treatment. Their attack rates and lab values were tracked before and after the trial. Baseline lab levels may help doctors judge when preventive treatment is warranted.
pmc-11668167:
Sameh Msaad, Rim Khemakhem, and Dorra Abdelmouleh studied sleep apnea that lingers in children in a 2024 paper, written in French. In this disorder, a child's upper airway partly or fully closes again and again in sleep, cutting airflow despite effort to breathe. Removing the tonsils and adenoids is the standard first cure.

For some children the apnea stays or comes back after surgery. The team hunted for traits that forecast that poor result, so high-risk children can be watched or treated in other ways. Grades of the disorder rest on how many airway events strike per hour of sleep. Their findings guide follow-up care after the operation.
pmc-11668267:
Seven researchers mine a national hospital database in a 2024 paper on septic shock and kidney care. Septic shock is a grave infection state where blood pressure stays low despite fluids and drugs. The treatment studied cleans the blood nonstop to support failed kidneys and calm the body.

The team used 2019 records and found close to sixteen thousand adults with septic shock who got the treatment. More than half of them died in hospital. Older age and high blood pressure went with higher death rates. Past kidney disease and prior diabetes, by contrast, went with better odds in this data set, a result the authors report as it stands.
pmc-11668567:
Jialing Li and co-authors inject a smart nanomaterial gel into jawbone defects to coax faster, stronger regrowth. Alveolar bone, which anchors teeth, heals poorly when defects are large, and solid graft blocks fit its irregular hollows badly, sometimes harming the site. An injectable filler that sets in place solves the geometry problem.

Their hydrogel blends silver-hydroxyapatite particles into a gel laced with MXene, a two-dimensional nanomaterial prized for conductivity and cell friendliness. The composite aims to beat standard substitutes on bone induction, degradation pace, inflammation, and strength. Mechanistic studies accompany the material tests, tracing how the gel persuades bone-forming cells to build where the body alone would stall.
pmc-11668667:
Hai and co-authors present in 2024 four cases of liver cancer with tumor clots reaching the large vein to the heart, or the heart chamber itself. Such spread worsens outlook a great deal. All four men had surgery to remove liver tissue and the clot at one center.

Targeted and immune drugs were given after surgery in the care plans. One man was alive 74 months after care. Another had a liver transplant at 54 months with no return. The other two stayed disease free at 27 and 22 months. The team argues surgery plus paired drug care may extend life in such advanced cases, while calling for more study.
pmc-11668767:
Pig lung macrophages are the known doorway for a costly swine virus, but belly macrophages were long thought safe from it. Kassandra Durazo-Martinez and co-authors test that belief in this 2024 study of porcine reproductive and respiratory syndrome virus. Belly macrophages carried the virus's two entry receptors, just at lower levels than lung cells.

Despite the lower levels, both major virus types infected the belly cells. Letting the cells mature one day in culture raised infection tenfold. Blocking the main receptor with an antibody cut infection sharply, proving the same door is used. The finding widens the map of where this virus can live in a pig. That matters for control, since hidden reservoirs help outbreaks persist.
pmc-11669167:
Shan Liu and co-authors watch a crystal framework flex around guest molecules in a 2024 study. Covalent organic frameworks are porous crystals stitched by strong bonds. Dynamic ones can reshape themselves as guests slip inside, but the motion's origin stayed guesswork.

A slow exchange method grew true single crystals of the framework COF-300. X-ray views then caught linkages rotating and sliding as guests entered. Several rotamer shapes and switching contacts between woven frames appeared. Steric crowding between frames shares credit with the famous pedal motion. Atomic proof of flexibility guides designs for sensing and separation.
pmc-11669867:
Carlos Almenara and co-authors map the top weight loss websites on Google in a 2024 study. People seek diet advice online, and what they find shapes health choices. Prior work checked few queries by hand. A data-mining tool scales the search up.

Four hundred thirty-two queries came from autocomplete, common questions, and trend data. The tool pulled results with English and US settings. Sites were sorted by topic and checked for attack risk. The top five non-ad pages were healthline, webmd, verywellfit, mayoclinic, and womenshealthmag. All five showed accuracy statements and author credentials. Category counts and risks fill out the map of diet advice online.
pmc-11670667:
Eda Yilmazer, Zeynep Hamamci, and Fulya Turk test a self-rating scale in 2024 for use in Turkey. The scale gauges metacognition: how well a person reads and explains their own thoughts and those of others. Weak skills here link to worse social life, lower life quality, and stronger personality disorders.

Other Turkish tools exist, but none match this scale's mix of speed, ease, and breadth, the authors note. It scores four jobs, from watching one's own mind to holding its parts together. Their sample held 467 adults outside clinics, mostly women, aged eighteen to thirty-one. First checks found the scale sound and steady for Turkish use. A trusted local screen helps clinics spot thinking-style trouble early.
pmc-11671367:
Tonglin Sun and co-authors review a protein called ILF2 in a 2024 paper on its role in cancer. The protein helps control gene activity and partners with a related protein in many body tissues. Recent work finds far more of it in several tumor types than in healthy tissue.

High levels of the protein track with faster tumor growth, spread to new sites, new blood vessel growth, and worse outlook for patients. It also affects the cell cycle and a shift that helps cancer cells move. The review gathers these findings and weighs the protein as a marker for early diagnosis and outlook, and as a possible drug target. More proof is still needed before clinic use.
pmc-11672267:
Ai and co-authors review ways to switch diarylethene molecules with heat, acid, or electricity instead of light. These molecules are champion light switches, stable and hard to wear out. They serve in devices, data storage, smart materials, and imaging. Newer work drives their shape change with other triggers. A molecule that answers several triggers can do more jobs at once. Logic gates and denser storage are among the payoffs.

The review sorts advances by trigger type: acid, heat, and electric response. It stresses how molecular design makes each response possible. The flip and flip-back paths get close attention. The authors map a field moving past light-only control.
pmc-11672667:
Daniel Robertson and six co-authors describe a battery material that forms inside the cell as it first charges, in a study published in two thousand twenty-four. The starting oxide mixes vanadium and molybdenum. Once charged, it shifts into a disordered rock salt form that can store and release lithium fast. Such fast charging is prized for cars and grid storage.

Using X-ray tools that watch the cell as it works, the team saw the shift happen in a single step. Fine imaging showed the product forms thin, bent layers inside grains that stay fairly large. In spite of that size, the material charged fast and behaved like much finer powders. The work helps explain what lets these formed-in-place materials charge quickly.
pmc-11672767:
Ádám Kerek and co-authors profile drug resistance in harmless gut bacteria from Hungarian chickens, in a 2024 study. Bacteria that cause no disease still hoard resistance genes and can pass them on. Poultry carry enterococci widely, making farms a natural watch post.

Nearly five hundred isolates from farms were tested against fifteen antibiotics. Resistance to a common first line drug stayed near twenty percent. Alarmingly, resistance to vancomycin, a reserve drug for the worst human infections, hit about twenty-eight percent. Patterns in one species matched Hungarian hospital isolates closely. The authors urge steady farm level monitoring beside hospital tracking.
pmc-11672967:
Karol Rycerz, Aleksandra Krawczyk, Jadwiga Jaworska-Adamu, and Marcin Arciszewski wrote this research paper, published in 2024. It shows that feeding rats monosodium glutamate, the flavor enhancer, switches on the star-shaped support cells of a deep brain movement center.

Glutamate is the brain's main excitatory messenger, but in excess it can poison neurons and their astrocyte partners. Fifteen rats got salt water or one of two glutamate doses for three days. Brain sections through the caudate nucleus were stained for two astrocyte marker proteins. Treated animals showed denser astrocytes and stronger staining for both markers, most clearly at the higher dose. The cells' process counts, though, stayed the same. The authors read the change as astrocytes reacting to a glutamate flood, an early response that could protect or harm. The work links a food additive's brain chemistry to glial behavior.
pmc-11673167:
Hong and co-authors test whether computer traits of bone marrow cells can spot abnormal blood cell growth, in a study from 2024. The condition, myelodysplastic syndrome, warps how marrow cells form and lowers blood counts. Digital pathology and pathomics turn cell images into hundreds of numbers per cell.

The team studied marrow smears from 24 patients and 21 healthy peers, sorting 12,360 cells into normal and warped types across three lineages. Each cell yielded 476 features of brightness, shape, and texture. Two classifier pairings sorted the cells with fair accuracy in cross-checks. Warped red cell and white cell precursors stood out with lower heat map values on key traits. The authors propose the traits as a helper marker, pending larger studies.
pmc-11673867:
Arjun Vyas, Nantapong Butakhieo, and Lina Vyas study pandemic effects on mental health of NHS health workers in 2024. The UK health system faced staff exits and shortages at the time. Pandemic work added fear of infection and long hours. The team asks how frustration, fear, and hours drive plans to quit. They use both surveys and online interviews.

Frustration raised quit intent through raised fear of infection. Hours changed that path in a surprise way. The path was strongest for staff with short hours, not long ones. Interview data add depth on why staff want to leave. The authors point to steps firms and policy makers can take to keep staff.
pmc-11673967:
Maize varieties differ in how well they fit a given climate, and Ding and co-authors test seven of them in the Alar region of southern Xinjiang over two growing seasons. Nineteen traits were measured, from antioxidant enzyme activity to ear and leaf form.

All seven varieties grew robustly, though their trait profiles differed. Two, Jin'ai 588 and Denghai 3672, yielded steadily across both years. A statistical reduction picked out five traits carrying most of the information, including kernel weight and a stress enzyme. Composite scores put Xinyu 66 and Denghai 3672 on top as the best fits for the region, while Xinyu 24 scored lowest and was judged unsuitable. Clustering sorted the seven into three groups that matched the scoring, giving local growers a short list.
pmc-11674067:
Sara Azevedo and co-authors review a survey system that lets young bowel patients speak for themselves. The ill, a long-term gut swelling, hits life quality hard and runs a harsher course in kids than in adults. Reports from patients or parents catch what lab tests miss: pain in daily life, mood, and social strain. The system in view, PROMIS, was built for use across ills and across the life span.

Surveys span body, mind, and social health, plus life quality as a whole. Tools exist for both grown patients and kids. Their 2024 review weighs how the system has been used in youth bowel care and where gaps stay. The team backs its wider use to guide care talks, while proof of gain in this group is still young.
pmc-11674267:
Elżbieta Bartoszewska and co-authors introduce three little-known ways cells die and ask what cancer therapy can do with them. The famous deaths, apoptosis and necrosis, no longer exhaust the catalog. Methuosis drowns the cell in its own vacuoles. Alkaliptosis rides a lethal rise in internal alkalinity. Oxeiptosis answers oxidative stress through a sensor-driven path. Their 2024 review gathers what is known of each mechanism's molecules and outcomes.

Each death has a distinct morphology and trigger set. Cancer cells that evade the famous deaths might still fall to these. The review weighs early evidence for drugs that provoke each route. Better cell death biology, the team argues, is a direct road to new neoplasm management.
pmc-11674567:
Galvany-López and co-authors review dog-assisted therapy for children and teens with autism spectrum disorder. Animal therapies are used widely to lift quality of life. The team searched eight databases for studies on dogs with this group. The review plan was registered in advance. Nineteen papers met the bar for inclusion. Most, 84%, found gains in communication and social interaction.

Dogs often act as a bridge that draws the child's attention and rewards contact. Emotional gains also appeared across studies. The review weighs how feasible such programs are to run. Limits include small samples and varied methods. Still, the signal favors the dogs.
pmc-11674667:
Altrawy leads a large team reviewing gut microbes and breast cancer, in work from twenty twenty-four. Breast cancer is a major cause of death in women. Beyond genes and environment, gut bacteria now look like a real factor in how tumors grow.

Helpful and harmful gut species make small chemicals that affect hormones, immunity, and cell signals in breast tissue. An unbalanced gut mix has been linked to higher risk. The review maps how those microbial chemicals reprogram the tumor surroundings and may change treatment response. The authors argue that diet and microbe care deserve a place in future breast cancer plans.
pmc-11674767:
Amalia Făgărășan and co-authors ran a pilot study of heart function in children born with a bicuspid aortic valve, which has two leaflets instead of three. The usual pumping measure, ejection fraction, can look normal while the heart muscle already weakens. A speckle-tracking ultrasound method measures muscle stretch directly and is thought to catch trouble earlier.

The study followed seventy-three children with the defect and fifty-five healthy controls over one year at a Romanian referral center. Ejection fraction was normal in the patient group. Stretch analysis, though, showed reduced values in the heart's inferior and anterior segments and in one standard view, compared with controls. The authors ask whether these early dips predict later heart failure and whether spotting them early can cut illness.
pmc-11675267:
Chloe Lisette Jones and co-authors ask in a 2024 study whether weather and air quality move the daily symptoms of women with a chronic fatigue illness. Patients have long said bad air or odd weather worsens pain and exhaustion, but no study had tested the claim day by day.

Fifty-eight women rated their pain and fatigue daily for about two months. The team matched those ratings with weather and pollution records for the Birmingham, Alabama area. Worse pain tracked with worse air quality scores, more fine particles, and calmer winds. Fatigue rose with more particles and lower air pressure. The effects were small, but they back patients' reports with numbers for the first time.
pmc-11675567:
Jiho Lee and six co-authors test whether voice features can flag cognitive decline in Korean speakers. A cheap, noninvasive screen would aid early detection as dementia grows worldwide. Speech data came from two hundred twenty-three patients who completed eight speaking tasks, grouped by scores on a standard mental test.

Four learning models were tried on three sorting tasks. A deep network led on two tasks, and a forest model led on the third. Certain voice traits, such as shimmer in a vowel task and pitch variation in a syllable task, recurred as useful signals. The authors call the work preliminary. Age and other personal factors sway the voice measures, so matched groups are needed next.
pmc-11675767:
Daibin Zhong and co-authors trace insecticide resistance in an invasive malaria mosquito in Ethiopia in a 2024 study. The mosquito, Anopheles stephensi, has spread through Africa and thrives in cities, unlike the native malaria carriers.

Field mosquitoes from one town survived standard doses of two pyrethroid sprays at high rates. Gene readings showed resistant and even unexposed field groups switching on detox genes far above a tame lab strain. Two esterase genes stood out, one running up to 70 times higher. These enzymes break down the poison before it can kill. The finding matters because bed nets and sprays lean on this drug class. Control programs, the authors imply, need new tools for city mosquitoes.
pmc-11675867:
A semi empirical method for judging how well a model fits sea clutter radar returns is proposed in a 2024 paper, with future Adriatic Sea measurements in view. Radar echoes from the sea surface follow heavy tailed distributions, and checking a model against data usually needs histogram binning, which distorts the fit.

The method compares the data and model distribution functions directly, measuring two standard divergence scores without binning. Proofs show the estimates converge to the true values. Examples test the scores on synthetic data and on a widely used measured data set. The Adriatic, with its many islands, may need its own models.
pmc-11675967:
Charlotte Werndl and co-authors, writing in 2024, ask where the Boltzmann equation belongs in the foundations of statistical mechanics. The field is usually split into two camps, one following Boltzmann's line and one following Gibbs, and the famous equation fits awkwardly in both. The authors first restate the Boltzmann-style approach using local field variables to define the large-scale states of a system. On that restatement, the equation appears as a special case of the approach.

They then turn to the Gibbs-style side, working through a chain of linked equations. The version of the equation that drops out of that chain counts as Gibbsian only in a thin sense, they argue: it uses a steady measure over the whole system's state space. The paper sorts concepts rather than reporting data. Its claim is that a clearer statement of each camp dissolves much of the puzzle.
pmc-11676067:
Samantha Bastow and five co-authors report a 2024 national survey of controlled substance diversion in hospital pharmacies in the United States. Diversion means drugs meant for patients are stolen or misused by staff. Pharmacies guard those drugs, but how they watch for theft varies a lot by site.

The survey drew replies from dozens of sites in many states. Most leads were pharmacy chiefs or staff in set diversion roles. Most sites had a watch team and software for the task. Big sites met the rules best, the team found. Checks on stock flow were the weak point in most replies.
pmc-11676167:
Xiaoping Shao and co-authors worked in 2024 on making mine backfill stronger by adding silica fume to a fly ash and cement mix. Backfill fills mined-out space, and using fly ash cuts cost and carbon output. The drawback is weak strength in the early and middle stages, which matters when mining and filling run side by side.

The team varied the silica fume share and measured flow, strength, and fine structure. A moderate share gave the best mid-term strength, a clear gain over the mix without it. Too much hurt both flow and strength. Study of the fine structure showed the additive helped form a binding gel and filled tiny pores at the best dose.
pmc-11676267:
Corina Eugenia Budin and co-authors run a pilot study of lung cancer patients at a hospital in Romania, sorting risk factors and other diseases by cancer type. Lung cancer is a top cause of cancer death worldwide. Records for patients admitted across most of 2023 were reviewed, and 115 patients met the study rules.

Most had the non-small cell type, split evenly between its two main forms, and the rest had the small cell type. Lung airway disease and heart disease were the most common other illnesses. The authors argue that airway disease shares roots with lung cancer, such as smoking, and stands as its own risk factor. Body weight showed no link to cancer type.
pmc-11676367:
Autoimmune diseases are hard to treat because drug levels and responses vary widely from patient to patient. Świerczek and co-authors review how pharmacometrics, the science of modeling drug behavior, is reshaping therapy for these conditions. They survey two decades of work on model families that simulate drug absorption, link dose to effect, and chart disease progression over time.

Population models and model-based meta-analysis help personalize dosing and improve safety. Quantitative systems pharmacology adds a view of the disease machinery itself. Newer work folds in artificial intelligence and machine learning to sharpen the predictions. The authors see the toolkit as a bridge from lab findings to tailored care.
pmc-11676667:
Cristina Sempio and ten colleagues measured how the body processes an oral dose of a lesser-known cannabis compound. The compound, delta-8 tetrahydrocannabivarin, occurs in cannabis and may have useful drug properties. Its behavior in humans after dosing had never been studied. The twenty twenty-four analysis came from a two-phase, placebo-controlled, dose-ranging trial in healthy volunteers. Doses ran from 12.5 to 200 milligrams in an oil formulation.

Twenty-one participants completed sessions, and blood samples from fifteen were analyzed up to eight hours after dosing. A carboxy metabolite of the compound was the main breakdown product detected in plasma. Mapping these pharmacokinetics is basic groundwork for any future medical use. It tells researchers how fast the compound appears, converts, and clears in people.
pmc-11676767:
Per Milberg and co-authors related bumblebee numbers in species-rich Swedish grasslands to the makeup of the surrounding landscape, in a 2024 study. Bumblebees pollinate crops and wild plants, and their decline is tied to farm intensification and lost grasslands. The team surveyed 476 semi-natural grassland sites across southern Sweden and measured land use at several distances around each.

More arable land nearby meant fewer bumblebees at every scale, hardest on short-tongued species and early-emerging colonies. Surprisingly, more semi-natural grassland within a kilometer also linked to fewer bees in some groups. The authors urge farm changes such as fewer pesticides and richer field margins.
pmc-11676967:
Hadi Darawsheh and co-authors study how skull variation shifts the position of the mandibular foramen, in an anatomy paper from 2024. The foramen is the entry point for the nerve that dentists block for lower jaw work. Its place varies with skull and face shape, so a one-size rule can miss the nerve.

The team measured one hundred six certified cadaver heads of both sexes. Skull, face, and jaw shapes were classified with standard indices. Foramen position was then compared across shapes. Key jaw indices tracked with foramen place in a significant way. The data support a personalized read of anatomy before nerve block and jaw surgery, rather than a fixed landmark rule.
pmc-11677167:
Chengqu Fu and co-authors review whether the chemistry of metabolism can forecast a colorectal cancer patient's future. Tumors rewire how they burn sugar, fats, and amino acids, and the small molecules left behind circulate as potential signals. If those metabolites foretell relapse or survival, doctors could aim follow-up care and extra treatment at the patients who need them most.

The review gathers studies that tie specific metabolites and metabolic patterns to outcomes after diagnosis. It sorts which candidates repeat across cohorts and which remain one-off sightings, and weighs how ready each is for the clinic. Future trends and hurdles, from standardizing assays to proving added value over staging, close the survey. The authors see prognosis by metabolite panel as promising but unfinished.
pmc-11677267:
Bile salts ball up in gut juice to ferry fat wares, and their balls grow in two steps that no eye had caught at the speck scale. Fatmegyul Mustan and co-authors run that growth in a 2024 set of atom sims. First balls of near ten specks form fast and hold.

Past a set span, the first balls fuse to balls of near twenty. Skin bare to the juice drops in the fuse, which is the push. Fat salts then join: two stiff kinds sink to the ball's core, with the bile specks as a shell. The bent kind stirs through the whole ball. That stirred ball, the team say, is a prime host for fat drugs.
pmc-11677367:
Tai-Ti Liu and co-authors report lab work in a 2024 paper on mushroom sugars changed with gallic acid. The sugars come from an edible mushroom and already draw interest for health uses. Adding gallic acid, a plant compound, was meant to boost their power against cell damage and germs.

Tests showed the changed sugars cleared harmful free radicals better than the plain sugars and bound iron more strongly. In one iron test, the changed sugars even beat gallic acid on its own. A version paired with zinc killed two common bacteria far better than the changed sugars alone. The results point to food and health uses for the changed sugars, pending further tests.
pmc-11677567:
Hyunsoo Jang and co-authors tested a probiotic strain in obese mice in a 2024 study. The strain, a Lactobacillus type, had shown promise for fatty liver disease linked to metabolism, but had not been confirmed in a living system. Mice fed a high-fat diet served as the model.

After twelve weeks on the diet and twelve weeks of treatment, supplemented mice weighed less and had lower insulin and insulin resistance scores. Blood fat fell without change in total cholesterol, while liver fat and cholesterol buildup reversed. Liver injury scores, scarring, and a function marker improved. A key energy signalling step also rose. Gene expression for fat handling changed little.
pmc-11677767:
Márk Váradi and colleagues built iron-bearing molecules that grab a partner molecule and report the catch electrically. Their host compounds pair a ferrocene unit with a urea-bearing ring that can hydrogen-bond to guests. They studied one guest closely: 2,6-diaminopyridine.

Nuclear magnetic resonance at low temperatures revealed how the hosts fold and bind. Adding a pyridine arm to the host changed both its shape and its grip on the guest. Electrode tests agreed: coated surfaces responded when the guest arrived. Such hosts could become chemical sensors that signal what they catch.
pmc-11677867:
Tatiana Kekeeva and co-authors wrote a 2024 paper on ovarian cancer tumors that share one trait but act in different ways. These tumors have a broken DNA repair system, which makes them sensitive to platinum drugs. The team asked whether the cause of the break splits patients into groups with different outlooks.

They tested three hundred fifty-two tumor samples for gene mutations, repair scores, and chemical silencing of repair genes. About two thirds had the repair defect. The group with true gene mutations responded best to platinum, gained most from a targeted drug, and lived longest without the disease returning. Splitting the patients this way can guide which drug each woman should get first.
pmc-11677967:
A cut nerve needs a bridge that guides the regrowth and then gets out of the way. Abdulla Yergeshov and eight co-authors built such a bridge in 2024: a spongy gel core, laced with a short protein scrap that nerve cells love, wrapped in a slow-fade shell. The scrap is tied into the gel as it sets, so its spread can be steered. A dyed twin of the scrap let the team watch that spread.

The parts left skin cells unharmed in dishes, and the scrap's dose set how nerve-like cells grew and shaped. Sewn into rats across a nerve gap, the bridge held the stumps for eight weeks while the shell thinned. Electric tests and flesh reads showed the core did real repair work. The team call it a proof of build for gel bridges.
pmc-11678067:
Jing Yin and seven co-authors warm a subalpine meadow at several altitudes in a 2024 paper. Mountain grasslands are sensitive to climate shifts, and most warming studies use one altitude. On a high mountain site, warming eased cold limits on grass, raising biomass, height, and coverage. Richer plant matter fed more soil carbon, which in turn reshaped the soil fungal community measured by gene sequencing.

Fungal diversity rose at low altitude under warming but fell higher up, as community assembly turned more deterministic. Nutrient-cycling fungi grew more common and better connected. Yet grass pathogens also increased, a risk the authors say needs long-term watching.
pmc-11678467:
Benjamin Tutolo and co-authors study two small alkaline lakes in British Columbia and what they say about early Earth. Such lakes are thought to help build the first blocks of life, since they can stock key feedstocks like phosphate. Yet the needs of key steps clash with each other, and with the needs of early cells. Past work had not traced how water and land shape the lakes over time.

Field tools, water tests, and models show what drives the pair, Last Chance Lake and Goodenough Lake. Strong loss of water to air is what lets phosphate build to high levels. The clash between salty lake water and fresh inflow stirs strong mixing. That mixing may let one lake both feed early reactions and shelter early life.
pmc-11678667:
Adina Andreea Mirea and co-authors examine, in a 2024 study, whether tooth and gum damage tracks with small-vessel harm in people with type 2 diabetes. Diabetes and gum disease feed each other: mouth infection and poor sugar control form a hard circle to break. The team asked whether worse dental lesions go with more vessel complications and weaker control.

The study enrolled 112 patients who had a dental exam. Half had deep, complicated lesions and half had shallow ones, matched by age and sex. The deep-lesion group showed higher blood sugar, higher long-term sugar marks, and more inflammation signals, along with worse kidney function. Nerve damage and eye damage from diabetes were both more common in that group. The authors built a score from these signs that predicted complicated lesions well.
pmc-11678767:
Sydney Chase and three co-authors tested how well an Apple Watch Series 9 reads energy use and heart rate, and whether skin tone changes the result, published in two thousand twenty-four. Thirty young, healthy adults were grouped by a standard skin tone scale. Each walked a ten-minute treadmill routine at mixed speeds and slopes while wearing the watch, a lab breathing mask setup, and a chest strap.

Energy use readings missed the lab values in every group. Heart rate readings drifted more for darker skin than for lighter skin, and drift grew and shrank with effort level. The authors warn that watch numbers should not be taken as exact, least of all for users with dark skin.
pmc-11678867:
Ignacio Diaz-Lorenzo and co-authors present a 2024 review of CT pulmonary angiography in lung clot care. The scan is the main test for pulmonary embolism, a clot that blocks lung arteries. The review covers clot burden scoring and death risk prediction. It also weighs new scan techniques and clot makeup reading. Artificial intelligence tools for the scan get a section.

One scan finding is firmly validated for prognosis so far. A right-to-left heart chamber width ratio above one links to far higher death risk. Other burden scores remain unproven by comparison. Radiologists get a disciplined account of what the scan can and cannot promise. Clot age reading from makeup could one day match treatment to clot stage. The review separates proven signs from hopeful ones, which busy clinicians need.
pmc-11679067:
Mingze Ma and co-authors study stress that builds inside electric motor insulation as its varnish hardens. Their 2024 study treats hair-pin motors, whose flat wire windings need a sound coat to guard against sparks and early failure. Stress left from hardening can crack that guard, yet the process had drawn little study.

The team pairs fiber sensors that track heat and strain with lab tests of how the resin sets. Their math model, which treats the set as self-speeding, matches the sensor data well. Retuning the bake cycle cut peak stress from about forty-five to about thirty-nine pressure units. The late hot phase drives much of the stress, they find. The model can guide coat design for other resins too.
pmc-11679367:
Weny Rinawati, Abdulloh Machin, and Aryati Aryati test whether routine blood counts taken at admission can predict which stroke patients will develop an infection, in a 2024 study. Infections after a stroke worsen outcomes, and cheap early warnings would help wards act fast. The team reviewed records at a brain hospital in Jakarta, Indonesia.

The study covers 163 patients with a first ischemic stroke, admitted between October 2023 and March 2024, all with blood counts drawn within a day. Twenty-four patients developed an infection. Simple counts did best as predictors: total white cells, neutrophils, and monocytes each separated the groups with fair accuracy. Ratios built from those counts are also examined. The authors argue these everyday measures, read early, can flag patients who need closer watching for infection.
pmc-11679567:
Wenqin Yan and co-authors present a camera method for reading heart rhythm from the face in a 2024 paper. Tiny color shifts in the skin track each heartbeat, but shifting light and head motion muddy the signal, and the best current models are too heavy for everyday gear.

Their network, MFF-Net, is built to be light. It splits the raw signal into parts by rhythm speed and cleans each part with its own settings. Two added blocks widen the view across time scales and sharpen the signal's spectrum. The design aims to recover the pulse wave cleanly even in messy rooms, fast enough for clinics, phones, and other small devices to run it live.
pmc-11679667:
Elizaveta Sigova and a large team assembled complete genomes of a flax infecting fungus in a 2024 paper. The fungus causes heavy yield losses in flax. The team read the DNA of four highly harmful strains with two sequencing platforms and compared two assembly tools built for end to end genomes. Reads from long read sequencing were first corrected by a dedicated algorithm.

One tool gave genomes that were complete but broken into more pieces, while the other gave true end to end assemblies. All four assemblies had ten core chromosomes plus two or three extra ones, at much the same total size. Extra polishing with short reads stopped helping once coverage with corrected long reads passed a set level. Core chromosomes were highly alike across strains. The authors say their approach may work for other fungi and will aid the hunt for strain level differences.
pmc-11679967:
Janusz Kirenko, Anna Prokopiak, and Maciej Wodziński compare how parents and teachers rate the everyday skills of autistic young people, in a 2024 study. The Polish study used a standard adaptive behavior system that gathers ratings from both home and school. Ninety-nine people on the spectrum, aged five to twenty-one, were assessed; seventy were boys and twenty-nine girls. The two rater groups disagreed significantly about the same children's skills.

The predictors of overall adaptive scores also differed by who was rating. A child can genuinely function differently at home and at school, and each observer sees only one stage. The results argue for planning support from both views at once, rather than treating either report as the whole truth.
pmc-11680167:
Jose Angel Santiago-Cruz and co-authors test a plant latex against a mosquito borne virus in a 2024 dish study. The virus can spark pandemics and has no approved drug, so plant leads draw real interest.

Step guided screening split the latex into parts and tracked which part kept the virus down. A plain alcohol extract already worked at low harm to cells. Its cleaned active part worked far better, at a dose more than fifty times lower. Timing tests hint the part blocks one of the virus's work proteins. The part also killed cancer cells while sparing a dengue virus, a sign of narrow aim.
pmc-11680367:
Barbara Platschek and co-authors examine the post-acute COVID vaccination syndrome through drug safety records in a 2024 paper. Some vaccine recipients report a severe, lasting syndrome much like long COVID, yet it still lacks official recognition as a disease.
