The authors argue the syndrome differs from normal vaccine reactions only by duration, and that safety monitoring tracks duration poorly. Syndrome-specific signals were in fact logged faithfully by European systems, but authorities did not act on them. Estimates clash: dose-based math suggests a vanishingly rare outcome, while workplace studies of young and middle-aged staff suggest near one in a hundred. The paper calls denial of recognition unjustified and asks for proper study of affected people.
pmc-11682767:
Amal Aboelmaaty and co-authors track fertility signs across the heat cycle in old mares. Their twenty twenty-four study compares five mares over twenty years old with six young native mares. Aging dulls fertility in horses as in people, yet daily hormone patterns in old mares were little mapped.

Doppler ultrasound watched the lead follicle, the corpus luteum, and the womb across six cycles. Blood drawn at each scan gave hormone, enzyme, and antioxidant levels. The anti-Müllerian hormone, a marker of egg reserve, was a core read. Shifts in blood flow and chemistry show how the old ovary copes, guiding breeding vets who manage aged mares.
pmc-11683367:
Yonghui Cheng and co-authors trace how one gene helps lung cancer spread in a 2024 study. The cancer type is non-small-cell lung cancer, the most common form. Spread to new sites, more than the first tumor, is what kills most patients.

The gene, XRN2, chews up RNA strands in the cell. Lab tests raised and lowered its levels in cancer cells. Cells with more of the gene moved and invaded more; cells with less moved less. The gene boosted a growth signal path named EGFR, which pushes cells to change shape and travel. Adding that signal back restored the spread that gene loss had cut. Mouse tumors backed the lab story, as the authors report.
pmc-11683567:
Hyun-Jin Na, Mi-Jeong Sung, and Joung-Sun Park used fruit flies to study kidney stones and cell faults tied to age and stress in 2024. Kidney disease is rising worldwide, and stones are a major risk for long-term kidney harm. The fly kidney-like tubule system shares traits with the human kidney and is easy to test.

With age and oxidative stress, the tubules showed more centrosome faults and more stone formation. Centrosomes are cell structures that organize division, and extra copies are a cancer hallmark. A high-sugar diet also raised stone formation. The authors argue the links among aging, stress, and chronic disease run deep, and offer the fly as a tool to hunt for new kidney drugs.
pmc-11683667:
Malcolm McDonald and co-authors report in 2024 a surprising ally in brain cancer: a marker on some tumor cells that helps the immune system fight back. Glioma, the deadliest brain cancer, usually hides in an immune suppressed setting that blocks clearance.

Gene data from single cells showed a small set of human and mouse glioma cells carrying CD83, a marker of mature immune presenting cells. In a mouse model and in human samples, tumors with the marker grew less and drew a stronger killer T cell profile. Forcing the marker up raised pro immune signals and long term T cell responses. The team thinks tumor made CD83 talks to T cells and reshapes the local immune scene.
pmc-11688067:
Jing Kang and co-authors run a randomized trial of a potassium-lowering drug around parathyroid surgery, in a 2024 study. Patients on long-term dialysis with overactive parathyroid glands often face dangerous potassium spikes after surgery. The drug tested, sodium zirconium cyclosilicate, binds potassium in the gut. Patients took it just before their operation in the treatment group.

Blood tests were taken before and after surgery in both groups. The hormone targeted by surgery fell sharply in everyone. Potassium levels matched early on, but by that evening the treated group ran clearly lower. Three control patients needed emergency treatment for severe potassium highs. No treated patient needed such rescue care.
pmc-11688367:
Yamina Alioui and co-authors test a mushroom extract against gut inflammation in mice. Their 2024 paper uses polysaccharides from the golden chanterelle, a well-liked edible mushroom. Colitis harms the gut barrier, stirs the immune system, and upsets gut microbes. The extract was fed to mice after a chemical brought on colitis.

Treated mice kept more weight and had a stronger gut lining. Levels of a key mucus protein and of proteins that seal the gut rose. Harmful immune signals fell, while calming signals rose. Gene checks on stool showed the microbe mix moved back toward balance. The authors see the extract as a candidate path for colitis care, acting on barrier, immune response, and microbes at once.
pmc-11688867:
Catherine Clair and co-authors present a 2024 study on the personal care networks of older adults living with type 2 diabetes. Some elders draw on family and friends for daily help; others face the disease alone. The team mapped those networks with a name-by-name survey of 58 community-dwelling adults.

The participants averaged 73 years old, and most were women and non-White. About one in six reported no family or friends involved in their care at all. Those isolated adults were more often never married. People with networks named about three helpers on average, who shared daily tasks, errands, and medical chores. Patterns differed between Black and White participants. The findings argue for screening that asks who helps, not just what hurts.
pmc-11688967:
Yoon Chung Kim, Michael Lepore, Nancy Kusmaul, and Sarah Holmes asked care workers how they give person-centered care to residents with dementia, and whether experience changes the craft, in a 2024 study. About half of nursing home residents live with dementia. The team interviewed twenty direct care workers in four low-resource homes in two states. Workers averaged about nine years in the job.

The shared playbook ran: affirm feelings, build trust, bring families in, honor tastes and life stories, know each resident's triggers and past wounds, and tailor activities to the person. Everyone stressed that training matters. Old hands and newcomers named the same moves. The split was inward: long-tenured staff reported more emotional distance from residents, while newer staff felt more attached. The authors say support should differ by tenure to keep care warm and workers well.
pmc-11689067:
Jason Wong and co-authors ask whether caring for grandchildren pulls older adults out of social life or pushes them into it. Their 2024 study uses three waves of a Chinese ageing survey covering more than 11,000 adults. Both strain and reward stories are plausible, so the data must decide.

Nearly every form of grandchild care raised informal social life, like meeting and helping friends. Formal activities such as clubs showed no link. The gains split by sex and care type: some forms helped only grandfathers, others only grandmothers. Living in a three-generation home was the exception for the general rise. The authors credit linked family lives across generations in later life.
pmc-11689167:
Dale Dannefer, Chris Phillipson, and Jessica Kelley introduce a symposium honoring sociologist Carroll Estes in this 2024 paper. Her emancipatory gerontology imagines a society where people of all ages hold dignity and access to essentials. Reaching it means changing institutions and the stories told about class, race, gender, and age.

The papers span how long life is shared out, especially in cities, and how age and race intertwine. One coins the term rageism for that intersection and traces its effects across generations. Another argues long lives are becoming a privilege of the wealthy. Others probe city-driven divides and the uncritical use of agency in aging theory. The editors frame the set against market-first policies and renewed exclusion.
pmc-11689267:
Christina Victor asks whether faith links to loneliness in older adults in England, in a 2024 study. Past work, mostly from North America, hints at a link, but the topic is rarely studied in the United Kingdom. Victor used a long running survey of ageing for the test.

The sample held 6,225 adults aged 50 and over from one wave of the survey. Most called themselves Christian, about one in five had no religion, and near half had not been to worship in the past year. About 19 percent scored as lonely. Going to worship looked linked to less loneliness at first, but the link faded once other traits were held fixed. Faith labels and private practice showed no link.
pmc-11689367:
Carlisle Shealy and Pamela Teaster recount in 2024 the story of the Virginia Tech Center for Gerontology as it marks forty-five years. The center runs two graduate certificates, one for campus students and one online for leaders in an aging society. Its reach spans five core faculty, ninety-five affiliated faculty, and about twenty funded projects at a time.

Over its life the center has trained one hundred forty certificate holders and built a futures board drawn from across the state and nation. The talk covers the center's history, the hardships it weathered, and the paths it sees for the next fifty years of aging research and teaching.
pmc-11689667:
Caregivers who mix several substances show more abusive behavior, Jessica Hernandez and co-authors find in a 2024 study. Four hundred fifty-three family caregivers of people with dementia reported daily for twenty-one days. Statistical models tracked substance use against harsh acts day by day.

Polysubstance use clearly raised the odds of both psychological and physical aggression. The mix of being male and using multiple substances stood out as especially risky. Models also weighed care hours, family relation, emotion control, age, and ethnicity. Screening caregivers for combined substance use, with an eye on gender, could flag homes where support must arrive early.
pmc-11689767:
Xiao Qiu and co-authors study many-drug use and mood in older adults in this 2024 paper. Polypharmacy means taking five or more prescription drugs at once. It is common after age sixty-five and has been tied to more depressive symptoms.

They used national survey data on 3,143 community-dwelling older adults. More than forty percent met the many-drug mark in the study waves. Overall, polypharmacy linked to more depressive symptoms. The link split by gender in a sharp way. Among women it tied to fewer symptoms, while among men it tied to more. The authors call for care plans that account for that split.
pmc-11689867:
Wenxing Wei and co-authors review, in a 2024 paper, what protects older adults with dementia from elder abuse, and what harm the abuse leaves behind. People with dementia are abused more often than their sharper peers, yet research on their specific risks and shields is thin.

Following standard review practice, the team searched four databases through mid-2023 and kept eight studies. Protective factors clustered around the caregiver: coping strategies, rewards in the prior relationship, and informal support from family and friends, tested during the pandemic. Documented harms included more medical problems and poorer medication safety. The thin evidence base itself is a warning.
pmc-11690367:
Allen Glicksman and co-authors examine how birthplace and language shape older immigrants' use of formal health care, in a 2024 paper. Meeting the health system is hard for any older adult, and harder still for immigrants facing language gaps, cultural differences, and an unfamiliar system. The team studied service records for patients who spoke Chinese, Spanish, or Russian, comparing clinic visits, emergency department use, and hospital stays among people with similar insurance and diagnoses.

Chinese speakers stood out, above all for using emergency departments far less than other groups, including white and Black English speakers. The authors also warn about a data problem: health records usually capture the language spoken at the visit, not the patient's birthplace, which blurs exactly the differences researchers want to study. The paper calls for attention to both origin and encounter type in aging and migration research.
pmc-11690567:
Keran Chamberlin and co-authors test whether a poor sense of smell predicts coronary heart disease in older adults. Their 2024 study draws on the ARIC Neurocognitive Study, following 5,142 people free of heart disease at the start. Smell was scored with a twelve-item odor test in 2011 to 2013 and classed as good, moderate, or poor.

Over up to 9.6 years, 280 people, about five percent, developed coronary heart disease. Poor smell went with higher risk in the first six years, with risk roughly doubled at the two-year mark. The link faded over time afterward. The authors account for deaths and dropouts in their models.
pmc-11690667:
Lucas Hamilton and Eric Allard use network science to track how emotions move together across adult life, in a 2024 paper. Studies of emotion dynamics have grown fast with phone-based sampling. One approach builds networks where each emotion is a node. Links show how strongly two emotions rise and fall together.

Such networks can be built for one person or compared across groups. Earlier work by the team showed the method can measure emotional reactivity across the lifespan. Here they used video clips to stir emotions in 531 people aged from the teens onward. The paper explains the planning and reading such networks demand. It aims to help researchers use the tool with care.
pmc-11690767:
Steffi Kim, Lena Thompson, and Jordan Lewis hear elders on giving in a 2024 study of Alaska Native towns. West school lore on elder town life dwells on clubs, help shifts, and votes. What towns mean from the Native side was far less heard.

The talk set is vast: well past a hundred talks with town elders and a small set in the big town, across more than a decade. Themes from the talks show a two-way road. Elders both take part and lead, and both ways knit kin and keep old ways alive. Town teams gain the elders own tale of why giving is joy.
pmc-11690867:
Claudia von Bastian and co-authors present first findings, in a 2024 conference paper, from a large study of speed training across adult life. Speed training is one of the few brain training types that seems to lift untrained skills. Yet why it works is unclear, and the role of attention demands in the tasks is untested.

The study enrolled 476 healthy adults aged eighteen to eighty-five at sites in three countries. Groups trained on tasks with rising attention demands over ten sessions. Gains were checked right after training and three months later, across memory, reasoning, and daily thinking skills. Early results were shared in this talk, with close to four hundred adults finishing the study.
pmc-11690967:
Amy Eisenstein and Kenneth Hepburn introduce a symposium on adapting proven caregiver support programs for diverse families, in this 2024 piece. Many evidence-based programs exist to help people who care for ill or aging relatives. Yet the cultural and language needs of the highly varied caregiver population are often ignored when those programs are designed.

The symposium gathers four projects. One built and tested a culturally tailored anxiety program for Latinx caregivers of older adults with cancer. A second translated and tested an online program for Latinx relatives caring for people with dementia, and a third adapted a teaching program for Black dementia caregivers. The fourth reviewed family-centered programs to find the shared core parts that could ground new designs for any background. A closing discussion draws lessons on when to adapt, when to build fresh, and where the research gaps remain.
pmc-11691067:
Sydney Hoel and six co-authors field test a website that connects rural dementia caregivers to local help, in this 2024 study. Rural caregivers carry heavier loads and thinner support than city peers. The platform, built with rural caregivers and community groups, tailors its listings to each user's needs and location.

Fifteen caregivers used the site for thirty days and then sat for interviews. They liked having everything in one place, the need and location matching, alerts about new resources, and contact with fellow caregivers. Barriers were also plain: little spare time, listings that missed the right disease stage, and a plain lack of local services to list. The team plans design fixes before a large effectiveness trial. The study shows a platform can be welcome yet still hit real world limits.
pmc-11691267:
Karen Kopera-Frye, Lyn Holley, and Cassandra Ford gathered field lessons in 2024 on working with older adults in rural and Indigenous communities, where distance and culture shape what good care looks like. Their symposium shared studies rather than a single trial.

Talks covered how health conditions, race, and rural life steer the course of frailty in national data. One project tapped older farmers' know how to sharpen emergency decisions in a Canadian valley. Work with Alaska Native elders stressed that trust and mutual benefit must come before research questions. A program with Latino elders built bridges to care through family centered respect. Mobile pain apps for diverse elders were also weighed.
pmc-11691367:
Duo Wei, Joseph Morales, and David Burdick report a class project that pairs students with older adults in a 2024 paper. University students in a medical informatics class ran tech workshops across South Jersey. Older adults learned to use smartphones and AI tools for chat, fun, and health tasks. Sites ranged from health centers to a canoe club and a clubhouse.

Both sides gained from the swap. Older adults built tech skills and trust with new tools. Students acted as mentors yet also learned from the life views of their elders. Feedback came from student notes, surveys of the older group, course scores, and press reports. All signs pointed the same way: the project built a learning culture on both sides. It also drew the town and the university closer in trust and support.
pmc-11691567:
Lillian Hung and seven co-authors published this study in 2024. It gathers staff views on virtual team-based care during one of care's riskiest handoffs: moving an older patient from hospital to long-term care. Video-linked teams promise coordination across sites, but the transition's success depends on the humans using the screens.

Fifty-two participants, clinicians, leaders, and patients with families, joined interviews, focus groups, and a policy review. Staff called the model acceptable, efficient, and cost-saving. Enablers were engaged teams, training and support, and access to equipment. Barriers were the mirror image: shaky infrastructure, scarce resources, and privacy worries. Families' involvement emerged as the pivot: their complex knowledge of the patient makes or breaks the plan, and virtual planning must include them. The authors ask for policies to standardize the practice. They frame virtual transition care as promising but unfinished, pending family-centered design.
pmc-11691667:
Older adults with memory and thinking problems face a higher risk of being neglected by the people meant to care for them. Amy Shaw, Alyssa Elman, and Tony Rosen examined case records from a hospital-based elder mistreatment team, covering 146 patients where the team judged neglect likely. The typical patient was eighty-two, and more than three quarters were women.

Nearly half also showed signs of another form of mistreatment, such as verbal, physical, or financial abuse. The neglecting caregiver was most often the patient's own child, then a partner, then a paid aide. Seven themes ran through the cases, including delayed medical care, poor supervision, caregiver impairment, and conflicts between caregivers. The authors argue that neglect has varied roots, so responses must be just as varied.
pmc-11691767:
Ling Han and co-authors track how physical activity unfolds in the years after a stroke. Getting moving again is a core goal of stroke rehab, yet long term data are scarce. The team followed close to three hundred patients in a Norwegian study. Thigh sensors logged upright time over six day spans at three points across three years.

Upright time slid down slowly month by month, even after many health factors were counted. Men logged less upright time than women, and each year of age cut time further. Worse stroke scores at the start also meant less movement later. Spread between patients was wide. The authors call for longer follow up and rehab shaped to each person.
pmc-11692067:
Ajla Basic and Mushira Khan asked whether being born in the United States changes how Latinx adults age well. They surveyed 141 community-dwelling adults over fifty in the Chicago area. The forms covered aging satisfaction, cultural blending, and feelings of connection, control, and growth.

Birthplace changed how several factors tied to successful aging. The link between aging well and age, sex, autonomy, and self-rated health all ran differently for US-born participants than for immigrants. The authors point to migration history, cultural views of aging, and uneven access to resources. Programs for older Latinx adults, they argue, should not treat the group as one.
pmc-11692167:
Jun Chu, Christine Mair, and Michel Boudreaux examine whether hearing trouble raises the risk of dementia among older adults living in the community in the United States. Their research article, published in twenty twenty-four, follows the question over time rather than at a single moment, using nationally representative survey data.

Drawing on the National Health and Aging Trends Study from twenty eleven through twenty twenty-two, the authors apply a Cox proportional hazards model. They adjust for demographics, chronic conditions, hearing aid use, and social isolation. Older adults with hearing trouble faced more than double the risk of developing dementia over eleven years. The link did not differ significantly by race or ethnicity. The authors suggest that policies promoting hearing tests and hearing aid use might help delay or prevent dementia.
pmc-11692267:
Jae Jun Lee and co-authors measure, in 2024, how common early muscle loss is among older adults in Korea who have fallen. Muscle loss raises the risk of poor health, and a simple screening stage was defined in 2019 for use across Asia. The study covered one hundred eighty-four adults aged sixty-five or older living at home, each with a fall in the past two years.

About one in four met the screening stage, based on calf size, grip strength, and a sit-to-stand test. Doing little physical activity and fearing another fall both linked strongly to the condition. Other factors, such as mood and memory, did not. The authors urge activity programs for this group.
pmc-11692367:
Pain paths over ten years among older veterans are traced by Chiyoung Lee and co-authors in a 2024 study. Chronic pain affects about one hundred million Americans, and veterans face higher risk. Six hundred nineteen veterans in a heart health cohort gave pain scores at two, five, and ten years.

Two paths emerged: a low pain path and a high pain path, both fairly steady over time. The team then hunts traits that predict landing on a worsening course, using learning models. Knowing who is at risk early could steer support before pain sets in hard. The study fills a gap, since long pain courses in veterans were poorly mapped before.
pmc-11692467:
Four authors report a 2024 survey study of midlife adults in Korea. Their topic is how views on aging, a sense of purpose, and healthy habits fit together, and whether those links differ for men and women.

The team surveyed 298 adults aged 50 to 64 who lived in the community. People with more negative views on aging tended to report less purpose, and more purpose went with healthier habits. Purpose also carried part of the link from aging views to habits for both sexes. The link from aging views to purpose was stronger in men, so the authors urge programs that build purpose and treat men and women with care for that gap.
pmc-11692767:
George Daniel and co-authors show that plain poverty, measured by income and daily hardship, predicts weaker thinking in older Americans. Most research ties mental decline to schooling or wealth. Their 2024 paper uses the Health and Retirement Study to test two blunter measures: falling below an income poverty line, and material hardship, the lived struggle to cover basics.

The sample held nearly eleven thousand adults averaging seventy-four years old. About nine hundred sixty lived below the poverty line, and they were younger, less schooled, less wealthy, and sicker than the rest. Poverty proved the strongest single predictor of poorer cognitive scores, and the link ran stronger in Black participants and in women. Hardship measures added their own signal. The authors argue that money stress in old age is not background noise for brain health, but one of its clearest measurable drivers.
pmc-11692967:
Channing Tate and co-authors gather hospice views from older Black Americans in a 2024 paper. One hundred forty-four adults aged sixty-five and over wrote responses. Each described hospice care in their own words.

Misconceptions about hospice are common in every group studied. Black Americans use hospice less than others, for reasons worth naming. Responses were checked for errors across four eligibility dimensions. Cultural barriers to enrollment were a central concern of the team. Knowing what people believe is the first step to fixing it. Readers learn how end-of-life care is understood inside a community it underserves.
pmc-11693067:
Jethro Raphael Suarez and co-authors test whether anxiety shifts how older adults sway, in work from 2024. Balance loss is a known harm of anxiety, but which sway path it drives was unclear. The team measured sway in one hundred seventy adults aged sixty-one to ninety-one with a simple board test, eyes closed, and sorted them by a short anxiety survey.

Adults with mid-to-high anxiety swayed more from side to side than calmer peers. Front-to-back sway did not differ by group. The authors note that past injury or low mood could sway the results too. They call for more work that weighs those factors in anxious older adults.
pmc-11693167:
Ruth Melo and seven co-authors follow frailty in Brazilian older adults over nine years. Their study came out in 2024. Frailty, a state of weakness and low reserve, predicts disability and death, but its long-term course in Latin America is little studied.

At follow-up, the share of frail participants had risen while the robust share fell by more than half. New frailty appeared in about a quarter of those at risk. Older age, cognitive impairment, illiteracy, male sex, and giving up advanced daily activities each predicted decline or death. Living alone, somewhat surprisingly, protected against frailty. The authors call for more long-term studies to pin down which risks can be changed.
pmc-11693267:
Woo Jang, Drew Krull, Seonhwa Lee, and Merril Silverstein wrote a 2024 paper mapping health care access for older people in Minnesota. The state's oldest group, those eighty-five and up, is set to more than double in thirty-five years. Rural counties will age even faster than cities. Yet clinics and hospitals are spread thin in rural areas.

Using 2020 census data and map-based methods, the team measured how social and money factors shape access for people sixty-five and older. Their maps show detailed patterns of where care is hard to reach. Naming those pockets helps the state plan clinics, transport, and home services before the wave of older residents arrives.
pmc-11696667:
Li and co-authors wrote a study from 2024 on injecting a chemotherapy drug into the spinal fluid of lung cancer patients whose disease had spread to the membranes around the brain. That spread is hard to treat, since most drugs reach it poorly. The patients all had a mutation-driven form of lung cancer and had failed targeted pills. Fifty patients at one cancer hospital in Hunan received the spinal injections.

About two in three patients improved in nerve symptoms and function scores. Survival without growth inside the skull ran about five months, and overall survival about a year. Responders lived far longer than non-responders. Side effects were mainly lowered blood counts and liver strain, none fatal. The team calls the route a workable option after targeted pills fail.
pmc-11699567:
Supawadee Patathananone and co-authors profile ripening karanda fruit to judge its promise as a functional food. The fruit carries plant chemicals with varied biological effects. The team extracted those chemicals at low temperature and measured the fruit's phenolic content, antioxidant strength, sugars, and vitamin C. They also checked whether the extracts harm human blood cells.

Repeated ultrasonic extraction worked best at four rounds. Extracts from fresh fruit and from freeze-dried powder both showed antioxidant activity. The extracts did not kill white blood cells at moderate doses, though they damaged red blood cells at higher ones. Fresh fruit extract held 0.27 percent total sugar and a small amount of vitamin C. Chemical analysis named the extract's main components. The authors say the profile supports developing supplement foods built on ripening karanda fruit, with dose care guided by the blood cell results.
pmc-11704367:
Mahie Patil, Sanjana Konda, and Latha Ganti mined United States mental health records for ADHD patterns in a 2024 study. The dataset held nearly 5.9 million patients from a national services database in 2022. Just under eleven percent carried an ADHD diagnosis. Rates ran highest in children under twelve and fell with age and with education level.

People outside the labor force showed the highest rates, pointing to work struggles. Black patients had the highest prevalence by race and Asian patients the lowest, and the Midwest and South led the regions. Men and the never-married were overrepresented. ADHD traveled most with defiant, developmental, and conduct disorders. The authors call for coordinated support across schools, workplaces, clinics, and policy.
pmc-11704867:
Yun and co-authors write a reply letter on drug resistance and the One Health approach, in a letter from 2024. The letter answers a commentary on their report about antibiotic use in Korean hospitals from 2018 to 2021. The authors agree that resistance is a grave threat to public health worldwide.

They note that resistance grows not only from drug use in care settings but also from farm chemicals, waste, and contact among livestock, wildlife, and people. That web of links is the heart of the One Health view. Still, their own data spoke only to hospital use, so their firm claims stay with stewardship in care facilities. They call for shared global data systems and joint work across human, animal, and environmental health.
pmc-11705367: The hosted text is a compiled roster of the Poultry Science Association's honors and awards, published in 2024. It lists recipients year by year for many named prizes, among them student research manuscript awards, egg research awards, and nutrition research awards. The tables run from the late nineteen forties to 2024, with a few years marked as having no award. As a reference list it records who was honored in each year rather than reporting a study.
pmc-11709367:
Luis Santos and four co-authors set out a pilot study of remote brain testing for older adults in Panama and Florida. Video based testing spread during the pandemic, but proof from low and middle income countries is scarce. The team built a Spanish friendly battery and a parallel cohort to a Florida study.

So far eighty adults over fifty have been assessed across both sites, with one hundred planned per cohort. Screening checks dementia risk and basic device access. The battery comes from a national Alzheimer center set, paired with surveys on daily function. The authors expect a feasibility picture for both places. They note the study is a first of its kind in Panama.
pmc-11709467:
Vonk and co-authors test whether a short speech sample recorded at home can flag a behavioral form of frontotemporal dementia, in a 2025 study. Fifteen patients and nineteen healthy volunteers used a phone app to talk freely about a happy memory. Recordings were transcribed automatically and mined for ninety-eight language features.

Three features did the separating: longer silences, fewer complex noun clauses relative to all clauses, and more restarts mid-sentence. Together they classified the groups with about eighty-five percent accuracy. The authors present remote speech analysis as a quick, scalable screening approach for this dementia, which is notoriously hard to diagnose early.
pmc-11709567:
Mark Dubbelman and nine co-authors test a new digital way to check sense of time, place, and self in older adults with no thought loss. Their study appeared in twenty twenty-five. A chat tool asked about past events, places, and close ties, then posed short quiz items in each of the three areas. Scores mixed right replies with speed of reply.

Fifty-one adults took the test and also had brain scans for amyloid and tau. High amyloid linked to worse sense of place. Sense of time linked to amyloid plus tau in two brain areas. Sense of self showed no such link. The team sees place and time sense as early signs worth tracking.
pmc-11709667:
A protein that carries fats in blood and brain comes in three forms, and one form strongly raises Alzheimer risk. Bilal Ersen Kerman and co-authors study how that risky form clumps in living cells in a 2025 paper.

The team tagged the protein forms with glowing markers and used a light method that senses when tagged copies sit close together, a sign of clumping. The risky form clumped more than the common form in hamster cells. Boosting a fat-loading protein cut the clumping. X-ray checks backed the light results, and the protein left cells riding on fat particles. Tests in human neurons extend the work toward the brain cells that matter in disease.
pmc-11709767:
Anna Aaronson and co-authors study clashing memory reports in aging research in this 2025 paper. Studies of Alzheimer's disease ask both participants and study partners how thinking has changed. The team asked whether disagreement between the two flags mild cognitive impairment.

Pairs from two large cohorts filled a daily cognition scale. Four disagreement measures were built from their answers. Bigger gaps, and partners reporting more decline than participants, tied to higher impairment odds. A model picked from one cohort's pairs held up in the second cohort. The authors suggest disagreement itself is a useful early signal.
pmc-11709867:
Jeanne Gallée and co-authors offer a 2025 conference abstract on language skills in subgroups of Alzheimer's disease. Some patients show clear language loss early, while others show no single weak area. The team asked whether a known language pattern, tied to a form of aphasia, shows up more often in the language-weak group.

The team studied 642 people from three long-running aging studies. They scored word understanding, naming, and phrase repetition, then sorted each person into one of eight language patterns. The patterns differed sharply between the two groups. The aphasia-like pattern appeared far more often in the language-weak group, as the team expected.
pmc-11709967:
Cassidy Molinare and co-authors study a quiet memory failure that may flag Alzheimer's disease before symptoms. Some people recall new material fine after half an hour, then lose it over weeks. That pattern is called accelerated long-term forgetting. Their 2025 study tests it in sixty-one cognitively healthy older adults using a remote, at-home program called BRANCH.

Volunteers took the tests on their own devices over seven days, while brain scans measured amyloid and tau. The design lets forgetting be timed at several gaps, which clinic visits cannot do well. Linking the forgetting curve to scan markers shows whether the trait tracks silent disease. Dementia researchers get a home-based tool for catching decline at its faintest stage.
pmc-11710067:
Anil R Wadhwani and co-authors report a 2025 conference abstract on chemical marks on DNA in two tau conditions. Alzheimer's disease spreads tau tangles across the cortex, while a related condition, PART, keeps them near the hippocampus. The team asked whether methylation marks help explain why tangles spread in one and stall in the other.

The team profiled frontal cortex from 398 donors and checked the findings in a second cohort of 707. Marks tied to tangles did not overlap with marks tied to amyloid plaques in the first cohort. Shared marks in the second cohort pointed to T cell and transport genes, while tangle-only marks pointed to synapse genes.
pmc-11710167:
Li Sun and four co-authors apply causal network analysis to multi layer data from Alzheimer brains. The disease affects more than six million Americans, and most cases have no clear single cause. Recent antibody drugs that clear amyloid give only modest benefit, so deeper mechanism work is needed.

The team built probability network models from two hundred eighty-seven donated brain samples with clinical and gene and protein data. Fake perturbations traced which factors drive outcomes. Gene groups tied to mitochondria, the cell's power plants, stood out strongly among drivers. Paths from known risk factors to memory scores ran through those groups. The finding revives an old hypothesis placing mitochondria near the disease core.
pmc-11710467:
Ipsit Vahia presents a talk summary in a 2025 piece on early dementia signs. Behavior change can herald Alzheimer's disease up to three years before memory symptoms show. Such changes are often mistaken for primary mental illness. Mild behavioral impairment names the pattern, and the talk argues for measuring it with precision.

Data from three studies show sensor based markers that can quantify subtle behavior shifts. Case stories show how tracking helps sort dementia linked change from psychiatric illness. Getting that call right steers patients to the right clinic years earlier. The talk maps a field moving from checklists toward continuous, measured behavior.
pmc-11710567:
Yi-Chien Liu, Chia-Ju Chou, and Chia-Ying Lee follow memory clinic patients in a 2025 study. Alzheimer's progression varies widely between people, and spotting fast decliners early matters. The team asked whether walking and speech, both cheap to record, forecast who will progress. Ninety-nine patients in Taiwan joined from 2021 to 2023 and faced full workups, from amyloid scans to blood tests.

Follow up ran two years with repeat diagnoses. Gait and speech measures from the start were weighed against later change. Cheap signals that predict decline could spare patients costly scans until they are truly needed. The design, rich baseline plus long follow up, is what gives such small signals a fair test.
pmc-11710767:
Rick Zirkel and co-authors test whether raising brain blood flow calms faulty nerve activity in Alzheimer's mouse models, in a 2025 paper. In these mice, white blood cells plug tiny vessels and cut flow across the brain. An antibody that clears those plugs restores flow in minutes and improves mind function within hours.

Visual cortex neurons in the mice showed widened tuning to moving patterns, a sign of deranged activity. The team used calcium markers to watch neurons before and after flow treatment. Their hypothesis is that better flow can normalize at least part of that activity. Such a result would show some disease linked nerve harm is reversible, not fixed.
pmc-11710867:
Miyuki Nemoto and co-authors test in 2024 how six kinds of exercise change mood in people with mental disorders. Their group held twenty-four patients, aged twenty to seventy-seven, with mood disorders, schizophrenia, and other states. Each kind of session ran an hour, once a week, across many months in 2018 and 2019.

Patients rated their mood before and after each bout. Pleasant feelings rose and bad feelings fell after most kinds of exercise. Yoga gave the largest gains in calm and ease and cut worry the most. Work with two tasks at once helped least. The results can guide staff who plan activity for such patients.
pmc-11711967:
Caring for a relative with Alzheimer's at home is relentless, and falls and hospital trips are constant risks. Rosemary D Laird and Jason Abrevaya describe a Florida pilot program that gave 50 family caregivers a personal licensed social worker by video or phone. An opening survey of 80 questions, plus a standard burden scale, shaped a personal risk plan for each family.

Monthly meetings worked through the flagged risks, with a fresh assessment every three months. After nine months, caregivers reported 75 percent fewer falls and 68 percent fewer hospitalizations, and patients' mood, legal planning, and finances also improved. Caregiver burden stayed level despite the disease advancing. The partners now plan to study the cost of expanding the model. The pilot appears in 2025.
pmc-11712067:
Arlene Astell and co-authors tour the homes of people living with dementia to log their technology in a 2025 study. Everyday devices already hold helpful tools, from stored phone numbers to calendar reminders. Nine people walked the researchers through their homes room by room, naming each device, its use, and how they got it.

Residents used far more than phones and tablets: televisions, stoves, mobility aids, and voice assistants all featured. They used tech to keep up valued activities, stay in touch, and stay independent. Ease of use and safety features mattered to them. Many wanted more from their devices but found learning new functions hard. The authors say the tours dispel myths about dementia and digital tools.
pmc-11712167:
Shulla Cose, Fitzgerald, LaFleur, and Ruge give voice to young people whose parents developed dementia early in life. Writing in 2025, the authors describe these youth as the softest voices on the hardest road. Their project, run through a community called Lorenzo's House, teaches a three-step model for meeting stigma: recognize it, respond to it, and let the exchange empower both sides.

At an international youth summit, nearly one hundred young people shared stories of stigma at parties, shops, parks, and hospitals. The model gave them tools to answer with teaching rather than fight, flight, or freeze. The group expects more than two hundred youth at its next summit. The piece is a community report, not a clinical study.
pmc-11712367:
Sori Kim Lundin and seven co-authors link a blood pressure drug class to lower dementia risk in a 2025 study. Angiotensin receptor blockers had shown hints of brain protection, but reads clashed. Their pool is huge: more than six million people with high blood pressure in a United States claims trove, sorted by drug class and by whether the drug crosses into the brain.

Users of the blocker class showed the lowest hazard curves of all groups. Against the sister class, their adjusted risk of Alzheimer's and kin dementias ran a fifth lower; against other drugs and non users the gaps ran wider still. Brain crossing blockers beat the rest of their own class too. The authors say the class looks brain kind, with crossing types ahead.
pmc-11712467:
Marina Ritchie and co-authors ask what helps people join early Alzheimer disease trials, in a research paper from 2025. New drugs are in tests, yet sign-up is slow. The team looks at how trial design shapes the choice to take part for people with mild memory loss and their families.

People rated sample trials on a scale of one to seven. The trials varied in drug type, scan result sharing, and whether a study partner had to attend in person. A risk of brain swelling was also varied. The results show which perks draw interest. Trial teams can use the findings to plan fair sign-up.
pmc-11712567:
Gabrielle Lincoln and co-authors compared two classic paper tests of executive function, the mental skills used to plan, switch tasks, and hold rules in mind. One test sorts cards by shifting rules, and the other connects numbered and lettered circles in turn. An adapted card test from Emory removes cards with several possible sorts, making it a cleaner measure.

Data came from 864 adults in a long-running Michigan study of memory and aging. Earlier work found the trail test more sensitive to executive problems than the original card test. The new study asks whether the cleaned-up card test now beats the trail test. Sharper tests help clinicians spot early decline in thinking.
pmc-11712667:
Xinyi Xia, Qi Qin, and Yi Tang compare blood signs of Alzheimer's disease by age of onset in a 2025 study. Blood tests promise a kind, cheap way to spot the disease. The early-onset form may run on partly distinct tracks, which blood could reveal.

Ninety-five people took part: early-onset patients, late-onset patients, and matched healthy peers. Eighteen blood markers were read, next to spinal fluid tests, mind tests, gene status, and brain scans. Patients showed higher levels of nerve harm and stress marks and lower stores of a key fragment. Early-onset blood ran lower on three swelling marks than late-onset blood.
pmc-11712767:
Roisin McManus and co-authors study an immune sensor that shapes how brain support cells use fuel in Alzheimer disease, in a 2025 paper. The sensor, NLRP3, triggers inflammation when it meets disease-linked peptides. Mice that model the disease but lack the sensor are protected from its brain harm, and the team ask what else changes without it.

Single-cell gene and access data found a distinct group of microglia, the brain immune cells, in protected mice. Those cells showed stronger eating of debris and a raised transporter for a brain chemical. Cells without the sensor also had better energy function and more of a key metabolite. That metabolite was required for their stronger clearing of amyloid, via control of gene switching. The pattern held in human cells, and drugs that block the sensor copied it in mice.
pmc-11712867:
Christopher Schwarz and co-authors compare in this 2025 paper two programs that erase faces from brain scans. Shared scan data must not let face-matching software name the people scanned. The team ran both programs, mri_reface and MiDeFace, on two large scan sets and then tried to match the cleaned scans to face photos with a commercial tool.

Untouched scans matched almost every time, while both programs cut matches to near one in ten. The older program hid faces a bit more fully and missed fewer patches. Effects on later brain measures, though, were small for both and near equal. The authors give labs a clear basis for picking a tool that fits their sharing rules.
pmc-11712967:
Avi L Benitah and co-authors present a 2025 drug design study aimed at an enzyme called Lyn, which sits inside microglia, the brain's immune cells. Blocking the enzyme may switch these cells into a state that clears toxic amyloid from the brain. No strong, selective blocker that reaches the brain was available to test this idea.

The team screened known drugs, took one as a starting point, and reshaped it on a computer model of the enzyme. They built new compounds, tested how well each blocked the enzyme, and checked the best ones in cell tests. The work produced a new set of blockers ready for testing in animals.
pmc-11713067:
Thamara Tapia-Muñoz and Claudia Miranda-Castillo measured loneliness among people living with dementia in England. Their 2025 study notes that research usually treats loneliness as a risk factor for dementia, not as something felt by those who already have it. They drew on a long running survey of older adults in England.

Across nine waves, they found 181 people who said they had been told they have dementia, plus 775 people without it for comparison. The start point for the dementia group was the wave when the diagnosis was first reported. That group averaged about 76 years old and scored 4.71 on loneliness, against 4.07 for the others. A smaller set gave loneliness scores from two years before as well.
pmc-11713167:
Amanda Lima and co-authors follow young rats bred for mind loss to catch a brief phase when brain sugar burn runs hot, in a study from 2025. Scans, maze tasks, and spine fluid were read at four ages through the first year. Clump seeds of the ill showed in the brain from month six.

At month nine the rat brain crust burned sugar past sound peers, three months past first clump sight. Star cells in crust and deep brain drew in more of a feed good at that age, and their marks rose and fell in step. Maze scores slid at months nine and twelve. Nerve and germ marks held still while star marks moved. The hot phase looks like a star cell act.
pmc-11713267:
Hyena Kim and co-authors asked in 2025 whether stiff arteries, measured before any symptoms, already track the spinal fluid markers of Alzheimer's disease. Their sample held 751 cognitively normal adults in a healthy brain study, average age sixty-two. Stiffness was read as pulse wave velocity, with a standard cut-off marking the stiff group.

People with stiff arteries had clearly higher odds of testing positive on both Alzheimer's marker ratios. After adjusting for age, race, sex, schooling, and heart risk factors, one link stayed solid and the other faded to borderline. The authors read stiffness as an early companion of silent Alzheimer's chemistry. They call for follow-up studies to test whether the simple pulse measure can screen for the disease before memory slips.
pmc-11713367:
Ackley and co-authors examine in 2025 how the link between brain tau buildup and cognition shifts with age. Tau scans are now common, yet age patterns across samples were unknown. They joined two cohorts to span ages 55 to past 90.

Tau uptake by brain stage was set against two cognition scores, a mental status exam and a dementia rating sum. Groups split into four age bands in one cohort, plus the oldest old cohort. Models adjusted for age, race, gene risk count, schooling, and gender. Bootstrapped fits tested how steady the tau cognition link stays as age climbs.
pmc-11713467:
Fonov and co-authors map amyloid and tau build-up in living brains using PET scans, in this 2025 paper. In Alzheimer's disease these two proteins spread through the brain in known stage patterns. Past work matched the tau stages in living people using hand-drawn scan regions.

The team instead let the data speak, with no regions set in advance. Their scans came from young adults, healthy older adults, people with mild impairment, and patients with the disease, all seen at a Montreal aging center. Two tracers lit up amyloid and tau in turn. The joint patterns they found track disease progress and may help stage patients without guesswork.
pmc-11713567:
Hyejin Kim and co-authors study how stand-in decision makers choose life-sustaining treatment for older patients with dementia in South Korean long-term care hospitals. Their 2025 study draws on interviews with twenty-four care providers and seven family surrogates. Such hospitals are the main setting for dementia care in the country, yet they face thin resources and awkward rules around end-of-life care.

The team maps how choices actually get made, what helps the process, and what blocks it. Providers ranged from doctors and nurses to social workers and traditional medicine doctors. Families who had faced the choice shared their side as well. The authors close with directions to improve these hard decisions.
pmc-11713667:
Huang and a large team (2025) tested a drug delivery approach meant to slow the spread of tau. In Alzheimer's disease, a harmful form of this protein travels between brain cells. Some of that travel happens inside tiny vesicles that cells release. Blocking the enzyme that helps make the vesicles can slow the spread. The team attached a potent blocker of that enzyme to a branching carrier. The carrier homes to microglia, the brain's immune cells.

Mice with a tau-related brain disorder were dosed for 20 weeks. The treatment reached microglia and switched the enzyme off there. It also lowered the vesicles that activated microglia shed into the blood. Yet total tau, harmful tau, memory scores, and brain shrinkage were unchanged. The authors conclude that tau spreads mainly through neurons in this model. A microglia-only treatment therefore cannot stop it.
pmc-11713767:
Johanne Stümpel, Marlena van Munster, Annika Dörrhöfer, and Björn Schmitz-Luhn explore what dementia patients and caregivers need in a 2025 paper. Alzheimer's cases may grow fourfold by the year 2050. Care often falls on families, and their views are key to good care design. The team worked with people who have Parkinson's disease, whose care needs overlap with dementia care.

Ten talks and group workshops were held with patients and caregivers. People picked cards about resources, tools, and human contact to picture their future care. The team compared what came up with past Alzheimer's research. Heavy feelings and upset daily routines stood out across the disease course. The themes can guide care plans that fit real family life.
pmc-11714067:
Taylor Kimberly tests a portable low power brain scanner for use in Alzheimer's disease, in a 2025 conference paper. A scanner that can travel to the patient could open brain imaging to far more people. The trade off is a weaker signal and fuzzier images than standard hospital machines.

The team enrolled 45 clinic patients with mild loss or dementia, plus 23 controls from an emergency unit. Each had a scan on the portable machine, which runs at a fraction of standard strength. Smart software rebuilt the images and measured brain areas and scar spots. The same measures from standard scans matched closely, with whole brain size nearly exact. The author says the portable scans are sound enough for point of care use.
pmc-11714267:
Naaheed Mukadam and twelve co-authors gather everything meta-analyses say about everyday medicines and dementia risk, in this 2025 umbrella review. Sixty reviews were included, spanning blood pressure drugs, statins, antacids, anti-inflammatory drugs, diabetes and hormone treatments, and more, with participant counts from hundreds to over nine million.

The trend lines pointed both ways. Blood pressure treatment, statins, anti-inflammatory drugs, anticoagulants, and vitamin E leaned toward lower dementia risk. Androgen deprivation, benzodiazepines, and anticholinergic drugs leaned toward higher risk. Almost all the evidence was observational, open to biases like sicker patients getting more drugs, and few reviews scored well on quality. The rare trial data supported blood pressure treatment against dementia and hinted hormone therapy might raise risk. The authors are plain: no medicine should yet be prescribed just to prevent dementia.
pmc-11714367:
Fernanda Souza Andrade and co-authors test whether wearable sensors can gauge chronic pain in older adults with Alzheimer's disease. Their 2025 pilot study starts from a care gap. Pain often goes untreated in dementia because patients cannot say where or how much it hurts. A cap that reads brain waves and a screen tool that tracks gaze supply the signals. Eligible patients have early to mid-stage disease plus pain lasting months.

Screening proves steep. Of dozens of applicants, only a handful meet all the terms, and fewer still finish the single test session. Those who finish span the late seventies to early nineties. Self-rated pain runs mild to moderate for most of them. Early data show the setup can be run and tolerated in this group. The authors present the work as a first step toward fair, signal-based pain checks.
pmc-11714467:
Laura Willers Souza and co-authors link the stress hormone cortisol, measured in spinal fluid, to brain thinning across the Alzheimer's continuum. They studied 310 people from the ADNI cohort with hormone measures, brain scans, and the standard fluid markers of the disease. Whole-brain maps tested the hormone against cortical thickness, and follow-up scans tracked change over time.

At a single visit, higher cortisol meant thinner cortex in several regions, regardless of diagnosis or marker status. Over time the story sharpened: cortisol alone did little, but in people already positive for disease markers it sped thinning in the signature regions. The authors suggest stress chemistry makes a vulnerable brain wear faster, a possible lever for future therapies.
pmc-11714567:
Tristyn Hall and co-authors report a 2025 account of side effects in a large trial aimed at preventing dementia. The trial ran for two years at more than one center. It enrolled five hundred and thirteen adults aged sixty to eighty-five. All had high blood pressure, a family history of dementia, memory complaints, or some mix of these. People were split into four groups by chance.

The groups got hard exercise training, strong drug care for blood pressure and blood fats, both, or usual care. Groups on strong drug care had more odd lab results and more leg cramps, swelling, and feeling faint or tired. Groups that exercised had more muscle and joint complaints. Rates of serious harm and death were low and much the same across groups. The report helps readers weigh the costs of each plan.
pmc-11714767:
Anna Rosenberg and co-authors describe a 2025 lifestyle trial to protect brain health in older adults across Europe. An earlier Finnish trial showed that a mix of diet, exercise, and training helps the aging brain. The new trial, called LETHE, adapts that mix with digital support. It enrolls adults aged sixty to seventy-seven who face a raised risk of loss but still think well. Sites in four countries take part in the two-year study.

Half the group gets the full program, with staff-led sessions and a phone app that gives personal tips. The other half gets general health advice and a simple form of the app. All wear smart watches that track activity and sleep in the background. The main checks are whether people stay in the trial and follow the plan. Changes in risk scores, habits, and quality of life are also tracked.
pmc-11714867:
Sayaka Kuwayama and co-authors present a 2025 study of how well daily thinking complaints can be predicted in Latino adults. They used health study data from more than four thousand people first seen in their late fifties on average. A follow-up visit about seven years later asked how people felt their thinking worked in daily life. The team tested thirty-seven early measures from health, habits, mood, and home life.

Three kinds of statistical models were compared, and the best one still explained only a small share of the later complaints. Physical health scores and air flow limits were among the top early signs. Adding a score for overall thinking at the first visit changed the results only a bit. The authors note how hard it is to predict such complaints ahead of time.
pmc-11714967:
Adults with Down syndrome make too much of a protein that forms plaques, so Alzheimer's disease strikes them often and early. Patrick Lao and co-authors tracked a brain scan marker of small vessel disease in seventy-eight adults with Down syndrome. Each person had two MRI scans, a bit over a year apart. The marker was the volume of bright spots in white matter, which signal vessel damage.

Bright spots grew faster in the temporal and occipital lobes for people who stayed in the Alzheimer's group at both visits. Growth in the frontal lobe did not differ by diagnosis. The pattern matters for drug trials, since a marker that changes at a known rate can show whether a drug slows the disease. The study gives trial planners those rates by brain region and diagnosis.
pmc-11715167:
Wendell Lima Rabelo and four co-authors examine death rates among older adults with dementia in Brazil, in work from 2025. They use a large long-term study of aging that follows people over time. Past work in Brazil leaned on death records, which are often filled out poorly.

The team looked at more than five thousand people aged 60 and older and checked who was still alive. People with dementia died at much higher rates than those without it. Rates were higher for men than for women in the group with dementia. Age and years of schooling also shaped the gaps the team found.
pmc-11715267:
Pei-Ning Wang and three co-authors built a blood-based way to find early Alzheimer's disease patients for drug care. New drugs can slow the disease at its first stage, when thought slips just a bit. But proof of amyloid in the brain is a must before care starts, and brain scans are scarce and dear. A cheap blood screen could sort who should get a scan.

The team ran a multi-site study of people with mild memory loss or early dementia. Two blood scores, each built from amyloid and tau levels, sorted the early stage with more than eighty-five percent accuracy. A blood amyloid score plus a known gene type then foretold a clear brain scan in more than eighty-four percent of cases. The flow could ease the jam in clinics and widen the reach of the new drugs.
pmc-11715367:
Tahmida Sharmin and seven co-authors search blood chemistry for early companions of an Alzheimer's marker, in a 2025 study. The marker, P-tau181, hints at brain amyloid years before symptoms. What travels with it in healthy elders was unclear.

The study sampled 100 cognitively intact older adults, 65 with normal brain amyloid and 35 with raised levels. Several fat transport molecules rose alongside the marker in the whole group. The amino acid citrulline and three other small molecules also tracked it. In the raised amyloid group, one molecule stood out alone. Adding it sharpened the marker's ability to sort brain status. Such partners may refine early screening.
pmc-11715467:
Greta Keller and co-authors test a cognitive score for early Alzheimer's disease, in a study published in 2025. The score blends three tests: word learning, a timed connecting task, and word fluency. It aims to flag brain changes before dementia sets in. The team, working with a South American cohort, asked whether the score predicts spinal fluid markers equally well in women and men.

They studied 112 patients with mild cognitive problems, matched across the sexes on age, schooling, and test scores. A learning model using the score did modestly overall. In women, though, its accuracy fell below chance level, while results in men were stronger. The timed task carried the most weight in women. The authors warn that one score may not read risk the same way in both sexes.
pmc-11715667:
Yaqun Yuan and co-authors link major pesticide exposure accidents to later memory complaints among older American farmers, in a 2025 study. The analysis drew on 2,365 mostly white male farmers in Iowa and North Carolina, enrolled in a long-running farm health study in the 1990s and rechecked in 2020 and 2021. Memory decline was scored with a fourteen-item questionnaire.

Farmers who had lived through a high-exposure event, such as a spill soaking the skin, reported significant memory decline more often than those who never had one. The link held across every survey wave in which the events were recorded. Careful weighting handled the study design and missing answers. The authors urge prevention of such accidents as brain protection.
pmc-11715767:
Lowering blood pressure hard might slow the amyloid build-up behind Alzheimer's disease, and one trial is testing that idea in older adults. Jordan Zaenglein and seven co-authors report in 2025 how the IPAT study recruits its participants and what the early returns look like.

The trial aims for 180 volunteers aged sixty to eighty-five with systolic pressure at or above 130. People with major stroke history or dementia are excluded. Brain scans then follow the volunteers for two years. Recruitment mixes hospital databases, online sources, referrals, and community outreach. From late 2022 through 2023, 718 people responded, and the team tracked how each channel performed through consent and randomization. The paper doubles as a playbook for prevention-trial recruitment.
pmc-11715867:
Takashi Kudo and Shoshin Akamine develop a blood test route for Alzheimer's disease based on vesicles shed by neurons. Tiny extracellular vesicles from the brain drift into the blood, and catching the neuron-born ones could give a window on disease. The team first grew neurons from stem cells to learn the surface marks of their vesicles.

In their 2025 paper, one mark, APLP1, stood out as neuron-specific. Blood plasma held vesicles that carried it, sorted first by size and then pulled out with an antibody. Vesicles from patients with Alzheimer's disease were read with a digital assay. Their tau levels tracked the known markers in spinal fluid, a sign the blood route may serve as a biomarker.
pmc-11715967:
Changzheng Yuan and six co-authors search tears for protein signs of memory loss and dementia, in this 2025 exploratory study. Tears are easy to collect without needles and may reflect changes in the brain. The team compared tear proteins from older adults with dementia, mild impairment, or normal thinking, matched by age, sex, and schooling.

Seventy tear proteins differed between the dementia group and healthy controls, and all pointed the same way in the mild impairment group. The strongest signals clustered in pathways for nerve cell growth and protein building. Adding thirteen of the proteins to a standard risk model sharply improved its accuracy at flagging dementia. The authors stress the work is early, but tears could one day offer a painless screening sample.
pmc-11716167:
A brain-scan index that tracks water flow along the drainage sleeves around blood vessels has been floated as a marker of small-vessel dementia. Xiaodan Liu and co-authors put it through a formal validation in this 2025 study. They drew on five hundred and seventy-eight participants across seven sites of a national consortium built for exactly this purpose.

Each person received the scan plus repeated tests of memory, general cognition, and executive skill. The index was computed by a fixed pipeline and set beside two rival white-matter measures of damage. Validation here means showing the marker tracks the disease it claims to track, across sites and scanners, which is the bar regulators and trial designers require. The paper reports the consortium's test of whether this drainage-based number earns a place among dementia biomarkers.
pmc-11716267:
Polina Shichkova and co-authors published this study in two thousand twenty-five on how aging changes proteins in blood and spinal fluid. Age is the top risk factor for Alzheimer's disease, yet healthy aging and disease aging are hard to tell apart.

The team took paired blood and spinal fluid samples from ninety-three people at Johns Hopkins clinics, both young adults and healthy older adults. A mass spectrometry method counted tens of thousands of protein pieces in each fluid. The reads covered paths tied to amyloid, tau, nerve harm, swelling, and iron damage. The team paid close heed to protein pieces cut or joined in ways that mark disease steps. Their map gives a base line of normal aging that later disease studies can measure against.
pmc-11716467:
Raul Vintimilla published a study in 2025 on white matter damage, dementia risk scores, and thinking in Mexican American elders. Both brain white matter spots and the CAIDE risk score are known to affect cognition, but their joint role in this group was unclear. The analysis covered one hundred and twelve cognitively normal elders from a brain aging study, split by a risk score cutoff.

The high-risk group was older, less educated, and scored lower on every thinking test. White matter load tracked worse memory, executive skill, and processing speed. The risk score alone tracked no test directly, yet it partly carried the white matter effect on two skills. The author calls for follow-up on whether this pattern forecasts decline.
pmc-11716567:
Wiesje Pelkmans and co-authors linked fluid biomarker patterns to brain volume changes in people with no symptoms but early Alzheimer changes, in work published in 2025. The catalog byline ends one name earlier than the head byline, so team framing is used. More than six hundred adults had spinal fluid tests and repeat brain scans over about three and a half years.

Six marker patterns were extracted from the fluid panel. A pattern of pure amyloid change tied to wide volume loss and faster decline. A star cell pattern tied to volume gains in some regions yet faster decline when amyloid was present. A mixed tau and injury pattern tied to shrinkage in front and side regions. The authors say several cell processes drive early brain change at once.
pmc-11716667:
Reem Neal, Zhiyi Yang, and Ihab Hajjar hunt early Alzheimer's signals in 2025 in spinal fluid. Most protein studies focus on late disease, yet the silent preclinical stage may be the best window to intervene. The team measures 276 proteins tied to nerve injury, vessel function, and metabolism in 354 study participants.

Comparing people by a spinal fluid marker ratio that flags Alzheimer's risk, they find hub proteins linked to disease markers and clinical traits. Six key genes differ by risk status, and several are adhesion proteins that help cells stick and signal. The authors argue these early protein patterns could guide intervention before symptoms.
pmc-11716767:
Paulina Orellana and co-authors hunt blood marks in 2025 that split two dementias which mimic each other. Alzheimer disease and frontotemporal dementia ask for different care, and blood tests for either are scarce. Tiny parcels shed by cells into blood carry small RNAs whose levels shift with disease.

Plasma parcels came from twenty-five healthy controls, twenty-five Alzheimer patients, and ten frontotemporal patients in Chile, the team reports. Their small RNAs were read and fed to learning models that sort the groups. Marks found in parcels could one day make the split with a simple blood draw. That would spare families the long, costly road of scans and spinal taps, and start the right care sooner.
pmc-11716867:
Ya-nan Ou, Lan Tan, and Jin-Tai Yu published a study in 2025 on heart and vessel health and the later risk of dementia. Evidence on single heart conditions has been patchy, so the team took a broad view in the UK Biobank. They tested both a standard heart-risk score and a long list of vessel diseases against several kinds of dementia.

More than four hundred thirty thousand dementia-free adults were followed for about nine years, during which nearly five thousand developed dementia. Higher heart-risk scores went with higher risk across the dementia spectrum. The high-risk group carried the heaviest burden, above all for vascular dementia. The results strengthen the case for guarding heart health to protect the brain.
pmc-11716967:
Yue Cai and co-authors use a 2025 imaging study to test a puzzle about schooling and Alzheimer's disease. Past work found that people with more schooling tend to show less brain damage at one point in time. Far less was known about how damage builds up over time.

The team drew on a large national cohort and split people by years of schooling around a middle value of sixteen years. Brain scans tracked amyloid and tau, the two proteins that mark the disease. Follow-up scans let them watch tau spread in each group. Comparing the paths side by side helps explain why schooling can look protective at first yet pair with faster change later.
pmc-11717367:
Colin Ihrig and co-authors test in 2024 whether blocking an enzyme can save erection function in mice with high cholesterol. The state grows more common as obesity and heart disease rise. A drug that blocks the enzyme is tested in a model of vessel harm from cholesterol.

Mice split into three groups, with two groups given a virus trick plus a fatty diet for eighteen weeks. One treated group got daily shots of the blocker, while others got plain shots. Pressure tests and tissue bath checks grade function at the end. Marker checks test whether cell cleanup paths explain any gain, and the title reports they do not.
pmc-11720167:
Vanmaele and co-authors follow mood and life quality in patients whose abdominal aortic swelling nears the size where surgery is advised. Such patients live under watch for years, and the toll of that watch was poorly known. Their study, published in 2024, mails standard surveys to 124 patients at the start and after one and two years, or until surgery or death.

On average, life quality, anxiety, and depression held steady over time. Patients who reached surgery saw anxiety and depression scores fall by amounts patients and doctors would notice. Those with only primary schooling fared worse on mood scores. Having a close relative with the same condition raised the risk of clinical anxiety. The authors say support should target those subgroups during the long watch.
pmc-11723567:
Julian Morano and Samer Kholoki report the care of a 68-year-old woman whose blood pressure stays high despite full drug care in a 2024 case paper. The state, called resistant hypertension, is set apart from plain missed doses: this patient took her drugs and kept the lifestyle rules, yet her day-long reads stayed up. Her exam was steady and her labs plain save one kidney gauge on the low side.

The report walks through the choices made at each step and why. The authors stress that such cases call for steady checks and fine tuning over time, since genes, habits, and other ills tangle the cause.
pmc-11724767:
Mirjana Ždraljević and co-authors report a rare pair of ills in a new mother and review past cases. The report appeared in 2024. One ill harms blood, liver, and platelets in late pregnancy. The other swells the brain for a short time and can be reversed with care.

The patient was a healthy woman aged thirty-one in her late term. High blood pressure led to an urgent birth by surgery. Two days later she had a harsh headache, blurred sight, and fits. Brain scans fit the brain ill, and care for pressure and swelling followed. A later scan was clear, and she left with no lasting harm. The review adds thirty past cases.
pmc-11726767:
Devaraja and co-authors retrace how cancer immunotherapy grew from a bacterial toxin in the 1890s to the first approved therapeutic vaccine. Their 2024 historical review opens with reports of tumors shrinking after feverish infections, the observation behind Coley's toxin, the field's first deliberate immune treatment. Head and neck cancer serves as the running example.

The tour passes the immune surveillance theory, the discovery of T cells and dendritic cells, tumor antigens, and the tumor microenvironment. BCG's anti-tumor use and Melacine, the first engineered therapeutic vaccine, mark the middle chapters. Immunoediting and immunophenotyping theories frame the modern era, ending with Provenge, the first FDA-approved therapeutic vaccine. The authors argue today's hot field stands on a century of near-forgotten work.
pmc-11726867:
Heba Elkhodary and co-authors present a 2024 study of weight and tooth decay in Saudi kindergarten children. The team examined 347 children in Jeddah during the early years of the national Vision 2030 health push. Each child's height and weight were measured, and dentists counted decayed, missing, and filled baby teeth.

About fifteen percent of the children were obese and another ten percent overweight, with no clear gap between public and private schools. Tooth decay was widespread, averaging nearly three affected teeth per child, and public kindergarten children fared significantly worse. Surprisingly, heavier children did not show more decay. The authors say current initiatives are not yet bending either curve and call for sharper, targeted programs.
pmc-11726967:
Catalin Pestrea and co-authors track heart health after a new style of pacemaker lead is placed, in a study from 2024. The style, conduction system pacing, taps the heart's own wiring, so beats stay in step. Old styles can weaken the heart over time in a small share of cases.

The team enrolled 128 patients whose pump strength was fair or good at the start. Two lead sites were used, with most patients on the left bundle branch area kind. After near two years, pump strength rose a bit and chamber sizes shrank in a good way. Right side work got better too. Just three patients met the mark for pacing-caused weakness. Both lead sites did as well, which the team reads as a shield for the whole heart.
pmc-11727567:
Leónides Fernández and co-authors review the safety of probiotics for pregnant and nursing women in a 2024 paper. Probiotics are live germs sold to aid health, and many women use them for minor or major issues in pregnancy. Yet most products were never tested in this group, so claims of benefit and safety often rest on thin ground.

Trials in pregnant and nursing women mostly find the products well tolerated and safe, though side effects can occur. The authors say staff who care for these women should know what is being used and watch how it works. They urge that advice rest on solid proof. Only products made for the exact need, and tested in this group, should be advised.
pmc-11727767:
Charlotte Nichol and co-authors ask why so few patients in their eighties take up cardiac rehabilitation. Rehab after heart care lifts function and cuts repeat hospital stays. Yet uptake in the United Kingdom sits near half of those offered it. Their 2024 study speaks with 20 patients who have aortic stenosis, a stiff heart valve. The patients came from one large health trust in the North East of England.

Four themes ran through the talks. Patients weighed what rehab was for, how and where it was given, and what exercise might do. Travel and life changes at home also shaped their choice. Clear offers, plain accounts of the gain, and family support helped people say yes. The team urges programs shaped to older patients' real lives.
pmc-11728167:
Chenlong Fan and four co-authors build a camera-and-learning system that estimates how many maize kernels break during harvest. Their 2024 study addresses a costly gap: broken kernels invite fungal damage, yet crews lack a fast way to measure breakage as machines run. The team photographed kernels with high moisture and pulled seven shape features from each.

Two models were trained, one to sort kernels as broken or whole and one to predict each kind's weight. The sorting model passed ninety-five percent accuracy. Weight models from two algorithms tracked true weights closely. Predicted and real broken rates lined up in a strong straight relation. The authors offer the setup as an objective, on-line gauge for gentler harvesting.
pmc-11728467:
A research team reviewed what is known about hepatitis E infection in people with beta-thalassemia, in this 2024 paper. Thalassemia is an inherited blood disorder treated with frequent transfusions, which can carry the hepatitis E virus. For most people the infection passes, but in thalassemia patients it can turn chronic and dangerous.

Reported infection rates vary widely by country. Risk climbs with age, with where a patient lives, and with the total volume of blood received over years of care. Several countries now screen donated blood for the virus, either for everyone or for high-risk groups. The authors call for close watching of thalassemia patients and antibody checks, so infections are caught and treated early.
pmc-11728667:
Exosomes and other tiny cell-made particles are promising medicines, but batches can hide stray proteins and look-alike particles.
