Hirotaka Nishimura and co-authors test in 2024 whether a combined method, size-exclusion chromatography with multi-angle light scattering, can police that quality. The setup sorts particles by size, then reads their size and amount with scattered light.

The method separated particles more sharply than two rival sizing tools and matched their accuracy on standard beads. Paired with ultraviolet detection, it also measured dissolved protein impurities. Protein analysis of the sorted fractions found distinct markers for true vesicles and for fat particles. The authors propose it as a quality check for therapeutic batches.
pmc-11728767:
Karolina Przepiórska-Drońska and co-authors test whether a common sunscreen filter harms the developing brain across generations, published in 2024. The chemical, benzophenone-3, is used in personal care products and as a stabilizer. It is suspected of disrupting hormones, yet its effects on brain growth over more than one generation were little studied.

The team exposed mother mice to levels like those found in the environment. They then checked markers of cell damage and cell death in two brain regions, in both the first and second generations. Effects differed by sex and by region. Signs of death through an external cell pathway rose most, and effects were stronger in the first generation than the second.
pmc-11731667:
Meiyanti and co-authors review tuberculosis care outcomes in one Indonesian province in this 2024 study. Beating the lung disease takes months of steady drug taking, and success cuts its spread. The team uses national registry data for patients treated in one year.

More than two thousand patients were tracked, and just over nine in ten finished care cured or complete. Older age and heavy germ loads in spit tests linked to worse outcomes. Patients without HIV and those found by symptoms rather than lab tests did better. Longer courses, past three months, linked strongly to success. The authors urge support programs that keep patients on their full course.
pmc-11736367:
Ritika Ritika and co-authors add turmeric's curcumin to buffalo embryos growing in the lab, in a 2024 paper. Buffalo supply about half of India's milk, but summer heat pushes their body temperature high enough to spawn damaging oxygen radicals and spoil reproduction. Curcumin is an antioxidant that might shield young embryos.

Embryos were produced in vitro under normal warmth and under heat stress, with no curcumin or two doses of it in the culture. The study tracked how many embryos developed well and how key genes behaved in each condition. The setup tests whether a cheap plant compound can rescue embryo quality when the mercury rises, a practical question for dairy breeding in a warming climate.
pmc-11744467:
Richard E Field wrote an editorial in 2025 on levels of evidence in medical research. He recalls advice that an editor should ask if a paper brings new facts and if it can guide care. Strength of proof is the key test for the second question.

Field traces grading systems from a 1979 Canadian task force to later ranked lists. He notes that one database of such lists now holds close to two hundred entries. Reviews and pooled studies tend to draw the most cites in his journal. He asks if they in fact change how surgeons treat hip cases.
pmc-11748067:
Christoph Schindler and colleagues run a first-in-human phase one study of a multi-target gene therapy for diabetic foot ulcers. Their 2024 open-label dose-finding study uses bacteria engineered to produce three healing factors.

Sixteen patients aged in their fifties to eighties with non-healing ulcers joined four dose cohorts. Treatment ranged from a single low dose to repeated higher doses three times weekly for six weeks. A standard dose-escalation scheme monitored safety, tolerability, and efficacy in each cohort. The therapy demonstrated a favourable early profile in the reported results. The study aimed to judge safety, wound healing, quality of life, and to select a recommended dose for phase two testing.
pmc-11748267:
Meng Nie and Zeping Hu review how metabolism sustains drug-tolerant persister cells in cancer in 2024. These rare, slow-growing cells enter a reversible quiet state that lets them survive the first rounds of therapy, then later seed relapse and full resistance.

Persisters have been found across many cancer types and treatments. While their gene-control rewiring is well described, their metabolic adaptations are less charted. One defence stands out: the enzyme ALDH clears toxic reactive oxygen species, and blocking it lets the toxins build up and damage DNA. The authors survey the metabolic wiring of persisters and the weak points it may expose for future combination therapies.
pmc-11784867:
Akira Matsui and Emilio Ferrara survey how social scientists use word embeddings, in a 2024 review paper. Word embeddings turn text into compact number vectors that capture meaning, and the method has spread far beyond computer science. No single overview covered its use across social science fields.

The authors gather recent studies that mine human behavior with embeddings and sort them into a taxonomy. The map shows what questions each field asks with the tool and which techniques dominate. They aim to give newcomers a concise but complete picture of the trend. The survey doubles as a guide for scholars planning embedding-based research on society.
pmc-11788367:
Tianze Hou and co-authors study a plant pigment under fake low gravity in a study listed in 2025. Anthocyanin gives leaves color and adds to food and health value. The plant is Dendrobium catenatum, an orchid used for food and medicine. Long space flights will need plants that stay useful in changed gravity.

Clones grown for 20 days under simulated low gravity held more anthocyanin than clones in normal gravity. Gene work pointed to one gene, DcaWRKY2, as a likely control switch. When the team silenced that gene, leaf pigment rose and related pigment genes grew more active. Gravity seems to shape that control.
pmc-11790667:
Shuiping Ni leads a team that improves a light net for tomato leaf disease. Their work deals with ShuffleNetV2, a small deep learning model. Fast, true disease spotting is key for tomato yield.

Large models are sharp but too heavy for edge devices. Their trick builds many shallow models at varied depths. A joined feature map blends maps from all those models. A light convolution layer then pulls more useful traits. The joined model teaches the small model in a dynamic way. That keeps key traits while the model stays light.
pmc-11799267:
Quitting smoking is hard, and intensive programs help, but where they run may matter. The authors test whether Denmark's six-week Gold Standard Program works as well outdoors in nature as in the usual clinic setting. Their feasibility study, published in 2024, follows 81 participants in the nature setting. It also covers a large national group of 56,480 in the standard setting, all registered in the Danish STOPbase from 2018 to 2023. Everyone received the same intensive program.

Six months after the program, 43 percent of the nature group had quit, against 37 percent in the standard setting, a gap that was not statistically significant. Quit rates at the end of the six weeks, plus compliance and satisfaction, were also similar in both settings. The authors conclude that running the program in nature is feasible in real life and appears to give results much like the standard setting.
pmc-11801267:
Judit Tomsen-Melero leads a large team packaging a missing enzyme into targeted nanoliposomes for Fabry disease. Patients lack working alpha-galactosidase A, so fatty material accumulates across organs, and standard enzyme infusions distribute poorly and never reach the brain. Their formulation aims a recombinant enzyme at the tissues that need it.

In a Fabry mouse model, the nanoformulation cleared more of the stored material than free enzyme at the same task, including deposits in the brain. That reach into the central nervous system addresses one of replacement therapy's biggest blind spots. European regulators have granted the product orphan drug designation. The authors present it as a platform for other lysosomal storage disorders with brain involvement.
pmc-11810567:
Yongke Zhang and co-authors published a case report, with the head dated 2024, on managing a rare twin blood disorder in two shared-placenta pregnancies. In this condition one twin turns anemic while the other grows overloaded with blood. The first case was confirmed at stage three after a cesarean birth at thirty-three weeks. The second was caught at stage two, early at eighteen weeks.

The early case received laser surgery inside the womb to seal linking vessels. Scans then tracked blood speeds in both twins, with one twin growing slower than its sibling. Both newborns developed normally after an early spontaneous birth. The authors stress matching treatment to each case's stage and course.
pmc-11821967:
Mengmeng Shi and ten co-authors map, in work published in 2024, a family of scaffold-cutting genes in alfalfa and how they answer salt and drought. The cutters trim the cell's inner frame, which shapes growth and stress replies. Alfalfa, a top feed crop, had not had its set charted.

Nine such genes were found, spread on five strands and sorted into four kin groups with like shapes. Their start zones carry cues for hormones, defence, and stress. Most switch on by organ, and most rose more than twofold under salt or drought, four of them sharply. The team reads them as stress guards and offers the map for crop work.
pmc-11831567:
A dentist numbing the palate needs to find one small hole in the bone: the greater palatine foramen. Alma Voljevica and co-authors measure its position in skulls from Bosnia and Herzegovina. Using fine calipers on dry skulls, they recorded the foramen's distance from the midline suture, the incisive fossa, and the back edge of the palate. Both sides of each skull were measured.

The foramen sits about sixteen millimeters from the midline and about forty from the incisive fossa. It lies only a few millimeters ahead of the palate's rear border. In nearly three quarters of skulls, it aligned with the third molar. Population-specific numbers like these steady the hand of any clinician aiming an injection, and they refine anatomy teaching for the region.
pmc-11832467:
Elizabeth Edrich and co-authors aimed drug-like chains straight at a deadly fungus's power plants, in a study published in 2024. Cryptococcus neoformans causes meningitis in people with weak immunity, and drug resistance is rising. The fungus leans on an alternative oxidase enzyme for stress survival that human cells lack. The team modified a natural compound that blocks that enzyme, tethering it to a mitochondria-seeking group with alkyl chains of differing length.

Two derivatives blocked the target enzyme and a second respiratory complex in the lab, and both crushed the fungus's growth and survival. Chain length decided how each killed, steering the mode of cell death. Targeted chains look like a new antifungal class in the making.
pmc-11847667:
Wabi Temesgen Atinafu and Kefyalew Naniye Tilahun survey diet adherence among diabetic patients in Addis Ababa in this paper, published in 2024. Diet control is central to type 2 diabetes care, yet adherence in Ethiopia is poorly documented. Four hospitals joined the study in mid 2024. Systematic sampling recruited 420 patients.

Questionnaires measured how closely patients followed dietary advice. Analysis searched for traits linked with good or poor adherence. Results were summarized with standard statistical reporting and odds ratios. Income, education, and support often decide whether advice is followable. Hospital based data miss patients who never reach care, a limit to keep in mind. The findings guide counseling and food support in urban clinics.
pmc-11935667:
A study by de Frutos and co-authors, published in 2024, describes children with a weakened, stretched heart muscle caused by one gene. Changes in that gene are the most common inherited cause of this disease in children, yet no study had charted the condition itself. The team gathered records for 44 young patients across many centers. The median age at diagnosis was about half a year. Slightly more than half were boys.

They mapped where in the gene each child's change fell and how the illness unfolded. They hunted for signs that predict a poor course. A clear picture of this disease helps doctors counsel families at diagnosis. It may also guide how closely each child is watched and when stronger treatment starts. The study, backed by a European initiative, gives the condition its first full portrait.
pmc-11970167:
Wangbing Xu and co-authors probe two growth factors that drive scarring in spinal discs. Disc decay stiffens the soft core as scar matrix builds. Both factors are known scar promoters in other tissues. The team read their levels in human disc tissue at unlike decay stages and in lab grown disc cells.

Both factors ran high in late stage decay and rose together. Raising either one lifted the other, plus scar collagens, and suppressed the core's healthy proteins. Silencing either cut its partner and the scar output. The authors say breaking the pair's mutual boost could slow disc scarring, a target worth drug hunting.
pmc-12082667:
I Chukwu and five co-authors count what emergency bowel surgery costs Nigerian families in a 2024 study. In young children, one loop of bowel can telescope into another, blocking it. Surgery saves the child, but families pay out of pocket in a system where insurance is rare and late arrival is common.

The team followed seventy-eight children treated at one teaching hospital over four years. Nearly all needed operations, some twice. Only four families held national insurance; they arrived days sooner than the rest. The typical uninsured bill topped ten percent of the national yearly income per person, the study's ruin threshold. The authors frame such bills as a policy emergency.
pmc-12171967:
Amirhossein Alirezaie, Habibeh Ahmadipour, and Mina Mobasher grade a medical ethics course through students' eyes, in a 2024 study. Ethics teaching aims to keep the human side of medicine alive as schools try varied formats. The authors use a four-part evaluation model that judges a program's setting, inputs, delivery, and results.

They surveyed 136 senior medical students at an Iranian university with a tailored questionnaire. Results scored highest: students felt the course conveyed ethical ideas and deepened understanding. Inputs scored lowest, pointing at materials and resources. The authors urge better alignment with cultural norms and stronger support for student engagement. The study gives curriculum committees a map of where a valued course still leaks.
pmc-12331167:
Torres and colleagues published in twenty twenty-four a lab study of debris pushed out of tooth roots during root canal work. Material extruded past the root tip can cause pain and slow healing. Before shaping a canal, dentists carve a glide path with a starter file. The team compared three glide path files in curved molar roots. Twenty-four extracted human roots were split into three groups. Roots sat in gel-filled tubes that were weighed before and after.

All three files extruded some debris through the root tip. The WaveOne Gold Glider extruded the least by a clear margin. The R-Pilot file came next, and the hand file extruded most. Differences between groups were statistically significant in their tests. The authors suggest powered glider files may reduce postoperative problems. The bench setup cannot prove clinical benefit, but it ranks the tools.
pmc-12381767:
Neri Niccolai, Edoardo Morandi, and Andrea Bernini published a simulation study in two thousand twenty-four on long-range electric effects inside proteins. Proteins must find their partners in crowded cells without random luck. The authors propose that surface charges, arranged in clusters, broadcast electromagnetic signals.

Molecular dynamics simulations on two very different proteins, small human ubiquitin and a large insect enzyme, tracked charged side chains moving in concert. Their motions create charge proximities that could guide recognition at a distance. The authors frame protein electrodynamics as a lens on long-range interaction. They suggest the findings could steer design of proteins with programmed recognition patterns.
pmc-12384267:
Suicide attempts among older adults are a grave concern in South Korea. Hye Jung Jun and Jun Hee Jang dig into a national health survey from twenty twenty-one to find what raises the risk. Their sample covered seventy-three thousand three hundred and twenty-six older adults living in the community. About zero point three percent reported a suicide attempt.

Thoughts of suicide stood out as the strongest factor, raising the odds more than fifteen-fold. Depression raised them about three-fold, and low life satisfaction about two-fold. Schooling and region mattered too, with more schooling linked to lower odds. The authors call for screening that catches depression and suicidal thoughts early, plus nursing care that lifts life satisfaction in older adults.
pmc-12453567:
Kiersten Fullem and seven co-authors describe two new bacterial species found on watermelon leaves in Florida that showed leaf spot disease. Their paper appeared in two thousand twenty-four. Three fluorescent strains were isolated from the sick foliage. Sorting them took a full battery of lab and genome tests.

Phenotype checks covered classic biochemical traits and whether the strains sicken watermelon and squash seedlings. Genome trees placed the isolates in two separate branches of the Pseudomonas genus. Similarity scores against all known relatives fell well below the species cutoff. Other ID systems, from chemical profiling to mass spectra, also failed to name them. The combined evidence says the strains are two species new to science. They are named for Florida and for their watermelon host.
pmc-12659067:
Chen Liu and six co-authors report a 2025 study on weight gain and the timing of puberty in girls in Shanghai, China. Puberty has been starting earlier in many countries, and early starts carry health and mood risks later. Extra body fat is one factor that can be changed, yet most past work took a single snapshot rather than tracking girls over time.

The team followed just over one thousand first-grade girls, checking their weight, waist size, and development each year. Girls who were heavy before puberty faced a higher risk of early development, and steady or fast gains in weight or waist size raised the risk further. Girls whose measures rose slowly had the lowest risk. The authors say that watching weight paths over years, not single readings, gives the best warning of early puberty.
pmc-12659267:
Phuong Nguyen and co-authors optimize helicopter base placement for Icelandic emergency care in a 2025 study. Total time to hospital, not just response time, decides outcomes for the worst injuries. Iceland's spread-out population already leans on fixed-wing air ambulances, and helicopters could serve spots far from airports.

Models weighed three transport modes and candidate second bases atop the existing network. Two towns emerged as contenders, with similar coverage. Which one wins depends on the destination rule: one shines if everyone flies to the capital's hospital, the other if patients go to the nearest hospital. The method, the authors note, travels well to other countries with hard geography.
pmc-12660867:
Dalia Sanchez, Analí Sulca, and Liz Pacheco-Pumaleque test whether strong leadership pushes firms toward greener, more digital business models, in a 2025 study. Companies face twin pressures: cut waste through circular practices and adopt new technology such as artificial intelligence. The authors ask if the person at the top is the lever.

They surveyed 146 companies in metropolitan Lima and modeled the answers statistically. Leadership, defined as mobilizing a firm toward strategic change, promoted the adoption of circular practices. It also drove uptake of AI solutions by fostering adaptability and openness. Decisiveness, a shared vision, and skill at handling resistance stood out. The findings argue that model change starts with who leads, not just with budgets or rules.
pmc-12660967:
Yuncheng Bai and co-authors test whether blocking a calcium gate helps cells clear a clumping protein tied to Parkinson's disease. Their 2025 study uses a toxin-treated rat cell line that mimics the disease. The toxin raised the gate's levels, cut cell survival, and piled up the harmful form of the protein.

Silencing the gate reversed each of those effects, the team reports. A drug blocker of the same gate did much the same. Cell cleanup flow, stalled by the toxin, ran again, and key markers of the cleanup path returned toward normal. Extra protein was broken down faster as a result. The gate thus looks like a drug target worth chasing for this disease.
pmc-12661667:
Oyun-Erdene Batgerel, Melda Akkitap, and Rafat Sasany test how well senior dental students spot tooth decay on panoramic X-rays, with and without AI help. Finding decay between teeth early guides treatment and prevention. One hundred thirty-two students in their fourth and fifth years at a Turkish university took part.

Each student read sixty images twice, first alone and then with software that boxes suspect areas and gives odds. Fifth years beat fourth years overall. Deep decay reaching the pulp was spotted most often, while shallow enamel decay was mostly missed. The AI system itself reached about ninety percent accuracy, well above both student groups. The authors see the tool as a strong teaching and clinic aid.
pmc-12661767:
Mengting Wang and co-authors rank immune drugs for advanced stomach cancer in a 2025 analysis. The drugs block a brake on immune cells called PD-1, freeing them to attack the tumor. Several such drugs are used for stomach and junction cancers that cannot be cut out or have come back. No trial has tested them against each other directly.

The team pooled nineteen trials with close to ninety-five hundred patients, using a network method that links drugs through shared rivals. One drug alone, nivolumab, ranked first for survival and tumor response, but worst for severe side effects. Drug plus chemo pairs beat control care and did not raise severe harm. A distinct drug alone proved safest but weakest. The authors advise chemo plus immune therapy first, with nivolumab pairs giving the best balance.
pmc-12663267:
Clare Webster and co-authors published this data paper in 2025. It presents SwissRad10, a set of maps that give the light reaching the ground across Switzerland, hour by hour for a full year. Each cell of the map spans ten meters. The maps count both direct sun and soft sky light, and they are built from laser scans so fine that the shade of each tree is cast.

Forest plots come in two forms, with leaves on and with leaves off, and bare-ground values are given as well. Light at ground level shapes where plants and animals can live, how snow melts, and how forests trade carbon and water. The team offers the set as a base for ecology and land work across the country.
pmc-12663367:
Tan and seven co-authors ferment pumpkin juice with a mix of yeast and bacteria to boost its health value, in a study from twenty twenty-five. Pumpkin juice is rich but plain, with room to improve flavor and nutrients. The mix pairs one yeast with two milk bacteria used in yogurt. Together they turn sugars into new acids, scents, and active compounds.

The fermented juice held high counts of live microbes after brewing. Vitamin C, plant pigments, and protective compounds all rose versus plain juice. New fruity and floral scent compounds gave it a richer aroma. Color stayed nearly the same, and texture pleased tasters most among test batches. Sensory panels gave the mixed ferment the top score overall.
pmc-12663567:
Sebastiano Vaccarella and co-authors build tumor organoids from womb cancer patients to test drug response, in a study from two thousand twenty-five. Womb cancer rates and deaths have climbed over the last decade. The mini-tumors grown in the lab matched their source cancers in looks, gene faults, and activity patterns.

Organoid responses to standard and targeted drugs matched the patients' own responses, guided by each tumor's drug-sensitive gene faults. Matched support cells from the tumor's surroundings were also grown and profiled. Unlike the organoids, those support cells barely responded and aged into an inflamed state under standard drugs. The platform pre-tests therapy on tumor and surroundings alike.
pmc-12664267:
Dai reports fast relief of depression with extra potassium in a single patient, in a case report from twenty twenty-five. Most drugs for depression act slowly, and they do not work the same way for all. A woman of thirty-two has mild anxiety that came on not long ago, and severe depression. She is given potassium ions, based on the idea that her body holds too little of them for its needs.

Her signs of illness clear fast and in full once the extra potassium starts. The report looks at how low potassium might link to depression. Too little of the ion, for the body's needs, may play a part in the core of the illness. One case cannot prove a treatment, no matter how good it looks. More care notes and group studies are needed to test the claim.
pmc-12670267:
Mohammed Kanan and eight co-authors surveyed care providers in Saudi Arabia in two thousand twenty-five about their confidence in managing chronic kidney disease. Kidney disease is rising there as diabetes and high blood pressure spread. Their survey ran for six months and drew three hundred ninety-one health workers, about half of them pharmacists.

Diabetes specialists showed by far the highest confidence in picking the right kidney care. They also scored highest on grasp of key drug classes used to slow kidney damage. Other groups scored lower on screening, diagnosis, and treatment points. The results show where training should focus so front-line staff can catch kidney disease early.
pmc-12683467:
Moving cell power parts into tissue as a cure for erection failure is reviewed by Caiyuzhu Wen and co-authors in work dated 2025. Standard pills fail or cause harsh effects for close to a third of patients. Faulty power parts, called mitochondria, drive much of the failure through low energy and cell death signals. The team searched three data banks across twenty-five years of work.

From a large first haul, fifty-eight key papers shaped the review. In animal models, moved power parts restored energy, cut damage signals, and improved blood flow in key tissue. New ways to free, carry, and place the parts are charted. Dose and safety gaps still block clinic use.
pmc-12691067:
Stoyan Kostov and co-authors review a rare cancer of a small gland near the birth canal in a 2025 paper. The cancer makes up a small share of cancers of the outer female parts. Since cases are so few, firm proof on best care is thin, and doctors borrow rules from kin cancers.

The review sums up how often the ill strikes, what its main forms look like, and how gene tests can help sort them. One form linked to a common virus tends to strike younger women and run a kinder course. Care plans are laid out by form. Clinicians who may see one case in a career get a full map in one place.
pmc-12693867:
Yejin Kang, Katherine Dillon, Danielle Levitt, and Arturo Figueroa test an amino acid supplement in people with type 2 diabetes in a 2025 trial. High blood sugar, both steady and spiking, stiffens arteries and harms their lining, raising heart risk. Sixteen middle aged and older patients took either the supplement, citrulline, or a placebo daily for four weeks.

The supplement group improved artery dilation, leg artery stiffness, aorta pressure, and fasting glucose compared with placebo. After a glucose drink, the same advantages appeared: better dilation, softer arteries, lower pressure and sugar. The authors conclude citrulline helps vessel function and glucose control in both chronic and acute high sugar states in this group.
pmc-12697267:
Wei Feng, Pingping He, Zhimin Wang, and Weishuai Li review ultrasound-burst microbubbles to treat heart reperfusion harm. Their review from twenty twenty-five covers a way to carry drugs to the heart. When blood flow comes back after a heart attack, it can harm the muscle yet more. Oxygen stress, inflammation, and failure of cell power units drive that harm.

Sound waves pop aimed microbubbles right at the heart. The pop, called cavitation, pushes drugs past walls of tiny vessels. Aim grows exact and more of each drug gets through. One path this way grows new blood vessels. A second calms a key alarm knot for inflammation. Drugs in use stay narrow in reach and raise safety doubts. This way aims for exact hits, not brute dose size.
pmc-12698067:
Huijuan Lu and co-authors report a boy whose rare kidney disorder wore the mask of another illness for years, in a 2025 case report. The disorder, type 1 Bartter syndrome, wastes salt through the kidneys. This child instead showed high salt levels and vast urine output, which pointed doctors toward a water balance disease.

Born early after excess fluid in the womb, he had low potassium and seizures by age nine. Gene tests found faults in a salt channel gene and cleared the water disease genes. A standard drug fixed his salts and urine output. He later stopped the drug on his own, and by seventeen his kidneys were scarred. The case warns against missed follow-up.
pmc-12698867:
Erlin Chen and co-authors build in this 2025 study a pocket test for an enzyme whose activity flags nerve disease. Acetylcholinesterase levels matter in disorders like Alzheimer's, and its blockers are candidate drugs. Their platform pairs a microneedle patch with iron-based nanozyme rods that mimic an enzyme and drive a color change.

The target enzyme's product switches the nanozyme off, so color fades in proportion to activity, read by a phone camera. The sensor proved keen and selective, with a very low detection limit and a range spanning five orders of size. It matched the standard lab method and served to screen a plant compound as a blocker. Clinics could run the test at the bedside.
pmc-12699867:
Laura Elisa Streck and co-authors track recovery in the first month after hip surgery, in a study published in 2025. Patients chose among three operations for worn hip joints: full replacement through the front, full replacement through the back, or resurfacing of the joint. Debate over which is best is heated, and early patient reports can inform the choice.

The study covered 207 hips in 199 patients treated from 2020 to 2022. Patients used a phone app to report pain, opioid use, walking, swelling, and wound drainage for thirty days. Nearly all had stopped opioids by day twenty. Scores for hip function rose sharply in all three groups, and pain, drug doses, and problems did not differ by approach. The authors say early recovery looks much alike across these operations.
pmc-12700367:
Lingling Wu, Weiwei Cai, Fei Wang, Yazhuo Wang, and Chang Wang surveyed obstetric nurses in China in two thousand twenty-five. The nurses care for women in pregnancy and birth, and many now also offer care through online services. The authors asked how a strong sense of work identity links to quality of work life.

Nurses came from thirty-three large hospitals in Anhui Province that run such online services. The study found that mental resilience, the ability to cope with strain, helped carry the link from identity to work life. Willingness to join the online services also shaped that path. The authors urge managers to support both resilience and willing participation.
pmc-12700667:
Five authors, led by Jun Jean Ong, revisit in 2025 the value of overseas training fellowships in child development and behavior care, seen from Malaysia. Such posts let young doctors learn new skills abroad and meet peers from other lands. Fellows from poorer countries often return with stronger leadership and go on to teach others at home.

Yet the path has real costs and hurdles, the authors note. Time away, money, and gaps in home services all shape what a fellow can bring back. The paper weighs these gains and strains for Malaysia. It asks how training abroad should fit the future of the field at home.
pmc-12700767:
Xiaohui Xie and co-authors report, in a 2025 case study, a rare thymus tumor that first showed up as swollen neck glands. Tumors of this type arise from hormone-like cells in the thymus and are uncommon. The patient presented with neck lymph node swelling as the main sign, which can point to many other causes first.

The authors stress that early notice and a team-based diagnostic path were key to finding the true source. Correctly locating the tumor opened the way to full surgical removal, the main hope of cure. The case adds a warning for doctors who see lone neck gland swelling: rare chest tumors belong on the list of possible causes.
pmc-12700967:
Robert Biney and seven co-authors shared a study in twenty twenty-five. It is about stigmasterol, a plant sterol found in every vegetable oil. They test it as a candidate antidepressant. Computational network analysis first mapped forty genes. At those genes, the compound's predicted targets meet the genes of depression. A handful of hubs stood out. They include AKT1 and the monoamine enzymes.

Docking simulations checked the fit of the compound. Then came the animal work. Mice given stigmasterol struggled less in two tests. Those were the standard swim and suspension despair tests. When the team blocked monoamine production or storage, the effect went away. That confirmed the predicted mechanism in an experimental way. The pipeline is the template here. Computation proposes, and animals dispose. The authors present a dietary molecule with a traced, testable antidepressant pathway.
pmc-12701067:
Xiren Zhou and co-authors present a computer model for finding hidden flaws under city roads, in a study published in 2025. Ground radar can picture what lies below the surface, but cracks and cavities are hard to mark: labels are scarce and edges are fuzzy. Radar traces also carry wave patterns that plain image tools ignore.

Their model extends a well-known image-cutting tool with a memory-like step that studies how waves change near a suspect spot. It first flags likely flaw areas by sight, then refines them using the wave evidence. In real-world tests it beat older methods, scoring above eighty-five percent, while needing very little training data. The system can run on its own or with light human guidance, cutting the effort of road checks.
pmc-12701567:
A 37-year-old man with an inherited skin-fragility disease needed a new kidney, a pairing surgeons rarely attempt because fragile skin heals badly and tubes threaten the airway. Sasho Dohchev and eight co-authors report his successful living-donor transplant in a 2025 case report from a resource-limited setting. A full team planned around the risks: numbing the spine with light sedation avoided airway tubes, and gentle handling protected the skin.

Surgery and recovery went smoothly, and the new kidney still worked a year later. The authors argue that careful planning and teamwork can make even very complex transplants possible where resources are thin.
pmc-12701867:
Denis Laloë and a large team compare the fluid left behind by cow embryos grown in the lab with fluid from embryos grown inside the cow, in a twenty twenty-five study. Lab-grown embryos are now more common than natural ones in cattle breeding, but their quality lags. The fluid an embryo grows in can hint at its health and sex. The team wanted to know what drives the mix of small chemicals in that fluid.

Embryos grown in the lab showed far less spread in their fluid chemistry than those grown in the cow. Stage and grade explained a fair share of the spread for natural embryos but almost none for lab ones. The authors say lab growth flattens the very differences that might help pick the best embryos.
pmc-12702267:
Jun Wu and eight co-authors profile blood chemistry in narcolepsy type one, a sleep disorder, focusing on its link with unhealthy blood fats. Their multi-center study was published in twenty twenty-five.

Forty-four patients and forty-four matched comparisons took sleep lab tests overnight and a nap test by day. Fasting blood was checked for the main fats and scanned broadly for small molecules. Patients showed higher total and harmful cholesterol and lower protective cholesterol than comparisons, even after adjustments. Certain chemical pathways, above all those around the amino acid arginine, differed between groups. The team split samples into discovery and validation sets to firm up the pattern. The signatures may help explain why this sleep disorder strains the heart.
pmc-12703267:
Canty, Gartner, Hoek, and Hefler scan in twenty twenty-five how countries regulate shops that sell smoked tobacco. Shop density and closeness to schools run higher in poorer areas, and easy access normalises smoking and undermines quitting. The team gathered laws, reports, and expert leads from every world health region to map what rules exist.

Many places set a minimum buying age and limit shop-window promotion, but few attack availability head-on. Some use licences with fees, caps on licence counts, or rules on shop type and distance from youth spaces. A very few places have ended tobacco retail outright. The authors urge licensing, caps, and distance limits at minimum, backed by monitoring and enforcement.
pmc-12704067:
Priyanka Madaan, Santosh Kumar Mishra, Jithangi Wanigasinghe, and Jitendra Kumar Sahu weigh how a new gene therapy for Duchenne muscular dystrophy should reach South Asia. Their 2025 commentary explains the disease: a faulty dystrophin gene causes progressive muscle weakness, loss of walking in the teens, and early death. No cure exists, so a one-shot gene therapy raised families' hopes worldwide.

Regulators first approved the therapy broadly, then narrowed it after two non-ambulatory patients died of acute liver failure, adding a boxed warning and limiting use to patients who can still walk. The authors review the therapy's current status and the region-specific hurdles: cost, diagnosis delays, and thin specialist infrastructure. Their aim is a realistic path forward for South Asian health systems.
pmc-12705267:
Wentong Lan and co-authors describe a rare gut defect found in an adult woman in a 2025 case report. She had faced gut bleeding for a month, and scans plus standard scopes found no clear source. A camera pill then showed a raised spot with active bleeding high in her small bowel.

A deep scope exam found three channels where one would be normal, a sign of a doubled tube in the jejunum. Surgeons cut out the short doubled stretch, and lab checks on the tissue proved the call. The case shows how deep scope work can pin down a birth defect that hides from scans for years.
pmc-12705767:
Lukas Urbanschitz and four co-authors ask whether surgical residents can learn to place spinal screws inside virtual reality as well as on plastic bones. Four neurosurgery residents with under a year of spine experience each placed screws from the first lumbar to the first sacral vertebra in three rounds. Everyone started after self-instruction alone.

Before round two, one pair trained conventionally on a synthetic bone model and the other in VR; for round three everyone had both. After self-instruction, forty-four percent of screws were misplaced, worst in the VR-bound pair. After training, errors collapsed: one misplaced screw in the VR group and none in the conventional group. The pilot suggests VR training is a legitimate alternative for this skill.
pmc-12706067:
Sheikh Shafaet Islam, Selim Hossain, Shariful Islam, and Rakibul Hasan design a radar beamforming scheme for spotting several moving targets in noisy settings, in a 2025 paper. Standard radar beams blur when interference is strong. The team first validated a simpler 16-element line array with a plain beamformer in calm conditions. Their hybrid design then merges two classic beamformers with diagonal loading on a large 30-by-30 phased array.

The simple setup reached about 90 percent detection accuracy but failed in noise. The hybrid array reached 99.29 percent accuracy in simulation while rejecting interference. The authors present the design as a step toward tracking many movers at once in cluttered airspace.
pmc-12706467:
Taito Kitano and Sayaka Yoshida compare two added antibiotics for staph infection of an artificial heart valve in 2025. Guidelines have backed adding rifampicin or gentamicin, but hard data on which works better are thin.

Using a large records network from US centers, the authors matched patients who got one drug but not the other. Death within one year was lower in the rifampicin group than in the gentamicin group. Other outcomes, such as return of infection or kidney failure, did not differ clearly. The authors urge caution, since records can hide key details such as treatment length.
pmc-12706967:
Tessa van der Meer and co-authors write a critical letter in a 2025 journal exchange. They challenge a study that used target trial emulation on heart-lung machine patients to compare liberal and strict blood transfusion thresholds. The original authors reported a small early survival edge for the liberal strategy.

The letter argues the groups were never truly comparable. Baseline severity scores and prior blood levels went unadjusted, and sicker patients likely landed in the strict group. Defining time zero at machine start, while assigning strategies later, added immortal time bias. Readers get a methods caution for emulation studies.
pmc-12707667:
Xiajing Chu and co-authors set out the plan for a review asking which eye scan features predict vision after membrane surgery in a 2025 protocol. An epiretinal membrane is a thin film that grows on the retina, blurring and warping sight, mostly in older adults. Surgery peels it away, but outcomes vary widely between patients.

Optical coherence tomography gives cross-section views of the retina before surgery. The review will pool studies testing whether features in those scans forecast the vision patients regain. A validated forecast would sharpen consent talks and target follow-up care. Publishing the protocol first locks the methods in public, guarding the review against cherry-picking later.
pmc-12708667:
Emmanuel Nyaaba and co-authors link social support to sleep and self-rated health among Ghanaian artisanal miners, in a 2025 study. Small-scale mining is hazardous work, yet little was known about how miners' support networks relate to how they sleep and feel. The team surveyed 664 miners and tested whether depression carries part of the association.

Miners with stronger support reported better health and somewhat better sleep, after accounting for background and health factors. Depression explained about a third of the support-sleep link but only a sliver of the support-health link. The authors argue that strengthening community support and treating depression could lift well-being in mining communities where formal health services are thin.
pmc-12708867:
He and a large team dope perovskite crystals with lanthanide ions to pin phase separation and enable dual-color lasing, in a study from twenty twenty-five. Mixed-halide perovskites can split into domains with different band gaps. Uncontrolled splitting harms devices, but pinned splitting may be useful. Vapor growth yields high-quality microplates across halogen pairs.

Each plate emits two stable light bands under steady excitation. Pairwise halogen mixes cover red, green, and blue regions together. Dual-wavelength lasers with high performance result from the plates. Domains are tens of nanometers wide with sharp boundaries. Calculations show doping drives splitting, then blocks ion drift to pin it. Stability and tuning improve at once.
pmc-12709767:
Predicting survival helps doctors plan care for advanced cancer of the food pipe. A seven-author team built a scoring chart for patients with locally advanced disease treated with strong chemotherapy and radiation, some also receiving immunotherapy. From CT scans of 200 patients at three centers, machine learning extracted image features from each tumor, which the team combined with standard clinical facts.

The image-based score alone predicted survival only modestly, though it did separate high-risk from low-risk patients in both the training and check groups, and in two outside cohorts as well. The combined chart beat models using either part alone and showed promise for guiding real decisions. Within the subgroup that also received immunotherapy, the image score still predicted survival. The authors see the tool as support for tailoring treatment plans to each patient's outlook.
pmc-12712067:
Jinjing Ma and four co-authors published a computer vision study in twenty twenty-five on reading facial expressions in real time without heavy computation. Existing recognizers are expensive to run and miss the subtle features that separate expressions. Their network, SPAYOLO, rebuilds the YOLOv8 detector around a new module mixing space and frequency information.

Three paths work together: multi-scale convolutions catch fine and mid-level facial changes, a Fourier path extracts high-frequency texture and micro-expression cues, and a gated attention step fuses the streams. Accuracy reached about seventy-one percent on one standard dataset and sixty-eight on another, at real-time cost. The authors pitch the design for live affective computing.
pmc-12713267:
Gianluca Villa and co-authors report how a blood purification membrane called Oxiris is actually used in intensive care units, drawing on a multicenter registry. The device filters inflammatory mediators and bacterial components from the blood of critically ill patients. Three patient clusters were tracked: kidney patients with inflammation after surgery, patients needing immune modulation alone, and abdominal sepsis patients needing both.

Four days after treatment began, observed death rates in all three groups ran far below the rates predicted by a standard severity score. Early death tracked instead with needing blood-pressure support drugs and with poor blood oxygen levels. The authors frame mediator removal as an emerging target in critical care and present the registry as real-world evidence of practice and outcomes.
pmc-12714267:
Amine Ben Safta and co-authors set out a trial protocol on gallbladder surgery in this 2025 article. Keyhole removal of the gallbladder is the standard cure for painful gallstones. Surgeons inflate the belly with gas to see inside, usually at a pressure of twelve to fourteen units, but that pressure may add to pain after surgery.

The trial will assign patients at random to a low pressure of eight units or the standard fourteen. Neither patients nor assessors will know which pressure was used. Pain six hours after surgery is the main measure, with later pain, sickness, stay length, and complications also tracked. Enrollment runs through the end of 2025 at one center. The authors say a win for low pressure would give surgeons a simple comfort gain.
pmc-12714767:
Yumi C Del Rey and co-authors test a new surface for dental implants in a paper from two thousand twenty-five. Titanium implants are strong and safe, but germs stick to them more easily than to ceramic, and infection is a main cause of implant failure. The team made a titanium surface coated with zirconium using an electric process that leaves tiny pores.

They compared the new surface with plain and acid-treated titanium worn in the mouth. The coated surface had moderate roughness, lower surface energy, and less wetting. Films of mouth germs grown on it held far fewer germs in total, with fewer harmful types and more harmless ones. The authors say such coatings could cut implant infection.
pmc-12715167:
Anne Melzer and co-authors pilot a text message program to help lung patients quit smoking, in work from 2025. People with chronic lung disease gain greatly from quitting, yet many are not ready to try. A gentle, proactive program could reach them where clinic offers fail.

Adults who smoke were enrolled whether or not they wanted to quit. Two-thirds got twelve weeks of motivational texts that tapered over time, plus phone help to reach treatment. The rest got a mailed offer of standard services. Of 697 people invited, 125 joined the trial. Main readouts were uptake and treatment use over six months. The pilot tests whether texting can start quit attempts at scale.
pmc-12716467:
Jihong Jiang and co-authors ask if a body that ages fast on paper also sags in blood pressure mid-surgery. Low pressure in big operations is common and tracks with harm post-care. A pace-of-aging score, built from plain body marks, sums years of wear. Their 2025 study pools just under one hundred and seventeen thousand adults from three big centers in east China.

Drops are counted when mean pressure sits past a set floor, with depth and span both scored. Fast aging links strong to those drops in the part of the sums shown, once key traits are weighed. The score is cheap and drawn from ward facts at hand. Such a flag could let teams prep fluids and drugs for the frail pre-cut, not scramble mid-case.
pmc-12716567:
Ahad Mahmud Khan and co-authors test a video panel for child pneumonia checks in this 2025 study. Breathing rate is a key sign when judging pneumonia in young children. Expert panels can read that rate from videos of chest movement.

Six trained doctors formed the panel and read videos from health sites in Bangladesh. Of 605 videos, most were judged readable with close agreement on the count. Agreement between readers ranged from high eighties to mid nineties in percent. Each reader matched the final panel call at a similar rate. Repeat reads by the same doctor agreed almost fully. A check against senior child doctors supported the method.
pmc-12717067:
Chordoma, a rare bone cancer, resists treatment partly because its driver protein, brachyury, has long resisted drug design. Shifaa Alshammari used AI-assisted screening to search a desert plant, Aizoon canariense, for a way in. Starting from the plant compound beta-sitosterol, the search produced a family of analogs, and one, AI-Ligand 2, bound the target most strongly.

Simulations showed the pairing stayed stable over 500 nanoseconds of molecular dynamics. Predicted drug-like properties looked workable, including gut absorption and blood-brain barrier crossing, with moderate predicted toxicity. Alshammari presents the compound as a candidate for lab validation, not yet a drug.
pmc-12717167:
Vallely, Weadick, Treacy, and O'Reilly surveyed sleep in breast cancer patients for this short report from twenty twenty-five. Earlier Irish work found insomnia twice as common in cancer patients as in the general public. Breast cancer itself predicted clinical insomnia. The team widened the lens to a larger group of patients with early-stage disease.

Three hundred fifteen patients completed a forty-item questionnaire. Over half said their sleep had changed since diagnosis. More than half met the bar for near-clinical or clinical insomnia. Two thirds agreed sleep should be part of cancer assessment. Yet only a third recalled ever being asked about sleep, and about a quarter felt their problems were handled well. The authors call the gap a target for care.
pmc-12717267:
Alexis Sullivan and co-authors read three decades of life from air filters in a 2025 study. DNA shed into the air by organisms, called eDNA, can reveal what lives in a place without seeing it. Past checks of whole ecosystems across all life forms were too costly and hard to attempt at scale.

Archived aerosol filters spanning thirty-four years yielded weekly traces for more than twenty-seven hundred genera. The air record matched classic monitoring on abundance shifts. It also showed a regional decline in variety tied to land use in a northern boreal system. The authors present airborne eDNA as a single frame for watching whole ecosystems over long spans.
pmc-12717467:
A large team in Norway reports field proof that salmon make vitamin D in sunlight in a 2025 paper. Fish were long thought to get the vitamin only from food, with plankton as the source up the food chain. Salmon are a rich food source of the vitamin, yet blood levels were little known.

Fish in open sea pens held much higher levels than fish raised indoors. Over eighteen months, levels rose and fell with day length. Indoor fish moved outside for 52 days on the same feed gained five times the body vitamin. The team warns that indoor farms may leave fish short of the vitamin.
pmc-12717767:
Min Yang and four co-authors test a tiny camera for teeth feared to have cracked roots, in a 2025 study. A vertical root fracture often ends in pulling the tooth, yet it is hard to confirm, and the usual three-dimensional scan can mislead.

The team examined 115 suspect teeth with a periodontal endoscope, a thin camera slipped along the gum line. Each tooth's plan, set before the camera by two specialists, was then re-set by what the camera saw. The camera cut needless root treatments by about forty percent and needless surgery by about two thirds, while lifting accuracy sharply. It caught about eighty-four percent of true fractures, confirmed at surgery or over a year of follow-up.
pmc-12718267:
Haoyun Mao and colleagues published a 2025 study asking whether low blood oxygen worsens kidney injury in sepsis. Sepsis often damages the kidneys. Low oxygen is common in these patients too. The team analyzed thousands of intensive care records. Mice experiments tested the mechanism directly.

Patients with lower oxygen looked sicker at first glance. Careful adjustment removed the independent link. Kidney markers matched that pattern. Mouse groups combined sepsis, low oxygen, or both. Tissue and protein measures tracked the injury. The combined evidence argues low oxygen is a warning sign. It may not itself drive the kidney damage.
pmc-12718367:
Zhongwei Yuan and seven co-authors study nutrient limits on plankton growth in the South Pacific in this 2025 paper. Phytoplankton are tiny drifting plants that anchor ocean food webs. Their growth can be capped by one nutrient or by several at once. Telling the two apart matters for models of ocean growth. The team ran twelve experiments on surface seawater drawn from across the subtropical South Pacific.

Each sample got a matrix of added nutrients, with the water strongly diluted to slow grazing and nutrient drawdown. Across the nutrient poor gyre, growth was capped by nitrogen alone, even though nitrate, phosphate, and iron all ran low. Along the eastern edge of the gyre, nitrogen and iron limited growth together or in sequence. There, growth responses varied from site to site. The authors say models need to handle this shifting mix to predict ocean growth well.
pmc-12718567:
Mahiro Sazawa and co-authors measured what happened when Japan restarted active promotion of the HPV vaccine in a 2025 study. Japan had paused its recommendation for eight years, and coverage fell below one percent, among the lowest in the world. In April 2022 the government resumed promotion and added a catch-up program.

Using registry data from one municipality, the team tracked vaccination across girls born from 2003 to 2011. The 2006 cohort reached the highest coverage by mid 2023, about one third for the first dose. A time series model showed first-dose rates jumped by about half right when promotion resumed. The trend after the jump stayed nearly flat. The study offers rare hard evidence that government recommendation itself drives vaccine uptake.
pmc-12720667:
Wenhui Qiu and co-authors review research on histone deacetylases, enzymes that steer gene activity, in the peritoneal fibrosis that can follow long-term peritoneal dialysis. This scarring of the belly lining can end dialysis by blocking fluid exchange. Most fibrosis work targets liver and kidney, leaving the peritoneum understudied.

The review covers how these enzymes and their inhibitors affect inflammation and scarring in the peritoneum. It sets out the enzymes' traits, their links with the extracellular matrix, and their part in whether fibrosis can roll back. Future study paths toward treatments are also weighed. The authors aim to give the field a firmer base for finding anti-fibrotic targets.
pmc-12721367:
Qianqian Chen and co-authors wrote a 2025 set of clinical guidelines from China on a gentler way to treat tumors of the digestive tract. Standard surgery removes whole organs or key valves in the gut, which cures the tumor but often leaves patients with lasting problems like reflux or poor digestion. The new approach aims to cure the disease while keeping the body's normal layout.

The method, called super minimally invasive surgery, works through scopes passed into the body rather than large cuts. The guidelines describe its routes and the cases each route suits. They come from China's digestive endoscopy society with an international committee. Shared standards help more hospitals adopt the approach safely and train surgeons the same way.
pmc-12721967:
Sadri and colleagues validated in 2025 a Persian version of a screening questionnaire for REM sleep behavior disorder. In this disorder, people act out dreams, and it often precedes diseases like Parkinson's. Their study enrolled patients and healthy controls at Tehran sleep centres. The translated questionnaire was checked for internal consistency and repeat reliability.

Scores were highly consistent, and a cutoff separated cases from non-cases with perfect sensitivity and strong specificity in their sample. The authors say the tool can improve first sleep assessments for Persian speakers. They recommend testing it in broader patient groups before wide use.
pmc-12722167:
Eight clinicians report an unusual rescue for severe bleeding during fibroid surgery in a case report from 2025. The patient was a woman with a two-year history of symptomatic uterine fibroids. During removal of a fibroid, heavy bleeding began deep in the pelvis from low-pressure vessels. Standard methods could not stop it, and the loss threatened her life.

The team packed the pelvis with surgical mops through the vagina, cutting bleeding sharply. A further mop pressed from the abdomen stopped it fully. The packs were removed after forty-eight hours, and she recovered without further problems. The authors present combined packing as a life-saving option for deep pelvic bleeding.
pmc-12722267:
Mohammad Nadi and six co-authors test, in a 2025 study, a clay and iron-mineral mix as a liner for low-level waste landfills. A safe liner must block water flow and hold its strength. It should also shield radiation. The team blended goethite, an iron mineral, into bentonite clay at shares from ten to fifty percent.

Lab measures, computer simulation, and database checks all pointed the same way. The blends blocked gamma rays better as the goethite share rose. Gains reached about a fifth to a quarter at the tested energies. More goethite halved cohesion but doubled the friction angle. Strength peaked at a thirty percent blend, while water flow rose with goethite share. The mix looks promising where radiation shielding matters most.
pmc-12722367:
Maria Arioli and co-authors traced in 2025 the white matter wiring behind loss aversion, the tendency to feel losses more than equal gains. Brain activity studies had already named regions that track how loss-averse a person is. The wiring between regions was unmapped. The team scanned 130 healthy young adults and measured each person's behavioral loss aversion outside the scanner.

A connectometry analysis linked higher loss aversion to stronger coherence in bundles tied to attention toward negative cues, aversive feeling, and avoidance drive. The opposite link sat in bundles tied to reward sensitivity reaching frontal-striatal circuits. Stronger reward wiring may soften loss aversion by making gains shine brighter. The authors read loss aversion as a stable trait built from two opposing networks. That frames it as a lasting feature of decision style, not a passing fear.
pmc-12722467:
Leyna Díaz and co-authors published this genomics study in 2025. Malassezia yeasts live on the skin of warm-blooded animals and cannot make their own long-chain fatty acids, so they normally need fats supplied. One species, common on pets, usually manages to grow on standard lab agar anyway. A few odd strains cannot. The team sequenced three of those atypical, fat-demanding strains and compared them with the reference genome.

They found 397 small genetic changes with likely effects on proteins, concentrated in fat-handling genes. Twelve of the thirteen genes for secreted lipases, enzymes that harvest fats from the surroundings, carried changes. So did a gene unique to this species in its genus. The pattern suggests the atypical strains have a blunted ability to scavenge fats, forcing them to demand richer food. The authors link the variants to how flexibly the yeast adapts to different environments.
pmc-12723867:
Jianlin Xu and seven colleagues published a real-world analysis in two thousand twenty-five on lung cancer after targeted drugs fail. A mutation called C797S commonly defeats third-generation EGFR inhibitors. What to give next was guided by little evidence.

Forty-four patients with the mutation and full records were compared across follow-up regimens. Chemotherapy-based care beat non-chemotherapy care on time without progression, five point five versus three point four months. Adding a blood-vessel blocker to chemotherapy did best. Subgroup patterns differed by whether a second mutation coexisted; one subgroup fared better on targeted drugs. The authors conclude chemotherapy remains the backbone for most of these patients.
pmc-12724067:
Matthew Stamets and a large team of co-authors surveyed how young Europeans use digital devices, in this 2025 study. In 2023, four thousand people aged sixteen to twenty-five in Italy, Poland, Spain, and Switzerland reported which gadgets they used, for what, how long, and how they held them. The authors aimed to refresh a fast-aging picture of youth device habits.

Smartphones ruled: about ninety-one percent used one. Laptops reached about sixty-nine percent, tablets a third, and wrist trackers just under a quarter. Old cordless phones clung on at about twelve percent. Older youths and women reported more use of most devices. The team also weighed schooling, work, and home place, aiming to guide later work on radio exposure and health.
pmc-12725567:
Alex Bhattacharya and co-authors review, in a 2025 paper, phone and digital tools meant to raise childhood vaccine uptake in nineteen African countries set to roll out new malaria vaccines. Multi-dose vaccines only work if families return on time, so reminders and records matter. The team searched eight databases plus grey sources for trials of such tools.

Fourteen studies met the bar, but they covered only four of the nineteen countries. All tested appointment reminders in some form. Evidence strength and bias were graded with standard tools. The patchy map shows where proof exists and where it does not. Digital reminders help, the authors suggest, but most target countries still lack direct trials.
pmc-12727767:
Fish that know each other may react to danger as one body rather than as scattered individuals. Ryohei Nakahata and Hideaki Takeuchi test this in groups of six medaka fish, some raised together for a month and some thrown together just before testing. A looming shape, mimicking a predator's rush, plays before each group while the researchers sort behavior into fast flight, normal swimming, and freezing.

Familiar groups split into all-freeze or all-swim outcomes, forming clear group styles, including a freezing-dominant style. Stranger groups lacked that style, and their members more often settled back to normal swimming after a startle. The authors conclude that familiarity promotes unified, consensus-like decisions under threat. The assay, reported in 2025, offers a route from fish behavior to brain science.
pmc-12727867:
Daniel Metcalfe and a large international team of co-authors show that tropical science is unevenly spread across the tropics. Their 2025 paper argues that sound environmental policy needs accurate, representative data, yet sampling is patchy.

The team mapped sampling locations and citations from 2,738 published studies in natural terrestrial settings across the tropics. Some biomes and some parts of key environmental gradients are poorly covered, in both field sampling and later citation. Such gaps can lead to flawed scientific paradigms and poor policy choices. The paper makes the case for directing new work and credit toward the places that are now missed.
pmc-12727967:
Nocardia farcinica causes stubborn infections, and some strains shrug off the antibiotic ciprofloxacin for reasons that gene sequencing alone missed. Six researchers study 20 strains in 2025. The usual suspects, two genes whose changes often block the drug, show no resistance mutations. Blocking the cell's efflux pumps with inhibitors, though, slashes the drug level needed by up to 64 times. That result points at pumps that spit the drug back out.

Of 26 candidate pump genes, three switch on hard under drug pressure. One, named nfa56470, stands out as the steadiest and strongest in resistant strains. The authors name it a prime target for future work on beating this resistance.
pmc-12728067:
Fei Li and co-authors test whether immune drugs can work a second time in advanced stomach cancer, in a study from two thousand twenty-five. Most patients worsen after first immune-plus-chemo care. Records covered eighty-three patients at one Chinese hospital who moved to second-line care.

About half got the immune drugs again, and the rest got chemo alone. The immune group responded far more often and lived longer on median. Grave side effects were less common in the immune group. A marker of immune activity split the gain: those above the cut gained, those below did not. The authors see real promise in the second try.
pmc-12728167:
Abbas Rahdar and co-authors blend machine learning with physics rules to design better curcumin carriers, in a 2025 study. Curcumin, a plant compound, holds medical promise but rides poorly in the body. Tiny composite carriers can ferry it, yet tuning their recipe takes many lab trials. The team built a joint model to forecast two scores: how much drug a carrier holds, and how well it traps the drug.

They trained on 74 lab-made recipes. A gradient boosting model foresaw the scores best on its own. A physics-informed network then added rules from colloid science and diffusion, which lifted broad accuracy by about a quarter. Clue analysis named the polymer ratio and the surfactant dose as the top levers. The best recipes used mid-sized particles with a strong surface charge. The authors claim large cuts in lab screening cost.
pmc-12729067:
Yuan Fang and six co-authors single out a primitive stem cell group in the womb lining, in a 2025 study. The lining rebuilds itself each month and depends on resident stem cells. Standard markers catch the broad stem cell pool, but the quietest, most original cells had not been pinned down.

Reading genes cell by cell, the team found a subgroup marked by a receptor called LEPR sitting at the root of the family tree. These cells rested in the dormant phase of the cell cycle yet outgrew their peers when asked to found colonies or renew themselves. A signaling path called Notch, fed by two partner proteins, kept them in that poised state. The authors suggest guarding this pathway could help efforts to regrow a damaged lining.
pmc-12729167:
Peiwei Zhao and co-authors describe the gene variants and clinical traits of 20 Chinese patients with congenital disorders of glycosylation. Published in 2025, the paper covers a family of rare metabolic diseases where the tagging of proteins and fats with sugars goes wrong. Signs vary widely, even within one subtype.

Whole exome sequencing, backed by other checks, found 28 distinct variants across many genes. Eleven of them had not been reported before. Three genes each accounted for three patients. The team traced links between where a variant sits in a gene and how severe the illness is. One gene's variants at one end caused a muscle related syndrome, while variants at the other end caused a different form.
pmc-12729567:
Bingqing Gao and co-authors test, in a 2025 study, whether the alkaloid part of a traditional Chinese herb can fight ovarian cancer, and how. The herb has broad reported effects, but its alkaloid share was unmapped. Chemical scans found thirty-eight nitrogen-bearing compounds in the fraction. Lab assays then tracked cancer cell growth, movement, and death.

The fraction slowed cell growth and spread in a dose-wise way and pushed cells into programmed death. A stress and guardian protein pathway sat at the center of the effect. In mice carrying human tumors, the fraction repeated its good showing. Tissue and blood checks backed the lab story. The authors pitch the fraction as a lead for new ovarian drugs.
pmc-12730167:
Mingjun Zhang and five co-authors grade chatbots answering stomach infection questions in Chinese, in a 2025 study. Helicobacter pylori infects much of the world, and patients increasingly ask language models for counsel. Whether the answers are trustworthy in a Chinese medical context was untested.

Twenty questions spanning definition, diagnosis, treatment, and prevention were put to several models three times each, and scored on accuracy, relevance, completeness, clarity, and reliability. In the first round about a third of answers rated good and almost none poor, with no clear winner overall, though one Chinese-developed bot led on reliability. A later round, over a year on, showed marked improvement, with seventy percent good and a different model on top. Accuracy and completeness were relative strengths; clarity and reliability lagged. The authors see promise, with reservations about consistency.
pmc-12730767:
Joong Min Lee and co-authors track causes of cardiac arrest inside a Korean hospital in this 2025 study. Arrest in hospital carries high death rates and grave brain harm. Alert systems have improved, but their power to change how often arrest occurs, or why, is limited.

The study covered 1,994 adults with 2,121 arrest events from 2011 to 2019 at one large hospital. The mean age was 63, and about two thirds were men. A heart rhythm fault was the most common cause, at about 15 percent, followed by breathing failure at about 13 percent. Arrests from breathing failure fell sharply over the decade, from a high rate in 2011 to a much lower one later.
pmc-12730867:
Paola Viganò and co-authors lay out, in a 2025 protocol, a trial testing whether an anti-inflammatory diet lifts IVF success for women with endometriosis. The disease inflames the body and often blocks pregnancy. Assisted reproduction helps only partly, and no firm therapy targets the infertility itself, so many women try diet changes on hope alone.

The DANTE trial will randomize infertile patients at one center to the diet or usual care before in vitro fertilization. Fertility outcomes will show whether the eating plan earns its place. Solid evidence here would give clinics a low-risk tool to offer beside drugs and surgery. The protocol also fixes in advance how success gets judged, guarding the result against wishful reading.
pmc-12731067:
Rodrigo Vargas and co-authors published a 2025 study on the genetics of tuco-tucos, burrowing rodents of the Andes in Chile. These rodents are famous for how much their chromosome counts vary between species. Much of that variety comes from repeated DNA stretches being gained, lost, or moved. The team focused on two closely related forms living side by side.

One form has twenty-six chromosomes and the other twenty-eight. Using several lab methods that light up repeated DNA, they mapped where those repeats sit in each form. One form lacked rich repeat blocks on four chromosome pairs; the other lacked them on nine. Neither form showed a fresh burst of its own repeats. A family tree built from a gene sequence dated their split to the late ice age period. The authors argue that repeat loss, tied to chromosome splitting, drove the change in chromosome number.
pmc-12731167:
Micol Lupi and co-authors map women in England who carry both anal and genital HPV disease in a 2025 study. Women bear two thirds of the global anal cancer burden. Registry data covered two decades of diagnoses for women over twenty-five. The team found women whose anal disease came with genital disease in the same window.

Eight percent of women with anal disease also had genital disease records. Those with cervical disease first faced higher late stage anal cancer risk. Multi site disease struck ten to twenty years earlier than single site reports suggest. First site and timing thus shape later danger. The findings back current screening guidance and hint cervical risk is underrated.
pmc-12731367:
Yunxiao Wang and four co-authors test robot help for dental implants in a lab study from 2025. They printed jaw models with two sites: a fresh socket after tooth removal and a healed site. A robot drilled the sites and placed implants under two levels of guidance, with or without an extra thread step.

Healed sites gave more exact placement and lower drill forces than fresh sites. In fresh sites, the extra thread step and full guidance each cut placement error a great deal. In healed sites, full guidance helped less. The findings guide how dentists should plan robot work by site type.  Force on the drill was logged by a sensor on the robot arm during each placement.
pmc-12731567:
Inês Gil-Santos and Luís Guedes-Martins review how blood flows through the unborn baby's liver and how ultrasound can read it, in a 2025 paper. The hepatic artery supplies only a small share of the fetal liver's blood. Yet it reacts sensitively when other inflows falter, widening to compensate. That buffer response makes it a window on fetal adaptation.

Doppler ultrasound can now measure the artery's flow patterns before birth. Softer resistance readings signal the compensating widening in action. Such patterns appear in growth-restricted fetuses and some chromosomal conditions. No standard reference curves exist yet, and screening does not include the vessel. The authors argue the measure deserves a place in fetal well-being checks.
pmc-12731667:
Eleni Geladari and co-authors review liver injury in sepsis in a 2025 paper. Sepsis can damage the liver early, in a pattern called sepsis-associated liver injury. The injury unfolds in two phases: a fierce inflammatory phase and a later immune-suppressed phase.

In the first phase, signaling storms harm liver cells and track with worse survival. Immune cells in the liver add to the damage with harsh chemicals. In the second phase, weak defenses invite new infections and slow repair. Liver cells also lose their normal fat-burning program. The review frames these phases as a base for immune treatments tailored to each patient.
pmc-12731867:
Xanthan gum is a thickener used in foods and industry, but the powder dissolves poorly and its texture is hard to control. Lei Zhang and co-authors studied how ultrasound travels through xanthan solutions and changes them. They compared single frequency ultrasound with dual and triple frequency setups, using a curved flat plate device. In thick solutions the single frequency field faded fast, while the combined frequencies kept a stronger, more even field across a wider range of concentrations.

The treatment paid off. Dissolved share rose from about sixty-three percent untreated to nearly eighty-six percent under the dual frequency setting. The solutions also grew less viscous, their surface tension fell, and their chains moved more freely. Microscope images showed broken fibers and a porous network, most clearly after multi-frequency treatment. The authors conclude that keeping sound energy alive in thick fluids is the key to the improvements.
pmc-12731967:
Ultrasound is the first tool doctors reach for when checking the kidneys, since it is safe and involves no radiation. Yadav and co-authors review what healthy kidneys look like on these scans and what their normal measurements are.

Drawing on sources from the 1950s to 2025, the review sets out reference ranges for kidney size, cortical thickness, brightness, and blood-flow measures. It shows how these values shift with age, sex, body build, and ethnicity, and notes common anatomical variants. The authors then tie the numbers to real cases, such as chronic kidney disease, narrowed kidney arteries, blockages, and transplants. Used with lab results, the measures help clinicians spot disease early and follow its course.
pmc-12732267:
Krisztina Martha and colleagues study how infant feeding links to tooth decay in young children, in a twenty twenty-five paper. Early childhood decay is one of the most common long-term conditions in preschool children. Feeding in the first months shapes the germs that settle in the mouth. The team examined 103 children aged three to five and asked parents how each child was fed as a baby.

Children fed only formula had the worst decay scores, and breastfed children had the lowest. Mixed-fed children fell in between. Decay was also tied to feeding type in group tests. The authors say early feeding habits leave a mark on teeth years later, so guidance for new parents should cover oral health too.
pmc-12732467:
Metal-filled gels for diabetic wound care are summed up by the authors in work dated 2025. Diabetic wounds stall in a harsh bath of high sugar, long flare, and germ risk. Gels hold the moist cover wounds heal best in. Metal parts add germ kill, flare calm, and oxygen waste soak. The review sorts build tricks into plain mixing, chemical bonds, and blends.

Kill paths span waste bursts and heat therapy. The gels also steer immune cells toward calm and spur vessel growth and skin rebuild. Safety, scale-up, and clinic entry still block the way. The map gives builders a full field view.
pmc-12732667:
Chenxi Cheng and co-authors combine a new antibody with engineered immune cells to attack lung cancer, in a study from 2025. The cells, called CAR-T cells, are a patient's own T cells fitted with a synthetic receptor that homes to cancer. They work well in blood cancers but fade too fast in solid tumors such as lung cancer.

The team first built an antibody that binds tightly to a brake protein on T cells and blocks its partners. They then fitted CAR-T cells to release IL-7, a growth signal that helps T cells persist. In mouse models, the engineered cells fought tumors better than plain CAR-T cells. A blended form of the antibody boosted the engineered cells further. The pairing offers a path to longer lasting cell therapy.
pmc-12732967:
Mikhail Savelyev and nine co-authors improve a conductive gel in 2025 meant to coat metal electrodes that stimulate nerves.
