The gel mixes carbon nanotubes and graphene flakes into a body-safe polymer; clumping of the carbon fillers throttles its conductivity. Sound-wave treatment was used to break the clumps apart.

Light scattering tracked the dispersion while conductivity probes measured the payoff. The team also followed swelling and mass loss over eighty days to gauge how the gel ages. A laser curing study found a cold working point that gives the most repeatable setting with no raw patches. The one-to-one carbon blend is presented as the coating candidate.
pmc-12733267:
Ziyan Shu and co-authors build a bendy pressure sensor from a gel laced with ink-born carbon and a conducting polymer, in a 2025 study. Wearable sensors must be light, quick, and sharp. The team stirred carbon nanospheres made from cuttlefish ink into a polyvinyl alcohol gel. Strands of polypyrrole kept the spheres from clumping and wove a web that carries charge through the film.

The sensor answered pressure in a blink and snapped back just as fast. It kept its poise through nearly six thousand press cycles. The film also sheds water and resists flame better than plain gel. On skin, it tracked finger bends and face movements with ease. It even read the faint taps of a mouse click, enough to write by touch. The authors pitch the recipe for next-wave wearables.
pmc-12733767:
Weichen Gong and co-authors review how two slime parts team up to shield germ films from drugs in a 2025 paper. Germ films, the mats behind long infections, are held by a web of goods the germs shed. Two of those goods star here: loose DNA and stiff protein ropes.

Each alone stiffens the mat and blunts drugs. Side by side they do more: the DNA seeds rope growth, and the ropes guard the DNA from decay. The dense web blocks drugs, hides killer peptides, shelters sleepy germs, and passes resistance genes around. The pair is a hidden driver of drug failure, the team argues.
pmc-12734767:
Researchers compare three simulation models in 2025 for solute spread in alloy casts spun in a centrifuge. As a two-metal cast hardens, the mix can drift apart in large patches, a flaw called macro-segregation. All three models share one heat base but treat flow drag in the mushy zone in unlike ways.

Runs on lead-tin casts at varied spin force and tilt show the pictures hinge on the drag model in use. The tip-tracking model, checked against a known test case, gave the most true-to-life maps. Stronger spin widened the even zone yet made solute channels worse.
pmc-12734967:
Lingyue Zhong and co-authors make immune active peptides from oyster protein by fermentation. The team ferments the protein with a lactic acid bacterium and tunes time, heat, and dose of starter culture. Best results came at 30 hours with a set heat and starter share, giving a high degree of protein breakdown.

The peptides are mostly small, rich in water avoiding amino acids, and stable through simulated digestion. In mouse immune cells in culture, they boosted engulfing activity and nitric oxide output. They also raised levels of three inflammatory signals. Tests show the effect runs through one branch of a known signaling cascade. The work supports fermented oyster peptides as a candidate food ingredient for immune support.
pmc-12735067:
Xin Wang reports a fossil plant that blurs the line between the two great seed plant groups, in a paper from 2025. Flowering plants are defined by seeds wrapped in a case, while their kin bear naked seeds, so a plant caught mid shift has long been sought.

The fossil, named Lingyuanfructus, comes from an early chalk age layer in Liaoning, China. In one plant, young seeds sit both naked and wrapped, just as shift theory would predict. Wang argues the find defies clean placement in either group. It gives the shift account its first direct fossil match.
pmc-12735167:
Cracks and other flaws in concrete threaten safety, yet checking structures by eye is slow. Ali Mahmoud Mayya and Nizar Faisal Alkayem trained an image model to sort concrete flaws into five classes. They built a dataset of two thousand twenty-nine photos of damaged and sound concrete. Their model extends a known image network with modules that fuse meaning and place, plus a step that highlights key features.

The new model beat the base network, gaining five point six percent in accuracy. It also located flaw regions, not just named them. A simple screen lets users run the model like a measuring tool. Such tools could speed routine checks of bridges and buildings while keeping records consistent.
pmc-12735467:
Moswane and colleagues read the full genomes in twenty twenty-five of vaccine-strain bacteria that caused disease in patients. The TB vaccine is made from a weakened cattle strain, but decades of uncontrolled growing split it into many gene variants. In rare cases the vaccine strain itself makes people ill, and telling it apart from true TB matters for care.

The team sequenced seven samples from a national TB lab and compared them with reference strains. The samples differed widely from each other and from the references. One sat close to a standard vaccine strain, and one near a TB strain, hinting at a wrong first diagnosis. Two samples showed possible resistance to a TB drug. The authors urge routine gene testing in such cases.
pmc-12735567:
Sirinthip Phuwayanon and co-authors compare guided and unguided podcast production for nursing students in work from 2025. Nurses need strong English to reach knowledge and support evidence-based care, and making podcasts is a promising way to practice.

Seventy-eight third-year students in northern Thailand split into two groups of thirty-nine. One group got detailed production guidelines, the other worked without them. Both improved, but the unguided group reported higher gains in perceived English reading skill. The guided group still rated the guidelines positively. The authors suggest freedom may boost autonomy and engagement.
pmc-12736167:
Qian Zou, Rafael Ogaz-González, Gerton Lunter, Eva Corpeleijn, and Christian Ritz link lifestyle patterns to chronic disease in this two thousand twenty-five prospective cohort study. Lifestyle factors interact in tangled ways, so the authors derived patterns from baseline self-reports in the Dutch Lifelines cohort. Diet, activity, substance use, sleep, stress, and social ties were each graded healthy, middling, or unhealthy, then combined into patterns and summation scores. Disease-free adults were followed a median of eight years.

The analysis covered over one hundred thousand people per disease, with thousands of cases of diabetes, cancer, respiratory disease, and cardiovascular disease. Against the unhealthy pattern, both a balanced healthy pattern and a healthy-but-inactive pattern were protective. One pattern, unhealthy overall but without substance use, raised diabetes risk while lowering cancer risk. The study shows whole-lifestyle patterns predict disease in ways single habits cannot.
pmc-12736267:
Nava-Solis and co-authors test a plant extract against harmful bacteria in a 2025 study. The plant, Neltuma laevigata, is a dry-land tree used in folk care for eye, stomach, and skin infections. The team drew the alkaloid part from its flower clusters, gathered in Puebla, Mexico. Tests ran against staph and cholera bacteria in dishes and broth.

The extract fought both germs well. Leakage tests and glowing dye views pointed to damage at the cell membrane. Sorting the mix yielded a known compound, julifloridine, found in this species for the first time. The authors back the folk use and flag the extract for deeper study.
pmc-12736467:
Mateus Pena and co-authors present a 2025 study on how cannabis plants handle drought. Dry conditions limit yield of both plant material and the active compounds people harvest. The team compared two contrasting types: one rich in THC and one rich in CBD, the two best-known compounds in the plant.

Plants were grown in a greenhouse, and water was cut at early flowering. The CBD plants built more biomass but did not photosynthesize faster when water was plentiful. Under drought, the THC plants mainly closed their leaf pores to save water. The CBD plants showed deeper internal limits and a stronger drop in photosynthesis. Both types ended with similar cell damage, so sun-protection tricks did not explain the gap.
pmc-12736567:
Trent Yamamoto and co-authors compared balance training styles in college football players, in this 2025 trial. Poor balance raises injury risk, yet slackline training had scarce tests in elite athletes. Thirty male players were split into standard training, slackline board training, and no training for eight weeks.

Both trained groups improved standing and moving balance over the control group. The slackline group beat the standard group on wobble-board sway, one reach direction, and total reach scores. Sessions ran three times a week. The authors present slackline work as equal or better than standard drills for this squad. Wider trials can test the claim.
pmc-12736667:
Beyza Toprak and colleagues set out a study protocol for testing whether a chest wearable can catch lung flare-ups early, in a 2025 paper. Flare-ups of chronic obstructive pulmonary disease drive emergency visits and erode quality of life. Catching one days earlier could let community teams act before a hospital stay becomes likely.

The retrospective mixed-methods study examines records from volunteers with the disease who wore the Frontier X2 device and later had flare-ups. Continuous signals such as heart and breathing measures will be checked for patterns that preceded each event. Interviews add the patients’ side of wearability. The protocol fixes the questions and methods in advance, so the eventual verdict on the device rests on a transparent plan.
pmc-12736767:
Yessenia Ibeth Paucar and colleagues map out how to print graphene strain sensors with a cheap diode laser. Laser-induced graphene, formed by irradiating polyimide film, promises low-cost flexible sensors. The team varied laser power, focal length, and number of passes using a blue diode laser. They then evaluated the resulting sensors in three-point bending tests.

Shape checks, Raman spectroscopy, and electrical measurements gauged conductivity, bending stability, and sensitivity. Laser power proved the key factor for graphene quality and sensor performance. Focal length had almost no effect. Extra passes in fact reduced material quality and sensitivity. That is a useful negative result against the gut sense that more processing helps. The work shows working, low-cost graphene strain sensors from a commercial diode laser. It offers a route to make them at scale, cheaply.
pmc-12737767:
Jeanine Guidry and co-authors follow vaccine views over time in a 2025 study of United States adults. They asked about COVID shot plans before any shot existed, then checked who got one once shots were wide open.

One hundred forty two adults answered at both points. Felt risk, gains, and hurdles shaped early plans, while trust in government did not. A year on, trust did join gains and hurdles as a driver of who got the shot. Trust and self belief rose between the rounds, while felt threat and hurdles fell. The team urge readiness work that builds trust before the next crisis.
pmc-12738067:
Basil Baby Mattamana and co-authors tuned a prep method for cell culture fluid in a 2025 paper. The fluid cells grow in holds the proteins they shed, a rich source of disease marks and signals. Big volumes, over five milliliters, defeat standard prep: proteins are scarce, serum floods the mix, and losses mount.

Their workflow stacks three steps: a fine filter that keeps the mid-size proteins, a column that pulls out the flood proteins, and a solvent crash that gathers the rest. The stack keeps both rare and common shed proteins for the mass spectrometer. Labs can scale it to large culture runs.
pmc-12738767:
Jiali Shou and co-authors present a 2025 study on using ultrasound to detect muscle loss in heart patients. Sarcopenia weakens people with cardiovascular disease, but standard checks of mass and strength can be slow. The team tested whether standard ultrasound plus a stiffness method, shear wave elastography, could flag the condition.

They enrolled 114 patients with heart disease or stroke. Thirty-six had sarcopenia by the standard measures of mass, grip, and walking speed. Ultrasound features of the front thigh muscle were taken at rest and stretched. The muscle loss group showed thinner fat and muscle layers and smaller muscle area. Correlation checks and a combined model then weighed which scan features predict sarcopenia on their own.
pmc-12739867:
Vincent Luong and co-authors chart what happens to Swedish myeloma patients once the two workhorse drug classes have been used up. Their 2025 real-world study reviews 218 patients at one center whose disease returned after proteasome inhibitors and lenalidomide in early treatment lines. The key split is whether the cancer had stopped responding to lenalidomide.

Refractory patients fared worse: survival medians were shorter, and their overall survival median sat near twenty months while the comparison group's was never reached in follow-up. Response to the next treatment line was similar in both groups, around six in ten, which makes the survival gap more pointed. Most patients next received drug classes they had partly seen before. The authors call the refractory group's outcomes suboptimal in plain terms. Real-world studies like this one set the bar new drugs must clear, measured in clinic corridors rather than trial brochures.
pmc-12740967:
Oveys Ziya, Laxmi Sushama, and Husham Almansour present a 2025 study of flood loads on road overpasses in Montreal. A warmer climate can bring more short, intense rain bursts. Such bursts cause flash floods that can strain city structures, yet overpasses have been little studied in this regard.

The team paired fine scale climate runs with a two dimensional water flow model of the city. They built design storms for current and future climates under several paths for gas emissions. The storms matched the kind of rain expected once in a hundred years. Then they weighed the push, drag, and debris hit loads that flood water would place on overpasses.
pmc-12741067:
Liang and ten co-authors show a medicinal chrysanthemum extract protects skin from ultraviolet A damage, in a study from twenty twenty-five. Sunlight's UVA triggers stress in the cell's protein-folding compartment, causing cell death. The plant, Coreopsis tinctoria, is rich in antioxidant flavonoids. Over twelve hundred metabolites are profiled in the extract.

In human skin cells, the extract cuts death, inflammation, and reactive oxygen. All three stress branches are suppressed while Nrf2 defenses activate. Removing Nrf2 abolishes the protection, proving its central role. Topical use also protects UVA-exposed mouse skin in tests. A natural photoprotective agent candidate emerges.
pmc-12742067:
Classrooms pack children into shared air, which makes them prime spots for spreading respiratory viruses. Runar Solberg and co-authors lay out a trial plan in 2025 to test whether portable air purifiers with high-grade filters cut school absence. The trial will run in Norwegian primary schools across two winters, with schools randomly assigned to real or sham units.

Each classroom gets two units; in control rooms the units run at a whisper of the real cleaning rate, so the trial stays blinded. Absence days form the main outcome over a twelve-week span, with a planned mid-trial look that can stop the study early for clear benefit or futility. The authors detail the statistics that keep error rates in check under that design.
pmc-12742167:
Chiara Bernardi and thirteen co-authors present a 2025 study asking whether the time of day a stem cell graft is given changes transplant results. The body clock shapes blood formation and immune control. An earlier study had linked afternoon grafts with more graft versus host disease and worse survival.

The team checked that claim in their own center's records. They reviewed 368 patients who got donor stem cell transplants in Geneva from 2015 to 2024. Timing patterns at their center differed from the earlier report, which gave a clean test of the link. The study weighs disease rates and survival by infusion time.
pmc-12742767:
Linen Li, Hao Chen, Feng Zhou, and Yanqing Shi sort, in a 2025 study, stomach cancers into immune subtypes using two genes from a cancer-testis family. The immune surroundings of a tumor decide much of its course and its answer to immunotherapy, but epithelial genes that flag those surroundings were poorly mapped. The team crossed single-cell data with a large tumor atlas to find such genes.

Two genes, MAGEA3 and MAGEA6, split the tumors cleanly. Cancers high in both were immune cold, thinly infiltrated by immune cells, while cancers low in both were immune hot. Two further genes, BCL11B and PAEP, tracked closely with infiltration and immune regulation, marking them as candidate levers. The authors propose the pair as a simple subtyping test for stomach cancer, and the extra genes as targets worth probing for therapy.
pmc-12743267:
Jialei Zhang and ten co-authors present a study from twenty twenty-five on a rare gut illness tied to the IgG4 disease family. The illness scars and thickens the mesentery, the fold that holds the gut. It is little known and may be missed. The team drew on a large cohort at a Beijing hospital, with close to thirty such cases, plus cases from past reports.

Cases skewed to older men with more organs hit and higher disease scores than kin cases with no gut form. Scans showed a range from misty haze to soft masses in the mesentery. Their cohort had less belly pain but more gland swell than past reports. Drug care in the cohort matched surgery in past cases on relapse rates.
pmc-12743467:
A poisoned child can crash fast, so early signs of who will fare worst are worth a great deal. Asmaa Sharif and three co-authors build risk charts from three years of cases. Their 2025 study covers 1,328 children seen for acute poisoning.

The death rate was 1.7 percent, and 1.3 percent of children needed intensive care. Age split the cause in a stark way: nearly all infants and small children were exposed by chance, while most teens took the substance on purpose. One farm chemical stood out as a top driver of deaths and intensive care. Poisoning by non-drug goods brought worse signs than drug cases. The charts aim to flag, at the door, which children need the closest watch.
pmc-12744867:
Gu and four colleagues track the global burden of psoriasis from nineteen ninety to twenty twenty-one in a twenty twenty-five study. Psoriasis is a long term skin disease marked by inflammation. The team drew rates of new cases, total cases, and years lost to disability from a global disease database. They also forecast trends for the next fifteen years.

Rates of new cases rose over the study period, and total case rates rose as well. Rates were higher in men than in women. In twenty twenty-one, new case rates peaked in the fifty-five to sixty-nine age group. Rates were highest in wealthy regions, in Western Europe, and in Germany. The forecast sees rates rising further, so the authors urge plans aimed at high risk groups.
pmc-12745467:
Chao Huang and co-authors test blood-based scores for early detection of Alzheimer's disease in this 2025 paper. The three scores combine routine blood values tied to inflammation and nutrition. They are named HALP, PIV, and SII, and all are cheap to compute.

The study compared more than two hundred patients with about one hundred seventy-six healthy controls. Matching methods built balanced pairs for a fair comparison. The team checked how the scores link to dementia severity as well. Cheap blood scores could help clinics flag patients who need fuller testing. They might also help track how the disease moves over time. More study in wider groups is still needed before clinic use.
pmc-12745967:
Sanjiao Liu and five co-authors present a summary from twenty twenty-five of best care before pregnancy for women with rheumatoid arthritis. The disease often starts in the childbearing years. Its chronic inflammation plus drug effects raise the risk of poor pregnancy outcomes. Yet the evidence for care before conception is scattered across many sources. The team hunts it down in a set order.

Eleven sources made the cut: guidelines, expert accords, and reviews. From them came a set of best practice points in seven areas. Areas span fertility risk checks, screening, drug tweaks, fertility saving, weight and food, and mind support. Most points won a strong backing grade. The set is meant as a bench guide for nurses.
pmc-12747067:
Yangyang Wang, Jin Xu, and Wenjing Li review cases of severe whooping cough in children treated at one hospital during 2024. Their 2025 study notes that pertussis, a sharp respiratory infection, is rising worldwide as vaccine protection fades and the bacteria change. Severe cases can end in breathing failure and death, mainly in young infants.

The records cover 76 children, split into severe and non-severe groups. The highest rates fell in babies aged six weeks to three months. Severe cases stayed in hospital longer and needed longer drug courses. The standard antibiotic family still leads treatment, though resistance has appeared in some regions. Costs were compared too.
pmc-12748367:
Satoshi Naruse and co-authors report an emergency caesarean delivery in a pregnant woman with uncorrected diabetic ketoacidosis, in work published in 2025. The condition, where blood turns acidic from uncontrolled diabetes, is rare in pregnancy but often fatal for the baby. Standard care stabilises the mother first, yet the baby's distress can force immediate delivery.

The patient was a 24-year-old first-time mother at thirty-five weeks with poorly controlled type 2 diabetes. Her baby showed a worrying heart pattern, so surgery went ahead before her blood chemistry was fixed. A combined spinal-epidural block was used, with insulin and glucose therapy running and blood gases checked through an arterial line. Both mother and baby recovered and went home without complications. The case shows a coordinated path for this rare emergency.
pmc-12748567:
Xinpai Liu and co-authors test a plant compound against tooth pulp inflammation in a 2025 study. Inflamed pulp causes severe tooth pain and is hard to calm. Carnosol comes from herbs and is known for calming effects. The team tested it in human pulp cells and in rats.

In cells, the compound cut the output of several inflammatory signals. It also lowered a sensor protein and blocked a key inflammation switch. Silencing that sensor copied much of the compound's calming effect. In rats, dosing the inflamed pulp eased the inflammation visibly.
pmc-12748867:
Jolanta Nowak and six co-authors published a muscle biology study in twenty twenty-five on myosin VI, an unconventional motor protein, at the junction where nerves meet muscle. The protein already had known roles in muscle building and heart function. Its job at the neuromuscular junction, the synapse that triggers contraction, had never been examined.

The protein concentrates at the junction's receiving side in young and adult animals. Mice lacking it showed delayed junction maturation in both fast and slow muscles, and smaller junctions in the soleus. The normal pruning of extra nerve inputs, though, proceeded on schedule. Grip strength suffered in both sexes. The authors conclude myosin VI is a genuine regulator of junction size and timing.
pmc-12749367:
Lokman Damar and Birgül Otludil examine, under the microscope, what a common farm pesticide does to a freshwater snail, and whether vitamin C can shield it. Imidacloprid, a neonicotinoid insecticide, washes into waterways and threatens aquatic life. Their 2025 study exposed Melanopsis snails to three low doses for up to twenty-one days, with and without ascorbic acid alongside. Slices of the digestive gland and mantle showed the damage: swollen and hollowed cells, fat buildup, and dead tissue, worse at higher doses and longer times.

Tissue pictures make pollution visible in a way water chemistry cannot. If a cheap vitamin blunts the harm, that hints at an oxidation-driven mechanism and a possible buffer for wild populations. The authors use a humble snail as a sentinel for its ecosystem. Their design pairs dose and duration, the two axes of real exposure. It is environmental toxicology at bench scale.
pmc-12749867:
Tinghao Wang, Yuheng Li, Weiping Li, Lijuan Zhou, and Ning Luo build in a 2025 paper a tool to spot fake goods text. Fakes often copy a brand name with a sound alike or shape alike character swap. That text trick fools buyers and is hard to catch at scale online.

Their network pairs a corrector with a detector helper built on a language model. A light transformer block first flags suspect characters so they warp meaning less. Shape, sound, and sense traits of each character are fused to lift fix accuracy. A new data set of 289,851 samples was built to end the data drought in this niche. The tool topped past methods on that set and held up on three public sets.
pmc-12750267:
Smita Dey and co-authors package two approved drugs into lipid particles for glioblastoma care in a 2025 study. The brain tumor is aggressive and resists treatment. The standard drug often fails and harms the body at useful doses. Earlier work showed the two repurposed drugs killed tumor cells at lower doses in the lab.

Free drugs still harmed healthy cells. Packing them into solid lipid particles lowered the dose needed, raised uptake by tumor cells, and reduced harm to healthy cells. Tests in flat and three dimensional tumor models probed how the particles work against the cancer.
pmc-12750567: Xiaoyun Ye and co-authors report a jaw infection in a healthy child caused by Legionella maceachernii in a 2025 case paper. Infections from this germ outside the lungs are very rare, above all in children with sound immune systems. The child recovered fully on azithromycin plus a sulfa combo drug. The report details diagnosis and care to alert doctors that odd germs can drive soft tissue infections in children.
pmc-12750667:
Nienke de Graef and co-authors plan a review asking not whether shared decision-making works, but how, for patients who struggle with health information. Their 2025 protocol describes a realist review focused on people with limited health literacy, over a quarter of European adults. Such patients face worse outcomes partly because medical information is hard to find, grasp, and use.

Realist method hunts mechanisms: which contexts trigger which responses to produce which outcomes. The team has drafted initial program theories with expert input. Next they will search and appraise the literature, then refine the theories with patients and clinicians at the table. Shared decision-making is often prescribed as a universal good. The reviewers suspect its benefits hinge on recognition, since clinicians routinely miss limited literacy. The finished review aims to tell designers which levers make participation real for this group.
pmc-12750767:
Video and phone visits grew fast during the pandemic, including for allied health care such as physio and speech therapy. Senyel and seven co-authors asked Australian users how these remote visits felt and what helped or hindered them. They ran eight focus groups with 57 people, drawing in groups often left out of such studies, including deaf people, young disabled people, and Pacific Islander community members.

Five themes stood out. The person's own situation shaped whether remote care fit. The worker's skill and the bond between worker and patient shaped quality. Remote visits improved access but suited talking-based care best. Technology access could make or break the visit. The authors say services should keep remote care as a real choice, keep the tools easy to use, and hold quality standards, rather than treating video visits as a cheap stand-in.
pmc-12751267:
Tevfik Akol and co-authors run a pilot test in 2025 on breathing masks worn during hard interval training by young soccer players. Such masks claim to mimic training at height, here set to mimic six thousand feet. What they do to blood and body stress in youth players was unclear.

Twelve male amateur players each ran the same hard session twice, once masked and once not, in random order. Heart rate and blood oxygen were tracked through the work. Blood drawn before and after gauged sugar, fats, stress hormones, and muscle harm marks. Both sessions raised heart rate and cut oxygen, the head reports. Pilot data like this help coaches judge whether mask claims rest on body facts or on effort alone.
pmc-12751567:
Ilechukwu Agu and co-authors test whether a cancer drug that blocks a host growth pathway can change flu virus output. Their 2025 study starts from a known fact: flu makes many flawed genome copies, and those flawed copies can soften infection. Most past work blamed virus proteins for how many flawed copies form.

The team blocked the host pathway in infected cells and tracked flawed genomes and non-infectious particles. One flu strain sharply raised its flawed copies under the drug, while a second strain did not. The second strain instead made slightly more non-infectious particles. The authors argue that host cell state shapes virus output. Strain gaps point to a virus-host contact worth probing next.
pmc-12751867:
Tianlin Wang and colleagues test a head-start training plan for new clinical pharmacists in China, in this trial from twenty twenty-five. Standard training lasts a year and leans on drug knowledge, but new hires without a clinical pharmacy degree often lack job readiness and soft skills. The team's plan adds three months of adaptability training before the standard year.

Twenty new pharmacists were split at random into two groups. One group took the extra training, covering career awareness, teamwork, clear thinking, and coping with stress, and the other did not. After the shared year of training, expert panels rated both groups. The head-start group scored higher on career awareness, fitting in with ward demands, reasoning through cases, and working across fields. It also won praise for sound analysis and care for patients. The authors urge wider use of the plan.
pmc-12751967:
Andrea Duarte-Díaz and colleagues pooled dementia therapy trials in 2025. Dementia brings fading memory and heavy emotional strain. Emotion-oriented care targets feelings and psychological needs directly. Such care skips drugs entirely. Forms include supportive talk therapy and reminiscence work. Sensory programs and simulated family presence also count. The team searched seven databases for randomized trials. Thirty-four trials entered the combined analysis. Bias checks used standard Cochrane tools.

Treated patients improved on several fronts. Thinking scores and depressive symptoms both got better. Life quality and daily function also improved. Gains looked largest where few other options existed. Results varied against active comparison therapies, though. The specific method and setting shaped the effect. The authors call these therapies a valuable complement. Low-resource settings may gain the most from them. More work must set long-term value and delivery rules.
pmc-12752967:
Cecere and co-authors share a protocol for moving a standard genetic tool into wild strains of a glowing marine bacterium. The bacterium, Vibrio fischeri, lives in symbiosis with the Hawaiian bobtail squid. Tools built for the lab strain often fail in its wild relatives.

Their workaround first inserts the desired DNA into the lab strain at the usual landing site. DNA from that strain then transforms the target strain, whose natural uptake is switched on. As proof, they restored a broken gene in another strain using an inducible copy. The authors offer the method to anyone studying symbiosis genes in hard-to-edit strains.
pmc-12753367:
Saskia Wildi and eight co-authors weigh the safety of hormone therapy for women who have cavernous malformations in the brain or spine. These tangles of blood vessels can bleed into the brain, causing stroke or nerve damage. Birth control and menopause hormone treatment are not withheld from such patients, yet proof of their safety here is thin. Their 2025 study searched a hospital's prospective records for all such patients. It compared bleeding and new nerve deficits between those on hormone therapy and those not.

A clear risk number would help women and doctors make a hard trade-off with open eyes. Hormones help many patients, so a blanket ban has costs too. The authors aim to replace guesswork with rates drawn from real follow-up. The study adds to a small pool of data on this group.
pmc-12753867:
Jesús Endara-Mina and co-authors map how menopause is experienced across ethnic groups, in a 2025 scoping review. The review followed standard scoping methods across several databases, with no language or date limits. From four hundred forty-six records, twenty studies met the criteria. The team read them for recurring themes in how symptoms are felt, described, and handled.

African American and Hispanic women carried a heavier load of emotional and hot-flush symptoms. Asian and Indigenous women more often framed the change as a natural stage of life. Belief systems and social position shaped what was reported as much as biology did. The authors conclude menopause is a culturally embedded experience, not a uniform biological event, and they urge care that asks women what the transition means in their own community's terms.
pmc-12754467:
Six researchers pool studies on shockwave therapy after knee ligament surgery in a review from 2025. The surgery rebuilds the anterior cruciate ligament, a key knee stabilizer. Recovery is often slow even with standard rehabilitation. Shockwave therapy sends pressure pulses into tissue and may speed healing. The team gathered six studies, five of them randomized trials, comparing added shockwaves with rehab alone.

One knee function score improved modestly with shockwaves, though studies varied widely. Focused shockwaves looked better than radial ones. Other scores, including pain and knee looseness, showed no clear gain. The authors note signs of publication bias. They call for larger, placebo-controlled trials with standard methods.
pmc-12754967:
Support workers who care for people with disabilities in group housing are rarely trained to coach chronic disease care. Han Nah Park and co-authors map what such training should teach in this 2025 study from South Korea. Thirty-two workers joined focus groups, and 193 more answered a survey, rating both how much they know and how much each topic matters.

Thirteen topics came out as top needs, led by exercise programs matched to each disability type and diet guidance for overweight residents. Skin and mental health, communication, challenging behavior, and sex education also ranked high. So did support for the workers' own mental strain. The results now guide a draft curriculum for this workforce, which sits at the front line of daily health care.
pmc-12755067:
Muscle cells fuse to build fibers, and a fusion gene's changing role across life is traced in zebrafish by Dhar and co-authors in a 2025 study. Two fusogen proteins drive that fusion in vertebrates. The team imaged gene activity and used a knockout fish line that lacks one of them.

Early muscle formation uses the gene in a patchy pattern across the whole segment, not just along one axis. Without it, segment shape warps and both cell and tissue form suffer. Later growth leans on the two fusogens in different measure. The split matters for repair, since adult muscle regrows by the same fusion steps. Fish offer a clear window on those steps.
pmc-12755767:
Anup Talukder and three co-authors surveyed in 2025 the mental health of women with polycystic ovary syndrome in Bangladesh. The hormone disorder is common in women of childbearing age, and mental care often lags in poorer countries. The team sampled 212 women and diagnosed the syndrome by standard criteria. Screens measured depression, anxiety, stress, and poor sleep.

About half the women met the syndrome criteria, and rates of each distress measure ran near or above half. Women with the syndrome showed more distress than those without it. Rural women met the criteria more often and reported more anxiety and poor sleep. Meeting more of the criteria raised the odds of distress further. The authors urge joint checks of body and mind in care for this group.
pmc-12756467:
Jie Chen and co-authors report a 2025 case of a rare breast cancer form that spread fast, against its usual slow course. The form grows with bland spindle cells and lacks the three standard markers, which class it as triple-negative. Most cases stay mild, so a fast, drug-proof course breaks the known pattern and needs a cause.

The patient, a woman aged 57, had a mass in her left breast that tissue tests named as this rare form. Gene checks found a change in the switch region of a gene that keeps cell growth caps in repair. Despite surgery, radiation, and many rounds of drugs, the cancer reached her lungs at five months and her bones at fifteen. The team urges closer watch and gene profiling for such cases.
pmc-12757267:
Weihua Zheng and co-authors present a 2025 review that pools past trials of short, hard interval training for children and teens. The work asks whether brief bouts of hard exercise can improve body shape and heart health in less time than steady exercise.

Across twenty three studies with close to one thousand young people, the training lowered body mass, fat, waist size, weight, and blood pressure. It also raised fitness, measured by oxygen use. Gains were much like those from steady training. Dose, age, and weight status shaped the results, so the review helps schools and families judge a time saving option.
pmc-12757967:
Bárbara dos Santos and co-authors test denture materials in this 2025 study. Full dentures can be relined with hard acrylic to restore their fit. Many wearers also use adhesives to keep dentures in place. The team asked how adhesives and aging change the reliners' color, hardness, and surface roughness.

They tested three reliner brands with three adhesives on 120 samples. Samples were checked fresh, after two months, and after heat-cycle aging. Time changed every property, with hardness and roughness rising. One brand held its color and hardness best, a trait tied to elements in its makeup. Its surface, though, grew roughest. The results help dentists weigh looks and durability by brand.
pmc-12764967:
Ronnie Serfa Juan and Alison Gerken present a 2025 data set built to help computers name beetle fragments. The six species covered are stored-food pests from two beetle families. Staff often find only broken bits of these insects, so a tool that can sort fragments by species would speed up pest checks.

Each fragment photo was taken through a digital microscope and cleaned with a set process. Four numbers were drawn from each image, summing up texture and shape traits such as spread and roughness. The set holds 3,423 images, each tagged with its species, body part, and a matching number profile. The data follows open reuse rules for pest research.
pmc-12766767:
Maiar Elhariry and a large team swap paper consent for digital consent in a 2025 project. The work sat in a trauma and bone ward of an English hospital group. Paper forms suffer bad script, gaps, and weak legal worth. The team set base reads from mid 2024, then ran the digital form for three months. Change ran in plan-do-study-act loops. Forms from 619 patients and 24 staff fed the grades.

Script clarity hit 100 percent on digital forms, from under half on paper. Notes of other care paths leapt from near none to near all. Risks and gains sat in all digital forms. Staff and patients scored the tool high on ease forms. Hurdles stayed for low-tech patients and small screens. The swap saved over two and a half thousand pounds in seven months.
pmc-12767667:
Kaleab Tegegne and co-authors pool world evidence on early birth and cerebral palsy in this 2025 paper. Cerebral palsy is the most common childhood movement disability, and babies born before 37 weeks face an immature, fragile brain. The team reviewed sixteen observational studies covering over thirty thousand children. Only studies passing a quality bar entered the pool.

For the broad preterm group, the pooled risk sat close to that of full-term children. The picture changed when births were split by how early they came. Risk climbed steeply with greater prematurity. Bias checks found no sign of missing studies. The authors urge care and follow-up weighted toward the earliest-born infants, where the danger concentrates.
pmc-12768667:
Jo Watson and co-authors described in 2025 how Australian patients and the public were put in charge of reshaping their own role in health technology assessment. The process grew from a five-year pact between the health department and the drug industry body. A consumer reference group designed the co-design, tilting membership toward consumers and choosing them through peer selection.

An independent facilitator ran the work against principles the group set itself. The resulting report, Enhance HTA, carries ten recommendations on partnership, openness, and evidence. Its vision puts Australians' lived experience at the heart of assessment decisions. The authors call the consumer-led design a strong signal of intent. They expect the plan to be built into the pathway from drug development to funding.
pmc-12768767:
Lais da Silva Barbosa and co-authors report a 2025 conference study on how Brazil's health technology committee turns science into terms that decision makers can use. Even experts can struggle to grasp and apply research proof. Knowledge translation is the craft of reshaping that proof for different audiences, and of bringing the right people into the process.

The committee judges which health technologies the public system should adopt. The study set out to trace how it uses this craft at each stage of its judging work. The team searched the committee's website for the materials it produces for different audiences. They listed the main items and discussed their impact. As a short conference item, the report focuses on mapping practice rather than on measured outcomes for patients.
pmc-12769567:
Shuping Chen, Jinwen Wu, and Hongxiao Zhao built a layered model for plates made of materials that grade smoothly from one mix to another in a 2025 paper. Such plates serve in aircraft and other high-end gear, but their bending is hard to compute when the grading follows no simple rule. Any smooth curve, though, can be traced by short power-law pieces.

The model stacks thin layers, each with its own power-law grading, keeping stress and displacement smooth at the seams. For a plate held at its edges under a wavy load, all bending values follow in closed form. Tests show how layer count trades against accuracy, and how grading shapes compare. The authors offer the model as a fast, exact-leaning tool for plate design.
pmc-12770067:
Mobina Nakhaei Shamahmood and co-authors review the diabetes drug metformin as a partner drug against acute myeloid leukemia, in this 2025 paper. The leukemia kills many patients through relapse and drug resistance. Metformin alone does little, but studies hint it sharpens other drugs. The team sifted over a hundred papers down to thirty-two that tested real combinations.

Partners ranged from targeted agents to classic chemotherapy. Across studies the pairs drained cell energy, stalled growth cycles, and pushed leukemia cells into death, trimming disease burden and lengthening survival in models. Effects like blocked sugar burning and lowered power output recurred. The authors conclude metformin can add real synergy to leukemia regimens. They call for clinical testing to sort which pairs deserve patients first.
pmc-12770467:
Martina Schiavello and ten co-authors hunt tiny RNA strands in blood that could flag COVID-19 and warn who will worsen. The illness ranges from mild to lung failure, and early sorting saves lives. Their 2025 study took blood at the ER door from forty suspects, thirty of whom had the virus.

Four strands ran high in virus patients against healthy peers. Two of them also split virus cases from like illnesses. Four more strands ran high in patients who later fell into lung failure. Map work tied the strands to immune and swelling paths. The authors call blood strand reads a hopeful, needle-light tool. Bigger groups must prove the marks, they add.
pmc-12771067:
Raviprakash T. Sitaram and Börje Ljungberg reported a tissue study in 2025 on the most common form of kidney cancer. A protein that normally keeps oxygen sensing in check is often lost in these tumors. Losing it frees oxygen-response proteins and may weaken a protein that helps cells stick together. The team measured all three in tumors from many patients, alongside normal kidney tissue, and linked the patterns to stage, size, and survival.

The control protein was lower in tumors than in normal tissue. One oxygen-response protein rose in the most advanced tumors, while another rose with tumor size. The sticking protein fell in tumors, above all in larger and later-stage ones. Higher levels of that protein tracked with better survival only when the control protein stayed high. The authors read the chain as a driver of tumor growth and a possible source of drug targets.
pmc-12771767:
Qiang Ji and Yawei Hou review environmental drivers of brain bleeding in older adults in a 2025 paper. Bleeding in the brain is often fatal and claims a large share of stroke deaths in this group. Beyond biology, the authors focus on context, such as air pollution, traffic gases and noise, heat swings, and heavy metals.

They argue these stressors act through arousal, broken sleep, inactivity, and poor heat control, which strain fragile small vessels. Exposure is uneven across communities due to social and commercial forces. The review appraises policies, such as cleaner urban transport, that could lower risk.
pmc-12772367:
Maiko Jao and Karen Joy Kimseng report Weber-Christian disease in a twelve-year-old girl in the Philippines. The disease, a relapsing fever with inflamed fat under the skin, mostly strikes women in mid and later life. Cases in children are rare, and only one had been reported in the country before. Their 2025 case report traces four months of facial lumps, thigh pain, and recurring fever.

Tests ruled out allergy, autoimmune disease, infection, and blood problems, and standard care did not help. A biopsy of firm abdominal lesions fit the disease at last. Steroids, hydroxychloroquine, and a topical drug then shrank the lumps step by step. Pediatricians get a reminder to biopsy stubborn nodular fevers.
pmc-12772567:
Anouk Olthof and seven co-authors grade a new second-step test in Dutch newborn screening for an adrenal disorder, in a 2025 paper. The disorder stems from a missing enzyme and can endanger babies. Screening first measures a hormone in heel-prick blood, with a second prick when the first is unclear. Since late 2021, a different hormone test on the same spot replaced that second prick.

Over two years, the new test ran on 147 babies. It sent twenty to a specialist on strong first results, fifteen of whom truly had the classic disorder. Of the unclear group, only three tested positive, and none had the disease. The new path spared 127 second heel pricks and cut needless referrals from about eight percent to about two percent.
pmc-12772967:
Yohei Mineharu and co-authors link blood GATA2 expression to mutation impact in moyamoya disease in a 2025 study. A founder mutation in RNF213 raises risk for this brain artery disease, yet many carriers never fall ill.

Blood gene profiling in families found modules tied to fat handling, white cell growth, and growth signals switched up in patients. One network around GATA2 stood out and was retested in a larger case-control set. GATA2 levels ran higher in patients than in healthy carriers. Among mutation carriers, higher GATA2 tied to earlier onset, both-side disease, and symptomatic start. The marker may help predict which carriers need close watch.
pmc-12775367:
Josep Carbonell-Roig and a large team of co-authors studied faulty signal flow in a mouse model of autism, in a 2024 paper. The model carries raised levels of a protein that controls how cells build other proteins. Altered dopamine signaling in a deep brain area has been linked to autism traits. The team joined gene, behavior, and imaging methods to trace the fault.

Mice with raised levels of the protein showed rigid behavior. Their dopamine release in the named area was impaired. The fault traced to a receptor pathway that uses a related brain chemical. That pathway normally tunes calcium flow in dopamine cell branches. When it failed, release fell out of tune. The findings link the protein, the signal fault, and rigid behavior in one chain. The authors say the chain offers targets for future treatment work.
pmc-12776867:
Shwethapriya Rao and six co-authors published a study in 2025 on a blood signal that warns of organ failure in patients whose lungs have failed. In acute respiratory distress syndrome the lungs fill and stiffen, and other organs often follow. A molecule called eNAMPT, part enzyme and part alarm signal, rises with inflammation and was already suspected as a treatment target.

Ninety patients at one center had their eNAMPT levels, oxygen readings, lung ultrasound scores, and heart measures tracked. Higher eNAMPT predicted severe multi-organ dysfunction, and a cutoff value separated high-risk patients with decent accuracy. Non-survivors carried clearly higher levels than survivors, and crossing a second cutoff nearly quadrupled the death hazard. A single blood draw early on may flag who needs the closest watch.
pmc-12781267:
Alvin Chai and co-authors review lymphoma care outcomes at a Malaysian tertiary hospital. Diffuse large B-cell lymphoma is the most common lymphoma in Malaysia and worldwide. Records covered 202 patients treated from 2015 to 2020 with the R-CHOP drug mix. Median age was fifty-eight, and most patients were men.

Complete response came for about fifty-eight percent of patients. Three-year survival sat near sixty-one percent, with progression-free survival close behind. High prognostic index scores and B symptoms both marked worse paths. Low blood albumin stood alone as an independent death risk in deep analysis. The authors call for bigger prospective trials with longer follow-up.
pmc-12784267:
Emily Morris and Oliver Rider review obesity as a target in heart failure care in a 2025 article. Obesity is rising worldwide and drives heart failure with both preserved and reduced pumping function. It acts through blood flow stress, hormone signals, metabolic problems, and inflammation.

Weight loss surgery gives consistent benefits across heart failure types. Diet and drug approaches also show promise, especially a class of diabetes drugs now used for weight control. Structured exercise helps too. Gaps remain on long term effects and on combining drug classes. The authors argue treating obesity is essential for this high risk group.
pmc-12784667:
Xi Chen and co-authors report a 2025 study on breeding small-grained rice. Small grains help machine seed production for hybrid rice and are valued in food markets. The team aimed to shrink grain size while also lifting cooking and nutrition quality, a hard pair of goals.

Using gene editing, the team altered a gene called OsVIN2 in a high-quality rice line. Edited plants made seeds notably shorter and narrower, and total grain weight fell sharply. Quality moved the right way at the same time. Starch type linked to texture dropped, protein rose, and chalkiness, a flaw in grain look and milling, fell steeply. The authors say the edit offers breeding stock for fine small-grain rice.
pmc-12784867:
Junnan Ding, Yingjian Wang, and Shaopeng Yu study how microbe communities change as salty, alkaline wetlands break down, in a 2025 paper. They sampled four habitats, from untouched wetland to converted farmland. As wetlands degrade, soil dries out, nutrients fall, and salt stress grows, but bacteria and fungi may not respond in the same way.

Soil water and nutrients were highest in the untouched wetland and lowest in the harshest habitat. Bacteria were ruled more strongly by soil traits such as acidity, carbon, and moisture. Under stress, bacterial grouping followed set rules driven by selection. Fungal grouping stayed mostly random, and fungal networks held up better under extreme damage. The split shows the two groups follow different rules during wetland loss.
pmc-12785467:
Nam Hee Kim and co-authors ask what drives anxiety and low mood in older adults living at home during a long disease outbreak. The study surveyed 178 adults aged sixty-five and older in South Korea. It measured stress tied to the outbreak, kinds of support from others, and signs of anxiety and low mood.

Trouble keeping up with distancing rules was the stress factor most tied to both anxiety and low mood. Warm, caring support from others was the strongest shield against both. Help with goods and money eased low mood in particular, and older adults with chronic illness faced higher risk. The authors urge support that guards daily contact, not just safety from infection.
pmc-12786567:
Tianyi Feng and co-authors study how iron and silicon impurities shape the strength of aluminum-copper-lithium alloys, metals prized for aircraft. Trace iron and silicon sneak in, above all when scrap is recycled. The team made five alloy mixes with iron and silicon each held between 0.03 and 0.12 percent by weight. All went through the same chain of heating, extrusion, solution treatment, and aging.

Iron pushed the growth of coarse, skeletal iron-bearing crystals. Silicon favored blocky iron-silicon phases and plain silicon grains. More iron cut strength, ductility, and fracture toughness. The harm runs two ways: the iron phases persist, act as stress points, and start cracks; and iron eats up copper that would otherwise form the key strengthening particles. Silicon hurt less. For makers of recycled alloys: control iron tightly; silicon is the lever to trade for lower cost.
pmc-12786867:
Soyeon Jung, Sodam Yi, and Seokchan Eun evaluated using a flap of tissue from the upper arm to rebuild heels after skin cancer removal, in a 2025 study. Heel repairs must withstand body weight, pressure, and rubbing, which makes them demanding. Eight patients treated between 2014 and 2020 received a free lateral arm flap after wide excision of their tumors.

The defects averaged thirty-two square centimeters, and operations lasted about three hours. Function was scored at least a year later by an examiner who had not operated, using two standard scales for leg and foot function. The authors set out to judge whether this flap's mix of durability and appearance serves heel patients well in practice.
pmc-12787167:
Barr and four co-authors test treated dietary protein in mice on high fat diets, in work from twenty twenty-five. Fatty liver disease linked to metabolism is rising, and diet change is hard to sustain. A protein treatment with ammonium hydroxide may soften liver harm without strict dieting.

Mice ate high fat diets built on beef or casein protein, with or without the treatment. Liver metabolism signaling was tracked by sex and age. Effects differed between males and females and across ages. Molecular evidence like this is an early step; it does not yet show the approach works in people.
pmc-12787367:
Marius Nicolae Baba and Mirela Camelia Baba map the review literature on wood and polymer mixes. Their paper from 2025 notes that these mixes draw wide interest for their range of uses and green appeal. Many reviews exist, but no one had joined the reviews themselves into one map.

A search of a major database up to June 2025 gave fifty one review papers after screening. Network tools traced how the reviews cite each other and group by topic and key words. Three linked themes lead the field: stronger joints between wood and polymer, how making shapes traits, and green design. Machine based making and recycled inputs stand out as growth areas.
pmc-12787967:
Giulia Moretto and co-authors study a lemon verbena leaf extract for its power to block harmful sugar-protein reactions, in work published in 2025. Those reactions build up products called AGEs in the body, which are linked to ageing and degenerative disease. Plant compounds can interfere with the chemistry at several steps.

The extract proved rich in several families of plant metabolites. In lab tests, it strongly blocked AGE formation at the middle and end steps of the reaction, and it trapped two reactive sugar fragments at high rates. Computer docking suggested the compounds can bind the receptor that AGEs activate. Simulated digestion broke down much of the extract, leaving about forty percent accessible. The bioaccessible part kept some protective activity. The work weighs promise against losses in digestion.
pmc-12788267:
Qinghua Zhang, Zhenxing Liu, Jianbo Wu, Ping Sun, and Hanwen Zhang design a flexible pressure sensor with a graded porous layer, in a research paper from 2025. Pressure sensors usually trade sensitivity against range: keen sensors saturate early. The team aimed to keep both wide range and sharp response.

The sensing film mixes plastic with carbon nanotubes over printed silver electrodes. Mixed sugar grains of two sizes form uneven pores when washed away, building the graded structure. Tests showed near-perfect linearity and high sensitivity across a wide pressure span. The sensor answered in fifty milliseconds and survived over five hundred cycles with little drift.
pmc-12788467:
Shaji Varghese and co-authors model tooth movement with braces, in a study published in 2025. When front teeth are pulled back and pushed up at once, the anchor molars can drift forward, a loss called anchorage loss. Small implants in the front are meant to hold that drift. The team tested whether the implants help, using a computer model built from scans.

Their model of an upper jaw compared setups with and without the small screws, under a steady pull and three levels of upward force. Pulling back without upward force gave the least molar drift. Adding upward force raised drift in all setups, and the implant setup at the strongest force drifted most. The authors caution that more force is not always better in this common extraction plan.
pmc-12788567:
Mohammad Alam and five colleagues used artificial intelligence to track jaw growth in teenagers, in a 2025 study. Orthodontists plan treatment around how a young face will grow. Hand tracing of skull X-rays is slow and varies between observers, so the team tested an AI method that overlays images taken eighteen months apart.

The study followed ninety adolescents aged eleven to sixteen, split evenly among horizontal, vertical, and average growth patterns. The AI overlays proved highly repeatable between runs. Jaw length grew most in the horizontal group, while lower face height grew most in the vertical group. Standard measures separated the groups clearly. The authors conclude that AI overlay analysis is reliable and fast. They suggest it could sharpen diagnosis and growth forecasts in everyday orthodontic practice.
pmc-12794367:
Taryn Fuentes-Castillo and co-authors present a method for mapping forest carbon in fine detail, tested in the old-growth forests of Chilean Patagonia. Honest carbon credit systems need maps that show where carbon sits and how it moves, not just rough totals. The method fuses three streams: tower sensors that breathe with the forest in real time, airborne and satellite images, and computer models. Together they pin down the model's settings and spread its readings across the landscape.

The output gives carbon stored in above-ground wood at 30 meter detail. It also gives the forest's net carbon exchange at 30 meters every half hour. Because ground truth steers the spread, the maps carry less doubt than inventory-based estimates. The authors offer the recipe as a repeatable tool for climate policy, conservation planning, and nature-based finance.
pmc-12795767:
Ulfi Hida Zainita and co-authors present a 2025 qualitative study on social media disorder among Indonesian college students. Nearly half of Indonesia's population used social media in 2024, and heavy passive use can slide into disorder. Most research blames personal habits, so this team explored the social and cultural forces around the habit.

They interviewed 12 students aged 18 to 22 from twelve faculties at the Universitas Indonesia. All used the same six major apps. Nine shared themes emerged, starting with sheer duration of daily use. The analysis reads the disorder through a socio-ecological lens, from family norms to platform design. The findings suggest fixes must reach beyond willpower. Campus programs and cultural change both have roles to play.
pmc-12796367:
A breast cancer subtype once lumped with the untargetable now has its own drug class, so telling it apart matters. Junzhong Liu and co-authors test whether a synthetic MRI measure can spot HER2-low tumors without a biopsy in a 2025 study.

Scans from one hundred fifty patients at one hospital formed the training set, with ninety-eight patients from a second hospital for outside validation. Of the many values the scanner reports, one relaxation measure, T2, separated the groups best. It distinguished low from over-expressing tumors and zero from low with moderate accuracy in both cohorts. The authors present the quick, noninvasive measure as decision support for tailoring therapy, not a replacement for tissue testing.
pmc-12799067:
Abrar-Ahmad Zulfiqar, Rezika Bellazouz, and Minh Huynh report a rare cause of sudden breathing trouble in an older man, in a 2025 case. The man, aged eighty-seven, came in with hard breathing on the in-breath and a worsening voice. A bone growth along the front of his neck spine was pressing on his airway. The condition is known as Forestier's disease.

A scope exam showed one side of his voice box was paralyzed. Swelling was also present in the throat area. Scans revealed the large bone growth squeezing the airway. Old nerve paralysis, new swelling, and steady pressure combined to block airflow. The authors stress fast imaging and scope checks in such cases. Early recognition allows quick and effective care, they conclude.
pmc-12799267:
Pedro Almeida and co-authors tell the case of a young adult whose lung illness first revealed a weak immune system in a 2025 report. The patient, aged nineteen, had mild flu-like signs, yet scans showed many lung spots and swollen glands. Her spleen was large, and blood counts were low.

Her past held repeat infections as a child, and tests showed very low antibody levels. A lung sample confirmed a lung disease tied to a known immune defect. Antibody therapy kept her lung spots stable with no new infections. The case urges doctors to test immune health when scans look far worse than symptoms.
pmc-12800067:
Tomoyo Sawada leads a large team studying a gene tied to schizophrenia in this twenty twenty-five paper. Rare broken copies of the gene raise the risk of the illness. What the working gene does in the brain, and why its loss matters, were unclear. Its role for patients without the rare change was also unknown.

Working with human fetal brain tissue and lab-grown nerve cells, the team mapped where the gene's protein binds and which genes it controls. It favored the start sites of genes tied to mental illness risk, DNA repair, and nerve signaling. The results link one rare cause to pathways shared by the wider illness.
pmc-12802067:
Eunjin Bae reviews how a class of diabetes drugs also lowers uric acid in the blood, a side benefit with heart and kidney implications. SGLT2 inhibitors, which block sugar reabsorption in the kidney, cut serum urate in trials. Humans, lacking the enzyme uricase, handle urate differently from most mammals, so the route matters.

Bae walks through how the kidneys and gut share urate excretion, and how excess urate drives gout, stones, and wider disease risk. The drugs appear to block a kidney exchanger that reclaims urate, letting more escape in urine. The review ties a glucose drug's hidden plumbing to protection beyond blood sugar.
pmc-12802167:
Mingjie Xu and co-authors asked in 2025 how thinning a subtropical conifer plantation in China affects its carbon budget. China has planted vast forests that soak up carbon, but aging plantations need management. Thinning helps in the long run yet disturbs the forest at first, which can cost carbon.

The team compared three ways of measuring carbon flows, and judged the two-tower method most dependable for tracking seasonal patterns. All three agreed that moderate thinning raised the forest's carbon uptake, its breathing, and its net gain. Uptake rose more in the second year, but breathing rose even faster then. The study gives managers a firmer basis for carbon accounting after thinning.
pmc-12804867:
Laurence Howe and a large team ask a plain question in a 2025 study: when do cell tests in a dish match traits in people? They use gene screens where genes are switched off in cells. They also use human data on loss of gene function.

Their frame, called GPAT, checks if a gene change moves the cell trait and the human trait in the same way. It compares both the path and the size of the effect. The aim is to judge which lab models can stand in for real illness. That helps teams pick models for drug work with more care and less guesswork.
pmc-12804967:
Sara Mogedano-Cruz and seven co-authors map two leg nerves with ultrasound and test which body measures forecast their depth, in a 2025 study. Guided shots and pain work need exact nerve spots. Depth varies by person, which can sink a procedure. Thirty healthy adults had both nerves scanned and their bodies measured in detail.

No left-right gaps appeared for any measure. Fat layer depth and limb girth tracked nerve depth closely. Models using fat depth, limb length, and girth explained most of the spread in nerve depth for both nerves. The authors say simple body measures can help plan safer guided work. The thigh fat layer stood out as the top clue.
pmc-12806567:
Baloch, Javed, and Grosu audit tool-assisted births at Bedford Hospital. Forceps and vacuum cups help when labor stalls or the baby is at risk. Rates have fallen worldwide, yet the skill stays vital. Good notes and rule-based care guard mother and baby.

The audit covered all 62 attempted tool births in late 2024. Records came from electronic maternity files and a data hub. The team checked tool type, success rate, and time to birth. Consent and note quality were also graded in full. Care was weighed against national and local rule sets. Gaps point to training and form fixes.
pmc-12808167:
Chengfei Zhang and eleven co-authors show a growth part, PRAS40, feeds colon cancer stem traits by way of sugar burn. Their study appeared in twenty twenty-five. Stem-like cells drive this cancer's growth and cure shrug. The part ran high in tumor cuts and tied to short life. Its cut-out curbed tumor birth in mice.

With the part, cells made more balls, bore more stem marks, and seeded tumors with ease. It binds and wakes a sugar burn step and draws in a tag crew that tags that step, which fires the burn. Block of the tag step cut stem traits and tumor birth in tests.
pmc-12808267:
An Arctic peat core keeps the shells of tiny amoebae for centuries, and Alexis Stansfield and three co-authors read those shells for a climate story in a 2025 paper. One amoeba species hosts algae inside itself and can feed two ways: by sunlight, through its guests, or by hunting like other amoebae.

Carbon isotope ratios in the shells betray which way the amoeba fed, since the two diets leave different signatures. A mixing model against the peat moss record put numbers on the split through time. The shells show a clear turn after the late 1980s toward more sun feeding. The species then spread, and shell sizes in several amoeba kinds shrank. Set beside plant and climate records, the shift reads as a living response to a warming Arctic, captured in a jar of peat.
pmc-12808367:
Nan Jiang, Yanchun Ma, Huijun Chen, and Chengjia Li review work, given in the head as a 2025 paper, on a toxic fat-breakdown product as a target in diabetic heart disease. The disease creeps up in people with diabetes, first stiffening the heart, then killing cells and laying down scar, on the path to heart failure. No therapy yet hits its core mechanisms.

The product in view forms when the fats packed in heart cells oxidise under the strain of diabetes. It attacks the cell's inner parts at once: draining energy, flooding calcium, blocking waste cleanup, and sparking an iron-linked cell death. The review maps those hits across the power units, storage nets, and cleanup sacs of the cell. Candidate therapies span a detox enzyme booster, cell guards aimed at power units, and blockers of the iron death path.
pmc-12810067:
Jesspreet Kaur and co-authors report a devastating surgical complication in a 2025 ophthalmology case report. A seventy-two-year-old man with advanced pseudoexfoliation glaucoma, unresponsive to maximal drops, received a PreserFlo MicroShunt implant to drain fluid and cut eye pressure.

The operation overshot: pressure fell too low, the macula wrinkled, and within three weeks his sight collapsed to bare light perception despite a healthy-looking drainage bleb. Attempts to repressurize the eye swung pressure wildly high instead. The authors present the sequence as wipe-out syndrome, a feared sudden loss of remaining vision, and review the risk signs in eyes like this one.
pmc-12810167:
Divya Singh and co-authors compare herbal extracts with a standard mouthwash in this 2025 lab study. The target germ causes tooth decay, and the standard rinse, chlorhexidine, works well but has side effects with long use. Most people in poor countries lean on plant remedies for basic care.

Plates of the germ were treated with tulsi, a three-fruit blend called triphala, aloe vera, and the standard rinse. Growth-free zones were measured after a day. The standard rinse won clearly, but all three herbs showed real killing power. Tulsi led the herbs, then triphala, with aloe vera last. The authors suggest the extracts could form a herbal rinse for people who prefer natural options.
pmc-12812567:
Mengjie Mao, Mengling Hu, Qingxiu Tao, Zhuo Zuo, and Bin Liu report a rare lung cancer that mimics bowel cancer under the microscope. The head of the text dates the report to 2025, though the catalog lists 2026. Pulmonary enteric adenocarcinoma grows gland structures like colorectal tumors, and here it appeared in both lungs of an elderly man at once, a presentation barely documented before.

Stains for bowel markers came back positive while lung markers were negative, complicating the call between a lung primary and spread from the gut. Gene tests found KRAS, TP53, and APC mutations together, pointing to a bowel-like growth program. Surgery plus chemo and radiation brought short-term stability. The case argues for joint molecular and stain profiling.
pmc-12812667:
Yue Dan, Qian Li, Ting Xu, Xuemei Tu, and Li Yan study life space mobility in older patients after a heart procedure to open a blocked artery. How far older adults move through their daily world ties to healthy aging and quality of life, yet its drivers after such care are not well known.

Their cross-sectional study enrolled older outpatients at a large hospital in Chongqing. Surveys measured social support, health literacy, and intrinsic capacity, next to life space mobility. The team tests if the last two sit in the middle: that is, if support lifts mobility in part by lifting knowledge and inner capacity.
pmc-12812867:
Breeders now predict crop traits from DNA and spectral data, and deep learning can catch nonlinear patterns that older statistical methods miss — but few breeders can build such models from scratch. Freddy Mora-Poblete and co-authors introduce MTMEGPS in this paper (published 2025). It is an R software package that wraps deep learning genomic and phenomic selection into a full workflow, from data preparation through training and evaluation.

The package handles single or multiple traits across single or multiple environments. Tested on built-in maize and eucalyptus datasets and on an independent public trial, it beat benchmark models in most scenarios, especially for single-trait prediction internally and multi-trait prediction on the external set. Prediction errors stayed in a moderate range throughout. The authors present the tool as a practical way to bring deep learning into breeding programs without heavy programming.
pmc-12813067:
Xin Liu and co-authors present a study, published in 2025, that maps sugar coats on a worm vaccine candidate in fine detail. The target is a gut enzyme set from a blood feeding worm that drains farm animals. Sugar chains on such proteins shape how the host immune system sees them, but site by site maps were missing.

Mass tools that read whole sugar tagged pieces found seven enzymes of the set, with 19 sugar sites and 31 sugar shapes among them. Rich core fucose marks stood out. Thirteen tagged pieces were grabbed by the guard antibodies that shield animals. Docking models place those pieces on the protein face or near its intake channel. The map guides a smarter vaccine build.
pmc-12813567:
Akira Morimoto and co-authors test a pain-control method in a 2025 study of balloon angioplasty for dialysis access. Widening a narrowed forearm fistula with a balloon often hurts enough to make patients flinch or resist, yet doctors want pain relief without paralyzing the arm or causing body-wide side effects.

The retrospective study covers seventy-seven patients treated at one center. Ultrasound-guided blocks of the skin nerves in the forearm, using lidocaine, were applied before the procedure. The authors recorded block time, procedure time, drug volume, complications, and how well pain was controlled. Their aim was a targeted block that numbs the skin while leaving movement intact.
pmc-12815567:
Mamata Kene and five co-authors charted child emergency visits for breathing ills before, through, and after COVID in a 2025 study. The pandemic warped both germ spread and how families seek care. Their data came from twenty one emergency rooms of one large health system in Northern California across six years.

Near one hundred fifty two thousand visits fit the study. Visits sank each month in early 2020 to a low of a few hundred in June. After child vaccines landed, visits roared back and peaked far above the old norm in one month. The mix of ages, ills, and past health shifted across the three spans. The authors say the swings matter for staffing plans ahead of future surges.
pmc-12815767:
Peiqin Li and colleagues test a traditional Chinese herbal mix against lung cancer in mice, in this study published in twenty twenty-five. The mix, called Jinfu'an decoction, is already used to treat lung cancer and has shown anti-tumor effects in past work. Here the team asks how it works, by joining two tools: body chemistry profiling and gut microbe analysis.

The team grew human lung tumor cells under the skin of mice, then split them into groups. Three groups got low, medium, or high doses of the mix by tube feeding for twenty-one days, next to an untreated tumor group and a healthy group. By tracking tumor growth along with blood and tissue chemistry and gut microbes, the study maps the paths through which the mix may slow tumors. The design gives later work a base for testing single active parts.
pmc-12815967:
Korry Wirth and co-authors kill drug-resistant bacteria from children's appendix infections with light and dye, in this 2025 study. Ruptured appendicitis is the top cause of belly abscess in children and breeds hard-to-treat germs. The team grew bacteria from thirty young patients' surgical fluid, soaked them in methylene blue, and lit them with a red laser.

The treatment cut the main species by over ninety-nine point nine percent, matching its power on resistant and sensitive strains alike. One species, Pseudomonas, proved hardier. The authors propose the method as a helper beside antibiotics in surgery.
pmc-12816267:
Raif Cavolli and Dogan Kahraman report long-term results for a root repair of the main heart artery, dated 2025 in the head. The repair swaps the swollen root and valve for a graft that keeps the root shape. The team tracked forty-eight patients treated over more than a decade for one root ill.

One patient died from the surgery itself, and three more died late from heart, brain, or lung causes. About ninety-six in a hundred patients lived five years, and about ninety-five in a hundred lived ten years. Bleeding was the main late ill, and the authors call the graft safe for this use.
pmc-12816667:
Olivia Maurice, Caroline Jones, and Celia Harris study multilingualism and thinking in later life in a 2025 paper. Speaking several languages has been linked to delayed dementia in population studies, but lab evidence for working memory, control, and attention effects is mixed. Task and measurement choices may explain the conflict.

Ninety four adults aged eighteen to eighty three completed memory, control, and attention tasks in sound and visual forms. Language experience was measured continuously with a questionnaire. Models found no link for auditory tasks and most visual tasks. A selective effect did emerge for visuospatial working memory in later life.
pmc-12817667:
Sandra Milena Castellar-Leones and co-authors report twin sisters with Fabry disease and nerve pain in a 2025 case study. The inherited disorder harms many organs, including small skin nerves. Both girls carry one faulty gene copy and showed burning limb sensations plus gut trouble. Sensory testing gave hard numbers for their small fiber function.

One twin showed altered heat, pain, and vibration thresholds. The other showed only dulled vibration sense. Both patterns back small fiber damage as the pain source. Such signs are often missed or blamed elsewhere in children. Early testing can speed enzyme therapy and slow disease harm, the authors argue.
pmc-12817767:
Zewditu Denu and thirteen colleagues measured whether mothers in Ethiopia give birth with skilled help at hand, and whether that care works in fact. Skilled help at birth cuts deaths of mothers and newborns, but only when sites are ready and care is good. The study covered the population. It used a cascade with four steps toward coverage adjusted for quality. Site readiness came from a 2019 check of services. The final figure was built step by step: attendance, readiness, care given, quality of process.

Crude coverage for skilled delivery stood at fifty-four percent. Each cascade step then cut that figure down toward true coverage that works. The gap between contact and quality is the heart of the story: many women reach a site that lacks key supplies or skills. For planners in Ethiopia, the 2025 numbers show where the chain breaks, supplies, skills, or follow-through.
pmc-12819167:
