Xiang Han proposes a graph-based offline learning method for robot path planning. His study from twenty twenty-six tackles long-horizon navigation. Sparse rewards make ordinary reinforcement learning inefficient here. Hierarchical methods split the job into subgoals and steps.

Earlier latent-space subgoal methods search a continuous space wastefully. Training instability and slow convergence follow from that search. Han's design places subgoals on a learned latent graph instead. A proven policy algorithm runs at both hierarchy levels. Offline training uses logged data rather than live trials. Structured subgoal spaces should stabilise the learning process. Warehouse and service robots need exactly this reliability.
pmc-12819467:
Qianzhi Wang and co-authors warn that harsh low-yield spans for sun and wind power will swell world-wide as the air warms. Green growth is the core cure path, yet the cure's own yield can sag in bad runs. Their 2025 study casts low-yield odds in three fate paths, from low to high gas pour. Low-yield risk climbs in a third of lands even on the kind path, and in near two thirds on the harsh one.

Wind low-yield is near set to climb in most built yards by late age. Sun odds split by path: down on the kind path, up wide on the harsh one. Poor lands bear risk at near twice the world rate on the harsh path. Grid plans must bank spare yield for bad runs.
pmc-12820167:
Qiu and coauthors build a stiff scope frame that stops drift in fine imaging. Single-molecule imaging can locate points at nanometer scale. Sample drift during shots blurs that sharp result. Most fixes correct drift after shots or add marker beads.

Their frame stops drift at its source in the hardware. Holed parts linked by tungsten steel rods form the cage. Bench tests showed lateral drift near five nanometers in two hours. Single-molecule runs held drift to a narrow band in 15 minutes. No axial drift could be measured in those runs. The design may ease super-fine imaging in plain labs.
pmc-12820267:
Hans Petter Sejrup leads a team of seven authors in 2025 in reading two and a half centuries of ocean history from the shells of tiny sea creatures. Warm Atlantic water flowing into the Nordic Seas carries heat toward the Arctic and forms a key limb of the great Atlantic overturning circulation.

From oxygen isotopes in foraminifera shells, the team built a year-by-year record running from 1750 to 1992. The record tracks the temperature of the surface inflow waters. It reveals a sharp rise in temperature instability starting in the mid twentieth century, a shift not recognized before. Such records help test whether the modern ocean is behaving unusually.
pmc-12821167:
Semin Jang and three colleagues weigh the cost and benefit of adding acupotomy to a spinal steroid injection for a painful back condition, in a 2025 study. Acupotomy blends acupuncture with a small cutting tool that frees stuck soft tissue.

In a trial of fifty patients, the combined care cost less overall than the injection alone over eight weeks. It also gave slightly better quality of life, so it won on both cost and benefit. Savings came mostly from less lost work time. The authors warn that the trial was small, short, and run at one center, so wider proof is still needed.
pmc-12821267:
A blood marker for prostate cancer is itself shaped by gene variants, and two of those variants tie to cancer risk. Srilakshmi Srinivasan and co-authors modeled how the variants change the marker's motion in this 2025 study. The marker, PSA, is a protein-cutting enzyme made by the prostate. The two variants each swap one building block of the protein and lower its activity.

Computer modeling found no drastic shape change from either swap. Long motion simulations told a subtler story, though. Two loops on the normal protein stayed near their starting pose for the full run. In both variants those loops came loose, and the protein flexed more. Extra flex could explain the lower activity and the risk link. The work shows risk can hide in dynamics, not just shape.
pmc-12821867:
Shun Yoshida and nine co-authors hunt what drives early grave infection in old folks with a vessel flare ill tied to MPO-ANCA. Their study appeared in twenty twenty-five. Drugs that calm the immune set have lifted life odds in this ill, yet infections early in care stay a top risk in the old. Fifty patients aged past seventy-five at one hub were checked, all with the small-vessel form.

Grave infections hit one third of them in six months of care start. A drug pair used to guard lungs, TMP-SMX, tied to a sharp drop in infection risk, and held past checks for sex. The team pitch lung guard use for high-risk old folks, with care for the watch-only design.
pmc-12822267:
Anne-Marie Burn, Hayley Gains, Poppy Hall, and Joanna Anderson ask schools how to meet self-harm whole in a 2025 study. Self-harm is rife in the teen years, and schools are a first place a cut or a burn can be seen, yet staff oft feel bare of craft.

Seven talk rounds with staff and young folk drew one shared tale. A school must first grasp what self-harm is and how wide it runs. It must then build the whole staff's craft to act. Last, it must make the school a place where a teen can speak and be held. The team turned the tale to rules of work a school can pick up and use.
pmc-12823567:
Ana Paula Azambuja, Megan Rothstein, Tatiane Y Kanno, and Marcos Simoes-Costa show that the embryo's chromatin landscape is patterned in space during gastrulation, in a 2025 study. How cells record their position in the early embryo was unclear. Using spatially resolved genomic methods in bird embryos, the team watched the regulatory DNA landscape as the body plan forms.

They found that chromatin openness and activity form gradients along the embryo's axes. These gradients appear at developmental gene sites right as gastrulation begins, and they are precise enough to infer a cell's position from its chromatin alone. The authors conclude that laying down the body plan includes organizing the epigenome in space.
pmc-12824267:
Ntelekwane Khasapane and co-authors study drug resistance in bacteria taken from cows with hidden udder infection, in work from 2025. The infection lowers milk output and can shelter hard to treat germs. Two Enterococcus species are a growing cause of this infection in dairy cows.

Samples came from milk and cow dung. Standard tests found the hidden infection in a large share of cows and udder quarters. Lab methods named the species and checked which drugs still worked against them. The team also looked for genes tied to harm. Local data like this guide farm level control and drug choice.
pmc-12824367:
Chiara Herzog and co-authors set out guidance in 2025 for how firms that work on aging should collect marker data in clinical trials. Markers of aging could help sort trial participants, pick treatments, and track whether a treatment works. Without shared practice, data from different trials is hard to compare or reuse.

The authors propose common standards for what to collect and how. Shared tools and early alignment across firms would let the field check and rank markers together. They argue this would raise the quality of trial data at little extra cost. It would also help the wider science of aging, beyond any one firm's program.
pmc-12824467:
Sakher Ja'anini and Aseel Al-Ma'ai'a report a 2025 case of a heart attack that announced itself without chest pain. A sixty-year-old man with diabetes, high blood pressure, past heart attack, and a weak heart arrived after fainting, with severe belly pain. Nothing hurt in his chest, which could easily have sent doctors down the wrong path.

An electrocardiogram told the true story: a major heart attack in the lower wall of the heart. He received blood-thinning drugs and was rushed for vessel imaging, which found his right coronary artery blocked. The authors warn that heart attacks can wear disguises, above all in patients with diabetes and other risk factors for atypical signs. Fainting or belly pain alone should still trigger heart checks. Fast suspicion matters, since delays in reopening the artery raise the risk of death and lasting damage.
pmc-12826567:
Giovani Burgos and Alex Trillo study how discrimination is measured in Latino health research, in a paper from 2025. Feeling discriminated against is tied to worse health. Most studies, though, flatten Latino groups into one bloc and use a single score. That habit can hide real gaps and bend the results.

Using a national survey of Latino and Asian Americans, they test a common discrimination scale group by group. The scale split cleanly into two sides: subtle slights and overt acts. That two-sided form fit every Latino group in the data. When the scale was modeled that way, its link to depression and chronic illness grew stronger. The authors say finer scales give truer answers. Splitting the bloc also reveals how each group fares on its own.
pmc-12827067:
Haitao Xie and co-authors examine a blood fat ratio and a heart stress marker in a study published in 2025. The ratio compares all cholesterol except the protective kind against that protective kind, giving a broad view of fat balance. The marker, NT-proBNP, rises when the heart is strained.

Data came from a national survey group from 1999 to 2004 and from hospital inpatients treated in early 2025. Women showed a higher rate of raised marker levels than men after age adjustment. As the fat ratio rose, the rate of raised marker levels fell in the survey group. The authors used layered models, curve fits, and subgroup checks to test whether the link held across groups.
pmc-12827567:
Paola Gobbi and co-authors update the genetic map of small ruminant lentiviruses in Italy, in a study first shared in 2025, though the catalog lists 2026. These retroviruses infect sheep and goats and vary a great deal. They cause a range of slow illnesses and cross between the two hosts with ease. Samples came from routine watch work in sixteen of Italy's twenty regions.

Family tree analysis of samples from 2019 to 2024 showed wide variety across the country. Some virus clusters stayed locked to single regions. The clusters did not match the current naming scheme for subtypes. That mismatch suggests the scheme needs an update. The authors call for steady watch work with full gene reads. A fresh classification would help vets track how these viruses spread and change.
pmc-12827667:
Xinfu Lian and co-authors probe how a senna plant fights brain swelling in Parkinson's disease, in a 2025 paper. The slow brain illness ties tight to swelling, yet strong anti-swell drugs are few. The team used network methods to map the plant's active parts against disease targets.

More than one hundred candidate targets surfaced, with three swelling paths standing out. One lead compound, rhein, docked tight to a master swelling switch in the sums. In dish tests on brain immune cells, rhein cut swelling outputs and dimmed that switch's firing. The authors read the plant as a multi-target anti-swell agent and a fair lead for deeper study.
pmc-12829067:
Sara Paparini and five co-authors explored in 2025 why people with HIV in the United Kingdom joined, or declined, a study of long-acting injectable treatment. Trials often fail to recruit people who match the patients the drugs serve, which deepens health gaps. The team interviewed and surveyed both joiners and decliners of the study.

Three themes ran through the answers. Solidarity with others living with HIV pulled people in. The wish for a normal life cut both ways, since injections free people from daily pills but add clinic visits. Trust in their own clinicians tipped many choices. Trial designers can act on all three.
pmc-12830667:
Zaagan and three co-authors improve a process control chart with machine learning in a paper from 2025. Control charts watch a factory process and flag shifts, but charts that trim extreme values can miss real changes, while classic charts assume tidy data. Their hybrid chart lets an anomaly model weigh each new reading before it enters the running average.

Simulations across dirty-data settings and shift sizes showed the hybrid kept false alarms lower than classic charts. It also caught moderate shifts faster. A case study on real contaminated process data backed the lab results. The authors offer the chart for robust monitoring where outliers are common.
pmc-12830867:
Naike Su and co-authors promote a small carp, called Juji, as a cleaner model for studying how fish sex organs develop, in a 2025 paper. The usual model, zebrafish, has quirks that muddy results, including lost sex genes in lab strains. Juji keeps a genetic sex system. The team built a glowing reporter line that lights up germ cells for life.

Early brightness of the glow, not the number of germ cells, foretold adult sex. Gene scans of young ovaries and testes found the expected master switches among the differing genes. Knocking out one switch, dmrt1, turned young males into females, and transplanted male germ cells also became female inside mutants, proving the switch acts through the support cells.
pmc-12830967:
Shiva Raj Acharya, Sudarshan Subedi, and Diwash Timilsina link two common conditions to suicidal thinking in Korean adults, in a study published in 2025. Drawing on three years of a national health panel, they analyzed over thirty-two thousand adults. About thirty percent were obese by the Korean cutoff, fourteen percent had diabetes, and five and a half percent reported suicidal ideation.

Each condition alone raised the odds of suicidal thoughts modestly, and having both raised them similarly. The links ran stronger in some groups: diabetic and obese women, and younger obese adults, showed notably higher odds. The authors argue that clinics treating diabetes and obesity should treat the combination as a flag for mental-health screening, an often-missed pairing in a country with high suicide rates.
pmc-12831267:
Rashid Nasr and a team of colleagues published a headache survey in two thousand twenty-five among Sudanese health sciences students. Migraine and tension headaches are common in students and hurt study performance. Data from Sudan were scarce.

The questionnaire reached nearly one thousand eight hundred medical, dental, and pharmacy students. About forty-two percent reported recurring headaches. Migraine made up about twenty-four percent and tension headache about eighteen percent. Light sensitivity came with most migraines. Stress and lost sleep were the top triggers. Nine in ten students treated themselves with shop-bought painkillers, and few saw a doctor. About a fifth had missed classes or exams because of headaches.
pmc-12832567:
Rachid and co-authors detail a stubborn case of heart artery spasm in a 2025 report. A 46-year-old woman suffered night chest pain with fleeting heart trace changes. Her right heart artery clamped shut hard enough to slow her pulse. Standard drips eased then failed her, and a camera inside the artery showed the spasm directly.

A shot of vessel relaxant into the artery freed the clamp. Blood tests then found low phosphate and low vitamin D. After phosphate top-up, no new spasms came. The authors suggest low phosphate can feed vessel spasm by starving heart muscle of energy. They urge metabolic checks in hard vasospasm cases.
pmc-12834867:
Marc Kidess and co-authors pilot a new scan for germ cell tumors in a 2025 study. These tumors, most often in the testicle, are the most common cancer in young men, and survival runs high thanks to surgery and drug therapy. Standard CT is the usual staging tool, but a PET scan that targets a protein switched on in tumor support tissue may spot hidden spread.

The pilot tests the tracer-based scan in tumors of the gonads and in the rarer cases that start elsewhere in the body. The paper sets the stage with how these cancers present: most at stage one, a fifth with spread to belly nodes, and a tenth with distant spread. Early proof on where the new scan helps would guide larger trials.
pmc-12835267:
Jeeyoung Kim and co-authors test sphingolipids as markers of long-term air pollution exposure in a 2025 metabolomics study in South Korea. Blood fat shifts from dirty air were reported before, but long-term targeted proof was thin.

Plasma from close to two hundred adults in a dusty-area lung cohort was profiled for sphingolipids and amino acids. Yearly particle and nitrogen dioxide levels at each home came from a national model. Long-term particle exposure tied loosely to higher sphingomyelins before strict correction. In the lung disease subgroup, several sphingomyelin links passed the strict bar. Nitrogen dioxide tied to one ceramide and glutamate. The authors call for larger cohorts to confirm.
pmc-12836767:
Sareh-Sadat Heydari and co-authors pool trials of carotenoids on liver enzymes in a 2025 review. These plant pigments act as antioxidants, and liver enzyme levels hint at liver strain. Past trial results on the pair clash, so the team graded the full proof with the GRADE method.

Searches to late 2024 found 15 trials with 757 adults, a mix of healthy people and patients. Pooled sums showed no firm shift in any of the four enzymes tracked, from ALT to GGT. Dose response and bias checks ran beside the main sums. The flat result says pigment pills alone do not move liver marks much.
pmc-12836867:
Wang-Sheng Lin and five co-authors tracked fitness trends in older adults who live at home in Taiwan. Their study, from twenty twenty-five, starts from the worth of fitness for free life in old age. Long term proof on many sides of fitness in Asian elders was thin. The group held four hundred three adults of age sixty-five and up. They joined a community health drive and took the same tests at three points in time.

Tests spanned grip strength, arm curls, chair stands, balance on one leg, timed up and go, step and walk endurance, and reach and stretch marks. The team read which way each trait moved and what traits pushed the change. Readers in elder health get a rare long view of fitness drift.
pmc-12836967:
Yang and coauthors study a gene that may drive heart harm in sepsis. The gene, called JunB, was high in hurt heart tissue. Its role in sepsis heart harm had not been probed yet. The team built cell and mouse models of that harm.

Toxin-treated heart cells and septic mice both served as models. The team lowered JunB in each model and tracked results. Cell death, swelling signals, and stress marks all fell. A growth path in cells switched on as JunB fell. A blocker of that path erased the gains in cells. The work names JunB as a drug target worth study.
pmc-12837067:
Shiqi Zhang and six co-authors screen close contacts of lung TB patients in Shanghai, in a 2025 study. Catching the disease early in household and close contacts is a core brake on its spread. Over two years the team checked about 1,040 contacts in one district with symptom forms, chest images, and a blood test for hidden infection. Positive screens went on to spit tests to confirm live disease.

Most contacts were cleared, with a small set flagged by each screen type. The sharpest risk sat with contacts of patients whose spit grew the germ, and with contacts whose own symptom screen raised a flag. The pairing of those two raised risk further still. The authors urge follow-up teams to spend their closest watch on those two groups, where new cases are likeliest to surface.
pmc-12837667:
Ferraris and co-authors compare throat microbes in people before and after chronic lung disease sets in, in a 2025 study. The pharynx hosts a microbial community that guards the airways, and its disruption tracks with respiratory illness. Swabs came from three small groups: people with pre-COPD, pre-COPD patients with an acute infection on antibiotics, and people with stable severe COPD. Gene sequencing profiled the microbes in each swab.

Diversity stayed full in the pre-COPD group but collapsed to a quarter or less in the infected and severe groups. Community makeup differed sharply across groups, above all at the broad phylum level. Functional profiles shifted little by comparison. The authors read the throat ecosystem as an early marker that frays as disease advances.
pmc-12837967:
Julia Keiner and three co-authors test why people remember words for living things better than words for objects. Their 2025 study examines the animacy advantage, a steady finding in memory research. The team suspected the edge comes from effort: people naturally pay more attention to living things while learning a list.

Two experiments attached point values to words, pushing learners to try harder on some items. Overall, living words were recalled better, and high-value words were recalled better. Under high effort, though, the living-word edge vanished, because recall of object words rose to match. The authors say effort during learning, not the words themselves, explains much of the classic effect.
pmc-12838067:
Shuguang Yang and seven co-authors built risk models in a 2025 study of patients admitted to intensive care with suspected infection. Such patients can slide into sepsis, and drug-proof infections raise the danger further. The team took data from 2,963 patients in 67 hospitals across China. They trained several machine learning models to flag, at admission, who might die or carry a drug-proof infection.

A simple model beat the fancier methods, scoring 0.87 for death and 0.86 for resistant infection. Recent surgery, a severity score, and blood infection flagged the risk of death. Certain bacteria, above all two hardy kinds, flagged resistant infection. Lung infection was the most common site, and deaths ran near 11 percent overall. The models could help units act sooner on the riskiest patients.
pmc-12838267:
Yuqing Meng and Mingpeng Huang ask why a kind work air breeds good rule bends in staff, in a study from 2025. Good bends break norms to fix or lift the work, a seed of fresh craft in firms. Polls from over four hundred staff in one large city fed a twin path model.

Kind air fed both a will to risk and a sense of home at work. Each of those then fed good bends in its own lane, with risk will the hinge of the pair. Home sense bridges air and act where risk will can not reach. The pair urge firms to grow back and home feel if they want bold good acts.
pmc-12839167:
Trukhin and co-authors fish specific antibodies out of blood serum with a gentle soap-like rinse instead of harsh acid. Studying disease-targeted antibodies is hampered because standard column methods eat costly antigen and acid baths can damage the catch or make it sticky. Their 2025 method anchors antigen on hydrogel chips or magnetic beads at tiny scale, then tries detergents as release agents.

One detergent, sodium lauroyl glutamate, freed up to seventy-eight percent of working antibodies. After a gel cleanup step, isolated antibodies kept most of their activity and stayed specific, with no detergent-induced stickiness. The workflow caught virus, food, and self-targeted antibodies plus total antibody stock. The authors offer it for deep antibody profiling.
pmc-12840167:
Ryoichi Sato, Mitsuki Fujiwara, Yasuyuki Nogami, Md Arshad Ali, and Yuta Kodera tune a chip-based random number maker in a 2025 study. Such makers spin tiny rings that flip states at high speed, then mix the outputs into random bits. Uneven bit mixes weaken the locks and codes built on them. Past work traced some of the unevenness to shaky signals entering the mixing gate.

The team asked how many latch stages after each ring clean up the signal. Models covered plain two-state signals and a third, in-between state that real circuits show. Tests on a real chip, checked against a standard test suite, told the same story. Two or more latch stages settled the signals and evened out the bit mix. The result gives chip designers a small, cheap fix for fairer random numbers.
pmc-12840467:
Rodrigo de Miguel uses a simple grid model to teach the ideal gas law in a paper from 2025. The law links the pressure, volume, and warmth of a gas. Textbooks often derive it by assuming a huge system at low density. De Miguel instead places free particles on a grid with a set number of boxes.

The analysis shows the gas law emerging as the gas settles into balance with its surroundings. No extra assumptions about size or density are needed. A second version treats volume as split into small steps and reaches the same result. The paper aims to give students a clearer view of what the law assumes.
pmc-12840667:
Wenhao Gao and co-authors tested food gels blending pork and soy for people who struggle to swallow, in a 2025 paper. Soft, water-holding gels make eating safer in dysphagia care. Three gums were mixed into a pork and whole soy milk gel. Levels ran from low to high for each gum.

The gums disrupted protein cross-links and softened the gels. At the same time, water holding improved a lot. One percent xanthan gum gave the best overall balance. Soft yet water-rich is exactly what swallowing diets need. The study guides recipe choices for care kitchens.
pmc-12843167:
Akram Khan and co-authors pool trial results on personal programs that ease doctor burnout, in a 2025 meta-analysis. Burnout shows up as exhaustion, detachment, and a lost sense of achievement. The team asked whether programs aimed at the individual doctor, rather than the workplace, move those scores. They searched medical databases for studies from 2009 to 2023 that used a standard burnout scale.

Seventeen studies fit the review, and six with 585 doctors could be pooled. The programs covered mindfulness courses, professional coaching, and peer discussion groups. Pooled results showed lower exhaustion and detachment, and higher sense of achievement, in the program groups. The authors note real limits: few trials, mixed program styles, and bias risk in many studies. They call the evidence promising but early.
pmc-12843467:
Ching-En Lin and four co-authors test a probiotic aimed at the gut-brain link in adults who feel their memory slipping. Subjective cognitive decline, where tests are still normal, is seen as a window to prevent Alzheimer's disease. Their 2025 study gave a supplement called ExoBDNF, built around a brain growth factor idea, for nine weeks in an open-label design. Before and after, participants took questionnaires on memory complaints, mood, and sleep, plus standard and computerized thinking tests.

The computer battery probed stopping, switching, and holding information in mind. An open design without a placebo group can show promise but not proof. The authors present the results as a case for a blinded trial. Gut-based routes to brain health are drawing wide interest, and this adds one tested product.
pmc-12844567:
Miae Oh and Sukhee Ahn test a class program that teaches fifth graders to prevent digital sexual violence, in a school in Korea, in work from 2025. Children meet sexual harm online earlier than many adults expect. Four weekly sessions covered the harm itself, digital citizenship, and gender sensitivity.

Two classes, twenty-seven children, took the program. Two other classes, twenty children, served as the control with no lessons. Tests before and after measured safety knowledge, self-protection habits, and digital citizenship. Scores in the taught group rose more than in the control group. The authors present the program as a workable school model for upper elementary grades.
pmc-12844967:
Elshafie, Kattoor, Kelly, and Wilkes adapted this test panel in twenty twenty-five for disease watch in wild meat-eating animals. Standard tests each hunt one germ at a time and can miss mixed infections. The team moved a targeted sequencing panel onto a small portable sequencer, the MinION. They merged it with a full-genome test for the virus behind COVID-19.

Spiked samples showed the panel could find the virus at low levels and read nearly its whole genome. It also spotted other pathogens in the same run. Accuracy tests gave high marks for both finding true cases and clearing true negatives. All one hundred sixty-one real wildlife samples tested negative. The authors offer the workflow as a cheap, flexible tool for wildlife surveillance.
pmc-12845367:
Anna Pikuła and co-authors track a chicken bronchitis virus clan in Poland in a 2025 study. The clan, genotype II, sat calm for years, then rose of late. The team read the full S1 code of eight field strains from 2011 to 2021. Two sat in known sub-clans. Six formed a fresh twig on the tree. A wider test then weighed if that twig earns a clan of its own.

Full marks fell short of a new clan call; the six sit in the lead sub-clan. Part reads of 15 more strains show fast drift in the clan. Long-lived layer and breeder hens bear the brunt. Drift may hide spread, the team warn, and mask as farm yield loss.
pmc-12845567:
Plastic dust and a farm pesticide wash into the same rivers, and fish hearts may pay for the combination. Guanghua Xiong and eight co-authors exposed zebrafish, larvae and adults, in 2025 to polystyrene microplastics plus avermectin at levels the environment actually holds.

Pairs of exposures stunted the larvae: fewer hatched, fewer survived, and heart muscle cells thinned. Defender enzymes dropped while inflammatory signals rose. Adult hearts showed disordered muscle and swelling between cells. Gene activity pointed to suppressed cell division, raised cell death, and a stress pathway driven by reactive oxygen. The authors warn that judging pollutants one at a time understates what mixtures do to aquatic life.
pmc-12846367:
Maria del Mar Villanueva Guzman, Zhenlan Yao, Melody Li, and Maria Gabriela Noval review how alphaviruses, long cast as hit-and-run infections, can linger in the body for months or years. Their 2025 synthesis gathers cell and animal evidence that viral RNA and proteins persist after symptoms clear. Persistence, they argue, is an active standoff, not leftover debris.

Three interlocking processes build the hiding places: infecting the right cellular niches, rewiring host pathways, and softening immune attack. The viruses infect many cell types, and each niche supports survival differently. Whether that lingering presence drives the chronic joint and nerve complaints seen after infection remains unresolved. The authors map the open questions and the experiments that could settle them. Chronic disease, in their frame, may be persistence's price.
pmc-12847467:
Shihao Huang and five colleagues study a gene called CTHRC1 in mouth cancer and its link to a rust-like cell death, in a twenty twenty-five paper. The gene is overactive in many cancers, including oral squamous cell carcinoma. The team measured it in three cancer cell lines and then silenced it. They tracked growth, cell death, and iron-driven damage markers.

Silencing the gene slowed growth and pushed cells toward both normal suicide and the rust-like death, ferroptosis. It also quieted a growth pathway called TGF-beta Smad. A drug that wakes that pathway reversed the death effect. The authors name this gene axis as a possible treatment target.
pmc-12847967:
Klaudia Kołodziejska and eight co-authors published a 2025 study on how worms release tiny vesicles when they sense danger from pathogens, before any infection. Animals meet pathogen chemicals in nature long before microbes invade. Extracellular vesicles carry signals that tune immunity and stress responses, but anticipatory control of them was unknown.

Working with the roundworm Caenorhabditis elegans, the team split pathogen cues into airborne and dissolved kinds. Dissolved cues, including one small peptide, switched on vesicle release through immune pathways. Airborne cues triggered release without immunity. Both routes needed the same three sensory neurons and fed into one neural circuit. Certain receptor proteins handled the dissolved cues, one acting from the gut. Offspring of exposed worms survived later infection better.
pmc-12849167:
Stefanie Braig and co-authors present a 2025 study of work ability two years after a COVID-19 infection in Germany. Lingering symptoms after the illness can cut work capacity and stretch sick leave. The link is tangled, since symptoms vary widely and work ability has many sides.

The study followed 5,422 adults aged eighteen to sixty five in the southwest of the country. All had a confirmed infection. The team tracked self rated work ability and sick leave at six to twelve months and again at twenty four months. About 1.1 percent stayed on sick leave from the first infection onward, they report.
pmc-12849267:
Nicholas M Kiger and three co-authors separate the jobs of two near-twin signaling proteins in a social amoeba. Dictyostelium cells chase chemical signals to gather, guided by G proteins that pass messages from surface receptors inward. The Gα2 subunit was known to drive the chase toward the signal cAMP, switching on a kinase and moving a gene regulator. Yet some responses persist without Gα2, hinting at a stand-in. Its closest relative, Gα1, is the natural suspect. Their 2025 study expresses Gα1 in cells lacking Gα2 and watches which responses return.

The rescue fails for chemotaxis, showing the twins are not interchangeable there. Related subunits dividing labor, rather than backing each other up, sharpens the map of the pathway. The authors test both movement and gene control readouts. Their amoeba is a stand-in for signaling logic used across life.
pmc-12852767:
Yujie Peng and five co-authors dig into why rock bursts erupt as mine tunnels are cut. A burst is a sudden rock failure that can kill, and its roots in shifting energy were unclear. Their 2025 study mixes lab tests with computer models of the rock around a fresh tunnel.

Stored stretch energy in the wall rock lets go at once, crushing the weak shallow zone and firing the burst. Side stress from the land raised risk in a steady climb. Push from mining raised risk first, then lowered it as it grew. Shocks from afar deepened harm and raised burst odds. The team pairs relief cuts with added support as a guard. Mines can tune that pair by energy zone, they say.
pmc-12853067:
Bhagvat Maheta and co-authors studied which numbers on a residency application best predict matching in a 2025 study. The match weighs many factors, but scores and counts are the most objective and consistently reported. The team asked which quantitative variables track match success most strongly.

They used national data on residents from 2013 to 2021 across all approved fields. Candidate predictors included licensing exam scores, research experiences, publications and presentations, and volunteer and work histories. Tracking these over time and by field shows which credentials actually move the needle. Such evidence helps students spend effort where it counts instead of padding every line.
pmc-12855267:
Yanan Wang and colleagues follow what happens when prenatal testing finds a genetic variant nobody can classify, in this study from twenty twenty-five. Copy number variants of unknown significance turn up in amniotic fluid tests and leave parents in limbo. The team tracked one hundred thirty-two such findings from over three thousand six hundred samples.

Most parents, nearly nine in ten, chose to continue the pregnancy, and even brand-new variants rarely led to termination. Of one hundred fifteen live births, three babies had abnormalities, none provably tied to the variant. Checking whether a variant came from a parent helped counsel families. The authors conclude that most such variants end in healthy babies. They recommend a shared database and steady follow-up of these children, so tomorrow's parents get evidence instead of a shrug.
pmc-12857067:
Cong Wang and co-authors asked in 2025 whether the shape of a patient's kneecap affects how they feel after a partial knee replacement. The kneecap joint is a known source of lasting symptoms after this surgery, and kneecaps fall into three classic shape types.

The team reviewed 327 patients treated from 2020 to 2023 and followed for three to five years. All groups improved after surgery. Still, clear gaps emerged. Patients with the third shape type reported worse scores on a scale for how forgotten the new joint feels. They also reported more pain at the front of the knee than the second type. The first type sat between. Shape, the authors argue, should enter planning and counseling.
pmc-12859867:
Jie Yu and six co-authors sort patients with chronic lung disease into self-care profiles, in a 2025 study. Self-care is key in COPD, yet patients vary much in how they manage. A survey of 315 inpatients at a hospital in Hebei, China, fed a class-finding method. Forms gauged self-care, breath strain, fatigue, mood, and social backing.

Three profiles emerged. The largest group was weak across all areas. A second group handled symptoms well but lagged in daily life and mood care. The smallest group was strong across the board. Schooling, disease length, and social backing forecast the strong profile. Anxiety pulled the other way. The authors urge tailored care over one-size plans.
pmc-12859967:
Nasim Sadeghi and co-authors test probiotics in smokers in a randomized trial from 2025. Smoking links to metabolic problems and to poor mental health. Gut microbes may play a role in both, so live microbe capsules might ease nicotine dependence, anxiety, and low mood while improving blood markers.

Seventy-four adult smokers in Kashan, Iran, took probiotic or placebo capsules for twelve weeks. The active capsules held four Lactobacillus and Bifidobacterium strains. Standard scales tracked mood, anxiety, and dependence. After twelve weeks, the probiotic group showed drops in fasting blood sugar, triglycerides, and an inflammation marker, among other shifts. The trial tests a gut route to smoker health.
pmc-12860067:
Marion Ravit and co-authors compared cesarean rates across hospitals in four lower-income countries, in a 2025 meta-analysis. Birth surgery rates vary wildly between facilities. The Robson system sorts mothers into comparable groups. The study covers the four lowest-risk groups in that system.

Thirty-two hospitals in Argentina, Burkina Faso, Thailand, and Vietnam shared 2020 records. Rates differed sharply even within the same Robson group. Hospital traits linked to the gaps were hunted by regression. Fair comparisons can now target outlier practices. Safer birth care starts with knowing where rates stray. Mothers in these groups usually expect a vaginal birth at admission.
pmc-12860467:
Ling Sun, Xin Feng, Xingru Li, and a wider team wrote this meta-analysis, published in 2025. It pools studies of a surgical trick for dialysis patients: inflating a balloon inside a narrow wrist artery before sewing it to a vein, so the access port survives longer.

Dialysis needs a durable port, and a self-made vein fistula is preferred, but thin arteries make fistulas fail often. The review gathered twenty-five studies covering 2,450 patients. Balloon-assisted fistulas stayed open without help in about eighty-eight percent of cases at six months and seventy-five percent at twelve months. The pooled rates beat traditional surgery, and the review also tracked procedural success, ripening of the fistula, and complications. The authors say widening the artery first is an effective and safe way to rescue an otherwise doomed access.
pmc-12860567:
Daniela Soares and three co-authors wrote this 2025 case report on a rare hormone lack hiding behind an unrelated complaint. A man of thirty was referred for breast pain and swelling of both breasts. Blood work showed an underactive thyroid with autoimmune markers. More unusually, it showed very low levels of follicle-stimulating hormone, with normal testosterone and normal levels of its sister hormone.

A stimulation test confirmed the pituitary barely answered for that hormone. That is the signature of isolated FSH deficiency, a rare inherited disorder usually found during fertility work-ups. Genetic testing found no change in the hormone's beta subunit gene. Full exome sequencing found no known culprit either. The authors note the condition is probably missed often in men, since testosterone stays normal and manhood masks it. They urge clinicians to keep it in mind.
pmc-12866067:
A strong cancer drug, doxorubicin, can damage the heart even as it saves lives. Johan Guthormsen and co-authors tested a tiny RNA that might shield heart cells from that drug in this 2025 study. The RNA, called miR-210, had already shown heart-protective effects in low-oxygen heart disease. Whether it guards against drug damage was open.

The team raised or lowered the RNA in lab-grown heart cells, then dosed the cells with the drug for a day. Cell death was read by a leakage test, and programmed cell death was checked apart. The title gives the finding: more of the RNA meant less programmed death under the drug. A shield like this, if it holds in animals, could widen the safe use of a key cancer drug.
pmc-12867167:
Guangzong Chen and co-authors strip image translation networks down to their core, in a 2025 paper. Tools that turn one image style into another often stack complex parts and many loss terms. That bulk makes them hard to read and costly to run. The team asked whether a basic adversarial network suffices on its own.

Their streamlined model drops the extra losses that leading systems rely on, such as cycle consistency. Theory and tests together show the plain design still gives high-quality translations. A link drawn between adversarial networks and autoencoders explains why content survives while style changes. On standard data sets, the simple model matched far heavier rivals. The result clarifies what the adversarial loss truly does.
pmc-12872167:
Plant psychedelics like ayahuasca and huachuma, the San Pedro cactus, are studied for mental health, yet their link with the gut microbiome is barely studied. The seven authors present a single-patient case study. A thirty-five-year-old woman who had used them before took part in two ceremonies, one per plant. Stool samples came before and after each, plus depression and connectedness scales and talks with the team.

Both sessions cut the depression scores sharply, from eighteen to six after ayahuasca and from twelve to two after huachuma. Scores for feeling close to others climbed. Each plant shifted gut microbes in its own way, but both trimmed pro-inflammatory species and boosted butyrate producers. The authors frame the case as a source of ideas for later tests: shifts in gut microbes may help explain the mood lift, through the gut-brain axis.
pmc-12872567:
Hao Jing and co-authors compare two ways of catching harmful drug reactions in cancer care in a study published in 2025. Hospitals often rely on staff filing reports when they spot a problem, which misses many cases and acts late. The team instead used a Chinese hospital system that scans patient data actively to flag reactions.

The study followed five hundred patients on chemotherapy, targeted therapy, or immune therapy. About thirty-seven percent had a drug reaction, and active scanning found far more cases than staff reports did. It also found them days sooner. Blood, gut, and skin problems were most common. Older age, many drugs at once, and liver or kidney problems raised the risk of severe reactions. The authors back wider use of active scanning in hospitals.
pmc-12872867:
Tian and co-authors report a rare soft tumor inside a jaw muscle. The patient had a painless lump under the jaw. A CT scan showed a cyst-like lesion in that area. The growth came from the mylohyoid muscle under the tongue. Lab review of the removed tissue confirmed an intramuscular myxoma.

Such tumors are benign but rare, at about one case per million people per year. Growths in the jaw muscles are rarer still and can mimic gland cysts. Scans alone can mislead, so tissue review stays the sure test. Full removal is the standard cure for this tumor type. The patient healed well after surgery, and outlook is good.
pmc-12873267:
Huawei Tan and co-authors present near complete, two version genomes for the cacao variety CCN51, in work from 2025. Cacao underpins the global chocolate trade and supports millions of livelihoods. CCN51 is the most widely planted hybrid in Latin America, prized for yield, disease resistance, and adaptability.

Long read sequencing plus chromosome contact data built the two versions. Each spans a bit over four hundred million letters, with very high completeness. Gene counts came to just under twenty-three thousand per version. Mobile DNA made up a large share of the genome, classified far better than in past reports. The resource supports breeding of hardier cacao.
pmc-12874767:
Jiayu Liang and seven co-authors turn marine waste into prized sugar chains with a reworked bacterium, in a 2025 paper. Chitosan, drawn from shell waste, can be cut into short chains valued in medicine and farming. The usual cutting uses harsh chemistry. Their route engineers Bacillus subtilis, a workhorse microbe, with the CRISPR gene editor to serve as a clean factory.

They first deleted the bacterium's own cutting enzyme, then added a borrowed one tuned for export out of the cell. With the brew conditions tuned by a surface-fitting method, a five-liter fed tank reached high enzyme output. The enzyme cut chitosan into chains of two to four sugar units, a defined mix. The team frames the setup as a green upcycling path for sea waste.
pmc-12879467:
Hande Baba Kaya and seven co-authors examine brain, body, and mind after knee ligament surgery, in this 2025 paper. Tearing the anterior cruciate ligament, a key knee stabilizer, affects more than the joint. Athletes may think and react differently, and feel less ready to return. The team compared healthy athletes with those after first-time and repeat reconstructions.

Sixty men aged 18 to 30 took brain-wave tests, reaction tests, and standard questionnaires on fear of movement and readiness to play. The repeat-surgery group showed the highest frontal brain ratios, the slowest reactions at 293 milliseconds, the most fear, and the lowest readiness scores. First-time patients sat between them and controls on every measure. The measures also moved together. The authors argue rehab should train brain and confidence, not just muscle.
pmc-12882367:
Tingting Xia and five co-authors test a bacterial acid against a yeast that plagues women in a 2025 study. Candida albicans drives vulvovaginal candidiasis, a common and often returning ill, and drug resistance is thinning the standard cures. D-lactic acid, made by friendly vaginal bacteria, was a candidate shield with an unclear mode of attack.

In dishes the acid curbed the yeast's switch to thread form and its biofilm building, dose by dose. Film mass and living activity both fell hard. Stains showed the cell skin leaking, and gene reads mapped the pathways hit. In a mouse model of the ill, the acid eased the infection in step with the dish work. The authors offer it as a fresh antifungal lead.
pmc-12896067:
Lucía Pérez Rodríguez and eight colleagues test a quick infrared tool for typing a hospital germ group, in a twenty twenty-five study. Typing tells staff whether infections share one source, but classic methods are slow and costly. The team checked the IR Biotyper on seventy-two drug-resistant strains of the Enterobacter cloacae complex. They compared its groupings with two gene-based methods.

The infrared tool sorted strains at least as sharply as the older gel method and near the level of full gene reading. Its groupings matched both methods closely. Results came in under three hours at low cost. The tool also performed well in a real outbreak check, backing its use in routine hospital labs.
pmc-12901467:
Xiu-Long Niu and a team of co-authors hunt for tiny RNA markers of high blood pressure in younger adults. Their study is from two thousand twenty-five by its journal record. High blood pressure in this age group raises the risk of heart disease, yet its molecular roots are still murky. Tiny RNAs that tune genes are one place to look.

The team first sequenced blood samples from six patients and six healthy peers. They found fifteen tiny RNAs whose levels differed between the groups. Five of them held up in a second, more exact test. Pathway checks tied the raised RNAs to low-oxygen response and inflammation signals. A genetics method then probed whether proteins targeted by these RNAs help cause the condition. The markers may aid early detection in time.
pmc-12913167:
Liba Sokolovska and thirteen colleagues published a cancer study in two thousand twenty-five on the viruses behind cervical disease in Latvia. Latvia has some of Europe's highest cervical cancer rates. The team typed the high-risk human papillomaviruses in tissue samples spanning two thousand sixteen to two thousand twenty-four.

They tested one hundred forty-five samples from precancer and cancer cases. Nearly all carried at least one high-risk virus type, and many carried several. Type sixteen stayed the most common across the years. Type eighteen fell sharply over the period. Several other types became more common instead. Worse disease stages carried heavier virus loads and more types. The authors say these shifts matter for screening and vaccine planning in Latvia.
pmc-12914967:
Geoffrey Barnes and co-authors trial a quiet way to fix risky blood thinner prescriptions, in a 2025 study. Prescribing slips for direct oral anticoagulants are a leading cause of harm, often arising after the first order as patients change. Alerts that interrupt work annoy clinicians and get ignored.

Their trial sent calm, non-interruptive record notifications when a prescription broke label rules or clashed with other drugs. Each notice went either to the prescriber or to a specialist pharmacist, assigned by prescriber. Nearly four hundred notices were tracked for whether any fix followed within a week. About twenty-three percent drew a change in the study window.
pmc-12922367:
Senjeet Sreekissoon and eleven co-authors study a mouth cancer that comes with a scarring condition of the mouth lining, in this twenty twenty-five paper. Both are common where betel nut is chewed, in parts of Asia. Whether cancer with the scarring behaves worse than cancer without it was debated.

The team followed patients treated at a dental hospital in China over about a decade, sorted by whether they had the scarring. Checks every three months tracked return of disease and problems after care. The study also probed immune cells and checkpoints around the tumors, which seemed to form a suppressive shield. The findings may guide how these patients are watched.
pmc-12930467:
Silvia Camporesi and four colleagues published a critical essay in two thousand twenty-five on sex testing in women's sport. For decades, all women athletes faced forced sex tests, a practice that ended in the nineteen nineties after strong objections. The essay examines a two thousand twenty-five policy shift by World Athletics.

The new rules bring back blanket screening of elite women runners for a single gene. The authors note the rules call women's events female events, putting biology ahead of gender. They also merge rules for women with sex variations and transgender women into one set. The authors argue these choices repeat past harms flagged by medical, ethics, and human rights experts. They warn today's athletes face the same risks.
pmc-12932167:
Italo Messias Ferreira de Souza and co-authors review in work whose head dates it to 2025 how heat stress shows in cattle and how herds can be judged for welfare. As the world warms, heat loads on cattle grow. Signs in body, acts, and yield can flag when beasts suffer before losses mount.

The review sets two great cattle kinds side by side: the European kind and the Zebu kind bred for hot lands. It pulls from fresh studies of body replies, acts, and farm output in heat. Zebu traits for heat bear come out as a key split. Herders in hot zones gain a sign list tuned to a warming world.
pmc-12951467:
Hardened tooth roots block the files dentists use, and a printed guide can steer the drill to the canal. Bruna de Athayde Casadei and co-authors review their guided cases in a 2025 study. One hundred teeth with severe pulp hardening were treated between 2019 and 2021. Three-dimensional scans planned a virtual drill path for each tooth. A machined template then held that path in the mouth.

Success meant reaching the canal space without straying from the plan. The reported success rate topped ninety-nine percent. Deep fillings, dead pulp, and past trauma led the case histories. Two-thirds of teeth had already failed a normal attempt elsewhere. The authors back the guided route for hardened canals.
pmc-12952367:
Abduletif Haji Ababor Abagojam and four co-authors report appendix trouble in an odd place in a paper whose head dates it to 2024. The appendix hangs off the start of the large gut, most often low on the right side. In this man it sat high under the liver, where its flare can mimic other ills and slip past doctors.

The twenty seven year old came in with upper right belly pain, mild fever, a racing heart, and diarrhea. A scan showed a swollen high appendix with a small stone inside. Surgery found it on the edge of bursting, and it was removed in time. At follow up the man had healed well with no pain. The authors urge scans when the picture does not fit the classic spot.
pmc-12955767:
Giulia Simonetti and Gianfranco Taruschio survey premenstrual mood symptoms during lockdown in this 2025 paper. A severe form of premenstrual distress affects a small share of women, with mood, thought, and body symptoms that fade after each period. The COVID-19 quarantine added stress that may have swelled those symptoms.

An anonymous online survey in May of 2020 drew just over one hundred Italian women. More than three quarters reported premenstrual symptoms. Over a third met the symptom count for the severe form, far above the usual share. The authors say the clash with past rates needs care in reading, since the sample is small and self-chosen. They urge more heed to women's mental health in hard times.
pmc-13001767:
Mitsuru Tonosaki and six co-authors probe how two brain arousal systems shape ketamine's pain relief in rats, in a 2024 study. Orexin neurons drive wakefulness and talk to a noradrenaline hub in the brainstem. The team used transgenic rats whose orexin neurons are genetically degraded, plus normal rats for comparison. Pain responses were measured with hotplate and tail-flick tests after ketamine injections.

Some groups received a toxin against the noradrenaline hub, or brain injections of orexin, a receptor blocker, or both. Brain levels of orexin and noradrenaline were measured in untreated animals. If ketamine's analgesia rides on arousal circuitry, then sleep and alertness states may tune how well the drug works, a link anesthesiologists could exploit.
pmc-13036067:
Shan and colleagues report in 2025 that the human blood fluke Schistosoma japonicum carries virus-like RNAs that are not part of its own genome. Blocking these RNAs cut embryo survival and egg output.

Similar RNAs appear in a free-living flatworm, where the enzyme keeps the worm alive. The team combined large-scale sequencing, single-cell data, and gene silencing to map the system. They propose these RNAs as fresh targets for controlling schistosomiasis.
pmc-13089367:
Geert Rutten and colleagues studied citizen involvement in integrated care networks. Their 2026 participatory research follows three community care networks. Rising demand pushes health systems toward cross-domain models. Networks that include citizens may fit local needs better. The team tracked what helps or hinders such networks as they grow.

A four-stage framework charted each network's development path. Documents, observations, talks, and twenty interviews supplied the data. All networks moved forward by one development stage. One advanced only in professional collaboration, not citizen depth. Shared urgency and communication strength aided progress. Advisory and steering groups kept reflection built into the work. Lessons serve regions building community-rooted care systems.
pmc-13094567:
Miller, Chawla, Pierson, and Johansen Taber wrote this 2026 study of pregnancies that screen positive for tiny missing chromosome pieces. A blood test in pregnancy can screen for five microdeletions, small gaps tied to named syndromes. A positive screen raises hard questions about what happens next.

The team linked test results to insurance claims to follow care and outcomes. They compared 119 patients who screened positive with 287,169 who screened negative. Statistical models adjusted for past high-risk pregnancy and payer type. During pregnancy, the positive group was more likely to have excess amniotic fluid, one of several outcomes tracked. The study maps how often follow-up tests, extra care, and birth outcomes follow a positive screen, data that counselors need when they explain the test.
pmc-13100267:
Alice Coelho and co-authors report a scan pitfall after a vessel growth drug is stopped in a patient with a returned brain tumor, in a case report from 2026. The drug is wide used for such tumors since it chokes new vessel growth.

A fifty year old man on long term use showed a patch of high blood flow in the brain crust after the drug ended. No seizure, stroke, high pressure, or tumor return explained the patch. The team reads it as a brief rebound as vessel control resets once the drug block lifts. Readers of scans should know this trap, they warn.
pmc-13101767:
George Sun and co-authors link, in a 2026 study, features of local climate to how long people live across the United States. Climate change is widely seen as a health threat, yet it rarely enters health policy in a direct way. The authors set out to measure which weather traits track with life expectancy. They combined three modeling methods, including machine learning and models that let effects vary by place.

Moist air, higher heat, and more water loss from land and plants all tracked with shorter lives. More sunshine, by contrast, tracked with longer lives. The patterns held across all three methods, which the authors take as a sign of robustness. They argue that health planning should treat climate as a core input, and they offer their results as evidence for joining the two policy worlds.
pmc-13105767:
Yi-Heng Liu and co-authors ask whether a past Covid-19 infection raises the risk of confusion after surgery, in a study published in 2025. Delirium after an operation is a serious problem, and the role of prior infection was unclear. The work reuses data from an earlier cohort study of adults having planned, non-heart surgery.

People who had surgery within seven weeks of a Covid diagnosis faced about three times the risk of delirium. Those who waited longer did not show the added risk. Infections with symptoms, not silent ones, carried the link, and the pattern held in patients under sixty-five. The results may help surgical teams time operations after an infection and watch high-risk patients more closely.
pmc-13126567:
Men who take part in reproductive health care can help their partners use services on time, which can save mothers' lives. The team gave a structured survey to 366 married men aged 20 and older, picked at random. Men who said they intended to take part had about three times the odds of actually doing so. Two factors cut the odds down. Men who lived in rural areas were less likely to be involved than town dwellers. Men with two wives were also less likely to take part than men with one wife. The authors say health programs should build intention and reach rural men.
pmc-13127667:
Jason Martin, Davis Reina-Guerra, and Leslie Stone-Roy survey undergraduates who volunteer for Brain Awareness Week outreach, asking what draws them and what they gain. Their 2025 study notes that outreach deepens knowledge and sharpens teaching and communication skills. Entry and exit surveys frame the work.

Motives sorted into three themes: career growth, communication training, and science advocacy. Most students joined from love of outreach and neuroscience, or to polish applications. Younger students leaned hardest on career motives and felt the most need for communication training. Prior teaching boosted advocacy scores at every level. Exit answers tied career motives to bolder contact with faculty and wider audiences. The authors advise tailoring training to student background.
pmc-13132967:
Xuyuan Ma and five co-authors traced in 2026 how a placental protein helps blood vessels remodel, and how that help fails in preeclampsia. The protein, SPP1, ferries signals between the placenta's invading cells and the vessel lining. The team measured it in placentas from healthy and affected pregnancies, then stressed placental cells with low oxygen in the lab.

A signaling chain running through a cell-surface anchor and a growth switch ended at a vessel-cutting enzyme. Giving the protein to rats with a drug-induced form of the disease eased it. The chain offers new targets for a dangerous pregnancy disorder.
pmc-13135567:
Dániel Keliger and Illés Horváth explain a puzzle in epidemic modeling: the curve is easier to predict than the network behind it. Their 2026 paper studies a standard model where people cycle between susceptible and infected states on a weighted contact graph. Earlier work showed a learned stand-in network can forecast the curve well even when it looks nothing like the true network.

The pair give a rigorous account of that odd fact. For large networks, curve prediction is robust, while rebuilding the true network from the same data is ill-conditioned. They also give an explicit formula for the network in cases where rebuilding is possible. Their proof leans on a classic regularity result from graph theory. The lesson guides modelers to trust forecasts while doubting reverse-engineered contact maps.
pmc-13136767:
Vera Cruz and co-authors survey in 2026 how willing people are to use game based tools to strengthen mental health and emotion control. Such apps are proposed as low barrier aids, but uptake is not given. Responses came from people across diverse countries.

Most respondents showed mid to high willingness. Cluster analysis split them into a high group, at 43 percent, and a moderate group, at 57 percent. Youth, male gender, frequent gaming, and some emotion control traits raised the odds of the high group. Impulsive traits and low emotional awareness lowered openness. People were less keen to use such tools to prevent problems than to react to them.
pmc-13138667:
Momtaz Esfahani and co-authors build a fair read of patient tales in a 2026 paper. Wards drown in tales of care told in free words, and a tool that sorts them must not learn to sort by the teller's kind.

Their line reads feel, themes, and care terms in each tale. Three de-bias crafts were tried on word tools of four kinds. One craft, which cuts song, cut feel scores as it cut bias. The next two held the scores whole while the bias fell. The best of them cut the gap in fair odds and in word-pair bias by clear marks. It also took most of the marks adepts had tagged. The authors own that kind gaps past the sex pair run more hard to mend.
pmc-13138867:
Shohei Yano and co-authors report a 2026 case of lung inflammation of the pleura linked to the cancer drug brigatinib. Their patient, a woman in her late seventies with a gene marked type of lung cancer, began the drug as a third line of care. Soon after, she developed breathlessness, fever, raised inflammation markers, and fluid on both sides of the chest.

Fluid tests showed an immune rich fluid with no sign of cancer or infection, pointing to the drug as the cause.
