Restarting the drug at a low dose shrank the tumor without bringing the pleuritis back, and a higher dose was also borne well. The authors flag drug caused pleuritis as a cause to weigh when fluid appears on this therapy.
pmc-13139567:
Yang Xu, Yuqi Tang, and Quan Li wrote a 2026 perspective on molecules that switch shape when light hits them. Most such switches flip between two states, like a lamp on or off, and each state has its own traits.

Switches with many states are drawing growing interest because they offer more settings to control with light. The authors trace how the field grew, set out the basic rules behind these molecules, and review the main design plans. They give leading examples and survey new uses in materials and devices. A final part covers the open problems, such as stability and control, and where the field may go next.
pmc-13139767:
Edward Gilbert and co-authors track what sets telomere length in a Canary Islands lizard, and find drought years leave a mark. Their study appeared in 2026. Telomeres, the caps on chromosomes, signal aging and population health. The team measured them in the western Canaries lizard across varied habitats over ten years. Built-in traits dominated: males carried shorter telomeres than females, and larger females had shorter ones than smaller females.

Weather and habitat factors mattered less, but dry years lined up with shorter telomeres across the population. The authors read this as a cumulative burden from harsh conditions, laid on top of each animal's own baseline. The work warns that climate stress may quietly age wild populations even when individuals look healthy.
pmc-13144967:
Isabella Püschel and eight colleagues report the LUMOS study, a conference abstract on skin blood flow after acute ischemic stroke. Working at a German tertiary stroke center, the team asked whether weakened limbs show worse small-vessel circulation than the other side. They also asked whether that weakness predicts recovery.

Sixty-six patients had laser Doppler imaging of both forearms at admission and again on day three. Blood flow was lower in the weakened limbs, and it fell over time on both sides. Early impairment did not predict function at ninety days, however. The authors suggest the pattern points to body-wide autonomic disturbance, and that bedside imaging could help monitor it.
pmc-13145067:
John Volpi and co-authors set out a trial of a new drug for stroke patients who miss out on standard clot care. Their conference abstract from 2026 covers a made version of a human protein. It may raise blood flow in the brain and help vessel repair, which could cut both harm and repeat stroke.

Adults seen within a day of onset, with mid level stroke scores, will get the drug or a dummy drug plus standard care. Those with a large vessel block or fast early gains after clot drugs are left out. The drug is given once by vein, then by shots twice a week for three weeks. Top recovery at ninety days is the main check.
pmc-13145167:
Curtis Amankwah and co-authors present a 2026 case report on stroke in a man with a chronic skin disease. The skin disease causes painful abscesses and is now seen as a body wide condition tied to heart and vessel risk. Stroke reports in such patients, though, are rare, and the pathways are poorly mapped.

The patient was a 48 year old man with diabetes, high pressure, high blood fats, and tobacco use. He came in after six days of growing speech loss and right side weakness. Scans showed twin blockages of a neck and brain artery and many small strokes in low flow zones. During the stay, sepsis from skin abscesses led doctors to the skin diagnosis, which had been missed before. His nerve signs improved with standard care.
pmc-13145267:
When bleeding strikes inside the brain, surgeons must judge fast who needs an operation. Mocco and co-authors mine a large trial cohort for those cues in a 2026 report. Of 626 patients, 54 went to surgery.

Surgical patients were younger and scored worse on brain function tests. Their bleeds were bigger, with more push on nearby tissue. Bleed size and midline shift held up as lone predictors after adjustment. An early clotting drug did not change who went to surgery. Outcomes after surgery also matched across drug arms. Size and shift, the team says, drive the call.
pmc-13145467:
Cliff Oguk, Benjamin Okanga, and Annie Kariuki set out in 2026 to map stroke imaging in Kenyan referral hospitals. Stroke is a top cause of death in the nation. Most sites can run a plain CT scan, but the sharper vessel and flow scans that pick out patients for clot pulls are rare. Their survey asks stroke care staff in all forty-seven counties what gear and rules they have and what blocks the sharper scans.

At the time of the report, replies were still coming in. The form had been checked by clinicians and sent out through pro networks. A national ethics pass was in its last steps. The team plans to close the poll and chart the gap, to give the nation its first base line for stroke imaging policy.
pmc-13145567:
Guo and co-authors report a conference study on using brain network imaging to spot sleep problems in people with cerebral small vessel disease. This disease damages the brain's smallest blood vessels and often harms sleep and thinking, but the link between vessel damage and poor sleep is hard to measure in clinic.

The team studied one hundred and two patients and built models from neurovascular network features. Their full model identified sleep disturbance with an area under the curve of 0.854, a strong score for this kind of test. If confirmed in larger groups, such a model could help doctors flag patients who need sleep assessment and treatment earlier in their care.
pmc-13145667:
Olli Mattila and co-authors report a 2026 conference study on a blood test that may spot brain bleeding before patients reach the hospital. The test measures a protein released when brain cells are hurt. Fast sorting matters because bleeding and blocked-vessel strokes need very different care.

Blood samples came from more than nine hundred emergency stroke cases within six hours of onset. With cut points set by age and sex, the test ruled out bleeding with high trust in about half the group. It ruled bleeding in for a small share with fair trust. Many cases fell in a gray zone, so the authors say extra tests will still be needed.
pmc-13145767:
Hussain Binamir and co-authors compare brain scans before and after stem cell transplants for sickle cell disease in this 2026 paper. The disease scars the brain with silent strokes and vessel damage. Transplant can cure the blood side of the illness. Its effect on the brain picture was unknown.

The team matched 134 scan pairs from the same patients. No brain measure changed clearly after transplant once strict statistics were applied. Scar and stroke shares crept up slightly, without reaching significance. Vessel problems and shrinkage stayed flat. White matter grades and microbleed counts also held steady. The authors read the scans as stable, neither clear gain nor clear harm.
pmc-13145867:
Clustered mini-strokes that fool a risk score are studied by Ali Mahyaei and co-authors in work dated 2026. Crescendo TIA means brief attacks that pile up fast. One hundred such cases faced four hundred seventy-nine single attacks at one center. Risk traits matched near point for point across the groups. Attack length split them, though.

Cluster cases ran far shorter, most under ten minutes. Short length cut their ABCD2 scores, so fewer read as high risk. The score thus plays down a plainly risky form. The team urges triage by pattern, not score.
pmc-13145967:
Huma Fatima Ali and co-authors pilot a fast MRI method that reads stiffness in the brain's arteries. The method, dynamic inflow magnitude contrast imaging, times the pulse wave between the neck carotid and a front brain artery. Pulse wave speed gauges stiffness, a suspect in small vessel disease. Their 2026 feasibility study scans 51 patients seen for suspected stroke or mini-stroke. Heart-gated images slice the cycle into two-millisecond steps. Burden of small vessel disease and thinking scores are set beside the speeds.

Median pulse wave speed lands near five meters per second. No tie to single disease markers or total burden reaches significance. Thinking scores also show no link to speed. A borderline trend ties heavier vessel disease to lower cognition. The team reads the method as workable, the biology still open.
pmc-13146367:
Amar Valentin and co-authors present a 2026 conference study on a protein sign in patients with a vessel disease that stiffens brain arteries with protein deposits. The sign is a hallmark of Alzheimer's disease in spinal fluid. Whether it means the same thing in this vessel disease was unclear.

The study set more than eighty vessel disease patients beside matched Alzheimer's patients at two centers. Those with the protein sign thought much like those without it, bar weaker naming. Both vessel groups kept far better memory than the Alzheimer's group. Brain shrinkage scores also split the vessel group from Alzheimer's. The authors suggest the sign may not simply mark added Alzheimer's disease here.
pmc-13146567:
Miriam Kempter and co-authors test very early aerobic training after stroke in high-risk patients, in a 2026 trial report. Guidelines urge early exercise for fitness and recovery, but a big earlier trial raised safety doubts for patients with heavy cardiometabolic risk. The Early-Fit study asks whether carefully dosed training is at least feasible in that group.

Forty patients in inpatient rehabilitation, three to twenty-one days post-stroke and carrying diabetes risk or atrial fibrillation, were randomized to treadmill training or usual care. Training intensity followed heart rate reserve, aiming at six or more sessions. Glucose sensors watched metabolic stress in both groups. The report covers recruitment, adherence, and safety, groundwork for judging whether early exertion helps or harms fragile hearts.
pmc-13146667:
Ibrahim Serag reports a 2026 conference review on how low to push top blood pressure after a brain bleed. Hard lowering is widely used, yet the best target stays in dispute. The review pooled trials that set a hard target against a standard one.

Eight trials with near sixty-nine hundred patients fed the pool. Hard lowering did not lift function at ninety days by any firm step. Bleed growth, though, fell clearly under hard lowering. Death rates matched between the paths. Kidney harms ran higher with hard lowering, while early brain worsening leaned lower. The author backs targets shaped to the patient rather than one hard rule for all.
pmc-13146767:
Huangwenyi Huang's 2026 conference abstract hunts for blood signs of acute ischemic stroke, the kind caused by a blocked brain vessel. The work reads tiny RNA strands carried in serum exosomes, small packets cells shed into the blood. Samples from stroke patients were compared with samples from healthy controls, first by RNA sequencing and then by targeted checks.

Three strands ran low in patients, and two of them, miR-23a-3p and miR-375-3p, could directly steer three clot-related proteins in vessel cells grown in the lab. Those proteins ran high in patient blood. Pairing the strands with the proteins predicted stroke with moderate accuracy. Huang offers the pair as candidate markers for faster diagnosis and as a window on how stroke unfolds.
pmc-13146967:
Five authors check trial results for carotid stenting against real world practice in this 2026 conference abstract. A major trial had found that placing a stent in the neck artery beat medicine alone for selected patients with no symptoms. The team asked whether United States practice matches that result.

Using a health record database for 2015 to 2025, they emulated the trial's design in 9,050 treated patients without symptoms. Stroke or death within forty-four days hit 6.10 percent, far above the trial's 1.30 percent. Later stroke rates are also reported. The gap between trial and real world care is the paper's core warning.
pmc-13147967:
Zaid Akram Thabit and co-authors read the full genome of a gut germ found on fresh vegetables in Baghdad, in work published in 2026. Raw greens are a healthy plate staple, yet outbreaks tied to fresh produce have grown, with Escherichia coli the top cause. The team tested fifty market vegetable samples for the germ.

Three samples, two cucumbers and one celery, carried it. The genomes ran near five million letters with a balanced letter mix. Two strain types turned up, kin to a known outbreak strain. The germs held many drug-proof tricks, from pumps to gene tweaks. The authors urge steady genome watch on produce germs.
pmc-13148467:
Marcela Xiomara Rivera Pineda, Jaakko Lehtimaki, and Guillaume Jacquemet present a customisable three-dimensional printed mould for orienting zebrafish larvae during live imaging. Their 2026 methods article improves on standard agarose mounting, which makes precise orientation difficult.

The mould is printed by fused deposition modelling and coated with resin for a smoother surface. It creates consistent larva-shaped wells that hold larvae in a belly-to-back orientation. Designed for standard glass-bottom dishes, the moulds are cheap to print on desktop machines. Open design files let users adapt them to different imaging setups. The approach enables reliable long-term imaging of multiple larvae, extending low-cost manufacturing in zebrafish workflows.
pmc-13148967:
Gani Oruqaj and co-authors published a 2026 study of a freezing-cut way to take tissue samples from chest lymph nodes, set against the standard suction-needle way. The needle way is the norm for such nodes. It can fall short on rare tumors, benign diseases, and blood disorders, and for detailed cell analyses. The freezing way takes a bigger, intact sample.

Ninety patients had both ways done in the same node, one after the other. Two tunnel paths were used, with two needle sizes. The freezing way found the diagnosis in over nine of ten cases, for both tunnel paths. The needle way found it in nearly seven of ten for one path, and over three in four for the other. Procedure times and sample sizes were nearly the same for both tunnels. The advantage of the freezing way was firm in statistical checks.
pmc-13149767:
Raffaella Pisapia and co-authors present a 2026 case report on severe malaria and a gene variant that may have shaped its course. Malaria from the falciparum parasite stays a major global threat, above all in sub Saharan Africa.

The patient was a forty year old woman from Seychelles who lived in Ivory Coast. She developed severe malaria with a very high parasite load, kidney injury, and acid buildup in the blood, plus a blood clot. Gene tests found a variant in the ACE gene, along with other variants tied to clotting. The authors add the case to debate on whether such variants worsen malaria, and they call for wider studies in endemic areas.
pmc-13150067:
Shubh Saraswat and four colleagues launch CytokineProfile, a web tool that walks researchers through cytokine data from start to finish. Multiplex assays that measure many immune signals at once are common in biomarker hunts. Most analysis sites were built for other data types and demand heavy reformatting.

The tool takes plain tables and guides preview, quality checks, missing-value fixes, and filtering. Its modules span charts, group tests, multivariate models, and machine learning classifiers that rank key signals. A prediabetes case study matched rival tools on the same data while adding views they lack. Speed tests on up to a thousand samples showed practical run times.
pmc-13150967:
Qinwen Qin, Wenjun Jia, and Semonti Nandi report a 2026 case of inflammatory breast cancer treated with chemotherapy before surgery. This rare form of breast cancer shows as skin swelling and redness, with tumor cells blocking the skin's lymph channels. The patient had locally advanced disease. A team from several fields planned her care together.

She first got a series of chemotherapy rounds, then had the left breast removed with a skin graft. Tests on the removed tissue showed no cancer left, a complete response to the drugs. After surgery she got radiation, a short course of hormone therapy, and a further drug course. Two years of follow up showed no return or spread of the disease. The authors stress that close teamwork across fields was central to the good result.
pmc-13151167:
El Ghoul and colleagues review care at a trauma stop point in Khan Younis, Gaza, in twenty twenty-six, using records from early twenty twenty-four. Such stop points, borrowed from army practice, give fast first care and sorting close to where people are hurt. Civil systems in war zones often lack that speed, so the model was brought in to fill the gap.

Nearly two thousand patients were logged over about ten weeks. Just over half came with non-injury problems, and most arrived stable. Care was mostly basic, such as stitching wounds and giving fever drugs. Four in five patients went home the same day, while one in five moved to a working hospital. The authors say the site eased pressure on hospitals and ambulances.
pmc-13152167:
Qian He and Xu Huang study a blood marker for immune shutdown in sepsis in a 2026 paper. Sepsis can leave the immune system too weak to fight later infections, a state tied to many deaths. A blood enzyme called cholinesterase drops in sepsis, but its tie to immune weakness was not well mapped.

The team combined patient data, gene data mining, and mouse experiments. Low enzyme levels went with worse severity scores and fewer key immune cells. Their gene work singled out RORA as a hub gene linking the enzyme, sepsis, and immunity, and mouse data matched the pattern. The authors propose the enzyme level as a handy marker for tracking immune state in sepsis care.
pmc-13153167:
Reda Attia tested in 2026 whether corn cob treated with citric acid can pull thorium out of water. Thorium is a radioactive metal that needs safe removal from waste streams. The treated plant material is cheap and kind to the environment, which makes it appealing if it works well.

Tests of the material's surface showed more area, more pores, and more of the chemical groups that grab metal ions after treatment. In lab runs, the best removal came at a set acidity and dose, with balance reached in under half an hour. The material could be cleaned and reused several times with only a small loss. The study also maps how speed and heat affect the process.
pmc-13155667:
Ida Sutrisni leads a large team on COVID vaccine uptake in three Asian lands. Their study from twenty twenty-six covers Indonesia, Nepal, and Vietnam. Vaccine doubt is a top world health threat, WHO says.

Talks with folks in town and rural zones were held. Themes were risk sense, trust, logistics, and social norms. Each theme was shaped by local context and changed with time. Rollout tales give clear lessons for new vaccine work. Trust should be built as early as one can. Local norms must be embraced, not fought.  The study ran as part of mixed methods work.
pmc-13156367:
Light-emitting threads could weave displays into clothing, but their standard charge-injection layer is acidic and drags on performance. Jae Ho Kim and ten co-authors swap that layer for a single-molecule carpet in this 2026 paper. The carpet, a phosphonic acid that assembles itself, tunes the surface energy step so charges enter more easily.

Fiber-shaped diodes built on it lit at lower voltage and converted current to light more efficiently, gaining about seventeen percent for green and thirteen for red over the standard layer. The same carpet lifted fiber solar cells from about five point seven to six point five percent efficiency. Fiber gas sensors wearing it also responded more strongly. One surface trick thus improves three thread-like devices at once, a hint for wearable electronics.
pmc-13156467:
Roshun Sangani, Param Shukla, and Miriam Habiel report a glaucoma rescue after a cosmetic iris implant went wrong. A 42-year-old woman with implants in both eyes came to the emergency room with corneal failure and mixed mechanism glaucoma in her left eye, caused by the implant chafing the iris. The implant was removed, yet her eye pressure stayed high afterward.

An off-label Xen Gel Stent, placed from outside the eye, then brought pressures under control. She needed no extra glaucoma drops for 13 months and kept a look she was happy with. The authors propose the stent as a safe option for implant-related glaucoma.
pmc-13156567:
Hugo Turner and co-authors weigh the cost of three leaner ways to cure hepatitis C, in a 2026 study based on a trial in Vietnam. Standard cure uses antiviral pills for twelve weeks, but access stays limited in many places. The trial tested shorter or lighter plans that need fewer pills and clinic visits, and all matched the standard cure rate.

One plan adjusts length based on virus levels after one week. One lowers dose frequency in later weeks. One adds four weekly doses of an older immune drug to a short pill course. In the base case, each plan cost less per cure than the standard, by roughly twelve to eighteen percent. Which plan was cheapest depended on the local price of the pills. In some cases, savings for clinics came with higher costs for patients, a trade-off the authors flag.
pmc-13156967:
Jing Li, Huilu Zhang, Peng Zhang, and Jie Hu test whether fixing gut microbes can ease chronic lung disease in this 2026 paper. The gut-lung axis links the two organs' health. Patients and smoke-exposed mice both showed altered, less diverse gut communities.

Wiping out gut microbes with antibiotics worsened lung damage and function in the mice and tired out a regulatory immune cell type. Restoring the gut by transplant brought the changes back toward normal. A signaling chemical, acetylcholine, ran high in sick mice and highest after antibiotics, tracking certain bacterial groups. Pathway analysis flagged fat building and purine routes. The authors propose gut care as a new treatment angle for the disease.
pmc-13157367:
Gabriel Pérez-Tierra, Jessica Calo, Ayelén Blanco, and José Soengas study white fat tissue as a target of secondary bile acids in rainbow trout. Their 2026 paper deals with hormone-like signals whose role in fish fat is largely unexplored.

Four compounds were tested: two secondary bile acids and their taurine conjugates. Six hours after stomach administration, the team measured gene expression plus glucose and lipid handling in the fat tissue. One acid stood out as the main metabolic modulator. It raised the activity of enzymes that start sugar breakdown and shifted energy-sensing genes. Fat metabolism adjusted in a coordinated way as well. The results open fish nutrition questions.
pmc-13157567:
Wenhao Chu and co-authors report a 2026 case of a severe kidney infection that looked like a stomach illness. The infection destroys kidney tissue and fills it with gas, and it usually shows classic urinary signs. Their patient, a woman in her sixties with type 2 diabetes, had only vomiting and diarrhea at first. No urinary complaint pointed to the true cause.

Within two days she fell into septic shock with a clouded mind. A CT scan showed advanced infection with wide destruction of the right kidney. Drugs alone were failing, so the team removed the kidney in an emergency operation. That step stopped the collapse, and she stabilized and recovered. The authors warn that in diabetic patients, stomach signs plus fast decline should trigger an immediate scan. When gas spread is wide, bold surgery can be the life saving call.
pmc-13157667:
Hospital stays in the last decade of life depend on more than age alone. Gabriele Doblhammer, Elena Rakuša, and Anne Fink followed a German birth cohort of over seventeen thousand people from age eighty-five to ninety-five in 2026, using insurance claims. They modeled how sex and dementia status, along with care needs and other illness, shifted the chance of a hospital stay.

Men were hospitalized more than women at every point, and dementia raised the risk for both. Among people without dementia the risk climbed with age; among women with dementia it slowly fell. Needing long-term care cut women's hospital risk sharply but barely moved men's. The authors press for care strategies that respect these splits.
pmc-13158367:
Motlagomang Khantsi and Olubukola Babalola wrote a review from 2026 on how cowpea plants shape the bacteria that live around their roots. Cowpea is a key food crop in much of Africa south of the Sahara. Its roots host a rich mix of germs. Some fix nitrogen from the air, some free up phosphorus, and some break down dead matter, all of which feed the plant and build the soil.

The review gathers what is known about this root zone. Soil traits such as acidity, salt, and food levels steer which germs thrive. Studies do not yet agree on how acidity alone shapes the mix. New gene-based tools have shown both common and rare germs at work near the roots. The authors say gaps remain on how the mix shifts under stress, and they call for joined studies that read genes, proteins, and small chemicals at once.
pmc-13160367:
Some molecules are chiral around a carbon-oxygen bond, a twisted axis that resists being set because the bond spins too freely. Yanbo Zhang and co-authors report building such axes from scratch rather than reshaping ready-made ethers. Their cobalt catalyst, cheap and earth-abundant, activates a carbon-hydrogen bond and closes a ring in one motion, creating the ring and the twisted axis together.

A helper group that steers the reaction removes itself during the process, leaving clean products. Many variants carried several stereogenic elements at once, all set with excellent selectivity, and the products held their twist without racemising under test. The authors extend the products into a library of unusual scaffolds, opening fresh ground for drug-like molecule design.
pmc-13161967:
Timothy Westbrooks and co-authors report gunshot caused Galeazzi fractures in a 2026 case series. A Galeazzi injury breaks the forearm radius shaft and dislocates the joint near the wrist. Such breaks most often come from falls or blunt force, since twisting force is thought key to the joint harm.

Six patients, aged 25 to 52, took low speed gunshot wounds that gave this pattern, and some bore further wounds. All had the radius fixed with rigid plates, and the wrist joint then proved stable in theatre with no extra fix needed. Short splints gave way to early motion. All bones healed with pain free forearm turns at review.
pmc-13162667:
Lulu Kong and co-authors review cell therapy prospects for a bone marrow disease in 2026. Myelofibrosis scars the marrow, enlarges the spleen, and drives body-wide inflammation. Current drugs ease symptoms but rarely clear the faulty clones or reverse scarring.

Engineered T cells have shown strong results in other blood cancers. The authors map targets on faulty cells and on the scarred niche around them. Hitting both could control clones and reshape the niche at once. Targets include surface markers, a scar protein, and signal paths that sustain the disease setting.
pmc-13162967:
Zhang and co-authors silence a sex gene in swimming crabs to watch growth and gonads. The IAG gene guides sexual development in decapod crustaceans. The team mapped the gene in Portunus trituberculatus first. Its build matched the standard B-C-A pattern of its family. Gene activity showed as early as the zygote stage.

The insulin receptor gene fell in males but was absent in the ovary. The authors call IAG a broad growth and maturation coordinator.
pmc-13164167:
Kazuyuki Yusa and co-authors ask, in a 2026 pilot study, whether scans taken before jaw surgery can predict how long the operation will take. The surgery splits and resets the lower jaw on both sides. The team reviewed forty-six patients treated over seven years at one hospital.

Body weight and bone density in the jaw's upright part, read from scans, both rose with operating time. Men also had longer operations on average. Once other factors were accounted for, bone density kept its link with time. Denser bone likely resists the cut more, which slows the work. Scan readings could help teams plan theater time and staffing.
pmc-13164667:
Kelei Zhu and co-authors bake bricks from fake moon soil in a microwave and test them for building on the Moon, in a 2026 study. Shipping bricks from Earth is unthinkable, so lunar bases must use local soil, called regolith. Microwave sintering fuses that soil into solid blocks with modest energy.

Bricks baked at different heats were checked for inner structure, crushing strength, and wear. The batch sintered at one thousand degrees reached a density near three grams per cubic centimeter and a strength of 260 megapascals. The team also tested how well the bricks pass radio waves and how cracks grow, mixing lab work with simulation. Strong, signal-friendly bricks could serve as walls and landing pads alike.
pmc-13164967:
Douglas Lamounier Faria and co-authors stiffen paper boards with nano additives in a 2026 study. Boards of pressed paper layers serve in industry and as green concrete formwork, but the sodium silicate glue that binds them is weak. The team dosed that glue with a pinch of nanoclay, nanosilica, or kaolin.

Boards were built from 20 layers of recycled kraft paper and pressed hard. Density stayed the same across mixes, so the additives did not bulk the boards. Nanoclay stood out, lifting toughness by a quarter over plain glue boards. Checks on fine build rounded out the reads. The tweak offers a cheap grade lift for paper composites.
pmc-13165267:
Muhammad Rao and a large team compare wild and farmed strawberries in a 2026 study of health related compounds. Phenolic compounds give fruit much of its protective value, yet breeding for yield and looks has often thinned their variety. The team paired chemical profiling with gene activity data for one wild type and three farmed varieties.

The wild fruit had stronger antioxidant activity and a far richer mix of these compounds, including forms largely missing in farmed fruit. Each farmed variety kept a narrower, specialized profile. Gene checks found a family of control genes more active in the wild type, tied to key compounds. The authors say wild stock is a valuable source for breeding healthier fruit.
pmc-13167767:
Graham P Schmidt and co-authors study a light harvesting complex from a marine purple bacterium. These bacteria catch light with antenna proteins and pass the energy to a reaction center. The marine type studied here holds an extra pigment that boosts blue light capture, where sea light peaks.

To fit that pigment, its antenna has only seven parts, fewer than the eight or nine seen in other types. Using fast light based tests, the team found slower energy moves both within the antenna and likely between them. The trade off makes sense for its sea niche: better fit to local light, at the cost of slower transfer. The work shows how form tunes function.
pmc-13172667:
Chuang and co-authors present a 2026 review on a lipid signal system that tumors hijack. The signal, called S1P, works through five receptors on cell surfaces. Tumors rewire the system at many levels, from gene switches to receptor placement, the authors show. Extra fuel for making S1P teams up with those receptor changes to lock in the cancer state. The review sorts each receptor's role one by one. It ends with drug strategies aimed at the axis and the resistance it breeds.
pmc-13173267:
Shiloah Kviatkovsky and co-authors set out in 2026 a study protocol to profile nutrition status in joint replacement patients and link it to recovery outcomes. Nutrition is a fixable yet overlooked driver of healing after hip, knee, and shoulder replacement. Poor status may raise infection and revision risks.

The plan enrolls 800 elective surgery patients. Blood tests, body scans, and grip strength gauge readiness before surgery. Blended scores turn those measures into simple indices. Infections, hospital returns, revisions, and long stays are tracked at three months and one year. The team aims to prove which food-related metrics truly forecast trouble, so clinics can screen and feed patients before the operation.
pmc-13175267:
Jie Li and nine co-authors trace how an unusually small vertebral artery raises stroke risk over twenty years, in a two thousand twenty-six neurology cohort study. The artery variation was suspected to act partly by bending the basilar artery it feeds.

The retrospective study followed fourteen hundred sixty-four people from two thousand four to two thousand twenty-four, five hundred forty-seven with the hypoplastic artery. Ninety-one developed posterior circulation infarctions. Both the artery variation and worsening basilar bending independently raised the odds of infarction. Mediation analysis attributed about half of the variation's effect to the bending progression. The result identifies a measurable intermediate step on the path to posterior stroke.
pmc-13175967:
Marc Jones and co-authors test a stress chemical in the spit of police firearms officers in a study from 2026. Neuropeptide Y in blood tracks with calm performance under pressure. Saliva would be far easier to collect in the field. Whether spit levels mean the same was unknown.

Fifteen male officers on a tough selection course gave samples by passive drool. Sampling came one hour before a pass-or-fail shooting test. Self-rated mental states were gathered beside the samples. Shooting scores supplied the performance measure. If saliva mirrors blood, stress resilience could be screened without needles. Elite units and clinics both prize such shortcuts. The small elite sample keeps the question sharp.
pmc-13176167:
Pengfei Chen, Denian Miao, and seven co-authors test a new vaccine for a pig virus. Their paper, from twenty twenty-six, targets the 2d strain of porcine circovirus type 2. This virus causes one of the costliest diseases in pig farming worldwide. The 2d strain is now the most common, which raises doubts about older vaccines.

Their shot uses hollow shells built from the virus coat protein. Pigs that got the shot and then the live virus fared far better. They ran lower fevers and kept gaining weight. Virus levels in blood and organs dropped sharply. Strong antibody levels show the shot fired up the immune system well.
pmc-13176267:
University gym classes that blend movement with science and art are tested in a 2026 trial by Daoqing Zhang. The study asks whether a STEAM-based course can build both motor skill and the drive to keep learning in first-year students.

Seventy students were split by chance into an eight-week STEAM course built around Roliball, a racket sport, or a standard course. The STEAM group used phone video at high frame rates to study racket paths and link body mechanics to their play. Judges who did not know the groups rated skill, and tests covered course knowledge and drive to learn. The design gives a fair test of whether the mixed approach beats plain instruction.
pmc-13177167:
Yu Nagai Kanasaki, Yuki Kohno, and Takashi Makino study membranes that pull carbon dioxide from air in a 2026 paper. Capturing the gas at the faint levels found in air is a hard but needed step toward carbon neutrality. Their membranes use ionic liquids, salts that are liquid at room temperature, with carrier molecules that grab the gas and ferry it across.

The team blended carriers of varied shapes into the membrane and measured how much gas dissolved and how fast it crossed. Too much dissolving slowed crossing, while too little starved it; a middle range worked best. Tweaks to the carrier shape, plus the right heat, moisture, and mix, pushed results into that sweet range. The findings give design rules for air capture membranes.
pmc-13177567:
Danielle Southern and co-authors published a report in 2024 on tracking drug use through wastewater in Alberta. A university team adapted a system first built to track a virus during the pandemic. The joint effort with Alberta towns aims to give early warning of shifts in the drug supply. The warnings serve health workers, officials, and people who use drugs.

The system now tracks many substances, both the drugs and the traces the body leaves behind. Samples are taken up to three times a week at treatment plants, neighborhoods, and shelters. Spikes in strong drugs in the water matched rises in emergency calls for overdoses in 2023. The team is building a shared display that adds more data sources.
pmc-13177867:
Emre Demirsoy and co-authors test AI-found germ-killing peptides as a stand-in for antibiotics in broiler chickens, in a study from 2026. Heavy antibiotic use in farming breeds resistant bacteria, which drives the hunt for new options. Peptides are short protein chains that can kill germs and calm immune overreaction. A machine learning screen had picked candidates from hundreds of options.

Three lead peptides went into egg and pen trials. Infected chicks given one peptide showed fewer germ-positive organs and gained far more weight. In farm-scale pens, two peptides raised survival rates by day thirty-five. Growth and feed use stayed normal across the trials. One peptide also tamed a fierce immune signal in lab cells. The authors call the pair promising for poultry use.
pmc-13177967:
Rachel McCarter, Michael Rosato, and Gerard Leavey examined social mobility and health in Northern Ireland in a 2024 study. Three census waves linked to death records let them track disadvantage over twenty years. The question was whether moving up or down the social ladder changes the health penalty of disadvantage.

Nearly two hundred ninety thousand people aged twenty-five to seventy-four were followed. Those stuck in disadvantage showed the worst mental health and death rates, as expected. People who moved up still carried part of the pattern from the level they left, and the gap grew with the distance moved. Downward movers fared worse than upward movers at the same distance. Health stayed tightly bound to social circumstance.
pmc-13180167:
Janaína Santos Nascimento and co-authors present a 2026 paper on a digital record system for palliative care in Brazil. Good records keep end-of-life care joined up, above all in poor areas. Standard systems rarely hold social or personal detail, which blocks team planning. The team built a web platform with secure login, standard care assessment tools, and links to other systems.

From 2022 to 2025 the platform was built with an agile, user-led method. A trial inside a Rio de Janeiro favela project ran through early 2025. By then, 71 health workers had filed 520 records during home visits. Watchers logged ease of learning, clarity, and fit with daily work. Use became routine, though varied users strained some features.
pmc-13180567:
Chaoming Li and co-authors report, in a 2026 case study, how a benign belly adhesion was mistaken for returned cancer after rectal cancer surgery. The patient, a fifty-seven-year-old with advanced rectal cancer, had surgery and radiation. A later scan showed a bright nodule on the abdominal wall, and the care team suspected spread to the peritoneum, the lining of the abdomen. Such a finding would normally mean the cancer had returned.

The team chose surgical exploration and removed the lesion. Laboratory analysis showed it was a fold of fatty tissue, the greater omentum, stuck down with local inflammation, not cancer at all. The authors review why scans mislead here and what else should be weighed: past trauma, tumor markers, symptoms, and scan details together. They present the case as guidance for similar puzzling lesions.
pmc-13180767:
Sılanur Aydoğdu and co-authors studied a tomato gene that acts as a brake on ripening in 2026. Tomato ripening is driven by the hormone ethylene and a network of control genes. The gene they found, SlERF-RD1, belongs to a large family of such controls.

Plants made to overuse this gene ripened late, made far less ethylene at the peak, and stored pigments in altered patterns. Two master ripening genes were turned down in those plants. Fruits also stayed firmer late in ripening, as genes that soften cell walls were held back. The same gene shapes plant form and flowering time, which hints at use for shelf life and yield.
pmc-13181367:
Sui-Lung Su and seven co-authors report a 2026 study of air pollution and early memory loss in older adults in Taiwan. Mild memory and thinking problems often come before dementia, and they are hard to reverse once set. Dirty air has been named as a risk, but large national studies were lacking.

The team used data from the Taiwan Biobank for people over sixty, gathered between 2008 and 2021. Thinking was checked with a standard short test, and cut scores for problems varied by schooling level. Home sites were mapped so that each person could be matched with local air measures. The study then looked for links between the air measures and test scores.
pmc-13182567:
Five vets, led by Valentina Dazio, report in 2026 on four dogs with a sudden nerve illness that weakens the legs. The illness has no set cure in dog care, though a blood-cleaning method is standard for a like illness in people. That method, plasma exchange, takes out part of the blood fluid and replaces it.

All four dogs had three rounds of the treatment on back-to-back days. Each dog moved better after the first round, and all were near normal when they left care. No side effects were seen. Over the next two to twelve months, three dogs stayed well, and one relapse cleared. The cases suggest the method may speed recovery in severe cases.
pmc-13182967:
Cameron Thompson, Michael Andrews, and Douglas Adler mine the United States adverse event reporting system for the side-effect profiles of five drugs used against advanced gastrointestinal stromal tumors. These cancers, when metastatic or inoperable, are treated with avapritinib, imatinib, regorafenib, ripretinib, or sunitinib, and the team analyzed every report filed from each drug's approval through June 2025.

Fatigue and nausea or vomiting topped the lists across the drugs, but each had a signature. Avapritinib stood out for swelling around the eyes and face, imatinib for anemia and bleeding, regorafenib for a painful hand-foot skin reaction, ripretinib for hair loss, and sunitinib for bleeding and diarrhea. The authors also flag findings shared across all five, including headache and gait problems, plus low blood counts with imatinib. They present the comparison as a practical safety map for clinicians choosing among the options.
pmc-13183467:
Selim Sevim, Chadi Hajar, and Snehal Sonawane survey in 2026 what is new in digital pathology, where tissue slides are scanned and read with computer help. Growth is fast worldwide, driven by whole-slide imaging, AI tools, and better digital systems. Remote work and shared diagnosis add to the push.

The review covers rising adoption in the United States and abroad, backed by professional guidance and new payment paths. Shared data standards, clearer rules, and regulator approvals have firmed up clinical use. Large shared image banks and training methods that keep data at home site support stronger, privacy-safe models. New foundation models and AI copilots are reshaping diagnosis support, outcome forecasts, and trial work. The authors frame the field as moving from pilot projects toward daily clinical practice.
pmc-13184567:
Maxwell Voorn and co-authors compare how much bacteria wiping cloths transfer to clean surfaces. Their study deals with cross-spread in health care, a little-noted route for germs.

Staphylococcus aureus and Pseudomonas aeruginosa both persist in wards. The team tested hydrogen peroxide, a quaternary ammonium compound, and an alcohol cleaner with cotton, microfiber, and meltblown polypropylene wipes. Wipes were loaded heavily, then used on clean counters. Polypropylene cloths moved far less than the other two. The work focuses on transfer when cleaning is incomplete. Such transfer is one way infections spread between patients in care settings.
pmc-13185567:
A lung virus that hits children hard gets into cells by two doors at once, and the doors help each other. Lihua Ye and ten co-authors prove the pair in 2026 for adenovirus type 7. Past work had named each door alone for kin viruses; this one's picks were in doubt. The team threw every test at the ask: extra doors grown in cells, doors hushed, doors blocked by antibodies, and pure grip measures.

Both doors at once let the virus in far better than either alone. Mice bred to carry both human doors sickened worse than one-door or plain mice. The virus's grip knob holds both doors at once, at split spots and split strengths. The team say the pair is a mark for drugs, and a map for taming the virus into a delivery tool.
pmc-13185767:
Chengfeng Zhang and co-authors build a nanoparticle treatment meant to break the cycle that keeps chronic pain going. Their 2026 study targets the loop between nerve inflammation and oxidative stress in the spinal cord and brain. The platform packs selenium-doped carbon dots, which act as artificial enzymes, plus a plant anti-inflammatory compound into fat bubbles called liposomes.

In cell tests the particles neutralized harmful reactive species and calmed overactive immune cells of the nervous system. A single dose eased inflammatory pain in mice for up to three days, far longer than a standard shot. The treatment also helped in nerve injury and chemotherapy pain models. Safety tests looked clean. The authors pitch the platform as a long-acting option for chronic pain care.
pmc-13185867:
Taymaz Akan and five co-authors apply a flexible neural network to muscle disease images, in this 2026 paper. Computational pathology uses AI to read tissue slides, but standard networks apply the same fixed filters everywhere. Diseased tissue varies a lot in pattern, stain, and structure, so fixed filters can miss the signs that matter.

Their network, ODConv, adjusts its filters along four axes at once: position, input channel, output channel, and filter choice. They trained it from scratch, with no borrowed pretraining, on stained muscle images from mouse models of ALS and type 1 diabetes. It matched seven fine-tuned rival networks that had the head start of image pretraining. Scores also showed it handled class balance well. The authors offer it as a sturdy base for automated diagnosis of muscle disorders.
pmc-13187067:
Life frozen in Himalayan ice is cataloged in a 2026 study by Sonia Tamang and co-authors, who drilled cores from two glaciers in Sikkim. The Himalayas hold the largest ice fields outside the poles, yet the microbes in Sikkim's ice were barely known.

Gene-based analysis found a spread of bacterial groups, led by four major phyla. A machine learning model pointed to elements such as sodium, magnesium, potassium, calcium, and zinc as the strongest shapers of microbe diversity in the ice. The team also read the genes for antibiotic resistance and for the jobs the microbes can do. The study gives a baseline for a region where glaciers are shrinking fast.
pmc-13189067:
Mauricio Danckers and co-authors offer a 2026 review on support for LGBTQ+ trainees in medical training. Support varies a lot across specialties and schools. Gaps persist in course content, in mentors who affirm trainees, and in school-level backing. The team searched three sources for work from 2019 to early 2026 on trainee life and training practice.

Three themes ran through the finds. Teaching on LGBTQ+ health was uneven and often thin on trans health. Mentors and role models shaped how safe trainees felt to be open. School climate set whether support felt real or just a show. The authors urge aligned work on teaching, mentors, hiring, and daily practice.
pmc-13189767:
Luke Liu and Deborah Duricka report a man's twenty-eight years of severe motion sickness vanishing after neck nerve blocks for arm pain, in work from twenty twenty-six. Motion sickness springs from sensory conflict plus autonomic overdrive. The sixty-eight-year-old receives stellate ganglion blocks for complex regional pain. The blocks quiet a major sympathetic relay in the neck. His travel sickness was never the treatment's target.

After several block rounds he reports complete, lasting relief. Twelve months on, repeated boating brings no symptoms back. No motion sickness medicine is needed during follow-up. The block's brief drug action suggests lasting reflex rewiring. Overactive vestibulo-sympathetic reflexes fit the sickness pattern well. An accidental cure opens a research door for sufferers.
pmc-13191267: A sore, aching prostate with no clear infection can defy drug after drug. Leandro Reina Alcaina and Jesús Rodríguez Martínez report one hard case in 2026: a man of forty-four whose pain had beaten standard care. He tried a home routine of targeted vibration to the gland. Twelve weeks on, his symptom score fell from 26 to 14, pain eased most, and no ill effects came up. One case proves little, but a cheap, drug-free home option merits a fair trial.
pmc-13191367:
Yanting Zhang and colleagues review the measurement traits of the revised Richards-Campbell Sleep Questionnaire, a tool to assess sleep in intensive care patients. Sleep in such care is known to be poor and counts for health, so the quality of the tool matters. The review used standard guidelines, and graded studies with the COSMIN risk-of-bias checklist and mate quality rules.

Fourteen studies were taken in, covering eight language versions of the revised questionnaire, most from Asian countries. Samples went past intensive care to older inpatients, orthopedic patients around surgery, and acute stroke patients. Scores held up well inside most versions, but content validity, structural validity, and validity across cultures were thin, as was measurement error. The quality of methods showed some risk of bias. Proof across versions did not line up well.
pmc-13191467:
Roberto Godoy and co-authors report a 2026 first: spores of root fungi found inside moss balls in southern Chile. The moss Rigodium implexum rolls into loose balls, ten to twenty centimeters wide, that mass on the floor of Valdivian rainforests. Inside balls from two forest sites, the team found spores of four fungi that normally partner with plant roots.

The four species were named by their shape under standard keys. How the spores travel with the moss is an open question, and the authors flag shared dispersal as a topic for more work. They also share a method for pulling such spores out of this kind of plant matter, which other field teams can reuse.
pmc-13191767:
Wittaya Chaiwangyen and a team of co-authors test a plant extract for shielding placenta cells from stress, in a paper dated twenty twenty-six. The plant, Elsholtzia kachinensis, is rich in rosmarinic acid. One extract fraction showed the strongest antioxidant power and the richest store of plant chemicals. The team treated human trophoblast cells, which form the placenta's outer layer, with a bacterial toxin plus the extract.

The extract saved cell growth, movement, and invasion that the toxin had harmed. It cut cell suicide, oxygen waste, and swelling signals. It worked by lowering a small RNA that the toxin raises and restoring its target gene. The authors see a lead for guarding pregnancy health.
pmc-13193667:
Xiaohong Xu and co-authors pool the trial evidence for internet self-help programs for irritable bowel syndrome, in a 2026 review. The condition is common, drags down quality of life, and loads clinics. Online self-help is flexible and easy to scale, but the evidence was scattered.

Seventeen randomized trials from seven countries, with 2,289 participants, met the criteria. Against control groups, the online programs significantly eased symptom severity, improved quality of life, and reduced gut sensitivity and depressive symptoms. Anxiety results did not reach significance in the visible portion of the analysis. The team graded evidence quality formally and used a conservative statistical model suited to few trials. Effects varied between studies, with prediction intervals crossing zero for some outcomes. The authors conclude the approach helps, while calling for more uniform and rigorous trials.
pmc-13193967:
Yadan Ye built a deep learning model that reads feelings in dance therapy in a 2026 paper. Dance therapy helps mental health, but feelings shift fast and are hard to track live. Past tools read just the face or just the body, and miss much of the change.

The model, DanceEmoNet, joins face reads with body pose reads in one net. It spots faces and poses, tracks them over time, and fuses the two streams. In tests it beat bench mark models on many scores, ran faster per frame, and cost less to run. Gains ran from five to ten percent, which suits live therapy use.
pmc-13194167:
Pooya Eini and co-authors review tiny RNA markers for a dangerous aortic swelling in a 2026 paper. An abdominal aortic aneurysm can rupture without warning, and doctors lack a blood test to catch it early. MicroRNAs, small gene regulators shed into blood, are promising candidates.

Thirty-nine studies met the review's bar. A consistent panel emerged: several microRNAs ran high in patients, including miR-21 and miR-155, while others, like the let-7 family, ran low. The changes showed in plasma, serum, and vessel tissue, and the molecules feed into pathways for inflammation and vessel wall breakdown. Reported accuracy varied a lot between studies. The authors call the panel promising for screening, pending standard methods and prospective validation.
pmc-13194467:
Wen He and colleagues describe a two thousand twenty-six case report of a high-grade neuroendocrine carcinoma that masqueraded as squamous lung cancer. Some of these tumours switch off their usual marker proteins. Their squared shape then misleads pathologists toward a different diagnosis and treatment.

Biopsies from lung and liver showed poorly differentiated tumour with all classic neuroendocrine markers negative. Rapid liver spread, a soaring marker enzyme, and fierce growth rate contradicted the first diagnosis. A ninety-gene expression test reclassified the tumour. The case warns that marker-negative results demand molecular backup when behaviour disagrees.
pmc-13195267:
Ning Tian and co-authors report a study from two thousand twenty-six comparing stool chemistry in children with and without migraine. Most gut research on migraine covers adults, leaving children's metabolic patterns largely unmapped. The team used targeted chemical profiling to look for a signature tied to the childhood form of the disease.

They enrolled thirty children with migraine and thirty healthy peers, aged five to fourteen, in Hebei Province, China. Eight amino acid compounds ran higher in the migraine group, including valine, leucine, and phenylalanine. Those changes clustered in pathways that build and break down key amino acids. Short-chain fatty acids differed too, though most single comparisons fell short of clear significance. The authors call the work exploratory.
pmc-13197067:
Cristina Aldaz-Barreno and co-authors track hospital stays for neglected tropical diseases in Ecuador in a 2026 study. Twenty-one such diseases burden millions worldwide, yet trends in their most severe cases are little known. The team mined twenty-five years of national discharge records.

About one hundred eighty thousand discharges tied to these diseases appeared from 2000 to 2024. Five conditions made up nearly all of them, led by dengue and a related viral illness, then snakebite. Deaths were rare, and patients skewed young and male. Viral cases drove an overall rise, while snakebite, worm, and tapeworm stays fell steadily. Coastal and Amazon provinces carried the heaviest burden.
pmc-13197767:
Yu'e Sun and co-authors take stock of the live monitoring that guards the nervous system during brain and spine surgery. Electrodes watch motor and sensory signals while the surgeon works, warning when a cut threatens movement or feeling. The review weighs what is settled practice, what is still argued, and where the field is heading.

Good results rest on two pillars, they say: combined signal monitoring and an anesthesia style built on intravenous drugs with careful muscle relaxation. The method cuts nerve damage in spine deformity, tumor, and hearing-nerve surgeries. Yet alarms are often false, and turning a signal dip into the right action stays hard. The authors look ahead to artificial intelligence dashboards that predict trouble instead of merely reporting it, while urging common standards and team-wide training.
pmc-13197867:
Pishoy Gouda and co-authors run a randomized trial on how to recruit people into research by message, in a paper from 2026. Recruitment shapes who joins a study and how far its results apply. Digital invites are now common, but proof on the best channel and wording was thin.

The trial sat inside a larger heart disease prevention study at one large academic health system. Invites were sent either by email or through a patient portal. The message text appealed either to helping others or to personal gain. The main measure was interest, shown by logging on to the study site. The design lets each factor be judged on its own and in combination. The authors frame the work as evidence for a routine but understudied step in research.
pmc-13198067: Federica Vernacchia and four co-authors present a 2026 case report on a heart tracing that seemed to show a block but did not. A sixty-five-year-old man came to hospital with fever, belly pain, and tiredness and was treated for abdominal sepsis. He had no heart symptoms and stayed stable. His electrocardiogram, though, showed odd conduction patterns. Review found the machine's signal had briefly saturated, faking a pattern that mimicked advanced atrioventricular block. The authors stress checking a tracing's internal agreement before diagnosing a heart wiring fault.
pmc-13198367:
Hamza Chraibi and co-authors report a case where a routine heart procedure tore both main coronary arteries, in a paper published in 2026. Catheter-caused dissection happens in fewer than one in a thousand procedures, and tears in both arteries at once are rarer still. Their patient was a forty-year-old woman with no medical history, admitted with a non-ST-elevation acute coronary syndrome.

Her first angiogram showed no blockages. Afterwards she developed crushing chest pain and went into ventricular fibrillation, needing electrical cardioversion. A second look revealed simultaneous dissections of the left main and right coronary arteries. Emergency stents sealed both tears, tests for vessel disease came back negative, and she went home four days later. The case stresses instant recognition and stenting.
pmc-13198467:
Kirsi Manz and colleagues tested a new iron marker in blood cancers in a 2026 study. Myeloproliferative neoplasms are cancers where the marrow makes too many blood cells. Inflammation and anemia blur standard iron tests there, so the team checked zinc protoporphyrin, a marker that rises when red cells lack iron.

They studied 445 patients and compared them with a large general cohort. Standard iron patterns flipped in cancer patients: higher stored iron went with lower blood counts, the reverse of healthy people. About twenty-eight percent had high marker values showing true iron shortage. Values varied by cancer subtype and tied to blood counts more than to stored iron. The marker may sharpen iron checks in these cancers.
pmc-13199067:
Kenjiro Kaneko and colleagues review balloons and stents for leg artery disease in a 2026 article, translated from a 2024 Japanese journal paper. Endovascular therapy treats narrowed leg arteries from inside the vessel. Better balloons and stents have widened who can be treated and improved results.

The review covers basic device topics for daily practice. Balloon catheters vary by wire size, length, and how they ride the guidewire. Choice depends on vessel width, lesion length, and access route. Stents prop vessels open after balloon widening. With device variety growing, selection has grown more complex. The authors lay out core traits to guide sound picks for each lesion.
pmc-13200567:
Ulcerative colitis can be controlled with modern drugs for many patients, but some still lose their colon to surgery. Sandro Ferreira and co-authors reviewed two hundred thirty-two patients at a Brazilian referral center to learn who ends up needing a colectomy. About one in five had the operation. The leading reasons were disease that no longer answered to medicine, and sudden severe flares.

Longer disease duration raised the odds of surgery. So did inflammation spanning the whole colon, compared with disease limited to the rectum, and severe findings on endoscopy at diagnosis. Patients who started on biological drugs early also went to surgery more often, most likely because their disease was the most aggressive from the start. Sex, race, smoking, and steroid use showed no link. The authors conclude that wide and severe disease at diagnosis marks the patients most likely to need surgery later.
pmc-13200667:
Jae Hyun Park examines how white hair makes scalps look thinner in a 2026 clinical article. White hair lacks pigment, so it contrasts weakly with the scalp and can look translucent under magnification. The scalp then seems exposed even when hair density and thickness are unchanged, a visual illusion with real clinic effects.

The article lays out the optics of scalp show-through and its non-linear rise as white share grows. Misreading it can lead to overtreatment for hair loss that is not progressing. Transplant work also suffers: pale hairs complicate strip dissection and graft harvest and placement. Five dyeing principles for white-haired patients close the piece. The claims rest on clinical experience, not yet on measured trials.
pmc-13202167:
Premature babies often need repeated blood transfusions, and a 2026 retrospective study authored by Malavika Krishnakumar builds a tool to predict that need from two simple measures. The research article analyzes transfusion patterns in a South Indian neonatal intensive care unit and models requirements from gestational age and birth weight.

The study covered preterm babies born at twenty-three to thirty-two weeks who received at least one transfusion during 2023. In total, 422 transfusions went to 118 babies, with smaller and earlier babies needing the most blood and the most donors. A Bayesian model using the two birth measures reduced projected multi-donor exposure, offering better planning for blood banks.
pmc-13202267:
Ryan Kilburn, Rachel Gomez, and Steven Evans describe a new lab test for checking the caps on RNA molecules, in a 2026 paper. RNA medicines need a cap at one end to work well, and makers must measure how many molecules carry it. Older tests depend on the exact RNA sequence, which slows work when many products are in development. The new test works for any RNA sequence.

The method digests the RNA with an enzyme, then measures capped and uncapped ends against known standards. A paired check corrects for leftover reagents, and the machine run takes ten minutes. The test covers a wide range of amounts using standards that labs can buy. It is built to support quality control as RNA therapies move through production.
pmc-13202767:
Hiromi Kumamaru and co-authors blame quiet spinal fluid for a surgical complication in a 2026 neurosurgery study. After lumbar decompression, blood can pool around the spinal cord's sac, an epidural hematoma that sometimes compresses nerves, and why some patients bleed this way was unclear.

Ninety-four patients had their spinal fluid pressure measured before surgery and their spines scanned after. Nearly a third showed a significant hematoma. Lower fluid pressure predicted it independently, alongside the number of levels operated on: with less internal pressure, the sac resists the blood less. Because pressure is potentially modifiable, the finding hints at prevention, not just prediction.
pmc-13202867:
Davies and co-authors build a shared guideline in 2026 for a quiet corner of drug trials: the run-in phase. Some trials use a run-in to keep only patients likely to take the study drug as told. How those phases are run and reported varies widely, with no clear rules, the team notes.

First, a review of past trials yielded draft items in two sets, methods and reporting. Experts in drug-taking research then rated and sorted the items over two survey rounds, with free comments in the first. Pilot work sharpened the wording before the vote. A shared rule set could make run-in phases fairer to judge, since readers could see who was kept out and why, and compare trials on equal terms.
pmc-13203067:
Matthew D Galsky and colleagues present a two thousand twenty-six trial design paper for bladder and urinary tract cancer that has advanced after standard therapy. A leading first-line drug pair now sets the standard. What to give after it stops working lacks randomized guidance.

The global trial tests an antibody-drug conjugate plus platinum chemotherapy against a standard pairing. A first phase picks between two doses in a small group. A larger phase then compares the chosen dose head-to-head in hundreds of patients. The design aims to settle post-progression treatment with solid evidence.
pmc-13203567:
Haotian Li and five co-authors compared gut bacteria in two thousand twenty-six in wild and captive horses and their kin. Captivity can harm the health of Equus species, yet which harmful bacteria they carry was poorly mapped due to thin databases. The team sampled three species, including Przewalski's horse, across wild and captive settings.

Gene sequencing plus a broad pathogen database showed captive animals from distinct places grew alike in their harmful gut bacteria. Captive animals carried more bacteria that can pass to humans, while wild ones carried more animal-only pathogens. The authors warn captivity may raise cross-species infection risk and urge care in zoo management.
pmc-13204067:
Panayiotis Gavriil and colleagues test a joint fluid marker for infection around tumour limb implants, in work from 2026. Infection after megaprosthesis repair is hard to prove due to past surgery and blurred standard scores. Calprotectin in joint fluid is a fast marker from white cells that may sharpen that call.

Twenty patients with suspected infection at a sarcoma centre in Athens were tested. A lateral flow test read the marker against a fixed positive cut off value. Thirteen patients met the set standard for true infection in the cohort. Common germs were skin staphylococci, with mixed germ cases also present. The study checks the marker against standard scores and in unclear score cases.
pmc-13204567:
Laura Del Gaudio, Stefano Lattanzio, Roberta Di Pietro, and Silvia Sancilio review how engineered materials coax the body to regrow tissue. Their review appeared in 2026. A good scaffold must invite cells to settle, grow, and specialize, and its chemistry, stiffness, and surface all matter. The authors survey natural and synthetic options, how the body answers them, and the tricks used to tune their surfaces.

Special weight goes to cold atmospheric plasma, which rewrites just the topmost layer of a material, making it wetter, stickier for proteins, and better at holding drugs. Stem cell behavior on these materials and AI tools that predict performance close the survey. The authors see design and surface treatment converging.
pmc-13205367:
Xiaonan Ma, Hua Yang, Yanli Xu, and Naoki Wakamiya wrote this 2026 study on drone relays for emergency communication at sea. Ships in trouble often sit beyond shore coverage, so drones acting as flying base stations can be sent out fast. The catch is a hard joint choice: which drone serves which ship, and where each drone should hover, as ships move and batteries drain.

The team splits the joint problem in two. A search method with priority rules assigns ships to drones, honoring load caps, urgency classes, and a floor on signal strength. A learning method with several cooperating agents then steers the drones over time, with tricks to keep training stable. Ships are classed by how urgent their need is. The authors report that the paired methods squeeze more long-run value from the fleet than simpler plans.
pmc-13205467:
Six authors, led by Andrea Chellini, tested a wellness program for women that mixes food, movement, breath, and touch in this 2026 study. Modern life loads the body with stress, and both physical and mental measures suffer. The program, called e-Motion training, bundles nutrition advice, physical activity, breathing practice, and hugging into one routine.

Thirty-three women, average age about forty-one, took part for six weeks; some trained and some served as controls. Before and after, the team measured heart rate patterns, surface fat, and trunk flexibility. Thinking tests checked attention and memory span. The trained group improved on several heart measures and other markers the report details. The study weighs a gentle, low-cost routine against hard outcomes, not just how participants felt.
pmc-13206267:
Yachen Xie and co-authors report a 2026 chemistry study on DNA strands that grab folate, the vitamin also known as B9. Folate matters most in pregnancy, and sensors that spot it fast and surely have clear medical value.

The team used a method called Capture-SELEX to fish out DNA aptamers, short strands that fold around a target. Their best strand bound folate tightly, with a dissociation constant of 640 nanomolar. Built into a glow-based sensor, it detected folate at very low levels, even in diluted blood serum. Look-alike molecules such as caffeine and adenine barely registered. The work gives food and health testers a sturdy new sensing part.
pmc-13206667:
Anushree Nagaraj and Ali Seyfoddin print cheek films that carry weed goods through the cheek skin, in a study from 2026. Cheek dose skips the gut and the liver first pass, which suits drugs that fade there. Two film bases, one smooth and one sour, host the goods in sugar ring packs.

Plant scent goods were tried as skin keys, solo and in blends. Blends beat solo scents and a lab made key at push of the calm good through cheek flesh. The smooth base gave strong films with a slow, odd pace of drug leak and fine push. The sour base stuck best but wore fast and broke weak. Print films can dose by cheek, the team finds.
pmc-13206767:
Zach Pennington and co-authors find what predicts solid bone fusion and wear at neighbouring levels after front-approach lower spine fusion, in a 2026 study. Records covered 177 patients treated at 245 levels, all with at least a year of scan follow-up.

Most levels fused, with added back fixation beating standalone cages. Front placement of the cage and use of a bone growth protein raised fusion odds. Wear at the next level hit about eighteen percent of levels and led to reoperation in about six percent. Older age, repeat surgery, a collapsed disc, and a gas sign in the joint predicted that wear. Nothing predicted reoperation itself. The authors back combined fixation for fusion odds.
pmc-13207467:
Lisset Herrera-Isidron and co-authors study how a growth regulator swells potato microtubers in a study from 2026. The chemical, paclobutrazol, blocks the making of gibberellins, plant hormones that drive stem growth. Treated plants stay compact yet grow bigger storage organs. The gene-level chain behind that trade was unclear.

Potato plants grown in the lab formed microtubers under the treatment. Shoots called stolons shrank while the tubers expanded. Tissue slices and full gene scans tracked the shift. Whole pathways for metabolism and signaling changed their activity. The results frame the effect as a full developmental reprogram, not just stunted growth. Seed potato producers may use such control to raise uniform microtubers.
pmc-13207567:
Shriyeta Biswas and co-authors set the two great joint diseases side by side in a 2026 review. Osteoarthritis wears cartilage down; rheumatoid arthritis is an immune attack on the joint lining. Shared pain and stiffness make early separation hard, and delay costs function.

The review contrasts how each disease works, cell by cell. Wear disease turns on matrix breakdown, tired cartilage cells, and mechanical stress. The immune disease runs on faulty activation, self-attack antibodies, and stubborn lining inflammation. Diagnosis blends exams, advanced imaging, and new molecular markers. Care spans pain drugs, steroids, immune-targeting medicines, biologic agents, therapy, lifestyle change, and surgery. The aim is earlier, better-matched treatment.
pmc-13208367:
Jin, Feng, Tong, Li, Huang, and Peng test in twenty twenty-six how welding heat changes joints between two different magnesium alloys. Welding helps these light alloys reach wider engineering use. But fast heating and cooling can coarsen grains near the weld, making that zone the weak point where joints fail.

The team welded thin sheets at several heat levels and checked strength and structure. One mid-level heat gave the best overall result, with the finest, most even spread of hard particles near the weld. All breaks still occurred on the same side's heat-affected zone. The findings give welders a target heat for strong, sound joints in such mixed alloys.
pmc-13208767:
Soobin Lee and co-authors report a new way to build light sensors in this 2026 paper. Their sensor rests on a flake of a layered crystal that soaks up visible light well. Moving such flakes into large, neat films has been hard, which held back low-power devices.

The team uses a gel pad to lift and lay the flakes onto a glass base coated with a second material. The gel doubles as the thin control layer of the device. The finished sensor ran on low voltage and switched sharply between dark and light. It answered most strongly to violet light in their tests. The authors offer the gel route as a base for next-round light gear.
pmc-13208867:
Nikolaos Martinos and co-authors tested whether blood markers can spot hidden gut inflammation in bowel disease patients whose gut lining looks healed, in a 2026 study. In ulcerative colitis, the surface can look calm through a scope while tissue samples still show active disease. That hidden activity raises the risk of relapse. The team measured two signaling proteins and one standard inflammation marker in blood taken before a colon exam.

The main group held thirty-one patients whose colitis looked quiet. Nearly half of them still had active tissue disease. One marker, interleukin-10, sorted them best: low levels flagged the hidden activity with good accuracy. A second marker added little alone but refined the risk groups when paired with the first. The combined ladder ran from seven percent active in the lowest group to all active in the highest. The authors call for bigger trials.
pmc-13209167:
Yang Li and co-authors tackle a noise problem in very precise laser measuring systems in a 2026 study. When a steering device tilts a beam, the tilt can leak into the length reading and fake a signal. This flaw is called tilt-to-length coupling, and it plagues instruments that must measure tiny changes over huge distances.

The team wiggles the beam in a steady cycle and compares the length signal with the tilt signal at that rhythm. That trick separates a sideways misalignment from other noise and lets them measure it. Correcting the offset cut the tilt noise by ninety-four percent, and the device's own stray motion fell by more than half. The method suits space-grade instruments that track gravitational signals.
pmc-13209467:
Zebrafish embryos are see-through at first, but pigment soon clouds the view of their inner organs. Muhammad Farooq Khan and Mohammad Ahmad Wadaan test a plant extract as a gentler way to keep embryos clear. The usual blocking chemicals, PTU and kojic acid, carry real toxicity concerns.

Extracts of lady's mantle were made with four solvents and compared for clearing power and safety. The ethyl acetate version cleared pigment best and proved least toxic, and it still worked when applied two days after fertilization, after pigment had formed. Chemical analysis found it rich in linoleic acid, fatty esters, and phenolics. The authors propose it as a natural stand-in for long imaging studies.
pmc-13210267:
Star ratings hide how hard a product is to live with, and a 2026 study headed by Shoukat Ullah builds a model that reads reviews for complexity instead. The research article pairs a transformer language model with a recurrent network to judge Amazon reviews along two appraisal dimensions: user-friendliness and judged effectiveness.

Human annotators first labeled reviews by perceived complexity, and an explanation method cross-checked those labels for consistency. The hybrid model then learned both context and word order, reaching higher cross-validated accuracy than the forest, transformer-only, and large language model baselines cited. Built-in explanations show which words drive each judgment, making the scores auditable for shoppers and sellers.
pmc-13210567:
Kubra Kose and co-authors built a drone testbed for hardware flaws in two thousand twenty-six. Drone software is often tuned inside simulators. Real hardware behaves differently in telling ways. Their testbed compares simulated and real flight logs. Both run the same PX4 flight stack. A shared pipeline extracts the telemetry streams.

Vibration, sensor noise, and signal interference diverged sharply. Real flights exposed faults invisible in simulation. Resource strain on board also differed. Baselines now quantify the sim-to-real gap. Security checks can validate against those baselines. Hardware attacks leave traces the testbed can catch. The work serves safer drone certification.
pmc-13210667:
Silvia Garofalide and co-authors tested whether gold particles coated with fat bubbles can protect the brain, in a 2026 zebrafish study. The gold particles were made by a chemical route, then exposed to natural green light. A fat layer drawn from a common membrane fat was added by simple contact, which also partly wrapped some particles.

The coated mix held together better in fluid, with a stronger surface charge and larger size. The team then gave it to zebrafish whose memory had been impaired by a drug. Tests of behavior and body chemistry weighed anxiety-like acts, memory, and oxidative stress, with a known drug as a yardstick. Under normal conditions the mix caused no clear harm.
pmc-13211067:
Na Zhang and nine co-authors study why coal dust scars the lungs, focusing on a protein that links two cell structures. Coal workers' pneumoconiosis is a leading job disease in China, marked by stiffening lung tissue. Tiny contact zones between mitochondria and the endoplasmic reticulum govern calcium flow and cell energy, and their breakdown is tied to scarring diseases. Their 2026 study centers on MFN2, a protein that holds those contact zones together.

Raising MFN2 levels in their models eased the dust-driven scarring. The effect ran through keeping the contact zones intact and cutting programmed cell death. The authors present MFN2 as a possible drug target for a disease that now has no cure. The work joins a shift toward treating fibrosis by repairing cell structure, not just symptoms.
pmc-13211767:
