Doris Chirinos-Peinado and colleagues assess lead and cadmium risk in raw milk from Peruvian Andes farms. Their risk study from twenty twenty-six covers small-scale dairy systems. Milk nourishes children, but mining pollution can taint it. Metal transfer into the food chain needs local measurement.

Forty-five milk samples were tested with emission spectrometry. Average metal levels stayed below legal limits overall. Hotspots near smelters showed much higher lead levels, though. Risk was modelled for ages from toddlers to the elderly. Three consumption levels covered light to heavy milk drinkers. The findings separate general safety from localised danger. Targeted monitoring near industry protects families best.
pmc-13211867:
Remote monitoring only works if patients can and will use it, and a 2026 qualitative study headed by Syed Mustafa Ali listens to a group often missed by such research. Seventeen Pakistani adults in the United Kingdom with rheumatoid or early inflammatory arthritis, none with English as a first language, joined interviews or a focus group about monitoring technology.

None had used remote monitoring before, yet many saw value in it, especially where current services dissatisfied them. Needs split by generation: first-generation immigrants leaned more on family and community help with technology than later generations did. Language support and relatives' involvement emerged as design requirements, not afterthoughts, for equitable rollout.
pmc-13212367:
John J. Tyson published a 2026 correction to his paper revisiting Alan Turing's chemical theory of pattern formation in development. The notice repairs formatting faults that crept in during production and distorted several mathematical statements in the published version.

Readers are shown the faulty lines beside their repaired forms for three places in the paper, covering a steady-state condition, a matrix equation, and a set of inequalities. The equations render poorly in print, with markup and stray characters mixed into the maths. Even so, the notice lets anyone checking the model use the intended symbols rather than the corrupted print.
pmc-13212767:
Anisha and colleagues explore in 2026 whether future electron-positron colliders could detect signs of a violent early-universe transition involving two Higgs fields. Such a transition might explain why matter outnumbers antimatter today, a puzzle the standard model cannot solve.

The team checked model settings that allow a strong first-order transition against expected precision from planned machines in Europe and China. Even when current collider data look standard, the rate of Higgs production alongside a Z boson should shift by more than the planned machines' tiny measurement error. Precision Higgs measurements could therefore expose hidden physics indirectly, long before any new particle appears directly.
pmc-13212867:
Enhui He and colleagues review in 2026 how nanotechnology is reshaping neuroprostheses, devices that restore lost senses or movement by linking electronics to the nervous system. The weak point remains the junction where hard electronics meet soft living tissue.

The review covers six device classes, from motor and visual systems to memory and smell, and proposes an architecture built around two key interfaces. New materials promise gentler, sharper electrodes and better sensors, while brain-inspired computing could process signals on the device itself. The authors look toward two-way, adaptive systems that adjust in a closed loop, aiming for a far more natural fit between machine and nerve.
pmc-13213167:
Hiroko Otake and co-authors test in 2026 whether adding a moisture-holding polymer to glaucoma eye drops helps the drug work longer. Timolol lowers eye pressure, but tears wash drops away quickly, so keeping the drug on the eye surface could improve its effect.

In rats and rabbits, the polymer additive formed tiny particles in a clear, stable drop and caused no damage with repeated use. More timolol stayed on the eye, crossed the cornea, and reached the inner fluid than with ordinary drops. In rabbits with raised pressure, the combined drop lowered pressure more strongly and for longer. The additive looks like a safe route to longer-acting glaucoma treatment.
pmc-13214267:
Ziqi Shang and ten co-authors traced how breathing machines and sepsis hurt lungs through one shared path in a 2026 study. Both harms leave lasting oxidative stress and a weak vessel lining. The team joined population data, gene profiles, and single cell reads to find the shared program and a plant compound that may block it.

Survey data tied more intake of the compound, kaempferol, to better lung function in men. Lab work showed it binds a stress enzyme in the cell wall and shuts a chain that breaks the vessel lining. In cells and animals it cut stress damage and raised survival in a sepsis lung model. The authors name it a lead drug for both kinds of lung harm.
pmc-13215167:
Suqin Q. Duan and co-authors examine in 2026 the statistics of extreme rain across the world's weather systems, asking whether the worst downpours follow one pattern. Models struggle with these events, which drive floods and infrastructure damage.

Using high-resolution hourly observations split by system type, they found the intense tails of rain distributions share a typical shape set mainly by storm dynamics. Heat and moisture conditions scale how big the tail gets. Because dominant storm types share similar environments, overall extremes largely inherit their shape. Exceptions appear where intense tropical lows or overlapping storm clusters stack the odds. Risk assessors, the authors say, can often skip fine weather typing.
pmc-13215467:
Tsebaot Tesfaye and co-authors report a balloon procedure that relieved a narrowed pulmonary valve in a woman whose rheumatic disease had touched all four heart valves, in this 2026 case report. She had already received two replacement valves and one repair, so another open operation carried high risk. Scans showed the pulmonary valve squeezed tight, with pressure across it near 97 millimeters of mercury.

Guided by X-ray imaging, the team inflated a balloon inside the valve and stretched it open. The pressure gap fell to about 35 at once, and her breathlessness eased. Three months on she stayed symptom-free with the gain holding. The authors present the balloon route as a safer stand-in for repeat surgery in well-chosen patients.
pmc-13215667:
Roy van den Heuvel and co-authors present a 2026 mixed methods study of an app that helps people with diabetes check their own feet for ulcer risk. Foot ulcers are a serious diabetes complication, and podiatry services face rising demand.

Twenty-four patients with type 2 diabetes used the Feetchecker app for three months, logging 393 checks and sending nine photos that all prompted podiatrist follow-up calls. Patients rated the app positively and valued how easily a photo could reach a professional. Engagement fell into steady, frequent, and minimal patterns, shaped by ease of use, social support, and digital skills. Podiatrists liked the faster reporting but found promoting the app in consultations difficult.
pmc-13216167:
Toru Nakai and co-authors present a 2026 case report, with a literature review, on treating a ruptured aneurysm of a tiny perforating branch of the basilar artery. These aneurysms cause bleeding around the brainstem and are notoriously hard to even see on first scans.

Their patient, a 75-year-old woman, showed no clear aneurysm on day one; repeat angiography on day four revealed a small saccular bulge that later grew. On day sixteen the team threaded in two overlapping LVIS Blue stents to divert flow while keeping the perforator open. She recovered without symptoms, and imaging at one month showed the aneurysm completely closed. The authors argue the overlapping stent approach suits aneurysms arising from the basilar trunk.
pmc-13218167:
Kavindhaya Karunarathna and co-authors present a 2026 protocol for a qualitative systematic review of family caregiving in cancer palliative care across countries. In low-income and lower-middle-income countries, formal palliative services are scarce, so relatives deliver most care for adults with advanced cancer. Their experience is the foundation the system rests on, yet it is rarely gathered together.

The review will search PubMed, Embase, CINAHL, and PsycINFO with no language or date limits, plus an open repository for grey literature. Studies of family caregivers of adults receiving end-of-life cancer care in these countries will be appraised with Joanna Briggs Institute tools. Findings will be combined through meta-aggregation, or narratively if pooling proves unworkable, and reported under the ENTREQ framework. No ethics approval is needed for published data. The team will publish openly and carry the recommendations to policymakers and organizations that run palliative services.
pmc-13219267:
Liyun Wei, Lemuge Qi, Xiaoqian Yu, Aiping Shi, and Zhu Zhu review a candidate gene in breast cancer in a 2026 paper. The gene, TNNT3, normally helps muscle contract as part of the troponin set. The team's past work linked it to triple-negative breast cancer, a hard-to-treat form. Cancer growth is now seen as shaped by forces too: how cells pull, stick, and sense stiff tissue.

The review sorts proof into three piles. Direct breast cancer proof is thin. Wider proof from force-based cell biology is broader. Pure models of how the gene might act are marked as guesses. The authors do not claim the gene drives the cancer. They frame it as a low-proof but intriguing lead that needs tests in real tissue settings.
pmc-13219667:
C. C. Loeff and colleagues track how the Netherlands adopted MRI scanning before prostate biopsy in a 2026 study. Guidelines recommend the scan first, because it can spare men biopsies and target sampling better, but uptake had never been measured nationwide. The Netherlands Cancer Registry supplied the data.

The cohort held 50,987 men diagnosed with biopsy-proven prostate cancer between 2019 and 2023, with a historical cohort from 2015 and 2016. Use of pre-biopsy MRI climbed from seventeen percent at the start of the period to seventy-four percent by 2023. Men over seventy, men with high PSA values, and men with signs of advanced disease were less likely to be scanned first, which matches guideline logic. Hospitals differed early on, with rates spanning ten to eighty-six percent, but by the post-implementation years the spread had narrowed to the sixties through eighties. The authors read this as implementation maturing into consistent, targeted practice.
pmc-13219867:
Pallavi V. Menon and colleagues describe a forty-five-minute session that asks students to name their purpose, in a 2026 report. Medical training front-loads skill and leaves professional identity, the process of becoming a doctor in one's own values, to chance. The Finding Your North Star session was built to give that identity an anchor.

One hundred thirty first-year students discussed values in groups led by senior students and deans, reflected with guidance, and wrote purpose statements printed on cards decorated with artwork. Of the 101 students who answered the survey, eighty-five percent said the session deepened their grasp of purpose in medicine. Over ninety percent valued hearing senior students' reflections and sharing their values with peers. Students asked for more discussion time and more voices, such as alumni and physicians. The authors present the exercise as insurance against the disorientation and burnout that stalk training.
pmc-13221167:
Lara de Souza Cruz Lizardo and co-authors study tooth loss among Brazilian adolescents in a 2026 multilevel analysis of a national oral health survey. Their dataset covered 8,053 teenagers aged fifteen and nineteen from the SB Brasil 2023 survey. Factors were examined at individual, municipal, and state levels together.

About one in seven adolescents had lost a tooth. Risk rose with age, toothache, use of public dental services, and receiving social program benefits. Wider primary care oral health coverage and richer, more developed areas showed lower rates. The authors argue that prevention and fairer access matter more than the mostly curative care many teenagers currently receive, especially for vulnerable groups.
pmc-13221767:
Mohamed Abdelgalil presents a 2026 case of heart valve infection caused by Achromobacter xylosoxidans, paired with a literature review. The patient was a 69-year-old woman with heart surgery history, kidney failure on dialysis, chronic breathing failure, and a persistent vegetative state after cardiac arrest. She was staying in a long-term acute care unit.

Blood cultures kept growing the bacterium despite targeted antibiotics and catheter exchange. Heart imaging first showed a small growth on the mitral valve, then new aortic valve involvement a month later. Surgery was judged too risky given her frailty. She later developed resistant pneumonia, septic shock, and a fatal arrest, illustrating how stubborn this rare infection can be.
pmc-13221867:
Lieke van Susante and three co-authors ask whether how patients rate their own health before heart surgery predicts who survives the month after, in this 2026 study. Quality of life surveys are common in heart research, but their link to hard outcomes like death is rarely tested. A clear link could earn the surveys a place in standard risk checks.

The team studied 2,259 adults having planned heart surgery at one Dutch center between 2018 and 2023. Patients sorted into the lower health group died at nearly triple the rate of the higher group within thirty days. The link held after adjusting for other risks, and it was driven by physical, not mental, health scores. Among patients with complications, the lower group also died more often, hinting at thinner reserves.
pmc-13222167:
Jonas Korb and co-authors raise production of aurachin D, a promising antibiotic compound, in engineered Escherichia coli, in a 2026 biotechnology study. The compound comes from myxobacteria and also acts against protozoa. A membrane enzyme performs the final building step, and an earlier engineered strain made only small amounts.

Switching to a glycerol-based minimal medium and tuning the starting material lifted output roughly sevenfold in a microbioreactor. Glycerol did not mainly help growth or dissolve the substrate better. Instead it increased the supply of correctly folded enzyme, until osmotic stress began hurting the host. Medium design, not new genes, delivered the gain.
pmc-13222367:
Wagner and co-authors study how people balance habits against goal-driven choices when they must act fast. Theories hold that two control systems run side by side, one careful and one automatic, but their interplay under time pressure was unclear. Their 2026 study gives 60 adults a task that builds a repeated action pattern, then asks for goal actions that either match or clash with that pattern.

Computer models showed that habit strength grows with the number of repeats, rather than staying fixed. People also used context well: they blocked the habit when it clashed with their goal and leaned on it when the two agreed. Choice and timing models showed a shift in response bias when habit and goal aligned. The authors see control as flexible, not a fixed tug of war.
pmc-13222767:
Yubo Zhang and co-authors shorten a uterine fibroid symptom and quality-of-life questionnaire, in a 2026 validation study across twenty Chinese centers. The cohort held 1,939 premenopausal women with symptomatic fibroids facing surgery or focused ultrasound treatment, split into development and validation halves. Classical and modern test theory together chose which items survived.

The result, an eleven-item form, cut administration burden by seventy percent from the original thirty-seven items. One whole subscale was dropped, and sexual functioning kept a single item. Scores correlated strongly with the full form in every domain, with comparable sensitivity to health changes. Reliability was excellent. The short form promises faster assessment in clinics and trials, pending checks in new populations.
pmc-13223167:
Dorey Glenn and thirteen co-authors study how well COVID-19 vaccination works in people whose immune systems are medically suppressed, in a two thousand twenty-six immunology paper. Patients with immune-mediated diseases take drugs that can blunt vaccine responses, and their protection was poorly characterized.

The study measures both arms of vaccine immunity in this population: antibodies, the humoral response, and T-cell based cellular responses against SARS-CoV-2. Healthy people mount responses that protect against severe disease, but whether patients on immunosuppressants reach similar levels, and which drug regimens interfere most, needed direct evidence. The authors set out to supply that evidence for clinicians advising some of the most vulnerable vaccine recipients.
pmc-13223867:
Altevogt and co-authors re-measure how much manganese broiler chickens need when an enzyme joins the feed, in this 2026 study. Manganese is added to poultry diets to prevent deficiency and keep growth on track. The enzyme phytase frees up trace minerals in corn and soybean feeds, so the old supplement levels may overshoot. The team crossed two enzyme settings with five manganese levels to find the true need.

Six hundred forty day-old male chicks were raised in battery cages, eight birds to a cage with eight repeats per diet. All began on a manganese-poor diet for a week, then switched to the test diets for three weeks. Growth and health measures across the grid show where extra manganese stops helping. Leaner, evidence-set levels cut feed cost and mineral waste alike.
pmc-13223967:
Eleonora Pero and colleagues report a 2026 study of red blood cells in cystic fibrosis, a genetic illness caused by faults in the CFTR chloride channel. Although CFTR is usually studied in airway and gut tissue, it also appears in red blood cells at lower levels in patients. Whether that reduction changes how the cells bend and squeeze through small vessels was unknown.

Using a technique that stretches cells under shifting salt conditions, the team compared 70 people with cystic fibrosis or related disorders against 46 healthy controls. Cell deformability differed clearly and consistently with CFTR dysfunction. Treatment with strong CFTR modulator drugs partly restored normal behaviour, suggesting deformability could serve as a measurable sign of disease activity.
pmc-13224267:
Khalid Bajunaid and co-authors review brain abscess cases in Saudi Arabia in this 2026 study. A brain abscess is a pocket of infection inside the brain that can kill or disable despite better scans, surgery, and antibiotics. Data from the Middle East were thin, so the team gathered cases from two large hospitals in Jeddah treated between 2010 and 2020.

Thirty-four patients were included, with a mean age near thirty-one and most of them male. Nearly all had a single abscess, most often in the frontal or parietal lobes. Germs were grown from under half the samples. About seven in ten patients left the hospital with a good functional outcome. Older age and low consciousness at arrival were the main signs of a poor outcome, while abscess size and site did not predict it.
pmc-13224667:
Dandan Hong, Jialin Dai, and Xinyi Zhou sorted bowel cancers into types based on genes tied to a sugar based signaling system, in work published in 2026. This system helps control cell signals, and its role in this cancer had not been mapped in a systematic way.

Using gene and clinical data from two large databases, the team found two cancer types with distinct outlooks and drug sensitivities. One type, with stable DNA markers, had better outcomes. The other showed more invasive traits. A score built from the genes predicted who would do well, and low scores went with better drug response. One gene stood out as a key marker between the types.
pmc-13224767:
Camilla Molinari and Nicholas J. Talbot review a 2026 account of rice blast fungus, Magnaporthe oryzae, the agent behind the most damaging disease of cultivated rice and a growing threat to wheat. Because blast control is central to food security, the review concentrates on how the fungus breaks into plant tissue and then keeps the plant's defences down.

A specialised cell builds enormous internal pressure and punches a peg through the leaf's tough outer layer. Once inside, the fungus deploys secreted proteins that suppress host immunity and support rapid colonisation of neighbouring tissue. Understanding each stage, from surface breaching to immune evasion, identifies weak points that breeders and fungicide designers can target.
pmc-13225167: Shingles can leave behind more than pain: in a rare turn, the healed skin grows into thick, raised keloid scars. Punam Sawakar and Pawan Itankar present a forty-two-year-old woman with that outcome in this 2025 image report. Two years after herpes zoster across both armpits and arms, she had darkened, thickened scars on both arms, with itching, pricking pain in the rainy season, and mild discharge. The scars tightened the skin and spread past the rash borders, the hallmark of hypertrophic keloid.
pmc-13225267:
Ifrah Zawar and co-authors ask whether the two sides of the brain's memory structures differ in shape when epilepsy comes with cognitive impairment, in a 2026 multicentre study. Epilepsy is common in Alzheimer's disease and related dementias, and both conditions reshape the hippocampus and amygdala deep in the temporal lobe. The team drew people from thirty-nine American Alzheimer's centers, spanning records from 2005 to 2021.

Patients with cognitive impairment and epilepsy were matched to patients without epilepsy and to healthy controls. Software split the brain scans, and the team worked out left-minus-right asymmetry for volume and surface shape of each structure, using hundreds of surface points. Comparisons split Alzheimer's cases from other dementia cases in each group. The study tests whether mesial temporal asymmetry is a clear imaging sign of epilepsy here. The sign is little studied and could help flag which dementia patients live with seizures.
pmc-13225767:
Ximing Xiao ran a trial on whether one active recess can sharpen students' attention in a 2026 paper. Junior high students were assigned either twenty minutes of moderate-to-vigorous play at recess or a quiet, seated recess. Attention was tested before and after with a standard sustained-attention task, alongside measures of executive function and class engagement.

The active group improved significantly more on attention, executive function, and engagement than the control group. Boys moved at higher intensity, and ninth graders showed stronger executive function, but the recess effect stood across groups. The analysis traced a chain in which better executive function and engagement carry the activity boost into attention. The author offers the results as guidance for planning school recess.
pmc-13227367:
Astrid Bergmann and colleagues compare a 2026 anaesthesia question in catheter-based aortic valve replacement: does full general anaesthesia raise lung infection risk compared with lighter sedation? The patients are elderly and frail, and no earlier study had used infections as the main endpoint. Records covered 3,313 patients at a large heart centre in Western Europe, with matching producing over a thousand comparable pairs.

Pneumonia after the procedure did not differ much between the two approaches, and neither did heart attack or stroke rates. Temporary dialysis and thirty-day death, though, were both lower in the sedation group. The authors recommend sedation as the default in experienced centres, while keeping the full option on hand when patients need it.
pmc-13228567:
Jorge Mínguez-Martínez and co-authors map a 2026 gene-control network that gives lung macrophages their specialised identity. Macrophages living permanently in tissues take on local jobs, and those in the air sacs clear pathogens while managing the fatty lining fluid. Identity is installed by signals from the surrounding niche acting through transcription factors, proteins that switch gene sets on and off.

The study shows that receptors called RXRs steer the differentiation of these alveolar macrophages by opening chromatin and coordinating gene activity with partner factors. Three local signals, DLL4, GM-CSF, and TGF-beta, organise the wider network around them. Together with a partner axis involving PPAR-gamma, they establish the population and keep its identity stable over time.
pmc-13231467:
Iman A Mohammed Ali and Ali Ben Ahmed review in 2026 metal particles that can both kill bacteria and calm harmful oxidation. Tiny particles of metals such as silver, copper, zinc, and iron, plus their oxides, attack germs by releasing ions and tearing membranes. Some also mimic natural antioxidant enzymes, which helps protect healthy tissue.

Traits like particle size, shape, surface charge, and coatings decide how strong each effect runs. Strong germ killing often pairs with weak antioxidant power, so one particle rarely does both jobs well. Mixing materials, tuning surfaces, and pairing particles with standard antibiotics are offered as fixes. Safety over long use and germ resistance still block the path to clinics.
pmc-13231567:
Yoshiyuki Kobayashi and co-authors report a rare tear in the left atrium of the heart after removal of a benign heart tumor, in a 2026 case report. This dissection is very rare after heart surgery and rarer still after this tumor type. An eighty-year-old woman had the tumor removed.

The tear came with a slow, oozing rupture. More surgery carried prohibitive risk, so the team managed her without repairing the tear directly. Repeated ultrasound through the esophagus guided care. Prior reported cases with oozing rupture had needed surgery. The case shows a conservative path can work when guided by close imaging.
pmc-13232267:
Adrián Infante Valenzuela and eight co-authors reported a nerve disease that began in a woman late in pregnancy, in a case report published in 2026. The disease is an immune attack on the protective coating of nerves, and its first sign is often an inflamed optic nerve. In pregnancy, its signs can resemble high pressure inside the head or blood pressure disorders. Their patient was 39, at 31 weeks, with diabetes and high body weight.

She arrived with head pain, then dim vision in both eyes and sharp vision loss in the right eye. Scans of head and spine looked nearly normal. Eye tests showed swollen optic nerve heads and slow signals on both sides. Blood tests found the antibody marker for this disease and ruled out its close relatives. Steroids helped little, so plasma exchange followed, and vision slowly returned with no harm to mother or child.
pmc-13232567:
Eirini M Poulaki and colleagues report in 2026 drilling results that tie granite intrusions to fast lifting of deep mantle rock. Cores from a young ocean basin near Italy mixed deformed granite layers with slivers of mantle rock called peridotite. Water-altered mantle rock dominated a second core set, with granite appearing only in places.

Dating shows the granites hardened about four million years ago several kilometers down, then reached the surface within half a million years. That pace needs uplift near two centimeters a year, which is swift for geology. The soft granite layers took up much of the later strain and focused slip on the big fault. Water alteration came afterward, once the fault had done its work.
pmc-13233267:
Anjali Yadav wrote a paper from 2026 on how one Indigenous people in India guard their hills through family life. The Dongria Kondh live in the Niyamgiri hills and hold the land sacred. Policy often treats families as passive receivers of green plans. Yadav argues the reverse: the household is where care for the land is taught, law is felt, and duty to kin and grove is passed down.

The paper reads laws, court rulings, field accounts, and policy texts, among them a landmark case on the hills. It coins a term for the pattern: family-based rule over the living world, held by rite, care, and joint choice. Yadav is frank about strains inside families, such as uneven power by sex. The paper urges green rule to treat families as co-rulers of the land.
pmc-13233667:
Francisco Pinto-Santos and co-authors joined two AI styles in 2026 to hunt flaws in software code. Deep networks find flaw shapes well but act as black boxes that give no reasons. Their frame adds a knowledge graph built from each function's code, with edges for how control and data flow line by line. A graph network reads that map while a code model reads the text, and the two reads are fused for the call.

On a large real-world flaw set, the frame scored on par with a strong blend of past tools. It gave far fewer false alarms on clean code. Best of all, the graph gives a trail a human can check to see why a flaw was flagged. The team pitches that trail as the true gain.
pmc-13233767:
Shuning Tan and colleagues published a 2026 theoretical physics study of an exotic superfluid state on an optical lattice, a grid of light used to hold ultracold atoms. In the Fulde-Ferrell-Larkin-Ovchinnikov state, atom pairs carry momentum instead of sitting still, and measuring that momentum has been a long-standing challenge. The team modeled a two-dimensional spin-polarized gas with attraction between atoms under an effective magnetic field.

Their calculations of density and spin response showed a phonon mode plus a new low-energy spin mode tied to quasiparticles on a special surface in momentum space. At half filling, a roton dip in the spectrum reshaped into a ring shifted by exactly the pairs' momentum as the system crossed into the exotic state. That shift offers experimenters a practical way to measure the momentum and confirm the state exists.
pmc-13233967:
Hitomi Inano and colleagues published a 2026 analysis of mother-to-infant bonding difficulties in Japan's national birth cohort. Bonding problems are often blamed on postnatal depression, yet they also occur without it. The study examined 64,938 mother-child pairs registered between 2011 and 2014, setting aside mothers whose depression scores stayed high at both one and six months, then measuring bonding with a standard scale.

Among mothers without prior postnatal depression, 7.7 percent showed bonding difficulties. The strongest links were struggling to hold a baby who arches or fusses, and having felt negatively about the pregnancy. Strong social support cut the odds roughly in half. The authors argue that screening should watch for bonding trouble even when depression screens come back clean.
pmc-13234367:
Ali Alqahtani and co-authors presented in 2026 a greener lab method for testing three allergy drugs at the same time. Cetirizine, fexofenadine, and loratadine have UV spectra that overlap heavily, so direct measure cannot split them. The team built a math approach that uses spectral traces to resolve the overlap. Test mixes covered a small range of amounts for tuning and checking.

The new approach gave lower prediction errors than a related method that works from amount traces. Formal checking showed exact recovery, tight precision across days, and low finding limits for all three drugs. Results on commercial tablets matched those from standard liquid chromatography methods. Spiked tap water samples also gave strong recovery after a simple removal step. Sustainability scores were high because the method avoids organic solvents and runs many samples per hour.
pmc-13234467:
Frank Jessen and co-authors analysed in 2026 how donanemab performs in the population eligible for the drug in Europe. Donanemab is an antibody treatment that targets amyloid plaques in the brain in early Alzheimer's disease. The analysis drew on the TRAILBLAZER-ALZ 2 trial and its long-term extension. European eligibility excludes people carrying two copies of a gene variant that raises side effect risk.

Highlights report that the drug significantly slowed disease progression in the eligible group. Benefit grew over three years of follow-up in the analyses presented. People who finished a fifty-two-week course kept amyloid clearance for two further years. Rates of a brain imaging side effect called ARIA were lower when the highest-risk gene group was excluded. The work supports the European dosing approach while stressing careful patient selection.
pmc-13235167:
Mona A. Hegazy and colleagues measured in 2026 a selenium-carrying blood protein in Egyptians with fatty liver disease tied to metabolic problems. The protein, selenoprotein P, is made by the liver and supports antioxidant defence. One hundred sixty participants joined the study, half with the liver disease and half healthy. Liver stiffness scanning split the patient group into milder and more significant scarring.

Protein levels ran much lower in patients than in healthy controls in the blood tests. Levels were lowest in the group with significant liver scarring. Lower levels tracked with higher body mass, stronger insulin resistance, and higher fasting insulin. Body mass and insulin resistance independently predicted having the disease in the models. The authors propose the protein as a simple blood marker for severity and scarring risk, pending further study.
pmc-13235267:
Stabler and colleagues set out a Cochrane review protocol on ischaemic conditioning in kidney transplantation. The method briefly restricts and restores blood flow, hoping to shield the new kidney from injury. A kidney transplant is the finest option for kidney failure that needs dialysis, the authors note, improving lives and saving health services large sums each year.

As a protocol, the paper fixes the question and methods before results are gathered. The review will weigh benefits and harms for both patients and grafted organs across trials. Publishing the plan first guards against cherry-picking later. Transplant teams get a promise of a careful, unbiased verdict on a cheap technique that might protect scarce donor kidneys.
pmc-13235467:
Sotirios Tsiodras and co-authors examined a hantavirus outbreak on a polar cruise ship in a 2026 editorial. The ship, the Hondius, was linked to at least eight confirmed cases and three deaths by May 9, 2026. Three ill passengers were taken off at Cape Verde. The ship then reached Tenerife under a deal between the World Health Organization and Spanish authorities.

Andes hantavirus can pass between people, which raises the stakes on a crowded ship. The editors review the rules for ship health checks and who holds duty among flag, port, and coastal states. Past cruise outbreaks showed fuzzy duties and uneven port health capacity. They argue the event exposes gaps that future outbreak plans must close.
pmc-13235567:
Merve Gurler and four co-authors weigh fast gene panels for brain and spine infections in a 2026 study. Such panels test spinal fluid for many germs at once, which can name a brain ill in hours, not days. Their use grows fast, yet real-world yield and worth in clinic had thin data.

The team looked back at five years of panel use at a large hospital, from 2019 to the end of 2023. Each first hit per patient was set next to case files and the acts doctors took. The study shows how often panels hit, and when hits changed care.
pmc-13236467:
Kang, Jeong, and Kim present a 2026 study of pregnancy loss in dairy cows and its cost to farm output. Loss risk may differ before and after the placenta firmly sets, around day sixty. Records covered 6,444 pregnancies confirmed by ultrasound at day thirty-one after breeding. Losses were split into an early band and a mid-to-late band.

Early loss struck about six percent of pregnancies and later loss about eight percent. Early losses made up over two-fifths of all losses. Fat condition at calving slightly cut early loss risk, while breeding protocol choices mattered strongly. The team also tracked how fast cows became pregnant again by day four hundred after calving.
pmc-13237267:
Morgan R Dillon and colleagues mined public records for 1,445 Major League Baseball pitchers from 2015 to 2025 in a 2026 study of shoulder and elbow injury burden. The pitchers, each with at least a thousand career pitches in the window, accumulated about 148,000 injured-list days. Models linked that lost time to performance numbers and pitch-tracking traits while accounting for workload and starting role.

Higher strikeout rate, faster four-seam fastballs, and higher fastball spin each came with greater combined shoulder and elbow burden. The joint-specific signals split: longer release extension tied to less shoulder trouble, while bigger pitch-to-pitch velocity swings tied to more elbow trouble. The findings give medical and coaching staff measurable traits to watch in prevention planning.
pmc-13237367:
Hoda S M Abdel-Ghany and colleagues tested essential oils from dill, lime, and wormwood against larvae of the mosquito Culex pipiens in 2026, seeking plant-based replacements for chemical insecticides. The team analyzed each oil's chemistry, tried blends, and made nanoemulsions, tiny oil droplets meant to improve delivery. Young larvae were exposed for up to 48 hours.

Dill oil killed larvae fastest and at the lowest dose, with its main components identified as apiol, carvone, and limonene. Surprisingly, the nanoemulsions did not beat the plain oils, and blends needed much higher doses than dill alone. Enzyme measurements in the larvae shifted in mixed directions depending on the formulation. The authors back dill-based products as biodegradable candidates, while asking for toxicity and environmental checks before wide use.
pmc-13238267:
Wang and colleagues replace animal serum in sheep embryo culture with a defined substitute. Labs growing sheep embryos in vitro rely on fetal bovine serum and ewe serum, which vary batch to batch, raise ethical concerns, and face supply limits. Those swings make experiments hard to repeat and hard to scale for breeding programmes.

The team tested a commercial serum replacer, called XRS, as a complete stand-in for both serums across maturation and fertilisation steps. They then judged embryo yield and quality against the old recipe. A chemically defined system that performs as well would clean up sheep embryo science and ease its move into routine farm breeding.
pmc-13238767:
Xu Zhang, Rongyang Wang, and Zhongyou Zhou redesigned a rotary drum screen for sorting fresh tea leaves in 2026, using particle simulations joined with statistical optimization. Conventional drums clog and tangle leaves, and their settings are usually guessed. The team compared the usual small-to-large hole sequence with a new alternating pattern that repeats small and medium holes before the large ones.

The alternating layout reduced entanglement and clogging in simulation and in bench tests. Experiments then tuned drum speed, tilt, and feed rate together, landing on thirteen revolutions per minute, a gentle tilt, and a modest batch size. Under those settings the machine sorted about 70 percent of leaves correctly on average. The authors offer the coupled method as a foundation for standardizing early tea processing.
pmc-13239367:
Shashi Gujar and co-authors wrote a 2026 commentary on an unexpected cancer finding linked to COVID-19 vaccination. A recent study by Grippin and others found that people receiving an mRNA COVID vaccine near the start of checkpoint inhibitor treatment lived notably longer.

Checkpoint inhibitors release brakes on immune cells, yet many tumours still resist them by keeping the surroundings hostile. The vaccine's early immune jolt appears to undo several of those defences and rally tumour-killing T cells. Gains were largest in lung cancer, melanoma, and even tumours classed as immunologically cold. Because such vaccines already exist, pairing them with cancer drugs could move to clinics quickly.
pmc-13239867:
Leonardo López and co-authors test whether weather shaped the Omicron wave of COVID-19 in a 2026 global analysis. Early pandemic debates asked whether temperature and humidity helped the virus spread, and the team checked whether the later variant showed the same climate signature once immunity was widespread.

Combining worldwide case and climate data from 2021 and 2022, they found incidence rose as temperature and absolute humidity fell, especially in mid-latitudes during cold months. Transmission seemed favoured within a moderate temperature band rather than at extremes. A model letting infection rates vary with temperature reproduced epidemic curves far better than fixed-rate versions, cutting errors by roughly half.
pmc-13240167:
Hu and colleagues build microscopic helices that form and move on command, copying a trick from climbing plants. A plant tendril coils when one side of it swells more than the other. The team recreated that uneven swelling in tiny hydrogel fibres, using electric fields to drive water in or out of one side and so bend the fibre into a helix.

Flipping the field's polarity and patterning the surface let them control where and when each helix formed, and reverse it. The moving helices could rotate and could catch and release a tiny sphere. Precise, reversible micro-coils like these point toward soft micro-robots and artificial muscles that work at scales fingers cannot reach.
pmc-13240467:
Fuyuki Yamagata and co-authors report three patients whose TP53-altered blood cancers stayed in remission after a carefully timed transplant strategy. Such cancers relapse stubbornly even after a donor stem cell transplant, and no standard recipe exists. Each patient first got only two to three rounds of therapy, aimed at shrinking the TP53-carrying clone, then moved quickly to transplant.

Tracking showed the altered clones fading before transplant and vanishing after it. Within about two months, all three began azacitidine maintenance at adjusted doses, continued for twenty-seven to fifty-three cycles as tolerated. All three remain in complete remission. The authors argue that shrinking the clone first, transplanting early, and then holding the line with long maintenance can tame this feared cancer type.
pmc-13240767:
Pilar Cataldo-Miranda and colleagues publish a 2026 umbrella review of beta-blocker treatment after heart attack. Beta-blockers are a long-standing part of care after myocardial infarction. Doubt remains about their value when heart pumping strength is midrange or preserved in the modern treatment era.

The authors gathered recent systematic reviews and pooled data from unique primary studies. Trial evidence showed a clear drop in repeat heart attacks but no significant drop in overall or cardiovascular deaths. Observational studies tended to report larger benefits, which may reflect bias. Patients with preserved pumping strength gained no clear survival benefit in trials. The review supports tailoring long-term beta-blocker use rather than assuming equal benefit for everyone.
pmc-13240867:
Aynalem's team looked at how adults in Addis Ababa meet preconception care, years after Ethiopia issued its first national guideline in 2024. Such care still sits outside routine practice. The team spoke with eighteen adults, ten women and eight men, at two public hospitals. Talks explored social, cultural, and structural pressures around preparing for pregnancy.

Seven themes showed knowledge came late, often only after complications struck. Marital gatekeeping, faith beliefs, stigma, and poverty all narrowed access, and single women felt shut out. Men mostly paid the bills but wanted a larger role. People asked for simpler messaging, easier clinic entry, and visible state backing.
pmc-13241767:
Ma del Rosario García Calderón and a large team report a 2026 case of a benign blood vessel tumor inside the chest wall muscle of a 54-year-old woman. Routine breast imaging showed one breast larger than the other and raised suspicion of a breast lesion. Such muscle tumors are rare and often mimic breast disease.

Mammography, ultrasound, magnetic resonance imaging, and computed tomography together located the mass in the pectoralis major muscle, separate from breast tissue. The combined imaging features fit an intramuscular hemangioma. The patient declined a biopsy, so no tissue confirmation was obtained. The authors stress that cross-sectional imaging can prevent a wrong breast-centered workup when a chest wall tumor hides behind breast asymmetry.
pmc-13241967:
Bing Jie Zheng and a large team report a 2026 imaging analysis from a breast cancer treatment trial. Women with triple-negative breast cancer received combined immune and chemotherapy before surgery. Their scans showed a curious pattern the authors name tumor flare-like response: new bright nodules appearing away from the main tumor, then fading.

The pattern appeared in most patients in the small trial group. Nodules were usually oval with smooth edges, often in both breasts, and first showed after two treatment cycles. The pattern alone did not predict complete tumor disappearance. Size did matter: patients whose largest nodule passed a set threshold cleared the tumor far more often. The authors suggest nodule size could help forecast treatment success.
pmc-13242367:
Lannon's team in Belfast asked fourteen nurses why weak students pass clinical placements anyway. The nurses assessed students on the wards. Long online interviews probed the 'failing to fail' pattern head-on. All were in postgraduate nursing courses while assessing students. Careful sorting split their accounts into four groups.

Failure carries a stigma that graders dread pinning on a student. Time pressure and thin workplace support squeeze honest skill grading. Close bonds, low grader confidence, and fear of blowback complete the barrier set. Kind workplace cultures, school teamwork, training, and clear guidance enabled firmer calls.
pmc-13242467:
Simone Giovacchini and co-authors tested whether water samples could guide conservation work across freshwater sites in central Italy. Their study appeared in Environmental Management in 2026. Using a DNA test on water from 53 sites, they searched for 11 endangered species, four invasive aliens, one harmful fungus, and one moved fish at the same time. European law already requires member states to track many of these species.

From the results they built three scores that rank sites for protection, for invasive-species removal, and for further survey work. The scores flagged 39 sites as protection candidates, 22 for eradication work, and 33 where DNA surveys would help most. The survey also recorded the target species in 53 map cells where they were not known before. The authors say one combined test can serve several legal duties at once.
pmc-13242767:
Jianning Lan and co-authors publish a 2026 retrospective study of scalp nerve blocks during deep brain stimulation surgery for Parkinson disease. Blocking scalp nerves may smooth the long procedure, which implants electrodes in a movement-control nucleus. Records came from one Chinese teaching hospital across several years.

Patients treated after the block was adopted had shorter electrode implantation times than the earlier local anesthesia group. Lung infections after surgery were less frequent in raw counts. Once other factors were weighed, the block itself no longer predicted infection, while longer time to breathing tube removal did. The authors note that era differences and selection bias limit the comparison. They frame the block as helpful for workflow, not proven protection.
pmc-13242967:
Hiroshi Kiyomatsu and co-authors used three-dimensional CT planning to ask which ball size suits reverse shoulder replacements in small shoulder sockets. Their study appeared in Bone and Joint Open in 2026. The patients were Asian women with small glenoid anatomy, a group where implant fit is tight. The team simulated three glenosphere sizes and three amounts of downward overhang in every patient, measuring how far the joint could move before bone met bone.

The smallest ball, thirty-two millimeters, gave the widest arcs in bending, lifting, and rotation, while the largest consistently restricted motion. Placing the ball with at least three millimeters of overhang also helped in every plane. The authors recommend downsizing with adequate overhang for small sockets. They caution that soft tissue and stability, absent from the simulation, must confirm the choice in the operating room.
pmc-13243067:
Chao Meng and co-authors present a 2026 review on how heart muscle heals badly after a heart attack, a process called ventricular remodelling that can lead to heart failure. Their focus is DNA from mitochondria, the cell's energy units, which can leak out and act as an alarm signal.

The authors propose a three-threshold model covering how this DNA escapes, how it travels between cells, and how strongly it switches on an immune alarm pathway. It can move as bare DNA, in tiny cell-made bubbles, or inside whole mitochondria. They suggest timed drug combinations aimed at each step, while noting parts of the model still need direct proof.
pmc-13245067:
Robert Connacher and colleagues asked whether a fruit fly developmental protein must actually grip RNA to do its job. Their study appeared in RNA Biology in 2026. The protein, Brat, guides neural stem cell development and is named for the brain tumors its loss causes. Lab work showed its NHL domain binds specific RNA sites, untested inside a living animal. The team used CRISPR to edit single amino acids at the binding surface, directly in the fly's own gene.

Three independent RNA-binding-defective versions resulted, and each behaved as a strong loss of function. Flies carrying only the edited gene died, mostly as late larvae or pupae, just like flies missing Brat entirely, and the edits failed to rescue known brat mutants. The verdict is clean: RNA binding is not an accessory to Brat's work but its essence. The alleles give biologists a precision tool for separating Brat's roles.
pmc-13245267:
Zacharie Cloutier and seven co-authors asked colorectal cancer patients how they felt about a common, doubted step in their care: a second endoscopy before surgery. Doctors often repeat the scope to check the tumor, but the step is criticized as wasteful and delaying. The team interviewed twenty patients who had been through it at one academic center.

Most patients were fine with the repeat. Eighty percent called the overall experience positive, and three quarters saw a clear benefit. The scope built trust and gave a reassuring second look for planning the operation. Patients also accepted it as a normal part of the road to surgery, bowel preparation and all. The weak spot was communication: understanding the plan and handling the logistics confused many. The authors say the patient's view deserves a seat in efficiency debates.
pmc-13245467:
Yiwen Lu and co-authors explain why a blood fat called lipoprotein(a) is so hard to measure fairly in a 2026 review. Levels of this particle are set mostly by genes and raise heart risk on their own. Yet its odd structure fools common lab tests.

Copies of one protein segment vary by person, which skews tests that count by weight. The review favors reporting in moles, the count of particles, and warns against fixed swaps between units. High levels can also inflate standard cholesterol scores and mislead risk calls. Automated tests suit screening, while lab-grade methods anchor accuracy. Fair measurement matters more as drugs aimed at this particle near the clinic.
pmc-13246467:
Hasan and co-authors designed an off-grid power system for a coastal island community in Bangladesh, in this 2026 Global Challenges study. Char Ishwar, in Noakhali district, has weak grid access and growing demand. Using planning software, the team modeled a hybrid microgrid combining solar panels, wind turbines, batteries, and a hydrogen loop with an electrolyzer, storage tank, and fuel cell to cover calm, cloudy spells.

Of three designs tested for one hundred eighty households, the full hybrid won, delivering power at a modest cost per unit with near-zero net emissions. Wind speed and demand growth most affected the economics. The authors present the design as a practical template for reliable, low-carbon electrification of isolated coastal settlements.
pmc-13246767:
Hongjie Qiu and eleven colleagues propose KnitLoRA, a denser way to fine-tune large language models cheaply. Low-rank adaptation inserts small trainable matrices into a frozen model. In deep stacks of these blocks, signals and gradients can fade before reaching the last layers. That fading slows training. KnitLoRA weaves dense connections between each block and many earlier blocks, borrowing the DenseNet idea.

Feature reuse improves, and gradients flow more freely to early layers. The authors report faster convergence and better results than standard low-rank adaptation and its variants. Crucially, the extra connections vanish at inference time, so the deployed model costs nothing extra to run. The twenty twenty-six method targets practitioners who fine-tune large models on modest hardware budgets.
pmc-13247167:
Gong, Fan, Fang, and co-authors built swimming microrobots from living algae in this 2026 Microsystems and Nanoengineering paper. Synthetic microrobots struggle to squeeze through the body's tight, complex spaces, a requirement for reaching tumors. The team instead harnessed Euglena gracilis, a soft, shape-shifting single-celled swimmer, fitting it with magnetic structures so external magnets could steer, propel, and deform it on command.

The biohybrids threaded through dense three-dimensional biological matrices and gathered around tumor spheroids, guided both magnetically and by their own drift toward tumors. The algae themselves add therapy: their chlorophyll supports light-driven tumor killing, and their natural products modulate immunity. The authors present the platform as precision medicine that needs no loaded drug cargo.
pmc-13247267:
Sayed Sabir Shah, Slawomir Koziel, and five co-authors published a 2026 engineering paper on a low cost antenna that folds out for use. The design borrows from kirigami, the art of cutting and folding sheets. It sends and receives in two polarizations and points its pattern in more than one direction.

The antenna works at 2 gigahertz and sits on a foldable stepped sheet of plastic. Each of its two crossed units has a main strip, a helper strip that aims the signal, and a reflector at the back. Tests showed strong gain, a wide working band, and very low cross talk between units. Total efficiency stayed above eighty percent across the band. The authors stress that it is cheap and easy to make.
pmc-13247967:
Mehmet Mavi and Seyfettin Ilgan report a silent focal thyroid inflammation case that can mislead two imaging methods, in a paper from 2026. Subacute thyroiditis usually announces itself with neck pain and overactive thyroid signs. Ultrasound is the first check, and glucose scans can also light up inflamed tissue.

This case was found by chance with no symptoms, in a focal patch rather than the whole gland. Such a patch can mimic a nodule or tumor on ultrasound and take up tracer on scans like cancer would. The authors review the confusing imaging traits and urge clinicians to keep inflammation on the list before invasive steps.
pmc-13248967:
Zhang reviewed ultrasound for diagnosing rheumatoid arthritis in this 2026 article. The disease inflames joints and destroys them slowly, and early treatment changes its course. Blood tests miss some patients, especially those whose marker tests come back negative, so imaging that can see inflammation directly has drawn growing interest.

Musculoskeletal ultrasound can reveal swollen joint lining, fluid, increased blood flow, and early bone erosion in real time. It excels at catching hidden inflammation before damage shows elsewhere. Results still depend on the operator's skill, the author notes, but shared scoring systems, standard scanning routines, and early artificial intelligence tools are tightening the method for everyday clinics.
pmc-13249167:
Katayama and colleagues compared two ways blood vessel cells grow old, in a 2026 PLOS One study. Cells can senesce by dividing until they wear out, or early under stress. Both states appear in aging vessels, which grow prone to clots, and the team asked whether the two aging routes affect clotting control differently.

Worn-out cells unexpectedly boosted the vessel lining's anti-clotting behavior in dish tests, while stress-aged cells did not. Mice engineered for stress-aged vessel cells formed worse vein clots, closely matching naturally old mice. Gene patterns agreed. The authors conclude stress-driven aging, not division-driven aging, is the main culprit behind age-related clotting trouble.
pmc-13249567:
Pickersgill and a large drilling expedition team dated the hot water system inside the Chicxulub crater, in a 2026 study. The crater, in present-day Mexico, was blasted out sixty-six million years ago by the asteroid linked to the dinosaur extinction. Heated water circulated through its fractured rock long afterward, the kind of setting where life may first have arisen.

Rock dating and computer simulation together show the hydrothermal activity lasted at least eight million years. That is roughly four times longer than earlier estimates from rock magnetism and mineral studies. The authors call Chicxulub the longest-lived impact-driven hydrothermal system yet documented on Earth, with implications for how life might start on other worlds.
pmc-13249867:
Sato and a Japanese team found a protein that helps the spinal cord rewire after stroke, in a 2026 mouse study. Surviving corticospinal fibers, the brain's movement command lines, sprouted into the emptied side of the neck cord and reconnected with V2a interneurons, relay cells for premotor circuits. Silencing those new links chemically weakened the recovered movement, proving they carried real function.

A secreted protein, secretogranin II, rose after injury in helper astrocytes and in the relay neurons during rehabilitation. It pushed axons to grow through familiar growth signals, and removing it blunted rewiring. The authors nominate the protein as a therapeutic lever for stroke and other central nervous system injuries.
pmc-13250167:
Lorenté and co-authors film shock waves moving through a safe stand-in for an explosive. Their 2026 Scientific Reports experiments used compressed sucrose, ordinary sugar pressed into a solid, instead of real energetic material. A short green laser pulse struck the sample to launch each shock wave.

Because the granular material is opaque, the team used high-speed synchrotron X-ray imaging to watch the shock form inside it. Follow-up tomography let them estimate the shock pressure and speed, which reached about four times the speed of sound in the material. Adding aluminum nanoparticles made the sample absorb more laser light and raised the pressure. The results point toward detonators triggered by light rather than by impact.
pmc-13250267:
Seven researchers ask whether the timing of a back scan affects surgery results, in a paper from 2026. The scan is an MRI taken before lumbar decompression, an operation that eases pressure on spine nerves. Some patients are scanned a month or more before surgery, and others just before. The team used a large shared health record network to compare the two paths.

After matching, each group held more than thirty-seven thousand patients. Rates of repeat surgery and nerve problems were nearly the same in both groups. Patients scanned earlier had a slightly lower rate of infection after surgery. The authors think scan timing may reflect care paths rather than cause the gap.
pmc-13250767:
Ruchama Charles and co-authors recount a cancer scare that ended well in this 2026 case report. A 68-year-old man treated two years earlier for colon cancer had rising blood marker levels, and scans found a growing mass inside a hip muscle.

The lump lit up on a PET scan, which raised fears the cancer had spread. Two needle samples gave no answer. Tissue study after closer work showed nodular fasciitis, a harmless, fast-growing knot of repair cells that often mimics cancer. A gene test confirmed it. Since removing such lumps cures them, the authors stress firm diagnosis to spare patients needless cancer treatment.
pmc-13250867:
Lee, Shin, and Song test ear-based nerve stimulation as a drug-free helper for eczema-like skin inflammation in mice. Their 2026 Annals of Medicine study uses a chemical called DNCB to trigger atopic dermatitis on mouse skin. Gentle electrical pulses on the ear stimulate the vagus nerve, a pathway known to calm immune responses.

Stimulated mice showed healthier skin structure and lower inflammatory markers than untreated dermatitis mice. Blocking acetylcholine receptors partly erased the benefit, pointing to cholinergic signaling, including one nicotine-type receptor, as part of the mechanism. Treatments ran a few minutes every two or three days for one or two weeks. The authors call the approach a promising add-on and ask for deeper mechanism and translation studies.
pmc-13251167:
Karin Dalhammar, Maria Schelin, and Marie-Louise Möllerberg compare end-of-life care settings in Sweden in this 2026 study. About half of Swedes who die receive municipal care first, and people at home face more emergency hospital trips than those in care facilities.

The study covered 50,219 people in the national palliative care register during 2023 and 2024, all in their last week of life. Facility residents were more likely to get symptom checks than people in ordinary housing. Yet they were less likely to receive end-of-life information, support for relatives after death, or outside pain advice. The authors say each setting has distinct weak spots needing targeted fixes.
pmc-13251767:
Stephanie T.D. Pham and colleagues characterize human kallistatin, a blood protein that restrains an enzyme involved in blood vessel control, in a 2026 study. Kallistatin belongs to the serpin family, whose members can link into inactive chains called polymers. Its sugar decorations, tissue locations, and tendency to polymerize were poorly mapped before this work.

The team built custom antibodies and a sensitive test that measures kallistatin in plasma and in fluid from cultured tissue, including vessel tissue from patients with aortic aneurysm. Mass spectrometry confirmed a predicted sugar attachment site on the protein. Experiments showed kallistatin does polymerize, and that stripping its sugars sharply increased polymer formation, meaning the sugars act as stabilizers. Polymerized kallistatin lost its ability to block its target enzyme, while sugar-stripped protein still worked. The authors say the tools and maps they built open the way to studying this protein in disease.
pmc-13252267:
Vaibhav Sharma and co-authors compared, in a 2026 clinical study, guided against freehand root canal treatment in teeth whose canals had calcified shut. Blocked canals invite drilling errors, wasted dentin, and failure. Sixty teeth in 48 patients were split evenly between a planned, guide-assisted approach and the conventional one.

The guided route found the canal in 96.7 percent of cases against 73.3 percent freehand. It also negotiated faster, removed less dentin, and suffered fewer mishaps like perforations and broken instruments. Patients reported less pain and higher satisfaction at one week and three months. The authors argue the guide turns a dreaded case type into a precise, gentle routine. Wider adoption could set a new standard for calcified canals.
pmc-13252767:
Isa Spiero and a large team compare Dutch language models for mining medical notes in this 2026 study. Health records hold rich symptom detail in free text, and automated extraction could save hours of hand labelling, but most tools are built and tested in English.

Two Dutch models were tried on primary care notes from patients with chest infections, against hand-labelled examples. Used as direct classifiers, both did well after enough training, the medical one slightly ahead. Prompt-style use failed badly, with very low scores. pmc-13253767:

pmc-13253867:

pmc-13255167:

pmc-13255667:

pmc-13255767:

pmc-13256067:

pmc-13256767:

pmc-13256867:

pmc-13257067:

pmc-13258167:

pmc-13258567:

Engineers weighing food waste treatment options get a combined risk and cost view of the concept.
pmc-13258767:

pmc-13258867:

pmc-13259167:

pmc-13259767:

pmc-13260067:

pmc-13260567:

pmc-13262167:

pmc-13262367:

pmc-13262567:

pmc-13262667:

pmc-13263867:

pmc-13264867:

pmc-13265167:

pmc-13266067:

pmc-13266267:

pmc-13266367:

pmc-13266567:

pmc-13266767:

pmc-13266867:
