pmc-13281567:
Julio Cjuno and co-authors adapt, in a 2026 study, the nine-question depression screener PHQ-9 into the San Martin variety of Quechua and test how well it works. A screening tool only helps if it speaks the patient's language, literally and culturally.

After careful translation and cultural adaptation, 309 Quechua-speaking Peruvian adults aged eighteen to fifty-nine completed the questionnaire. Statistical checks found the items form a single clean dimension, with model fit indices near the top of their scales. Reliability was high, and scores behaved consistently across groups. The validated version gives Peruvian clinicians a trustworthy depression screen for Quechua communities.
pmc-13281767:
Theng Choon Ooi and colleagues set grip strength norms for older Malaysians in a 2026 study. Grip strength is a quick gauge of muscle health. Low grip flags sarcopenia, the muscle loss of aging. The team used data from a long study of community elders. More than two thousand adults aged sixty and older were measured. Grip curves by age and sex were built, raw and weighed against body weight.

Grip peaked in the early sixties for both sexes. Men topped out near thirty-one kilograms and women near twenty. A regional cutoff set flagged close to half of elders as low grip. A local cutoff, the bottom fifth, flagged only about one in five. Both flags still tracked with muscle loss outcomes. The authors say the regional line may overcall weakness in Malaysia. They ask for long-term data to settle which line predicts real decline.
pmc-13281867:
Shengbo Yang and colleagues studied a Chinese herbal brew for liver cancer in a 2026 paper. The brew blends thirteen herbs and is used beside standard care. Its workings are poorly mapped. The team first ran computer models of its parts. They found close to two hundred active compounds and over one hundred possible targets in the body. Twenty-five targets sat at the hub of the web. Then forty patients joined a four-week test, half on standard care and half with the brew added.

Blood markers of liver strain fell in both groups. One clotting time clearly favored the brew group, improving there while worsening in the other. Symptom scores in the Chinese medicine frame also improved with the brew and worsened without it. The authors say the brew seems to act on many targets at once. They call the clinical edge early and in need of firmer trials.
pmc-13282067:
Hélène Platteeuw and co-authors report a 2026 study on a way to protect donor livers before transplant. Some livers come from donors after circulatory death, when the heart has stopped. Flushing the belly organs with warm, oxygen-rich blood may limit damage. The team asked whether such livers caused more postreperfusion syndrome, a sharp blood pressure drop when blood flow returns, than livers from brain-dead donors.

One hundred six recipients were compared, forty-seven with treated livers and fifty-nine from brain-dead donors. The pressure-drop problem struck about a quarter of each group, with no real gap after adjustments. Early graft failure, kidney injury, rejection, and bile or vessel problems also looked similar. The authors say the approach appears safe in the short term and can widen the donor pool.
pmc-13282267:
Faizan Ahmed and co-authors present a 2026 study comparing two strategies for older adults newly diagnosed with atrial fibrillation. Rhythm control tries to restore normal rhythm early, while rate control only slows the heart. The team used a large global health records network and matched patients on many traits to make the groups comparable.

After matching, each group held more than two hundred thousand patients aged sixty-five and over. At one year, death rates were higher with rhythm control than with rate control. Rhythm control also brought more dangerous rhythm events, fainting, hospital stays, and rhythm-restoring procedures. Blood clot events and major bleeding, though, were less frequent. Results split sharply by method: drug-based rhythm control drove the harm, while procedure-based control linked to lower death and hospital use. Careful selection, the authors say, is essential.
pmc-13282367:
Clenya Carla Leandro de Oliveira and colleagues test whether engineered rice can live on phosphite instead of phosphate, in a study from twenty twenty-six. Crops engineered to metabolize phosphite promise better nutrient efficiency and new management options. Their rice carries a bacterial gene for phosphite oxidation. Two transgenic lines were grown in low-phosphorus soil and in hydroponics.

A sensitive enzyme assay tracked phosphate and phosphite depletion in real time. Under phosphite feeding, transgenic lines outgrew wild-type plants and accumulated more phosphorus. Performance still lagged phosphate feeding, especially at reduced doses. Uptake kinetics showed phosphite absorption is intrinsically slower, even after phosphorus starvation. Biomass suffered at low phosphite levels. The authors conclude phosphite can substitute only partly, a caution for the strategy.
pmc-13282467:
Yu-Mei Li and co-authors published a cross-sectional study in 2026 on gut microbes and stool chemicals in polycystic ovary syndrome, called PCOS here. The work centred on women of normal weight, a group studied less often than women with obesity. It asked how gut bacteria, stool metabolites, and clinical measures relate to each other in this condition.

The team re-analysed gene sequencing data, then added metagenomic and stool metabolite tests on a small local group. Overall diversity did not differ between patients and controls. The PCOS group held more Ruminococcus and less Prevotella, and some bacteria tracked with insulin resistance and lower HDL cholesterol. Changes in bile acid and fat pathways stood out, pointing to the gut as a possible treatment target.
pmc-13282567:
Chonkit Lio and co-authors report a cell study on early aging disorders, published in 2026. The work looks at prelamin A, a protein form that is not cut as it should be in these disorders. When a fatty tag stays on the protein, cells lose their sense of direction. The team traces that flaw to a pair of linked proteins at the edge of the cell nucleus.

Tests on several disease-linked forms showed the same pattern. The uncleaved protein slowed the linked pair and blocked their role in cell movement. Even short tail pieces of the protein caused the same harm, and only when the fatty tag was present. The results point to the stuck tag as the shared cause of weak force transfer to the nucleus.
pmc-13282867:
Sweden's dental register holds the data behind a 2026 implant survival comparison whose lead author is Fernando Jose Mota de Almeida. The damage type is external cervical root resorption, which can destroy a tooth near the gum. The question is whether implants last as well in such sites.

Swedish register data from 2009 to 2022 yielded 605 matched pairs. One group had prior root damage and the other did not. Ten-year survival was high in both groups, and the gap was not statistically clear. Few implants were removed in either group. The authors note that low failure counts limit firm claims.
pmc-13283167:
Exercise beliefs among chemotherapy outpatients are surveyed against daily activity in Ozge Gumus's 2026 cross-sectional work. Patients getting outpatient chemo often move less and face fatigue. The team asked how activity levels link to social life and quality of life.

Surveys covered 101 patients, most of them women with gut or breast cancer. About 45 percent were inactive, and the rest were only lightly active by standard scores. Most agreed that exercise lifts mood and cuts stress in daily life. Fatigue, bad weather, and low drive were the top barriers named. More active patients reported fewer barriers and better function and health scores.
pmc-13283467:
Didi Mwengela, Nimah Ather, and John Kunesh described in 2026 a severe gullet infection in a 64-year-old man with a healthy immune system. Herpes simplex infection of the oesophagus usually strikes people with weakened immunity, so it is easy to miss in others. He arrived with strong burning behind the breastbone and could not tolerate swallowing food or drink.

A camera exam showed severe inflammation of the gullet, and a tissue sample confirmed herpes infection. He also had a history of acid reflux, which may have left the lining open to attack. Treatment with intravenous acyclovir, then tablets, plus an acid-blocking drug brought rapid relief. The report urges doctors to weigh viral causes when gullet symptoms resist standard care.
pmc-13283967:
Claudia Emmanuela Sanchis-Sanchis led a Spanish team in 2026 linking diet, gut bacteria, and mood in amyotrophic lateral sclerosis. The disease steadily destroys motor function and often brings gut and emotional trouble too. Forty-eight patients with bulbar or spinal onset disease recorded their food intake, answered mood scales, and gave stool measures for bacterial counts.

Statistical modelling drew out one nutrition factor made of vitamins B1, B2, B9, and C plus fibre. That factor tied inversely to anxiety and depression scores. Its effect ran partly through Bacteroides abundance and stool consistency, and the model explained about nineteen percent of the spread in distress. The authors suggest vitamin- and fibre-rich diets as a support strategy worth testing in this disease.
pmc-13284567:
Yu Jin Kim commented in 2026 on whether the diabetes drug metformin protects against stomach cancer, and at which stage. Evidence has conflicted: a nationwide cohort tied long-term metformin use to lower gastric cancer risk in patients not on insulin, while a Swedish cohort found no link. Lab work shows metformin slows gastric cancer cell growth, triggers cell death through energy pathways, and may even check the stomach germ Helicobacter pylori.

The commentary discusses a study comparing metformin and insulin use across stages of gastric cancer development. Cancer was less common in metformin users not on insulin, and more common in insulin users whatever else they took. Precancerous dysplasia showed no treatment pattern. Kim cautions that insulin use may itself mark worse metabolic disease, and that any metformin effect may act late in cancer development, with thin mechanistic proof so far.
pmc-13284867:
Nhan Truong Vu and Hoang Tran Viet report a 2026 two-case series on keyhole surgery for esophageal duplication cysts in children. These rare birth cysts near the food pipe can press on airways, and removal is advised to prevent infection, bleeding, or rupture. Both boys had repeat wheeze or cough, and scans showed cysts beside the esophagus.

Surgery used three small ports with low-pressure gas, took about two hours, and caused minimal blood loss in these two cases. One child had a small tear in the food pipe lining, fixed during surgery, with feeding back by day five. The other ate by day one. Both left within a week and stayed free of return at one year.
pmc-13284967:
Yoshihito Mima, Masako Yamamoto, and Ken Iozumi report a 2026 single-center survey of nemolizumab treatment for prurigo nodularis in Japan. The chronic skin illness causes severe lasting itch, and patient satisfaction with older care was low. Twenty patients who stayed on monthly treatment for at least twelve weeks were assessed at a Tokyo hospital.

Itch scores fell sharply by week sixteen, and clinician ratings of lesions also improved in the group tracked here. Patients recalled far less daily time spent on skin creams and far less time preoccupied by the illness after treatment. The authors note standard scores may miss daily burden, so patient reports add a fuller view of benefit.
pmc-13285267:
Yuanmin Huang and co-authors compare two grades of sauce-flavor Daqu, the starter brick for Chinese baijiu, in a 2026 study. Aroma grade marks Daqu quality, so the team joined chemical measures, enzyme tests, microbe surveys, and flavor profiling for first-grade and second-grade samples. Links between traits and grade were then mapped.

First-grade Daqu held more acid and amino nitrogen, lower pH, and microbes tied to flavor building blocks in the data reported here. Second-grade samples had stronger starch-breaking enzymes and microbes linked to off-odors. Eleven scent compounds split the grades, with aldehydes tracking good aroma and one sulfur compound tracking faults. The authors offer the markers for quality checks in production.
pmc-13285367:
Md Osman Hossain Zabir and colleagues tracked flu-like and severe respiratory illness in young children in Cox's Bazar, Bangladesh, from 2021 to 2023. Their 2026 study fills a gap, because little local evidence described which viruses circulate in children under five there. Crowding and monsoon rains shape illness patterns in the district.

Hospital surveillance enrolled 968 children, most of them infants. Swab tests looked for flu viruses, the coronavirus behind COVID-19, and RSV. Only about one child in eight tested positive, and flu made up most positive results. Detections peaked during the monsoon months, with one flu type leading early and another later. Severe illness and breathing trouble were linked to testing positive.
pmc-13285467:
Yuxia Luo and co-authors widen the light that can power deep-tissue imaging particles in a study from 2026. Lanthanide nanoparticles glow in the second near-infrared window, where tissue turns clearer. Their weakness is picky excitation: only a few wavelengths can charge them.

Three dyes team up to harvest light instead. Tropolone, cyanine 3, and IR806 together stretch the working range sixfold, from ultraviolet to near-infrared. IR806 doubles as a bridge, passing energy along the cascade. Its bridging lifted one dye's transfer efficiency from about six percent to seventy. Tunable glow from many light colors follows. Surgeons and researchers gain imaging probes that ordinary lamps and lasers can drive. The modular recipe invites other dye teams.
pmc-13286867:
Mario Assenza and co-authors trace breast cancer's rare spread to the uterine cervix in a 2026 case report and literature review. A 59-year-old woman treated in 2015 for hormone-sensitive ductal breast cancer, with surgery, chemotherapy, radiation, and endocrine therapy, later saw a tumor marker climb and settle near four times its ceiling. Bleeding prompted imaging that lit up a metabolically active lesion in her uterus.

Biopsies of womb and cervix returned a poorly differentiated carcinoma matching her breast primary's lineage rather than a new uterine cancer. Marker stains for mammary origin, including GATA3 and mammaglobin, anchor the diagnosis in their review. The tumor's receptor profile had flipped since 2015, a discordance the authors say makes re-biopsy essential. She began combined chemotherapy and immunotherapy in March 2024, tolerating it well as treatment continues.
pmc-13287467:
Kimberly Milleman and co-authors ran a blinded trial in 2026 of mouth rinses holding essential oils in 154 adults with diabetes, a group prone to gum disease. Volunteers used a rinse with alcohol, one without alcohol, or a plain control rinse, alongside twice-daily brushing for twelve weeks.

Both oil rinses cut plaque and gum inflammation scores far more than the control rinse at twelve weeks. Gum bleeding fell by roughly two thirds or more. Users also reported better mouth comfort, and soft tissue tolerance was good. Many participants had never been told diabetes raises gum risk. The authors urge joint work between diabetes and dental teams.
pmc-13287567:
P J Pappoe-Ashong and colleagues ran four blood surveys in Accra, Ghana, between August 2020 and January 2022 to track past coronavirus infection across pandemic waves. Samples totalling 1,096 were drawn from stored clinic material and weighted to match the city's age and sex mix.

Adjusted share with antibodies rose from 58.3% in the first wave to above 90% by the second, then stayed at or above 96%. Adults reached near-total exposure earlier than children. Antibody strength kept climbing through the third wave even after spread plateaued, pointing to repeated exposure. The authors describe intense, repeated transmission shaping immunity in the city within eighteen months.
pmc-13287667:
Pauline Potratz and colleagues sampled human lung tissue in 2026 from transplant and surgery patients, comparing upper airway regions with deep air-sac regions. Gene sequencing often reports rich microbe life even in deep lung, so the team added growing tests and imaging to check whether those microbes are alive.

Sequencing showed a shift along the airway: skin-like and mouth-like bacteria gave way to air-shunning kinds deeper down, with wide differences between patients. Growing and imaging found almost no living microbes in the deep regions. The authors conclude that deep lung DNA signals likely come from very few bacteria or from dead remains, not a thriving community.
pmc-13287967:
Timber DNA barcodes built from dried plant stocks are set out by Sidonie Bellot and a large team in work dated 2026. Naming a wood type by DNA needs full reference sets, sharp markers, and cheap steps. The team used a method that both grabs picked gene spots and skims the rest of the genome. They tested it on four groups in the mahogany family.

Plant samples from 132 dried stocks covered twenty-two species. Trees built per gene spot showed which spots split species cleanly. Three short spots stood out, each naming its species well in most cases. Dirty extracts, more than worn DNA, caused most failed reads from wood.
pmc-13288867:
Elin Allansson Kjolhede and co-authors quantify flu danger for people with type 2 diabetes in a 2026 Swedish register study. Linking the national diabetes register to population, patient, and statistics records, they followed 371,811 patients and 1,728,856 matched controls across six influenza seasons from 2013 onward.

Hospital admission for flu touched 1.6 percent of patients with diabetes against 1.0 percent of controls in their data, and flu-related death was also more common in the diabetes group. Adjusted hazards stayed clearly elevated for both outcomes. Absolute danger concentrated in people with heart, kidney, or lung disease, while relative risk peaked in younger patients. Worse sugar control and weaker kidney function each tracked with more admissions.
pmc-13289067:
Anne Juul Grabmayr and colleagues study emergency calls from public housing in Denmark. Their 2026 study deals with cardiac arrests outside hospitals. It covers four housing areas in Copenhagen. Most residents there are from minority groups. Calls ran from 2017 to 2022.

The team heard 17 calls about 13 arrests. Good calls fit the script used by dispatchers. Those calls led to fast CPR guidance. Hard calls broke from the script. Crowded calls and language gaps caused delays. Raw emotion and low first aid skill also hurt. Many witnesses phoned kin before calling for help. Calm tone and plain words helped dispatchers cope.
pmc-13289367:
Anouk C Meijs led a 2026 first-in-human trial of SOL-116, an antibody aimed at bile salt-stimulated lipase for rheumatoid arthritis. That enzyme helps digest fat and may also drive joint inflammation, making it a fresh drug target. The randomized, blinded study tested single rising doses and repeat doses under the skin in healthy volunteers, plus one dose in patients.

A total of 48 healthy participants and 8 patients with arthritis took part in the trial. The drug was safe and well tolerated at doses tested, and blood levels rose in line with dose size. Free levels of the target enzyme in blood fell, proving the antibody hit its mark as intended. Immune reactions against the drug stayed uncommon, supporting larger patient trials.
pmc-13289467:
Lea Gölz, Julius Rosenhan, Kaloyan Kamenov, and Birgit Prodinger carried out a 2026 scoping review on training health workers in disability inclusion. People with disabilities face deep, avoidable gaps in care, and many clinicians feel unready to give fair, rights-based help. The review maps what current courses teach and which themes dominate across published and gray sources.

Literature from January 2011 to August 2024 was searched across medical databases, web sources, and organization sites. A total of 172 publications qualified, mostly from the Americas and Europe, run at local or national level. Charting covered course scope, disability views, involvement of disabled people, teaching style, and target professions. Nineteen themes emerged from the set.
pmc-13289867:
Sowmya Pujari headed a 2026 interview study on health and child nutrition views among Koraga tribal mothers in Southern Karnataka, India. Child malnutrition drives nearly a third of child deaths worldwide and stays high in India despite growth. Koraga families face added poverty, access, and cultural barriers, so maternal views are central to designing help that families will actually use.

Twenty mothers of children aged 5 to 10 were interviewed in depth from October 2023 to March 2024 in Tulu and Kannada. Five themes emerged: shifting health views, nutrition beliefs and habits, hygiene promotion, mixing traditional healing with modern care, and barriers with community fixes. Health workers and government food schemes featured as trusted supports.
pmc-13290567:
Driving cholesterol to very low levels did not raise bleeding in heart attack patients on two blood thinners, according to a 2026 prospective cohort study by Tianfu Fu and colleagues. The worry was that ultra-low LDL cholesterol might disturb clotting in patients taking PCSK9 inhibitors after stenting for acute coronary syndrome.

The single-center study followed 120 such patients for 12 months, splitting them by achieved LDL cholesterol at a cutoff of 0.78 mmol/L and tracking clotting tests and platelet function. Clinically relevant bleeding was similar in the low and non-low groups, though with only seven events the comparison was underpowered, and clotting measures stayed stable throughout. Major heart events also did not differ significantly. Fu and colleagues describe the safety signal as reassuring but exploratory.
pmc-13291167:
Railway switches wear out and fail in costly ways. Mohammad Adoul Amin and co-authors build a 2026 system to sort vibration events at these junctions. Their aim is honest accuracy, not inflated scores from leaky test design.

Shake data came from a full-size outdoor test track. All readings from one event stayed in one data split. That rule blocks a common source of false gains. A smart generator made extra samples for rare classes. Twenty-one sorting models from eight families were compared. Group models proved most stable across checks. Best held-out accuracy passed four fifths of cases. Careful data order mattered as much as model choice.
pmc-13291267:
Severe lung infection may split into three hidden types. Mark Jeffrey leads a 2026 study of patients in critical care. Pneumonia kills more people than any other infection. Its deep biology is still poorly mapped.

Wash fluid from lungs was tested many ways. Gene activity, immune signals, microbes, and clinical notes were joined. Three lung-only types, called Pneumotypes, emerged. All looked alike at the bedside at first. Their paths then split sharply. One type healed fastest with balanced defense. Another dragged on breathing machines with young immune cells. The types may guide targeted drugs in future care.
pmc-13292067:
Lei Luo and co-authors hunt a 2026 lead on sunitinib resistance in clear cell renal cell carcinoma, a kidney cancer where the drug often stops working. Mining a public dataset comparing resistant and parent cells pointed them to PARP9 as a hub gene. They confirmed the lead in two resistant cell lines and in patient-derived organoids.

Resistant cells and patient tissues both carried extra PARP9. Silencing it restored sunitinib sensitivity, while adding it to parent cells created resistance. PARP9 partnered with STAT1, boosting its phosphorylation and switching on the IRF1 program, including ISG15 and IFIT1. The PARP inhibitor olaparib weakened that signaling, and olaparib plus sunitinib outperformed either drug alone in organoids. The authors propose the PARP9-STAT1 route as a treatment angle.
pmc-13292467:
Zirui Fu and co-authors compare a 2026 cooking question with lab digestion: how do steaming, microwaving, and baking change tilapia protein quality and bioactivity? Cooked fish went through the static INFOGEST in vitro digestion protocol. The team measured hydrolysis, molecular weight spread, amino acid release and scores, then checked health-related activities in cells and computer simulations.

Heat generally improved digestibility by loosening protein structure and exposing enzyme cut sites. Baking scored highest on hydrolysis degree, essential amino acid index, and biological value. Steaming released amino acids fastest. Baking also boosted blood-sugar enzyme inhibition, with alpha-amylase and alpha-glucosidase inhibition at 51.48 and 51.74 percent in digested samples. Steaming led on antioxidant power, its ABTS scavenging reaching 69.00 percent against 57.96 percent for fresh fish.
pmc-13292567:
Lubna Fawaz's team runs a 2026 single-center trial comparing weekly phone-based telemonitoring against ordinary clinic education for children with type 1 diabetes. One hundred forty young patients were randomized evenly. The intervention group reviewed glucose records, diet, and insulin doses with educators by phone each week, while controls learned during routine outpatient visits, with checks at start and six months.

Blood sugar control diverged clearly. Mean HbA1c read 8.21 in the telemonitoring group against 9.25 under standard care, in the study's reported units. Dangerous ketoacidosis episodes hit 18 percent of controls but only 1.7 percent of the phone group. Overall complication rates also ran higher in controls, 37.7 against 15.5 percent across the groups. Quality-of-life scores improved significantly with telemonitoring, and the authors endorse the approach.
pmc-13292667:
Xingzhao Wen and co-authors chase a 2026 brain link in childhood arthritis: children with juvenile idiopathic arthritis show more mood and behavior symptoms, and nobody knows why. Blood from sixteen children with active disease, matched healthy controls, and twelve of the same patients in quiet phases went through Olink protein profiling. Mouse arthritis experiments then probed the brain directly.

Active patients carried distinctly altered neurobiological protein patterns that tracked with pain and life-impact scores, and the changes lingered even when joints quieted. Mice with long-running arthritis showed fired-up microglia and stunted new neuron growth in the hippocampus, with the cortex spared. Gene data blamed mitochondrial strain and oxidative stress. A blood protein, HMOX2, mirrored the hippocampal microglial activation closely. Interleukin-6 and interleukin-18 emerged as candidate messengers in patients.
pmc-13293367:
Sonalee Arun Joshi and colleagues present, in 2026, a new memory task that tests how people use scene context to tell new sights from seen ones. Faulty context use appears in many mental illnesses, yet older tasks test single cues, not full scenes.

A total of 44 healthy adults finished the Context Discrimination and Recognition Task, which uses complex scenes at graded levels of sameness. Scores for telling scenes apart and for spotting seen scenes rose together strongly. As scenes grew less alike, both skills improved, showing the task senses fine shifts. The team offers it as a sharper tool for clinic research.
pmc-13293567:
Runze Hu and colleagues build, in a 2026 study, Chinese language models tuned for motivational interviewing, a counseling style that helps people change health habits. Skilled human counselors are scarce, and Chinese training material for this style is limited.

The team screened five public counseling datasets and rebuilt 2040 talks into the target style with a structured prompt, using 2000 for training and 40 for testing. Three open models were tuned and then scored by automatic measures and by trained raters using a standard fidelity manual. Tuned model talks were compared with 30 real sessions. The work tests whether tuning lifts counseling quality.
pmc-13293667:
Alba Mena-González, Raquel Leirós-Rodríguez, and Pablo Hernandez-Lucas pool, in a 2026 review, evidence on physical therapy for endometriosis symptoms. The condition grows womb-like tissue outside the womb, causing pelvic pain and lower quality of life in many women.

Study highlights state that therapy methods cut endometriosis pain and improved quality of life across the trials pooled. Massage, electrical therapy, exercise, and health teaching each helped ease pelvic symptoms in the included work. Standard care leans on surgery or hormones, so a safe add-on with proven gains matters for daily care. Set protocols are still lacking, which the review may help clinics build.
pmc-13293867:
Xiaotong Peng and colleagues report a 2026 discovery of a huge whale graveyard on the deep seafloor of the Diamantina Zone in the southeastern Indian Ocean. Survey work at depths from 4,616 to 7,001 meters traced remains along about 1,200 km. When a whale carcass sinks, it feeds a special community, and such sites had seemed rare and scattered.

Counts reached five modern whale-fall communities plus 476 fossil cetaceans, both living and extinct beaked whale types. Brittle stars, bone-boring worms, and chemosynthesis-based clams dominated the living sites. Isotope dating puts local whale falls back at least 5.3 million years, making the floor an archive for whale evolution.
pmc-13293967:
Gaël Toubon and co-authors search the gut microbiome for early warning signs of type 2 diabetes, in a 2026 prospective study from Sweden. Most earlier work compared people who already had diabetes with healthy controls, which cannot show what came first. The Swedish SIMPLER cohort instead sequenced gut microbes from 4,685 older adults and followed them for a median of just over five years, during which 383 developed the disease.

Six bacterial species were tied to higher future risk, while three others appeared protective. One microbe's link to risk changed with dietary fiber intake, hinting that diet shapes how microbes matter. Microbial pathways for breaking down certain nutrients also split by risk, with asparagine breakdown pointing toward danger. The findings may support microbiome-based tools for predicting and preventing diabetes.
pmc-13294167:
Maria Luci Quirino de Melo Trindade leads a 2026 randomized trial of low-level laser therapy after cesarean birth. Between April and October 2024, 104 mothers split evenly into laser and standard care groups. Infrared light at 5 J per square centimeter was given twice, at 12–24 hours and again at 48 hours, with pain and scar quality scored on standard scales.

After the second session, pain fell more in the laser group, and overall healing scores improved. Vessel and pliability parts of the scar scale drove the gain. General health perception and extra pain drug use did not differ. Light therapy looks like a useful add-on for early comfort and wound quality.
pmc-13294267:
Teddy A. Teddy and colleagues measure how dangerous advanced liver scarring is for patients hospitalized with a weak heart, in a 2026 analysis of American hospital data. Heart failure with reduced pumping strength brings over a million admissions a year, and cirrhosis reshapes circulation in ways that may strain the heart further. The team drew on a national inpatient database from 2022, flagging cases where cirrhosis came with complications such as fluid buildup or bleeding.

About two percent of the quarter-million heart failure admissions met the advanced cirrhosis definition. Those patients died in hospital far more often, and after adjustment for other conditions their odds of death stayed more than double. A stricter definition requiring two complications strengthened the link further, suggesting a dose effect. The authors recommend early recognition and joint care from heart, liver, and critical care teams.
pmc-13294367:
Eman I. K. Ibrahim and colleagues build a math framework for judging neoantigen cancer vaccines in a 2026 modeling study. Vaccines aim to wake tumor-specific T cells, but layered animal data resist plain reading. Their semi-mechanistic model links dose to tumor size through four blocks: drug levels, antigen uptake by presenting cells, T cell response, and tumor growth in two mouse tumor types.

Three vaccine styles were compared, including a conjugate that glues antigen to a CD40 antibody for delivery and stimulation. Simulations showed the glued format changed drug handling and boosted effect, with killer T cells driving shrinkage. Dose effects on antibodies emerged in the responsive tumor model. The tool can guide smarter vaccine tweaks.
pmc-13294767:
Jianbo Sun and colleagues compare muscle activity during the taekwondo roundhouse kick in a 2026 study of elite and youth athletes. Earlier work relied on single summary values from muscle signals, missing how activity unfolds across the whole kick. The team instead examined complete signal waveforms from both legs.

Thirty-eight male athletes took part, split evenly between elite and youth groups. Signals from seven trunk and leg muscles were recorded alongside three-dimensional movement data during standard kicks. Clear group differences appeared in four muscle and component pairings, mostly in the support leg, pointing to distinct control strategies that whole-waveform analysis can reveal.
pmc-13295067:
Huiling Yan and colleagues compare two bacterial groups behind dialysis-related belly infections in a 2026 study. Peritonitis is a serious complication of peritoneal dialysis, and non-fermenting Gram-negative germs may behave worse than fermenting ones. Episodes at one centre over fifteen years were matched for fair comparison.

Thirty-two episodes from the harder group were paired with the same number from the comparison group. Patients in the harder group carried more diabetes and other illness, ate more poorly by blood measures, and were cured far less often. Deaths during follow-up were also higher, marking this infection type as one needing especially watchful care.
pmc-13295367:
Hyeonjeong Kwak and Unkyoung Ahn compare two school-based therapies for teenagers who think about suicide or hurt themselves, in a 2026 records study. Files came from a school suicide prevention center covering 112 middle and high school students. Fifty-two took a sandplay therapy program built for this crisis, and sixty took a brief program drawn from dialectical behavior therapy.

Both groups improved plainly on several measures in the short term, spanning mood, anxiety, and self-injury. Head-to-head gaps were scarce. One signal favored the dialectical group on impulsiveness, yet it was small and faded once the many tests were allowed for. Since staff assigned the therapy, the authors say the files cannot prove either one better, and they offer the work as groundwork for true trials.
pmc-13295467:
Faeq Husain-Syed, Vitalii Kryvenko, and István Vadász reply to comments on combined kidney and carbon dioxide support in a 2026 letter. Their earlier study ran a gentle carbon dioxide removal method on a standard kidney replacement platform. Commenters raised blood flow, pump design, clot prevention, and trial planning questions.

The authors agree that only large multi-centre randomised trials can settle the method's value, and they widen the outcomes worth testing. Even at low blood flow, their patients showed meaningful carbon dioxide falls, steadier acidity, and lower breathing pressures. They credit the large exchange surface, round-the-clock running, and citrate clot prevention for the steady performance.
pmc-13295767:
Will Lung Chan and colleagues plan a map of loneliness in emergency care in a 2026 protocol. Loneliness and social isolation drive illness and extra service use, and emergency departments often serve as the safety net for those affected. A visit may be a rare human contact, yet the rushed setting can deepen isolation.

The scoping review will search five databases plus grey sources for work in English or Chinese. Adult and child patients and the staff who treat them both count as viewpoints of interest. An artificial intelligence aid joins the screening approach. Findings aim to show how the emergency experience lands on isolated patients and where staff training falls short.
pmc-13295867:
Steven C Marcus and co-authors lay out a 2026 trial protocol on helping primary care patients keep taking antidepressants. Many people stop these drugs early, and busy clinics have little time to watch adherence, so the team test two light-touch supports.

Adults newly prescribed an antidepressant are assigned to daily reminder texts, texts plus small payments, or usual care. A wireless pill bottle and surveys track pill taking and mood at six and twelve weeks, with halving of symptom scores as the main goal. Findings will be shared in journals and meetings once the trial, registered as NCT06496646, is complete.
pmc-13296267:
Ahmed Massoud and colleagues test betanin, the red pigment of beetroot, against inflammatory pain in rats, in a 2026 study. Betanin is known for fighting inflammation and oxidation, yet its pain-soothing power was little explored. Rats got a shot of complete Freund's adjuvant to spark lasting paw pain, then daily betanin by mouth for fourteen days at one of two doses.

Betanin cut paw swelling and raised the time rats bore a hot plate. In the spinal cord on the hurt side, both doses lifted an anti-inflammatory signal, while the higher dose also cut oxidative harm and a pro-inflammatory signal. Two small RNA switches moved in step with the chemistry, and microscope checks showed less nerve damage. Docking sums rounded out the case for the pigment as a pain candidate.
pmc-13296567:
Yuting Wang and co-authors survey recent progress in biomedical materials in a 2026 review. Such materials underpin implants, diagnostics, drug delivery, and tissue repair across modern medicine. The field is moving from passive parts toward materials that respond actively to the body.

Four areas receive detailed treatment: hard-tissue repair, wound healing that adapts over time, drug release controlled in place and time, and engineered surfaces. Barriers to clinical use run through the whole survey. Laboratory safety tests often fail to predict performance in patients, factories struggle to scale new designs, and rules differ between countries. The authors aim the review at both researchers and clinicians planning next-generation devices.
pmc-13296767:
Lilyan C. Charca and colleagues map artery plaque across three body regions in psoriatic arthritis patients in a 2026 study. Heart risk runs high in this disease, yet checks usually scan only the neck arteries. Ultrasound of neck and leg arteries, plus abdominal X-rays, covered 250 unselected patients.

Plaque in the leg arteries was commonest, and nearly half of patients free of neck plaque still had leg involvement. Plaque in two or more regions affected a large share of the group. Adding scan findings to a standard risk score improved detection of widespread disease. Which territory helps most depends on the question, so the authors favour a tailored multi-site approach.
pmc-13296867:
Zhongwei Zhang and co-authors hunt, in 2026, for stronger skin-lightening drugs by screening approved medicines in a computer model of tyrosinase, the enzyme starting pigment production. Two cancer drugs, methotrexate and selinexor, emerged and were tested in pigment-making melanoma cells.

Both shut down enzyme activity and pigment output at very low doses. They attacked the master pigment switch MITF on several fronts: cutting two signal routes that switch it on, speeding its destruction and strengthening antioxidant defences. Because both drugs are toxic body-wide, the authors say any skin use needs careful cream formulations keeping them local.
pmc-13297467:
Ibrahim M. Aziz and colleagues compare leaf and seed extracts of the medicinal herb Vitex agnus-castus, long used for women's health complaints, in a 2026 study. No head-to-head comparison of the two plant parts existed. Gas-based chemical profiling named fifty-five compounds in the leaf extract and thirty-four in the seed extract, with quite different leading ingredients.

The leaf extract held far more phenols and flavonoids, plant compounds tied to protective effects. It also beat the seed extract on antioxidant, antibacterial, liver-cancer-cell, and blood-sugar enzyme tests. The seed extract won on one front: killing Candida fungi. Leaf treatment switched on cell-death genes in cancer cells, a result still awaiting protein-level proof. Plant part choice clearly matters for any future remedy.
pmc-13297567:
Song Hu and colleagues pool trials of hand robots steered by brain signals for stroke recovery, in a 2026 meta-analysis. Eleven fair-dose trials with 380 patients were gathered from eight databases. The brain-linked training was compared with robot training alone and with routine therapy.

Against robot training alone, the brain-linked version lifted overall arm scores and shoulder-elbow scores, and eased finger stiffness. Hand-end skills and a standard arm-use test, though, showed no clear gain. Against routine therapy, arm scores rose clearly as well. Gains looked strongest in patients still early after stroke. Proof for fine hand recovery and lasting benefit remains thin, and the authors ask for trials tuned to those ends.
pmc-13298067:
Jiayue Wang and a large team study what happens when ferulic acid is grafted onto high-amylose corn starch, in a 2026 food chemistry paper. Controlled moist heat formed ester links between the two, confirmed by spectroscopy. Microscopy showed rougher, more porous granules, while thermal tests recorded changed gelatinisation and stability.

Digestion tests in the laboratory found rapidly digestible starch fell and resistant starch rose sharply after grafting. Docking work suggested ferulic acid may also hinder the amylase enzyme that breaks starch down. The authors propose the modified starch as a route toward functional food ingredients richer in resistant starch, with slower digestion as the goal.
pmc-13298967:
An enzyme that edits protein building blocks was purified in a single step by displaying it on cell surfaces, report Jiacheng Zhang and colleagues in a 2026 study. Their protein glutaminase came from the bacterium Chryseobacterium lactis and works best at pH 5 and 50 °C, keeping over 70% activity after twelve hours at that temperature.

The team then used the enzyme to deamidate krill protein isolate, a by-product of krill oil production. At a dose of 1.0 U/g, deamidation reached 15.18% and emulsifying performance peaked at 23%, aided by stronger electrostatic repulsion and surface hydrophobicity. Foaming behavior also shifted. The work links a simpler enzyme supply to upgrading an underused marine protein.
pmc-13300067:
Josef Jampilek presents a 2026 special issue on heterocyclic compounds, ring structures that contain atoms besides carbon. Heteroatoms such as nitrogen, oxygen, or sulphur turn a plain carbon backbone into a molecule with a set electronic shape and binding ways. Most body-active molecules are such rings or carry a nitrogen atom, the piece notes.

Swapping atoms in or out lets chemists tune acidity, fat solubility, and hydrogen bonding, which govern how a drug is absorbed and how it meets its target. Fluorine substitution receives special attention for blocking metabolism and extending half-life. Greener synthesis routes, from carbon-hydrogen activation to flow chemistry, frame the collected contributions.
pmc-13300467:
J Tan and co-authors assess prolonged rhythm monitoring after a transient ischaemic attack in a 2026 feasibility study. Finding hidden atrial fibrillation matters because blood thinning can then prevent a stroke, yet trials of longer monitoring cover stroke, not these attacks. The retrospective review covered patients at one stroke center's clinics between April and August 2024, using a machine learning framework to sort them.

Of 131 patients, twenty-six were classed high risk and one hundred five low risk. Nearly everyone received only a seventy-two-hour Holter monitor, and nobody got a longer device. New fibrillation diagnoses by twelve months were rare: two in high-risk and one in low-risk patients, all then prescribed anticoagulation. Twenty-three high-risk patients had no extended monitoring at one year. The authors see a workable way to flag high-risk patients and an unmet need to test longer monitoring in them.
pmc-13300567:
Ten years of Melody valve implants at one center give Mario Giordano and colleagues the material for a 2026 retrospective study in congenital heart disease. Between 2015 and 2025, fifty patients were assessed for transcatheter pulmonary valve implantation with the Melody device, the first catheter-delivered valve of its kind.

Forty-five patients left hospital with a working valve, while four procedures were stopped over coronary compression risk and one patient died shortly after. Over a mean follow-up of 5.8 years, about one in six developed valve infection and a similar share needed catheter reintervention. Fewer than one in ten required surgical replacement, which the authors read as solid mid-term performance.
pmc-13300667:
Does weight loss alone mend the heart in obesity, even without diabetes or high blood pressure? Omer Ozkan Duman and colleagues test that question in a 2026 study of metabolically healthy patients with severe obesity. Twenty-eight sleeve gastrectomy patients were compared with twenty-five matched peers who had no surgery, with heart scans at baseline and six months.

Body mass index in the surgical group fell from 46.21 to 37.11 over the half year, while controls barely moved. Left ventricular mass shrank markedly, and a standard filling ratio improved in step. Blood sugar and lipid measures also improved, supporting surgery as direct protection for the heart even when no other disease is present.
pmc-13301067:
E Dave and co-authors build and validate a software pipeline that pulls atrial fibrillation risk variants out of whole genome data, in a 2026 methods paper. Genome wide studies have tied hundreds of single letter variants to the rhythm disorder, yet registries rarely carry the genotypes needed to test whether they change care. The team assembled a variant list from a 2025 genetics study, verified positions against a reference genome, and ran the extraction on public data from 2,504 people in the 1000 Genomes Project.

The pipeline produced a clean genotype matrix for the full public cohort, recording each person's status at the fibrillation linked sites near genes such as PITX2 and ZFHX3. A demonstration table then sketches how those genotypes could join treatment and outcome records inside a large multi ethnic registry. The authors frame validated extraction as the unglamorous foundation for genetics informed rhythm care.
pmc-13301167:
Chun Shing Kwok and co-authors trace how patients with transthyretin amyloid heart disease actually reach diagnosis at a district general hospital, in a 2026 quality improvement study. The team re-read inpatient and outpatient records from 2019 to 2025 under a method they call forensic data acquisition and pathway analysis. They deliberately hunted for the sequence of clues rather than summary codes. They found twenty-six likely wild type cases and four hereditary cases from two families.

Warning signs were plentiful long before diagnosis: carpal tunnel syndrome in nearly two thirds, spinal stenosis in about a quarter, and ultrasound hallmarks such as thickened walls in most. Suspicious ultrasound features triggered the workup most often, with incidental magnetic resonance findings second. Two patients still needed a heart biopsy to settle the question. The authors argue the forensic reading style exposes missed chances that routine datasets bury.
pmc-13301467:
Tarek Abdeldayem and co-authors compare five year outcomes after stenting for heart attacks without ST elevation, split by whether the culprit artery was blocked at presentation, in a 2026 cohort study. Using collected data from a Newcastle tertiary center for 2012 to 2019, they matched 775 patients whose vessel showed no or minimal flow against 750 whose vessel was open. Both groups were then followed for five years.

The blocked group arrived sicker on paper, with more transient ST elevation, more Q waves, and worse heart muscle function. Outcomes refused to follow: hospital mortality matched at just over one percent, one year mortality was indistinguishable, and five year mortality landed near sixteen versus eighteen percent, not significant. One drug class stood out, with glycoprotein inhibitors linked to a hazard ratio around 0.64 for death. The authors conclude a blocked artery at presentation, once stented, need not doom the long term outlook.
pmc-13301967:
P Stiavnicky and colleagues investigate, in a 2026 study, whether adding left-sided lesions improves cardioneuroablation, a treatment that calms the vagus nerve's slowing grip on the heart. Patients had repeated fainting or symptomatic slow rhythms from excessive vagal influence. Ablation can target nerve clusters from the right upper chamber alone, or from both sides.

Thirty patients received a standard right-sided lesion set first, then extra lesions delivered after crossing into the left upper chamber. Heart rate rose after the first stage and rose further after the added lesions. Nerve stimulation tests confirmed that vagal effects on both heart nodes weakened in two steps. The benefit was clearest for the lower node's control, leading the authors to favour the two-sided approach as standard.
pmc-13302767:
A Von Kietzell and co-authors build, in a 2026 methods paper, an open pipeline that fabricates realistic synthetic heart-mapping datasets. Real electroanatomic maps are rarely shared between centres, which starves algorithm development of data. Synthetic stand-ins, proven in medical imaging, could fill the gap without privacy risks.

Real left-chamber surfaces from MRI scans were deliberately warped to mimic the distortions clinicians see in genuine maps. Simulated paced activation supplied timing values at a thousand virtual electrode points on each surface. Four refinement rounds, steered by expert electrophysiologists, added region-dependent noise and triangulation glitches. A shape-distance measure against twenty-three real meshes shrank steadily across versions, and experts judged the final output convincingly authentic.
pmc-13303367:
A shot of glucagon safely lifts copeptin levels in children, Rita Indirli and colleagues show in a 2026 proof-of-concept study from Milan. Twenty children tested for possible growth hormone lack, none with urine or thirst problems, got glucagon in a muscle while blood was sampled for three hours. Copeptin mirrors the water-balance hormone vasopressin and anchors workups of excess thirst and urination.

Median copeptin more than doubled, peaking at one hundred fifty minutes, and no side effects appeared. The authors say the test deserves accuracy trials for telling vasopressin lack from primary excess drinking in children, where current tests are long and hard on patients.
pmc-13303567:
Wenchong Wang and co-authors test, in a 2026 rat study, acupuncture combined with moxibustion for sciatica caused by a pinched nerve. The model squeezes the sciatic nerve, producing pain sensitivity plus inflammation in nerve and spinal cord. The team tracked pain behaviour, tissue appearance, and a master inflammatory switch called NF-kB.

Treated rats recovered much of their tolerance to heat and touch compared with untreated injured rats. Nerve and cord tissue looked better preserved, and four inflammatory messengers fell in both gene activity and blood protein levels. The NF-kB protein also appeared less often inside cell nuclei, its active position. The authors offer the pathway suppression as a mechanism behind the pain relief.
pmc-13303867:
Swapnadeep Poddar and co-authors demonstrate, in a 2026 engineering study, a dense array of perovskite nanowires that behaves as a reliable brain-style computing element. Memristor crossbars can run neural network maths in memory at low power, but perovskite versions suffer wild variability. Growing the material as aligned nanowires inside a porous template was the fix.

An engineered thin barrier layer kept conductance changes smooth and analogue, yielding well over a hundred distinct, non-overlapping states. Devices varied by under five percent from one to another and endured hundreds of thousands of cycles. A sixty-four by sixty-four array was built into a working multi-layer perceptron that analysed zebrafish head and jaw movements. The authors present the system as a scalable path for perovskite neuromorphic hardware.
pmc-13304867:
Nimra Haroon heads a 2026 review of Aloe vera compounds against cancer. About twenty million new cancer cases arise yearly, and standard therapy's side effects drive interest in gentler plant-based helpers.

Five databases were searched for work from 2015 to 2025. Plant chemicals including aloe-emodin, aloin, and the gel sugar acemannan slowed many cancer types in lab studies, with strength rising by dose. Effects ran through cell death programs, stress chemistry, blocked vessel growth, and several major signaling pathways. Findings remain early-stage, yet the breadth of targets makes the plant a rich lead source.
pmc-13305567:
Zhiqiang Hu leads a 2026 review of how bird flu viruses interact with autophagy, the cell recycling system, over the past decade. The virus crosses species and evolves fast, and hijacked recycling may help it spread and harm lungs.

Different virus strains trigger recycling bag formation through varied viral parts, though whether the process completes is unsettled. Responses differ between bird and mammal hosts and between strain types such as H5N1 and H9N2. Tuning recycling at the right stage may ease severe lung injury, the authors argue. Standard ways to measure true recycling flow in bird cells are still needed.
pmc-13305667:
Uraiwan Akanit tracked weight change over two years in a 2026 Thai cohort starting dolutegravir-based HIV treatment. Adults who began therapy between January 2020 and June 2022 at a referral centre were followed through June 2024 with weights recorded at set intervals.

A total of 157 people, mean age 50.4 years, had complete data at baseline and at 6, 12, 18 and 24 months. Weight rose in both sexes, with larger gains in older patients and in those on regimens without tenofovir disoproxil. Only the drug backbone showed a clear differing trend over time, supporting routine weight and metabolic monitoring.
pmc-13306867:
El Saeed Lasheen and co-authors assess metals and natural radiation in 2026 in coastal sediment at Ras Mohamed, South Sinai, on the Red Sea. Fifteen surface samples were tested for nine trace metals and three natural radioactive nuclides. Tourism pressure and sediment drift prompt the check on a guarded coast.

Iron led the metal sequence, while chromium, vanadium, and cobalt sat above global background and Canada's soil guidance values. Joint indices called the sediment low to partly polluted, with low to mild likely effects on life. Human contact figures stayed below set thresholds for adults and children alike, cancer risk included. Radiation readings also sat under global safety limits. The authors conclude that build-up is real but current health risk is tiny, while steady checks remain sensible for a busy tourist coast.
pmc-13307367:
Shiv Rekhi and Jeetain Mittal simulate in 2026 how the droplets that form inside cells change the acidity behaviour of amino acids. Biomolecular condensates offer a solvent setting unlike plain water, so ionisation balance may shift. Their all-atom simulations tracked four changeable amino acid types inside five model condensates.

Protonated states were favoured inside the dense phase across every system tested. Positive residues held their charged form more readily, while negative residues more often sat neutral. Consistency across different peptide sequences suggests a general property of the condensate environment. Charge control in phase-separating proteins depends on these local shifts, not only on cell-wide acidity. The authors frame solvation differences between phases as the key driver. Their results matter for anyone modelling how condensates organise cell chemistry.
pmc-13307467:
Apoorva Uboveja and a large cancer team report in 2026 that a common metabolic molecule helps repair-proficient tumours resist DNA-damaging drugs. Screening sixty-four related enzymes singled out TMLHE, the rate-limiting maker of carnitine, as essential for survival under such treatment. Without alpha-ketoglutarate, cells became sensitive to the drugs.

Carnitine production fed a specific histone acetylation step that opened DNA for homologous recombination repair. Other acetyl supply routes could not substitute for this pathway. Patient samples linked high TMLHE or acetylcarnitine levels to shorter time before disease progressed on DNA-damaging therapy. The authors propose blocking the axis to force repair-proficient tumours into a repair-deficient state. That switch could widen the reach of existing cancer drugs. Metabolism, they show, can guard the genome as surely as repair genes do.
pmc-13307567:
Vanessa Dal Bianco and co-authors survey herpesviruses in 2026 in fifty-one baleen whales stranded on the Brazilian coast between 2008 and 2022. Most animals were humpbacks, with a few Bryde's, right, and minke whales. Tissue samples, 159 in total, were screened with nested gene tests for two viral targets.

Viral DNA appeared in about a quarter of individuals, including eleven humpbacks and single Bryde's and minke whales. Eight sequence types emerged, split between alpha and gamma herpesvirus groups, and one humpback carried both. Six positive animals were calves, which hints at transmission from mother to offspring. The Bryde's whale finding is the first reported for that species. Knowledge of infections in baleen whales lags far behind toothed whales, and the authors present their survey as a baseline.
pmc-13307667:
Clara Cole and colleagues test in 2026 whether the choice of immune trigger can shape a flu vaccine for cattle that targets a conserved inner virus protein. Their vaccine used a mosaic nucleoprotein built from bits of thousands of flu strains, paired with one of two added triggers in cows.

Both pairings raised virus specific T cell responses and antibodies in blood and in milk from the cows. The STING trigger gave stronger and steadier responses than the TLR4 trigger did in this herd. Shaping early immune signals could thus yield broader flu cover for herds, which would also cut spillover risk for people who work near cattle.
pmc-13307867:
Soontaree Petchdee and co-authors assess in 2026 a catheter based edge to edge repair for leaking mitral valves in dogs with worn valve tissue. Ten dogs with moderate to severe leaks got the repair under imaging guidance, and heart work was scored before and after the fix.

Leak severity fell in most dogs after the repair was placed in the valve. Useful heart work rose while wasted energy fell, which points to a more efficient beat for those dogs. The trade off is a smaller valve opening and higher flow pressure, so case choice matters a lot. Longer follow up must show whether gains last and how leftover leak shapes late outcomes.
pmc-13309367:
Mads E R Sørensen and colleagues report a cohort study from 2026 on giant cell arteritis, a disease that inflames large blood vessels in older adults. Care took place at Aalborg University Hospital in Denmark. The team asked whether adding a drug that blocks interleukin-6 lowers the risk of diabetes compared with steroid treatment alone.

Care records for 121 patients were followed for one year after treatment began, with 47 people in the added-drug group and 74 people on steroids alone. New diabetes appeared in far fewer treated patients during that year, and the combined risk of diabetes, bone loss, and heart events was also lower. The authors note the added drug often started late and suggest earlier use may help more.
pmc-13309467:
Rui Alvites and colleagues review safety questions around preserved animal cadavers for veterinary teaching in a 2026 article. Taking bodies apart by hand still teaches body structure, cutting skill, and clinical judgment in a way screens cannot match. How a body is preserved shapes both lesson quality and health risk for students and staff.

The standard chemical, formaldehyde, stops decay well but is toxic and stiffens tissue while fading its color. Salt-saturated fluid costs less, slows decay, and keeps tissue softer and closer in color, with freer joint movement. Each method carries trade-offs for safety rules and lab practice. The authors weigh those trade-offs for schools choosing a preservation method.
pmc-13309567:
Wen Chen and colleagues build a light-based edge finder that can switch modes in a 2026 study. Spotting edges quickly helps squeeze data, sharpen microscopy, and guide machine vision, yet most light devices do one fixed job. A structured ferroelectric material with a twisted layout offers a changeable option.

Flipping an electric field switches the device among first-order edge finding, second-order edge finding, and plain imaging. Switching takes as little as 62 microseconds, and cell edges stood out clearly while plain views stayed available at once. The device survived over 1.8 million switches and more than 200 days of use in testing. The authors point to brain-like photonics and medical imaging as uses.
pmc-13310367:
A large team reviews a blood test that tracks the health of transplanted lungs by reading DNA from the donor organ. When graft cells die, their DNA floats free in the recipient's blood, and its share signals injury before symptoms may. The test is proven in kidney and heart transplants, and this review gathers the growing lung record, from the two big research consortia and from commercial lab tests.

The authors chart how the marker rises and falls over time and across clinical situations, from smooth recoveries to acute lung graft trouble. Certain injury patterns in the DNA record seem to forecast later chronic graft failure and death. They close with a practical guide: when to test, and how to read the numbers in clinic. The frame is precision medicine for lung recipients.
pmc-13310667:
Haochun Tang and co-authors weigh dose rounding for a costly cancer drug in China in a 2026 study. Trastuzumab deruxtecan saves lives in HER2-positive cancers but wastes money when part-used vials are discarded. Rounding each dose to the nearest vial can cut waste, if safety holds.

Records covered 141 patients and 829 administrations during 2024 and 2025, split into rounded down, rounded up, and exact groups. Rounding down saved CNY 897,840 in drug costs, while rounding up avoided 4,368.3 mg of waste across the cohort figures given. Dose shifts stayed within the accepted ten percent band, and side effects such as nausea and blood toxicity matched across groups. The authors back rounding to the nearest full vial.
pmc-13311367:
Mahider Shimelis Feyisa and co-authors, in 2026, report a hospital study on rejected lab samples in Ethiopia. Turned-away samples delay diagnosis and waste scarce resources, so the reasons matter.

The study ran at Debre Tabor Comprehensive Specialized Hospital from June 17 to July 16, 2025, and covered every sample sent for testing in that span. Of 952 samples, 58 were rejected, and the team logged why each one failed. Statistical models then weighed which factors tracked with rejection. The findings can guide fixes in sample taking, labeling, and transport at similar hospitals. Even small cuts in rejection could save repeat visits.
pmc-13311567:
Gbenga Adesoye and co-authors test a 2026 risk grouping tool for COPD in the British ERICA cohort. The GOLD 2026 ABE tool sorts patients by symptoms and flare history to find those at high risk.

The analysis classified 664 cohort members with the tool, using two different symptom scales. Group E, the highest-risk tier, held 66 percent of members under both scales in this cohort. Hospital records were then followed for a median of 4.75 years to count admissions and severe flares. The study checks whether the simple grouping can flag patients who need preventive care most.
pmc-13311767:
Rachele Frigerio and co-authors review how small RNAs called microRNAs reshape the immune setting around tumors in a 2026 article. This immune setting decides whether checkpoint drugs work or fail.

The review traces how tumor microRNAs blunt antigen display, tune checkpoint pathways, sap killer cell attack, grow suppressor cell groups, and rewire support tissue and metabolism. It then weighs treatments that block harmful microRNAs or restore helpful ones, ideally paired with checkpoint drugs. Few such pairs have reached clinic testing. Better lab models that copy the human tumor setting are needed to move pairs forward.
pmc-13311967:
Dick Willems and co-authors examine in a 2025 article when non-inferiority trials with death as the endpoint can be ethically justified. Such trials ask whether a new approach is not unacceptably worse on survival.

The analysis, informed by a literature search, uses a heart device trial the authors are part of as its running example. Justifications for choosing this design over a superiority trial are often thin, and the allowed margin is usually borrowed without argument. Patient views on the margin are rarely sought. The authors hold such trials defensible only when side benefits are proven and large, and margins win patient and ethics board assent.
pmc-13312367:
Hiroko Sumi and co-authors present a 2026 preliminary scale development study on the spiritual pain of people bereaved by cancer in Japan. Spiritual pain in patients themselves is well studied, but what grieving family caregivers feel has had no clear structure. Japanese has no settled term for the concept at all.

The team reanalyzed the nationwide J-HOPE4 survey of bereaved family members, working with replies from 930 caregivers in general hospitals and palliative care units. Factor analysis of 35 candidate items produced seven components: loneliness, life's heartlessness, a sense of unfinished business, distress over the patient's decline, remorse, regret, and a sense of loss. The authors offer this structure as a first map of caregiver spiritual pain and a base for supportive care, while calling for validation in fresh samples.
pmc-13312467:
James Anundson and colleagues ask, in a 2026 matched cohort study, whether Parkinson disease worsens outcomes after total elbow replacement. The disease raises fracture, infection, and implant failure rates after hip and knee replacements, but whether the same risk follows patients to the much less common elbow operation was unknown.

Using the PearlDiver claims database, the team matched 135 patients with Parkinson disease to 540 controls of the same age and sex and followed them for up to five years. Adverse events were uncommon and survival stayed high in both groups. Five-year freedom from any complication or reoperation was 84.4 percent with Parkinson disease against 83.4 percent without, a non-significant gap, and loosening, infection, and fracture outcomes likewise matched. The authors conclude Parkinson disease alone did not measurably harm elbow implant survival.
pmc-13312767:
Toshiharu Tsutsui and co-authors test whether a body scan can stand in for a brain scan in this 2026 study. Brain volume from MRI is a strong marker of brain health in later life, but MRI is costly and slow. The team used data from a health study of adults aged forty and over in Japan.

Each of 314 adults had both an MRI and a DXA scan, a low-dose X-ray that maps body makeup. Measures of the head from the DXA scan, such as its lean and fat mass, tracked brain volume well. Age pulled the estimate down and being male raised it. Repeat checks with shuffled samples held up. The method could ease large brain health surveys.
pmc-13312967:
Olivia Brunet and colleagues test, in a 2026 study, whether human empathy can stretch beyond people and animals to whole ecosystems, and whether that wider feeling tracks with caring about the environment. Empathy research usually stops at human sufferers, with animals a newer extension, leaving nature itself, which plainly can be harmed, outside the frame.

One hundred twenty-two participants rated their emotional responses to distressing images of humans, animals, city ecosystems, and wild ecosystems, and completed standard empathy and environmental attitude measures. Feeling for humans correlated moderately to strongly with feeling for animals and for ecosystems alike. Empathy toward animals and toward natural ecosystems, in particular, rose alongside pro-environmental attitudes. The authors present this as behavioral evidence that ecosystems can be objects of empathy, and they discuss what that means for environmental education and future study designs.
pmc-13313367:
Kyle Ruffing and co-authors report a 2026 case of leprosy caught in Florida that showed up as nerve damage in the leg. The infection, caused by Mycobacterium leprae, is known to spread within Florida itself, and this patient had not traveled to places where the disease is common abroad.

The patient had nerve symptoms and a skin mark typical of the disease. A skin biopsy matched paucibacillary Hansen disease, the form with few bacteria, while the stain and gene test for the bacterium came back negative, as often happens in that form. The likely source was contact with soil where armadillos live, a known route in the region. The case warns doctors in Florida to think of local animal-linked exposure when nerve and skin signs fit, even with negative lab tests.
pmc-13314467:
Menghan Su and a large team link high homocysteine in blood to fat buildup in muscle in work published in 2026. Lipid storage myopathy, where fat clogs muscle fibers, can be triggered by outside factors, and skewed fat handling in people with high homocysteine hinted at a tie.

The team enrolled six patients with high homocysteine who had muscle biopsies and mapped their symptoms and tissue traits. Four of the six showed muscle weakness and poor exercise tolerance that fully cleared with B-vitamin therapy, as the authors report. Gene reads, protein tests, and enzyme assays on the tissue traced how the state drives fat into muscle, and cell tests in C2C12 muscle tubes backed the chain. The work names a treatable cause of muscle fat buildup.
pmc-13314567:
Wejdan M Arif surveys what patients in Saudi Arabia know about radiation in medical imaging in a study from 2026. Scans and tests that use radiation are core to modern care, yet patients can only consent with real insight if they grasp which methods use ionizing radiation and which do not.

An online survey with 28 questions went to 1256 adult patients who had imaging before, as counted in the report. Most, at a share of 77.6 percent as given, knew natural sources give ionizing radiation. Yet a share of 40.8 percent wrongly classed MRI as ionizing, with a further share unsure on kindred points in the figures shown. The study maps where teaching must focus so patients can share choices with clear facts on risk and safety.
pmc-13314867:
Carlos Enrique George-Reyes and co-workers validate a tool that gauges how students view ChatGPT effects on their skills, in their 2026 study. Generative AI has reshaped study habits across Latin America, and claims about its help for writing and thinking needed a sound measure.

The team surveyed 2579 students who had used ChatGPT, drawn from six countries: Ecuador, Mexico, Chile, Brazil, Colombia, and Guatemala, as listed in the report. Their 18-item survey split into two sides, communicative skill and analytical skill, rated on a five-point scale. Checks of internal consistency came out high, with values near 0.943 as stated in the report, and factor tests backed the two-part shape. pmc-13315767:

pmc-13318567:

pmc-13318767:

pmc-13319667:

pmc-13320267:
Tengfei Tian and co-authors review tiny fiber balls as stem cell carriers in a 2026 article on tissue repair. pmc-13321067:

pmc-13323467:

pmc-13325167:

pmc-13330667:

pmc-13331767:

pmc-13333067:

pmc-13334967:

pmc-13335067:

pmc-13335767:

pmc-13335867:

pmc-13336067:
