The review pulls together old and new studies on how kinases steer both processes at once. It covers harm to cell power plants and waste sacs, stress from reactive oxygen, and signals aged cells send to nearby tissue. Because kinases are common drug targets, the author argues that learning how they run both processes could lead to better treatments for aging and cancer.
pmc-13360467:
Smita Kumari and co-authors wrote a 2026 review of antibody-drug conjugates, a fast-growing class of cancer treatment. These drugs join an antibody, which homes in on cancer cells, to a cell-killing drug it carries along. The review traces how the field has moved from early proofs of concept to drugs in routine use. It focuses on how each part of the design has improved.

Better targets, antibody building, linkers, drug payloads, and joining methods have all raised how well these drugs work and how safe they are. The authors also weigh open problems: side effects, drug resistance, and hard manufacturing. Computer and AI methods now help guide design choices. The review offers a clear frame for building the next wave of these targeted drugs.
pmc-13360567:
Jinkimoni Singha and co-authors report a 2026 case of a sinus growth that looked like a tooth-root cyst. The patient was a 38-year-old man with pain and swelling at the back of his upper jaw. The true cause was a mucopyocele, a rare mucus-filled growth in the maxillary sinus that had become infected. Such growths expand slowly and can wear away bone over time.

The case shows how closely a sinus mucopyocele can copy a cyst that starts from a tooth. The team reached the right answer by combining the man's symptoms, a hands-on exam, scans, surgery, and tissue study. Their report warns dentists and surgeons to keep sinus causes in mind when jaw swellings appear. A full workup guards against treating the wrong disease.
pmc-13361467:
Feng Xu, Jinjiang Li, Wei Zhao, Shijing Ding, and Jing Cao show that tracking a nutrition score over time predicts sepsis death better than one reading at admission. Their 2026 study follows 492 adults with sepsis. The score joins blood protein and immune cell counts into one index.

Admission scores alone split survival weakly and lose force after adjustment. Repeated scores from the first week tell a stronger story. In time-aware models, higher moving scores link to lower 28-day death risk. The two parts of the score, taken alone, show no such link. Joint models that handle early death or discharge confirm the tie. The authors advise watching the trend, not the snapshot, when judging nutrition-linked risk.
pmc-13362767:
Md Sofiqul Islam and colleagues report a 2026 lab study on universal-shade dental fillings, the one-shade resins that promise to match any tooth and save chair time. They compared five such products with one classic multi-shade resin, testing hardness, stiffness, slow bending under load, color, and gloss after a day in water and after a simulated year of aging.

The classic resin stayed harder and stiffer and crept less than every one-shade rival. Yet the one-shade products matched it on color stability, and some kept a better gloss after aging. The authors advise picking by need: the classic for heavy-load spots, and one-shade products where looks and speed matter most, since quality varies by brand.
pmc-13363467:
Renfei Gao and colleagues report a 2026 study on toughening geopolymer mortar, a low-carbon stand-in for cement, with basalt fibers. The binder blends metakaolin, slag, and fly ash, but plain geopolymer cracks easily. The team dosed basalt fiber from zero to just over one percent and tracked flow, bending and crushing strength, and crack growth live with a camera method that maps surface strain.

A mid dose, half a percent, gave the best bending strength and slowed cracks the most, while squeezing strength peaked at a lower dose and faded past the mid dose. More fiber always hurt flow. Microscopy showed good grip between fiber and binder at the sweet spots. The authors mark the mid range as the practical window for tougher, greener mortar.
pmc-13364067:
Zhonghui Zhao and colleagues present a 2026 study on steering antenna beams when only the signal phase can be set and the noise picture is skewed. Real arrays estimate their interference map from few snapshots, which corrupts the math behind classic beamforming. Their cascaded network first runs the faulty map through a denoising autoencoder. That rebuilds a clean version and squeezes it into compact features. Then a residual network turns those features into phase settings directly.

Splitting the job this way skips the slow repeated optimization of older robust methods at run time. Tests under short snapshot counts and noisy estimates showed stronger tolerance of map mismatch and output quality that rivaled the classic approaches. The authors aim the method at radar and wireless arrays on tight budgets.
pmc-13364367:
Ayesha Mariam and co-workers review the 2026 state of knowledge on Firmiana colorata, a drug tree of South Asia. Old healers use it, yet its plant facts and drug traits had not been drawn into one place. The review pulls its naming, range, form, genes, and plant compounds into one account.

Lab work hints at use for pain, swelling, germs, and cell growth ills, but most tests use crude plant draws and weak dose proof. Safe use data are thin. The team calls for set plant standards, firm dose work, and harm checks before any clinic use.
pmc-13364667:
Fin Brown and co-authors test a drug pairing against head and neck cancer cells in a 2026 study. These cancers often resist chemo and radiation, and a survival pathway helps the cells hold out. The drug b-AP15 blocks part of that pathway and can kill such cells on its own. The team asked whether it also makes cells weak to TRAIL, a signal that tells cancer cells to die.

Lab tests said yes. The drug raised levels of a TRAIL receptor called DR5 on the cells. That rise needed stress signals inside the cell, namely reactive oxygen species and the JNK pathway. Blocking a survival gene also played a role. Pairing the drug with a second class of blockers killed even more cells. The authors call for animal studies next.
pmc-13365067:
Riddhesh B Doshi and others tuned hydrogel workings and microstructure to max outside vesicle making from mesenchymal stem cells, in 2026. Stem cell sacs are hopeful therapeutics due to firmness and size suited to crossing biological barriers, but reproducible, scalable making remains a biotechnology challenge. Culture problems may control vesicle output.

Gelatin methacryloyl gels at varied concentrations were used as soft microcarriers for adipose-derived and other mesenchymal stem cells, with workings and microstructure fully tuned. Best gels much increased vesicle making. Biomanufacturers gain a scalable culture platform for healing sacs.
pmc-13365967:
Kalyan Mondal and co-workers check in 2026 if math models of beam harm risk for head and neck care hold up at their India site. Such models must be proved on local folks prior to clinic use. The team runs past charts of 51 patients through two code paths and two classic models.

Both code paths match near full. Classic models rank harm grade well and score high truth. Yet the dose that harms half of glands at the site runs low next to book worth. Smart learn tools add some call power for spread organs. Local proof must come first, they stress.
pmc-13366967:
Honghui Yu, Lin Cheng, and Hongbo Zheng report sleep care in a child heart surgery. Their case from twenty twenty-six deals with a girl of nine. She had a thick heart muscle that blocked blood flow.

Her surgery cut the thick septum through the heart tip. The heart kept beating through the whole procedure. No past case told of sleep care for kids in this surgery. She had low pressure and off rhythm despite full prep. Her heart stopped when the device was turned mid surgery. Chest pressure, a pacer, and team work saved her.
pmc-13367967:
Michelle Hua and co-workers tie in 2026 faults in a gene named CELF2 to brain growth ill, fits, and learn loss. New gene faults in this code had just been tied to the ill, with dim cause. The team reads 18 folks and tests cells and mice.

Faults that trap the protein out of the cell core track with fits, while faults that void it do not. Trapped protein stirs nerve cells too much and rules codes for nerve links. A drug hunt flags a cell path that can free the trap. Fit care may aim at that path.
pmc-13369067:
Chenyang Han and co-authors cut scan time and dose in child PET imaging with a deep learning method in a 2026 study. PET scans map body activity but use a tracer dose, so less dose and less time help children most. Standard smart denoise tools need huge training sets. Their patch-based method learns from one clean scan, cut into small patches. It then cleans short, noisy scans to match.

Tests used a lab phantom and 88 child scans cut from 90 seconds per bed to 20. The method kept sharpness and contrast while it cut noise in the phantom. In blind reads, cleaned short scans matched or beat full scans in over 85 percent of cases. A small low bias showed in some uptake scores, with no firm gaps in key spots. The work may let clinics scan children faster at lower dose.
pmc-13369767:
Mengting Zhu and co-workers show in 2026 that world warm skews the build energy counts at the heart of climate plans. Most plan mods hold past weather set when they guess heat and cool needs. The team feeds fresh warm day counts from world climate mods into a big energy mod.

Skip of warm trends cuts cool need by up to a fifth in low warm paths and near four fifths in high ones, while heat need reads too high. Counts of gas out shift by huge sums in 2100. Cool gas leaks in warm poor lands read too low as well.
pmc-13369967:
Sonia Dupuis, Nando Metzger, Konrad Schindler, Frank Göttsche, and Stefan Wunderle built a forty-two-year Arctic land temperature dataset in two thousand twenty-six. Land surface temperature is a key climate variable, especially in the fast-warming Arctic. Older satellite records are long but coarse, which blurs fine surface processes like permafrost change.

Their method sharpens the coarse record to one kilometer using a deep diffusion model trained on finer modern data. Land cover, elevation, and vegetation height maps guide the sharpening. The result gives twice-daily readings for the whole pan-Arctic across four decades. Uses include permafrost modeling, air temperature reconstruction, and Greenland ice sheet studies.
pmc-13370867:
Romana Ďuráčiová and co-workers launch in 2026 Foldify, a free web app that lets any lab call protein shapes with no own gear or code skill. Top shape tools ask for strong chips and tech hands. Foldify joins five such tools in one plain web face on a shared big compute sys.

Users paste a code line and run one or more tools on it. Shapes show in a web view or save to disk. A side by side way stacks shapes in one view with like scores. No log in is need, which drops the gate for small labs.
pmc-13371267:
Petr Birke and colleagues describe parvovirus B19 crises in Czech children with hereditary spherocytosis in a 2026 study. In this inherited anaemia, red cells are sphere-shaped and break down early, and parvovirus B19 can halt red cell production, causing a sudden aplastic crisis. Twenty-three children hospitalised in early 2024 at Olomouc and Brno were reviewed.

The average age was just under seven years. Fever, pallor, tiredness, vomiting, pain, and cough were the most common signs, while the classic rash of parvovirus was rare. Average haemoglobin was very low, near 4.9 grams per decilitre. The series helps clinicians recognise crises early, when transfusion and close monitoring can prevent severe harm.
pmc-13372067:
Aoumar G Chamma and co-authors report a rare mix of heart and artery ills in a 2026 case report. A man aged 84 had lived 30 years with a swelling disease of the large arteries. He took low-dose steroid pills and a weekly drug to calm his immune system.

Routine checks found wide spots on his heart arteries and a large soft growth in the top left chamber of his heart. The growth was about 3.5 cm wide and mildly blocked blood flow. Scans also showed his artery disease was still active. The case shows how two rare ills can meet in one person and test the care team.
pmc-13373267:
Abiodun O Adewuya and co-authors mapped faith leads as mind care gate staff in Nigeria in a 2026 study. Few Nigerians who need mind care get it from clinics. Pastors and imams are, in truth, the first port of call for most homes.

The study sorts faith leads by what they hold true about mind ills and how they act on those views. Some mix faith and clinic paths, and some hold one path alone. Named types help health teams train and team up with the right leads. The aim is a bridge where faith care and clinic care back each other, not clash.
pmc-13375267:
Tyler C Prinkey and colleagues study limited health literacy in Finland's general and migrant-origin populations in a 2026 paper. Limited health literacy tracks with worse health outcomes, yet which factors drive it in diverse populations was unclear. Surveys Terve Suomi and MoniSuomi from 2022 to 2023 covered 9,717 adults aged 20 to 74, with literacy measured by the HLS19-Q12 scale.

Limited literacy affected 15 percent of the general population and 42 percent of the migrant-origin population. Across both groups, risk rose with migration background, unemployment or student status, income strain, living alone, lower education, and fair or poor self-rated health. Among migrants, language skills and length of residence also mattered. The findings argue for plain-language services and targeted support for newcomers.
pmc-13376067:
Marina Barba-Aliaga, Lianqi Chi, and co-authors show a yeast build aid runs both gene read and gene build for its own marks, in work from 2026. The aid frees stuck build lines at hard code runs in cells. It roams twixt core and cell sap, but its core acts were dim till now.

Core aid grips gene strands and blocks the read head from its marks. Those marks are the same genes the aid helps build in the sap. Hard run marks in a gene call for both aid acts at once. Sap build work must run for the core brake to hold, they find. Twin rule keeps end counts trim and true.
pmc-13376167:
Daniela Münch and eight colleagues published a 2026 study on how zebrafish regrow sense organs. Fish can replace lost hair cells in their lateral line, a sense organ along the body. Regrowth starts after cells die, but deaths can happen in more than one way.

The team compared two kinds of cell death, a neat programmed death and a harsh death by cell bursting. The neat death drew a milder response from immune cells, with fewer white blood cells rushing in. Even so, both paths ended at the same core set of regrowth genes. Blocking immune cells even sped up healing after harsh damage, a result that may guide repair research.
pmc-13376367:
Yashar Salami and three co-authors propose a 2026 scheme for swapping secret keys safely over future 6G wireless links. Two sides need a shared secret before they can talk in private, and open airwaves let spies listen in. Their design mixes a classic key-swap method with signals at terahertz rates.

A two-layer graphene sheet shapes the signal, its tuning giving a way to stamp bits onto the wave. Proof of who is who, plus freshness values, ride inside the wave itself. Tests across a wide range of signal strength showed clean reading of the wave and matching keys at both ends.
pmc-13376567:
Veryer and five co-authors grow two germ-fight dusts from a shelf fungus broth in this twenty twenty-six study. Fine zinc and magnesium oxide dusts can eat dye waste under light. Green growth paths skip harsh brews and use live broth in their place.

Inside, beam and scope checks proved both dusts formed as the team meant. Zinc dust grew as nail shapes spread in an even field in the checks. Light tests ate near all dye for zinc dust in just past two hours. The mag dust ate most of its dye load in a bit more time. Both dusts curbed all six test germs, most hard on one lung germ.
pmc-13377067:
The high Qinghai-Tibet plateau teems with wildlife whose viruses nobody had cataloged. Hao Zhou and co-authors sequence that hidden world in a 2026 survey of twenty-two wild species, hunting for the next spillover threat before it spills.

Birds carried richer virus loads than mammals. Greylag geese and Himalayan vultures held many cross-species viruses and sat at the hub of the transmission network the team mapped. Thirty-six virus genera with potential to infect people or livestock turned up. Rotavirus A and a parainfluenza virus ranked as high zoonotic risks. The plateau vole carried the most high-risk viruses of any host, including an early-branching rotavirus line. Surveillance, the authors argue, should start with those hub species.
pmc-13377167:
Inha Hwang and nine co-authors test if sleep span links to thirst in a large Korean survey. Their study appeared in twenty twenty-six. Thirst flags a shift in body water state. Near twenty-five hundred adults from a state sleep and head pain survey were weighed, split by thirst rate and by sleep span bands.

Short sleep, at six hours or less, tied to high thirst against the mid band. In adults past fifty, a band just past six hours also tied to high thirst. Diabetes, loud snore, and low mood shaped the links in probe checks. Low mood flagged high thirst in each run. The team reads a mixed web of sleep, thirst, and water state.
pmc-13377667:
Five vets led by Anja Suter report eyelid surgery that cured sore eyes in a giant pet rabbit. The two-year-old male rabbit had eye surface sores that kept coming back in both eyes. Its upper lids were too long and rolled both in and out at once. Its third eyelid, a side lid rabbits hold, was also too long and folded over the eye.

Surgery cut a wedge from each upper lid to firm its edge. The third eyelid cartilage was cut short in the same work. After surgery, the sores healed in full and stayed away for a whole year of checks. The team offers the paired fix for like cases in pet rabbits. Shape faults of the lids, they note, are a cause of sore eyes that is easy to miss.
pmc-13377867:
Hamidreza Mortazavy Beni and co-authors built a checked sim of a gas heat box in a 2026 study. The box warms gas at town gate posts through a water bath, a fire tube, and a coil. A full 3D sim tied heat in solids and flows in one solve.

Two load rates were run, and sums held when the grid grew fine. The bath swirled soft, warm at top and cool at its core, while gas in the coil rose from cold to set heat most on its first pass. Fire side peaks kissed the top wall. A checked sim lets staff tune burn sets with no field risk.
pmc-13378367:
Fu-Kwun Wang, Fantahun Tsegaw, and William Gomez propose a 2026 method for forecasting wind speed over the medium term. Accurate forecasts help wind farms run steadily, but wind is uneven, random, and changes at several time scales at once. Their approach blends methods that pull out wind patterns with methods that track sequences over time.

Tests used data from a weather station at Pacific Grove and a second data set called VALHALL_A. The new model explained the observed wind very well and cut forecast error by more than one fifth compared with standard models. It also included features that show how it reaches a forecast, which helps users trust and check its output.
pmc-13379467:
Giulia D'Arcangelo and colleagues discuss a 2026 review on getting the treatment balance right for children with inflammatory bowel disease. New drugs have improved care, but matching the right treatment to each child at the right time remains an unmet goal. Decisions still lean on broad guidance and imperfect predictors of risk.

Treating too strongly can expose a child with mild disease to powerful immune-suppressing drugs, with side effects and heavy monitoring. Treating too weakly can let severe disease cause lasting damage before effective therapy starts. The review weighs both risks and argues for judging each child's likely course early. Its aim is care sized to the child, not to the average patient.
pmc-13379867:
Maulik A Patel and colleagues present a 2026 study of more than a thousand tunnelled dialysis catheter placements at one centre over four years. These catheters give access for blood cleaning when a surgically made access point is not possible or dialysis must start urgently. Where the catheter enters the body may affect safety and outcomes.

The study compared four entry sites, most often the large veins on either side of the neck. For 1,050 patients it checked complications during the procedure, plus blood tests and clinical outcomes at later follow-ups. Baseline features were similar across groups. The comparison helps clinicians weigh which site serves patients best.
pmc-13380167:
Tang and colleagues examine whether blood in the urine, tracked over time, predicts kidney decline in IgA nephropathy, in 2026 nephrology research. The disease, where antibody deposits inflame the kidney filters, shows hematuria, yet readings have given muddy prognostic answers. The study followed 1,771 biopsy-proven patients, sorting visit urine red cell counts into four bands. Statistical models for time-varying risks linked the hematuria level to a composite outcome of filtration loss or kidney failure.

During a median follow-up of 48 months, the outcome struck 487 participants, or 27.5 percent of the cohort. Baseline hematuria showed no significant association once adjusted. Time-updated hematuria told a different story: counts at or above 100 cells per microliter carried a hazard ratio of 1.53 for progression. In patients with proteinuria, moderate levels, 20 to under 100 cells, carried a hazard ratio of 1.89 in subgroup analysis. Tang argues repeated checks, not one-off readings, carry the prognostic signal.
pmc-13381367:
Ayushi Singh and co-authors report a 2026 study of two tissue stains that help diagnose prostate cancer and judge its behaviour. One stain highlights the basal cell layer that cancer usually lacks. The other, called NKX3.1, is found almost only in prostate tissue and marks cancer cells directly.

The study examined 58 prostate tissue samples received over two years at a specialist institute. NKX3.1 staining was scored by how many tumour cells were positive. The team then checked whether stronger staining tracked with adverse features of the cancer, using blood PSA values where available. Combining both stains may sharpen diagnosis in difficult prostate samples.
pmc-13381767:
Gen Xu and co-authors probe why hybrid corn outgrows both of its parents, a puzzle called heterosis or hybrid vigor. Their 2026 study joins gene activity data with trait data across many maize hybrids. About 30 percent of active genes in hybrid seedlings sat above or below the midpoint between the parents, a pattern called incomplete dominance.

Genes whose activity was set nearby mostly behaved in a simple additive way. The off-midpoint genes, by contrast, were often run by distant control spots that cluster into hotspots, each steering hundreds of genes. The team proved one hotspot's role by testing a switch gene called ZmR1, which shifted seedling and field traits alike. Their model gives breeders a clearer map of how hybrid vigor arises.
pmc-13382067:
Muhammad Adeel Zafar and colleagues present a 2026 cross-sectional study from Pakistan on high blood pressure medicines. It asks whether patients take them as prescribed, and whether that links to control of their pressure. Poor adherence is a major reason control rates stay low in the country. The study ran in outpatient clinics in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa province.

In total 436 patients were recruited from large hospitals and completed a structured questionnaire plus a validated medication questionnaire. Blood pressure was measured with standard methods, and control was defined against a standard threshold. The analysis compares adherence levels with achieved control. Results can guide clinics toward the adherence problems that matter most.
pmc-13382967:
Zhenzhen Lin and a large team present DFA-YOLO, an image system that finds maize leaf stomata at any angle, in 2026 work. Stomata, the pores that trade carbon gain against water loss, are dense and tilted in microscope images. Standard box detection often places them poorly, so the team used rotated boxes instead.

Trained on 3,597 images, the system adds knowledge transfer, a reweighted loss for hard cases, and a new feature module. It reached strong accuracy scores and ran at close to 45 frames per second on an automated platform. The tool supports fast counts of stomata and early measures of size for crop studies.
pmc-13383067:
Tengyu Liu's team reports a photocatalyst that turns biomass-derived oxalic acid fully into carbon monoxide, in a 2026 study. Green photocatalysis often wastes carbon, but the team's two-in-one design uses electron-rich cadmium sites near sulfur vacancies on a Bi2S3/CdS yolk-shell structure. The shell oxidizes water while the yolk drives oxalic acid cleavage.

The catalyst converted oxalic acid to CO at 1671 micromoles per gram per hour with selectivity above 99 percent, beating prior CO2-to-CO photocatalysts. Mechanistic work showed shell and yolk cooperating through hydroxyl radicals and carbon dioxide radical anions protonated in place. The route upgrades a biomass waste stream into a useful chemical feedstock.
pmc-13385367:
Hulda Ingvarsdottir's team tracked five-year stability of blood proteins in older adults, in a 2026 study. Circulating proteins reflect health and aging, but their long-term stability was little known. The team measured 7288 serum proteins in 3093 participants averaging 75 years old in the AGES-Reykjavik study, with a plasma subset checked in the Cardiovascular Health Study.

Stability varied widely and independently of tissue RNA stability. Stable proteins tended to be extracellular, secreted, and tissue-specific, while variable ones handled intracellular housekeeping. Levels generally steadied with age, and some proteins differed by sex. Genes and disease swayed stability broadly, yet the co-regulation structure of the proteome largely held over time.
pmc-13385967:
Catarina Pereira's team built trainable spin hardware that learns on-device, in a 2026 study. Spin nano-neurons promise energy-efficient neural hardware, but training relied on oversimplified device models sensitive to variation. The team showed magnetic tunnel junctions can generate tunable complex nonlinear responses, then implemented analog finite-difference gradient generation on-chip.

Device-in-the-loop training in a magnetic tunnel junction network with one and two hidden layers reached 93.3 percent classification accuracy despite marked device variation. Gradients from the analog neurons closely matched numerical values. The design removes the training bottleneck for spin neural networks, bringing hardware learning closer to practice.
pmc-13386467:
Theresa A. L. Ehret and colleagues build live-cell assays for a family of signaling kinases in 2026 work. The six PAK kinases steer cell survival, movement, and shape, yet no assay could track drug binding for all forms inside cells. Light-based tags now report both drug engagement and pairing of the kinases in living cells.

Testing with those tools produced a surprise: group I PAK inhibitors appear to push the kinases into paired, dimeric forms. That finding changes how inhibitor action may be read in cells. The assay set gives drug designers a direct way to watch on-target effects across the whole family.
pmc-13386867:
Shea A. Lowery and co-authors review knotted DNA structures inside herpesviruses in a 2026 article. G-quadruplexes form when guanine-rich DNA folds into stacked blocks instead of a helix. Herpesvirus genomes carry unusually many sequences that can fold this way, across all three human-infecting subfamilies.

These folds can steer both active replication and the latent state that lets herpesviruses persist for life. Their shifting shapes in living cells make them hard to pin down and harder to drug, the authors note. The review gathers conserved roles across viruses and lists what tools the field needs next.
pmc-13387867:
Erasmo Barbante Casella read the Global Burden of Disease 2023 numbers on child brain development disorders in a 2026 commentary. Such disorders are common and shape whole lives, yet surveillance often misses them, above all where services are unequal. The underlying study tracked trends from 1990 to 2023 across twelve South American countries, offering a rare long, comparative view.

Three patterns stood out. Autism rates rose modestly, ADHD held steady, and unexplained intellectual disability declined steadily. Casella warns these lines mostly mirror how well systems detect, classify, and record cases, not just true change. Autism's small rise, far below rich-country growth, likely reflects underdiagnosis where specialists and standard tools are scarce.
pmc-13389067:
Valdés Olmos and colleagues review how nuclear medicine guides surgeons in the operating room. Their 2026 paper traces radioguided surgery from the sentinel node procedure, developed over three decades ago. That procedure combined pre-operative scans, a hand-held gamma probe, and blue dye. Together they find the first lymph node draining a tumour. That procedure became standard in melanoma and breast cancer and founded interventional nuclear medicine.

Modern scanners such as SPECT/CT and PET/CT now give surgeons precise roadmaps before the operation. The review describes expansion into gynaecological, urological, head and neck, and gastrointestinal cancers, plus robot-assisted procedures targeting sentinel nodes and small clusters of metastases. Hybrid tracers that are both radioactive and fluorescent are highlighted as the coming step. The authors comprehensively assess current applications and the technology's trajectory.
pmc-13390367:
Qiang Gao's team presents ProtSeqGen, a deep-learning model for the protein inverse folding problem: designing an amino acid sequence that folds into a specified backbone shape. Existing methods struggle to optimise hit rate, stability, efficiency, and generalisation together across diverse folds.

ProtSeqGen encodes shapes as local geometric graphs, models residue interactions with a message-passing network, and predicts amino acids with a multilayer perceptron. Trained on the CATH 4.2 data set, it beat state-of-the-art methods on sequence recovery and made accurate, designable sequences for nine shape-diverse proteins, establishing a robust, scalable tool for de novo protein design.
pmc-13391367:
Andrii Bugai and a large team uncover, in 2026, how the cell nucleus decides which newly made RNAs to export and which to destroy. Cells produce many polyadenylated RNAs, packaged with proteins, but only functional packages should reach the cytoplasm while faulty ones are degraded in the nucleus.

The study centres on UAP56, also called DDX39B, a core part of functional RNA packages that docks them to a pore-linked export machine. The team traces how that docking hands the transcript over for release and export. Molecular biologists gain the missing decision step in RNA quality control, explaining how faithful gene expression is protected from a flood of defective transcripts.
pmc-13391467:
Sérgio Cavalheiro's team used a working drug-response assay to guide treatment for a four-year-old with repeat spread clival chordoma, a rare, locally fast-moving tumour considered chemotherapy-stubborn in children. Tumour cell balls were tested ex vivo on the Bioverso rig.

The assay showed broad resistance with relative response to irinotecan, and an irinotecan course made marked medical and scan shrinkage of brain and lung lesions after three cycles, without severe harm. Response held for fourteen months, illustrating working exact cancer care for rare, stubborn child tumours where gene targets are scarce.
pmc-13391767:
I. S. Alam's team weighed open, keyhole, and robotic total belly colon removal with end ileum opening for immune bowel disease, using matched national records data from 2022. Lightly cutting techniques have better bowel results, but head-to-head evidence for this extensive operation was limited.

Among 581 matched patients, eighty-three robotic, four hundred fifteen keyhole, and eighty-three open, overall thirty-day illness did not differ clearly. Robotic surgery took clearly longer than keyhole surgery, and secondary results including stay, return stays, and exact complications round out a comparison surgeons can weigh against surgery time.
pmc-13392367:
Ziling Liu's team built a sound time crystal from ringing meta-atoms in a one-axis acoustic wave guide, creating a time-varying meta-stuff that boosts sound at motion band gaps. Selectively harnessing Floquet band structure and opening multiple gaps had challenged experiment.

Dynamic squeeze swing made boosted passage and strong output boost for a compact Floquet slab at the gap rate. A time super-cell design then bent motion bands to create multiple gaps, yielding two boosted passage ranges near half and quarter of the original swing rate, opening routes to higher-axis time crystals.
pmc-13392467:
Connor Prosty, Mark Sorin, Emily G McDonald, and Todd C Lee pooled the trial evidence on giving vancomycin by mouth to stop Clostridioides difficile infection coming back. The risk returns whenever a past patient needs antibiotics again. A past bout of this gut infection makes a repeat episode much more likely during later antibiotic courses. Their review updated a search of MEDLINE and Embase to March 2026.

Only two randomised trials qualified, covering 102 patients in total, both judged at low risk of bias. Pooling them gave odds of recurrence modestly below the control level, with an eighty-eight percent chance of some benefit on the authors' Bayesian reading. Uncertainty stays wide, though, and the pair of small trials cannot settle the question, so larger studies are called for.
pmc-13392867:

The paper frames the hormone as a tolerance booster through antioxidant and defense regulation. Growers on copper-rich soils get a candidate treatment, still at the pot-trial stage.
pmc-13440567:
An and colleagues built a tumour-based printing ink in 2026 for modelling glioblastoma, an aggressive brain cancer.  The team grew glioblastoma cells in gels tuned to tumour stiffness and squeezed them to mimic pressure inside the skull. This workout pushed cells to release their own matrix, which was collected as a bioink, a cell-friendly printing material.

The ink carried stronger tumour signals than plain gel controls, including higher levels of GDF15, MMP2, and MMP9, all linked to tumour spread. Printed models made from the ink grew faster and switched on more invasion-related genes. Adding vessel cells or fibroblasts, which are support cells, recreated stromal activation and matrix change seen in real tumours. The authors present the ink as a repeatable platform for glioblastoma-on-chip studies and drug tests.
pmc-13441167:
Silvia Piunno and co-authors follow patients with a puzzling form of lupus: blood tests show active disease, yet they feel clinically well for long periods. Their 2026 longitudinal study asks whether two blood markers, anti-dsDNA antibodies and complement C3, can predict future flares in this group.

Sixty patients from a London lupus cohort contributed 531 visits over an average follow-up of 3.3 years. Despite their quiet clinical picture, 63.3 percent experienced at least one flare. Visit-by-visit analysis showed that rising anti-dsDNA levels and falling C3 independently predicted a flare or sustained activity at the next visit, including moderate-to-severe flares. Patients who flared were also more often anti-Ro positive. The authors argue this state is rarely benign and needs close clinical and blood monitoring.
pmc-13442867:
Prabakar Vaittinada Ayar and colleagues report a 2026 laboratory study of how blood-pressure drugs used in septic shock affect Escherichia coli, a gut bacterium often involved in sepsis. The team tested norepinephrine, vasopressin, and angiotensin II on 21 diverse strains plus a urinary sepsis model strain, growing them in fluids meant to mimic serum and urine.

Norepinephrine boosted bacterial fitness across strains, body sites, and virulence backgrounds in both fluids, while the two alternative drugs showed little or no such effect. The pattern matters because the first-line drug may unintentionally aid the very microbe doctors are fighting. The authors call for animal studies next, since dish results alone cannot settle how these drugs behave in patients.
pmc-13443767:
Francis Smit and colleagues argue that specialist training is a national asset for South Africa in a 2026 essay. Training a specialist takes 12 to 15 years of public funds, deep in wards where trainees also carry real patient loads. Universities, provinces, hospitals, and councils share the build.

Since training lives inside care, ward quality and school quality rise or fall together. Staff gaps, broken gear, and weak rule hit both patients and pupils at once. The authors say pass marks on school checks now double as a gauge of system health. A specialist's worth spills past one career into leadership, research, and service reach. They urge leaders to fund and guard training as core national wealth, not a side cost.
pmc-13444267:
Gabriel França Toledo Pinto and colleagues measure food insecurity in children and teens with type 1 diabetes in a 2026 study. The clinic sat at a Rio de Janeiro child institute, and a Brazil food scale graded home food stress. The pool held 130 young patients, most of them girls, with mothers as main carers in most homes.

Food insecurity touched 67.4 percent of the group in the count. Mild stress led at 50.4 percent of cases, while severe stress sat at 5.4 percent of cases. Income, carer schooling, and benefit receipt each tied to food stress in the checks. Most children held healthy weight for age, and height ran on track. The authors call for joint health and social policy, since tight food budgets fight the strict meal plans diabetes demands.
pmc-13444367:
Ting Xie and colleagues link felt stress, symptoms, and hippocampus part sizes in first-episode schizophrenia in a 2026 study. The pool held 97 patients at first break and 47 healthy peers. Stress scales, symptom scales, and 3.0-T MRI scans fed subfield maps of the hippocampus.

Patients felt more stress than peers in the checks. Their fimbria zones ran smaller, while tail zones ran larger, after head size and trait fixes. In healthy peers, many zone sizes rose with felt stress in tidy lines. Those lines broke or vanished in patients. In patients, felt stress rose with positive symptoms and with worry-low mood marks. The authors read the break as a sign that stress wiring itself is off in the illness.
pmc-13445567:
Yoko Akazawa-Ogawa and seven co-authors watch alpaca antibodies evolve in real time and find that getting better at binding often means getting worse at staying folded. Their technique tracks antibody sequences from the same starting genome as somatic mutations accumulate after immunization. Mutation-heavy clusters bound antigen more strongly but lost thermal stability, by up to twenty-one degrees in the extreme.

Binding strength and stability, notably, correlated only weakly. Mutations concentrated in the binding loops and one framework region. Less thermally stable clones paradoxically resisted acid and alkali better. The picture reframes affinity maturation as a trade-off managed by selection, with stability acting as an adjustable dial rather than a fixed virtue.
pmc-13445767:
Jinxin Gao and coauthors uncover a 2026 account of how the RNA helicase Dbp7 loads the centromere mark CENP-A in fission yeast, guarding chromosome splitting. Using a visual genetic screen, the team found Dbp7 prevents harmful R-loop buildup at centromeres and traced its pairing with the RNA exosome part Dis3.

Cutting the Dbp7 gene mislaid CENP-A, broke chromosome splitting, and cut centromere muting, with both the helicase domain and a tail motif needed. Dbp7 and Dis3 jointly bind centromere transcripts and recruit CENP-A through its helper Sim3. The work reveals a new loading route with weight for genome steadiness research.
pmc-13446367:
Murat Ferhat Ferhatoğlu and colleagues compare two cold storage tricks for kidneys from living donors, in a 2026 prospective study at an Istanbul transplant clinic. A graft must stay cold and viable between removal and implant, and plain cold storage still rules in living donation for its ease and low cost. The rivals were a chilled sponge wrap and a bag of ice.

Graft results at six months matched between the two methods. The ice bag showed a modest edge in the first days after surgery, in early lab signs of graft work. The authors count both as sound picks, with the bag a touch kinder at the start. Their data fill a gap on early chemistry reads for living donor grafts.
pmc-13447067:
Zhenyu Lu and colleagues open a journal collection on sensing, learning, and control for robots that work with people, in a 2026 editorial. The field is shifting, they argue, from robots as tools to robots as partners that read people and settings, learn from feedback, and act with care. The collection prizes whole-loop builds over lone clever algorithms.

Four contributions show the range. One has robots ask people smart questions to learn reward from feedback. Others cover long action reading, farm perception, and self-running medical scanning. Shared ground runs through all four: better senses, learning that takes user taste on board, and control that holds safety while work gets done. The editors frame the set as a step toward robots fit for human spaces.
pmc-13447267:
Linlin Fang leads a team mapping new antibody targets on a cattle coronavirus protein in 2026 laboratory work. The virus causes calf diarrhoea, winter gut illness in adults and breathing disease, with heavy farm losses. Its nucleocapsid protein, the most stable viral protein, suits early diagnosis and vaccine design, provided exact binding spots are known.

Lab-made protein was used to immunise mice, yielding two specific antibodies through fused-cell methods. Both reacted only with the target virus in blot and cell tests and shared the same antibody class. Cutting the protein into pieces pinpointed two short stretches that each antibody grasps, both lying on the protein surface and stable across strains. Those mapped spots give concrete starting points for targeted diagnostic tests.
pmc-13447367:
Víctor Carballo-Uicab and colleagues build synthetic gene switches to detect Listeria bacteria in raw milk in 2026 proof-of-concept work. Listeria can cause severe foodborne illness, yet direct detection in complex foods without lab amplification had not been shown. Toehold switches are RNA devices that turn on a signal only when a matching RNA sequence appears.

Analysis of a variable gene region found a short trigger stretch unique to Listeria among related bacteria. Three switch designs were built, and the most stable was tested against synthetic triggers across a wide dose range. RNA extracted from pure cultures and from spiked raw milk both activated the switch, while clean milk gave a clearly different signal. Activation stayed modest, yet detection without amplification in a messy food matrix marks a step toward cheaper food safety tests.
pmc-13447667:
Su and colleagues tackled in 2026 a stubborn flaw in cryo-electron microscopy, where sample particles stick to the grid in one preferred pose, leaving missing views that blur the final structure. Fixes such as detergents or tilted imaging are slow and case-bound. Their approach varies the temperature at which samples are frozen, which shifts how particles settle, then merges data sets taken at different temperatures.

Su merged heat-loving ribosome data from several temperatures and rebalanced the particles using a draft three-dimensional model. The merged set gave smoother quality curves, higher roundness scores, and a narrower blind zone than single-temperature data. They proved the method on a protein complex known for severe posing problems, winning a high-quality reconstruction. The authors offer the recipe as a simple, widely usable cure for a bottleneck that limits high-resolution structure work.
pmc-13447867:
Nicole M. Antczak and coauthors test a 2026 side-by-side study of active-site loops in E. coli DinB and human DNA copier kappa, two damage-bypass enzymes with matching bypass patterns. The team scanned loop spots by alanine gene change, assaying primer growth and thermal steadiness for both proteins.

Most variants matched wild-type work, but a few gene changes caused sharp work and steadiness losses, with notably similar effects at aligned spots across species. Less active variants also gained less steadying from DNA or building blocks. The kept loop governs damage toughness in both enzymes, feeding copier biology and blocker design.
pmc-13449367:
Liang and colleagues study anakinra, an immune calming drug, for the brain toxicity that can follow CAR T cell therapy. That treatment reprograms a patient's immune cells against blood cancer. The syndrome, shortened to ICANS, can be life threatening, and steroids fail many severe cases. Their 2026 study reviews 101 patients treated with anakinra at two centers and asks whether improvement in the first three days forecasts the course.

Early response was far from assured. Only about 43 percent reached neurologic improvement by seventy two hours. The median time to resolution ran eight days. Treatment related death at twenty eight days touched about one in eight. Yet the seventy two hour mark proved decisive. Patients who hit it cleared the syndrome faster, needed less steroid exposure, and died less often. The authors propose that checkpoint as the moment to judge whether anakinra suffices or escalation must begin.
pmc-13449567:
Shanshan Xu and colleagues built a deep-learning tool in 2026 to stage cervical cancer from MRI scans automatically. Staging guides treatment, but radiologists now rely heavily on personal experience, which can lead to errors. The team wanted a system that outlines tumors and nearby structures and then assigns a T stage.

A dataset of 17,479 MRI scans from 144 patients across stages T1 to T4 was hand-outlined to train the system. A new segmentation network called CPANet beat UNet, UNet++, DeepLabv3+, and UperNet-Swin on overlap scores for tumor and nearby tissues. Staging models built on those outlines were then compared, with the best chosen by accuracy. Clinics gain a faster, more consistent staging aid.
pmc-13449867:
Rik Dawson and co-authors build a fall-prevention exercise site with older users at the table in a 2026 study. Falls hit older people hard, and exercise cuts them, yet many elders fall short of activity goals. The team ran three rounds of co-design with elders in care, care staff, and physios.

Round one shaped a first site from talks and checks. Round two had elders think aloud as they used it, rating ease and clarity. Eight design themes rose: plain words, easy reach, true-to-life feel, safety, and choice, among them. Elders liked shaping the tool and praised its ease. The site now backs the TOP UP program.
pmc-13449967:
Fu and colleagues presented in 2026 a step-by-step protocol for mapping where long non-coding RNAs bind, with fine spatial detail. These RNAs guide gene control by gripping chromatin, the packaged DNA in the cell. The classic mapping method needs huge cell numbers, suffers noisy background, and shreds the RNA it hunts during preparation. Their variant, ChIRP-Tag, swaps the shredding step for an enzyme that tags DNA in place.

Fu lays out each stage. Cells are softened so probes can enter. Tagged probes latch onto the target RNA. Antibodies then fetch a cutting enzyme that builds the sequencing library at the binding sites. The swap cuts the needed cell input sharply, spares the target RNA, and speeds library preparation. Sensitivity and spatial detail stay high across cell types, the authors report. The protocol aims to serve studies of rare samples the older method could not handle.
pmc-13450567:
Alvaro Andres Saavedra and co-authors relate a 2026 case where lasting clots in the penis hid a rare cancer for two years. Their patient, a man aged 36, had clots on both sides of the erection chambers with steady pelvic pain. Scans at the time found no tumor, and his care stayed cautious and drug based.

Later a fast-growing mass appeared with spread to groin nodes, and surgery plus tissue tests named it synovial sarcoma, a cancer almost never seen in the penis. The disease came back soon after surgery, and he died eight months later. The team urges doctors to suspect hidden cancer when such clots persist with no clear cause.
pmc-13451867:
Kelsey McAlister and co-authors review in 2026 outcomes for adults who got online therapy for gambling disorder through one provider. Few people with the disorder seek care, and real-world proof for virtual care is thin. Records covered 1,305 adults treated between mid 2024 and spring 2026, with weekly scores of gambling symptom weight.

Patients arrived with mid-level symptoms, and over half carried another mental health condition, most often anxiety. The study tracks how scores moved over the first twelve weeks and which starting traits tied to faster gains. It also times when a gain large enough to matter in daily life first shows. The authors frame the cohort as a base for judging virtual gambling care at scale.
pmc-13452767:
Luka Flegar and five co-authors reflect on their nationwide study of surgery for urachal cancer, a rare cancer of a leftover bladder cord. Their 2026 piece sums up German hospital billing records from 2006 to 2022, covering 2,593 cases. Care for this cancer usually removes part or all of the bladder along with the cord and navel.

The share of cases treated by removing only part of the bladder rose over time and reached 74 percent in 2022. Stays after that smaller operation fell from 14 days in 2006 to just 9 days in 2022, and robot help shortened them further. The piece flags uneven care coverage across the country as a worry. Since the cancer is rare and harsh, the authors call for joint work across centers and countries to test whether the smaller operation stays as safe.
pmc-13453467:
Kaveh Ebrahimzadeh, Mohammad Mirahmadi Eraghi, and Farahnaz Bidari Zerehpoosh report a rare spine tumor that crushed a vertebra in a young man. The tumor, called pseudomyogenic hemangioendothelioma, grows from blood vessel tissue and sits between benign and cancerous. Their 2026 report covers a 24 year old with a burst fracture at the T12 vertebra, growing back pain, tingling legs, and weakness.

Surgeons removed the whole T12 vertebra from behind, freed the spinal cord, and rebuilt the front column with an expanding cage and screws. Lab checks on the removed tissue confirmed the rare tumor type. Two years on, the patient had no return of the tumor or new problems. The authors stress that this tumor can mimic other bone tumors on scans, so tissue proof and full removal matter.
pmc-13453567:
Xu Xiaomin and five co-authors report a prostate cancer first read as an abscess in a 36 year old man with a transplanted kidney. Transplant patients face a two to four fold higher cancer risk from drugs that mute the immune system. Their 2026 case report follows a man 16 years past his transplant who came in with pelvic pain, fever, and a rising PSA level.

A needle draw from the prostate pulled bloody fluid instead of pus, which pushed the team to biopsy at once. The tissue showed a poorly formed prostate cancer with changes in three DNA repair genes, among them BRCA2. Surgeons removed the prostate with a reshaped laparoscopic plan that kept clear of the graft kidney. One year on, his PSA was undetectable and the kidney worked steadily. The authors urge fast biopsy when a presumed abscess bleeds.
pmc-13453667:
Ryoma Oda, Takeshi Kinoshita, Nobuo Tomizawa, and Minoru Tabata report a case where a moving CT scan exposed silent poor blood flow to the brain. Their 2026 report follows a 72 year old woman with a chronic tear in her aorta, the body's main artery, forming a 53 millimetre bulge found by chance. The tear squeezed the true channel of two neck bound arteries, starving the right side of her brain.

The four dimensional scan, which shows flow over time, caught a delayed peak on the right side that plain scans would miss. Guided by that map, surgeons rebuilt the brachiocephalic and right carotid arteries, the vessels feeding that side. Scans after surgery showed the flow delay had eased. The authors present the moving scan as a planning tool for tears that quietly threaten the brain.
pmc-13454067:
Ghina Fakhri and nine co-authors chart childhood heart muscle disease at a single major center in a resource limited setting over twenty years. Their 2026 review covers 244 children diagnosed before age 18, with an average age of 5.9 years. Dilated cardiomyopathy, where the heart stretches weak, led at 62.7 percent, ahead of the thickened form at 30.3 percent.

Half the children had no symptoms and were found by chance. Suspected inflammation drove most of the stretched cases, while inherited causes led the thickened ones. Five year mortality reached 13.1 percent, concentrated in the stretched group. Two signs at diagnosis predicted death on their own: badly reduced pumping power and high pressure in the lung arteries. Subtype, age, and sex did not. The authors stress early pumping and lung pressure checks.
pmc-13455267:
Yin and co-authors profiled the immune checkpoint TIM-3 in tumors from 117 patients with intrahepatic cholangiocarcinoma, an aggressive bile duct cancer usually found too late for surgery. They stained tumor tissue for TIM-3 and companion checkpoints, counted infiltrating immune cells, and linked the patterns to clinical outcomes for these patients.

High TIM-3 expression in tumor cells appeared in 61 patients, 52.1 percent of the cohort, and correlated significantly with poorer tumor differentiation in the pathology analysis. Those patients relapsed and died sooner, and high TIM-3 independently predicted shorter disease-free survival with a hazard ratio of 1.589 after multivariable adjustment. TIM-3 levels also tracked with the density of CD4 and CD8 tumor-infiltrating lymphocytes in the tissue samples examined. The authors propose TIM-3 staining as a prognostic and inflammation biomarker and TIM-3 blockade as a therapeutic strategy worth testing in this cancer.
pmc-13455367:
Tambaro and colleagues pooled real-world results for 132 patients with advanced urothelial cancer treated with second-line pembrolizumab immunotherapy. The patients came from six centers of the Campania oncology network in Italy, treated between January 2021 and November 2023. Trial populations are fitter than everyday patients, so the network tested whether trial benefits survive routine practice.

The median age was 67 years and 73.5 percent were men, with most patients still reasonably fit at performance status zero or one. Median progression-free survival came to 3.75 months on the standard 200 milligram, three-weekly dosing schedule used. Median overall survival was 7.3 months across the full cohort, and the objective response rate was 13.5 percent, with disease control in 33.9 percent of patients treated. The authors present the figures as a realistic benchmark for counseling patients outside trials.
pmc-13456467:
Faith often goes unspoken in therapy, and a 2026 study by Rumena Islam asks Muslim clients in the UK what that silence costs and how to fix it. The study explored how clients feel when religion is played down or shut out of their sessions.

Interviews were held with twenty-five Muslim adults who had therapy in both public and private settings. Two broad themes came out. As barriers, clients named therapists' low confidence and knowledge about faith, service rules that keep therapy secular, and their own habit of holding back. As fixes, they asked for faith-aware skills, open talk about religion from the start, and service-level change so faith counts as a real part of care.
pmc-13457067:
Hee-Jung Hong and Ju-Dong Jang analyze, in a 2026 national study, how daily habits line up with how older Koreans rate their own mouth health. The data came from a community health survey of 210,212 adults aged sixty and over, gathered across 2022 and 2023. Self-rated mouth health is a practical stand-in for pain, chewing trouble, and unmet care in this age group.

Schooling showed the steepest gradient: college graduates had more than double the odds of rating their oral health well. Brushing after dinner or before bed lifted the odds by about half. Low stress and regular walking also helped. Smoking, low income, and above all unmet dental needs dragged ratings down; unmet need cut the odds to under a quarter. The authors argue that mouth health in old age mirrors social position as much as toothpaste.
pmc-13458267:
Liang and Song review in twenty twenty-six a class of targeted drugs for breast cancers that lack one key growth receptor. The drugs pair an antibody that homes to a surface marker found on many tumours with a toxic payload. That design delivers the poison mainly to cancer cells, sparing healthy tissue better than standard chemo.

Three such drugs are in active trials for advanced breast cancer, including the hardest triple-negative form. One has shown strong results against standard chemo, with tolerable side effects. The review covers pairing these drugs with immune therapy and other targeted drugs. It also covers use when cancer has spread to the brain. Hurdles remain, the authors note, despite clear progress.
pmc-13458567:
Wanli Zhu and colleagues let algorithms pick a biomarker for prostate cancer, and the machines chose HOXC4, a developmental gene better known for body patterning. Their 2026 study merges 258 samples from four datasets, finds 123 genes differing between tumor and normal, and runs three selection methods whose overlap leaves five candidates. Ten diagnostic models compete, interpreted with SHAP values showing each gene's push.

A partial least squares model won with an accuracy area of 0.977. HOXC4 stood out as a risk-raising feature; patients with high levels relapsed sooner, confirmed in an independent Memorial Sloan Kettering cohort. Tumors high in HOXC4 leaned on energy metabolism and protein-processing pathways, hosted a suppressive immune mix of regulatory T cells and M2 macrophages, and tied to checkpoints such as CD40 and SIGLEC-15. Expression varied across cancers in a pan-cancer scan. The authors offer HOXC4 as a diagnostic and prognostic candidate wired into immune escape.
pmc-13458667:
Harutake Sawazaki weighs what the EMBARK trial's final analysis should change for men whose prostate cancer returns as rising PSA after surgery or radiation, with no visible disease. Roughly half of men relapse this way within a decade, yet guidelines still split between watching, continuous hormone therapy, and intermittent therapy. Hormone therapy exacts a toll: hot flashes, weight gain, sexual dysfunction, and low mood.

The commentary walks through enzalutamide, the second-generation androgen receptor blocker EMBARK tested, alone and with leuprolide, against leuprolide alone. The drug binds its target ten times more tightly than older bicalutamide and carries no partial agonist activity, properties underpinning its approvals across prostate cancer. Sawazaki frames high-risk recurrence, marked by PSA doubling and high Gleason grade, as the subgroup where intensified therapy earns its keep. He argues the standard of care is being rewritten around risk-stratified treatment, not reflex hormone suppression.
pmc-13458767:
Timo-Daniel Voss and colleagues dissect NLRP10, the odd member of the inflammasome family that lacks the usual sensing tail. Working in human epithelial cells and skin keratinocytes, their 2026 study shows NLRP10 clumping into oligomers after treatment with two activating compounds. It asks which parts of the protein make that possible and where in the cell it waits.

Neither its energy-burning ATPase activity nor its pyrin domain proved necessary. The short basic tail at the protein's end was required and sufficient, a finding confirmed by swapping tails between human and mouse versions, which preserved clumping while changing protein stability. Conserved lysine residues in that tail steer most protein onto lipid droplets, the cell's fat-storage organelles, and losing them scrambles localization and oligomer formation. NLRP10 also handles the scaffold protein ASC differently from its cousin NLRP3. The authors propose lipids help switch this skin-expressed sensor on.
pmc-13458967: Giuseppe d'Orsi and co-authors issued this 2026 correction concerning their article on tailored use of cenobamate for epilepsy that resists standard drugs. The notice is a correction only: it supplies an acknowledgements section that the published article had left out. The added text credits two researchers at Children's Mercy Research Institute in Kansas City for sequencing the CYP2A6 gene and testing it for copy number variation. Readers are told the original article has been updated with that section.
pmc-13459167:
Rafael Gutiérrez-López and co-authors asked whether mosquito species living in Spain could spread Oropouche virus, an emerging pathogen from South America and the Caribbean. Imported human cases have reached Europe, but biting midges, not mosquitoes, are the known carriers. In their 2026 study, the team fed three mosquito types on virus laden blood, including the tiger mosquito and the common house mosquito. They then checked over three weeks whether the virus infected them, spread through their bodies, and reached their saliva.

Results were reassuring for Spain. The tiger mosquito showed low infection rates with only rare spread. The other two species became infected and sometimes carried virus beyond the gut, but never transmitted it in these experiments. A second plain blood meal changed nothing, mosquito survival was unaffected, and no virus passed to offspring. The risk of the virus establishing in Spain through these mosquitoes looks low.
pmc-13459267:
Wan Tang and colleagues survey availability, price and affordability of negotiated diabetes drugs in China in a 2026 study. Diabetes affects nearly one in nine adults worldwide, and China's negotiated drug list aims to cut costs, yet access gaps persist. Monthly usage data from 2018 to 2023 covered 804 public general hospitals in 31 regions, 537 tertiary and 267 secondary, for 12 negotiated antidiabetic medicines. WHO and Health Action International methods were used.

Drugs with availability above 50 percent rose from 1 to 5, and tertiary hospitals stocked more than secondary ones. Daily dose costs fell by about 23 to about 90 percent, and affordability improved by about 43 to about 98 percent. By 2023, 7 of 12 drugs were affordable, though rural residents fared worse than urban residents. Most drugs still sat below 50 percent availability, so negotiation alone has not yet secured equal access.
pmc-13459767:
Jiajia Mai and co-authors ran an early phase trial of HTD1801, a compound pairing the plant alkaloid berberine with a bile acid. It was tested in patients who have both type 2 diabetes and fatty liver disease. The drug is designed as a gut and liver modulator. In their 2026 phase Ib study, forty eight patients took the drug or placebo twice daily for twenty eight days across doses of 500, 750, and 1,000 milligrams. Twelve patients were already on stable metformin. The team tracked safety, drug levels, blood sugar, lipids, and liver enzymes.

The drug was generally well tolerated, with mostly mild to moderate side effects and no serious events reported. Metabolic gains grew with dose. In the metformin group, the top dose beat placebo clearly: fasting glucose fell by 1.271 units against a rise on placebo. Post meal glucose fell by 4.167 units in the reported comparisons. Cholesterol measures and liver enzymes also improved.
pmc-13459967:
Juan Zhang and co-authors tested in 2026 whether calycosin, an active compound from the herb Radix astragali, can protect the heart after a heart attack. Heart attacks are the commonest route into heart failure, and the compound had shown promise in earlier work. The team used heart cells starved of oxygen and glucose, plus rats whose coronary artery was tied off, measuring oxidative damage, iron levels, and cell-death markers.

Calycosin lowered harmful oxygen radicals and iron accumulation, restored cell energy, and revived protective proteins. Those benefits flowed through a defense pathway switched on by the protein NRF2, since silencing NRF2 undid much of the effect. In rats, treatment eased scarring, improved pumping, and limited mitochondrial damage, suggesting a candidate therapy worth further study.
pmc-13461367:
Sina Fathieh and a large team showed in 2026 that faint traces of a heart injury protein in the blood can reveal silent coronary artery disease on CT scans. Their study covered 1,613 adults who underwent coronary imaging, comparing high-sensitivity troponin I levels against calcium scores and plaque measurements. A level above a low threshold enriched strongly for actionable disease, defined by a calcium score of at least one hundred, especially among people lacking the usual risk factors.

Dividing troponin by heart muscle mass, with age and kidney function factored in, sharpened prediction further and explained why baseline levels vary. A two-stage pathway, blood test first and scans only for those flagged, raised diagnostic yield while cutting the number of scans needed. Prospective trials are the authors' stated next requirement.
pmc-13461567:
Katerina Kyriakouli and co-authors report a 2026 interview study with partners of people who received a kidney transplant. Care centers on the patient, yet partners carry much of the daily support work at home. The authors wanted to hear how partners live through illness, surgery, and the months after. Their study sits in one social and cultural setting.

Twelve partners took part in interviews, and the team grouped what they said into five themes. Partners often felt pushed into the background, even while taking on hard emotional roles. They spoke of moving from illness toward a new normal, of wanting clearer talk and more support from health staff, and of rethinking their life as a couple. Transplant also struck many as a lesson that changed how they saw life. The authors argue that care should treat the couple as a unit and give partners a voice of their own.
pmc-13462067:
Rodothea Amerikanou leads a 2026 UK study of trametinib, a drug, for adults with histiocytic neoplasms, rare disorders where immune cells called histiocytes grow in a tumor-like way. Many such diseases are driven by faults in a cell growth pathway. Patients whose disease resists standard chemotherapy often need pathway-blocking drugs. Trametinib blocks a pathway step called MEK. Cases came through a national expert panel.

Thirty-seven adults who started the drug before May 2024 were included, some alone and some paired with a second drug. At a median follow-up of about twenty-one months, roughly four in five patients showed a clinical response: their disease signs improved. Scans showed a response in two in three patients. The diseases covered included Erdheim-Chester disease, Langerhans cell histiocytosis, histiocytic sarcoma, and Rosai-Dorfman disease. The authors offer the results as wider evidence for trametinib across this disease family.
pmc-13462367:
Zhuona Zhang and colleagues adapt, in a 2026 study, an empathy fatigue scale for Chinese intensive care nurses. Intensive care nurses face patient suffering, death, and hard moral choices daily, which raises their risk of empathy fatigue: exhaustion from caring deeply too long. China lacked a tool for that specialty setting. The team translated the professionals' scale with two translation frameworks and checked it in 300 nurses at a hospital in Inner Mongolia.

All 21 items were kept, yet the version split into factors, emotional load and exhaustion state, covering most of the score variation. Scores were consistent, stable on retesting, and steady across split halves. A check against a compassion fatigue scale gave a moderate positive link, supporting the tool's target. Factor testing favored the two-part structure over the original form. The authors offer the scale as a screen to guide health support for intensive care nurses.
pmc-13462767:
Jingjing Yin and colleagues review, in a 2026 article, two keyhole approaches to breast cancer surgery: endoscopic surgery through small cuts and robot-assisted surgery with the Da Vinci system. Both aim to match open surgery's safety while leaving patients with better cosmetic results. The team searched four databases through spring 2026 for studies comparing the new approaches with standard ones.

Endoscopic surgery, first developed in East Asian centers, gave better cosmetic results in early-stage disease with acceptable short-term outcomes. Robotic nipple-sparing removal adds a 3D view, wristed tools, and tremor filtering. Pooled data show fewer deaths of skin flap and nipple tissue than open surgery, with similar short-term results, though operations run longer and cost more. pmc-13463367:

pmc-13463967:

pmc-13464767:

pmc-13465067:

pmc-13465167:

pmc-13465467:

pmc-13465767:

pmc-13466367:

pmc-13466667:

pmc-13467167:

pmc-13467467:

pmc-13467767:

pmc-13467967:

pmc-13468067:

pmc-13468467:

pmc-13469967:

pmc-13470267:

pmc-13470567:

pmc-13472167:

pmc-13472867:

pmc-13473267:

pmc-13473467:

pmc-13473567:

pmc-13473967:

pmc-13474567:

pmc-13474867:

pmc-13476567:

pmc-13478467:

pmc-13479867:

Engineered reporter strands turn that shredding into a measurable signal.
