The approach proved itself during COVID-19 as a fast, low-equipment alternative to laboratory PCR. The review then turns to cancer, where detecting faint mutation signals in blood could enable earlier diagnosis, and weighs sensitivity limits that still separate promise from practice.
pmc-13480267:
Zhongjie Shi and co-authors describe a 2026 test of a mixed reality headset that guides brain stimulation to the right spot. Magnetic stimulation works only when the coil lands on the correct scalp target, and cap-based guessing can miss by a wide margin. Their system runs on a HoloLens 2 headset with three hand tools, and three researchers aimed at ten points on each of five model heads, standing and lying.

Errors sat near two to two and a half millimetres in both postures, far tighter than manual guessing. Scores differed between researchers but stayed steady within each person across repeats. The team frames the rig as a portable, low-cost guide for stimulation clinics. Tests on real patients, with moving heads and varied hair and skull shapes, remain the next hurdle.
pmc-13481567:
Jr-Wei Wu and co-authors report a 2026 study of narrowed brain arteries in people with lasting headache or brain fog after COVID. The team gathered 108 patients whose symptoms ran past three months, plus controls free of nerve symptoms after recovery. A scoring system graded artery narrowing in front and rear brain circuits, adjusted for both sides.

Narrowing scores rose step by step with the load of symptom types, peaking in patients who carried both headache and fog. Pure fog cases leaned toward front-circuit narrowing, while fog severity itself tracked rear-circuit scores. Headache severity showed no tidy vessel link. The pattern hints that poor front-brain flow may feed fog, while headache draws on wider causes. Vessel checks may deserve a place in long-COVID brain work-ups.
pmc-13481967:
Luis Mario Castellanos-Alvarenga and co-authors describe a 2026 check of a money wellness scale among young adults in Chile. The scale gauges whether people can meet bills, feel secure about the future, and enjoy choices that money allows. The adapted form went to 624 university and technical students aged eighteen to twenty-nine, most of them women.

Scores split cleanly into two parts, money distress and money well-being, with sound consistency. The scale read the same way for men and women in full. Across ethnic and job groups it held with minor item tweaks, which the team freed one by one. In a country where many households lean on store credit, a trusted early-warning tool can steer campus support toward students sliding into money distress.
pmc-13482867:
Jingwen Liang and co-authors describe a 2026 study of how helper cells around pancreatic tumours push cancer cells toward a nerve-like identity that resists drugs. Tumour samples with strong nerve-like markers fared worse, and single-cell maps fingered a factor made by the helper fibroblasts, called PTGDS. Lab tests then fed that factor to cancer cells.

Treated cells grew, moved, and invaded faster and shook off the standard drug gemcitabine more easily. The factor works through a surface receiver that fires a growth pathway inside the cell. Blocking that pathway or removing the receiver undid the nasty shift. The chain gives drug hunters a stromal target, since starving the tumour of helper signals may restore drug sensitivity.
pmc-13483467:
Spancerski and colleagues ran a large contest among vision models to name tree species from photos of cut wood, a skill that helps police illegal logging. Their 2026 benchmark tested 15 versions of the YOLO detector family across three generations and five sizes. The dataset held nearly 78,000 image patches covering 73 forest species, drawn from three different photo collections.

Four models tied at the top, each classifying about 99.9 percent of test patches correctly in the benchmark results. Every model placed the right species in its top three guesses for all test patches. A medium model from the newest generation offered the best speed trade-off, processing over 200 frames per second. Voting across patches from one wood sample pushed that model to perfect image-level accuracy. Spancerski also verified the models looked at real wood anatomy, like pore patterns.
pmc-13483567:
Yu Chen and co-authors report a striking eye injury case in a 2026 paper. A sixty-two-year-old man with diabetes used a percussion massage gun on his closed eyelids to ease dryness, pressing it there for days. Weeks later his vision faded and headaches grew, and tests found very high pressure in both eyes.

Scans showed the lens of each eye had slipped forward, its supports torn all around, blocking fluid flow and causing glaucoma. No inborn or other cause fit the picture. Surgeons removed both lenses and fixed new ones in place. A year later his corrected vision was strong in both eyes. The authors note that no safety rules govern such devices near the eyes, and past reports involved milder harm.
pmc-13483667:
Iwelunmor and colleagues laid out the plan for a trial testing whether a youth-led HIV prevention program in Nigeria can keep running after its first funding ends. The 2026 protocol describes the 4 Youth by Youth program, where young people design and spread HIV services, now moving into a sustainment phase. The trial spans 40 community sites run with 18 community organizations, assigned by cluster to different support strategies.

The study is a hybrid design, judging both whether services survive and whether the surviving program still prevents infections cost-effectively. Earlier work showed the youth approach raised uptake of HIV prevention services among Nigerian teenagers and young adults. Outcomes will include how faithfully sites keep delivering the package over time. Iwelunmor expects the results to teach funders how community-grown programs can outlast their launch grants.
pmc-13485267:
Beatrice Dal Passo and a large team review what atrial strain can tell doctors about heart muscle disease in this 2026 paper. Atrial strain measures how much the heart's upper chambers stretch as they fill and empty. It can be read from ultrasound images or from heart scans, and it is now used across many kinds of cardiomyopathy.

The review finds the strongest proof in diseases where the heart wall grows thick. There, strain values help tell one disease from another, with amyloid disease showing the lowest values. Low strain also warns of rhythm problems and of major heart events ahead. In wide, weak hearts, strain helps predict recovery and tell causes apart. In right-heart disease, strain in the right upper chamber flags risk even before the chamber grows. The paper maps where this measure is ready for clinic use.
pmc-13485667:
Rhodora Therese Gumabao Torres checks whether camera-based motion tracking without body markers can replace the marker gold standard in knee arthritis. Published in 2026, the comparison records 22 participants with mild to moderate disability walking at chosen and fast speeds plus standing up from a chair. Both systems run simultaneously alongside force plates.

Differences between systems stayed small, with angle errors under six degrees and joint center offsets under five centimeters. Agreement was excellent for knee loading impulse at both walking speeds and for the second loading peak at fast walking. Several angle and moment peaks scored good rather than excellent agreement. Markerless tracking promises cheaper, clinic-friendly gait assessment, and these results show which knee measures can already be trusted from video alone.
pmc-13488267:
Winchana Srivilaithon and colleagues present a 2026 protocol for a trial of carbon dioxide targets during resuscitation in Thailand. End-tidal carbon dioxide, measured in exhaled breath during chest compressions, mirrors blood flow and predicts whether the heart restarts. Whether pushing compressions to hit a higher target improves outcomes is untested. The single-center trial at Thammasat University Hospital will enroll three hundred emergency department cardiac arrest patients.

They will be assigned at random to one of three targets, a standard level, a higher fixed level, or a level tied to a blood gas measure. All care otherwise follows international resuscitation guidance. The main outcome is sustained return of circulation. Results are not yet available, since recruitment defines the planned work.
pmc-13488567:
Nurten Arslan, Aysel Topan, and Meltem Kurtuncu study problem solving and kind, helpful behavior in Turkish adolescents in a 2026 cross-sectional survey. One thousand students aged ten to fourteen from secondary schools in one province capital took part through face-to-face interviews. Validated scales measured problem-solving skill, with subscales for confidence, self-control, and avoidance, alongside a prosociality scale covering sharing, helping, and empathy-driven action.

Stronger overall problem-solving scores went with higher prosocial scores in the reported correlations. Confidence showed the tightest positive link of the subscales. Higher self-control and avoidance scores instead went with lower prosocial scores, a pattern the authors call negative influence. They propose school programs that build problem-solving confidence to support social and emotional growth.
pmc-13488667:
Jiang-Ying Li and co-authors interview heart failure patients about what shapes how well they understand their medicines. Their 2026 study covers young and middle aged patients who had a stent procedure. Twenty one patients, aged eighteen to sixty five, were chosen on purpose from one hospital. Interviews ran from October to December 2024. Answers were coded and grouped into themes by a directed method.

Four themes captured the barriers. First, basic drug knowledge was thin, fed by overly simple teaching. Second, contact channels with clinicians and family were weak. Third, patients lacked skill at judging health claims, leaning on unchecked online sources. Fourth, daily management was hard amid work, travel, and mood strain from treatment. The authors call for richer, interactive teaching. They also urge stronger support systems and direct work on patients' mistaken beliefs.
pmc-13489567:
Ebrahimi and colleagues examined what influences screening among newly diagnosed colorectal cancer patients in Iran's Isfahan Province, in 2026 public health research drawn from a larger cohort study. The parent study follows new breast and colorectal cancer cases across several centers. This analysis covered patients diagnosed between January 2020 and January 2022, gathering background, lifestyle, and psychological information through questionnaires about each participant.

The study included 78 patients with colon cancer and 69 with rectal cancer in its final sample. Most patients were aged 45 to 75, married, educated, urban residents, and covered by insurance, and most reported normal stress levels. Screening behavior, especially colonoscopy, rose with higher age, which reached statistical significance in the analysis reported. Higher anxiety scores and a past history of colorectal surgery were also linked to more screening. Ebrahimi argues that awareness efforts should target younger and less anxious patients.
pmc-13490467:
Demsie and a large team surveyed 420 adults with type 2 diabetes in northwest Ethiopia about herbal medicine use and compared their long-term blood sugar control. Herbal cures are common in the region, yet their effect on glycated hemoglobin, the three-month sugar average, is rarely measured. Their 2026 study combined structured talks with medical record reviews across clinic patients sampled systematically during the first half of 2025.

Herbal use proved highly common among the patients surveyed, forming part of routine self-care for many. Users showed clearly poorer sugar control than non-users in the adjusted analyses reported. Urban residence, shorter disease duration, and having no other chronic conditions instead predicted favorable control. Talks suggested many patients never disclose herbal use to their doctors. Demsie recommends doctors ask about herbs directly and study which cures help or harm, rather than ignoring a practice patients will continue anyway.
pmc-13490567:
Xu and team taught a reinforcement-learning agent to schedule three kinds of 5G resources at once for mobile broadband users: subcarriers, transmit power levels, and computing capacity. Schedulers must balance speed, energy, and fairness while channels change constantly, and deciding everything jointly explodes the choice space. Their 2026 design splits the decision into synchronized branches, one per resource, and replays the agent's most instructive past experiences first during training.

In massive MIMO simulations the scheduler reached aggregate throughput of about eleven gigabits per second across the system modeled. Energy efficiency hit about fifty-four bits per joule while learning stayed stable across runs. Branching turned an exponentially growing action space into a linearly scaling one, speeding convergence in the reported experiments. Xu presents the framework as a practical scheduler for dense broadband cells.
pmc-13491067:
Julius W. Jaeger and Robert F. Schwabe comment on how support cells direct liver cell behavior in fatty liver disease in a 2026 article. Fatty liver conditions, driven by metabolism, alcohol, or both, affect a large share of the world, and treatments remain few. Liver cells do the metabolic work, yet two neighbor types, vessel-lining endothelial cells and star-shaped stellate cells, constantly instruct them through released factors, organizing the liver into zones along its blood flow.

The commentary centers on new work naming an endothelial receptor, HEG1, as a gatekeeper of fat balance and zonation, tested in gene-deleted mice across three disease diets. A famous growth signal pathway sits at the network's core, fed by both neighbor types. The authors frame support cells as conductors worth targeting.
pmc-13491167:
Amit Kandhari and co-authors chart a shift in how newborn sepsis is treated in a 2026 review. Early sepsis in newborns is rare but can kill fast. Its signs mimic normal first day change, so many healthy babies get drugs just in case.

That habit costs bonding time, needless tests, and germ drug strain. Drug proof bugs grow as new drugs lag behind. Gut germ balance in babies may also suffer long term from early drugs. Care now aims to treat the truly ill fast while sparing the well. The review traces how watch scores and stop rules made that balance real.
pmc-13491667:
Chunfan Xiang and others assemble and analyze the complete power unit genome of Aucklandia lappa, a valued medicinal herb in China. In 2026, the study joins Illumina short reads with Nanopore long reads to build a single circular genome of about 437,000 base pairs, containing fifty-four genes. The dried rhizome supplies volatile oils and sesquiterpenes used in traditional medicine.

Analysis reveals strong AT bias in frequent codons, 431 RNA editing sites, and twenty-six fragments transferred from chloroplast DNA. Phylogenetic comparison with twenty-seven other taxa clarifies the plant's place within the Asteraceae family. The genome provides a high-quality resource for studying evolution and working genomics of medicinal Asteraceae species.
pmc-13492167:
Julianna R Cresti and Lyle A Simmons review in 2026 the most common copying error in DNA: the wrong sugar. When cells duplicate their genomes, the copying enzymes grab RNA building blocks roughly once every few thousand letters, because those blocks vastly outnumber the DNA versions. Each stray ribonucleotide twists the DNA and, if left in place, invites mutations and instability.

An enzyme family called RNase H spots these errors and starts a repair pathway that cuts the mistake out and patches the strand with proper DNA letters. Repair failures bring mutation buildups, neurological disease, and death before birth in severe cases. The review compares how bacteria, archaea, and complex cells each run this cleanup, highlighting Bacillus subtilis as a window into the bacterial version.
pmc-13492367:
Sevón and colleagues in Finland tested in 2026 thin fat based films that could slow water loss from open reservoirs. Drought is set to worsen with climate change, and stored water leaks away as vapor each day. A film just one molecule thick can curb that loss if it spreads well and holds tight. The team checked four types of fat like compounds, from fatty alcohols to wax esters, alone and in blends.

They used a Langmuir trough, a shallow bath that lets a film be spread and squeezed while gauges track its strength. Some blends beat the best films now in use at blocking vapor. The mix could be tuned: a dash of one fat type fixed spread, while another firmed the layer. The authors say the lab results give a firm base for field grade covers that waste less water.
pmc-13493767:
Geeta S Boora and five colleagues build in 2026 a blood test workflow that sorts the tumor cells shed by oral cancers into their disguises. Circulating tumor cells drive spread, and they travel as plain epithelial cells, shape-shifted mesenchymal cells, or clusters armored with platelets. Sorting blood from thirty-three mouth cancer patients by surface markers, after stripping away ordinary blood cells, resolved all three states.

Spike-in tests proved the method could find a single cancer cell in a milliliter of blood. Seven in ten patients carried detectable circulating cells, sometimes hundreds per milliliter. Platelet-cloaked clusters dominated the catch at roughly five sixths, a population that epithelial-only tests would largely miss. Pure mesenchymal cells were rare. The authors set a positivity threshold and argue that future liquid biopsies must count the cloaked majority.
pmc-13493867:
Michal Brzus and others present an automated imaging platform that predicts individual mental results after blood-starved stroke. In 2026, the system processes raw MRI data from varied scanners, segments lesions with deep learning, and builds location- and network-based traits to forecast results. Models trained on 604 lesion cases were tested on an independent cohort of 153 patients.

Multiple mental predictions reached reasonable rightness with ninety-six percent agreement with manual methods, and a language-model report delivers patient-specific prognoses in about three minutes. Doctors gain imaging-informed guidance for healing planning and for counseling patients and families about likely recovery, where human prognostication is often variable and imprecise.
pmc-13494167:
Weilong Gu and Rachel F. Tyndale study age and sex effects on a liver enzyme, CYP2A6, in African green monkeys. In 2026, the study tests fifty-six monkeys of both sexes across five developmental stages, testing formation of 7-hydroxycoumarin from coumarin and cotinine from tobacco drug. CYP2A6 is the main human enzyme for both compounds, but human developmental patterns are inconsistent.

Per milligram of microsomal protein, per gram of liver, and per whole liver adjusted for body weight, younger monkeys showed higher action, with no sex effect. Once extrapolated to the whole liver without body-weight adjustment, older and male monkeys showed higher total velocity, mainly because their livers are larger. The distinction matters for translating monkey data to human tobacco drug and drug fuel use.
pmc-13495167:
Chuntao Wu and co-authors examine, in a 2026 analysis, how often two ways of judging migraine treatment success disagree in the same patient. Antibody drugs that block the CGRP pathway are standard migraine preventives. Success is often counted as a set cut in monthly migraine days, yet patients also judge gain by disability and by how hard attacks hit daily life.

The team reworked public patient-level data from 417 people on their first such drug. Just under a third met all three success marks, while about half were split: classed as responders by one measure and not by another. Feeling-based gains without a frequency gain were far more common than the reverse. Gains on the scales moved together only moderately. The authors do not crown a winner; they argue that judging response by diary counts alone misses real relief some patients report.
pmc-13495667:
Avni S Patel and colleagues measure, in a 2026 geochemistry study, how amorphous carbonate minerals change inside water films only nanometers thick. Shells and other natural carbonates often start as shapeless precursors that later crystallize, and damp air alone can drive the shift. The team tracked how much water vapor these calcium and magnesium carbonates soak up across humidity levels, then watched them age for months in humid air.

Water uptake soared once humidity passed roughly four fifths saturation, and the films settled just a few nanometers thick. Over seven months at near-full humidity the minerals kept recrystallizing, growing varied crystal shapes that hint at pockets of different chemistry. Mixed minerals also split into separate calcium and magnesium crystals, proof that ions travel through the films. The authors discuss ripening and diffusion as the engines of the change.
pmc-13499067:
Efrain M Castillo and colleagues ask in 2026 whether receiving a donor heart that already has coronary artery disease harms transplant outcomes, and whether donor age or treatment era changes the answer. Donor hearts are scarce, so centres increasingly accept organs with existing artery disease. Using a national transplant registry, they followed adults who received heart transplants between 2000 and 2025 and compared survival by donor artery status.

Of 21,805 recipients, about one in eleven received a heart with artery disease, and overall that group showed no clear survival disadvantage. Risk did rise with older donors, however, reaching a clear increase by donor age 60 in their model. Era mattered too, since the same donor feature linked to higher death rates only after 2018, when recipients tended to be sicker. The authors urge a fresh review of donor selection rules.
pmc-13499167:
Bernard Schockaert and co-authors classified the causes of heart muscle injury found after surgery in high-risk patients, and linked each cause to outcomes. Such injury, detected by a blood marker called troponin, is common after non-heart surgery and often silent. It can arise from several mechanisms, from oxygen starvation to direct strain, and the mix in high-risk patients was unclear.

The team reviewed one hospital's records from 2017 to 2022, taking injury as a troponin level above a set threshold within three days of surgery. Testing had targeted selected high-risk patients. Applying an existing ranked framework, they sorted cases by likely cause. Knowing the cause mix guides prevention and follow-up.
pmc-13499667:
Riya Mukherjee, Ramendra Pati Pandey, and Chung Ming Chang synthesise in 2026 animal evidence on tiny parcels released by stem cells as a cell-free treatment for osteoarthritis, the wear-related joint disease. These extracellular vesicles carry molecular cargo that may protect cartilage without transplanting living cells. Their meta-analysis pooled preclinical studies in living osteoarthritis models and graded reporting quality against current field standards and a bias tool for animal work.

Cartilage damage scores improved after vesicle treatment in studies using human-derived vesicles. The benefit looked larger still in the smaller set using animal-derived vesicles, with statistical checks suggesting missing studies were unlikely to explain the gains. Results varied widely between studies, however, and dose reported by particle count or protein weight failed to predict benefit, exposing weak standardisation. The authors argue that standard dosing, tracking in the body, and cargo checks must come before regulatory approval.
pmc-13499867:
Julyana Ribeiro and others analyze Y-chromosome variety across Colombian groups to reconstruct father history. In 2026, the study types twenty-three Y-STR markers in 975 men from five regions, Andes, Pacific, Caribbean, Orinoquía, and Amazon, with a subset of 175 men sequenced for 859 Y-SNPs. Colonial-era gene flow among Native, EU, and African groups created complex admixture.

Haplotypic variety was very high, and expanding from seventeen to twenty-three markers sharpened regional change. Caribbean and Orinoquía groups clustered nearer EU and admixed groups, Pacific nearer African groups, and Amazon with Peru and Ecuador. EU father ancestry predominated in Caribbean and Andean regions, backing region-specific forensic databases.
pmc-13499967:
Durga A Jagdale and Sandeep Shinde review in 2026 newer rehabilitation technologies and training methods for sports-related knee injuries, which sideline athletes with pain, weakness, and slow return to play. Their search kept randomised trials published between 2021 and 2026, and twelve studies qualified. The set covered ligament reconstruction, kneecap tendon pain, and other athletic knee problems, with study quality checked against a standard bias tool.

Interventions ranged from nerve-muscle training with external focus cues and heavy slow tendon loading to Nordic hamstring work, balance and jumping drills, and accelerated schedules. Criteria-based progression also featured, where athletes advance by meeting test targets rather than by calendar. Most approaches improved function, strength, balance, pain, and readiness to return compared with usual care alone. Tendon-focused eccentric loading shone for kneecap tendon pain, while criteria-based programmes stood out after ligament surgery.
pmc-13500467:
Zheng Chen and colleagues run in 2026 a prospective nested case-control study of deep vein thrombosis, dangerous leg vein clots, after hip fracture surgery during the hospital stay. Patients admitted with hip fractures between January 2023 and December 2024 were followed. Those who developed clots were matched two-to-one with clot-free patients of the same department, fracture type, and similar surgery timing. The matched set held 72 cases and 144 controls, compared across background, clinical, and laboratory measures.

Three factors stood as independent predictors in adjusted analysis, namely older age, longer delay from injury to surgery, and higher D-dimer, a blood marker of clot breakdown. Each carried a calculated risk threshold. A curious ward observation, sweating heavily enough after fever medicine to soak a gown, linked to clots in simple comparisons yet faded after adjustment, which the authors flag for further study. The thresholds aim to flag high-risk patients early.
pmc-13501467:
A single material that can both kill resistant bacteria and speed chemical production would serve clinics and factories alike. Narjes Sadat Mireei and co-authors build such a hybrid in a 2026 study, doping a zinc oxide and framework composite with niobium.

The doping shrank the crystal grains and set the pore size to a fine scale, opening more active surface. The composite attacked both major classes of bacteria, with strong zones of clearing and a steep drop in living cells within a day. The team credits stress from reactive oxygen inside the bacteria. The same material also worked as a catalyst for building a class of ring-shaped drug-like compounds. Early yield reports round out the dual-use claim.
pmc-13502167:
Monika B Dolinska leads a large multi-author team reporting a 2026 drug screen that found an activator of tyrosinase, the enzyme that starts melanin production. Pigment loss disorders, from albinism to acquired pigment loss, carry skin cancer risk, poor vision, and heavy social stigma, yet medicine has tyrosinase blockers in clinics and almost no activators. The team built high-throughput assays around a human tyrosinase construct, confirmed hits in cells using carbon-13 labelled tyrosine tracing, and modelled the chemistry by computer.

The winner was ampyrone, also called 4-aminoantipyrine. It raised the catalytic activity of normal tyrosinase and of a weakened variant, Pro406Leu, that causes a form of albinism. Melanin rose in healthy and albinism-model pigment cells, in mouse pigment cells of another albinism type, and in 3D human skin cultures. The authors nominate ampyrone as a lead compound for therapies that switch pigment production back on.
pmc-13502667:
Miguel A. Medel leads a seven-author team reporting a 2026 synthesis of graphene nanoribbons with a fresh edge shape and record length for their class. Nanoribbons are graphene strips whose electronics hinge on width, length, and edge topology, yet undoped versions had no iterative synthesis, so lengths stayed short and many edges unrealized. The team's route repeats a two-step cycle, borylation then a merged Suzuki coupling and cyclodehydrogenation, adding one pyrene-coronene unit per pass.

Iteration delivered a family of ribbons with a new edge topology at unprecedented length for undoped molecular ribbons. The products absorb light and fluoresce efficiently, with absorptivity and brightness on the order of one hundred thousand on the reported molar scale. Charge carriers move through them at a mobility measured at 475, give or take 32, square centimetres per volt-second. Precision at this length lets physicists test predictions about how ribbon properties scale.
pmc-13502867:
Li and colleagues reported a fifteen-year-old girl whose lupus flare was complicated by a virus-triggered disorder, in a 2026 case report. She arrived with ten days of abdominal pain and four days of fever, a facial rash, and swollen neck glands, after years of sun-worsened facial redness. Testing pointed to systemic lupus erythematosus with macrophage activation syndrome, a state in which immune cells attack tissues.

Li's workup found Epstein-Barr virus triggering Evans syndrome. In Evans syndrome the immune system destroys red blood cells and platelets. The combination is rare and is often mistaken for an immune storm called hemophagocytic lymphohistiocytosis. Treatment combined antibiotics, an antiviral, steroids, an immune suppressant, acid protection, and immunoglobulin, and after twenty days she had improved and was discharged for follow-up. The authors stress that history, testing, and diagnosis separate this entity from its look-alikes.
pmc-13503267:
Stefan Fritze and others test a Ta carbide tiny-ceramic coating for mishap-tough nuclear fuel cladding. In 2026, the study lays a dense tiny-crystal coating onto ZIRLO cladding by magnet spray, then checks fine build, beam-hit toughness, and rust. Zr cladding can rust wildly during loss-of-coolant mishaps, making blast gas.

Heavy-ion beam hits to about eight shifts per atom gave no glass change, phase breakdown, or splitting, with only limited grain growth and tiny xenon bubbles. Current tests in borated water showed rapid shielding, very low rust currents, and high block over long contact. The coating emerges as a robust, scalable pick for safer fuel rods.
pmc-13503867:
Yuta Nakaniida leads a team comparing how the cornea bends in two forms of glaucoma, in a 2026 study. A device called Corvis ST puffs air at the eye and films how the clear front window dents and rebounds. Earlier work found gaps between the two glaucoma types, but the groups also differed in eye length and sex.

The team matched 48 eyes of each type on key traits, then compared twelve measures from the device. Three measures looked higher in the closed-angle group before full statistical checks. After those checks, none of the gaps held up as firm. The authors call the early trends exploratory and say matched designs are key for such work.
pmc-13503967:
The tree Vernicia montana has separate male and female plants, with sex set by a ZW chromosome system. Xiang Dong and co-authors built a complete genome for a female tree, separating its two chromosome copies. They scanned the genomes of one hundred seventy-eight wild trees to find the stretch of DNA that tracks with sex. The signal narrowed to a small region on one chromosome, about sixty-one thousand letters long, found only in females.

That region is a tangle of inserted, duplicated, and flipped segments, with complex repeats inside. Lab tests confirmed several female-only pieces inside. Two conserved genes sit at its borders, and one shifts activity during flower development. Moving that gene into a test plant disturbed its flowers. The authors propose that sex comes not from a new master gene but from structural shuffling at the region's edge.
pmc-13504567:
Yufei Chen, Yan Zhang, and Wei Wang review a study of harmful byproducts in disinfected desalinated water, in a 2026 commentary. Desalination now supplies drinking water to more than 300 million people. Plant processes strip out most natural matter but leave traces of bromide and iodide, which cleaners can turn into toxic byproducts.

The study under review sampled three large plants in the United Arab Emirates and ran lab disinfection trials. Fine chemical screening found 55 byproducts, some never before reported in desalinated water. Bromine and iodine forms are known to harm cells and DNA more than chlorine forms. The authors stress that spotting which compounds drive the toxicity is key to safer treatment choices.
pmc-13505167:
Jostein Rødseth Brede and Andreas Jørstad Krüger answered critics of their cardiac arrest trial in a 2026 response. The REBOARREST trial tested a balloon catheter that blocks the aorta from inside during resuscitation for out-of-hospital cardiac arrest. A comment questioned balloon sizing and trial conduct. The authors reply point by point, starting with approvals: all ethics, institutional, and device permissions were in place before the trial began.

They concede one limit. Patients excluded for missing deferred consent may skew the sample, since consent failure tracks with early death; the rule came from ethics committees, not the team. On sizing, they set the cited thirty-millimeter aorta estimate against pooled data nearer twenty-four to twenty-six millimeters.
pmc-13507067:
Fadhila Fitriana and a large team check two malaria parasite proteins as shot candidates, in a study from 2026. The parasite still kills many people, and strain shifts can blunt shots, so stable targets are prized.

In samples from Tanzanian adults with no symptoms, both genes varied very little and showed signs of strong constraint. Nearly all carriers held antibodies to both proteins, and the two antibody levels rose together. One common swap stood out in one protein. The team says the stable form and strong immune reply merit more work on both proteins.
pmc-13507167:
Yueming Chen and co-authors trace a cause of drug resistance in kidney cancer, in this 2026 study. The cancer type they study often stops responding to a class of drugs that block growth signals. Once that happens, treatment options shrink fast. The team searched for what changes inside tumor cells when they learn to resist these drugs.

A protein called P4HA3 stood out, rising sharply in resistant cells. Raising it made cells grow faster and shrug off two common drugs, while cutting it restored drug response. The protein steadies a second protein that guards cells against a form of iron-driven cell death. By blocking that death route, P4HA3 helps tumors survive treatment. The work names a target for drugs that might break this resistance.
pmc-13507667:
Shainur Premji leads a ten-author team weighing whether a nurse-led violence support team in Welsh emergency departments is worth its cost, in 2026 work. Such teams meet victims and others hurt by assault and help them tackle risks that could lead to repeat harm. Violence injuries cost the British health service billions each year. The analysis compared the Welsh Violence Prevention Team with standard care for patients aged 11 and older hurt in assaults.

The team built a model that followed patients for ten years after a first assault visit, tracking later emergency visits. Routine Welsh health data supplied the rates and costs behind the model. Outcomes were counted in years of healthy life, and costs were judged from both health service and wider social views. Readers get a framework for deciding whether early support in the emergency room pays off over time.
pmc-13507867:
Valentina Barrera and seven co-authors test a natural compound for muscle healing after blood flow injury in a 2026 study. When blood rushes back into starved muscle, the return itself harms fibers, dulls self repair, and slows strength gains. Their compound, a lanthionine kin, is known to stir cell clean up, and the team asked if it shields the stem cells that rebuild muscle.

Rat stem cells dosed with the compound cleaned house faster and lived better, while a standard drug slowed their growth. Under a harsh oxidant that killed near two thirds of cells, the compound pulled survival back toward normal. In a leg injury model, dosed rats regained grip strength faster in the first week. Gene reads echoed the clean up boost. The authors call it a proof of concept for early recovery.
pmc-13508267:
Yangjia Cao and six co-authors sort stem cells from umbilical cords to find the subgroup best at supporting blood cell growth, in 2026 work. These mesenchymal stem cells are prized for therapy, yet growth in the lab makes batches uneven, which complicates quality control. The team read gene activity cell by cell in more than 78,000 cells and found 14 subgroups. Cells at a middle stage of lab growth performed best overall. One subgroup, labeled C8, stood out for stem-like qualities, blood support, and calming immune effects.

Cells rich in both markers supported blood growth and curbed immune activity better than cells low in them. The markers give makers a handle for picking premium cells for treatment batches.
pmc-13508367:
Congai Chen leads a thirteen-author review of how helper T cells cross the blood-brain barrier after a stroke, and how that traffic might be controlled, in 2026 work. The barrier normally shields the brain, letting nutrients in while keeping toxins and most immune cells out. A stroke tears that shield, and helper T cells flood in. Depending on their subtype, these cells can protect tissue or deepen the injury, and they can loosen the barrier further.

The review walks through the entry steps in detail: capture, sticking, and squeezing through the vessel wall. Named adhesion molecules handle each stage, and the authors explain their roles. They also survey immune-suppressing drugs already used in clinics that limit immune cell entry into the brain. The aim is finer control, blocking harmful traffic while sparing helpful cells, as a companion to standard stroke care.
pmc-13508467:
Ozoemena Eje and five co-authors extract an enzyme from papaya fruit peel and test it as a cleaner for dye-polluted water, in 2026 work. Industrial dyes in wastewater threaten health, and enzymes offer a greener cleanup than harsh chemical methods. The team partly purified the enzyme, a peroxidase, from peel waste in two steps. Tests pinned down its size, its best acidity and heat, and how strongly it grabs two test chemicals.

The process concentrated the enzyme twenty-four-fold while keeping about a fifth of the starting activity. Copper and zinc salts switched it on, while several other metals slowed it. The enzyme held nearly all activity after half an hour at mild heat and kept about half after ninety minutes. It stripped color from several dyes, clearing one green dye by up to about nine tenths.
pmc-13509367:
Abugharsa and colleagues compared gene activity in 2026 in leg veins from people with chronic venous insufficiency, a fault where weak vein valves let blood pool in the legs. They focused on three genes in the Wnt pathway, a signaling route that helps control how blood vessel walls grow and repair. No earlier study had checked how these genes work together in diseased vein tissue.

What changed was the pairing: two of the genes rose and fell together far more tightly in diseased veins than in healthy ones. That shift hints that faulty teamwork among genes, not single-gene change, may help drive vein wall damage.
pmc-13509567:
Yang Ren and co-authors probe in 2026 how tuberculous meningitis injures the brain's ventricle lining, using a mouse model driven by the BCG vaccine strain. The lining cells, called ependymal cells, keep spinal fluid moving with tiny beating hairs, and their failure adds to this disease's heavy toll.

A gene named Hmgcs2 emerged as a core casualty: its loss shortened the cells' hairs and raised cell death. Sodium butyrate, a gut-derived compound, restored that gene, preserved the hairs, and cut cell death, pointing to a possible protective treatment.
pmc-13510267:
Hairui Li and co-authors review, in a 2026 paper, how diffusion MRI methods for studying chronic pain have changed over time. Chronic pain is common and varied, and its workings are still not fully understood. No proven body marker exists to sort patients, explain the pain, or judge treatment, which holds the field back.

Diffusion MRI tracks how water moves in tissue, without cutting or dyes. From that motion, it infers the fine structure and wiring of nerves and brain. The review follows the method from its tensor form to newer multi shell scans. Those add richer models of tiny fibers and their spread, plus links to other scan types. The authors searched two major databases for pain studies through late 2025. Their aim is a method map for researchers choosing tools.
pmc-13510667:
Ronja Marquardt, Simon Hundeshagen, Felix Tilsen, Frank Tavassol, and Waldemar Reich report a 2026 case of neuroblastoma spreading to the jaw in an infant, paired with a review of past cases. Neuroblastoma is a common solid cancer of early childhood, yet jaw spread is rare and can mimic tooth or gland infection. The case concerns an eight-month-old girl with swelling beside the left jaw first taken for gland inflammation.

Imaging showed a destructive jaw lesion, and tissue tests confirmed the cancer. Staging found a left adrenal primary tumor, wide bone marrow spread, and a high-risk gene change. She received a high-risk treatment program and reached remission on scans. She then developed severe lung problems and died shortly before a planned next step. Past cases shared jaw swelling, mouth masses, pain, and loose teeth. The authors urge imaging and biopsy for fast-growing jaw swelling in children.
pmc-13510767:

Musashi proteins bind RNA, the working copies of genes, and guide stem cell growth. They were long seen as switches that turn protein making off, yet at times they turn it on, and no one knew how.

Working with frog eggs, the team removed a helper called ELAVL4 and found that egg ripening stalled and key Musashi target RNAs stayed unused. Adding the helper back fixed the fault. The helpers grip Musashi directly, without RNA in between. The same pairing showed up in mouse and human cells, and removing the human helper in a cell line shut down Musashi-driven activation. The mechanism seems shared across species.
pmc-13511167:
Xue Yan and six co-authors review a helpful bacterium as a probiotic that raises disease resistance in farmed aquatic animals, in 2026 work. Intensive fish and shellfish farming faces frequent outbreaks and heavy antibiotic use. The bacterium reviewed forms hardy spores, fights a wide range of germs, and steadies host immunity, which makes it a candidate green alternative.

The review groups its actions into four routes. Its actions fall into four routes. It releases fatty compounds that attack pathogens directly. It jams the chemical chatter germs use to coordinate attacks. It reshapes gut communities toward helpful kinds, and it switches on the host's built-in defenses and related markers. Trials also link it to cleaner water and better growth. The authors flag open questions on how strains differ, on safety for wild microbe communities, and on thin long-term evidence in farm settings.
pmc-13511467:
Wong, Kendzerska, and Mak reviewed in 2026 a nightly pill for obstructive sleep apnea, a disorder where the throat closes repeatedly during sleep. Air pressure masks are the standard cure but many patients cannot tolerate them. The pill, called AD109, pairs atomoxetine with aroxybutynin. During sleep, nerve drive to the tongue muscle fades and a braking signal rises, so the targeted pair aims to restore throat muscle tone at its root in the brainstem.

After 26 weeks, the pill cut the hourly count of breathing pauses and shallow breaths by roughly 44 to 47 percent more than placebo, and night oxygen levels improved. Side effects were mostly dry mouth, poor sleep, nausea, and hesitant urination, with no serious treatment-linked events. Longer data and direct comparison with masks are still needed.
pmc-13511767:
Mirella Vinci and ten co-authors report a gene finding in a boy with attention deficit hyperactivity disorder and oppositional defiant disorder, in 2026 work. Both parents were healthy and unrelated. The team read the protein-coding genes of the child and both parents, sorting the found change by standard medical genetics rules and checking it with prediction tools and protein structure models.

The child carried two copies of a rare change in a gene called LNX2, which is active during brain development and helps guide nerve cell growth and connection. The change sits in a region that handles protein partnerships. It was classed as a variant of uncertain significance, since population records list it without any tied condition and the doubled state has been seen only once before. Structure models predicted a local reshaping of chemical bonds. The authors offer the gene as a candidate needing far more proof.
pmc-13513167:
Yazan Omari and co-authors published this liver study in 2026. People with cirrhosis who await a transplant often run low blood pressure, and rules of thumb urge keeping the mean arterial pressure at sixty-five or above. The team asked whether that pressure at listing foretells death on the waitlist. They read records of 103 adults at one center from 2019 to 2023, all with mid-range severity scores.

Survivors had come in with clearly higher pressure than the nine who died. Each extra point of pressure cut the odds of waitlist death a touch. Low pressure also tied to a grave kidney syndrome of liver failure. It did not tie to confusion, fluid build-up, or bleeding. With so few deaths, the authors urge care in reading the result and call for larger cohorts to test it.
pmc-13513767:
Hafid Sid-Ahmed and co-authors measure brain responses to sound during hypnosis in a 2026 study. Hypnosis sees growing medical use, yet doctors lack a firm signal to tell how deep a patient's trance runs.

Twenty volunteers heard mostly repeated tones with rare odd ones mixed in, under three states: alert focus, distraction by a story, and hypnotic trance. A magnetic brain scanner tracked the responses in the hearing cortex and at the scalp. Responses shrank in both trance and distraction compared with alert focus. Trance and distraction differed only slightly. The authors suggest the shrunken response could serve as a rough gauge of the hypnotic state.
pmc-13513867:
Junke Nan and co-authors report a 2026 study on how the map area of species records shapes range forecasts. Forecasts of where a pest can live guide farm defense. Models built from one region alone may miss parts of the range a pest could fill, since the records clip the true niche.

The team modeled a crop pest moth in China with a shared modeling platform. One model used world records and the other used China only records. Both drew on climate, land shape, and plant cover data, and both were run for current and future climate paths. The world model scored very high on skill tests and drew on a more even mix of factors. The split shows record scope can shift the forecast map.
pmc-13514367:
Shun-Xin Deng and six co-authors set out in 2026 to build a quality-checking framework for Wolfiporia extensa, a fungus long used in Traditional Chinese Medicine. Its underground mass yields four drug parts, each prescribed for different purposes, yet makers have lacked clear markers to tell them apart. The team measured seven triterpenoid compounds, mapped sugar profiles, and recorded colour values for each part.

Distinct chemical fingerprints emerged: one acid peaked in the outer skin part, another in the red part, and a third in the inner white part, which also carried the most sugars. Simple ratios between two compounds, paired with lightness readings, separated the parts reliably. Extracts behaved differently in cell tests, with the white part shielding nerve-like cells from peroxide damage and the skin part protecting a second cell line. Readers gain a practical grading scheme for a classic remedy.
pmc-13514767:
Chen and colleagues wrote a 2026 survey of Microbispora, a little studied genus of rare actinomycetes, bacteria famed for making useful natural products. These microbes live in soils, seas, plants, and insects, yet drug hunters have largely passed them by. The survey lists every compound reported from the genus so far.

Eighty-one compounds are now known, spanning quinones, chromones, macrolides, alkaloids, peptides, and other groups of molecules. Chen notes effects ranging from killing microbes and cancer cells to guarding nerves and boosting plant growth. Gene studies predict many more chemical factories in Microbispora genomes that remain untested. The authors argue the genus is a rich, little explored source for new drug hunting.
pmc-13515067:
Nina Dimitrijevic Jovanovic leads a twelve-author team documenting oral health among hospitalised patients treated for heroin-related opioid use disorder in a 2026 cross-sectional study. Ninety-seven inpatients received structured interviews and dental examinations, including standard counts of decayed, missing, and filled teeth plus a hygiene index. They also rated how mouth problems affected daily life on a fourteen-item questionnaire.

The average tooth index showed extensive lifetime decay experience, hygiene scores pointed to poor cleanliness, and quality-of-life scores were markedly impaired, worst in psychological and social domains. Worse mouths meant worse lives in the data: quality-of-life scores climbed steeply alongside tooth damage and with poorer hygiene. Longer heroin use tracked more damage on all fronts. Regression pinned poorer quality of life on accumulated tooth damage, hygiene, and unstable housing.
pmc-13515567:

Cervical cancer is largely preventable, yet Romania records the European Union's highest death rates from it, and vaccination runs on a passive opt-in basis. Only about twenty-nine percent of the women were vaccinated. Knowledge about HPV and trust in health authorities each tracked a stronger intention to vaccinate. Leaning on official sources went with seeing the vaccine as safer. Negative online content linked weakly to lower knowledge but did not directly move vaccination intent. Nati's team argues that health literacy and institutional trust are the pillars of acceptance.
pmc-13515767:
Yaqian Liang and seven colleagues characterise three bacteria-eating viruses, called phages, that attack Staphylococcus aureus, in a 2026 study. This germ threatens people, food safety, and livestock, and phages are candidate weapons against drug-resistant strains. The team isolated three phages from sewage and profiled them with electron microscopy, killing assays, and full genome sequencing.

The myovirus-like phage killed the widest range of strains and kept killing longest, and it also weathered heat and ultraviolet light best. All three stayed infectious across a broad span of acidity and cool-to-room temperatures. Their genomes ran to roughly forty-four thousand letters, with no antibiotic resistance genes found. Some genes hinted at a dormant lifestyle, though, so the authors say safety checks must go further before any farm or clinic use.
pmc-13516167:
Elaine de Jesus and co-authors map ritual healers and plant knowledge across regions in a 2026 scoping review. In many Brazilian communities, prayer healers pair spoken blessings, gestures, and faith with plant remedies. Their work forms a full local care system, not a mere folk extra.

The review pooled a core set of studies plus a wider layer found by chasing citations. Dozens of healer titles and hundreds of plant entries emerged, spanning many plant families. Plants served as drugs, ritual aids, shields, and place markers at once. Uneven records across regions show where field work should go next.
pmc-13516367:
Petar Vasilev and co-authors present two case reports, published in 2026. Both infants came from the same family. Each developed severe hepatitis. The cause was linked to hepatitis B virus. Liver infection from this virus is rare in infancy. It is usually mild there. The siblings fell ill two years apart. Their outcomes differed sharply.

The first infant was a five-month-old girl. She suffered fulminant liver failure. She died before full testing could confirm the cause. Her brother fell ill at four months old. His acute infection was confirmed. Other possible infections were present too. He needed prolonged hospital care. He recovered, and the virus later cleared. Testing relatives found chronic hepatitis B in the mother and grandmother. Hepatitis D virus was also present.
pmc-13517167:
Monica-Daniela Padurariu-Covit and five colleagues track blood counts and survival in people newly diagnosed with HIV in a 2026 cohort study. Low blood counts are common at diagnosis, but their warning value is fuzzy. The team reviewed patients diagnosed between 2018 and 2024 at one centre, comparing blood, immune, viral, and inflammation measures at entry and after twelve months of therapy.

pmc-13518367:

Past trials and cohort studies mostly show no added fracture risk, but bone events are rare and doubts persist.

Most checks found no link to fractures or bone loss. One database gave slightly raised estimates that faded after correction for multiple testing. Bone density gaps were small and not significant.
pmc-13518867:
Shuyi Sun and a large team report in 2026 an optical sensor method that adds up wireless data without demanding tight timing between senders. Internet of Things networks drown in data, and over-the-air computation normally requires signals to arrive in lockstep, which costs overhead. pmc-13518967:
Burke J Minsley leads a nine-author team mapping salty groundwater hidden beneath coastal Louisiana in 2026 with airborne electromagnetic surveys. Managers usually blame modern seawater creeping inland, yet geology can strand ancient salt underground. Their surveys reveal a buried pattern spanning more than 10,000 square kilometers.

As post-glacial seas rose, the Mississippi's incised valley flooded into a paleo-estuary, trapping seawater that still lingers under the delta plain. Minsley and colleagues offer the finding as a framework for spotting legacy salt along other coastlines, where it can threaten wells.
pmc-13519667:
Seven authors report a greener way to make sulfonamides in 2026 with a plant-based solvent called Cyrene. Sulfonamides are a broad drug and chemical family, and standard routes use harsher solvents. Their method runs at room heat and ends in about half an hour to an hour for most cases.

Twenty products came out in good to high yields, up to 90 percent, by simple settling from cold water with mild acid. No column cleanup was needed. About 79 percent of the solvent was caught back and reused with like yield, which cuts waste for scale-up.
pmc-13519867:
Pavithra R and co-authors recount in this 2026 case a painless tearing of the aorta in a thirty-four year old man, a presentation that hides a deadly emergency. Aortic dissection usually announces itself with severe tearing chest pain, but about one case in ten has none.

pmc-13519967:

Cells in the hippocampus and its neighbors fired in a pattern tied to errors, which backs a role for that region in the error watch. During wandering, that pattern ran clearly weaker. The authors read it as proof that a drifting mind impairs both the watch and the fix.
pmc-13520167:

pmc-13520367:

pmc-13520767:

pmc-13520867:
Leslie Michielsen and co-authors ask what skills primary care needs for patients with many chronic illnesses in a 2026 study. Care programs for single diseases often miss complex, whole-person needs. pmc-13520967:

Many patients got a second treatment, and some a third, under a protocol that aims for the best distance and near vision in both eyes. Follow-up ran to 24 months. pmc-13521467:

Chosen simple models predicted dry weight well across species, with noisier results for the diluted optical target. Paired full and pocket-calculator versions suit both automated plants and manual operations.
pmc-13521567:

The authors accept points about regression to the mean, changes in adherence, and confounding by indication. They stress the study was not built to prove the drug beats all rivals under controlled conditions. Findings, they say, show an association in routine care, not proof of drug superiority.
pmc-13521767:

Most earlier work looked at whole organizations, not individuals, and rarely in multicultural universities. Cultural values went hand in hand with stronger innovation, and transformational leadership partly carried that link. A small interaction suggested the link shifts slightly with leadership level. The study speaks to managers of mixed teams in education and beyond.
pmc-13521867:

The review searched eight databases through late 2025 and weighed seventy-eight papers, favoring multicenter and guideline evidence. Child adaptations of adult criteria appear in single center reports, with thresholds for stomach residual volume, belly pressure, and feeding intolerance. Higher grades consistently track worse outcomes and shape feeding plans. The authors call for a validated pediatric scale to guide nutrition and prognosis.
pmc-13522567:

Matching sequences leaves those gaps even in well-studied species.

In tests, known labels were hidden on purpose. WASP recovered them better than leading sequence-based tools. It labelled a fifth to a third of proteins with no known function. This held across twenty species of practical interest. The authors show its use in curating genome-scale metabolic models for biotechnology.
pmc-13522767:

The work draws on cases seen in one hospital emergency department in Wenzhou between January 2024 and June 2025.

The team compared survivors and non-survivors among 216 patients, and 27 of them died during the stay. They tracked several measures of blood pressure change and used statistical models to test each link. Systolic measures, including spread and average real change, differed clearly between the two groups. Readers get a careful look at which simple bedside measures may flag higher risk.
pmc-13522867:
Ameena M Khan Sullivan and colleagues test how simulated night shifts alter responses to meals in a 2026 laboratory study. Four identical meals were eaten per shift, and blood glucose, insulin, and fats were measured hourly alongside hunger ratings.

Night shifts raised glucose and insulin responses after meals, while insulin failed to fully compensate, signaling lower glucose tolerance. Time of day mattered in both schedules, with early evening meals producing the highest glucose responses. The authors propose mistimed eating as one route by which shift work raises metabolic disease risk.
pmc-13523267:
Yujie Shi, Ye Jin, and Hui Yu investigate a small RNA as a marker for newborn breathing disease in a 2026 study. Neonatal respiratory distress syndrome is a major cause of illness and death, especially in preterm infants. Blood and amniotic fluid from thirty-five affected newborns and thirty-five healthy controls were compared for levels of one microRNA, and cell experiments tested its effect on lung surface cells.

The microRNA was elevated in both blood and amniotic fluid of affected newborns, and each fluid distinguished cases from controls with good accuracy. Blocking the microRNA in lung cells improved cell survival and raised output of a key surfactant protein, whose gene it directly regulates. The authors suggest the molecule participates in fetal lung development and could serve as a biomarker for the syndrome.
pmc-13523367:

Breakdown products behaved less cleanly: they were biased in capillary blood, needing correction factors, and rarely detectable in oral fluid. The authors support the new sampling routes for the parent drug.
pmc-13523467:
Muhammed M. Faiz and colleagues report a 2026 randomized trial comparing two drugs added to a scalp nerve block for awake brain surgery. The authors call for larger multicenter trials to settle the best choice.
pmc-13523567:

Their 2026 study adds heat burns to the pulse line for a through-wall seal.

Heat work in the heart's drain vein stays a must in near half the cases for a same-day seal. Late checks test if the seal holds. Few redo cases let the team read where seals fail. Mix craft may give the line both speed and stay.
pmc-13524367:
Apps, wearables, and video programs now promise to guide scoliosis rehab from home, but the evidence is a patchwork.
