They judged bias, reporting quality, and certainty alongside outcomes.

Spinal alignment, flexibility, breathing, posture, and quality of life mostly tilted favorable, while trunk rotation, pain, and body image results were mixed. Sticking with the program depended more on how much supervision came with it than on the gadget itself. No serious harms appeared, but certainty was low throughout. The authors urge better trials before clinics lean on these tools.
pmc-13524967:
Vishesh Jain, Matthew Kwan, and Marcus Michelen published a 2026 mathematics paper on quantum entanglement. Two partners, Alice and Bob, share one quantum state between them. By acting only on their own parts and talking freely, they may turn that state into a new one.

A famous result, Nielsen's theorem, gives an exact rule for when such a change can happen. Nielsen also guessed that in large systems, almost all pairs of states cannot be changed into each other at all. The authors take up that guess in their title's claim: entangled states are typically incomparable. Their work uses the natural measure on states to say what typical means. The result shapes how scientists think about handling quantum states.
pmc-13525167:
Ong and colleagues tested in 2026 whether swinging reduces academic stress in nursing students. Swinging stimulates the vestibular system, the inner-ear balance sense, and is linked to relaxation. The quasi-experimental study enrolled seventy-eight student nurses in Baguio City, split into swinging and control groups. Stress was measured with a standard academic stress scale, and the team varied swinging duration and body position.

The swinging group showed a significant drop in academic stress compared with controls. How long students swung, and in what position, changed how much stress fell. They recommend building vestibular stimulation into nursing education. That includes campus spaces designed for swinging breaks. The study adds a low-cost, non-drug option to the student stress toolkit, tested across year levels of the nursing programme.
pmc-13525667:
Shiqiong Huang and colleagues run a 2026 retrospective study of adverse drug reactions among hospitalized patients with HIV and AIDS in China, using a variable-selection regression method to hunt for risk factors. Such reactions add heavily to hospital burden in this population. Suspected reactions were judged for causality with an international monitoring system.

Among 918 patients, 210 experienced a reaction, an incidence of 22.88 percent. Blood and lymphatic disorders were the commonest manifestation class. Antibacterial drugs caused the largest share, followed closely by antivirals. The selection model singled out one clear factor, the number of medications given during hospitalization, which raised the odds of a reaction substantially. The authors propose the count as a simple flag for closer monitoring and regimen review.
pmc-13525967:
Salvatore Alessio Angileri leads a large team in a 2026 review of interventional radiology for slipped discs, a common cause of spinal pain and nerve pain. Most patients recover with rest and basic care, yet lasting cases need options between drugs and open surgery. Needle techniques guided by imaging fill that middle step.

A structured search of PubMed and Scopus covered mechanical, thermal, chemical, and healing methods for cervical, thoracic, and lumbar slipped discs. Noted results included pain relief, recovery, complications, and repeat procedures. Findings suggest needle procedures can give real short- and medium-term gains in chosen patients whose symptoms match imaging, with less cutting and faster recovery in skilled hands. The authors note the findings are mostly observational and call for trials across many centers with uniform reporting.
pmc-13526367:
Gi Jeong Park, Do Yun Kwon, and Kwang-Ryeol Kim reported in 2026 a rare case where a slipped neck disc caused a partial spinal cord syndrome. It also caused a nerve syndrome of the face. A man aged thirty-seven came in with neck and shoulder pain and growing weakness in his right arm. He also had trouble walking and face signs on the same side, including a drooping lid and small pupil.

Scans showed a large disc bulge in the neck pressing hard on the cord. Surgery from the front removed the disc piece and joined the bones. Afterward his arm strength and walking fully returned. The face signs also cleared, which the authors use to stress this rare cause.
pmc-13528067:
Yongyi Pan and eleven colleagues test a plant compound against obesity-linked male infertility in a 2026 mouse study. Puerarin comes from the kudzu plant root. Mice on a high-fat diet gained weight and made less testosterone. Their sperm counts and movement fell. The team combined gene scans with protein hunting to find the compound's target.

Puerarin trimmed weight gain and fat, and it cleaned up blood lipids. Testes kept a healthier shape, and testosterone, count, and motility rose. The compound latched onto a helper protein called GRP78. That grip steadied StAR, a protein that starts testosterone making. Blocking GRP78 in cells undid the benefit. The authors name the GRP78 to StAR route as the mechanism. Human testing would be a distant next step.
pmc-13528167:
Csilla Kurdi and nine colleagues compare amino acid patterns in egg follicle fluid across three infertility-linked conditions in a 2026 study. The fluid bathes the egg and mirrors body metabolism. Samples totaled 171 from IVF patients. Groups covered insulin resistance, endometriosis, and thyroid trouble. Twenty amino acids were measured with precise lab methods.

Overall patterns looked alike across groups. Disease still left a modest but real fingerprint. Insulin resistance came with lower glycine and arginine. Thyroid trouble came with lower histidine, tryptophan, and lysine. Endometriosis stood out for higher histidine. The shifts held after accounting for body weight. Single amino acids sorted the groups poorly. The authors favor whole-pattern readouts. They say the follicle senses whole-body metabolic health in a quiet, spread-out way.
pmc-13528667:
Omer Othman Abdullah explores whether conception by IVF and long breathing support track with severe eye disease in premature infants, published in 2026. The study covers babies with established retinopathy of prematurity sent to a specialist retina center in Erbil, Iraq. The outcome was disease severe enough to need laser treatment, injections, or surgery.

Sixty consecutive infants were included over two years. Treatment-requiring disease appeared in the large majority of IVF-conceived infants, a much higher share than in the others. Long support on a pressure breathing device was the second exposure examined. The author is careful about limits: the data were sparse, the two exposures overlapped, and twins broke the independence of observations, so adjusted models were not shown. The work is framed as exploratory.
pmc-13528767:
Durjoy Lahiri argues in a 2026 letter for a fast-track path to disease-modifying treatment in early Alzheimer's disease. The letter replies to a commentary on strain in Canadian brain health care. Critics called the new amyloid-targeting drugs a niche fix for a tiny share of patients. Lahiri disputes the math behind that claim.

The low share counts all comers to a memory clinic, Lahiri notes. Among true early-stage patients without safety blocks, the share climbs to near one in five. Slow expert checks also push some patients past the window before they are seen. The letter draws a likeness to stroke clot-busting care, which also serves a small share yet reshaped the system.
pmc-13528867:
Lucy Hughes and five co-authors tested what adds value to story based word teaching for children with language disorder. Their study, from twenty twenty-six, deals with developmental language disorder and like states. Such children find word learning hard. Word programs often mix three parts: words in a story, clear direct teaching, and sign or gesture with speech. Which parts carry the gains was not known.

Eighteen children took part in a design where each child met each mix. All had a language disorder, most of the set kind. The team gauged the boost from clear teaching, from signing, and from both at once. Readers who treat child language get facts to build leaner, stronger word programs.
pmc-13529267:
Yuichiro Hara and seven co-authors hunt for an HIV cure compound in a 2026 paper. Modern therapy controls the virus but cannot clear hidden reservoirs of infected cells. A shock-and-kill strategy wakes the virus so the cells can be destroyed. Most known waking agents only shock, without the kill. Screening a small-molecule library turned up a compound that seems to do both.

The compound reactivated hidden virus and selectively harmed the reservoir cell lines. At single-cell level the two effects looked independent, so one did not simply cause the other. It also switched on viral activity in cells taken from treated patients. More validation in primary cells is urged.
pmc-13529867:
Shimosato and Goyama review a rare but instructive form of acute myeloid leukaemia driven by rearrangements of the NPM1 gene. The common NPM1 story is a small mutation found in up to two fifths of adult cases, with well-mapped behaviour. Rearrangements, where NPM1 fuses with partners such as MLF1 or RARA, are far rarer and were long neglected. Their 2026 synthesis gathers the emerging evidence on how these fusions look clinically and how they cause disease.

Reassuringly for drug developers, the fusions work through the same machinery as the common mutation. The NPM1 protein ends up stranded in the cytoplasm, partners with the export protein XPO1, and holds developmental HOX genes switched on, driving the leukaemia. Clinically, rearranged cases skew younger and may carry a worse outlook, though the authors flag the small numbers behind that claim.
pmc-13530167:
Vera Weisbecker, Andrew Pask, Axel Newton, and Douglass Rovinsky study the skull of the extinct Tasmanian tiger, in a 2026 paper. The thylacine was the largest modern marsupial predator, and its wolf-like skull is a famous case of similar evolution. The team measured skull shape in detail.

Their data show a mix of traits not seen in dogs or other living meat-eaters. Thylacines had large heads, tall slender snouts, a flared canine area, and unusually large openings near the eye socket. The authors link that mix to fast, high-impact snapping at prey. They warn that its hunting style may not be inferable from living mammals alone.
pmc-13530267:
Mohammad Khorsandi and colleagues test in 2026 green solvents that could dissolve a poorly soluble drug ingredient called 4-hydroxycoumarin. Three acidic deep eutectic solvents, each built from choline chloride plus a simple acid, competed against plain water. Standard shaking-flask measurements spanned a small temperature range.

The propionic acid version lifted solubility more than five hundredfold over water, beating the acetic and lactic versions. Math models fit the data closely, and heating analysis showed dissolving absorbs heat. Cell tests on colon cancer cells found moderate killing power that varied with solvent mix, supporting early drug formulation work.
pmc-13531267:
Thomas Jeanne and co-authors ask whether soil microbes can predict a field's carbon and structure better than chemistry alone, in this 2026 study. Standard formulas estimate soil behavior from fixed physical traits and ignore the organisms that actively build soil structure. The team assembled over two thousand farm soil samples from Quebec, with microbe censuses spanning bacteria, fungi, and tiny eukaryotes, plus texture and climate data. Four learning algorithms competed on three targets.

The targets are the soil's stored carbon, its crumb stability, and its pore space. Interpretable models let the authors say which life signals carry the predictions. If biology truly forecasts function, soil maps and carbon accounting both gain a living layer they have been missing.
pmc-13531667:
Silva-Ramos and co-authors combed fleas from rural dogs across 24 municipalities of Cundinamarca, Colombia. They checked them for two bacterial genera that fleas carry to people: Rickettsia, which causes spotted fevers, and Bartonella, behind cat-scratch disease and other illnesses. Colombian data on dog fleas were thin. Their 2026 field study examined 116 dogs in 2019 and 2020, identified the fleas, pooled them, and screened the pools with sensitive DNA tests, following up positives for species identification.

About two fifths of dogs carried fleas, and nearly all the fleas were the cat flea species that happily bites dogs and humans alike. Rickettsia turned up in the large majority of pools, mostly Rickettsia asembonensis with some Rickettsia felis. Bartonella appeared in over a quarter of pools, though sequencing could not pin its species down.
pmc-13531867:
Hongchun Li and colleagues show in 2026 that silencing the Tau protein protects young mice from lasting thinking damage after newborn sepsis. Infection in the first month of life often leaves survivors with cognitive harm into adolescence. Tau, a nerve fiber protein, was the suspect mediator in this mouse work.

Turning Tau down softened memory loss after early inflammation. Brain checks showed reshaped branching in a memory region and renewed birth of nerve cells there in adulthood. The authors nominate Tau as a treatment target for sepsis-related brain injury, with structure and cell renewal as the routes.
pmc-13531967:
Jiangyuan Liu, Johan H Gibcus, and Job Dekker present in 2026 a workflow that calls DNA loops jointly across related chromosome-folding datasets. Loop calls from Hi-C maps vary wildly between similar samples, muddying comparisons. Their tool, UnionLoops, first builds one shared candidate set, then applies uniform filtering and scores support sample by sample.

Joint calling found more shared loops, trimmed spurious one-off calls, and matched independent protein occupancy evidence better than single-sample routes. Cleaner loop maps sharpen reading of how genome folding shifts across conditions, a basic need for studies of development and disease across sample groups.
pmc-13532167:
Arun Pal and co-authors build a molecular wheel that flips into a small cluster and back in this 2026 paper. The wheel holds twenty molybdenum atoms in a ring with a hollow center about two nanometers wide. Depending on the salts used, the cavity sits empty or traps two guest molecules. A battery of crystal, spectroscopic, and scattering tests confirmed the structure.

In water the wheel breaks down cleanly into a four-molybdenum cluster. The change is fast, complete, and fully reversible. Drying the solution regrows the wheel without loss. Computer modeling backed the switch. The authors present it as a rare, tidy case of host-guest chemistry driving reversible rebuilding.
pmc-13532267:
Yuyuan Xue and a team of co-authors tune a rapid PCR test for skin and nail fungal infections. Their study appeared in twenty twenty-six. Microscopy misses cases, culture takes weeks, and patients wait in limbo.

One hundred thirteen suspected cases ran through all three methods plus the new multiplex assay. A receiver-operating analysis set the positivity cutoff at a cycle threshold near thirty-two point seven. Resampling a thousand times confirmed the cutoff was no fluke. The assay read two major fungus genera with strong accuracy. Pairing microscopy with the rapid test caught sixty-six percent of cases, beating microscopy alone, and answers landed within three hours instead of weeks.
pmc-13532367:
Caroline Cushman and co-authors report, in a 2026 case study, a usually harmless kidney tumor that invaded the heart of a thirty-six-year-old woman. Such tumors rarely grow into veins, and reaching the heart's right side without the linked genetic syndrome is rarer still. She arrived with belly and back pain plus nausea.

Scans showed a huge left kidney mass with a tumor cord running up the great vein into the heart, dipping through a valve with each beat. Gene tests ruled out the syndrome. A multi-team operation removed kidney and cord together and rebuilt the vein. Final checks confirmed full removal with clean margins.
pmc-13532767:
Giovanna Pazin and co-authors study accidental ureter injury during bowel surgery, in a 2026 cohort analysis. The ureter is the tube that carries urine from kidney to bladder. Injury to it is a rare but serious mishap in belly and pelvis operations. The team reviewed elective colorectal cases at a large teaching hospital over many years.

Among more than two thousand operations, nineteen injuries were found. Most patients were in their mid fifties, and most had prior belly surgery. Rectal cancer was the most common reason for operating. Injuries were more frequent in keyhole surgery than in open surgery, and in repeat tumor cases. The left ureter was hurt most often. Risk factors and guard steps are set out for surgical teams.
pmc-13532867:
Yanqiu Wang and colleagues tested what happens while focused ultrasound is beamed at the brain's movement area, rather than after it ends. They measured how strongly one side of the brain reins in the other, a balance key to smooth movement.

Fifteen healthy volunteers received ultrasound to one movement area while magnetic pulses measured the cross-brain braking at two time gaps. Ultrasound weakened the long-gap braking from the treated side to the opposite side during the beaming. The short-gap braking stayed unchanged, and the opposite side's own excitability did not shift either. Wang reads this as ultrasound tuning a complex circuit, and offers it as a probe of how the two brain halves interact.
pmc-13534467:
Minmin Xiang, Shuang Liu, Desheng Xiao, and Yongguang Tao wrote a review in 2026 on immune checks and how they shape both body-weight ills and cancer. Such ills as fat gain, high blood sugar, and thyroid trouble have grown much more common in recent years. Standard drugs help many people but can bring side effects and lose force over time.

The review explains how signals that calm immune cells also shape heat burn, fat tissue, and long-term swelling. One key path can shift cells in fat toward a calmer state and ease harm. The authors map what is known for each ill and point to new drug ideas. Readers gain a clear view of a fast-growing link between two fields.
pmc-13534667:
Mengyue Wei and colleagues optimise in 2026 an ethanol extract of Litsea cubeba fruit and probe how it kills Staphylococcus aureus. The plant has a long history as a spice and folk remedy, and natural germ killers are sought for food and drug use. Response surface methods tuned heat, time, and liquid ratio for the best yield.

Best settings gave a high antibacterial rate, and chemical scans found 20 compounds led by fatty acids. The extract killed germs at low doses and broke their walls and membranes, leaking cell contents. The work supports the fruit as a natural antibacterial source.
pmc-13534767:
Mónika Koós and a large global team develop in 2026 the Paraphilic Disorders Short Screen, a brief tool aligned with current ICD-11 rules. No reliable screen existed for these disorders under the new guidance. Data came from 82,243 adults across 42 countries in 26 languages, with expert-led item design.

The screen covers seven paraphilias in 21 items, with cut scores set per guidance. Voyeuristic interest was most common, and groups meeting disorder cut-offs showed worse depression and anxiety than others. Clinicians and researchers gain a validated way to flag at-risk people across cultures.
pmc-13535367:
Gwendolyn Stark and co-authors publish the genomes of two North American dung beetles, in a 2026 paper. Dung beetles aerate soil, bury nutrients, and keep pastures and wild lands working, yet their family has few sequenced genomes. The team collected the two species in eastern Tennessee and read their DNA with long-read technology. Both assemblies came out highly complete by standard gene checks.

Software predicted roughly twelve to thirteen thousand genes in each beetle. Comparing their proteins with a relative and a distant beetle cousin revealed a few hundred protein clusters unique to each species. Those clusters are leads for what makes each beetle distinct. The authors offer the assemblies as resources for comparative genomics, evolution, and family-tree studies across dung beetles, a group whose ecological services are easy to overlook.
pmc-13535467:
Soki Kashima and twelve co-authors ask whether a kidney cancer drug dulls the immune cells meant to help it, in a 2026 conference abstract. The drug blocks a low-oxygen sensor that tumors use to grow, and it already extends life in treated patients. Trials now pair it with drugs that free immune cells to attack. Mouse work warns that the same oxygen signal helps killer T cells do their job, so blocking it might cut both ways.

The team built a lab model of the cancer to test the drug on human T cells. They drew T cells from healthy donors and also bred cells with the sensor knocked out. The cells then worked in normal air and in low oxygen, while the team read out gene activity and killing power. The setup aims to show whether the pairing is wise before big trial results land.
pmc-13536067:
Sophie Faber and co-authors lay out a study protocol in a 2026 paper for a parent group program in Germany. When a parent dies of cancer, the surviving parent must grieve while also carrying the children through their own loss. A proven group program from abroad supports such parents, but no adapted version existed for Germany.

The team will translate and adapt the program for cancer loss, train experienced grief workers to lead it, and run pilot groups for about thirty parents. Parents will meet every two weeks, in person or online, for ten sessions. The study will check whether the plan is workable and welcome, and will track early signs of change in well-being, family coping, and communication.
pmc-13536267:
Michael Rouse, Yumna Kaleem, and Justin M Yeung discuss in 2026 how artificial intelligence can lower barriers to research for surgical trainees. Research is now core to training, yet cost, time, thin mentoring, and ethics delays block many juniors. Their view maps AI help across each research stage.

Tools can aid idea shaping, literature search, protocol drafting, ethics forms in plain language, data extraction, and analysis code. The authors stress that AI should support, not replace, core skills like design judgement and critical reading. Risks and limits must stay in view for safe trainee use.
pmc-13536567:
Shixin Ding and co-authors review the brain's lymphatic drainage network, a system long thought not to exist. The brain was held to be immune-privileged, with no lymph vessels in its tissue. Fresh work has redrawn that picture, joining the glymphatic flow, meningeal lymph vessels, and drainage paths along cranial nerves.

Their 2026 review lays out the anatomy, the molecular controls, and the daily work of this network. It clears metabolic waste and hosts immune cells that steer nerve activity through their signals. In aging and in degenerative disease, the network falters: a water channel sits out of place, valves weaken, and immune mixes shift. The authors weigh cures that might flow from repair.
pmc-13536767:
Laura Barberán-Bernardos, Miguel Ángel Ariza-Gracia, and David P Piñero compare two eye imaging devices in a 2026 agreement study. Both devices measure front eye shape, corneal thickness, and chamber size used in diagnosis and surgical planning. Fifty-five healthy eyes were measured with each device by the same examiner. Paired tests and agreement plots assessed whether readings could be swapped in practice.

Front corneal curvature agreed well enough for shared use, with no clear average gap. Other measures differed clearly, including back curvature, chamber depth, thickness, and chamber angle, with one device tending toward deeper chambers and narrower angles. Thickness agreement ranges were wide. The authors warn against swapping devices freely for thickness checks before lens surgery or for chamber measures guiding implant choices.
pmc-13536867:
Zichun Wang and colleagues track care delays for migrant tuberculosis patients in suburban Shanghai in a 2026 review of cases from 2015 to 2024. Two delays matter, the wait before a patient first seeks care and the wait before the system confirms diagnosis. Records held 3,178 lung tuberculosis cases, split almost evenly between locals and migrants in Fengxian District. Trends and risk factors for each delay were compared.

Migrants waited fewer days before seeking care than locals, yet waited longer for confirmed diagnosis. The first wait among migrants rose steadily from 2017 onward. Female sex, middle age, and first seeking care outside the district raised the first wait, while test results and care location shaped the second wait. The authors urge better cross-district coordination and stronger local lab testing.
pmc-13537267:
Fatemeh Tavakoli Joorabi and six co-authors published a study in 2026 on how the feel of the surrounding jelly shapes collagen fibers. Collagen threads build themselves from loose molecules inside the body's crowded, sugar-rich matrix. Earlier work watched them in plain gels, missing the push and give of a second, woven-in network like the real one.

The team grew collagen inside alginate networks tuned from runny to firm by recipe and cross-link style. Firm, less giving networks slowed and shrank fiber growth, seen under a special microscope that images collagen without stains. Flow through the gels also dropped as give dropped. Simulations of the mechanical grip between network and growing clumps matched the trend, offering tissue engineers a dial for fiber structure.
pmc-13537567:
Cai Xu and co-authors study loneliness and capacity in older Hispanic adults in 2026. Intrinsic capacity sums the body and mind powers that let older people thrive. Social isolation may erode that capacity over time. The team used a national retirement study wave with hundreds of Hispanic adults aged sixty and over.

Capacity scores drew on five domains, and isolation was scored by a composite index. In the full group, isolation showed no clear link with capacity. Subgroup checks by region, community type, and birthplace told a more mixed story. The results hint that place and social setting shape how isolation bites.
pmc-13537867:
Huai-xue Mi and Peipei Zhang write a letter weighing a new scan method that gauges pressure in the heart's left atrium without a catheter. The study under discussion used contrast timing on magnetic resonance scans before ablation for atrial fibrillation. A noninvasive pressure read would spare patients a risky tube procedure.

The letter praises the design, then presses three points from imaging practice. First, scans were taken in steady rhythm, while many real patients stay in fibrillation during imaging, which warps contrast flow. Second, blood flow factors beyond pressure can shift the timing signal. Third, the patient mix may not travel well to other clinics. The writers ask for tests in messier, real-world cohorts. Their aim is to firm the method's place in pre-ablation workups.
pmc-13538167:
Roberta Borg-Bartolo, Maurus Jaeggi, Martin Schimmel, and Hendrik Meyer-Lueckel review oral health in older adults in Switzerland in work dated two thousand twenty-six. The review spans studies from nineteen seventy onward, for people aged sixty-five and up. It tracks tooth loss, gum disease, false teeth, and chewing function over time.

Toothlessness fell sharply, from near half of older adults in the nineteen eighties to a small share in recent years. The mean count of missing teeth fell by more than half across the same span. People living at home had better mouth health and chewing than those in care homes. Mouth cleanliness stayed middling to poor in all settings, and data on life quality tied to oral health were scarce.
pmc-13538567:
Abdalla Elbialy presents a framework that sharpens spot-based tissue gene maps to single-cell detail without outside references in a 2026 study. Spot platforms average several cells per reading, while rival sharpening tools need reference data or fresh training per dataset. The morphology-guided system works training-free, validated on one colon cancer sample measured across four platforms, including a true single-cell reference.

On the finest spot input, the system matched the single-cell reference more closely than any rival tested. Across six distribution checks on a shared gene panel, its variants led most metrics with no rival winning any. Trained rivals merely tracked raw readings on matched regions. The authors highlight per-cell records with coordinates as output no raw spot reading can supply.
pmc-13538767:
Fujishiro and co-authors argue that apathy deserves more attention when doctors try to spot Lewy body dementia early. This dementia is the second most common kind, yet at the earliest stage it is often mistaken for Alzheimer's disease. Post-mortem studies show about a third of early Alzheimer's diagnoses actually hide Lewy body disease.

Apathy, a loss of motivation, is a listed supportive feature of the disease but has been little studied as an early sign. The authors review evidence that persistent apathy in older adults predicts later dementia and may appear early in Lewy body disease. They make the case for assessing apathy systematically so the two diseases can be told apart sooner.
pmc-13539067:
Aylar Afshari, Zahra Mohandes, and Shabnam Ajami report a 2026 study that compares an AI tool with hand tracing for jaw X-ray measures. Such measures guide braces care, and spot picking is extra hard in children with cleft lip and palate. Hand tracing is the gold standard but slow and tied to the tracer.

The study used side head films of 45 children with repaired one sided clefts and 30 matched peers, all aged 8 to 12. Seven angles from 14 spots were read both ways. The AI tool failed on about a fifth of films in both groups. Where it worked, agreement ran from weak to good by angle, with two angles scoring well.
pmc-13539467:
Stéphane Gooré and co-authors profile trunk bark oil from an Ivorian tree across fifty trees in eight places, in a study from two thousand twenty-six. Three lab methods split the oils into eighty-three parts. Scent oils of this species are reported here for the first time.

Pine-type scents rule the oils, led by one form that swings from near a third to three quarters. Cluster math split the oils into two groups, one with a split pair of subgroups. Mixes differ by which pine forms lead and which side notes join. Place and tree both seem to shape the oil. Readers get a first chemical map of a little-known bark oil.
pmc-13540267:
Olivia Shay and co-authors measure how a belly compression belt shifts anatomy between radiation sessions. Their 2026 paper deals with MR-guided therapy for belly and liver cancers. The belt limits motion from breathing during a session. But daily belt placement varies, and its effect across sessions was little known.

They reviewed daily MR images from 17 belt patients and 17 matched controls. Shape match scores at the target were lower in the belt group, and distance errors were higher. At the squeeze zone, outlines shifted by a clear median amount from the first session. Organ shifts ran in a like range in both groups. Age, sex, and body size explained only a small share of target shifts. Most variation was patient-specific.
pmc-13540867:
Weishan Lin leads a 2026 study explaining part of the bone fragility seen in spinal muscular atrophy, a genetic disease that wastes muscle and leaves many patients with osteoporosis. Muscle talks to bone partly through tiny parcels called extracellular vesicles, and patient muscle samples hinted that this traffic was disturbed.

Patients and model mice both showed muscle releasing far fewer vesicles. Those vesicles, when supplied in adequate doses, encouraged bone-forming cells and restrained bone-eating cells just as well as vesicles from healthy muscle, and replenishing them rescued bone in the mice. The chain ran from the missing SMN protein down to a release protein, SNAP23, whose fall throttled vesicle secretion.
pmc-13540967:
Laura L Jelliffe-Pawlowski leads a 2026 California study building an index of preterm birth risk that only counts risk factors medicine can actually act on. Preterm birth is the leading killer of young children, and proven interventions for many maternal conditions reach fewer than half of eligible women.

Linked records for 1.9 million singleton births between 2016 and 2020 were split into training and testing sets. Eighteen candidate risks with evidence-based responses, spanning clinical, behavioural, and social domains, fed the index. Conditions such as chronic hypertension, diabetes, anaemia, asthma, and mental illness anchor the list. The study examines how well the index flags risk through pregnancy and which factors combine most dangerously.
pmc-13542067:
Hilal Kalkan and seven colleagues monitor, in a 2026 field study, whether pole vaulters keep their run-up speed across repeated attempts as effort builds inside the body. Approach speed in the final metres is the main mechanical driver of jump height, so any fade matters to coaches.

Eleven competitive vaulters, four women and seven men, made four jumps twenty centimetres below their personal bests with short rests. Blood lactate and heart rate stayed statistically flat between attempts, while felt exertion rose only late in the set. Run-up speed and every step measure held steady throughout. The authors conclude that this submaximal protocol preserves speed even as internal signals climb unevenly.
pmc-13542567:
Ravinder Saini and co-authors present a 2026 computer-based study of coatings for dental implants. A good implant must bond with the jaw bone, a process called osseointegration. The team studied a mixed coating of two materials. One is graphene oxide, which grips proteins well but can harm cells at high doses. The other is hydroxyapatite, a bone-like mineral that is gentle on tissue but grips less well.

Using docking, modelling, and motion simulations, the team watched how the blended coating met proteins that guide cell attachment. The blend formed more bonds and held the proteins steadier than either material alone. Early safety screening raised more alerts for graphene oxide than for the mineral. The authors stress that these are computer results, and lab and animal tests must come next before any clinical use.
pmc-13543167:
Yunxiao Ji and five co-authors asked if salt intake drives bone loss risk. Their study, from twenty twenty-six, pairs two kinds of proof. Osteoporosis is a world health load, most for older adults. Salt is a diet trait that could be changed, but past finds clash. The team used a big United States health survey with just over three thousand adults across three wave spans.

Survey math weighed the salt and bone link with other traits held in check. A gene based method then tested if the link could be causal, through variants tied to salt handling. Readers who guide diet learn if the salt and bone tale holds past plain links. Two proof paths make the read stronger than one.
pmc-13543367:
Hyejung Han, Khammany Phommachanh, and Sung Hye Kim measure completion of the maternal and child health care continuum in two Lao provinces, in a study from twenty twenty-six. Laos has among Southeast Asia's highest maternal and neonatal mortality. Remote provinces like Xiengkhuang and Huaphanh are underserved. A household survey covered women with a recent live birth.

pmc-13546667:

pmc-13546767:

pmc-13548267:

pmc-13548467:

pmc-13548567:

Gijs Geleijnse and co-authors argue in a 2026 article that Europe's cancer registries need strong backing. These lists track every cancer case in a set area by shared world rules. They show how many new cases arise, how long patients live, and how many live with the disease.

Fed into a shared European system, the data reveal gaps in cancer burden between places. Spending on cancer is set to rise 59% by 2050, so good data can steer funds where they help most. Still, many lists struggle to gather fast, sound, and full data in daily practice. The authors call for stronger systems and laws so each patient counts in plans for control and care.
pmc-13571567:
Jason Rall and co-authors test whole blood transfusion in a pig trauma model in a 2026 study. Thirty-two pigs received fracture, liver injury, and controlled blood loss. A thirty-minute shock period followed the injuries.

Whole blood is returning to trauma care, but survival results are mixed. Component therapy is the main alternative in hospitals. Citrate exposure from stored blood can drop calcium levels. The team tied citrate, calcium dosing, and stability to survival. Animals were assigned at random to transfusion plans. Readers learn which chemical details may decide whether whole blood saves or harms.
pmc-13571867:
Siheng Ma and four co-authors present a 2026 study of how diabetes and low mood combine to affect thinking in older adults. The team compares two large health surveys, one from the United States and one from China. All of the people studied were aged sixty or older.

The United States survey covered twelve hundred people and the China survey fifteen hundred. Diabetes and signs of depression each raised the risk of weak thinking on their own. In the China group, the two together added extra risk beyond either one alone. That added effect did not appear in the United States group. The authors suggest screening for both body and mood health to protect thinking in later life.
pmc-13571967:
Martijn Heleven and co-authors find a gentle way to hold flatworms still for live imaging. The planarian Schmidtea mediterranea can regrow its whole body, making it a favorite for regeneration studies, but imaging a moving worm at high resolution is hard. The team tested linalool, a fragrant plant compound, as a reversible sedative.

At the chosen dose, worms stilled quickly, recovered fully, and showed no stress signs. Short sedation before cutting, or daily short doses during regrowth, left regrowth, stem cell activity, and brain shape intact. Constant exposure throughout regrowth, by contrast, caused stress and poorer healing. The paper defines safe exposure windows and notes the method works alongside fluorescent dyes, opening steady imaging from whole worm to single cell.
pmc-13572067:
Rule Du and co-authors link paths of healthy aging to heart disease risk in this 2026 study. How aging unfolds over years, not just at one checkup, may steer chronic disease. Proof on that point was thin.

The team drew on three big aging cohorts from Europe, England, and China. All participants were at least 50 and free of heart disease during the path-finding years. A healthy aging score, built from 41 signs of inner capacity, sorted people into trajectories. The study then asked which paths led to new cardiovascular disease. Steady healthy paths, it turns out, matter for the heart as much as any single measure.
pmc-13572167:
Guo and co-authors fed a 2026 comparison of dietary oils in Pekin ducks, testing soybean oil against flaxseed oil and rubber seed oil for omega-3 enrichment. One hundred and forty-four day old ducks were split into three groups and fed the diets for six weeks. Fatty acid make-up, antioxidant status, and liver gene activity were measured at the end.

Both alternative oils cut liver and abdominal fat indices and enriched omega-3 fats in blood and liver while lowering the omega-6 to omega-3 ratio. Rubber seed oil outperformed flaxseed oil on most measures Guo reports, dropping blood triglycerides, cholesterol, and a liver enzyme significantly. It also lowered a fat damage marker in blood and liver while boosting several antioxidant enzyme activities. Liver genes for fat burning fell and protective genes rose under both alternative oils.
pmc-13572367:
Hemant Kumar Sharma presents a 2026 theory study of charge flow through a tiny device made of three quantum dots set in a triangle. Such a device works like a very small transistor built from a single molecule. The study asks how three forces shape the flow: electrons pushing on each other, electrons linked to shaking in the dots, and loss of that shaking to the base below.

Sharma uses a math model that treats the link to shaking in full, not as a small tweak. A Green's function method then yields the charge spectrum, the current, and how current changes with voltage. The results show how charge push-back, reshaped energy levels, and damping act together. The work maps when flow stays smooth, when shaking helps it, and when loss to the base dulls it.
pmc-13572567:
Anjali Rathee, with ten colleagues, reports a 2026 study of loneliness and care satisfaction in stem cell transplant patients. Transplant patients spend weeks in protective isolation to dodge infection, and that confinement can weigh on mood and trust in care. The team asked who feels isolation most, and what softens it.

The study enrolled 47 adults at a large hospital in India after autologous or allogeneic transplants. Set scales gauged felt isolation and satisfaction with care. Near half the patients fell into a high-isolation group, and a like share scored low on satisfaction. A caregiver who was not the patient's partner was the strongest marker of high isolation. Being unmarried marked the lowest satisfaction. The caregiver effect on satisfaction ran fully through how patients felt about their ties with others.
pmc-13572667:
Kar, Zaccaria, Šebek, and van Gastelen present a study from twenty twenty-six on microbes inside the cow rumen. Six dairy cows with rumen ports give fluid samples. Three rumen regions are sampled twice each for comparison. Gene sequencing profiles the microbial communities. Which cow a sample comes from explains the largest share of variation. Sampling region shifts almost nothing in overall community shape. Core microbe groups dominate every region alike.

A few rare microbes do differ by region. Diversity scores stay flat across regions and repeats. The authors call the rumen community stable within each animal. Vertical layers may still differ, they caution.
pmc-13572767:
Home workouts help liver donors recover, and Ilker Demir and Kezban Yigiter compare formats in a 2026 trial. One hundred seventeen donors who gave part of their liver were split into three arms: no program, paper-guided home exercise, and video-guided exercise. Sessions ran twice weekly for eight weeks.

Hospital tests before and after the program score strength and function. All three groups changed over time, and the trial weighs which format wins. Donors are healthy volunteers who accept real surgical cost for another's life; their recovery deserves the same rigor as patients'. A proven home format cuts travel while rehab continues.
pmc-13572967:
Alba Diaz-Rodriguez and co-authors review enzyme use in drug making at AstraZeneca in a 2026 paper. Biocatalysis uses enzymes to run chemical steps under milder conditions with less waste. The company now treats it as a strategic skill, tied to its net-zero goals.

Growth spans people, sites, and tools: more experts, shared high-throughput testing rigs, and university partners. Case studies show how finding, tuning, and evolving an enzyme yields a sturdy process for a drug ingredient. The authors close with next steps, led by end-to-end automated workflows and artificial intelligence. Other drug makers can borrow the playbook for greener production lines.
pmc-13573367:
Ramachandran and co-authors test a heart measure called myocardial work in liver disease patients. Cirrhotic cardiomyopathy is heart dysfunction tied to advanced liver scarring. A common strain measure exists for it, but myocardial work, which adds pressure to the strain picture, had not been assessed in this group.

The team used standard heart ultrasound at rest and stress ultrasound with dobutamine, a drug that makes the heart work harder. They compared work values with strain results in cirrhosis patients. The aim is to judge if this measure finds hidden heart weakness that rest tests alone might miss.
pmc-13574167:
Leeana Peters and co-authors study immune cells in the lymph nodes near the pancreas in type 1 diabetes, in a 2026 paper. These nodes drain the organ that the disease attacks, so they may hold early clues. The team used mass cytometry and single-cell gene reading, plus receptor profiling, on human node tissue.

Nodes from people with the disease held more stem-like memory CD8 T cells than expected. Their killer T cells also showed a hot, active gene pattern, with signs of a signal called IL-15 driving the state. Some cell clones were shared between the nodes and the pancreas itself, and the pancreas cells looked more worn into their killer role. The work maps how these cells may mature before they strike.
pmc-13574267:
Heat, pollution, and a shifting climate may all bear on human fertility, but the research is scattered across fields and places. Mrunali Zode and co-authors lay out a plan in this 2026 protocol for a scoping review that will map the worldwide evidence on such exposures and fertility outcomes.

The team will search major databases, screen studies in pairs, and chart which exposures and outcomes have been studied and what links were reported. Screening was already underway when the protocol appeared. The finished map should show where evidence is strong, where it is thin, and which questions deserve fresh studies.
pmc-13574567:
Da-Wei Wei and co-authors found a gene-copy trick that helps a hospital pathogen thrive inside hosts in a 2026 study. The germ, Acinetobacter baumannii, adapts readily to hospitals and to the human body, making it hard to clear. Understanding its adaptation genes is vital for control.

A mobile DNA element called ISAba1 flanks a gene cluster named crp-osmC in the germ's genome. Copies of that cluster can amplify, raising gene dosage. The team shows the amplification boosts fitness in host-like conditions. Such copy-number tricks let bacteria adapt fast without new mutations. Tracking them could predict which strains will persist in wards and patients.
pmc-13574667:
Hoofs and co-authors tested, in a 2026 proof-of-concept study, whether paired skin sensors can catch failing small-vessel flow early in sepsis. When inflammation turns severe, the tiniest vessels falter first, starving tissue of oxygen. Skin gas sensors read oxygen and carbon dioxide through the surface, and warming the skin changes what they see.

Thirty pigs were split into control, inflammation, and inflammation-plus-fluids groups. Each ear wore two sensors, one heated and one not, logging gases around the clock while blood samples checked the readings. Comparing the pair may expose the vessel response to warming, which sepsis blunts. An early skin signal of vessel failure could speed treatment in intensive care. The animal work lays groundwork before any patient trial.
pmc-13574767:
Liangbo Sun leads a twelve-author team uncovering a molecular switch that starts cellular self-eating during starvation, in a study published in two thousand twenty-six. Autophagy recycles cell contents when nutrients vanish. Its initiation circuitry was incompletely known.

The switch centers on the protein OTUB1. During starvation, the kinase ERK adds a phosphate to OTUB1 at one specific site. That change lets another protein bind, shielding OTUB1 from destruction. Stabilized OTUB1 raises levels of DEPTOR, which throttles the growth regulator mTOR and releases autophagy. In animals, fasting used the same circuit to counteract a Western diet's effects. The pathway even ameliorated fatty liver disease progression in their models.
pmc-13574867:
Sílvia Costa Dias leads a large team in testing how reliably two scans grade knee swelling in child arthritis. The paper is from two thousand twenty-six. The scans are contrast ultrasound and contrast MRI, both done on the same day. The young patients have juvenile idiopathic arthritis.

Two readers grade each scan on a short scale, twice, and the grades match very well within and between readers for both scans. Number-based measures of blood rush also match well between readers. Yet the exact spread of those numbers is wide, so precision is poor. The scans are thus trusty for rank, less so for fine cuts. The work ran across two years with school-age and teen patients.
pmc-13574967:
Praveen Athauda-Arachchi and co-authors study a year of drug searches on a national health site in Sri Lanka. The study appeared in 2026. The site lists all drugs cleared by the national board. In its first year it logged close to one and a half million searches.

The team cleaned the search logs and matched them to a list of near twelve thousand drugs. Vitamin and mineral searches led, with germ drugs and sugar drugs next. The study also flags gaps between what the public seeks and what key drug lists hold. Site speed and energy use were tracked as well. The work shows what big search logs can teach health planners.
pmc-13575067:
Michael Hoberger and colleagues used machine learning to find what predicts survival once soft tissue sarcoma reaches third-line treatment and beyond. Evidence for sequencing later-line therapies is thin, leaving clinicians to guess which drug order helps. Their retrospective study analysed 90 patients with advanced sarcoma receiving third-line or later systemic therapy, using gradient-boosted models to rank predictors.

Progression on second-line therapy predicted worse survival, while lipo- or leiomyosarcoma type and a long first-line benefit predicted better survival. Sequencing hints emerged: trabectedin kept activity in later lines, and earlier pazopanib use looked better, while gemcitabine plus docetaxel showed no timing effect. The authors caution that these sequencing signals are exploratory, but argue that prior response and tumour type should anchor later-line decisions.
pmc-13575167:
Rain on a lens, a fence in front of a camera, dust on a drone's eye: nearby clutter ruins faraway pictures. Seungwoo Yoon and co-authors build a flat metalens that erases the clutter itself. Their lens splits each color channel into pass and stop bands. Distant scenes shine through the pass bands and focus sharply. Light from near obstructions lands in the stop bands and gets rejected.

A neural network then polishes what remains. Against a standard metalens viewing the same blocked scenes, image quality rose by about a third. Object detection and scene segmentation improved markedly too. Flat, self-cleaning vision of this kind suits the places washing cannot reach: mobile robots, drones, and endoscopes working inside the body.
pmc-13575267:
Sounira Mehri and Josef Finsterer wrote this 2026 letter responding to a study by Oh and colleagues. That study used exome sequencing and mitochondrial DNA analysis in 77 children with blood or protein in the urine and a family history of kidney disease. It reported a yield of 55 percent, with COL4A-related kidney disease the commonest finding. Mehri and Finsterer welcome it but challenge how gene variants were judged harmful.

They argue that prediction tools alone cannot prove a variant causes disease: tools disagree, and their accuracy is low for several variant types. Proof needs patient features, population frequencies, family segregation or lab function tests. They fault the handling of a symptom-free carrier of a mitochondrial variant known for multi-system disease. Such carriers need brain, eye, ear and heart screening, they write. Low mutation levels in blood do not rule out illness, so follow-up is essential.
pmc-13575467:
Andrew Tuckey and co-authors rebuild an ancient plant hormone receptor and test how it works in a study published in 2026. Strigolactones are signals that shape shoot branching and help plants talk to fungi and neighbors. The receptor, called D14, arose long ago from a gene copying event in early seed plants.

The rebuilt ancestral receptor behaved much like the modern one found in a common lab plant. Its taste for signals was nearly the same, despite a reshaped active site and different reaction speed. One key part thought to be essential proved not to be needed for signaling. The ancient version was also sturdier and easier to produce, which suits it for engineering uses.
pmc-13575867:
Bhekinkosi Sibanda and co-authors review the status and ecology of the cattle egret in southern Africa, in a 2026 paper. The bird lives across wetlands, grazing land, irrigated farms, and town green spaces, and reacts quickly to environmental change. The review gathers 173 studies from the 1940s to 2025.

Habitat and feeding studies dominate the record, ahead of population and breeding work. Atlas data show the bird spreading and holding steady or growing across much of the region over three decades. Diets lean on grasshoppers, and breeding follows rainfall with fair fledging success. Threats include lost nesting sites, storm wrecks of colonies, and chemical contamination. The authors urge tracking, screening, and wider citizen counts.
pmc-13577267:
Pierluigi Diotaiuti and co-authors review eye tracking studies in post traumatic stress in a 2026 paper. The disorder warps attention toward threat, though newer work shows the bias flips with context and load. Eye tracking records those shifts with fine timing, especially when paired with brain measures.

Across antisaccade, free viewing, and search tasks, patterns proved mixed and personal. Some patients locked onto threats; others avoided them under load, explored less, and scanned shorter paths. A wobble measure between vigilance and avoidance tracked illness severity in several studies. Trauma type and symptom mix reshaped the picture further. The authors argue gaze measures may out sense reaction time tests and deserve wider clinical study.
pmc-13577567:
Lijun Zhang and colleagues classify lung nodules from three viewing angles at once. Their deep learning study from twenty twenty-six targets early lung cancer detection. A single scan slice shows too little of a nodule shape. Multi-view methods help, but they often merge views clumsily.

The system reads axial, coronal, and sagittal slices together. A lesion-guided attention step sharpens features near the nodule. A weighted fusion step then learns each view value per case. Tests used a public lung image collection with hundreds of nodules. Accuracy and related scores beat standard comparison methods. Balanced benign and malignant cases make the test fair. Radiologists gain a second reader tuned to nodule shape.
pmc-13577667:
Yibo Wang and co-authors describe a new software tool from 2026 that pulls neat facts out of messy papers and files. Pulling data by hand is slow and prone to error, yet shared databases need clean, ordered records. Their tool, called OmniExtract, uses a large language model to do the pulling.

Users set up the task with plain config files, and the tool tunes its prompts on its own to raise accuracy. It works on both text and tables in many forms and sizes. In tests it reached about ninety percent accuracy, with still higher scores on tables. A free test site and open code let other teams try it for their own database work.
pmc-13577767:
Betina Biagetti and co-authors check whether a simple urine measure can separate two causes of excess cortisol, in a 2026 study. In ACTH-dependent Cushing syndrome, the hormone excess comes either from a pituitary tumor or from hormone-secreting tumors elsewhere, and telling them apart is a hard step. The team used a Spanish registry of 269 patients, 208 with the pituitary form and 61 with the ectopic form.

Urinary free cortisol, scaled to its normal ceiling, separated the groups well, as did a late-night saliva measure. No ectopic case fell below three times the ceiling, while at ten times the ceiling about forty percent were ectopic. Patients with the ectopic form were also older with far higher values. The authors validate the urine cutoff for Spanish practice.
pmc-13577867:
Mostafa Kamal, Efehan Ulas, and Yesim Senayli map in 2026 where childbearing runs high in Bangladesh and what drives it. The land's birth rate fell from 6.3 in 1975 to 2.3 in 2011, but it has not hit the swap level of 2.1, and regions split sharply. The team used a 2017-18 health survey of married women aged 15 to 49.

Birth counts clump in clear hot spots in Sylhet and Chittagong, with cold spots in the northwest and southwest. Child marriage and low schooling for mothers raised counts at the level of the woman. Poor towns and strong local norms for large families raised them too, on their own. The team says national drives no longer suffice. Local plans must meet the blocks in each hot spot.
pmc-13578167:
Elizabeth Dudnik leads a 2026 phase II trial of first-line chemo-immunotherapy for advanced large-cell neuroendocrine lung carcinoma, a rare and aggressive cancer with little trial data. Patients received durvalumab, an immune therapy, plus platinum and etoposide chemotherapy for four cycles, then durvalumab alone on a monthly schedule. The main goal was the share of patients free of progression at twelve months.

The trial closed early for slow recruitment after twelve of twenty-two planned patients joined. Median time without progression was 4.4 months, while the twelve-month progression-free share reached 25.0 percent, above the bar the design set. Half the patients' tumours shrank measurably, and all three patients with untreated brain spread saw it clear completely inside the skull. Side effects were mostly mild, with no treatment-related deaths. The authors call the results consistent with their hopes, while stressing the small numbers.
pmc-13578267:
Wonyong Kwun and co-authors describe a 2026 rapid test for scabies, the itchy skin disease caused by a tiny mite. Standard checks rely on scraping skin and hunting for mites under a lens, a method that misses many cases. Their test copies mite DNA at one steady heat, so it needs little gear and no full lab.

A quick lysis step frees DNA straight from scrapings, skipping the usual extraction work. Two mite gene targets each lit up within about half an hour, and neither fired on human DNA or on dust mite DNA. Scrapings from patients with classic and crusted forms tested positive, while control skin stayed negative through many repeat runs. The team pitches the kit for clinics and field care.
pmc-13578667:
Julia Oh and co-authors compare chicken and human forelimb muscles in a 2026 study. The chicken embryo is a classic, low cost model for limb development and for human conditions such as extra digits and thalidomide effects. New genetic tools in chickens now allow modeling of human congenital limb conditions, including muscle changes.

No direct muscle by muscle comparison existed, blocking translation from chicken models to human surgery. Combining literature with their own observations, the authors map homologies between the two species. Muscle homology is broadly conserved, and the upper arm and forearm sections are detailed in the work.
pmc-13579367:
Omayma El Maabiche and co-authors tune solvent mixes in 2026 to pull the most protective compounds from cannabis leaves and flowers. The plant's phenolic compounds draw interest for food, drug, and cosmetic uses. Three solvents, water, alcohol, and acetone, were blended by design to test how mix polarity steers yield from each plant part.

Five lab tests gauged protective strength, and fine instruments profiled the extracts, the team reports. Flowers peaked with an acetone-rich blend; leaves with an alcohol-acetone blend. Best all-round mixes differed by part: equal thirds for flowers, a water-heavy blend for leaves. One recipe will not fit a whole plant; part-wise tuning is the practical lesson for makers.
pmc-13579467:
Morgan Birabaharan and Annie Cowell present a case of tuberculosis of the brain lining caused by a cattle linked form of the germ, in a paper from 2026. This form of TB is devastating, strikes children and people with HIV hardest, and is often found late. Outcomes stay poor even with care.

Their patient lived near the United States and Mexico border, where the cattle form is common. That form is born resistant to one of the few first line drugs that reach the brain well. Drawing on the case, the authors review proof for adding brain reaching backup drugs early when this TB form is suspected in such regions. Waiting for firm proof of the germ type can lose the narrow window in which added drugs help most.
pmc-13579667:
Irene Kindole and co-authors published this study in 2026 from a large teaching hospital in Tanzania. They asked how well two tools flag sick children who may get worse in the emergency ward. One tool is PEWS, a score built from a child's vital signs. The other is a doctor's gut call, given as a percent chance on arrival.

The team tracked 250 children classed as top urgency, and 48 of them had a bad event, such as a move to high care or death. The gut call proved the sharper tool, sorting cases with more accuracy than the score. Both tools rarely missed a child who stayed safe. The authors back gut calls as a triage aid in low-resource wards, but they warn that a single training hospital may not speak for all settings.
pmc-13579767:
Luyao Ma, Tongxi Hu, and Jinjuan Huang report gut bacteria carrying a plasmid with a potent drug breaking gene, found in a patient with a torn intestine, in a 2026 study. Three strains of an environmental species, Comamonas thiooxydans, grew from diarrheal samples on plates laced with a last line antibiotic. Gene checks confirmed each strain carried a metal based enzyme that disarms that drug class.

Full genome reads placed the gene on a movable plasmid, not the main chromosome. One early strain also held an extra DNA insert with a regulator gene. Set against 481 related genomes, the isolates proved distinct from one another yet closest to a strain from the environment. The authors warn this species may warehouse and shuttle resistance genes inside the human gut, and they urge watch lists to include it.
pmc-13579967:
Hillel Lehmann and co-authors run a small trial that varies the dosing schedule of a multiple sclerosis drug on purpose. The drug, dimethyl fumarate, often loses effect or is dropped for side effects and poor adherence. Their 2026 trial tests a constrained disorder idea: small planned variation may dodge the body's compensation habits.

Seven patients used an app that set personal doses and times within safe preset ranges for 12 weeks. The feasibility checks were app setup, adherence to the shifting schedule, trial completion, and no grave adverse events. Disability scores, a nerve damage blood marker, and MRI scans were tracked as early signals only. The study is framed as proof of concept.
pmc-13580067:
A protein called Nrf2 runs the cell's antioxidant defenses, and in colorectal cancer it plays both sides: it keeps chemical balance in healthy tissue, yet it also helps tumors resist chemotherapy. Yichen Yu and co-authors review in this paper (published 2027) how that defense system talks to the cell's programmed death pathways. Those pathways — apoptosis, ferroptosis, and autophagy — are largely steered by reactive oxygen species.

Many drugs and natural compounds kill cancer cells by forcing those reactive molecules to pile up, and cells that lean hardest on their defenses suffer most. The review gathers recent work on switching Nrf2 up or down within death-focused treatment plans. The authors propose pairing Nrf2 blockers or boosters with standard regimens to break drug resistance. They frame Nrf2 as a central node for redesigning redox-based therapy against this cancer.
pmc-13580367: Bei Zhou and co-authors read the full mitochondrial genome of a small fly, Sapromyza sexpunctata, and place it on the family tree of its group. Mitochondrial genomes are handy markers for sorting species, and this fly family had few on record. Their 2026 study reports the sequence and compares it with relatives to test how the groups within the wider superfamily connect.
pmc-13580967:
Claire Birkenheuer, Terri Edwards, David Bloom, and Joel Baines used a human nerve cell model to track how herpes simplex virus 1 changes gene activity, in a study from 2026. They grew LUHMES cells, which can be turned into mature neurons, and compared healthy cells with infected ones. Two lab methods let them separate brand-new RNA from the total RNA already present in the cell.

Infected neurons turned on viral genes far more slowly than other cell types do. During the quiet latent phase, the virus kept starting new RNA copies on all its genes, yet almost none of that RNA built up. Healthy neuron genes also kept a pause in their reading that the virus removes in skin-type cells. The contrast shows that neurons handle this virus in their own distinct way.
pmc-13581467:
Louiza Papantonatou and colleagues compare two gum thickening methods placed with dental implants in the smile zone, in a 2026 trial. Twenty five patients were assigned by chance to a collagen matrix, a graft of their own connective tissue, or no thickening. Ultrasound tracked gum thickness and cone beam scans tracked the bone plate, at placement and six months on, with tissue samples and patient reports added.

Both graft types thickened the gum clearly over doing nothing, with the matrix slightly ahead on paper. The bone plate thinned over time in every group, so thickening the gum did not save bone. Patients rated both routes much alike, though the own tissue graft stung a bit more. Lab views showed both materials settling in well. The authors call for bigger trials to settle the pairing.
pmc-13581567:
Xiuyu Zhang and co-authors pin a cattle lung outbreak in Xinjiang on a known virus type. Their 2026 study responds to a harsh winter outbreak in brown cattle in Yili. Tests found bovine parainfluenza virus type 3 in every sick animal's sample, and the team grew the virus in the lab. Full genome reads sorted the isolates into genotype C, the line now dominant in Chinese herds.

Key surface marks on the virus matched the approved vaccine strain in full. That match hints the stock vaccine may still shield herds against this line. The authors call for tighter watch and fast preventive steps in the region, as this is the first such proof there.
pmc-13581667:
Haini Wu studies how taking part in traditional music relates to mental health among ethnic minority communities in Southwest China. The study covers members of the Dai, Yi, Miao, and Dong communities, for whom the music is woven into identity and daily life. Wu asks whether taking part connects with recovery-oriented functioning, feeling supported by others, and the ability to bounce back from hardship.

The design mixed methods in sequence: surveys from 503 people came first, then interviews with 32 adults to deepen the picture. Taking part, cultural identity, joining community life, and expressing feelings through music all linked positively with recovery-oriented functioning and perceived support. Those two factors in turn linked with resilience, and the model explained about seventy-three percent of its variance. Interviews added themes of expressing feelings, cultural continuity, community cohesion, and hope for the future.
pmc-13581867:
Rojin Adabdokht and co-authors validate in 2026 a commercial AI tool that segments teeth in intraoral scans, comparing it with expert markings and with a transparent method of their own. Automated tooth segmentation could speed digital dental work, but commercial tools are black boxes with unclear reach. Their two-level check used 126 expert-annotated clinical scans with crowding, gaps, and missing teeth.

The open method paired an object detector for tooth finding and numbering with a 3D segmentation network. It trained on eighty open scans. Scores used overlap measures and numbering accuracy. Comparisons were made per scan and by region, front versus back teeth.
pmc-13582367:
Misaki Hamashima and co-authors break test crowns for baby teeth to learn which designs hold in this 2026 paper. Children's molars get computer-made crowns milled or printed from several materials. The team varied the crown's edge shape: knife-edge, chamfer, and deep chamfer. One hundred eighty crowns were bonded to standard test teeth and loaded until they cracked.

Material and edge shape interacted strongly. One milled material topped the load chart with knife-edge margins, yet its failures wrecked the tooth below. Another printed material led with deep chamfers but split between layers. Softer options broke at lower loads but in repairable ways. The authors advise weighing failure style alongside strength.
pmc-13582767:
Shir Ginosar Yaari, Noa Boker Segal, and Maya Tamir test whether feeling worse makes a person worse at cheering someone else, in a 2026 study. Two experiments paired a helper with a person facing an upsetting stimulus. In one, sixty four pairs of strangers took part; in the other, one hundred ten pairs of closer partners. Helpers rated their own feelings, then tried to lift the other person's mood.

The pattern held in both rounds. Helpers who reacted more strongly left their partners feeling worse than calmer helpers did. Strong reactors also reached for fewer tactics, a sign of lower effort. The authors borrow the airplane rule for their advice: settle your own feelings first, then turn to the other person's. The finding matters for support work, care roles, and close bonds alike.
pmc-13583067:
Donna Ruth, Margaret Hammersla, and Andrea Tanner report a 2026 quality project from a rural elementary school in Montana. Children with anxiety often show up at the school health office with aches that have no clear cause. The school nurse began watching for pupils who came in three or more times in six weeks with such complaints. Those pupils were then offered a standard anxiety check, filled in by both the child and a parent.

Of 430 pupils, eight met the visit rule, six finished the check, and five screened positive for anxiety. Each of those five got a short talk with the nurse and a referral for counseling. The authors present the plan as a workable way for school nurses to spot anxiety early where mental health care is scarce.
pmc-13583167: Gen Matsuura and co-authors report a heart ablation case in a 2026 paper. Pulsed field ablation treats atrial fibrillation with electric pulses, but its safety beside a leadless pacemaker was unsure. Their patient needed wide ablation that reached the left atrial back wall and both great veins, including a persistent left superior vena cava. The work went ahead in full with no interference to the pacemaker, which supports careful use of the method in such patients.
pmc-13583267:
Elona Bebla and Attiya Haroon report a case in 2026 of rapidly spreading skin calcification in a 52-year-old woman with dermatomyositis. Calcium deposits under the skin affect roughly one in five adults with this muscle and skin disease at most. Her case moved unusually fast despite ongoing immune-suppressing therapy.

Biopsy confirmed calcification within three months of first presentation. Deposits spread to both armpits, the front chest wall, and upper thighs, limiting function. Antibody panel results were still pending at report time. The authors stress limited treatment options once calcification sets in, and the need for early firm disease control.
pmc-13583467:
Dapkutė, Laurinavičius and their co-authors present a national case study of Lithuania's digital health system, listed for 2026. Lithuania is one of few European countries with a fully centralized national platform, making it a useful case for others.

The study used long-range document analysis of policy, law, audits and official statistics over twenty-five years. The system grew from scattered projects in the early two thousands into a nationwide platform running since the middle of the next decade. Use of electronic records then became required, and all reimbursed medicines moved to electronic prescribing. Lessons cover governance, data sharing and adoption hurdles.
pmc-13583667:
Yaqi Feng, Jingxia Zhang, and Rong Zhang review what is known about the brothers and sisters of autistic people, and how they fare. Searching three databases for work from 2021 to 2026, the authors organise findings by setting, by age, and along a line from risk to resilience. The picture is mixed by design: the same sibling may report loneliness, anxiety, and strain from extra duties, yet also empathy, maturity, and pride in the role.

What tips the balance includes the autistic child's own difficulties, the sibling's age and sex, parents' mental health, family openness, and support at school, with culture shaping what the role means. Support groups and play-based training proved workable, and one proper trial improved relationship quality, but firm proof of benefit is still missing. The authors call for long-term studies and care not to paint ordinary mixed feelings as illness.
pmc-13583767:
Mousavi leads a team setting out a trial of gut-focused help for mood in pregnant women with diabetes of pregnancy, in a 2026 protocol paper. This form of diabetes raises the risk of anxiety and low mood severalfold. Signaling between gut and brain offers a possible route to prevent them.

About a hundred women will be assigned to a capsule of live bacteria plus fiber, a diet aimed at gut health, or a dummy capsule. Care runs from diagnosis in mid-pregnancy until a month after birth. Main outcomes are low mood and pregnancy-related anxiety near term, with mood after birth checked later. Measures of metabolism and birth outcomes are also tracked. Everyone receives standard healthy diet teaching. The plan has ethics approval and public registration. Results will test whether gut-targeted care prevents mood problems around birth.
pmc-13583867:
Andrea Bernasconi and co-authors wrote a study from 2026 on how WhatsApp quietly became a channel for children's health advice in Pakistan. Parents and doctors increasingly consult by instant message, outside any formal system. Little was known about how that practice works day to day. The team interviewed nineteen parents and twelve health providers across Punjab who already used the app this way.

Access ran on social ties and provider goodwill, filling gaps the formal system leaves. Consultations worked by what the team calls digital auscultation: photos, voice notes, and video standing in for the exam room. Parents and providers jointly weighed uncertain calls and informal thresholds for escalating care. The channel clearly widened access and convenience. It also traded away privacy, blurred safety lines, and loaded providers with unpaid, always-on work. The team urges guidelines and training shaped to this grassroots reality.
pmc-13583967:
Navyte, Gillmeister, and Kumari link partner touch to later health in older adults. Touch is a form of social support tied to stress control. Data came from a U.S. aging study with 787 adults. The mean age was 73.34 years. Health was read at two points five years apart.

Health load was split into metabolic, heart, and hormone domains. Frequent partner touch tied to a better metabolic score over time. The link held after adjusting for other factors. Touch from other close adults showed weaker ties. The authors say daily touch may leave a long mark on body systems in old age.
pmc-13584167:
Cristabella Fortna and Lisa Fredin present a theory study, published in 2026, on iridium compounds used as photocatalysts. These metal compounds soak up light and drive chemical reactions, and they are prized for lasting long in their excited state. Most past work focused on just two parent forms, leaving other shapes poorly mapped.

Using quantum calculations, the pair charted the excited-state surfaces of six parent compounds and their variants. They tested how adding nitrogen links, turning links around the metal, and stiffening the outer parts changed behavior. Some excited states help reactions, while others waste the light as heat. Their maps explain why these compounds work so well and give design rules for longer-lived states. Chemists planning new light-driven catalysts can use the results as a guide.
pmc-13584967:
Bashir A Akhoon, Lakshay Anand, and Kendall R Corbin build a gene base for pulp-making germs in a 2026 paper on germ data. Such germs spin a prized pulp used in a wide span of craft goods round the world. They sit in one germ clan yet spread wide across its lines in kind and form.

No base yet served this group's study next to kin germs, the team notes in the work. Their base joins genome sets, gene notes, and joint read tools in one home on the web. Two germ lines form the core of the base at launch in the end.
pmc-13585067:
Teng Yang and Longxiang Li model indoor radon exposure across the United States in a 2026 study. Radon gas is the top cause of lung cancer in nonsmokers, yet past maps used only averages that hide local spread. The team set out to model the full spread of radon levels for each postal area.

They drew on more than six million short term radon tests from 2000 to 2021. About half of all areas had at least one in five homes above the national action level. High exposure areas clustered in the Midwest. The data set lets residents judge their own risk and lets health teams aim fixes where they count most.
pmc-13585567:
Bo Youl Choi marks a special issue in a 2026 editorial for a Korean public health weekly. Four papers in the issue cover three diseases passed from beasts or bites, plus a joint human-animal health view. Choi traces how the journal has covered each theme since 2008 and what the new papers add.

Malaria takes the longest thread. The disease near died out in the Republic of Korea by the late 1970s, then came back near the border zone in 1993. A new paper maps a Korean plan to certify local wiping-out, zone by zone, toward a 2030 goal. Choi also notes how malaria there tracks patterns in North Korea, a call for joint watch. Other threads sum past work on brucellosis and a tick fever.
pmc-13585667: Rieza Soelaeman and five co-authors surveyed United States adults in August 2025 about wastewater surveillance, the practice of testing sewage to track viruses in a community. About half of those surveyed had heard of the practice. Nearly four in five said that information about viruses from such testing was important. The authors argue that health agencies should engage communities more about how the testing works and why it matters, so the data are understood and trusted.
pmc-13585967:
Alessandro De Vita and co-authors reviewed this 2026 state of gene sequencing in sarcoma research. Sarcomas are rare, varied cancers where microscope work alone often cannot pin the type. Fast sequencing now finds the fusions, mutations, and copy changes that define subtypes and sometimes point to drugs. The review maps where the technology genuinely helps.

Sequencing has widened detection of both common and rare changes, including druggable rearrangements. Yet its clinical value depends on the subtype, sample quality, and expert interpretation at reference centers. Older tests still complement it. The authors urge care in drawing the line between research findings and bedside decisions, presenting sequencing as powerful but context-bound rather than a universal answer.
pmc-13586067:
