Did the last common ancestor of apes and humans walk on its knuckles? Laura Hunter and co-authors test that idea through wrist bones in this 2026 study. They measured carpal shapes across many primates with varied gaits, using a math method that captures curved surfaces, then compared distances between species grouped by how they move.

Nearly all traits once called knuckle-walking traits turned up broadly across primates, and several were shared with Asian apes. A few African ape traits were shared only with humans, which could hint at knuckle-walking ancestry. Still, African ape wrists look far from specialized for that gait. Few changes would be needed to evolve it, and an ape-like wrist remains a sound model for the ancestor.
pmc-13586467:
A blood test for stomach wear could spare many people a camera exam, and one such test reads a pair of stomach-made proteins in the blood. Sun-Young Lee reviews how to read that test in a 2026 paper, since its meaning shifts with the kind and spread of stomach wear. Two very different diseases wear the stomach down: immune attack and a common germ infection.

In immune-driven wear, the first protein sinks hard and a stomach hormone climbs, marking deep wear of the stomach's main body. Germ-driven wear gives a softer, patchier signal. The test shines at spotting severe wear and grading risk, but it misses early wear too often. Lee notes that test brands use quite different cut-offs, so a number means little without knowing the kit. Paired with the hormone reading, the test helps rank cancer risk.
pmc-13586567:
Vaneli Colombo Rossi, Ana Carolina Constantini, and Carlos Takahiro Chone test a device that helps people speak again after their voice box is removed. Their 2026 study enrolls fifteen patients who had a total laryngectomy and had failed to learn esophageal voice, speech made by burping air through the throat, with standard therapy.

A thin catheter, passed through the nose to the throat segment, directly stimulates the tissue over twelve weekly sessions. Nine of the fifteen patients gained an effective speaking voice, and the rest produced usable sound. Patients rated their own voices better afterward, though expert ratings did not shift clearly. The device offers a new aid for a hard skill.
pmc-13586667:
Simon Ntumi surveyed more than a thousand Ghanaian senior high school teachers in 2026 about the psychology behind fair grading. A teacher who is exhausted or distressed may mark differently from one who is settled, and fairness in assessment decides students' futures. The study, correlational in design, recruited teachers from public and private schools by stratified random sampling. It measured them with checked instruments. These covered mindfulness, psychological distress, general mental health, and emotional exhaustion. They also covered job satisfaction. And their own perceptions of grading bias and fairness.

Mindfulness emerged as the hub factor. Teachers scoring higher on mindfulness also noted better mental health, greater job satisfaction. And a stronger sense that their assessment was fair. While scoring lower on distress, emotional exhaustion, and grading bias. The pattern suggests teacher well-being is not a private matter but an input into the justice of the grades students receive.
pmc-13586867:
Qiang Tao and co-authors package an immune stimulant inside heat-generating nanoparticles to attack liver cancer on two fronts. Their 2026 study concerns hepatocellular carcinoma, the commonest liver cancer, whose advanced stages resist treatment. The drug they carry, resiquimod, wakes both arms of immunity but dissolves poorly, clears fast, and poisons at dose.

A copper framework particle loads the drug and releases it in acid, as found around tumors. Shone with light, the particles heat the tumor while the freed drug rallies immune attack. The design answers the drug's flaws with a carrier and adds a second weapon, aiming to make a cold tumor hot in both senses.
pmc-13587067:
Dominik Linz and Dobromir Dobrev gather recent highlights on atrial fibrillation care from their journal's pages. Their 2026 update stresses a stubborn fact: the rhythm disorder stays partly understood, and even with ablation gains, drugs remain the backbone of therapy for most patients. Success tracks the time spent in the abnormal rhythm more than its surface form.

The roundup walks through outcomes data, from heart failure patients, where new or old fibrillation raises risk, to stroke prediction sharpened by imaging the atrial appendage and blood markers. Possible links to cognitive decline through reduced brain blood flow get attention too. Better detection and finer sorting of patient types, the editors argue, should unlock tailored therapy. The piece doubles as a map of where the field's open questions sit.
pmc-13587567:
Yong Feng and co-authors published a research paper in 2026 comparing two strains of the monkeypox virus in mice and testing antiviral drugs against both. The newer strain spreading in Africa seems harsher than the one that circled the globe from 2022. The team built a nose-infection mouse model to compare them fairly.

The newer strain killed at about a tenth of the dose the older one needed. It also advanced faster, loaded the lungs more heavily late on, and damaged them worse. Single-cell reads showed unlike immune landscapes in the lungs. Both standard antivirals worked, though one needed a higher dose against the new strain.
pmc-13588967:
Maria Ilenia De Bartolo and co-authors test, in a 2026 study, whether a steady infusion of a dopamine drug calms the overexcitable motor cortex seen in Parkinson's disease. The drug, apomorphine, is pumped under the skin and is known to ease symptoms in moderate to advanced disease. Whether it also fixes the cortex's abnormal excitability and plasticity was unknown.

Patients were tested before treatment and again after one, twelve, and twenty four weeks on the infusion. Magnetic stimulation over the motor cortex measured how easily it fires, through recruitment curves and response sizes at several intensities. Paired pulse protocols probed inhibition and facilitation inside the cortex. Plasticity protocols tested how the cortex rewires after stimulation. If a symptom drug also normalizes cortical behavior, it may slow the maladaptive side of the disease, not just mask it. The study links bedside benefit to brain mechanism.
pmc-13589167:
Carlos Rivera Lopez and co-authors published this 2026 study on a simpler MRI scan for men watching prostate cancer. Many low-risk patients choose active surveillance over quick treatment. They need repeat scans to catch any turn for the worse. The standard scan uses three parts, while a shorter version uses two, dropping the contrast dye step.

The team compared both scans in 129 men at their center, with about 29 months between scans. The later short scans found more flagged spots, yet the spread of risk grades looked much the same. A matched subgroup also had repeat biopsies after each scan type. The study checks whether the shorter scan changes risk grades at the same rate, which would let clinics save time and skip the dye.
pmc-13589267:
Dongning Chen and co-authors uncover an unexpected second career for the XIST RNA. Their 2026 study starts from XIST's famous job, silencing one X chromosome in females. It then asks whether XIST also steers the adhesome, the network of genes that glue cells to their surroundings and feed cancer stemness.

Knocking XIST down in ovarian cancer cells rewired adhesome gene expression and the pathways below it. Across normal and tumor tissue data sets, XIST levels correlated with adhesome genes in patterns tied to stemness. Network analysis places XIST in the nucleus alongside specific adhesion genes, and survival analysis links the pairings to patient outcomes. Among well-mapped long RNAs, the authors conclude, XIST stands out as a modulator of the adhesion network.
pmc-13589367:
Le Liu and five co-authors test a tweaked fat-burn diet plus drills gainst drills lone in young kids with autism. Their chance trial appeared in twenty twenty-six. Sixty-two kids at a Hefei mother-child ward in twenty twenty-four to twenty twenty-five were split to two packs of thirty-one. Both had ward drills on week days and home drills on rest days for two months.

The diet pack also ate a set fat-burn plan with a food powder. Both packs eased on two set sign forms. The diet pack eased more on both. The team call the diet fit in the short run.
pmc-13589867:
Anja Schroff and co-authors track radioactive iodine in rats in a 2026 study, with an eye to human risk. Iodine-131 is used in thyroid therapy and is also a fallout hazard; after Chernobyl, thyroid cancer rose among children in contaminated areas, above all young girls. Why age and sex shape the harm is not fully clear.

Male and female rats were exposed at five or seventeen weeks of age, roughly childhood and late adolescence. The team measured where the iodine traveled and the dose each organ absorbed. If young females concentrate more dose in the thyroid, that fact could explain part of the Chernobyl pattern and sharpen emergency guidance.
pmc-13589967:
Haotian Zhang and five co-authors published a cohort study in twenty twenty-six on how depression shapes frailty over time in older Chinese adults living with chronic pain. Pain and low mood often arrive together, and frailty raises the risk of falls, disability, and death. The team wanted to find who slides fastest.

Using eight years of a national aging survey, they followed four thousand seven hundred seventy-eight people aged forty-five and older. Three frailty paths emerged: low, moderate, and high. Over sixty percent had depressive symptoms, and those symptoms raised the odds of landing in worse trajectories. The results argue for treating mood as part of frailty prevention in people with pain.
pmc-13590267:
Shuting Li and Rongrong Bai mapped a drug target where fat meets power plants in two thousand twenty-six. Fat droplets and mitochondria touch at regulated sites. Those contacts now look measurable and druggable. Liver and muscle studies mapped the toolkit first. Lung disease has lagged despite deep lipid dependence. Surfactant making and fat handling define lung work.

The review builds a matrix across lung cell types. Evidence is graded direct, indirect, or borrowed. Scaffold proteins and tether molecules anchor the sites. Their shapes and switches behave like drug variables. Translation routes for lung therapy are laid out. Spatial pharmacology gains a respiratory beachhead.
pmc-13591067:
Buse Bekar and Handan Sevim Akan test a plant compound against cancer in this 2026 study. The compound, bergaptol, belongs to a family found in plants such as figs and citrus. The team treated three cancer cell lines, from breast, liver, and cervix, plus vessel-lining cells, and used healthy skin cells as the comparison group.

Bergaptol killed cancer and vessel cells selectively, sparing the healthy cells. Treated cells died by the cell's self-destruct path and their division cycles stalled. In three-dimensional tumor balls, the compound shrank the balls and cut their vessel cell content. A test on chick embryo membranes confirmed fewer new vessels formed. The authors argue the dual action, against tumors and against their blood supply, merits further study.
pmc-13591167:
Sara Penrod, Zoe Samson, and Stephanie C Chan describe, in 2026, how 68 adults with disorders of consciousness fared in acute care after severe brain injury. Such patients range from coma to near wakefulness, and most prior work looks at later rehab stages. At a major trauma hospital the team tracked awareness with a standard recovery scale. They also tracked breathing, throat tube care, and swallowing.

On arrival most patients were in unresponsive wakefulness, yet by discharge none stayed in coma and many had emerged. Most patients with breathing tubes tried speaking valves, and over two thirds had the tube removed. Penrod and the team argue that structured checks and rehab should start in the first days, not weeks later.
pmc-13591367:
Abbas Hussain and co-authors review why combo therapy stalls in head and neck cancer in a 2026 paper. Locally advanced squamous cell cancer of the head and neck stays hard to cure even with layered care. Immune checkpoint drugs added to chemoradiation gave thin survival gains in big trials, blocked by tangled resistance.

The review sorts the blocks: suppressive tumor surrounds, weak DNA damage replies, low oxygen shifts, metabolic rewiring, and HER family signals. Counter moves span nano delivery, dual blocks on growth receptors, and marks like PD-L1 and tumor DNA in blood. Fresh checkpoints and cell therapies join the list.
pmc-13591767:
Israa Ismael, Xin Luo, and Sen Li study a 2026 program that pairs new English teachers in Egypt with online mentors, with help from an AI tool. The study asks whether this kind of support can raise the trainees' belief in their own skill and their grasp of feelings in the classroom. Fifty trainees took part in the work.

Half of the group got structured mentoring, shared online tools, and feedback from the Gemini AI system. The other half followed the normal training routine. The first group showed large gains in both self-belief and emotional skill. Their own accounts also showed a shift toward teaching that puts students at the center and gives more room for thought and change.
pmc-13591967:
Narangarav Nyamdag and co-authors reviewed this 2026 record of drug prescribing for COVID-19 pneumonia in Mongolia. Border closures and shortages left Mongolian hospitals short of the globally advised antiviral drugs, so clinicians improvised with alternatives and heavy antibiotic use. The team pulled charts for 1,012 adults treated at the country's two largest referral hospitals during 2021.

Antibiotics reached 87.6 percent of patients, a striking rate for a viral illness. One antibiotic family, cephalosporins, went to nearly nine in ten patients, with a second family reaching over a third. The study compares the two hospitals' habits in detail. Its real-world record helps future planners judge where stewardship and supply planning failed during the pandemic.
pmc-13592667:
Serena Kao and three colleagues gather what remote care did for women's mental health during and after the pandemic. Phone and video therapy spread fast, yet results for women stayed scattered across small studies. Their review searched five databases through March 2026 and kept 57 studies with 13,457 women in 24 countries. Trials were pooled for depression, anxiety, and stress outcomes, while other designs fed summaries of acceptability and satisfaction.

Remote care beat waiting lists and usual care on all three outcomes. Depression improved most, with a moderate effect, anxiety close behind, and stress gains modest. Results swung widely between settings, so certainty stayed moderate. Benefits held in women only samples. Kao and the team call telehealth a scalable route to care while demanding stronger trials.
pmc-13593067:
Ojemolon and co-authors report in a 2026 case study a rare cause of troubled swallowing in a patient with Goltz syndrome. The syndrome, also called focal dermal hypoplasia, is a rare gene disorder that warps skin, bone, and other tissues as a child develops. Growths like those in this case often dot the mouth and throat, but rarely the food pipe.

Here, several large wart-like growths in the food pipe blocked swallowing. Doctors removed them through a scope threaded down the throat, a method called endoscopic mucosal resection, and the blockage eased. The case widens the map of where this syndrome can strike.
pmc-13593567:
Eleanor Hammond and co-authors audit big food firms in a 2026 UK study. The makers of packaged food and drink can speed or block the shift to diets that are good for bodies and for the planet. How much room they have to improve, using their own product lines, was not well measured.

The team scored the full ranges of 44 major UK makers for nutrition and footprint. Scores varied widely between firms selling the same kinds of goods, and even within one firm's own range. Swapping the mix toward each firm's better lines could bring large gains. The headroom sits inside portfolios that already exist.
pmc-13593867:
Wenjie Zhu, Wenping Zhu, and Yizhuo Fan traced how heavy internet use links to a wandering mind in college students, in a 2026 study. Phones keep students half-present in class, and mind-wandering marks weak attentional control. Nearly three and a half thousand Chinese students filled in scales for internet addiction, mind-wandering, physical activity, and self-control. The team modeled the paths among the four.

Addiction scores rose with mind-wandering and fell with activity and self-control. Activity and self-control each tied to less wandering, and active students showed stronger self-control. The model found a direct path from addiction to wandering, plus indirect paths through activity alone, self-control alone, and a chain of the two. The authors suggest that campus programs pairing exercise with self-control training could steady attention. They stress the data show links, not proof of cause.
pmc-13594467:
Alba Rio-Ropero and co-authors map persulfidation in lung lining cells in a 2026 study of defense against a harmful fungus. Persulfidation adds a sulfur group to proteins and can change how they act during stress and infection.

The team listed which proteins gain the mark when cells meet Aspergillus fumigatus, with or without a sulfide donor. The mark seems to shape immunity through RNA handling and protein making. One key protein, calprotectin, needs the mark to keep its antifungal power under stress. The findings link a small chemical change to broad and targeted immune strength in the lung.
pmc-13594567:
Jiani Liu and co-authors study early life antibiotic use and later kidney cancer in a 2026 cohort study. Antibiotics have been linked to cancer risk, but proof for kidney cancer from early use was thin. The team used a large British biobank with about one hundred forty eight thousand people who reported long or repeated use in childhood or youth. All were cancer free at the start.

Such early use linked to a forty eight percent higher risk of kidney cancer after adjustment for other factors. Part of the link ran through adult body fat, from a small share by waist measures to a larger share by body fat percent. The authors call for studies with recorded prescription data to confirm the finding. Readers see a long shadow from early drug exposure.
pmc-13594867:
Al Jumlat Ahmed and co-authors review speck-born boosts for heat-to-charge stuffs, where the speck kind, host match, and seam craft rule the gain. Mixed stuffs let smiths bend charge flow and heat flow at once, the pair that sets the worth mark. Their 2026 review walks two speck clans, the coal clan and the boron clan, cross four host kinds: bismuth mixes, a copper salt, oxides, and bend films.

Each host takes seams at its own price. Bismuth hosts spoil swift if specks pile; the copper salt hosts wide seams and keeps top marks. Oxides gain charge flow yet leak heat too fast to cash it. Bend hosts must weigh force, wear, and yield as one.
pmc-13595167:
Irianti Bahana Maulida Reyaan and co-authors translate and test a pharmacy satisfaction survey for Indonesia. Their paper from 2026 deals with the PSPSQ 2.0, a form that asks patients how they rate pharmacist services. No fit, tested Indonesian form had been reported before.

Patients came from town pharmacies and public health centers, filling an anonymous online form; two hundred took part. The form went through two way translation, expert review, and trial talks with patients. Content scores were high, and a fit index showed the items hang together well. Factor tests probed the form shape, and two scales checked inner consistency. The authors present the form as ready for wider use and study.
pmc-13595267:
Faraz Pathan and Kathryn Williams review how obesity tangles with heart failure in mechanism, diagnosis, and treatment. Their review was published in twenty twenty-six. The two conditions now overlap so often that each complicates the other.

Fresh definitions of obesity open the discussion. Direct and indirect paths from excess weight to heart failure are laid out. Obesity also distorts the usual tests, clouding both scan images and the standard blood marker. Treatment evidence is weighed for both heart failure types, weak and preserved pumping. New gut-hormone-based weight drugs get a safety review. The paper gives clinicians one map of a double burden.
pmc-13595467:
Vojtěch Mýlek and co-authors tracked how teens judge meeting online contacts in person in this 2026 study. The team surveyed 2,500 Czech adolescents, aged eleven to sixteen, three times over a span of time. They asked how risky and how rewarding the teens saw such meetings, and how common they took them to be among friends.

Seeing meetings as more dangerous in outcome led teens to meet less; seeing likely benefits led them to meet more. Experience fed back the other way: teens who met more came to see more benefit and less danger. Feeling that a meeting might happen raised meeting counts, against the team's guess. Friends' habits, oddly, predicted nothing. Prevention work must handle this two-way pull.
pmc-13595567:
Ying Dai and Bo Han review smart materials as a way to tune the immune response in viral heart inflammation, published in 2026. This illness is a leading cause of sudden heart death in young people. It can also lead to a stretched, weak heart over time.

Good outcomes hinge on clearing the virus while stopping immune attack on the heart. Broad immune-suppressing drugs often fail, since they cannot act at the right place and time. The review covers new platforms such as fitted heart patches, engineered cell vesicles, and materials that respond to force. These aim to calm harmful inflammation early, without weakening the body's own defense against the virus itself.
pmc-13597167:
Rahmi Canbar, Tugba Melike Parlak, Muhittin Uslu, and Enver Yazar test a drug's safety in sheep, in a study published in 2026. The drug, mefepronic acid, aids bile flow in several species and is used in sheep without a label for them. Little was known about its safety in sheep, so the team checked blood signs of organ strain.

Ten sheep got the drug by muscle injection once a day for three days. Blood taken over three days showed brief shifts in stress markers and one heart enzyme, plus drops in urea and two fat measures. A key heart damage marker did not rise, and liver and kidney values stayed sound. The authors judge the drug free of major harm in sheep at this dose, while noting the brief shifts deserve watching.
pmc-13597267:
Ke Liu and seven co-authors study leadership and innovation among intensive care nurses in a paper from two thousand twenty-six. Responsible leadership may spur nurses to innovate, but the path was unclear. The team tested whether feeling like an insider and speaking up carry that effect.

They surveyed three hundred seventy-two nurses in three large hospitals in northern China in early two thousand twenty-five. All four traits were positively linked. Responsible leadership raised innovation both directly and through the two middle steps, each carrying about a fifth of the total effect. The two steps also chained together for a smaller share. The authors advise leaders to build belonging and open communication so nurses share ideas.
pmc-13597367:
Yuan Xu and five co-authors study in 2026 restless legs syndrome in patients whose kidneys have failed and who depend on dialysis. The syndrome brings an urge to move the legs that wrecks sleep and daily life, yet it is often missed because doctors and patients know little about it.

The team gathered clinical and lab data from one hundred forty-seven dialysis patients at Xiangyang Central Hospital. They counted how many had the syndrome, hunted for factors that raised the risk, and measured its effect on sleep and quality of life. The study aims to help dialysis units spot and treat a problem patients quietly endure.
pmc-13597467:
Marina Ritchie and eight co-authors ask trial volunteers how satisfied they feel about taking part. Their 2026 study draws on a preclinical Alzheimer's trial. Participants had no symptoms yet faced years of study visits. Their experience data can shape how future trials are run.

A satisfaction survey ran from the first week to week two hundred forty. Over ninety percent answered every item positively. Helping others was the motive most often affirmed. Design features drew the most complaints. Social motives grew warmer over time. Those lukewarm about joining at the start were likelier to quit. Early satisfaction checks may flag who needs support to stay.
pmc-13598567:
Maitikuerban and colleagues build and validate a questionnaire that measures how people with chronic disease look for health information, a habit that shapes daily self care. Existing tools cover only active searching, missing the passive ways information reaches patients through feeds and pushes. Their 2026 study, published in Chinese, grounds the design in Wilson's model of information behavior. Items are drafted from literature and team debate, refined through expert consultation, and fielded with 368 patients across six Zhejiang cities.

The instrument holds thirty items in four dimensions: information needs, channels used, searching and obtaining, and judging what was found. Reliability ran high, and experts backed nearly every item. Factor analysis pulled out three shared factors covering three quarters of the variation, and a confirmatory model fit well. Nurses and doctors, the authors argue, now have a sound tool for spotting where a patient's information habits need coaching.
pmc-13599667:
Cuong and co-authors build and check a lab test that puts a number on antibodies attacking the body's own interferon gamma. These antibodies mark an adult-onset immune disorder seen mostly in southeast Asia, where patients suffer repeated severe infections. Current tests give rough readings that vary between labs, which makes tracking patients hard. The new test is a quantitative ELISA reporting a standard inhibitory measure, validated over eight months of routine service.

The assay stayed linear across a wide range of antibody levels and held steady under quality-control checks. It also separated active cases from inactive ones more accurately than the older semi-quantitative method. The authors present the test, with its built-in quality-control plan, as ready for routine lab use. For clinical labs in the region, the gain is a standard measure that can follow a patient over time and across hospitals.
pmc-13600767:
Ghari and four co-authors report a 2026 study of how udder infection changes the trace elements in goat milk. The team infected one udder half in nine healthy goats with one of two strains of the bacterium Staphylococcus aureus. One strain forms biofilms, sticky layers that help germs persist, and the other does not. Milk was sampled many times over hours and days, before and after antibiotic treatment.

Eight elements were measured in the milk, including calcium, selenium, zinc, and potassium. Goats given the biofilm-forming strain released more calcium and selenium into their milk at several time points. Their milk also held more potassium and phosphorus just before treatment. The authors link the pattern to stronger gland damage from biofilm strains.
pmc-13601067:
A single gene can yield many protein variants through RNA splicing and editing, but bulk sequencing hides which cell types do what. Magnus Harnau and co-authors present two tools that read these processes inside single cells using fluorescence ratios. The first, CRYSPER, reports on standard and unusual splice site use. The second builds on it to switch on protein production in response to a specific kind of RNA editing.

With the first tool they found unusual splice choices varying by cell type, including a wobble base at a spot textbooks treat as fixed. The patchy use of hidden splice sites points to cell-specific control of splicing. The second tool is the first to let a human editing enzyme trigger protein expression on demand, which could counter faulty editing or deliver any chosen protein inside the right cells only.
pmc-13601267:
Chelangat Sitonik and co-authors test early maturing, drought tolerant maize hybrids across many sites in a 2026 paper. Breeders need hybrids that yield well and stay stable when weather and soil change from place to place. The team grew three way hybrids in six test settings in Tanzania over two wet seasons in 2018 and 2019.

Sites ranged from no drought to severe drought, and yield data were split by stress level. Two linked models were used to separate hybrid effects from site effects and their interplay. The work picks out hybrids that hold up across settings and those that fit a set stress level, which guides seed choice for dry areas.
pmc-13601367:
Katharina Platzgummer and fifteen co-authors present a 2026 study of two sand fly borne infections in dogs in Austria and Germany. The parasite behind one disease is common around the Mediterranean, where dogs serve as its main reservoir. The second group, a set of viruses, matters mostly for human health, but dogs make good sentinels for its spread.

Neither country is thought to have local spread of these agents. The team tested blood from 1,520 dogs, split evenly between the two countries. They looked for antibodies that mark past exposure to each agent. The results gauge how far the risk has crept into central Europe.
pmc-13601867:
Vesa Putkinen, Maya Rassouli, and Lauri Nummenmaa reviewed in 2026 how music expresses emotion and how listeners share those feelings. Music stirs strong emotion even though it carries no direct news about survival. The review covers brain and mind studies of how musical emotion works in social life.

A combined analysis of brain imaging studies found overlap between brain systems for making music and for emotion. Yet musical expression differs from faces, bodies, and speech in its timing, context, and live back-and-forth feel. Words and other cues can also shift what a piece seems to express. Readers get a broad account of why people use music to reach each other. It can guide work on therapy, teaching, and social bonding through sound.
pmc-13602367:
An interview with Igor Limaev, a research pathologist in Moscow, published in 2026 in the journal Biology Open. The journal's First Person series speaks with first authors of selected papers about their careers. His paper profiled skeletal muscle in mice carrying a gene fault that causes dysferlinopathy, a muscle-wasting disease, at the stage when the illness first shows.

Limaev did that research as an undergraduate in a lab at Kazan Federal University and now studies rare muscle diseases at a national surgery research center in Moscow. He explains that he became a pathologist out of a childhood drive to organize knowledge into one logical system, calling pathology the trunk from which other medical sciences grow. He chose muscle disease because the field is still largely uncharted. The interview pairs his personal path with a plain account of the muscle study.
pmc-13602467:
Ting Pan and three colleagues check in 2026 whether two questionnaires measure self-directed weight stigma in women after childbirth. New mothers face intense pressure to lose pregnancy weight quickly, and turning society's weight bias inward can harm mental health. Two scales exist for this, the Weight Self-Stigma Questionnaire and the Weight Bias Internalization Scale, but neither had been validated in postpartum women. The team gave both to 476 Chinese mothers averaging about 31 years old.

Both scales proved internally consistent and tracked with body mass index, felt stigma, worse psychological outcomes, and restrained or emotional eating. Their structures differed: the self-stigma questionnaire's two-factor structure held up, while the bias scale's single-factor structure did not. The authors recommend the self-stigma questionnaire for postpartum use now. The bias scale needs revision and fresh validation before it can be trusted with new mothers.
pmc-13602767:
Qiong Wu and co-authors build food-grade nanoparticles from black fungus extract in a 2026 paper. They first compared two ways to extract the fungus polysaccharide: ultra-high pressure and hot water. The pressure method gave better emulsifying power and stronger anti-inflammatory action in lab tests.

They then paired the extract with soy protein to form composite nanoparticles using ultrasound. The best recipe used equal parts, mid-level power, and ten minutes of treatment. The particles were small, stable, and evenly dispersed. Bonds of several kinds held the network together. The authors propose the particles as carriers for functional foods.
pmc-13602967:
Shroog M Al-Shahrani, Abdulaziz A Al-Askar, Kevin D Hyde, and Fatimah Al-Otibi study, in a 2026 paper, friendly fungi that may protect coffee roots from a damaging rival. Root disease caused by Fusarium fungi is spreading on Saudi coffee farms. The team collected Trichoderma fungi from coffee root zones and tested how they fight two Fusarium strains, probing three suspected weapons at once.

In paired cultures, the Trichoderma isolates grew about three times faster than their rivals, crowding them for space. Two strains blocked the worst Fusarium by over seventy-seven percent. Chemical analysis found sixty-nine scent compounds released by the defenders, some with known antifungal action. Math modeling split the credit among fast growth, scent diversity, and single key compounds. The authors frame the native fungi as a greener shield for coffee roots.
pmc-13603167:
Lee and co-authors present a lab device that pumps fluid in a loop through tiny channels where barrier tissues grow on chips. Such tissues, like blood vessel linings, stay healthy only under the right flow pressure, and one-way flow at the right strength is hard to achieve while reusing small fluid volumes. Their 2026 design covers a wide range of flow rates in a single system.

The team grew human vein lining cells in the device and confirmed the cells aligned with the flow, as healthy lining should. A math model lets users compute settings for any tissue they wish to grow. The system can recirculate as little as a tenth of a milliliter or as much as five. The authors pitch it for testing rare cells and costly compounds.
pmc-13603267:
John Dangerfield and two co-authors describe two hard cases of chronic wounds in a 2026 case report. Both patients were older adults whose wounds had failed to heal despite standard care and advanced products. The team treated them with a gel-like carrier holding the secretome, the mix of signals released by stem cells from Wharton's jelly.

One patient was a 95-year-old woman with poor blood flow and a two-year ankle ulcer. The other was a 69-year-old man with a foot ulcer that had lasted a year. Both wounds closed fully after about 27 and 28 weeks of care. The authors note that two cases cannot prove the treatment works.
pmc-13603367:
Evgeny Pislyagin and co-authors report a 2026 study of trans-vitisin B, a compound from grapes, in models of Parkinson's disease. Current drugs such as L-DOPA ease symptoms but do not protect brain cells. The team tested the compound in cell models and in mice with a poison-induced form of the disease, tracking swelling, rust-like cell harm, and behavior.

In cells, the compound cut swelling signals and stress markers while restoring a guard protein. In mice, it eased movement faults and memory slips, and spared the brain cells that make dopamine. It also cut a harmful form of the tau protein. Unlike L-DOPA, it worked without causing the jerky side effects seen in rodents.
pmc-13603667:
Five authors report a 2026 veterinary case of a benign bone cyst in a puppy that grew again after surgery. Aneurysmal bone cysts are rare in dogs and can return after care. A four-month-old Labrador had a fast-growing, bone-thinning cyst in the left ulna, checked by X-ray and CT scans.

First surgery scraped the cyst, packed graft bone, and fixed the shell with screws, and the limp cleared. Scans six weeks later showed growth past the first site, so a wider second surgery followed. Checks out to 35 months show steady bone rebuild with no new growth.
pmc-13603767:
Zhending Gan and co-authors test whether adding glutamate to feed shields young piglets' guts from an inflammatory hit, in a 2026 study. Weaned piglets often suffer gut damage when bacteria toxins strike, which slows growth. Glutamate, an amino acid, fuels gut lining cells, but how it protects at the RNA-tag level was unclear.

Piglets given the toxin showed harmed gut walls, fired-up inflammatory signals, and disturbed bile handling. Glutamate feed partly reversed each effect: walls healed, tight seals between cells rose, and bile uptake improved. The team trace the gain to a bile transporter gene whose RNA tags glutamate helps reset, backed by cell tests. The pathway gives feed makers a concrete target for protecting weaned animals.
pmc-13604467:
Shuo Ding and co-authors review, in twenty twenty-six, acupuncture as a precise treatment for nerve damage caused by chemotherapy. That damage causes pain and numbness, and can force doctors to cut drug doses. It affects a wide share of cancer patients, and no treatment yet reverses it. Lab studies suggest electric acupuncture can calm nerve swelling and stress pathways. Trials with fake-needle controls suggest real acupuncture may ease pain, sensory symptoms, and quality of life.

The review is frank about gaps. A high success rate for ear acupuncture comes from an uncontrolled case series. Studies vary much in method, and the key needle sensation is judged by feel. The authors call for trials that sort patients better and track lab markers and costs.
pmc-13604767:
Amro Tuffaha and co-authors map a target protein in parathyroid tumors in this 2026 study. Overactive parathyroid glands must be located before focused surgery, but small or hidden glands can evade standard scans. A new scan tracer targets a surface protein, and early results in this disease look strong.

The team stained 56 removed parathyroid adenomas and, where available, nearby normal tissue for that protein. About 80 percent of tumors and 94 percent of normal samples met the positive mark. The median share of stained tumor cells was 42.5 percent. The authors compare tumor and normal staining to judge whether the tracer's target is common enough to justify the imaging approach.
pmc-13605067:
Marina Conesa-Molina and three co-authors gather parent views on sports for autistic boys in a 2026 study. The boys had finished a twelve-week activity program in Valencia, Spain. Children at this support level face barriers to sport that research has barely mapped.

Interviews with seventeen parents of boys aged eight to twelve fed a thematic analysis. Seven themes captured both barriers and helpers. Parents described their own fears and past bad experiences with programs. Bullying and exclusion pushed many boys away from activity. Non-adapted teaching and staff without autism training added further blocks. Few programs exist for this group at all. The findings point to design changes that could open sport to these children.
pmc-13605467:
Amonnat Sukhamwang and co-authors profile two growth genes in Thai stomach cancer in a 2026 study. Stomach cancer weighs heavily on northern Thailand. Two signals that drive blood vessel growth and inflammation often run high in these tumors. The team measured both in tissue from eighty-three patients with advanced disease.

The inflammation gene ran high in more than four fifths of patients, the vessel gene in over two fifths. Starting levels did not predict survival on their own. After chemo, both signals fell in about a third of patients. The authors suggest profiling may pick who could gain from early vessel-targeted drugs. Readers get a biomarker lead for tailored care.
pmc-13605867:
Thomas Corfield and Denice Higgins review the glow of teeth and tooth-colored fillings in a 2026 paper. Real teeth shine faintly blue under ultraviolet light, mostly from the dentine within. A filling that lacks that glow can betray itself in nightclub light, so makers now stir glow agents into their resins.

The review pulls studies from 2004 to 2025 on human teeth and direct fillings. Real teeth glow in a band the eye reads as blue-white, dentine brighter than enamel. Fillings lean on rare-earth powders for their shine. The authors weigh how the glow is measured, what dims it over time, and how close the match to nature runs.
pmc-13606367:
Eleven authors survey awareness of diabetic ketoacidosis in the Jazan region of Saudi Arabia in a 2026 paper. The crisis is a complication of diabetes that can kill, and quick spotting can blunt its harm. An online survey ran from late 2024 to mid 2025 among adults who had the disease or a family member with it.

Four hundred seventeen people answered, and about a third had the disease. The questions asked how well people could spot it. They covered what raises the risk, what sets it off, what harm it can do, how to prevent it, and what to do in an emergency. Scores ran out of ten, with six or more counted as appropriate awareness. Group tests and regression models hunted for factors tied to good awareness. The study maps where education should aim in a group with close ties to the disease.
pmc-13606767:
Han Yang and four co-authors build a soy glue with a salt web and clay to gain both fire block and shear hold. Their study appeared in twenty twenty-six. Soy glues are green but weak in wet and hold. An epoxy in water fixes those flaws, yet fire rules for plywood grow strict. A web of chitosan and a P-N-S salt was dried and set in the glue with clay.

Plywood with the new glue hit a high fire mark and shed far less heat in cone tests. Dry and wet shear holds both met the state rule for in-room plywood. The team offers the mix as a green high-force glue path.
pmc-13606867:
Şelale Öncü Glaue, a solo author, studies puddings made from a melon seed drink set with various gums, in work listed for 2026. Seeds from a local Turkish melon are an underused by-product, and the author asks if they can form a plant-based pudding without starch.

Four gums were tested at two doses, with starch-set seed and milk puddings as controls. Gum type and dose interacted on every texture measure, so equal weights of different gums were not interchangeable. One gum at the lower dose gave the most balanced texture response. The strongest gel at high dose was squeezed out of the test gap under shear, the author notes.
pmc-13607367:
Lynch, Mauricio, Palomino, and Brown compared immune defenses in male and female cat fleas after a body-wide bacterial challenge. Both sexes drink blood all their adult lives, but past immunity work studied mostly females. The team injected Escherichia coli bacteria into the body cavity and tracked infection levels, survival, and the blood cells that eat bacteria.

Females cleared the bacteria better: fewer stayed infected and their loads were lower a day later. Infection cut survival in both sexes but far more in males, and even sterile injury alone hurt males. Females carried more circulating blood cells, raised their numbers after injury or infection, and had a larger share of cells actively eating bacteria. The authors say sex is a real variable in flea immunity and should be tested under natural exposure routes too.
pmc-13607567:
Rosa Gemma Viterbo and five colleagues review how the immune system may shape autism's wide variety. Autistic people differ greatly in language, attention, thinking skills, and long-term outcomes, and genetics alone does not explain the spread. Their review gathers the molecular and cellular routes by which immune disturbance and autoimmunity could modify development.

Topics range over immune activation in mothers during pregnancy, maternal antibodies reacting with the fetal brain, cytokine signaling, and brain immune cells, microglia and astrocytes. Complement-driven pruning of synapses and gut-immune-brain pathways also feature. The authors are careful: immune dysfunction looks like a modifier of autism's shape in some people, not a universal cause. Direct long-term studies tying immune profiles to thinking trajectories remain scarce, above all in adults. Joining molecular, immune, and psychological data, they argue, could define subgroups and guide biomarker work.
pmc-13607767:
Cho Lau, Khadija Khan, Dora Kwong, Wei Dai, and Ngar Kam review chemical marks on a key protein in throat cancer, in work from 2026. Nasopharyngeal carcinoma links closely with Epstein-Barr virus and with deep gene control changes. The protein HMGB1 binds chromatin inside cells and can also act as an alarm signal outside cells.

Marks such as added acetyl, phosphate, and sugar groups steer where HMGB1 sits and what it does. Higher HMGB1 levels in this cancer link with worse features and poorer outcomes. The review splits facts proven in this cancer from ideas drawn from other diseases. Clear gaps remain where proposed steps still lack direct proof in throat tumours.
pmc-13607867:
Silvia Abril, Alex Lopez, and Mara Moreno-Gomez test which baits draw six pest ant species across seasons, in a study from 2026. Toxic baits work only if ants haul them home, and taste for protein or sugar shifts by species and time of year. The team set out protein, sugar, and mixed baits in fall and spring, with ten tries per species and season.

Three species leaned to protein baits, while two invader species leaned to sugar. One species showed no clear lean. Spring brought shifts, with two species taking more protein and one taking still more sugar. The authors map bait blends to species and season. Protein rich baits suit the first trio, sugar rich baits suit the invaders, and spring tweaks lift the haul.
pmc-13608167:
Fahad Alsudairi and co-authors traced how students' confidence in their own skill shapes their engagement with AI learning tools, in a study published in 2026. Investment theories of intelligence say ability grows when learners wrestle with hard material themselves. Yet students may instead hand the thinking to the tool. The team surveyed 185 business undergraduates at a Saudi university who used generative AI in coursework. A modeling method tested a chain from self-belief through motivation and enjoyment to perceived usefulness.

All nine hypotheses held. Confidence strongly fed both motivation and enjoyment, but motivation was the main route to finding the tools useful. Enjoyment played a smaller role, and a serial path ran from confidence through motivation to enjoyment. The model explained over half the variation in intention to keep using the tools. The authors warn that design should build student competence, not replace it.
pmc-13608867:
Oğuzhan Çağlayan and co-authors test how allergy syrups wear down children's tooth fillings in a 2026 lab study. Kids' liquid medicines are acidic and bathe fillings often. Three filling types went through a set soak routine with two common syrups.

Disc samples first aged through five thousand heat cycles. They then soaked in syrup or plain water for five minutes, twice a day, for six days. Surface roughness and color shift were measured at each stage. Both syrups changed surface shape and color in clear ways. A glass hybrid filling roughened and shifted color most, though much of that came from the heat aging. The study helps dentists pick fillings for kids on long syrup courses.
pmc-13609067:
Junaid Saleem, Zubair Moghal, and Gordon McKay published an environmental assessment in two thousand twenty-six on a sorbent made from electronic waste. The non-metal part of old circuit boards can be activated to soak up heavy metals from water. The team measured the production footprint of making it.

Making one kilogram of the sorbent caused about five point eight kilograms of carbon dioxide equivalent and a set energy demand. They then divided those burdens by how much lead, copper, or zinc the material can hold. Per kilogram of metal captured, lead looked cheapest environmentally. Shop-bought activated carbon had slightly lower production impacts but held far less lead, so its per-capture burden ran higher. Use and disposal stages were left out.
pmc-13609367:
Harsh Goel and co-authors map gene changes in a rare child blood cancer in a 2026 study from India. The cancer, which affects young children, grows fast and almost always involves a signal path that tells cells to divide. The team read the full coding part of genes in tumor samples from 35 patients, paired with cheek swab samples from the same children.

The study lists which genes changed, which changes drive the cancer, and which paths those changes affect. It also checks which changed proteins sit in spots that drugs could reach. By sorting real driver changes from harmless ones, the work points to drug targets worth testing. It adds data from a group that is rare in most gene databases.
pmc-13610267:
Madison Wise and Abdel Alli review how a diabetes pill protects kidneys and the wider body beyond sugar control in a 2026 paper. Dapagliflozin began as a way to spill glucose in urine. Trials then showed slower kidney decline and fewer heart failures, even without diabetes.

The review walks from the drugs plant-derived ancestor to modern selective versions. Inside kidney tubules it retunes several sodium and phosphate handlers at once. It also damps inflammation and scarring signals, steadies cell power plants, and eases stress responses. The authors frame the pill as a system drug, not a sugar drug.
pmc-13610667:
Levent Yorulmaz and co-authors read cross patterns in fast bred wheat in a 2026 paper. Speed breeding rushes wheat lines in lit chambers. Most past work tuned the chamber, not the genes shown inside it.

Their F2 flock held over eight hundred plants from three parent wheats. One parent bears heat well, the other two wilt in heat. Crosses in both directions let parent sex effects show. Twelve traits were scored under long day chamber light. Wide trait spread and rich out of range heirs showed in all crosses. One cross pairing threw the most top heirs for grain and yield marks.
pmc-13611367:
Prachid Saramolee and co-authors published this wearable technology study in 2026. It presents a smart insole made largely of natural rubber, designed to measure body load remotely and cheaply. Each insole carries four load sensors under high-pressure spots of the foot. A small chip streams left and right loads over Wi-Fi to a cloud service. The team tested the insole against reference weights, then compared walking in thirty adults, half with flexible flatfoot and half with normal arches.

Body weight came out with an average error under three percent, and the small bias left over could be removed by one calibration factor. While wearing the insoles, the flatfoot group walked with a wider base but matched the other group in step length and speed. At fast walking, only a drop in cadence survived strict statistical correction. The authors see the insole as fit for remote monitoring.
pmc-13611767:
Zhiwei Si and colleagues design a training scheme for sensor networks that learns together without leaking data or trusting the server, in this computing paper from twenty twenty-six. In federated learning, devices train a shared model locally and send only updates. But updates can leak private facts, and a dishonest server can fake the combined result.

Their scheme, VCFedAdam, compresses each update into a small masked sketch, so little travels and little can leak. A commitment check then lets devices verify the server's combined answer rather than take it on faith. At a quarter of the original size, computing cost fell by about ninety percent and traffic by about three quarters, against standard secure methods. Accuracy on two standard image tests dipped by about one percent. The authors aim the design at the small, battery-bound sensors that need such thrift most.
pmc-13611867:
A fierce blood-vessel cancer in dogs mirrors a rare human cancer, yet its drivers are still poorly known. Yishan Liu and co-authors build a living model of the dog disease in a 2026 study. They grow flat organ-like cultures from patient tumors and also plant them in mice.

Gene scans of the cultures flagged one gene, PLAAT3, as far more active than in benign growths. Muting that gene, or blocking it with a drug, cut the cells' power to invade. When the cultures were placed in mouse spleens, they formed tumors that spread like the real disease. The model gives labs a test bed for new drugs for both dogs and people.
pmc-13611967:
Philip Buck and co-authors measure what congenital cytomegalovirus costs US families in this 2026 paper. The virus can damage hearing, vision, and development before birth. Care burdens fall heavily on households, not just insurers. Web surveys ran from August 2024 to April 2025.

Respondents included 227 caregivers, 211 affected children, and 173 siblings. Total yearly family costs averaged about 83,140 dollars, counting care spending and lost work. Lifetime home adaptation and special schooling added about 4,713 dollars out of pocket. Caregiver quality of life scores matched general population norms. Scores for affected children varied widely by severity. Sibling scores were near normal on average. Family level data completes the case for prevention and early support.
pmc-13612067:
Jie Tao and six co-authors wrote a 2026 study on the emergence of porcine sapelovirus, a gut virus of pigs in China. The virus is tied to diarrhea in pigs, yet its spread and genetic diversity in China were poorly mapped. The team gathered all reported Chinese strains from papers and gene banks.

They built a distribution map and checked which other viruses travel with it. It often appears alongside three other pig gut viruses. Gene analysis of 74 strains found no clear regional clustering. A striking 85 percent of strains showed signs of recombination, gene swapping that speeds evolution, mostly near one gene region. Timelines suggest the pig virus and a bird cousin arose around 1985. The authors call for sustained genomic watch on this pathogen.
pmc-13612467:
Yang argues in twenty twenty-six that weaving AI into company decision-making quietly drains the raw material of innovation. Efficiency rises, he grants, but the odd, hard-to-measure ideas that seed new products get filtered out. His lens is the institutional interface: the joint effect of AI design choices, human-AI routines, and company norms on what the organisation notices.

He names a failure mode of automatic execution that runs unseen, strips human agency, and dulls self-questioning. Leftovers that defy the statistical mainstream, called residuals, get dropped at the thinking, acting, and valuing stages alike. Guards like non-optimised zones and outlier paths can help, but each carries stubborn dilemmas of isolation, authority, and judgement. The piece offers testable claims for governing AI-fed firms.
pmc-13613067:
Silvia Ferrara and co-authors link two signal systems that control biofilm growth in a common bacterium. Their twenty twenty-six paper studies Pseudomonas aeruginosa, a germ that forms tough biofilms in lungs and on devices. One system is a small messenger called cyclic di-GMP, and the other is a small RNA named ErsA.

Past work showed ErsA blocking a gene needed for biofilm sugar building blocks. That seemed odd, since high messenger levels push biofilm growth. The team shows high messenger levels lift the ErsA block on that gene. The same release works on other ErsA targets tied to cell envelope care. A seeming clash resolves into one switch.
pmc-13613267:
Jing Li, Ziheng Lin, and Chengqun Qiu probe a personalization paradox in AI-tutored college study, in a 2026 paper. Platforms that tailor lessons to each student spread fast through universities. The worry is that leaning on the algorithm dulls the student's own grip on their learning. The team tracked 486 Chinese undergraduates across one term, asking about the AI setting, their feelings, and study habits.

Students who felt the setting as more adaptive reported weaker self-regulated learning. Feelings carried over half the effect: joy, anxiety, and boredom each formed part of the bridge. One guard stood out. Students with strong AI literacy felt the setting's pull on their feelings far less, a shield on every path. The authors urge schools to teach AI literacy for credit and to build platforms whose steering stays in user hands. They note the survey design caps causal claims.
pmc-13613467:
Krishna KC and seven co-authors tuned tungsten oxide nanostructures in two thousand twenty-six to store more charge in supercapacitors. Tungsten oxide comes in several oxygen ratios, and lower oxygen brings better conductivity plus open channels in the crystal. Making each phase precisely is the hard part, so most work sticks to the common fully oxidized form.

A hot-wire oxidation method let them set the oxygen ratio and shape at will. One phase, rich in fine nanostructure, stored charge mainly at its surface. A more oxygen-poor phase mixed surface storage with diffusion-based storage, thanks to wider channels and more charge carriers. Performance tracked crystal phase, shape, and electrolyte ion size.
pmc-13613567:
Garnett and a large team asked in twenty twenty-six how species name work is used in the Red List of species at risk. Names set the units that care work tries to save, and name shifts can shake those plans. No broad view yet showed how risk judges use names in their work.

They asked the heads of expert groups that run risk checks for each life group. Ways of work varied a lot, from one judge to full boards that set all name calls. Lists used in Red List work can clash with lists used by other care pacts. More shared rules could help, but may curb the flex that judges need.
pmc-13614067:
Sucheta Kundu and coauthors published a 2026 chemistry study of a flexible two-unit dye molecule, built from two linked porphyrin rings. It serves as a small model for how plants harvest light. The pair can twist around the link between its units. The team asked how that twisting shapes the way absorbed light energy moves and fades. They tracked the molecule with ultrafast laser methods that watch energy states rise and fall in trillionths of a second.

At low light levels the pair behaved much like the single unit. Stronger pulses revealed fading steps lasting about one picosecond and eighteen to twenty-eight picoseconds. Calculations showed that the link between the units depends on the twist angle. The pair sits in a weak-coupling regime. The extra fading fits a process in which two excited states meet and one is lost, driven by overlap between emitted and absorbed light.
pmc-13614167:
Renato D. dos Santos, Guilherme Colherinhas, and Wesley B. Cardoso test in 2026 whether HIV drugs could be reused against West Nile virus, a mosquito-borne virus that can attack the brain and has no approved drug treatment. Working fully on computers, they docked ten HIV protease blockers into the virus's own protease, an enzyme it needs to copy itself, then ran motion simulations to see which drugs stayed bound.

Two drugs, indinavir and atazanavir, held on firmly, with steady contact, lasting hydrogen bonds, and favourable binding energy. Several others scored well in the still docking test yet drifted loose once the simulation moved. The lesson for drug hunting is plain: a good first fit means little until the pairing survives motion. The two winners now merit testing in real lab experiments.
pmc-13614267:
Mark Naslund, Sungil Kim, Ambar La Forgia, Riley League, Ryan McDevitt, Xingzhi Wang, and Kelly Kaili Yang published a 2026 study of private equity ownership of United States hospitals. The topic draws heated debate. Yet patchy deal data made even basic facts hard to pin down. The team built a harmonized public dataset of acquisitions, checked against exit records.

They traced ownership spells for all short term acute care hospitals from 2000 to 2024. First, private equity never held more than seven percent of such hospitals, and the share sat below four percent in 2024. Second, most firms exit within five years, usually by selling to another firm or a strategic buyer; closures are rare. Third, most Americans live in regions with no private equity hospital at all.
pmc-13615067:
Bingjie Li leads a team on how drive to work hard adapts. Their study from twenty twenty-six uses a new task called CoMET. It varies how much control folks have and how rich rewards are.

Folks were more keen to work hard when they had control. They also tuned effort fast as control changed in the task. Rich reward settings drew more effort as well. The team held mean reward rate fixed while control varied. Poor tuning of effort shows in many mind disorders. The task helps map how that tuning works.
pmc-13615167:
Chenlong Xie and co-authors test electric needle care as a shield for lungs hurt by heart attacks in rats in a 2026 study. When blood flow returns to heart muscle, the lungs can take damage too, a known snag after heart surgery. Rats got the needle care at two body points once a day for three days before the harm was induced.

Treated rats breathed better and showed less lung damage and swelling. Two linked signal proteins tied to the harm fell under the care. When the team forced those signals back up with a lab dose, the shield broke. The care seems to work by muting that signal pair.
pmc-13616467:
Compounds in a knotweed plant that block the COVID-19 virus's main enzyme are fished out by Huang and co-authors in a 2026 study. Traditional plant extracts hide their active parts in complex mixes. The team ties the virus enzyme to magnetic beads, letting it grab its own blockers from the extract.

Eight compounds were caught and named by precision mass tools. Six blocked the enzyme in dose tests, led by resveratrol, a well-known plant compound. Further measures rank the main actives by amount. Computer docking suggests how they sit in the enzyme's grip. The bead method can speed blocker hunts in other medicinal plants.
pmc-13616667:
Sushma Salethoor and co-authors report Ayurvedic care for severe dry eye before cataract surgery in a 2026 case paper. A seventy-three-year-old woman had eye irritation, a gritty feeling, and blurred distance vision for three months. Tests showed very low tear flow and cataracts in both eyes, with surface damage that made surgery unsafe at once.

She also lived with diabetes and high blood pressure, both controlled. The report describes traditional Ayurvedic management used to restore the eye surface so surgery could proceed. Such cases interest clinicians who blend traditional and modern care, though one case cannot prove a method works.
pmc-13616767:
Hamza Boukeffa, Selman Djeffal, and Abdelhamid Ghoul present a 2026 study on early warning of market swings. A useful warning must give sound odds, stay simple, and turn into a safe position. The team set all of that as one task with seven goals. Eleven nature-inspired search methods tuned the system on stock and fear index data from 2015 to 2020.

Each method ran 30 times, against random search and nine standard plans. In training checks, the nature methods won clearly, and one took the best rank. On fresh data, the gap vanished. No tuned method beat random search, and a simple fixed model matched them all. The lesson is to judge search quality and choice quality apart.
pmc-13617067:
In Alzheimer disease and kin disorders, a protein called tau builds up in the brain and many genes go quiet. Kendall Cottingham and co-authors use fruit flies in a 2026 study to learn why long brain genes fall silent.

Flies bred to make a harmful form of human tau in nerve cells showed a clear pattern. Long genes in nerve cells were turned down the most. The enzyme that reads genes piled up near gene starts and was scarce along gene bodies, as if it stalled before it could finish the job. The longer the gene, the stronger the stall and the deeper the drop. The work names stalled reading as a key source of stress in these disorders.
pmc-13617267:
Sebastian Ullrich and co-authors tested whether practicing with virtual patients improves nurses' professional language skills in a 2026 study. Nurses recruited from abroad must pass a demanding German exam to work in Germany. Talking with patients is the hardest part to practice in a classroom.

Twenty-five international nursing staff took part at one language school. Thirteen gained access to a digital tool with interactive patient and colleague scenarios, on top of the same 600 hours of standard training the control group received. The main measure was the fail rate at the first exam attempt. Supervisors were also interviewed a year later about workplace integration.
pmc-13617367:
Paoletti and colleagues published in twenty twenty-six a review of allergy treatment given under the tongue. Sublingual immunotherapy slowly trains the immune system to tolerate allergens. It is the only treatment that can change the course of allergic disease. Tablets for grass and dust mite allergy have strong trial support. They cut symptoms and medicine use, with benefits lasting after treatment ends.

Real-world studies agree and add lower risk of new asthma. Effects on day-to-day asthma control are less steady across trials. Children's results mostly mirror those in adults, with good safety. Reviews confirm overall benefit but note wide differences between products. The authors stress standardized doses and at least three years of adherence. Better product-specific trials remain a priority.
pmc-13617467:
Abdelrahim Shaaeldin and nine co-authors audit how fast elderly hip fracture patients reach surgery in Saudi Arabia's Medina region in a 2026 study. Guidelines worldwide urge operating within two days; delays cost lives and independence. Local data on why waits happen were scarce.

The team reviewed 400 patients aged sixty and up at two hospitals. Only twenty-two percent made the two-day mark; the typical wait topped eighty-eight hours. Older age and sicker patients waited longer. Weekend arrival and a pile-up of pre-surgery consultations predicted delay too. The authors call it a systems gap, not a surgeon gap, and point to weekend cover and consult queues as fixable bottlenecks.
pmc-13617767:
Yongbin Xu and seven colleagues describe a pectin-like polysaccharide from the pollen of Typha angustifolia, a cattail plant used in traditional medicine, and test how it steers immune cells. Plant pectins are promising immune modulators, yet their tangled makeup has hidden which parts do the work. The team mapped the molecule's size, sugar building blocks, and branching with chemical analysis and magnetic resonance methods, then exposed mouse dendritic cells to it.

The polysaccharide, about ten kilodaltons in size, mixes smooth pectin regions with richly branched side chains and rare structural motifs. It matured dendritic cells without poisoning them, raising surface activation markers and inflammatory signals while reducing their appetite for swallowing particles. Treated cells then activated antigen-specific killer T cells more strongly, boosting their growth and interferon output. Tests against clipped versions suggest the intact, complex branching underlies the activity, though molecule size may also play a part.
pmc-13617967:
Cannabis compounds are moving from street stigma to the rehabilitation ward, and Ozlem Balbaloglu and Evrim Coskun survey the shift in a 2026 review. Their question is no longer whether cannabinoids belong in the conversation, but how to use them rationally for patients rebuilding function after multiple sclerosis, spinal cord injury, stroke, or brain trauma.

Rehabilitation succeeds by mobility, daily activity, participation, and quality of life, not pain scores alone. So the authors ask whether these agents help patients engage with therapy itself, beyond easing symptoms. The endocannabinoid system, the body's own cannabis-like signaling web, links brain, body, and immune system in ways that make the idea plausible. Against that promise they weigh the field's open uncertainties and safety concerns, arguing the evidence now justifies careful clinical integration rather than reflexive rejection.
pmc-13618067:
Mansoore Shahabi and two colleagues build a magnetic nanocatalyst pairing nickel and copper for two jobs: converting toxic nitroaromatic compounds into useful amines, and forming carbon-nitrogen bonds in a single pot. Industrial nitro compounds pollute water and resist breakdown, while their amine products feed dyes, drugs, and polymers. The catalyst sits on silica-coated magnetite particles, so a magnet can fish it out afterward.

A battery of imaging and analysis methods confirmed the layered structure. Reactions ran in water, a green solvent, finished within about two hours, and gave high yields. The nickel-copper pairing outperformed what either metal suggests alone, a synergy the authors credit for the activity. Most importantly for practical use, the catalyst survived seven consecutive runs of nitro reduction without significant loss of activity, supporting the design as a cost-effective, environmentally friendlier route to amine chemistry.
pmc-13618267:
Nicole Lardini Freitas and eight colleagues profile spinal fluid proteins in COVID-19 patients with acute neurological problems, hunting for the biology behind them. They compared patients grouped as stubborn headache alone, encephalopathy, or inflammatory brain disease, against controls with non-inflammatory conditions. Protein patterns were read for the processes they reveal.

Altered proteins clustered around the complement system, an immune attack cascade, plus microglia and macrophage activity, inflammation, and nerve-cell housekeeping. Complement and clotting cascades were switched on, with raised levels of two complement products backing the signal. Synaptic pruning pathways appeared in the encephalopathy and inflammatory groups. The inflammatory group also showed glial activation and immune cells moving into the brain, plus more microglia-related proteins. The authors propose that complement-driven inflammation, driven by glial cells, disrupts the blood-brain barrier and produces these distinct syndromes.
pmc-13618767:
Xunzhuo Dong and seven colleagues separate the effect of soil acidity itself from everything else that changes when farmers swap some synthetic fertilizer for organic amendments. Using two complementary global field datasets, they partitioned how much soil carbon gain and yield gain trace specifically to pH moving toward neutral, rather than to the added carbon or other shifts.

Organic substitution consistently nudged pH toward neutrality in acidic, neutral, and alkaline soils alike. The pH improvement alone explained fifteen percent of carbon accrual in acidic soils, about nine percent in neutral soils, and about four percent in alkaline soils, working mainly by boosting microbial biomass. That pH-linked carbon gain underpinned yield rises of roughly five to nine percent across soil types, strongest and most durable in acidic soils and peaking regionally in Africa. The authors urge pairing organic substitution with deliberate pH management.
pmc-13618967:
Dayou Cui and five colleagues build a lightweight neural network that diagnoses bearing faults in rotating machinery under noise and changing speeds. Bearings account for roughly half of rotating machinery failures, yet harsh conditions defeat many models. Their design, MDW-Mamba, decouples noise from fault features in stages. A three-channel input, a multi-scale convolution backbone, and a dual-scale wavelet module model long-range patterns efficiently.

Across three public variable-speed datasets, the network beat current best methods and kept average accuracy above eighty-seven percent even when noise exceeded signal. It does this with about a quarter-million parameters and answers in about a millisecond. That is small and fast enough for real-time diagnosis on small edge devices mounted on the machines. The authors position it for wind turbines, aerospace propulsion, and heavy manufacturing, where catching a failing bearing early prevents downtime and loss.
pmc-13619067:
Andrew J. Webb and seven colleagues show that chewing sugary gum can amplify beetroot juice's blood-pressure benefit, in a 2026 crossover experiment. Dietary nitrate is concentrated in saliva, where tongue bacteria convert it to nitrite, the step to vessel-relaxing nitric oxide. Fourteen volunteers drank a beetroot shot on two visits, chewing either sugary acidic bubble gum or sugar-free gum, and were tracked for seven hours.

The sugary gum dropped salivary acidity, by one and a half pH units. Nitrate delivery did not change, yet salivary nitrite production jumped forty-five percent and plasma nitrite rose a quarter, showing mouth bacteria work faster in acid conditions. Blood pressure followed: systolic fell nearly three points and diastolic nearly two, both significant. The authors note the trick could potentiate other nitrate benefits, such as exercise performance. It reframes an everyday habit, gum choice, as a lever on a body pathway.
pmc-13619467:
Wenming Shao and a team of co-authors report a pilot study of a robot surgery training system in China, in two thousand twenty-six. Robot systems give surgeons three-dimensional views, force feedback, and precise control. Yet few Chinese medical colleges build them into training so far.

Students at one medical college trained on a home-grown multi-port robot for belly surgery tasks. They rated the system's usability highly on a standard scale. Questionnaires showed good acceptance and a sense that learning felt faster and more fun. Male students rated ease of use higher than female students did. The authors note that felt gains are not proof of real skill gains.
pmc-13619567:
Hannah Meinert led a large team searching for a brain wiring pattern tied to social anxiety across diagnoses. Social anxiety runs on a spectrum, from mild shyness in healthy people to a full disorder. The researchers scanned 160 participants across that spectrum and rebuilt each person's structural connectome, the map of white-matter links between brain regions.

A predictive modeling method found a network of forty-six connections whose pattern tracked how socially anxious each person was, regardless of diagnosis. Key hub regions sat in visual and parietal areas and in part of the frontal lobe. Sixty-four participants had social anxiety disorder and ninety-six did not, and the shared network still held across the groups. The authors present the result as early evidence that one brain network underlies social anxiety wherever it appears on the spectrum.
pmc-13620167:
Kyungbin Yoo and eight colleagues built a brain stimulator for mice that runs entirely on radio waves, with no battery and no wires. Tools for nudging brain circuits in freely moving animals usually need batteries or special cages wrapped in power coils. Their device pairs a flexible antenna that catches radio-frequency power from almost any angle with circuits that turn it into steady direct current for stimulation.

In mice moving freely around a normal cage, the device held its output voltage steady for most of the session, dipping only briefly when a mouse twisted sharply. Aimed at a motor area of the cortex, the stimulation reliably made mice circle, proving the current reached the brain with behavioral effect. The authors say radiative power transfer can free neurostimulation experiments from tethers and coil-lined arenas.
pmc-13620267:
Zikang Guo, Yunwen Wu, Yuhui Guo, and Shenghong Ju introduce Q-LEAP, a design system that uses quantum annealing to invent optical metamaterials, artificial structures that steer light in ways natural materials cannot. The search space is enormous, holding more design candidates than any team could test one by one. A factorization machine first learns the landscape, then quantum tunneling jumps across it to promising corners.

One optimization step finished in a few milliseconds and landed close to the theoretical best score for the target. By the team's combined measure of speed, sampling, and quality, the system beat the best conventional optimizer by a wide margin. A physics-guided machine learning partner predicted how candidate materials respond across the light spectrum, extending reliable estimates beyond the cutoff of standard calculations. The target design emits selectively in one infrared band while suppressing others, a trick useful for heat management.
pmc-13620467:
Six reviewers assess artificial intelligence for corneal endothelial disease in a 2026 paper. The cornea's inner cell layer yields rich imaging and follow up data, well suited to machine learning. The review follows AI along the whole care path and grades each use by readiness for clinic, not accuracy alone.

Measurement tasks lead: cell segmentation, image quality checks, swelling maps, and graft detachment grading all perform strongly. Prognostic tasks lag, and models often drop when moved across devices or centers; one detection score fell from 0.96 to 0.77 on outside data. Few studies add calibration checks or head to head human comparisons. Donor cell counting in eye banks stands as the most mature use.
pmc-13620867:
Pan Li and eleven colleagues ran a randomized trial of 5G cloud follow-up for heart failure patients living far from specialist centers. These patients carry implanted defibrillators that need regular checks and sometimes remote reprogramming. Two hundred six patients at five centers were assigned to a year of remote platform care or standard clinic visits.

The remote group got help far sooner after a clinical event, with response time cut from well over a week to a few days on median. Quality of life scores improved more in the remote group at twelve months. Unplanned visits and intervention rates matched between groups, and no complications came from the remote procedures. The platform links community hospitals to implant centers over 5G, so specialists can direct care while patients stay local. The authors call it a workable model for underserved regions.
pmc-13621467:
Adam Daly and five colleagues, writing as early-career researchers joined by an experienced public contributor, examine why involving patients and the public in research is hard at the start of a career. Done badly, involvement becomes token decoration that shuts contributors out. The authors organize the problem into three areas: teaching, practice, and data governance.

On teaching, they argue involvement belongs inside research training itself, with patients helping to teach it. On practice, thin budgets and narrow recruitment shut out diverse voices, so they push creative methods that meet people where they are. On data, junior researchers often feel lost deciding ownership and safety with contributors, so the paper proposes a framework for working those questions through together. Their shared message: the barriers are real, yet each one hides a workable opening.
pmc-13621567:
Xiaochen Ji, Zhiqiang Niu, and Yabo Wang report a suspected nerve injury following a stellate ganglion block given for stubborn insomnia.
