The procedure injects local anesthetic beside a neck nerve cluster to calm the autonomic nervous system, and its use has spread into sleep medicine. Their patient, a forty-nine-year-old woman, felt radiating shoulder pain the moment the block was placed.

Her right upper arm went numb on its outer side and her deltoid muscle weakened, a pattern pointing to the fifth cervical nerve root. Electrical testing of muscle and nerve supported an acute injury at that root. The authors stop short of claiming proof, since timing alone cannot establish that the needle caused the damage. They use the case to press practical cautions: watch the needle tip continuously under imaging, halt at the first radiating pain, check neurology promptly, and report uncertainty honestly when publishing complications.
pmc-13623267:
Diego Berlingeri Collazo and three co-authors describe a skin cancer that changed its identity papers after immunotherapy. Their case report appeared in twenty twenty-six. Merkel cell carcinoma usually stains positive for the marker CK20, a signature pathologists lean on.

The patient, a woman in her eighties, first had surgery and radiation for an arm tumor. Node recurrence brought dissection, then a checkpoint inhibitor drug. A year later, liver and lung lesions appeared. The liver biopsy read as a fast-growing neuroendocrine cancer with CK20 missing entirely. Standard chemotherapy for such tumors failed to slow it, and she moved to hospice care. The authors warn that treatment can strip the classic marker, so history must guide diagnosis.
pmc-13623367:
Nevin Karakus, Elif Donmezoglu Kutukcu, and Sumeyye Yildirim look for blood signals that warn of pregnancy complications, using tiny gene regulators called microRNAs that float in the mother's blood. Such markers could one day allow a simple blood test instead of waiting for symptoms. The prospective study ran at a university clinic in Tokat, Türkiye.

Thirty-nine pregnant women took part: twenty-eight healthy and eleven with complications, split between blood pressure disorders and pregnancy diabetes. Lab tests measured two candidate microRNAs in plasma. One of them, MIR375-3p, ran clearly lower in women with complications than in healthy women, while the other showed no firm difference. The authors propose the lowered marker as a possible early indicator worth pursuing. They are candid about the small group size and call for larger studies before any test could be trusted in practice.
pmc-13623467:
Reinhilde Jacobs, Rellyca Sola Gracea, and Dhanaporn Papasratorn published a 2026 commentary on the images behind artificial intelligence in dentistry. Most dental AI tools learn from scans and X-rays, and the authors ask whether those training images are good enough for the claims made. With dentists scarce worldwide, the pressure to automate is real.

The authors sort dental imaging by task. For single-tooth X-rays, taken and read in seconds, they warn that AI overlays and boxes can hide the fine detail that makes the image useful. Panoramic views, which show the whole jaw at once, present a different balance of risks and gains. Three-dimensional scans add another case. Their common thread is that image quality, fit to the task, and honest clinical testing decide whether a tool helps or distracts. At present, they say, those conditions are rarely met, so enthusiasm should wait on proof.
pmc-13623567:
Mohammed Almeshari and co-authors surveyed health students on AI chatbots in two thousand twenty-six. Large language models are spreading through health education. Saudi evidence on student use was thin. The team sent an online questionnaire across universities. Students in health fields formed the sample. Responses were collected over several months in twenty twenty-five.

Just over four hundred students entered the final analysis. Awareness and attitudes toward the tools were measured. Actual usage patterns were recorded as well. Comparisons by sex were part of the analysis. The instrument was adapted from a published one. Results show how future clinicians meet AI early. Educators can plan guidance from such baselines. Integrity and accuracy concerns frame the discussion.
pmc-13623667:
Thomas Murchie, writing alone, works out a maths puzzle about effective arterial elastance, a single number summarising the load the arteries place on the heart. Older formulas split that load into a resistance part and a stiffness part joined by a fudge factor, yet published values for the factor disagree, and some studies claim stiffness barely matters.

Murchie derives a cleaner approximation from a model of the arterial tree by simplifying its exponential term. The result says the fudge factor is not fixed: it grows with the share of each heartbeat spent in diastole, the resting phase, squared and halved. He checked the formula across hundreds of combinations of resistance, stiffness, and heart rate in a virtual population numbering more than four thousand adults from a vessel model. The approximation tracked the full model exactly and beat earlier versions. The work explains why past estimates scattered.
pmc-13623767:
Chiara Paolin and colleagues study brain injury found before heart surgery in children with complex congenital heart disease at the University of Padova in Italy. Such injuries, present from fetal or newborn life, predict later development problems. The team compared children with genetic syndromes against those without, a group rarely separated in earlier work.

Fifty-four children who had brain scans before surgery between January 2020 and October 2024 were followed, with development checks up to eighteen months. Brain lesions appeared in forty-four percent overall, and rates were similar in syndromic and non-syndromic children. Stroke in an artery was the most common lesion, followed by bleeding under the skull and clots in brain veins. Syndromic children, though, had rockier newborn courses and clearly worse development, above all in movement and language. The authors conclude that the syndrome itself, not extra brain injury, drives the added risk.
pmc-13624367:
Hong Luo and co-authors compare acupuncture and moxibustion treatments for subthreshold depression. Their 2026 review covers a mild stage that can come before full depression. Both therapies come from traditional Chinese medicine, and the authors ask which form works best on standard mood scales.

Eight databases were searched for randomized trials, yielding seventeen studies and six therapies. A Bayesian network method ranked the options on two depression scales. Needling plus moxibustion and needling alone beat placebo, no treatment, and Western medicine on the main scale. The combined therapy also beat herbal patching and talk therapy. The authors offer the ranking as guidance for clinicians choosing among these options.
pmc-13624467:
Braces that pull the upper front teeth back can change the gum tissue around them, and thin gums may react worse than thick ones. Muhammad Ihtisham Munawar and co-authors measured that reaction in this 2026 study. Patients had a bite fault where the upper teeth jut forward. Fifty patients aged eighteen to thirty took part at a dental institute in Karachi.

Thirty-five patients had thin gum tissue and fifteen had thick tissue. A standard gum probe measured gum height, pocket depth, and width before and after the teeth were drawn back. The study ran for one year, from June 2023 to July 2024. Knowing how each gum type answers tooth movement helps orthodontists plan pullback in stages. Gum checks before treatment could flag patients who need gentler handling.
pmc-13624767:
Shawn Teoh and Anthony Teoh review two ways to drain a blocked bile duct in a 2026 article. Blockage often comes from cancer in the head of the pancreas. The standard route uses a scope passed through the mouth and gut. A newer route uses ultrasound guidance to create drainage.

The newer route was first used when the standard route failed. It may offer higher success, shorter procedure time, lower risk of pancreas inflammation, and longer stent life. Yet trials comparing the two as a first choice disagree. The authors weigh that trial evidence to help clinicians choose.
pmc-13624967:
Kim, Choe, and Kang sorted United States adults into digital health profiles in twenty twenty-six and linked them to exercise habits. Digital tools, from wearables to patient portals, are often studied one at a time. The team instead looked for patterns of combined use within people.

Using a twenty twenty-four national health survey, they classed over five thousand eight hundred adults by seventeen indicators across five domains. Four profiles emerged: broad engagement, wearable-centered, portal-centered, and limited engagement. Broad users had nearly triple the odds of meeting both aerobic and muscle-strengthening guidelines versus limited users. Wearable-centered users also fared well. Portal use alone showed no clear link. The authors back profile-guided support but call for long-term studies first.
pmc-13625767:
Nematullah Kordi Koosheh and co-authors feed laying quails in 2026 to test guards against spoiled oil in feed. Oxidized oil, fat that has gone rancid, harms birds' health and egg output. The team added a plant essential oil, vitamin E, both, or neither to quail diets, with or without the bad oil.

Four hundred eighty quails took part over seven weeks in eight diet groups. The spoiled oil cut egg output, thinned shells, and stressed the gut and blood. Either supplement blunted most of that harm, and the pair together sped blood recovery and lowered blood fats. The authors back the combo as a shield for laying birds fed risky oil.
pmc-13625967:
Enric Petrus, Diego Garay-Ruiz, Thomas Weymuth, Markus Reiher, and Thomas Hofstetter present a software tool for exploring chemical reaction networks in this two thousand twenty-six paper. Computer-led quantum chemistry now builds large reaction networks, but the data stay locked inside niche software, with no bridge to other chemistry tools. VizChemoton, an open-source module in the SCINE framework, closes that gap. It draws networks and converts structures, among them radicals and molecular complexes, into string forms through RDKit.

Across four test networks built with density functional theory and tight-binding methods, over ninety percent of compounds converted well. Compounds missing from public databases were mainly molecular complexes and unstable intermediates, just what computer-led searches find. Data ship in CSV and JSON for machine learning, and networks render in a browser page. The tool targets researchers mining reaction networks by computer.
pmc-13626067:
Konstantina Bachtalia, Veatriki Athanasiou, Aikaterini Athanasiadou, Maria Mavrommati, and Sotiria Palioura tested a stepped treatment plan for a scarring eye disease, in a 2026 study. The disease is an immune attack on the eye's surface lining, proven by biopsy in every patient. Treatment strength was matched to the worst inflammation grade in either eye. Care ran forward in time from 2018 to 2025.

Forty-eight patients with ninety-six eyes took part. Mild cases got a gentler immune drug, while worse cases got stronger infusions. Nearly half the patients reached full quiet in both eyes within about nine months. A few patients later stopped drugs entirely without the disease returning. Relapses occurred in six patients and were tamed by stronger treatment. Side effects stayed manageable throughout.
pmc-13626167:
Weidong Jin and co-authors build a sensor that sniffs out pancreatic cancer from a droplet of blood fluid. Tumors shed tiny parcels called exosomes, and catching them early could save lives in a cancer usually found too late. Their probe pairs two grippers. Magnetic beads carry one antibody, and MXene sheets, a flaky conductive material, carry another. The pair grips matching parcels in a sandwich, and a terahertz metasurface reads the catch with boosted resonance.

The sensor found as few as hundreds of parcels per milliliter, beating gold particles as an amplifier. In mice it tracked early tumors and treatment response, and in sixty people it separated patients from healthy controls almost perfectly, outscoring the standard CA19-9 blood test in early-stage cases. Ten microliters and a few dollars per test make the design clinic-friendly.
pmc-13627067:
Zhang and co-authors sort patients with brain glioma into groups by their psychological resilience, in this 2026 study. Coping strength shapes how patients weather a serious brain tumor. The team surveyed 224 patients at a large hospital using standard scales for resilience, mood, quality of life, and support.

Three groups emerged: a low-resilience group covering a quarter of patients, a middle group of about a third, and a high group above forty percent. The groups differed clearly in anxiety, depression, symptom burden, and family support. Older age, higher tumor grade, and return of the disease all raised the odds of landing in the low group. The authors suggest screening resilience to target support.
pmc-13627167:
Alessandra Gambineri and co-authors argue that a simple body measure beats the classic diagnostic boxes for sorting women with polycystic ovary syndrome. Their 2026 study uses a national Italian registry of over 1,300 women. The standard Rotterdam scheme sorts patients into four phenotypes, and the team asked whether those four, or body mass index, better separate metabolic risk.

The phenotypes barely separated anything: rates of blood fat problems, glucose trouble, high blood pressure, and metabolic syndrome were flat across them, though anxiety peaked in one group. Body weight told a clean story instead. Women with obesity, or above a mid-twenties index cutoff, carried more of every metabolic complication, plus stronger male-hormone signs. The authors urge folding weight into the classification itself, since the risk that matters most to long-term health follows the scale, not the phenotype.
pmc-13627667:
Maximilian Fascher, Krzysztof Krasowski, and Markus Muehlhan pool brain scans to ask what drug-cue studies really prove about addiction, in a 2026 meta-analysis. In these studies, people with substance use disorders view drug images while their brains are scanned, and results often clash between labs. The team focused on case-versus-control contrasts, which dodge some design quirks.

Across studies, one region lit up reliably: the ventral anterior cingulate cortex, tied to reward, reasoning, and social thought. Alcohol studies fed that cluster less, and its signal faded when drug cues were compared with natural rewards. The result tempers claims that cue reactivity maps addiction in a simple, general way.
pmc-13627867:
Jaqueline Hersch-González and colleagues compare three lineages of the laboratory worm Caenorhabditis elegans to learn what decades on the bench do to a model animal. Their panel joins a fresh isolate from Mexico City, the standard N2 strain kept in labs today, and an ancestral N2 line frozen since 1969. Life history, stress survival, and gene activity were measured side by side under the same conditions.

The Mexican worms lived shorter lives and bred less, yet survived a bacterial pathogen better, while the ancestral line shrugged off oxidative stress but wilted in heat. Gene profiles of the Mexican and ancestral strains resembled each other more than either resembled today's N2, and only a small core of heat shock genes answered in all three. Strain history, the authors warn, is a hidden variable in worm experiments.
pmc-13628167:
Mingfang Zhan and Ruigang Wu review in 2026 sequence-to-function models for plant gene control, with stress on true causal spread. Such models read DNA and predict gene control outputs, guiding variant hunts and design work. Most are trained on one or a few reference genomes, which narrows their reach.

Plant genomes add hurdles from vast diversity, jumping genes, doubled sets, and long-range control. The authors urge grading by shifts that matter in biology, not just reference accuracy. Gene editing, reporter tests, and active learning could close the loop between models and lab proof. Pan-genome and multi-layer data get a central role.
pmc-13628567:
Ivan Šitum and eight colleagues pooled trial evidence on two ways of keeping day-surgery patients asleep. One way gives the drug propofol through a vein. The other uses sevoflurane gas. Their review gathered fifteen trials with 1,345 adults having outpatient surgery. The trials came out between 2014 and 2025. The team compared waking speed, sickness, and pain after surgery.

Patients on vein propofol had far less sickness and vomiting after surgery. They also reported slightly lower pain scores. Waking told a mixed story, though. One trial found faster readiness to go home. Time in the recovery unit did not differ overall. Waking times varied too much to pool. The authors advise picking the method by patient needs and local resources. Neither way wins clearly on speed.
pmc-13628667:
Mengxia Wu and co-authors present a 2026 profile of the small compounds in fruits of seven Prunus cultivars grown in Xinjiang, China. The mix of such compounds sets each fruit's flavor and worth, and thus what buyers pick. The team used a joined extraction plan to pull two fractions from the same samples.

In all, about eight hundred compounds were named, with phenols the top bulk group and esters rich among the scent group. One dark cultivar stood out for antioxidant strength, tied to a few compounds at fourfold levels. Network checks linked the compounds to several diseases.
pmc-13629567:
Zhilei Zhang and two colleagues examined 104 Chinese college students. They untangled how body size, grip strength, and bone density connect. Skeletal muscle was the suspected middleman. Students are still building peak bone mass. The team measured forearm bone density. They also measured height, weight, grip strength, and muscle mass.

All the measures moved together in a positive way. Modelling then showed that muscle carried a real share of the effect. Both body weight and grip strength acted on bone density through muscle. Sex predicted muscle mass directly. It did not predict bone density itself. Height showed no indirect route through muscle once sex was counted. The authors conclude that building and keeping muscle is a practical lever. It can mean stronger bones in young adults.
pmc-13629767:
Miao-Miao Chen and six colleagues assembled the full mitochondrial genome of Rhynocoris altaicus. This predatory assassin bug of the eastern Palearctic hunts moth and butterfly pests. The work supplies the first full genetic reference for this wide-ranging species. Its kin help control pests in farms and forests.

The circular genome runs just over sixteen thousand DNA letters. It is rich in adenine and thymine. It carries the standard thirty-seven mitochondrial genes plus a control region. Family tree analysis used thirteen protein-coding genes. It placed Rhynocoris as the closest kin of Sphedanolestes within its subfamily. That confirms earlier hints from the one published relative. The sequence sits in a public database. Workers in taxonomy, evolution, and conservation can use it.
pmc-13630767:
Chao Li and co-authors published this study in 2026. It records follower-arm muscles during the golf driver swing. The follower arm is the trailing arm, long overshadowed by the lead side in coaching. Sixteen male golfers, split between two national skill levels, swung while surface sensors read five arm muscles. The swing was cut into five phases, and muscle activity was compared across levels and tied to shot results.

Top-level golfers fired some muscles less and others more at precise moments late in the swing. A wrist flexor stood out, working harder in the better group near impact. Its early-swing activity also tracked carry distance. Backspin linked to biceps timing, and attack angle to a forearm rotator. The authors say the follower arm has a timed, skill-marked role. Coaching that ignores it may miss real gains.
pmc-13631067:
Wang and a team including Rong study brain network changes after acupuncture in patients with disorders of consciousness in twenty twenty-six. Such disorders involve severe disruption of large brain networks. The team used near infrared spectroscopy to record resting brain activity. Thirty patients were scanned just before and after one acupuncture session.

The session targeted three standard acupuncture points on the head and face. After treatment, average positive connectivity across the cortex rose. Global efficiency and clustering of the network also rose. Connectivity grew within the left hemisphere and between front and back regions. Nodes in language, touch, and movement areas gained strength. Single edge changes did not survive strict correction. The authors call for controlled long term studies.
pmc-13631667:
Jing-Feng Huang and co-authors build tiny drug carriers that calm the immune cells driving rheumatoid arthritis, in work published in 2026. Current drugs for the disease target joints poorly and can harm the whole body. In arthritic joints, overactive macrophages and high levels of reactive oxygen drive damage.

Their carriers are micelles loaded with an anti-inflammatory drug. The outer coat homes to a receptor found on activated macrophages, so the cells take the carriers up. A linker inside breaks under oxidative stress, releasing the drug where the joint is most inflamed. In cells and in arthritic mice, the carriers shifted macrophages from attack mode to calm mode. Drug exposure more than doubled versus the free drug, and joints showed less swelling, cartilage loss, and bone erosion.
pmc-13632667:
Jordan Gipper, Kritika Gour, Nattamai Bhuvanesh, and Manar Shoshani report a route to mixed-metal compounds that carry hydrogen atoms. Their 2026 chemistry paper starts with a building block that holds aluminum and two hydrides, meaning hydrogen atoms bound to a metal. They react this block with salts of nickel and of iron, two metals known for rich chemistry.

The two metals take the starting block down different paths. With the nickel salt, the parts join in a step that adds electrons and builds a three-metal product. With the iron salt, a hydride and a chloride trade places instead. Both paths give products that mix three metal centers with hydrides. Such compounds are of interest as models for catalysts and for storing hydrogen in solid form.
pmc-13632967:
Ogasawara and co-authors try out smart glasses that can check a patient's identity by face. Fourteen urologists wear a prototype with a tiny camera and face-matching software in a mock clinic, where patient details appear on the right lens. Afterwards they fill in a survey on comfort, clarity, and symptoms.

Most say the glasses help with clinical work and make care safer, and most would wear them again. Some report tired eyes, and a few find the glasses heavy or awkward over their own spectacles. Many also find the shown patient details a bit hard to read. The team reads this pilot as a promising start that still needs design fixes.
pmc-13633167:
Kadri Ozer presents a repair method for tough finger back wounds in a 2026 case series. Such wounds can bare bone and the tendon gear that straightens the finger, a hard mix to fix. New maps of the blood supply on the finger back now let fat and fascia flaps follow set vessel lines, which makes them more sound.

Seven fingers with wounds on the mid and end bones were treated with a three part local plan. A turned over fat fascia flap covered the wound, tendon links from between the knuckles rebuilt the gear, and skin from the wrist closed the surface. All flaps lived, and finger motion stayed fair after six months or more.
pmc-13633467:
Anne-Marie Roque-Afonso and seven colleagues, writing for the Demosthenes research group, tracked hepatitis A severity in French hospitals from 2013 to 2024. Hepatitis A is a liver infection spread through contaminated food, water, or close contact. It usually passes mildly in children but hits adults harder. As infections fall across Europe, cases shift to older ages where danger grows. The team used the national hospital discharge database to find every admitted case.

Nearly eight thousand cases were identified, with a median age of thirty. Well over a quarter developed severe disease with organ failure, and a small share died. Older age, male sex, smoking, and existing liver problems raised the odds of severity. Death tied most strongly to heavy overall illness burden and to cirrhosis. Severe disease and death both grew more common in the most recent period. The authors suggest wider, perhaps universal, vaccination deserves consideration.
pmc-13633867:
Takafumi Matsunaga and colleagues published a 2026 nationwide study of a parasitic worm infection in Japan. The worms normally infect dogs and cats. Humans catch them from soil or food. Adult cases seem to be rising there. Hospital records from a national database were analyzed.

Only forty-one hospitalized patients appeared over seven years. Most were middle-aged men. No patient was under ten years old. Eye involvement was the commonest presentation. That pattern differs from classic childhood disease. Foodborne transmission may explain adult cases. Eye disease can cause severe vision loss. Clinicians should consider this parasite in unexplained eye inflammation.
pmc-13634267:
Pavlina Lenga and six colleagues reviewed outcomes for patients with cerebral cavernous malformations at one large center. These tangles of blood vessels in the brain can bleed, yet removing them carries its own risks. Doctors lack solid rules for choosing between watching and operating. The team analyzed two hundred sixty-eight patients treated between 2014 and 2021, recording symptoms, scans, treatments, complications, and daily function scores.

Most patients arrived after a bleed, and most were managed without surgery. About a quarter of the treated group had operations, usually within seven weeks of diagnosis. Roughly a quarter of surgical patients suffered a new neurological complication afterward. Function scores in the surgical group improved by last follow-up, except that brainstem lesions left deeper disability. Bleeds during watchful waiting were rare in the recorded years. The authors say the numbers support careful, case-by-case choices rather than any single rule.
pmc-13634367:
Maria Osório, Ana Guiomar, and Pedro Macedo report a brain tumor case in a paper from 2026. A man of sixty-four was first treated for a stroke in the left middle brain artery. Days later he showed strong jealousy, wild mood swings, and acts of harm toward his wife.

At first the signs were blamed on the stroke and on past alcohol use. Careful checks then found a glioblastoma, a fast-growing brain tumor, as the true cause. The case shows how a tumor can look like a pure mental illness. It warns teams to scan for brain causes when psychosis starts late or changes fast.
pmc-13635467:
Daiki Hatakeyama and colleagues studied how the liver expels its own injured cells. The liver keeps itself healthy both by regrowing tissue and by pushing abnormal liver cells out into the blood channels, where they die and get eaten by scavenger cells. A growth switch called YAP marks the cells chosen for expulsion. The team read the gene activity of such cells and mapped which DNA regions stood open in them.

The doomed cells switched on genes for halting division and reshaping their skeletons. They also released signals that summon and activate the scavenger macrophages. Open DNA regions clustered around binding sites for a shape-organizing protein called CTCF. Lab tests showed the YAP partnership physically associates with that protein in the nucleus. The authors describe a three-part axis that remodels DNA packaging to run the expulsion program, a fresh angle on how livers stay clean.
pmc-13636167:
Zarqum Masood and co-authors study shared meals among hospital doctors in a 2026 qualitative paper. Modern hospitals leave doctors few chances to build collegial ties, and isolation follows. Eating together, called commensality, has been proposed as a way to rebuild the relational fabric of clinical life.

Earlier meal programs showed modest effects on burnout in numbers. Less was known about how doctors experience the gatherings and what cultural work they do. Through interviews, the team explores those meanings. The findings may help hospitals design simple rituals that restore community, not just feed staff.
pmc-13637267:
Kil Yong Choi and Ho-Hyun Kim published this 2026 cohort study of air pollution and illness near industrial zones in South Korea's Gyeonggi province. Residents breathe emissions from big plants and small workshops alike. The team modeled how particles drift on local winds and linked exposure to national health records. Winds blew mostly from the west and northwest, letting coarse particles pile up near the complexes.

Peak particle levels in the worst season far exceeded the annual standard. Respiratory illness struck the exposed population clearly more often than the comparison group. One oddity ran the other way: rhinitis rates were sky high in both groups and slightly higher in the control area. The authors still read the pattern as long-term industrial exposure raising respiratory risk, with possible cancer and chronic disease links. They offer the work as baseline data for environmental health policy in industrial regions.
pmc-13638767:
Courtney E. Harris and eight colleagues wrote a 2026 field report on starting a career in transplant infectious diseases. This small specialty deals with infections in patients whose immune systems are weakened by organ transplant treatment.

Drawing on their own early years, the authors cover mentorship, training junior doctors, building skills, and choosing research projects. They also discuss time management during unpredictable clinical work, keeping up with new science, and staying visible in a transplant team. Their shared theme is that young specialists must align clinical, academic, and personal goals deliberately if they want lasting impact rather than mere survival.
pmc-13639067:
Manu Suvarna and eight colleagues describe a 2026 project that fine-tunes a large language model to write recipes for single-atom catalysts. These catalysts, with isolated metal atoms on a support, are hard to design because knowledge sits scattered across fast-growing literature.

The team trained the model on 2,964 publications and built an interface where researchers request procedures by metal, support, and target reaction. Human reviewers checked 150 generated protocols and found the steps coherent and chemically sensible, though with clear limits. The authors stress that model output must be reviewed critically and used as an assistant, not an authority.
pmc-13639967:
Abir Manni, Yacine Zouirech, and Mounir Kisra report a knee injury in a 14-year-old girl hurt in a high-speed electric scooter crash. She landed on both bent knees. The injury broke the bump of bone where the knee's main ligament anchors, the teen form of a ligament tear.

First X-rays at a local hospital were read as normal, though she had pain, swelling, and a leg she could not use. Fresh comparison films showed the bone bump lifted slightly. A detailed scan confirmed the break, reaching into the growth plate, with a second flat break nearby. She was treated without surgery, with gentle repositioning under sedation. The case warns that this break is easy to miss on first films. A missed call can leave a knee unstable for years.
pmc-13640867:
Lisanthini Naidu and co-authors test in 2026 a quick urine test for a key HIV drug in a community treatment program in South Africa. Urine levels show recent drug use, while a dried blood measure shows use over a longer span. The team checked the quick test against a precise lab method and linked both measures to virus levels and staying in care.

Of 196 adults, almost all had drug found by the quick test. The test caught almost all true high results, though its rule out rate was only moderate. The authors also assess how these measures relate to virus in the blood at entry and to staying in care by sixteen weeks.
pmc-13641967:
Maria Fernanda Silva Andrade-Bortoletto and six colleagues present a 2026 laboratory study comparing two imaging routes for finding a hidden second root canal in lower front teeth. Missing such a canal is a known cause of root canal treatment failure, and a nearby zirconia implant might distort the images.

Twenty extracted incisors, some with one canal and some with two, were set in a human jaw beside an implant. Five evaluators read angled X-ray pairs and two cone-beam scan protocols. All routes performed comparably, and the implant did not reduce accuracy. The authors say the simpler X-ray technique remains a valid choice here.
pmc-13642167:
Yanqiu Zou and co-authors built ultraviolet light antennas that can read the fingerprint of a single protein, in a study published in 2026. Raman scattering reveals molecular structure, and metal nanostructures amplify it enormously at hotspots. DNA origami scaffolds can park one molecule exactly in such a hotspot, but gold and silver antennas only resonate in visible light. Biomolecules absorb strongly in the ultraviolet, so the team switched to rhodium nanocubes.

Pairs of the cubes self-assembled on the DNA scaffold, forming a dimer antenna with the protein target held in the gap. The setup detected the Raman signal of a single streptavidin molecule. Rotating the light's polarization modulated the signal exactly as expected only when a protein occupied the hotspot, confirming the reading. The authors present a sensitive, tunable platform for label-free study of single biomolecules in the ultraviolet.
pmc-13642367:
Ah-Reum Lee and two colleagues present a 2026 study of what happens to the health of spouses after their partner receives a first major diagnosis of cancer, stroke, or heart disease. Most earlier work looked only at caregiving strain or jobs.

Using the United States Health and Retirement Study from 1992 to 2020, the matched event study covered 29,166 people. Spouses reported poorer health more often, accumulated more diagnosed conditions, and showed more depressive symptoms, with effects lasting over time. Burdens fell hardest on women and on spouses with less education or fewer assets. Daily health behaviors barely changed.
pmc-13643167:
Ryusei Yoshida, Kazutoshi Kasho, Shogo Ozaki, and Tsutomu Katayama test how flexibly germs can lay out their start site for copying DNA in a 2026 study. In a common gut germ, copy work starts at a set zone with grip sites for a starter protein. Kin germs lay that zone out in far apart or flipped forms, though.

The team rebuilt the gut germ's zone to copy those odd forms. Both forms still worked, letting copy work start and a loader protein land. The odd forms leaned more on side aids and kept a weaker grip on the start step. Cells with them grew slowly, which hints why the standard form wins in fast life.
pmc-13643567:
Brunilda Alushi and Alexander Lauten argue, in a 2026 review, that some failing tricuspid valves still fall beyond every current repair option. The leak was long dismissed as a bystander in heart failure. It affects roughly 1.6 million people in the United States and kills many within a few years.

Catheter repair and replacement have widened choices for high-risk patients in the past decade. A distinct subset remains stranded, though: gaps too wide to clip, rings too large for devices. The review surveys what might serve them next. Naming the leftover group precisely is the first step toward trials and tools designed for their anatomy.
pmc-13645967:
Samuel Leslie and five co-authors analyze bariatric surgery data in two thousand twenty-six. The duodenal switch is a weight-loss operation, and robotic assistance is growing in this field. Whether the robot changes readmission risk, and how surgery length interacts with it, was not known.

They studied over seventeen thousand cases from a national quality database spanning two thousand fifteen to two thousand twenty-four. About thirty-one percent used robotic help. Readmission within thirty days was higher after robotic cases than after standard laparoscopic ones. Both robotic use and longer operations raised readmission odds in adjusted models. The disadvantage centered on the earlier years. The authors say faster robotic surgery alone will not erase the gap.
pmc-13646067:
Dilara Faderl and co-authors speed up early drug screening in this 2026 paper. Magnetic resonance scans can hunt for drug leads, but the classic tool tests one sample at a time, which is slow. Their method takes images instead, reading many tiny samples at once.

A honeycomb holder lets the scanner resolve up to sixty-one samples in one run. The test watches a tagged stand-in molecule to see if test compounds push it off a target protein. Smarter scan settings cut run time further without losing accuracy. Tests on two proteins sorted close to five dozen compounds by grip strength. The authors say the method can lift the pace of early drug hunts.
pmc-13646167:
Li He and eleven colleagues scan the brains of twelve people with chronic shoulder pain to map faulty connections and test whether a hands-on muscle treatment shifts them. Chronic pain can rewire the brain's pain pathways, a process called central sensitization. Patients received ten sessions of a peripheral muscle stimulation treatment, with brain scans before and after. Eighteen healthy volunteers supplied comparison data at the start only.

At baseline, patients showed a trend toward weaker coupling between the thalamus and the touch-sensing cortex, tied to how heavy their disease burden felt. After treatment, one connection between a frontal control area and the brainstem quieted, though that result did not survive the strictest correction. Changes in the thalamus link tracked changes in pain intensity. The authors frame the small pilot as a mechanism sketch that larger trials should test properly.
pmc-13647367:
Seongran Cho and four colleagues trace a three-part circuit that helps lung cancer spread, built around a switch protein and a circular RNA. The switch, ZEB1, drives cancer cells into a mobile, invasive state. Gene reading of cells flooded with ZEB1 found twenty-five circular RNAs changed, and one, named circDennd1b, dropped sharply. The team then raised and lowered that circle to watch what it does.

Lowering the circle sped cell growth, movement, and invasion, while raising it held migration and invasion back. The circle works by soaking up a small regulatory RNA family, miR-181, freeing that family's targets. Since ZEB1 suppresses the circle, the chain from ZEB1 through the circle to miR-181 forms a single axis pushing progression. The authors propose the axis as a treatment angle for a cancer that badly needs new ones.
pmc-13647467:
Tinghui Shao and Jin-Ming Liu run a small pilot on whether intermittent fasting reshapes gut microbes through eating rhythm alone, apart from what is eaten. Five healthy adults from one family ate shared, identical meals while following a sixteen-eight fasting pattern for four weeks. Stool gene sequencing and chemical profiling tracked the gut community over time. A mouse arm then tested a candidate bacterial mechanism with a probiotic supplement.

The adults lost about two kilograms without clearly eating less. No bacterial genus survived strict statistical correction, though one group, Lacticaseibacillus, drifted downward in step with predicted changes in microbial energy handling. In mice, fasting raised a ketone marker and cut weight, while daily doses of the probiotic strain reversed both effects. The authors label the human work hypothesis-generating and demand larger cohorts. The mouse result at least shows the bacterial lead can act, not merely correlate.
pmc-13648267:
Diego R. Perinelli and eleven colleagues study how amino-acid-based surfactants, soap-like molecules built from natural building blocks, arrange themselves where air meets water. How tightly such molecules pack at a surface may predict how they behave against cell membranes, which matters for drug and biomedical uses.

Using surface tension and neutron reflectivity, the team compared three ten-carbon surfactants differing in their head groups. All formed layers of similar thickness, but the serine version packed most tightly while the bulkier leucine version spread widest. Tighter packing matched earlier findings of deeper membrane entry and better tolerance. Measurements at two temperatures agreed, supporting packing as a useful guide for designing gentler surfactants.
pmc-13649767:
Ya-li Yan and two colleagues plead for equity-first AI in the fight against low mood after birth. This ill hits one to two in ten new mothers round the world. Most cases pass unseen and uncared for, above all in poor groups. AI tools, from risk scores to chat care, are sold as the cure.

The authors warn of four traps. Scores may not turn into real gains for whole groups. Training data may shut out the very groups most in need. Machine care may thin the human ties that guard new mothers. Weak rules may let tools spread with no one to blame. They call for design with mothers at the table, hard proof rules, tiered checks, and clear safety paths, all before wide launch.
pmc-13650967:
Alexander Muacevic and three colleagues report a woman in the United Arab Emirates whose HIV had outworn nearly every drug class after more than a decade of incomplete viral control. Resistance testing showed her virus had defeated all drugs in three major families and almost all in a fourth, leaving salvage options nearly exhausted.

After a viral rebound in 2023 and further failed combinations, clinicians started lenacapavir in 2024, a first-of-its-kind drug that attacks the virus's capsid shell and stays active against heavily resistant strains. They paired it with an optimized background regimen built around a modern integrase inhibitor combination. Her viral load fell quickly to undetectable and has stayed suppressed since. The authors present the case as real-world evidence that capsid inhibition can rescue patients whose treatment history has closed almost every other door.
pmc-13651567:
Zhongjun Shen and co-authors studied why glioma cells resist a form of cell death under low oxygen in 2026. Glioma is among the most aggressive brain tumors, with high return rates and strong treatment resistance. The death process, ferroptosis, depends on iron and could be a treatment lever if tumors did not evade it.

Low oxygen raised a factor called HIF-1α in the cells and made them resist a ferroptosis trigger. That factor switched on a fat-handling regulator, which raised two enzymes that build fats and thereby cut the fat damage that drives this death. A drug that blocks the oxygen factor reversed the resistance. In animals, pairing that drug with the trigger gave strong anti-tumor effects.
pmc-13652467:
Assefa and co-authors report a rare case of extreme breast growth in pregnancy that ended in emergency surgery. The disorder makes both breasts swell fast and out of proportion. It can bring severe pain, skin breakdown, infection, and lasting distress.

Their patient was a 24-year-old mother who arrived two days after birth. Her breasts had grown fast over five months of pregnancy, and two days of pain had become disabling. A hormone-blocking drug and strong pain care failed to ease her. Surgeons removed both breasts as an emergency step. Lab study of the tissue confirmed the disorder, and she recovered without problems. The case shows how far medical care can fall short in this rare condition. It also records surgery as the last resort that worked.
pmc-13654167:
Wang and co-authors use resting brain scans to ask whether hearing loss changes how the brain rewires itself in people with ringing in the ears. Ringing without a sound source is common, and many who have it also lose hearing. Whether that loss alters the brain pattern was unclear.

The study scanned 38 patients with ringing, split into those with and without hearing loss, plus 28 healthy adults. Three scan measures were compared: local signal strength, local teamwork, and links from the hearing centers to the rest of the brain. The team also tied scan traits to clinical features. If hearing loss steers the rewiring, care may need to treat the two together. Hearing aids, for instance, might matter beyond sound alone.
pmc-13654567:
Elgharably and co-authors report fixing a heart artery fault during a double lung transplant. Their patient was a 42-year-old man with scarred lungs. Other centers had turned him down for transplant, in part because one heart artery arose from the wrong side with a slit-like opening.

Scans showed the artery ran a short course inside the artery wall, a setup that can choke blood flow. He also had high pressure in the lung arteries and a weakened right heart. At transplant, the team opened the slit segment of the artery to free its path, in the same operation. Doing both at once avoided a second major surgery. The case shows how a center can widen who qualifies for transplant. Careful planning across heart and lung teams made it possible.
pmc-13655467:
Su-Yeon Lee and co-authors issue treatment recommendations for infections by Candida auris, a drug-resistant fungus, tailored to Korea, in a 2026 guideline paper. The fungus causes invasive infections with high death rates and resists many standard drugs. Korean cases were long dominated by one strain family, but a more resistant family has begun causing invasive disease, changing the calculus.

The panel advises no antifungal treatment for mere colonization, and a drug class called echinocandins as first-line therapy for invasive infection. A different standard drug is preferred for newborns and young infants. Susceptibility testing should start whenever invasion is suspected, without delaying first treatment. Refractory cases merit specialist input, and the authors urge continued surveillance as patterns shift.
pmc-13655567:
Jiayu Shi and co-authors pool in 2026 past studies of a cat virus that causes upper airway illness in mainland China. Reports from single places varied a lot, so a shared estimate was missing. The team searched five large databases and checked lists by hand.

Thirty studies with more than seventeen thousand samples met the rules for the pool. The shared rate came out near twenty three percent, with wide spread between studies. The authors split results by age, sex, breed, season, time, and region to find what drove the spread. Such a pooled view helps vets and owners judge risk and plan control steps for cats.
pmc-13655967:
Manon Peeters and three co-authors ask in 2026 whether deep behavior patterns forecast who gains from talk therapy for anxiety and obsessive-compulsive disorder. Talk therapy helps most patients, but three to four in ten gain too little. Early signs of poor response could guide care changes.

One hundred patients rate their schema modes, or deep mood states, before therapy starts. Distress is tracked before and after care. Harmful child-like modes at the start predict more distress after therapy, though the effect is small. Helpful modes add little forecast power once starting distress is counted. The results hint that softening harsh early modes may help therapy land better for some patients.
pmc-13656967:
Christian O'Donnell and co-authors track, in a 2026 study, how the heart's right side recovers after a lung transplant reached via a heart-lung support machine. Severe lung disease strains the right ventricle, the chamber that pushes blood through the lungs. Some patients survive to transplant only on external oxygen support.

The team reviewed adults bridged to transplant on that support between 2015 and 2022. Ultrasound scans were compared from before transplant to early and late points after. Paired tests measured within-patient change in chamber size and function. Whether the right heart remodels back matters for long-term survival and for deciding who should receive scarce donor lungs.
pmc-13657467:
Oral Ospanov and co-authors weigh cost and benefit of two weight loss surgeries in a 2026 study. Both operations shrink the stomach and reroute food to cut weight in people with metabolic syndrome. One adds a wrap at the top of the new stomach pouch. Past trial results favored the wrapped form, but its value for money was unclear.

The cost study ran beside a trial of a thousand patients followed for up to three years. Success meant reaching a body mass index below a set target at the last visit. The team counted surgery, hospital, follow up, and late problem costs. They then compared extra cost against extra success to judge value for the health system.
pmc-13657567:
Manasa Kuppireddy and Dikshitha Bai present a case report, published in 2026, on a bleeding disorder first found in adulthood. Glanzmann thrombasthenia is an inherited fault in platelet clumping that usually shows in childhood with mucosal bleeding. Their patient, a young adult man, came in with repeated gum bleeding and severe iron deficiency anemia, yet no childhood bleeding history.

Routine clotting tests and platelet counts were normal, which can mislead the first workup. Special aggregation studies then showed platelets failing to respond to nearly every trigger, confirming the diagnosis. Care was supportive, with transfusion when needed. The authors urge doctors to consider inherited platelet faults in adults with unexplained mucosal bleeding and normal first line tests.
pmc-13658567:
Maby M Martínez-Garzón and co-authors build a green trap for sex hormones in hospital waste water in a 2026 study. The trap blends a clay with fungus threads grown from an oyster mushroom kin. Stuck to a spinning disk, it pulls four target hormones from the water for lab reads.

Weak bonds at clay edges and fungus walls hold the targets, helped by charge play in the clay core. The trap beat a standard trap, with low find limits and near-full yields. Real waste samples held clear traces of the hormones, and green scores for the method were strong.
pmc-13659267:
Pushpamala Ramaiah and co-authors build a brain wave model for depression signs in a 2026 study. Brain wave records at rest may hold signs of low mood, but models often need huge labeled sets. Their model first learns from unlabeled records by hiding parts of the signal. It then fine tunes on labeled records to sort people by symptom level.

The model sorted people with high symptom scores from others with fair accuracy. It topped the other methods tested on the main score, though margins overlapped. Maps of model focus and feature weights showed which head sensors drove its calls. The authors warn that false alarms were common in this small high symptom group.
pmc-13659467:
Justin Wang and co-authors asked whether the dying phase of lung donors harms transplant outcomes, in a study published in 2026. Lungs donated after circulatory death are used cautiously because the agonal phase, when oxygen and blood pressure crash before death is declared, may injure the organ. The team analyzed 1,305 recipients in a national registry from 2016 to 2024. Donors were split at fifteen minutes of agonal time into long and short groups.

After adjustment, agonal time showed no significant link to the combined early recovery outcomes. Recipients of long-agonal lungs did show worse oxygenation at seventy-two hours and higher long-term graft failure and retransplant rates. Overall survival, though, matched the short group. The authors conclude that a longer agonal phase alone should not disqualify donor lungs. Its exact share in later graft failure remains unclear and needs targeted study.
pmc-13660767:
Mariarita Sciume and co-authors study a leukemia drug mix in daily practice in a 2026 paper. The drug blocks a survival protein in cancer cells and pairs with gentler agents. It is now standard for patients too frail for strong chemotherapy. Fungus prevention drugs clash with it, forcing dose cuts with no agreed target.

The series covered patients treated first line and after relapse at their center. Remission rates were higher in first line use than in relapsed disease. Patients reaching remission lived about the same span in both groups. A low daily dose paired with one fungus drug linked to much shorter survival in the analysis.
pmc-13662467:
Lukas Goderbauer and co-authors link radiation dose to urinary harm in prostate brachytherapy in a 2026 study. Two hundred eighty men treated from 2012 to 2020 receive internal radiation alone or as a boost after beam therapy. Doses to the prostate, bladder, rectum, and both urethral sphincters are mapped from ultrasound plans. Side effects are graded over a median follow-up near eight years.

Five-year survival and disease control run high in both groups, they report. Severe urinary burning stays rare, while severe incontinence reaches about seven percent by two years. Dose-response checks tie sphincter dose to urinary trouble, guiding safer planning. The study refines dose limits for this treatment.
pmc-13666567:
Willian Lazarini-Lopes and co-authors review deep brain circuits and seizures in a 2026 paper. The circuits, called the basal ganglia, are best known for starting and shaping movement. Past work over many years hints they also act as a brake on seizures. The review pulls that work together and asks how the brake works across brain regions.

Old drug and lesion studies showed that quieting one output hub could stop many seizure types. Newer work adds more hubs and maps the exact cell types and paths involved. The authors frame the whole circuit as a gate that can hold back seizure spread. That view may point to care that boosts the brain's own seizure control.
pmc-13668767:
Tian Zhao and co-authors study a protein that blocks drug delivery in solid tumors in a 2026 paper. Tiny drug carriers often fail to reach deep tumor cells. Dense tumor scaffolding and stiff cells both bar their path. The team names a grip protein as the shared switch behind both blocks.

Tumor scaffolding from patients was stiffer and richer in collagen, and carriers barely penetrated it. Removing or blocking the grip protein loosened the scaffolding and boosted carrier entry. It also softened cells and reshaped how they swallow outside material. In animals, blocking the protein plus chemotherapy gave strong anti tumor effects.
pmc-13669367:
Yuanzhe Liang and co-authors build a bendy magnet joystick for wearable controls in a 2026 study. Wearable gear needs many commands from few wires, but the usual fix is a grid of sensors that tacks on bulk and messy leads. Their stick packs many outputs into one channel by design.

Laser cuts in a magnet block split its ring tones by push path, and the tone's sign adds a second split. One stick thus gives four clear outputs from flat pushes. More cuts, sizes, or stuff choices can grow that count, and sticks can team up with no wire clash. Demos ran a game, slides, a robot car, and a fingertip adding tool.
pmc-13669767:
Jasmine Ho and Clarissa Hjalmarsson debate dental teaching in medical school in this 2026 article. Ho argues the proposition: dental health is so vital that it belongs in the medical curriculum. Hjalmarsson presents the other side of the question.

Both sides ground their case in patient welfare. They weigh how care is delivered now, what doctors are expected to know, and the policy pressure for joined-up care. Teaching time is scarce, so any addition must earn its place. The debate lays out the gains and costs of tying medicine and dentistry closer. It asks how future doctors should be trained for whole-person care.
pmc-13670267:
Vets in Italy tested a hazelnut skin extract as an add-on cure for scouring in young dairy calves. Calf diarrhoea kills and stunts many calves in their first weeks of life. Worry over drug resistance has pushed interest in plant-based aids. Hazelnut skins are a sweet-shop waste rich in plant compounds that fight cell stress, yet their worth in sick calves was untested before this trial.

Sixty female calves in a vet hospital were split by chance into two groups of 30. One group got the extract in milk for five days, and both got standard care with fluids and drugs. Staff tracked fever, stool scores, thirst, milk intake, weight, and blood stress marks. No clear edge showed for the extract group on any of these checks. Stay length and death rates were alike as well.
pmc-13670367:
Naser Alshamsi is the subject of a short interview in the First Person series from Biology Open, published in 2026. The series talks with first authors about their work and their path in science. Alshamsi led a paper on a growth factor called DNT-2 and how it helps nerve cells survive and take shape as the visual system forms.

He did that work as a doctoral student in Alicia Hidalgo's lab at the University of Birmingham, where he first joined for a master's project. There he learned gene editing in fruit flies and moved toward brain science. He now teaches in Dubai and studies how nerve cells stay alive, grow, and link up.
pmc-13671367:
Ran Xiang and co-authors report a cohort study, published in 2026, on whether the shine of retinal artery walls predicts future heart and vessel disease. The retina offers a direct view of small arteries, and reflectivity measured on eye scans may capture wall change earlier than symptoms. More than six thousand adults in a Japanese community study had the measure taken and were followed for about seven years.

One hundred and twenty-five new cases of cardiovascular disease, including stroke and coronary disease, appeared during follow up. Across the whole group the reflectivity showed no clear independent link to events. An age interaction emerged, though, with possible risk signals under age seventy in exploratory models. The authors urge caution, treating the under seventy signal as a lead, not a verdict.
pmc-13672267:
Tamara Rushovich and co-authors measure public health by city council district in Philadelphia, in this 2026 study. Health data are usually mapped by census tract or county, not by the districts that elect local lawmakers. The team argues district-level numbers help advocacy, since council members vote on local policy. They report two measures for every district and tract: tree canopy cover and health insurance coverage.

Both measures varied widely across the city, and also within single districts. That inner spread matters: a district average can hide sharp local gaps. The authors describe putting the data on a public online dashboard. Residents and advocates can then bring their own district's numbers to local politicians, the team suggests.
pmc-13672967:
Medical journals rarely publish jokes on purpose, but Robert Holzman and Cynthia Wong argue in a 2026 editorial that a well-aimed satire can teach. They discuss a companion study that pretends to test ventilator settings based on prime numbers against oxygen levels, using the full machinery of a real database study.

The fake study finds differences that are statistically significant and completely meaningless. That is the point. The editorial uses the piece to examine how clinicians think: mental shortcuts, arbitrary groupings, and huge datasets can combine into findings that look solid and mean nothing. Holzman and Wong present satire as a teaching tool for clinical reasoning, one that trains readers to ask whether a result could possibly be real.
pmc-13673067:
Ceramics are strong but usually snap rather than bend, and Chang Liu and co-authors show a 2026 route to making one bend. Their material is a medium-entropy oxide, a crystal mixing four metals with oxygen, made without cobalt. By letting a copper-rich second phase form inside, they planted ready-made defect sources in the crystal.

The team squeezed microscopic pillars of the material while watching under a microscope, at room temperature and at 400 and 600 degrees. Cold pillars cracked with little flow. Hotter ones let crystal defects glide and pile up, hardening as they deformed. Strain before fracture rose from about two percent when cold to nearly sixteen percent at the top heat. The authors call the trick controlled entropy destabilization.
pmc-13673367:
Sea cucumbers defend themselves with an immune system that researchers have mostly studied in two separate halves. Noé Wambreuse and co-authors review the whole field, counting 108 immune genes reported so far, seventy-four of them functionally characterised, and ten main kinds of immune cells, only five firmly confirmed. Most work centres on one farmed species prized in Asian markets, leaving the family's diversity unexplored.

Genes are usually studied apart from the cells that use them, which blocks a functional picture of how defence actually runs. The authors argue for linking gene activity to specific cell types, building a classification based on what cells do. The stakes are practical as well as scientific: disease outbreaks, notably a skin ulcer syndrome, hammer farmed sea cucumbers worldwide.
pmc-13674167:
Four doctors in Iran report a new gene variant behind a brain development disorder in a 2026 case paper. Their patient is a seven year old boy with a small head, stiff legs, crossed eyes, and moderate learning disability. The disorder also brings autism like behaviors in his case.

Gene sequencing found a fresh change in CTNNB1, a gene that makes a protein key to brain growth. The change arose new in the boy, not passed from a parent, and the team judges it likely harmful. No cure exists for the disorder, and care is supportive. The case adds one more variant to the map and backs early sequencing for such children.
pmc-13675167:
Marleen Trapp and co-authors report a 2026 cell study on how insulin reshapes hair-like structures in a brain tissue called the choroid plexus. That tissue makes the fluid that bathes the brain. Its cells carry many small hairs whose odd layout is still not well understood.

The team grew mouse choroid plexus cells and exposed them to insulin for up to six days. They then used staining, gene tests, and protein checks to track changes in the cells. Long insulin exposure raised the share of cells showing altered hair patterns. The work is basic science, but it links a hormone best known for blood sugar to the brain's fluid system. That link may matter for understanding hormone effects on the brain.
pmc-13675367:
Enrique Vazquez-Mendoza and co-authors put forward a theory paper from 2026 about the brain spot that drives breathing in newborn and adult mammals. That spot, a small cluster of nerve cells, sets the rhythm for each breath in. Models of the rhythm need a base level of cell readiness, but no one has pinned down what sets that level in the body.

The authors suggest that a steady background level of glutamate, a common signal chemical, could play that role. They review how the chemical is released, spread, cleared, and sensed near cells in the breathing cluster. They stress that direct proof is still missing. The paper ends with tests that could tell a true cause apart from a mere side effect of network activity.
pmc-13677767:
Taiyo Hashimoto and six co-authors test whether treating bull sperm before fertilization improves calf embryos made in the lab, in a study from 2026. Lab embryo work aims for more high-grade embryos that survive freezing and transfer. A sperm surface sensor that responds to a lab activator is the focus here.

Sperm treated for a short time before joining eggs gave more split eggs and more embryos at the key growth stage, lifting yield by about a tenth. Those embryos had more cells and less cell death. Calcium levels and cell cleanup paths shifted in helpful ways. Top-grade share and thaw survival stayed about the same.
pmc-13678067:
Santhalakshmi Angappan, Joseph Brisson, and Nakul Kumar report cases of sudden lung white out after the start of a lung support machine, in a 2026 paper. The machine, called VV-ECMO, takes over gas exchange when breathing fails despite a ventilator. Its value and risks in blocking airway diseases are still not well mapped. The cases here involve patients whose lungs blocked rather than stiffened.

Within hours of starting the machine, the patients' lungs turned fully opaque on imaging, a sign of collapse. The authors tie the event to the lung rest settings used while the machine runs. Use of the machine for asthma and chronic blocking lung disease is growing, they note. Intensive care teams should know this risk so they can spot the change fast and act early. The series is offered as a warning drawn from a small set of cases.
pmc-13678167:
Olinto da Fonseca and co-authors review unsaturated fats as immune-metabolic modulators in risky pregnancies. High-risk pregnancy mixes metabolic strain, low-grade inflammation, and placenta faults. Omega-3 fats like EPA and DHA reshape cell membranes. They damp NF-kB signals and inflammasome firing. They also aid mitochondria and yield pro-resolving mediators.

Clinical proof spans cohort studies, trials, and pooled analyses. Omega-3 intake links to lower preterm birth risk in the data. Gains look strongest in women with low baseline intake. The review maps mechanisms cell by cell. It weighs how fat intake could ease placenta inflammation.
pmc-13679367:
Bénédicte Stengel and co-authors report in 2026 on poor sleep among people with long-term kidney disease in France. The team followed close to three thousand patients who were not on dialysis, drawn from forty clinics across the country. They asked how often troubled sleep and daytime sleepiness occurred.

At the start, about one patient in five reported troubled sleep, and about one in seven reported daytime sleepiness. Over five years of checks, the team weighed kidney markers against symptoms, habits, other illness, and drug effects. Their work helps doctors see which factors track with poor sleep, so care can target the causes that matter most.
pmc-13679867:
Soheil Hashtarkhani and co-authors study whether distress reported by cancer patients predicts breaks in their radiation treatment, in a 2026 retrospective study. Unplanned breaks harm tumor control and survival. Clinical and social factors have been studied, but the role of psychosocial distress was less clear.

The cohort holds 1,953 patients who had external beam radiation from 2020 to 2024 at one institution. Distress screening data were joined with clinical and socioeconomic records. The team use both standard regression and machine learning models to find predictors. The work aims to flag patients who may need support to finish treatment without breaks.
pmc-13680567:
Manu Krishnan, Kimneihat Vaiphei, Pracheth Raghuveer, and Prabha Chandra study mental health in expectant fathers from tribal groups in India. Their 2026 paper notes that fathers can face distress during a partner's pregnancy. Data on tribal fathers are scarce. The team surveyed 80 men in Attappady with standard scales for mood, anxiety, well-being, and support.

About one in six men reported depressive symptoms, and one in ten reported anxiety. Two in five had poor well-being. Seasonal migration for work and financial debt tied strongly to depressive symptoms. A planned pregnancy tied to lower anxiety, while a past pregnancy loss tied to higher anxiety. Low mood and anxiety both tracked with lower support. The authors urge father-inclusive screening.
pmc-13681467:
Jingfang Song, Ailan He, Shuyu Li, and Qiong Wu published a study in 2026 on a drug that shields rat brain-like cells from amyloid damage. Alzheimer's disease advances as amyloid clumps kill neurons. The team blocked an enzyme whose levels rose in amyloid-treated cells, using its inhibitor TPPU. Survival, death signals, and cell powerhouses were then measured.

The inhibitor cut cell death and restored viability. It normalized a key executioner protein and revived the membrane charge of the powerhouses. Natural fat messengers from the same pathway partly copied the protection. The drug also calmed a stress signaling switch tied to cell death. The authors propose the enzyme as a treatment target.
pmc-13681967:
Anselm Schneider and co-authors find a dye that lets drug hunters run heat tests on membrane proteins, the hardest targets in the business. Thermal shift assays watch a protein unfold as it warms and are cheap to set up, but the usual glow dyes fail on membrane proteins floating in detergent. A workaround uses dyes that light up when they grab cysteine, a building block common inside membrane spans. Their 2026 study trials several new candidates.

One dye, called Naph-EA-Mal, read melting points reliably at low amounts and across many buffers and protein classes. The team used it to tune the buffer for an ion channel and to screen small fragments against a carrier protein called Spns2. The screen surfaced a new binder shape that could seed future Spns2 blockers. The authors offer the dye as a practical key to a locked screening room.
pmc-13682367:
Ilenia Sana and fourteen co-authors charted the genes controlled by a signaling protein in leukemia in a 2026 paper. The protein, IκBζ, switches on after immune receptors fire and shapes inflammation. Its targets in normal and malignant B cells were poorly mapped, so the team profiled chronic lymphocytic leukemia cells with two genome-wide binding methods.

Binding patterns shifted after stimulation in both cell types. Key genes such as NFKB2, BATF, and FOXP1 gained binding in both, while CXCR5 was bound mainly in leukemia cells. Blocking the protein's pathway stopped those genes from switching on. The authors cast IκBζ as a central tuner that links inflammatory signaling to the B cell's own receptor and movement programs.
pmc-13688367:
Jushawn Macon and nine co-authors audit where diverse patients drop out of two large precision health trials, step by step, in a two thousand twenty-six implementation study. Trials that fail to engage everyone compromise validity and equity.

Over twenty-four thousand patients were approached for smoking and lung cancer screening studies. Race, social vulnerability, insurance, and distance shaped each cascade stage differently. Black patients were reached and screened at higher rates than white patients, yet consented and completed genetic testing at lower rates. Portal recruitment flipped some patterns, favoring distant patients and disfavoring Black patients. The authors call for stage-specific engagement strategies rather than generic outreach.
pmc-13688867:
Ignacia and co-authors map the genes behind yeast clumping in lager brewing in a 2026 study. Clumping, called flocculation, decides how well yeast settles and how beer turns out. The lager yeast is a hybrid with two tangled genomes, which had blocked clear gene work.

The team re-read the full gene set for clumping in one strain and found thirteen genes. One was new, with a grip part unlike the rest. Light-switched gene control in a blank yeast showed two genes drive clumping most. During a real wort ferment, those genes woke up as clumping began. Deleting both in the strain only delayed settling, and sugar use improved. Moderate gene action, not max, fits the strain's style.
pmc-13689167: Marc Moussan, Mariam El Arab, Nancy Fayad, and Mireille Kallassy Awad report draft genomes of nine Bacillus strains from Lebanese soil. Eight are Bacillus thuringiensis and one is Bacillus mycoides, all within the close-knit cereus group known for varied capacities including antimicrobial production. Their announcement from twenty twenty-six shares the sequences and genomic features within a project hunting for new bioactivity, giving other researchers raw material to mine for useful compounds.
pmc-3218867:
Mermel, Schumacher, Hill, and co-authors present GISTIC2.0, a method for locating the targets of focal copy-number changes in human cancers. Cancers gain or lose pieces of DNA, and some of those changes drive tumour growth. The task is separating driver changes from background noise.

Their methods improve power and specificity by splitting copy-number profiles into broad arm-level changes and narrow focal ones. Better background estimates make true focal targets stand out. Finding those genes points drug research at the alterations cancers actually depend on.  Focal gains pointing at known growth genes confirmed the method recovered real biology.
pmc-4190567:
Housman, Byler, Heerboth, and their co-authors gave an overview of drug resistance in cancer in 2014. Cancers can learn to survive drugs that once worked against them. As resistant cancers have become more common, the need for new research and treatments has grown.

The overview sets out the known ways cancers gain resistance. These include pumping drugs out of cells, repairing damage faster, and switching growth pathways. It also covers how resistance can spread within a tumor as hardy cells survive treatment. Knowing these routes helps doctors plan drug combinations and helps labs design drugs that are harder to evade.
pmc-5411767:
Koren, Walenz, Berlin, and their colleagues presented Canu in 2017, an assembler for long-read sequencing. Long-read single-molecule sequencing had revolutionized genome assembly and enabled automated reconstruction of reference-quality genomes. Its relatively high error rates, though, made efficient and accurate assembly of large repeats hard.

Canu tackles this through adaptive k-mer weighting and repeat separation. It weighs sequence pieces by how informative they are and pulls apart repeated stretches that confuse assemblers. The result is a scalable tool that can assemble large genomes from noisy long reads. Reference-quality genomes for complex species became far more attainable with such methods.
pmc-6324067:
Randi Vita, Swapnil Mahajan, James Overton, and coauthors gave the 2018 update of the Immune Epitope Database. The database pulls experimental epitope data out of papers and makes it searchable. Epitopes are the exact pieces of a pathogen that immune cells recognize.

Coverage spans infectious disease, allergy, autoimmunity, and transplant settings across many species. Each record keeps the assay and context, since an epitope claim means little without them. Vaccine and immunotherapy teams search it before designing new candidates. Free public access turns scattered literature into one working tool. Users can query by pathogen, host, or assay type and export result tables for their own work.
pmc-6450067:
Russell Glasgow, Samantha Harden, Bridget Gaglio, and coauthors revisited the RE-AIM framework in 2019. RE-AIM guides planning and evaluation of health programs. Two decades after its launch, it ranks among the most used frameworks in implementation research.

The letters stand for reach, effectiveness, adoption, implementation, and maintenance. The paper traces how use of the framework grew and changed, drawing lessons from thousands of studies. It urges fuller reporting of who is reached and whether gains last. Program planners read it to design rollouts that work outside trial conditions. Updated examples in the paper show the framework applied to digital health and community programs.
pmc-6859567:
Matthew Dodson, Raul Castro-Portuguez, and Donna Zhang reviewed the NRF2 pathway in ferroptosis in 2019. NRF2 is a master switch for the cell's antioxidant defenses. It turns on genes that counter oxidative and chemical stress.

Ferroptosis is cell death driven by iron and oxidized membrane fats. NRF2 controls many of the genes that hold that process back, from iron storage to fat repair. When the pathway fails, cells grow far more sensitive to ferroptotic death. The link matters for cancer, where raising or blocking NRF2 could tilt tumors toward survival or death.
pmc-7619567:
Stephanie Williams and four colleagues show that a long spell of winter cold leaves a lasting mark on the daily clock of Arabidopsis plants. Many plants require vernalisation, weeks of cold, before they can flower in spring, and the circadian clock helps time flowering to day length. The team found that cold exposure changes how clock genes behave, and that the changes persist after the plant returns to warmth, giving the clock a memory of winter.

The effect required Polycomb Repressive Complex 2, a gene-silencing system, yet it did not depend on FLC, the famous flowering repressor that vernalisation is known to switch off. Clock-controlled outputs, including flowering responses to day length, shifted as a result. The finding links two timing systems, the daily clock and the seasonal calendar, through a memory mechanism separate from the textbook pathway.
pmc-8081667:
Arang Rhie and the Vertebrate Genomes Project team set out in 2021 what it will take to produce complete, error free reference genomes for all vertebrate species. High quality reference genomes underpin work in biology, medicine, and conservation. Yet at the time, such assemblies existed for only a handful of species beyond microbes and model organisms.

Working through an international consortium, the authors describe the sequencing and assembly standards they developed and the lessons from their first flagship genomes. They argue for quality targets that future projects should meet before a genome is called a reference. The paper is both a progress report and a blueprint for one of the largest undertakings in modern biology.
pmc-8333067:
Dan Li and Minghong Wu reviewed in 2021 the pattern recognition receptors, the immune system's front line sensors. These receptors directly detect the molecular shapes found on pathogens, on dying host cells, and on damaged aging cells. By sounding the alarm, they link the fast, general immune response to the slower, targeted one.

The review describes the main families of these receptors, where each sits in the cell, and what each is tuned to notice. It then follows their roles in health and in diseases where the alarm system misfires or is exploited. Because these sensors decide what counts as danger, they are prime targets for vaccines and for drugs that calm harmful inflammation.
pmc-8938267:
Yan Xie, Evan Xu, Benjamin Bowe, and Ziyad Al-Aly studied in 2022 the long term effects of COVID-19 on the heart and blood vessels. The heart related complications of the acute illness were already well documented. What happened to survivors' cardiovascular health in the year after infection was much less clear.

Using national health care databases from the United States Department of Veterans Affairs, the team followed huge numbers of survivors and comparison groups. They report raised risks of many cardiovascular problems long after the initial illness, including in people who were never hospitalized. The study widened the frame of long COVID to include the heart, and it argued for follow up care that watches for these late effects.
poems-pg1567:
T. S. Eliot published his first book of poems in New York with Alfred A. Knopf in 1920, dedicating it to Jean Verdenal, 1889 to 1915, his friend killed in the war. Some pieces had already appeared in little magazines such as Poetry, Blast, and the Little Review. The contents announce a new kind of poetry: ironic, allusive, urban, and weary, written in voices that trail off into quotation and doubt.

Gerontion opens the book, an old man in a dry month meditating on history. The Love Song of J. Alfred Prufrock stands at the center, with Preludes, Rhapsody on a Windy Night, and Portrait of a Lady around it, while the Sweeney poems add a coarser music-hall note.
